Late Devonian to Early Carboniferous palaeomagnetic 
poles from the Armorican Massif, France 
Meridee Jones Deparrment of Geology and Mineralogy, University ofMichigan, 
Ann Arbor, Michigon 48109, USA (currently employed by USGS, Denver, 
Colorado 80225, USA)

Received 1978 December 1;in original form 1978 March 24 
Summary. In order to test plate tectonic hypotheses for the Hercynian 
orogeny in western Europe, Late Devonian and Cambro-Ordovician redbeds 
and volcanics have been palaeomagnetically studied. The Late Devonian 
redbeds show nearly univectorial remanent magnetizations during stepwise 
thermal, chemical and alternating field demagnetization and yield a pole 
position at 19.8' N, 144.2' E. All three Cambro-Ordovician units studied 
yielded characteristic directions of magnetization that are interpreted as 
remagnetizations of Late Devonian-Early Carboniferous age on the basis of 
negative fold tests, similarities with the directions of the Late Devonian 
redbeds, reset K/Ar ages of 345 MA, or the occurrence of significant high- 
temperature magnetizations. A comparison of a mean Late Devonihn-Early 
Carboniferous pole for all four formations (28.1' N, 146.4" E, dp = 3.87", 
drn = 7.50") from the Armorican Massif with contemporaneous poles from 
stable ('extra-Hercynian') Europe indicates that there was little or no 
separation between Hercynian and stable Europe in that time. A significant 
separation between the Armorican Massif and Gondwanaland, on the other 
hand, suggests that an intervening middle Palaeozoic ocean existed which 
subsequently was consumed by subduction somewhere to the south of the 
Armorican Massif. Those high-temperature directions from the Cambro- 
Ordovician redbeds and volcanics that are relatively well grouped are 
interpreted as original Cambro-Ordovician magnetizations. They show 
shallow inclinations and north-westerly declinations, but are not sufficiently 
substantiated to give more than the tentative interpretation that their palaeo- 
latitudes also are roughly in agreement with the data from stable Europe for 
that time.

Introduction 
Interpretation of past orogenies in a plate tectonic context is valuable in expanding 
knowledge of plate tectonic theory and of specific orogenic processes. Some orogenies 
readily lend themselves to a tectonic subduction and/or collision interpretation. Others, 
such as the Late Palaeozoic Hercynian orogeny of western Europe, are enigmatic. The 
Hercynian orogenic belt lacks many of the typical tectonic indicators of subduction and 
collision and has characteristics not easily explained in plate tectonic terms. The Hercynian 
belt has few or no high-pressure, low-temperature metamorphic indicators, ophiolites or 
ultrabasites. Nappe structures are rare. Metamorphism is shallow. In addition, the orogenic 
belt is very wide (approximately 1000 km) and contains abundant granites and migmatites 
(Zwart 1967). The difficulty in placing the Hercynian orogeny into a plate tectonic model 
can be seen in the number of locations of proposed subduction zones (Fig. 1) and the 
suggested styles and timing of closure. 
The plate tectonic models can be divided into three groups: (1) those proposing the 
closure of an ocean to the north of the Armorican Massif separating stable or northern 
Europe from Hercynian or central and southern Europe ending in a continent-continent 
collision (Johnson 1973, 1974; Dewey & Burke 1973; Burrett 1972; in part, McKerrow & 
Ziegler 1972; in part, Burne 1973), (2) those proposing the closure of an ocean to the south 
of Hercynian Europe in an Andean-type subduction, later the site of the Alpine orogeny 
(Nicolas 1972; Floyd 1972), and (3) those proposing the existence of more than one ocean 
where Hercynian Europe or parts of it acted as microplates between or attached to stable 
Europe and the Gondwana continents (Laurent 1972; Riding 1974; Badham & Halls 1975; 
in part, Floyd 1972). In general, proponents of subduction maintain that closure of an 
intervening ocean or oceans was occurring during the Late Devonian and/or Early 
Carboniferous with final collision in the early Late Carboniferous. Krebs & Wachendorf 
(1 973) and Ager (1 975) dispute the palaeontological, structural, geochemical and sedimento- 
logical arguments and maintain that the Hercynian orogeny did not involve any large-scale

The existence of an ocean or oceans separating Hercynian Europe from stable Europe 
and/or the Gondwana continents during the Middle to Late Palaeozoic is testable palaeo- 
magnetically. Comparison of the palaeolatitude of Hercynian Europe with respect to stable 
Europe and Gondwanaland during a given time in the Palaeozoic can show the latitudinal 
extent of any such oceans at that time. Although sparse within certain ages, enough palaeo- 
magnetic data exist for stable Europe and the Gondwana continents for such a comparison 
through most of the later Palaeozoic. The present study was undertaken to obtain palaeo- 
magnetic data for Hercynian Europe to complete the comparison. 
The Armorican Massif was selected for sampling due to prevalence of relatively un- 
metamorphozed Palaeozoic sediments preserved in the synclines of Normandy and Brittany. 
The Massif is divided into a series of domains separated by fault systems trending E-W to 
ESE-WNW (Fig. 2, inset). The two northernmost domains, the Domnonean domain and the 
Mancellian domain, are thought to have been virtually unaffected or only moderately 
affected respectively by the Hercynian deformation and metamorphism (CognB 1974), and 
thus they appeared to be well suited for palaeomagnetic investigation. Devonian redbeds 
were sampled from the Syncline of Montmartin (Group A) in Normandy, Cambro- 
Ordovician redbeds and trachyandesites were sampled in the areas of PaimpolLBrBhec 
(Group B) and Erquy-Cap Frkhel (Group C) in northern Brittany. Samples of Late 
Cambrian to Early Ordovician redbeds were taken from the Syncline of the Zone Bocaine 
(Group D) in Normandy. The geology and relative ages of the individual areas will be 
discussed with the results. 
Sampling and laboratory techniques 
All sites but one were drilled in the field and oriented with a standard geological compass. 
For two sites within the trachyandesite, orientation errors increased from ?2' to a

approximately 200 nanoTesla (nT) It: 200 nT after effects of the Earth's field were observed

analysed by vector subtraction. All directions so obtained as well as sampling localities and 
lithologies are given in more detail in Jones (1978).

Results 
GROUP A - LATE DEVONIAN OF THE SYNCLINE OF MONTMARTIN, NORMANDY 
Five redbed sites were sampled on the south limb of the Syncline of Montmartin (Fig. 2). 
Three sites are within the redbeds of Hyenville which are assigned a Late Devonian age by 
Doubinger & Poncet (1964) and Doubinger, Drot & Poncet (1966) on the basis of micro- 
fossils. The remaining two sites (B and C) are within the finer-grained layers of the basal 
conglomerate in the eastern portion of the Syncline. The age of these beds is questionable 
since some authors claim the fault separating the eastern and western portions of the 
Syncline (and the two sets of sites from each other) to be a delineation between Late 
Devonian to the west and Late Ordovician or Early Silurian to the east (Cognt? 1974; 
Robardet 1973). In addition, there is controversy about a conformable versus tectonic 
contact in the east between the (sampled) basal conglomerate and the (unsampled) overlying 
sandstone which contains fossils of tentative Ordovician/Silurian age (Robardet 1973; 
Doubinger et al. 1966). Because of the uncertainty of the age determination of the basal 
conglomerate, we are following Graindor & Roblot (1966) in taking the entire sampled 
portion of the Syncline of Montmartin as Late Devonian. The mean direction for the red- 
beds is given with and without these two possibly Ordovician sites. It can be seen in Table 1 
that this does not make any appreciable difference. 
Thermal, chemical and alternating field demagnetizations were performed on the Late 
Devonian redbeds. The demagnetization curves are generally of good quality and show 
nearly univectorial decay (Fig. 3). In almost all cases the chemical demagnetizations agree 
well with thermal and alternating field demagnetizations in both the component removed 
and the final 'stable' component (the endpoint at which direction and intensity changes 
cease). The direction and coercivity of this final component was determined by further 
demagnetization in alternating fields of one of the chemically demagnetized samples 
(following the technique used by Park (1 970)). The direction obtained by vector subtraction 
of the final component was very similar to the characteristic direction seen in all other 
samples from Group A that were thermally or chemically demagnetized. The final 
component was of low coercivity since approximately 50 per cent of the remaining 
magnetization was removed by peak alternating fields of 50 milliTesla (500 Oe). The low 
coercivity and resistance to acid leaching would imply that the final component was carried 
by magnetite of relatively large grain size.

High-temperature directions were observed in some samples. The high-temperature com- 
ponent was seen either as an over-shoot of the origin at intensities above machine noise level 
(as in sample A7b, Fig. 3) or as a small final component decaying to the origin but barely 
above machine noise level (as in sample A 10 of Fig. 3). When statistically analysed the high- 
temperature directions are very poorly grouped (with a Fisher precision parameter of 2 
(Table 2)) and consequently are taken to be insignificant. 
Fig. 4 is an equal-area plot of the characteristic directions of magnetization after 
structural correction. Due to the similarity of bedding corrections a fold test of these 
characteristic directions of magnetization is not significant at the 95 per cent confidence 
level. However, the nearly univectorial decay during thermal, chemical and alternating field 
demagnetizations (excluding the scattered high-temperature magnetization) documents the 
existence of only one significant direction of magnetization recorded in the redbeds, regard- 
less of the blocking temperature, solubility and coercivity of the carriers of magnetization. 
Since no conclusive evidence for remagnetization is seen, the resulting pole position of 
19.8' N, 144.2" E is taken to be the Late Devonian pole for the Syncline of Montmartin. 
GROUP B - CAMBRO-ORDOVICIAN OF PAIMPOL-BREHEC, BRITTANY 
Three sites of redbeds and five sites of trachyandesites were sampled in the Paimpol-BrBhec 
area (Fig. 5, top). The three redbed sites were sampled from the redbed of la RocheJagu, 
one of which was quartzitic (site D). Three of the trachyandesite sites are within a flow 
intercalated with the redbeds. Of these three, sites F and G appear weathered in outcrop. 
The remaining two trachyandesite sites (I and Y) were sampled from two dikes cutting the 
redbeds. 
The redbeds contain no fossils; therefore an age assignment is made on the basis of radio- 
metric dating of the intercalated trachyandesite flow and dikes. Recently these have been 
assigned a Rb/Sr whole-rock isochron age of 472 ? 8 MA (Mac6 et al. 1979). In addition, 
two much younger Late Devonian K/Ar ages have been found (Mac6 et al. 1979; Rochette- 
Pinel, Giot & Dumesnil 1965) for the trachyandesite flow; these appear to record a younger 
thermal event which has affected these rocks. 
Most of the redbed specimens from Group B were demagnetized thermally. Of these, 
some were demagnetized in alternating fields before thermal treatment. The remainder was 
chemically leached and/or demagnetized in alternating fields. The quartzitic site D showed 
erratic or inconsistent behaviour during thermal, alternating field and chemical'treatment. 
Consequently, the site has been omitted from the group average, even thou& its mean 
direction is not very different from those of the other sites (Table 1). The two other redbed 
sites showed thermal behaviour similar to that of the Late Devonian from the Syncline of 
Montmartin in Normandy with the addition of a low-temperature component. As in Group 
A, a high-temperature component is seen in some of the samples. 
Unlike Group A, the chemical demagnetizations of the Group B redbed samples were in 
apparent disagreement with the thermal and alternating field demagnetizations. Eight 
specimens of tine-grained red sandstone from site H were partially or wholly chemically 
demagnetized. In all but one case the inclination steepened as leaching proceeded. Slicing 
of one specimen showed that the red pigment was being removed throughout the core and 
therefore the steepening of inclination could not be caused by incomplete penetration of the 
acid which, in turn, would cause increasing predominance of the NRM from unleached 
portions of the core. Alternating field demagnetization of two of the chemically leached 
samples that had not yet been completely demagnetized showed removal of a 'soft', low- 
coercivity component of steep inclination (more than 50 per cent of the intensity remaining

steep, ‘soft’ component was only partially removed during chemical demagnetization while

The trachyandesites from Group B were demagnetized thermally and with alternating 
fields. Initial intensities were low, ranging from 10-’A/m (10T4emu ~m-~) to 10-3A/m 
(lO-bemu ~m-~). All samples showed at least two components of magnetization, several 
showed three (see Fig. 7). One dike sampled (site Y) records the only normal polarity in 
Group B. Five of the six samples from this dike had characteristic magnetizations almost 
exactly antipodal to the rest of Group B (Fig. 8(a)). 
In addition to demagnetization studies, polished thin sections of seven trachyandesite 
samples were examined. The thin sections showed a preponderance of a hematitic alteration 
product, a scarcity of original magnetite, as well as a very fine-grained (< 1 pm in diameter), 
optically unidentifiable, opaque phase. The low initial intensities observed in the 
demagnetization studies are in agreement with the predominance of hematite. However, 
the low-temperature and characteristic components were removed below or by the Curie 
temperature of magnetite (c. 580°C). Thus, the hematite may be the result of two different 
alterations and be rich in titanium. The latter is also suggested optically by occasional inter- 
growths of hematite and rutile. The high-temperature component seen in Fig. 7 was removed 
near the magnetite Curie point. In other samples it was removed near or above 580°C. 
Thus, the carrier of this high-temperature component must be relatively pure iron oxide 
and may be associated with the unidentified fine-grained opaque phase, perhaps ‘primary’ 
in origin.

Let it suffice now to say that they show the greatest directional consistency of high- 
temperature directions of any of the areas sampled - they pass a fold test at the 95 per cent 
confidence level (McElhinny 1964) and yield a mean declination/inclination of 325,0'/

The characteristic direction of magnetization seen in all Group B samples has a 
declination/inclination of 210.5'/+6.6' and yields a pole position of 31.6" N, 140.5' E. 
However, this characteristic magnetization is most likely a remagnetization. The presence of 
a small, although consistent, high-temperature direction and the oxidation of the trachy- 
andesites examined in polished thin section suggests that the characteristic direction is not 
primary. In view of the reset K/Ar ages (345 MA) and the proximity of this pole to the Late 
Devonian pole of Group A from Normandy we interpret the pole position to be'Late 
Devonian(?). 
GROUP c - CAMBRO-ORDOVICIAN(?) OF ERQUY-CAP FR~HEL, BRITTANY 
Various lithologies were sampled within the redbeds of Erquy-Cap FrChel in Brittany. A 
corresponding variation in magnetic behaviour and results was observed. Two of the four 
Group C sites (site S and T) are located in relatively coarse, quartzitic pink sandstone. 
Samples taken from site J were of pink sandstone, of red siltstone lenses within the pink 
sandstone and of well-indurated arkosic sandstone. Samples at site K were of somewhat 
fissile, fine-grained, very red sandstone (see Fig. 5 for sampling localities). 
The Erquy-Cap FrChel redbeds are taken to be Late Cambrian-Early Ordovician in age. 
This age is based on: (1) a stratigraphic correlation of the Erquy-Cap FrChel redbeds across 
the Bay of St Brieuc with the redbeds of la RocheJagu of Group B and an overlying sand- 
stone, and on (2) a Rb/Sr isochron of 482 f 10 MA for the Erquy spilites and supportive 
microfossil evidence below the conformable overlying redbeds of Erquy-cap FrChel (Vidal

All but three of the redbed samples from Erquy-Cap Frkhel were thermally de- 
magnetized. The three remaining samples were chemically leached. Site J generally hows 
good demagnetization curves, initial intensities from 2.9 to 0.3 x 10-3A/m, good grouping 
of characteristic directions at the site mean level and little evidence of a high-temperature 
component. Site S, of quartzitic pink sandstone, showed a wide range of blocking 
temperatures and initial intensities from 2.0 to 8.0 x 10d3A/m and at least two distinct 
components of magnetization. The lower, and larger, component is taken as the 
characteristic direction of magnetization since the higher-temperature component is very 
scattered. Site T, also of quartzitic pink sandstone, consisted of samples with generally low 
blocking temperatures (most below 45OoC) and inconsistent directions of magnetization; the 
one high-temperature direction (600°C) is similar to those seen in sites S, J and the 
'Devonian' directions. However, the site as a whole has been eliminated from the group 
mean, even though its mean direction is very close to those of the other sites (Table 1). 
Site K is anomalous with respect to the other Erquy-Cap Frkhel results. The highest 
temperature components of magnetization are within the hematite blocking temperature 
range, in most cases being removed between 655OC and 66OoC and often within a 2" or 3'

GROUP D - LATE CAMBRIAN-EARLY ORDOVICIAN OF NORMANDY 
The Cambro-Ordovician redbeds of the Syncline of the Zone Bocaine are definitely re- 
magnetized. As seen in Table 1, they fail a fold test, even at the 99 per cent confidence 
level (McElhinny 1964), and hence prove to have been remagnetized during, or subsequent 
to, the time of folding of the Syncline. 
Seven sites of red siltstones of the redbeds of St. RCmy were sampled within the Syncline 
of the Zone Bocaine (Fig. 5, bottom). In the eastern and western portions of the Zone 
Bocaine, the 'syncline' is, in fact, a synclinorium made up of two synclines separated by an 
anticline (Robardet 1973). Sites are located on both north and south limbs of the synclines. 
Consequently, the collection encompasses considerable structural variation with strike/dip 
ranging from 73"/80" to 302"/45". 
In the explanation of the Coutances geological map, Graindor (1 966) calls the redbeds 
of St RCmy (whch are included in the 'schistes et grks rouges') Tremadocian in analogy 
to other Armorican redbeds of that age. An age discrepancy arises in both the placement of 
the Tremadocian as a stage and in other authors' age assignments of the same beds. DorC 
(1 969, 1972) and Robardet (1 973) assign a Cambrian age to these redbeds since they under- 
lie the Grks de Montabot of latest Cambrian age. The Tremadocian age, although of little 
significance in light of the complete remagnetization, has been used in this study and is 
taken to be latest Cambrian to earliest Ordovician. 
Site Q was the only site of all the Cambro-Ordovician sites in Normandy that showed two 
distinct components of magnetization. The higher-temperature component was large enough 
and, although somewhat scattered, consistent enough to be taken as the characteristic 
direction (D = 200.8", I = + 30.5" before unfolding; D = 200.8', I = - 27.5" afder unfolding). 
This component was of mixed polarity, containing the only normal polarities seen in Group 
D. The lower-temperature component showed a steep negative inclination (D = 187.4", 
I= -42.3') before structural correction, and an anomalous direction (D = 67.6", I= 
- 74.2") after structural correction. The in situ lower-temperature direction could represent 
a Late Mesozoic-Early Cenozoic remagnetization since the resulting pole of 64.8" N, 
163.5" E is in close agreement with poles of this time for Western Europe and the Russian 
Platform (McElhinny 1973, table 29, p. 244). 
The mean of all in situ directions for the redbeds of St RCmy (Figure 8(c)) yields a

High-temperature directions - further discussion 
All four groups within the collection of Devonian and Cambro-Ordovician rocks showed 
some evidence of high-temperature components of magnetization. Few of these high- 
temperature components were well defined for the following reasons: (1) low intensities

samples picked up spurious laboratory magnetizations as susceptibilities changed at high 
temperatures, and (3) there may have been an overlap of blocking temperature spectra of 
the Characteristic direction and the high-temperature direction in some of the samples. 
Laboratory methods were used that minimized the first two problems. The Cryogenic 
magnetometer with sensitivity to lO-’A/m for a 10 cm3 sample was used for all samples 
of low initial intensity, as well as for many of the rest of the samples. The spurious 
magnetization observed was most frequently the result of the sample being in the Earth’s 
field during transfer from furnace to magnetometer and particularly while held stationary 
in an upright position during insertion in the sample holder of the Cryogenic magnetometer. 
Once placed in the field-free space of the magnetometer this magnetization decayed 
exponentially. Since the largest portion of the Earth’s field is in the vertical component at 
the latitude of our laboratory, an averaging technique was used to cancel out the introduced 
magnetization. The sample was measured in the upright position, then inverted (which had 
to be done in the Earth’s field again) and measured again; the two measurements were then 
averaged, 
If the blocking temperature spectra of the characteristic direction and that of the high- 
temperature direction were discrete and it was possible to measure the sample up to the 
blocking temperature of the high-temperature component without interference of the 
spurious magnetization or noise-level intensities, then the high-temperature direction was 
seen as a univectorial decay to the origin. Criteria of reliability were set to correspond with 
this situation. If the high-temperature magnetization was defined by at least three roughly 
co-linear points, decayed to the origin, and was different from the characteristic direction, 
it was taken to be reliable. Group means of the reliable high-temperature directions are 
shown in Table 2 without parentheses. However, if the blocking temperature spectra of the 
two components overlapped, and either there was interference by the spurious magnetiza- 
tion or intensities were too low, then the high-temperature component was never seen 
without some contribution from the characteristic direction and univectorial decay would 
not be observed. These directions are averaged with the reliable directions, but the results are 
entered in Table 2 in parentheses. 
Halls’ (1 976) least-squares method of determining convergence of remagnetization circles 
was used in an effort to isolate the high-temperature component. Best-fitting great circles 
were defined for those portions of the demagnetization that involved the high-temperature 
components. As Halls (1976) has noted the method only works when the recorded pdrtions 
of the high-temperature directions approach a tighter cluster than that of the characteristic 
direction. This is not the case, as was seen in the Syncline of Montmartin and also the 
Cambro-Ordovician of Normandy, even after unfolding where characteristic directions show 
a large dispersion. Thus, it was not possible to define the high-temperature component by 
the converging great circle method. 
Group means were calculated for the high-temperature components meeting the criteria 
of reliability set above. Only Group B (Cambro-Ordovician of Paimpol-Br6hec) yields a 
Fisher precision parameter value greater than 10. This group of high-temperature directions 
passes a fold-test (as seen in Fig. 10 and Table 2). Group means were also calculated for all 
final high-temperature components whether they passed the reliability criteria or not and are 
seen in Table 2 in parentheses. Most of the group means showed very poor grouping (see 
Fisher precision values in Table 2). 
Despite the large scatter in the high-temperature directions, the group mean directions all 
lie between the Devonian characteristic direction and the reliable high-temperature direction

Discussion 
The present results from the Devonian and Cambro-Ordovician of Normandy and Brittany 
can be divided into three groups: (1) those from the Late Devonian redbeds (Group A) 
with a south-south-westerly declination and shallow positive inclination, (2) the 
remagnetized directions from the Cambro-Ordovician redbeds and volcanics (Groups B, C 
and D), and (3) the set of directions obtained from the high-temperature components of 
magnetization (Groups B and C). 
The Late Devonian redbeds of the Syncline of Montmartin, Normandy, yield a group 
mean declination/inclination of 213.4"/+ 27.7" after unfolding and a pole position at 
19.8" N, 144.2" E. This result from Group A is the only result for which there is no evidence 
for remagnetization. Although some high-temperature directions were observed, these were 
essentially random. Chemical, thermal and alternating field demagnetizations all agreed 
with each other and revealed only one characteristic direction of magnetization. Unfortu- 
nately, a fold test is not possible because of a lack of different structural corrections. 
The second set of results is obtained from the Cambro-Ordovician redbeds and volcanics. 
The redbeds from Normandy (Group D) were remagnetized during or after the folding of 
the synclinorium as seen in the failure of the fold test. The pole position obtained from the 
in situ directions corresponds to the pole at the time of remagnetization and is located at 
33.4" N, 15 1 .5" E (see Fig. 11). The other two Cambro-Ordovician collections from 
Paimpol-BrBhec and Erquy-Cap Frkhel in Brittany are probably remagnetized as well. 
Because of the lack of different structural corrections, fold tests are inconclusive for 
Groups B and C, and we have, therefore, plotted two pole positions for these groups in 
Fig. 11 -one pole corresponding to the directions before unfolding, the other pole 
representing the directions after unfolding (see also Table 1). Even though there is no palaeo- 
magnetic indication whether the directions of magnetization of Groups B and C are pre- or 
post-folding, there are some geologic arguments that point to a post-folding age. The folding 
phases in Brittany are the Bretonian (c. 360MA) and Sudetian (c. 320MA) phases (e.g. 
Rutten 1969). Post-tectonic dikes, however, cut the formations along the northern coast of 
Brittany, and have recently been dated at The University of Rennes as 325 MA old, which 
indicates that the Bretonian phase is probably responsible for the deformation of Groups B 
and C. If we assume that the secondary K/Ar age of 345 MA obtained from the Paimpol- 
Brbhec trachy-andesite corresponds to the age of the remagnetization, we can assume also 
that the magnetization is of post-folding age. Consequently, we have favoured the pole 
positions for Groups B and C calculated for the in siru directions. 
A mean direction calculated from the site means of Group A (after tectonic correction) 
and the site means of Groups B, C and D (before tectonic correction) gives a declination/ 
inclination of 207.8"/+ 15.9" (N= 21; k = 19.9; ag5 = 7.3"). This direction results in a 
combined pole position at 28.1" N, 146.4" E (dp = 3.87"; dm = 7.50°), which can be 
compared with poles from the part of Europe north of the Hercynian fold belt ('stable 
Europe'). A stable-European Late Devonian mean pole at 30.2" N, 161.4" E (N= 14, Ag5 = 
4.8") and a nearby Early Carboniferous mean pole at 28.5" N, 163.6" E (N = 16, Ag5 = 6.5") 
are based on data from Norway, Great Britain and the Russian Platform (French 1976). 
The time of the polar wander shift between Early and Late Carboniferous is not well 
documented. Russian Platform data of Early and Middle Carboniferous age (the Russian

collision tectonics could be the source of the Hercynian orogeny if microcontinents existed 
within Hercynian Europe or if subduction took place south of Hercynian Europe and the 
remnants of the zone were incorporated into the Alpine belt. 
The third set of results yielded pole positions significantly different from the other data 
sets. These poles were obtained from the six reliable high-temperature directions from the 
Cambro-Ordovician of Paimpol-Brdhec and from site K from the Cambro-Ordovician(?) 
of Erquy-Cap Frdhel. A discussion of the implications of these poles has limitations that 
must be emphasized before proceeding. Both poles are based on a few samples, and in the 
case of Erquy-Cap Frdhel they are all from a single site. Consequently, the poles cannot be 
taken as representative of the entire collection.

The mean declination/inclination after unfolding of the six reliable high-temperature 
directions from Paimpol-BrBhec is 325'/+ 37', is taken to be of normal polarity, and yields 
a pole position at 50.4' N, 234.4' E. High-temperature components of site K give a mean 
declination/inclination of 312'1- 1" and a pole position at 25.9" N, 233.2' E. These mean 
directions and pole positions could, with the above-mentioned reservations, be taken as 
representative of the Late Cambrian-Early Ordovician palaeomagnetic field. A comparison 
with contemporaneous poles from Great Britain reveals that the areas may have had entirely 
different positions. This is particularly apparent in their palaeolatitudes as indicated by their 
inclinations. Whereas the Armorican Massif was at latitudes between the equator and 20", 
Great Britain occupied Early Ordovician latitudes of at least 30'. Current interpretations 
of the British ('Caledonian') apparent polar wander path make this a southern hemisphere 
palaeolatitude, implying that the Armorican Massif was more northerly than Great Britain! 
It should be noted, however, that the Caledonian mobile belt may not be representative of 
the stable part of Europe (the Baltic Shield and the Russian Platform) at that time and that 
a comparison between the Armorican Massif and the Caledonides may not be very meaning- 
ful. The few Cambrian and Ordovician poles from the Russian Platform are rather un- 
substantiated, but they do agree favourably in latitude with our results and would not 
indicate the need for a large ocean between stable Europe and the Armorican Massif. As 
these conclusions must be rather tentative, and since other studies on Cambrian and 
Ordovician rocks of the Armorican Massif are in progress at the Universities of Rennes, 
Leeds and Michigan, we will not elaborate at this point. 
Based on the bulk of data from this study of redbeds and trachy-andesites of Normandy 
and Brittany, there appears to be no significant separation of Hercynian Europe from stable 
Europe in the Late Devonian and Early Carboniferous. A plate tectonic model calling on 
Late Palaeozoic subduction of a large ocean separating the two areas and ending in a 
continent-continent collision is not supported. A separation of Hercynian Europe (i.e. the 
Armorican Massif) and the African and South American continents in the Devonian and the 
subsequent collision of the two land masses would suggest the possibility of a subduction 
zone to the south of Hercynian Europe. An ensialic cause of the Hercynian orogeny in 
southern England, northern France and Belgium remains a possibility, although our data 
do not present the resolution needed to decide whether a small ocean could have existed 
there.

1 Introduction
The Fongen-Hyllingen complex is a synorogenic layered gabbro intrusion, situated about
75 km south-east of Trondheim in the Norwegian Caledonides (Fig. 1). A preliminary
account of the complex has been presented by Wilson & Olesen (1975). The present study
has been undertaken to add to the scanty palaeomagnetic results from the Scandinavian
Caledonides.

2 Geology
2.1 REGIONAL SETTING OF THE FONGEN-HYLLINGEN COMPLEX
The Fongen-Hyllingen complex is emplaced in rocks belonging to the allochthonous
Western Complex (e.g. Gee 1975) of the southern Scandinavian Caledonides. The gabbro
intrudes metasediments and metavolcanics of the Fundsjd group, which may correlate with
the Stq5ren group to the west (eg. Roberts, Springer & Wolff 1970), and the Ordovician
(Tremadocian) fossil Dictyonema flabelliforme has been found in rocks of the aureole
(Vogt 1940). The gabbro hornfelsed tightly folded rocks and has inclusions of folded
country rocks, so the intrusion clearly post-dates at least one fold phase. A contact meta-
morphic aureole with index-minerals cordierite, sillimanite and andalusite is developed, with
additional garnet present throughout. The peak of regional metamorphism was reached
shortly after the emplacement of the complex and was accompanied by the main deforma-
tion phase in the area (Olesen et al. 1973). In the western part of the aureole the contact
metamorphic assemblages are overprinted by regional assemblages such as andalusite being
replaced by kyanite and sillimanite by staurolite and white mica.
During regional metamorphism, large parts of the Fongen--Hyllingen complex were
altered to hornblende metagabbros, though often retaining igneous microstructures, and
foliated amplvbolites were produced where metamorphism of the gabbro was accompanied
by penetrative deformation. The gabbro and its envelope were later folded during the
Selbu Tydal phase (Olesen et al. 1973) and the present form of the Fongen-Hyllingen
complex (Wilson & Olesen 1975) is to some extent influenced by its situation in the Tydal
synform which is overturned towards the east. The gabbro can thus with certainty be
regarded as synorogenic.
The Fundsjd Group rocks enveloping the complex occupy a controversial tectono-
stratigraphic position but are interpreted by Zwart (1974) and Gee (1975) as part of the
Kdli (Supergroup) of the Seve --Kdli Nappe complex. Orogenic deformation of this nappe,
with folding, metamorphism and thrusting is considered by Gee & Wilson (1974) to have
both started and finished in Silurian times. Important evidence as to the timing of the end
of the Caledonian orogeny in this region is found at Rdragen, some 50 km SSE of Fongen,
where rocks probably belonging to the Kdli Supergroup are unconformably overlain by
continental conglomerates and sandstones, identified from plant fossils as of Lower
Devonian age (Halle 1916; Hdeg 1936). These Devonian rocks have however been affected
by a late phase of the Caledonian orogeny since they are folded, faulted and show evidence
of low grade metamorphism (Holmsen 1963), and the possibility remains that they were
transported along with the pre-Devonian rocks of the Seve-Kdli Nappe during the final
thrusting.
2.2 PETROLOGY OF THE COMPLEX
Rocks of the Fongen-Hyllingen complex vary from ultramafics, through olivine gabbros,
gabbros and norites to diorites, monzonites and quartz-bearing syenites. Rhythmic layering
is widely developed and there is an extensive cryptic variation (Esbensen, Thy & Wilson
1978). The deepest levels of the intrusion occur in the north where layering is arranged in
a saucer-like form, emphasized by later folding. In the southern part of the complex around
Hyllingen mountain, described by Kisch (1962) and Nilsen (1973), the rhythmic layering
strikes roughly north--south and dips east, the rocks younging consistently to the east.

three parts. These are the Fongen and Ruten sequences in the north (Fig. 1) and the

2.3 OPAQUE PHASES FROM THE FONGEN-HY LLINGEN COMPLEX
The primary oxides in the northern part of the complex are titanomagnetite belonging to
the magnetite- ulvospinel solid solution series, and ilmenite belonging to the ilmenite-
haematite solid solution series. Titanomagnetite (30 mol per cent ulvospinel) normally
dominates over ilmenite (0-2 mol per cent haematite). Two microstructural varieties can be
distinguished; ilmenite and titanomagnetite occurring as intercumulus grains interstitial to
silicates, and subhedral to euhedral cumulus grains in which titanomagnetite dominates
over ilmenite. The grain size of the cumulus Fe-Ti oxides ranges from 1 mm to below
0.05 mm.
Two types of titanomagnetite are found, the first indicating an early stage of ulvospinel
exsolution and the second a sub-solidus oxidation of ulvospinel at high temperature during
magmatic or late-magmatic conditions (Buddington & Lindsley 1964). Ulvospinel can be
completely or partly replaced by magnetite/ilmenite intergrowth and is found in one third
of the samples where it occurs in a fine cloth-like microstructure with possible single or
pseudosingle domain magnetite in the micron-range. The most common microstructures are,
however, a subhedral coarse ilmenite/magnetite intergrowth or an intergrowth of fine
ilmenite lamellae in magnetite corresponding to oxidation class 11-111 (Ade-Hall et al. 1968).
Similar assemblages have been described, among others by Vincent (1960) and Mathison
(1975). Fine acicular Al- Fe spinel is found in the magnetite and, as proposed by Turnock
& Eugster (1 962), results from exsolution.
Ilmenite occurs as mm-sized interstitial grains, sometimes with tapering twins. Ilmenite
can replace titanomagnetite when they have mutual grain boundaries. Equivalent micro-
structures have been interpreted as resulting from replacement during crystallization (Gierth
& Krause 1973) or as a sub-solidus reaction (Krause & Pape 1975). Haematite exsolution
is not observed, which according to Ramdohr (1969) indicates less than 6 per cent Fe203
in the ilmenite-haematite solid solution series.
Sulphides occur in amounts less than 2 per cent of the total opaque phase in the cumulus
magnetite zone. Pyrrhotite is the dominant sulphide and may contribute to the remanence
in a few cases. It occurs in interstitial to subhedral aggregates with minor amounts of pent-
landite and chalcopyrite with sub-solidus exsolution microstructures.
Secondary magnetite, and to a lesser extent ilmenite, is formed during late-magmatic
replacement of olivine with magnetite- orthopyroxene symplectites or by reactions between
olivine and plagioclase. The magnetite occurs with the silicates in a vermicular to tabular
symplectic intergrowth or as irregular grains from a few microns to mm-size often surround-
ing partly or completely altered olivine. Magnetite and ilmenite are also found as tabular
to acicular grains along the prismatic cleavage in the pyroxenes. Magnetite is only altered to
a relatively minor degree with a weak marginal decomposition to goethte in some instances.
The opaque phases hence record a prolonged crystallization and sub-solidus re-equilibra-
tion history. The ilmenite/magnetite intergrowth clearly post-dates the ulvospinel/magnetite

3 Palaeomagnetic investigations
A total of 1 11 palaeomagnetic samples were collected from eight sites in the gabbro around
Fongen mountain (Fig. 1, sites 1-7 and 1 l), two sites in strongly deformed and amphiboli-
tized gabbro (sites 8 and 9) and one site in a trondhjemite intrusion (site 10).
In the field 10 hand samples were collected from each site with an areal coverage of
typically 30 x 100 m2. Unmetamorphosed sites were selected from previous knowledge.
Unweathered hand samples were loosened by a hammer, the north direction was measured

The compass measurements were individually controlled by topographical sights and no

strike are estimated to be about ? 1" and ? 2" respectively.

Site 1, however, behaves in a different way. It converges against a subhorizontal SW-
direction, and when taking a closer look at the demagnetization stereograms of the other
gabbro sites, it appears that a characteristic SW-component is present in all the other sites,
although not as clearly depicted as in site 1 which only sporadically shows the NW-direction
(except specimens 8 and 10, Fig. 3).
The SW-direction is obviously not as well defined as the NW-direction, and a formal
palaeomagnetic stability index such as that of Symons & Stupavsky (1974), which applies
well for the NW-direction is of but little help in defining the SW-direction. In 17 cases the
SW-component is revealed in or even dominates the NRM, and the remanence migrates to
the NW during progressive af cleaning. In some cases the SW-component emerges in a
moderate demagnetizing field between 200 and lOOOOe, but stable high coercivity SW-
components are only found in a few cases, notably in site 6. The coercivity spectra of the
NW- and the SW-components apparently overlap, and both cover a wide range, probably
reflecting the wide range in grain size of the magnetic phases present.
The best evidence for the relative magnetic chronology is seen in sites 3,4 and 7 (Fig. 3),
where the SW-component is clearly removed by cleaning in higher ac fields, thus illustrating
the dominance of the high coercivity components of the NW-direction. In site 4 younger
viscous components are nearly absent, making the picture even more clear. In this site, it
also appears that the blocking period of the magnetic recordings was of sufficient duration
to capture normal as well as reverse polarity of both directions.
As all the petrological events of relevance to the magnetic blocking of the remanence
occurred below the respective Curie-points (G 575°C for titanomagnetite), the magnetizing
processes must have occurred during the postmagmatic and metamorphic (and tectonic)
history of the gabbro.
Further, the local temperature of the gabbro during the blocking of the SW-component
was not higher than the blocking temperatures of the NW-component, otherwise the NW-
direction could not have been preserved; both remanences appear to be carried essentially
by titanomagnetites of equivalent Curie-points. The generally higher coercivities of the NW-
component probably also indicate that at least part of the carriers of the NW-component
are more fine-grained than those of the SE-component.
Finally, it should be noted that in site 1 only, five specimens (Fl-5) have relatively high
content of pyrrhotite as compared to magnetite; the Curie-point of pyrrhotite is fairly low
(300-325"C), and site 1 is the only one in which the SW-component is completely
dominant. This supports the other indications that the SW-component is younger than the

244 N. Abrahamsen et al.
As a first approximation, the pole - P2, corresponding to a reversed SW-direction, may
readily be interpreted as a reversely polarized palaeomagnetic pole of Caledonian, Upper
Silurian-Lower Devonian age, as it is not far away from other known poles of this age (see
further discussion below).
The position of the pole PI of the NW-direction corresponding to the dominant NW
magnetization of the gabbro is, however, not readily explained. It is situated about 90"
away from the P2 pole, and is placed in the NE-Pacific area (Fig. 5). The pole PI cannot be
explained as a much younger magnetization because of the absence of any correlation with
post-Palaeozoic poles, bearing in mind the dominant nature of the PI pole over the Pz pole
and their apparent relative age.
As components of both polarities appear to be present in some specimens (notably 22.3,
24.31, 31,32, 38, 41.2, 42.2, 52.2, 58, 68.21, 105.21 and 107) it could be argued that the
NW-direction is just the accidental mean of two shallow SW-subcomponents of opposite
polarity (SW and NE) combining to a NW-direction, possibly supplied by a steep normal
component of a recently induced viscous component. This is quite unlikely, because the
convergence of the NW-direction is so well pronounced (it would be expected to show
a random variation confined to the vertical plane orthogonal to the SW-NE axis) and
because the recent viscous remanent magnetization, if not completely destroyed by the
cleaning process, would tend to parallelize the combined directions in a steep northerly
downdip (or southerly updip in case of a reversed field) direction in the vertical plane
containing the SW-direction.
It would therefore appear that both poles must be explained in a Palaeozoic context.
One possibility is that the PI pole could be an original Silurian/Devonian TCRM, the
apparent palaeomagnetic field having made an excursion of about 90" to the pole PI in Late
Caledonian time, which was stable long enough to cause the NW-direction to be locked in
firmly at the expense of the (probably slightly younger) P2 pole of the general Caledonian
SW direction. Considering the dimensions of the gabbro, the depth of emplacement (15-
20 km) and particularly the synorogenic environment, the total cooling time of the gabbro
to below the active blocking range of the TRM, of which the thermomagnetic blocking range
is a considerable part, must have been of the order of several millions of years (e.g. Jaeger
1968). This palaeomagnetic polar excursion explanation is not very plausible, as out of
about 50 published palaeomagnetic investigations of NW-European Palaeozoic formations
(e.g. Creer 1970; McElhinny 1973) there are only two poles in the vicinity ofPl. These are
Nos. 3 and 9 in Table 2, both of which are too old and with a high scatter (ag5= 20°), the
palaeomagnetic reliability of No. 3 in addition being questionable (McElhinny 1973, note
p. 289). The Late Ordovician (Caradocian) probably non-axial dipole field, which appears
to have been recorded by some hypabyssal intrusions in North Wales and in dyke swarms in
northern England (Piper, private communication, 1978) is also too old for our case.
Another interesting possibility is that the two directions record the rotation of a block
within the Scandinavian Caledonides. A block including the Fongen-Hyllingen complex
must then be supposed to have rotated anticlockwise around a subvertical axis by an angle
of about 90' relative to the normal NE or NNE updip Palaeozoic field direction after cooling
down below the effective blocking temperatures (say c. 500-550°C) of the titano-
magnetites present. This rotation could presumably have taken place during the nappe
emplacements. During or shortly after the rotation, and after a reversal of the field polarity
(both polarities are known from other investigations of Caledonian rocks), the SW-direction
was then induced as a secondary TCRM, which now defines the 'Caldeonian' pole Pz of the
gabbro complex. As the -P2 pole lies some 10-20" W of the main cluster of other Upper
Silurian-Lower Devonian poles (Fig. 9, it could be postulated that this direction was

According to this hypothesis the dominant NW direction does not define a true palaeo-
magnetic pole but rather the local rotation of the pertinent block. Rotation in the opposite
(clockwise) direction of about 90' is an equally possible alternative; in this case no reversal
needs to have taken place between the two recording times.
it would be useful to try to relate the possible timing of the acquisition of the two
magnetic components to the geological events in which the Fongen-Hyllingen complex
has been involved. Contact metamorphic assemblages surrounding the complex indicate
emplacement at about 5 Kb, equivalent to a depth of 15-20km, and intrusion was shortly
followed by the peak of regional metamorphism at up to about 7 Kb and 650°C (Olesen
et al. 1973). In view of the well defined nature of the NW-direction and the high tempera-
tures involved during regional metamorphism, it seems likely that this magnetic component
was established during cooling after the regional metamorphic peak. Broadly speaking the
peak of regional metamorphism and deformation was followed by two phases of mesoscopic
folding (Olesen et al. 1973), which appear to have had little effect on the competent gabbro
complex. These were followed by a major fold phase, the Selbu-Tydal phase of Olesen et al.
(1973) which influenced the shape of the gabbro complex (Wilson & Olesen 1975) and had
the effect of steepening the dips of the rhythmic layering around Fongen mountain where
most of the palaeomagnetic samples were collected. This Selgu-Tydal phase comprises
essentially open folds with no associated axial plane foliation. The temperatures prevailing
during this fold episode are poorly known, and it is not clear whether the NW and/or the SW
components pre- or post-date this fold phase and should consequently be corrected for dip.
The closest and hence most relevant palaeomagnetic results from Scandinavia at present
available are from the upper Ordovician synorogenic Sulitjelma Gabbro some 500 km to the
NNE (pole 11 in Fig. 5), from the Upper Silurian Ringerike Sandstone 350 km to the south
(pole 19), from the Lower or Middle Devonian sediments at Roragen 50 km to the south
(pole 22), and from the Middle Devonian Kvamshesten Sandstone some 350 km to the
south-west (pole 23).
The palaeomagnetic pole from the (older) Sulitjelma Gabbro, when uncorrected for dip,
is in good agreement with those from the British Isles (poles 6--lO), and the Sulitjelma pole
clearly lies outside any block possibly involved in only a 'local' rotation in the southern
Scandinavian Caledonides. The precision of pole 11, however, is quite low (k = 6, ag5=
28", N= 6), the sites sampled being metamorphosed, tectonized and folded (Piper 1974,
1975a; Mason 1975), and the constraints from this pole on possible rotational interpreta-
tions hence would be rather broad.
The Devonian Roragen Old Red Sandstones (pole 22) are late orogenic; deposited on rocks
of the nappe which contains the Fongen--Hyllingen complex; they may therefore post-date
the possible rotational movements of the block containing the gabbro. The palaeomagnetic
poles for the Roragen Sandstone, the Ringerike Sandstone (pole 19) and the Kvamshesten
Sandstone (pole 23) are mutually consistent and define an 'Old Red' Norwegian pole close
to 20" N, 160" E. A moderate rotation of 15" anticlockwise for the Kvamshesten area was
suggested by Storetvedt (1967), because of the unconformity and slightly younger age of the
sediments as compared to the base, to make a better coincidence of the Norwegian Old Red
poles. Considering the Fisher statistics of pole 23 (ags= 9"), however, a rotation of only a
few degrees may suffice in this case. The poles of four supposed Palaeozoic dykes on the
island of Bornholm (pole 16) are also close to this Devonian Old Red pole. The Roragen
pole position therefore appears to have been established essentially after the suggested
rotation of the pertinent block containing the Fongen -Hyllingen complex.

5 Conclusions
In the Fongen -Hyllingen gabbro complex two characteristic palaeomagnetic directions are
recorded, a well defined NW direction (P,)a nd a less well defined but distinct SW direction
(Pz), and it appears that the NW component predates the SW one. The -Pz pole of the SW
(reversed) direction lies fairly close to late Caledonian poles from Scandinavia. It seems that
the PI pole was established during cooling after the peak of regional metamorphism and may
record either a persistent geomagnetic excursion during Late Caledonian time, or a roughly
90" rotation of a crustal block in the Scandinavian Caledonides.
In the last decade numerous palaeomagnetic investigations have been published,
suggesting azimuthal block rotations of crustal segments of local to regional scales in
orogenic collision zones. In most cases the field geologist had no observations to corroborate
such ideas prior to the palaeomagnetic evidence. Some minor or medium scale examples in
the Mediterranean mobile belt are the Northern Calcareous Alps showing about 45" clock-
wise rotation with respect to Eurasia since the Jurassic (Mauritsch & Frisch 1978), the
Corso-Sardinian Plate showing about 50' anticlockwise rotation during the Early Miocene
(De Jong et al. 1973; Storetvedt & Markhus 1978), and the Iberian and Italian peninsulae
also showing anticlockwise rotations of between 35 and 70" since the Triassic. These and
other examples from Turkey and Japan are summarized by McElhinny (1973).
Probably the most detailed sampled Palaeozoic region is the British Isles, the older
Palaeozoic palaeomagnetic data of which are known to be quite complex. During the
Caledonian orogeny the isles appear to have behaved as a separate crustal plate (Piper 1978),
and in a recent palaeocontinental reconstruction Morel & Irving (1978), although with some
hesitation, suggest that between 450 and -400 Ma the British Isles (perhaps in part)
-
rotated over 90' relative to Gondwanaland about a local axis. The Fongen- Hyllingen
gabbro complex may have recorded the rotation of a comparable orogenic plate within the
Scandinavian Caledonides.
Other apparently anomalous Palaeozoic palaeomagnetic results from Europe have been
reported, such as two Irish palaeomagnetic directions from the Mid-Ordovician Mweelrea
ignimbrites and the Connemara gabbros (Morris et al. 1973) which may be interpreted either
as 40' anticlockwise and clockwise local rotations, respectively, or as geomagnetic
excursions. It is hardly possible at this stage definitively to decide which hypothesis
--
geomagnetic excursion or block rotation -is to be preferred to account for the palaeo-
magnetic results from the Fongen-Hyllingen complex. Further palaeomagnetic investiga-
tions from the Scandinavian Caledonides, as well as structural evidence related to possible
azimuthal rotation, may throw more light on this interesting problem.

The Middle Jurassic Camaraca Formation, Arica, Chile: 
palaeomagnetism, K-Ar age dating and tectonic 
implications 
H. c. Palmer and A. Hayatsu Department ofGeophysics, 
The University of Western Ontario, Lmdon, Ontario, Canada N6A 5B7 
W. D. MacDonald Department of Geological sciences, 
State University of New York, Binghampton, New York 13901, USA 
Received 1979 November 6; in original form 1979 May 21 
Summary. Palaeomagnetic and K-Ar whole rock age studies are reported 
from samples of the Camaraca Formation exposed near Arica (18.6"S, 
70.3' W), Chile. The Camaraca Formation is composed of andesites and inter- 
bedded marine shales which yield a fauna placing the formation in the 
Bajocian-Callovian stages of the Jurassic. Our sampling sites span a strati- 
graphic thickness of 2 km and yield a reversal stratigraphy of: N-R-N. 
The K-Ar isochron method, applied to least altered samples from the 
formation, gives a sharply defiied age of 157 Myr which is in agreement with 
the palaeontologically assigned age of the formation. Normal and reversed 
directions of remanent magnetization, isolated by af and thermal de- 
magnetization methods, are statistically antiparallel. The pole position, 
computed from these directions of magnetization, is at 010" E, 70%"S 
(Ag5= 6.0'). This pole position, when compared with the wellstudied Chon 
Aike Formation of Argentina, suggests that the sampling region has under- 
gone a 28" ? 28" counter-clockwise rotation about a local vertical axis. The 
large uncertainty (between 0' and 56") in this estimate is due to the large 
scatter in the South American reference data. When compared with African 
Jurassic palaeopoles, with allowance made for the opening of the South 
Atlantic, a counter-clockwise rotation of 44" -I 14" is indicated. 
Introduction 
The pioneering work of Creer (1965) demonstrated that the pole with respect to South 
America in Mesozoic time was close to its present position. Thus, the Mesozoic magnetiza- 
tion in rocks from equatorial South America would have shallow inclination and be 
characterized dominantly by the horizontal component. Such conditions are optimal for 
applying the pdaeomagnetic test for the orocline hypothesis (Carey 1955); an orocline being 
an orogenic system which has been flexed in plan to a horseshoe or elbow shape. The 
essential part of the oroclinal hypothesis is that the change in trend is an impressed strain

(Carey 1955, 1976) rather than an original feature. One of the best examples claimed as an 
oroclinal bend is the change in trend of the Andean structures from near north-south to 
NW-SE at the Chile-Peru border. This orocline has been termed the Bolivian orocline by 
Carey (1958) and also referred to in his Fig. 27 as the Peruvian orocline. The initial objective 
of this study was a test of the oroclinal bending hypothesis using the palaeomagnetic 
technique as a tool. 
Middle Jurassic andesites of the Camaraca Formation strike north-south in the extreme 
north of Chile, near Arica (Salas et al. 1966). In the immediately adjacent region of Peru 
the South American coastline changes abruptly from north trending to north-west-trending. 
Probable correlatives of the Camaraca Formation there are the Chocolate Volcanic 
Formation and the Guaneros Formation (Jaen & Ortiz 1963). The latter formations have a 
north-west regional tectonic strike. Accordingly oriented samples were collected from these 
formations to test whether the Bolivian orocline is indeed an impressed strain feature or 
whether the change in tectonic grain merely reflects a change in trend of the original de- 
positional basin. Unfortunately, the rocks from the Peruvian exposures proved to be very 
unstable magnetically and no meaningful palaeomagnetic information could be extracted 
from them. On the other hand, the majority of samples from the Chilean Camaraca 
Formation proved to be moderately stable and we here report those results, together with 
the results of a K-Ar age study of some of them. 
H. C. Palmer, A. Hayatm and W. D. MacDonald 
Geology 
The rocks of the Arica Group consist of two formations: the primarily volcanic Camaraca 
Formation and the primarily sedimentary LQS Tarros Formation (Salas et al. 1966). 
Ammonite assemblages place the Camaraca Formation in the Bajocian- Callovian stages of 
the Middle Jurassic whereas the Los Tarros Formation is assigned to the Oxfordian stage of 
the Upper Jurassic. The Arica Group is overlain discordantly by the Neocomian AtajaEa 
Formation. All of our sampling sites are in the andesites of the Camaraca Formation. The 
thickness of the Camaraca Formation has been estimated at 1900 m (Salas et al. 1966) and 
2800 m (Tobar, Salas & Kast 1968). Much of the uncertainty in the thickness of the forma- 
tion stems from the fact that it is severely broken by numerous north-trending faults and 
also intruded by dykes neither of which are illustrated on Fig. 1, The stratigraphic relation- 
ship of the Camaraca Formation to older rocks is not known as the base of the formation 
is below sea-level. Older rocks represented by mica schists and gneisses of the Pre- 
cambrian (?> Belen Schists are brought up in fault slices 100 km to the east of the main 
outcrop belt of the Arica Group (Salas et al. 1966). These schists are overlain uncon- 
formably by the Cretaceous-Tertiary Lupica Group rocks. However, because of the 
intervening cover of ignimbrite sheets of the Middle Tertiary Oxaya Formation, the relation- 
ship of the Lupica Group to the Arica Group is not known and thus the relationshp of the 
Camaraca Formation to Andean basement is an open question. We dwell on this point 
because one of the results of this study is evidence that the Camaraca Formation has under- 
gone an anticlockwise rotation in addition to the 20"-30" eastward tilting which is 
geologically observable. 
Sampling sites (Fig. 1) are priiarily in andesite flows of the Camaraca Formation. A few 
sites are in related diabase and microdiorite sheets and dykes. The flow rocks are grey, 
brownish grey and brownish red rocks commonly porphyritic in plagioclase and less 
commonly in pyroxene or the alteration products of pyroxene. Amygdular phases of flows 
are sparse. A few flows exhibit pillow structure. Mineralogically the flows consist mainly 
of plagioclase, clinopyroxene and oxides. Scarce biotite is in part altered to haematite.

Olivine or the alteration products of olivine, serpentine and oxides, are sparsely present 
in a few flows. The intensity of secondary mineral alteration varies generally increasing 
from north to south. The least altered samples were taken immediately south of Arica, 
with chlorite, calcite and sparse sericitic alteration of the plagioclase being the only 
obvious secondary minerals. Southward across the east-west faults shown in Fig. 1, clino- 
pyroxenes are partially replaced or wholly replaced by calcite, chlorite, epidote and possibly 
pumpellyite. Alteration of the plagioclases to the same assemblage of minerals together with 
white mica becomes more pronounced from north to south. Tremolite-actinolite as a 
replacement mineral appears in the south of the area (site 20, Fig. 1) in a dyke rock near 
Caleta Vitor. The mineralogical evidence is consistent with the contention of Salas et al. 
(1966) that most of the east-west faults cutting the Camaraca Formation are down-thrown 
to the north, the more southerly exposures thus representing deeper levels. Although lacking

metamorphism to conditions approaching the greenschist facies. 
The iron-titanium oxides, now greatly altered to maghaemite and haematite, were 
titanomagnetites in which the level of original hgh temperature deuteric oxidation was 
generally low. The majority of samples examined in reflected light with oil immersion 
exhibit relict titanomagnetite dominated by oxidation classes 1 to 3 as defined by Wilson & 
Haggerty (1966), Ade-Hall et al. (1968) and Haggerty (1976). In the extreme northern part 
of the sampling area, ‘exsolved’ ilmenite is still present, whereas in the southern part of the 
sampling area the included ilmenite lamellae are totally replaced by black sphene, a 
characteristic burial metamorphism feature typical of conditions from the base of the 
laumontite zone to the epidote zone (Ade-Hall, Palmer & Hubbard 1971). Thus the iron- 
titanium oxide petrography is consistent with that found in transmission microscopy and 
supports the view that the southern exposures of the formation have suffered more intense 
burial metamorphism. 
H. C. Palmer, A. Hayatsu and W. D. Madonuld 
Sampling and laboratory methods 
An early collection of block samples (AR series) was made in 1967 as part of a recon- 
naissance sampling of various Mesozoic units of northern Chile. Preliminary analysis of core 
samples drilled from these 18 block samples yielded an encouraging result with both 
polarities being present and reasonably good grouping of the sample directions within each 
of these two polarity groups. A second collection (CA series) was made in 1974 using 
portable rock drills in which generally four independently oriented cores were obtained at 
each of 26 sites. In the second collection, most of the sampling was concentrated in two 
profiles (sites 3-12 and 18-26 of Fig. 1) where uninterrupted stratigraphic successions 
could be obtained. This sampling scheme attempted to gain some knowledge of the reversal 
frequency in the part of the Middle Jurassic represented by the Camaraca Formation. The 
azimuthal component of orientation of the field-drilled cores was determined with a sun 
compass and checked with a Brunton compass corrected for the local published magnetic 
declination. Agreement of the sun and magnetic bearings to within 3” indicates that there is 
no orientation problem with the older.collection of block samples (AR series) which were 
oriented by magnetic methods only. 
In the laboratory two to six specimens were drilled from each block sample and one or 
two specimens could be obtained from each field-drilled core. One polished thin section 
from each of the block samples and from one of the cores from each of the 26 field-drilled 
sites was prepared. In addition, small chips each weighing 0.5-1 g were machined for use in 
a Curie balance. 
The early stages of the palaeomagnetic measurements were performed using a PAR 
spinner magnetometer. All measurements of remanent magnetization intensity and direction 
subsequent to the 30 mT af demagnetization step, and all measurements subsequent to 
thermal demagnetization steps, were performed with a Schonstedt DSM-I spinner magneto- 
meter. Alternating field demagnetization was carried out to a maximum of 110 mT (peak) 
using a three-axis tumbler and coil apparatus similar to that described by Roy, Reynolds & 
Sander (1973). Two to four specimens from each block sample and one specimen from each 
of the 102 field-drilled core samples were progressively demagnetized in steps to a routine 
maximum of 80 mT. The most representative value of the mean direction for a site or a 
sample was made by choosing the data set from the demagnetization level for which the 
specimen directions were most tightly clustered provided that the field exceeded 10 mT. In 
a few cases, a less well clustered level was chosen where visual inspection of the data

Step-wise thermal demagnetization was carried out on selected samples and sites. In some 
experiments the thermal demagnetization was performed on specimens which had previously 
been subjected to the partial alternating field demagnetization treatment; in other experi- 
ments the thermal demagnetization was done on specimens which had not been so treated. 
The thermal demagnetization experiments were done in furnaces employing nested mumetal 
shielding. One of these demagnetizers is a Schonstedt TSD-I model; the other is a hand- 
crafted model in which the specimens are slowly rotated along one axis during cooling. This 
rotation minimizes the possible acquisition of small PTRM's in one plane due to incomplete 
dc field cancellation. Temperature calibration experiments, temperature gradient measure- 
ments and duplicate runs in this furnace and in the TSD-1 indicate that temperatures (given 
on the thermal demagnetization plots) are conservatively estimated to be accurate to 5°C. 
Jsat versus T curves were obtained by heating and cooling small chips in air in a constant 
gradient field by a null method in a horizontal translation balance; at the null position the 
applied field used was 0.8 T. 
Palaeomagnetic results 
Approximately 35 per cent of the samples in the collection have median destructive fields 
(mdf) of 5 mT or less and only about 15 per cent of the collection have mdf's exceeding 
40 mT. On the whole the collection was not an easy one to work with and the data from a - 
number of sites had to be rejected (as noted in Table 1). This is particularly true in the 
field-drilled collection (CA series) which emphasized continuous section coverage which in 
some outcrops meant collecting from poorly exposed and weathered outcrops. The block 
samples (AR series) were taken from well exposed outcrops, all of which provided usable 
palaeomagnetic information.

An inspection of Fig. 2(a) and (b) reveals that the treatment methods employed improve 
the grouping, and the sites can be classified as either normally or reversely magnetized. The 
application of the structural tilt correction (Fig. 2c) improves the clustering of each group 
but only marginally; the improvement is not statistically significant (Table 2). A significant 
Downloaded from https://academic.oup.com/gji/article/62/1/155/620380 by Curtin University Library user on 21 September 2025

Palaeomagnetism of the Camaraca Formation 163 
improvement is not to be expected however as the dips of the flows, as measured from flow 
contacts and the attitude of interlayered sedimentary rock, are all shallow and homoclinal. 
Excepting CA-21 and CA-22 (Fig. 2b and c) the normally magnetized flows are con- 
siderably better grouped than the reversely magnetized ones. CA-21, 22 and 23 are in 
stratigraphic order. CA-21 is very stably magnetized and is on the periphery of the normal 
group; CA-22 is a poorly grouped site and is excluded from the summary statistics of Table 
2. CA-23 is a rejected site consisting of three unstable cores and one very stable reversely 
magnetized core. It seems probable that CA-21, 22 and 23 represent a poorly documented 
(normal to reverse) field transition, 
Much of the detailed laboratory work was directed in searching for additional com- 
ponents of remanence which might possibly account for the greater dispersion of the 
reversed group. Examples from the results of these experiments are presented below. In 
Fig. 3 are shown two Zijderveld diagrams where the specimens have been treated by thermal 
demagnetization subsequent to partial af demagnetization. The directions move into the 
reversed group at very low af fields and then follow somewhat jagged paths to the origin. 
However, if one examines companion specimens from the same samples the nature of the 
deflections is not systematic. In Fig, 4 the effects of thermal demagnetization alone are 
compared with af plus thermal treatment for specimens from a reversely magnetized site. 
Specimens 46-2, 47-2 and 48-2 were examined by thermal demagnetization and it is noted 
that 300-400°C treatments serve to bring the specimen directions into concordance. It is 
inferred from the Jsat versus T curve, shown inset in Fig. 4, that over this temperature 
range maghaernite is demagnetized and/or converted to haematite. The directions remain 
reasonably well grouped to a temperature of 650°C after which scattering sets in without 
any systematic trend for the site as a whole. Repeat measurements of 49-1 subsequent to 
the 80 mT af step indicate that ARM'S are troublesome. Subsequent thermal treatments fail 
to undo this effect and for the site as a whole the 550°C thermal result gives the best 
grouping (Table 1). The important point, however, is that using any higher temperature data 
set up to and including the 650°C run, would produce a very similar result. 
Fig. 5 illustrates similar behaviour in a normally magnetized specimen from a normally 
magnetized site. For the site as a whole the 80 mT or the 500°C thermal treatment produces 
almost identical results. At temperatures above 500°C the mean site direction has lower 
precision but does not move significantly or systematically until 660°C, when final un- 
blocking is obtained and the directions become random. 
In summary, extensive laboratory analysis fails to detect unwanted secondary com- 
ponents of magnetization other than those which are eliminated at low af fields and at low 
blocking temperatures. Although the original high-temperature magnetic mineralogy has 
been modified by weathering the burial metamorphic processes, the initial directions of 
remanence can be recovered. Similar conclusions for similar rocks were reached by Marshall 
& Cox (1972). They showed that extensive mineralogical changes in weathered submarine 
basalt are accompanied by a number of changes in magnetic properties but, significantly, 
the primary remanence directions can still be recovered. A second argument that the 
directions obtained in the present study are indeed Middle Jurassic magnetic magnetizations 
is that the normal and reversed groups are statistically antiparallel (Table 2).

examination, were crushed to pass 20 mesh. Powder finer than 100 mesh was discarded.

method range from 105 to 153 Myr. Conventionally, the low ages would be attributed to

Figure 6. Isochron plot of the whole rock data indicates an age of 157 Myr for the Camaraca andesites. 
The slope and the intercept of the isochron were calculated by the method developed by 
York (1969). The calculated initial ratio is close to the primordial 40Ar/36Ar ratio, suggesting 
that the argon was derived from the Earth's interior where the 40K/36Ar ratio would have to 
have been less than 700. Elements other than argon, however, may well have been derived 
from partial melting of, or contamination by, lithospheric plate material. Further study on 
the rare gas abundance pattern of these samples would seem fruitful. 
Reversal stratigraphy and comparison with other South American poles 
Both reversed and normally magnetized samples were used in constructing the K-Ar 
isochron of Fig. 6 and there is no resolvable difference in age between normal and reversed 
samples. Our field data suggest that the reversal stratigraphy from the exposed base to the 
highest stratigraphic samples is: N-R-N. We have no defmitive evidence that more than one 
reversed zone is present within the Camaraca Formation. It is premature to make any 
attempt in correlating this reversed magnetozone with those that have been indicated from 
an analysis of global palaemagnetic data (McElhinny & Burek 1971 ; Creer 1971; Pechersky 
& Khramov 1973) as these reversal schemes tend to be more generalized than is revealed by 
the more continuous record of reversal history given from the interpretation of marine 
magnetic anomalies (Larson & Pitman 1972). To date, linear magnetic anomalies have been 
assigned in time from the beginning of the Late Jurassic stopping just short of Camaraca 
Formation time. Should the stratigraphic limits of the formation be further refmed by 
future palaeontological findings it may be possible, however, to integrate our magnetic data 
with Jurassic reversal history. 
Well-controlled palaeomagnetic poles from rock units of undisputed Jurassic age are 
relatively scarce for South America (Table 4; Fig. 7a). The best studied unit is the Chon Aike 
Formation of Argentina (Valencio & Vilas 1970; Creer, Mitchell & Abou Deeb 1972; Vilas 
1974). A Jurassic pole for Kimmeridgian sedimentary rocks, also from Argentina but based 
on untreated NRM data (Creer 1962) has large error limits (pole 3, Table 4). The older dyke 
suite of the Rio de 10s Molinos area, Argentina with an age of 140 Myr (bares & Valencio 
1975) lies near the Jurassic-Cretaceous boundary (pole 4, Table 4).

Figure 7. (a) Summary plot of Jurassic poles for South America. Older Jurassic poles (6,7, 8) lie closer to 
the continent than younger Jurassic poles (1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 9). Both groups are spread along approximately 
arcuate trends. (b) Africa and its mean Jurassic pole (M) rotated about the Euler pole which best closes 
the South Atlantic (Bullard et al. 1965). Individual African poles are as follows: 1 Stromberg lavas 
(9.46, 9.47 and 9.48); 2 Mateke Hills Complexes (9.57); 3 Marangudzi Complex (9.59); 4 Hoachanas 
basalts (9.175); 5 Liberian diabase dykes and siUs (9.172) and, 6 dolerite sills, Sahara (14.249). Pole 
reference numbers beginning with the number 9 are from Irving ef aZ. (1976) and reference number 
(14.249) is from McElhinny & Cowley (1977). (c) The error in the rotation angle 6 by which the sampling 
site must be rotated to bring the Camaraca pole into coincidence with the African reference pole is taken 
to be e, + e2. 
Much older poles, radiometrically dated and previously assigned to the Triassic, may also 
be Jurassic (poles 6, 7, 8, Table 4). The Triassic-Jurassic boundary, previously thought to 
be about 180 Myr (Kulp 1961; Harland, Smith & Wilcock 1964) has been recently assessed 
at about 210 Myr (Hedberg 1976; Armstrong 1978). Therefore, because of age uncertainty, 
the following units are also thought to be Early Jurassic: sills of the Las Cabras Formation, 
at 204 Myr, from Argentina (Valencio 1969; Valencio & Vilas 1972), the Bolivar dyke set,

Paheomagnetism of the Camaraca Formation 169 
199 Myr, from Venezuela (MacDonald & Opdyke 1974) and the Guacamayas Group at 
195 Myr, also from Venezuela (MacDonald & Opdyke 1974). 
Spanning the Jurassic- Cretaceous boundary, but not included in the present compilation 
of Jurassic poles, is the Botucatu sandstone of Brazil (Creer, Embleton & Valencio 1970), 
and its stratigraphic equivalent, the Tacuarembo sandstone of Uruguay (Creer 1958). The 
reported Botucatu pole is based on NRM results and has large error limits (Creer et al. 
1970). The Tacuarembo samples are of baked contacts affected by basalt flows of the 
younger Serra Geral Formation. The age of the magnetization therefore presumably 
represents the emplacement of the Serra Geral, and is post-Tacuarembo. The Botucatu and 
Tacuarembo might yet yield useful Jurassic data with further study. 
Palaeomagnetic results from redbeds of possible Jurassic age from northern South 
America have been excluded from the present compilation. The Giron Formation of 
Colombia, for example, has been assigned to the Triassic (Creer et al. 1970) and to the 
Jurassic (Cediel, Ujueta & Caceres 1970). For want of more precise age data, both the Giron 
Formation and its possible correlative the La Quinta Formation of Venezuela are excluded 
for the time being. 
Tectonic implications and conclusions 
Jurassic poles of South America (Fig. 7aj reveal two trends: both older (poles 6, 7 and 8) 
and younger (poles 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 9) Jurassic poles are scattered along approximately arcuate 
trends; and, older poles are closer to South America than are the younger poles. These 
results indicate: (1) significant tectonic rotation between sampling areas and (2) a northward 
shift of South America away from the south pole between Early and Late Jurassic times of 
about 10". 
The jurassic poles of South America were compared with those from Africa as compiled 
by Irviig, Tanczyk & Hastie (1976) and McElhinny & Cowley (1977). The section of the 
African data was based on the following criteria: (1) that the stability of the magnetization 
was examined by one or more of af, thermal or chemical demagnetization techniques, (2) 
that the number of samples exceeded eight, (3) that the error about the calculated pole was 
less than 20", (4) averages of previously reported poles were excluded, and (5) that localities 
from areas of Africa which have undergone post-Jurassic folding were excluded. 
The poles so selected are plotted in Fig. 7(b). By rotating this African pole (83"E, 
67" S, A%= 6.8") about the Euler pole which best closes the South Atlantic (Bullard, Everitt 
& Smith 1965) an estimate of the expected Jurassic pole for South America was obtained 
near 143" W, 68" S (M of Fig. 7b). Relative to this expected Jurassic pole for South America, 
the Camaraca strata have been rotated 44" k 14" in a counter-clockwise sense. The error in 
this estimate is taken to be + f2 of Fig. 7(c). The African reference pole is, however, based 
on data which have an average age about 20 Myr older than the rocks of the Camaraca 
Formation (Fitch & Miller 1970; Foland & Henderson 1976; Manton 1968; Gidskehaug, 
Creer & Mitchell 1975; Dalrymple, Gromme & White 1975). The discrepancy between the 
observed and expected poles might be attributed in part to age difference rather than local 
tectonic rotation. 
The Camaraca Formation is close in age to the Chon Aike Formation of Argentina 
(Table 4). Although there is considerable scatter in the Chon Aike poles (poles 1,2 and 5 of 
Table 4), a comparison of the mean of these (186" E, 82" S, A9,= 21") with the Camaraca 
pole also indicates a counter-clockwise rotation of smaller amount but with considerable 
error (28" k 28"). Thus it would appear that only part of the discrepancy between the 
rotated African reference pole and the Camaraca pole is possibly due to an age difference.
