& Dunlop 1978) that span the interval 1050-800 Ma (Berger et al. 1979). 
The Grenvillian orogeny in the Hastings area thus had at least three phases. First there 
was deformation, largely monoclinal tilting, of thick volcanic and sedimentary sequences, 
followed by their burial to 10-1 5 km depths, perhaps by thrust-slice stacking (Rivers 1983), 
between 1300 and 1250 Ma. Then came intrusion of post-kinematic epizonal and mesozonal 
plutons around the time of deepest burial, between 1250 and 1200 Ma. Finally erosion, 
uplift and slow cooling occurred, either continuously or discontinuously, from 1200 to 
900 Ma or later. 
D. J. Dunlop and J. M. Stirling 
AN ALTERNATIVE VIEW OF THE GRENVILLIAN OROGENY 
If uplift and cooling were continuous, the cooling rate must have been only 1-2°C Myr-’, 
about an order of magnitude lower than estimated cooling rates in the Alps over the past few 
tens of million years (Baer 1981a). For this reason, and because of the concentration of 
1100-1 150 Myr old whole-rock Rb/Sr ages in the central part of the Grenville where the 
structural grain is NNE and oblique to the Grenville Front, Baer favours a compound cooling 
history with separate thermal events around 1150-1 100 and 950-900 Ma. 
The Central Metasedimentary Belt containing the Hastings region is one of the areas that 
should have felt the effects of a penetrative 1150-1 100 Myr event, but the palaeomagnetic 
data do not bear this out. All palaeopoles so far reported seem to fall in the 1050-820 Myr 
interval and are very different from 1150-1 100 Ma poles for rocks of the Lake Superior 
Keweenawan rift sequence (Fig. l), which may be genetically related to the Grenvillian 
event or events (Donaldson & Irving 1972; Baer 1981 b). 
The palaeomagnetic observations do not rule out an 1150-1100 Ma event followed by 
reheating around 1050-1000Ma to a temperature of about 650”6, which would be 
sufficient to erase all pre-existing magnetization. 40Ar/39Ar stepheating data for the Thanet 
complex (Berger & York 1981) are compatible with this compound model: one hornblende 
with an Ar closure temperature of 700°C gave an age of 1200 Myr whereas another with 
a closure temperature of 600°C gave an age of 1050 Myr, similar to ages of biotites that 
closed below 400°C. However hornblendes from the Cordova gabbro (Lopez-Martinez & 
York 1983) record simple cooling from 500°C around 1150 Ma to 350°C at 1050Ma 
and rule out a reheating to 650°C just before 1050Ma. For this reason, although the 
possibility of thermal pulses to moderate temperatures will be considered in what follows, 
a simple, very slow cooling history will be preferred at the outset. 
Palaeomagnetic background 
Grenvillian palaeomagnetic data and models for their interpretation have been reviewed 
by Symons (1978), Irving (1979), Roy & Robertson (1979), Dunlop (1981), Irving & 
McGlynn (1981) and Park & Emslie (1983). More specialized reviews of the palaeo- 
magnetism and geochronology of the Hastings-Haliburton region have been given by 
Dunlop et al. (1980), Dunlop & Schutts (1983) and York (1984). Early studies were aimed 
at testing two different views of the ‘Tibetan model’ of the Grenville orogen. In the first 
view, the Grenvillian analogue of the Himalayan collision zone would lie near the southern 
edge of the Grenville Front Tectonic Zone (Fig. 1) and much of the Grenville would be an 
exotic terrane, with a pre-collisional apparent polar wander path (APW) different from 
that of the remainder of Laurentia. In the other view, ‘Grenvillia’ and ‘Interior Laurentia’ 
form part of a single plate and the collisional zone lies to the SE of both.

Palaeomagnetism of the Cordova gabbro 525 
The discovery of multivectorial magnetizations in the Haliburton intrusions (Buchan & 
Dunlop 1973, 1976), the Morin complex (Irving, Park & Emslie 1974) and the Whitestone 
anorthosite (Ueno, Irving & McNutt 1974) lent impetus to the search for a pre-orogenic 
magnetic record. Individual samples recorded both an A magnetization with a palaeopole 
near Australia and a B magnetization with a palaeopole in the equatorial Pacific. The A 
magnetization was demonstrably older than the B, and the A-B sequence seemed to mark 
a convergent juncture with the Logan Loop or Keweenawan Track of the Laurentian APWP. 
McWilliams & Dunlop (1978) hypothesized, however, that the A and B poles form part 
of a post-orogenic Grenville Track that is younger than any part of the Keweenawan Track. 
This conjecture was confirmed when the A and B poles were dated by 40Ar/39Ar thermo- 
chrononietry (Berger et al. 1979; Berger & York 1981) and were shown to be about 
1000-950 and 850-800 Ma respectively. 
The Hastings Lowlands is one of the few parts of the Grenville from which pre-orogenic 
magnetizations might possibly be recovered. The discovery of primary K/Ar ages of 11 50- 
1200 Myr for hornblendes from the Thanet and Cordova gabbros (Berger & York 1981; 
Lopez-Martinez & York 1983) intensified the search. Of course, whether a pre-metamorphic 
magnetization in either of these intrusions would be strictly pre-orogenic depends on 
whether the Grenvillian collision coincided with the 1150- 1100 Ma event proposed by Baer 
(1981a) or with the earlier deformational event which predated these intrusions. 
When a novel C component of magnetization was discovered in the Cordova gabbro 
(Dunlop et al. 1980), it was suggested on the basis of preliminary results that it might 
represent a pre-orogenic magnetization, or at any rate a remanence older than any previously 
uncovered. The detailed results presented in this paper show that this speculation was wrong. 
The C magnetization is a low-temperature Silurian or late Ordovician overprint, dated at 
445-450 Ma by 40Ar/39Ar on plagioclase (Lopez-Martinez & York 1983). This is the first 
palaeomagnetic evidence for a possible ‘echo’ in the Crenville of Acadian-Caledonian 
events in the Appalachian Orogen. 
Field and laboratory procedures 
One hundred and thirty block samples were collected from 23 sites in the Cordova gabbro 
(Fig. 2). Samples were oriented by magnetic compass and strike readings were checked 
1-2 m above the outcrop. Two sites (14 and 21) yielded no useful results, but almost 
all samples from the other sites behaved stably. The contact is poorly exposed, being covered 
by the Crowe Kiver on the SW, by Crowe Lake on the south and by swamp to the east 
and NE. Paragneisses near the contact at site 14 and mafic metavolcanics near site 20 were 
collected for a baked contact test, but these samples proved to be weakly and erratically 
magnetized. Sixteen drill cores from the gold and sulphide mineralization zone of the former 
Cordova Mine near site 15 were stably magnetized, although interpretation of these results 
is more problematic since the cores were unoriented in azimuth. 
Five 2.5 cm cylindrical specimens were drilled in the laboratory from each block sample 
or mine drill core. A full programme of stepwise alternating field (AF) and thermal demag- 
netization was carried out on every sample. Normally three specimens were AF cleaned in 
12 steps to 1000 Oe (0.1 T) using a Schonstedt single-axis demagnetizer and one or two 
specimens were thermally cleaned in 50°C steps to 500°C and then in smaller steps to 660 
or 670°C using either a home-built non-inductive furnace or a Schonstedt shielded furnace. 
Magnetizations were measured with Schonstedt and Digico spinner magnetometers. Results 
were accepted if specimen magnetizations reached a stable endpoint during cleaning with

Thin-section studies 
Thin-sections of 23 samples were examined in transmitted light by L. D. Schutts. Average 
composition was 50-55 per cent clinopyroxene (augite), 40-45 per cent calcic plagioclase, 
<1 per cent biotite and the remainder coarse opaques, often rimmed by hornblende. The 
quantity of opaques averaged higher in samples with a C magnetization (10 sections 
examined) or C and an underlying A (four sections) than ;in samples with only an A 
magnetization (nine sections): 1-3 per cent of A sections, 2-3 per cent of C +A sections 
and 2-4 per cent of C sections.

Pyroxenes in A sections are sometimes uralitized to a hornblende-hastingsite only along their

One possible model of the alterations (L. D. Schutts 1982, private communication) is 
that uralitization and sericitization are deuteric while saussurite and scapolite formed 
hydrothermally. Uralitization at an early stage is reasonable enough: amphiboles that formed 
in this way are invariably chloritized to some degree (see below) and must have formed prior 
to regional metamorphism. There is no clear-cut evidence for the time of sericite formation. 
The association of sericite, saussurite and scapolite with the C magnetization, which is likely 
a low-temperature post-metamorphic overprint, favours a late hydrothermal origin for all 
three minerals. Furthermore alteration visibly associated with late-stage calcite-quartz veins 
was seen in about one-third of the C sections but not in A sections. 
Biotites and uralites are lightly to extensively altered to chlorite, the degree of chloritiza- 
tion being unrelated to magnetization type. Several fine-grained calcite-albite-chlorite pods 
were also noted. These rocks must have partially re-equilibrated during regional greenschist 
metamorphism, in contradiction to the interpretation of Lumbers (1964. 1969) that the 
Hastings mafic stocks were intruded after the culmination of regional metamorphism.

Thermomagnetic curves 
Thermomagnetic curves were measured in air using a recording Curie balance for 20 samples, 
of which 12 exhibited principally A or B natural remanent magnetizations (NRMs) and 8 
principally C NRMs. The field applied was about 5 kOe (0.5 T). A few typical results are 
shown in Fig. 3. 
Samples with C NRMs, like CG16 and 18, have practically reversible thermomagnetic 
behaviour and show a single Curie point near 580"C, indicating titanium-free magnetite as 
the only important magnetic phase. Although opaques are abundant in thin section, they 
tend to be altered and these samples have relatively low saturation magnetizations. The 
strong magnetite curve of CG18 is exceptional. Curves like that of CG16, with marked 
low-temperature paramagnetic curvature, are typical. 
The curve for CG57 is fairly typical of results from samples with A or B NRh4s. The 
magnetite Curie point is poorly indicated; there may be hematite present blurring the 
transition. Cooling curves almost always fall well below heating curves, so that magnetite 
has been destroyed, presumably by oxidation. There is also an indication, sometimes vague 
but occasionally quite pronounced as in CG57, of a magnetic phase with a Curie point or 
inversion temperature of 300-350°C. This phase could be pyrrhotite, maghemite or titano- 
magnetite. It is destroyed by heating, since cooling curves never show a low-temperature 
inflection.

After AF and thermal cleaning, the NRMs of 49 samples from 18 sites reached stable 
endpoint directions with NW declinations and intermediate to steep upward inclinations

Fig. 9 gives a few examples in which the B vector is cleanly resolved by AF demagne- 
tization. The A magnetization in these samples is atypical: it resides entirely in hematite 
with coercivities > 1000 Oe that do not overlap those of the B remanence. Thus between 
250 Oe (whch is sufficient to erase the PEF component) and 1000 Oe, only the B vector 
is attacked. In CG101/2, where the A and B vectors are of comparable magnitude, all B 
remanence is eliminated by 1000 Oe and the resultant vector approaches the A direction. 
In CG2/2, the resultant is midway between A and B at 1000 Oe, but this is a result of the 
small magnitude of A compared to B rather than of unusually high B coercitivites. 
In general, A and B coercivity spectra are rather similar, although the B spectra are more 
variable (Fig. 6a, b). However, whenever A and B are superimposed in a sample, whatever 
the overlap of their coercivities, the resultant vector always migrates towards the A direc- 
tion, showing that B is softer than A. 
Similarly, in thermal demagnetization of multicomponent samples, the B vector is 
erased at lower temperatures than the A (Fig. lo). However, there are not many examples 
in orthogonal vector plots of non-overlapping A and B blocking temperature spectra. 
Single-component A and B blocking temperature spectra are also very similar (Fig. 6a, b). 
B therefore cannot be a simple thermal overprint of A.

It was anticipated that it would be possible to use soft PEF overprints to determine north

One specimen of each core was AF cleaned to 1000 Oe and a companion specimen 
of most cores was thermally cleaned to 620°C. A selection of the more interesting AF 
results is given in Fig. 16. NRM intensities dropped to low levels and directions tended to 
randomize at fields of 200-300 Oe. Five cores, including CM5/l and 14/1 in Fig. 16,

higher fields. With the exception of one weakly magnetized sample, the remaining cores had 
similar soft intensity decay curves and were either directionally stable or followed great- 
circle swings, but the directions could not be confidently interpreted as combinations of A, 
B and C vectors, usually because there was no steep PEF component to fix the sample 
orientation. 
Directional behaviour during thermal cleaning resembled AF behaviour for each core. 
PEF overprints were eliminated by 300°C and stable components had blocking temperatures 
extending to 560-580°C. 
The Cordova Mines cores do not have particularly conspicuous C magnetizations and do 
not support the idea of a genetic relation between Palaeozoic sulphide mineralization and 
acquisition of the C magnetic overprint.

Palaeopoles and apparent polar wander 
Fig. 17(a-c) is a compilation of palaeopoles with Grenvillian affinities from within and 
outside of the Grenville Province. A few poles from formations just north of the Grenville 
Front have not been shown because of space limitations, but are plotted by Hyodo & 
Dunlop (1985). All published poles from the Grenville Province are shown in Fig. 17(a). 
They form a linked sequence from about 1020 to 820 Ma (the Grenville Track), followed by 
two probably later groups of poles, the Tu/TuA/SM grouping and the single pole COC of the 
present study. 
Selected Keweenawan poles from the time window, 1150-1050 Ma, appear in Fig. 17(b). 
They link satisfactorily with the older end of the Grenville Track, except for primary poles 
MRp, EP and FLp (Watts 1981), which fall well to the west of the Keweenawan Track 
among later Grenville poles. Fig. 17(c) summarizes Grenvillian or just pre-Grenvillian poles 
from Arizona, Montana, Wyoming, the Mackenzie Mountains and Baffin Island. Unfortu- 
nately, few of these poles are well dated radiogenically, but it is clear that Grenville-like 
poles are by no means confined to the Grenville Province. 
Palaeopoles CoA, CoB and Coc corresponding to the mean Cordova A, B and C magne- 
tizations respectively appear in Tables 1, 3 and 4. These poles were calculated without 
corrections for tectonic rotations, since COA and COB resemble Grenvillian poles which are 
known to date from post-tectonic uplift and cooling and since COC is argued to be an 
even younger overprint. In Fig. 17(a), CoA, COB and Coc are compared explicitly to other 
Grenville Province palaeopoles. 
CoA does not fall in the southerly = 1000 Ma group of A poles with HbA and ThA of 
the Haliburton and Thanet intrusions of the Hastings-Haliburton region. Instead COA 
resembles more northerly poles about 900 Ma in age from the Wilberforce pyroxenite, the 
Umfraville gabbro and the Whitestone anorthosite, all of southern Ontario. However, COB 
does resemble HbB and ThB. It is probably about 850-800 Myr old. 
Fig. 17(d) compares Ordovician, Silurian and Devonian palaeopoles from cratonic North 
America with the Grenville Track. Coc is virtually coincident, both in its position and in its 
95 per cent confidence oval, with pole B1 of the Silurian Bloomsburg Formation (Roy, 
Opdyke & Irving 1967). It falls well west of most Ordovician poles and south and west of 
most Devonian poles, although it does resemble two Devonian poles (Do and PS1) that 
diverge from the main grouping. In view of the wAr/39Ar plagioclase age of about 445 Ma 
determined by Lopez-Martinez & York (1983) for the Cordova, an upper Ordovician- 
Silurian age for Coc is most likely.

Discussion 
A AND B NRMs: POST-GRENVILLIAN COOLING HISTORY 
The Cordova A and B magnetizations are definitely not primary, and tell us nothing about 
the nature of the Grenvillian event or events. Like other Grenville A and B poles, they were 
acquired during post-tectonic uplift and cooling following the Grenvillian orogeny, in the 
general time interval 1000-800 Ma (Patchett & Bylund 1977; Berger et al. 1979; Dallmeyer 
& Sutter 1980). Judging by the paleopole positions, CoA is about 900 Ma and Cog is about 
850-800 Myr old. 
According to the regional cooling curve established by Berger & York (1981) and Lopez- 
Martinez & York (1983) from 40Ar/39Ar mineral ages and Ar closure temperatures, the 
Cordova and Thanet gabbros had cooled to around 500°C by 1150-1 100 Ma and to 
around 300°C by 1000 Ma. If the Cordova A and B magnetizations were TRMs or partial

either below 250°C during slow continuous cooling or below about 400°C in a brief thermal 
pulse. 
The cause of these postulated discrete NRM overprinting events is unknown, but the 
suggestion is clear that there may be unresolved ‘fine structure’ in present Grenvillian cooling 
curves. Brief events or pulses around 900 and 850-800 Ma, superimposed on general uplift 
and cooling, would account for the marked clustering of palaeopoles around these times on 
the Grenville Track (Fig. 17a). It has long been puzzling that Grenvillian magnetizations 
with broad ranges of laboratory blocking temperatures should fail to record APW if they 
were indeed acquired during continuous slow cooling. They are typically resultants of 
discrete A and B remanences, not continuously evolving vectors that track the changing 
Earth’s field direction during slow cooling. Vectors of the latter type are well documented 
in slowly cooled rocks from west Greenland (Morgan 1976; Piper 198 1). 
It can be argued that the very segregation of data into A and B groups, like those of 
Figs 4 and 8, suppresses any between-site record of APW, and authors have occasionally 
plotted site-mean poles to make the point that they span much of the Grenville Track 
(see, e.g. Roy & Robertson 1979, fig. 1). However, there is no escaping the fact that discrete 
A and B remanences are resolved quite routinely in orthogonal vector plots of individual 
specimen data (e.g. Fig. 9). Discrete pulses superimposed on general Grenvillian cooling 
would account for this observation. 
THE C NRM: PALAEOZOIC REACTIVATION IN THE GRENVILLE 
The C magnetization tends to occur in samples with pronounced silicate alteration and its 
blocking temperatures are lower on the average than those of A and B NRMs (Fig. 6), 
although there is considerable overlap among A, B and C spectra. On this evidence, C is a 
low-temperature CRM younger than either A or B. Despite its low AF coercivities and its 
association with samples containing abundant visible opaques of multidomain size, the C 
component is probably carried mainly by very fine, nearly superparamagnetic secondary 
magnetite. Only such fine-grained material has low blocking temperatures as well as low 
coercivities. 
Results from the Cordova Mines cores do not support a genetic relation between early 
Palaeozoic mineralization and the C magnetization, although they do not rule out such a 
relation. The C component is certainly no more widespread in these cores than in the 
general sampling. 
There was definitely a late Ordovician or early Silurian (about 445 Ma) event that 
outgassed argon from plagioclases in the Cordova samples (Lopez-Martinez & York 1983). 
It is plausible that the temperatures reached did not exceed 200°C or so, and that the C 
magnetization was produced thermochemically in this event. The good agreement of the 
CoC palaeopole with known Silurian and late Ordovician poles for cratonic North America 
makes such an origin almost certain. 
The timing of this event suggests an echo of the Taconic orogeny in the Appalachian 
region. If so, the relation between the two is subtle. Middle Ordovician sediments just 
south of Crowe Lake (Fig. 2) and for at least 100 km to the south and east are flat lying 
and undisturbed. Alternatively, mild reheating due to burial by these sediments, which 
must once have overlain the Cordova body, or alteration related to seawater infiltration 
during sediment deposition could have caused the C overprinting (D. T. A. Symons 1984, 
private communication). 
Whatever the exact nature of the C magnetization, if one accepts that it is a late over- 
print and that its age is fixed beyond reasonable doubt by the 40Ar/39Ar plagioclase date of

Summary. Study of the palaeomagnetism of two complexes from the Newer 
Granite Suite in Scotland, at Ratagan (NW Highlands) and Comrie (central 
Highlands), reveals the variable nature of the natural remanence encountered 
in granodioritic intrusions and the surrounding metamorphic country rock. 
Forty-eight specimens from Ratagan, dated at 415 Itr 5 Ma, gave a mean direc- 
tion: D= 8", I= - 32", and a palaeomagnetic south pole: 1S0S, 346"E 
(6p= 5", Fm=9"). Twenty-eight specimens from Comrie, dated at 40855 Ma, 
gave a mean direction: D = 75", I= - 30", and a palaeomagnetic south pole: 
6"S, 287"E(6p = 4", 6m = 7"). These results have been compared with the 
established apparent polar wander path (APWP) for Britain. The Ratagan pole 
improves the reliability of the APWP but doubt remains as to whether the 
primary magnetization from Comrie represents a true late Silurian direction 
or whether it has been affected by post-cooling rotation, possibly associated 
with the nearby Highland Boundary Fault.

1 Introduction 
The newer igneous rocks in the Scottish Highland region which post-date the main Grampian 
metamorphism and tectonism range in composition from basic to granitic. Two members of 
this suite were chosen for palaeomagnetic study in an attempt to refine the apparent polar 
wander path for Scotland in the Palaeozoic. 
This paper describes the results of the detailed palaeomagnetic analysis which has been 
carried out. Thermal and alternating field (af) demagnetization was supplemented by rock 
magnetic experiments on a limited selection of specimens from each sampling site to help 
characterize the remanence carriers. These consisted of thin-section observations and the 
measurement of thermomagnetic and hysteresis properties. Each complex provides an 
example of the widespread variability in remanence behaviour which may be encountered in 
a single intrusion.

the age of the rock is required. Brown, Miller & Grasty (1968) give a poorly defined K-Ar

2 Method 
Processing methods adopted were the same for all the palaeomagnetic samples. Individual 
specimens from each site were thermally demagnetized in steps of 50°C or smaller intervals 
depending on the behaviour of the rock. Another specimen from each site was af demag- 
netized in steps of 5-10mT. After a definite pattern of behaviour had emerged for each site, 
the rate of processing was increased by using fewer, appropriately chosen temperature and 
field intervals. 
Components of magnetization together with their blocking temperature ranges were esti- 
mated with the aid of orthogonal projections of the demagnetization data. As a result of 
minimizing the number of field/temperature intervals, the remanences removed at low steps. 
which were considered to have no ancient geological significance, were often defined by only 
two points on the orthogonal projections. 
Generally, orthogonal projections of demagnetization data reveal straight-line segments 
which are associated with single components of NRM. In any assessment of such vector 
plots, some decision must be made as to which points should be included in the definition of 
a particular component. In this study, it was found that minimization of the 95 per cent 
confidence angle on vector differences (Arss of Briden & Arthur 1981) resulted in a tighter 
grouping of the removed vectors. Therefore, this was used as a guide to obtaining ‘best- 
estimates’ of the direction of magnetization components (cf. Turnell & Briden 1983). 
Listings of all the components from each specimen used in this study, including blocking 
temperature/coercivity ranges and the error parameter, are available from the author. 
3 The Ratagan Complex 
3.1 GEOLOGY AND SAivlPLING 
The Ratagan Complex is a composite intrusion situated approximately 10 km east of Glenelg 
in Inverness-shire, east of the Moine thrust. To the north-east the igneous rocks intrude 
Lewisian paragneisses and elsewhere the country rock comprises Moinan gneisses interrupted 
by pelitic bands. Immediately east of the pluton, the country rocks are crushed and shattered 
along faults of the Strathconon-Ben Sgriol system (Nicholls 1950). Parallel, SW-NE 
fractures cut the igneous rocks but have littie effect on the igneous boundaries. 
Fig. 1 is a sketch map of the intrusion showing the four main phases. From west to east 
these are classified as granite, diorite, syenitic hybrids and adamellite (Nicholls 1950). Each 
phase itself shows considerable variation in both composition and grain size and, taken as a 
whole, the body has an unusually high alkali element content compared with intrusions in 
the central and eastern Highlands. Nevertheless, Ratagan has been classified as one of the 
Newer Granites of Scotland. Nicholls (1950) concluded that the body is derived from a 
parental dioritic magma through differentiation and hybridization and more recent major 
and trace element analyses (Turnell 1982) have revealed low Nb/Y ratios relative to within- 
plate alkali basalts suggesting that they are not intra-plate. 
There is little evidence on the form of the intrusion and, because it post-dates the main 
cleavage seen in the country rock, no structural correction has been applied to the palaeo- 
magnetic directions obtained. 
A total of 18 sites were drilled in the intrusion itself, in road cuttings, the river bed and 
along forestry tracks. The distribution of sites is shown on the sketch map (Fig. 1). Nine

3.2 RESULTS 
For most sites, natural remanent magnetizations (NFWs) clustered close to the direction of 
the Earth’s present field. Values of Koenigsberger ratios (Qn) calculated for samples from 
the adamellite, syenite and diorite were below 0.5, reflecting the presence of coarse-grained 
magnetite. For specimens from the diorite phase Qn values were higher, suggesting single 
domain (sd) or pseudo-single domain (psd) magnetite. 
Af demagnetization of a large proportion of pilot samples failed to isolate any consistent 
direction of magnetization which might be geologically ancient. This unstable behaviour is 
attributed to multi-domain (md) magnetite which is affected by stray fields during 
measurement or in the demagnetizer. Typical demagnetization results are shown in Fig. 2(a). 
Stable specimens from the diorite had coercivities in the range 100-140 mT corresponding 
to sd or psd magnetite. Stable specimens from the syenite contain haematite with coercivities 
exceeding 200mT. The corresponding stereograms show southerly downward or north- 
easterly upward directions for the diorites and exclusively north-easterly upward directions 
for the syenites. 
Thermal demagnetization revealed that most specimens contained some proportion of 
low blocking temperature (Tb) material. Stereograms and orthogonal projections showing 
the directional changes of the NRM during demagnetization are shown in Fig. 2(b). The 
stable specimens were classified into three groups: (1) Most syenite specimens appeared to 
contain only one (ancient) component of remanence (Tb > 580°C) in a northerly, upward 
direction, presumably carried by haematite, e.g. R48-3. (2) The dioritic specimens contained 
two (ancient) remanence components, one in a northerly upward direction, and the other in 
a southerly downward direction, e.g. RR6-2, RR7-7; both had Tb < 580°C and are pre- 
sumably carried by magnetite. Specimen RR5-2, of diorite composition, was atypical in

3.3 MAGNETIC PROPERTIES 
Twp types of thermomagnetic behaviour were observed as shown in Fig. 3(a): (a) the convex 
curves are typical of specimens containing nearly pure sd magnetite which dominates the 
results even for specimens with a high proportion of primary remanence carried by haematite 
(e.g. R44, R48); (b) the concave curves indicate the presence of superparamagnetic grains 
(Radhakrishnamurty 1973) although this does not appear to affect the stability of the 
specimen on thermal demagnetization in every case (e.g. RR7-3). Possibly the relaxation 
time is comparable to the laboratory measurement time. 
Most specimens gave saturation isothermal remanent magnetization (IRM) curves (Fig. 3b) 
with B,, (the coercivity of maximum remanence) between 20 and 50 mT, typical of nearly 
pure magnetite. Haematite bearing specimens, e.g. R48-2, failed to achieve saturation in field 
strengths of around 0.7 T. Unstable specimens tended towards much higher saturation 
magnetizations, indicating a higher concentration of coarse, probably md magnetite. 
Thin-section studies revealed that, while all the material shows some degree of hydro- 
thermal alteration in the form of brown-red iron staining and sericitization of feldspars, this 
was seen to be more extensive in the syenitic rocks. In general, the highest proportion of 
coarse-grained magnetite was observed in specimens from sites which showed the poorest 
magnetic stability. The total ferromagnetic content observed in the stable dioritic rocks was 
small compared with the stable syenitic specimens, reflecting their relatively lower NRM 
intensities (< 20 x 10-3Am-'). Observations suggest that the source of the stable haematite

3.4 IN TE R P R E TAT ION 
Confidence circles associated with the two pole positions derived independently from the 
normal (N) and reversed (R) directions in each site show that they are not significantly 
different from normal and reversed indicators of the same magnetic field direction and are 
compatible with other known lower Palaeozoic poles from Scotland (e.g. Piper 1979). 
Therefore, all the data have been combined to produce a single pole position. 
The simplest explanation for the origin of the magnetization is that it is a TRM recorded 
during the cooling of the intrusion through regional uplift. Considering the magnetite 
remanence, the consistently higher blocking temperature of the reversed component suggests 
that it is older than the normal component. Such an argument would not hold if either of 
the magnetite components is not a pure partial thermoremanent magnetization (PTRM). The 
haematite remanence, which is of normal polarity, could be a thermochemical remanence 
(TCRM) formed during haematite growth during the later stages of cooling when the lower 
Tb magnetites were acquiring their PTRM. It is unlikely to be much younger because of the 
agreement with the lower Tb magnetite component. 
3.5 COUNTRY ROCKS 
Fig. 4 shows the thermal demagnetization behaviour of specimens from the metamorphic 
rocks west of Ratagan. Reasonably well-grouped remanences were found within the Lewisian 
in amphibolitic material (site R55) identified as part of the pre- or syn-tectonic amphibolite 
suite (Smith 1979), in high-grade gneiss, permeated with granitic veins (sites R50 and R52) 
and in reddish Moinian quartzite (site R54). Other samples, from lower-grade Lewisian 
psammite and some Moinian gneiss were found to be weak and unstable.

Apart from a few scattered points, corresponding to poorly defined, contaminated or 
anomalous magnetizations, the data define two palaeomagnetic directions, A and B (Fig. 5). 
Blocking temperatures and coercivities indicate haematite remanence carriers for A and both 
magnetite and haematite carriers for B. The A Component is similar to that in the Ratagan 
complex; the B direction is better defined from a larger population. It is significantly 
different from the Ratagan direction and by comparison with the established apparent polar 
wander path (APW)for this period (e.g. Turnell & Briden 1983) must be younger. However, 
the source of this component is unclear. 
4 The Comrie intrusion 
4.1 GEOLOGY AND SAMPLING 
A simplified geological map of the Comrie area is shown in Fig. 6. The major part of the 
body is composed of diorites which are themselves intruded by a plug of medium to fine- 
grained pink granite. The country rock comprises hornfelsed slate and greywacke of the 
Dalradian series. Because of the observed variation in both composition and grain size, 
sampling sites were restricted to the finer-grained, most basic phases, which are most suitable 
for palaeomagnetic work. Some cores were also drilled in the country rock up to 6 km from 
the diorite body making a total of 17 sampling sites in the area. These are shown on the 
sketch map (Fig. 6). 
4.2 RESULTS 
NRMs (except the country grit) measured between 50 and 500x 10-3Am-' and the direc- 
tions of magnetization grouped around the Earth's present field. For most specimens, 
Koenigsberger ratios, Qn, were close to 0.2 indicating a high proportion of md magnetite.

of magnetite obscures the detection of haematite by the Curie balance because of the 
susceptibility contrast. However, it is clear from the low B,, values and saturation field 
strengths measured in the IRM experiments (e.g. Fig. 9b) that there is none present in any of 
the samples tested. The high saturation magnetization measured in all specimens is due to 
the grains larger than 100pm in diameter observed in the microscope studies. 
Thin-section studies revealed some clear differences in the character of stable and 
unstable rock-types: (i) the grain size of the stable material is generally finer; (ii) the stable 
rock is fresher, showing less evidence of sericitization in the feldspar or oxidation of 
magnetite to haematite; (iii) there is a higher proportion of single phase magnetite without 
ilmenite exsolution lamellae in the stable material; (iv) the stable rock types show a higher 
proportion of small grain sizes among the magnetites. It is likely that these differences are 
shared by grains of sub-optical dimensions in the rocks. The coarsest material probably lacks 
any sd remanence carriers (with grain diameter below 15 pm). Significantly, only the stable 
rocks contain magnetite whose size range extends to the limit of resolution of the microscope. 
4.4 INTERPRETATION 
The C component is not precisely defined. It is restricted to the hornfels and some diorite 
specimens in site K17 suggesting that magnetite grains of the appropriate relaxation time 
must be limited to these rock types. Unfortunately, this renders the hornfels useless for clari- 
fying the tectonic interpretation of the primary diorite magnetization. The direction does 
not correspond closely to any British magnetization since the Devonian. The only specimen 
with both C and A components reveals that C has the lower blocking temperature although 
this does not necessarily imply that C represents a younger magnetization than A. Maybe C 
is a combination of the present field direction and a post-Devonian magnetization, perhaps 
Tertiary or Carboniferous. 
Comparison of the characteristic direction of magnetization (A) with those derived from 
other Highland intrusions of comparable age, e.g. Garabal Hill-Glen Fyne and Arrochar 
(Briden 1970) reveals a considerable discrepancy in declination. However, a similar primary 
magnetization with easterly declination has been reported from the Cwmbran Old Red 
Sandstone (Chamalaun & Creer 1964) and, more recently, westerly palaeomagnetic poles 
have been derived from metamorphic rocks in the Moines north of the Great Glen, Scotland 
(Watts 1982). If these directions represent true Devonian magnetizations, the primary com- 
ponent, A, found in Comrie is not anomalous but confirms a large westerly swing in the 
APWP for Britain at the end of the Silurian. 
Alternatively, the Comrie characteristic direction may be a primary TRM comparable to 
magnetizations in other Newer Granites, which has been affected by the post-cooling rota- 
tion of the intrusion. The geology of the country rock north of the fault is structurally 
complicated. The Dalradian grits are part of the inverted limb of a large recumbent fold, the 
Tay Nappe. Detailed mapping by several different workers has shown that, at different 
localities adjacent to the fault, the inverted grits and slates have suffered varying degrees of 
folding (Harris 1972; Harris, Bradbury & McGonigal 1976; Shackleton 1958). The Tay 
Nappe itself is related to the Grampian metamorphism which ended long before 408 Ma, but 
the later folds may well be the result of movement of the Highland Boundary Fault which, 
because of its proximity and strike, could also have caused the displacement of the Comrie 
palaeomagnetic pole. Bulk rotation of the intrusion about a horizontal axis (strike 050") 
parallel to the fault during vertical, downward faulting would produce the appropriate 
rotation (60"). This requires that the intrusion lies in the core of an antiform structurally 
between the Aberfoyle synform to the SE and the synform at Callander. While this is com-

The results are presented in Tables 1 and 2. High values (> 1) of the mean square of weighted 
deviates (mswd) result from the failure of all points to lie on an isochron within error. This 
may be related to the sericitization of the feldspar, implying mobility of Sr near the feldspar

the diorite and the surrounding grits.

408 ? 5 Myr for Comrie and probably dates the cooling of the intrusions below about

that the ages are comparable. i.e. the intrusion cooled quickly. The spread of poles to the 
west of the Ratagan result indicates a period of rapid apparent polar wander after 415 Ma, 
including a large rotational component, which supports the hypothesis that the field reversal 
observed in the Ratagan results occurred during the initial cooling of the body. It is clear 
that the NRM of the metasediments west of Ratagan gives a pole far from any Ordovician 
data (i.e. in positions which might have been anticipated from the 430-480 Ma ‘chrontour’ 
ages (Dewey & Pankhurst 1970)). Therefore, it is assumed that the magnetization of these 
rocks is related to a younger event associated with prolonged Newer Granite activity. Similar 
ideas have been discussed in relation to palaeomagnetic results from the heavy mineral seams 
about 20km south of Glenelg (Watts 1982) which also fail to agree with the published 
chrontour pattern. 
The lack of reversed magnetization components among the Comrie results is unusual 
compared with the alkaline Newer Granites of the Assynt area (Turnell & Briden 1983) and 
Ratagan. It is assumed that, in this particular rock, evidence of reversed components with

istic high blocking temperature A component of natural remanent 
magnetization (NRM) of the Tudor gabbro of southern Ontario has a mean

temperature reached locally during = 1050 Ma Grenvillian regional meta- 
morphism. The A NRM therefore predates metamorphism and is probably a

and this is the best estimate of the age of the A remanence. Successful 
Thellier-type palaeointensity determinations on 1 1 Tudor samples confirm

Introduction 
Penetrating the Grenvillian ‘metamorphic veil’ (Berger & York 1981) to recover the pre- 
orogenic palaeomagnetic and drift history of Grenvillia has proved unexpectedly difficult 
(Dunlop et al. 1980; Park & Emslie 1983). Numerous palaeomagnetic poles that were at first 
believed to ‘see through’ the Grenvillian orogeny almost certainly date from post-meta- 
morpluc regional uplift and cooling (e.g. Irving, Emslie & Uena 1974; Buchan & Dunlop 
1976; Symons 1978). They fall on the Grenville Loop of the Laurentian apparent polar 
wander path (APWP) in the approximate time interval 1000-800 Ma (Berger, York & 
Dunlop 1979; Dallmeyer & Sutter 1980). A recent example is the A palaeopole of the early 
Palaeohelkian (FJ 1700 Ma, U/Pb zircon) French River anorthosite (Stupavsky & Symons 
1982), which falls on the Grenville Loop around 950 Ma. 
In parts of the Hastings Lowlands of southern Ontario (Fig. l), the metamorpluc grade is 
unusually low for the Grenville Province and pre-metamorphic 40Ar/39Ar hornblende ages 
have been recovered. The Thanet gabbro has hornblende ages as old as 1200 Ma (Berger & 
York 1981), the Cordova gabbro has ages as old as 1150 Ma (Lopez-Martinez & York 1983) 
and hornblendes from the Tudor gabbro define an 11 10 Ma isochron (Baksi 1982). These 
ages are essentially identical to the U/Pb zircon emplacement ages of the plutons. However, 
primary magnetizations have apparently not survived for the Thanet and Cordova bodies. 
Their high and medium blocking temperature natural remanent magnetizations (NRMs) give 
palaeopoles that fall on the usual Grenville path (Buchan 1978; Dunlop & Stirling 1985) and 
are therefore younger than 1000 Ma. 
The Tudor gabbro, on tne other hand, has long been known to have an anomalous palaeo-

Grenville poles. Hayatsu & Palmer (1975) determined a K/Ar whole-rock isochron age of 
670 Ma for the Tudor body, which Baksi (1982) has shown dates the time of post-meta- 
morphic cooling of plagioclases to abour 200°C. This age has come to be associated with the 
palaeopole as well, and most palaeomagnetists have incorporated the Tudor pole on a post- 
Grenvillian extension of the APW (e.g. Irving 1979; Roy & Robertson 1979; Buchan et al. 
1983). 
There are two problems with this traditional interpretation. If the Tudor NRM was frozen 
in thermally at temperatures around 200"C, it could hardly have escaped viscous over- 
printing in later geomagnetic fields (e.g. Pullaiah et al. 1975). If the NRM was acquired 
thermochemically, producing laboratory unblocking temperatures considerably higher than 
2OO0C, the marked difference between the Tudor pole and late metamorphic B poles of the 
neighbouring Cordova, Thanet and Haliburton intrusions (Fig. 1) is hard to account for. All 
four bodies must have had parallel uplift and cooling histories. Apart from their proximity, 
40Ar/39Ar step-heating analyses of plagioclases indicate cooling in all cases to -2200°C 
around 700-800 Ma (Berger et al. 1979; Berger & York 1981; Baksi 1982; Lopez-Martinez 
& York 1983). 
The other possibility is that the Tudor pole is unique because it alone is pre-metamorphic. 
This possibility is worth considering, since the Tudor lies in the lowest metamorphic zone in 
the Hastings Basin (Fig. 1) and was not reheated to as high temperatures as the Thanet and 
Haliburton stocks. The Cordova gabbro, which was reheated to temperatures similar to those 
experienced by the Tudor, has unmistakably suffered post-metamorphic thermochemical 
resetting of its entire NRM (Dunlop & Stirling 1985). A pre-metamorphic origin for part of 
the Tudor NRM cannot be taken seriously, therefore, unless this NRM fraction can be shown 
to be a thermoremanent magnetization (TRM) with blocking temperatures 2 5OO0C, the 
peak metamorphic temperature reached locally. 
Palmer & Carmichael(l973) unfortunately did not thermally demagnetize their samples. 
We therefore undertook a palaeomagnetic restudy of the Tudor gabbro and its contact rocks, 
concentrating on detailed thermal analyses of palaeofield directions and intensities. 
Geological setting and sampling scheme 
The regional geology of the Tudor gabbro (Fig. 2) has been described in detail by Lumbers 
(1967, 1969) and only a summary will be given here. The Grenvillian orogeny in the 
Hastings area had at least three phases. The first was deformation, largely monoclinal tilting, 
of thick volcanic and sedimentary sequences, of which the Tudor rnetavolcanics and Hastings 
marble are examples, between 1300 and 1250 Ma. This was followed by intrusion of post- 
kinematic granitic stocks like the Glanmire complex around 1250 Ma (Silver & Lumbers 
1966) and of trondjemitic and mafic stocks like the Tudor gabbro around 1100-1200 Ma 
(S. B. Lumbers, cited in Symons 1978; Berger & York 1981; Baksi 1982). Finally erosion, 
uplift and slow cooling, either continuous or discontinuous, occurred from perhaps 1050- 
800 Ma or later. 
Lumbers (1969) believes that burial and regional metamorphism coincided with the 
kinematic phase and preceded intrusion of all granitic and mafic stocks. Baer (1981) favours 
two separate thermal pulses. Whatever the timing of events, the area surrounding the Tudor 
gabbro was evidently never buried very deeply compared to other parts of the Grenville 
Province. The Tudor stock lies below both the oligoclase and zoned albite isograds (Lumbers 
1969, chart A) and cannot have experienced metamorphic temperatures greater than 500°C 
at most. A reheating this mild would not necessarily have destroyed the contact meta-

The main reason for favouring a pre-metamorphic age of intrusion is the following. Baksi 
(1982) finds that hornblendes in the Tudor gabbro cooled through 590°C around 11 10 Ma. 
This temperature is about equal to the maximum blocking temperatures of the characteristic 
NRM observed in the present study. If the NRM is primary, its age must be approximately 
11 10 Ma, since the Tudor body was never subsequently reheated above about 500°C. We 
observe that the NRM is very consistently overprinted or remagnetized in the blocking 
temperature range below about 500°C. This overprinting we attribute to regional meta- 
morphic heating. 
This scenario, if it can be substantiated, is important because it would date the peak of 
Grenvillian metamorphism (in this area at least) more precisely than has been possible 
previously. The best proof would be to demonstrate a primary NRM by means of a positive 
baked contact test with the country rocks intruded by the Tudor. Failing ths, the next best 
proof would be a demonstration that the characteristic NRM has the properties of a TRM, 
either primary or secondary, so that laboratory blocking temperatures are a reliable guide to 
peak temperatures experienced in nature. 
Sixty-eight block samples were collected from 12 sites in the Tudor gabbro (Fig. 2). Sites 
were concentrated in the eastern lobe of the stock, which has a marked negative aeromag- 
netic anomaly, in fresh roadcuts along Hwy. 62. As in Palmer & Carmichael's (1973) study,

our best results came from these sites; samples taken along the former Hastings Settlement 
Road tended to have unstable behaviour. 
We also made three traverses through the contact metamorphic aureole into unbaked or 
only slightly baked country rocks. Thirty-two samples of the Glanmire and Hastings marbles 
were collected at sites MI -M10, and 55 samples of the Tudor volcanics from sites V1-V9 
were studied. Samples from seven of the volcanic sites were collected in an earlier field 
season by K. L. Buchan, C. J. Hale and J. M. Stirling. 
Analytical procedures 
Three or four 2.5 cm cylindrical cores were drilled in the laboratory from each block sample. 
NRMs in the course of stepwise alternating field (AF) and thermal demagnetization were 
measured on Schonstedt SSM-1 and modified Digico spinner megnetometers, both 
computer-interfaced. Except in cases where the NRMs were below instrumental noise levels 
(<lo4 A m-') or behaved erratically in the course of cleaning, every specimen was 
subjected to a full programme of thermal or AF demagnetization. The usual programme was 
12 steps from 0 to 100 mT using a Schonstedt GSD-1 demagnetizer for AF cleaning and 16 
steps from 20 to 640°C using a Schonstedt TSD-1 furnace for thermal cleaning. 
Twenty-four Tudor gabbro samples had predominantly univectorial NRMs throughout 
thermal cleaning. Fresh specimens of these samples were used for Thellier-type determi- 
nations of palaeofield intensity. The procedure was to heat a specimen twice to the same 
temperature, cooling the first time in zero field and the second time in a field of known 
direction and intensity, in ths case 50 pT. The purpose of the first heating is to demagnetize 
the NRM in steps, while the second heating allows one to deduce the partial TRMs acquired 
over the same temperature steps. The NRM lost and the partial TRM gained in a given 
temperature interval are proportional to each other only if the NRM itself originated as a 
TRM. If this turns out to be the case, the slope of the graph of NRM lost versus partial TRM 
gained gives the ratio of ancient field to laboratory field. The Thellier experiment was used 
in the present study mainly as a test of the TRM nature (or otherwise) of the NRM, but the 
palaeointensities are of considerable interest for their own sakes. 
In the initial trial run of eight specimens, relatively rapid double heatings to temperatures 
of 150, 250, 350, 400, 450, 490, 520, 540,555 and 57OoC were used. Higher temperatures 
were of little interest since thermal demagnetization had shown that magnetite with blocking 
temperatures ~570°C was the major NRM carrier in all samples. In the second and third 
runs (eight specimens each), four more heating steps were added above 400°C and longer 
individual heatings were used to ensure uniform and identical specimen temperatures in each 
pair of double heatings. Unfortunately chemical alteration increased as a result of the greater 
length and number of heatings, and the results were less successful than in the trial run. 
AF and thermal demagnetization data and NRM demagnetization results from Thellier 
experiments were displayed and analysed on both stereographic and orthogonal vector 
projections (Zijderveld 1967). The latter method is particularly useful because it preserves 
information about both the direction and the intensity of NRM. Results were considered 
acceptable if NRM vectors of individual specimens reached a stable endpoint grouping at 
higher AFs or temperatures, with <20° divergence between the directions recorded by 
different specimens of the same sample, or if NRM vectors swung in a coherent fashion 
upon demagnetization. In the latter case, the path followed was usually a great circle, the 
trace of a bivectorial resultant. Great circles were fitted by eye to individual NRM swings 
and their point of intersection (Halls 1976; Bailey & Halls 1984) gave an estimate of one of 
the two vectors (usually the more stable one).

Baked contact test results 
The results of the contact test were discouraging. The NRMs of virtually all the marble 
samples were at or below the noise levels of the spinners. The only exceptions were baked 
samples from site M2 at the northern contact with the Glanmire marble. Two examples are 
illustrated in Fig. 3. The results are noisy because of the weak moments of these specimens, 
but the NRM vector of GL6/2 unmistakably swings from an initial orientation near the 
present Earth’s field (PEF) towards the NW and up ‘A’ direction that is the characteristic 
endpoint of most Tudor gabbro samples. GL5/2 has a very soft NRM that is initially NW 
and shallow, like typical Grenville ‘B’ directions, and swings to negative inclinations at 10 
and 15 mT. Even if we were able to demonstrate convincingly that all marbles from the 
baked zone are overprinted by the Tudor A remanence, there is no indication of a stable pre- 
intrusion remanence in samples outside the baked zone.

We propose instead that contact overprinting in and even beyond the mapped contact 
metamorphic zone was thermochemical rather than purely thermal. This is a common 
situation near intrusive contacts (Dunlop & Schutts 1983; K. L. Buchan 1984, private 
communication). We note that Tudor gabbro samples from sites 3, 4 and 8 at or very near 
the contact are severely altered and gave uninterpretable palaeomagnetic results, whereas 
samples from all but one of the interior sites gave stable, consistent results. Circulation of 
hydrothermal solutions along the intrusive contact during emplacement therefore seems 
probable. 
On the basis of the contact test results alone, it is not possible to choose between (i) con- 
tact overprinting of NRM in some, but not all, contact rocks at the time the Tudor gabbro 
was emplaced and acquired a primary A TRM, and (ii) later regional overprinting of both 
gabbro and country rocks. The results reported in the rest of this paper favour the first 
alternative.

Proof of thermal overprinting: blocking temperature spectra 
The A magnetization of Tudor gabbro samples is carried mainly by magnetite with discrete 
high blocking temperatures (TBs). TGG/C, 49/2/1 and 60/1/2 (Figs 7, 8 and 9) are typical 
examples. In these samples and 27 others like them, the orthogonal vector diagram of thermal 
demagnetization data is ideal: both vector components define linear segments that intersect

Palaeopoles and Grenvillian continental drift 
Despite the failure of the baked contact test, it seems fairly certain that the characteristic A 
magnetization of the Tudor gabbro is the hlgh blocking temperature portion of a primary 
TRM. It has survived later thermal overprinting during Grenvillian regional metamorphism 
and must predate the metamorplum. Since hornblendes from the Tudor closed to Ar 
diffusion at a temperature of about 59OoC around 11 10 Ma (Baksi 1982), and the magnetic 
blocking temperatures range from 570 to about 520°C (Figs 7-9, 12), a maximum age for 
the A remanence is about 1100 Ma. A minimum age of about 1050 Ma is imposed by the 
oldest known ages, about 1000 Ma, of post-Grenvillian uplift and cooling magnetizations 
(Fig. 13). The age of Grenvillian metamorphism, in the Tudor area at least, is bracketed by 
the same dates. 
How then is one to interpret the Tudor gabbro palaeopole (Fig. 13), which must now be 
regarded as older, not younger, than other Grenvillian poles? Poles from Interior Laurentia 
(mainly from the Lake Superior Keweenawan succession) in the age interval 1100-1050 Ma

One tectonic model that would reconcile the results is shown in Fig. 14. In this 
reconstruction, the Tudor A magnetization was impressed while a small ocean (< 1000 km) 
existed between ancestral Grenvillia and Interior Laurentia. Because of the indeterminacy of 
palaeolongitude, a host of similar reconstructions are possible, but all require a pole of 
closing near the (present-day) eastern tip of Grenvillia. That is, the discrepancy between the 
Grenvillian and other Laurentian data can be largely accommodated by a small-angle 
rotation of Grenvillia with respect to Interior Laurentia, rather similar to that suggested for 
the northeastern Grenville by Roy & Fahrig (1973) on quite different grounds. (A local 
rotation of the Tudor gabbro and its surrounding country rocks would of course also 
accommodate the results, but there is no geological evidence that this occurred.) 
The cartoon of Fig. 14 would imply that the collisional phase of the Grenvillian orogeny 
followed emplacement of the Tudor gabbro and acquisition of the A magnetization during 
initial cooling. This picture is inconsistent with the fact that the Tudor volcanics and 
Hastings and Glanmire sediments (Fig. 2) were already steeply dipping at the time they were 
intruded by the Tudor gabbro. A more reasonable model is that collision first occurred at or 
before 1200 Ma, that the Tudor gabbro and related stocks were intruded after deformation 
was complete, but that convergence continued for another 100 Myr or so with extensive 
underplating of the Interior Laurentian protocontinent by Grenvillian crust, in the manner

The exact chronology of Grenvillian orogenic events is only as certain as the 40Ar/39Ar 
and other ages that pinpoint key events, most notably in the present model the initial 
cooling of the Tudor gabbro (Baksi 1982). Once the time framework is established, provided 
pre-burial magnetizations can be demonstrated to have survived, palaeomagnetism places 
quite close constraints on the relative rotations and palaeolatitude shifts of the colliding 
continents. 
In fairness, we should point out that incorporating the Tudor gabbro pole on a younger 
extension of the Grenville Loop, as has been done in the past, is a perfectly reasonable join- 
the-poles approach. Pole SM of the Steel Mountain anorthosite of western Newfoundland 
(Murthy & Rao 1976), which lies in granulite terrain and has a K/Ar chlorite age of 450 k 35 
Ma, is probably a late post-metamorphic overprint that belongs on such an extension. 
However, the burentian APWP appears to have made two or more loops through this 
general area between 700 and 400 Ma (Irving 1979; Dunlop 1981b) and we do not regard 
the agreement of SM with Tu and TUA (Fig. 13) as compelling evidence of contemporaneity. 
If, despite the contrast in metamorphic conditions, the SM and Tu poles are actually of 
similar ages, the Tudor A magnetization would have to be a low-temperature CRM, since the 
Tudor was not reheated sufficiently around 1000 Ma, let alone around 700 or 450 Ma, to 
acquire TRM in the TB range 520-570°C. The very sharp and consistent upper TBS of the 
overprinting remanences, which we find suggestive of the leading edge of an -500°C thermal 
event, would then be no more than a curious coincidence. We do not favour this interpret- 
ation, but the magnetic evidence is not yet compelling enough to rule it out.

Conclusions 
D. J. Dunlop et al. 
(1) The palaeopole of the Tudor gabbro characteristic A magnetization, first determined 
by Hood (1958) and Palmer & Carmichael (1973), is indeed anomalous compared to other 
Grenvillian poles. Our determination, using stable endpoint magnetizations and intersecting 
great circles, places the pole at 12'N, 133"E (dp = 4", dm = 6'). 
(2) The baked contact test with surrounding volcanic and sedimentary rocks was incon- 
clusive. It neither proved nor disproved that the A is the primary NRM of the Tudor gabbro. 
(3) Thellier-type palaeointensity determinations were successful in samples that did not 
alter severely during heating and indicated a palaeofield strength about one-half of that of 
the present-day field at the same latitude. Although this evidence is not conclusive, the A 
magnetization is likely a TRM. 
(4) The A remanence is overprinted by a secondary magnetization which superficially 
resembles the C magnetization of the Cordova gabbro (Dunlop & Stirling 1985) but is rather 
erratic in intensity and direction. The upper blocking temperatures of this 'C' magnetization 
are consistently between 5 15 and 525°C and have no overlap with blocking temperatures of 
the A magnetization. The A magnetization has therefore been thermally overprinted at peak 
temperatures in nature of 470-500°C, presumably during regional burial metamorphism 
which locally produced maximum temperatures in this range. The A magnetization is thus 
pre-metamorphic, in contrast to other reported Grenvillian remanences, which date from 
post-metamorphic uplift and cooling. 
(5) The anomalous Tudor gabbro palaeopole records either local rotation or, more likely, 
pre-metamorphic continent-wide rotation of Grenvillia with respect to Interior Laurentia on 
a scale sufficient to close a small ocean and underplate continental crust in Himalayan 
fashion. A tentative chronology of events is as follows: initial collision and deformational 
phase of orogeny around 1200Ma; intrusion of post-kinematic plutons like the Tudor 
before 1100 Ma; continued continental convergence until about 1050 Ma; and slow uplift 
and cooling lasting until at least 800 Ma.

The palaeomagnetism of the Tertiary igneous 
complex of Ardnamurchan 
P. Dagley, A. E. Mussett and R. R. Skelhorn 
The Sub-Department of Geophysics, Oliver Lodge Laboratory, The University of 
Liverpool, Oxford Street, PO Box 14 7, Liverpool L69 3BX 
Received 1984 May 25; in original form 1984 January 30 
Summary. Samples have been taken systematically through the intrusive 
sequence for the three centres which form the Tertiary central intrusive ring 
complex. Palaeomagnetic measurements show that all the units are reversely 
magnetized as are the earlier lavas - an extension of those of Mull and 
Morvern - which they intrude. This is in contrast to Mull. Skye and Arran, 
where the igneous sequences have been shown to span at least three polarity 
intervals, but is similar to Rhum where the only normal units are a few late 
dykes. Since Rhum and Ardnamuchan both lie on the dyke swarm which 
passes through Muck, the two complexes are considered to be closely related. 
If the Ardnamurchan central complex was formed in a single reversed interval 
the total duration of igneous activity was less than 3 Myr. 
Introduction 
Ardnamurchan is the site of a classic, Tertiary central intrusive complex, made famous by 
the work of Richey & Thomas (1930). Excellent summaries of the geology have been given 
by Richey (1933), Deer (1969), Gribble, Durrance & Walsh (1976) and Emeleus (1982). 
The aim of the work reported in this paper was to sample as completely as posslble from 
the well-established igneous sequence (Table la) in order to determine the magneto- 
stratigraphy and to relate the Ardnamurchan central intrusive complex to the neighbouring 
ones of Mull (Mussett, Dagley Clr Skelhorn 1980), Rhum (Dagley & Mussett 1981) and Skye 
(Dagley & Mussett 1980). 
The central intrusive complex has been intruded into Moine schists, and overlying thin 
Sequence of Jurassic and Triassic sediments and Tertiary basaltic lavas which are considered 
to be an extension of the Mull-Morvern plateau lavas; the base of the lavas can be seen on 
the eastern flanks of Ben Hiant. Richey & Thomas (1930) recognized three successive 
centres of intrusion, Centre 1 to the east, Centre 2 to the west with Centre 3 between, and 
Suggested a sequence of events on which Table 1 is based. However, there is some debate 
about the sequence, particularly within Centre 1.

Richey considered the Ben Hiant complex (events 2 and 3) to be early, and either 
between the plateau lava and Centre 1 or part of the Centre 1 with possibly the youngest 
unit, the quartz-dolerite, contemporaneous with the Centre 1 cone-sheets (event 6). Gribble 
(1 974, p. 76), as a result of a petrochemical investigation, has indeed suggested that the Ben 
Hiant quartz-dolerite represents several cone sheets which have coalesced within the earlier 
event. Field evidence shows that the quartz-dolerite cuts the porphyritic dolerite plug but 
there is no indication of the time interval. 
An alternative interpretation for the Ben Hiant complex has been put forward by Green 
& Wright (1969, 1974). They argue that, assuming there has been negligible movement, the 
question arises as to how the subaerially-formed agglomerates, tuffs and pitchstone lavas of 
Ben Hiant can be preserved at a lower topographical level than the ostensibly younger but 
deeper-level intrusions of Centres 2 and 3, which are thought to have solidified beneath at 
least 1000 m of overburden. Thus they propose that the Ben Hiant sequence results from a 
flank eruption younger than either Centre 2 or 3, and that many of the so-called Centre I 
cone sheets were emplaced late in the development of the central intrusive complex. How- 
ever, we believe that the Ben Hiant sequence is part of Centre 1 and field observations 
suggest that the inter-bedded agglomerates and tuffs, along with the andesitic pitchstone laws 
which occur in the upper part of the bedded pyroclastic sequence, have been downfaulted 
into a small caldera, termed by Richey & Thomas (1930) the South-West Vent. This 
sequence of agglomerates, tuffs and pitchstone lavas is younger than the plateau lavas and 
may represent the surface manifestation of the Northern Vents. 
There is one minor difference in our interpretation of the Ben Hiant sequence compared 
with that of Richey & Thomas (1930). We believe that the porphyritic dolerite plug post- 
dates the agglomerates. tuffs and pitchstone lavas whereas Richey & Thomas (1930, p. 15 1 ). 
on the basis of devitrification textures in the adjacent pitchstones, thought that the plug 
post-dated the lowest two pitchstones but pre-dated pitchstones 3 and 4 of this study. In a 
stream section (540 626) the porphyritic dolerite plug is seen to have an intrusive. chilled 
margin against tuffs and agglomerates which overlie the lowest two pitchstone lavas. 
Although no contacts are exposed between the porphyritic dolerite and the pitchstone lavas 
3 and 4 the scarps formed by these pitchstones are terminated to the SW by the margin of 
the porphyritic dolerite.

The trachyte plug (event la) is difficult to place precisely in the sequence; although it is 
intruded into Moine rocks and must be early because it is cut by Centre 1 cone-sheets. 
The only previous palaeoniagnetic work had been limited to specific problems. Khan 
(1960) sampled the Hypersthene Gabbro for comparison with gabbro bodies in Rhum and 
Skye. He found it to be reversely magnetized. Wells & McRae (1 969) undertook four radial 
traverses across the Hypersthene Gabbro intrusion to ascertain whether the dips of the 
layering were a primary feature or produced by post-consolidation deformation. They con- 
cluded that because there was a close clustering of the palaeomagnetic directions about that 
found by Khan the layering had suffered little 01- no deformation after cooling below the 
Curie temperature of about 570°C. 
Watt (1966) sampled some of the cone sheets to investigate the correlations of the 
magnetic properties with the fabric. His samples were reversely magnetized, 
lntrusions from the three centres have been dated by the K-Ar method (see discussion for 
details) and the dates obtained suggest an age about 00 Ma. i.e. the same as most of the rest 
of the British Tertiary Igneous Province (Mussett 1980). 
Sampling and results 
Sampling was carried out using portable drills. orienting the cores by means of sunsights or 
geographic bearings. The 73 sampling sites are shown in Fig. 1 and listed according to the 
established sequence in Table l(a). Only dykes which have a cross-cutting relationship 
with intrusions belonging to the central intrusive complex were sampled (Table I b). The 
directions of magnetization of at least four cores from each site were determined using a 
parastatic magnetometer and incremental alternating field demagnetization. Thermal 
demagnetization was also used for samples from most units. 
For some samples the magnetization was so strong that it is almost certain that the 
locality had been struck by lightning. In a few of these cases demagnetization uncovered 
a primary direction of magnetization on which the directions for several individual cores 
converged; in other cases no agreement was achieved. 
In general, the results after thermal demagnetization are in good agreement with those 
following magnetic cleaning. However, frequently the change of direction was less than 
occurred during magnetic cleaning and in several cases there was no change from the NRM 
direction so that the primary direction is not revealed. Those units with noticeably different 
directions after demagnetization by the two methods are V005, V009B, V013, V020, V022, 
V043, V048, V060, V062 and V068. 
The detailed results are listed in Table 2 (see also Figs 2 and 3). Several features of the 
results are worth pointing out. 
The acid and basic components of each of the composite bodies sampled (V2 in Fig. 3c, 
V9 in Fig. 3b and V44 in Table 2) are significantly different. It is not uncommon for the 
acid parts to give more uncertain directions because of their weaker magnetization, as with 
V009 but for V002 it is the basic part which has the less well defined direction. 
Similar differences occur between core clusters (sites) from different parts of the same 
body; thus V016 and V017 from the Quartzgabbro of Faskadale (event 17) and VO18 and 
9047 from the Great Eucrite (event 18) do not agree well. In these cases it may be naive 
(0 regard these bodies as simple intrusions. The Quartz-gabbro of Faskadale varies from a 
basic variety in the east to a more acid variety in the west (Richey & Thomas 1930). At 
Faskadale, the rock (V016) is an olivine-gabbro whereas the rock sampled (V017) to the east 
of the Achnaha-Kilchoan road is a quartz-gabbro with well-developed interstitial granophyric 
htergrowth. Because of the presence of internal contacts, combined with considerable petro-

The thermomagnetic behaviour of samples from each site was determined using a strong 
field Curie balance. There was no evidence for 'double' Curie points and for some samples 
the Curie transition was very poorly defined. Curie points generally lie in the range 
500-580°C (Table 2) suggesting titanomagnetite as the principal carrier of the remanence. 
Discussion and conclusions 
It is our contention that the primary polarity of all the bodies sampled is reversed and that 
the igneous sequence was formed during a single reversed interval of the geomagnetic field. 
However, before interpreting our results further the alternatives involving slow cooling 
and/or overprinting must be considered. 
If, during the evolution of the three centres, the regional temperature never fell below the 
Curie point, the magnetic polarities will reflect only the post-Centre 3 cooling event. A 
reason for such slow cooling could be that. at the present level of erosion, the Ardnamurchan 
central intrusive complex represents a deeper level than for instance, the Mull complex. The 
Ardnamurchan complex is characterized by an abundance of basic intrusions with only one 
acid intrusion of any size, the Grigadale Granophyre measuring 0.5 kni in diameter. whereas 
at the present level of erosion acid intrusions comprise 40 per cent of the Mull complex. 
We consider this hypothesis of slow cooling unlikely because of the small size of the 
intrusive complex. From the interpretation of gravity anomalies, Bott & Tuson (1973) have 
shown that the Ardnamurchan complex is probably underlain by a cylinder of mafic 
material having a dianiter of 12km extending to a depth of 4.5 km beneath the present 
surface. This is much smaller than is found for the Mull and Skye complexes for both of 
which the underlying cylinders are estimated to be 20km in diameter and 14km in depth.

sions they may have been reheated and magnetically overprinted by later intrusions, 
particularly those of Centre 3, to give the common reversed polarity. 
With this possibility in mind, intrusions belonging to both Centre I and 2 were sampled 
geographically as far away and as close as possible to Centre 3. For example, Centre 1 basic 
cone sheets were sampled to the east of Ockle Point, Port Ban and Faskadale, respectively 
5. 1.2 and 340m from the margin of Centre 3. Within Centre 2, a 2.5 km long traverse was 
carried out from the Point of Ardnamurchan (lighthouse). through Grigadale to Achosnich 
in which various major intrusions and cone sheets were sampled. We think that this 
geographical disposition of the sampling sites is greater than the likely width of the zone of 
reheating. In Mull, we have shown (Dagley, Mussett & Skelhorn 1983) that the zone of 
magnetic overprinting produced by the major intrusions of Centre 2 has a width of 
approximately 1 km. 
Those intrusions in the Ardnamurchan Centre 2 traverse. the Older Quartz Gabbro of 
Beinn Bhuidhe (V041), a member of the Inner Set ot' cone sheets (V040), the Grigadale 
Granophyre (V039) and the Older Gabbro of Lochan an Aodainn(V037, V038), which are 
nearest to Centre 3 all exhibit evidence of metamorphism as shown by intense clouding of 
the plagioclase and the development of iron oxide in the ferromagnesian minerals, similar 
to that which in Mull is associated with magnetic overprinting. However, all the intrusions 
in this traverse give reversed polarity, and thermal demagnetization of cores from V039, 
V040 and V041 shows that a secondary normal component is removed by 300°C. There is 
similar, but weak. evidence for overprinting by normal magnetization in some of the later 
intrusions. Thus this evidence suggests that the reversed polarity of the unnietamorphosed 
intrusions of Centt-e 2 is primary. 
We believe, therefore, that all the intrusions we have sampled, as well as the dykes and 
lavas. are reversely magnetized. The reversed polarity of the lavas is consistent with the 
belief that they are an extension of the Mull-Morvern lavas. Seven of the eight dykes 
sampled are reversed; the other VOGO gave an unreliable result. 
Though the Ardnamurchan complex consists of three consecutive centres, because of its 
small size, the whole complex may have been emplaced quite rapidly, so that the whole 
igneous sequence was formed during the same reversed interval of the geomagnetic field. 
Thus there is a marked contrast with the central intrusive complexes of Skye, Mull and 
Arran. The former with four centres was emplaced over at least three polarity intervals 
(Dagley & Mussett 1980), whereas Mull with three centres was emplaced over two polarity 
intervals (Mussett et al. 1980; Dagley et al. 1983) with a third polarity interval being 
recognized in the reversely magnetized, NW-trending basic dykes which cut the Loch Ba 
Felsite, the last major intrusion of the central intrusive complex. In ' Arran a polarity 
succession of at least R-N-R has been demonstrated by two stratigraphic sequences 
(Hodgson 1981). 
Ardnamurchan is more like Rhum in being a small compact complex. Although Rhum has 
one of the largest gravity anomalies of all the centres the basic cylinder is estimated to be 
only 8-10km in diameter (McQuillan & Tuson 1963). Rhum, too, is entirely reversely 
magnetized except for a few late dykes (Dagley & Mussett 1981). The overall mean direc- 
tions for the two centres lie within 5' of each other and are the same at the 95 per cent 
confidence level (see Table 2). We think that the similarity is not fortuitous because the two 
centres lie along the same regional linear dyke swarm (Speight et al. 1982) which probably 
controlled the duration of igneous activity in that the mafic cylinders which underlie the 
central complexes are merely the higher-rising components of a more fundamental structure, 
namely the proposed extensive magma ridges from which the regional dyke swarms arose.

These dates suggest that the Ardnamurchan activity took place at more or less the same 
time as that in Mull and Rhurti and we suggest that the reversed interval recorded in 
Ardnamurchan is the same as that recorded in Rhuni. Both the Ardnamurchan and Mull 
central complexes followed the same plateau basalt sequence and we suggest that the 
reversed interval recorded in Ardnamurchan (and Rhum) is the same as the first reversed 
interval recorded in Mull. Other evidence (Meighan etal. 1983) shows that the Rhum centre 
preceded the lavas and central intrusive complex of Skye. The Skye lavas (Wilson. Dagley & 
Ade-Hall 1977,) and the early Basic centres (Dagley & Mussett 1980) are reversely 
magnetized and dates for the centre (Dickin 1981, unpublished work of this laboratory) 
show it was contemporary with both Ardnamurchan and Rhum. Thus it is most probable 
that both these centres were intruded during the first reversed interval recorded in Skye. On 
the time-scale of Harland et al. 1983,) this common reversed interval recorded in Rhum and 
Ardnamurchan and by the lavas and early intrusions of Mull and Skye would be Chron 26r, 
which lasted from 61.00 to 58.19 Ma.

A palaeomagnetic investigation of a Permian redbed 
sequence from a mining drill core 
M. E . Evans Institute of Earth and Planetary Physics, University ofAlberta,
