Summary. Samples spanning 66 m of Permian redbeds were collected from a 
vertical, but azimuthally unoriented, drill core obtained during a uranium 
exploration programme in the Lodhe Basin of southern France. Inclinations 
are well grouped @= - 6.5", k = 121.5) and consistent with the known 
Permian palaeolatitude of Europe. Declinations have been estimated by using 
a sedimentological model involving tectonically-rotated cross-bed laminations. 
The results are very encouraging and suggest a pole at 151°E, 53"N (6p = lo, 
6m = 2", N = 43), which agrees well with the Eurasian apparent polar wander 
curve. The small polar discrepancy could well be due to secular variation, 
which is consistent with the small variance and presumed short time spanned 
by the sequence. Fully oriented surface samples confirm these findings, and 
support the validity of the orientation model. Temporal variations revealed 
by the stratigraphic ordering can be interpreted as slow dipole wobble, on a 
time-scale of lo5 yr or more, on which is superimposed a more rapid non- 
dipole secular variation. It appears that the core stores of the world could 
become - at least under favourable circumstances - an important source of 
palaeomagnetic information. 
Key words: palaeomagnetism, Permian, drill-core, cross-bedding, von Mises 
distribution 
Introduction 
There is a growing need for long sequences of stratigraphically ordered palaeomagnetic data 
in order to describe the temporal behaviour of the geomagnetic field. Over the last decade, 
investigations of recent lake sediments has led to considerable progress in this direction, but 
the bulk of the results available refer to the most recent lo4 yr, or so, of geological time. 
Comparable data for earlier periods is much more sparse, and this prompted the present

412 
attempt to extract useful palaeomagnetic data from a vertical, but azimuthally unoriented 
mining drill core. Apart from the notable exception of reversal stratigraphy studies on 
DSD?/IPOD cores, this type of material has attracted little attention; but even if the success 
rate turns out to be quite modest the core stores throughout the world offer a potential 
dataset well worth exploiting. 
M. E. Evans and J. M. Maillol 
Procedure and results 
The entire core is some 470 m long and was obtained during a uranium exploration 
programme in the Lodeve Basin of southern France. This particular study involves a 66 m 
sequence of Permian redbeds which comprise the uppermost portion of the core. Two series 
of measurements are involved - magnetic and geometric. The first is straightforward and 
simply involves determining the remanence vector of each specimen relative to an arbitrary 
reference line scribed on the core. Specimens took the form of horizontal cylinders (25 mm 
diameterx 25 mm long) drilled perpendicular to the axis of the original 35 mm diameter 
core. Initial measurements made in the Montpellier laboratory employed a portable Molspin 
spinner magnetometer; the project was completed in the Edmonton laboratory using a 
Digico spinner magnetometer. The geometric measurements consisted of relating the 
arbitrary reference line to the stratification visible in each core segment, the intention being 
to relate this to the known bedding in the area to obtain an absolute reference frame. This 
was done by least-squares fitting of sinusoids to the stratification traces on the cylindrical 
surface of the original core. The actual data consisted of several - usually about 12 - 
distances between the selected stratification trace and an arbitrary horizontal circumference. 
Measurements were made with the aid of a graduated transparent plastic cylinder which 
fitted snugly over the core. This technique is applicable only to segments with simple 
stratification; zones of massive or contorted bedding were avoided. The sediments were 
deposited in a continental environmenl and exhibit abundant cross-bedding. This

DECLINATION DATA 
These sediments were formed in an intermittently fluvial sub-desert environment, and cross- 
bedding is consequently ubiquitous. Following a detailed study of the sedimentology, 
Kruseman (1962) concludes that the direction of transport was from west to east. Potter & 
Pettijohn (1977) have made an extensive survey of published data and conclude that 
averages for the dip of cross-bedding generally fall between 18 and 25". We combine these 
conclusions and propose that, on average, the original cross-bed laminations inclined 20" to 
the East. The geological map of the area, and our own measurements in the vicinity of the 
drill hole, indicate a tectonic dip of 16" towards N165"E. Tilting the cross-bed mode axis 
appropriately leads to a maximum-likelihood strike of N211"E (see Fig. 3a). We assign this 
value to the stratification in each measured core segment and obtain the distribution of 
magnetic declinations shown in Fig. 3(b). 
Since the magnetic vectors are close to the horizontal we adopt a circular normal (von 
Mises) distribution to analyse the declinations obtained by the above procedure. This yields 
b= 197.2" with a standard deviation of 28.4". Assuming k = 121.5, as deduced from the 
analysis of inclinations, one expects an angular standard deviation (81/v/k) of 7.3"; the 
excess reflects real variation in cross-bed orientation. The amount of azimuthal variation

Poles corresponding to the drill-core samples (151°E, 53"N, 6p = I", 6m = 2", N= 43), 
the surface samples (148"E, 47"N, 6p = 2", 6m = 4", N= 15), and Kruseman's Saxonian 
data are plotted in Fig. 5, where they are compared with the Eurasian apparent polar wander 
curve proposed by Irving & Irving (1982). Agreement is good. The differences observed 
could well be due to secular variation which is discussed more fully in the next section. For 
the moment we reiterate that Kruseman's result represents an average over some 1500 m 
whereas our data represent only 66 and 10 m for the drill-core and surface samples 
respectively. Moreover, our two datasets may be distinct in time since there is a mapped 
fault running between the two sampling localities. It is also possible that Kruseman's average 
is slightly offset by the failure to completely remove recent overprints from all his selected 
samples. Be that as it may, it appears that reliable palaeomagnetic results can be obtained 
from unoriented cores - at least when circumstances are favourable.

To investigate the temporal variation of the geomagnetic field which occurred during 
deposition of this sedimentary sequence one requires declination and inclination for each 
horizon. This is not possible here because the attitude of the cross-bedding at each individual 
horizon is unknown. Such success as the above orientation procedure enjoys results from the 
use of averages, not individual data. Nevertheless, a pattern in the uncorrected inclination 
data is clearly apparent (Fig. 6). The results fall into two distinct clouds with an abrupt 
break near a depth of 32 m. Subsequently, the drillers' log was obtained and it was gratifying 
to discover that there is a 50 cm coarse gravel at this level. Furthermore, it is the only such 
gravel recorded in the entire 66 m of sediment. It presumably reflects a hiatus of unknown 
duration. The inclination trends above and below this break may be due to dipole wobble, 
with the higher freqtiency content then being attributed to secular variation of the non- 
dipole field. The smoothed curves obtained from a S-point moving average indicate the 
possible form of the dipole wobble. Observed deviations up to 10" then represent non-dipole 
effects - certainly an acceptable magnitude for such perturbations. Although a pattern 
emerges when viewed over tens of metres, there is very little sequential ordering on a scale of 
1 or 2 m. This suggests that the sample spacing is too coarse to yield smooth secular variation 
paths. If these took place on a time-scale of -lo3 yr, as is the case for the recent past, then

Palaeomagnetic investigation of a Redbed sequence 419 
we can perhaps associate a time span of this order with our typical sampling interval; this in 
turn leads to an order-of-magnitude estimate of 1 mm yr-' for the deposition rate. Each 
30 m section would then represent some 3 x lo4 yr, which would imply a time scale of 
210s yr for dipole wobble. Three of the longer core segments were investigated in more 
detail to test this general interpretation. As with the other core segments these cannot be 
azimuthally oriented a priori, but relative orientation between individual specimens is 
possible. As can be seen in Fig. 7, successive vectors do fall on smooth curves, and this 
supports the idea that the high-frequency scatter does represent a real geomagnetic 
phenomenon. 
Van den Ende (1977) reaches very similar conclusions from his study of fully-orientated 
samples of Permian redbeds from the DGme de Barrot which is situated some 300 km to the 
East of the LodBve Basin. A detailed study of two particular sequences (1.3 and 2.3 m 
thick) reveals field-vector trajectories that sweep out open loops which are very reminiscent 
of the recent secular variation. Exploiting this analogy, van den Ende deduces a 
sedimentation rate of 1 mm yr-'. A more widely-sample section (26 horizons spanning 38 m, 
four samples per horizon) suggests longer-period variations which he interprets as dipole 
wobble on a time scale of 1-5 x 104yr. Without adequate dating control all these 
conclusions - both our own and those of van den Ende - must be regarded as rather 
tentative, but the nature of these sedimentary sequences makes it unlikely that the absolute 
chronology will be significantly improved in the near future. Nevertheless, it does seem that 
the gross properties of the geomagnetic field in the deep geological past is recoverable and 
that appropriate enquiry will pay dividends.

The results of thermal and alternating field demagnetization of 13 specimens from a fully oriented mafic 
igneous core taken from a depth of 5.32 km near the center of the Michigan basin give a pole position at 
9øS, 159øE (k = 69, a95 = 5ø). This pole is close to'late Hadrynian and Cambrian pole positions from the 
North American craton. Furthermore, one specimen was cut from each of three vertical red bed core 
segments, unoriented in declination, from depths of 4.59, 4.09, and 4.08 km. Thermal demagnetization 
revealed a large secondary magnetization in these samples, which was fully eliminated at 480øC. Further 
thermal demagnetization revealed closely grouped characteristic inclinations that averaged 8 ø . By assum- 
ing the secondary magnetizations to be parallel to the present-day geomagnetic field direction it was 
possible to obtain characteristic declinations as well. The pole from the red beds is located at 7øN, 174øE 
and agrees well with the pole obtained from the late Keweenawan sediments (Freda sandstone and 
Nonesuch shale) of the Upper Peninsula in Michigan. These results suggest that the red beds acquired 
their characteristic magnetization before the igneous basement rock. If the igneous rock is an extrusive 
body of Keweenawan age, its characteristic magnetization must be entirely secondary. 
INTRODUCTION 
As part of the geophysical and geological studies associated 
with the Michigan basin borehole project (McClure-Sparks 1- 
8 well in Ithaca, Gratiot County, Michigan), paleomagnetic 
studies were undertaken on red bed and medium- to coarse- 
grained mafic igneous rock samples. The red beds are found as 
a 1500-m-thick and relatively undisturbed sequence below the 
lowest identifiable Cambrian strata of the Michigan basin; a 
Late Precambrian age is assumed, but the upper part could be 
as young as Early Cambrian. Within the red bed sequence of 
me borehole, igneous bodies of manc composition were en- 
countered at two levels; gravity studies within the borehole 
[Bradley and Hinze, 1976; Bradley et al., 1976] indicate that 
more igneous bodies may exist at other depths. The borehole 
bottomed at 5.32-km depth in the lower igneous unit, from 
which our samples were taken. The three red bed samples were 
obtained to complement the paleomagnetic studies of the ig- 
neous core; these samples were drilled from the shallower 
depths of 4.59, 4.09, and 4.08 km. 
The goals of this study were to find out whether paleomag- 
netism can assist in dating the sequence and to study the effects 
of burial temperatures on the magnetization. The experimental 
results will be presented here, and the age implications will be 
discussed. The effects of the burial temperatures have been dis- 
cussed elsewhere [Van der Voo et al., 1978]. The igneous core 
was oriented azimuthally in situ at a depth of 5.32 km by a 
camera-clock-compass-level bubble system attached to knives 
scribing the core. Thirteen specimens, distributed along at 
least 5 m of the core, were measured and used for statistical 
analysis and pole position determination. Nevertheless, it\" 
should be realized that statistically, the borehole paleomag- 
netic results cannot be equated with results from surface out- 
crops, where it is usually possible to obtain a larger number of 
individually oriented _samples from several sites. 
MEASUREMENT AND DEMAGNETIZATION 
The natural remanent magnetization (NRM) of the 13 ig- 
neous specimens was measured with a Schonstedt spinner 
magnetometer and a ScT cryogenic magnetometer. Intensities

DISCUSSION 
Since our main goal in studying the paleomagnetism of the 
borehole samples was to assist in dating the rocks involved, it 
is important to ascertain whether the characteristic magnet-

izations are original, i.e., whether they were acquired when the 
rocks were formed. For the red beds we see no reason to 
question the assumption that the magnetization is the initial 
one, acquired during or shorly after deposition. Their magnet- 
ization, which is carried by hematite, has a very high stability 
and blocking temperatures of up to 675øC or more. The result- 
ing pole position, as discussed below, agrees well with the age 
expected from the regional tectonic setting of the red beds in 
the Michigan basin. The igneous rock, on the other hand, has 
undergone hydrothermal alteration or even metamorphism to 
greenschist facies according to E. W. Heinrich (personal com- 
munication, 1977), and complete remagnetization cannot a 
priori be excluded. The red beds do not show any magnet- 
ization which is similar to the magnetizations of the igneous 
core other than the steeply inclined components attributed to 
remagnetization in the present-day field. Therefore complete 
remagnetization, if it occurred, appears to have been restricted 
to the igneous rocks. 
The pole positions of the igneous and red bed samples are 
plotted in Figure 5, together with published Late Precambrian 
and Cambrian poles for North America [Irving and McGlynn, 
1976; Henry et al., 1977; French et al., 1977]. These pole 
positions fall into two groups. The older group, with ages 
between about 1100 and 1000 m.y., forms the K eweenawan 
trend (Table 1; Figure 5, circles). The other group, with ages 
between about 700 and 500 m.y., forms the late Hadrynian- 
Cambrian trend (Table 1; Figure 5, squares). The intervening 
period between 1000 m.y. and 700 m.y. has yielded to date 
only a limited number of poles (not plotted). These fall mostly 
in the general area between the above mentioned groups [Mor- 
ris, 1977], though Morris and Roy [1977] recently advocated a 
Hadrynian age for some poles that fall close to the present-day 
pole. Synorogenic poles from the Grenville province have 
not been plotted, since its position with respect to cratonic 
North America is controversial [Buchan and Dunlop, 1976].

are very different and since the Michigan borehole rocks are 
relatively undisturbed and do not belong to the Grenville 
province. It is, on the other hand, quite reasonable to assume 
that the rocks penetrated in the Michigan borehole are analo- 
gous to the Keweenawan suite as exposed in the Lake Superior 
region. This assumption is supported by the similarity between 
the pole position of the Michigan borehole red beds and the 
poles of the late Keweenawan red beds (Nonesuch shale and 
Freda sandstone, poles 11 and 12 in Figure 5). The pole of the 
igneous rock of the borehole, however, is different from the 
middle and late Keweenawan poles of the Lake Superior re- 
gion and falls near the late H adrynian-Cambrian poles (Fig- 
ure 5, squares). An interpretation of the petrography of the 
rock (E. W. Heinrich, personal communication, 1977) suggests 
that the igneous body at the base of the borehole may be an 
altered lava flow, with Keweenawan affinities. If this is the 
case, the characteristic magnetization is secondary and has 
replaced any initial magnetization. The mechanism by which 
the igneous body could have acquired the secondary magnet- 
ization is difficult to explain, as the overlying red beds, 700 m 
above, were not affected by late Hadrynian-Cambrian re- 
magnetization. The thermal demagnetization curves for the 
igneous rock (Figure 1) show the highest blocking temper- 
atures to be near 560øC for the carriers of the characteristic 
magnetization, suggesting that magnetite is the dominant car- 
rier. A regional thermal event of sufficient intensity to re- 
magnetize the magnetite would have very likely remagnetized 
the hematite in the red beds overlying the igneous body to a 
large extent. A possibility which cannot be excluded is that the 
characteristic direction of the igneous body (Figure 2) is not 
one of a single remanence vector but rather the resultant of the 
decay of two vectors of equal coercivity spectra. 
In summary, our studies indicate that a late Keweenawan 
age (about 1000 m.y.) for the Michigan basin red beds is not 
unreasonable. The magnetization of the basic igneous rock is 
likely to be entirely secondary and may have been acquired by 
the unit during late Hadrynian or possibly Cambrian time. 
The remagnetization of the igneous body is not necessarily 
evidence for a thermal event, as the overlying red beds do not 
show any remagnetization at this time; tentatively, we suggest 
that the remagnetization is of chemical origin. No paleomag-

The palaeomagnetism of the main zone in the western Bushveld Complex 
P. J. Hattingh 
University of Pretoria, Pretoria 0002 (Republic o/South Africa) 
Received November 20,1985; revised version accepted June 19.1986 
Sampling was done at thirty-four sites in the main zone of the western Bushveld Complex, South Africa. Alternating 
field (AF) and thermal demagnetization of specimens indicated a multicomponent NRM in the majority of specimens. 
A primary magnetization direction (D = 357.8”; I = 70.9O; ag5 = 2.8O; k = 80) was recovered from thirty-two 
sampling sites. Fold tests indicate that the igneous layering was emplaced in a horizontal position and that the NRM 
predates tilling of the layered sequence. Two sampling sites situated in the lower part of the main zone yielded 
magnetization directions approximately antipodal to the above mentioned magnetization direction. The palaeomagnetic 
pole position (9.2ON; 27.3OE), calculated for the main zone of the western Bushveld Complex, indicates that this part 
of the main zone had acquired its magnetization later than the main zone in the eastern Bushveld Complex and later 
than the underlying critical zone. 
1. Introduction 
Recent palaeomagnetic investigations on cer- 
tain layered intrusions such as Sudbury [1,2] and 
Skaergaard [3], have shown that palaeomagnetic 
data can be an important indicator of the 
tectono-intrusive history of layered intrusions. For 
this reason, a comprehensive palaeomagnetic in- 
vestigation of the Bushveld Complex was initiated 
in order to extend the study of Gough and Van 
Niekerk [4] and to relate the new palaeomagnetic 
results from the layered sequence to more modern 
concepts of the genesis and structure of the Com- 
plex [5-71. 
In this report palaeomagnetic data from the 
main zone of the western Bushveld Complex are 
presented. The geographical and stratigraphical 
positions of thirty-four sampling sites are shown 
in Figs. 1 and 2. The majority of sites is situated 
in quarries and road cuttings. The resultant rela- 
tively unweathered samples enabled the extraction 
of consistent and stable magnetization directions 
from all sampling sites and it was unnecessary to 
reject any data. . 
2. Laboratory measurements 
Samples were taken with a petrol driven porta- 
ble core drill. The core samples are 25 mm in 
diameter and up to 250 mm in length. Four core 
samples were taken at each sampling site. Each 
core was cut into five or more 25 mm long cylin- 
drical specimens. Core orientation was done with 
a sun compass [8] which allows orientation to a 
precision of lo [9]. 
The remanent magnetization of specimens was 
measured using a Digico “Complete Results” 
fluxgate spinner magnetometer. In practice it was 
found that to measure a reliable direction of mag- 
netization to within one degree, a minimum inten- 
sity of magnetization of 0.5 X 10m3 A m-’ was 
required. 
Continuous thermal demagnetization of speci- 
mens was done with a slightly-modified form of 
the spinner magnetometer. It was possible to mea- 
sure remanence at high temperatures without the 
need for cooling the specimen in a field free space. 
Operating the instrument in this mode, however, 
led to a decreased sensitivity, and it was found 
that the minimum intensity of magnetization that 
could be measured reliably was in the region of 
4 X 10s3 A m-‘. 
Alternating field (AF) demagnetization of 
specimens was done with an apparatus built at the 
Geological Survey of South Africa following a 
‘description by McElhinny [lo]. This apparatus is 
capable of creating a peak alternating magnetic 
field of 120 mT.

5. Stepwise alternating field demagnetization of 
pilot specimens 
During stepwise AF demagnetization of speci- 
mens at progressively higher AF values, magneti- 
zation directions from virtually all the sites in 
group B exhibited a slow change in direction. At 
low AF values the magnetization vectors remain 
stable with very little movement, but at AF values 
higher than approximately 40 mT the directions 
start to change, with the directional change and 
divergence of vectors becoming larger as the AF 
values increase. This type of response is illustrated 
in Fig. 5 with the aid of specimens from sites 56 
and 62. From this it must be concluded that the 
magnetization directions in groups A and B are 
not primary magnetization directions, but rather 
resultant magnetization directions due to primary 
and secondary magnetization. 
In Fig. 6 remagnetization circles [17] fitted to 
AF demagnetization data from four sites, are 
shown. A comparison of the orientation of these 
remagnetization circles and the dip and dip direc- 
tions of the layering at each site (Table 1) indi- 
cates that there is no correlation between the 
secondary magnetization(s) and the dip of the 
igneous layering at each site. 
The magnetization component responsible for 
the grouping of the magnetization vectors into 
group B, dominates the magnetic characteristics of 
the specimens and this primary magnetization 
component almost certainly was acquired by all 
the specimens at more or less the same time. With 
this and the previous arguments on the effect of 
the dip of the igneous layering in mind, only one 
plausible explanation for the diverging circles of 
remagnetization can be postulated, namely that 
the secondary magnetization component was 
acquired at a different time at each site, resulting 
in a different direction of secondary magnetiza- 
tion for each site. It must, however, be emphasized

6. Thermal demagnetization 
The directional response of the NRM vector of 
specimens from group A to continuous thermal 
demagnetization (Fig. 10) is similar to the re- 
sponse to AF demagnetization. At low tempera- 
tures the magnetization directions remain virtually 
constant, but at higher temperatures the magneti- 
zation directions start to change, with the change 
becoming larger at high temperatures. The vectors 
do not describe remagnetization circles as in some 
instances during AF demagnetization but, as dur- 
ing AF demagnetization, the directions diverge 
more and more as the demagnetization process 
proceeds. From this it appears as if there are 
mainly only two magnetization components. The 
dominant primary magnetization is removed at 
slightly lower temperatures than the smaller sec- 
ondary component, which is possibly different for 
each site. 
A typical normalized thermal intensity response 
curve of a specimen from group A, is shown in 
Fig. 10B. On this curve two separate Curie points 
are evident. The lower of these, at approximately 
575°C indicates magnetite as the source of rema- 
nent magnetization, while the higher Curie point 
in the region of 6OO”C, possibly indicates haema- 
tite [20] as the source of magnetization.

7. Mineralogy of opaque minerals 
All the specimens from sites with reversed mag- 
netization directions (positive inclinations, group 
B) contain similar opaque minerals. Magnetite 
occurs as lamellae in both the pyroxene and 
plagioclase crystals similar to the magnetite in 
specimens from the main zone in the eastern 
Bushveld Complex [ll]. Magnetite lamellae seem 
to be less abundant in specimens from the western 
Bushveld Complex. It must be concluded that the 
lower Curie point of 575°C observed for these 
specimens, can be attributed to these magnetite 
lamellae. Discrete magnetite grains, although they 
do occur in the specimens, are very rare. 
Ilmenite generally occurs as discrete grains with 
diameters up to 0.1 mm. These grains commonly 
exhibit haematite exsolution lamellae. No other 
haematite is present in the specimens and the 
second observed Curie temperature of approxi- 
mately 600°C, could be the result of these exsolu- 
tion lamellae in the ilmenite. 
Sulphide grains occur commonly, but are less 
abundant than the ilmenite grains. Some of the 
sulphide grains were identified as pyrrhotite. 
The opaque mineralogy of sites 75 and 76, 
differs considerably from that described for sites 
in group B. No magnetite grains could be found in 
either pyroxene or plagioclase crystals and it is 
noteworthy that the intensity of the NRM of these 
specimens is two orders of magnitude less than the 
intensity of the NRM of specimens from sites in 
group B. Small discrete magnetite grains do occur 
in these specimens, but are very rare. 
A similarity of the opaque minerals in these 
specimens with respect to specimens from sites in 
group B, is the occurrence of ilmenite grains with 
haematite exsolution lamellae. Although no Curie 
point could be obtained for these specimens due 
to the low intensity of magnetization, it is possible 
that the haematite lamellae are the carriers of a 
primary magnetization in the specimens from sites 
75 and 76, as well as the carriers of the hard 
secondary magnetization in specimens from group 
B. This will explain the observed magnetic polar- 
ity difference which can be the result of a geomag- 
netic field reversal or a self-reversal of magnetiza- 
tion resulting from a mechanism operating in the 
haemo-ilmenite grains. However, this possibility 
can not readily explain the apparent difference of 
the secondary magnetization components of sites 
in group B. 
8. Summary of results 
Fold tests applied to palaeomagnetic directions 
from the main zone in the western Bushveld Com- 
plex, yield results indicating that the main zone 
possibly acquired its present dip after cooling to 
temperatures below the Curie points of the respec- 
tive ferromagnetic components. 
The NRM of the main zone comprises a num- 
ber of magnetization components, but the primary 
magnetization dominates over the small secondary 
components to such an extent, that when correc- 
tions for these secondary components are applied 
the mean magnetization direction does not change 
substantially. This mean magnetization (corrected 
for the dip of the igneous layering) of the main 
zone in the western Bushveld Complex is as fol-

The apparent polar wander (APW) path for 
Africa for the interval circa 2070-1800 m.y. with 
selected pole positions is shown in Fig. 11. Morgan 
[21] regards this as a particularly well defined 
APW segment - 80” long with f10” lateral un- 
certainty. A comparison of radiometric ages and 
pole positions (Fig. 11) certainly confirms this 
with the exception of two poles, namely the Los- 
berg Gabbro (LB) and the younger Phalaborwa 
(PA2) poles. 
The radiometric age of the Losberg Gabbro is 
1841 + 276 m.y. [21]. The relative large uncer- 
tainty associated with this age however renders 
this pole position compatible with other poles on 
the APW path. The Phalaborwa (PA2) pole repre- 
sents dolerite dykes and syenite which are younger 
than the carbonatite and phoscorite of the Phala- 
borwa Complex. A previous minimum age of 1520 
m.y. for the dolerite dykes was given by Morgan 
and Briden [22], but in a later publication Morgan 
[21] gives an age of 2012 f 19 m.y. for the PA2 
pole. This age is difficult to accommodate with the 
PA2 pole position, and the progressive younger 
radiometric ages manifested from east to west by 
all other poles on the APW path. 
The pole position of the main zone, western 
Bushveld Complex (pole B, Fig. 11) lies on the 
APW path to the west of poles BMZ and BCZ 
which represents the main zone eastern Bushveld 
Complex [ll] and the critical zone of the Bushveld 
Complex [23] respectively. This implies that em- 
placement and subsequent cooling of the critical 
zone was the first phase in the genesis of the 
layered sequence of the Bushveld Complex. Pole 
positions (Fig. 11) further indicate that this event 
took place before or simultaneously with the onset 
of deposition of Waterberg sediments and the 
451 
emplacement of the Phalaborwa Complex. This 
was followed by the emplacement and cooling of 
the main zone in the eastern Bushveld Complex 
and only then, the emplacement of the main zone 
of the western Bushveld Complex. 
This is in concordance with the view held by 
Sharpe et al. [7], based on work in the eastern 
Bushveld, that the layered rocks were derived from 
two magma series. The position of pole B (western 
Bushveld Complex, Fig. ll), however, indicate a 
possible third influx of magma to form the main 
zone of the western Bushveld Complex.

ABSTRACT 
Mauritsch, H. J. and Pondaga, M. M., 1985. Paleomagnetic investigations on the East African Rift in 
Northern Tanzania, Journal of Geodynamics, 2: 265-274. 
Near Lake Manyara and north of Monduli, Northern Tanzania, Precambrian gneisses and Neogene 
basalts on the East African rift were sampled. Rock magnetic and microscope investigations established 
coarse and fine grained magnetite as carrier of the NRM in the basalts, and hematite in the gneisses. In 
all three sections only reversed magnetization directions were found. The Precambrian gneisses show 
very hard magnetizations which is known to be prefolding and possibly of Proterozoic age. 
INTRODUCTION 
Within a mineral prospecting program in Northern Tanzania, sponsored 
by UNDP and Tanzania, the possibility arose to take paleomagnetic sam- 
ples on the eastern branch of the East African Rift. The two major targets 
were to test the suitability of different rock types like Precambrian gneisses 
and Neogene basalts for paleomagnetic purpose and the application of 
reversal stratigraphy as an aid to interpreting the geology. Three sections 
were chosen. The first one near Lake Manyara runs down the small Marera 
Valley north of Manyara hotel. From the top to the bottom, where the talus 
deposits start, one can distinguish 16 layers. Sometimes they are separated 
by thin (0,5 m) tuffite layers. The thickness of the basalt flows varies 
between 3 and 10 meters. 
Stratigraphically, they belong to the informally named "Older Extrusives" 
from the lowermost part of the Noegene (R. Pickering, 1963). Absolute age 
data are not available so far. The rocks are basaltic lavas, sometimes olivine 
basalts. Under the microscope, the olivines show strong weathering effects 
as evidenced by brown edge zones. West of this section, carbonatites and

The two sections N of Monduli are nearly opposite each other. The W-sec-

ROCK MAGNETIC EXPERIMENTS 
From the samples, which were taken by hand drills, a large number of 
pilot samples were selected, representing the great variety of rock types. The 
pilot samples were selected to investigate their suitability for paleomagnetic 
purposes. Thermal and alternating magnetic field (AF) cleaning, isothermal 
remanent magnetization (IRM) aquisition and saturation magnetization 
versus temperature (Js-T) experiments were carried out, establishing 
magnetite as the main carrier of the natural remanent magnetization 
(NRM). The observed blocking temperature was nearly always around 
570°C (Fig. 2a-d). Figure 2a shows the data for the carbonatites. In the vec- 
tor diagram, three components of remanence directions can be seen, a stable 
end direction being obtained above 400°C. As the outcrops are dislocated, 
they are not discussed any further. In the Manyara section a very soft com- 
ponent or viscous remanent magnetization (VRM) was noticed, and above 
50°C nearly 90% of the NRM intensity was lost. This soft component is 
thought to be due to ironhydroxide. The Zijderveld diagrams in Fig. 2a-d 
show two components, which demonstrates successful thermal cleaning. AF- 
cleaning also shows a removal of the soft secondary component up to

A magnetic overprint aquired during the time of Pleistocene volcanism 
seems to be impossible, as the directions before tectonic correction (F-corr) 
shows no correlation with Neogene directions. The Neogene basalts, as 
mentioned before, show a magnetically soft behaviour, which is the 
probable cause of the partly unstable results of the sampled sections. 
Starting off with the Manyara section, one can see that the best grouping 
of site means is reached at 100°C, after eliminating the influence of 
ironhydroxide. At 300°C the scatter increases and at 500°C just 8 sites 
remain more or less stable (Fig. 6). This stability is seen in the Zijderveld 
plots (Fig. 2). 
The Matunginni Scarp section is the only one which shows a successful 
cleaning with a good fitting average direction above 500°C. Just 3 sites 
increase in scatter and reduce the quality of the mean direction shown in 
Fig. 6.

In contrast, the Tarosero Scarp section appears successfully cleaned at 
100°C and increases in scatter above that temperature. This behaviour 
seems to be similar to that seen in the Manyara section. 
As the pilot samples (Fig. 2a-d) show, there is no indication of a com- 
plicated multi-component magnetization. After eliminating weathering 
effects, a good grouping is obtained, which is thought to be the result of a 
PTRM from one of the last thermal events during the Pleistocene tectonism. 
The scatter of vector direction above this temperature is explained by 
relative motion between different parts of the sampled profile. This idea is 
supported by the direction in which the points scatter. They scatter towards 
a direction more or less perpendicular to the rift (Fig. 6). Whether this is 
due to recent downward creeping or bending during rifting or both, is dif- 
ficult to decide.

Preliminary paleomagnetic data are reported for Archean metavolcanics, felsic and mafic 
intrusives, gneisses, and iron formations from the Quetico, Shebandowan, and Wabigoon belts in 
the western Superior Structural Province. Eleven of the 23 formations sampled have been studied 
in detail using stepwise alternating-field demagnetization and, in some cases, thermal demagneti- 
zation. Two characteristic components of magnetization are revealed. One is widespread in 
occurrence and reasonably well grouped (D = 43, 1 = +55.7", k = 17.9, a,, = 5.4", N = 40 
samples for the Shelley Lake granite for example). It is a regional magnetic overprint due to the 
Kenoran orogeny, acquired. according to the position ofits paleopole (71.7"E, 77.3"N, Fp = 5.Y, 
Frn = 8" for the Shelley Lake granite) on the Laurentian apparent polar wander path and to 
independent radiometric evidence, about -2600 Ma. The second magnetic component is spotty 
in occurrence, more prevalent in the Wabigoon belt than elsewhere, and everywhere rather 
scattered. The only fully reliable determination is D = 66.0'. I = -5. lo (k = 10.2, a,, = ISo, N = 
11 samples)for the Wabigoongabbro. The corresponding paleopole is either 17.8"E, 13. ION (Fp = 
7.5", Fm = 15") falling at about -2800 Ma on the apparent polar wander path orthe antipole of this 
direction, dating between - 1350 and - 1250 Ma. The younger date, implying a late Proterqzoic 
metamorphic event in the region, is more likely than the older age, which would require that the 
magnetization be primary or a pre-Kenoran overprint. The metamorphism seems to have oc- 
curred too early to have been caused by igneous activity ca. 1 100 Ma in the nearby Keweenawan 
basin. About -2600 Ma, the region was in its present orientation, but at a latitude of 20 to 35"N 
and probably drifting northward. About - 1250 Ma, the region was equatorial but rotated 90". so 
that presently east-west trending greenstone belts were north-south. It is possible, but un- 
proven, that a paleoocean existed between the Wabigoon subprovince and the other belts about 
- 1250 Ma, the Wabigoon region having since moved >SO0 km westward (present-day direction) 
to its present location.

"original" (not necessarily primary) NRM and not 
variations in magnetic mineral content. Decay of 
NRM, whether spontaneous or due to thermal or 
chemical overprinting, in turn reflects grain size of 
the magnetic minerals or effective size of exsolved 
and subdivided grains. Rather small shifts in mean 
grain size spell the difference between paleo- 
magnetic stability and instability. 
If regional trends or consistent differences be- 
tween structural subprovinces exist in this area, 
they have no obvious expression in the magnetic 
results of Table 1. Felsic intrusives from the 
Quetico, Shebandowan, and Wabigoon belts had 
similar high induced and remanent magnetizations. 
Magnetic variation from site to site in individual 
greenstone belts was orders of magnitude greater 
than differences in ARM or k from one greenstone 
belt to another. 
The regional grade of metamorphism in the 
southern geotraverse area is middle to upper green- 
schist. Even this relatively mild degree of meta- 
morphism has profoundly affected the magnetic 
minerals. Basalts forming in the oceans today and 
fresh Tertiary basalts in general have magnetite or 
titanomagnetite contents of 1% or so, induced 
magnetizations of - lop3 emu cmP3, and en's > 1 
(often >> 1). Their NRM's tend to be about 10 times 
those of related mafic intrusive rocks. The meta: 
volcanic rocks in Table 1 have emu I k 
I emu ~m-~: they contain 10 to 1000 times less 
magnetite than their modern-day equivalents. On 
average, their en's are very low, indicating a coarse 
grain size. Greenschist-facies metamorphism has 
been responsible for destroying the finer-grained, 
high-stability fraction of the magnetic minerals in 
the volcanics. Mafic intrusives have fared some- 
what better, presumably because of their larger 
initial grain sizes. Their k and JNRM values are about 
twice those of the volcanics. 
It is more difficult to say what magnetic minerals 
may have been added to these rocks in the course 
of metamorphism. The felsic intrusives as a class 
are remarkably magnetic (Table I), although the 
sampling procedure of course has the bias that the 
more magnetic formations are sampled in more 
detail. Certain] y from the point of view of anomaly 
interpretation, felsic plutons in this area are more 
likely to have aeromagnetic expression than mafic 
ones. Greenstone belts can almost be ignored ex- 
cept for their associated iron formations. Felsic 
intmsions often have Q, fairly close to 1, in con- 
trast to the mafic rocks. The remanent component 
cannot, therefore, be ignored in interpreting 
anomalies. The same is true for the iron formations. 
The felsic intrusions also turned out to be more 
promising candidates for paleomagnetic study than 
other rock types, as the following sections will 
show. 
Stable Remanent Magnetizations 
The NRM's of three specimens of each sample in 
Table 1 were AF cleaned in 11 steps to 1000 Oe 
(7.95 x lo4 A/m). Twelve formations were rejected 
because of the high proportion of magnetizations 
that were either unmeasurably weak, directionally 
unstable during cleaning, or directed near the local 
geomagnetic field direction (D = 4"E, 1 = +70") and 
of probable recent viscous origin. 
The remaining 11 formations were sampled in 
detail in the third and fourth field seasons. They too 
have their share of weak, soft, viscous, or unstable 
samples-not surprising in view of the generally 
low en's. The stably magnetized samples contain, 
in addition to a possible viscous remanence erased 
at low AF's, one or both of the characteristic stable 
paleoremanences whose directions are plotted in 
Figs. 3 and 4. Group 1 directions tend to have north 
(or south) declinations and intermediate (40-65") 
inclinations. Group 2 directions tend to have shal- 
low inclinations with east to northeast (or west to 
southwest) declinations. Reversals of the paleofield 
are recorded in both groups. The proportion of 
normal and reversed samples is variable and not 
close to 50:50, suggesting infrequent reversals. 
A few formations show only group 1 or only 
group 2 NRM's, but most have examples of both, 
frequently superimposed in individual samples. 
Superimposed (or multicomponent) NRM's were 
separable in two cases: (I) if one component was 
completely demagnetized at high AF steps, so that 
the remanence vector reached a stable endpoint 
direction or (2) if one component was not demag- 
netized at all over some AF range, usually at low 
AF steps, so that the direction of the other compo- 
nent could be deduced by the Zijderveld diagram 
vector-subtraction technique (Zijderveld 1967). 
Otherwise, although the magnetization vector fol- 
lowed a "remagnetization circle" (Halls 1976) 
joining groups 1 and 2, neither component could be 
isolated from the data and used in defining the mean 
group directions. 
Sample mean directions of stable or isolated 
NRM's are plotted in Figs. 3 and 4. Each is the 
average of three specimen directions at the AF step 
where these directions grouped best. If specimen 
directions diverged 220°, the sample was rejected, 
even though the specimen results were often indi- 
vidually stable. (Such results usually indicated 
lightning strikes and had anomalous directions as 
well as high between-specimen dispersion.)

At least a hint of a group 1 NRM is common to 
every rock type sampled (felsic and mafic intru- 
sive~, mafic and intermediate metavolcanics, para- 
gneisses, and, more dubiously, iron formations) 
and to all three tectonic belts. Furthermore, the 
Burchell Lake, Shelley Lake, and Watcomb gran-

significantly different and are barely distinct from 
those of the Poohbah Lake complex and the Huro-

these various units formed are not known in any 
detail but they likely span a sufficient interval-100 
to 200 Ma-for significant apparent polar wander to 
have occurred. On these grounds, the group 1 
magnetization is unlikely to be primary. It repre- 
sents a pervasic remagnetization or magnetic over- 
printing of regional extent. 
The group 2 magnetization is also imprinted in 
many different rock types and there are examples 
from all three structural belts. However, many 
formations lack any trace of a group 2 component. 
It is rare in the Quetico belt but widespread in the 
Wabigoon volcanic subprovince. From this evi- 
dence, the group 2 NRM could be primary and 
confined to older units in all belts or it could be a 
late overprint due to a relatively mild metamorphic

There is a suggestion in Fig. 4f that group 2

Multicomponent Magnetizations and Relative Ages 
of NRM Components 
One specimen of selected samples (28 from the 
Shelley Lake granite, 18 from the Burchell Lake 
granite, and nine from the Sapawe iron formation) 
SCI, VOL. 16, 1979 
have been thermally cleaned to 600°C. Thermal 
cleaning has three aims: (I) to identify the minerals 
carrying NRM and the NRM fraction carried by 
each; (2) possibly to reveal a new NRM component 
or components or to isolate superimposed compo- 
nents not separable by AF cleaning, and (3) to 
determine the relative ages of thermally over- 
printed NRM components. 
This last deduction is possible because thermal 
demagnetization reproduces, in reverse and on a 
reduced time scale, the thermal remagnetizing pro- 
cess in nature. The first NRM component erased 
(the one with the lowest blocking temperatures) is 
the youngest, and the last to be erased is the oldest. 
Clearly this conclusion does not hold for chemical 
overprints, which can have blocking temperatures 
vastly in excess of temperatures experienced in 
nature during remagnetization. Thermal over- 
prints, being partial TRM's (thermoremanent mag- 
netizations), cannot have overlapping blocking 
temperature ranges (Thellier 1938). This consti- 
tutes a minimum test of thermal overprinting. 
In the Shelley Lake granite, an average 35% of 
the NRM is carried by a mineral with Curie point 
between 250 and 300°C, 60% by a mineral with 
blocking temperatures from 300-580°C and a Curie 
point between 525 and 580°C, and 5% has blocking 
temperatures >600"C. In 20 thin sections examined 
in reflected light by L. D. Schutts, these minerals 
were identified as being, respectively, homoge- 
neous unexsolved titanomagnetite (no pyrrhotite 
was seen), nearly pure magnetite subdivided by 
exsolved ilmenite lamellae, and hematite. 
To date, no new components of NRM have been 
revealed by thermal cleaning, nor has resolution of 
superimposed components been much improved 
compared to AF cleaning. 
To test for overlapping blocking temperatures of 
group 1 and group 2 NRM's, single-component 
samples carrying one NRM or the other were first 
compared. For the Shelley Lake granite at least, 
overlap was considerable and all three minerals 
were carriers of either component. 
A second approach to the same question is illus- 
trated in Fig. 5. In these Shelley Lake samples, the 
magnetization swung from a group 2 toward a 
group 1 direction on both AF and thermal demag- 
netization. Curiously enough, both normal and re- 
versed group 1 components evidently coexist, the 
normal one being isolated by AF and the reversed 
one by thermal cleaning. 
The group 1 component has the higher blocking 
temperatures in both samples, but the group 2 com- 
ponent possesses some blocking temperatures 
>600"C, since a stable group 1 endpoint has not

thereby invalidated. Even if group 1 blocking tem- 
peraturesshould prove to lie entirely above those 
of the group 2 component, this would merely indi-

Both group 1 and group 2 NRM's are likely

Nothing can be deduced from thermal demagneti-

Paleopoles and Absolute Ages of the NRM 
Components 
Paleomagnetic poles together with their ovals of 
confidence are calculated in Tables 2 and 3 and 
plotted for comparison with Tracks 3B, 4A, and 6 
(Irving and McGlynn 1976; Irving and Naldrett 
1977) of the North American APWP in Fig. 6. As 
noted earlier, only the group 1 results for the Shel- 
ley Lake and Burchell Lake granites and the 
Poohbah Lake complex (poles 1,4, and 11 at the left 
of Fig. 6u) are of sufficient quality to serve in de- 
fining the APWP. The purpose of Fig. 6 is rather to 
use the APWP to date the group 1 and 2 poles. 
The Poohbah Lake complex has been dated by 
Mitchell (1976) using KIAr. He finds 2706 f 23 Ma 
for the cooling age, with a later thermal event at 
2556 f 36 Ma. Berger and York (1979, this issue) 
have applied step-heating 40Ar/39Ar dating to the

The Poohbah Lake complex has only a group 1

granite anyway, is unlikely to be a primary TRM 
dating from initial cooling. Therefore, the group 1 
NRM is probably about 2600 Ma in age, making it a 
metamorphic overprint associated with the cooling 
phase of the Kenoran orogeny. This inferred age 
agrees well with the approximate age calibration of 
Track 6 (Fig. 6n), whose tie point in the neighbour- 
hood of the group I poles is the 2690 Ma (Gates and 
Hurley 1973) Matachewan diabase. 
Assigning an age to the group 2 NRM is a more 
difficult problem. Figs. 6 cr and b illustrate the pos- 
sible alternative models. In model 1, the poles fall 
along Track 6 and the age assignment is about 
2800 Ma. In model 2, the poles lie at the older end of 
Track 3B, with ages of 1250-1350 Ma. If we knew 
the relative ages of groups 1 and 2 from thermal 
demagnetization, the choice would be easy, but 
the best we can do is assess probabilities. 
Model 1 implies a late Archean but significantly 
(-200 Ma) pre-Kenoran age for group 2. Favouring 
this model is the fact that group 1 NRM is ubiquit- 
ous and well-grouped while group 2 NRM is spotty 
in occurrence and more scattered in direction. A 
specific comparison is between the Shelley Lake 
granite, which has a group 2 component, and the 
Poohbah Lake complex, which lacks it. The 
Poohbah intrusion cuts across the grain of the 
Quetico gneiss belt and seems to be younger than 
the steeply-tilted (MacKidd 1973) Shelley Lake 
body, which conforms to the grain and must have 
been intruded before the sediments were deformed. 
On the other hand, if group 2 remanence is pre- 
Kenoran, we would expect to have to apply a 
structural correction to allow for the change in at- 
titude resulting from the Kenoran orogeny. In the 
Shelley Lake remanence, the group 2 component 
happens to lie nearly along strike and "untilting" 
the body has little effect on magnetization direc- 
tion, but this cannot be true in general. The group 2 
directions, however, group without any structural 
corrections, implying a post-Kenoran origin. 
Model 2 implies a late Proterozoic remagnetiza- 
tion. Local tectonic events cannot be responsible 
because rocks of all belts have a common group 2 
imprint. K/Ar ages in potassium feldspars from the 
Shelley Lake granite have been partially reset 
ca. 1100 Ma (Berger and York 1979, this issue). It 
would seem most natural to associate this resetting 
with the thermal effects of rifting and volcanism in 
the Keweenawan basin immediately to the south- 
east. The observed minima in 40Ar/39Ar spectra of 
potassium feldspars are, however, explicable if the 
heating event actually occurred about ,- 1250 Ma 
(G. W. Berger, personal communication, 1978). A 
Mackenzie age is favoured by the magnetic data.

According to Fig. 6b, the magnetic overprinting 
predates the onset of Keweenawan igneous activity 
by at least 100 Ma. Furthermore, the overprinting 
increases with distance from the Keweenawan rift. 
The possibility of a regular progression of mean 
group 2 magnetization directions from one struc- 
tural belt to the next was noted earlier. The same 
progression is seen in the corresponding paleopoles 
(Fig. 6). If the trend is real, there are two pos- 
sibilities: (1) group 2 NRM was acquired at the 
same time in all belts, but the belts were not then in 
their present relative positions or (2) group 2 NRM 
was acquired at slightly different times in different 
belts, and the trend reflects drift of the Laurentian 
protocontinent during this time interval. 
Radiometric dating does not have the precision 
for a direct test of simultaneity. Geometrical con- 
straints on the first possibility will be considered in 
the section that follows. The second possibility can 
be ruled out if the sequence of poles obviously cuts 
across the trend of the APWP. (A well-known 
example is the pole for the Dogrib dikes of the Slave 
Province (McGlynn and Irving 1975) which is dis- 
placed from the contemporaneous Matachewan 
diabase pole in a direction normal to the APWP.) 
Whether model 1 or model 2 holds, however, the 
group 2 poles trend along the APWP. The age pro- 
gression is (from oldest to youngest) Shebandowan 
to Quetico to Wabigoon according to model I but 
the reverse according to model 2 . Such a trend 
might express, for example, burial metamorphism 
of the region, with uplift either beginning later or 
continuing longer to the northwest in model 1 or to 
the southeast in model 2.

Figure 76 illustrates the overall and relative 
paleopositions of some Shebandowan, Quetico, 
and Wabigoon belt formations about 2.8 Ga ago. (If 
model 2 is accepted, the paleopositions 1.25- 1.35 Ga 
ago can be obtained by inverting Fig. 7b and 
redefining the south pole as the north pole.) 
Laurentia was nearly equatorial and rotated almost 
90". If the implied relative displacements of the 
belts are real, they involved substantial differential 
rotation, small differences in paleolatitude, and un- 
known differences in paleolongitude. 
Since paleonorth is present-day east, cir- 
cumstances are unfavourable for detecting opening 
or closing of oceans between presently east-west 
(paleo-north-south) belts: such motions would 
have changed only paleolongitude. Paleolatitude 
changes would record paleo-north-south motion, 
i.e., shear between the belts. The only significant 
paleolatitude difference in Fig. 7b is between the 
Gulliver greenstone result and those for the other 
formations. If real, the difference implies that the 
Wabigoon belt at the time was > 500 km east of the 
Shebandowan and Quetico belts, reaching its pres- 
ent location by westward (sinistral) shear, counter- 
clockwise rotation of -20°, and an unknown 
amount of convergence. 
The geological evidence, however, favours dex- 
tral rather than sinistral shear on the Quetico fault 
(Mackasey et 01. 1974), with displacements of at 
most 200 km. A fundamental objection is that 
large-scale movements, eastward or westward, 
would degroup the older group 1 poles, unless the 
movements represented the second half of a Wilson 
cycle and reassembled the subprovinces in their 
Kenoran configuration. 
The more likely explanation is that these relative 
paleopositions record successive locations of the 
entire Laurentian continent at different times or 
that they are an artifact resulting from noisy data. 
i Conclusions 
 he main conclusions of this study are the fol- 
lowing: 
(1) As a result of greenschist-facies metamor- 
phism, volcanic rocks from the southern Superior 
Geotraverse region are weakly and rather unstably 
magnetized compared to modern oceanic basalts. 
Mafic intrusions are more strongly and stably mag- 
netized than their volcanic equivalents, felsic and 
intrusions sometimes much more so. 
(2) No simple criteria were discovered relating 
magnetic intensity and stability to either rock type 
or degree of metamorphism. 
(3) Two stable ancient NRM's are preserved in 
many different types of rocks from the area. One is 
SCI. VOL. 16, 1979 
a ubiquitous metamorphic overprint dating from 
the Kenoran orogeny. The other could be Archean, 
either a primary remanence or a pre-Kenoran over- 
print, but it is more likely an overprint acquired 
during late Proterozoic time. 
(4) Thermal demagnetization failed to determine 
the relative ages of the two NRM's. Both compo- 
nents are probably chemical or thermochemical 
overprints. 
(5) Paleopoles for the two NRM's when com- 
pared to the Precambrian APWP for North 
America suggest an age of -2600 Ma for the Keno- 
ran orogeny, in agreement with two radiometric 
dates from the area, and a mild metamorphic event 
about 1250- 1350 Ma ago, probably not related to 
Keweenawan igneous activity. 
(6) At the time of the Kenoran orogeny, the 
Wabigoon, Shebandowan, and Quetico belts al- 
ready formed a single unit within Laurentia. During 
the orogeny, Laurentia was in its present orienta- 
tion and the geotraverse area was located between 
20 and 35"N. 
(7) At the time the second characteristic NRM 
formed, either 2800 Ma or, more likely 1250- 
1350 Ma ago, Laurentia was equatorial and rotated 
about 90" from its present orientation. 
(8) The Wabigoon subprovince may have been 
displaced from the Quetico and Shebandowan belts 
about 1350- 1250 Ma ago, having reached its pres- 
ent position by major sinistral shear and an un- 
known amount of convergent motion. 
(9) Alternatively, 1350-1250 Ma ago there may 
have been no relative displacement of belts but the 
second NRM may have been acquired later in the 
Shebandowan and Quetico belts than in the Wabi- 
goon belt.

W. A. MORRIS

Positive fold tests are reported on two remanence components resolved from the same Nipissing diabase sills. These tests 
conclusively indicate that the region south of the Sudbury Basin in the Southern Structural Province has been subjected to 
two distinct deformational episodes subsequent to the intrusion of the Nipissing diabase. One event precedes (1850-2150 Ma) 
and one event postdates (1250-1850 Ma) intrusion of the Sudbury irruptive. Some evidence also exists for a third event that may 
be related to the development of the Sudbury structure, around 1850 Ma. Evidence that the Nipissing was intruded into already 
folded Huronian sediments confirms previous suggestions of four separate orogenic pulses in the period 2300-1250 Ma.

Figures 2 and 3 summarize the demagnetization 
characteristics of the various remanence components 
found in this collection. The west-northwest direction 
shown in Fig. 3 a and b is probably the least commonly 
found direction. As in these examples it invariably has 
low to moderate unblocking temperatures (<500"C) and 
low coercive forces (<20 mT). In other specimens it is 
also found to exist with the opposite polarity. In Fig. 3 a 
and b it exhibits simple linear paths on orthogonal 
demagnetization plots. Directions similar to this have 
been found in the Sudbury irruptive (N4) where they are 
often associated with mineralization (Morris 1980). 
Here these directions will not be considered further. 
A more common direction is the shallow positive 
southeasterly A direction (Figs. 2 a, b, 3d). Upon thermal 
demagnetization this direction generally unblocks in the 
interval 250-400°C. At site L, where BSY 140 AC was 
collected, all specimens show similar characteristics: 
little direction change up to 400°C, and no meaningful 
direction with further demagnetization. Yet this latter 
characteristic is often associated with a less pronounced 
but clearly defined Curie point between 530 and 550°C. 
Figure 3d shows a similar property. The intensity plot 
shows that a large portion of the A remanence is 
removed after 325"C, but the vector diagram shows that 
A is still present up to 540°C. During the interval 
400-540°C both the A and B directions are being 
demagnetized, but it is the A component that is 
preferentially being destroyed. AF demagnetization 
(Fig 2b) shows that the A direction resides in some 
mineral with a substantial resistive force. The direction 
is only unblocked after 50 mT. 
The B direction (tilt-corrected, it is oriented shallow 
positive to the southwest; Figs. 2 a and b, 3 a, b, and d) 
which is extremely stable under thermal treatment, is 
carried by two remanence phases. One phase with 
unblocking temperatures in the range 550-570°C (Figs. 
2a, 3b) is probably low-titanium magnetite. In other 
specimens this direction shows only minor unblocking 
up to 620°C (Fig. 34. Usually this high Curie tempera- 
ture is associated with an extremely stable remanence 
direction upon demagnetization. This phase of B rema- 
nence seems to be somewhat resistant to later alteration. 
The identity of this remanence carrier is uncertain. It is 
known to coexist in some specimens with the 570°C B 
remanence phase. Possible candidates for remanence 
carrier are NiFe alloys, aluminum-doped maghemite, or 
hematite. The extremely high specific magnetization, 3 
Alm, could argue against hematite but at the moment it 
is impossible to decide.

Two bodies of Nipissing diabase were sampled. Sites 
H, J, K, and L are in a sill that is presently dipping to the 
south. Sites A-G are in the limbs of an asymmetrical 
syncline that is gently plunging to the north. The attitude 
of the beds at each sampling locality was measured from 
the nearest sedimentary unit and verified by comparing 
with the values given on the published geological map of 
the area (Ontario Department of Mines Map 2017). Tilt 
corrections were made by simple rotation of the mag- 
netization about the locally measured horizontal strike 
direction. It is possible that a minor plunge correction 
should be applied but the effect would be negligible 
(Ramsay 1967). 
As discussed in the previous section a number of 
distinct remanence phases could be resolved. In general 
the A magnetizations have lower blocking temperatures 
than the B magnetizations. Assuming that these rema- 
nences were acquired purely by thermal overprinting 
then the acquisition sequence would be B + A. Later it 
will be shown that the sequence A + B would lead to a 
geologically implausible reconstruction. 
Within the A remanences, three groups of directions 
can be identified (Table 1). Sites H and K have a mean in 
situ direction, irrespective of polarity, around D = log0, 
I = +31° (ag5 = 8" specimen unit weight). This is not 
significantly different from the Grenville Front overprint 
direction of D = 11 lo, I = + 27" (ag5 = 7") reported by 
Palmer et al. (1977) from this same region and there is 
no reason to suppose that the overprint reported here has 
a different origin. Sites D and G in the southern limb of 
the syncline and L in the main Sudbury sill have a mean 
in situ direction of D = 149", I = +54" (ag5 = 60). 
Comparison of Fisher precisions before and after tilting 
indicates that this remanence postdates the folding at the 
99% confidence level. Similarly sites A, B, and C in the 
north limb of the syncline have a mean direction of D = 
103", I = +73" (ag5 = 60); this remanence also appears 
to postdate the folding with the same degree of confi- 
dence. The A magnetizations from each limb of the 
syncline are, however, directionally quite distinct (Fig. 
4a). If the A magnetization was acquired synchronously 
on each limb then there has been relative rotation 
between the two fold limbs subsequent to the time when 
correction. The former unblocks between 300 and 350°C, and 
the latter unblocks between 500 and 550°C. (d) Thermal 
demagnetization of a specimen 186 AC from the top of the sill. 
Two directional components are observed: an A magnetization 
to the southeast and a B magnetization to the southwest. The 
intensity decay curve and the X-Y plot suggest that A may 
reside in two remanence phases. Some A component is 
unblocked between 300-325°C but some still remains up to 
540°C, at which point a pure B direction with an unblocking 
temperature of 620°C is found.

A was acquired. Since the total relative rotation (2S0) 
permitted by the data does not allow either limb to be 
rotated to the present horizontal, the question arises: 
How much rotation should be apportioned to each limb? 
Paleomagnetic investigations of the 1250 Ma Sud- 
bury dike swarm do not reveal any evidence for folding 
in the Sudbu~y region (Larochelle 1966; Palmer et al. 
1977). Therefore the overprint must be older than 1250 
Ma, The most likely candidate iu the Sudbury region is 
thermal overprinting by the intrusion of the nearby 
Sudbury irruptive. The portion of the Sudbury irruptive 
that is closest to this locality is the noritic phase of the 
South Range. In Fig. 4a the two overprint magnetiza- 
, tions are compared with the initial norite magnetization 
I (Morris 1980), which has been corrected for the same 
fault-block rotation that the south range has undergone 
relative to the remainder of the Sudbury irruptive. All 
three points lie close to the same great circle, but the two 
overprint magnetizations are on the same side of the 
corrected norite direction. This indicates that both limbs 
of the syncline have been rotated in the same sense, the 
north limb by 14" and the south limb by 40". After this 
correction the syncline is more open and the axial planar 
surface now dips to the north. The sill must also be 
rotated by 40°, which means that at this point it was 
slightly overturned (Fig. 4c(ii)). 
To further unravel the fold sequence one must first 
correct the B magnetizations and calculate the residual 
dips by using the rotations as just defined by the A 
magnetizations (Fig. 4b). Applying the residual tilts to 
the corrected B magnetizations produces a clustering in 
the southwest quadrant. To apply the fold test the normal 
polarity direction for site F has been adopted. A fold test 
on the corrected B magnetizations of sites A, B, C, F 
(norm), H, I, J , and K is positive at the 99% probability 
level (McElhinny 1964). It would appear that the site F

596 CAN. J. EARTH SCI. VOL. 18. 1981 
magnetization is crucial to the validity of this test. It is 
the only site from the north dipping limb of the syncline. 
All others are from south facing strata. However, there 
is some difference in the amount of dip between the two 
south facing strata. Upon repeating the test, but exclud- 
ing site F, a positive fold test is still found, but the 
probability is reduced to 95%. As further confirmation 
of the validity of this test, we note that the mean 
direction (D = 199", I = + 33", ag5 = 7") is quite similar 
to other directions reported from the Nipissing diabase 
(Symons 1970; Symons and Londry 1975; Moms 
1979). These tilt corrections suggest that when the 
Nipissing sills were first intruded they approximated 
flat-lying sheets. That some tilt corrections appear to be 
too great by small amounts and the mean inclination is 
slightly too shallow are compatible with the diabase 
having been intruded into already gently folded Huro- 
nian strata, as seen now on the Cobalt plate. This is one 
possible explanation for the minor divergence of the 
normal F magnetization; others include polar drift 
between polarity reversals, and more probably inexact 
tilt correction, possibly involving rotations about fold 
axes that were not exactly horizontal or similarly 
inclined, as assumed here (Macdonald 1980). 
Finally, there are three B magnetizations (at D, G, J2) 
that have not yet been considered. A ready explanation 
of the G magnetization is not apparent. Both D and 
J2 are in the more coarse-grained central portions of sills. 
J2 as discussed above has low blocking temperatures 
(<350°C) and has a direction relative to the present 
horizontal surface that is identical to the totally tilt- 
corrected directions in sites H and K from the margins of 
the same sill. J1, the high-temperature direction at site J, 
is identical to the site H and K direction. Unless J2 is a 
much later overprint it is necessary to find some 
geological explanation for the identity of the tilt- 
corrected high-temperature direction and the in situ 
low-temperature direction. Folding of an intrusive sheet 
that is slowly cooling provides the best explanation. The 
sites at the margins would be cooled much more quickly 
than the centre. If syntectonic intrusion were important 
the high blocking-temperature magnetic fraction at the 
centre of the sill could record the local geomagnetic field 
direction prior to any tilting, whereas the lower blocking- 
temperature fraction could record nearly the same local 
field direction after folding had been completed. This 
would result in the high and low blocking-temperature 
phases at the centre of the sill having different rema- 
nence directions that were acquired with approximately 
the same ambient field direction. From this information 
it is possible to define the sense and magnitude of 
rotation the body underwent while cooling. 
The agreement between the tilt-corrected B direc- 
tions, the in situ J2 directions, and the accepted 
Nipissing directions (Morris 1979) indicates that the sill 
was approximately flat lying when initially intruded. 
When it finally cooled after undergoing tectonic rotation 
it then occupied its present-day orientation (Fig. 
4c(iii)). A corollary of this interpretation is that the 
region between the Sudbury Basin and the Grenville 
Front was tilted to the south prior to the intrusion of the 
norite, but after the initial folding of the diabase. During 
this event the sill was rotated by some 60". Further 
evidence for a pre-norite intrusion and post-initial-fold- 
ing tilting in the Nipissing comes from site D, which 
also forms the central portion of a sill. Rotating (by 
approximately 30") the fold axial plane of the recon- 
structed syncline (after removal of the post A magnetiza- 
tion folding) brings the axial plane back to vertical and 
brings the DB direction into closer agreement with the 
mean Nipissing direction (Fig. 4c(iii)). This suggests 
that the central portion of this sill too only cooled below 
the effective Curie point (here 425°C) after the initial 
folding, and that it was subsequently tilted prior to the 
second later post A magnetization folding event. It 
might be noticed that the proposed tilting is greater 
(60") near the irruptive margin, and less (30") further 
away. 
The above interpretation assumes that the remanence 
acquisition sequence was B + A. By adopting this 
sequence it has been possible to construct a tectonic 
history for these Nipissing sills that fits the geological 
record; the preferred older direction (the tilt-corrected B 
magnetizations) agrees with a direction (N2) that dates 
from the original intrusion of the diabase (positive 
contact test, Moms 1979). With the alternative se- 
quence A + B the A magnetizations must date from 
the time of intrusion, yet there is no possible way to 
bring the A magnetizations in agreement with either of 
the two most commonly observed Nipissing directions 
(NlatD =27O0,I=65",orN2atD =04O0,1= -40"). 
Hence with this sequence it is necessary to accept that 
either there is yet another real Nipissing direction (not 
yet reported in any other studies) or the supposedly older 
A remanence was acquired as an overprint. Neither of 
these seems likely. This is further emphasized by 
considering the B magnetizations. In situ the B direc- 
tions have close similarity to the N1 directions (D = 
270°, 1 = +65") found in the Nipissing on the Cobalt 
plate. This produces the improbable situation where the 
supposedly older A magnetization was an overprint, and 
the younger B magnetization records an intrusive event. 
A requisite of this is that the A magnetization be imposed 
by a regional metamorphic event, after which the sills 
were folded and rotated. Following this the B magnet- 
ization records a subsequent intrusive event that was not 
followed by tectonism. This scenario cannot be valid for 
two reasons. Firstly, if the metamorphic event was pro- 
duced by the norite it requires that the second Nipissing 
intrusive event (B) postdate intrusion of the norite.

Secondly, it requires that these sills exhibit evidence of 
multiple intrusions. No evidence to support either of 
these two observations exists. .Therefore we can 
discount the sequence A + B and accept the history 
defined by the sequence B + A as outlined above. 
Regional tectonic significance 
Card (1979) and Brocoum and Dalziel (1974) agree 
there has been only one tectonic event in the region south 
of the Sudbury Basin after formation of the Sudbury 
irruptive. Brocoum and Dalziel (1974) consider this 
event to have produced all the structures in the Sudbury 
region. Card (1979) conversely suggests that these 
structures represent the summation of four distinct 
tectonic episodes. 
From the evidence presented in the previous section it 
would appear that paleomagnetism appears to favour the 
second alternative. It was shown that the Nipissing 
diabase in the region south of the Sudbury Basin shows 
conclusive evidence of two, and possibly three, tectonic 
events affecting this region. The oldest tectonic event 
appears to be related to the initial intrusion of the 
Nipissing at some time around 2150 Ma. (The exact age 
of this event is uncertain because it is uncertain as to 
which of the two Nipissing poles (N1 and N2, Moms 
1979) the radiometric age should be attributed.) The 
next youngest event is a regional tilting of locally 
variable degree, which possibly records the Sudbury 
event; radiometric age constraints on this event are 
1840-2150 Ma. The youngest tectonic event is a 
regional folding event that postdates the intrusion of the 
noritic phase of the Sudbury irruptive. A preferred time 
interval would be 1700- 1840 Ma. This suggests that the 
Grenville event imposed little or no regional folding on 
this area. 
It is possible to proceed one step further back in time 
with this regional tectonic analysis. Paleomagnetic fold 
tests on Nivissing diabase from localities where it 
outcrops outside &e Sudbury region have consistently 
shown evidence for no significant deformation of the 
Nipissing (Symons 1970, 1971; Symons and Londry 
1975), but there is a positive fold test on Gowganda 
argillites, the unit into which many of the Nipissing 
diabases are intruded (Morris 1977). Therefore, there is 
evidence of a fourth tectonic event affecting this 
region of the Southern Structural Province. Time 
bounds on this older event are crudely set by the 
intrusion of the Nipissing at 2150 Ma and the deposition 
of the Gowganda at approximately 2300 Ma. 
The four tectonic episodes recognized paleomagnet- 
south of the Sudbury Basin it occupies tightly fol 
synclines and anticlines. A paleomagnetic study of two 
sills from this zone (one dipping uniformly to the south, 
and the other occupying an asymmetrical syncline) 
suggests that it has undergone a complex tectonic 
history. Positive fold tests of remanence indicate that 
there have been two quite distinct folding episodes. The 
younger event, which postdated the intrusion of the 
norite (ca. 1850 Ma) but predated the intrusion of the 
Sudbury dyke swarm (1250 Ma), tightened an initially 
more open syncline, and rotated the other sill from an 
overturned position to a uniform southerly dip. The 
older deforrnational event predated the intrusion of tl 
norite and must therefore have occurred during tl 
period 1850-2150 Ma. Pnor to this event the sil 
approximated flat-lying sheets. Conclusive evidence 
exists, therefore, for at least two separate folding events 
in the Nipissing. 
Support also exists for a third event between the two 
phases outlined above. The equivalence of the low- 
temperature in situ directions from the centre of the sills 
to the high-temperature directions from the sill margins 
is compatible with the concept of syntectonic intrusion. 
This interpretation requires that, upon completion of the 
first folding event when remanence blocking of the 
low-temperature components of the B magnetization 
(J2, DB) was finalized, the main Sudbury sill must have 
had an orientation similar to its present one. To produce 
this special structural geometry at the time of acquisition 
of the A magnetization requires that the sill be over- 
turned by some other tectonic event. This indicates there 
have been three deforrnational events affecting the 
Nipissing in the Sudbury region. This intermediate 
event must have occurred prior to the intrusion of the 
norite. One could speculatively interpret this event as 
the extrabasinal signature of the so-called Sudbury event, 
be it meteorite impact or crypto-explosion.

Paleomagnetic results are reported for six Archean volcanics and six Proterozoic diabase dike sites in the La Grande Riviere 
basin using AF and thermal demagnetization. The area is now flooded so that future work is not possible. The limited geological 
and statistical data base makes interpretation of the results necessarily tentative. The dikes yield an A component pole at 84W, 
74% from magnetization residing in higher stability domains, which likely reflects emplacement either at -2150 or -1825 or 
- 1650 Ma ago, and a B component pole at 33W, 4"s residing in lower stability domains, which likely reflects metamorphism 
during the Hudsonian Orogeny at - 1725 Ma, or, less likely, during Grenvillian uplift at -975 Ma. The volcanics appear to yield 
a prefolding C component pole at 28"W, 49"s that dates extrusion at -2900 Ma and a postfolding D component pole at 306W, 
37"N that dates metamorphism by the Kenoran Orogeny at -2600 Ma.

Introduction and geology 
Samples for this paleomagnetic study were collected 
in 1978 prior to flooding of the La Grande Riviere basin 
(Fig. 1) by Hydro QuCbec power projects. The conclu- 
sions are very tentative because details on the geologic 
relationships between the units are not known in detail 
and because no radiometric age dates are available. 
The La Grande Rivikre area is in the Superior 
Structural Province (Eade 1966). The Archean meta- 
volcanics and metasediments occur in a few east-

1974a,b, 1975,1976,1977,1978). They were intruded

-2.5 Ga, the Archean strata were deformed into tight 
east to east-northeast trending folds that plunge at 35 +

and quartz veins. Gently dipping pink orthoquartzites 
of the lower Aphebian Sakarni Formation unconform- 
ably overlie the Archean basement in several outliers.

Sampling and measurement 
The Archean metavolcanic sites include four flow 
sites of massive komatiitic basalt (Vl, Fig. I), koma- 
tiitic basaltic pillow breccia (V2), high-magnesium 
basalt (V3), and massive spinifexed komatiitic peridotite 
(V4), and two sill sites of serpentized peridotites (V5, 
V6). All six dike sites (Dl-D6) are in massive diabase 
with ophitic texture. From two to five oriented hand or 
core samples were collected at each site, and from four 
to 20 specimens were cut from each sample. The 17 
volcanic samples yielded 129 specimens and the 20 dike 
samples yielded 157 specimens. 
The natural remanent magnetization (NRM) of each 
specimen was measured using a Schonstedt DSM-1 
spinner magnetometer. The NRM intensities ranged 
between lo2 and 10' A m- ' and the NRM directions were 
broadly scattered for both the. volcanics and dikes. 
Alternating field (AF) step demagnetization was done 
using equipment described by Seguin (1975) in 5 mT 
increments up to 75 mT. The characteristic direction, 
isolated in several steps between 30 and 60mT, was 
determined for each of 34 volcanic and 64 dike 
specimens. Thermal demagnetization was done using a 
Schonstedt TSD- 1 oven at steps of 200,300,400,450, 
500,540,550,565,570, and 600°C. The characteristic 
direction isolated in the 540-565°C range was deter- 
mined for each of 95 volcanic and 93 dike specimens.
