Volcanics 
The C and D components of the Archean volcanics are 
both thermally unblocked at -555 + 15°C. Although 
the C component is more prevalent than the D, both 
appear equally stable, and hence either may be older. 
Also, their high blocking temperatures suggest that both 
were set before or during the Kenoran Orogeny, which 
deformed and regionally metamorphosed the volcanics 
prior to -2450 Ma. The volcanics strike at 260 + 10" 
and dip at 62 + 8"s at all sampling sites, so that the fold 
test is equivocal. Microfold structures show that the 
volcanics plunge at 35 + 5W. The pole positions for the 
C and D components are given in Table 2 both before 
and after tectonic correction for attitude and plunge.

Prominent north- to northwest-trending dikes (herein termed the Hearst swarm) west of the Kapuskasing Structural Zone

the southem KSZ as first proposed in 1983 by Percival and Card.

Introduction 
In northern Ontario a north-northeast-trending zone of 
faulting cuts sharply across the east-west Archean grain and 
exposes deep crustal rocks at surface (Bennett et al. 1967; 
Thurston et al. 1977; Percival and Coe 1981). This feature, the 
Kapuskasing Structural Zone (KSZ), separates two Archean 
terranes with distinctly different geological and geophysical 
characteristics (Bennett et al. 1967). Diabase dikes of this 
region show a roughly orthogonal pattern (north to northwest 
and northeast). Their orientation, however, changes dra- 
matically once the KSZ is crossed. The dike pattern on the 
western side is rotated up to -40" counterclockwise compared 
with that on the eastern side (Fig. 1). An accompanying change 
in the trend of the Archean structural grain also occurs and 
suggests that relative rotation between two crustal blocks has 
occurred as a result of fault movements associated with the 
KSZ (Bennett et al. 1967). Such a rotation, however, is not 
apparent in the extreme northern part of the KSZ where dike 
aeromagnetic anomalies appear to cross the KSZ with little 
change in trend. 
The regional metamorphic grade increases eastwards from 
greenschist grade in the Michipicoten greenstone belt (near 
Wawa) to granulite grade within the KSZ northeast of 
Chapleau. This observation, amongst others, suggests that 
upthrusting along the eastern margin of the southern KSZ has

Dikes on the eastern side of the KSZ comprise: (1) 2.6 Ga 
north-trending Matachewan quartz tholeiites, (2) 2.15 Ga 
northeast-trending Preissac tholeiites, and (3) 1.15 Ga east- 
northeast-trending Abitibi alkali olivine basalts (Fahrig 1972; 
Card 
et al. 1981; Gates and Hurley 1973; Hanes and York 
1979). Although several paleomagnetic studies have been done 
on these dikes (e.g., Strangway 1961, 1964; Larochelle 1966; 
Irving and Naldrett 1977; Buchan and Schwarz 1981; Schutts 
and Dunlop 198 l), a clear picture of variation in primary direc- 
tion and polarity within any one swarm has yet to emerge. 
Comparatively little is known about the dikes west of the 
KSZ. Information is largely confined to reconnaissance petrog- 
raphy and petrochemistry (Siragusa 1977; Thurston et al. 
1977; Card et al. 1981). K-Ar ages on NW-trending dikes 
range from 2.4 to 1.4 Ga (Wanless et al. 1966; W. F. Fahrig, 
personal communication, 1984). On the basis of aeromagnetic 
data Watson (1980) correlated the northwest- and northeast- 
trending dikes with the Matachewan and Preissac (or Abitibi), 
respectively, whereas Thurston 
et al. (1977) considered the 
northwest-trending dikes to be part of the 1.25 Ga Mackenzie 
swarm (located to the northwest mainly in the northwest Supe- 
rior, Churchill, Slave, and Bear provinces, Fahrig and Jones 
1969). 
This paper focuses on the north- to northwest-trending dikes 
west of the KSZ, assessing their (1) paleomagnetic charac- 
teristics, (2) relationship to the Matachewan swarm, and (3) 
implications for the tectonic history of the KSZ.

Petrography and structure 
The dikes of this study have near-vertical dips and thick- 
nesses that range from less than 0.05 m to more than 70 m; the 
average thickness is about 30 m. Lengths of individual aero- 
magnetic dike anomalies reach 200-300 km. The calculated 
crustal extension indicated by this swarm is 1.0%, based on an 
average dike thickness of about 30 m. 
Dike interiors are fine to medium grained with intergranular 
to subophitic textures that consist of subequal amounts (about 
40% each) of weakly zoned saussuritized plagioclase (labra- 
dorite) and clinopyroxene (mostly augite with minor pigeon- 
ite). Pyroxenes are variably altered to chlorite and uralite and 
many are also rimmed by blue-green amphibole. Interstitial 
quartz is always present and composes up to 7% of the rock, but 
olivine is absent. Minor biotite and apatite also occur. Opaque 
phases (up to about 10%) include Ti magnetite, ilmenite, and 
trace sulphides. The Ti magnetite usually shows ilmenite ex- 
solution lamellae and may contain fine hematite rods, sug- 
gesting a low-level deuteric oxidation state of C3 (Haggerty 
1976). Phenocrysts of greenish plagioclase up to 3 cm diameter 
are common but their distribution is very heterogeneous when 
viewed on the scale of outcrop, dike, or swarm. They are 
frequently concentrated near dike margins or apophyses (e.g., 
dike 1 l), but some dikes (e.g., 8 and 15) have a median 
phenocryst-rich layer that may be a final phase of injection. 
Dike 4 contains alternate plagioclase-free and -poor layers, 
about 1 cm wide, that parallel the dike margins. 
The north- to northwest-trending dikes are classified as 
plagioclase - porphyritic quartz tholeiites on the basis of 
modal mineralogy. Their textural and mineralogical simi- 
larities suggest a single intrusion event, identified in this paper 
as the Hearst swarm.

During demagnetization the remanence vector commonly fol- 
lows a great-circle path on the stereonet (e.g., Fig. 3a), indi-

remagnetization circles have no consistent orientation within a 
site, signifying that the soft component (probably a viscous

paleomagnetic significance. In some samples remagnetiza-

site directions are computed using both SEP and remag- 
netization circle data according to the method of Bailey and 
Halls (1984). Thermal demagnetization proved less capable 
than AF of isolating the characteristic component because over- 
prints sometimes survive the highest unblocking temperatures 
(see Fig. 3). 
The characteristic component is considered to be primary 
because it is typically isolated at the highest coercivities 
(50- 100 mT) and unblocking temperatures (550-570°C) and 
is best preserved in fine-grained and chilled margin samples 
having the least silicate alteration. 
In order to further test the primary nature of the remanence, 
baked and unbaked country rock samples were also collected at 
three dike sites (5, 11, and 12) but the results were inconclusive 
(Emst 1981). Apart from four anomalous dikes, all in the 
vicinity of the KSZ, the directions of the characteristic com- 
ponent fall into two approximately antiparallel populations 
(Fig. 4, Table 1). For any one dike the polarity of the com- 
ponent is the same for all samples, suggesting that intrusion of 
the Hearst swarm spanned a reversal of the Earth's magnetic 
field. In some samples there is a soft, intense component, 
opposite to the characteristic one (e.g., Fig. 3 a and e) that may 
be due to self-reversal. Although there are about equal numbers 
of normal and reversed polarity dikes, there is some suggestion 
of a higher proportion of normal ones closer to the KSZ.

Discussion 
Correlation of Hearst and Matachewan swarms 
The Hearst and Matachewan dike swarms are paleo- 
magnetically very similar: they yield matching mean site direc- 
tions (Table 1) and have a comparable disposition to normal 
and reversed polarities (Ernst 1981). Both swarms are quartz 
tholeiites with characteristic saussuritized plagioclase pheno- 
crysts and have similar mineralogy and alteration. On average, 
dike thickness and spacing are also comparable for the two 
swarms (Emst 1981). 
These paleomagnetic, petrologic, and structural similarities 
indicate that the Hearst dikes represent a northwest con- 
tinuation of the Matachewan swarm as previously proposed by 
Watson (1980). A series of almost unbroken linear aero- 
magnetic anomalies extends northwestwards from the area 
sampled to near the Berens-Uchi subprovince boundary west 
of James Bay (see ODM-GSC 1970). Some of these anoma- 
lies can be correlated with individual dikes of this study. On 
this basis, the Hearst-Matachewan swarm has a longitudinal 
extent exceeding 700 km and covers an area greater than 
2 x lo5 km2. 
Tectonic implications 
There is a positive correlation between dike trend and the 
declination of the characteristic component. Northwest- 
trending Hearst dikes have a mean remanence direction rotated 
- 15" counterclockwise from both north-trending Hearst dikes 
near the southern KSZ and the north-trending Matachewan 
dikes (Table 1). The directions are statistically different at the 
0.05 confidence level (statistics from Tarling 1983). One pos- 
sible explanation is that the northwest dikes have been rotated 
counterclockwise relative to the north dikes during deformation 
along the KSZ, as suggested by Bennett et al. (1967). How- 
ever, the declination difference (- 15") is less than the change 
in dike trend (25-40"), so some of the variation in dike trend 
must be primary. Other explanations for the paleomagnetic 
data are that the northwest-trending dikes are of a slightly 
different age, or that the remanence vector is biassed into the 
plane of the dike (Strangway 1961). This latter possibility 
needs to be checked by detailed rock magnetic studies but was 
not revealed in a statistical study of worldwide paleomagnetic 
data obtained from dikes (Evans 1968). 
Structural and paleomagnetic data from the Hearst dikes 
support the model of crustal tilting associated with KSZ 
thrusting proposed by Percival and Card (1983) and indicate 
that this deformation occurred at least in part subsequent to dike 
intrusion (i.e., after 2.6 Ga). The region affected by tilting is 
marked by a dike-dip reversal from steeply southwest to east as 
the KSZ is approached (Table 1, Fig. 5b) (Emst 1981, 1982). 
Sites 17, 18, 19, and 20 are all within this region of easterly 
dips. The paleomagnetic direction of these north-trending 
Hearst dikes differs by 12" from the mean direction of the 
Matachewan swarm as determined by Schutts and Dunlop 
(1981) (directions are statistically different at the 0.05 level)

Hearst dikes tend to be thinner and less numerous in the 
vicinity of the KSZ and are conspicuously absent from the 
Shawmere anorthosite and other granulite facies rocks of the 
KSZ (Figs. 2,5) (Emst and Halls 1983; Thurston et al. 1977). 
A possible cause is that the dikes taper downwards and finally 
pinch out entirely at crustal depths corresponding to granulite 
grade conditions. 
Conclusions 
A reconnaissance paleomagnetic and petrographic study of 
north- to northwest-trending dikes west of the Kapuskasing 
Structural Zone suggests their correlation with the 2.6 Ga 
old north-trending Matachewan swarm to the east. The 
Hearst-Matachewan swarm is thus more than 700 km long and 
is characterized by a gradual change from north- to northwest- 
trending dikes as it is followed northwards across the 
Kapuskasing Zone. This change in trend may in part be caused

Palaeomagnetism of Australian Hematite Ore Bodies-I1 
Western Australia 
H. Porath* and F. H. Chamalaun 
(Received 1967 October 1l)t 
Summary 
Iron ore deposits of the Lake Superior type within the Archaean and 
Proterozoic banded iron formations of Western Australia show consistent 
and stable directions of remanent magnetization. The palaeomagnetic 
poles of the ores do not correlate with poles of Post-Cambrian Australian 
rocks, which suggests a Pre-Cambrian age for the ore formation. Mag- 
netic anisotropies of the ores are low and the distribution of the principal 
susceptibility axes tends to reflect the magnetic fabric of the host rocks. 
1. Introduction 
In a previous publication (Chamalaun & Porath 1967) we reported the results 
of a palaeomagnetic study on the hematite ore bodies of the Middleback Ranges in 
South Australia. It was found that these were consistently and stably magnetized 
with a Pre-Cambrian direction. We therefore extended the study to the Western 
Australian ore bodies, the results of which are reported here. 
A large number of high-grade hematite ore bodies are known to occur in the 
Archaean and Proterozoic banded iron formations of Western Australia, but in 
order to obtain fresh subsurface samples we have sampled only those that are actively 
mined. The localities of the ore bodies sampled are shown in Fig. 1. The Mt 
Goldsworthy and Koolyanobbing deposits occur in Archaean banded iron forma- 
tions, whilst the host rocks for the Mt Tom Price and Mt Newman ore bodies are 
Proterozoic iron formations. 
2. Results 
(a) Mt Goldsworthy. The Mt Goldsworthy deposit is located at the northern 
extremity of the Western Australian Archaean shield. A folded and faulted banded 
iron formation, which consists of alternating layers of silica and hematite, forms the 
host rock of a number of high-grade hematite ore bodies of varying origins. Brandt 
(1964, 1966) makes a distinction between lode ore and crust ore deposits. Lode ores 
are deep lenses of massive finely crystalline hematite (average grain size about 20p). 
The major deposit at Mt Goldsworthy consists of lode ore and is controlled by a 
steep angled transcurrent fault. Pebbles of massive hematite ore occur in the basal 
Proterozoic conglomerate indicating that the ore formed in Pre-Proterozoic times 
(Brandt 1964). Brandt (1966) favours a hypogene origin of the lode ore along the 
lines suggested by Dorr (1965) for the Brazilian ores. 
Crust ores form shallow cappings of hematite and goethite on the upturned

overlie the lode ores in some places and are therefore younger. They have probably

of silica by iron (Brandt 1964). 
Sixty samples were collected from surface exposures and adits of the banded 
iron formation, lode ore and crust ore. The NRM directions, which are stable 
against partial demagnetization by thermal and alternating field methods, are shown 
in Fig. 2. Lode ores show a discrete blocking temperature with a Curie temperature 
of 695 “C, which is characteristic of hematite (see Fig. 3). The crust ores, however, 
show a spectrum which includes lower blocking temperatures, but their magnetiza- 
tion directions remain stable with remanent coercivities exceeding 750 oersteds. 
A statistical test (Watson & Irving 1957) shows that the directions of magnetiza- 
tion of the lode ore do not have a Fisher (1953) distribution. (xi,, = 22.9; 
xl”,, = 18.3.) The magnetization directions form two clusters, the majority (31) 
having moderate to steep inclinations and northwesterly declinations, whilst eight 
samples have steep inclinations and southeasterly declinations. Of these eight 
samples three come from a surface exposure of the ore body and another three from 
parts of the ore body which are near the fault zone and the contact zone with the 
banded iron formation. 
Polar wandering is suggested as a possible explanation of the observed pattern 
of magnetization directions of the lode ore samples. The relative age of the two 
groups of directions is not known, but it is possible that the ore formation progressed 
from these zones inward, so that the minor group of directions represents the early 
stages in the ore-forming process. As each of the two clusters separately obeys the 
rules of Fisherian statistics (major group: xiec = 9.5; xl”,, = 9.3; minor group: 
xi,, = 10.0; &, = 2.4), the magnetization of the lode ore is represented by two 
mean directions and their corresponding palaeomagnetic poles (see Table 1). 
The mean direction of the crust ore samples is significantly different from that of 
the lode ore. The circle of confidence of the mean direction is, however, rather 
large due to the fact that only a few samples could be collected from the extremely 
friable ore. Samples from the banded iron formation have magnetization directions 
similar to those of the main group of lode ore samples. The significance test of 
Watson & Irving (1957) shows that the two mean vectors are not significantly different.

(b) Koolyanobbing. A number of iron ore bodies occur as irregular lenses in the 
folded parts or along straight limbs of the extensively metamorphosed banded iron 
formation of the Koolyanobbing Hills of South West Australia. Dowd’s Hill and 
the A-deposit are the largest ore bodies and have been sampled for magnetic studies. 
The mineralogy of the Koolyanobbing ores is much more complex compared with 
other Lake Superior type ores. Four types of iron oxides can be distinguished in 
the Dowd’s Hill deposit. Cryptocrystalline goethite is predominant and always 
accompanied by varying amounts of magnetite and hematite in the form of martite.

The high-grade hematite ores of Mt Goldsworthy, Mt Newman and Mt Tom Price 
show the characteristic magnetic properties of fine grained hematite, i.e. a discrete 
blocking temperature and high coercivities. Similarly the low temperature transi-

The NRM intensities of the ores are remarkably low and represent only 1 per 
cent or less of the TRM developed by cooling in a magnetic field of H = 0.6 oersteds. 
Using the same reasoning as in the previous paper, we suggest that a CRM rather 
than a TRM is responsible for the natural remanence of the ores. 
4. Discussion of results 
The Lake Superior ore bodies reported here carry a consistent and stable direc- 
tion of remanent magnetization. Magnetic anisotropies are low and will not have 
seriously affected the direction of the magnetization vector. By comparing the 
palaeomagnetic poles of the ores with the Australian polar wandering curve it should 
then be possible to estimate the age of the ore formation. Reliable palaeomagnetic 
poles have, however, only been obtained from Post-Cambrian Australian rocks and 
the poles for the iron ores, which are shown in Fig. 10, do not correlate with the 
established Australian polar wandering curve. This suggests a Pre-Cambrian age of

Cambrian rocks (Irving & Green 1958) shows the palaeomagnetic pole of the Dowd’s 
Hill deposit to be in good agreement with the pole of the Nullagine Lavas, if sign is 
disregarded (see Fig. 10). Although the exact sampling sites have not been described 
by Irving & Green, the Nullagine Lavas probably form part of the Lower Proterozoic 
Fortescue Group which is older than 2100m.y. (Leggo et al. 1965). A lower Pro- 
terozoic age would therefore result for the formation of the largest Koolyanobbing

Because of the lack of Australian Pre-Cambrian palaeomagnetic poles equivalent 
to the poles of the Mt Goldsworthy and Hamersley deposits, it is not possible to 
arrive at a more accurate age for the formation of these ores. The distribution of the 
magnetization directions of the Mt Goldsworthy deposits suggests that the ore 
formation covered a considerable period of time. The difference in age between the 
lode ore and the crust ore, which was suggested by Brandt (1964) on geological evi- 
dence, is confirmed by the magnetic results. Samples from the banded iron formation 
have similar magnetization directions to the ores. The iron oxide of the Archaean 
banded iron formation at Mt Goldsworthy is formed by hematite in similar crystalline 
form as in the hematite ore bodies. It is therefore likely that the remanence of the 
banded iron formation dates from the formation of the ore and that the hematite in 
the iron formation signifies the first phase of the formation of an ore body. The

ore deposit represent early Pre-Cambrian poles. 
The position of the palaeomagnetic poles of the Hamersley ore bodies, Mt Tom 
Price and Mt Newman, does not support a Mesozoic age of the ore formation as 
was suggested by McLeod (1963), but indicates that, similar to other Lake Superior 
type ores, they are Pre-Cambrian in age. It appears therefore that the old land 
surface, to which concentrations of iron ore are confiend in the Hamersley Province, 
dates from Pre-Cambrian times. To assign a more accurate age for the ore formation 
fails again because of the lack of palaeomagnetic data from Australian Pre-Cambrian 
rocks.

4. Discussion 
Partial remagnetization is a problem often encoun- 
tered during palaeomagnetrc investigations. Rather than 
affecting preferred horizons (especially in sediments) 
degrees of remagnetization may be inhomogeneously 
distributed within individual beds and even, as in the 
case of the Pound Quartzite, within a single hand 
sample. Luck [7] encountered similar problems du- 
rmg his study of Lower Palaeozoic sediments from 
northern Australia. Also, during a study of the Permian 
red-beds from the Colorado Plateau, Farrell and May 
[40] rejected 90% of the specimens from their Monu- 
ment Valley collection. The implication is that infor- 
matron relating to the primary magnetization might be 
retrievable if results are scrutinized at the specimen, 
rather than sample, level. This procedure was adopted 
with the palaeomagnetic data obtained by Briden [12, 
131 from an earlier extensive study of South Australian 
late Precambrian and Cambrian formations. Giddings 
and Embleton [ 151 discuss those results more fully m 
terms of their particular relevance to the structural 
history of the Lower Palaeozotc in South Australia. 
Briden’s material suffered severe remagnetization 
during the Late Cambrian-Early Ordovician erogenic 
activity and our interpretation of that data supports 
results presented here for the Late Cambrian-Early 
Ordovician of South Australia.

Supergroup, N.W.T.) and the Coronation loop1 
J. C. MCGLYNN

The Pearson Formation is the youngest unit of the Great Slave Supergroup of the Coronation 
Geosyncline. Study of samples from 22 locations shows that the dominant magnetization has a 
direction 329", -08" (a,, = 10") and corresponding pole at 19S0, 077"W (A,, = 9"). This magnetiza- 
tion is considered to have been acquired at the time the rock was formed about - 1800 Maago. In 
addition, there are two, possibly three, overprints. One of the two well-established overprints is 
attributed touplift following deep burial at about - 1600 Ma. The other has no known explanation. 
These results, together with others from the Coronation Geosyncline, are used to construct a 
polar loop (the Coronation loop) that is apparently the paleomagnetic signature of the orogeny 
that affected the geosyncline. The Coronation loop straddles the boundary between the Aphebian 
and Paleohelikian, and it is tentatively suggested that the physical boundary between these two 
eras could be placed between the Great Slave Supergroup and the overlying Et-Then Group.

Introduction 
The Athapuscow Aulacogen is part of the Coro- 
nation Geosyncline that developed in Aphebian 
time along the western margin of the Slave Struc- 
tural Province in the northwestern part of the 
Canadian Shield (Hoffman 1973). Rocks of the au- 
lacogen are exposed in the East Arm of Great Slave 
Lake, N.W.T. The Great Slave Supergroup com- 
prises about 8000 m of sedimentary and volcanic 
rocks, and forms the bulk of the fill of the aulaco- 
gen. The Great Slave sequence was deposited in 
Aphebian time between about - 1800 and -2200 
Ma. It rests unconformably on the Union Island 
Group, is younger than the Wilson Island Group 
and is overlain unconformably by the Et-Then 
Group. The lower part of the sequence is intruded 
by quartz-diorite laccoliths, and all the rocks are 
intruded by Mackenzie diabase sills and dikes. The

and the major Mackenzie sills, is shown in Fig. 1. 
The stratigraphy and geochronological data are 
summarized in Table 1. 
One of the major problems in paleomagnetic 
studies is the determination of the ages, both rela- 
tive and 'absolute', of pole positions. In the 
Athapuscow Aulacogen there are only a few 
radiometric ages from the stratigraphic sequence 
itself, but the relative order of rock units is well- 
known from super-imposition. The sequence is one 
of the best in the Canadian Shield for magneto- 
stratigraphic work. The first unit to be studied in 
the stratigraphic sequence was the Et-Then Group, 
which was shown to have a magnetization older 
than the 1250 Ma old Mackenzie intrusions (Irving 
et al. 1972). Subsequent work on the Kahochella 
Group was important because it showed that the 
magnetization history of Great Slave Supergroup is 
complex. Its magnetization consisted of a pre-

Geology of the Pearson Formation 
The Pearson Formation has a maximum thick- 
ness of 165 m and consists of flows of basalt with a 
few thin beds of grey or red mudstones. It is of 
limited areal extent, being confined mainly to the 
region of the inset in Fig. 1. It is autochthonous, 
being north of the zone of nappes described by 
Hoffman et al. (1977). No radiometric age determi- 
nations have been published from the formation. Its 
stratigraphic position indicates that it is about 1800 
Ma old (Table 1). Most flows are massive and have 
columnar jointing. Many flows are amygdaloidal I 
and have vesicular contacts. The rocks are com- 
posed of saussuritized plagioclase lathes in 
pyroxene that is partly altered to light green actino- 
lite or chlorite. The plagioclase is albite but many 
lathes have more basic cores. Carbonate occurs 
along with pumpellyite and the amygdules are filled 
with quartz and chlorite. Although the presence of 
prehnite was not confirmed, the mineral as- 
semblage is typical of prehnite-pumpellyite facies 
metamorphism. This facies is often associated 
with burial metamorphism and, according to 
Turner (1968). may indicate a temperature range of 
100-250°C and pressures of 2-6 kbars (1 x lo1 to 6 
x 10' kPa), which correspond to depths of burial of 
8- 20 km. Liou (1971) suggests arange of 20(t350°C 
and similar pressures, but notes the presence of this 
assemhlage in vertically zoned sequences at depths 
of 5 km. These depth estimates were made assum- 
ing normal thermal gradients, and may be too high 
because the thermal gradients could have been 
higher in the past in this deep sedimentary basin. 
Zen (1974). however, considers these ranges dubl- 
ous as a general rule and notes that Sigvaldson 
(1962) has reported pumpellyite in drill holes in the 
thermal area of Iceland as an alteration product of 
mafic lavas at depths of only a few hundred metres. 
Therefore the assemblage in the Pearson lavas may 
be the result either of deep burial or of deuteric 
action shortly after the lavas were extruded. Its 
presence is important in this context, because if it 
reflects deep burial. then it sets an upper limit to 
subsequent reheating of the Pearson rocks. 
The flows are gently folded about easterly- to 
northeasterly-trending axes. Dips do not exceed 
20" and average ahout 10". Samples were collected 
over about 20 km (Fig. 2). Sampling sites 8-13 and 
107-1 11 are probably from opposing limbs of one 
fold. The remaining samples are collected from the 
north limb of a different fold. About five oriented 
cores were obtained from each site and two speci- 
mens cut and studied from each core. 
Paleomagnetic Results I 
The experimental procedures used have been 
explained previously (Irving and McGl ynn 1976~). 
Thermal demagnetization curves were obtained 
from 23 specimens. There are two distinct types of 
curves (A and Dl. and also intermediate types, 
which are referred to as A + , B and C. 
Specimens with A magnetization exhibit ideal 
behaviour. Their thermal demagnetization curves 
are square-shouldered, the magnetization first de- 
creasing slowly up to 5W°C, and then falling 
rapidly, all of it being lost at 550°C (Fig. 3). The 
blocking temperatures are mainly between 500 and

I (550-570°C) was not observed. After heating to 
temperatures in the range 300-500"C, the reman- 
ence directions are north-northwest with low gen-

creases regularly, and the median destructive field 
(mdf) always exceeds 200 Oe (15.9 x lo3 Alrn). The

The D phase is the least stable magnetization. It 
has very low blocking temperatures, generally 
below 300°C (Fig. 3). The directions are initially

I tion in the same specimen. The mean direction at 
sites with D magnetization is shown in Fig. 6.

yields consistent west-northwest directions (Fig. 
6), but on thermal demagnetization the directions

has a shallow.positive inclination.

The A magnetization has high rernanent coercive 
force and square-shouldered thermal decay curves. 
It is presumably carried by the unaltered magnetite 
observed in polished section. The results of Pul- 
laiah et al. (1976) suggest that such magnetization 
would become unblocked in about lo7 years at 
temperatures of about 400°C. This indicates that 
the A magnetization could have resisted heating 
associated with prehnite-pumpellyite facies meta- 
morphism. Since the lavas do not exceed this 
metamorphic grade the A phase is probably the 
original magnetization, acquired at the time the 
lavas were extruded at approximately - 1800 Ma. 
This argument is supported by all the known field 
relationships. The A direction is very different 
from that observed in the Et-Then Group (the pole 
positions PA and ET of Fig. 8 differ by more than 
three times the 95% error) and cannot be matched 
with any known secondary magnetization that has 
been observed from the region. The only known 
subsequent heating event is that associated with the 
massive Mackenzie intrusions (Fig. 1). Overprints 
identifiable with that event are found close to the 
intrusions (Irving et al. 1972), and sometimes at 
distances of the order of a kilometre (Evans and 
Bingham 1976; Irving and McGlynn 1978; poles TS 
and DS, Fig. 9). These overprints are readily re- 
moved at temperatures (usually about 300°C) much 
lower than the blocking temperatures of the A mag- 
netization. Moreover, the A directions are over 60" 
different from the Mackenzie directions (Fig. 6). 
There is therefore no evidence that the A magne- 
tization is secondary. The precision, before correc- 
tion for tilt, is 21, compared with 15 after correc- 
tion, but the change is not significant at P = 0.05 
using Watson's test (Watson 1956); the dip con- 
trasts are clearly too small to carry out a fold-test. 
Tilt corrections have no effect on the mean direc- I 
tion. The pole PA corresponding to the A rnagne- 
tization is listed in Table 3 and plotted in Fig. 8. 
The B, C and D magnetizations are probably 
secondary because they have lower blocking tem- 
peratures, and lowerremanent coercivities, thanthe 
A magnetization, and because B and C can be ten- 
tatively identified with post-depositional events. 
The D magnetization presumably reflects a very 
mild reheating event because its blocking tempera- 
tures are mostly below 300°C. The pole (PD) 
corresponding to the D magnetization falls on the 
polar curve at about - 1100 Ma (Fig. 9). Its origin is 
unknown. The pole (PB) for the B magnetization 
falls close to the pole for the Et-Then Group and 
could have been acquired during burial by the over- 
lying Et-Then sandstones. The pole (PC) for the C 
magnetization falls in the Caribbean, and agrees 
with the poles for the overprints commonly found 
in rocks of the Coronation Geosyncline as first ob- 
served by McMurry et al. (1973). McGlynn et al. i 
(1974) argue that these overprints were acquired 
during uplift and cooling followed the Hudsonian 
orogeny; it might be more precise to consider them 
to be caused by uplift and cooling following the 
orogeny in the Coronation Geosyncline (see be- 
low). 
Coronation Loop I 
In Fig. 8 the poles obtained from the Canadian 
Shield in the interval -2200 to - 1800 Ma are plot- 
ted. They are connected by a broad swath that is 
considered to describe the general motion of the 
pole relative to Laurentia. It is becoming obvious, 
however, as more detail becomes available, that 
the true path is more complicated. But it is not yet 
clear to what extent these comvlications are real 
irregularities in the path, or arise from local rota- 
tions in fault blocks, or are owing to the practical 
difficulties in getting accurate determinations of 
such old magnetizations. The polar sequence given 
by the stratigraphy of Table 1 is shown by arrows 
on Fig. 8. The Seton, Gibraltar and McLeod poles 
are in reasonable agreement, but there is a sig- 
nificant easterly trend. Whether this represents 
true ~olar movement. or relative rotations of blocks 
within the ~tha~uscow Aulacogen, is unknown.

Further evidence for the rotation idea has recently 
been obtained from the Takiyuak Formation (Irving 
and McGlynn 1978). The Takiyuak Formation is 
situated 400 km to the north outside the aulacogen 
and is autochthonous. It is the approximate strati- 
graphic equivalent of the Tochatwi (Hoffman 
1973). Its pole is near the Douglas Peninsula pole 
and well to the east of the Stark and Tochatwi 
poles. Another possibility is that the polar path 
truly made a large swing westwards into the Pacific 
(Irving and McGlynn 1976b) or eastwards as far as 
Africa using the antipole of the poles (ST and TP) 
plotted in Fig. 8 (Roy and Lapointe 1976), meaning 
that all of Laurentia rotated about a nearby axis by 
about 60" between the deposition of the Stark and 
Pearson Formations. This could have happened, 
but, on the basis of present paleomagnetic evi- 
dence, the suggestion of Bingham and Evans (1976) 
that the Stark and Tochatwi poles are the result of 
local rotations, is the more reasonable one. 
The polar paths of Figs. 8 and 9 are referred to as 
tracks 5 and 4. They correspond in time to the 
middle and late Aphebian and the Paleohelikian of 
Stockwell (1972). They are set out schematically in 
Fig. 10, which gives a summary polar path for 
Laurentia during the middle Proterozoic. The later 
part of track 5 and the early part of track 4 together 
comprise the Coronation loop. The loop is re- 
corded by the magnetizations of the deposits of the 
Coronation Geos yncline and associated aulacogen. 
These deposits record the phases of a classical 
geosynclinal cycle for which Hoffman has provided 
a beautiful interpretation in terms of an ocean-con- 
tinent plate interaction (Hoffman 1973). The Coro- 
nation loop appears, in part at least, to be the 
paleomagnetic signature of this cycle. The rate of 
motion relative to the pole, that is the rate of change 
of latitude, is about 5 cm year-'. The major defor- 
mation phase occurs during and after the deposi- 
tion of the Great Slave Supergroup, but before the 
deposition of the Et-Then Group, so the bend or 
hairpin of the Coronation loop corresponds to that 
deformational phase. During this deformational 
phase, the Coronation Geosyncline was in latitudes 
of about 25" (Seton Formation), moved to equa- 
torial latitudes (Christie Bay Group) and then back 
to a latitude of about 25" (Et-Then Group). Thus the 
major deformation phase of the Coronation Geo- 
syncline corresponds to a large change in direction 
of the motions of the Laurentian plate as recorded 
paleomagnetically between the Pearson and the 
Et-Then. 
The orogenic phase of the Coronation Geosyn- 
cline, which is dated about - 1800 Ma, appears to 
post-date certain Hudsonian events in the central 
part of the Churchill Province, because the Du- 
bawnt Group, which post-dates the major deF orm ma- 
tion of the central part of the Churchill Province, 
has a radiometric age and pole position that agrees 
with those of the Seton Formation in the lower part 
of the Great Slave Supergroup. The age of the 
Seton corresponds to ages of syntectonic granitic 
rocks (- 1870 Ma), and are younger than the upper 
Hurwitz volcanic rocks of the Churchill Province 
(- 1910 Ma, Wanless and Eade 1975). This suggests 
that the orogeny, and much of the depositional 
phase of the Coronation Geosyncline, are younger 
than the orogenic and depositional phases of the 
central part of the Churchill Province. It is unwise 
therefore to use the term Hudsonian orogeny to 
describe the orogeny in the Coronation Geo- 
syncline.

PALEOMAGNETISM IN ABITIBI GREENSTONE BELT, AND 
ABITIBI AND MATACHEWAN DIABASE DIKES: 
EVIDENCE OF THE ARCHEAN GEOMAGNETIC FIELD1,2 
E. IRVING AND A. J. NALDRETT 
Earth Physics Branch, Department of Energy, Mines and Resources, Ottawa and 
Department of Geology, University of Toronto, Toronto 
ABSTRACT 
Paleomagnetic results are described from three Archean rock units, and two sets of diabase dikes 
that intrude them. The magnetization of the country rocks is reset by intrusion of the diabase up to 
distances of about 80 m from contacts. The temperature reached during intrusion at this distance 
determined from thermal demagnetization is about 400°C, which is also the approximate temperature 
predicted from Jaeger's cooling curves assuming intrusion into cool rock. At greater distances other 
and presumably older magnetizations are found with a westerly direction. The oldest dykes (the 
Matachewan) have an age of - 2.6 Ga so that this westerly directed magnetization was acquired 
during the Archean. Its age, other than the fact that it is Archean, is not known, but by comparison 
with results from the Stillwater Complex it is estimated to be about - 2.8 Ga. The results are used 
along with previously published data to define in tentative fashion an apparent polar wandering 
curve for the late Archean and early Aphebian which is referred to as Track 6. Track 6 has a simple 
form, and there is no indication that the horizontal mobility of the crust in the late Archean was 
any greater than during the Proterozoic. 
INTRODUCTION 
The purpose of this paper is to describe 
new paleomagnetic results from the Abitibi 
Greenstone Belt, and then to use them to 
construct a path of apparent polar wander 
(APW) for late Archean and early Aphe- 
bian time (approximately -2.3 to -2.8 
Ga, Ga = 109y). This polar path is of 
potential importance for stratigraphic 
correlations and for the tectonic history of 
late Archean time. For instance, it would 
provide information relating to the nature 
of the Kenoran Orogeny. Sampling was 
carried out during the summers of 1970, 
1971, and 1973. 
The Abitibi greenstone belt is relatively 
weakly metamorphosed, the grade of 
metamorphism varying from lower green- 
schist to prehnite-pumpellyite facies (Jolly 
1974). In Munro township, where much of 
our work has been done, it is prehnite- 
pumpellyite (Arndt et al. 1977). Because 
the rocks have undergone only low-grade 
metamorphism it does not necessarily

have been retained. Rocks that are 
essentially unaltered geologically, can have 
had their original magnetization replaced 
partly or entirely by secondary magnetiza- 
tion. This phenomenon of partial or 
complete resetting of magnetizations is 
widespread in Precambrian terrains. (See 
documentation of magnetic overprints, 
figs. 9, 10, and 11, Irving and McGlynn 
1976.) The temperatures achieved during 
low-grade metamorphism (say 300°C) are 
lower than the blocking temperature of 
rocks commonly observed on laboratory 
time scales (typically 500 to 600°C), but 
magnetization can be destroyed if these 
temperatures are applied for long intervals 
of time. Time itself becomes an effective 
agent of demagnetization. Such secondary 
magnetization has been shown by blocking 
temperatures, ranging from the Curie 
temperature of the constituent minerals 
down to room temperatures, whereas the 
magnetization that has survived is 
characterized by a small discrete range of 
blocking temperatures withih 50° or so of 
the Curie temperature. The theoretical 
explanation of this phenomenon has 
recently been given by Buchan and

Dunlop (in Pullaiah et al. 1975). The 
magnetization of single-domain pure mag- 
netite and hematite should survive the 
prehnite-pumpellyite and low greenschist 
facies metamorphism provided there has 
been no chemical change of the iron 
minerals. It ought to be possible to 
retrieve original magnetizations in the 
Abitibi Greenstone Belt provided that 
magnetizations with high discrete blocking 
temperatures (that is square-shouldered 
thermal decay curves) can be located. The 
key observations required are the thermal 
decay characteristics. 
The metamorphism associated with the 
Kenoran Orogeny, is however not the only 
possible cause of remagnetization. Long- 
term mild reheating may have accom- 
panied either the intrusion of Proterozoic 
dikes, or burial beneath Huronian sedi- 
ments which may once have blanketed 
this area. Thus studies of dike contacts 
have been made, and one of the by- 
products of this work has been that we 
have been able to show, for the first time, 
that the characteristic magnetization di- 
rections of the Abitibi and Matachewan 
dike swarms were acquired at the time 
they were intruded. 
The first important study of palaeo- 
magnetism of Archean rocks of Laurentia 
was made by Berg (1970) on the Stillwater 
Igneous Complex. Estimates of the age of 
emplacement of the complex have been 
obtained by Nunes and Tilton (1971) who 
obtained -2.75 Ga by the U-Pb method 
from zircons in the basal zone, and by 
Mueller and Wooden (1976) who obtained 
-2.75 + 0.05 Ga for an Rb-Sr isochron 
from the contact aureole. (Rb-Sr ages in 
this paper are quoted for SRb decay 
constant of 1.39 x 10-11y-1.) Berg ob- 
tained some consistent magnetization 
directions, but the layering at his sites is 
approximately uniform so that it is not 
possible to use Graham's fold test (Graham 
1949) to determine whether the magnetiza- 
tion was acquired before or after deforma- 
tion. Berg believed that the magnetization 
was acquired before deformation. It is 
equally possible that the magnetization 
was acquired after deformation. For 
example the thick Archean sills of the 
Chibougamau Greenstone Belt have mag- 
netizations which structural evidence 
shows were acquired after deformation 
(Ueno and Irving 1976). Ueno and Irving 
therefore considered these magnetizations 
to be somewhat younger than the Kenoran 
Orogeny, which in this area is determined 
by Rb-Sr isochrons to be about -2.6 Ga 
(Jones et al. 1974). Ridler and Foster 
(1975) have given results in abstract from 
the Skead Group. Although they do not 
report any thermal studies, they do report 
that they have carried out a fold test 
indicating that the magnetization is 
Archean in age. Symons (1967) has 
reported work on the Ely greenstones of 
Minnesota but no thermal studies were 
made and only nine samples studied; the 
data do not fulfil the minimum reliability 
criteria of Hicken et al. (1972) and are 
therefore not considered further in this 
paper. Preliminary results have been 
reported from the Shebandowan volcanic- 
plutonic belt at the Superior Geotraverse 
Conferences by Dunlop and Buchan (1975, 
1976) and by Halls (1975), and abstracts 
of work by Londry and Symons (1976) and 
Dunlop and Buchan (1976) have appeared 
but no thermal studies have been reported, 
and the results are not therefore con- 
sidered further in this paper. 
REGIONAL GEOLOGY 
Goodwin and Ridler (1970) have defined 
the Abitibi Greenstone Belt as a crudely 
parallelogram-shaped structure extending 
from the Grenville Front in the east 
through Noranda and Timmins to the 
belt of gneisses associated with the 
Kapuskasing gravity high in the west. It 
is bounded to north and south by areas of 
metasedimentary and gneissic rocks, which 
are intruded by a variety of felsic plutons, 
one of which was dated by Krogh and 
Davis (1971) at -2.7 Ga using the U-Pb 
method on zircons. Much of our work has 
been in Munro and Dundonald townships

in the western part of the belt (fig. 1). In 
the vicinity of Munro, the oldest rocks 
constitute a dominantly south-facing suc- 
cession and occur within and to the north 
of the township. They belong to the 
Kinojevis Group (Dimroth et al. 1973; 
Jensen, in prep.) and consist largely of 
Fe-rich tholeiitic basalts with a small 
proportion of intermediate to felsic vol- 
canic rock, and a succession of ultramafic 
lavas and mafic-ultramafic intrusions 
which are referred to by Arndt et al. 
(1977) as the Munro Formation. The 
Kinojevis Group is overlain by the Blake 
River Group, a thick succession of 
dominantly calc-alkaline volcanic rocks 
that outcrop over a large, crudely elliptical 
area extending from Nighthawk Lake in 
the west to east of Noranda. The Blake 
River Group is overlain by the Skead 
Group. 
In Munro and adjacent townships the 
Munro Formation has been folded about 
east-southeast trending axes and disrupted 
by a series of early faults with similar 
strike. Gabbros have been injected along 
these faults and, at first sight, appear to be 
concordant, although Arndt (1976) has 
demonstrated that they cut across con- 
cordant strata of the Munro Formation at 
the noses of folds. These fault-controlled 
gabbros are cut by north-south dikes of 
Matachewan age (-2.69 ± 0.93 Ga, Gates 
and Hurley 1973) which, in turn, are cut 
by east-northeast trending Abitibi dikes. 
The latter have yielded an Rb-Sr isochron 
of -2.15 ± 0.68 Ga (Gates and Hurley 
1973).

The Dundonald sill (Naldrett and 
Mason 1968), sampled by us in Dundonald 
township 50 km west of Munro, is identical 
to the sills in Munro township (MacRae 
1969), and probably lies within the Munro 
Formation, although poor outcrop and 
complex structure in the intervening area 
leave this an open question. The Kamis- 
kotia complex sampled in Robb township 
15 km northwest of Timmins, differs from 
the sills of Munro and Dundonald town- 
ships in that it contains less peridotite and 
pyroxenite and more anorthositic gabbro. 
It is intrusive into a volcanic succession 
that is capped by felsic rocks. Poor 
outcrop has prevented correlation of this 
succession with rocks east of Timmins. 
The Kamiskotia complex belongs petro- 
logically to a group of anorthositic 
magnetite rich intrusions including the 
Dord Lake and Bell River complexes 
(Class I subclass ii(b) of Naldrett and 
Cabri 1976), which are probably com- 
parable in age to the basement. 
METHODS 
Samples were cored by gasoline drill and 
oriented by magnetic and solar compass. 
About five cores were drilled at each 
collecting site, and two cylindrical speci- 
mens were cut from each core. The 
remanent magnetization of the specimens 
was measured by spinner magnetometers. 
All specimens were demagnetized by 
step-wise heating, or by alternating fields 
(a.f. peak field strength are quoted) using 
the apparatus described by Roy et al. 
(1969, 1971, 1973). Demagnetization was 
carried in fields of less than two gammas. 
In some samples, particularly from the 
Dundonald sill, no coherent magnetization 
could be found; if the directions in 
specimens from the same sample disagreed 
by more than 40°, the results were 
rejected. Eight percent of samples collected 
were rejected on this basis. Results from 
each specimen are averaged to give means 
for each core. The core means are averaged 
giving each unit weight to obtain the mean 
for each sampling site. The overall 
averages for each rock unit are calculated 
giving unit weight to the mean of each 
sampling site. 
ABITIBI DIKES 
In their unaltered state these dikes 
consist of 50-60 modal percent plagioclase, 
30% augite, 5-10% quartz and 5-7% 
opaques. The plagioclase is fresh and 
occurs as stubby to acicular laths up to 
2 mm long, bearing an ophitic to sub- 
ophitic relationship to the enclosing 
augite, which is mostly replaced by 
chlorite, brown and green amphibole, and 
biotite. Quartz occurs interstitially to the 
plagioclase and pyroxene. Magnetite was 
the original opaque mineral occurring as 
equant grains up to 1 mm in diameter 
with ilmenite exsolved around the margins 
and parallel to [111]. In most samples this 
primary magnetite has been totally al- 
tered, leaving only the ilmenite lamellae 
with a matrix of very fine-grained poorly 
reflecting material that could not be iden- 
tified in polished section. Small amounts 
(0.5%) of pyrite are present, commonly 
associated with biotite. Trace quantities 
of pyrrhotite and chalcopyrite are also 
observed. 
A study of the natural remanent 
magnetization (n.r.m.) of the Abitibi dikes 
has been described by Larochelle (1966). 
He reported a dominant westerly magneti- 
zation (W) with steep inclination from 
sampling sites immediately to the north- 
east of figure 1. In addition he reported 
two subordinate magnetizations, with 
directions to NNE and 8 W. The W 
magnetization has been assumed by most 
workers (e.g. Robertson and Fahrig 1971) 
to be the primary magnetization. McGlynn 
et al. (1975) and Pullaiah and Irving 
(1975) have recently questioned the age of 
magnetization of the Abitibi dikes, and 
Roy and Lapointe (1976) have argued 
that the similarity between directions of 
the NNE and SW magnetizations and 
what they regard as a secondary magneti- 
zation of the Nipissing diabase, suggests 
that they too are really secondary mag-

also that the W magnetization was 
acquired during cooling, and is the 
primary magnetization as previous workers 
have assumed it to be. Using the above 
thermal demagnetization results and the 
approximations of Pullaiah et al. (1975), 
the temperature attained at a distance of 
about 80 m may be estimated to be about 
400°C. Consideration of Jaeger's (1957) 
cooling curves applied to a diabase dyke 
equal in thickness to the dike studied by 
us (100 m) and intruding material of 
similar conductivity and density to itself, 
suggests that the maximum temperature 
reached at a point 80 m from the contact 
would be 360°C higher than the temper- 
ature of the country rocks at the time of 
intrusion. Provided that the temperature 
of the country rocks was low, this is 
consistent with the conclusions from the 
magnetization studies. The change from 
Abitibi to Matachewan directions ap- 
parently occurs suddenly within a matter 
of metres since at site M of figure 2 both 
magnetizations occur. There is no evidence 
of a transition zone where both magnetiza- 
tions occur, and in neither sample is there 
a change during demagnetization from W 
Abitibi to Matachewan directions; the 
magnetization appears to be either com- 
pletely Abitibi W or completely Mata- 
chewan. This is consistent with the 
observed presence of very narrow discrete 
range of blocking temperatures. Unfor- 
tunately, because of heavy bush, sampling 
on either side of site M was not practicable.

diabase are in excellent agreement. 
MATACHEWAN DIKES 
The Matachewan diabase dikes form an 
extensive swarm of north-trending vertical 
dikes (fig. 1). The samples studied by us 
resemble the Abitibi dikes in that they are 
composed of 50-60% plagioclase, 30% 
augite, 5-10% quartz and granophyric

intergrowths, and 5o% opaques. The 
plagioclase is lath-like, but the augite 
differs from that in the Abitibi dikes in 
that in addition to developing interstitially 
to the plagioclase, much of it occurs also 
as equant grains. The principal oxide 
mineral is magnetite, now largely altered 
to a fine grained poorly reflecting material, 
and containing ilmenite lamellae and rims. 
The remanent magnetization of the 
Matachewan dikes has been studied pre- 
viously by Strangway (1964) and Fahrig 
et al. (1965) who carried out magnetic 
cleaning in fields of about 100 Oe, but who 
reported no thermal or contact studies. 
These workers found directions of opposite 
polarities, but they were not antiparallel, 
the misalignment being on average 40°, 
and in the sense expected from incomplete 
removal of viscous magnetizations caused 
by the present geomagnetic field. Incom- 
plete cleaning in these early studies is 
probably the cause of the misalignment, 
because we find that after cleaning in 
fields of 300 or 400 Oe there is no evidence 
of misalignment.

DUNDONALD SILL 
The Dundonald sill is a simple differen- 
tiated sill ranging from peridotite at the 
base through pyroxenite to a gabbro 
which contains occasional zones of grano- 
phyric gabbro (Naldrett and Mason 1968). 
Since layering within the sill correlates 
closely with interflow contacts in the 
enclosing volcanics, it is thought to have 
crystallized with a sub-horizontal orienta- 
tion, but it has since been deformed into a 
W-shape consisting of two synclines 
flanking a central anticline (fig. 12). The 
peridotites are mostly completely ser- 
pentinized, but pseudomorphic textures

The primitive is the present horizontal plane. 
indicate that it was originally composed of 
olivine and augite in the proportions of 
4 to 1. The pyroxenites consist of 60-95 
modal percent of relatively fresh diopsidic 
augite with chloritic alteration after 
plagioclase. Fresh to moderately altered 
intercumulus plagioclase is common in the 
upper part of the pyroxenite horizon 
towards the contact with the gabbro, 
although it is usually saussuritized. The 
gabbros consist of cumulus plagioclase 
(now partially saussuritized), cumulus 
augite, and up to 10% of altered cumulus 
magnetite containing both large and 
extremely fine exsolution lamellae of 
ilmenite. The proportion of magnetite 
decreases upwards to less than 5% in the 
upper half of the gabbro. 
Samples were obtained from eight sites 
from the north limb and three sites from 
the south limb (fig. 12). Opaque minerals 
in the peridotite are primary chromite and 
secondary magnetite, distributed through- 
out the serpentine as a fine dusting, and 
also as small granules concentrated along 
cross-cutting serpentine veinlets. Chromite 
is the principal oxide at the base of the 
pyroxenite horizon, but this.gives way to 
magnetite in the central and upper 
portions of the unit. While the chromite is 
fresh in all samples examined, the magne- 
tite is largely altered and contains fine 
lamellae of ilmenite. Fine flakes (<3 
microns) of oxide, probably magnetite, 
occur along the cleavage in the pyroxenes. 
The main oxide in the gabbro is magnetite, 
occurring as 1 mm diameter grains 
containing up to 40% exsolved ilmenite, 
some of it exsolved on such a fine scale as 
to subdivide the host magnetite into areas 
a few tens of microns in dimensions. The 
magnetite is now largely altered. 
Coherent magnetization was obtained 
from four of the five pyroxenite sites 
sampled and one oxide-rich gabbro site 
distinguished by solid dots in figure 12. 
During a.f. demagnetization the directions 
migrate away from the present field to a 
west-northwest direction and remain ap- 
proximately constant up to 1,000 Oe 
(fig. 13). The thermal decay curves show a 
narrow range of blocking temperatures 
between 500 and 600°C, suggesting that 
fine-grained titanium-free magnetite is the 
carrier of the remanence. There is only one 
sample with coherent magnetization from 
the south limb, so that a fold test cannot 
be made. The directions in all samples 
after cleaning are shown in figure 11. The 
directions differ strongly from directions 
in Matachewan diabase, but are similar 
(although more scattered) to those of the 
Kamiskotia complex, indicating that the 
remanence is pre-Matachewan in age. 
ULTRAMAFIC LAVA 
Ultramafic lavas were sampled from the 
locality in Munro Township described by 
Pyke et al. (1973). Many of the flows 
consist of a basal zone (B zone) rich in 
cumulus olivine, overlain by a zone (A 
zone) composed of skeletal olivine and 
pyroxene displaying spinifex texture. 
Other flows do not show this zonation and 
are characterized by a uniform distribution 
of olivine phenocrysts. Although fresh 
olivine and pyroxene occur, secondary

DISCUSSION 
The results show that the magnetiza- 
tions of the Abitibi and Matachewan 
dikes were acquired during cooling and 
have not been altered subsequently. The 
magnetization of the Kamiskotia complex 
was acquired prior to the intrusion of 
the Matachewan dikes and is therefore 
Archean. The magnetization of Dundonald 
sill is less easily interpreted, but the 
directions are similar to those in the 
Kamiskotia complex and therefore it is 
probably that its magnetization is also

directions in all specimens are given on the left, and typical changes in direction during a.f. de- 
magnetization in samples 15 and 26. P is the present filed direction. The primitive is the horizontal. 
Archean. The Dundonald sill magnetiza- 
tion is probably post-deformational, but 
this deformation may have occurred soon 
after formation so the magnetization may 
also date from that time. Rocks with high 
blocking temperatures in a range 500 to 
600°C and square-shouldered demagnetiza- 
tion curves occur in the Dundonald and 
Kamiskotia bodies indicating that this 
material is unlikely to have been reset by 
heating during regional metamorphism to 
the prehnite-pumpellyite grade prevalent 
in this region (Pullaiah et al. 1975). The 
group I samples from the ultrabasic lavas 
give consistent directions with high block- 
ing temperatures, but until results are 
available from other localities no weight 
can be placed on them and they are not 
considered further. 
A summary of the results is given in 
table 2. The Archean poles together with 
those from Aphebian rocks are plotted in 
figure 16. A smooth curve can be drawn 
through them, the one exception being the 
pole for the Dogrib dikes which falls near 
Japan. A prominent bend in the curve 
occurs in NE Siberia at about -2.3 Ga. 
To conform with the classification of 
Irving and McGlynn (1975) we may refer 
to this bend as hairpin 50. The polar path 
following this bend is referred to as 
track 5 and the path before as track 6. 
Track 5 has been discussed previously 
(Irving and Lapointe 1975; McGlynn 
et al. 1975; Roy et al. 1975; Irving and 
McGlynn 1976; Roy and Lapointe 1976). 
Track 6 is the first recorded attempt to 
provide an APW curve for the late 
Archean based on magnetizations that are 
of Archean age. It is obviously very 
tentative indeed, both in form and 
timing. The age calibration at -2.6 Ga is 
given by the age of the Matachewan 
dikes. The calibration at approximately 
-2.8 Ga for the Dundonald sill and 
Kamiskotia complex is suggested, very 
tentatively, on the basis of the agreement 
of their poles with that for the Stillwater

factory calibration of track 6 but seems 
the most reasonable on the basis of the 
present scanty evidence. 
One of the main problems in Pre- 
cambrian work is to determine whether 
the remanence directions should be referred 
(a) to the horizontal at the time the rock 
was formed on the assumption that the 
magnetization was acquired prior to 
deformation, or (b) to present horizontal 
on the assumption that it was acquired 
after deformation, or (c) to some other 
plane on the assumption that the magneti- 
zation was acquired at some intermediate 
stage of deformation. (This problem does 
not of course arise in studies of vertically 
inclined diabase dikes.) If (a) or (c) are the 
proper procedures, then study of deformed 
rocks of this very great age (and most are 
deformed) is severely limited, because in 
most situations the correct reference 
plane cannot be accurately determined. 
One of the redeeming features of Pre- 
cambrian work in the Canadian Shield, 
which apparently makes this aspect of 
paleomagnetic work simpler than it might 
at first sight appear, is that coherent 
polar tracks can be obtained when 
directions are referred to present hori- 
zontal. This amounts to a negative fold 
test on a continent-wide scale. It is a 
feature, not only of highly deformed and 
metamorphosed terrains where it is to be 
expected (Ueno and Irving 1976; Mc- 
Williams and Dunlop 1976), but also of 
rocks that have undergone little or no 
alteration (McGlynn et al. 1974). In the 
present context an item of interest is the 
agreement between pole for the Stillwater 
complex (SU) and those for the Kamiskotia 
and Dundonald bodies, when all the 
directions are referred to present horizontal 
(fig. 16). It is therefore possible that 
the present horizontal (hypothesis (b)) is 
the correct plane of reference, and that the 
bodies have not undergone very much 
relative movement since they were magne- 
tized. This point if substantiated by 
further observations, is of considerable 
interest, because it implies little or no 
relative movement between the Stillwater 
block and the Superior Province. 
There is no polar bend (or hairpin) 
associated with the Kenoran Orogeny. 
This is different from Proterozoic and 
Phanerozoic orogenies that are character- 
ized by polar loops and hairpins. This 
result could mean that the Kenoran 
Orogeny is entirely unlike Phanerozoic and

Proterozoic orogenies, or it could simply 
reflect the inadequacy of the record 
available at present. There does, however, 
appear to be a hairpin at about -2.3 Ga 
and this could be the polar signature of a 
mid-Aphebian orogeny. Further evidence 
for this is to be found in the divergence of 
the Dogrib pole (-2.6 Ga) from track 6. 
If this is indicative of movement between 
the Slave and Superior Provinces then 
this movement appears to have been 
mid-Aphebian in age and was completed 
by about -2.1 Ga, because poles of this 
age from Slave and Superior available at 
the present time and are in substantial 
agreement (McGlynn et al. 1975).

Paleomagnetism of the Great Slave Supergroup, Northwest Territories, 
Canada: the Tochatwi Formation 
M. E. EVANS AND D. K. BINGHAM' 
Institute of Earth and Planetary Physics, University ofAlberta, Edmonton, Alberta T6G 2EI 
Received 7 August 1975 
Revision accepted for publication 13 January 1976 
The Tochatwi Formation comprises some 800 m of fine-grained red to buff sandstone in the 
upper part of the Great Slave Supergroup. Recent geological work indicates an age of 1700 m.y., 
but this is not yet known with certainty. Results from 29 sampling sites stratigraphically covering 
the Tochatwi Formation are presented. Standard paleomagnetic techniques indicate that post- 
folding remagnetization is common, and this is confirmed by analysis of the magnetic vectors 
removed as partial thermal demagnetization proceeds. Two phases of remagnetization are 
recognized, one of which can be attributed to nearby Mackenzie-age intrusions. ihe other phase 
is equivalent to a remagnetization observed by other workers in Kahochella Group strata at 
localities70 km away. As yet, the source of this remagnetization event cannot be identified. Eight 
sampling sites have escaped total remagnetization and an earlier, pre-folding remanence has been 
isolated from these (D = 030, I = - 11, k = 14, a,, = 15"). The corresponding pole position (144W, 
18s) is remote from those deduced from North American rocks of similar age, and possible 
explanations of this problem are discussed.

Introduction 
The Great Slave Supergroup comprises some 
12 000 m of unmetamorphosed sedimentary and 
volcanic rocks preserved in the East Arm Fold 
Belt of Great Slave Lake (Hoffman 1968). As 
many of the sedimentary strata contain red beds 
the area is well suited to studying the Proterozoic 
paleomagnetic record. 
The Christie Bay Group is the uppermost of 
four groups (Sosan, Kahochella, Pethei, Christie 
Bay) into which Hoffman (1969) divided the 
Great Slave Supergroup. It consists of four 
conformable formations, which are, in order of

decreasing age, the Stark, Tochatwi, Portage 
Inlet, and Pearson Formations. Paleomagnetic 
results from the oldest of these, the Stark Forma- 
tion, are reported in a companion paper (Bing- 
ham and Evans 1976). The present paper con- 
cerns the Tochatwi Formation, which con- 
formably overlies the Stark Formation. Geo- 
logical details can be found in a comprehensive 
report by Hoffman (1968). Briefly, the Tochatwi 
Formation consists of fine-grained red-to-buff 
sandstone up to 800 m thick. Cross-bedding, 
mud cracks, and ripple marks are common and 
a few beds of shale or conglomerate occur. 
Hoffman (1969) concluded that the formation is 
largely fluviatile, except at the base, which may 
represent a tidal marine environment.

556 CAN. J. EARTH SCI. VOL. 13, 1976 
In many localities, strata of the Great Slave 
Supergroup are tightly folded. The sedimentary 
rocks comprising the Et-then Group rest un- 
comfortably on the truncated folds of the Great 
Slave Supergroup and are themselves only 
gently folded (Barnes 1951). This implies that 
the bulk of the folding of the Christie Bay Group 
and older strata pre-dates the deposition of Et- 
then Group rocks, an observation that will 
become important in connection with the ages 
of the various magnetizations found in these 
rocks. 
Methods and Sampling Details 
Standard orientation, measurement, and de- 
magnetization procedures were employed (see 
Bingham and Evans 1976, for details). The 
study involved about 1000 measurements of 
remanence. 
Two to six samples were collected at each of 
29 stratigraphically distinct sites (Fig. 1). Where 
possible, these samples were drilled, but at four 
sites the friable condition of the material pre- 
cluded drilling, and hand samples were therefore 
collected. In sedimentary strata sampling was 
carefully confined to a single stratigraphic 
horizon at each sampling site. The sites are 
located in four separate areas, representing 
four stratigraphic sections: section A (6 sites), 
section F (5 sites), section G (2 sites), and section 
N (16 sites). The N section lies about 14 km 
east of the other sections (Fig. 1). It spans the 
entire Tochatwi Formation, which at this 
locality is approximately 600 m thick. The A and 
G sections each contain one site in igneous 
rocks probably intruded during the Mackenzie 
igneous events at about 1200 m.y. (Fahrig and 
Jones 1969); site AA is located in a 1.5 m thick 
shallowly dipping intrusive sheet cutting 
Tochatwi rocks; site AB is a baked contact less 
than 0.5 m from this intrusion; sites AD, AC, 
AE, and AF lie roughly 25, 75, 125, and more 
than 200 m away from the contact. As these 
distances were measured horizontally across the 
outcrop and as the sheet dips at about 20" their 
perpendicular separation from the intrusion is 
difficult to determine, but is likely to be con- 
siderably less than the figures given. In fact, if 
the sheet was originally irregular in the area from 
which it is now eroded the separation is un- 
known. A total stratigraphic thickness of about 
100 m is represented, but how it correlates 
with sections N and F is not known. Site GA 
is in a large (- 50 m thick) sill, whereas GB is in 
Tochatwi rocks about 50 m distant; the contact 
itself is obscured by soil and vegetation. The F 
section represents the lowest 90 m of Tochatwi 
sediments, and is thus laterally equivalent to the 
lower part of section N. 
From each site two pilot specimens were 
selected: one for detailed alternating field (a.f.) 
and one for detailed thermal demagnetization 
experiments. In all cases, the thermal treatment 
is preferred because where a.f. and thermal 
results disagree significantly, the thermal result 
is always farther from the natural remanent 
magnetization (NRM) direction. In fact, the a.f. 
result often differs little from the NRM. It 
appears that thermal treatment more success- 
fully removes secondary components of mag- 
netization. 
According to the quality of the thermal end- 
points of pilot specimens one or several tem- 
peratures were chosen for blanket treatment of 
one specimen from every sample collected. For 
sites at which several temperatures were used the 
data obtained from that treatment yielding 
highest within-site precision were selected as 
the site mean (Irving et al. 1961). 
Discussion 
Directions of Magnetization 
For discussion, it is convenient to divide the 
results according to sampling locality or section. 
N Section 
During pilot thermal demagnetization 16 
specimens (one from each site) move system- 
atically along great circles by 20 to 50°, or 
more, before reaching reasonable end-points 
(McElhinny and Gough 1963) between 500 and 
600 "C. They also show markedly distributed 
blocking temperature spectra (Irving and Op- 
dyke 1965), with intensities after 200 "C heating 
lying between 5 and 35% of NRM (Fig. 2). The 
vectors removed by the first heating step 
(200 "C) are loosely grouped (266, + 85, N = 16, 
k = 8, a,, = 14") about the present field at the 
sampling locality, suggesting that a recently 
acquired magnetization is being removed. 
On the basis of the pilot study, one specimen 
from each sample (N = 46) was heated to 500 
and 600 "C. In four cases site means were random 
(Watson 1956a) at both temperatures; 11 of the 
remaining 12 possess higher within-site precision 
at 500°C and these yield the data given in

graphic section records the legacy of the same 
post-folding remagnetization event as that found 
in the Kahochella Group sampled some 70 km 
to the east. At the present time not much can be 
inferred as to the nature of this event. Its areal 
spread favours a thermal process such as might 
accompany burial and uplift or widespread in- 
trusive activity. In the latter category there exist 
two likely possibilities : Mackenzie-age intru- 
sions, and the earlier quartz-diorite laccoliths, 
both of which occur commonly throughout the 
area. A Mackenzie reheating can be ruled out 
because the direction diverges by almost 70" from 
that necessary (Fahrig and Jones 1969; Irving 
et al. 1972). To date no paleomagnetic informa- 
tion is available on the quartz-diorite laccoliths, 
but an investigation is currently in progress. It 
will be of some interest to see if these intrusions 
are indeed the remagnetization source, as they 
are thought to have been emplaced during upper 
Christie Bay Group times (Hoffman 1969); in 
fact, they are not reported actually cutting any 
strata higher than the Stark Formation, which 
underlies the Tochatwi Formation. Thus they 
offer a potential means of considerably re-

and, in turn, an earlier magnetic component 
discussed below. A third possible source of 
reheating could be associated with the extrusion 
of the Pearson Volcanics, which are the youngest 
formation of the Christie Bay Group. Here again 
no data are available, but their restricted areal 
distribution renders them a less likely source for 
widespread reheating. 
A Section 
Site AA represents an intrusive sheet cutting 
Tochatwi strata. Pilot demagnetization indicated 
highly stable remanence, and a site mean 
direction southwesterly with shallow positive 
dip is found (Fig. 5a). Similar directions were 
obtained from sites AB, AE, and AF, and again 
angular movements were very small, except for 
two specimens, which at high temperatures 
begin to show systematic movement towards the 
northeast quadrant. The meaning of this be- 
haviour becomes clear when the two remaining 
sites (AC, AD) are scrutinized. Two specimens 
from site AC migrate along great circles and 
reach end-points in the northeast quadrant, 
whereas a third specimen moves in like manner 
but fails to reach a good end point before its 
highest blocking temperatures are exceeded 
(Fig. 5b). From site AD, one specimen attains a 
similarly directed end-point and the other two 
migrate to the same direction at 660 "C. Thus 
sites AC and AD provide strong evidence for 
the presence of two magnetic components. The 
one with lower blocking temperatures apparently 
represents a remanence acquired at the time of 
heating by the intrusive sheet (or unexposed 
equivalents), whereas the high temperature com- 
ponent presumably reflects an earlier magnetiza- 
tion. On the other hand, sites AB, AE, and AF 
have been almost totally remagnetized. 
The age of the intrusive sheet (site AA) can 
be reasonably well inferred from the magnetic 
data itself, as its direction of remanence lies 
close to that expected for Mackenzie age in- 
trusions (- 1200 m.y.; Fahrig and Jones 1969; 
Irving et al. 1972). This is further substantiated

EVANS A1 
by the site means for the baked sites (AB, AE, 
AF). Furthermore if the vectors removed 
between NRM and 500 "C are calculated this 
Mackenzie remagnetization can also be recog- 
nized in the partially reheated sites (AC, AD). 
The five site means for the removed vectors 
have a mean of 249, +29 (k = 35, a,, = 13"), 
which does not differ significantly from the ex- 
pected Mackenzie direction (Fig. 6). Since the 
Mackenzie intrusions were emplaced after the 
folding the above comments obviously refer to 
directions of mametization prior to any correc- 
tion for Iocal geological tilt. 
The meaning and significance of the earlier 
magnetic component revealed at sites AC and 
AD are more conveniently discussed after the 
F and G section results are described. 
G Section 
During thermal demagnetization specimens 
from sites GA and GB show systematic move- 
ment and reach good end-points at or prior 
to 500 "C. Inspection of Table 1 indicates that 
the sedimentary site (GB) strongly suggests a 
Mackenzie reheating, but the intrusion itself 
is somewhat divergent (- 30°), although not 
beyond the limits of reasonable secular varia- 
tion. 
F Section 
Of six samples collected at site FA, two are 
excluded owing to inconsistent behaviour during 
test demagnetization runs (one exhibited er- 
ratic behaviour, and the other yielded an end- 
point diverging widely from the rest of the data). 
The remaining four show excellent end-points 
between 600 and 630°C after having migrated 
along great circle paths by more than 90'. The 
other four sites (FB-FE) possess very good 
within-and between-site grouping at tem- 
peratures from 300 to 500°C (Table 1). It will 
be noted that site FA has a magnetic polarity 
opposite to the other four sites. Inverting it and 
averaging a11 five yield a mean direction of 
038, -03 (k = 31, a,, = 14"). This result rep- 
resents the data after correction for local 
geological dip. Before dip correction (D = 199, 
Z = +56, k = 36, a,, = 13") they offer no 
evidence of remagnetization by either of the 
two possible causes identified above. The 
presence of a reversal emphasizes this point 
because both potential remagnetization sources 
possess only one polarity (Fahrig and Jones 
1969; Reid 1972).

Pole Position and Magnetic Polarity 
Detailed thermal demagnetization studies 
coupled with analysis of the magnetic vectors 
removed by such treatment indicates that most 
of the Tochatwi Formation samples collected 
have undergone some form of remagnetization. 
However, eight sites appear to have escaped 
such influence. These are sites FA-FE, AC, AD, 
and NA, and their mean directions of remanence 
are illustrated in Fig. 7. Before dip correction 
they are widely scattered, and their resultant 
indicates randomness (Watson 1956a), but after 
allowing for local geological tilt a coherent 
group emerges with a mean direction of 030, 
-11 (k = 14, a,,.= 15"). The between-site 
precision parameter increases by a factor of nine 
when bedding attitude is allowed for, thus 
providing strong evidence that magnetization 
preceded folding, which is known to have oc- 
curred before deposition of Et-then group 
strata. As the Stark direction is the same as the 
Tochatwi direction (Fig. 7), this in turn im- 
plies that the Stark magnetization is also pre-Et- 
then in age. 
On the usual assumption of a geocentric 
dipole the mean direction maps to a paleo- 
magnetic pole at 144" W, 18" S. However, it is 
stressed that Bingham and Evans (1976) have 
argued that a small crustal block containing

Formations may have been rotated about a

obtained should not be incorporated into polar

Poor effective stratigraphic coverage resulting 
from widespread remagnetization means that 
very little can be deduced about geomagnetic 
polarities in Tochatwi times. One interesting 
point does emerge, however. Reference to 
figs. 2 and 8 in the companion paper (Binpham 
and Evans 1976) shows that the polarity of 
sites SEA and SEB, which occur at the very top 
of the Stark Formation, is normal (i.e. south- 
west and shallow). The same polarity is re- 
corded at sites FA and NA, which are separated 
laterally by some 14 km but which both lie in 
the bottom 20-40 m of the Tochatwi Formation. 
Between sites FA and FB, a reversal occurs 
indicating that the normal polarity magnetozone 
which starts near the top of the Stark Formation 
occupies a limited stratigraphic thickness and 
was therefore probably short-lived.

Paleomagnetic results from 55 sampling sites throughout the Stark Formation are reported. 
The known stratigraphic sequence of these sites enables the behaviour of thegeomagnetic field in 
these remote times ( 1750 m.y .) to be elucidated. Two polarity reversals are identified and these 
represent potentially useful comtative features in strata devoid of index fossils. One of these is 
investigated in detail and indicates that hehaviour of the geomagnetic field during polarity 
reversals was essentially the same in the early Proterozoic as it has heen over the last few million 
years. The pole position (145" W. 15"S. dp = 3.5, dm =6.9)!ies far to the west of that anticipated 
from earlier results, implying further complexity of the North American polar wander curve. 
Possible alternatives 10 this added complexity are discussed.

Introduction 
On the Canadian Shield there are a number 
of basins containing great thicknesses of 
relatively fresh sedimentary and volcanic rocks 
of Precambrian age. Since the stratigraphy in 
some of these basins is well known and since 
some of the formations consist primarily of red 
beds, these basins provide good access to 
portions of the Precambrian paleomagnetic 
record for North America. 
The present study is part of a program of 
paleomagnetic sampling of Lower Proterozoic 
rocks preserved in the East Arm Fold Belt of 
Great Slave Lake, N.W.T. This foldbelt lies 
within the Churchill Province and is bounded 
on the north by the Slave Province of the Cana- 
dian Shield. The nearby granites of the former 
province are Hudsonian in age (1450-2010 m.y.); 
those of the latter are of Kenoran age (2300- 
2640 m.y.) (Hoffman 1969). The 12 000 strati- 
graphic metres of sedimentary and volcanic

rocks comprising the Great Slave Supergroup 
have been mapped by Stockwell (1936) and more 
recently by Hoffman (1968, 1969), whose nomen- 
clature is followed here. Unconformably over- 
lying the Great Slave Supergroup are strata of 
the Et-then Group, whereas the final geological 
element consists of diabase dykes and sills 
correlated with the Mackenzie igneous events 
(- 1200 m.y.). 
The Great Slave Supergroup has been sub- 
divided by Hoffman (1968) into four groups: in 
order of decreasing age these are the Sosan, 
Kahochella, Pethei, and Christie Bay Groups. 
The Stark Formation is the lowest member of 
the Christie Bay Group, and it consists of at 
least 600 m of finely bedded red mudstones. 
Frequent discontinuous pale green layers and 
blotches up to a few centimetres thick give 
outcrops a striped appearance. Ripple marks, 
cross bedding, and hopper-shaped halite crystal 
casts are common. Hoffman (1969, p. 453) 
suggests that the Stark Formation was "de- 
posited in a shallow sublittoral marine environ- 
ment of high aridity".
