The age of Stark sedimentation can be in- 
ferred from its relationship to several radio- 
metrically dated quartz diorite laccoliths, and 
also from the broader interpretation of the 
evolutionary history of the so-called Coronation 
geosyncline. For details, the reader should con- 
sult Hoffman (1968, 1969, 1973) and Hoffman 
et al. (1970); these authors conclude that the 
best available estimate of the age of the sedi- 
mentation phase to which the Stark Formation 
belongs is 1750 m.y. Conformably overlying the 
Stark Formation is the Tochatwi Formation, a 
paleomagnetic survey of which is reported in a 
companion paper (Evans and Bingham 1975). 
Methods 
A total of 160 hand blocks were collected from 
55 stratigraphically distinct sites. Forty-five 
of these represent a sequential sampling of a 
single 600 m thick section consisting of nearly 
vertically dipping beds along the shore of 
Christie Bay, Great Slave Lake (Fig. I). The 
historical details of sampling this section have 
resulted in site names starting with SB, SC, SK, 
and AJ; this entire section is hereafter referred 
to as the "main section". The other stratigraphic 
sections are called the SD and SE sections, in 
accordance with the first two characters ap- 
pearing in the site names.

At all but a few sites, beds that are pre- 
dominantly red were sampled. Hand samples 
were collected because the generally friable 
nature of the rocks made field drilling impossible. 
For the most part, 3 blocks were collected at 
each site, but occasionally 2 or 4 blocks were 
taken; full details are given in Table 1. Orienta- 
tion was by solar bearings and/or by geo- 
graphical sight points tied to solar bearings. 
The complete study involved about 1700 
measurements of remanence which were made 
on a PAR model SM-1 spinner magnetometer. 
Routine partial demagnetization was carried 
out on all specimens used in the final analysis. 
AIternating field (AF) demagnetization was 
performed with the apparatus described by 
Murthy (1969), which is similar to that of 
McElhinny (1966). Thermal cleaning was ac- 
complished using a small oven in a room- 
sized magnetic shield (Patton and Fitch 1962; 
Reid 1972); the magnetic field over the volume 
occupied by the specimens during thermal 
cleaning studies is less than 5 y and temperatures 
are controlled to + 5 "C.

Alternating Field Demagnetization 
Detailed step-wise AF demagnetization studies 
up to 1800 Oe peak field were carried out on 
pilot specimens from 32 of the 45 sites. With 
few exceptions, the behaviour of all specimens 
is both remarkably uniform and very stable. 
The magnetization vectors of specimens from 
all but 6 of the 32 pilot specimens moved less 
than 15" between NRM and 400Oe. Between 
400 and 1800 Oe, very little further angular 
change was observed; in only two cases did 
movement exceed 8" (SBM, 14"; SCE, 32"). 
On the basis of the uniformity of behaviour 
throughout the section, 400 Oe has been chosen 
as that AF treatment which best removes 
secondary components without unduly de- 
grading the primary remanence. However, it is 
clear from the stability of the remanence direc- 
tions throughout AF cleaning that this choice 
is not critical. One specimen from each hand 
block from all SB- and SK- sites (32 sites, 99 
samples) was therefore treated at 400 Oe peak 
field. 
Under AF demagnetization the intensities of 
magnetization follow two distinct patterns, one 
for reversed specimens and one for normal 
specimens. All but one of the pilot specimens 
from the reversed sites show a decrease in 
J/Jo (to between 77 and 96% at 400 Oe) (Fig. 
3a). The aberrant site, SKZ, is green and is 
magnetically much softer. On the other hand, all 
but three of the normal sites show an initial 
intensity increase (100 to 172% at 400 0e) 
(Fig. 3b). Two of the three exceptions, sites 
SBN and SCE, possess anomalously large, soft 
components that are removed by 100 to 200 Oe, 
and thereafter they behave like the others (SCE, 
being somewhat greener than the others, is very 
weakly magnetized, and thus J/Jo appears to 
vary more erratically). The remaining site, SBQ, 
is lithologically different and will be discussed 
in a later subsection. 
The observed pattern of intensity behaviour 
is readily explicable in terms of small secondary 
components of magnetization parallel to the 
present field at the collecting locality. In order 
to facilitate discussion of common features, we 
return to this point below, after results from 
other stratigraphic sections have been discussed.

Thermal Demagnetization 
Uniformity of the lithology and magnetic 
behaviour under AF treatment led us to restrict 
detailed thermal demagnetization studies to 
pilot specimens from 11 sites, spread throughout 
the main section. Three of these sites are litho- 
logically distinct (SBA, SKZ, SBQ) and behave 
differently; they will be discussed separately in 
the next subsection. Between NRM and 500 "C, 
six of the remaining eight moved less than 20", 
while the other two moved 27" and 55". From 
500 to 660 "C, they all moved less than 8"; but 
above 660 "C, movements were large. 
As with the AF treatment, the exact choice of 
temperature for blanket cleaning is not critical; 
500 "C was chosen, although any temperature 
between 300 and 550 "C would probably produce 
statistically indistinguishable results when ap- 
plied to the section as a whole, for the end- 
points are generally well defined within that 
interval.

Discussion 
Secondary Magnetization Removed by Partial 
Demagnetization 
The remarkable pattern of intensity be- 
haviour during AF cleaning suggests that a 
secondary component of magnetization, ap- 
proximately parallel to the magnetization of the 
reversed sites but opposing the normal sites, is 
being removed by fields up to 400 Oe. A re- 
cently acquired remanence directed along the 
present geomagnetic field at the collecting 
locality and with the strata in their present 
attitude is an obvious candidate. This suggestion 
has been tested by analyzing the magnetic 
vectors removed during 'cleaning'. Of the 55 
sites sampled, 42 have been subjected to AF 
treatment. The vectors removed between NRM 
and 400 Oe form a coherent group, the mean of 
which lies close to the present field. Details 
are as follows. Site level statistics on the re- 
moved vectors indicate that at 8 sites, these 
are random (Watson 1956~). Considering the 34 
non-random sites, it may be preferable to weight 
in favour of those with higher within-site 
precision. Seventeen of the 34 have within-site 
precision parameters greater than 10, and their 
mean direction is D = 013, I = + 83 (k = 17, 
a,, = 9"); inclusion of the 17 sites which have 
k t I0 moves the mean only 4" and yields 
D = 347, Z = +87 (k = 18, a,, = 6"). Neither 
of these directions differ significantly from the 
present field (D = 030, 1 = +83) at the col- 
lecting locality. 
The 34 sites used in this analysis represent 
both normal and reversed polarities and transi- 
tional directions, but it is clear that vectorial 
subtraction succeeds in isolating a secondary 
magnetization common to the various groups. 
Application of Graham's (1949) fold test in- 
dicates that the removed vectors are signifi- 
cantly more scattered after restoring the strata 
to the horizontal, thereby demonstrating that 
they were imposed after folding. For the 17 sites 
having within-site k > 10, we obtain k = 8 
(cf. k = 17 before structural correction); where- 
as for all 34 sites, we obtain k = 7 (cf. k = 18 
before correction). After structural correction, 
the 17 sites with k > 10 are significantly more 
scattered at the 95% confidence level, whereas 
all 34 sites are more scattered at the 99% level 
(McElhinny 1964). 
The negative fold test and close proximity of 
the overall mean for the removed vectors with the 
present field at the sampling locality leave little 
doubt that most specimens possess a secondary 
magnetization acquired in very recent times. 
However, demagnetization to 400 0e success- 
fully erases this magnetic component and re- 
veals an underlying magnetization whose nature 
is discussed further below. 
A similar analysis of the vectors removed by 
heating to 500 "C has been carried out. Again a 
coherent grouping emerges with 5 1 non-random 
sites yielding a mean direction of D = 239, 
I = +80 (k = 22, a,, = 4"). After correction 
for local geological dip, scatter increases signifi- 
cantly at the 99% confidence level (k decreases to 
6), and a post-folding secondary component is 
indicated. However, the mean of these removed 
vectors lies 17" from the presznt field and 12" 
from the mean of the 34 magnetically treated 
sites described above. It is not clear at the 
present time whether this small offset has any 
geophysical significance.

All the results quoted thus far were computed 
under the assumption, commonly followed in 
paleomagnetic studies, that the folds involved 
do not plunge. Since most of the strata under 
study here possess steep dips, the possibility 
of plunge represents a serious potential problem. 
To test the possible significance of plunge, an 
analysis of bedding plane poles has been carried 
out following the method of Watson (1960), 
outlined by Cruden (1968). 
The data used consisted of 62 bed orientations 
measured in the field during paleomagnetic 
sampling and strikes and dips measured from 
Barnes' (1951) map. The 26 strikes and dips 
from Barnes' map are more or less randomly 
distributed over the area included in the left 
half of Fig. 1. The 36 bed attitudes measured 
in the field are distributed along the coast line 
between the main and SE- sections (the 45 
closely spaced main section attitudes have been 
combined into a single datum to avoid over- 
representation) and on the south arm of Pearson 
Point (just off the north edge of Fig. 1). Because 
it is not known exactly where Barnes measured 
his bed attitudes, it is possible that there is 
some duplication within this set of data; how- 
ever, such doubling of points appears to be 
limited to a maximum of 5 points. Excluded 
from the analysis are two small areas that give 
widely scattered bedding poles and thus appear 
to represent tectonically disturbed areas. No 
samples were collected from one of the areas, 
but the second area covers the East half of the 
island where the SD section lies (Fig. 1). Al- 
though this part of the island appears to be 
tectonically complex, the six sites of the SD 
section themselves represent a homoclinal 
sequence (Table I), and this is important to the 
interpretation of their paleomagnetic data (see 
below). 
The 62 bedding poles yield the eigenvector 
corresponding to the minimum eigenvalue of 
the variance-covariance matrix of direction 
cosines (Cruden 1968) and the rr-diagram shown 
in Fig. 9. The distribution of points clearly 
indicates approximately cylindrical folding. The 
eigenvector associated with the minimum eigen-

of the overlying Tochatwi Formation. This 
the different sedtions, and the interpretation 
given (Fig. 2) leads to the simplest sequence of 
geomagnetic polarities. Thus, there appears to 
have been two full field reversals during Stark 
times: one recorded in the middle of the main 
section and one somewhere between the SD and 
SE sections. It is perhaps worth pointing out 
that the polarity pattern emerging has con- 
siderable potential in regional and possibly 
global correlation, particularly in sedimentary 
sequences devoid of index fossils and sparsely 
endowed with datable igneous material. 
The virtual geomagnetic poles (VGP's) corre- 
sponding to the intermediate sites (SKI through 
AJD) follow an approximate great circle path 
(Fig. lo), as has been found for studies of more 
recent polarity transitions (e.g. Creer and Ispir 
1970a; Dunn et al. 1971). Furthermore, strata 
in the transition zone are less strongly mag- 
netized than the rocks above and below. This 
point is more clearly revealed when five point 
running (geometric) means of the thermal 
results (excluding sites SKZ and SBQ, which are 
lithologically distinct) are computed (Fig. 2). 
While it is recognized that the relationship 
between measured remanent intensity and 
paleointensity of the geomagnetic field is not 
necessarily simple, the marked lithological 
uniformity of the section makes it not unlikely 
that the drop in intensity recorded during the

transition represents a real drop in paleointen- 
sity. A decrease in paleointensity during more 
recent reversals by a factor of about 4 or 5 has 
been noted by several workers, as reviewed by 
McElhinny (1971). The decrease observed in the 
Stark Formation represents a factor of about 2 
or 3. This feature, along with the path of 
transitional poles, indicates that in some ways 
this reversal closely resembles those recorded in 
much more recent rocks. 
The polarity transition occupies approxi- 
mately 25 m of section (Fig. 2), and it therefore 
contrasts markedly with results from several 
Phanerozoic reversals, which occupy only 1 or 
2 m of red beds (see Baag and Helsley 1974, for 
a recent review), and sometimes as little as a 
few centimetres (McElhinny 1970). Thus it is 
tempting to suggest that our results favour a 
slower reversal mechanism in the early Protero- 
zoic, but a correspondingly rapid sedimentation 
rate cannot be ruled out. Of course, it is im- 
portant to distinguish between the rate at which 
the sediments in question were deposited and the 
rate at which they acquired their remanence, 
since the two are not necessarily the same. We 
return to this point below, when the origin of 
the magnetization is discussed. If we accept, for 
the moment, that magnetization occurred at or 
shortly after deposition, and also that the time 
required for a field reversal was similar to that 
involved in geologically recent reversals (i.e. 
1-2 x lo3 years, McElhinny 1971), then a sedi- 
mentation rate of about 1-2 cm/y is implied. 
Although this is rather high compared to ob- 
served contemporary rates of accumulation 
(Kukal 1971), it cannot be ruled out, partic- 
ularly if a deltaic environment be envisaged. 
However 1 or 2 cm/y is likely to represent the 
upper limit, and this being so, the entire sampled 
sequence (>800 m, see Fig. 2) represents at 
least 4 x lo4 years, and perhaps as much as 
8 x lo6 years. 
Site SCA lies roughly in the middle of the 
normal part of the main section and has a VGP 
about 90" from the section mean (Fig. 10). This 
solitary intermediate direction is interpreted as 
a field excursion event similar to those observed 
in the more recent geologic record (e.g. Doell 
and Cox 1972; Barbetti and McElhinny 1972). 
It is noteworthy that this VGP lies close to the 
path subsequently traced out by the subsequent 
transition zone. This proximity to the later 
reversal path may be entirely coincidental, or it 
may be due to a persistent non-dipole source 
such as that hypothesized by Watkins and 
Nougier (1973) to explain the similarity of two 
separate Bruhnes epoch field excursions recorded 
in rocks from the Indian Ocean; alternatively, it 
may be a consequence of the three dipole model 
proposed by Creer and Ispir (1970b) to explain 
parallism of pole paths during several different 
polarity transitions. 
As pointed out above, the SD section lies in a 
tectonically disturbed zone. However, the scatter 
of the six site means cannot be attributed to 
structure because the entire section forms a 
homoclinal sequence (Table 1). The results are 
therefore interpreted as representing a period 
of geomagnetic instability consisting of a pos- 
sible excursion (4 coplanar sites, SDF-SDC), 
followed by a brief attempt to return to reverse 
polarity (SDB-SDA), before swinging through 
the ANR direction to the normal polarity of 
SEB and SEC (Fig. 8). It is worth noting that 
although structural complexity cannot be in- 
voked as a cause for the scatter of the results, 
it may explain the offset between the SDB-SDA 
data and the main section reversed directions 
(Fig. 8).

Origin of the Magnetization Revealed by Partial 
Demagnetization 
The AF and thermal demagnetization experi- 
ments indicate that, except for predominantly 
green sites, the 'cleaned' magnetic remanence 
lies largely in a high coercivity, high Curie 
temperature magnetic fraction. Coercivities in 
excess of 1800 Oe (Figs. 3 and 5) and Curie 
temperatures between 660 and 700 "C (Figs. 4 
and 6) point to hematite as the significant mag- 
neticmineral, and this is confirmed by IRM build- 
up curves (Fig. 11). Slight drops of about 10% in 
J/J, between 550 and 600 "C indicate that small 
amounts of magnetite may also be present. 
The means of the 20 reversed and 19 normal 
sites (entries 4 and 5, Table 2) are within 10" of 
being exactly reversed, and this provides evidence 
that later secondary magnetic components super- 
imposed on an underlying magnetization are 
unimportant. However, this underlying mag- 
netization is probably a chemical remanent 
magnetization, and it is therefore important to 
enquire when it was acquired. The well known 
fold test (Graham 1949) can discriminate 
between pre- and post-folding magnetization 
episodes, but in the present case there is not 
enough variation in the attitudes of the strata 
sampled to cause a significant difference in 
statistics when mean directions are calculated in 
the present and ancient coordinate frames 
(entries I and 2, Table 2).

section strongly suggest that the strata were 
magnetized sequentially, either progressively 
upwards or progressively downwards. This is 
most readily achieved during diagenesis, either 
upon deposition or as lithification proceeds 
vertically through the sediment pile. Indeed, in a 
recent review, Baag and Helsley (1974, p. 3308) 
concluded that "most paleomagnetic literature 
concerning red beds supports the view that the 
stable primary NRM of red beds was acquired 
at and/or soon after deposition". Furthermore, 
these authors point out that the presence of a 
gradual trend of intermediate directions between 
opposed polarity zones favours syndepositional 
acquisition of remanence. Despite these favour- 
able points, it is, of course, possible to devise 
later remagnetization schemes (e.g., movement 
of an isotherm or chemical front) that could 
give rise to the observed facts, and the problem 
cannot be completely resolved by reference to 
the Stark Formation data alone. The possibly 
primary nature of the remanence was discussed 
further in a companion paper (Evans and 
Bingham 1975), where results from strati- 
graphically adjacent formations were described. 
There it is shown that the remanence does in- 
deed pre-date the folding which, in turn, pre- 
dates deposition of the overlying Et-then Group. 
Pole positions 
The main section mean direction, which best 
represents the true mean paleomagnetic field 
direction during Stark times (entry 1, Table 2), 
yields a pole position at 145" W, 15" S in the 
equatorial mid-Pacific. Sites SDA, SDB, SEB, 
and SEC are not included, since they are closely 
associated with periods of geomagnetic in- 
stability, and they represent insufficient data to 
warrant the assumption that stable dipole posi- 
tions had been achieved. A paleolatitude of 8" is 
implied and this is consistent with the abundant 
occurrence of halite casts. The pole position 
falls more than 60" to the west of both the Et- 
then Group pole (Irving et al. 1972) and the 
Kahochella Group pole (McMurry et al. 1973), 
which are known to lie stratigraphically above 
and below the Stark Formation, respectively. 
Taken at face value, the Stark result requires an 
additional large loop in the polar wander path 
for North America. Although the time period 
involved for the new loop (- 200m.y.) is 
probably long enough to accommodate it at 
recognized rates of polar wandering (e.g.

BINGHAM 
Creer et al. 1957), this added complexity in the 
total curve begins to make the polar wander 
curve more difficult to use as a stratigraphic or 
geotectonic tool. Therefore, it is worthwhile to 
consider possible alternatives. 
(a) The Stark pole is not significantly different 
from the 'Elsonian pole' of 1300-1475 m.y. 
(Spall 197 1 ; Evans et al. 1975), but an 'Elsonian' 
age is at variance with all the geological facts 
(see, e.g., Hoffman 1973). 
(b) It is always possible to explain any ap- 
parent anomaly in a polar wandering curve by 
supposing that for the time in question the geo- 
magnetic field was non-dipolar in character. 
Evidence for the dipolar nature of the geo- 
magnetic field during Stark or earlier times is 
lacking, but evidence exists for such behaviour 
at later times, the earliest of which is the Elsonian 
Pole (Evans et al. 1975). At the present time it is 
unwise to appeal to such ad hoc hypotheses 
until all simpler suggestions are firmly ruled 
out. 
(c) Introducing an additional loop can be 
avoided by drawing the polar wander path 
through the Stark Formation anti-pole. Instead 
of producing a new loop across the Pacific, this 
alternative stretches the presently accepted 
northern South American loop 90" further east- 
ward to a point near Khartoum, Sudan. In like 
manner, one could use the other end of the Et- 
then pole as the normal pole, thereby producing 
a westward loop over New Guinea. Either (or 
both) of these possibilities are viable suggestions, 
and a final decision will only be possible as more 
data become available. 
(d) Perhaps some additional tectonic correc- 
tion to the paleomagnetic data is necessary, such 
as rotation of a small block about a vertical axis. 
This mechanism has previously been proposed 
to account for divergent paleomagnetic poles 
(e.g. Fahrig and Larochelle 1972; Roy and 
Fahrig 1973). Such suggestions require extreme 
caution since, used arbitrarily, they can readily 
give rise to misleading interpretations. However, 
in the present case there exists evidence that such 
a rotation may have occurred. Examination of 
the geological map (Geological Survey of 
Canada, Map 1 122A, 1968) indicates that the 
general trend of the East Arm Fold Belt is 
approximately NE-SW, but that in the area 
covered by Fig. 1 fold axes trend more E-W or 
even south of east. Quantitative analysis of 
bedding attitudes (Fig. 9) confirm this dis- 
AND EVANS 577 
crepancy. If this change in strike represents a 
tectonic bending by some 50-60", then ap- 
propriate allowance must be made for it. The 
intriguing situation then arises that the paleo- 
magnetic pole is shifted to a position much 
more consistent with those derived from North 
American rocks of similar age. For example, 
rotation by 60" about a vertical axis yields a pole 
at 83" W 18" S. A firm decision cannot be made 
on this problem until the possibility of rotation 
is tested by adequate sampling in areas where 
the tectonic 'grain' is conformable with that of 
the entire basin.

The Palaeomagnetism of Precambrian Igneous and 
Sedimentary Rocks of the Orange River Belt in 
South Africa and South West Africa 
J. D. A. Piper 
(Received 1974 November 4)* 
Summary 
Palaeomagnetic results are presented for a variety of Precambrian rocks 
from south-western Africa. Oldest rocks studied are the Orange River 
Lavas (> I850 My) from which the three least altered sites give a VGP at 
254" E, 19" N near the polar wander curve for Africa at c.2100 My. Five 
sites from basic intrusions believed to be about 1200 My in age at Ookiep, 
Namaqualand, give a pole at 155" E, 15" S. Nineteen sites in lavas of the 
Barby Formation (Sinclair Group, < 1200 My) in South West Africa 
yield a significant direction after cleaning with five sites reversed with 
respect to the remainder; grouping is improved after correction for folding 
(> 1020 My). Palaeomagnetic results are also given for lavas of the over- 
lying Guperas Formation (< 1020 h.ly), sediments of the succeeding 
Auborus Formation, basic dykes at Klein Karas (878+41 My), and six 
dolerite dykes from Namaqualand (probable age of 653 A- 70 My). Nine 
sites from the Fish River Formation (probable Lower Cambrian age) give 
pole positions correlating with a late Precambrian to Ordovician polar 
shift recognized from other Gondwanaland data. The Doornpoort 
Formation of Central South West Africa gives a direction of magnetization 
which a fold test dates as originating from the Damaran folding 
(550-500 My). 
The results define a loop in the polar wander curve for Africa between 
1200 and 1000 My which can be matched in size, shape and age to a Ioop 
in the North American curve implying that the two regions were in 
juxtaposition at this time. 
1. Introduction 
Palaeomagnetic studies of African Precambrian rocks were concentrated during the 
last decade on rocks of the Rhodesia/Kaapvaal (Transvaal) cratons, and have been 
summarized by McElhinny et aZ. (1968) who define an appaient polar wander (apw) 
curve for the intervals 2700-2300 My and 1970-1300 My. From late Precambrian 
palaeomagnetic results from Tanzania (Piper 1972) and Kenya (Brock, Raja & Vise 
1972), Brock & Piper (1972) proposed an apw path to connect the Precambrian and 
Phanerozoic paths. Uncertainty surrounded this interpretation because there still 
remained large gaps in time coverage of the data and it was uncertain whether later 
tectonic activity had caused large relative movements between the cratonic regions of

central and southern Africa where the separate portions of the apw curve were 
derived. This study is concerned with pre- and post-orogenic igneous rocks from the 
northern part of the Namaqualand Complex incorporating a region of varying 
structural trends but yielding a preponderance of age dates around 1100 My (Nicolay- 
sen 1962; Clifford 1968) known as the Orange River or Namaqualand Belt; it abuts 
against the western margin of the Rhodesia-Kaapvaal craton. The study gives several 
new palaeomagnetic poles which help to resolve these uncertainties. 
2. Geological background 
Precambrian rocks of the region outcrop below Karroo and younger rocks in a 
strip of country running between the coast and 300-400 km inland (Fig. 1). Oldest 
rocks form a basement of metasediments and metavolcanics collectively known as the 
Kheis Group and intruded by large masses of granite-gneiss (Martin 1965; Haughton 
1969; Joubert 1971). The Orange Riker Lavas sampled for this study at Vioolsdrif 
belong to this Group and are intruded by granite-gneiss giving an age of 1850+ 50 My 
(de Villiers & Burger 1967) although they may be considerably older because granite 
intruding the Marydale Series of the Kheis in the type are given an age of 2600 My 
(Nicolaysen & Burger 1965). 
In the western part of the southern South West Africa folded and largely un- 
metamorphosed rocks lie on probable Kheis basement subdivided as the Kunjas, 
Sinclair and Auborus Series by Beetz (1923) who grouped them as the Konkip System. 
A predominantly volcanic formation below the first series was subsequently recognized 
as the Nagatis Formation (Martin 1965) and was intruded by granites including the 
Tumuab granite (1290 k 30 My) before deposition of the predominantly-clastic 
Kunjas series. Radiometric data suggest a possible age of 1200 My for acid volcanics 
of the Nagatis Formation (von Brunn 1969). The overlying Sinclair Group is pre- 
dominantly volcanic and granites intrusive into it but predating the overlying Auborus 
Formation, include the Rooikam granite dated at 1020+80 My (von Brunn 1969). 
At the top of the Sinclair Group and separated from it by angular unconformity is a 
suite of rocks including lava flows and sediments distinguished (Martin 1965) as the 
Guperas member how considered to be a formation). These lavas were erupted after 
the bulk of the folding of the Sinclair Group was completed (B. R. Watters 1971, 
private communication). 
Folding and intrusion of the Sinclair series was followed by deposition of a thick 
succession of conglomerates, breccias, red sandstones, and siltstones known as the 
Auborus formation. In the type area this formation was laid down in a N-S synclinal 
basin with thick conglomerates at the base and characterized by large lateral changes 
in lithology and thickness. Sedimentological studies (Miller 1969) suggest deposition 
under strongly oxidizing conditions with frequent exposure and formation of dessica- 
tion features. Mild deformation and block faulting of the Auborus formation took 
place soon after deposition and was followed by erosion to the flat surface on which 
the overlying Nama Group was deposited. This Group comprises shallow water shelf 
sediments divided into three foimations with which this paper is concerned only with 
the top (Fish River) Formation. The Nama is predominantly arenaceous or argil- 
laceous but includes limestones and glacial horizons (Kroner & Rankama 1972). The 
Fish River Formation is a very shallow water sandstone and siltstone succession 
deposited in strongly oxidizing conditions. Germs (1972) suggested a Cambrian age 
for these beds on account of the presence of the trace fossil Phycodespedum. 
In the north-central part of South West Africa rocks belonging to the Damara 
System have a NE-SW Structural trend acquired during the Damaran episode of the 
Pan African orogeny which cuts across the trends imposed by earlier episodes to the 
south and north (Fig. 1). The Damara System is underlain, locally unconformably,

3. Palaeomagnetic results 
3.1 Field and laboratory techniques 
Except for the dykes of Klein Karas which were lump sampled, all the palaeo- 
magnetic samples were collected using a portable coring drill (Doell & Cox 1967).

Up to seven cores were sampled at each site and oriented by sun sights. They were cut 
into inch-long cylinders in the laboratory, and one or two pilot samples were selected 
from each site for stepwise af demagnetization. As a rule steps of 100 Oe up to 1000 
or 1600 Oe were chosen and samples were measured before and after treatment with a 
PAR Model SM-2D spinner magnetometer. A stability index (Briden 1972) was 
computed for each step and an optimum alternating field chosen from the behaviour 
of the pilot for treatment of the remaining samples from the site. 
3.2 Orange River Lavas, Vioolsdrif, Cape Province 
Palaeomagnetic sites were taken through a pile of lavas dipping to the north of 
NNW at angles which increase from 25" in the south to 50" in the north of the outcrop.

sequence through the succession, sites are 46, 47, 112, 111, 110, 109, 51, 50, 48 and 
49, the lowest site (46) being 20m above the intrusive contact with granite gneiss 
(Fig. 2). The Orange River lavas are included in the Wilgenhout Drift Formation of 
the Kheis (de Villiers & Sohnge 1959) but a correlation with the Ventersdorp System 
should also be considered (J. H. W. Ward and A. Kroner 1972, private communica-

fall in moments; the other three samples of this site give scattered directions both 
before and after cleaning although vectors move towards that of the three stable 
samples which are used in computation of the site mean. Site 49 has closely grouped 
total NRMs with a mean near to that of site 46. On demagnetization however, the 
vectors become scattered but three of the samples move to westerly negative inclina- 
tions near to that shown by site 51. After cleaning sites, 46, 48 and 51 are moderate 
to well grouped, 47, 109, 11 1 and 112 are less well grouped and site 49 is significant 
before cleaning; three samples from each of sites 49 and 50 are well grouped after 
cleaning (Table 1).

(Figs 2 and 4). Sites near the base and top have easterly negative directions while 
sites near the middle have westerly declinations with shallow positive or steeper

3.3 Basic intrusions, O'okiep, Cape Province 
In the O'okiep region of the Namaqualand Copper Field metamorphosed sedi- 
mentary rocks possibly belonging to the Kaaien Formation of the Kheis (Haughton 
1969) have been folded along east-west axes and intruded by later granites and 
copper-bearing norites. These latter bodies are associated with sharp folds super- 
imposed on the regional foliation and are confined to certain levels in the stratigraphy 
(Benedict et al. 1964). The O'okiep mining company have kindly provided the author 
with samples drilled from single surface sites in five of these basic bodies (A. F. Lom- 
baard & J. A. Muller 1971, private communication). The bodies are: Wheal Heath 
(site 34), Kliphoog (35), Fonteintjie (36), Hoits (37) and Ring Dyke (38). Two age 
determinations of 101OMy and 1060My with a preferred mean of 1042My have 
been made on these rocks (Nicolaysen & Burger 1965). According to Dr A. Kroner 
(private communication 1972) this age probably reflects a strong thermal episode 
associated with extensive and large scale lateral shearing in this region; new work 
suggests a slightly older age (Professor F. N. Clifford 1972, private communication).

3.4 Lavas of the Sincluir Group, Barby Formation, South West Africa 
Basic lavas of the Sinclair Group (Barby Formation) outcrop over a large area to 
the north-west of Helmeringshausen and have been folded to acquire dips between 
25" and 90" mostly to the east or north. They are predominantly feldspar-phyric 
varying between andesite and basalt in composition and are associated with sub- 
ordinate acid lavas and tuffs. Deuteric alteration is practically ubiquitous and 
volcanism was evidently discontinuous since interbasaltic horizons are common. The 
sampling sites span most of the thickness of the outcrop and although sites 69-80 
form a general stratigraphic sequence (Fig. 6) it is not possible to erect a simple 
stratigraphy because of extensive faulting (von Brunn 1969); similarly it is impossible 
to make a precise estimate of thickness of the Barby series. According to B. R. 
Watters (1973, private communication) the Barby Formation is at least 3000 m and 
probably as much as 5000 m thick.

Intensities of magnetization of thcse lavas show a wide range of values between

notably the pilots from sites 75, 78 and 82 show practically no decrease in their

All these samples are however stable, and show little change in directions of magnetiza- 
tion after cleaning in fields of 200-300 Oe. Stability indices reach optimum values 
mostly between 300 and 500 Oe and continuing demagnetization to 1000 Oe does not

generally improve within-site grouping. The only systematic feature of direction 
changes during demagnetization is a tendency for some samples to move away from 
the direction of the present Earth's field, and grouping is improved by af cleaning for

When the af cleaned site mean directions are corrected for the local dip of the

variation at this palaeolatitude (Irving 1964, page 146) and might be improved if it 
were possible to correct for plunge components. Furthermore most of the sites are 
situated within small fault blocks and differential rotation of these blocks may 
contribute to between-site scatter. 
Five sites (59, 62, 69 and 93) are magnetized in the opposite sense to the 
remainder (Table 3) and the first four imply that there are at least two approximate 
reversals in the lower part of the Barby Series (Fig. 3). Sites 81, 82, 83, 91 and 93 are 
from opposite sides of a synclinal structure and the single reversal represented by 
site 93 may represent the same horizon as 59, 62 and 69, although the lava of site 93 
is petrographically distinct, being markedly feldspar phyric.

Petrology of these lavas has been treated in detail by von Brunn (1969) and only 
relationship between petrology and magnetic properties is considered here. They are 
mostly slightly undersaturated and near the junction between andesite and basalt in 
composition; the bulk are zeolitized. The state of alteration varies from greeschist- 
amphibolite facies metamorphism (e.g. sites 60-65) where the feldspar and pyroxenes 
are pseudomorphed by sericite, and chlorite and actinolite respectively, to zeolite- 
greenschist (e.g. sites 82, 83) in which a primary igneous texture is visible but the 
pyroxenes and olivines are pseudomorphed, to zeolite facies (e.g. sites 90-93) in 
which the igneous minerals are entirely fresh. Thus in general degree of alteration 
diminishes northwards across the sampling area (Fig. 6), and has affected the magnetic 
minerals to varying degrees. Unoxidized titanomagnetite grains in the more highly 
altered rocks are surrounded, and sometimes completely pseudomorphed, by altera- 
tion rims of rutile and haematite; grains also show variable amounts of granulation 
(Ade-Hall et al. 1968, Part I) within their area. Lavas with an intermediate degree of 
alteration are at the most marginally granulated and titanomagnetites, generally with 
oxidation states 1-2, are preserved with slight marginal alteration. Sites 90-93 show 
an absence of granulation and subdivision by ilmenite lamellae equivalent to oxidation 
states 2-3, and locally, a pesudomorphing of the ilmenite lamellae gives oxidation 
states 4 and 5. Site 92 shows two stages of titanomagnetite growth with large, partially 
resorbed, grains and fine elongated grains in the groundmass and some other sections 
(e.g. 91 and 93) have fine-grained magnetite pseudomorphing olivine. Although the 
Barby Formation lavas exhibit degrees of low-grade alteration the magnetic evidence 
suggests that remagnetization has not been widespread. Firstly the positive fold test 
demonstrates that the magnetization of these lavas predates that of the Guperas lavas 
(post folding) and secondly reversals (sites 59 and 62) are found even in the highly 
altered rocks. Any remagnetization therefore must have been at least pre-folding and 
local in its effects, and the observation of Ade-Hall et al. (1968, Part 11) that titano- 
magnetite granulation does not apparently produce remagnetization seems to receive 
some support here.

These are basalt lavas with vesicles infilled with carbonate and zeolites. Plagioclase 
phenocrysts are slightly sericitized with primary mafic minerals entirely converted to 
secondary minerals. Large grains of haematite occur as late-stage magmatic minerals 
enclosing feldspar laths and are themselves marginally overgrown by fine-grained 
haematite. Haematite is also a prominent constituent of the groundmass where grain 
size goes down to the limit of microscopic resolution; a few relict titanomagnetite 
grains have also been observed in a sample from site 86. Predominance of haematite 
as an opaque phase in these lavas explains the high magnetic coercivity and stability, 
and the petrographic relationships suggest that it developed under strongly oxidizing 
conditions at a late magmatic-early deuteric phase.

These dykes show variable degrees of alteration from slight sericitization of the 
feldspars (sites 41 and 42) and marginal chloritization of the pyroxenes (43) to 
practically complete pseudomorphing of silicates by secondary minerals (45). Opaques 
present in these rocks include pyrite and large, generally unoxidized, titanomagnetites 
intersertal with respect to the silicates. These titanomagnetites have irregular, 
probably resorbed, outlines and represent an early magmatic phase, and at site 45 
they are largely replaced by secondary aggregates. Titanomagnetite also occurs in all 
sections as fine acicular grains in the groundmass which appear to be largely un- 
oxidised. The low magnetic stabilities of this collection are probably attributable to 
the unoxidized state of the bulk of the titanomagnetite. 
3.10 Fish River Formation, Nama Group, South West Africa 
This series was sampled in a tributary canyon to the Fish River Canyon between 
10 and 15 km west of Seeheim (17.7" E, 26.8" S). The samples are entirely medium 
to fine-grained sandstones dipping uniformly at 10" in a direction 120" E and the 
formation has a strong red colouration throughout.

direction of NRM moves systematically away from the present Earth's field and af 
demagnetization appears to be successful in removing a secondary component near 
this direction. To test this possibility the entire collection has been demagnetized in 
fields of 500-600Oe and lOOOOe, and the overall grouping is slightly better after 
demagnetizing in the higher field than in the lower field, although the combined 
precision (k = 5.6) is considerably lower than that of the total NRM grouping 
(k = 26.5). Sites 98, 99, 101 and 102 move away from the present Earth's field 
direction and three of them improve their precisions with cleaning. Remaining sites 
stay close to their total NRM directions but their precisions deteriorate and in view 
of the possibility that the combined mean of Table 9 includes sites which have not 
been successfully cleaned by the af method, poles for individual sites are quoted. The 
distribution of mean directions from this formation is not Fisherian and an explana- 
tion for this is explored in the next section. 
4. Interpretation of virtual geomagnetic poles 
4.1 Orange River Lavas, Cape Province 
Since these lavas have been subjected to at least two later thermal events, age 
dating is likely to prove difficult, but is currently being attempted (D. L. Reid 1972, 
private communication). With a possible age between c.2600 and 1850 My the pole 
merits comparison with the apw curve for Africa during this interval (McElhinny et 
al. 1968; Piper, Briden & Lomax 1973) and falls close to the curve at c.2100My 
although the antipole also falls near the curve at c.2500My and the lavas might 
possibly be as old as this. 
4.2 Upper Proterozoic results 
The only published pole of similar age to the oldest Upper Proterozoic pole of this 
study is that obtained by Gough (1956) from five sites in the Pilanesberg dykes. An 
age for this pole of 1310+60 My is suggested by Rb-Sr determinations although an 
older age, possibly near 1420+70 My is suggested by associated rocks (see Clifford 
1968, page 345). An apparent movement of the pole is implied across central Africa 
between the times of intrusion of these dykes and the time of formation of the O'okiep 
intrusions (pole 3, Fig. 15) and the eruption of the Kisii series of Kenya (pole 2, 
Fig. 15). Further dating of the Kisii Series by the 40Ar/39Ar technique (Charlton 
1973) has suggested an age of approximately 1200 My for this pole. 
Relative movement of the pole away from Africa through at least 65" is implied 
by the pole for the Barby Formation (pole 5, Fig. 15) with a maximum age of 
1290+80 My and a minimum age of 1020+70 My. A single age of 500+20 My 
from the author's site 75 (D. C. Rex 1973, private communication) is most probably 
to be interpreted in terms of argon loss during the ' Pan African ' thermal-tectonic 
episode. This pole is not significantly different from the poles obtained from the 
Umkondo and Waterberg lavas and intrusions of Rhodesia and the Transvaal (poles 4, 
Fig. 15) and this palaeomagnetic evidence is an indicator to the true age of the 
Umkondo-Waterberg igneous activity. Johnson & Vail (1965) report a single age of 
1140 My for a dolerite cutting the Umkondo but Jones & McElhinny (1966) report 
inconsistent K-Ar ages ranging from 600-1300 My for Waterberg dolerites and 
650-1150 My for Umkondo dolerites. If the problem with this material is pre- 
dominantly argon loss we may suspect that the higher ages are near the true age of this 
material. The correlation with the pole from the Barby series defines a minimum age 
of 1020+70 My for this igneous activity. The Waterberg and Umkondo systems were 
originally thought to be pre-Upper Proterozoic in age (Johnson & Vail 1965) and this

conclusion still applies to the Waterberg system which is only intruded by these 
doierites, and may be older than 1720 My (Jones & McElhinny 1967). However, the 
pole obtained from Umkondo latins places a likely age on the Umkondo and makes a 
correlation of this System with part of the Upper Proterozoic of central Africa (Swift 
1961; Clifford 1967, page 45) again a probability. 
The poles 6 and 7 from the Guperas lavas and Auborus Formation respectively 
define by their superposed relationship with the Barby Formation a return movement 
of the pole towards Africa. They both postdate the Rooikam granite (von Brunn 1969) 
and hence the movement from pole 5 to pole 6 can be dated as taking place at some- 
time around 1020k80 My. The loop Bl-B2-B3 of Fig. 16 has been defined (Piper 
1972) from study of the Bukoban system of Tanzania, the Bukoba Sandstone pole B1 
has a probable minimum age of 990-1000 My and the pole B2 from the Kigonero 
Flags has a probable minimum age of 890 My (Dr N. J. Snelling, unpublished results; 
Professor L. Cahen 1972, 1973, private communications). This polar wander curve 
derived from the Tanganyika craton can be incorporated in the curve derived from 
south-western Africa because close agreement has been observed between poles 
c.2300-1950 My in age from cratonic regions of west and southern Africa (Piper et 
al. 1973); the Kisii and O'okiep poles and the Klein Karas (pole 8, Fig. 15) and 
Kigonero Flags (> 890 My) poles are also consistent with a single apparent polar 
wander curve. 
The position of the Auborus pole (7) in relation to the Bukoba Sandstone pole B1 
on the polar wai;der curve suggests that it is slightly older than this formation 
(> 990-1000 My). The palaeomagnetic information precludes it being greatly younger 
than the Sinclair Formation and this is in agreement with its post-orogenic nature; the 
pal~eomagnetic inclination shows that these haematite-rich sediments were deposited 
at a palaeolatitude of 18". Pole S3 is derived from the ' soft ' component shown by 
sites 46, 47 and 49 in the Vioolsdrif lavas is merely inserted here to show that its 
position is commensurate with acquisition in Late Precambrian times. It is known 
that this region was subjected to thermal events at this time including the activity of 
the Richtersveld complex (50 km to the west) and extensive intrusion of dolerite 
dykes in the iinmcdiate vicinity before deposition of the Nama System. There are 
thus several possible geological causes for remagnetization although no single one 
can be isolated. 
The pole 10 from the pre-Nama dykes of Namaqualand is removed by 63" from 
the section of the African polar wander curve at B3 dated at c.800 My. The pre- 
Nama dykes west of Vioolsdrif were dated by Kostlin (1971) at 653+70 My and tkis 
pole is therefore younger than the pole 9 (Fig. 15) from the Mbozi Complex of 
Tanzania dates at 743 30 My (Author, unpublished result). There is some doubt 
as to whether the five dykes used to compute this pole are all in fact pre-Nama in age 
and Dr S. R. Charlton (1973, private communication) has obtained Karroo ages 
from an earlier unsuccessful palaeomagnetic collection of dykes in Namaqualand 
made by Dr C. Snape. A Karroo age would not be inconsistent with the directions of 
magnetization derived from this material but cannot be substantiated for three of the 
dykes. In addition to tlieage data of Kostlin (1971), sites 44 and 45 predate the 
Nama unconformity and a sample from site 42 has been dated at 401 & 16 My by the 
K-Ar method (D. C. Rex, 1973, private communication) an age which is again most 
reasonably interpreted in terms of thermal overprinting and argon loss. There is no 
direct evidence bearing on the age of the other two dykes and in view of this the 
combined pole position should be treated as provisional. 
McElhinny, Giddings & Embleton (1974) recognize a large loop in the apparent 
polar wander curve for Gondwanaland between Late Precambrian and Ordovician 
times, which implies that the pole moved from a position close to that indicated by 
the pre-Nama dyke and Mbozi poles to the vicinity of West Africa as suggested by

340 J. D. A. Piper 
the pole from the Ntonya ring structure of Malawi (Briden 1968, 630+24 My). The 
pole then followed a large loop which took Africa to low latitudes in Lower to Middle 
Cambrian times and back to high latitudes in Ordovician times. The poles derived 
from the Fish River Formation of this study appear to match the part of the loop 
proposed by McElhinny et al. (1974) close to the portion falling between c.600 My 
and Lower Cambrian times consistent in part with the age inferred from palaeonto- 
logical data. The polar migration is also consistent with palaeoclimatic indicators 
which suggest that the climate ameliorated during deposition of the Nama Group with 
deposition of glacial horizons in the lower part and red sediments (Fish River Forma- 
tion) in the upper part (Dr A. Kroner 1973, private communication). 
The Doornpoort Formation from which pole 12 is derived is separate from the 
Nama Group by two unconformities and predates the Nosib and Gzriep Groups. 
It is therefore older than 800 My and may be as old as the Auborus Formation. It 
cannot however be matched to any part of the African apw curve from 1300 to 
600 My and since the negative fold test implies a post-tectonic magnetization it 
probably correlates with folding of the Damaran belt. In Late Precambrian and 
Lower Palaeozoic times in Africa Clifford (1967) distinguishes a Damaran episode 
with a main pulse between 500 and 550 My and a slightly earlier Katangan episode 
covering tectono-thermal events reflected by ages in the range 580-680 My. The pole 
from the Doornpoort Formation falls on the loop of McElhinny et al. close to poles 
of Middle Cambrian to Middle Ordovician age, consistent with a magnetization 
acquired in Damaran times. 
FIG. 16. Apparent polar wander curves for Africa and North America for the 
interval 1300-1000 My superimposed to show the distribution of Precambrian 
crust (stippled) and mobile belts belonging to this interval. The apparent polar 
wander curves shown in this figure are interpreted as south curves by McElhinny 
et a1 (1974).

Precambrian igneous and sedimentary rocks 34 1 
4.3 Intercontinental correlations between shield areas in Upper Proteroizoic times 
An attempt to reconstruct the positions of shield areas in Precambrian time was 
made by McElhinny et al. (1968) who found that their apw curve for the interval 
1950-1310 My could be fitted to the then-available data from the Canadian shield for a 
similar interval. Subsequent data have altered both the shape and the age control of 
the apw curves from each shield area, and the reconstruction suggested by McElhinny 
et al. (1968) cannot now be substantiated. Brock & Piper (1972) using data from Africa 
available up to 1971 compared the shapes of the African and North American apw 
curves and demonstrated that it was not possible to superimpose the curves over their 
whole length. The implication of this conclusion is that relative movement between 
the regions must have taken place during at least part of Precambrian time. 
With improved definition of the Precambrian apw curves for Africa and North 
America (Irving & Park 1972) it is possible to attempt a much more rigorous com- 
parison. Two major points emerge: firstly both the African and North American 
apw curves show tight loops of nearly identical size between 1300 and lo00 My, and 
secondly the two curves have quite different form after about 1000 My so that there 
is no possibility of superimposing them in Upper Proterozoic time. If the two loops 
between 1300 and 1000 My are superimposed for the two regions areas of known 
Precambrian crust are brought into close proximity as shown in Fig. 16. The 
1300-1100 My mobile belts (Grenville, Kibaran and Orange River) then lie on an 
arc close to a great circle. Palaeomagnetic data from the Fenno-Scandian shield are 
sparse but it appears that the Gothide orogenic line (c.1000 My) also belonged to this 
lineament, and Donaldson et al. (1973, Fig. 10) have made a palaeomagnetic recon- 
struction to demonstrate this point; this is included in Fig. 16 to demonstrate the 
alignment of the belts at the time of their formation.

Tectonic Results from Paleomagnetism of the Aphebian Nipissing Diabase 
at Gowganda, Ontario 
D. T. A. SYMONS AND J. W. LONDRY 
Department of Geology, University of Windsor, Windsor, Ontario N9B3P4 
Received October 29, 1974 
Accepted for publication February 4, 1975 
A total of 30 sites (150 cores, 300 specimens) of the 2165 ? -25 m.y. Nipissing diabase were 
collected from around the Miller Lake basin at Gowganda. After alternatingfield demagnetization 
a stable primary remanence was isolated at 10 sites of which eight were reversely polarized. A 
fold test shows that the basinal structure is primary at the 95% confidence level. The pole position 
of 1M0W, 14"s (P0,,,:9", 14") is statistically indistinguishable from previous Nipissing poles from 
the Cobalt and Elliot Lake areas. The evident conclusion is that the Superior and Southern 
geologic provinces have not undergone significant relative tectonic translation or rotation in the 
last 2165 m.y. Combining the remanence directions from the 37 available reliable sites of 
Nipissing diabase, they give a highly reliable pole position of 94. low, 14.5"s (Po.,,:5.7", 8.8") for 
Nipissing time on the polar wander curve for these two provinces of the Canadian Precambrian 
Shield. Only four of the 37 sites are normally polarized suggesting that the Nipissing event reflects 
a dominantly reversed paleofield.

furent collectionnes autour du bassin de Miller Lake a Gowganda. Apres une ddmagnetisation de 
champ alternatif une remanence primaire stable etait isolee a 10 sites, desquels huit etaient 
polarises en sens inverse. Un test de plissement montre que la structure du bassin est primaire a 
un niveau de confiance de 95%. La position du pBle de 1M0W, 14% (P0.,,:9", 14") est statistique- 
ment indistincte des p6les anterieurs du Nipissing des regions de Cobalt et Elliot Lake. La 
conclusion Cvidente est que les provinces geologiques Superieur et du Sud (Southern) n'ont pas

Introduction 
The town of Gowganda is about 190 km north 
of Sudbury, Ontario (Fig. 1). From 1908 to 
1972, native silver was mined near the town from 
narrow veins in the undulating Nipissing diabase 
sill. This mining activity has resulted in the sill 
being well mapped geologically and dated 
radiometrically. Elsewhere the Nipissing diabase 
gives good paleomagnetic results. This paleomag- 
netic study was made to test whether the Miller 
Lake basinal structure defined by the sill at 
Gowganda is a primary intrusive or a secondary 
deformational feature by using the fold test on 
the sill's remanence directions from sites around 
the basin (Fig. 2, sites 1-23). This study was also 
made to test for possible geotectonic movements 
within the enclosing Superior Geologic Province 
or between it and other Precambrian provinces 
by comparing the sill's paleomagnetic pole 
position to other coeval poles from North 
America. 
Can. J. Earth Sci., 12,940-948 (1975) 
Geology 
The Gowganda area has been mapped geolog- 
ically by Collins (1913), Burrows (1921, 1926) 
and Moore (1955). 
The Nipissing diabase intrudes Archean and 
Huronian rocks (Fig. 2). The Archean rocks 
include the Keewatin basic to acidic volcanic 
sequence and a few younger Haileyburian ser- 
pentine plugs. These units were severely de- 
formed during emplacement of the Algoman 
granitic stocks and batholiths. A few Mata- 
chewan porphyritic quartz diabase dikes were 
then intruded. After orogenic deformation, the 
early Aphebian (Huronian) Cobalt series sedi- 
ments were deposited. The lower part of the 
series consists of the conglomerates and grey- 
wackes of the Gowganda formation. This forma- 
tion is disconformably overlain by the feldspathic 
quartzites and arkoses of the Lorrain formation. 
The series is gently deformed with dips rarely 
in excess of 25". Fairbairn et al. (1969) dated the

Nipissing diabase plutons outcrop extensively 
throughout the Cobalt Plate in the Superior 
Province and throughout the Penokean Fold 
Belt of the adjacent Southern Province (Stock- 
well 1969). The plutons are dominantly con- 
formable sill-like bodies following structural 
trends in the Huronian sediments with the 
competent conglomeratic units often providing a 
barrier to the ascending magma (Card and 
Pattison 1973). These tabular, sill-like plutons 
commonly outcrop in elliptical basins and arches 
which may be entirely primary in origin as sills 
following folded strata (Miller 1910) or as cone- 
sheets (Love11 and Caine 1970). Alternatively, 
the basins and arches may be partly primary and 
partly secondary (Knight 1922; Thompson 
1957). The plutons are also found in transgres-

942 CAN. J. EARTH 
sive dike-like bodies that apparently follow 
pre-existing faults. 
At Gowganda the Nipissing sill is between 20 
and 190 m thick (Moore 1955). The sill dips 
gently (< 25") with occasional steep to vertical 
dips. It is composed of quartz diabase with a 
feldspar to pyroxene ratio of 1 :3 at the bottom 
varying to 3: 1 at the top of the sill. It contains 
no olivine and only minor biotite. Its ubiquitous 
titanomagnetite and ilmenite content varies 
between 1 and 3%. In a few places the quartz 
diabase has differentiated to granophyre (e.g., 
sites 14 and 15). The granophyre contains some 
monoclinic pyroxene and micrographic inter- 
growths of its quartz and feldspar. It is reddish 
due to hematite stain and its titanomagnetite 
content may increase to 5%. The sill's petrology 
and ferromagnetic mineralogy is about typical 
of the Nipissing as a whole (Card and Pattison 
1973). 
Fairbairn et al. (1969) dated the Nipissing 
diabase at Gowganda at 2162 f 27 m.y. using 
the Rb-Sr whole rock isochron method on 12 
samples from one 270 m core through the sill. 
This date agrees well with the 2155 f 80 m.y. 
Rb-Sr whole rock isochron determined by Van 
Schmus (1965) for the Nipissing diabase sheets 
at Blind River (Fig. 1). It also agrees with the 
Rb-Sr whole rock date of 2180m.y. (Van 
Schmus 1965) and the K-Ar biotite date of 
2095 m.y. (Lowden et al. 1963) determined for 
the Nipissing diabase sill at Cobalt. 
The Nipissing diabase was apparently em- 
placed in the late stages of the Penokean orogeny 
some 2165 + 25 m.y. ago (Church 1968). In 
adjacent areas to the south around Sudbury, the 
diabase has been regionally metamorphosed with 
updated radiometric ages. Thus, some deforma- 
tion during the Hudsonian orogeny some 1700 
m.y. ago is also a possibility. 
At Gowganda only a few quartz diabase dikes 
and one olivine diabase dike were emplaced 
after the Nipissing diabase and before deposition 
of the Pleistocene and Recent glacial drift and 
alluvium. This paucity of younger rocks has 
prevented determination of the amount of post- 
emplacement deformation in the Nipissing 
diabase sill. 
Experimental Procedure 
Five cores were drilled from each of 30 sites 
and were oriented in situ using a sun compass 
and/or Brunton compass with topographic 
SCI. VOL. 12, 1T5 
checks. Two 2.5 cm right cylindrical specimens 
were cut from each core. The natural remanent 
magnetization (NRM) of all 300 specimens were 
measured on a Schonstedt SSM-1A magnetom- 
eter. Using a Schonstedt AF demagnetizer, one 
pilot specimen per site with an average NRM 
direction and intensity was step-demagnetized 
in peak alternating fields (AF) of 50, 100, 150, 
225, 350, 500, 750 and 1000 Oe. For each pilot 
specimen the Paleomagnetic Stability Index 
(PSI) was calculated and plotted as in Fig. 3 
(Symons and Stupavsky 1974). This index mea- 
sures the rate of change of the remanence direc- 
tion in millidegrees per oersted (mdeg/Oe) at each 
AF demagnetizing step. In general, the lowest 
PSI value indicates the most stable endpoint 
direction and the optimum AF intensity (H,,,) 
for cleaning or removing unstable remanence 
components. For each pilot specimen, the ratio 
of the remanence intensity after each step (J,) to 
the original remanence (J,) was plotted (e.g., 
Fig. 4). For a stable remanence component this 
ratio gives a smooth and minimal exponential 
rate of decay. Based on the results for its pilot 
specimen, the remaining specimens from the site 
were AF demagnetized at a selected AF intensity 
and their remanence remeasured (Table 1). In 
26 cores, the remanence directions of the two ~ 
specimens diverged by more than 20°, thereby 
indicating inhomogeneous or unstable mag- 
netization, and so the data from these cores were 
rejected from further consideration. The mean 
direction was calculated for the remaining cores. 
In four sites, one core was rejected as anomalous 
because its remanence direction deviated by 
more than two times the radius of the cone of 
95% confidence (a,,; Fisher 1953) of the re- 
maining cores from their mean direction. Using 
the core mean remanence directions, the site 
mean directions were calculated along with their 
a,, values (Table 1). 
Pate1 and Palmer (1974) found that the stable 
remanence in the Nipissing diabase near Elliot 
Lake resides in magnetite-ilmenite exsolution 
and that unstable remanence resides in unex- 
solved titanomagnetite. This explanation is con- 
sistent for the mixture of stable and unstable 
sites found in this study.

Discussion 
There are four previous paleomagnetic studies 
on Nipissing diabase sills (Table 3). Two studies 
originate within the Cobalt Plate of the Superior 
Province. Symons (1967) studied at 65 m vertical 
section of the sill at the Silverfield Mine near 
the town of Cobalt (Fig. 1) and found reversed 
remanence directions only. A more extensive 
study of the sill around Cobalt revealed a stable 
reversed remanence in 11 of 14 sites (Symons 
1970). The other two studies originate within the 
Penokean Fold Belt of the Southern Province. 
Symons (1971) found a stable remanence in two 
normal and six reversed sites or in eight of 11 
sites between Elliot Lake and Matinenda Lake. 
Pate1 and Palmer (1974) sampled seven sites to 
the west of Matinenda Lake and found a stable 
remanence in five reversely polarized sites. 
The 'reverse' group of Nipissing diabase sites 
with a,, G25" at Gowganda have been sub- 
jected to a similar standard of data screening as 
used in the previous studies. This group con- 
tains eight reversely and two normally polarized 
site mean remanence directions. This result con- 
firms the earlier observation (Symons 1971) that 
the Earth's magnetic field was dominantly 
reversed during emplacement and cooling of the 
Nipissing sills with minor periods of normal 
polarity. This observation is true for both the 
Superior and Southern Provinces, and it also 
provides substantial evidence that the diabase 
sills retain a primary remanence of probable 
TRM origin. 
Finally, Symons (1967) used a contact test to 
show that the diabase sill at the Silverfield Mine 
retains a primary remanence. 
It is visually apparent from the overlapping 
ovals of 95% confidence in Fig. 6a and from 
using Watson's (1956) F-ratio test that the 
Gowganda Nipissing population of directions 
is not significantly different from either the 
Silverfields Mine or Cobalt area populations. 
Pate1 and Palmer (1974) have already noted that 
the Elliot Lake and Matinenda Lake populations 
of Nipissing directions are not significantly 
different at the 95% confidence level. It is further 
true that the combined Superior Province direc- 
tions are not significantly different from the 
combined Southern Province directions (Fig. 
6b). The concordance of these populations leads 
to three conclusions. First, the Nipissing sills in 
all five collections have retained a stable primary 
remanence. Second, these sills were emplaced 
during a single major igneous event. Third, the 
Superior and Southern Provinces have not 
undergone significant differential tectonic rota- 
tion or translation since emplacement of the 
Nipissing sills. 
The concordance of Nipissing sill directions 
also allows all the site mean remanence direc- 
tions to be combined to give a highly reliable 
overall pole position of 94.1°W, 14.1"s (P,,,, = 
5,7", 8.8") with an assigned age of 2165 + ~25

Geology and Sampling 
The Otto stock is situated in the Superior 
Structural Province near Kirkland Lake, Ontario 
(Fig. 1). Figure 2 is a schematic representation 
of its relationship with adjacent rock units and 
Fig. 3 is a map of the body showing sample 
locations. The stock is about 10 km in diameter 
and was intruded into Archean rocks. Its geology 
has been described by Lovell (1972). The stock 
has yielded an Rb-Sr whole-rock isochron of 
2160 + 80 m.y. (K. Bell, personal communica- 
tion, 1975).' Earlier radiometric work is reviewed 
in that paper. The Archean country rock con- 
sists mainly of metavolcanics and felsic intru- 
sions, both of which were intruded by unmeta- 
morphosed Matachewan diabase dikes, whose 
age is about 2600 m.y. (Gates and Hurley 1973). 
The latter are not observed to cut the Otto stock, 
although a dike that probably belongs to the

Matachewan swarm, occurs in the contact 
aureole (site 10 on Fig. 3) that extends around 
the stock. The aureole is about 300 m wide, and 
within it the metamorphic grade reaches amphi- 
bolite facies. The stock itself is unmetamor- 
phosed, and consists of syenite, locally contami- 
nated by country rock. The effects of contamina- 
tion range from slightly digested basic zenoliths, 
through diorite, to mafic syenite and lampro- 
phyre (Lovell 1972). Lamprophyre dikes, gener- 
ally a few metres in width, are abundant along 
Highway 112. In the center-west of the stock 
along Highway 11 is a large outcrop of basic 
rock, which is considered by Lovell to be a 
roof pendant or inclusion. This outcrop has 
been heated and metamorphosed to amphibolite 
facies by the intrusion of the Otto stock. It is 
referred to here as the west-central baked zone. 
The contact aureole, the west-central baked 
zone, and the lamprophyre dikes are obvious 
targets for paleomagnetic studies, because they 
might be expected to record the field at the time 
of intrusion.

The probable sequence of rock units is given 
below from youngest to oldest based mainly on 
Lovell (1972). 
1. Nipissing diabase (intrudes Huronian). 
2a. Huronian (overlies Archean and contains 
Otto-type boulders). 
2b. Otto stock (intrudes Archean, but is not 
seen to be cut by Matachewan dikes; relationship 
to Huronian uncertain, see above).

The Rb-Sr ages of the Otto stock and the 
Nipissing diabas; are statistically indistinguish- 
able (Bell and Blenkin~op)~ indicating that events 
'2b' and '1' span approximately 100 m.y. or less. 
The paleomagnetic sampling sites are marked 
on Fig. 3. Much of the area is wooded, access 
is difficult, and natural exposures are commonly 
weathered. Sampling was confined to highway 
cuttings and the lake shore where unweathered 
rock is available. Cores were obtained from 
28 sites. Two cylindrical specimens were cut 
from each core. The magnetization was mea- 
sured by a Schonstedt SMl magnetometer. 
Alternating field (AF) and thermal demagnetiza- 
tion was carried out using the apparatus 
described by Roy et al. (1972, 1973). The initial 
magnetization (NRM) directions in all speci- 
mens are plotted in Fig. 4. The most notable 
features are a strong condensation of directions 
not far from the present field, superimposed on 
a wide scatter of directions.

Lamprophyre Dikes 
Twelve lamprophyre dikes intrusive into sye- 
nite were sampled. The NRM intensities are 
low, of the order 10 pG. Site 7 was unstable and 
had random magnetizations in AF of 100 Oe. 
The magnetization at sites 12, 13, 15 to 18, and 
27 consists of small magnetization along the 
present field, together with much larger stable N 
magnetizations (Table 1). The blocking tempera- 
tures are predominantly between 550 and 650 "C, 
except at site 17, where 209, of the magnetization 
is retained at 600 "C. Polished sections have 
abundant sulfides, and ilmenite, both generally 
highly altered. There are many euhedral grains 
of magnetite (10 pm) with no intergrowths, and 
there are abundant smaller disseminated grains 
of magnetite. The latter are presumably respons- 
ible for the stable N magnetization. Hematite 
occurs at site 17 and correlates with high block- 
ing temperatures there. At site 21 there is a 
single reversed magnetization. 
At sites 14, 19, and 20, composite magnetiza- 
tion occurs. At site 14 the directions are southerly 
with moderate upward inclinations. The blocking 
temperatures are predominantly below 400 "C, 
but small magnetizations are retained at 500 "C 
(Fig. 9). The directions remained constant to 
500 "C. This shoutherly directed magnetization is 
referred to as S magnetization. At sites 19 and 20 
the thermal demagnetization shows a similar 
two-step curve, with some blocking temperatures 
below 400 "C, and others typically between 550 
and 600 "C. Specimens from site 19 show this 
two-step curve most clearly. During thermal 
demagnetization dramatic changes in direction 
occur. The initial directions are to the south- 
southwest with low inclinations, at temperatures 
of 200 and 300 "C they have shallow negative 
inclinations, and then between 400 and 550 "C 
they move sharply to a direction with steep 
positive inclinations. The final direction at site

Matachewan Dike 
Two sites were sampled in the contact aureole 
on Highway 11. Site 9 in amphibolite has no 
stable magnetization. Two thin diabase dikes 
occur close together in the aureole (site 10). 
They contain green feldspar phenocrysts charac- 
teristic of Matachewan diabase. Only a single 
stable magnetization is present, and the block- 
ing temperatures lie between 550 and 600 "C. 
After cleaning at 550 "C the directions are close 
to the N magnetization (Fig. 4 and Table 1). 
Discussion 
The syenite, which comprises most of the 
Otto stock, has low magnetic stability and pro- 
vides no information about the geomagnetic 
field at the time of intrusion. The lamprophyre 
dikes, which are late-stage products of the 
intrusive phase, the west-central baked zone, 
and Matachewan diabase within the aureole, 
typically have N or R magnetizations commonly 
with high coercivities, often exceeding 1000 Oe, 
and blocking temperatures between 550 and 
600 "C and occasionally exceeding 600 "C. The 
magnetization directions of the diabase of the 
aureole (site 10) are very different from these of 
I unaltered Matachewan diabase a few kilometres 
away (Strangway 1964; Fahrig et al. 1965). The 
dikes of the aureole appear to have been remag- 
netized more or less completely during the 
intrusion of the Otto stock, whereas those at a 
distance are unaffected. Hence the conditions of 
the contact test are satisfied, and the N and R 
magnetizations were probably acquired during 
cooling following intrusion at -2160 + 80 m.y. 
One or more reversals of the field may have 
occurred during cooling. The mean direction 
and pole is listed in Table 3, generally giving 
unit weight to each site (B = 18). At- site 28 
both Nand R can be recognized and unit weight 
is given to each. The pole and its error are 
plotted on Fig. 10. The aberrant result from 
site 21 (Table 1) is omitted. 
The S magnetization is characterized by low 
blocking temperatures. It occurs at only three 
sites, and dominates only at one. The S magne- 
tization could be a transitional field direction 
acquired during a field reversal, but it seems 
unlikely that such a magnetization should always 
be characterized by low blocking temperatures. 
It is suggested that this magnetization was 
probably acquired later than the N and R 
magnetizations during some subsequent mild 
reheating event. The pole for the S magnetiza- 
tion direction is given in Table 3 and Fig. 10, 
and is close to that observed in Matachewan 
dikes. Taken in isolation this result indicates 
that the stock is pre-Matachewan in age. This 
notion, however, is inconsistent with the fact 
that the magnetization of Matachewan diabase 
in the aureole (site 10) is close to the N magne- 
tization and therefore probably reset, and with 
the Rb-Sr age obtained by Bell and Blenkinsop4. 
The more probable explanation is that it repre- 
sents a later field direction. 
The paleomagnetic poles in the interval 2200 
to 1800 m.y. ago are compiled in Fig. 10. The 
poles form a reasonably coherent array stretching 
from what is nowadays the Mackenzie delta to 
Peru, with a possible extension farther south 
to include pole 0s. This array is referred to as 
track 5 (Irving and Lapointe 1975). We suggest 
that the sense of apparent polar motion is from 
north to south. The evidence for this is that the 
Dubawnt Group (pole D), the Kahocella For- 
mation (K), and the Martin Formation (MN) 
have ages between 1800 and 1900 m.y. and are 
younger than the Indin dikes (pole I), and the 
Otto stock. The dates of the results from the 
Mugford basalt, Wind River dikes, and the Otish

successful contact tests and detailed thermal 
demagnetization of the remanent magnetization, 
the presently available positions of the Abitibi 
and Nipissing diabase poles must be regarded as 
uncertain, and all that can be said is that they 
probably lie near to Track 5. This reinterpreta- 
tion of the paleomagnetic data in the interval 
2200 to 1800 m.y. given in Fig. 10 is, of course, 
tentative. The new polar track differs very con- 
siderably from the previous interpretations, 
which were based on much less information 
(see, for instance, Irving and Park (1972), or 
Fahrig and Chown (1973)). 
The poles of track 5 are derived from many 
different parts of the Laurentian Shield, includ- 
ing the main Archean blocks (Superior, Slave, 
and Nain Provinces, and the Bear-tooth uplift). 
The general coherence of these poles suggests 
that these Archean blocks did not move relative 
on one another by many thousands of kilometres 
during the Hudsonian orogeny, as has already 
been noted by McGlynn and Irving (1975) and 
Irving and Lapointe (1975). This result does 
not mean that relative movement did not occur, 
because there are still major uncertainties in the 
paleomagnetic data and in its time basis, for 
example, the unsatisfactory nature of the record 
from the Nipissing diabase. Nevertheless, if there 
had been large relative motions comparable to 
those among continents in the Phanerozoic, 
then it would be a remarkable coincidence that 
the poles should now form the coherent array 
that is observed. 
Finally a note is made about the geometry of 
Track 5, as a preview to a discussion that cannot 
be satisfactorily made until more precise data 
become available. Relative motion in a purely 
longitudinal sense cannot be detected paleo- 
magnetically; that is, if the pivot point defining 
the relative motion of two land masses coincides 
with the mean geomagnetic pole then the relative 
motions will have no paleomagnetic expression. 
This means, for example, that if relative motion 
of the Slave and Superior Archean blocks had 
occurred they would not be seen paleomagnetic- 
ally if the motion had been in a longitudinal 
sense relative to the paleomagnetic pole. If the 
pivot points defining the relative motions of the 
Archean blocks fell on Track 5 and migrated 
down Track 5 following the paleomagnetic pole, 
then such motions would go undetected by the 
paleomagnetic method. The presence of a single 
polar track does not therefore necessarily imply 
that there have been no relative motions among 
the Archean cratons; it simply means that the 
hypothesis of no motions is the simplest but not 
the only explanation of the results. 
Acknowledgments 
We gratefully acknowledge the help of Mrs. 
Jean Hastie in data processing, and helpful 
discussions with Jean Roy, H. L. Lovell, and 
J. C. McGlynn. Comments by referees were very 
useful. 
NOTE ADDED IN PROOF: In a very recent paper, 
Symons and Londry (1975) have described new 
results from the Nipissing diabase of the Gow- 
ganda area (47.7"N, 80.8"W). As has been found 
in previous studies, the magnetization is com- 
posite. There is a magnetization (A) with a pole 
(14"S, 100°W) near to previously determined 
Nipissing poles N2, N4, and N6, and there is a 
magnetization (B) with a pole (67"N, 11 low) 
near to the pole for the Otto stock. Both poles 
fall on Track 5 (Fig. 10). The information in 
Table 1 of Symons and Londry indicates that 
there is no significant difference between the 
remanent coercive forces of the A and B mag- 
netizations. No thermal studies or studies of 
igneous contacts are reported. Hence from the 
internal evidence from the Nipissing diabase 
itself, it is not known whether A is older than B, 
or B older than A. Symons and Londry state 
categorically that A is primary and older than 
B. It is equally possible that B is older than A, 
and this is consistent with the new interpretation 
of Track 5 (Fig. 10). This interpretation has the 
interesting corollary that the Nipissing diabase 
at Gowganda and the Otto stock are essentially 
contemporaneous because their poles agree, and 
this reconciles the age evidence which also indi- 
cates that they are of the same age (see above).

Magnetic and Paleomagnetic Studies of the Nipissing Diabase, 
Lake Matinenda Area, Ontario 
J. P. PATEL' AND H. C. PALMER 
Department of Geophysics, Universio of Western Ontario, London, Ontario 
Received September 17, 1973 
Revision accepted for publication November 6, 1973 
Samples of the Nipissing diabase were collected for rock-magnetic and paleomagnetic 
studies around and west of Lake Matinenda, Ontario. The specimens have been classified 
into three groups, based on their stability of natural remanent magnetism, using the 
alternating field demagnetization technique. 
Opaque petrological studies showed that the specimens which possessed magnetite- 
ilmenite exsolution were magnetically very stable. The specimens without any exsolution 
possessed weak and unstable magnetization. 
Sphene was identified in the alteration product of ilmenite using X-ray techniques. 
Curie point measurements indicated low titanium content in the specimens which con- 
tained exsolution of ilmenite in magnetite. 
The pole position, calculated from five significant sites located around and west of 
Lake Matinenda is 69.9" W, 15.6" S (Ass = 6.1 ").

Introduction 
The Nipissing Diabase outcrops over a wide 
area of the Northern shore of Lake Huron and 
in the Cobalt region in the Province of On- 
tario. The diabase is intruded either as near 
vertical dikes or as flat-lying to gently undulat-
