ing sill-like bodies into the Huronian sedimen- 
tary rocks. The diabase of the Lake Matinenda 
area, north of Blind River, shows no clear cut 
relationship between the sills and the dikes. 
The dikes were probably intruded at much 
the same time as sills or they may have acted 
as feeders to the sills from the same magma 
(Robertson 1963). 
The Nipissing diabase from the Cobalt area

354 CAN. J. EARTH SCI. VOL. 11, 1974 
has been dated at 2095 m.y. by K-Ar in biotite 
(Lowdon et al. 1963). The Rb-Sr age of the 
diabase from the Blind River area was given 
as 2155 2 80 m.y., based on whole-rock 
isochrons (Van Schmus 1965). In many 
areas, the sills show development of a grano- 
phyre or the 'red-rock' usually at the top due 
to differentiation in larger bodies (Robertson 
1962). The texture of this rock is medium to 
coarse and red colour is imparted by hematite 
in feldspar. This granophyre was dated at 
1700 * 50 m.y. on mineral separates (feld- 
spar) by Van Schumus (1965). This date is 
interpreted as a metamorphic event during the 
Hudsonian Orogeny. 
Earlier paleomagnetic studies on the Cobalt 
area diabase have been carried out by two 
authors. Strangway (1964) studied the inten- 
sity and the direction of the remanent mag- 
netism of the diabase sampled near Cobalt 
township, to estimate the age of the diabase 
on the basis of the rate of decay of the stable 
remanence intensity. Symons ( 1967) collected 
thirteen samples of the diabase, along with 
other Precambrian rock samples, from the 
Silverfields Mines near Cobalt, and showed 
that the paleomagnetic results were consistent 
with the sequence of geologic events for the 
Cobalt area. In 1970, Symons collected 
samples from fourteen additional sites from 
the CobaltSilver area. The remanence direc- 
tions of these samples were analysed to prove 
that the diabase acquired its remanence after 
the formation of the Kerr Lake Arch and the 
North Lorrain Basin structures. In 1971, 
Symons sampled 19 sites (sills and dikes) of 
the same rock in the Blind River-Elliot Lake 
area of Ontario. From the results of paleo- 
magnetic studies of the diabase, he tentatively 
concluded that the sheets and dikes of this 
area contained generally weak but stable pri- 
mary remanence components which tend to be 
masked by much stronger unstable components. 
He also concluded that the sheets were em- 
placed and cooled during several polarity in- 
tervals of the earth's- magnetic field about 
2155 m.y. ago. 
Sampling and Laboratory Procedures 
Eleven sites of the diabase sills were sampled 
using a portable diamond drill, taking four to 
five cores from each site. These sites are located 
around and west of Lake Matinenda as shown 
in Fig. 1, and include three sites of the grano- 
phyre and eight of the normal diabase. Sites 
M2A, M3A, M6A, M8A, and MllA of the 
diabase were sampled on the shores of the 
Lake. Site M36A of the diabase was sampled 
36 mi (58 km) from Elliot Lake on Highway 
639. The Nipissing granophyre was sampled 
at three locations. The samples of Site M34A 
were collected from the ferry 1andi.ng to St. 
Joseph's Island 1.5 mi (2.4 km) south of 
Highway 17. Site M35A was sampled from 
road-cut exposures 11.1 mi (17.9 k:m) north 
of Highway 17 on Highway 129. Th~e last site 
of the granophyre, site M37A, was located on 
a northwest tract 11.5 mi ( 18 km) away from 
a northerly turnoff from Highway 17, 2.5 mi 
(4 km) west of Blind River. 
The field-drilled core samples were oriented 
in situ by a device similar to that described by 
Helsley (1967). The bearing of t:he arrow, 
marked on the core, was read first using a 
magnetic compass and was checked using a 
modified Mark I1 astro-compass. If the dif- 
ference between the readings of the sun com- 
pass and the magnetic compass was less than 
3", then an average value of the two readings 
was taken as the azimuth of the arrow marked. 
At a few sites, the rock was strongly mag- 
netized. Consequently the magnetic: compass 
readings were appreciably distorted. In such 
cases, only the sun compass readings were 
relied upon. 
Direction and intensity of natural remanent 
magnetization of each of the specimens was 
first measured using a commercial spinner mag- 
netometer (Princeton Applied Research-Model 
SM-1). Any viscous secondary components of 
magnetization present were de- 
magnetized using an alternating field technique, 
on a three axis tumbler apparatus. The field 
which gave the best precision within a site was 
defined as the 'Optimum field' for that par- 
ticular site. The maximum field used for the 
treatment was 1200 Oe peak. One polished 
section was also prepared from leach core 
sample to study opaque grains under the micro- 
scope. The measurements of the Curie points 
were carried out on a Curie balance similar to 
that of Chevallier and Pierre (193:2) with a 
bifilar suspension. The field in which the mea- 
surements were made was 1640 Oe.

Site mean directions of the eleven sites be-

ward and their directions lie away from the 
general clustering area of the diabase sites. 
The inclinations of site MlOA and MllA 
(Nipissing diabase) aIso point downward, 
though their azimuths tend to group with other 
diabase site mean directions after 'cleaning'. 
The variations in within-site dispersion may 
be illustrated by plotting k/ksl, vs. the strength 
of the applied alternating field (Irving et al.

samples of size N, is less than or equal to Ro,

sidered random. When R exceeds Ro, k/kSi, 
is larger than unity and its value is a measure 
of the tightness of grouping. The eleven sites 
have been classified into three groups based on 
the above criterion.

second pattern of the ilmenite lamellae ex- 
hibits 'Herring-bone' type of structures as 
shown in Plate lc. In each polished section of 
this group, the ilmenite-hematite exsolution 
dominated the magnetite-ilmenite exsolution. 
The stable natural remanence and the coercive 
force greater than 1200 Oe observed in speci- 
mens of this group may be due to both the 
exsolved phases. The magnetic grains are pos- 
sibly broken into single domains by the fine 
herring-bone structure of ilmenite (Evans and 
McElhinny 1966). The fine elongated hematite 
lamellae in ilmenite grains may also have con- 
tributed to the high coercive remanence and 
the stable magnetism of the specimens (Car- 
michael 196 l ). 
In the case of Group B specimens, the 
magnetite grains were partly filled with broad 
ilmenite lamellae, about 25-30 p long and 2 p 
wide (Plate Id). Homogeneous magnetite 
grains were few. This exsolution possibly be- 
longs to Class I1 of titanomagnetite high tem- 
perature oxidation described by Wilson and 
Haggerty (1966) and Ade Hall et al. (1968). 
The natural remanence is carried by the mag- 
netite grains partly divided by the broad ilmen- 
ite lamellae. No other exsolved phases were 
observed in specimens of this group. 
Altered skeletal ilmenite and large angular 
pyrite grains were the only grains observed in 
Group C specimens. The alteration in ilmenite 
occurred on the periphery of the grains as 
shown in Plate le. The altered product of the 
ilmenite was suspected to carry a few minute 
grains of ferromagnetic material which might 
have been responsible for carrying the weak 
remanence. The altered products were analysed 
using an X-ray powder technique (Debye- 
Scherrer, 57.26 mm diameter camera). The 
procedure for the preparation of the specimen 
for this camera has been outlined by Patel 
( 197 1 ) . Strong lines of sphene, ilmenite, augite, 
and plagioclase were observed on the films. 
No trace of ferromagnetic material was ob- 
served in the altered product of the ilmenite. 
Pale yellow to whitish anisotropic irregular 
patches (Plate If) were also observed in some 
of the ilmenite grains. This may be initial de- 
velopment of a hematite phase and is perhaps 
responsible for carrying the weak and unstable 
magnetization.

Curie Point Analysis 
The typical saturation magnetization (Js) 
versus temperature curves for the three groups 
of specimens are shown in Fig. 9. The Curie 
point obtained for the Group A specimens 
(M3A3-3) was about 555 2 5 "C. It appears 
from this Curie temperature observation that 
the material of this Group is mainly magnetite. 
The ilmenite-hematite phase could give the 
same Curie temperature if it has a suitable 
composition, and if so, the self-reversing mech- 
anism in ilmenite-hematite solid solution is 
ruled out (Uyeda 1958; Carmichael 1961 ) . 
But it is possible that this solution will not 
show up on the Js/T curves, as it would be 
masked by magnetically stronger magnetite- 
ilmenite exsolution. 
The Group B specimens (M8A 2-2), with 
ilmenite lamellae exsolved in magnetite grains 
showed a single Curie point of about 570 * 5 
OC. It appears from this Curie point that the 
magnetite in these specimens has a low titanium 
content as the Curie point of pure magnetite is 
580 OC. The third type of thermomagnetic 
curve is shown by the specimen M11A1-1 
Group C category, which is extremely unstable 
magnetically. The curves have long 'tails' and

Pole Position 
The pole positions of the seven significant 
sites (Groups A and B) of the diabase are 
given in Table 1. The mean of the poles of the 
five sites (M2A, M3A, M6A, M8A, and 
M36A) is 69.9" W, 15.6" S (Ag, = 6.1"). 
Sites M35A and M37A (granophyre) were 
discarded for calculating the mean pole as the 
development of the granophyre may be a 
metamorphic event and their magnetic direc- 
tions diverge by more than 90' from the 
directions of the other five sites. 
The pole positions of the same formation in 
other parts of the Province have also been 
determined by Pate1 (1971). The mean of 27 
sites in the Cobalt area is 95.0' W, 10.1 S and 
Symons (1970) calculated a pole at 88.1' W, 
19.4" S from 11 sites. Symons (1971) also 
determined the pole position for the Elliot 
Lake area at 98.4' W, 0.8' S from eight sites. 
The comparison of mean directions was carried 
out with Patel's (197 1) results to that of Symons' 
(1970) results and Symons' (1971), results to 
that of this paper. In both the cases, the direc- 
tions are observed nonsignificantly different 
using Watson's (1956~) F-ratio test at the 5% 
significance point. 
Conclusion 
The correlation of the opaque petrology 
with the stability of remanence of the three 
groups of specimens appears to be significant. 
Sites M9A, MIOA, MllA, and M34A 
showed random distribution using the Watson's 
(19563) test. The stability of remanence of 
the individual specimens from these sites was 
in keeping with the opaque petrology. Sites 
M2A, M3A, and M6A were found to be ex- 
tremely stable. The specimens from these sites 
contained two exsolutions. The varied differ- 
ences in high temperature oxidation of the 
minerals of the specimens from the same area 
may be due to different oxidation environments 
to which the sills have been subjected. 
It is rather difficult to comment on the 
titanium contents from the Curie points of 
specimens of Group A as both the exsolutions 
are present in the same specimens. The mag- 
netite in Group B specimens has little or no 
titanium and has a Curie temperature of 
570" C. 
The mean pole position for the Nipissing 
diabase around and west of Lake Matinenda 
is calculated at 69.9' W, 15.6" S (Ag5 = 
6.1 O), using the pole positions of five signifi- 
cant sites.

the Rondane Mountains, Queen Maud Land, Antarctica

Eighteen samples from three different intrusive rocks from the S0r Rondane Mountains 
(East Antarctica) contained a NRM with consistent directions around 341 ø, +64 ø. This 
result is similar to the NRM direction of the gneisses from the Ongul Island and Liitzow- 
Holm Bay, which belong to the same complex. It is argued that the NRM dates from the 
latest thermal event in this region, which is indicated by the Rb-Sr age of the biotites of 
the rocks as being 480 m.y. for the S0r 1%ndane intrusives. If it is assumed that the NRM 
reflects the local geomagnetic field direction in the Lower Ordovician, some tentative con- 
clusions for the position of Antarctica in Gondwanaland can be advanced. 
INTRODUCTION 
Since little is known of the palcomagnetism 
of Antarctica, the author joined the summer 
party to the Sr Rondane Mountains during 
the second Belgian-Netherlands Antarctic Ex- 
pedition (1965), as organized by the Belgian- 
Netherlands Antarctic Committee. The Sr 
Rondane Mountains are situated in East Ant- 
arcfica, at the border of the polar plateau, and 
are approximately 200 km south of the 'Base 
Rot Baudouin,' constructed by the 1958 
pdition Antarctique Belge (leader G. de Ger- 
lache). During January 1965 only the western 
part of this 250 km long and 90 km wide moun- 
tain range could be visited. This area lies at 
72øS, 24øE. 
The Sr Rondane Mountains are a gneissic 
complex composed of an important series of 
gneisses and migmatites, containing marble beds, 
graphite-schists, and quartzites. It is a Precam- 
brian sedimentary sequence, isoclinally folded 
and strongly metamorphosed in the upper cata- 
zone, with varying anatexitic phenomena and 
with a slight retrograde metamorphism in the 
mesozone [Michot and Klerkx, 1966]. Younger 
and nonmetamorphic sediments are not found 
[van Autenboer et al., 1964]. These meta- 
morphic rocks appeared to be very unsuitable 
for a preliminary pale.omagnetlc research. 
The metamorphic complex is invaded, how- 
ever, by younger igneous massifs and dykes, 
many of which have been dated by radiometric 
methods [Picciotto, Deutsch, and Pasteels, 1964, 
1966], and these dated intrusive rocks were used 
to supply the palcomagnetic data. This post- 
orogenic and post-metamorphic igneous com- 
plex consists mainly of granites, syenites, and 
gabbroic rocks. 
ADIOlETRIC AGES 
Picciotto et al. [19'64, 1966] have determined 
the ages of nineteen samples, representing the 
principal types of rocks from the region, using 
various methods of isotopic geochronometry. 
The results are summarized in Table 1. Their 
collection included two samples of rocks that 
were used in the present palcomagnetic study 
(granite from Romnesfjellet and syenite from 
Lunckerygge). 
From five of the samples ad'ditional K-Ar 
whole-rock measurements were made by Ravich 
and Krylov in Leningrad; the ages obtained 
were from 350 to 500 m.y. 
Picciotto. concluded that the emplacement of 
the intrusive complex, based on the age of its 
zircons, took place approximately 530 m.y. ago 
and that the metamorphism of the gneiss and 
the migmatization would be approximately 550 
m.y. old and thus nearly contemporaneous with 
the magmatic intrusions. The 550-m.y. age is 
based on the Rb-Sr whole-rock measurements of 
two fine-grained anatexitic granites, considere.d 
as products of the principal migmatic phase and 
synchronous with the tectonic deformation. 
The low K-Ar ages were determined on gra- 
nitic whole rocks and are thus undoubtedly a

480 m.y. Micho attributed this 'biotite Rb-Sr

moreover, correlated this retromorphism with 
the final phase of the consolidation of the erup- 
tive masses [Mich.o.t and Klerkx, 1966]. In the 
Sr Rondane region this slight retrograde meta- 
morphism took place in the mesozone. 
Another interpretation of the observations 
might connect this second metamorphic event 
with the intrusion of the igneous masses them- 
selves, both events being approximately 480 
m.y. old. Since the igneous rocks contain xeno- 
liths of the gneiss complex, this could also be 
the source of its older zircons. 
Nevertheless, for the palcomagnetic study only 
the final thermal event in the rocks recorded by 
their biotite Rb-Sr age is important,. 
SAMPLING LOCALITIES 
The post-metamorphic igneous rocks are 
found as huge massifs and dykes of all sizes 
intruding the metamorphic series in the moun- 
tains, but they are also found as isolated 
nunataks to the north of the mountain range. 
Because of the restricted conditions of the 
summer party, no extensive palcomagnetic col- 
lecting was possible. Each of the sampled 
intrusives was collected at only one locality. 
The sampling sites were chosen by van Auten- 
boer, the local geologist and leader of the sum- 
mer party. A detailed geologic description of 
the sampling region is given by van Autenboer 
and Loy [1966,]. A total of eight intrusives 
were sampled, their locations are indicated on 
Figure i by numbers that refer to 
North o[ the mountain range: 
1. On Seal nunat.ak. Coarse-grained granite (7 
samples and 1 sample of light colored gneiss 
inclusion). This granite is identical t.o that 
of the nearby large nunatak Romnasfjellet. 
2. On the eastern slope of Vesthaugen nunatak. 
2.1 Massive monzonite (4 samples), inter- 
ealating gneiss. 
2.2 Kersantite dyke (4 samples), cutting 
the monzonite. 
3. On nunatak 1550. Thin 'basalt sill (7 sam- 
ples), intervening gneiss. 
In the mountains: 
4. Syenite from Lunckerygge (7 samples), on 
the eastern slope of the Jenningsbreen val- 
ley. 
5. Granitic dyke in syenite from Lunekeryggen 
(5 samples), to the southeast of the Luneke 
pass (western slope of the Gjelbreen valley). 
6. Granite from Lunkerygge on the eastern 
slope of the Jenningsbreen valley. 
6.1 Granite (5 samples). 
6.2 Older aplite dyke (1 sample) in the 
granite. 
6.3 Younger aplite dyke (3 samples) in the 
granite. 
7..Granite from Vengen (9 samples) in the 
west wall of the Vengen mountain, between 
hill 2500 and hill 2550. 
8. Itornblende-epidote rock (probably meta- 
morphosed diabase) in the east wall of 
Widerefjellet (6 samples). 
The local geomagnetic declination was 35.5øW

RESULTS 
The measurements and analyses of the NRM 
(natural reinanent magnetization) of the samples 
led to a division into at least three groups' 
1. Some rocks proved to be unsuitable for 
the paledmagnetic investigation: the granite 
from Lunckerygge, the granite dykes in the 
syenite and in the granite from Lunckerygge, 
the granite from Vengen, and the metamor- 
phosed diabase from WiderOefjellet. These rocks 
have a relatively high magnetic suscepti- 
bility but only a relatively weak magnetic 
remanence. This relation can be given by the 
proportion of the NRM to the total of both 
magnetic remanence and induced magnetization, 
the latter in a magnetic field being equivalent 
to the geomagnetic field. For the rocks under 
discussion this 'proportional Q value' is not 
larger than 15% and is generally less than 10ø% 
with a minimum of 255. The directions of the 
relatively weak NRM of these rocks, shortly 
after arrival and preparation, were close to the 
local present geomagnetic direction in the Sr 
Rondane region .'(see Figure 2). The scatter 
appeared to be learly a consequence of their 
viscous nature, because repeated measurements 
after some months' storage in the laboratory 
revealed appreciable changes toward the new 
ambient field direction, in some cases even out- 
rageous changes. The supposition that the NRM 
of these rocks is entirely a viscous remanence is 
redundantly supported by their progressive ac 
demagnetizations: this NRM was largely or

even entirely eliminated in ac magnetic fields 
as low as 100 to 200 oe. 
2. More promising was the NRM of the 
granite from the Seal nunatak, the monzonite 
from Vesthaugen, and the syenite from Lunck- 
erygge. The intensity of the NRM of these 
rocks was 10 times stronger than that of the 
other sampled rocks. Moreover, their 'propor- 
tional Q value' was very large (the granite up 
to 93%). 
'The directions of this strong NRM have a 
large within-site consistency, are similar in all 
three intrusives, and are strongly divergent 
from the present field in the Sr Rondane 
Mountains. Progressive alemagnetizations with 
ac magnetic fields showed that this NRM did 
indeed consist almost entirely of only one fairly 
hard remanent component (see Figure 3a). The 
lower ac magnetic fields eliminated a small 
anomalous component, resulting in a slight ad- 
justment of the magnetization directions. 
All samples from the three intrusives were 
carefully demagnetized with ac magnetic fields 
and the direction of the harder, characteristic 
reinanent magnetization was deduced. The re- 
sult is shown in Figure 3b and summarized in 
Table 2. It is clear that the characteristic NRM 
directions of the three intrusive rocks agree 
closely. 
3. The results of the samples of the rela- 
tively young basaltic dykes from Vesthaugen 
and from nunatak 1550 are less consistent. The 
'proportional Q-value' of their NRM was very 
low. Moreover, the NRM of the dyke from 
nunatak 1550 had a surprisingly low intensity. 
The directions of the NRM of these dykes 
diverge, however, from each other and from 
the present geomagnetic field in the Sr Ron- 
dane Mountains (the samples from nunatak 
1550 display a 'streaking' toward the present 
field). Some progressive ac magnetic field de- 
magnetizations showed that this NRM was hard 
for the greater part. These ac magnetic field 
demagnetizations failed, however, to reveal a 
distinct characteristic magnetization direction, 
largely owing to a scatter in the results. Conse- 
quently, no approximations of the NRM direc- 
tions of these rocks are attempted. We can only 
report that the ac demagnetization revealed that 
the directions of the NRM of the dyke from 
Vesthaugen tend to approach the characteristic 
direction of the previous group, to which its 
host rock also belongs, and that the directions 
of the NRM of the sill from nunatak 1550 tend 
to collect in the ESE corner with a moderate, 
negative inclination. 
DISCUSSION 
The common NRM direction of the granite 
from the Seal, the monzonite from Vesthaugen, 
and the syenite from Lunckerygge seems to be 
characteristic for the main igneous complex. 
This NRM cannot, of course, be older than the 
530 m.y. inferred by Picciotto et al. [1964, 1966] 
from the zircon ages as the time of emplace- 
ment of the intrusives. The characteristic NRM 
most likely dates from the final thermal event, 
however, which is recorded by the Rb-Sr age 
of the biotites. Heating experiments with our 
samples showed that the characteristic NRM 
decayed over a range of temperatures up to 
450ø-575øC, which corresponds to the range of 
temperatures in which the loss of radiogenic 
strontium from biotite during regional heating 
occurs [Hanson and Gast, 1967]. The age of 
the characteristic NRM is therefore most likely 
given by the Rb-Sr age of the biotites and thus 
is approximately 480 m.y., which corresponds 
with the Lower Ordovician [Kulp, 1961]. From 
the palcomagnetic point of view it is unimpor- 
tant whether the final thermal event was the 
regional mesozonal retrograde metamorphism, 
as suggested by Michot and Klerkx [1966], or 
the actual eraplacement of the intrusives. 
Although a post-intrusive tilting is unlikely 
(E. Picciotto and J. Michot, personal com- 
munication, 1966), the possibility could not be 
excluded with certainty. van Autenboer [1964] 
reported that the large-scale structure tends 
east-west and dips 40 ø to 50 ø to the south. 
From data in a more recent paper [van Auten- 
boer and Loy, 1966] it can be inferred that in 
the mountains on both sides of the. Gunnestad- 
breen (Teltet, Vengen, Widerefjellet, Walnum- 
fjellet) the orientation of the gneiss dips at 45 ø 
to 75 ø uniformly to the south (dip azimuth 
varies between N 175øE and N 195øE); this 
dip increases from north to south. In the region 
of Brattnipane this orientation dips 25 ø to 40 ø 
in a more westerly direction (dip azimuth varies 
between N 205øE and N 225øE). 
Knowledge of the structural setting of the 
nunataks to the north of the mountain range is 
poor. The only details reported are that at

ANTARCTICA AND OTttER GONDWANIC 
CONTINENTS IN PALEOZOIC ERA 
Since only a few Paleozoic paleomagnetic data 
are available for the Gondwanic continents 
(Table 4), no definite discussion of our Ant- 
arctic result is possible. Nevertheless, some gen- 
eral remarks might be of importance for paleo- 
geographic reconstructions of Gondwanaland. 
Creer [1964, 1965] showed that, when South 
America and Africa are placed adjacent to one 
another in their classical fit, the few Paleozoic 
poles for Africa match his Paleozoic polar 
wandering curve for South America. The paleo- 
magnetic data thus confirmed this reconstruc- 
tion, and, moreover, the outline of the Paleozoic 
polar wandering curve for Gon'dwanaland was 
thereby indicated. The tentative Paleozoic polar 
wandering curve for Australia [Irving, 1964] 
has, however, a rather different shape. It is not 
possible to match these two Gondwanic polar 
wandering curves satisfactorily (Figures 5 and 
6). The length of the upper Paleozoic Austral- 
ian polar wandering curve is appreciably shorter 
than the contemporaneous part of the South 
American-African curve. This difference might 
be explained by a drifting ,apart of Australia 
and South America-Africa in the late Paleozoic. 
The lower Paleozoic reconstruction is then ob- 
tained by bringing together the Silurian-De- 
vonian poles of Australia (6, 7, 8, and 9') and 
South America-Africa (16, 21, and 17). In Fig- 
ure 5 it is shown that, following this interpreta- 
tion, Australia was situated close to the (present

It should be kept in mind, however, that, al-

coast of Australia. The continents are indicated with their --1000-fathom contours, and, for 
clarity, the present coast lines of Antarctica and Australia are also shown. Index numbers 
of the palcomagnetic poles refer to, Table 4. The dotted curve is the usually accepted Aus- 
tralian polar wandering curve [Irving, 1964; Irving, 1966]; the dashed curve is the common

The Paleomagnetism of the Modipe Gabbro 
M. E. Ewes  AND M. W. McEIHNNY  
Physics Department, University College oJ Rhodesia 
Salisbury, Rhodesia 
Samples have been collected from eleven sites in the Modipe gabbro which crops out on 
the border of Bechuanaland and South Africa. After partial demagnetization in alternating 
magnetic fields, ten of these sites give almost vertical directions of magnetization, forming a 
close group which corresponds to a palcomagnetic pole at 33øS, 31øE. The gabbro is intruded 
by the Gabcrones granite, and samples from two sites in the granite show almost horizontal 
magnetization. On initial measurement gabbro samples collected near the contact yield direc- 
tions close to those of the granite, which suggests that the gabbro was reheated at the time 
of emplacement of the granite (2350 m.y. ago). After magnetic cleaning, some of these samples 
give directions which agree with those at the other gabbro sites. Together with detailed alter- 
nating field and thermal demagnetization studies, this agreement provides strong evidence 
that the magnetically cleaned directions are those of the TRM acquired when the gabbro 
originally cooled. The gabbro has an age of approximately 2600 m.y. and is to date the oldest 
rock unit that has been studied palcomagnetically; the results imply the existence of a geo- 
magnetic field in this early stage of the earth's history. Alternating field demagnetization ex- 
periments indicate that some of the magnetic grains have very high coercivities. Thermal 
demagnetization and IRM studies exclude the presence of hematite and show that the mag- 
netic mineral present is magnetite. Microscopic observations and theoretical considerations 
suggest that the high coercivities observed are due to the shape anisotropy of small elongated 
single-domain grains of magnetite. 
INTRODUCTION 
The Modipe gabbro lies some 250 km north- 
west of Johannesburg at 24.7øS, 26.2øE. The 
intrusion is exposed over a distance of about 
16 kin, half of which lies in the Bechuanaland 
Protectorate (now called Botswana) 16 km 
east of Gaberones and half in the western 
Transvaal in the Republic of South Africa 
(Figure 1). It is to date the oldest rock unit 
that has been studied palcomagnetically. 
The gabbro exhibits some interesting mag- 
netic properties and despite its great age still 
contains a stable component of remanent mag- 
netization which is believed to date from the 
time the rock originally cooled. 
GEOLOGY 
The gabbro is exposed as a line of isolated 
hills trending northwest-southwest. Apart from 
these hills exposure is very poor and the actual 
extent of the gabbro is not known; the recon- 
x Now at Department of Geophysics and Geo- 
chemistry, Australian National University, Can- 
berra, A.C.T. 
naissance map [Joes, 1963] is based to a large 
extent on variation of soil types (Figure 1). 
The gabbro is very uniform in composition, 
consisting almost entirely of plagioclase feld- 
spar and augitc with abundant accessory 
'magnetite' [Jones, 1963]. 
To the northwest the gabbro is partly sur- 
rounded by the northeastern extremity of the 
Gabcrones granite, the outcrop of which covers 
some 4500 km '. On the northwestern slopes of 
Modipe Hill the gabbro is sheared and pene- 
trated by veinlets of granitic material, and 
Joes [1963] therefore concludes that the 
Gabcrones granite postdates the Modipe gab- 
bro, although the actual contact is not exposed. 
The BechuanaIand Geological Survey regards 
the granite as post-Dominion Reef system and 
pre-Transvaal system in age. In terms of South 
African geochronology this places the granite 
between 2100 and 3000 m.y. old [Nicolaysen, 
1962]. 
In adjacent parts of South Africa, about 20 
km east of Wildebeest Kop, isolated outcrop 
of basic rocks along the Marico River have 
been correlated with the Modipe gabbro 
[Poldervaart, 1952]. Schutie [1963], in turn,

Eleven sites were sampled in the Modipe

20 and 25 km, respectively, due west of Mo-

two cores, 60 cm long and 2.5 cm in diameter, 
were drilled with a modified version of the 
portable equipment described by McElhinny 
and Neal [1966]. The cores were oriented with 
respect to the sun's azimuth and the horizontal 
using the method of Gough and Opdylce [1963]. 
From the remaining site hand samples were 
collected which were oriented with a Brunton 
compass-clinometer.

cm in length were cut. For the purposes of

This gradual decrease in magnetic moment 
demonstrates that the gabbro has a very broad 
coercivity spectrum, which presumably indi- 
cates a large range in grain and domain size 
[Stacey, 1963]. Similar high coercivities in 
coarse-grained dolerites have been reported by 
McElhinny and Opdyke [1964]. 
The same specimens were then heated to 
700øC and cooled in the earth's magnetic field, 
and the TRM acquired in each case was de- 
magnetized. The demagnetization curves for 
the NRM and TRM of one of these specimens 
are shown in Figure 6. The great similarity of 
these curves demonstrates that the NRM and 
TRM have almost identical coercivity spec- 
trums. This provides further evidence that the 
NRM is a primary TRM and suggests that 
heating these specimens to 700øC in air caused 
little or no alteration. 
High coercivities ( > 100 mw m -') are usually 
attributed to hematite [e.g., Creer, 1959], but 
this mineral is rare as an original constituent 
of igneous rocks [Kerr, 1959]. We therefore 
attempted to determine from thermal demag- 
netization and isothermal reinanent magnetiza- 
tion experiments how much hematite, if any, is 
present. 
Thermal demagnetization. Figure 7a shows 
that the thermal demagnetization curves of the 
NRM and TRM of specimen BO2A are almost 
identical, which again indicates that the NRM 
is a primary TRM and that heating to 700øC 
caused very little, if any, alteration. The curves 
show a very sharp decrease between 550 and 
600øC, in which range 94% of the initial mo- 
ment is destroyed. After heating to 600øC, 
0.4% of the NRM and 1.0% of the TRM are 
left. Similar results were obtained for speci- 
men BO1A, and 0.3% of the NRM and 0.5% 
of the TRM remained at this temperature. 
No systematic direction could be observed after 
heating to 600øC. Thus not more than 1% of 
the remanence can be attributed to a mineral 
having blocking temperatures in excess of 
600øC, whereas grains with coercivities greater 
than 100 mw m - account for 10%.

Isothermal remanent magnetization. Roquet 
[1954] has studied the isothermal remanent 
magnetization (IRM) of magnetite and hema- 
tite samples of various grain sizes. Her results 
show that magnetite is saturated after being 
placed in a field of 0.3 w m -2 (3 kilogauss) and 
hematite approaches saturation only in fields 
of 3 w m -2. The hematite curves start to 
flatten out above 2 w m -, and the main rise 
in the IRM occurs between about 0.4 and 2 
w m -'. If hematite were present in appreciable 
amounts in a specimen whose magnetic mineral 
is predominantly magnetite, one would expect 
to see a rise in the IRM of the specimen be- 
tween 0.4 and 2 w m -2 after the magnetite has 
been saturated.

The Paleomagnetism of the Precambrian Dolerites of Eastern Southern Rhodesia, an Example of Geologic Correlation by Rock Magnetism

M. W. McELHINNY AND N. D. OPDYKE1

Physics Department University College of Rhodesia and Nyasaland Salisbury, Southern Rhodesia

Abstract. Thirty sites have been sampled in dolerites which intrude the Precambrian shield and the Umkondo system of eastern Southern Rhodesia. The natural remanent magnetization is random at sixteen of the twenty-five sites used in the final analysis. In many cases it has been necessary to resort to the use of high alternating fields to successfully remove later components of magnetization, which are thought to be the result of isothermal remanent magnetization due to lightning currents. The directions of magnetization after treatment in alternating fields form two distinct groups about 90° apart, which indicates that these dolerites represent two quite distinct magmatic episodes. These directions are given by D = 292°, I = +51° (pole position 7°N, 20°W, As = 71½2°), and D = 182½2°, I = —10½/°(pole position 65°N, 42½2°E, Aøs = 6°). The former group, which intrudes the Rhodesian Precambrian shield, are termed the Mashonaland dolerites, and the latter, which are associated with the Umkondo system, are termed the Umkondo dolerites. Paleomagnetic evidence is presented to show that the Mashonaland dolerites have intruded the Umkondo dolerites, which are therefore the older of the two sets of intrusions. Potassium-argon age determinations on some of the samples of Mashonaland dolerite used in this study indicate that this group of intrusions is at least 1600 m.y. old. This would indicate that the Umkondo dolerites and therefore the Umkondo system itself are at least this old.

Introduction. Throughout the eastern part of Southern Rhodesia in an area between longitudes 30° and 33°E and between latitudes 17° and 21°S, a large number of dolerite dikes, sheets, and sills have intruded the Precambrian shield of Southern Rhodesia. The dolerites crop out over an area of 80,000 km² and are seen to intrude the Great Dyke, the basement granites and gneisses, and the Umkondo-Frontier system (Figure 1). In the southeast part of Southern Rhodesia, around Melsetter, the dolerites intruding the Umkondo system take the form of large sills up to 200 m thick which can be traced for many kilometers. The geology of this part of the Umkondo system, along with its intrusions, has been described by Swift [1962] and Watson [1964].

In the northeast part of Southern Rhodesia, around Inyanga, a further sequence of thick sills up to 450 m thick are associatedwith what are presumed to be remnants of the Umkondo system in this area [Tyndale-Biscoe, 1958]. The sheets and dikes intruding the granites, schists, and gneisses of the older Precambrian basement are mainly demarked by the occurrences of red soil which show up conspicuously in the sandy soil derived from the granite. Most of these intrusions (see Figure 1) have been mapped from aerial photographs, and their considerable extent has only recently been appreciated.

In the Umkondo system in the southeast corner of Southern Rhodesia, one of the dolerite sills is overlain unconformably by the local base of the Karroo system. Swift [1961], correlating the sills in the Inyanga district with those in the Melsetter district, believes that, because the north-south extent is comparable with that of the Great Dyke, the two are probably contemporaneous. On the other hand, Nicolaysen et al. [1962] think that the dolerites around Shawa [see Gough and Brock, 1964]intruding the basement granite are of Karroo age, mainly because of their wide occurrence. Before this investigation it was not known whether these intrusions represented one magmatic episode or several.

The investigation of these intrusions arose out of a study of the paleomagnetism of the Great Dyke by McElhinny and Gough [1963]. In this study one of the sites sampled in the norite at the Umsweswe River was found to have a direction of magnetization quite different from that characteristic of the rest of the

Great Dyke. The most likely explanation of this anomalous direction was that it occurred from the reheating of the norite at the time of intrusion of the dolerite sills, dikes, and sheets, remnants of which outcrop in the area. To test this hypothesis we sampled several of these sills, and we then decided to extend the sampling to include the rest of the dolerites in the eastern half of the country.

Sampling and field methods. Thirty sites, spread throughout the area of occurrence of the dolerites, were sampled. As a result of some preliminary sampling, two areas of interest were later sampled more extensively. These were the Inyanga district and the Melsetter district along the eastern border of Southern Rhodesia.

We used a Graham-Keiller type portable sampling drill [Graham and Keiller, 1960], usually drilling eight or ten cores, 15 to 20 cm long, at each site. At one site the cores were extended to a depth of 60 cm, and only four were taken. These cores were oriented relative to the sun's azimuth by the method descrıbed by Gough and Opdyke [1963]. The positions of the sites are shown in Figure 1 and the geographical coordinates are given in Table 1.

Because of the heavy oxidizing conditions which exist in tropical countries, good outcrops are often hard to find. Also, the high probability of lightning striking the ground in southern Africa makes the selection of good sampling sites difficult. Where possible the sites were located in road cuts, but in an underdeveloped country these are rare. The majority of the samples were taken from natural exposures. Experience has shown that the best types of natural exposure are in river beds, where the rock is reasonably fresh and where the river valley affords some protection from lightning The individual cores were usually taken at least 2 m apart in order to minimize the effect of a lightning strike [Graham, 1961].

The natural remanent magnetization. The directions and intensities of the natural remanent magnetization (NRM) were measured by means of a spinner magnetometer [Gough, 1964]. Directions were measured with an uncertainty of 1° and intensities within 5 per cent.

37.5 per cent of the NRM. Between 100 and 300 gauss little change in direction is observed, but the moment drops quickly to 1.67 per cent of its NRM value. Between 300 and 1000 gauss the direction of magnetization starts to move again, but now it moves along a great circle almost at right angles to its first motion. At a peak field of 1000 gauss the moment is only 0.09 per cent of its original NRMvalue.

The three specimens illustrated in Figure 5 were also heated to 700°C in a nitrogen atmosphere and cooled in the earth's field. The resulting TRM was then demagnetized in increasing alternating fields, and the resultant curves are also shown in Figure 5. The shape of the demagnetization curve in each case is typical of the demagnetization of stable TRM in dolerite or basalt [Stott, 1963; van Zyl et al. 1962]. In each case the direction of the TRM was parallel to the applied field and remained unchanged within the experimental error up to 800 or 1000 gauss. This latter observation clearly indicates the presence of high-coercivity domains.

The two demagnetization curves (c and e) in Figure 5 have the shape which typifies the behavior of an unstable rock when subjected to alternating-field demagnetization. Clearly these two curves do not represent the demagnetization of a TRM alone. It is most probable that they represent the demagnetization of IRM due to lightning. Several factors favor this viewpoint. To obtain random directions of NRM it is necessary for different magnetizing fields to have been operating over different parts of the outcrop sampled [Gough et al., 1964]. Viscous magnetization in the present earth's field would produce a planar distribution, and it is difficult to conceive of any mechanism other than lightning currents which could produce this randomizing of directions.

Lightning currents can produce magnetization of high coercivity, depending on the magnitude and proximity of the currents involved. The initial sharp drop in moment observed in Figure 5 in the two demagnetizing curves probably merely indicates that a very large component of IRM is present. This has required the use of high alternating fields, and it seems that it is possible to isolate a small minority of stable domains of high coercivity by randomizing the directions of magnetization of the other domains. By this means the use of high alternating fields has effectively removed the effect of those domains which have been reoriented by lightning currents. This often means that the residual moment is less than 1 per cent of the original NRM. Therefore it seems that the shape of the demagnetization curve has little bearing on the 'stability'of the rock specimen being subjected to alternating fields. In Figure 5, curve e, the change in direction observed in the specimen which moves along two great circles almost at right angles probably indicates the occurrence of two lightning currents at this site, each producing a different coercivity IRM.

In Figure 6 is shown a thermal demagnetization curve for an adjacent specimen from the same core at site D. This curve was obtained on the thermal demagnetization apparatus at Imperial College, London, described by Wilson [1962]. No change in direction occurs on heating the specimen up to its Curie point. This probably indicates that the blocking temperature for high coercivity domains isothermally remagnetized is either at or very near the Curie point. It seems unlikely, therefore, that thermal demagnetization will prove successful as a means of removing lightning IRM. The technique of thermal demagnetization is probably most useful where a partial thermoremanence is involved. In the present situation the only successful demagnetization technique was the use of high alternating fields.

At five sites it was impossible to gain any useful paleomagnetic data after applying alternating fields. In these cases it is likely that an insufficient number of high-coercivity domains were present in the specimens, so that on applying higher fields the situation was reached of the statistical resultant of the randomly oriented domain magnetizations being greater than that of the few high-coercivity domains. In these cases the lightning effects had completely remagnetized the samples.

Discussion of results. Table 1 gives the parameters at all the sites after alternating-field demagnetization. At a few sites one or two samples were excluded from the analysis. These samples had very high moments, which on demagnetization changed little up to 800 gauss either in direction or intensity. These odd samples were in contrast to the remainder at all the sites which tended to form a tight group. These few samples were probably the result of direct hits by lightning.

Figure 7 shows a lower-hemisphere stereographic projection of the mean directions of magnetization at the twenty-five sites listed in Table 1, together with their circles of 95 per cent confidence. The mean directions of magnetization form two well-defined groups differing by nearly 90° in direction. The set with a declination of almost 300°and an inclination of 50° are numbered 1 to 14 in Table 1 and Figure 1. This direction is characteristic of all the intrusions sampled in the basement granites and gneisses on the Rhodesian shield. These dolerites are almost entirely restricted to the Mashonaland district of Southern Rhodesia and are therefore here named the Mashonaland dolerites. The other directions, which are low in inclination to the south, are lettered A to J in Table 1 and Figure 1. These dolerites are always associated with and intruded into the Umkondo system and are here called the Umkondo dolerites.

The Great Dyke. Site 8 represents the exposure of norite from the Great Dyke in the Umsweswe River. Sites 6 and 10 from nearby dolerite sills are seen to give a similar mean direction of magnetization, which lends support to the hypothesis that the Great Dyke norite in this area has been reheated by these Mashonaland dolerites. A 200-m sill is exposed in the Umsweswe Mine immediately underlying the Umsweswe River at this point [Worst, 1960], but unfortunately the mine has been flooded and it was not possible to collect samples from this sill. The dolerite at site 6 forms a sheet resting on top of the Great Dyke. It is very strongly magnetic and represents the 'magnetite dolerite' of Hess [1950]. This sheet, as are most others in this area, is clearly not Great Dyke in age on the paleomagnetic evidence presented here, and it therefore cannot be the roof phase of the Great Dyke as Hess suggests. It is probably a coincidence that the mineral content for these dolerites falls on the mineral variation curves plotted by Hess for the Great Dyke rocks.

The Umkondo dolerites. The Umkondo dolerites have been found only in those areas in which the Umkondo system rocks are developed. The principal occurrence of this system is in the Melsetter area in the region south of Umtali (Figure 1). These dolerites again occur in the Inyanga mountains, 160 km to the north, where remnants of what have always been regarded as the northern extension of the Umkondo system are preserved. The correlation of the dolerites between these two areas confirms the supposition that the small sedimentary sequence in the Inyanga area can be correlated with the Umkondo system. In thin section these dolerites consist of pyroxene and feldspar with a well-defined ophitic relationship, and they are fairly coarse in grain. The pyroxene is dominantly colorless augite, pigeonite being rare, and the feldspar is andesine or labradorite. Subordinate amounts of quartz and apatite occur. In polished section the opaque minerals are predominantly ilmeno-magnetite. The ilmenite usually occurs exclusively as thick exsolution lamellas and granules intergrown with magnetite. At site A, however, the opaques are predominantly maghemite with ultrafine intergrowths of ilmenite.

In the Inyanga area the Umkondo dolerites form the cappings to the hills and are found to be in intimate association with the Mashonaland dolerites. Topographically higher horizons in these sills gave Umkondo directions (at sites A, B, C, and D), whereas the lower horizons (at sites 4 and 7) gave Mashonaland dolerite directions. One anomalous site (site 15) gave a direction which agreed with neither set of dolerites. This occurred in one of the lower horizons in the Mudzoro River on Gairezi Ranch, and it is interesting to note that the inclination observed is similar to that of the Mashonaland dolerites. It seems likely that the outcrop at this site has been rotated in a large landslide at some time after it was originally formed. The difference in declination between this site and that of the mean of the Mashonaland dolerites is 82°. This is the angle through which this outcrop may have been rotated.

The Mashonaland dolerites. These constitute the most extensively developed body of dolerite intrusions in Southern Rhodesia. Petrologically the Mashonaland dolerites are similar to the Umkondo dolerites. They consist of labradorite, hypersthene, augite, and some pigeonite. Biotite and apatite are often present as accessories. In polished section the opaque minerals are mainly ilmeno-magnetite. The ilmenomagnetite grains have both coarse laths of granules and a grid of very fine ilmenite intergrowth. Pyrite and chalcopyrite occur rarely as small grains. Extensive sampling shows that they are found to intrude all the basement systems, the Great Dyke, and the Umkondo system. This fact could only be observed on paleomagnetic grounds. At site 12 in the Nyhodi River valley, south of Melsetter, a direction of magnetization was observed which corresponded to the Mashonaland dolerites. This site was located in fine-grained basaltic material occurring in the center of a large sill regarded by Watson [1964] as being part of the same sill in which sites E, F, G, and H are situated. These latter sites, as well as site I, located 1 mile away, all give Umkondo dolerite directions. Site 12 is therefore regarded as a separate intrusion into the large Umkondo sill. On normal geologic considerations, therefore, it appears that the Mashonaland dolerites were intruded later than the

Umkondo dolerites. Site 12 is the only place where the Mashonaland dolerites have been found intruding both the Umkondo system and the Umkondo dolerites. It is probable that more exist.

In the Inyanga area the Mashonaland dolerites have been intruded along the same lines of weakness as the earlier Umkondo dolerites. The magma probably rose in the crust until its ascent was blocked by the earlier dolerite sheets. In the field it is impossible to distinguish between the two sets of dolerites, and future detailed mapping of this area must be based on the paleomagnetic direction of the dolerites.

The Mashonaland dolerites show both normal and reversed polarity in the ratio of 4:10. In the present instance 'normal' polarity refers to those directions having positive inclination. The mean directions of the two polarities differ by 168° ± 18°. This provides strong evidence in favor of the stability of the magnetization of these intrusions and the demagnetization techniques used in this study.

The ancient pole positions. The mean directions of magnetization for the Mashonaland dolerites and also for the Umkondo dolerites have been calculated giving each site unit weight and combining the directions irrespective of sign. These mean directions, together with the corresponding pole positions on the assumption of an axial dipole field, are given in Table 3. In the case of the Mashonaland dolerites, the sampling sites cover an area of 80,000 km², and the directions include both normal and reversed polarity. It seems likely that these sites became magnetized over an interval of time long in comparison with the secular variation, so that the mean pole position approximates the geocentric axial dipole position freed from secular variation. These dolerites intrude the Precambrian Rhodesian shield, which has suffered little tectonic movement since their intrusion. The geology of this part of the Rhodesian shield is known only on the basis of reconnaissance mapping, and it is difficult to determine the extent to which small tectonic movements have affected these dolerites. It seems likely, however, that very small tectonic movements of these dolerites would be randomized over the wide sampling area covered.

The Umkondo dolerites are not as widespread as the Mashonaland dolerites, but they occur over nearly 3° of latitude, and it seems likely that the ten sampling sites cover a sufficient time to average out the effects of secular variation. The dolerites intrude the Umkondo beds, which usually dip gently at about 5° in a southeasterly direction. The directions of magnetization have therefore been corrected in each case for the attitude of the adjacent sediments at each sampling site. The corrections are very small; Fisher's k for the directions changes from 57 to 58 on application of the corrections. This change is not significant, but the corrections are so small that this is to be expected. The directions cited for the various Umkondo dolerite sites in Table 1 refer to the directions after correction for the attitude of the sampling sites.

The age of the Umkondo system. Dr. J. A. Miller at Cambridge has kindly made K-Ar determinations on our samples of dolerite from the Mashonaland dolerites (sites 3, 9, and 10). The results are listed in Table 5. They show that the Mashonaland dolerites are at least 1600 m.y. old. Samples of Umkondo dolerite gave inconclusive results and apparently have suffered loss of Ar. However, the paleomagnetic evidence presented in this paper shows that the Umkondo dolerites are older than the Mashonaland dolerites; consequently, the Umkondo dolerites and therefore the Umkondo system itself must be at least 1600 m.y. old. This system is usually regarded as Upper Precambrian, but it must now be placed in the Middle Precambrian. Recent correlation by Swift [1961] of the Umkondo system with the Transvaal system in South Africa, mainly on lithological grounds, appears to be more tenable. Nicolaysen [1962] regards the Transvaal system as being approximately 2000 m.y. old, that is, just older than the Bushveld igneous complex and the Great Dyke.

ABSTRACT 
.%me areas of the Canadian Shield are profusely intruded by swarms of 
subparallel basaltic dykes. These typically have a diabasic texture and formerly 
were considered to be strictly the intrusive equivalents of tholeiitic fld basalt. 
About 650 oriented samples sere collected from about 25 dyke swarms and 
reliminary palaeomngnetic data from six of them are presented here. The 
Riackenzie swarm has a Ii-Ar age of 1295 million years, occurs throughout: 
the western Canadian Shicld, and is the most extensive swarm of basic dykes 
known anywhere in the world. The other swarms are the Molson dykes (1 445 
m.y.) in northeastern Manitoba, the Marathon dykes (1 810 m.y.) just north 
of Lake Superior, the Sudbury dykes (1 285 m.y.) of southeastern Ontario, the 
Matachewan dykes (2 485 m.y.) of western Quebec and northeastern Ontario, 
and the Abitibi dykes (1 230 m.y.), thich occur from Sault Ste. Marie, Ontario, 
to Lake Mistassini, Quebec. 
The palaeomagnetic virtual pole positions of six swarms were derived from 
the mean of their measured remanent magnetization directions. These directions 
of magnetization were determined from the samples after they were magnetically 
washed in an a-c. field of 80 or 130 oersteds. The reasons for the dispersion 
within the individual swarms are discussed. The pole positions of the Sudbury 
and Mackenzie dykes are almost identical and the two swarms are the same 
age within the limits of analytical uncertainty. However, basalt of the Sudbury 
swarm is alkalic and more undersaturated than basalt of the Mackenzie dykes. 
No evidence was found to contradict the usual assumption that unaltered 
basic igneous rocks of this type acquire and generally retain a stable magnetization 
which was parallel with the earth's magnetic field at the time of the dyke 
intrusion. 
INTRODUCTION 
This is the initial report on the results of an extensive study of the magnetic, 
and in particular of the palaeomagnetic properties of basaltic dykes of the 
Canadian Shield. These intrusives typically exhibit a diabasic texture and for 
this reason are commonly referred to simply as diabase dykes. Such rocks 
appear to be ideal subjects for palaeomagnetic study because some swarms 
extend over large areas of the Shield; the intrusion of an individual swarm is 
thought to have been an igneous event of short duration; they can be dated 
by the K-Ar method; they have intruded the Shield at numerous stages 
throughout the span of Precambrian time; and many lack any indication of 
having been metamorphosed or disturbed since they were emplaced. 
The first attempt to investigate and interpret the remanent magnetism of 
diabase dyke swarms of the Canadian Shield was made by D. W. Strangway 
(1961). He studied swarms in eastern Ontario and southwestern Quebec and 
concluded that the most stable component of magnetization in diabase dykes 
lies close to the plane of the dyke. He concluded from these results and a review 
of literature that a diabase dyke can be treated as an infinite cooling sheet

which, by virtue of its geometry, sets up a demagnetizing field within the dyke 
that tends to cancel the component of magnetization normal to the dyke. 
There are more than 20 major, readily recognizable diabase dyke swarms in 
the Canadian Shield. The present preliminary report deals with the palaeo- 
magnetism of 6. The study of the remaining swarms is in progress and will be 
reported on at a later date, 
The usual assumptions made in the investigation of the palaeomagnetism 
of igneous rocks is that the rocks under investigation contain a stable compo- 
nent of magnetization that is parallel with the earth's magnetic field at the 
time of their formation and that the earth's field configuration may be con- 
sidered to be that of a coaxial geocentric dipole over the period of time involved 
in the cooling of the dyke swarm. Our immediate objectives are then threefold: 
to examine this assumption, to derive a pole position from the thermoremanent 
magnetization of each swarm and study variations of palaeomagnetic directions 
and intensities within apparently homogeneous swarms, and from this to 
assess palaeomagnetism as a tool in the correlation of basic dykes. 
SAMPLE COLLECTION AND MEASUREMENT 
Six hundred and fifty oriented samples were collected from about 350 sites 
in the initial phase of the program; 225 of these samples are from the six 
swarms discussed in this report. At each site an attempt was made to collect 
at least two samples. It would have been desirable to collect more oriented 
samples at each site, but the additional time required would have meant that 
the swarms could not have been sampled throughout, a requirement for a 
concurrent systematic geochemical and petrographic study of the swarms. 
Two 1-in. cubes were cut from each sample and their magnetization was 
determined with either a spinner or astatic magnetometer. To eliminate the 
viscous component of magnetization usually present in igneous rocks, all cubes 
were subjected to an alternating field whose peak value was empirically set at 
80 or 130 oersteds. Since the apparatus (Larochelle 1962) used in this operation 
did not allow tumbling of the specimens during treatment, the demagnetizing 
procedure was repeated three times with the three axes of the cube successively 
aligned parallel wit11 the axis of the demagnetizing coil. The two cubes of any 
individual sample were purposely oriented in opposite positions (viz. +x, -y, 
-2 vs. -x, +y, +z) to detect the introduction of an anhysteric component 
in the sample. Since in 14% of the samples the magnetic vectors of the tnro cubes 
cut from the individual samples diverged by more than 30 degrees after the 
treatment, these samples were temporarily considered 'unstable'. In most 
samples, this apparent 'instability' was the result of the introduction of an 
anhysteric component of magnetization. Some of these 'unstable' samples have 
since been rewashed with improved equipment; the anhysteric component 
introduced into the samples was eliminated and the magnetization directions 
obtained conform well with results obtained on the original 'stable' samples. 
For the purpose of this preliminary paper, however, the magnetic vectors of

only the 'stable' samples have been used in calculating the mean magnetization 
directions. The magnetization direction for each 'stable' sample was obtained 
by averaging the measurements made on the two cubes cut from that sample. 
Generally, the dispersion of the magnetic vectors within a swarm decreased 
markedly after the alternating field treatment. 
STATISTICAL TREATMENT OF DATA 
The average palaeomagnetic direction of stable samples of each swarm, the 
precision parameter k, and the radius or of the circle of confidence about the 
mean at the probability level of 95% were calculated by the method introduced 
by Fisher (1953). For the Marathon swarm for which only 11 samples were 
available, two 'anomalous' directions were excluded in the computation of 
the mean because of their pronounced distorting effect. 
The stable samples of each swarm appear to represent two populations. One 
exhibits a normal Fisherian distribution with a precision parameter of about 
20 and the other comprises randomly oriented samples. The latter population 
forms 10 to 25% of the samples in a swarm and the samples making up this 
population will be referred to hereafter as 'anomalous'. The magnetization 
directions of the Abitibi swarm may be used in examining the above statement. 
A histogram representing the deviations + of the 58 individual observations 
from the mean is represented in Fig. la. The k calculated for this population 
was 3.5 and the histogram of 9 assuming a Fisherian distribution for the 58 
samples is represented in Fig. lb. The fit of the observed data to the theoretical 
was tested by a x2 test (Watson and Irving 1956) and it was found that the 
distribution of the samples was not Fisherian at the 0.01% probability level 
(Table I). On the other hand if it is assumed that 75% of the samples (44) 
belong to a normal population having a k of 20 and the remaining 14 samples 
are random (k = 0) the histogram of Fig. lc is obtained. The x2 test shows 
that this distribution fits the observed data much better (Table 11). 
The magnetization measurements of the other swarms are characterized by 
similar behavior. The values of k listed in Table I would thus be conservative 
estimates, and the same remark applies to the values of a for the radius of 
confidence, since these populations are all contaminated with random samples. 
It was also noted that if two samples from a site, collected more than 20 ft 
apart, have magnetization directions within 30 degrees of one another, almost 
invariably they are within 30 degrees of the mean magnetization direction of 
the swarm to which they belong. If two such samples differ in magnetization 
direction by more than 30 degrees, then 4 times out of 5, the magnetization 
direction of one sample will lie within 30 degrees of the mean direction of the 
swarm whereas the direction of the second sample is completely erratic, i.e. is 
considerably more than 30 degrees from the mean. This fact also suggests two 
populations, as postulated earlier. 
The measurements may suggest the existence of a primary magnetic popu- 
lation of normal distribution upon which lightning has imposed a second 
population of random orientation. About 25% of Abitibi samples are randomly

I Our data suggest that for purposes of correlation at least three samples more 
than 20 ft apart should be collected from each dyke. If the magnetization 
directions of these samples agree within 30 degrees, then their mean will 
virtually always be close to the mean of the swarm to which the dyke belongs. 
Much of the value of palaeomagnetic measurements in terms of correlation of 
Precambrian dykes will lie in the value of negative correlation. In other words 
if the magnetization direction of a dyke differs considerably from that of 
another body of rock then the two are unlikely to be the same age. On the other 
hand, the difficulty inherent in establishing polar wandering curves for the 
Precambrian means that concordant magnetization directions at present 
provide only supporting evidence of concordant age. 
Some of the above statistical generalization regarding the magnetization of 
Precambrian basic dykes may be appreciably modified with the application of 
improved magnetic washing techniques. 
ABITIBI DYKES 
Geological Setting 
The Abitibi dykes form a northeasterly trending swarm that extends 
roughly 500 miles from at least the Sault Ste. Marie (Ontario) area on the 
southwest to the Lake Mistassini (Quebec) area on the northeast. The name is 
derived from Abitibi Lake near which the dykes are particularly well exposed. 
This swarm contains a relatively small number of dykes, but individual 
dykes are remarkably large, up to 800 ft wide, and up to several hundred 
miles long. Most of the larger dykes are shown on the accompanying map 
(Fig. 2). 
The central parts of the wider dykes are very coarse-grained, and locally

The probable extent of these intrusions has been determined only recently

this body in the midst of Mackenzie dyke intrusions, a similarity of K-Ar

The Mackenzie dykes are rather wide, generally more than 100 ft. In coarse 
central parts of the dykes the plagioclase and pyroxene typically enclose a 
finer-grained pink matrix and very wide dykes typically contain reddish 
granophyric segregations. Biotite is megascopically visible in most of the wider 
members of the swarm. The chemical analysis (Table 111) is the average of 
20 analyses of samples from chilled margins of 20 Mackenzie dykes.

THE MATACHEWAN DYKES 
Geological Setting 
The Matachewan dykes form a northerly striking swarm extending from 
James Bay south to the 47th parallel, and from the Noranda area on the east 
to the Timmins area on the west. They are prominent in the gold camps of 
Ontario and the geological literature of these areas abounds in references to

292 CANADIAN JOURNAL OF EARTH SCIENCES. VOL. 2. 1965 
'R/Iatachewan type' dykes. Locally, for example in the Matachewan area of 
Ontario, these basalt dykes occur in greater profusion than do dykes of any 
other swarm anywhere else in the Shield. W. S. Dyer (1935) states, "the name 
Matachewan was first used by Miller for certain diabase dykes that cut the 
Algoman and earlier rocks but are overlain unconformably by the Cobalt 
conglomerate, because dykes of such relationships were first recognized in the 
Matachewan area by Burrows". 
Most of the known, wider, Matachewan dykes are shown on Fig. 2. The 
dykes are generally less than 100 ft wide and frequently have a porphyritic 
or a glomeroporphyritic texture consisting of either individual crystals or 
roughly spherical aggregates of white or pale green-weathering plagioclase 
crystals in a finer-grained, generally dark green matrix. The analysis (Table 111) 
is the average of eight analyses of samples of chilled marginal phases of eight 
Matachewan dykes. These dykes are referred to compositionally as quartz 
diabase. 
The pre-Cobalt age of the Matachewan dykes provided an exception to the 
once held view that diabase dykes are intrusives of Keweenawan age and 
Gill and L'Esperance (1952) correctly used this as an argument to suggest that 
the Keewenawan age designation of most diabase was, in fact, not correct. 
Fahrig and Wanless (1963) reported a single K-Ar whole-rock age of 2 485 m.y. 
on the chilled margin of a Matachewan diabase dyke. A hornblende age of 
1 740 f 200 m.y. (early Proterozoic) has been reported by Campbell (1962) 
on a northerly striking dyke that cuts the Noranda mine. Our palaeomagnetic 
data suggest that this is a Matachewan dyke (Archaean). If this is correct, 
the age obtained by Campbell must be the result of post-intrusion argon loss 
from the dyke rock. 
Matachewan dykes cause pronounced linear anomalies on the aeromagnetic 
maps of the region in which they occur. 
Palaeomagnetic Data 
Fifty-seven samples were collected from 25 sites on dykes thought to be 
Matachewan type. Four of these samples were considered unstable. The collec- 
tion sites of the remaining 53 samples are shown on Fig. 2 and the magnetization 
directions after washing are plotted in Fig. 10 (a and b). 
The Matachewan dykes appear to be divisible into two groups whose 
palaeomagnetic directions are roughly opposed. The magnetization direction of 
one group is to the northeast (Fig. 10a) and of the other group to the southwest 
(Fig. lob). This relationship suggests the presence of a pole reversal during 
the formation of the dyke swarm. 
Strangway published palaeomagnetic data on a few north-south dykes that 
confirm the mean magnetization directions reported here. 
DISCUSSION OF PALAEOMAGNETIC DATA 
1. In three of the six swarms described above (Mackenzie, Sudbury, 
Matachewan) the mean magnetization direction forms an angle of greater than

30 degrees with the plane of the related dyke swarm. The angle between the 
dyke plane of the Mackenzie swarm and the mean vector is 65 degrees. These 
data contradict Strangway's (1961) suggestion that a correlation exists between 
palaeomagnetic and dyke directions such that the magnetization direction is 
within 24 degrees of the dyke plane. If the magnetization directions of dykes 
are parallel to the earth's field at the time of dyke crystallization, magnetization 
directions should be randomly oriented with respect to the planes of the dykes. 
If the magnetization directions were completely random, then it can be cal- 
culated that 40% of all mean vectors would lie within 24 degrees of any chosen 
plane. There is therefore a 40% chance that the mean vector of any dyke 
swarm will lie within 24 degrees of the plane of the dyke swarm. The correlation 
between vectors and dyke planes suggested by Strangway is not significant 
because of the small number of dyke swarms he studied. 
2. The virtual pole positions (Table I) calculated from the mean vectors of 
the Mackenzie and Sudbury dykes are very close. This suggests that the two 
dyke swarms could have formed contemporaneously. 
The magnetization directions of samples collected widely throughout some 
dyke swarms are moderately well grouped, which suggests that the intrusion 
of these swarms were igneous events of short duration. For example, dispersion 
of the magnetization directions within the Mackenzie swarm (Fig. 5) is mod- 
erately low and these samples were collected over an area of several hundred 
thousand square miles from dykes which vary in strike by at least 30 degrees. 
This suggests that not only was the intrusion of the Mackenzie dykes an event 
of short duration, but that a large section of the western Canadian Shield, 
including parts of three structural provinces, has been relatively stable except 
for epeirogenic movements for at least 1 300 million years.

3. In some samples the reason for the dispersion of magnetization directions 
within a swarm may be found in the geological setting of the swarm. For 
example, Fig. 11 shows the magnetization direction of 14 samples obtained

from 13 different sites in the Sudbury swarm by a single collector. The 
magnetization direction of one sample appears to be 'anomalous'. On closer 
study this sample was found to have certain chemical characteristics that 
distinguish it from the average Sudbury dyke. This rock contains 7% more 
SiOz and less than half the TiOz content of the average Sudbury dyke rock. 
Furthermore, the olivine and pyroxene typical of Sudbury dykes have been 
replaced in this rock by blue-green hornblende. In other respects, trend of the 
dyke, alkali content, and high biotite content, this is a typical Sudbury dyke. 
This sample was taken from within 10 miles of the contact between the 
Superior and Grenville structural provinces. This suggests that the alteration 
of pyroxene and olivine was due to the regional metamorphic effects of the 
Grenville orogeny rather than to deuteric processes. In certain cases, regional 
metamorphic effect might be assessed from a study of dispersion of the 
magnetization directions within a dyke swarm. This may prove to be a delicate 
thermometer as dyke samples exposed to different conditions of regional 
metamorphism may respond to slightly different alternating field treatment. 
Differential rotation of dykes and dyke segments as a result of later crustal 
deformation may be an important factor in the dispersion of magnetization 
vectors within older dyke swarms. During an orogeny, a belt of craton adjacent 
to the mobile belt must experience severe stresses that result in innumerable 
movements along major and minor fault planes. The resultant jostling and

FAHRIG ET AL.: DIABASE DYKES OF CANADIAN SHIELD 295 
differential rotation of crustal blocks containing older dykes or segments of 
dykes may add a significant dispersion factor to the magnetization directions 
of the swarm. The Matachewan dykes, for example, are Archaean in age and 
predate both the Hudsonian and Grenville orogenies. The south part of the 
Matachewan swarm lies within 100 miles of rocks that were intensely deformed 
during both orogenies. It is likely that faulting related to these periods of 
mountain building contributed to the dispersion of the magnetization direc- 
tions of the Matachewan dykes. 
We intend to evaluate the dispersion of magnetization vectors in different 
parts of dyke swarms as a possible index of post-dyke regional deformation. 
CHEMISTRY OF THE DYKES 
The chemical and mineralogical as well as the palaeomagnetic characters of 
diabase dykes may be useful guides in solving problems of correlation of diabase 
dykes and of dyke swarms. Chemical and mineralogical work on the samples 
is being carried out but as this will not be completed for some time, a summary 
of chemical data that is particularly pertinent to the present palaeomagnetic 
study is presented here. The quality of the analyses included in averages 1-5, 
Table 111, is not discussed here; however, the writers feel that their com- 
parability with the results of other analysis and their duplicability are well 
within the range necessary in making the generalizations below. 
It is widely accepted that the diabases of continental dyke and sill swarms 
are strictly the intrusive equivalents of tholeiitic flood basalts (Turner and 
Verhoogen 1960, p. 209). Our preliminary chemical work has indicated that 
this is not so. The alkali-silica ratios (Fig. 12) of the Sudbury and possibly of 
the Mackenzie swarms place them in the alkalic basalt field as defined by

This has an important bearing on one facet of our palaeomagnetic investi- 
gation, namely, the possible correlation of the Sudbury and Mackenzie dykes. 
The two swarms are not significantly different in terms of both palaeomagnetic 
pole position and K-Ar age (Table I). Furthermore, the Mackenzie dykes have 
been traced southeast from the area shown in Fig. 4, across the western Cana- 
dian Shield to within a few hundred miles of Sudbury dykes of similar trend. 
The Sudbury dykes are decidedly more undersaturated than the Mackenzie 
dykes; however, our preliminary chemical data suggest that they belong to 
the same great alkalic suite of rocks. The two swarms will be examined for 
evidence of chemical convergence in passing along strike from one swarm to 
the other. 
CONCLUSIONS 
(1) The close grouping of remanent magnetization directions of samples 
collected widely throughout certain Precambrian basaltic dyke swarms suggests 
that the dykes of individual swarms were intruded over a geologically short 
period of time and acquired and retained a stable thermoremanent magnetiza- 
tion. The general absence of evidence of pole reversal suggests relatively rapid 
formation of the dyke swarms. 
(2) The lack of evidence of a relationship between the direction of magneti- 
zation and the orientation of the plane of the dyke supports the usual 
assumption that the magnetization was parallel to the earth's magnetic field at 
the time of the cooling of the dyke. 
(3) These facts make palaeomagnetic data of practical value in correlating 
diabase dykes and in correlating diabase dykes with intrusive and extrusive 
equivalents. For example, the pole positions of two swarms, the Mackenzie 
and Sudbury, are identical within limits of analytical uncertainty. 
(4) Preliminary pole positions have been determined for six Precambrian 
diabase dyke swarms (Table I and Fig. 13). 
(5) Some data on palaeomagnetic dyke data may be useful in distinguishing 
between late magmatic (deuteric) effects within dykes and the effects of low 
grade regional metamorphism on dykes. Caution should be used in sampling 
dykes near the boundaries of younger structural provinces. 
(6) The dispersion of magnetization directions within a swarm of basalt 
dykes is greater than that generally recorded in single basic volcanic layers or 
in single basic intrusive bodies. This is attributed to the great chance of 
lightning striking high dyke ridges; to the greater period of time involved in 
the intrusion of a dyke swarm; to the difficulty often encountered in correctly 
assigning dykes to a single swarm; to low-grade regional metamorphic effects; 
and to differential rotation of dykes and dyke segments during later crustal 
deformation.

(7) The more extensive diabase dyke swarms are probably indicative of 
great tensional zones and may be considered per se to be evidence of the small- 
scale disruption of continents and evidence of continental drift. 
(8) A requirement of any continental drift hypothesis is the correlation of 
ancient diabase dyke swarms between segments of the hypothetical disrupted 
continent. The palaeomagnetic poles of dyke swarms from different continental 
blocks should be determined to see whether palaeomagnetic poles coincide 
when continental blocks are rotated back into their suggested primordial 
positions. 
(9) Not all diabase dyke swarms are chemical intrusive equivalents of 
tholeiitic flood basalts. This is significant in terms of the origin of basalt and 
greatly enhances the possibility of correlating dyke swarms and correlating 
dykes with extrusive equivalents.
