A PALEOMAGNETIC STUDY OF CONCENTRATING 
IRON ORES FROM NORTHERN MICHIGAN 
D. T. A. SYMONS 
ABSTRACT 
Fifty samples were collected from the concentrating iron ores and 
associated rocks in northern Michigan, U.S.A. They came from: the 
Republic Mine, Marquette Range; the Groveland Mine, Felch Mountain 
District; and along the Menominee Range. Standard paleomagnetic pro- 
cedures were used to study the samples. The Negaunee and Vulcan iron 
formations are thought to have been deposited as primary sediments of 
the hematite-banded and magnetite-banded oxide facies with chemical 
reinanent magnetization (CRM) during the Middle Animikie. During 
dynamic or thermal metamorphism, the primary remanence directions 
were modified causing them to be rotated into the bedding plane to yield 
directions that are random in declination but which are uniformly dis- 
tributed about the bedding plane in inclination. The metamorphism was 
likely associated with the Penokean orogeny during which the iron forma- 
tions were tightly folded and then thermally metamorphosed. Paleo- 
magnetism suggests that the iron formation at the Republic and Groveland 
Mines has been folded into synclines. The Lower Keweenawan diorites 
have a post-folding thermal remanent magnetization (TRM). The over- 
lying Cambrian sandstones have a primary CRM or detrital remanent 
magnetization (DRM). The above paleomagnetic conclusions are con- 
sistent with the geologic evidence. The paleomagnetic pole position 
determined from the Keweenawan diorites and the Cambrian sandstones 
are thought to be fairly reliable. 
INTRODUCTION 
IN a previous study (31), the author found that unmetamorphosed iron 
formation from the Gunflint, Mesabi and Cuyuna iron ranges has a stable 
primary remanence. The purpose of this study was to see if metamorphosed 
iron formation from three localities in northern Michigan (Fig. 1) has a 
similar remanence and if paleomagnetism would prove useful in studying 
the genesis of the concentrating iron deposits in the iron formation. The 
three iron formations are thought to be contemporaneous; they have been 
subjected to low-, intermediate-, and high-grade thermal metamorphism, and 
to moderate and intense dynamic metamorphism; and they are mined as 
concentrating iron ores at two of the localities. Most of the samples for 
this study come from the iron formations and a few samples come from the 
associated Keweenawan diorites and Cambrian clastic sediments. Twenty 
samples come from the Republic Mine on the Marquette iron range, fourteen 
samples from along the Menominee iron range, and sixteen samples from 
the Groveland Mine in the Felch Mountain iron district. The samples from 
these three localities are identified by the prefix letters, "B," "C," and "D" 
respectively before the sample number. In this paper the results from each of

study of the Marquette Range by Van Hise and Bayley (33)'at the turn 
of the century. The stratigraphic sequence shown in Table 1 is taken from 
a recent geologic summary by Boyurn (4). This sequence has been fitted 
into the subdivision of Precambrian time which Goldich et al. (11) proposed. 
At the Republic Mine, shown in Figure 2, the Negaunee iron formation 
of Middle Animikie age is 1400 feet thick (4). Goldich et al. (11) report 
two K-Ar radioactive age determinations of 1.61 and 1.89 billion (109)

The jaspilite ore occurs with either iron formation of the nongranular silicate

The Goodrich quartzite is composed of quartzite with interbeds of slate

is in excess of 3000 feet thick. It represents the Upper Animikie system. 
The Keweenawan diorite intrusives occur as sills and dikes in the 
Negaunee iron formation. There are three prominent sills with an aggregate 
thickness of about 1400 feet and they appear conformable to the bedding of 
the iron formation. One sill occurs on the east side of the Republic Mine

Symons (32) has provided paleomagnetic evidence to show that these sills 
on the Marquette Range are post-folding intrusives rather than conformable 
extrusives as some geologists have proposed (34). 
Origin of the Ore.--James (18) believes that the jaspilite ore was 
deposited as iron formation of the hematite-banded oxide facies in an oxidiz- 
ing environment at the end of Middle Animikie. Subsequent high-grade 
metamorphism created the specular hematite. 
Royce (26) argues that surface waters oxidized the primary siderite in 
the iron formation to hematite at the end of the Middle Animikie. Subse- 
quent metamorphism converted the oxidized iron formation into jaspilite ore. 
Van Hise and Leith (with Mead) (34) state that meteoric solutions of

Upper Animikie age flowed down along a trough formed by the folded 
extrusive "diorite" sheet. These solutions oxidized the siderite in the pri- 
mary iron formation to hematite. Later metamorphic and intrusive activity 
converted the oxidized.iron formation into jaspilite ore. 
Gruner (15, 16) suggests that hydrothermal solutions, derived from an 
igneous source or from groundwater heated by an igneous source, circulated 
in the Negaunee iron formation between the impermeable diorite sill and 
Goodrich quartzite. The solutions oxidized the primary iron minerals in 
the iron formation to specular hematite. 
Boyurn (4) finds that the jaspilite ores of the Marquette Range are 
related to structural features such as folds and to diorite intrusives. Also, 
the ores show replacement features and a higher metamorphic grade than the 
containing iron formation. Therefore, he appears to support an epigenetic 
Symons (32) on paleomagnetic evidence concludes that the stratigraphi- 
cally equivalent and structurally similar hard hematite ore deposit of the 
Cliff-Shaft Mine, Marquette Range, is syngenetic. He believes that it was 
formed as a laterite on exposed iron formation of the magnetite-banded oxide 
facies at the end of the Middle Animikie. 
Paleoma#netic Results.--At the Republic Mine, seventeen samples (B-1 to 
17) were collected from within the mine open pit around the main synclinal 
fold, and three samples (B-18 to 20) from a drift-stripped subcrop around a 
subsidiary synclinal fold as shown in Figure 2. The magnetic character- 
istics of the samples are summarized in Table 2. 
Nine samples (B-i, 4, 5, 6, 9, 10, 14, 16 and 17) of jaspilite ore were 
collected. The ore is composed of fine bands of specular hematite and chert 
with some magnetite-rich and red hematite-rich laminations. The prominent 
preferred orientation in the distribution of the specular hematite is shown 
in Figure 3a. The jaspilite ore yields a stable remanence after AC (alter- 
nating field) demagnetization as shown in Figure 4a where the remanence 
intensity is unchanged between the 300 and 700 oersted (peak) steps. This 
unchanged remanence and the range of magnetic characteristics of the samples 
(Table 2) are consistent with the hypothesis that their remanence originated 
as a chemical remanent magnetization (CRM). Unfolding the synclinal 
structure causes the precision parameter to decrease from 1.3 to 1.2. Both 
values are so low that no statistical significance can be attached to either 
the prefolding or postfolding grouping of remanence directions. However, 
their mean inclination is only 3.5 ø ----- 15 ø (s.d.) from the bedding plane and 
their declinations are randomly oriented as shown in Figure 5b which indicates 
a strong bias of the remanence direction to the bedding plane of the jaspilite 
ore. These jaspilite ore samples exhibit a moderate magnetic anisotropy as 
shown by the susceptibility differences measured along orthogonal axes. The 
measurements show that on average, the maximum susceptibility is at least 
25 percent greater than the minimum susceptibility and approximately parallel 
to the bedding plane. The bias of the remanence direction to the bedding 
plane and the apparent anisotropy in the bedding plane suggest that the 
primary remanence direction has been modified and rotated into the bedding 
plane by metamorphism.

MENOMINEE RANGE 
Geology.--At the turn of the century, W. S. Bayley (3) mapped and 
reported on the geology of the Menominee iron range. Van Hise and Leith 
(34) summarized his work. Two useful summaries that incorporate more 
recent work are by Dutton and Lamey (8) and R. W. Bayley (2). The 
stratigraphy of the range given in Table 1 is taken from James (20). 
The Vulcan iron formation of Middle Animikie age is divided into three 
members on the Menominee iron range: the basal Traders member contains 
mostly iron formation of the magnetite-banded oxide facies; the middle Brier 
member contains slate with a minor graphite, carbonate and magnetite; and 
the upper Curry member contains mostly iron formation of the hematite- 
banded oxide facies (18, 20). James (19) considers that the iron formation 
belongs to the chlorite-biotite metamorphic facies. Goldich et al. (11) report 
one K-Ar radioactive age determination of 1.35 billion (109) years for a 
sample from the underlying sediments of the Chocolay group of Lower 
Animikie age. This date indicates the minimum age of the Chocolay group's 
last metamorphic event which is probably the Penokean orogeny. 
The Vulcan iron formation of the Menominee range has been regionally 
folded into a series of anticlinal and synclinal folds with northwesterly striking 
axes as shown in Figure 6. Superimposed on these regional folds are minor 
pitching troughs caused by cross-folding or faulting. These troughs in places 
contained soft hematite (marrite) deposits of direct-shipping grade in the 
Traders member. No deposits of concentrating iron ore have been exploited. 
The Cambrian is represented by red sandstones that are fiat lying and 
undisturbed and which unconformably overlie the Precambrian Animikie 
strata. 
Paleomagnetic Results.--Fourteen samples (C-1 to 14) were collected 
from along the Menominee Range as shown in Figure 6. All the samples 
were collected from well below the original surface in abandoned mine pits 
except for one sample (C-l) from a surface outcrop, one sample (C-2) from 
a road cut, and two samples (C-3 and 11) from the crests of mine pits. 
Thirteen samples (C-1 to 5 and 7 to 14) were collected from the magnetite- 
banded and hematite-banded oxide facies of the Vulcan iron formation. 
Their remanence directions proved to be quite stable after AC demagnetiza- 
tion removed the unstable components as shown by step-demagnetization 
(Fig. 4d) and reversed-orientation demagnetization tests. The latter tests 
on seven samples yielded an average change in remanence direction of only 
6 ø of arc. The remanence intensities of the samples are quite weak but 
fairly uniform (Table 2) whereas their induced intensities are much more 
intense and varied. Their average anisotropy of magnetic susceptibility is 
quite prominent with the maximum axis at least 25 percent more intense 
than the minimum axis. The precision parameter for their remanence direc- 
tions is 1.9 before unfolding and 1.5 after unfolding, neither of which is 
statistically significant. However, the inclinations of the remanence direc-

GROVELAND MINE 
Geology.--The classic geologic study of the Felch Mountain iron district 
was by Clements and Smyth (5). Subsequent and more detailed studies are 
reported by James et al. (21). Recently Cumberlidge and Stone (6) have 
given an excellent account of the geology of the Groveland Mine. The 
stratigraphic sequence given in Table 1 is taken from James et al. (21). 
At the Groveland Mine, the Vulcan iron formation of Middle Animikie 
age can be subdivided into four members (6) as shown in Figure 8. The 
basal quartzite member contains massive vitreous quartzite with minor mag- 
netite and hematite. It varies between 30 and 110 feet in thickness. The 
lower iron-bearing member belongs to the hematite-banded oxide facies. It

varies between 10 and 235 feet in thickness. The middle iron-bearing mem- 
ber is transitional and belongs to both the hematite-banded and magnetite- 
banded oxide facies. It varies between zero and 30 feet in thickness. Finally, 
the upper iron-bearing member belongs to the magnetite-banded oxide facies. 
It is over 300 feet thick. The iron formation has been thermally metamor- 
phosed to above the staurolite isograd (19) as indicated by the presence of 
diopside, Ca-Mg hornblende, cummingtonite, garnet and recrystallized chert 
(6). Up to 100 feet below the Cambrian-Precambrian unconformity, the 
iron formation may be oxidized to yield specular hematite, jasper and sec- 
ondary carbonate. Also, there is a zone of hydrated iron formation asso- 
ciated with intense fracturing, which contains limonite and carbonate, and 
which occurs immediately below a pyrite zone in the Cambrian sandstone. 
The Felch Mountain iron district is an infolded E-W belt of Animikie 
sediments surrounded by Early Precambrian granites and gneisses. At the 
Groveland Mine, the three iron-bearing members of the Vulcan iron formation

are mined as an iron ore of concentrating grade. The structure of the deposit 
has not been clearly established. Cumberlidge and Stone (6) favor the 
possibility that the structure is a tight overturned syncline with an axial 
plane that strikes E-W and dips at -60øN as shown in Figure 8. As evi- 
dence for the syncline, they cite the rapid thickening of the iron formation at 
the deposit and the apparent closure of the iron formation around the east 
end of the deposit. The second possibility is that the structure is a single 
monoclinal limb for, as Stone (27) states, the synclinal axis has not been 
found despite the complete rock exposure in the mine pit. There is a major 
E-W strike-slip fault cutting through the center of the deposit and there are 
several minor faults as shown in Figure 8. The deposit is cut by several

CONCENTRATING IRON ORES 131 
N-S granitic dikes too narrow to be shown in Figure 8. The deposit is 
partially and unconformably overlain by undisturbed, flatly-dipping Cambrian 
sediments. 
Origin of the Ore.--Cumberlidge and Stone (6) believe that thermal 
metamorphism altered the mineralogy but did not alter the bulk chemistry or 
oxidation state of the primary iron formation to form the concentrating 
iron ore. 
James (18, 19) and James et al. (21) believe that thermal metamorphism 
altered the mineralogy and changed the oxidation state, but that it did not 
change the bulk chemistry of the primary iron formation in forming the 
concentrating iron ore. 
Van Hise and Leith (with Smyth) (34) believe that the iron silicates 
and carbonates in the primary iron formation were oxidized by meteoric 
solutions, and then the altered iron formation was metamorphosed to form 
the concentrating iron ore. 
Paleomagnetic Results.--All the samples (D-1 to 15) were collected from 
well below the original surface in the mine open pit except for one sample 
(D-16) which was collected from a drift-stripped subcrop as shown in Fig- 
ure 8. The samples of Vulcan iron formation were collected from all four 
members and from both sides of the ore body. 
Fourteen samples (D-1 to 8 and 10 to 15) were collected from the Vulcan 
iron formation of which one sample (D-13) crumbled so that it could not 
be measured, and a second sample (D-7) from the E-W fault zone proved 
to have unstable remanence so that it was excluded. The four samples from 
the basal quartzite (D- 1 and 3) and lower iron-bearing (D-2 and 15) mem- 
bers have fairly uniform magnetic characteristics which include stable rema- 
nence moments of low intensity (Table 2) which suggest a CRM. Their 
remanence directions form a cluster with precision parameters of 11.8 and 
10.9 before and after unfolding, respectively (Fig. 7b). Either group may 
have statistical significance; however, the samples have similar tectonic cor- 
rections so that the fold test is not diagnostic. Eight samples came from the 
middle iron-bearing member (D-14) and its oxidized equivalent (D-8) and 
from the upper iron-bearing member (D-4, 5, 6, 11 and 12) and its hydrated 
equivalent (D-10). The single oxidized and hydrated samples do not appear 
to have any diagnostic magnetic property which warrents individual discussion 
and so they are included in the group of eight samples. These samples have 
a wide range of magnetic properties that reflects their mixed ferromagnetic 
mineralogy (as shown in Table 2). In particular, they have large unstable 
remanence moments due mostly to the presence of magnetite as shown in 
Figure 4e. Also, these samples have directions of maximum magnetic sus- 
ceptibility that exceed the directions of minimum susceptibility by at least 40 
percent in magnitude on the average. Unf. olding causes the precision param- 
eter for the remanence directions of those eight samples after AC demagnetiza- 
tion to decrease from 2.3 to 1.8 assuming the structure is a monocline and to 1.2 
assuming a syncline. None of these values for the precision parameter has 
statistical significance, which suggests the presence of more than one type

132 D. T. A. SYMONS 
of remanence. However, the remanence inclinations have an average value 
of 10ø--- + 9 ø (s.d.) relative to the bedding plane of the iron formation and 
randomly oriented declinations assuming a syncline as shown in Figure 7d 
whereas there is not a systematic pattern assuming a monocline. This 
remanence pattern indicates that the primary remanence directions of samples 
from the middle and upper iron-bearing members have been modified and 
thereby rotated into the bedding plane through metamorphism, and that the 
deposit has a synclinal structure. The co-existence of magnetite and hematite 
as shown in Figure 3b and noted by Cumberlidge and Stone (6), militates 
against any genetic hypotheses that advocate the alteration of the mineralogy 
by hydrothermal or meteoric solutions. 
Four Cambrian samples were collected from sandstone (C-6) on the 
Menominee Range (Fig. 6), and from sandstone (D-16) and basal con- 
glomerate (D-9A and 9B) at the Groveland Mine (Fig. 8). The two basal 
conglomerate samples yield divergent remanence directions as shown in 
Figure 7c. One sample (D-9B) has a specific gravity of 2.94 and a mod- 
erately stable remanence (Fig. 4f) which reflect the presence of the observed 
hematitic pebbles of iron formation. The other sample (D-9A) contains 
only a matrix material for it has a specific gravity of 2.68 which corresponds 
to values of 2.69 and 2.48 determined for the sandstone samples (C-6 and 
D-16, respectively). The latter three samples (C-6; D-9A and 16) have 
very uniform magnetic characteristics (Table 2) which include extremely 
stable remanence moments that are almost unchanged by AC demagnetization 
as shown in Figure 4c. The remanence directions of the three samples yield 
a post-folding precision parameter of 5.9 and the computed paleomagnetic 
pole position agrees closely with the other Cambrian positions (17). The 
remanence is probably a CRM associated with the ultra-fine hematite grains 
that surround the well-sorted quartz grains or oblites. The conglomerate test 
given by samples D-9A and D-9B is indicative of remanence stability since 
deposition of the. conglomerate during the Cambrian period. 
CONCLUSIONS 
tnimikie Iron Formations.--The remanence directions from these three 
examples of iron formation yield the same distinctive pattern in which the 
remanence directions are uniformly distributed about the bedding plane in 
inclination and randomly distributed in declination. Most geologists (20, 
22, 23, 34) agree that the Negaunee iron formation of the Republic Mine, 
Marquette iron range, and the Vulcan iron formation of the Groveland Mine, 
Felch Mountain iron district, and of the Menominee iron range are con- 
temporaneous sediments of Middle Animikie age. It is probable that they 
have somewhat similar geologic histories because they come from a small area 
in the same geologic province. 'Unmetamorphosed and slightly metamor- 
phosed iron formations of the same age and region (31) and elsewhere (24, 
35) have yielded well-grouped prefolding remanence directions from stable 
primary CRM. However, these three iron formations have been metamor- 
Downloaded from http://pubs.geoscienceworld.org/segweb/economicgeology/article-pdf/62/1/118/3482905/118.pdf by Curtin University Library user on 15 June 2026

CONCENTRATING IRON ORES 133 
phosed in the Penokean orogeny (19) after burial by the Upper Animikie 
Michigamme series. If, during metamorphism, new ferromagnetic minerals 
were formed or if the Curie temperatures of the ferromagnetic minerals were 
exceeded, then the iron formations would have well-grouped post-folding CRM 
or TRM directions. This leads to the second general conclusion. 
The primary remanence of these metamorphosed iron formations was to 
a large extent but not entirely modified during metamorphism. Most likely 
the iron formations were deposited during the Middle Animikie as chemical 
sediments of the hematite-banded and magnetite-banded oxide facies with a 
primary CRM. Several bits of evidence indicate that a residual of this 
primary component is still present. First, the prefolding remanence direction 
(74 ø, 41ø; a63- 14 ø) found for the basal' and lower iron-bearing members 
of the Vulcan iron formation at the Groveland Mine after tectonic correction 
is similar in inclination, though not in declination due to relative tectonic 
rotation, to that (169 ø, 19ø; 63- 20 ø) found for the primary Negaunee 
iron formation at the east end of the Marquette Range (32). Second, 
if the conglomeratic iron formation at the Republic Mine has a sedimentary 
origin, then the divergence of the remanence directions within and between 
its samples suggests that some of the primary remanence component has 
survived metamorphism. Third, the co-existence of hematite and magnetite 
in both the Republic and Groveland Mine deposits (Figs. 3a, 3b; reference 5), 
the superposition of the magnetite-banded oxide facies over the hematite- 
banded oxide facies at the Groveland Mine, and the preservation of unaltered 
and undeformed primary structures and textures in the iron formations (21), 
all suggest that the iron formations were not altered by groundwater or 
hydrothermal solutions before burial, during diagenesis, or later. Thus it 
seems probable that the primary remanence was significantly modified in 
some way during metamorphism to yield the distinctive pattern but not 
completely eliminated. 
The process of remanence modification is not clear but it seems likely that 
metamorphism caused a dominant stable PPRM, PTRM or PCRM (partial 
pressure, thermal, or chemical reinanent magnetization, respectively) com- 
ponent to be superimposed on the primary component (17). The process 
is obscured by the complexity of the geology which involves the interrelation 
of mixed ferromagnetic mineralogy with a complex stress and thermal his- 
tory. Such a combination of components could yield the required remanence 
pattern. James et a.1. (19, 21) consider that the metamorphism was domi- 
nantly thermal because they found that: (a) the primary o61ites in the iron 
formation of the Groveland Mine are undeformed by stress; (b) the crystal 
dimensions of the minerals in the iron formation increase steadily with 
increased thermal metamorphic grade; and (c) new mineral facies are pro- 
gressively developed in the iron formation to delimit the thermal meta- 
morphic grades. Also, they believe that the increased grain size made 
economic beneficiation of the iron formation possible. Such a transformation 
in the ferromagnetic minerals would result in a PTRM or PCRM. The 
author considers that dynamic metamorphism was very important because:

134 D. T. A. SYMONS 
(a) the remanence pattern of these three metamorphosed iron formations is 
independent of their thermal metamorphic grade, which reached the chlorite- 
biotite facies on the Menominee Range, the staurolite facies at the Groveland 
Mine, and the sillimanite facies at the Republic Mine which represent low-, 
medium-, and high-grade intensities, respectively (19); (b) all three iron 
formations have been strongly deformed to about the same extent by dynamic 
metamorphism, which caused them to be tightly folded into synclines at the 
Republic and Groveland Mines and into synclines and anticlines on the 
Menominee Range; (c) the finding of the remanence pattern is dependent 
on thecorrect structural interpretation which, incidentally, supports the syn- 
clinal structural interpretation for the Groveland Mine where the structural 
interpretation is in some doubt; (d) the prominent magnetic anisotropy 
illustrated by the magnetic susceptibility of the iron formations in which the 
average ratio of the maximum axis to minimum axis is about 1.5: 1.0 with the 
maximum axis closely parallel to the bedding plane, has a much greater 
magnitude than found in unmetamorphosed iron formations (30) and is 
probably a response to increased pressure; (e) extreme dynamic metamor- 
phism in similar Precambrian iron formation in the USSR has strongly 
affected the remanence and caused it to become unstable (36); and (f) as 
Nagata (25) has shown, even the magnetic properties of aggregations of 
simple ferromagnetic minerals behave unpredictably in stress fields. This 
evidence suggests that a significant PPRM component is present in' the 
remanence. Also, a combination of primary and secondary components sug- 
gests the explanation of why the remanence of the middle and upper iron- 
bearing members of the Vulcan iron formation at the Groveland Mine has 
been modified whereas that of basal and lower members has not been modified 
by metamorphism. The former contain mostly coarse-grained magnetite that 
is much more susceptible to dynamic and thermal remanence alteration than 
the latter, which contain mostly fine-grained hematite. This interpretation 
is supported by the evidence of the two samples (D-6 and 10) from the 
upper iron-bearing members that have hematite as a major constituent and 
which give remanence directions that are close to those of the basal and lower 
iron-bearing members (Figs. 7b, 7d). It is noted that the remanence of the 
middle and upper members may have been more affected than that of the 
basal and lower members by dynamic metamorphism because of the former's 
position in the center of the fold structure. The direction of the secondary 
component would depend on the relative orientations of the sample, the 
adjacent rocks and the Earth's magnetic field in addition to temperature, 
pressure, and chemical considerations. The bias of the remanence directions 
about the bedding plane could possibly be explained by the "infinite magnetic 
sheet" hypothesis of Strangway (28). Summarizing, there does not appear 
to be a thoroughly satisfactory explanation of how the primary CRM of the 
iron formations was modified during metamorphism to form the distinctive 
pattern although a PPRM component appears to be the most attractive 
explanation. 
Keweenawan Diorites.--The Keweenawan diorites have a post-foldin# 
TRM with a Lower Keweenawan direction. After the Penokean orogeny 
Downloaded from http://pubs.geoscienceworld.org/segweb/economicgeology/article-pdf/62/1/118/3482905/118.pdf by Curtin University Library user on 15 June 2026

CONCENTR.dTING IRON ORES 135 
and metamorphism, the Lower Keweenawan diorites were intruded into the 
folded iron formations as sills and dikes as shown at the Republic Mine, to 
yield a post-folding TRM with a Lower Keweenawan direction. The ferro- 
magnetic minerals in the iron formation adjacent to the diorites were heated 
through their Curie point temperatures and perhaps recrystallized as different 
minerals so that they now have a post-folding TRM or CRM of Lower 
Keweenawan age and belong to the magnetite-banded oxide facies. During 
the remainder of the Keweenawan period, the Grenville orogeny, and the 
infra-Cambrian period, the iron formation and diorites were not altered or 
subjected to significant structural rotation or deformation. 
Cambrian Sediments.--The Cambrian sediments have a very stable pri- 
mary CRM or DRM in a Cambrian direction. The Cambrian sandstones and 
conglomerates were deposited unconformably over the Precambrian forma- 
ti.ons with a stable primary CRM or DRM. They, and the older formations, 
have been essentially unchanged or unmoved since the Cambrian. 
Summary.--The paleoma.gnetic results are consistent with the geologic 
evidence. They support the hypothesis that the Negaunee and Vulcan iron 
formations of the Republic Mine, Groveland Mine, and Menominee Range 
were deposited as iron formations of the magnetite-banded and hematite- 
banded oxide facies during the Middle Animikie. During the Upper Animi- 
kie they were buried by the Michigamme series, and then during the Penokean 
orogeny they were dynamically and thermally metamorphosed. These meta- 
morphic events probably did not change appreciably the bulk chemistry, the 
oxidation state, or the ferromagnetic mineralogy of the iron formations 
although they did alter the texture and the magnetic domain structure of the 
ferromagnetic minerals through dominantly stress effects. Except for a 
narrow zone of contact thermal metamorphism associated with the later 
intrusion of the Keweenawan diorites, the iron formations have not been 
subsequently altered. This interpretation of the genesis of these metamor- 
phosed iron formations that form the concentrating ores of the Republic and 
Groveland Mines agrees most closely with that proposed by Cumberlidge 
and Stone (6) for the Groveland Mine. 
Only the paleomagnetic pole positions derived from the Keweenawan 
diorite and Cambrian sandstone are thought to be reasonably reliable, and 
they are given in Table 2. The Animikie strata are thought to have been 
rotated so that a tectonic correction cannot be applied to derive a reliable 
pole position.

A Study of the Palaeomagnetism of the Bushveld Gabbrot 
By D. I. GOUGH and C. B. VAN NIEKERK 
National Physical Research Laboratory, 
Council for Scientific and Industrial Research, Pretoria 
[Received November 7, 19581 
ABSTRACT 
Data are presented on the natural remanent magnetization at five sites 
of the Main Gabbro zone of the Bushveld Igneous Complex. It is found that 
the directions of N.R.M. at the five sites would agree more closely if the 
rock at each site were rotated about the strike of tho pseudo-stratification 
so as to make its dip zero. This indicates that the gabbro became 
magnetized before the crust subsided to form the basin in which the 
Complex now lies. The same results show that the N.R.M. of the gabbro 
has been stable since before the crustal subsidence. Stability of the N.R.M. 
is further dornonstrated by the highly consistent directions of magnetization 
making a large angle with the present field. After correction for dip, and on 
the assumption that the ga.bbro was magnetized in the field of a geocentric 
dipole, the mean north magnetic pole from the five sites lies at 23" N. 36" E. 
The age of the Complex is close to 2.0 x 108 years. The palaeomagnetic 
results show that the crust supported the load due to the gabbro intrusion 
without subsidence for at least the time taken by this intrusion to cool to 
the Curie temperature of its ferrimagnetic constituents. A lower limit to 
this time is estimated, on reasonable assumptions, to be of the order of 
105 years, so that the South African crust 2 x loe years ago appears to have 
had very considerable strength. 
0 1. INTRODUCTION 
THE Bushveld Igneous Complex is one of the largest systems of intrusive 
rocks known. Figure 1 
shows its general structure, as given by du Toit. A basin, some 200 miles 
long from east to west and about 90 miles from north to south, is filled 
principally with gabbro (often described as norite, as in fig. 1) and red 
granite, the gabbro being exposed round the flanks of the basin with the 
granite in the centre. The total area of gabbroic rock is nearly 20 000 
sq. miles. The metamorphosed sediments of the Transvaal System which 
surround and underlie the gabbro, show systematic dips towards the 
centre of the Complex. In its lower levels the gabbro itself is differentiated 
into banded mineral assemblages which are inclined like the underlying 
sediments. Higher in the intrusion, pseudo-stratification in the undiffer- 
entiated gabbro shows similar, though loss obvious, evidence of dip 
towards the centre of the basin. Such data have led to the conclusion 
that the intrusion caused an extensive subsidence of the crust at some 
time after crystallization was well advanced. 
Its main features are described by du Toit (1954).

The age of the granite of the Complex has recently been firmly established. 
Schreiner (1958) used rubidium-strontium decay measured in total rock 
and separated mineral samples. He gives the age 1920 million years for 
the Bushveld granite, using half-life 5-0 x 1O1O years, with 99% confidence 
limits & 130 million years. Nicolaysen et al. (in the press) used rubidium- 
strontium and uranium-lead decay in various minerals from the Bushveld 
granite and give a mean age of 1950 5 150 million years. A specimen of 
biotite-bearing pyroxenitic gabbro from the Merensky Reef in the differ- 
entiated zone of the gabbro was found to be 2050 5 50 million years old 
(Nicolaysen et al.), The Bushveld Complex is therefore one of the best 
dated of ancient rock systems. The age of the gabbro must be close to 
2.0 x 109 years. The known age, together with the relative accuracy 
with which strike and dip could be defined round the basin, led to the 
palaeomagnetic study here reported.

5 2. SAMPLING AND MEASUREMENT 
Samples were cores of diameter one-half inch drilled from the rock at 
the site by means of a portable field drill fitted with a diamond coring 
crown. Before removal each core was oriented in one of several ways. 
Most of the surface cores were oriented with reference to the sun’s azimuth, 
some with reference to survey beacons and a few from a magnetic compass, 
which was not appreciably deflected by the gabbro. The underground 
cores from chrome mines were oriented relative to the mine survey 
networks. From one to four specimens one-half inch long were cut from 
each core in the laboratory, the number being two in nearly all cases.

The natural remanent magnetization (N.R.M.) of each specimen was 
measured in direction and intensity by means of an electromagnetic 
‘spinner’ type magnetometer. The specimens from the Bon Accord 
quarries (Site 4) were measured with the magnetometer used for the study 
of the Pilanesberg dykes (Gough 1956). All other specimens were measured 
with a new and much improved spinner magnetometer which will be 
described elsewhere. 
Mean directions were found for each core from the specimens (normally 
two) cut from it, and the unit in the statistical data and in the stereograms 
of fig. 2 is the mean direction for a core. 
$3. FIELD WORK 
It has been found that, in general, rock samples from the surface in 
South Africa are of little or no use for palaeomagnetic studies (Gough 
1956, Graham and Hales 1957). Attention was therefore confined to 
exposures of fresh rock in excavations. A set of cores from a quarry 
in the Main Gabbro zone at Bon Accord, north of Pretoria (see fig. 1, 
Site 4) gave north-seeking poles directed near the downward vertical, as 
shown in fig. 2. This result immediately raised the question whether 
the directions of N.R.M. should be corrected for the dip of the gabbro, 
that is, whether the N.R.M. observed had been acquired with the rock in 
its present attitude or in some other. The obvious way to answer this 
question was to sample the formation elsewhere where its strike and dip 
were as widely different as possible from those at Bon Accord. Cores were 
therefore collected from chrome mines in the north-east and north-west 
flanks of the basin. No undifferentiated gabbro or norite was exposed in 
these mines, and the pyroxenite cores were found to be feebly magnetized 
with scattered directions. A set of cores from a dam site (Site 5) near 
Roossenekal, in the eastern flank of the Main Gabbro zone showed close 
grouping of directions of N.R.M. Thereafter sampling was confined to 
exposures of the Main Gabbro zone. Pive sites were sampled, including 
the two already mentioned. Site 1 is a 
group of three quarries near Rustenburg, and Sites 2 and 3 are quarries 
near Brits, all in the Main Gabbro. Careful search failed to discover 
any suitable exposures of gabbro in the west, north-west or north-east 
flanks of the basin. 
Table 1 gives the positions of the five sites, and the strike and dip of 
the pseudo-stratification at each. The determinations of dip and strike 
presented problems because the rock at this horizon is homogeneous and 
shows no bands of mineral assemblages such as produce visible layering 
lower in the gabbro. Lenticular xenoliths of quartzite, which are oriented 
parallel to the pseudo-stratification, were well exposed only in one quarry. 
The rock develops natural fracture planes on weathering which follow 
the pseudo-stratification, and where such planes were freshly exposed in 
quarry excavations they were used for determination of dip and strike. 
Similar fracture surfaces exposed as outcrops at the surface were found

Figure 4(a) shows the oval of 99% confidence for the position. of tha 
North magnetic pole given by the data from each site, on the assumption 
that the observed N.R.M. was produced by the field of a geocentric dipole. 
Figure 4 (b) gives the corresponding North magnetic pole positions after 
correction for dip. It is clear from figs. 3 and 4 that the consistency of 
the data improves markedly when the pseudo-stratification is made 
horizontal at each site. This amounts to Graham's stability test on a 
large scale (Graham 1949). The simplest explanation is that the gabbro 
acquired its N.R.M. before the development of the crustal subsidence 
and that the N.R.M. has remained stable since the subsidence took place. 
It is possible that subsidence did not take place until after the passage 
of an appreciable fraction of the total time since the intrusion of the 
gabbro. Apart from the evidence of stability afforded by th0 subsidence, 
there is a strong argument for stability in the consistent and closely 
grouped N.R.M. vectors making an angle of about 120' with the present 
geomagnetic field. It is reasonable to suppose that the observed N.R.M. 
is the original thermo-remanent magnetization acquired when the gabbro 
cooled. 
The m0an positions of the North magnetic pole, derived from the five 
sites after correction for dip on the assumption of a geocentric dipole field, 
are given in table 3. The mean of the five mean pole positions with equal 
weights gives a North magnetic pole at latitude 23"N., longitude 36" E. 
There is relatively little difference between this and the pole position at 
the time of the intrusion of the Pilanesberg dykes.

to have been intruded rapidly enough so that its whole thickness was 
near the magma temperature at one time. In order to derive a minimum 
time for cooling of the Main Gabbro it will be assumed that the highly 
differentiated Critical Zone of the gabbro was already in place below it. 
Above the Main Gabbro was cap-rock whose position is now occupied by 
granite. The inclinations of the Transvaal System floor, of the Critical 
Zone, of the gabbro and of the granite are similar, and it is reasonable to 
suppose that the Main Gabbro formed a parallel sided slab after intrusion. 
If the cap-rock was much thicker than the gabbro slab, a lower limit for 
the cooling time would be given by taking the cap-rock above and the 
Critical Zone below to have been at zero temperature when the gabbro was 
intruded. There is in fact evidence that the Critical Zone was still at a 
high temperature. Du Toit (1954, p. 184) gives 15000 feet as a repre- 
sentative thickness for the Main Gabbro zone. The five sites described in 
this paper are near the centre of the Main Gabbro. Assuming that the 
Main Gabbro was initially at 1000"~ and had great thicknesses of rock at 
ordinary temperatures above and below it, an estimate can be made of the 
time required for it to cool to 600"c. Jaeger has calculated curves for 
this case, with assumed values of the thermal constants, which give 
time in years = 0.0 1 6D2 
for the temperature near the centre of such a slab to fall from 1000"~ to 
600"c, where D is the thickness in metres. At a point D/20 from the 
contact the corresponding time is O~010D2, so that neither convection nor 
the position within the slab affects the order of magnitude. With 
D = 4700 m, the time is 3.5 x lo5 years. The simplifying assumptions 
which do not minimize the time are (1) that the cap-rock was thick compared 
with the intrusion, (2) that the intrusion extended beyond the sites at 
least two or three times its thickness. Unless these assumptions are 
greatly in error it seems reasonable to conclude that the gabbro at the 
sampling sites took longer than a time of the order of 105 years to cool 
from 1000"~ to 600"c. The crust apparently supported the gabbro for 
a time greater than this without subsiding into the present basin. This 
suggests that the crust in South Africa 2 x lo9 years ago had very consider- 
able strength. There is of course no evidence from the present work to 
show whether a block including the whole of the Bushveld Complex moved 
so as to reduce the stresses.

Iron-rich and magnesium-rich basaltic tholeiites of the latest Archean Kinojevis Group, central Abitibi Belt, northeastern 
Ontario, contain a natural remanent magnetization that is generally multivectorial. The components in all units reside in 
essentially pure magnetite, not the original titanomagnetites (where x for Fe3-,Ti,04 probably was 0.60-0.65). Any original 
TRM was lost by chemical reconstitution of the magnetic oxides in response to primary deuteric conditions, long-term burial, 
regional metamorphism to prehnite-pumpellyite facies, and possibly intrusion by Matachewan dikes. Data from contact tests 
with Matachewan dikes indicate that the units are indeed capable of retaining a very latest Archean - earliest Proterozoic field 
(e.g., D = 194.9, I = - 14.3", k = 8.1, a95 = 7.9"; n = 45 vectors, 38 samples). High-coercivity, high-blocking-temperature 
directions from samples from other flows, corrected for nearly penecontemporaneous downwarping, are in only crude agreement 
with those of Matachewan dikes, possibly suggesting that these components reflect a general Late Archean - Early Proterozoic 
field for the Superior Province. The paleomagnetic data from Kinojevis tholeiites indicate the emplacement, burial, and tight 
downwarping of the 10 km or so of Kinojevis stratigraphy were nearly synchronous with Matachewan intrusion. The Kinojevis 
data by themselves cannot be taken as statistically reliable indicators of the pre- (or immediately post-) Matachewan geomagnetic 
field nor can temperature-time relations for magnetic viscosity be used to predict the preservation of a statistically reliable TRM in 
any of these units. Individual magnetization components were blocked over geologically short periods of time, whereas the 
ensemble of data from discrete flows must record secular variations, field excursions, and possibly long-term polar wander.

Success in compilation of APW paths requires that the 
field be recorded as continuously as possible by the rock 
record. The intermittent nature of Archean plutonism, 
however, makes this task difficult. Alternatively, 
volcanic units fill many gaps in the Archean rock record 
(Goodwin and Ridler 1970; Goodwin 1974, 1978, 
1980). Although extrusives constitute a significant 
portion of Archean terranes, their paleomagnetism has 
been studied only infrequently and those few studies 
have often been unsuccessful in deciphering any totally 
consistent record (Halls 1975; Pesonen 1973; Schwarz 
1966, 1977; D. J. Dunlop, personal communication, 
1980), though exceptions exist (e.g., Ridler and Foster 
1981). The TRM in Archean metavolcanics, if it is 
retained and can be isolated (e,g., McElhinny and 
Senenayake 1980), might be used to fill in important 
gaps in Archean APW paths. "Primary" and secondary 
magnetizations in Archean metavolcanics may be of 
benefit in deciphering complex structures and in 
exploration for massive sulfide deposits by explaining 
the effects of ocean floor alteration, regional 
metamorphism, and massive sulfide mineralization on 
the NRM. 
In this and in companion contributions (Geissman et 
al. 1982, and in preparation; Letros et al. 1983; 
Tasillo-Hirt et al. 1982) we describe the NRM, magnetic 
properties, and aeromagnetic signature of metavolcan- 
ics and metasediments in the central Abitibi Greenstone 
Belt. Between Kirkland Lake and Lake Abitibi (Fig. l), 
the low degree of deuteric alteration and dynamothermal 
metamorphism (Dimroth and Lichtblau 1979) and the 
near absence of later intrusive activity all, in theory, 
imply the retention of at least the high-blocking- 
temperature portion of a TRM. The relatively simple 
tectonism of some units may allow corrections to be 
made for structure and "primary" magnetizations to thus 
be included in APW paths. Schutts and Dunlop (1981) 
reported magnetization data from "basalts and gabbros" 
in the central Abitibi Belt that they suggested are 
representative of a Late Archean geomagnetic field 
existing during volcanism and plutonism. They did not 
correct their data for regional structure, citing arguments 
that "structure in the volcanics developed during 
deposition" and quoting paleomagnetic data from 
sill-like gabbros yielding negative fold tests. This paper 
is concerned with tholeiitic basalts of the Kinojevis 
Group (Jensen 19784, 1979, 1981). We studied the 
AN ET AL. 437 
paleomagnetism of four geologically and petrologically 
well characterized "sites" in Kinojevis flows in order to 
determine in detail the nature of their NRM. Detailed 
mapping indicates that flows at all of these areas were 
deposited horizontally and deformed only by simple 
tilting. A "primary" remanence, if indeed one exists, 
should be corrected for regional structure. 
General geology I 
The area sampled (Fig. 1) is part of Goodwin and 
Ridler's (1970) Noranda-Benoit volcanic complex, in 
the central Abitibi Belt. As this paper represents our 
initial studies of the paleomagnetism of this belt, the 
geology of the area is described in relative detail here; in 
other papers only the most pertinent aspects are 
included. The Ontario portion of the complex is 
composed of three subalkalic volcanic cycles, each 
associated with sedimentation and intrusion of 
comagmatic units (Jensen 1978a, 1981). The strati- 
graphic sequence is illustrated in Fig. 2. The Kinojevis 
Group, of the second volcanic cycle, is well preserved 
on both limbs of a major east-west-trending 
synclinorium in the Noranda-Benoit volcanic complex. 
At the base of the second cycle, flows of ultramafic and 
basaltic komatiite composition are interlayered with 
calc-alkalic tuff and tuff breccias, conglomerates, 
greywackes, argillites, cherts, and iron formation. 
Ultramafic and mafic members of this sequence, 
collectively termed the Stoughton-Roquemaure Group 
in the north and the Larder Lake Group in the south I 
(Jensen 1979), become predominant upwards in the I I 
section. The Stoughton-Roquemaure Group is approxi- 
mately 10 km in thickness and is conformably overlain 
by the Kinojevis Group. The Kinojevis Group consists 
of a 10 km thick succession of alternating magnesium- 
and iron-rich tholeiitic basalts, with minor andesites, 
i 
I 
dacites, and rhyolites. Flows average about 65 m in I 
thickness and are often traceable for several kilometres. 
They generally consist of a basal zone of flattened glass 
shards (hyaloclastite) and spherulites, a central zone of 
coarse cumulate material, overlying granular basalt, and 
an often highly vesiculated, shard-rich flow top (Pearce 
and Birckett 1974; Jensen 1978b; Jackson 1980~). 
Individual flows either alternate between iron- and 
magnesium-rich compositions or are grouped into 
sequences of several iron- or magnesium-rich units. 
Pearce and Birckett (1974) suggested on petrologic and 
geochemical groups that each flow has experienced 
some degree of in situ differentiation. 
Above the Kinojevis lavas is 12 km of calc-alkaline 
volcanics and hypabyssal intrusives, which occupy the 
center of the synclinorium. These constitute the Blake 
River Group; they were formed by the partial melting of 
ultramafic and mafic rocks of the lower komatiitic and 
tholeiitic volcanics (Jensen 198 1). 
The third volcanic cycle is preserved on both the south

438 CAN. J. EARTH SCI. VOL. 20, 1983 
limb of the synclinorium, along the Kirkland Lake - 
Larder Lake Fault Zone, and on the north limb, along the 
Destor-Porcupine Fault Zone (Fig. 1). In the south, 
approximately 3 km of fluvial sediments and turbidites, 
trachytes, and syenite stocks (collectively the Timis- 
kaming Group) is either in fault contact or unconform- 
ably overlies volcanics of the second cycle. 
North-south-trending Matachewan diabase dikes cut 
all volcanic cycles. However, the dikes, usually 
recognized by their aeromagnetic anomalies, are rare to 
non-existent in the central part of the Noranda-Benoit 
synclinorium (Lumbers and Milne 1978; Pyke et al. 
197 1). Their concentration increases westward from a 
point approximately lOkm east of Highway 11, 
reaching a maximum density (approximately two dikes 
per kilometre) west of Timmins. 
Letros et al. (1983) have described the aeromag- 
netism of the area between Lake Abitibi and Kirkland 
Lake. The Kinojevis Group, in particular, appears as 
a conspicuous set of alternating high and low east- 
northeast-trending magnetic anomalies, corresponding 
to iron-rich and magnesium-rich flow sequences, 
respectively. 
The depositional and structural history of the 
Noranda-Benoit volcanic complex has been interpreted 
in several ways (Goodwin and Ridler 1970; Jensen 
1978a, 1979, 1981; Goodwin 1980). Flows of the first 
and second volcanic cycles appear to have been extruded 
within a shallow, ocean basin environment (Jensen 
1981). Flow thicknesses and percentages of silicic flows 
increase toward the center of the synclinorium on both 
limbs, suggesting that the source area was near the fold 
axis. Kinojevis flows were deposited on mild 
topography and were tilted downward in the center of 
the synclinorium to accommodate additional lavas. 
With Blake River magmatism, an irregular topography 
was created by volcanic centers near the, fold axis. 
Accumulation of approximately 30 km of lavas and 
hypabyssal intrusives and the withdrawal of a sizeable 
magma chamber at depth ultimately caused the gradual 
downwarping of the volcanic complex into its present 
form. A few kilometres north and south of the syncline 
axis, orientations of flows as measured on compressed 
shards and pillows are nearly vertical. Contacts between 
Kinojevis flows are generally conformable and thus 
major downwarping of the complex was continuous 
until the waning stages of Blake River magmatism. 
Vertical movements of several hundreds of metres 
occurred along the Kirkland Lake - Larder Lake and 
Destor-Porcupine Fault Zones. These faults were 
probably major mechanisms for subsidence during the 
deposition of the second volcanic cycle (Jensen 1981). 
During Timiskaming deposition, both fault zones acted 
as graben structures, trapping steeply dipping units 
within a narrow belt. Emplacement of Matachewan 
dikes followed development of the synclinorium. 
There is evidence to suggest that at least some of the 
units in some areas of the Noranda-Benoit volcanic 
complex may have preserved a detectable TRM. In 
addition, there are sufficient age data from these units 
and the field relations are such that proof (or disproof) of 
the existence of a TRM is achievable. The prehnite-pum- 
pellyite to subgreenschist facies (Jolly 1974, 1980) of 
regional and (or) burial metamorphism of the terrane led 
Irving and Naldrett (1977) to suggest that a TRM might be 
preserved if much of it were contained in high-blocking- 
temperature phases. Metamorphism, in more detail, is 
complex in history, and at least six phases have been 
distinguished in units of the central and eastern parts of 
the complex (Dirnroth et al. 1974). Pearce and Birckett 
(1974) indicated that temperatures never exceeded 
400°C in any metamorphic event and were probably 
much less. Volcanic textures, major portions of the 
original magmatic mineralogies, and original within- 
flow chemical variations are still preserved, especially 
in Kinojevis flows (Pearce and Birckett 1974; Jensen 
1978a; Dirnroth and Lichtblau 1979). In addition, in 
some parts of Kinojevis flows the original magnetic 
mineralogy is still preserved. 
Units of the second and third volcanic cycles were 
emplaced within a well bracketed, short time period. 
Dacites underlying Stoughton-Roquemaure units east 
of Munro Township (Fig. 1) give a U-Pb zircon date of 
2710 + 2 Ma, and volcanic and subvolcanic units 
forming the top of the Blake River pile give an age of 
2703 + 2 Ma (Nunes and Jensen 1980). Zindler et al. 
(1978) listed a Sm-Nd age of 2765 + 47 Ma for 
komatiites and related intrusives of the Stoughton- 
Roquemaure Group, MUNO Township. The Rb-Sr age 
of Matachewan dikes is 2690 + 93 Ma (Gates and 
Hurley 1973), in overall agreement with field relations, 
though most workers infer that the dikes are closer to 
2600 Ma in age (e.g., Irving 1979; Schutts and Dunlop 
1981). A small difference in age, if real, between the 
volcanic cycles of the Noranda-Benoit volcanic 
complex and Matachewan activity implies a similarity 
or near similarity in TRM (or depositional remanent 
magnetization (DRM)) directions among these various 
units. Post-depositional tectonism of the volcanics and 
sediments, prior to Matachewan intrusion, should have 
dispersed the directions. In turn, the preservation of a 
TRM in the volcanics and sediments might be implied if,

The structural history of the second and third volcanic 
cycle units is relatively straightforward. Development 
of the major east-west-trending synclinorium structure 
occurred during the deposition of the Kinojevis and 
Blake River Groups (Jensen 1981). In situ "primary" 
magnetization data from Kinojevis and older units 
should be corrected for structure because lava 
successions have been tilted into monoclinal sequences 
well after emplacement and original cooling. 
The data presented here and in companion papers 
(Tasillo-Hirt et al. 1982; Geissman et al. 1982, and in 
preparation) are results of our efforts to extract further 
information on the Archean field from units of the 
Abitibi Greenstone Belt. We assumed that an original, 
syngenetic component of magnetization of statistical 
significance was present in the lithologies examined, 
and tests are applied for the presence of this remanence 
in as many instances as possible. 
Methodology 
Samples were collected by field drilling techniques or 
by orienting blocks. A magnetic compass was used for 
orientation (accuracy of 1-2"). Generally, two to five 
specimens (2.5 cm long by 2.5 cm diameter) were 
prepared from each core or block sample. Details of the 
sampled areas are given with the paleomagnetic data. 
The remanent magnetization was generally measured 
with the prototype SCT rock magnetometer (Goree and 
Fuller 1976) having a 4 in. (10 cm) diameter vertical 
access and background noise of around emu (10-lo 
A m2). Specimens with greater intensities were measured 
on a portable Schonstedt magnetometer (model PSM-1) 
or a Schonstedt spinner magnetometer (model SSM-la).

These were eventually measured on the SCT when their 
moment was reduced sufficiently in demagnetization. 
Progressive alternating field (AF) demagnetization was 
carried out with a single-axis Schonstedt demagnetizer, 
model GSD-1. A Schonstedt thermal demagnetizer, 
model TSD-1, was used for most thermal demagnetiza- 
tions, but two home-built furnaces (one capable of 
heating in vacuums less than lW3 Torr (0.13 Pa)), were 
also employed. Hysteresis and Curie temperature 
properties were measured on a PAR vibrating sample 
magnetometer. For thermomagnetic runs, whole-rock 
samples or magnetic separates were run under a vacuum 
of about lW3 Torr (0.13 Pa) or less. An isothermal 
remanent magnetization (IRM) was imparted with an 
electromagnet capable of producing fields up to 1.8 T. 
Polished thin sections from representative samples of all 
lithologies were prepared. 
All components of the NRM in all samples were 
identified using progressive demagnetization diagrams 
(Zijderveld 1967; Dunlop 1979). For the vast majority 
of samples, magnetization components decayed in a 
linear fashion in demagnetization, and vector subtrac- 
tion methods could thus be used to calculate the 
direction of each component. Because a multivectorial 
NRM was generally contained in each sample and, as will 
be shown, the NRM from sample to sample was anything 
but uniform, demagnetization procedures were gener- 
ally quite lengthy. At high peak fields in AF 
demagnetization (generally greater than 50 mT), some 
samples acquired a spurious component of magnetiza- 
tion, often parallel to the last axis demagnetized. The 
method of French (1976) was used to verify that this 
component was usually an anhysteretic remanent 
magnetization (ARM); this method entails a six-step 
demagnetization of the specimen at any given field, 
assuming that the ARM is essentially acquired parallel to 
the last axis demagnetized. The method was 
consequently employed where necessary to adequately 
resolve linear decays of NRM components. 
Results 
Sampling in the Kinojevis tholeiites is concentrated in 
three areas selected on the basis of exposure, amount of 
geologic mapping and petrologic investigations, 
accessibility, and location with respect to the 
synclinorium axis and Matachewan dikes. 
Cook Township 
The first area is Lava Flow Mountain, Cook 
Township (Fig. 1) where Jackson (1980a,b) has

The components trending toward the origin in

site 300, are clearly not Matachewan dike directions 
(Fig. 5). Because their coercivities and blocking 
temperatures are similar to the well grouped components

blocking temperatures) to those in the low-iron flow 
(Fig. 4f). 
Laboratory storage tests (periods of greater than 1 
month, with the NRM direction perpendicular to the 
Earth's field) indicate that the secondary components 
common to the low-iron flow are not viscous in origin. 
The secondary components are removed by approxi- 
mately 15.0 mT or 250°C in demagnetization. Unfortu- 
nately, these components themselves are not well 
grouped and therefore cannot be correlated with younger 
thermotectonic events. 
Thackeray Township 
In Thackeray Township (Fig. l), no Matachewan 
dikes are exposed or inferred from aeromagnetic data. 
The area consists of a thick succession of high-iron flows 
overlain to the south by a succession of low-iron flows. 
Two sampling traverses were made through the exact 
flows described by Pearce and Birckett (1974). One was 
through a single, complete, high-iron flow in which 38 
samples were collected (sites 125 and 131, Fig. 6). At 
the other traverse, through a portion of a low-iron flow, 
23 samples were collected (sites 128 and 129, Fig. 6). In 
addition, in the central part of this area (Fig. 6), 
compaction features and contacts between high-iron 
tholeiite flows suggest that one block has been rotated 
nearly 80". Six samples were collected from this area 
(site 130) with the hope of recognizing this rotation. 
For the high-iron flow, the NRM was again found to be 
often multivectorial (Fig. 7 a and b). In many samples, 
where two or more components of magnetization were 
resolved in AF demagnetization, thermal demagnetiza- 
tion again yielded only one, indicating the substantial 
overlap of blocking-temperature spectra and implying 
that the secondary components (fully isolated in 
alternating field demagnetization) may be chemical in 
origin. The AF demagnetization was thus the preferred 
method of resolving all components. In AF treatment, 
however, the component trending toward the origin was 
not always completely removed at 100 mT. To ascertain

of the remanence, several samples were demagnetized 
by AF method to between 60 and 100 mT, then thermally 
demagnetized in vacuum or air beginning at room 
temperature. Two examples of the results are shown in

ultimate directions (k = 2.6 for NRM versus k = 1.9 for 
ultimate directions), storage tests for periods of greater 
than 1 month (with the NRM direction perpendicular to 
the Earth's field), the general presence of multicompo- 
nent magnetizations, and the grouping of NRM directions 
away from a present field value all suggest that the 
remanence at this site is not dominated by viscous 
components. 
High-coercivity, high-blocking-temperature mag- 
netization components are present in the majority 
of samples analyzed. In most cases, however, the 
directions of these components are scattered, and do not 
reflect a short period of time, as would be expected by 
the TRM of an individual flow.

1978). Steiner (1982), however, has demonstrated a 
significant variability in ulvospinel contents (x = 
0.5-0.75) in nearly fresh titanomagnetites of ocean 
floor basalts and diorites. The originally high titanium 
content of Kinojevis titanomagnetites has been 
confirmed in the present study (to be discussed shortly) 
and by Hanes (1973) who reported ulvospinel contents 
as high as 63% in titanomagnetites from Kinojevis 
flows. The Kinojevis basalts would then have had Curie 
temperatures below 200°C. Unlike modem layer 2A 
tholeiites, individual Kinojevis flows are thicker, more 
extensive, and more variable in chemistry than ocean 
floor tholeiites. The Kinojevis units thus have 
undergone chemical and mineralogical differentiation in 
situ, as well as important deuteric changes and 
interactions with seawater like modem ocean floor 
basalts. Cumulate silicate textures are indeed common 
in the interiors of flows (Pearce and Birckett 1974). The 
primary magnetic mineralogy and subsequent alteration 
products vary significantly within the Kinojevis units. In 
sinr differentiation and deuteric (local) alteration appear 
to be the causes of these variations, but regional burial is 
probably the most influential cause of the overall 
difference in magnetic properties between the Kinojevis 
tholeiites and layer 2A rocks. 
Results of alternating field and thermal demagnetiza- 
tion studies indicate that magnetite is the essential 
magnetic phase. Rock magnetic data are summarized in 
Table 1. Representative (at least triplicate) samples of 
all units were analyzed thermomagnetically and in most 
cases, excluding those where paramagnetic material 
completely dominated the J,- T curve, the presence of 
magnetite was confirmed (Fig. 11). Curie temperatures 
of the main magnetite phase were always between 
560 and 585°C. In very rare instances (e.g., the

The abundance and textural relations of the 
microscopically visible magnetic mineralogy of the 
Kinojevis tholeiites vary considerably, both within and 
between flow units. The best preserved textural relations 
occur in basal hyaloclastite and upper, fragmental 
portions of flow units. For example, in the low-iron flow 
at Thackeray Township (sample 129B, Fig. 12 a and 
b) completely fresh, euhedral, lath-shaped ilmenite 
and equidimensional magnetite grains are aligned with 
groundmass material and are compressed and deformed 
around shards formed by the distintegration of early, 
quenched glassy material. Representative magnetite 
compositions determined by electron microprobe (Table 
2, analysis 1) are too low in Ti (in agreement with the 
Curie-temperature data) to have been directly precipi- 
tated as homogeneous phases from a tholeiitic basalt. 
Homogeneous ilmenite laths (Table 2, analyses 2 and 3) 
are high in hematite component, however, suggesting a 
high temperature of formation (Buddington and 
Lindsley 1964; Lindsley 1977). Because both inter- 
growths and individual minerals are aligned parallel to 
primary compaction and flow features, often display 
crystallization relations with early formed silicate 
phases, and are not spatially related to low-grade silicate 
devitrification-alteration products, we infer that the 
oxide phases were formed contemporaneously with the 
flows. 
Magnetite and ilmenite are also quite fresh, albeit 
rare, in glomeroporphyritic layers common to low-iron 
Kinojevis flows. For example, in the McVittie 
Township flow sampled, fine, euhedral, relatively 
Ti-poor magnetite grains (Table 2, analysis 4) occur in 
the groundmass (Fig. 12c). 
In other parts of flow units, sizes and textures of 
magnetite grains are more varied. In the coarse-grained 
high-iron flow in Thackeray Township, magnetite 
grains display intercumulus outlines (Fig. 126) or 
quenched cruciform (Haggerty 1976, p. HG- 106) 
textures (Fig. 12e), or are found as inclusions in silicate 
phases (Fig. 12f). Sporadic portions of the low-iron 
McVittie flow and the high-iron Cook flow are 
extremely enriched in subhedral magnetite grains of 
diverse sizes (Fig. 12g). The distribution of magnetite 
grains in these enriched areas, conformable with flow 
textures in the groundmass, suggests that they were 
precipitated simultaneously with the rest of the 
surrounding tholeiite melt in an irregular fashion. 
The amount of ferromagnetic material in a flow is a 
function of both the primary crystallization-differentia- 
tion history and subsequent oxidation. Uniform 
variations of magnetization parameters (e.g., NRM 
intensity, intensity behaviour in alternating field 
demagnetization, Fisher precision parameter, and 
oxidation index) would be expected within a flow unit 
were both processes regular (Watkins and Haggerty 
1967a,b). A measure of the relative amount of 
ferromagnetic material in a rock and its variability is the 
ratio Xp/J, (Dunlop and Hale 1977) where Xp is the 
paramagnetic susceptibility (due largely to ferromag- 
nesian silicates) and J, is the saturation magnetization. 
The paramagnetic susceptibility is measured between 
300 and 800 mT in hysteresis (Collinson 1968) and J, is 
the y intercept of the tangent to the magnetization-H 
curve at maximum H. Dunlop and Hale (1977) argued 
that if paramagnetic and ferromagnetic materials are 
comagmatic, i.e., deriving iron from the same sources, 
then the ratio Xp/ J, should be relatively constant. Figure 
13 shows the results of this test for the traverse through 
the complete section of the Thackeray high-iron flow. 
The Xp/J, ratios do not show a good correlation with 
lithologic variations. The variability suggests that 
alteration events have irregularly affected the magnetic 
mineralogy. 
On the other hand, Xp/J, ratios from the low-iron 
McVittie flow are all very low, ranging from 0.44 X 
lW5 to 4.8 X 1W5. Magmatic and (or) alteration 
processes affecting the magnetic mineralogy must have 
been relatively uniform through the portion of the flow 
sampled. 
In general, alteration of the primary magnetic 
mineralogy appears to increase toward the centers or 
lower centers of flows, together with an increase in 
silicate grain size. In the central part of the low-iron flow 
at Cook Township and the high-iron flow at Thackeray 
Township magnetite is abundant as a coarse, 
intercumulus phase but has invariably undergone 
oxidation to hematite, rutile, and sphene (Fig. 126). 
Relict structures indicative of ilmenite-magnetite 
intergrowths probably formed during earlier, high- 
temperature deuteric oxidation-exsolution. The degree 
of clearly secondary, low-temperature oxidation varies 
even on a thin-section scale, and irregular patches of 
titanomagnetite (Table 2, analysis 5) commonly occupy 
centers of original titaniferous magnetite grains (Fig. 
124. Small magnetite inclusions in silicate phases 
appear homogeneous and unoxidized under the 
microscope. 
The most important aspect of the magnetic 
mineralogy of the Kinojevis basalts is the ubiquitous 
property of Curie temperatures greater than 550°C, 
indicative of nearly pure magnetite. Electron micro- 
probe data do not always support this observation, 
however. For example, most magnetite grains in the 
low-iron McVittie flow are homogeneous at the 
resolution of the optical microscope (approximately 1 
pm) and display shrinkage cracks at their edges, 
suggesting partial maghemitization. Some grains clearly 
display oxidation-exsolution intergrowths (Fig. 12h). 
The optically homogeneous grains are both chemically 
homogeneous at the electron microprobe level and

eventual precipitation of pyrite below 730°C. Titano- 
magnetites in regions devoid of pyrite or containing 
pyrite deposited in late-stage, low-temperature condi- 
tions show evidence of more intense high- and low- 
temperature oxidation. 
The proposed action of phase splitting clearly 
distinguishes the Kinojevis flows from typical modem 
ocean floor tholeiites. In situ ocean floor lavas with high 
Curie temperatures have been rarely reported (e. g . , 
Ryall et al. 1977; Rice et al. 1980). In contrast, work on 
ophiolite complexes has shown an abundance of 
high-Curie-temperature basalts (Butler et al. 1975; Levi 
and Banerjee 1977; Levi et al. 1978; Beske-Diehl and 
Banerjee 1979; Banerjee 1980). These results have been 
interpreted as indicating a reheating (metamorphic) 
event causing the unrnixing of titanomaghemites at 
some later, but unknown, time (Levi et al. 1978). 
High-temperature oxidation probably occurred in some 
Kinojevis flows because the flows were too massive and 
deposited and buried too quickly to be quenched 
instantaneously and crystallize fine-grained titanomag- 
netite. 
The magnetic mineralogy of the Kinojevis basalts has 
been more extensively altered (probably involving 
pervasive phase splitting of homogeneous titanomag- 
hemites, produced from original titanomagnetites) than 
that of normal ocean floor tholeiites; the remanence is 
entirely secondary in origin. 
Discussion 
Interpretations of the paleomagnetic data from the 
Kinojevis tholeiites must involve three important 
features. First, individual samples usually contain at 
least one magnetization component of intermediate to 
high blocking temperatures and coercivities. These 
components generally display linear decays in 
demagnetization and therefore represent a relatively 
discrete period of geologic time. Second, "contact" tests 
(this study; Pesonen 1973) indicate the ability of at least 
some units to retain a statistically well grouped 
secondary TRM imparted by Matachewan dikes. 
Additional magnetization components, some perhaps 
chemical in origin, have been superimposed upon the 
overprinted TRM. Third, we suggest that original 
titanomagnetites of all flows have been in part converted 
to nearly pure magnetites in a probably complex series 
of changes. 
As noted previously, the thermal history of this area is 
complex, but critical information bearing on the 
magnetization features listed above is available. 
Maximum regional metamorphic temperatures could 
have been less than 400°C; the upper stability limit of 
prehnite-chlorite-quartz assemblages (very common in 
Kinojevis units) is approximately 300°C at a pressure of 
3 kbar (300MPa), and decreases at higher pressures 
(Nitsch 1971). Schwarz and Buchan (1980), Buchan 
and Schwarz (1981), and L. D. Schutts (personal 
communication, 1980) reported that the ambient 
temperature of presently exposed country rock at Munro 
Township during "Abitibi" dike intrusion (approximate- 
ly 2150 Ma) was between 181 + 7 and 250 + 25"C, 
implying a prolonged deep burial for this area. Schwarz 
and Buchan (1980) and Buchan and Schwarz (1981) also 
suggested that the Abitibi Belt remained deeply buried 
through Middle Proterozoic time. Magnetic (Schutts 
and Dunlop 1981) and 40Ar-39Ar (Hanes 1979) data 
further suggest mild thermal activity in the Abitibi area 
during Hudsonian (approximately 1800- 1600 Ma) 
orogenic activity. Assuming a maximum duration of 
heating of 1.0 Ga, an original remanence residing in

essentially pure single-domain magnetite capable of 
surviving heating must theoretically have blocking 
temperatures in excess of 500°C (Pullaiah et al. 1975). 
For example, the Matachewan dike component present 
in Kinojevis tholeiites at sites 40 and 41 is isolated in 
thermal demagnetization between approximately 350 
and 580°C. If the Matachewan remanence was a 
complete TRM due to reheating, then Pullaiah et al.'s 
(1975) curves, if applicable, yield a maximum ambient 
temperature of 150°C for partial unblocking to 350°C. 
If low-titanium magnetite formed during prolonged 
heating, as might be the case, then the remanence would 
be far more complex and Pullaiah et al.'s (1975) 
blocking curves may not be applicable. A CRM of high 
blocking temperatures (greater than 400°C, as a 
compromise) would reflect the ambient field during its 
formation (Memll 1975). Magnetite grains of lower 
blocking temperatures would remain unblocked until 
uplift and would either acquire a scattered or well 
grouped remanence, depending upon the rate of cooling 
and scale over which cooling took place. 
In most Kinojevis units examined, both high- and 
low-blocking-temperature components are scattered and 
must have been acquired over a significant period of 
time; the formation of low-titanium magnetite continued 
during burial and metamorphism. Importantly, we have 
observed that the scatter of directions is not related to the 
general ranges of blocking temperatures or coercivities 
over which the magnetization components are removed. 
On the basis of electron microprobe results from oxides 
in Kinojevis units and Matachewan dikes in Pesonen's 
(1973) study area, Hanes (1973) suggested that most 
titanium loss (and phase splitting) took place prior to 
Matachewan dike emplacement. This observation 
supports Jensen's (1981) belief that downwarping and 
burial of the major Noranda-Benoit synclinorium 
occurred concurrently with the emplacement of the 
latest Kinojevis units and the Blake River Group.

suggested that their data represent an Archean field 
existing during deposition and concomitant deformation 
of basalts and gabbros in the central Abitibi Belt. Our

Deformation was essentially complete by the time of

Tasillo-Hirt et al. (1982) and Geissman et al. (in 
preparation) report a characteristic magnetization from 
Timiskarning sediments near Kirkland Lake that, when 
corrected for structure, yields a pre-Matachewan dike 
paleopole. We have likewise corrected the high-

components in samples from Cook, Thackeray, and 
McVittie Townships for post-emplacement synclino-

corrected assuming simple tilt about a horizontal, nearly 
east-west striking axis. Additional structural correc- 
tions (e.g., to account for an apparent shallow eastward 
plunge of the synclinorium or possible local structural 
effects (e.g., Verosub and Moores (1981)) are not used. 
The eastward plunge of the synclinorium in the sampling 
area was probably assumed during downwarping of the 
region, not at a later time, and conventional corrections 
for this feature may not accurately reflect the true defor- 
mation of the units (Jensen 1981). The corrected data in

it is conceivable that the Kinojevis flows have sampled a 
younger Archean field than the units investigated by 
Schutts and Dunlop (1981). We now explore that 
possibility. 
For this analysis, we assume that (1) proposed phase 
splitting in the Kinojevis flows took place until (and 
even possibly later than) Matachewan dike emplace- 
ment and (2) the characteristic Matachewan dike 
direction (approximately D = 27", I = 16", e.g., Irving 
and Naldrett 1977) accurately represents the paleomag- 
netic field during changes in the magnetic mineralogy. 
We compare the structurally corrected Kinojevis ulti- 
mate components with theoretical estimates of geomag- 
netic field behaviour (e.g., Harrison and Watkins 1977; 
Dodson 1980). The virtual geomagnetic pole (VGP) 
angular dispersion of the observed directions is 
significantly greater and more distributed than a 
theoretical histogram of VGP angular dispersion (Dodson 
1980) for the approximate latitude of the Abitibi Belt at 
latest Archean time (Fig. 16). The Kinojevis units 
sampled clearly do not yield data consistent with 
magnetization blocking during distinct, well defined 
geologic events. 
We contend that scatter in directions from individual 
Kinojevis flows is due to short-term secular variation 
and (or) polarity reversals in probable combination with 
long-term polar wander. It is difficult to evaluate the 
relative contributions of these effects, especially since 
we observe directional variations within discrete flows 
and the remanence is not a TRM, or "primary," in the 
strictest sense. Other investigations of Proterozoic 
terranes, for example those of Morgan (1976), 
Beckrnann et al. (1977), Piper and Steam (1976), and 
Piper (1981) in western Greenland, have shown that 
long-term remanence acquisition records apparent polar 
wander rather than secular variation, because the 
cooling-uplift rate is slow enough to average secular
