A palaeomagnetic study of the Umvimeela Dyke, Zimbabwe: evidence for a Mesoproterozoic overprint

M.F. Mushayandebvua, D.L. Jonesa, J.C. Bridenb

aDepartment of Physics, University of Zimbabwe, P.O. Box MP 167, Harare, Zimbabwe bDepartment of Earth Sciences, University of Oxford, Oxford OX1 3PR, UK

Received August 7, 1992; revised version accepted January 27, 1994

Abstract

Palaeomagnetic and magnetic susceptibility results are reported from sixteen new sites (complementing the previous seven) on the Umvimeela Dyke, one of the two major satellite dykes parallelling the Great Dyke of Zimbabwe. Four of the new sites are in the deformed northernmost section of the dyke with a further four just to their south. The magnetisation of the long cratonic section of the Umvimeela Dyke is characterised by a component P, carried principally by magnetite and considered primary, with a mean direction D=219.8°, I= -58.7° with k= 116.8 and α9s=3.3°. This direction is almost identical to those of the Great Dyke and two other associated intrusions. The angular dispersion of site mean directions for the Umvimeela Dyke is only 6.5°, suggesting a short time of emplacement and cooling.

A second component S, carried by magnetite, titanomagnetite and ilmenohaematite, is present at most sites but in bigger proportions as the Limpopo and Zambezi Belts are approached. Considerations such as geographical distribution, magnetic susceptibility and dyke geology suggest S is an overprint. Its direction (D≈ 195°, I≈ 10°) is similar to that of the \ 1100 Ma Umkondo dolerites and it is suggested that it was introduced chemically at or just before the onset of Pan-African activity in the region.

Of the four sites in the deformed section of the dyke one carries the P component, but the other three have been completely remagnetized. At two of these a component Z was detected which may have been introduced \650 Ma ago. This suggests that this section, and the accompanying Musengezi Complex of the Great Dyke, were deformed in the late Pan-African orogenic phase of the Zambezi Belt.

1. Introduction

The Great Dyke crosses the Zimbabwe craton in a NNE-trending direction for 550 km. Its surface geometry is misleading; it is not a true dyke at all but the remains of a series of near-contiguous layered igneous bodies emplaced 2461 ± 16 Ma ago (Hamilton, 1977) along a line of weakness in the Earth's crust. Igneous bodies associated with the Great Dyke include the Southern Satellite Dykes beyond the south end of the Great

Dyke and within the Limpopo Belt, the Umvimeela and East Dykes roughly parallelling the Great Dyke, gabbroic dykes intruding some of the NNE-trending major faults in the craton (Wilson et al., 1987), and, almost certainly, a sill at Nenga and a dyke at Ngundu Halt, both within the northern zone of the Limpopo Belt. The Great Dyke and its principal satellites are described and analysed by Wilson and Prendergast (1988).

The Umvimeela Dyke (Fig. 1), up to 100 m wide, is situated to the west of the Great Dyke at a distance varying from 1 km in the north to 18 km in the south (Worst, 1960). It continues some 100 km further south than the Great Dyke, crossing into the Limpopo Belt. For most of its length the Umvimeela Dyke is undeformed except for small offsets associated with crosscutting faults. At its northern end, however, within the Zambezi Belt, the Umvimeela Dyke imitates the southern section of the extensively deformed Musengezi Complex of the Great Dyke; it is concave towards the west and wholly displaced about 10 km to the east.

Fig. 1. Sketch map of Zimbabwe showing location of sampling sites from the Umvimeela Dyke. The stereonet shows the components of remanence (L, P, S and Z) isolated in various segments of the dyke. Distances in Table 1 are measured from the line with asterisk.

The Umvimeela Dyke is composed of quartz gabbro. The deformed section of the dyke is highly faulted and there is evidence of extensive shearing at dyke margins. There are marked variations in the degree of alteration of the rock in the deformed section; in some places only slight alteration is evident, but in others there has been extensive uralitization and saussuritization (Wiles, 1972).

McElhinny and Gough (1963), in their palaeomagnetic study of the Great Dyke, included results from a single site (MG8) in the undeformed northern section of the Umvimeela Dyke. The mean direction was not significantly different from that of the Great Dyke. Later Jones et al. (1975) reported results from six sites in the Umvimeela Dyke including two (L and M) from its extension into the Limpopo Belt. They concluded that sites L and M had been completely remagnetized during a thermal event some 1900 Ma ago (Van Breemen and Dodson, 1972). The mean direction of sites deeper into the craton (including MG8) was N=5, D=220.6°, I=-62.7° with k=128.6. The angular dispersion of directions was only 7.1°, smaller than the angular dispersion expected from secular variations of the present Earth's field, suggesting that the Umvimeela Dyke was emplaced over a very short period of time.

The present study extends that of Jones et al. (1975) and includes sites close to and within the deformed zone. It was hoped that a detailed study of the very long undeformed section would provide firmer information on the duration of emplacement and cooling, while sites in the deformed section might provide information on the time (or times) of deformation of the Musengezi Complex (and Zambezi Belt).

2. Sampling

Outcrop, particularly in the northern half of the Umvimeela Dyke, is often difficult to locate. Nevertheless sixteen new sites were collected including four sites (UA, US, UT and UU) within the deformed zone and four sites just to the south of the deformed zone (Fig. 1). At site UG a transect of sampling was conducted consisting of three samples from the fractured edge of the dyke, one sample 16 m away from the edge and four samples from the undeformed centre of the dyke. Two sites, UO and UP, are located slightly north of where the Umvimeela Dyke enters the Limpopo Belt. All samples were hand-drilled and oriented by sun compass. Between five and nine samples were cored at each site.

3. Measurements

Measurements of intensity and direction of magnetization of specimens were made using a PAR-SM1 magnetometer. Alternating field demagnetization (AF) was performed using apparatus similar to that of McElhinny (1966). One specimen per sample was demagnetized stepwise, usually up to 180 mT; to try to eliminate components of magnetization introduced by the tumbling method, above 30 mT double demagnetization was performed (Hillhouse, 1977). A second specimen per sample was used in thermal demagnetization experiments using a Magnetic Measurements MMTD1 apparatus. The initial magnetic susceptibility of one specimen per sample has been measured using a Bison 3101 apparatus; corrections have been made for both length and diameter of specimens.

Measurements have been analysed using the battery of techniques now available. These include the use of orthogonal vector plots and LI-NEFIND (Kent et al., 1983), demagnetization circles (Jones et al., 1975; McFadden and Mc-Elhinny, 1988), stereonet plots and Fisher (1953) statistics.

4. Results

Five components of magnetization have been identified within Umvimeela Dyke samples. First, the natural remanent magnetization (NRM) includes an isothermal (IRM) component, labelled R. Second, there is a component, labelled P, sometimes persisting up to 180 mT, that is not significantly different from the previously reported direction for the Great Dyke and Umvimeela Dyke. Third, at most sites, there is a component, called S, residing in high-coercivity grains which manifests itself by a southerly shallowing from the P direction at high demagnetizing fields. A further component, Z, is observed at two sites (UT and UU) in the deformed zone and is believed to be related to Zambezi Belt activity. Finally there is the component L, identified by Jones et al. (1975) at the two sites within the Limpopo Belt. The very different directions

4.1. Component R

This component is randomly directed and was the largest component in most specimens. It was usually removed by AF in fields of less than 20 mT while thermal demagnetization of specimens with a significant R component maintained their NRM directions to temperatures over 580°C before intensities dropped to noise level. The low coercivities and high blocking temperatures associated with R suggest that it is carried by multidomain magnetite (Bol'shakov and Shcherbakova, 1979). An IRM origin for R is suggested by its randomly directed nature and comparison of AF decay curves with those of artificially introduced IRMs in the same specimens (Mushayandebvu, 1991).

AF demagnetization directions converged towards the P direction during removal of R followed generally by linear segments on orthogonal plots (Fig. 2). In some cases the direction of P was obtained using demagnetization circle analysis. Site mean directions for the P component are listed in Table 1 and shown in Fig. 3. Thermal demagnetization was carried out on specimens after removal of most of R by AF. However, the high blocking temperatures associated with the fraction of R remaining, overlapped with those of P and this led to poorer definition of P using thermal treatment.

P is the dominant component in grains with coercivities ranging from 30 to 180 mT at almost all the sites. The blocking temperature spectra for

P show that pure or nearly pure magnetite is its main carrier. The very high coercivities suggest P is carried mainly by single-domain magnetite. However, a number of specimens maintained the P direction during thermal demagnetization up to 640°C after the intensity had dropped sharply just below 580°C, suggesting that ilmenohaematite is a (minor) carrier of the P component too.

4.3. Component S

Many samples at our sites (except UM on the cratonic section where component P itself was poorly defined, and UA, UT and UU in the deformed zone) show a systematic southerly shallowing away from the P direction during demagnetization. This must be indicative of a further component of NRM which we call S. The shallowing is particularly evident in demagnetizing fields over 100 mT (Figs. 4 and 5). Insights about the origin of S are gained from its within-site variability at site UG as well as its between-site variability. At UG, the three samples collected from the sheared edge of the dyke show the presence of S at 60 mT, whereas at the centre of the dyke P continues to dominate until 100 mT. S is progressively more noticeable as the (Pan African) Zambezi Belt is approached through sites UG, UH, UR and US. At UQ and UR, just south of the deformed zone, the presence of S is clear in fields less than 60 mT, while at US, which has no significant R component, sample NRMs contain P and S in comparable amounts. S becomes slightly more evident as the Limpopo Belt is approached at sites UP and UO (the direction of S is very different, 72°, to that of component L observed by Jones et al., 1975, at sites L and M within the belt).

Specimens whose directions had swung towards S during AF were heated to determine the blocking temperature spectrum of S. Most of these specimens maintained their directions in temperatures above 580°C, showing that the blocking temperature spectra of S and P overlap and that the carriers are the same. However, a number of specimens maintained their direction only up to 550°C and then swung northward back to the P direction which they maintained to over 600°C (Fig. 6). It appears that S is carried by titanomagnetite grains with blocking temperatures not exceeding 560°C. A few specimens showed a slight swing in direction from P to S between 585°and 600°C, suggesting part of S is carried by ilmenohaematite.

Two estimates can be made of the direction of S. Firstly, using demagnetization circle analysis of specimens showing clear movement from P to S, nineteen specimens gave a mean result of D=198.1°, I=-17.1° with k=19.0 and α95 =8.2°(Fig. 7). Secondly, the component removed in the northward swing from S towards P duringthermal demagnetization can be estimated by use of LINEFIND and ten specimens gave D=190.9°, I=-6.3°with k=18.4 and α95= 10.4°as an estimate of the S direction using this method.

4.4. Component Z

The NRMs of samples from the four northern sites within the deformed zone generally involve low magnetic moments (0.1×10-⁶A m²) and low initial susceptibilities. Most specimens were able to acquire a viscous remanent magnetization between sampling and measurements and had to be stored in Mumetal boxes. The specimens also tended to acquire rotational remanent magnetization in alternating fields less than 20 mT. The instability of the specimens made it difficult to determine the characteristics of NRM at these sites. Nevertheless, a distinct southerly downward component, which we label Z, was detected at sites UT and UU. At site UT an estimate of the Z direction was possible using demagnetization circle analysis and this gave D=172.8°,I=62.9 with k=35.6 and α95=30.0° (Fig. 1). The corresponding virtual geomagnetic pole is at 41.8°E, 61.7°S.

Site mean values for susceptibility are given in Table 1 and there are clearly two distinct groups. The first, involving seventeen of the sites, has values spread between 4.3× 10-³ and 18.6× 10-3 with a mean value of 8.2× 10-³ (SI), while the four sites within the deformed zone have values closely grouped around 0.73× 10-³. At site UG the three samples from the sheared edge of the dyke have a mean of 1.8× 10-3, while the mean of the other five is 16× 10-³.

5. Discussion

5.1. Component P

Contacts of the Umvimeela Dyke with country rock were not located preventing the primary nature of P from being established, or otherwise, by a classic contact test. Nevertheless there is other evidence that suggests that P, carried predominantly by magnetite and present throughout the long cratonic section, is the primary component. Its direction is not significantly different from those of the Great Dyke, East Dyke and Popoteke gabbro. Thus if P is a later overprint, an event of almost regional extent is required. The Mashonaland Igneous Event (Wilson et al., 1987) was certainly of cratonic proportions and, during this event, a single site in the norite of the Great Dyke was completely remagnetized by a Mashonaland dolerite sill (McElhinny and Opdyke, 1964). Therefore, if P is not primary, it was introduced during a large-scale event occurring between the emplacement of the Great Dyke and the Mashonaland Igneous Event and there is no evidence of such an event. Finally comparisons of the blocking temperature spectra of P and those of thermoremanent magnetizations artificially introduced into the same specimens show virtually no differences (Mushayandebvu, 1991).

5.2. Component S

Unlike P there are noticeable variations of S both within-site and between-site. At site UG, S is more prominent in the sheared margin of the dyke than towards the undeformed middle. The magnetic susceptibility is an order of magnitude lower in the altered rock than at the dyke centre. S is absent at some sites but present in bigger proportions as the (younger) Zambezi and Limpopo Belts are approached. This suggests an origin related to activity in the Belts. The direction of S is unlike any known direction within the region older than 2500 Ma, but is similar to that of the 1100 Ma old Umkondo dolerites and lavas located principally 250 km to the east (there is an Umkondo dolerite dyke only 100 km to the east). S is probably a chemical remanent magnetization associated with Umkondo activity.

5.3. Component Z

Z was identified at two sites but its direction is well defined at only one of them. The corresponding virtual geomagnetic pole position, when compared to the apparent polar wander path for the Congo and Kalahari cratons of McWilliams and Kröner (1981) (Fig. 8), is roughly consistent with an age of \650 Ma (i.e. the later part of Pan-African activity in the region; Mushayandebvu, 1991).

Fig. 8. A version of the Late Precambrian apparent polar wander path for the Kalahari and Congo cratons showing pole positions for the S and P components of the Umvimeela Dyke remanence and for site UT. The pole position for P coincides with that of the Great Dyke.

5.4. Analysis of dispersion

Using McFadden's (1982) technique, the P component of the Umvimeela Dyke has an angular dispersion of 6.5°with95% confidence limits of 5.2°and 8.7°. This compares with a value of 9.8°(with 95% confidence limits of 7.0° and 16.1°) for the Great Dyke (Jones et al., 1975, recalculated by Mushayandebvu, 1991). This suggests that the time of emplacement and cooling of the Umvimeela Dyke was indeed less than that of the Great Dyke and was too short to average out secular variations as suggested by Jones et al. (1975). This idea is reinforced by the observation that the angular dispersion of the Umvimeela Dyke is significantly less than the angular dispersion of the present geomagnetic field (12.6° at latitude 39°; Brock, 1971), whereas the angular dispersion of the Great Dyke is not.

5.5. Comparison of mean directions

The mean direction for the P component at the seventeen sites in the Umvimeela Dyke is D=219.8°, I=-58.7°with k=116.8 and α95 = 3.3°. That for the Great Dyke is D=220.4°, I=-58.3°withk=55.5 and α95=8.2 (Mc-Elhinny and Gough, 1963). The mean directions for the two dykes are less than a degree apart and the circle of 95% confidence about the Umvimeela Dyke direction falls wholly within that about the Great Dyke mean. Clearly the two mean directions are indistinguishable. Mushayandebvu (1991) shows that the same conclusion can be drawn for the East Dyke and Popoteke gabbro and the Great Dyke (Fig. 9), from comparisons of the mean directions.

Fig. 9. Equal angle stereonet showing circles of 95% confidence about mean directions of various components and igneous bodies. GD=Great Dyke. UD=Umvimeela Dyke P component. ED=East Dyke. PG=Popoteke gabbro.

The direction of the S component was estimated by two methods (see earlier) but it has not been completely isolated. The Umkondo dolerites, dated at 1080±140 Ma (Allsopp et al., 1989), are thought to be part of regional-scale igneous activity and their direction of magnetizationis D=183°, I=-10°with k=63 and α95=5.8°. Fig. 9 shows the similarity in the directions of the S component of the Umvimeela Dyke and the characteristic remanence of the Umkondo dolerites. It is possible that the S component is associated with the Umkondo episode that preceded, or perhaps coincided with, the onset of the Pan-African activity during which the northern section of the Umvimeela Dyke and the Musengezi Complex were deformed.

6. Conclusions

Component P has been identified and defined at seventeen sites spread over the long cratonic section of the Umvimeela Dyke and at site US in the deformed zone at its northern end. The P direction is carried by single domain magnetite and, to a lesser extent, by ilmenohaematite. It is probably a primary thermoremanent magnetization. Analysis of the dispersion of site mean directions strongly suggests that this long dyke was emplaced and cooled in a short period of time.

Component S, carried by magnetite and, to a lesser extent, by titanomagnetite and ilmenohaematite, is more evident at the extremities of the Umvimeela Dyke where it enters the Zambezi and Limpopo Belts. Allsopp et al. (1989) suggested there had been widespread igneous activity throughout southern Africa 1100 Ma ago, termed the Umkondo Igneous Event. The similarity of S and the Umkondo dolerite direction is consistent with this hypothesis. The event probably included the flushing of fluids through many of the rocks of the sub-continent resulting in chemical alterations and the acquisition of the S component. More thorough studies of pre-Mesoproterozoic formations in southern Africa may reveal a widespread occurrence of component S and hence help define the geographic extent of the Umkondo Event.

Introduction 
Fluids expelled from orogenic belts have received con- 
siderable attention as a potential agent of chemical 
remagnetization [e.g., Miller and Kent, 1988; McCabe and 
Elmore, 1989; McCabe et al., 1989; Bethke and Marshak, 
1990; Lu et al., 1991; Oliver, 1992; Saffer and McCabe, 
1992; Elmore et al., 1993a]. The link between chemical 
remanent magnetization (CRM) and orogenic fluids is based 
largely on a spatial association with orogenic belts and a 
temporal association with periods oforogeny [McCabe and 
Elmore, 1989]. Many of these CRMs are synfolding (e.g., 
McCabe et al. [1983], Scotese et al. [1985], Bachtadse et 
al. [ 1987], Kodarna [ 1988], Elmore et al. [ 1993a], and many 
others) which has also been cited as evidence for a connec-

Whereas orogenic fluids are a possible agent of

Direct links between CRMs, inferred fluids, and the mag-

are to provide useful insights into the diagenetic history of 
remagnetized rocks. The Pennsylvanian Belden Formation 
on a large asymmetric anticline in northwestern Colorado 
provides an opportunity to test the orogenic fluid model and 
to link an apparent synfolding Late Cretaceous-early Ter- 
tiary magnetization residing in magnetite to the processes 
which caused the magnetization using geology, geochemis- 
try, and paleomagnetism.

Sampling and Processing 
The complete range of carbonate and clastic lithologies 
exposed in the anticline were sampled. A portable gas-pow- 
ered drill was used to sample the rocks, and 2.5-cm-diam- 
eter cores were oriented in place using a magnetic compass 
and a clinometer. The oriented cores were then cut to a 
standard length of 2.2 cm in the laboratory. 
Approximately 200 oriented core samples were collected 
from 25 sites located along the Sweetwater anticline from 
three general areas: the highly mineralized and fractured 
hinge zone; the highly fractured and mineralized steep flank 
(westerly dipping flank); and the less fractured, generally 
nonmineralized beds on the easterly, shallowly dipping limb. 
Some samples were collected from the same beds in all three 
areas. Sites designated SWl 1A (steep flank), SWl lB (hinge 
area), and SWl 1C (shallow flank) are all from the same 
packstone-grainstone. Sites AM2 (steep), SAM2 (shallow), 
TAM2 (hinge) and TAMA2 (hinge) are all from the same 
wackestone bed; and AM1 (steep), SAMA1 (shallow), and 
TAM 1 (hinge) are from the underlying carbonate mudstone 
(sites are sorted by structural position in Table 1 a). Sites 
SW2S, SW3 and SW10 are from different mudstone beds 
on the steep flank, shallow flank and hinge positions, re- 
spectively. SWC samples are from a bed near the Minturn 
Formation contact, stratigraphically higher than the other 
beds sampled. 
Most magnetic measurements were made using a United 
Scientific three-axis cryogenic magnetometer, sensitive to 
10 '6 A/m, that is located in a magnetically shielded labora- 
tory which reduces the ambient magnetic field to less than 
300 nT. Magnetic directions were plotted as orthogonal 
projections [Zijderveld, 1967], and best fit lines were cal- 
culated for linear demagnetization trajectories using princi- 
pal component analysis [Kirschrink, 1980]. Paleomagnetic 
techniques used include thermal and alternating field (AF) 
demagnetization and selective destructive demagnetization 
(SDD), by which magnetic grains were removed selectively. 
For thermal demagnetization of the natural remanent mag- 
netization (NRM) the specimens were heated at increasing 
temperatures (12 steps up to 580øC) in a Schonstedt ther- 
mal specimen demagnetizer (model TSD- 1) oven for 30 min. 
AF demagnetization was performed using a two-axis tum- 
bling unit located inside a variable field electromagnet. The 
specimens were subjected to increasing AF strengths (10 
steps from natural remanent magnetization up to 125 mT) 
while rotating about two axes. 
Acquisition of an isothermal remanent magnetization 
(IRM) was performed by exposing specimens to increasing 
magnetic fields up to 0.65 T at room temperature. The IRM 
was thermally demagnetized following the same procedures 
for thermal demagnetization of the NRM [e.g., Lowrie and 
Heller, 1982]. Magnetic susceptibility was calculated us- 
ing a Sapphire Instruments SI-2 sensitive to about 10 '8 SI volume units. 
Hysteresis loops for representative samples were acquired 
with an alternating force magnetometer (AGFM) at the Uni- 
versity of Utah. For each hysteresis run the coercivity H c, 
saturation magnetization M s, and saturation remanent mag- 
netization Mrs were determined. Backfield demagnetization 
was also performed which allows a determination of coer- 
civity of remanence Hcr. 
Petrographic studies were conducted on the various car- 
bonate lithologies using reflected and transmitted light. Mag- 
netic mineralogy was studied on the scanning transmission 
electron microscope (STEM), by D. Suk at the University of 
Michigan. Strontium 87Sr/8tSSr and oxygen stable isotopes 
were measured by G. Gao at the University of Texas. 
Paleomagnetic Results and Interpretations 
Fourteen of the 18 carbonate sites sampled carry a well- 
defined, stable characteristic remanence and were used in a 
paleomagnetic fold test. Clastic lithologies had weak mag- 
netizations, and the decay was poorly defined with no con- 
sistent directions. 
Several magnetic components were found in Belden For- 
mation carbonates. At low demagnetization temperatures 
(<200øC) a northerly and steep postfolding component (Fig- 
ure 3) was removed from all specimens. At intermediate 
temperatures (200-400øC) a component with southerly dec- 
linations and negative inclinations was removed. All car- 
bonate beds sampled (18) on the fold, having sufficient NRM 
intensity to be measured (16), carry this reversed compo- 
nent. In several beds this was the only component found. A 
fold test on this component indicates that it is postfolding 
(Table lb); the grouping before tilt correction is statisti- 
cally significant at the 99% level using the McElhinny [1964] 
test. Before structural correction the mean declination for 
this component before is 186.7øE and the mean inclination 
is -54.6 ø (precision parameter (k)=44.8, radius of 95% prob- 
ability cone (*:95)=4.90). The results for this pervasive com- ponent suggest remanence acquisition in the Tertiary. 
A characteristic component with northerly declinations 
and moderate-to-steep inclinations (Figure 3) was removed 
at high temperatures (400-580øC) and is found in the major- 
ity of carbonate beds. The intensity of this component var- 
ies between sites by several orders of magnitude (9.0 x 10 '4 
to 9.0 x 10 '2 A/m). Applying the tilt correction suggests 
that this characteristic magnetization is synfolding (Figures 
4a and 4b and Table 1). 
Site directions from the steep westerly limb and the east- 
erly limbs were evaluated using the fold test proposed by 
McFadden and Jones [ 1981 ]. This test distinguishes whether 
the mean direction of a group of sites from one limb can be 
statistically distinguished from the mean direction of sites 
from another limb. For the Belden Formation the hypoth- 
esis of a true common mean in the McFadden and Jones for- 
mulation of the fold test can be accepted at the 95% confi- 
dence level for the 58-72% unfolding steps for the charac- 
teristic magnetization (Figure 5). It must be rejected for the 
mean directions before and after tilt correction. The 
McElhinny [1964] test shows a similar result with a best 
grouping (k) at 65% unfolding (Figure 5). At 65% unfold- 
ing the mean declination is 338.7øE, the mean inclination is 
62.5 ø (k = 54.9; *:95 = 5.9ø).

The northerly and steep postfolding component removed 
at low demagnetization temperatures is interpreted as a mod- 
em viscous magnetization. The postfolding component with 
southerly declinations that is removed at intermediate tem-

On the basis of the blocking temperature-relaxation time

is not a TVRM. The origin of this component is a crucial 
issue. Petrographic and geochemical studies, described in 
the following sections, were undertaken to assess this issue.

Petrography, Scanning Transmission Microscopy, 
and Selective Destructive Demagnetization 
Petrographic examination shows that magnetically strong

Discussion 
The petrographic evidence for authigenic magnetite and 
the low burial temperatures, which rule out a thermoviscous 
remagnetization mechanism, suggest that the synfolding 
characteristic magnetization in the Belden Formation is a 
CRM. When considering the origin of this magnetization, 
several issues need to be addressed. For example, there are 
a number of mechanisms [e.g., Hudson et al., 1989] that can 
produce a synfolding test result, and these mechanisms need 
to be evaluated for the origin of the characteristic magneti- 
zation. The chemical mechanism of magnetite authigenesis 
also needs to be addressed. 
In addition to remanence acquisition during folding, a 
number of other mechanisms can produce a synfolding test 
result [e.g., Hudson et al., 1989]. These include structural 
modifications of a prefolding magnetization and combina- 
tions of prefolding and postfolding (or synfolding) compo- 
nents. 
In terms ofremanence acquisition during folding, the most 
popular model for magnetizations (e.g., low burial tempera- 
tures, presence of authigenic magnetite) similar to the char- 
acteristic magnetization in the Belden Formation has been a 
chemical process triggered by orogenic fluids [McCabe et 
al., 1983; Oliver, 1986; Jackson et al., 1988; McCabe et 
al., 1989; McCabe and Elmore, 1989; Lu et al., 1991; Suk 
et al., 1990; Oliver, 1992]. The lack of a control on the 
distribution and intensity of the magnetization by the veins 
and structural position, however, does not support this hy- 
pothesis for the characteristic magnetization. in the Belden 
Formation. The magnetic characteristics of the Belden For- 
mation vary with primary lithologic characteristics and do 
not show a relationship to alteration as documented by iso- 
topic values or syntectonic mineralization. 
An alternative explanation, however, for the lack of a 
link between syntectonic mineralization/fluid access and 
magnetic intensity is that matrix permeability may have 
exerted a control on the distribution of fluids and thereby 
the remagnetization. For example, Grant et al. [ 1991 ] show 
that permeability is controlled by the stratigraphy of car- 
bonate parasequences. Relative matrix permeability to flu- 
ids as a control for a synfolding magnetization in the Belden 
Formation is considered unlikely for several reasons. For

example, the black carbonate mudstone bed with high in- 
tensities in the range of the packstones probably had very 
low matrix permeability. More importantly, the permeabil- 
ity of the Belden Formation was changed with the onset of 
deformation. Shattered mudstones in the hinge area had 
considerably higher permeability after deformation than 
relatively unfractured packstones on the shallow limb, yet 
the packstones have higher magnetic intensities. 
The characteristic magnetization in the Belden Forma- 
tion may be a CRM, but there is no evidence that it is re- 
lated to syndeformational fluids. Other mechanisms that 
have been proposed for true synfolding magnetizations in- 
clude stress-accelerated acquisition of a VRM and acquisi- 
tion ofa piezoremanent magnetization (PRM) [e.g., Hudson 
et al., 1989]. Experimental studies suggest that geologi- 
cally reasonable differential stress levels can cause acquisi- 
tion ofa PRM [e.g., Borradaile, 1994]. Other experimental 
studies, however, indicate that stress-induced changes are 
most likely in MD grains and in Ti-rich grains [e.g., Kean 
et al., 1976]. A PRM therefore might be a valid explana- 
tion in a elastic unit, such as the Jurassic Preuss Sandstone, 
where the magnetization apparently resides in detrital mag- 
netite [Hudson et al., 1989], but would seem less likely in 
the Belden Formation, where the characteristic magnetiza- 
tion resides in single-domain magnetite. A PRM that re- 
sides in MD grains could also overprint the characteristic 
component. 
Another argument against the stress-related mechanisms 
is that stress fields during folding were probably complex, 
yet during unfolding the sites from different areas on the 
fold all behave in a similar fashion. For example, sites from 
the steep flank show similar amounts ofoversteepening. On 
the basis of the different fracture pattems and variation in 
the degree of fracturing, the magnitude of stress and the 
orientation of the principal components of stress varied be- 
tween sites and changed during development of the fold. If 
stress had caused acquisition of a PRM, a less uniform 
synfolding test result might be expected. 
Several different models have been proposed for struc- 
tural modification of a prefolding remanence into a 
synfolding configuration [e.g., van der Pluijm, 1987; 
Kodama, 1988; Stamatakos andKodama, 1991]. Ifthe ge- 
ometry of the strain is correct to have rotated the magnetiza- 
tion into a synfolding configuration, a syntectonic remanence 
acquisition must be questioned [Kodama, 1988]. Only if 
the deformation is sufficiently understood to determine that 
the difference between a synfolding and prefolding rema- 
nence cannot be accounted for by strain or rigid body rota- 
tion can a definitive determination of a synfolding magneti- 
zation be made [van der Pluijm, 1987; Stamatakos and 
Kodama, 1991 ]. 
The characteristic component for the Sweetwater samples 
is dispersed along a great circle normal to the fold axis after 
tilt correction. The inferred sense of rotation of the rema- 
nence on the steep limb is opposite to the rotation of the 
beds. If the remanence on the steep flank had a similar ori- 
entation to bedding as the shallow flank remanence (sub- 
normal to the bedding surface), the directions would correct 
to a best grouping after tilt correction. It is possible that 
strain could account for the synfolding fold test. The ques- 
tion is therefore can it be established that the steep flank 
characteristic magnetization has been steepened relative to 
bedding during deformation? 
As one means to evaluate relative strain in the fold, frac- 
ture counts were taken for two lithologies: thinly bedded 
(5-8 cm) carbonate mudstone and a 50-cm thick packstone 
bed. Three meter counts along bedding strike were taken 
for each lithology in the steep flank, near the hinge and on 
the shallow flank. The values for the packstone are 36 (steep), 
29 (hinge), and 13 (shallow), whereas the values for the 
mudstone are 570 (steep), 1050 (hinge), and 240 (shallow). 
Clearly, both lithology and structural position affect frac- 
ture intensity. The fine-grained and thinly bedded mudstones 
in the steep flank and hinge show the greatest intensity of 
fracturing, and the coarse-grained thick packstone bed on 
the shallow flank shows the least. Most fractures on the 
shallow flank show little mineralization, whereas mineral- 
ized fractures are common in the other two locations. Inter- 
penetration of grains and stylolites are also more highly de- 
veloped in the steep flank samples than in the shallow flank 
samples. There is also a noticeably greater degree of calcite

The precision of grouping of sites in each flank can be 
used to help distinguish a true synfolding remanence from a 
strain-deflected prefolding remanence [e.g. Kodama, 1988]. 
At the Sweetwater locality the blocking temperature spec- 
tra, coercivity spectra, and relative intensity from bed to bed 
for the characteristic component are the same on the steep 
and shallow flanks. It is reasonable to assume that the rema- 
nence resulted contemporaneously from the same event 
across the fold and therefore would originally have had simi- 
lar precisions. In the incremental fold test for the Belden 
Formation, however, the k values for the precisions of sites 
on the hinge and flank positions are dissimilar in situ (25, 
175, 210) at the maximum grouping (65% unfolding) for all 
sites (80, 30, 302) and after complete structural correction 
(100, 20, 350). McFadden and Jones [1981 ] note that for 
their fold test to be valid the directions from various limbs 
must originally have been part of the'same population and 
should therefore have a common precision. The precisions 
of the site means from the two limbs and hinge area for the 
characteristic magnetization in the Belden Formation, how- 
ever, clearly do not meet this criterion. 
This analysis suggests the possibility that a prefolding 
CRM was altered into a synfolding CRM by deformation. 
The steep flank has higher amounts of strain than the shal- 
low flank, but the characteristic magnetization on both flanks 
may have been influenced by deformation. It should be 
pointed out, however, that studies which have demonstrated 
structural modification of a prefolding magnetization have 
found that the deflection of the magnetic directions occurs 
in discrete zones that have undergone relatively high strain 
[e.g., Starnatakos and Kodarna, 1991 ]. The Belden Forma- 
tion limestones sampled are not discrete zones that have 
undergone high strain. It is also not clear that strain levels 
in the Belden were high enough to have caused deflection 
of a prefolding component into a synfolding configuration. 
In addition, sites from different lithologies on the fold be- 
have similarly and show similar amounts ofoversteepening. 
If strain was an important factor, the different lithologies 
might be expected to behave in a less uniform way because 
the mechanisms of strain were different in the different 
lithologies (i.e., shattering in mudstones and twinning and 
pressure solution in packstones). 
There are a number of different combinations of compo- 
nents that could produce a synfolding test result. There is 
no evidence for detrital magnetite in the Belden Formation 
limestones, so it is unlikely that the magnetization is a com- 
bination of a prefolding detrital magnetization and a 
postfolding (or synfolding) component. A combination of 
a prefolding CRM and a postfolding (or synfolding) over- 
print is possible. As pointed out by Dunlop [ 1983] and Xu 
and Dunlop [ 1994], complete thermal demagnetization of a 
magnetization (i.e., modern viscous) carried in multidomain 
magnetite will occur only at temperatures near the Curie 
temperature. The characteristic magnetization in the Belden 
Formation could be overprinted by a modern viscous com- 
ponent that extends to high demagnetization temperatures. 
A prefolding magnetization overprinted by such a 
postfolding component could produce the synfolding test 
result. For example, if the characteristic magnetization in 
the Belden is overprinted by a northerly and steep-down 
modern component, the before-tilt directions, particularly 
from the steep flank, would be steepened and this could ac- 
count for the synfolding test result. A prefolding CRM over- 
printed by a synfolding PRM could also produce the same 
oversteepening. 
If a postfolding or synfolding overprint is present, the 
demagnetization results could provide some evidence for 
overlap between components. Examination of the demag- 
netization paths did not reveal any evidence of overlap; the 
characteristic magnetization decays in a linear fashion with- 
out any curved demagnetization paths. This would suggest 
that if an overprint is present at high demagnetization tem- 
peratures, it almost completely overlaps with the character-

istic component. Although this might be considered unusual, 
some magnetostratigraphic studies have reported charac- 
teristic magnetizations that have a systematic bias in the di-

a modern viscous magnetization [e.g., Claire et al., 1991 ]. 
It is not clear, however, that the magnetic characteristics (e.g., 
domain states, Ti content) in such cases are similar to those 
in the Belden Formation. 
It is not possible to unequivocally establish whether the 
characteristic magnetization in the Belden Formation is 
prefolding or truly synfolding. Although a deflection by 
strain, a PRM, or a stress-accelerated VRM may be unlikely, 
they cannot be ruled out. A prefolding CRM, overprinted 
by a modem VRM or perhaps a synfolding PRM, are also 
possibilities. 
Although the mechanism of remanence acquisition may 
be open to speculation, the original magnetization was a 
CRM, and there is no evidence that this CRM was related to 
the syndeformational mineralizing fluids. This observation 
is consistent with several other studies which report CRMs 
in limestones that have not been altered by externally de- 
rived fluids (other than meteoric fluids). For example, Elmore 
et al. [ 1993a] report that in the low-permeability Viola Lime- 
stone (Ordovician) in Oklahoma a Permian CRM in hema- 
tite is limited to a halo around mineralized fractures, as was 
an isotopic alteration signature by basinal fluids. In con- 
trast, away from the veins the organic-rich Viola Limestone 
carries a pervasive Pennsylvanian synfolding CRM in mag- 
netite and there is no isotopic evidence of alteration by basi- 
nal fluids. In addition, Plaster-Kirk et al. [ 1995] report that 
organic-rich lacustrine source rocks in the Devonian Old Red 
Sandstone in Scotland which have not been altered by an 
orogenic or basinal fluid contain a Carboniferous CRM re- 
siding in magnetite. 
The chemical mechanism responsible for magnetite 
authigenesis (and perhaps remanence acquisition) in the 
Belden Formation is also open to question and speculation. 
A prefolding oxidizing fluid, perhaps meteoric in origin, is 
one possibility. If such a meteoric fluid did enter the rock, it 
did not leave an obvious diagnostic signature that can be 
detected geochemically. An alternative model involves re- 
placement of pyrite during burial and maturation of hydro- 
carbons. In this model, ferric iron that is complexed by hu- 
mic ligands [e.g., Fontes et al., 1992] is released during 
maturation and triggers the oxidation of pyrite into magne- 
tite. This reaction has been successfully modeled in simula- 
tion experiments which correspond chemically to the equili- 
bration of pyrite in an organically encased, acidic microen- 
vironment (e.g., fecal pellets) surrounded by basic fluids in 
a carbonate rock [Brothers et al., 1994]. This model is also 
consistent with other studies which report an association 
between organic matter and authigenic magnetite [e.g., 
Elmore and Crawford, 1990; Elmore et al., 1993b]. 
Conclusions 
The Belden Formation carbonates at the Sweetwater 
Creek Anticline were evaluated for a link between mineral- 
izing (orogenic) fluids and an apparently synfolding rema- 
nence. The characteristic remanence for the Belden Forma- 
tion carbonates shows a crossing pattern upon stepwise un- 
folding and superficially could be linked to radiogenic 
syntectonic mineralizing fluids. Testing this hypothesis, 
however, does not reveal a connection between the extent 
of isotopic alteration or mineralization related to syntectonic 
fluids and the presence or intensity of the characteristic re- 
manence. In particular, there is no relation between a 
geochemical halo and the magnetization around veins. Fur- 
thermore, the same bed does not have a consistently higher 
characteristic magnetization when measured on the highly 
mineralized steep flank relative to the less mineralized shal- 
low flank. The characteristic magnetization in the Belden 
Formation is lithologically controlled in its distribution. The 
beds with the highest magnetization have concentrations of 
pyrite, with alteration rims of magnetite in fecal pellets con- 
taining clay minerals and organic material. Selective demag- 
netization indicates that the pellets contain the magnetiza- 
tion. Rock magnetic studies suggest the characteristic mag- 
netization resides in SD magnetite. 
It is not possible to unequivocally establish whether the 
characteristic magnetization is prefolding or synfolding. We 
can rule out a true synfolding component that was caused 
by the syndeformational fluids. A synfolding stress-related 
magnetization, such as a PRM or a structural modification 
of a prefolding component, are also possible, but they are 
not considered likely. A prefolding component overprinted 
by a modern VRM in multidomain grains is one possible, 
and perhaps likely, explanation for the synfolding test re- 
sult. 
The characteristic magnetization in the Belden was origi- 
nally a CRM, and remanence acquisition probably took place 
during burial, prior to deformation. The chemical mecha- 
nism responsible for magnetite authigenesis is unknown but 
could be a prefolding oxidizing fluid, or perhaps processes 
associated with maturation of hydrocarbons are possibili- 
ties.

Remagnetisation of Strata during the Hunter-Bowen Orogeny

M.A. Lackie 
CSIRO Division of Exploration and Mining 
PO Box 136 
North Ryde, NSW 2113

Abstract

Palaeomagnetic studies of strata within the southern New England Fold Belt show evidence of a northward migration of remagnetisation of the Belt during the Permian. In some rock units, such as the Kiah Limestone a syn-deformational remagnetisation is observed, while in others a pre-folding magnetisation is observed.

Key words: New England Fold Belt, Hunter-Bowen Orogeny, remagnetisation, Permian, Kiah Limestone, Werrie Basalt.

Introduction

The southern New England Fold Belt underwent a “single but complex compressive tectonic event, the Hunter-Bowen Orogeny" in the Late Permian (Collins, 1991). This event caused remagnetisation which is ubiquitous in sediments and very common in igneous rocks of all preceding ages (Klootwijk and Giddings, 1988). In light of the widespread magnetic overprinting, other aspects of the palaeomagnetic data from the New England Fold Belt require re-evaluation. The apparent polar wander path (APWP) for Australia (Fig. 1) indicates rapid movement of Australia from low to high palaeolatitudes between the Late Devonian/Early Carboniferous and the Late Carboniferous (Irving, 1966; Schmidt, 1988). Recent SHRIMP ion microprobe dating of zircons from Carboniferous volcanics of the southern New England Fold Belt (Roberts et al., 1991) show that the age of the Paterson Volcanics, and consequently the age of the base of the Seaham Formation, are about 330 Ma. Overlying the Seaham Formation is the Early Permian Dalwood Group (Roberts et al., 1991). This implies that the Seaham Formation may have been deposited over a period of 55 Ma. As rapid as the Carboniferous polar shift was previously thought to be (Schmidt, 1988; Li et al., 1989), this revised older date for the high latitude Paterson Volcanics implies plate velocities of \6.0%Myr, or >60cm/yr. This is an order of magnitude larger than average plate motions over the last 200 Ma, and given that the Gondwana continents were contiguous at this time, it is unacceptably large. It is noteworthy that although the Seaham Formation may represent 55 Ma, it apparently records no polar wandering during this period. In addition, the older date for the Seaham Formation pole requires backtracking of the pole path to the younger Late Carboniferous Alice Springs Orogeny pole. We propose that widespread magnetic updating of Devonian and Carboniferous strata in the New England Fold Belt during the Permian accounts for this enigma.

Results

Sixty oriented samples were collected from ten sites within the Kiah Limestone over a strike length of 100km (Fig. 2).

The Kiah Limestone is thought to be Late Devonian or Early Carboniferous in age (Voisey and Packham, 1969). Thermal demagnetisation of the samples reveals two components, a soft remanence directed in the present geomagnetic field direction which is usually demagnetised by 300°C and a second component which is usually demagnetised between 500°C and 550°C. The in-situ directions of the harder component of samples from the different sites are scattered (Fig. 3). On progressive correction for bedding tilt the site directions firstly converge and then diverge (Fig. 4). This phenomenon is common in folded strata that have been remagnetised and is attributed to syn-deformational remagnetisation (SDR, Schmidt and Embleton, 1987). If we apply a fold test that assumes a uniform rate of tilting (McFadden, 1990), then 62 percent of tilting yields the best correlation between the site mean directions. However, if we allow for non-uniform tilting, then a much better correlation between site mean directions is possible. That is, if we make the reasonable assumptions that the geomagnetic field axis did not change grossly while these rocks were being remagnetised, and that they acquired remanences parallel to the field at that time, then to satisfactorily explain these data we are led to the conclusion that the beds were remagnetised during different stages of deformation. In detail, there is a trend along strike suggesting that subsequent to remagnetisation more tilting has occurred in the south than in the north. Directions from sites in the north (KL02-KL06) require a small amount of untilting to bring them into agreement, while southerly sites (KL01,KL10) require almost complete untilting. Fifty percent untilting has been applied to sites KL07-KL09 (i.e. those between the most northerly and southerly sites) which produces a tight group of directions as displayed in figure 3. Thus, with respect to the time of folding, the time of remagnetisation appears to have migrated from the southeast to the northwest.

The Permian Werrie Basalt was sampled near Murrurundi, in the upper Hunter Valley (sites WB01-03, WB08-09, Fig. 2) and from the Warrigundi Complex (sites WB04-07, Fig. 2), which was recently shown to be of similar chemistry and age to the Werrie Complex (Flood et al., 1988). Fourty-five oriented samples were collected from 9 sites within the Werrie Basalts and the Warragundi Complex. Samples from sites WB04 and WB07, within the topographically prominent Warrigundi Complex have been affected by lightning and did not yield useful information. Another site, WB09 from within the Werrie Basalt proper, also failed to yield a useful result for an unknown reason. The other 6 sites provided internally consistent results that are discussed below.

Applying a fold test (McFadden, 1990) the magnetisation appears to have been acquired prior to significant tilting of the various flow units. In their present attitudes the directions yield a fold test statistic of 5.4, while after tilt correction the test statistic drops to 1.6, compared to 95% and 99% confidence values for the test that are 2.9 and 3.9 respectively. This shows that the magnetisation predates folding. After correction for simple bedding tilt the site-mean direction (Table 1) for the Werrie Basalt is Dec= 158.8°, Inc= 74.4°, k= 34.9, αg5 = 11.5°, yielding a pole position at Lat= 57.2°, Long= 170.3° and an Ag5 = 20.2°. We have no reason to doubt that the magnetisation of the Werrie basalt is not original, since it was magnetised before folding and therefore before the syndeformational remagnetisation in the northwest.

Discussion

The current APWP for Australia (Fig. 1) indicates large latitudinal movement of Australia from low palaeolatitudes in the Late Devonian/Early Carboniferous, as shown by the Worange Point (WP), Hervey Group (HG) and Mount Eclipse Sandstone (MES) poles, to high palaeolatitudes in the Late Carboniferous/Early Permian, as shown by the mean Alice Spring Orogeny pole (ASO comprises overprint poles referenced by Camacho et al. 1991) and the Early Permian Mount Leyshon pole (MTL). The Seaham Formation pole (MG), referred to previously as the Main Glacial Stage pole (Irving, 1966) falls quite close to the Early Permian MTL pole, suggesting an Early Permian age of magnetisation for the Seaham Formation rather than a Visean/Namurian age for the magnetisation.

The pole for the Paterson Volcanics (Irving, 1966), which are now considered to be 330 Ma old (Roberts et al, 1991), falls approximately 60° away from the mid-Carboniferous Hartley area/Bathurst Batholith pole (HB). As is discussed above for the Seaham Formation, such an early date for the Paterson Volcanics requires backtracking of the pole path from PT to the younger HB pole (Fig. 1). Thus, it is possible that the Paterson Volcanics have been remagnetised after Australia had moved to higher palaeolatitudes, although it is of normal polarity and would have hád to be remagnetised some time after the Seaham Formation (i.e. post-Kiaman). It should be noted that the Paterson Volcanics is a D-class pole (using the palaeomagnetic data quality filter of Li, 1993) and is therefore of questionable quality.

The results from the Seaham Formation show a positive fold test (Irving, 1966) indicating that magnetisation occurred prefolding. Data from the Kiah Limestone in the south of the Tamworth Belt are interpreted to indicate that magnetisation occurred just before, or at the beginning of folding. This is similar to the Werrie Basalt result. However, in the central part of the Tamworth Belt the Kiah Limestone results indicate that magnetisation was acquired at various stages of folding.

In the mid to Late Permian, meridional folds developed throughout the Tamworth Belt producing the Werrie and Gloucester Synclines and the Timor Anticline (Collins, 1991). If folding was synchronous within the Tamworth Belt then the Permian remagnetisation event progressively moves from the southeast in the Early Permian to the northwest in the mid to Late Permian. It can also be argued that if the remagnetisation was synchronous, then folding of the belt has progressed from the northwest to the southeast although this is not favoured on geological grounds. For instance, Čollins (1991) notes that deformation normally migrates towards the foreland, or east to west for the southern New England Fold Belt.

We hypothesise, therefore, that remagnetisation and deformation both began in the southeast, but that the remagnetisation predated the deformation. Both remagnetisation and deformation progressed northwest but at different rates with the latter catching up to the former, so that strata in the northwest were deformed at about the same time as they were remagnetized. The mechanism for remagnetisation in fold belts may be due to fluid movements as originally suggested by Oliver (1986) or if these fluids are related to granite intrusion, the ages of granites might also be expected to reflect the remagnetisation trends. We therefore speculate whether the age trend from the Barrington Tops Granodiorite in the southeast (265-270 Ma, Roberts and Engel, 1987) to the Moombi Suite granites (247-249 Ma, S.E.Shaw unpubl. data) in the northwest, is germane to remagnetisation.

The left diagram depicts the relationship between the degree of folding and remagnetisation within the Tamworth Belt during the Permian. In the southeast, remagnetisation occurs pre-folding, while progressively further to the northwest remagnetisation occurs during greater degrees of folding. The right side, shows the relationship of the remanence to the units with respect to the structure of those units. Note, that in the south (Seaham Formation) the remanence of the sediments is dissimilar between limbs (because it is a pre-folding remanence) while in the north (northern Kiah Limestone samples) the remanence is close to parallel between limbs (reflectíng the syn-folding remanence).

Diachronous remagnetisation along a fold belt is not unique to the New England Fold Belt. Remagnetisation data from the Appalachian Fold Belt in North America also indicate that remagnetisations were diachronous over the length of the belt (Miller and Kent, 1988). These workers observed prefolding remagnetisations in the southern Appalachians, synfolding magnetisations in the central region and postfolding remagnetisations in the north-central Appalachians.

The relationship between the sequence of folding and remagnetisation within the Tamworth Belt during the Permian is shown in figure 6. In the southeast remagnetisation occurred in the flat lying units, while further to the northwest, the remagnetisation occurred at the initiation of folding and still further northwest, remagnetisation was synfolding. As a consequence of the time of remagnetisation of the units and the corresponding attitude of the strata, the present in-situ remanence is steeply inclined in the northwest but only moderately inclined in the southeast.

Abstract 
One of the goals of the Pit093 cruise along the perimeter of the Easter microplate was to obtain oriented rock samples 
from the ocean floor for paleomagnetic study. Using a new orienting device, the Geoeompass, 14 oriented blocks were 
obtained during 6 dives conducted using the Ifremer DSRV Nautile. Paleomagnetic analysis shows that 13 of these 14 blocks 
give consistent results in thermal and AF demagnetizations, and reveals a mean Characteristic Remanent Magnetization 
(ChRM) direction within each block, with both normal and reverse polarities. After elimination of data from 5 blocks 
situated outside the microplate, and one block which bears an anomalous direction, we have computed a mean ChRM 
direction at D,,, = 49.0”, I, = - 39.0” (k = 10.2, ag5 = 19X’, n = 7). Although the mean inclination is in agreement with the 
inclination of the recent dipole magnetic field (D = 0”. I = - 43”), the average declination is significantly different from this 
direction, which we interpret as due to a bulk clockwise rotation of 48.5” f 11” (after the bivariate average) of the Easter 
microplate over the past 2-3 Ma. This value is in excellent agreement with previous estimates based on remote geophysical 
measurements and models. 
1. Introduction 
The Easter microplate is located on the East 
Pacific Rise, along the very fast spreading Pacific- 
Nazca boundary (Fig. 1). Numerous geophysical 
studies, including focal earthquake solutions, 
bathymetry, side-scan sonar imaging, Sea Beam and 
magnetic profiling, have shown that the microplate 
exists as a small rigid plate that is trapped and 
rapidly rotating between the diverging Pacific and 
Nazca plates. The east and west boundaries are two 
N-S trending, simultaneously active spreading cen- 
h-es, whereas the north and south boundaries are 
complex, transform-like fault zones with components 
of extension, compression and shear (e.g. [l-8]). 
This tectonic system has been approximated by a

Nazca and Pacific [2,9,10] (Fig. 1~). Due to the

Physique du Globe de Paris, Universitt de Paris 
7-Denis Diderot. Remanent magnetization was mea-

4.2. Theoretical versus observed dispersion 
Before making any selection of data based on the 
tectonic settings of the blocks, we can test a first 
hypothesis which is: (1) the magnetization of the 
blocks is primary; (2) it has been acquired in a 
direction close to the average long-term axial dipole 
field direction (D = O”, I = - 43”), with some disper- 
sion as discussed below; and (3) accounting for 
previous tectonic interpretations of the Easter mi- 
croplate, magnetization of all the blocks has under- 
gone some amount of clockwise rotation about a 
vertical axis. 
We may estimate two main sources of dispersion 
around a possible common mean direction: (1) scat- 
ter due to errors in measuring magnetization, which 
are dominated by errors in block orientation; (2) 
dispersion arising from the scatter of virtual geomag- 
netic poles (VGP) due to paleo-secular variation 
(PSV, [22]). Obviously, there is a third source of 
dispersion, which is the component of rotation around 
horizontal axes due to block tilting near spreading 
centres (e.g., Hurst et al. [12]). This will be discussed 
later. 
Let o2 be the variance about the average direc- 
tion, aO* the variance due to errors in block orienta- 
tions, and or* the variance due to the VGP scatter. 
Assuming that the two sources of uncertainty are 
independent, we have u = F ap + a: . Following the 
above discussion, we estimate a, as about 10”. VGP 
scatter is a function of paleo-latitude, and, according 
to the ‘G model’ of McFadden et al. [22], is about 
15” for a latitude of 25”. This results in AD = 20” 
and AI = 15” at the sampling location. We thus 
estimate directional scatter due to PSV as err = 17”. 
With these values u = 20”. This means that, if the 
observed scatter arises from these 2 sources, 95% of 
the data should lie in a cone with an aperture angle 
of 2a = 40” around their mean direction. 
To test the above hypothesis, we constructed a 
window consisting of 2 spherical shells with a 40” 
aperture around the expected normal and reverse 
dipole field directions (D = O”, I = - 43” and D = 
180”, I = 43”; Fig. 5a), and we scanned the sphere by 
rotating these shells about a vertical axis, from 0” to 
360”, by 10” steps. 
The result of this scan is illustrated in Fig. 5b, 
which displays the number of data falling in the 
2u = 40” areas as a function of rotation angle. The 
figure clearly shows a maximum of 9 out of 13 data 
when the window is rotated clockwise by 40-60”. 
The corresponding cluster of magnetization direc- 
tions is rather clear in Fig. 5a (almost no data in the 
second and fourth quadrants of the projection). Two 
small secondary submaxima in the curves of Fig. 5b 
are due to blocks 18-08, 02-02 and 02-03. 
The magnetization of 18-08 is obviously anoma- 
lous as it has a very steep downward northerly 
direction (Table 1, Fig. 5a); this may arise from 
either a local tectonic rotation, sampling of a dis- 
placed outcrop, or erroneous orientation. As far as 
blocks 02-02 and 02-03 are concerned, we note that 
dive 02 is located to the east of the northward 
propagating East Rift and to the west of the nearby 
failing rift (Fig. 1). This places the samples in a 
sinistral zone of shear, which should result in a 
counter-clockwise rotation of the nearby crust 
[6,8,21]. This could explain the counter-clockwise 
rotation of magnetic directions from these two blocks. 
Finally, although data from dive 06 match the 
above model, we note that: (1) this dive is situated 
on the northern flank of Pito Deep, and most likely 
pertains to the Nazca plate; and (2) data from this 
dive are very scattered (Figs. 4 and 5a), although the 
three outcrops sampled are situated a few hundred 
meters apart. Because these data appear to be sus- 
pect, we reject them from our paleomagnetic esti- 
mate of the Easter microplate rotation.

5. Conclusions 
Using a new orienting device, the Geocompass, 
carried by the submersible Nuutile, we were able to 
collect oriented rock samples from the ocean floor, 
on the Easter microplate, during the Pit093 cruise, in 
November 1993, allowing a paleomagnetic study to 
be performed. Our sampling procedure, which con- 
sists in orienting two planar faces of each block, 
whenever possible, allowed us to check for large 
errors in orientation and to estimate orientation un- 
certainties at about L- 10”. 
Fourteen oriented blocks were recovered during 6 
dives. Thirteen of these 14 blocks give consistent 
results in both thermal and AF demagnetizations, 
allowing us to define a mean characteristic remanent 
magnetization direction within each block, with both 
normal and reverse polarities. The resulting ChRM 
distribution for all the blocks appears quite scattered. 
An analysis of this scatter, taking into account 
paleo-secular variation, orientation uncertainties in 
sampling and location of the dives, leads to the 
conclusion that at least 7 of the 13 magnetization 
directions are consistent with the hypothesis that the 
ChRM is a primary magnetization and has been 
rotated clockwise by 48.5” f 11” since 2.5 k 0.5 Ma. 
Of course, the number and location of sites only 
allows an estimate of an average rotation, and not its 
detailed distribution, as presented, for instance, by 
Naar and Hey 161. 
We interpret this rotation as a net clockwise 
rotation of the whole Easter microplate around a 
vertical axis. The sense of this rotation is in agree- 
ment with the one predicted by the models of Engeln 
et al. [9] and Schouten et al. [lo] and its amount is 
consistent with previous estimates based on the tec- 
tonic fabric of the microplate, and the pattern of its 
magnetic anomalies (e.g., see [3,5,6,8]). The rotation 
rate of the plate is difficult to evaluate, because of 
the lack of radiometric age control of our samples, 
but is approximately 23.5” i 1 lo/Ma, consistent with 
published rotation rates for the Easter microplate. 
Although better estimates could certainly have 
been obtained with a larger number of blocks from 
each dive (to evaluate orientation errors more accu- 
rately) and a larger number of dives, particularly in 
the central part of the microplate (to avoid effects 
due to nearby active tectonic boundaries), this study 
appears very encouraging in that it demonstrates the 
feasibility of underwater sampling of oriented blocks 
for use in paleomagnetic studies. Also, it provides 
the first direct underwater field evidence of large and 
fast microplate rotation.

Paleomagnetic study of the northern Ford Ranges, 
western Marie Byrd Land, West Antarctica' 
Motion between West and East Antarctica 
Bruce Luyendyk, Stan Cisowski, Christine Smith, l Steve Richard, 
and David Kimbrough 3 
Institute for Crustal Studies, University of California, Santa Barbara 
Abstract. A paleomagnetic study of Paleozoic and Mesozoic 
crystalline rocks in the northern Ford Ranges of Marie Byrd 
Land, West Antarctica, has determined a middle Cretaceous 
(circa 100 Ma) paleomagnetic pole and provided constraints 
on possible clockwise rotation of these ranges and on the 
rifting of east Gondwana. The 4(IAr/39Ar thermochronology 
data from the Fosdick Mountains record a period of rapid 
cooling from -700øC beginning at-100 Ma. We relate this to 
extension, intrusion, and uplift associated with the beginning 
of rifting between Campbell Plateau and Marie Byrd Land. All 
rocks from the Fosdick and Chester Mountains are normally 
polarized. We interpret thermochronology and paleomagnetic 
data to infer that the region was extensively remagnetized in 
middle Cretaceous time. Inclinations in samples from the 
Chester Mountains are less steep than those from the Fosdick 
Mountains, which we interpret as -25 ø of south tilting of the 
Chesters. We interpret cooling age data for the time of 
magnetization to infer that the tilting began after 105 Ma and 
ended prior to 103 Ma. We further interpret this as 
constraining the beginning of extension between the 
Campbell Plateau and western Marie Byrd Land to the interval 
105 to 103 Ma. Virtual geomagnetic poles from samples of 
Early Carboniferous age granodiorite from the western Phillips 
Mountains lie on the late Paleozoic apparent polar wander path 
for Australia transferred to Antarctica. Directions from 29 
sites in the central and eastern Phillips and Fosdick Mountains 
give a Middle Cretaceous paleomagnetic pole at 222.3 ø E, 
70.5 ø S (A95 6.1ø, KAPPA 20.0). This pole is 
indistinguishable from other Middle Cretaceous poles for 
studies further east in Marie Byrd Land. Combining middle 
Cretaceous poles determined for three other studies of the 
Antarctic Peninsula, Thurston Island, and the Ruppert-Hobbs 
coasts with ours gives a Pacific West Antarctic pole at 215.2 ø 
E, 73.5 ø S (A95 4.0 ø, KAPPA 528.9). This pole is discordant 
by 5 ø to 10 ø from synthetic mid-Cretaceous East Antarctic

to the choice of the specific reference pole. The lack of native 
East Antarctic reference poles leaves this analysis 
inconclusive. Accepting 10 ø of discordance, we favor an 
interpretation where Pacific West Antarctic crustal domains or 
microplates have rotated clockwise 40 ø to 90 ø and translated a 
few degrees away from East Antarctica during Late Cretaceous 
time. 
Purpose of Study 
A paleomagnetic study of igneous and metamorphic rocks 
from outcrops in the northern Edsel Ford Ranges of western 
Marie Byrd Land (MBL) was undertaken as a part of a larger 
geological study of this region (Figure 1). A primary goal of 
the overall study was to determine whether metamorphic rocks 
exposed in the Raymond Fosdick Mountains could be a 
metamorphic core complex similar to Cretaceous complexes 
found in New Zealand [Gibson et al., 1988; Tulloch and 
Kimbrough, 1989]. Our study included geologic mapping, 
metamorphic petrology, U-Pb and 4()Ar/39A r 
thermochronology, paleomagnetism, and anisotropy of 
magnetic susceptibility. The paleomagnetic program had as 
its goals (1) determination of Carboniferous, Cretaceous, and 
Cenozoic poles for a Pacific West Antarctic apparent polar 
wander path (APWP); (2) testing whether western Marie Byrd 
Land was distinct from other West Antarctic microplates 
[Grunow et al., 1991]; and (3) testing whether Marie Byrd Land 
is tectonically distinct from Victoria Land in East Antarctica 
[Grindley and Oliver, 1983; DiVertere et al., 1994]. 
Geologic Setting 
Microplates in West Antarctica 
West Antarctica is proposed to comprise four separate 
geologic terranes or microplates [Dalziel and Elliot, 1982; 
Dalziel and Grunow, 1985]. These are the Antarctic Peninsula, 
the Ellsworth-Whitmore Mountains, Thurston Island-Eights 
Coast, and Marie Byrd Land. The basis for this division is the 
contrasting geology and tectonic histories between them, 
paleomagnetic data, subice deeps separating the terranes, and 
overlap of the Antarctic Peninsula with the Falkland Plateau in 
Mesozoic reconstructions. Paleomagnetic data have been 
interpreted to suggest that West Antarctic terranes have been 
fixed to one another since Middle Cretaceous time [DiVehere et 
al., 1994]. Pre-Middle Cretaceous paleomagnetic data suggest 
a history of complex relative motions among the terranes and

Pacific West Antarctic (excluding the Ellsworth Mountains) 
elevation and relief are subdued in contrast to the spectacular 
Transantarctic Mountains and the East Antarctic Polar Plateau. 
P,,,,,amb,,,n crust in West Antarctica is found in the Haag 
Nunataks of Ellsworth Land adjacent to Weddell Embayment 
[e.g., Storey et al., 1988; Tingey, 1991]. However, 
Proterozoic U-Pb inheritance ages from Phanerozoic plutons 
in western Marie Byrd Land suggest a Precambrian component 
in the crust underlying this region [Kimbrough and Richard; 
1991; Palais et al., 1993]. Most Pacific West Antarctica rock 
outcrops consist of Phanerozoic subduction-related intrusive 
and volcanic rocks. 
The Pacific margin of West Antarctica, including the 
microplates of Marie Byrd Land, Thurston Island-Eights Coast, 
and the Antarctic Peninsula, has been an active margin of east 
Gondwana for most of Paleozoic and Mesozoic time [Borg and 
DePaolo, 1991; Elliot, 1991; Barker et al., 1991]. This 
margin was once continuous from Australia to South America 
and was subducting me Phoenix plate dunng Mesozoic time 
[Bradshaw, 1989; Barker et al., 1991]. In Late Cretaceous time 
the continental masses of New Zealand, the Lord Howe Rise, 
the Chatham Rise, and Campbell Plateau (Zealandia 
[Luyendyk, 1995]), separated off from east Gondwana [e.g., 
Mayes et al., 1990; Lawver et al, 1992]. Seafloor spreading 
between Marie Byrd Land and the Campbell Plateau began 
about 85 Ma [Mayes et al., 1990; Lawyer et al., 1992] but this 
was preceded by about 20 million years of extension 
throughout Zealandia [Bradshaw, 1991]. The transition from 
subduction to extension along the margin occurred abruptly 
around 105 Ma in New Zealand [Bradshaw, 1989] and Marie 
Byrd Land [Weaver et al., 1994]. Luyendyk [1995] explains 
this sudden transition by capture of a microplate piece of the 
subducted Phoenix plate beneath the margin by the Pacific 
plate. Northward motion of the Pacific plate and captured 
Phoenix microplate extended the margin and Zealandia.

Southern Ocean basins. There is also evidence for extension

the East Antarctic craton. Marie Byrd Land is separated from 
East Antarctica by the Ross Embayment, a province of horsts 
and grabens which underlies the Ross Sea and Ross Ice Shelf 
and extends eastward between the Transantarctic Mountains 
and Marie Byrd Land (Figure 1). The Ross Embayment is the 
locus of the majority of extension. Cooper et al. [1987, 
1991], interpreting marine seismic reflection data, suggest 
two phases of extension here, a major one in Jurassic and 
Cretaceous time followed by a lesser one beginning in Eocene 
time. Marine geophysical data suggest that the second 
extension phase in the Ross Embayment ended in the eastern 
Ross Sea by mid-late Oligocene time but continues in the west 
within the Victoria Land Basin to present day [Cooper et al., 
1991]. Middle Jurassic continental flood basalts of the Ferrar 
Group in the Transantarctic Mountains are believed to mark the 
beginning of Mesozoic extension between East and West 
Antarctica [Elliot, 1992; Heimann et al., 1994]. Extension in 
the Ross Embayment has also been related to uplift of the 
Transantarctic Mountains. Fission-track cooling data from 
these mountains can be interpreted as reflecting episodic uplift 
in Early and Late Cretaceous, Eocene, and Plio-Pleistocene 
time [Fitzgerald et al., 1986; Fitzgerald, 1992; Stump and 
Fitzgerald, 1992]. The major Tertiary uplift is likely related to 
a global plate reorganization near the beginning of Eocene 
time [Scotese et al., 1988]. 
The Ross Embayment and Marie Byrd Land are parts of the 
West Antarctic rift system [e.g., Behrendt et al., 1991] which 
has been active during Cenozoic time. Cenozoic extension 
was marked by bimodal volcanism [Behrendt et al., 1991]. 
Crustal thicknesses in the rift, including Marie Byrd Land, are 
half that of East Antarctica [Behrendt et al., 1991; Bentley, 
1973; 1991]. 
Geology of the Northern Ford Ranges 
Geologic ties can be made between western Marie Byrd Land 
and the Robertson Bay terrane in northem Victoria Land across 
the Ross Sea. The Lower Paleozoic Swanson Formation in 
western Marie Byrd Land comprising deep water quartzose 
sediments [Bradshaw et al., 1983], may correlate with 
sedimentary rocks of the Robertson Bay Group in northern 
Victoria Land [Wade and Couch, 1982; Adams, 1986; Muir et 
al., 1994]. Both regions were evidently deformed during the 
Cambrian Ross orogeny. The Carboniferous Ford Granodiorite 
(see below) in Marie Byrd Land may correlate with the 
Admiralty Intrusives of northern Victoria Land [Weaver et al., 
1991 ]. Borg and DePaolo [ 1991 ] argued that Marie Byrd Land 
amalgamated with terranes of northern Victoria Land including 
the Roberston Bay and Bowers terranes, at a location exotic to 
Gondwana from Ordovician through Devonian time. This

Permian time. 
The Phillips, Fosdick, and Chester Mountains are located in 
the northern portions of the Ford Ranges of western Marie 
Byrd Land (Figure 1). They trend east-west and are each 
separated by about 15-20 km. Plutonic rocks crop out in the 
Phillips and Chester Mountains, while the Fosdick Mountains 
comprise high-grade metamorphic rocks (Figures 2 and 3). 
The Ford Granodiorite (MDf) is a Devonian-Carboniferous 
granodiorite-tonalite found in the Phillips and Chester 
Mountains and the Denfield Mountains immediately to the 
south. It is a calc-alkaline and metaluminous to peraluminous 
I-type granitoid [Weaver et al., 1991]. Foliated hornblende- 
biotite tonali. te or granodiorite with enclaves of gneiss (MDf?) 
is found at Neptune and Griffith Nunataks. Kimbrough and 
Richard [1991] reported a U-Pb zircon age of 353 Ma for MDf 
from the Chester Mountains. A Permian two-mica granite 
intrudes the MDf in the Chester Mountains and Neptune 
Nunataks [Kimbrough and Richard, 1991; Richard et al., 
1994]. The Byrd Coast Granite (Kbc) is a Cretaceous granite 
which is ubiquitous in the Ford Ranges and Edward VII 
Peninsula to the southwest [Wade et al., 1977 a, b, c, 1978]. It 
has both A- and I-type characteristics [Weaver et al., 1991, 
1992, 1994].. Igneous textures indicate emplacement at 
shallow crustal depths. Ages determined by U-Pb analyses on 
zircons from Kbc at Mount Corey in the Chester Mountains are 
105 to 103 Ma (D.L. Kimbrough, unpublished data, 1992). 
These Middle Cretaceous ages indentify the Kbc in the 
northern Ford Ranges as the A-type suite II granitoids of 
Weaver et al. [1994]. Both MDf and Kbc may be present in the 
Ruppert Coast to the northeast [Sp6rli and Craddock, 1981; 
Bradshaw et al., 1991]. Although rocks similar to MDf are 
known in northern Victoria Land (Admiralty lntrusives), no 
rocks equivalent to the Kbc are known there. 
The Fosdick Metamorphic Complex comprises migmatized 
paragneiss and orthogneiss found in the Fosdick Mountains 
[Wilbanks, 1972; Smith, 1992]. Smith [1995] has determined 
peak metamorphic conditions corresponding to midcrustal 
depths (500 to 529+70 MPa) and temperatures of 632ø+78øC to 
699ø+67øC from geothermobarometry on paragneiss. Peak 
metamorphism and anatexis occurred at about 105 Ma 
[Kimbrough and Richard, 1991; Richard et al, 1994], 
contemporaneous with Kbc intrusion. In the northern Ford 
Ranges, mafic dikes intrude MDf, Kbc, and the Fosdick 
metamorphic rocks (FMR). Whereas dikes intruding the FMR 
are typically deformed and boudinaged, mafic dikes are 
undeformed within the other formations. In the central and 
eastern Fosdick Mountains, volcanic rocks of late Cenozoic 
age crop out. These are the westernmost outcrops of late 
Cenozoic age volcanic rocks in West Antarctica. Lavas from 
Mount Perkins are Pleistocene in age (4øAr/39Ar whole rock age 
courtesy of W. Mcintosh). We believe the Fosdick Complex 
has been uplifted rapidly from midcrustal depths in Late 
Cretaceous time [Richard, 1992; Richard et al., 1994]. A 
hanging wall-footwall fault relationship is suggested between 
the Phillips and Fosdick Mountains (Figures 2 and 3). 
Although the Fosdick Mountains have cooling ages similar to 
New Zealand core complexes, they lack brittle structural 
features and low-grade metamorphic overprint typical of 
Cordilleran-style metamorphic culminations in the western 
United States [Coney, 1980; Davis, 1980] and New Zealand 
[Tulloch and Kimbrough, 1989]. 
The Phillips and Fosdick Mountains trend subparallel to the 
Transantarctic Mountains (as viewed in a polar projection), as 
do other mountain ranges within the Ford Ranges. 
Furthermore, the individual ranges trend oblique to the passive 
continental margin here. The north scarp of the central 
Fosdick Mountains is defined by spectacular cliffs up to 500 m
