6. Discussion and implications for the tectonic 
emplacement of Sumba 
From the paleomagnetic analysis of the volcanics 
of the Jawila Formation one can conclude that in 
early Miocene times the island of Sumba had a 
position approximately at the same latitude as it has 
now. Moreover, the paleomagnetic data indicate that 
Sumba did practically not rotate since the early 
Miocene; if any, there could have been a clockwise 
rotation with a maximum of 4” (Tables 1 and 3). The 
a95 values of the data are rather large; therefore a 
N-S-directed shift of Sumba of 4” with respect to its 
present position cannot be excluded and a larger 
amount of rotation is possible as well. However, the 
preliminary results of a paleomagnetic analysis of 
the sediments from the middle to late Miocene-early 
Pliocene Sumba Formation are identical at a much 
lower a95 value (Van der Werff et al., 1995b) 
supporting the conclusion that at least since the 
Miocene the continental fragment of Sumba occu- 
pied approximately its present position. 
Therefore, the main stage of drift must have been 
prior to this time. Paleomagnetic studies on rocks 
from Sumba of late Cretaceous and early Tertiary 
age revealed that in pre-Miocene times the fragment 
must have performed large rotational and transla- 
tional movements. The original position of the Sumba 
fragment had a latitude of 18”, most likely in the 
northern hemisphere (Wensink, 1994; see also Table 
3). The majority of the geological arguments and 
recent isotopic evidence corroborates this hypothesis 
(Van der Borch et al., 1983; Audley-Charles et al., 
1988; Rangin et al., 1990a, b; Vroon et al., 1995). 
Simandjuntak (1993) reported striking similarities 
between late Cretaceous through Miocene strati- 
graphic sequences of Sumba and southern Sulawesi. 
He concluded that in late Cretaceous-Paleogene 
times the Sumba fragment was positioned east to the 
South Arm of Sulawesi, in the northern part of the 
present Bone Bay. However, his suggestion that the 
separation of the Sumba fragment occurred in early 
to middle Miocene times, is precluded by our results, 
according to which it had arrived at or very close to 
its present position by then. 
The geochemical signature of the Jawila volcanics 
indicates a subduction environment at the time of 
their formation, which implies that Sumba formed 
part of a volcanic arc in early Miocene times. This 
observation is of interest, because of the possible 
implications for the early stage of development of 
the East Sunda Arc. The East Sunda Arc can be seen 
as an eastward propagating extension of the older 
Sunda Arc of Sumatra and Java (Van Bemmelen, 
1949; Katitli, 1975; Abbott and Chamalaun, 1981). 
On Sumbawa, magmatism was initiated in the early 
Miocene; after an interruption in middle and late 
Miocene times volcanic activity resumed in the early 
Pliocene (Barberi et al., 1987). Fission-track dating 
of zircons in andesites from Flores yielded an oldest 
age of 21 Ma (Nishimura et al., 19811, but from 
central Flores ages of no more than 4 Ma have been 
reported (Abbott and Chamalaun, 198 I ). Further east 
the oldest dated igneous rocks are 12 Ma samples 
from the island of Wetar (Fig. 1) in the extinct sector 
north of Timor (Abbott and Chamalaun, 198 1). The 
active Banda Arc is considerably younger. 
The available geochronological data thus suggest 
that magmatic activity of an age similar to that of the 
Jawila volcanics occurred on Sumbawa and eastern 
Flores but may absent in the area between these two 
locations. We hypothesize, therefore, that Sumba and 
its surroundings formed part of the proto-East Sunda 
Arc during part of the Miocene. This leaves two 
options for the current position of Miocene arc vol- 
canics south of the present East Sunda Arc: 
(1) The Jawila rocks represent magmas from the 
(proto-) East Sunda Arc and originated slightly more 
to the north within the present domain of the vol- 
canic arc. Near the end of its drift from north to 
south, Sumba passed the zone of magma generation 
in this sector of the (proto-) East Sunda Arc, and 
carried the volcanics, detached from their mantle 
sources, over a relatively short distance (300 km at 
most) southward. This would imply that the Sumba 
fragment reached its final position when the volcanic 
arc already had started to develop, and that the 
western and eastern sides of the microcontinent are 
presently bound by major discontinuities across the 
arc system. In this case the East Sunda Arc is

28 H. Wensink. M.J. um Bergen/ Tectonophysics 250 (1995) 15-30 
assumed to have remained stationary at the same 
latitude since its formation. 
The statistical error in our paleomagnetic data on 
the Jawila volcanics permits such a minor southward 
drift since the early Miocene. On the other hand, the 
available data would also allow a slightly more 
southward Miocene position of the Sumba fragment 
rather than a northward one; the paleolatitude data 
derived from both the Jawila and the overlying Sumba 
Formation (Van der Werff et al., 1995b) would not 
be in conflict with a minor post early Pliocene drift 
of the Sumba block to the north (cf. Audley-Charles, 
1975). 
Therefore, relative to the present volcanic arc, 
slightly different positions of the Sumba fragment 
are conceivable: either within the region of the pre- 
sent arc at its current location, or somewhat more to 
the south. 
(2) The Jawila magmas originated at their present 
location after the drift of Sumba had come to a 
complete end. They represent an early manifestation 
of volcanic activity in this part of the East Sunda 
Arc. Assuming a single arc system, this would imply 
that in the early Miocene the volcanic front had a 
more southern position than in the adjacent sectors, 
and that it shifted northward to the present arc since 
then, perhaps after a period of volcanic rest. 
Such a shift has been proposed by Fortuin et al. 
(1994), based on the presence of abundant volcanic 
material in the Neogene deposits of the Sumba For- 
mation; the NNE-prograding submarine fans and 
outcrops along eastern Sumba’s south coast point to 
a provenance from a proto-volcanic arc to the south 
of the island. Seismo-stratigraphic research has con- 
firmed the eastward continuation of these deposits in 
the Sumba Basin, on the submarine Sumba Ridge 
and in the South Savu Basin (Van der Werff et al., 
1994a; Van der Werff, 1995). Since the front of the 
accretionary wedge has approached Sumba’s south 
coast at a distance of less than 50 km, it is unlikely 
that any trace of this presumed proto-volcanic arc is 
left (Van der Werff et al., 1995a). Eastward the 
wedge widens and backthrusts cut off the submarine 
continuation of Sumba in the South Savu Basin. The 
Jawila volcanics in western Sumba may represent a 
rather small advanced continuation of the same pos- 
tulated arc. 
Significant shifts of the volcanic front suggests 
changes in the subduction geometry since the 
Miocene, which are likely to have occurred in re- 
sponse to the arc-continent collision. They could be 
the effect of the transition in the subducting plate 
from oceanic to continental lithosphere. As long as 
subduction occurred in an entirely oceanic environ- 
ment, the downgoing slab of probably late Jurassic 
age, and therefore relatively cold and dense, was 
steep, resulting in a short arc-trench gap. Upon the 
arrival of the Australian continental margin, subduc- 
tion of its leading edge with much more buyoant 
material, may have caused a flattening of the dip and 
a concomitant widening of the arc-trench gap, which 
could explain the northward shift of the volcanic 
front. Sections across the present-day seismic Be- 
nioff zone in the collision region east of 116”E 
suggest such a change in dip: it is relatively flat in 
the shallow parts and steep at deeper levels to the 
north (McCaffrey, 1989). 
Furthermore, the gradually increasing supply of 
sedimentary material of the approaching passive 
margin has led to the formation of the voluminous 
accretionary prism south and southeast of Sumba. 
Sediment accretion, subduction and subduction ero- 
sion in areas with accretionary wedge formation may 
be accompanied by changes in the geometry of the 
subduction zone. Such features have been docu- 
mented for the Cenozoic tectonic history of northern 
Honshu in Japan by Von Huene et al. (19821, who 
attributed the presence of Tertiary volcanic rocks in 
the fore-arc area to changes in the geometry as well. 
Because a more southern position of the early 
Miocene volcanic front in the East Sunda Arc may 
have been limited to the Sumba area, the controls of 
the subduction geometry may have varied over rela- 
tively short distances along the strike of the arc 
system. Given the likely relation with the collision 
process, the variation could reflect irregularities in 
the outline of the approaching Australian margin, 
similar to those along its northwestern border with 
the Indian Ocean. 
We conclude from our paleomagnetic results that 
the drift of the Sumba fragment, which started at the 
eastern rim of Sundaland in late Cretaceous times, 
had practically ended in the early Miocene. Unequiv- 
ocal evidence on whether Sumba reached its final 
position shortly after or before the extrusion of the 
Jawila volcanics remains to be established. From

H. Wensink. M.J. mm Bergen/Tectonophysics 250 f1995115-30 29 
circumstantial evidence there is a slight preference 
for the second option. It should be noted, however, 
that both possibilities preclude the presence of arc- 
type magmatic rocks in the East Sunda sector to the 
north of Sumba with the same age as the Jawila 
Formation, except when two parallel arc systems 
existed simultaneously. Further verification requires 
detailed age dating of the Tertiary magmatic rocks in 
this part of the Sunda-Banda Arc.

Paleosecular Variation of Direction and Intensity from Two Pliocene-Pleistocene 
 Lava Sections in Southwestern Iceland
Hidefumi TANAKA', Maseru KONO2, and Shigetoshi KANEKO'
'Dept . of Earth and Planetary Sciences, Tokyo Institute of Technology, Tokyo 152, Japan 2Dept . of Earth and Planetary Physics, University of Tokyo, Tokyo 113, Japan
(Received January 22, 1994; Revised September 16, 1994; Accepted October 6, 1994)
 Two lava sections in southwestern Iceland were revisited; sectoin IG of Kristjansson et 
al. (1988) of Brunhes chron age and section K of Wilson et al. (1972) of early Matuyama 
chron age. Paleodirections obtained from 22 laves at the former section do not seem to 
have averaged out the secular variation completely because of their small angular standard 
deviation, and this suggests rapid accumulation of the lavas. The latter section consists of 
29 lavas and contains the Gauss to Matuyarna transition near its base. The time interval 
during which the laves at this section were erupted also seems to be short, judging from the 
small directional dispersion. Thelliers' paleointensity method was also applied to the samples 
from this section. A characteristic low paleointensity was obtained from the transitional lava 
flow. However, low paleointensities were also obtained from the lavas which erupted some 
time after the transition, and which record directions close to those of an axial geomagnetic 
dipole.
1. Introduction
 The remarkable basaltic lava sequences in Iceland have been the subject of many paleomag-
netic studies since the pioneering work by Jan Hospers in 1950's (see for example, Irving, 1988; 
Kristjiinsson, 1993). Paleomagnetic expeditions by several research groups since then have made 
substantial contributions to the study of geomagnetism. Paleomagnetic studies in Iceland are still 
worthwhile in spite of the largest paleomagnetic database ever obtained on the globe because; 1) 
previous measurements were often from only two or three samples per lava, 2) reliable paleoin-
tensity data are scarce, and 3) some of the lava sequences younger than 2-3 Ma have not been 
fully investigated. 
 Most of the paleointensity information from Icelandic lavas are estimates of relative pale-
ointensity; determined by the NRM intensity at a fixed level of AF demagnetization (first by 
Dagley and Wilson, 1971). The "relative" methods, unlike relative paleointensity methods often 
applied to sediment sections, do not take any account of magnetic mineral concentration. It is 
often supposed, however, that the relative paleointensity data from Icelandic lavas still reflect 
the real paleointensity, partly because the large number of data average out the differences of 
various rock magnetic factors, and partly because the Icelandic basalt lavas are relatively similar 
in rock magnetism. The relative paleointensity study gave intriguing results on the relation of 
pseudo-dipole moment versus VGP latitude, but this does not preclude the importance of the 
absolute paleointensity data. Early absolute paleointensity studies are due to Smith (1967) and 
Lawley (1970) in which 13 baked sediments plus 18 lava flows and 27 lava flows, respectively, 
were studied by the methods of either Wilson (1961) or van ZijI et al. (1962). Although it is 
now generally agreed that these two methods are less reliable than those by Thellier and Thel-
lier (1959) and Shaw (1974) due to the lack of an internal consistency test, the results of Smith 
(1967) and Lawley (1970) might be fairly reliable because they performed many tests to detect 
any magnetic alteration during heating. Some of the results of Smith (1967) are from the same

section at Mt. Reynivallahals as this study, and, as we will see later, his result from a lava which 
records a transitional direction is in good agreement with those obtained in this study. Shaw et 
al. (1982) and Roberts and Shaw (1984) applied the Shaw method to 277 late Tertiary lavas in 
Eastern Iceland to obtain 106 results, and in the latter paper some asymmetry between normal 
and reversed polarity data was found. It is noted that generally they obtained data from only 
one specimen per lava, and the reliability of some of the results, such as some very high paleoin-
tensities, is a matter of debate (Kristjansson, 1985b). Only few paleointensity studies using the 
Thelliers' method have been reported from Icelandic lavas. Two studies were made with regard 
to the latest Pleistocene geomagnetic excursion of about 40 ka (Marshall et al., 1988; Levi et al., 
1990), and one was on 17 Holocene lavas (Schweitzer and Soffel, 1980). Senanayake et al. (1982) 
obtained eleven late Tertiary paleointensities from one to three specimens per lava. 
 This study was aimed as a reconnaissance study for future extended works, such as a detailed 
magnetostratigraphy to establish the polarity time scale in Neogene period from Icelandic lavas 
which is considered to show more frequent reversals than those from marine magnetic anoma-
lies (Kristjansson, 1985a), or, thorough paleointensity studies to overcome the unbalanced data 
numbers between intensity and direction which are essential to establish a statistical model of 
paleomagnetic field. In this paper, we report on the paleosecular variation from two lava sections 
of Pliocene to Pleistocene age in southwestern Iceland which were previously studied by Wil-
son et al. (1972) and Kristjansson et al. (1988). Paleointensity experiments using the Thelliers' 
method was also performed on the samples from one of the sections, which includes the Gauss to 
Matuyama transition at its base. Special emphasis is put on these paleointensity results in this 
paper.
2. Lava Sections and Samples
 Samples were collected from 29 lavas of section K of Wilson et al. (1972) at Mt. Reynivallahals 
and 22 lavas of sectoin IG of Kristjansson et al. (1988) at Mt. Ingolfsflall, which locate about 30 
km northeast and about 50 km southeast of Reykjavik, respectively. Both sections comprise a 
sequence of basaltic lavas, mostly tholeiite type, of typical thickness of 2-20 m, and intermittent 
occurrence of sediment and hyaloclastite layers are recognized. The former, referred to as section 
RK in this study, covers the top of N4 and the lowest part of R3 using the polarity groups of 
Einarsson (1957), and this corresponds to Gauss to Matuyama chrons according to Kristjansson 
et al. (1980). Section IG (section RG in this study) was assumed to be in the Brunhes chron 
by Kristjansson et al. (1988), and recently this has been confirmed by K-Ar ages determined by 
Duncan (personal communication, 1994). He collected one and four samples from sections IE and 
II, respectively, of Kristjansson et al. (1988). Two normal lavas just above the reverse to normal 
boundary at the two sections gave 0.71 f 0.01 Ma and 0.57 + 0.18 Ma. One reversed lava below 
the boundary gave 0.83±0.27 Ma, and two lavas from much higher levels gave 0.29±0.03 Ma and 
0.54 ± 0.06 Ma. As the polarity boundaries of the two sections correspond to that of section IG 
because the lava layers are almost horizontal at Mt. Ing6lfsfjall, it is concluded that the normal 
of the section IG is in the Brunhes chron. 
 Samples were collected using a portable drill. Usually, five cores were drilled from each 
lava. The core orientations were ascertained by the sun azimuth or geographic sightings. A 
magnetic compass was also used as a subsidiary orientation method. However, the differences of 
measured azimuth angle between the magnetic orientation and other two methods varied between 
less than 5° and more than 25°, indicating that magnetic orientation is often compromised by 
the magnetization of the rock.

3. Paleomagnetic Results
8.1 Paleodirections 
 One pilot sample from each lava was subjected to stepwise alternating field (AF) demagneti-
zation, usually up to 80 mT. Stepwise thermal demagnetization was also applied to another pilot 
sample from each lava. Remanences were usually very stable to AF demagnetization while they 
were often less stable to thermal demagnetization. Nevertheless, analysis of the stable component 
on an orthogonal component plot was always straightforward for all samples from both sections 
RG and RK. Examples of the orthogonal component plot of AF and thermal demagnetization 
are shown in Fig. 1. As AF demagnetization was found to be more effective, all the remaining 
samples were cleaned by AF demagnetization at two or three steps up to the optimal level of 15-
25 mT. Primary remanence directions were also determined on the orthogonal component plot 
including the origins. Lava mean paleodirections were determined by combining these specimen 
directions with those of pilot samples. Lava mean directions and the corresponding VGP positions 
are summarized in Table 1 for section RG. For section RK, paleodirections are summarized in 
Table 2 with some paleointensity results which will be discussed later. No tectonic tilt correction 
was made to the paleodirections at section RG because at the Mt. Ingolfsfjall the lava layers are 
almost horizontal, while at section RK, an attitude correction was made to all the directions with 
a representative value (strike = 45°, dip = 4°).

3.2 Paleointensities 
 Two series of paleointensity experiments using the Thelliers' method were performed at 
University of Southern California (USC) and Tokyo Institute of Technology (TIT). As this 
was a good opportunity to check the inter-laboratory consistency of the experimental method, 
experiments were also made on the standard samples such as present-day lavas. The experimental 
procedure described by Coe (1967) in which samples are heated twice to each temperature (first 
in zero-field and second in a laboratory field) was adopted throughout both series of experiments. 
The first experiment at USC was made in air with a Schonstedt thermal demagnetizer using a 
laboratory field of 49 pT. In the second experiment at TIT, the laboratory field was selected 
to match the expected paleointensity, because it is considered that this yields minimum overall 
error (Tanaka and Kono, 1984; Aitken et al., 1989). Remanences were measured using spinner 
magnetometers; a Minispin of Molspin Ltd. at USC and a Schonstedt SSM-1A at TIT. 
 Results were analyzed on the NRM-TRM diagram or Arai diagram (Arai, 1963; Nagata et 
al., 1963) using the scheme of Kono and Tanaka (1984) which employs the least squares method of 
Williamson (1968). Some representative results are shown in Figs. 3(a) to 3(1). In the NRM-TRM 
diagrams, data points which were included (rejected) in the least squares fitting are shown by 
solid circles (open circles). A rectangle attached to each data point shows an error estimate based 
on Kono and Tanaka (1984). Triangles are the results of pTRM tests following the notation of Coe 
et al. (1978), in which solid and open symbols denote positive and negative results, respectively.

 Some examples of the inter-laboratory comparison of the method using the standard samples 
are shown in Figs. 3(a)-(d). Two results from the Kotaki Pyroclastic Flow from Asama Volcano, 
Japan are shown in Figs. 3(a) and (b). This flow is dated at 2200 years by (before present) by the 14C method (Kono, 1978) and has been frequently studied by both Thellier and Shaw methods 
(Kono, 1978; Tsunakawa and Shaw, 1994). A grand mean paleointensity is 86 ± 8 pT which 
was obtained by averaging 14 previous results. Figure 3(a) shows a result obtained in the first 
experiment at USC in which the laboratory field was 49 MT while Fig. 3(b) shows one from the 
second experiment at TIT where the laboratory field was 100 µT. The paleointensity of 78 pT 
resulting from the steep slope, of 1.58, of the linear part of the NRM-TRM plot in the former is 
in good agreement with the results in the latter experiment in which a laboratory field twice as 
large gave a slope of 0.83 resulting in a paleointensity of 83 µT. 
 Figures 3(c) and (d) are examples from the Hawaii 1935 lava. Results from the two series of 
experiment are in complete agreement giving about 35 µT. These values are reasonable according 
to DGRF45 which gives the total force of 37 pT at the site (Langel, 1992). Specimen level data 
are summarized in Table 3, in which some other results using 1951 and 1986 lavas at Oshima 
Volcano, Japan are also included. Consistency of the results between the two institutes is also 
good for the Oshima 1951 lava (the 1986 lava was studied only at USC). However, the lava mean 
paleointensities of 51-52 pT are larger than the expected total force of 46 pT at the site by about 
10%. As most previous results on this lava are also about 10% larger (Kono, 1978), we think 
the results obtained at both institutes are acceptable. The reason of the difference is unknown, 
but probably it is attributed to a local geomagnetic anomaly. Although possible rock magnetic 
problems have been suggested for similar inconsistencies of paleointensity results from the Hawaii 
1960 lava (Tanaka and Kono, 1991; Mankinen and Champion, 1993; Tsunakawa and Shaw, 1994), 
this is not likely in the case of Oshima lavas. 
 Paleointensity experiments on the samples from section RK were also made at both institutes. 
In the first experiment made at USC, no stability check of the remanence was made in advance to 
select suitable samples. Obviously this is the reason for the low success rate of the first experiment; 
only 19 out of 56 specimens (34%) gave successful results. In the second experiment made at TIT 
later, only those samples which gave successful results at USC were studied, giving 12 successful 
results out of 16 specimens. Several representative examples of the NRM-TRM plots from four 
lavas are shown in Figs. 3(e)-(1), and the specimen level data is included in Table 3. Two NRM-
TRM diagrams from the lowermost, normally magnetized lava, are shown in Figs. 3(e) and (f). 
The result obtained from the first experiment, shown in Fig. 3(e), was unsuccessful due to the low 
correlation coefficient, 0.938, of the linear portion of the data. However, three unsuccessful results 
obtained from the first experiment still suggested that the paleointensity might have been very 
high. So in the second experiment three further specimens were examined in a laboratory field of 
100 µT. All three specimens gave successful results as shown in Fig. 3(f). This pre-transitional 
normal lava gave a high paleointensity of 99 ± 19 µT. 
 The three overlying lavas had transitional directions and the NRM intensities were weak, as 
indicated in Table 2. Only one of these lavas gave successful results. An example from the first 
experiment with a laboratory field of 49 µT is shown in Fig. 3(g), in which a low paleointensity of 
22 MT was obtained. The second experiment on this lava was made with a smaller laboratory field 
of 30 µT, and low paleointensities were also obtained. An example from the second experiment, 
giving a paleointensity of 14 pT, is shown in Fig. 3(h). Unfortunately the consistency of the results

150 m above the transitional lava. Two low paleointensities, of 14 µT and 20 µT, were obtained

 A lava at an elevation of 340 m still gave a low paleointensity, as shown in the examples 
of NRM-TRM diagrams in Figs. 3(k) and (1). Results from the two series of experiment were 
in good agreement. Figure 3(k) shows an example from the first experiment giving 29 UT, and 
Fig. 3(1) shows one from the second experiment in which the laboratory field was 30 pT and a

quite low for Iceland, because a dipole field of 57 pT is expected at the high latitude of the site 
(64.4°N) if an axial dipole moment of 8 x 1022 Amt is supposed.
4. Discussion
 Kristjansson et al. (1988) suggested that the lavas of their section IG had accumulated over a 
short period of time, on the basis of the similarity in the mean paleodirections. This is confirmed 
by this study. The angular standard deviation (ASD) of VGPs from section RG, around the mean 
pole is 10.3° (N = 22), after correcting for the contribution of the within site dispersions (Doell, 
1970). The upper and lower 95% confidence limits (Cox, 1969) are 13.0° and 8.5°, respectively. 
This is a very low value when the high latitude of the site is taken into consideration, compared 
to the general trend for the last 5 my (McElhinny and Merrill, 1975; McFadden et al., 1991). 
A serial correlation test by Watson and Beran (1967) also supports the rapid accumulation of 
the lava flows. In this method, the sum of the cosines of the difference angles between the field 
directions of adjacent lavas (L) is the statistical parameter. This sum was 20.922 for 22 RG 
directions (L0). Randomization of the directions for 2500 permutations resulted in a distribution 
of L which is similar to a Gaussian distribution with no observation that exceeds Lo, suggesting 
that the RG directions are serially correlated. The mean time interval between lava eruptions in 
Iceland has often been discussed in the previous studies, and estimates range from 5000 to 40000 
years depending on the region and the age of the lava sections (e.g., Watkins and Walker, 1977; 
McDougall et al., 1984; Kristjansson, 1985a). It should be noted, however, that there are also 
lavas which are inferred to have accumulated more rapidly (e.g., Kristjansson et al., 1988). 
 It seems that the time span covered by the RK lavas is rather short, too. Although we 
collected only three transitional lavas at this section, Wilson et al. (1972) reported seven more 
lavas of "anomalous" direction which we missed. The facts that the paleodirections of these extra 
lavas are all similar and the presence of the large number of lavas which recorded the transitional 
directions suggest that these lavas erupted rapidly. The ASD of 25 VGPs from section RK, 
calculated after omitting the three transitional and one pre-transitional normal directions, was 
13.0° with upper and lower 95% confidence limits of 10.9° and 16.2°, respectively. This is again 
too small for the high latitude of Iceland. A serial correlation test on the 25 reversed field 
directions gave Lo of 23.704, and only ten observations out of 2500 permutations of the data 
exceed Lo. As these represent only 0.4% of the total observations of L, the possibility of the RK 
field directions being random is rejected at the 5% significance level. 
 The variation of the geomagnetic field is commonly pictured as a combination of usual, 
ordinary paleosecular variation and occasional abnormal behavior such as a transition or an ex-
cursion. However, this separation of usual and anomalous behaviour is not statistically necessary 
according to the analysis of the large number of Icelandic data (Kristjansson and McDougall,

100 H. TANAKA et al.
1982; Kristjansson, 1985a). The distribution of VGP latitudes of 2163 observations from Ice-
landic lavas was best fitted by a single Bingham distribution. This rather continuous picture of 
the geomagnetic field, also posed by Harrison (1995, this issue), will be one of the major issues 
to be solved in the near future. Paleodirections obtained from the section RK in this study seem 
to support the conventional idea, although the time span covered by the section is too short to 
conclude it as a general feature of the geomagnetic field. 
 The variations of inclination and paleointensity versus altitude at section RK are shown in 
Fig. 4. The dotted lines in Figs. 4(a) and (b) indicate the expected values of inclination and 
total force at the site for an axial geomagnetic dipole moment of 8 x 1022 Amt. A general 
paleointensity low is noted in the paleointensity variation curve. The low paleointensity observed 
in the transitional lava is typical for transitional fields. Actually, a low paleointensity of 11 pT 
was previously reported from one of the transitional lavas in this section in the study of Smith 
(1967). However, it is noted that the low paleointensity values extended up to some 300 m 
altitude although the field direction returns to the reversed dipole direction at about 150 m level. 
We interpret this as an indication of slower recovery of paleointensity after a transition. This 
is in contrast to the Steens Mountain polarity transition in which both direction and intensity 
changed almost simultaneously (Prevot et al., 1985). In the case of section RK, it is difficult to 
estimate the exact time span the lava sequence covers. Besides, rapid accumulation of the lavas 
is probable as discussed before. Still, the time span for recovery of paleointensity seems to be two 
or three times longer than that for paleodirection. We speculate that this phenomenon might be 
an indication of the idea of "dead time" in the statistical model of geomagnetic field reversals 
by McFadden and Merrill (1993). It is surprising that the pre-transitional normally magnetized 
lava gave a very high paleointensity. It is impossible to tell whether this high paleointensity was 
general for the latest part of the Gauss chron or was a temporary phenomenon associated with 
the transition. Considering the rapid lava accumulation at this section, the latter interpretation 
is more plausible.

5. Conclusions
 We revisited section K of Wilson et al. (1972) and sectoin IG of Kristjensson et al. (1988) 
in Southwestern Iceland which are Pliocene-Pleistocene age. The angular standard deviation of 
VGPs is 10.3° and 13.0° for the former and the latter sections, respectively. Both lava sequences 
seem to have erupted in a short time judging from these small angular standard deviations. 
A serial correlation test applied to the paleodirections of adjacent lavas also indicates possible 
correlation at both sections. Paleointensity experiments using the Thelliers' method were applied 
to 72 specimens from the latter section, which includes the Gauss to Matuyama transition at its 
base, giving 31 successful results. A high paleointensity, twice the present-day value, preceded 
the transition. It seems that low paleointensity prevailed not only during transition but also for 
some time after its completion.

Chile: Counterclockwise rotation in a dextral shear zone

Abstract--Relative motions of the southern Chilean foreare are assessed through a paleomagnetic study of the Eocene-Miocene 
Ayacara Formation. This marine voleanielastic unit was studied at three localities, all immediately west of the Liquitle-Ofqui 
fault zone (LOFZ), a 1000-km-long, NS-trending intracontinental shear zone with probable Cenozoic fight-lateral displacement. 
A paleomagnetic pole (74.8S; 44.0E; A-95, 8.5 °) was calculated by combining 11 site-mean VGP from the Ayacara Fm. with 
three sites from the nearby Oligocene Coeotue Beach basalts (previously published). When compared with a 20-40 Ma North 
American cratonic pole rotated into the South American reference framework this pole implies counterclockwise rotation of 
14.6+11.8. We speculate that this counterclockwise rotation results from processes that tend to impel a detached sliver of conti- 
nental crust northward along the continental margin, against a buttress. In our model, northward displacement of the trailing edge 
of the sliver is accomplished by segmenting the sliver into lens-shaped blocks which rotate counterclockwise as they move north- 
ward. The geometry of the LOFZ clearly supports this model, which may have application to other buttressed strike-slip fault 
zones. 
Resumen--Los movimientos relativos del antearco de Chile meridional son evaluados mediante un estudio paleomagnttico de la 
Formacitn Ayaeara (Eoceno-Mioceno). Esta unidad volcanocl~tica marina fue estudiada en tres localidades, todas elias ubicadas 
inmediatamente al oeste de la Zona de Falla LiquLeie-Ofqui (ZFLO): una zona de cizalle intracontinental de rumbo NS, con prob- 
able movimiento dextral cenozoico. Un polo paleomagnttieo (74.8S; 44.0E; A-95, 8.5 °) fue calculado a partir de la combinacitn 
de 11 PGV de la Formaci6n Ayacara y de ties sitios provenientes de los basalto~ oligocenos de Playa Cocotu6 (previamente pub-

obtiene una rotaeitn antihoraria de 14.6+11.8. Se especula que esta rotacitn antihoraria resulta de procesos que tienden a empujar 
un panel cortical despegado hacia el norte, a lo largo del margen continental, contra un obst~iculo. En nuestro modelo, el 
desplazamiento hacia el norte se logra mediante la segmentaei6n del panel en bloques lenticulares que rotan de manera antihoraria 
al mo'~erse hacia el notre. La geometria de la seccitn meridional de la ZFLO apoya claramente este modelo, el cual puede aplic-

INTRODUCTION 
PALEOMAGNETIC DATA provide evidence for many 
hundreds of kilometers of coastwise lransport of continen- 
tal slivers along the western North American Cordillera 
during the Mesozoic and early Cenozoic (e.g., Beck, 1980, 
1989; Irving et al., 1985). Oblique subduction has been 
proposed as a driving mechanism for such tectonic trans- 
port (Fitch, 1972; Beck, 1986; Jarrard, 1986) and is con- 
sistent with plate reconstructions for the northeastern 
Pacific (F_,ngebretson et al., 1985). Similar oblique sub- 
duction of the Farallon (Nazca) plate beneath the South 
American plate during the last 60 m.y. (Cande and Leslie, 
1986; Pardo-Casas and Molnar, 1987), and the existence 
of major trench-parallel lineaments along the Chilean 
Andes, suggest that north-south translation of outboard 
pieces of the Andean forearc also might have occurred. 
However, paleomagnetic studies to date have not reliably 
detected any such displaced blocks. The Chilean forearc 
south of about 42 ° S contains several outcrops of Eocene- 
Miocene marine volcaniclastic rocks, grouped into the 
Ayacara Formation by Levi et al. (1966). These all lie 
immediately west of the Liquifle Ofqui fault zone (LOFZ), 
a 1000-kin-long crustal lineament that cuts the main 
Andean arc and forearc between about 39 ° and 47 ° S 
(Herv6 and Thiele, 1987). The history of the LOFZ is not 
known in detail, and several current studies are attempting 
to unravel its tectonic evolution. Of great interest is the 
amount of lateral displacement and how that displacement 
is accommodated. 
REGIONAL GEOLOGY 
The Andes between 42 ° and 43 ° S are characterized by 
roughly defined north-south belts of igneous, metamorphic 
and sedimentary rocks (Fig. 1).

The westernmost belt, Chilo6 Island, is a prolongation 
of the Chilean Coast Range. It consists mainly of low 
grade metasedimentary rocks interpreted as a Paleozoic 
forearc aocretionary complex (Godoy et aL. 1984; I-lervt, 
1988). Locally this accretionary complex is overlain 
unconformably by Eocene-Miocene marine sedimentary 
and felsic volcanic deposits (Garcfa, 1968; Valenznela, 
1982; Garcfa et al., 1988). 
To the east, the Main Range consists mostly of plutonic 
rocks of the North Patagonian batholith (NPB). The west- 
era portion of the Nt'B is dominated by Mio-Pliocene gra- 
nodiorite and tonalite; to the east it consists mainly of 
monzogranite and monzonite that yield mid-Cretaceous 
radiometric ages (Panldaurst et al., 1992). Locally the 
western batholithic rocks intrude the Eocene-Miocene lay- 
ered rocks (Ayacara Fro.), although in other localities they 
are in fault contact (Cembrano, 1990). Locally Plio-Pleis- 
tocene volcanic deposits rest on all the lithological units 
mentioned earlier. 
The Liquiae-Ofqui Fault Zone (LOFZ) 
The LOFZ has been regarded by most researchers as a 
dextral strike-slip fault (e.g., Iterv6 et al., 1976; Forsythe 
and Nelson, 1985; Beck, 1988), although in many places 
(particularly where it runs through pint,nit rocks of the 
North Patagonian batholith) sense and amount of displace- 
ment are difficult to assess. A general description of the 
LOFZ is given by Herv~ and Thiele (1987). On the basis 
of distinctive structural and geologic features they have 
divided the LOFZ into the following segments: 
From 39*30' to 41"30' the LOFZ is represented by one 
main lineament striking N10E (Fig. 2). At Liquifle, it is 
described by Herv6 (1976) as a 3-kin-wide belt of mylo- 
nitic and cataclastic rocks. Right-lateral motion along the 
LOFZ has been inferred from mesoscopic faults within the 
mylonitic zone. A poorly constrained age of 28 Ma was 
obt_alned in a dacite porphyry which crosscuts the LOFZ- 
related mylonitization (Hervt, 1976). 
From about 41"30' to 42 ° the LOFZ shows more spo- 
radic and narrower cataclastic strips than further north. In 
this zone rex~nt geochronology (Drake et al., 1990) shows 
that the LOF-Z juxtaposes Miocene and Lower Cretaceous 
intrusive rocks. 
Between 42 ° to 43 °, the westernmost portion of the 
NPB and an associated 2-3 km wide aureole of medium to 
high grade metamorphic rocks are located within and east 
of the LOFZ. The plutonic rocks, which axe as young as 
Pliocene (Panldaurst et al.. 1992), show field relations and 
microstructural features consistent with brittle-ductile 
deformation in a dextral shear zone (Cembrano, 1990; 
1992). These relatively deep crustal levels are exposed 
immediately east of Eocene-Miocene volcaniclastic rocks 
and may indicate post-Pliocene fault-controlled differen- 
tial uplift.

From 43* S southward the LOFZ consists of a single 
linear feature that gives way to a series of en echelon NW 
and NE-trending lineaments, that (together with the main 
NNE,-trending LOFZ) outline a series of curved fault seg- 
ments that are concave toward the west. Isolated, rela- 
tively undeformed sequences of Paleogene (?) volcano- 
sedimentary rocks (Estratos de La Junta) and Pleistocene 
lacustrine sediments (Eatratos de La Silla) in places fill the 
glacial valley carved on the LOFZ south of 43*00' S. A 
1.2 Ma basaltic flow (I-Ierv~ et al., 1990) lies on top of this 
sedimentary fill at 43*30' S, overlapping the LOFZ's main 
trace. 
At its southernmost limit, the LOF'Z appears to origi- 
nate in the Golfo de Penas, which has been considered to

be an extensional (trailing edge) Cenozoic basin (Forsythe 
and Nelson, 1985). 
The tectonic significance of the LOFZ is hotly debated. 
Herv~ (1976), Leslie (1986) and Beck (1988) propose that 
oblique subduction of the Nazca plate beneath South 
America caused dextral shear in the leading edge of the 
overriding plate, leading to formation of the LOF-Z; the 
model invoked is similar to Fitch's (1972) explanation for 
the Sumatra fault. Leslie (1986) identified a period of 
highly oblique subduction during the Paleogene and sug- 
gested that the activity of the LOFZ might have reached a 
peak at that time. After a period of almost orthogomd con- 
vergence between 26 and 20 Ma, subdnction of the Nazca 
plate has been slighly fight-oblique (Pardo Casas and Mol- 
nar, 1987). This scenario may have favored dextral 
transpression along the LOF-Z until recent times. 
Forsythe and Nelson (1985), on the other hand, pro- 
posed that the LOFZ originated when the Chile Rise, act- 
hag as a rigid indenter, impinged on the South American 
plate. Their model predicts considerable Neogene offset 
on the fault. 
The Ayacara Formation 
Levi et al. (1966) described the Ayacara Formation as 
"a well consolidated volcaniclastic sequence cropping out 
in Caleta Ayacara" (Fig. 1). They identified two members: 
a lower member, 200 m thick, consisting of conglomerate 
and sandstone, and an upper member, 350 m thick, of tuff, 
dacitic volcanic sandstone and shale with synsedimantary 
structures suggesting turbidity current deposits. The same 
authors described a 150-m-thick sedimentary sequence, 
also assigned by them to the Ayacara Formation, that crops 
out on Isla Manzano (Fig. 1). Microfossils found at this 
locality suggest an Eocene-Miocene age (Martinez, 1961). 
Both the Caleta Ayacara and Isla Manzano exposures are 
gently to steeply dipping, nearly homoclinal, and show lit- 
tle evidence of internal deformation (cross-fanlts, etc.). 
There is no evidence of hydrothermal alteration, deep 
weathering, re-heating, or other processes that might lead 
to remagnetlzation. 
A third outcrop area, located on Isla Puduhuapi (Fig. 1), 
consists of a subhorizontal sequence of shale and andesite. 
This section was informally named the 'Tuduhuapi strata" 
by Levi et al. (1966) and was assigned a general Tertiary 
age on the basis of lithologic similarities with strata from 
the Ayacara Formation. 
Individual sections from the three Ayacara localities 
have never been formally correlated, although preliminary 
attempts to do so were made by Levi et al. (1966), Solano 
(1978), Araya (1979), and Fuenzalida (1979). During the 
present study, the lithology, age, and thickness of the For- 
marion at its type locality and at Isla Manzano were com- 
pared (Fig. 3). 
The section from Caleta Ayacara shows a 100m-thick 
lower member of conglomerate and tuffaceous sandstone. 
The upper member consists of 500 m of tuff, tuffaceous 
sandstone and tuffaceous siltstone. A facies analysis indl- 
cares that the lower member may have been deposited by 
debris flows. The upper member includes pyroclastic tur-

bidity current deposits interbedded with subaqueous pyro- 
clastic debris flow deposits (Cas and Wright, 1991). The 
presence of primary and reworked pyroclastic debris indi- 
cates penecontemporaneous volcanism and subsidence. A 
radiometric 4°Ar/39Ar age of 16.5=~0.5 Ma (F. Munizaga, 
written communication, 1991) obtained on plagioclase 
from a tuff near the top of the upper member constrains its 
minimum age to Early Miocene. 
The Isla Manzano section (Fig. 3) has a thickness of 
500 m. much greater than previously estimated. It consists 
of well-bedded tuff. tuffaceous and lithic sandstone, and 
tuffaceous siltstone deposited mainly by turbidity currents. 
Radiometric age determinations on samples from this 
locality yield no reliable results. 
No chronological data are available for the Isla Pudu- 
huapi strata. However, the presence of turbidite sequences 
similar to those from Isla Manzano suggests correlation of 
the two sections. 
Several features of the Ayacara Formation are similar to 
those described for strike-slip basins (Christie-Blick and 
Biddle, 1988). These include: 
(1) Geological mismatches with the surrounding 
area. For example, there appears to be no nearby 
source for clasts of andesite, dacite and shale, 
which reach diameters as great as I m in diameter 
in the lower member, and 
(2) Rapid vertical facies changes. In its type locality, 
the upper member has deep water facies interfin- 
gered with strata containing algae, suggesting 
rapid subsidence of the basin (Fnenzalida, 1979).

PALE*MAGNETIC STUDY 
During regional geologic mapping of the Andean 
forearc, 24 pale,magnetic sites (165 samples) were 
obtained from three localities within the Ayacara Forma- 
tion: 8 sites from Isla Manzano, 11 from Caleta Ayacara, 
and 5 from Isla Puduhuapi (Fig. 1). Six or more indepen- 
dently oriented samples were collected at each site. Sam- 
pies were oriented using a magnetic compass, checked by 
solar compass when weather permitted. The very weak 
magnetizations of these rocks, and the fact that sun com- 
pass and magnetic compass orientations were in good 
agreement when both were available, indicate that local 
magnetic anomalies were not a problem. 
In the laboratory magnetizations were measured on a 
Schonstedt spinner magnetometer. For each site, two rep- 
resentative specimens were selected to serve as pilot sam- 
pies for preliminary thermal (T) and alternating field (AF) 
demagnetization. The AF demagnetization range used 
was 2.5 mT and 100 roT; thermal demagnetization was 
performed between 1000 C and 680* C. All pilot demag- 
netizations included at least 10 steps. After pilot demag- 
netization, the remaining samples from each site were 
demagnetized by whichever method appeared to best 
define the characteristic remanent direction. Stable direc- 
tions were identified visually as straight line segments of 
demagnetization paths on orthogonal vector diagrams and 
then determined analytically by principal component anal- 
ysis (Kirschvink, 1980). Mean directions were calculated 
using the method of Fisher (1953). and also using the 
Bingham distribution (Onstott, 1980). As no significant 
difference between the two methods was detected, Fisher 
(1953) statistics axe used throughout the study. Site-mean 
directions were converted to virtual geomagnetic poles 
(VGP), and final analysis was conducted using VGP. 
To detect translations and/or rotations of sampling 
localities with respect to the stable interior of the conti- 
nent, we must compare our pale,magnetic poles with a 
reference pole from the South American craton. This is 
surprisingly difficult to do, because there are very few 
well-determined poles of the correct age available on the 
South American craton. For instance, the compilation of 
Irving and Irving (1982) lists no South American reference 
poles at all between 64 and 15 Ma. For this reason we 
used the North American 20-40 Ma pole of Diehl et al. 
(1988) (81.5N, 147.3E, A-95 = 2.4*), rotating it into the 
South American reference framework using the 37 Ma 
fixed-hotspot stage pole of Engebretson et al., (1985). 
Because our reference pole is for rocks that are predomi- 
nantly younger than the youngest stage pole given by 
Engebretson et al, (1985) we pro-rated the rotation angle 
(using 2.3 ° instead of 4.3*). This gives a southern-hemi- 
sphere mid-Tertiary (20-40 Ma) reference pole of 82.0S, 
308.3E (A-95 = 2.4*), only slightly different from the 
present spin-axis. Finally, rotations and poleward transla- 
tions were calculated in pole-space following Beck 
(1989). Site-mean directions and statistics are snmma- 
rized in Table 1; VGP calculations and statistics are given 
in Table 2. 
Pale,magnetic Results 
Here we first describe details of data selection, then dis- 
cuss results by locality. 
Data selection. Less than half the samples originally col- 
lected were used in the final averages. This resulted from 
acceptance criteria we applied at several levels. We reject- 
ed individual sample measurements if the estimate of pre- 
cision during measurement was consistently low during 
repeat measurement (ct-95 > 30*; Briden and Arthur, 
1981). We also rejected some samples because their initial 
magnetic moments were too low (typically < 5 x 10exp -5 
A/m) for us to obtain reliable demagnetizations paths in 
reasonable time. We also rejected individual sample mea- 
surements if the precision of line-fit was low (MAD > 20°; 
Kirschvink, 1980). Entire sites were rejected if their circles 
of 95% confidence (ct-95) exceeded 20*. In calculating 
site-mean directions we used anchored rather than free 
lines. Comparison of the two indicated that no systematic 
high-temperature/high-coercivity component was present 
(no systematic difference in mean direction was detected), 
and means calculated using anchored lines tended to be 
more precise. After application of these selection criteria 
we were left with 11 of our original 24 sites, representing 
72 of the original 165 samples. Thus, the attrition rate on 
this project was high, but internal (within-site) and external 
(between-site) consistency indicates that we have mea- 
sured a meaningful remanent direction. 
Isla Manzano 
Four (of 8) sites from this locality passed the screening 
criteria; these consisted of three sedimentary horizons and 
a sill. Stable directions in the sedimentary layers were iso- 
lated by thermal demagnetization, usually between 415 ° 
and 515" C (Fig. 4a). AF demagnetization was less effec- 
tive in removing a low-stability component, which tended 
to be northward and down (Fig. 4a,b). In the sill a single 
stable component of magnetization was isolated by AF 
demagnetization between 20 nat and 80 mT and also by 
thermal demagnetization between 1000 and 580 ° C. Site- 
mean directions from the sill and sedimentary rocks are 
similar; very shallow and northwesterly before tilt-correc- 
tion, much steeper and northwesterly after tilt-correction. 
Correction for tilt causes a slight increase in dispersion (k, 
the precision parameter of Fisher (1953) decreases from 
200 to 120). All sites have normal magnetic polarity. 
Caleta Ayacara 
Eleven sites were obtained from this locality but only 
five gave reasonably reliable results, and two of these were 
finally rejected because their circles of confidence slightly 
exceeded 20 ° (Table 1). Most samples had a low ceereiv- 
ity component that was removed by AF demagnetization 
at peak fields of up to 30 mT (Fig. 4c). At higher fields 
(generally 30 to 80 roT) a steady trend toward the origin 
indicated isolation of a single stable component. Thermal 
demagnetization between 415 ° C to 580 ° C gave a similar 
path. suggesting that titan,magnetite and/or magnetite car-

Isla Puduhuapi 
Four of five sites from this location gave reliable direc- 
tions. Sites 89FU58, 59, and 60 show similar AF demag- 
netization paths. A low coercivity component is removed 
at peak fields of 20 roT. and a single component is 
described thereafter, to peak fields of 70 mT. Site 90PA28 
shows a high-coercivity component (probably carried by 
pyrrhotite) which could not be removed by either AF (Fig. 
4e) or thermal demagnetization alone. However, a combi- 
nation of thermal demagnetization to 350 ° C, followed by 
AF demagnetization to 70 mT, effectively isolated a stable 
direction (Fig. 4f). This locality consists of three sedimen- 
tary layers and one dike; sedimentary layers have reverse 
polarity but the dike has normal polarity. Correcting for 
tilt (including a correction for the dike based on the atti- 
tude of its enclosing sedimentary layers) slightly decreases 
scatter (k increases from 54.5 to 65.2). We also computed 
a mean direction under the assumption that the dike was 
intruded after the sedimentary layers were tilted, but this 
result (D, 342.8; I, -55.1, k, 35.0) is more scattered than 
either the all-corrected or all-in situ scenarios.

DISCUSSION 
Isla Manzano 
The four sites from Isla Manzano all have normal mag- 
netic polarity and between-site dispersion is so low that it 
appears unlikely that the geomagnetic secular variation 
has been averaged. Dispersion increases when the tilt-cor- 
rection is made, which might suggest that the magnetiza- 
tion was acquired after tilting; that is, that the rocks are 
remagnetized. However, the change in dispersion is not 
significant at 95% confidence, using the chi-squared test of 
Cox (1969). Furthermore, there are no obvious signs of 
reheating or alteration, such as might suggest remagnetiza- 
tion. We suspect that the increase in scatter when the tilt- 
correction is made is simply the result of inaccuracy in 
measuring true strike and dip. Given the rotated Diehl et 
a/(1983) reference pole cited above, the direction one 
would expect to observe for mid-Tertiary rocks on Isla 
Manzano (assuming no post-magnetization displacement 
with respect to the South American craton) is: Dx = 355.5; 
I x = -67.0. (Here the subscript x denotes the "expected 
direction"; Beck, 1980). Both in situ and tilt-corrected 
mean directions for Isla Manzano have declinations that 
are rotated counterclockwise with respect to the expected 
direction. However, the in situ direction has an inclination 
that is extremely shallow, such as would be observed (for 
instance) if the rocks had moved several thousand kilome- 
ters southward relative to the South American craton. 
However, if the tilt correction is made, observed and 
expected inclinations are very similar and no large coast- 
wise displacements are required. It is very unlikely on

hence we will use the tilt-corrected directions for this

Caleta Ayacara 
As mentioned earlier, the polarity of the Caleta Ayacara 
sites defines an R-N-R sequence. Thus we have sampled 
across two polarity transitions, which suggests that our 
sites are spread out enough in time to adequately represent 
the longer frequencies of the geomagnetic secular varia- 
tion. Dispersion increases when the tilt correction is made, 
but the increase is not si~,nificant. Expected direction for 
this locality is: Dx = 355.6; I x = -67.0. Again, both in situ 
and tilt-corrected mean declinations are rotated counter- 
clockwise with respect to the reference direction. Both 
inclinations are more shallow than expected, but the in situ 
mean inclination is improbably shallow. As there is no 
geologic evidence to suggest remagnetization we will use 
the tilt-corrected data set in future calculations. 
lsla Puduhuapi 
The Isla Puduhuapi data set consists of three sedimen- 
tary units and a dike. The dike clearly is of a different age 
than the sedimentary layers because it has a different 
polarity. However, the dike's direction of remanent mag- 
netization falls within the grouping defined by the sedi- 
mentary units and there seems to be no reason to omit it 
from the final averaging process. Dispersion decreases 
slightly when the tilt-correction is applied, but the change 
is not statistically si£'nificant. The expected direction for 
this locality is: D x = 355.5; I x = -67.5, very nearly identi- 
cal to the mean in situ direction (Table 1). The tilt-cor- 
rected mean has a slightly shallow inclination and a 
declination that is rotated counterclockwise. Based on the 
slight decrease in dispersion when the tilt-correction is 
applied, the existence of two polarities, and the lack of any 
geological evidence for alteration or reheating, we use the 
tilt-cxmected directions in further calculations. 
To calculate a paleomagnetic pole for the Ayacara For- 
marion we averaged the 11 VGP listed in Table 2. This 
gives a mean pole at 79.6S, 344.9E, with a circle of 95% 
confidence (A-95) of 11.5" and a precision parameter (k) 
of 16.9. A similar mean using poies from in situ directions 
(54.8S, 29.1E) has much greater dispersion (K = 6.2) and 
a highly elongate distribution. The difference in precision 
is significant at 99% confidence (Cox, 1969). Overall pre- 
cision is somewhat low, probably reflecting random errors 
in measuring attitudes at the outcrop. 
Tables 1 and 2 also contain paleomagnetic results for 
three sites of Cocotne Beach basalts (Fig. 1). These results 
(early Miocene: 21.7:1:1.7 Ma; Garcfa et al., 1988) are the 
only other paleomagnetic data available from west of the 
LOFZ. The expected direction at Cocotue Beach. based 
on the rotated Diehl et al., (1988) reference pole, is: D x = 
355.4; I x = -66.6. The observed direction (Table 1) thus is 
concordant in inclination but rotated sharply counterclock- 
wise in declination. 
By including the Cocotue Beach data we can calculate 
a mean VGP for middle Tertiary rocks west of the LOFZ. 
This lies at 75.8S, 353.6E (A-95 = 10.0°; K -- 16.4). Fig.

In Fig. 5a we show virtual geomagnetic poles for the 
four localities discussed in this section. Locality mean 
VGP are shown in Fig. 5b, together with the overall mean 
pole and the rotated Diehl et al. (1988) reference pole. 
Clearly, all locality VGP and the resultant overall pole lie 
to the left of the reference pole, as viewed from the sam- 
piing area. This suggests that the region west of the Liq- 
uifie-Ofqui fault has rotated counterclockwise relative to 
stable South America. The amount of rotation can be cal- 
culated from the reference pole and the calculated mean 
VGP using the method of Beck (1989). For a location 
near the common center of the four sampling localities 
(42.25S, 287E) the rotation is 14.6°+11.9 ° counterclock- 
wise. Poleward transport is negligible; 3.3°+8.1" (error 
limits calculated after Demarest, 1983). These error limits 
clearly are minimum values, because any error that might 
arise from rotating the Diehl et al (1988) North American 
reference pole into South American coordinates is not 
included. 
TECTONIC INTERPRETATION 
The counterclockwise rotation shown by the Ayacara 
and Cocotue Beach rocks is small, but it appears to be real 
and tectonically significant. Westerly declinations (indi- 
caring counterclockwise rotations) are found throughout a 
broad area west of the LOFZ, whereas declinations mea- 
sured east of the LOFZ lie consistently clockwise of the 
expected direction (Cembrano et al, 1992). Moreover, 
most rocks spatially associated with the LOFZ in the Lake 
District, several hundred kilometers to the north, also are 
rotated clockwise (Garcia et al., 1988). Thus tectonic pro- 
cesses operating west of the LOFZ in our field area are dif- 
ferent in an important way from processes normally 
associated with dextral shear. 
In another paper we propose and describe in detail a 
speculative model that can account for counterclockwise 
rotations outboard of a dextral shear zone at the southern 
end of the LOFZ, as well as for other instances of "wrong- 
way" rotation in zones of strihe-slip faulting (Beck et al., 
1993). Here we will outline the model as it applies to the 
southern LOFZ. The model is suggested by the striking 
pattern of faults and other lineaments found along the 
southern end of the LOFZ. We believe that this instance of 
wrong-way rotation arises because the crustal sliver out- 
board (west) of the fault is prevented from freely moving 
northward by the presence of a buttress (Beck, 1991). 
The model is explained in Fig. 6. North-oblique sub- 
duction creates the conditions necessary to detach an out- 
board sliver from the leading edge of South America. 
However, owing perhaps to a steepening of subduction 
angle, or to a gradual decrease in the angle of obliquity, 
these conditions die out northward. A buttress therefore is 
present, preventing free movement of the sliver. The pat- 
tern of fjords and other lineaments in the southern LOFZ 
region suggests that northward displacement has been

A CAUTIONARY NOTE 
The results presented in this article must be considered 
preliminary, and the model we present thus is highly spec- 
ulative. In Fig. 5a the VGP representing normal-polarity 
and reverse-polarity sites are distinguished and it is clear 
that there is a difference between the two polarity-subsets. 
This could simply be an accident of locality, but it could 
also indicate that, despite careful laboratory demagnetiza- 
tion, some unremoved secondary magnetic component 
still remains. In the latter case the evidence for counter- 
clockwise rotation of crustal blocks west of the LOFZ is 
weakened, and our model severely compromised. How- 
ever, by presenting our data and model at this preliminary 
stage, we hope to encourage further paleomagnetic 
research on rock units having similar tectonic setting along 
the LOFZ or on other major strike-slip fault systems 
worldwide.

A 250-m thick volcanic sequence of some 63 Pliocene lava flows from Georgia (Akhalkalaki plateau) which was 
previously thought to record the Gauss-Matuyama reversal was re-studied in detail. About 400 oriented cores were sampled 
along four sub-vertical sections partially overlapping each other. At the base of the section, 16 consecutive lava flows were 
found to record intermediate directions. The overlying flows are all reversely magnetized. With the exception of the upper 
part of the sequence, four groups of three to 11 consecutive lava flows with strictly the same paleodirection can be 
recognized. The location of the intermediate virtual geomagnetic poles (VGPs) does not correspond to that of the VGP 
clusters previously proposed as indicating a long lasting near dipole configuration during reversals. The field paieointensity 
is close to one fifth of the present field at the bottom of the section and tends to increase uphill. Age determination 
(4°At/39At) provides an estimate of 3.6 + 0.06 Ma, which leaves us with two possible interpretations: the transitional 
vectors could correspond either to an excursion within chron 2Ar or to the upper (N-R) Cochiti-Gilbert reversal.

paleovalleys, later filled with the basaltic flows of 
the Akhalkalaki formation. This formation consists 
of two parts, separated by a second erosion surface. 
The lower Akhalkalaki sequence is approximately 
250 m thick. It consists of some 24 gray, massive 
and coarse-grained lava flows with a maximum 
thickness of 30 m. Several of these flows show 
evidence of weathering, with however relatively fresh

(1986) reported that the lower part of this sequence 
provides intermediate magnetization directions while 
the upper part is reversely magnetized. The upper 
Akhalkalaki sequence constitutes the upper part of 
the Thoki plateau and is approximately 150 m thick. 
The lava flows are fresh columnar dark gray fine- 
grained basalts only 2-3 m thick in general. They 
are reversely magnetized (Sologashvili, 1986). Due 
to the time needed for erosion, there is no doubt that 
some period of quiescence occurred between the 
emissions of the lower and upper Akhalkalaki vol- 
canic sequences.

3. 4°AR / 39AR geochronology 
3.1. Analytical procedure 
The plagioclase bulk samples (THOKI IW, 11Y 
and 16Y) were separated by the classical methods 
(magnetic separator and heavy liquids). The three 
final mineral separates (in the range 125-160 /zm) 
were obtained by hand-picking under a binocular 
microscope. The samples were irradiated in the Mc- 
Master reactor (Hamilton, Canada) with a total flux 
of 6.4× 1017 n.cm -2. The analyzed samples, 
wrapped in AI foils, were included in a narrow zone 
from the same level within the irradiation can to 
minimize the effects of flux gradient which is esti- 
mated, in this zone to be less than +0.5%. The 
irradiated standard was the biotite Bern 4B (17.25 
Ma; Hall et al., 1984, and subsequent analyses per- 
formed in the Toronto and Nice laboratories). The 
step heating procedure is described by F6raud et al 
(1986). 
The mass spectrometer consists of a 120 ° 
M.A.S.S.E.* tube, a B~iur Signer* source and an 
SEV 217" electron-multiplier (total gain: 5 × 1012) 
whereas the extraction and purification lines include 
a Ti-furnace (700°C), a SAES GP50W getter with 
Stl01* zirconium-aluminum alloy operating at 
400°C and a -95°C cold trap. 
Isotopic measurements are corrected for K and Ca 
isotopic interferences, mass discrimination and atmo- 
spheric argon contamination. All errors are quoted at 
the 1 o- level and do not include the errors on the 
4°mr *//39AI'K ratio and age of the monitor. The error 
in the 4°Ar * / 39ARK ratio of the monitor is included 
in the plateau age error bars calculation. To define a 
plateau age, we need at least three consecutive steps, 
corresponding to a minimum of 70% of the total 
39ARK released, and the individual fraction ages 
should agree within 2 0" with the 'integrated' age of 
the plateau segment. 
3.2. Results 
The results are displayed in Fig. 3 and 4. The 
plagioclase population THOKI 11Y displays an age 
spectrum (Fig. 3(a)) with a regular decreasing stair- 
case shape, from 25.4 Ma in the low temperature 
steps down to ca 7 Ma at high temperature, disturbed 
by a bump between 930°C and 1150°C. The shape of 
this age spectrum is partly well correlated to the 
evolution of the 37Arca//39AI'K ratio during the step 
heating experiment, for the intermediate and high 
temperatures (Fig. 3(b)). 
The plagioclase populations THOKI lW and 16Y 
display two age spectra with similar shapes (Fig. 
4(a)). Both age spectra show high ages in the first 
3% of the 39ARK released followed by a fiat age 
domain over 80-90% of the total 39ARK released and 
finally an increase of the ages for the remaining 10% 
of the degassing (Fig. 4(b)). The two fiat age do- 
mains allow the definition of two plateau ages at 
3.69_ 0.04 Ma and 3.53_ 0.04 Ma for samples 
THOKI 1W and THOKI 16Y, respectively. Despite 
similar age spectra, the two samples display distinct 
37Arca/39ARK spectra with a rather flat pattern for 
sample THOKI IW and a saddle shape for sample 
THOKI 16Y. 
3.3. Discussion 
The high ages in the low temperature steps and 
the decreasing staircase shape of the THOKI 11Y 
age spectrum are the most obvious signs of the 
presence of an excess argon component which prob- 
ably disturbs the whole experiment and does not 
allow us to obtain a valid age. The high temperature 
are bump (Fig. 3(a)) corresponds to a clear decrease 
of the 37Arca//39ARK ratio (Fig. 3) which could corre- 
spond to the degassing of either an alteration phase, 
contemporaneous of the cooling of the volcanic flow, 
or a contamination phase. 
The two samples THOKI 1W and 16Y display 
two 'distinct' plateau ages (Fig. 4a) which agree with 
their positioning in the volcanic sequence. Neverthe- 
less, as these two ages are concordant at the 20" 
level, it is not possible to confirm that the plateau 
age difference is significant. The validity of the 
measured ages, disregarding the respect of the plateau 
age criteria, is confirmed by (1) their concordance 
and (2) the very distinct shapes of the 37Arca//39ARK 
spectra with nevertheless similar age spectra shapes. 
The saddle shape of the THOKI lW 37 mrca//39mr K 
spectrum (Fig. 4(b)) probably corresponds to the 
simultaneous degassing of the plagioclase and a 
higher K-content alteration phase, which probably 
crystallized during the flow cooling.

So we propose that the mean age, 3.60 + 0.06 Ma 
(2 tr), is the best estimate of the time of emplace- 
ment of the lower Akhalkalaki sequence. 
4. Rock magnetic properties 
4.1. Experimental procedure 
Preferably, igneous rocks used for paleodirection 
and more especially paleointensity determinations 
must satisfy the following conditions: 
1. Be thermally stable at least in the 'active' 
temperature range where determinations are taken; 
2. For paleointensity, the remanence carriers must 
be fine, i.e. single-domain (SD) or small pseudo- 
single-domain (PSD) grains. Multi-domain (MD) 
grains usually give erroneous results (Levi, 1977) in 
relationship with a violation of the law of indepen- 
dence of partial thermoremanent magnetizations 
(PTRMs) (Borshakov and Shcherbakova, 1979). 
3. The part of natural remanent magnetization 
(NRM) used for paleointensity determinations must 
be a thermoremanent magnetization (TRM). 
4. The magnetic viscosity of the specimens must 
be small enough to obtain reliable and precise mea- 
surements of the remanence during the process of 
progressive thermal demagnetization. This require- 
ment can be readily fulfilled if the magnetic viscos- 
ity index v is lower than 5% (Prrvot et al., 1985). 
As for the last point, viscosity measurements pro- 
vided viscosity indexes generally less than 5% ex- 
cept for a few specimens from the very bottom of 
section W which were excluded from further consid- 
eration. To verify the fulfilment of other demands an 
extensive study of the magnetic properties has been 
carded out on selected samples: 
1. Strong field double heating thermomagnetic 
curves of induced saturation magnetization (Js-T). 
These experiments allowed us to determine the aver- 
age Curie point of the rock (corresponding to the 
temperature of the inflection point on Js-T curve) 
and check the thermal stability of the ferrimagnetic 
minerals by comparing the Js-T curves for the first 
heating (performed up to 600 ° to 7000C) and for the 
second one. 
2. Continuous thermal demagnetization of PTRMs. 
These experiments are crucial to distinguish between 
MD, PSD or SD carriers of TRM (and NRM as well 
so far as NRM is indeed a TRM). Bol'shakov and 
Shcherbakova (1979) were the first to suggest that 
the domain structure can be inferred from a 'thermo- 
magnetic criterion'. This criterion consists of testing 
the law of independence of PTRMs which implies 
that any PTRM(T], T2), in which T i is greater than 
T 2, must be entirely destroyed when heated to T I. 
They found that the law is valid for single-domain 
grains but not for multi-domain ones where a 
P'rRM(T i, T 2) is only completely demagnetized at 
temperatures significantly larger than T], sometimes 
reaching the Curie point. For small pseudo-single- 
domain magnetite grains with sizes lower than 5 
/.Lm, the PTRM(T) curves show a pronounced inflec- 
tion at T~. Thus such grains can be easily distin- 
guished from single-domain and multi-domain Gains. 
In addition, magnetic parameters such as the in 
situ Koenigsberger ratio Qa, the ratio of saturation 
remanent magnetization to saturation magnetization 
(JrJJs) and the ratio of remanent coercive force to 
coercive force (Hcr/H c) were also measured on 
adjacent unheated specimens. 
3. Continuous thermal demagnetization curves of 
NRM and artificial TRM acquired in a 50 /zT field, 
when the specimen was cooled down from the Curie 
point after demagnetization of NRM. These experi- 
ments were carried out in order to estimate the 
unblocking temperatures of NRM and to compare 
NRM and TRM. A similarity between these curves 
suggests in principle that NRM is actually a TRM 
provided that no noticeable changes in magnetic 
mineralogy occurred as a result of heating. Thermo- 
magnetic measurements were carded out using vi- 
brating sample magnetometers with a furnace built in 
Borok laboratory which allowed to the use of either 
weak or strong (up to 0.8 T) inducing fields. 
One to four specimens from each flow were 
chosen for each kind of experiment listed above, all 
heating being performed in air. We studied 51 sam- 
pies from the lower Akhalkalaki sequence and 18 
from the upper sequence. Moreover, several electron 
microprobe and scanning electron microscope analy- 
ses were carried out on samples selected from the 
paleodirection determinations.

4.2. Results 
4.2.1. Nature of magnetic oxides 
The Curie temperatures of the basalts from the 
lower Akhalkalaki sequence lie typically between 
550 ° and 580°C. In a few cases the Curie tempera- 
ture is higher (600°C) or lower (520°-530°C). We 
found a single occurrence (flow 19W) of a low-tem- 
perature Curie point (212°C), probably indicative of 
the presence of some Ti-rich titanomagnetite. 
Hematite is associated with magnetite in flow 14W. 
In general, the ferrimagnetic mineral appears to be 
magnetite or Ti-poor titanomagnetite, possibly 
slightly maghemitized in a few cases. Microprobe 
analyses confirmed these conclusions. They indi- 
cated the presence of inter-growths of Ti-poor titano- 
magnetite with an abundance of titanohematite 
lamellae. Such a high-temperature oxidation is usu- 
ally thought to take place at temperatures higher than 
600°C. Thus electron microprobe analyses provide 
decisive evidence that the primary NRM of these 
rocks is a TRM. For a few samples, however, no 
lamellae are visible. In view of the quite high-tem- 
perature Curie points of these rocks, close to that of 
magnetite, it is reasonable to suggest that a similar 
but finer spinodal decomposition of the original Ti- 
rich titanomagnetite occurred too. In the absence of 
any high-temperature exsolution phase which could 
be identified, we must consider the possibility that 
this process took place below the Curie point of 
magnetite (Gromm6 et al., 1969). If this is the case, 
then the primary NRM might not be a pure TRM. In 
contrast, the Curie temperatures of the basalts from 
the upper Akhalkalaki sequence are constantly low, 
between 130 ° and 200°C, which suggests that the 
remanence carrier is Ti-rich titanomagnetite.

(similar shape to the two Js-T curves and J~ values 
at room temperature within 10% of each other, Fig. 
5(b)). The other samples showed noticeable changes, 
although not too drastic in many cases (Fig. 5(a)). In 
contrast, the basalts from the upper Akhalkalaki

The thermomagnetic criteria for domain structure 
was applied to PTRMs (300 °, 20°C) which were 
acquired during the cooling down of the sample from 
the Curie temperature (initially demagnetized state). 
Both the basalts from the upper and the lower Akhal-

representative example is shown in Fig. 6. We note 
first that the NRM(T) and TRM(T) curves are rela- 
tively close to each other, which indicates the ab- 
sence of drastic magnetochemical changes due to 
heating. Obviously, the PTRM(300*, 20°C) is not 
completely demagnetized at 300°C. The remanence ~ 
left is slightly less than 25% of the value of the 
PTRM at room temperature. The PTRM(T) curves 
die out before reaching the Curie temperature. This 
behavior is typical of single-domain/pseudo-single- 
domain mixtures. 
Concerning the other magnetic characteristics, the 
in situ Koenigsberger ratio Qn was found to vary 
from 0.5 to 20 in the basalts from the lower se-

the first flow (IW). Typical values are between 2 
and 5. In contrast, the basalts from the upper Akhal- 
kalaki sequence provide Qn values averaging 50. In 
both sections the Hcr/H c ratio is about 2 and Jrs/Js 
Vary from 0.05 to 0.25. Altogether, these values are 
indicative of magnetic grain sizes mostly in the 
pseudo-single-domain range.
