samples, we used another version in which the re- 
maining NRM and the laboratory TRM intensities 
are measured at temperature, the double heating 
steps being performed first in zero field then under 
the laboratory field (Day et al., 1977). For this 
second method, the experimental procedure consists 
of heating the sample in zero field from T, to T, + i, 
at which temperature the remanent magnetization JI 
is measured. The sample is then cooled (always in 
zero field) down to a temperature T, and the rema- 
nent magnetization J2 measured. The second cycle 
consists of heating the sample again to T,+ I and 
then cooling it back in a controlled field (H = Hla b) 
to a temperature T, where the remanent magnetiza- 
tion J3 is measured. This procedure is repeated for 
successive increasing temperature intervals. The pa- 
ieointensity is then determined from a plot, at each 
temperature, of the sum of difference in NRM 
(~{Ji-J2}) against the sum of the consecutive differ- 
ences in TRM (~{J3-J2}). Thus the only difference 
with the usual Arai-Nagata plot is that the contribu- 
tion of the highest temperature intervals to the pale- 
ointensity determination is reduced as a result of the 
decay of spontaneous magnetization when T in- 
creases. For both methods, the NRM-TRM diagrams 
were statistically analyzed as recommended by Coe 
et al. (1978) following Prtvot et al.'s (1985) modifi- 
cations. 
All samples studied but one belong to the lower 
Akhalkalaki sequence. Due to practical problems for 
transferring the specimens from one laboratory to the 
others, the rock magnetic and the paleointensity ex- 
periments had to be carried out on a collection 
consisting of only one specimen per flow. Thus 
magnetic properties (except viscosity index) and pa- 
leointensity experiments were performed on different 
cores. As a result, no pre-selection of the cores was 
made before undertaking paleointensity experiments. 
6.2. Results 
Criteria for rejections of results were applied a 
posteriori. Only the paleointensities determined from 
a least five point segments and spanning at least 20% 
of the total NRM were accepted. Fig. 10 shows an 
example of NRM-TRM diagram obtained by the 
standard paleointensity procedure for each direc- 
tional group. 
In spite of the rather encouraging indications pro- 
vided by the rock magnetic experiments reported 
above, the quality of the paleointensity data is some- 
what poor. A paleointensity value was calculated for 
46 samples (Table 3). However, the quality factor 
(which can sometimes reach 100 or more, Prtvot et 
al., 1983) is low and not much confidence can be 
given to many of these individual data. We did not 
calculate flow averages because of the small number 
of determinations per flow (we often have only one 
determination) and the scattering observed in several 
cases within single flows. It is reasonable to consider 
that only paleointensity data corresponding to quality 
factors equal or greater than 5 can be reliable (bold 
font in Table 3). Thus, we have indications that the 
field intensity was particularly low (less than 10/zT) 
for the first DG. Then, the field magnitude varied 
between 20 and 40 p.T, which is almost twice less 
than expected at this latitude for the non-transitional 
field. This corroborates the results of Borisova and 
Sologashvili (1985) on the same section. This trend 
suggests a progressive recovering of a normal inten- 
sity during the end of either a reversal or an excur- 
sion. The low magnitudes obtained for the intermedi- 
ate field directions agree also with those reported for 
other volcanic records studied with the Thellier pale- 
ointensity method (Bogue and Coe, 1984; Coe et al. 
1984; Prtvot et al. 1985; Marshall et al., 1988; 
Roperch et al., 1988; Chauvin et al., 1990; Levi et 
al., 1990). The possibility that high intensities occur 
just after reversal, as suggested in some previous 
studies of volcanic records (Prtvot et al., 1985; 
Bogue and Paul, 1993), seems to be supported by the 
determination obtained from lava flow 17Y. How- 
ever, many more paleointensity measurements are 
needed to check this suggestion. 
7. Discussion 
The paleomagnetic results reported here qualita- 
tively corroborate the preliminary data of Borisova 
and Sologashvili (1985) and Sologashvili (1986) re- 
garding both the direction and paleointensity of the 
paleofield. However, we found no evidence that 
these intermediate directions are preceeded by nor- 
mal flows belonging to the Akhalkalaki sequence. 
Obviously, the polarity of the underlying Goderzi

P. Camps et al. / Physics of the Earth and Planetary Interiors 96 (1996) 41-59 57 
formation is of no help in this matter because of the 
hiatus in volcanic activity which is attested by the 
erosion surface separating these two formations. 
Thus, the geomagnetic event recorded in the Thoki 
section is not necessarily a N-T-R reversal, as 
previously supposed (Borisova and Sologashvili, 
1985). This might also he a R-T-R excursion. Also, 
the age of these intermediate directions is quite 
different from the Gauss-Matuyama age assumed by 
Borisova and Sologashvili (1985). 
The identification of the geomagnetic event 
recorded in the lower Akhallcalaki sequence near 
Thoki is uncertain. If one refers to the polarity time 
scale of Cande and Kent (1992), the age reported 
here (3.60 ± 0.60 Ma) does not correspond to a 
known reversal but rather to some (unspecified) ex- 
cursion which occurred during chron 2Ar of the 
Gilbert epoch. The existence of such an excursion is 
supported by some paleomagnetic observations in 
South West Iceland (Kristjansson et al., 1980) indi- 
cating the presence of one flpw (FA17) with an 
intermediate magnetization direction within a re- 
versed polarity zone believed to correspond to that 
chron. 
An alternative hypothesis is that the Thoki geo- 
magnetic event corresponds to the end of the Co- 
chiti-Gilhert reversal. This N-R boundary is dated 
at 4.0 Ma on the Cande and Kent (1992) time scale. 
Our paleomagnetic data might then be compared to 
the intermediate directions reported by Watkins et al. 
(1977) for the NP section in the BorgarfjiSrdur area 
(West Iceland) or/and to those found in the S and T 
sections of East Iceland (Watkins and Walker, 1977). 
Another point of interest is the origin of the VGP 
clusters observed during this transition (Fig. 11). 
Groups of consecutive flows with identical pale- 
ofield directions are commonly observed in volcanic 
records of geomagnetic reversals. In their detailed 
study of the Steens Mountain reversal, Mankinen et 
al. (1985) interpreted these groups as being due to 
the eruption of successive lava flows in a very short 
time interval. In contrast, Hoffman (1992) assumed 
that these clusters indicate long lived transitional 
states of the geomagnetic field. He also suggested 
that such stages are dominantly dipolar and have 
been persistent features of the geomagnetic reversals 
for the past 10 Ma. The question of whether the VGP 
clusters are of volcanic or geomagnetic origin is still

Abstract 
A detailed study of the ~ 2000 years old Xitle-Pedregal de San Angel volcanic field in the southern Basin of Mexico 
was undertaken to assess the reliability of the palaeomagnetic record as derived from fresh well-preserved and exposed lava 
flows. The Xitle vent is on the slope of the Ajusco volcano, which results in a topographic difference of over 800 m in less 
than 12 km of horizontal distance. Most sites present a mean direction, with a small within-site dispersion, around the 
dipolar direction for the locality, but some sites, particularly in the basin sector of flat relief away from the vent, show 
shallow inclinations. Anisotropy of magnetic susceptibility (AMS) shows normal 'flow' fabrics with horizontal foliation 
planes and small anisotropy degree. AMS lineations correlate with observed flow directions. The magnetic properties vary 
systematically across flow units, but directions do not show a consistent pattern. Secular variation effects do not apparently 
contribute to the shallow inclinations or directional scatter. Some lava structures like pressure crests and blocky fronts give 
shallow inclinations and scattered directions, respectively. The resulting overall mean direction is well defined and close to 
the dipolar direction (B ~ 26, Dec = 359.8 °, Inc = 32.8 °, k z 167, ot95 = 2.2°), but this excludes two apparent directional 
groups. The mean direction for one group, with B = 19, Dec ~ 359.0 °, Inc = 35.1 °, k~ 247, ot95 ~ 2.1 °, may be the 
representative estimate for the field. Shallow inclinations are considered anomalous and associated to a characteristic specific 
to given sectors of lava flows. Palaeointensity determinations have been obtained for six samples from five sites by using the 
Thellier and Shaw methods. Results agree well with previous studies, however, the standard deviation calculated for the 
mean value remains high after incorporation of the new data. Mean palaeointensity based on five new determinations and 
eight early data is N - 13, 56.50 + 6.16 mT (and the mean for the overall data set is N = 20, 60.50 + 9.21 mT). Results 
illustrate some practical considerations and limitations in methodology and the reliability of the palaeomagnetic record in 
volcanic rocks. 
I. Introduction 
The Xitle-Pedregal de San Angel volcanic field is 
formed by fresh, well exposed basaltic lava flows 
that originated from the activity of the Xitle cinder 
cone some 2000 years ago in the southern sector of 
the Basin of Mexico (Fig. 1). Earlier palaeomagnetic 
studies in the 1970s (Mooser et al., 1974; Urrutia- 
Fucugauchi and Valencio, 1976; Herrero-Bervera and 
Pal, 1978) reported data for the lava flows with small 
within-site dispersions but with different mean direc- 
tions. In particular, there were nine sites with inclina- 
tions close to the dipolar value and five sites with 
inclinations some 10 °- 12 ° shallower (Table 1). Only

2. Xitle-Pedregal de San Angel field and sampling 
The Xitle-Pedregal de San Angel volcanic field 
extends over a wide area in the southern sector of the 
Basin of Mexico. Lava flows cover some of the 
earlier pyramids and settlements in the region 
(Cuicuilco and Copilco archaeological sites). Nowa- 
days, Mexico City has extended over the lava field 
and the National University, including the Paleomag- 
netics Laboratory, is built on top of the flows. 
Organic material associated with the eruption of 
Xitle volcano was dated early during development of 
the radiocarbon method (Arnold and Libby, 1951; 
Libby, 1955). This date of 2422 + 250 years BP 
(before present, AD 1950) (C-200; Table 2) remains 
as the most widely quoted age for the Xitle eruption 
in subsequent studies; although there have been sev- 
eral additional studies reported (available data is 
summarized in Table 2), the age has remained a 
matter of controversy (Heizer and Bennyhoff, 1958, 
1972; Ortega et al., 1993). Some studies have sup- 
ported a much younger age for the Xitle; for in- 
stance, Cordova et al. (1994) have recently selected 
the date reported by Fergusson and Libby (1963) of 
1536 +_ 65 years BP (UCLA-228) which had been 
correlated with archaeological remains covered by 
the lava. Dates show three apparent groups, roughly 
around 2000, 2375, and 4000 years BP (Fig. 2). The 
group around 4000 years BP is mainly formed by 
dates obtained in the Cuicuilco archaeological exca- 
vations from horizons between about 4 and 7 m 
below the ground level and lava contact. They can be 
related to early archaeological occupation Tlalpan 
stages (Fergusson and Libby, 1963). The second 
group includes the date by Arnold and Libby (1951) 
which was obtained from a soil collected underneath 
the lava in Cuicuilco. The date of 2000 years BP for 
the first group has also been proposed as the age for 
the Xitle eruption (e.g. Heizer and Bennyhoff, 1958; 
White et al., 1990). We favour this date as represen- 
tative for the eruption, mainly because of the relative 
position of the material dated with respect to the lava 
and ash. A radiocarbon age determination on a burned 
wood fragment we collected beneath the lava (Ortega 
et al., 1993) in a quarry to the southeast of the 
Universidad Nacional Autonoma de Mexico (UNAM) 
campus gives a (C-13 corrected) date of 1960 + 65 
years BP (Geochron Laboratory, Krueger Enterprises

The lava flows correspond to pahoehoe type and 
display a young morphology with well preserved 
flow structures and little or no vegetation cover. 
Vesicles are very common, particularly towards the 
top of the flow units. There are several lava struc- 
tures including explosion tubes, lava channels, pres- 
sure crests, different types of vesicles and tumuli 
(Ordo~ez, 1890; Waitz and Wittch, 1911; Badilla- 
Cruz, 1977). The composition is basaltic and may be 
described as an olivine (augite) basalt (Schmitter, 
1953; Badilla-Cruz, 1977). As part of this study, we 
have obtained a chemical analysis for a sample from 
site CU-2 which corresponds to a high alumina 
basalt. Its calc-alkaline character is similar to data 
reported earlier (e.g. Gurm and Mooser, 1970; Pal 
and Urrutia-Fucugauchi, 1977; Perez et al., 1979). 
Emplacement of lava flows was controlled by the 
topography. The Xitle cone grew on the slope of the 
Ajusco volcano and lava flowed down the slope to 
the N-NE until reaching the basin floor (Fig. 1). In 
the basin itself there were hills and rivers that di- 
verted the flows and ponded the lava. In the out- 
crops, two and sometimes three flow units can be 
observed, with thicknesses varying from 2 to 6 m. 
Xitle may be described as a small scoria cone with a 
diameter of about 500 m and a height over the plain 
to the south of about 140 m. The southern rim is 
higher than the northern one. Some 100 m westwards 
there is a parasitic cone named Xicontle. Thick ash 
layers are exposed in the southern plain; layers a few

Previous studies have concentrated on the low 
areas in and around the university campus. Therefore 
sampling was extended into the Ajusco slope to- 
wards the Xitle vent (Fig. 1). Examination of these 
results then prompted additional sampling campaigns 
in the lower areas in order to evaluate some possible 
factors affecting the palaeomagnetic record and also 
to investigate particular structures (e.g. pressure 
crests and lava blocky fronts). A total of 14 new 
sites, with some five to 15 samples per site, were 
collected. 
3. Methods and results 
Previous studies used magnetic compass orienta- 
tion, therefore for this study both solar and magnetic 
compass orientations were used in order to evaluate 
the influence of the outcrop magnetizations on the 
orientation procedures. There were angular differ- 
ences of about +5 ° and up to 16 ° between the two 
orientation schemes. Angular differences do not seem 
to follow a simple trend as a function of initial 
magnetization intensity (Fig. 4). Magnetization direc- 
tions used for the site mean calculations (and statis- 
tics) below have been corrected using the solar com- 
pass orientations. However, site mean directions cal- 
culated using the solar and magnetic compass orien- 
tations are not significantly different, only within-site 
angular dispersion is less for the solar compass. 
The intensity and direction of natural remanent 
magnetization (NRM) were measured with a Mol- 
spin spinner magnetometer attached to an IBM com- 
puter. Low-field susceptibility was measured with 
the Minisep instrument. Vectorial composition, co- 
ercitivity and unblocking temperature spectra were 
investigated by detailed step wise alternating field 
(AF) and thermal demagnetization. AF demagnetiza- 
tion was completed in 8-12 steps up to 100 mT in a 
reverse tumbling Schonstedt demagnetizer. Thermal 
demagnetization was done in 8-10 steps up to 580°C 
in a Schonstedt TSD-1 demagnetizer. 
Characteristic magnetization directions were esti- 
mated from end-point analysis and the vector plots.

4. Discussion 
The new data from different parts of the volcanic 
field (Fig. 1) show well defined characteristic direc- 
tions with small within-site angular dispersions (Ta- 
ble 1). Particularly gratifying is the good coherence 
of directions over large horizontal distances, from 
close to the vent and farther away (over 12 km of 
horizontal distance). The overall mean direction (B 
= 26, Dec = 359.8 °, Inc = 32.8 °, k = 167, 0/,95 = 
2.2 ° ) is characterized by small angular dispersion and 
inclination close to the dipolar value for the locality 
(see also mean direction calculated for all 28 sites; 
Table 1). 
This overall mean direction can be considered as 
a reasonable result for a lava flow. Closer inspection, 
however, shows relatively large apparently consistent 
between-site differences, particularly in the mean 
inclinations. Discussion below concentrates on these 
between-site differences in directions and searches 
for possible explanations. First, we examine if the 
differences are statistically significant, and then we 
explore which directions, if any, may be considered 
as anomalous. By analysing the site mean directions 
and the apparent geographic dependence, an arbitrary 
cut-off inclination value of 30 ° was chosen to sepa- 
rate the data. The mean direction for sites with 
inclinations shallower than 30 ° is Dec = 1.5 °, Inc = 
26.7 ° (ct95 = 3.3 °, k = 338, B = 7) and for the other 
sites is Dec---359.0 °, Inc = 35.1 ° (ct95 = 2.1 °, k = 
247, B = 19). These two mean directions have cones 
of 95% confidence that do not overlap and are 
statistically different (McFadden and Lowes, 1981). 
To further investigate the site mean directional distri- 
bution, directions have been referred to the rotated 
space as defined by Hoffman (1984). This procedure 
was developed to study transitional data and permits 
the investigation of the pattern of angular deviations 
from the dipolar direction. Site-mean directions in 
the rotated space are given in Fig. 13. In this case, 
angular deviations are much smaller than for transi- 
tional directions. The sites with inclinations around

J. Urrutia-Fucugauchi / Physics of the Earth and Planetary Interiors 97 (1996) 177-196 189 
the dipolar value for the area are clearly more nu- 
merous. There is unfortunately no independent direc- 
tion for reference, and no way to conclusively esti- 
mate the corresponding geomagnetic field direction 
for the Xitle lava flow (and no way to conclusively 
identify any 'anomalous' directions). However, esti- 
mation of a direction for the locality calculated from 
the global virtual geomagnetic pole (VGP) compila- 
tion reported by Ohno and Hamano (1992) gives an 
inclination of 34.1 ° and a declination of 4.7 ° (refer- 
ence pole is 85.5°N, 358.0°E, N = 11, A95 = 4.4 °, 
for 2000 years BP (radiocarbon time scale); Table 1 
of Ohno and Hamano (1992). This calculated direc- 
tion agrees better with the direction estimated for the 
volcanic field using the results close to the dipolar 
inclination value. 
With the new data, the difference in the expanded 
data set between the shallow inclination and dipolar 
inclination sites decreased, but the two apparent 
directional groups remain. The distinction between 
the 'shallow' and 'dipolar' inclination sites which 
was clear in the earlier data set is not so simple in 
the expanded data set. Nevertheless, there are some 
additional indications. Sites with the shallow inclina- 
tions correspond to localities farther from the Xitle 
vent, in the low altitude, gentle slope (flat) terrain. 
This apparent correlation with the terrain character- 
istics that influenced the lava emplacement suggests 
that the magnetizations might be influenced by the 
lava emplacement process. The overall vector mean 
(Table 1) has an inclination close to the dipolar 
value. Plotting the inclination anomaly (Fig. 14(a)) 
(AI = observed inclination less the dipolar inclina- 
tion) or the site-mean inclinations as a function of 
site altitude (or distance from vent) shows a peculiar 
distribution as mentioned above, with the occurrence 
of 'anomalous' sites preferentially located in the low

Tanguy (1990) found very strong magnetizations, 
with values higher than 10 A m-1 and up to 35 A 
m- 1 in his studies, but the NRM intensities from the 
Xitle-Pedregal de San Angel flows are not that high, 
being between about 2.5 and 13 A m-~. The ex- 
pected deflection due to the shape of the lava flow 
will be too small to account for the angular differ- 
ence observed (Coe, 1979; Tanguy, 1990) and some 
characteristic specific to certain sectors of the Xitle- 
Pedregal de San Angel flow must be involved. There 
is, however, a relationship between site mean incli- 
nations and site mean NRM intensities (Fig. 16), 
with higher intensities corresponding to the shallow 
inclinations. 
Six palaeointensity determinations using the Thel- 
lier and the Shaw methods give a mean of 60.04 + 
9.62 mT. Deletion of one sample gives a mean of 
57.13 + 7.23 roT, which is close to the mean calcu- 
lated for eight samples reported earlier by Nagata et 
al. (1965) of 56.11 __+ 5.89 mT. The angular standard 
deviation is relatively high. The combined mean of 
the two data sets is 56.50+6.16 mT (N= 13), 
which also presents a high standard deviation that 
seems to be a characteristic of the flow (or the 
methods). Results obtained in this study give three 
lower palaeointensity values for sites in the campus 
compared with those three closer to the Xitle vent on 
the Ajusco slope. However, two of the low values 
have been obtained by the Shaw method, and it may 
be a methodological factor involved. Studies directed 
to compare the two methods have generally reported 
good agreement. For instance, Aitken et al. (1988) 
summarized results for 31 samples studied by the 
two methods and reported Shaw/Thellier ratios 
varying between 0.75 and 1.25, with a mean ratio of 
1.01 and a small standard deviation of 0.10. Addi- 
tional data reported in Gonzalez-Huesca (1992) give 
higher values, with a mean of 66.83 + 10.09 mT 
(N = 6). We note that in that study, the two results 
obtained with the Shaw method are also lower than 
those obtained with the Thellier method. Comparison 
of data obtained solely with the Thellier method 
shows a large standard deviation. There seems to be 
methodological factors involved, as well as factors 
related to the magnetic record of the lava flow (see 
e.g. Walton, 1988; Aitken et al., 1988). The number 
of palaeointensity determinations is relatively high 
for a single monogenetic volcano and the overall 
mean has a relatively large standard deviation (N = 
20, 60.50 + 9.21 mT; Table 3). 
Results show that careful analysis needs to be 
exercised when interpreting apparently anomalous 
data from young apparently 'quite suitable' volcanic 
lava flows. There are, for example, two directional 
groups for the Xitle-Pedregal de San Angel volcanic 
field. The group with more sites (B = 19) and which 
are distributed along the entire field shows an incli- 
nation close to the dipolar value and may be consid- 
ered representative for the Xitle-Pedregal de San 
Angel. The other group with shallow inclinations is 
less numerous (B = 7) and seems to have a restricted 
occurrence in a particular location of the volcanic 
field.

Paleomagnetism of Paleozoic strata, Brabant and Ardennes 
Massifs, Belgium: Implications of prefolding and postfolding 
Late Carboniferous secondary magnetizations for European 
apparent polar wander 
Roberto S. Molina Garza 
Department of Earth and Planetary Sciences, University of New Mexico, Albuquerque 
J. D. A. Zijderveld 
Paleomagnetic Laboratory Fort Hoofddijk, Utrecht, Netherlands 
Abstract. Paleozoic carbonate rocks of the Brabant Massif, Namur Basin, and Dinant 
Synclinorium, Belgium, are characterized by two secondary Late Carboniferous magneti- 
zations of uniform reverse polarity: a postfolding low unblocking temperature (300- 
375øC) component (LT) and a prefolding high unblocking temperature (400-550øC) 
component (HT). In the Namur Basin, LT magnetizations postdate late Westphalian 
deformation (-305 Ma); in the Dinant Synclinorium, HT magnetizations predate early 
Westphalian deformation (-316 Ma). LT magnetizations for the combined Brabant 
Massif and Namur Basin sites give a south paleopole at 42.3øS, 339.6øE (dp=l.9 ø, 
dm=3.8ø), consistent with the European cratonic reference. The LT magnetizations in the 
Dinant Synclinorium give a paleopole at 36.2øS 321.0øE (dp=2.4 ø, dm=4.7ø). The HT 
magnetization gives paleopoles at 34.1øS, 333.4øE (dp=2.6 ø, dm=5.1ø; Brabant and 
Namur) and at 25.9øS, 321.5øE (dp=3.5 ø, dm=6.8ø; Dinant Synclinorium). Declinations 
indicate -15 ø clockwise rotation of the Dinant Synclinorium with respect to the Brabant 
Massif after acquisition of the LT magnetization. Devonian red beds yield near 
univectorial apparent synfolding magnetizations of distributed unblocking temperature 
that we interpret as artifacts of the remanence acquisition or deformation processes. The 
HT paleopole for the Brabant Massif is indistinguishable from other early Late 
Carboniferous European paleopoles and is similar to poles interpreted to be derived from 
remagnetizations in the British Isles. Age constraints on the time of remanence 
acquisition of secondary mangetizations allow a refined calibration of the European 
apparent polar wander path. Inclinations of the LT and HT components indicate about 6- 
8 ø (700 km) northward motion during the Late Carboniferous. 
Introduction 
It is now widely recognized that sedimentary rocks in 
general, and shallow water carbonate rocks in particular, may 
acquire geologically stable secondary magnetizations. Late 
Paleozoic secondary magnetizations are widespread in 
carbonate rocks and red beds in the Appalachian and Ouachita 
belts and North America craton interior [McCabe and 
Ellmore, 1989; and references there in], Hercynian Europe 
and the Hercynian foreland [Edel and Coulon, 1984; 1987; 
Courtillot et al., 1986; McCabe and Charmell, 1994], the 
Russian Platform [Smethurst and Khramov, 1992], and north- 
ern Africa [Salmon et al., 1988]. Late Paleozoic remag- 
netization is a complex phenomenon, one not yet completely 
understood. Furthermore tectonic interpretation of late 
Paleozoic secondary magnetizations is hindered by problems 
in establishing the time of remanence acquisition.

has been the subject of several studies in which it has been 
concluded that these rocks carry postfolding or synfolding 
secondary magnetizations of late Paleozoic age [Thominski et 
al., 1993; Nowaczyk and Bleil, 1985; Edel and Coulon, 1987]. 
Thominski et al. [1993] interpreted a characteristic 
magnetization with distributed unblocking temperatures 
between 310 and 550øC as a thermoviscous remanence carried 
by detrital magnetite grains. Paleomagnetic directions were 
considered to reflect a small clockwise rotation (-15 ø) of the 
Dinant Synclinorium relative to the Inde Syncline, which has 
remained fixed relative to stable Europe since Late 
Carboniferous time. Nowaczyk and Bleil [1985] interpreted 
secondary magnetizations in Paleozoic strata north of the 
Stavelot Massif to indicate a small counterclockwise (-15 ø) 
rotation relative to parts of stable Europe not affected by the 
Hercynian orogeny. 
A more comprehensive study by Edel and Coulon [1987] 
found that the remanence of Paleozoic strata in the Ardennes 
is composed of two distinct components. Low unblocking 
temperature A magnetizations were regarded as post-folding

and Stephanian (latest Carboniferous) or Permian in age, high 
unblocking temperature B-magnetizations were regarded as 
postfolding or synfolding and middle-Late Carboniferous in 
age. Edel and Coulon [1987] associated B magnetizations 
with low grade metamorphism in the Ardennes Massif dated 
at about 316 Ma [Piqud et al., 1984] and concluded that-45 ø 
of clockwise rotation relative to the palcomeridian affected 
Hercynian massifs from Armorica to the Black Forest, 
including the Ardennes Massif, in Late Carboniferous times 
[Edel, 1987]. 
Paleozoic rock of the Ardennes and Brabant Massifs were 
indeed affected by late Paleozoic remagnetization. Further 
research shows, however, that the remanence is made of a 
prefolding, yet secondary, intermediate to high unblocking 
temperature magnetization and a postfolding, secondary, low 
unblocking temperature magnetization. Detailed 
palcomagnetic and rock magnetic data are reported here with 
emphasis on the character of magnetic carriers and the 
tectonic interpretation of palcomagnetic data for European 
apparent polar wander and Hercynian tectonics. 
Geological Setting 
Central Belgium is characterized by three main palc- 
ogeographic and tectonic elements: the Brabant Massif, the 
Namur Basin, and the Dinant Synclinorium, located at the 
southern margin of the mid-Paleozoic Old Red Sandstone 
continent (Figure 1). The Brabant Massif is a Caledonian 
realm not affected by the Hercynian orogeny. Its southern 
flank is covered unconformably by Middle Devonian through 
Upper Carboniferous strata dipping gently to the south. It is 
bordered to the south by the Namur Basin, which has been 
interpreted as an Hercynian foredeep basin. The Namur Basin 
is overthrusted from the south by rocks of the Dinant Syncli- 
norium along the Midi-Eifel-Aachen fault. The Dinant 
Synclinorium and the Namur Basin are part of the Ardennes; 
together with the Rheinisches-Schiefergebirge, these form the 
most northern units involved in the Hercynian orogeny in 
central Europe. 
The Dinant Synclinorium is made of a series of open, east- 
west trending, anticlines and synclines exposing Lower 
Devonian to Lower Carboniferous strata. The most important 
structures are attributed to the Asturian phase of the 
Hercynian cycle but there is some evidence of earlier 
(Sudetic?) deformation. Asturian deformation in the Namur 
Basin occurred sometime after the Westphalian B and before 
the Westphalian D, as suggested by the presence in 
Westphalian D strata in the Campine basin of detritus and 
conglomerate clasts derived from Devonian, Namurian, and 
lower Westphalian rocks [Bless et al., 1977, 1989]. The same

Earlier (late Namurian-early Westphalian) deformation in 
the Dinant Synclinorium is indicated by the contrast in 
tectonic styles between the Namur Basin and the 
synclinorium, the presence of karst surfaces on Upper Visean 
carbonate rocks and an angular unconformity with Namurian 
A rocks [Dressen et al., 1985], the start of fill-up in the 
Hercynian foredeep during the Namurian with influxing 
sediments from the south, and Namurian conglomerates in the 
northern part of the Ardenno-Rhenish Massif [Klerkx, 1966]. 
Low-grade regional metamorphism in the Ardennes Massif 
increases to the south and reached its peak at-316 Ma [Piqud 
et al., 1984]; younger radiometric ages have been obtained to 
the east in the Stavelot Massif at-310 Ma [Kramm et al., 
1985]. 
Sampling and Methodology 
Paleomagneti½ sampling includes a total of 36 sites (480 
independently oriented hand samples and drilled cores) of 
limestones, dolomites, and red beds from Lower Devonian 
through Lower Carboniferous strata (Table 1). Sites are 
distributed along the southern flank of the Brabant Massif 
along the Orneau Valley, the Samme Canal, and the river 
Dendre (Figure 1). Folded strata of similar age were collected 
in a series of folds exposed along the Meuse river between 
Yvoir and Namur. Additional sites in the Namur Basin were 
collected near Huy (Figure 1). The majority of the sites 
consist of hand samples collected within a quarry or a road 
outcrop from stratigraphic intervals of 5 to 20 m. 
Measurements of bedding dip and strike as well as sample 
orientations were done with a magnetic compass. 
Earlier collections (1963-1969) by J. D. A. Zijderveld were 
cast within paraffin cubes of 10 cm length. Their natural 
remanent magnetization (NRM) was measured with astatic 
magnetometers according to As [1960], and subjected only to 
alternating field (AF) demagnetization up to 100 mT. Later 
collections (1972-1975) were subsam.l?led as conventional 10.5 cm specimens, or a few as 85 cm cylinders. The latest 
collection (1991) consists of conventional paleomagnetic 
cores drilled in the field. Stepwise demagnetization was 
performed in noninductive furnaces or with an AF 
demagnetization apparatus, up to temperatures of 690øC or 
inductions of 300 mT, respectively. Their NRM was measured 
with either a three-axis 2G cryogenic or a modified JKL- 
spinner magnetometer, at the paleomagnetic laboratory Fort 
Hoofddijk. Vectorial components of the NRM were identified 
by inspection of orthogonal demagnetization diagrams 
[Zijderveld, 1967]; directions were calculated using principal 
component analysis (PCA) [Kirschrink, 1980]. 
The magnetic mineralogy was studied with various 
conventional techniques including measurements of bulk 
magnetic susceptibility during thermal demagnetization, 
anisotropy of magnetic susceptibility, isothermal remanent 
magnetization acquisition (IRM) up to inductions of 1.5 T, 
and thermal and AF demagnetization of the IRM [Lowrie, 
1990; Dunlop, 1972]. We also carried hysteresis 
measurements with a Micromag at the Institute of Rock 
Magnetism, University of Minnesota, thermomagnetic 
analysis on a horizontal Curie balance equipped with a 
cycling field system (200-400 roT), and microprobe and 
microscope observations. 
Paleomagnetic Results 
Carbonate Rocks 
Initial NRM intensities ranged approximately between 0.1 
and 20 mA/m, with a clear disposition to lower values in ' 
Lower Carboniferous rocks. Only about 75% of the samples 
had sufficiently high intensities to be stepwise demagnetized. 
NRM directions are well grouped at the site level. Typical 
demagnetization behavior is relatively straightforward (Figure 
2). AF demagnetization, however, fails to reveal the true 
multicomponent nature of the remanence, conversely thermal 
demagnetization isolates a low unblocking temperature (250 ø- 
375øC) and a high-temperature (400ø-550øC) magnetization. 
Magnetite-like minerals carry the magnetic signal, with a 
possible small contribution from magnetic sulfides. 
Median destructive fields range between-10 and 35 mT, 
and a small fraction of the NRM often remained after 
inductions of 100 mT (about 5% to 10%). At low inductions, 
AF removes a north directed and steep positive magnetization 
in the direction of the recent dipole field which has been 
partially overprinted by viscous and spurious magnetizations 
(Figure 2b). The north directed magnetization is largely 
removed with inductions of-20-25 mT, and it seems to have 
been completely eliminated with-50 mT. At higher induc- 
tions most samples show seemingly univectorial decay of a 
(in situ) shallow to moderately steep south-southwest 
remanence (Figures 2a-2b and 2h-2i). In detail, however, 
demagnetization trajectories show the inclination becoming 
progressively more shallow (Figure 2b); some fail to reach the 
origin and vector end points have shallow negative inclination 
(Figures 2c and 2h). In virtually all cases, maximum 
inductions of about 200 mT are sufficient to remove the 
remanence completely. 
In marked contrast to AF, thermal demagnetization 
(Figures 2d-2e and 2k-21) indicates that the south-southwest 
directed remanence results from the combined removal of two 
distinct components: a south-southwest and shallow negative 
magnetization (unblocked between 250 and 375øC) and yet 
another southwest directed magnetization with (tilt corrected) 
shallow predominantly positive inclination. Maximum 
laboratory unblocking temperatures for the latter range 
between 475 and 540øC. This NRM structure can be 
recognized in all carbonate samples of the three areas. We 
refer to the south-southwest shallow negative magnetization 
as the LT (low temperature) magnetization and the southwest 
shallow positive component as the HT (high temperature) 
magnetization. 
Comparisons of thermal and AF treatment for specimens 
from a single hand sample (e.g., Figures 2b and 2e, from site 
VIS2) or from the same bed (e.g., Figures 2a and 2d, from site 
FR6) suggest that AF demagnetization first removes the HT 
magnetization, and subsequently, in higher fields the LT 
component becomes removed. The LT magnetization is thus 
harder than the HT magnetization. In the Dinant Synclinorium 
(Figures 2h-2n), identifying the LT and HT components is 
straightforward, because in strongly folded strata they show a 
more obvious difference in direction. In general, however, 
demagnetization trajectories of samples from the synclinorium 
(e.g., Figures 21 and 2m) show greater overlap of unblocking 
temperatures than Brabant samples.

component was not completely isolated, great circles (GC) 
anchored to the origin were determined between the steps of 
300 ø and -450øC, rejecting GC data with MAD values greater

magnetization step) gave the best estimate of the HT 
magnetization. These data were combined with line segments 
and GC of other specimens, at the sample level, using the 
Bailey and Halls [1984] method. The majority of the samples 
that were AF demagnetized were excluded from the site mean 
calculations of the HT magnetization, except for samples 
where the intermediate coercivity HT magnetization was 
calculated using Hoffman-Day directions (e.g., Figure 2a) 
[Hoffman and Day, 1978]. For comparison, Edel and Coulon 
[1987] indicate that calculations of their B magnetization 
include the range of unblocking temperatures from 400 to 
580øC 
Measurements of magnetic susceptibility after partial 
demagnetization revealed a large increase starting at 
temperatures of about 420øCo We examined the possibility 
that the HT behavior might be related to thermal alteration 
using AF demagnetization after heating to 390øC. Linear 
trajectories to the origin suggest that this procedure isolated a 
magnetization virtually identical to that isolated using thermal 
demagnetization alone (e.g., Figure 2n). IRM acquisition 
curves of samples with this behavior are characterized by 
saturation at about 0.3 T. Although the HT magnetization can 
still be isolated in them, there are very few specimens where a 
bias in the demagnetization trajectory is caused by a third and 
still higher coercivity/unblocking temperature component. 
This component is small and resembles the recent dipole field 
direction (Figure 2g). Samples with this behavior are 
characterized by IRM acquisition curves which do not saturate 
with inductions of 1.5 T. 
A number of hand samples from earlier collections 
subjected only to AF demagnetization were retrieved from the 
laboratory archives, subsampled, and subjected to thermal 
demagnetization (Figure 2j). This technique removes the 
characteristic south-southwest LT magnetization between 250 
and 350øC, isolating a HT magnetization with (tilt corrected) 
southwest and shallow direction. 
Fold Test and the Relative Age of the LT and HT 
Magnetizations 
Sites collected in the syncline of Walgrappe of the Dinant 
Synclinorium (Figure 1) constrain the relative age of the LT 
and HT magnetizations. A single fold test indicates maximum 
values for k, the estimate of Fisher's precision parameter , at 
4% and 92% unfolding for the LT and HT magnetizations, 
respectively (Figure 3). The improvements in k values (from 0 
to 4%, as well as 92 to 100% unfolding) are not statistically 
significant. Therefore the LT magnetization was acquired after 
folding, while the HT magnetization was acquired before 
folding. 
Maximum concentration at values different from 0 or 
100% unfolding can be explained by incomplete application 
of the tilt correction, internal deformation affecting the 
remanence, incomplete separation of magnetic components, or 
a true synfolding age for the magnetization [MacDonald, 
1980; KligfieM et al., 1983; Kodama, 1988; van der Pluij'm, 
1987]. The syncline of Walgrappe is a simple structure with a 
very shallow plunge (-5 ø) to the west that was incorporated in 
the tilt correction. Evidence for internal deformation is not 
readily apparent at the outcrop scale. Magnetic anisotropy 
data, moreover, do not appear to indicate high strains. 
Contrary to other areas to the northeast [Kramm et al., 1985] 
and to the south [Piqud et al., 1984], the rocks we collected 
are not affected by metamorphism and magnetic fabrics are 
relatively simple. Most sites show \"sedimentary fabrics\" with 
the minimum susceptibility axis almost perpendicular to 
bedding. What is left as explanation is slightly incomplete 
separation of components. A regional fold test also suggests 
that HT magnetizations predate folding in the Namur Basin. 
On the Brabant Massif, the variations in the structure are 
insufficient to provide a significant fold test. For the HT 
magnetizations the k value estimated from the distribution of 
site means decreases from an in situ value of 132.2 to a tilt 
corrected value of 69.6 (Figure 4 and Table 2). The decrease 
in precision is not statistically significant but it could indicate 
that this magnetization was acquired after the slight southward 
tilt of the southern border of the Brabant Massif. Deformation 
on the Brabant Massif margin is not necessarily contemporary 
with deformation in the synclinorium; it is likely a flexural 
response to sediment loading in the Namur Basin. Both, in 
situ and tilt corrected HT inclinations in the Brabant Massif 
are statistically indistinguishable from tilt-corrected 
inclinations in the synclinorium. It is thus unclear whether HT 
magnetizations in the Brabant Massif were acquired when the 
rocks were horizontal (more on this below). As for the LT 
magnetizations in the Brabant Massif similarity reasons led us 
to infer that it postdates the final deformation as in the Dinant 
and Namur areas. 
Rock Magnetism of Carbonate Rocks 
IRM acquisition curves are dominated by magnetite (or 
maghemite) contributions, very small contributions from 
hematite or goethite are evident by small increase in remanent 
magnetization between 0.3 and 1.5 T (typically <5% of the 
total magnetization). Samples with larger contributions from 
high coercivity remanence are exceptional (Figure 5). In most 
cases when IRM curves indicate that hematite or goethite are 
present, these do not contribute significantly to the natural 
remanence because AF demagnetization completely removes 
the NRM (compare Figure 2). In some cases, IRM suggests 
that the high-coercivity material was probably derived from 
oxidation of pyrite or other nonmagnetic material. For 
example, the similarity in the shape and size of the IRM 
curves of samples 487 and 489 (from site FR4) below about

Three orthogonal IRM components of magnetization were 
induced and subsequently demagnetized in selected 
specimens according to the method of Lowtie [1990]. The 
intermediate coercivity IRM (0.3 T) is always the most 
prominent and the high-coercivity component (1.5 T) the 
smallest. In the most representative specimen for the 
collection (Figure 6a), for which hematite contributions to the 
IRM are very small, a significant fraction of the low 
coercivity IRM (<0.03 T) is removed at temperatures of about 
200øC, but generally, this component is not completely 
removed until about 500øC. At temperatures typical of the 
unblocking of the LT magnetization (275-350øC) the 
intermediate- and high-coercivity IRMs decay at a faster rate 
than the 1ow-coercivity IRM. Specimens with more complex 
behavior (Figure 6b) are a minority. In those, a considerable 
fraction of the high-coercivity IRM has unblocking 
temperatures greater than 600øC, evidently indicating the 
presence of hematite.

High-susceptibility magnetic material (most likely magnetite) 
is created when heating between 400 and 500øC. This newly 
formed magnetite is subsequently partly altered (oxidized to 
hematite), as indicated by magnetization values in the cooling 
curve below the peak value of the heating curve (Figure 6d). 
Also, IRM acquisition curves of samples subjected to thermal 
demagnetization show a significant increase in coercivity that 
indicates creation of hematite. The onset of alteration occurs 
at temperatures that are relatively close to typical inversion 
temperatures of titanomaghemites. We discount this 
interpretation because energy dispersion and microprobe 
analyses did not detect significant amounts of Ti in any of 
tens of grains analyzed. The alteration may result in part from 
breakdown of pyrite; abundant sulfide grains were observed 
in the petrographic examination. Erratic behavior of the NRM 
above 450øC can thus be related to creation of near- 
superparamagnetic magnetite during demagnetization 
experiments. Other thermomagnetic curves indicate a Curie 
temperature of about 575øC (near pure magnetite; Figure 6c) 
and lack the characteristic signal of alteration observed in 
other samples. These curves are not reversible above 600øC 
and are typical of samples for which IRM experiments also 
indicated the presence of significant amounts of hematite. In 
at least one example (Figure 6e), material with a Curie 
temperature around 350øC suggests the presence of magnetic 
iron sulfides. 
Magnetic hysteresis data (Figure 7) are characterized by 
constricted (wasp-waisted) geometry. Coercivity values are 
small (< 10 mT), and slope corrections to hysteresis loops 
include an almost equal number of curves with paramagnetic 
or diamagnetic signals. Hysteresis parameters for a small 
number of samples plotted in a log-log diagram fall along the 
general trend of remagnetized strata [clackson, 1990; McCabe 
and Channell, 1994]. Constrained hysteresis loops can be 
explained as mixtures of small amounts of hematite with 
magnetite (as suggested by the IRM results) or by the 
presence of a large superparamagnetic fraction (the presence 
of grains near the superparamagnetic-single domain threshold 
characterized by weakly prolate fabrics, by relatively low 
anisotropy (percent anisotropy ranges between 0.9 and 7.1%), 
and by \"sedimentary\" orientations (minimum susceptibility 
perpendicular to bedding). 
LT magnetizations unblock at temperatures typical of 
magnetic sulfides but in many instances, maximum 
unblocking temperatures exceed 350øC. The evidence in the 
thermomagnetic runs for material with a Curie temperature of 
about 350øC is only marginal (Figure 6e). The rock magnetic 
and microscopic evidence for pyrrhotite is relatively tenuous. 
An interpretation of demagnetization results combined with 
the rock magnetic experiments suggests that the LT 
magnetization is predominantly carried by small single- 
domain (SD) magnetite grains with low unblocking 
temperature and high coercivity and possibly by magnetic 
sulfides. The effective unblocking temperatures of small SD 
grains is possibly reduced by partial alteration (oxidation) 
during heating experiments. HT magnetizations are carried by 
large single-domain and pseudo-single-domain (PSD) 
magnetite grains with low coercivity and high laboratory 
unblocking temperatures. Large multidomain MD grains are 
the likely carriers of viscous overprints in the direction of the 
recent dipole field.

Ore microscopy and electron microscopy of carbonate 
rocks allowed identification of several iron-bearing phases. 
Iron oxides (based on the rock magnetic signature these are

features that suggest original euhedral morphologies over- 
grown by iron oxide groundmass (Figure 8). Iron sulfide 
grains occur disseminated and exhibit spherical and euhedral 
morphologies as well. Euhedral grains are concentrated along 
stylolite planes and microbreccias. Iron sulfides are typically 
homogeneous, but the rim of some grains is replaced by Fe-

High resistance to AF demagnetization, unblocking 
temperatures above 600øC, and IRM acquisition indicate that 
the magnetization of red beds is dominated hematite. 
Thermomagnetic curves indicate that hematite is the main 
ferromagnetic mineral and that contributions of magnetite are 
insignificant (Figure 60. Thermomagnetic curves are 
reversible; it thus seems that maghemite or other metastable 
phases are not present. The distributed unblocking 
temperature ChRM (between 300 and 650øC) is most likely 
carried by fine-grained hematite. 
In Brabant sites LT and HT directions from red beds are 
near those of the carbonate rocks (Figure 4) and the 
hypothesis of them sharing a common mean cannot be 
rejected with a 95% confidence [McFadden and Lowes, 
1981]. However, results from the synclinorium show the 
potential problems of separation of distinct LT and HT 
magnetizations; we have thus opted to exclude results of all 
red bed sites from the final interpretation. 
Discussion 
Age of the Remanence 
Paleomagnetic data for the Brabant Massif, Namur Basin 
and the Dinant Synclinorium are summarized in Table 3. 
Tectonic corrections incorporate an additional correction for 
the plunge of the fold axis except at sites where structural data 
are insufficient to determine the fold geometry (e.g., sites to9, 
fr10, gi6, and to8). The available data do not constrain the 
time of remanence acquisition of the HT component relative 
to southwards tilt of strata on the Brabant Massif. In the 
following discussion we assume that magnetizations predate 
tilting as in the Namur Basin but in Table 3 we include 
averages of Brabant sites in tilt corrected and in situ co- 
ordinates. Despite the fact that this assumption cannot be 
tested, we have assumed that mean calculations average 
sufficient secular variation and that they represent accurate 
records of the geomagnetic field. 
The age of deformation in the Namur Basin best constrains 
the age of LT magnetizations. LT magnetizations postdate 
deformation; therefore their age is at most Westphalian D as 
was also concluded by Edel and Coulon [ 1987]. According to 
the 1989 geologic timescale of Harland et al. [1990] they are 
not older than about 305 Ma (late Moscovian). The inclination 
of the LT magnetization correlates relatively well among all 
three areas (--10ø; Table 3). It thus seems logical to assume 
that magnetizations were acquired at similar times. The LT 
magnetization (Table 3) is of uniform reverse polarity which 
is consistent with a magnetization acquired during the Kiaman 
reverse polarity interval. The LT inclination is, however, more 
shallow than expected for the Early Permian reference for the 
stable European continent (-18 ø [after Van der Voo, 1990]). 
This suggests that LT magnetizations were acquired between 
290 and 305 Ma. The mean LT magnetization in the Dinant 
Synclinorium compares relatively well with the A 
magnetization of Edel and Coulon [ 1987] (i.e., their Ardennes 
sites A12, A13, A14, and A20). 
HT magnetizations predate Westphalian deformation. 
Several arguments, however, suggest that magnetizations are 
of secondary origin. The HT magnetization is also of uniform 
reverse polarity, its direction remains practically unchanged in 
rocks varying in age from Middle Devonian up to and 
including Early Carboniferous, and the pole derived from it 
falls on a younger segment of the apparent polar wander path 
(APWP), a generally accepted criterion for suspicion of 
remagnetization [Van der Voo, 1990]. Only a fiw sites in the 
red beds display normal directions, but the conglomerate test 
suggests they are secondary. Moreover, petrographic 
examinations revealed persuasive evidence of a secondary 
origin for the iron oxides. Because magnetizations were 
acquired when strata were horizontal they most probably 
predate the earlier (late Namurian-early Westphalian) 
deformation phase in the synclinorium. According to Harland 
et al. [1990] the age can be bracketed between 313 and 320 
Ma, which includes the age of peak metamorphism (-316 Ma) 
inferred in the southern Ardennes [Piqud et al., 1984].

remagnetization events, bounding, so to say, the orogenic 
episode. The first (and HT) remagnetization probably took

area during the early Late Carboniferous. Paleozoic rocks 
were remagnetized again after a second pulse of tectonic 
activity, the main (Asturian) deformation phase in latest 
Westphalian or Stephanian times. Interestingly, in nearly all 
sites the relative intensities of the LT and HT magnetizations 
are virtually the same; thus both episodes of remagnetizations 
appear to have operated with similar efficiency. The re- 
magnetizations are interpreted as chemical remanent 
magnetizations. Variation in the intensity of magnetization 
between Carboniferous and Devonian carbonate rocks may be 
related to the original supply of elements necessary for the 
diagenetic creation of the secondary magnetic minerals. 
Rotation of the Dinant Synclinorium With Respect to the 
Brabant Massif 
Declination of the LT magnetization indicates a small, yet 
statistically significant, clockwise rotation of the Dinant 
Synclinorium with respect to both the Namur Basin and the 
Brabant Massif of about 15 ø (Figure 4 and Table 3). 
Directions in the Namur Basin and Brabant Massif are 
indistinguishable. A major tectonic discontinuity in the region 
(the Midi Fault) separates the Namur and Dinant regions, but 
there is no distinct tectonic discontinuity between the Brabant 
Massif and Namur Basin. We thus combined data from 
Brabant and Namur in the final calculations. 
The HT magnetization indicates virtually the same 
magnitude of clockwise rotation of the Dinant Synclinorium. 
The rotation between Brabant and the Synclinorium cannot be 
explained as an artifact of the tilt correction or incomplete 
separation of magnetic components. Incomplete separation of 
vector components during demagnetization and principal 
component calculations would produce directions with 
declinations between those of the LT and HT, thus reducing 
the estimate of the amount of rotation. Consitent results from 
LT and HT magnetizations throughout the area suggest, 
however, that contamination of magnetic components does 
not affect overall means significantly. 
The HT magnetization is significantly different from both 
the B magnetization (D=236 ø and I=+2 ø) identified by Edel 
and Coulon [1987] and the characteristic magnetizations of 
Thominski et al. [1993]. This is because those authors used in 
situ directions in their calculations. Also, Edel and Coulon 
[1987] derived their data from a diversity of lithologies 
including lower Paleozoic metamorphic rocks and Late 
Carboniferous dikes. Without a more detailed evaluation of 
the demagnetization results of those areas, it is not possible to 
asses the significance of rotations proposed by Nmvaczyk and 
Bleil [1985] and Thominski et al. [1993]. 
Implications and Conclusions 
European Reference Apparent Polar Wander Path 
Van der Voo [ 1990], Torsvik et al. [ 1990], and Piper et at 
[ ! 99 ! ] have summarized the Paleozoic paleomagnetic data for 
stable Europe. A revised APWP (Figure 10a) is based on 
Early Devonian through Late Carboniferous data (Table 4) 
judged to be of adequate reliability and taken from the global 
paleomagnetic database [McElhinny and Lock, 1990]. The 
main criteria for data selection are the use of demagnetization, 
a statistically sufficient number of samples or sites, and 
reasonable statistics (k and c95 ). We calculated mean poles 
for five time intervals, Early Devonian, Middle-Late De- 
vonian, Early Carboniferous, early Late Carboniferous, and 
late Late Carboniferous (Figure 10a and Table 4). Improved 
calibration of the Carboniferous path is based on the time of 
acquisition of secondary magnetizations in the Brabant and 
Ardennes Massifs. 
We follow interpretations by Torsvik et al. [ 1990], Piper et 
al. [1991], and Srnethurst and Khramov [1992], who have 
suggested that Devonian results falling at latitudes greater 
than about 20øS are the product of early Late Carboniferous 
(-320 Ma) remagnetizations. This age assignment is 
somewhat arbitrary; the interpretation is based on their 
location on the APWP between the mean Early Carboniferous 
pole and Late Carboniferous poles. The constraints on the 
time of acquisition of HT magnetizations in the Ardennes and 
Brabant Massifs, and their similarity to dated early Late 
Carboniferous poles in the British Isles (Table 4), support the 
age assigned by Torsvik et al. [1990] to Carboniferous 
remagnetization. 
Unlike Torsvik et al. [1990] but following Van der Voo 
[1990], we combine data from the British Isles north of the 
Hercynian Front with data from the Russian platform and 
Baltic shield. The poles from the British Isles and Scandinavia 
suspected to be derived from remagnetized Devonian and 
Lower Carboniferous strata give a mean that is statistically 
different from either the Early Carboniferous or late Late 
Carboniferous groups. 
Poles B-LT and B-HT for the Brabant Massif (Table 3) are 
indistinguishable from the late Late Carboniferous and the 
early Late Carboniferous european means, respectively. The 
later includes the group of Devonian poles suspected to be 
derived from remagnetized strata. The discrepancy between 
poles D-LT and D-HT from the Dinant Synclinorium and the 
European reference is interpreted as a small (-15 ø) clockwise 
tectonic rotation of the synclinorium. The rotation is 
significantly smaller than that inferred by Edel and Coulon 
[1987]. 
Early Carboniferous paleolatitudes for the Brabant Massif 
of-24øS (e.g. those calculated using results for the -335 Ma 
Derbyshire lavas [Piper et al., 1991]) and early Late 
Carboniferous paleolatitudes of about 5øS indicate fast 
northward drift of Europe of-0.9 ø to 1.4ø/m.y. in the interval 
-335 to-320 Ma preceding Hercynian deformation events. 
The range is based on the limits assigned to HT 
magnetizations. The paleomagnetic data from the Brabant 
Massif and the Dinant Synclinorium indicate that significant 
APW occurred during the Late Carboniferous. A similar 
conclusion had been previously reached by Piper et al. 
[1991]. Late Late Carboniferous paleolatitudes of-3øN indi- 
cate, however, that the rate of poleward motion was noticably 
reduced to about 0.3 ø to 0.8ø/m.y. 
Paleogeographic Implications 
Alleghenian and Hercynian deformation are generally 
attributed to northward drift of Gondwana or peri-Gondwanan 
elements and their collision with Europe and North America 
(Laurasia). The relative motion between Gondwana and 
Laurasia is, therefore, a key factor in understanding late 
Paleozoic tectonics of the Atlantic bordering continents. 
Paleomagnetic data summarized here indicate that the 
southern margin of stable Europe drifted from tropical

massifs (Iberia, Armorica, Massif Central, Vosges, Harz,

tectonic elements situated in the Iapetus or other Paleozoic

The early Late Carboniferous reconstruction (Figure 10c) 
suggests that the intervening ocean had not been reduced in 
size significantly by that time. Early Late Carboniferous 
magnetizations in Armorica, such as interpreted for the Laval 
syncline [Edel and Coulon, 1984], for the Alba red beds 
[Bonhommet et al., 1981], and for dolerite dikes in Brittany 
[Perroud et al., 1986], indicate paleolatitudes of 8ø-12øS 
which are consistent with a position south of the margin of 
stable Europe. 
For the late Late Carboniferous, revised paleolatitudes for 
stable Europe and the northern margin of Africa (Figure 10d) 
suggest that reconstructing the margin using the upper 
Westphalian-Stephenian average (pole LC2, Figure 10a) of 
Henry et al. [1992] produces unreconcilable overlap of the 
African and European margins. A possible solution for this 
problem has been offered by Bachtadse and Briden [1991], 
who interpreted pole positions derived from Silurian and 
Devonian rocks, such as the AYr intrusives and Snowy River 
volcanics, falling near the B component Sudan Devonian ring 
complex (GB pole, Figure 10a) as Late Carboniferous 
remagnetizations. An average location for this pole is roughly 
at 42øS -15øE (pole LC1; Figure 10a). The reconstruction 
suggests complete closure of the ocean separating the 
Gondwanan and European continents by middle-late 
Westphalian times.

JOURNAL OF GEOPHYSICAL RESEARCH, VOL. 101, NO. B7, PAGES 15,819-15,835, JULY 10, 1996 
A Barremian-Aptian (Early Cretaceous) North American 
palcomagnetic reference pole 
Suzanne A. McEnroe 
Department of Geosciences, University of Massachusetts, Amherst 
and Norges Geologiske Underskelse, Trondheim, Norway 
Abstract. Four intrusive complexes from southern Maine, containing rocks ranging in 
composition from olivine gabbro to granodiorite, were sampled to determine an Early Cretaceous 
reference pole for the North American plate. Sampling included the Lebanon diorite, the Tatnic 
Complex, Alfred Complex, and the Cape Neddick Complex dated radiometrically by the 40Ar/39Ar 
or K-Ar method on biotite between 125 and 120 Ma. The majority of samples have unblocking 
temperatures between 550øC and 580øC and Curie temperatures between 550øC and 570øC, 
indicating that the dominant remanence carrier is titanomagnetite, which crystallized from the 
magma or was produced by deuteric oxidation alteration during post-magmatic cooling. 
Titanomagnetite occurs as discrete C1-C3 grains, as exsolution or oxidation-exsolution lamellae in 
the silicates, as a product of magmatic reactions forming magnetite-ilmenite symplectites with 
pyroxene or olivine, or as ultrafine dust. Hemo-ilmenite is present as a minor component in the 
Lebanon Diorite, and, in this case, the remanence direction carried by the hemo-ilmenite is 
indistinguishable from the titanomagnetite. Detailed petrographic observations and rockmagnetic 
experiments demonstrate that, despite the coarse average grain size of the oxides in these rocks, 
which might lead one to expect unstable magnetic remanence, the magnetic remanence in most 
samples is extremely stable and caused by single-domain or pseudo-single-domain behavior in 
magnetite containing fine oxidation-exsolution lamellae of ilmenite. The Tatnic and Alfred 
intrusions are of normal polarity (D = 333 ø, I = 62 ø, pole 70.5øN, 210.3øE, A95 = 3.7 ø, N= 24 
sites); the Cape Neddick and Lebanon intrusions are of reversed polarity (D = 161 ø, I = -57 ø, pole 
73.7øN, 185.7øE, A95 = 5.0 ø, N= 17 sites). Together these intrusions yield a mean paleomagnetic 
pole at 72.2øN, 198.9øE, A95 = 3.3 ø, N = 41 sites. The well-characterized reversed polarity 
recorded in the precisely dated Cape Neddick Complex may represent the best age for the magnetic 
polarity chron M0r, the last reversal before the onset of the Cretaceous normal superchron at the 
Barremian-Aptian stage boundary. 
Introduction 
A paleomagnetic investigation of Early Cretaceous igneous 
intrusive complexes from southern Maine (Figure 1) was 
carried out to expand the very limited Early Cretaceous 
database for North America and with a view to (1) establishing 
an Early Cretaceous reference pole for North America, (2) 
defining the nature and stability of the remanence carrier(s), 
and (3) examining the behavior of the magnetic field during 
this period of apparent low secular variation prior to the onset 
of the Cretaceous normal polarity superchron. The 
investigated complexes intrude Paleozoic basement of Silurian 
to Lower Devonian age. They form part of the New England- 
Quebec intraplate magmatic province of McHone and Butler 
[1984]. Southeast of this province in the Atlantic lie the New 
England Seamounts [Duncan, 1984], comprising a total of 
approximately 2000 km of Mesozoic igneous activity [Foland 
and Allen, 1992]. Both Duncan [1984] and Foland and Allen 
[1992] suggest that the magmatism was related to a stationary 
mantle plume that was overridden by the North American plate 
during Cretaceous time.

Apatite fission track studies indicate that this area has not 
been exposed to temperatures above 110øC since Cretaceous 
time [Zimmerman et al., 1975; Miller and Duddy, 1989]. 
Furthermore, results of recent paleomagnetic work on the 
Triassic Abbott and Agamenticus intrusions [Wu and Van der 
Voo, 1988] and the Early Jurassic dikes on Seward and Doyle 
Points [McEnroe and Brown, 1992] are generally consistent 
with other Late Triassic and Early Jurassic poles and argue 
against any significant Cretaceous or younger regional 
overprinting or tilting. Thus the paleomagnetic directions 
obtained from this study are likely to represent primary 
directions. The sampled intrusions were mapped in detail by 
Hussey [1962]. Three of the intrusions are composed of 
multiple pulses. These were sampled to examine possible 
tilting within the intrusive complexes and to ensure a time- 
averaged direction for the calculated poles. Radiometric ages 
from biotite and hornblende have recently been reported by 
Hubacher and Foland [1991]. The overall geochronology of 
the New England region has been reviewed by Zartman [1988]. 
Geology and Site Localities 
Alfred Complex 
The Alfred Complex (Figure 2) is described by Hussey 
[1962]. It intrudes the Lower Devonian (?) Rindgemere

Figure 1. Map of southwestern Maine and adjacent New Hampshire and Massachusetts showing Mesozoic 
intrusions is shown (modified from McHone and Butler [1984]). Cretaceous intrusions in Maine including 
the Alfred, Tatnic, Cape Neddick, and Lebanon of this study are indicated in solid black. 
Formation close to the northwestern contact of the Lyman 
pluton in the town of Alfred. The complex consists of four 
rock types in two major intrusions, an older cone-shaped 
intrusion 2.8 km in diameter of layered noritic gabbro with 
minor layers of anorthositic gabbro to the northeast; cut to the 
southwest by a circular complex 2.8 km in diameter consisting 
of outer monzodiorite and inner porphyritic granodiorite. 
Hubacher and Foland [ 1991] have obtained a 4øAr/39Ar age on 
biotite from the monzodiorite of the younger southwestern 
complex of 120.4-1-1.0 Ma, and Foland and Faul [1977] 
obtained a K-Ar age on biotite of 120-3:2 on the gabbro. 
Fourteen sites were collected (Figure 2), nine from the older 
northeastern layered gabbro and five from the younger 
southwestern intrusion. Sites in the older intrusion include 
four in gabbros and two small mafic dikes on a traverse along a 
stream pavement on the middle branch of Mousam River in the 
southern part of the intrusion (1-6), two gabbros from the bed 
of the Mousam River in the northern part of the intrusion (10- 
11), and one gabbro from a hilltop at the extreme northern 
limit of the intrusion (9). The five sites from the younger 
intrusion include a monzodiorite and a monzodiorite with 
included gabbro from a highway exposure in the southeastern 
part (7,8), a monzodiorite from a railroad cut in the southeast 
(13), a granodiorite from a railroad cut in the south (14), and a 
granodiorite from a pavement outcrop to the north (12). 
Tatnic Complex 
The Tatnic Complex (Figure 3) is described by Hussey 
[1962]. It is intruded into the Silurian (?) Kittery Formation 
and Devonian quartz monzonite and granodiorite of the 
Webhannet pluton [Fargo and Bothner, 1995]. The complex 
consists of six rock types emplaced in four igneous phases. 
The oldest phase consists of volcanics that are preserved as 
xenoliths through much of the intrusion. The next phase is a 
cone-shaped complex, 3 km in diameter, of fine-grained 
gabbro grading upward into anorthositic gabbro. Volcanics 
and gabbros alike were then intruded to the southwest by an 
irregular area of olivine gabbro and poikilitic gabbro about 
2.6 km in diameter, and this area was then further intruded by 
quartz diorite. Foland and Faul [1977] obtained a K-Ar age on 
biotite from the gabbro of 122-1-2 Ma and Hubacher and Foland 
[1991] obtained a 4øAr/39Ar age on biotite from the quartz 
diorite of 122+2 Ma.

Figure 2. Geologic map of the Alfred Complex is shown 
(modified from Hussey [1962]) with locations of 
paleomagnetic sites. Geologic contacts, solid lines, accurately 
located; dashed lines, approximately located. Key to rock 
units: Devonian metamorphic and intrusive rocks; Dr, 
Rindgemere Formation; Drl, calc-silicate member of 
Rindgmere Formation; Dp, Devonian pegmatite. Members of 
the Cretaceous Alfred Intrusive Complex: Kng, noritic gabbro; 
Kag, anorthositic gabbro; Kmd, monzodiorite; Kgd, 
porphyritic granodiorite. 
At the outer contact, the Kittery Formation is very strongly 
hornfelsed with development of cordierite-orthopyroxene 
assemblages in pelitic layers and wollastonite-diopside 
assemblages in calcareous layers. An 4øAr/39Ar age of 
120.6_+0.4 Ma on biotite from the gabbro is reported by 
Hubacher and Foland [ 1991]. 
The paleomagnetic localities are shown in Figure 4. All 
sites were collected as oriented blocks taken in inconspicuous 
locations so as not to mar the superb shore exposures. The 
sites include four of normal gabbro: three from near the 
northern contact (1,3,4) and one from the point opposite the 
Nubble (5); two of anorthositic gabbro from the northernmost 
shore exposures (6,7); two of cortlanditic gabbro, one from 
the eastern contact (8) and one from the western interior (11); 
two of dikes within the complex, one in normal gabbro near 
the northern contact (2) and one in anorthositic gabbro (9); 
two of dikes in country rock to the north of the complex (10, 
14); and two of variably hornfelsed Kittery Formation (12, 
13). Samples of the metamorphosed contact aureole and 
country rock were collected for a baked contact test. 
Lebanon Diorite 
The Lebanon Diorite is poorly exposed in an oval area (1.6 x 
1.2 km) centered around Philbrick Road in the eastern part of 
Lebanon and the western part of Sanford, Maine [Hussey, 1962]. 
It intrudes the Rindgemere Formation of probable Devonian age 
and has essentially no topographic expression. A K-Ar age of 
125 + 3 on biotite Ma was reported for the intrusion by Foland 
and Faul [1977]. The diorite was redated by Hubacher and 
Foland [1991] and yielded a 4øAr/39Ar age of 132 Ma on biotite 
Of a total of 10 paleomagnetic sites (Figure 3), six were 
obtained in a quarry in the northern part of the gabbro, 
including four sites in gabbro and two from fine-grained mafic 
dikes intruding the gabbro (1-6). Of the four remaining sites, 
one is a coarse mafic porphyry assigned to the volcanics by 
Hussey [1962] (7), one is of the olivine gabbro (8), and two 
are from the youngest quartz diorite near the south edge of the 
intrusion (9, 10). Hurley and Shearer [1981] collected and 
demagnetized 18 paleomagnetic samples from the gabbroic 
part of the Tatnic Complex as part of their regional study on 
mid-Paleozoic rock units in New England. 
Cape Neddick Complex 
The Cape Neddick Complex (Figure 4) at York, Maine, is an 
oval intrusion of layered gabbro 1.26 x 0.83 km [Hussey, 
1962]. It intrudes the low-grade, but vertically dipping 
Silurian-Ordovician Kittery Formation. Continuous coastal 
outcrops from the southeastern to the northern side of the 
intrusion provide the best exposures of any Mesozoic 
intrusion in New England. The complex involves five major 
rock types associated with two intrusive phases, plus a variety 
of mafic and felsic dikes. The earlier intrusive phase involves 
an intrusive agglomerate along some contacts, followed by 
normal gabbro that is chilled against it, and that grades inward 
to anorthositic gabbro. The later intrusive phase, confined to 
the interior of the complex, consists of olivine gabbro. This 
phase also grades inward toward higher plagioclase content.

Three sites in fresh diorite were collected in a very low 
exposure on the southeast side of Philbrick Road. Two 
additional diorite sites were obtained from large rounded 
natural exposures about 50m southeast of Philbrick Road near 
the Lebanon-Sanford town line. Samples of the contact- 
metamorphosed Rindgemere Formation were collected for a 
baked contact test. Thin sections and polished cores from the 
five diorite samples show that it is composed of plagioclase 
and dusty K-feldspar, augire, red-brown biotite, titano- 
magnetite, hemo-ilmenite, ilmenite, leucoxene, and minor 
chlorite, green biotite, hematite, pyrite, and apatite. 
Paleomagnetism 
A common conception in paleomagnetism is that stable 
remanence is held in grains of single-domain and pseudo- 
single-domain size (<8 gm), and that grains of multidomain 
(MD) size, such as would be expected in coarse-grained 
intrusive igneous rocks would not retain a stable remanence 
over a geological timescale. Nevertheless, several workers 
[Graham, 1953; Larson et al., 1969; Strangeway et al., 1968; 
Hargraves and Ade-Hall, 1975] have suggested features of 
multidomain-sized grains that may cause them to behave like 
single-domain or pseudo-single-domain material in terms of 
magnetic stability. Because the present study involves mainly 
coarse-grained rocks, it has required both routine alternating- 
field and thermal demagnetization procedures, and special 
investigations using reflected-light microscopy and rock 
magnetic experiments to verify the nature and stability of the 
magnetic remanence results. 
Field and Laboratory Procedure 
Samples were collected in the field using a portable 
gasoline-powered drill and oriented with a Brunton compass, 
and whenever possible, a sun compass. Oriented blocks were 
collected from sites where it was difficult to drill or where long 
traverses were necessary. 
The natural remanent magnetization (NRM) of the 237 
samples were measured with a Molspin spinner magnetometer 
at the Paleomagnetics Laboratory at the University of 
Massachusetts, Amherst, or the Paleomagnetics Laboratory at 
the Norwegian Geological Survey (NGU) in Trondheim, 
Norway. At least two specimens from each site were selected 
for detailed alternating field (AF) and/or thermal 
demagnetization treatment. For AF treatment, specimens were 
progressively stepwise demagnetized at increments of 5 or 10 
mT up to a peak induction of 100 mT using a three-axis 
tumbling (NGU) or a single-axis nontumbling Schoenstedt 
GSD-1 AF Geophysical specimen demagnetizer (UMASS). The 
alternating field demagnetization method was effective in 
isolating the characteristic remanence from secondary 
components in all samples. Remaining samples were AF- 
demagnetized in a minumum of three intervals. The fields 
selected were based on the detailed AF experiments. 
For thermal demagnetization, specimens were heated in air 
in steps between 50 ø and 100øC to temperatures of 585øC or 
630øC using a noninductively wound furnace with an accuracy 
of + 5øC and cooled in a field-free chamber at NGU and 
measured on magnetometer in an area with an ambient field of 
< 5 nT. Remanent magnetization was determined after each 
step. 
Hysteresis properties and Curie temperatures were measured 
on a vibrating sample magnetometer (Princeton Applied 
Research) at the Institute for Rock Magnetism, University of 
Minnesota. Hysteresis curves were measured at room 
temperature in a maximum field of 0.8T. 
Data were plotted on standard orthogonal vector end point 
diagrams [Zijderveld, 1967]. The primary remanent 
magnetization direction was determined by Spectrum 
[Srnethurst, 1987], or when necessary by Linefind [Kent et al., 
1983], or by standard paleomagnetic techniques. Site mean 
directions and the 95% confidence limits were calculated by 
standard Fisher statistics [Fisher, 1953]. Thirty-nine of the 41 
sites yielded site mean directions with 95% confidence (a95) of 
less than 10 ø. All sites were used in calculating the Early 
Cretaceous paleomagnetic pole.

Magnetic Mineralogy, Stability, and Relaxation 
Introduction. The palcopoles obtained in this study are 
significantly steeper than those obtained in many previous 
palcomagnetic studies of Cretaceous rocks in North America. 
To guard against a misinterpretation due to a contamination 
from the present-day field that would steepen the inclination, 
it is necessary to examine mechanisms that could produce a 
present-day overprint that was not removed by the extensive 
demagnetization procedures. Two hundred and sixty-seven 
samples were subjected to careful stepwise alternating field or 
thermal demagnetization. In general, a soft secondary 
magnetization, that was easily removed at low fields or 
temperatures, was followed by a linear decay representing the 
stable component. No evidence for additional overprints were 
observed. A question that needs to be addressed is whether 
these rocks could have been overprinted by relaxation of 
magnetic domains, by a thermal process, or by a chemical 
process, in a manner which is difficult to detect. Rock 
magnetic measurements made are on bulk samples (rock chips, 
powders, or cores) and are not representative of any individual 
feature. By combining optical observations, demagnetization 
spectra of natural remanent magnetization (NRM), Curie 
temperatures, and demagnetization spectra of isothermal 
remanent magnetization (IRM) and anhysteritic remanent 
magnetization (ARM), an attempt was made to understand what 
mineral phase or phases is associated with each component of 
the remanence. 
Petrographic observations related to 
demagnetization behavior. Sixty-four polished cores 
or thin sections representative of the palcomagnetic 
collection were examined to identify the magnetic carriers and 
to examine for alteration that could result in a change of the 
remanent magnetization. Observations of the opaque 
minerals, made in oil immersion in reflected light, included 
size, morphology, texture, degree of oidation, and exsolution 
features. Optical observations were combined with measured 
rock magnetic properties and demagnetization behavior to 
assess the reliability of the signal and the timing of 
acquisition of magnetization. 
When titanomagnetite grains are subjected to oxidation- 
exsolution of ilmenite, the remaining magnetite is more Ti- 
poor , and hence, has a higher Curie temperature than the 
original titano-magnetite. The oxidation-exsolution process 
may also produce a smaller effective magnetic grain size 
because the ilmenite lamellae parallel to the { 111 } planes of 
magnetite isolate the areas of Ti-poor titanomagnetite. The 
new compositions and the textures produced by oxidation- 
exsolution may have different and important rock magnetic 
properties as compared to the original titano-magnetite. The 
oxidation states of the observed titanomagnetites fall into 
classes C1 (unexsolved) to C3 (moderately exsolved) of 
Haggerty [1976]. Ilmenite intergrowths in the 
titanomagnetites are classified into three types: sandwich, 
trellis, and composite [Buddington and Lindsley, 1964]. The 
morphologies of the titanomagnetites range from skeletal to 
cruciform and herringbone, and to euhedral. 
Fine-grained titanomagnetites are found in the numerous 
dikes which cut the intrusions. Commonly, these dikes 
contain equant and skeletal homogeneous C1 titanomagnetite 
grains, and C2 grains with trellis ilmenite lamellae and minor 
sandwich-type lamellae. The C 1 grains are found in the chilled 
margins of the dikes. They progress from skeletal or herring 
bone to euhedral morphology. The palcomagnetic directions 
obtained from these dikes are very stable with a linear decay to 
the origin after the removal of a small overprint as is shown in 
the vector end point diagram (Figure 5) of a dike from the 
Tatnic gabbro (site 4). It is not surprising to have a high
