In the gabbros of the Cape Neddick Complex (Figure 8a) 
magnetite grains with oxidation-exsolution of ilmenite along 
{ 111 } plane of magnetite are observed. The ilmenite lamellae 
are either sandwich or trellis type. Many samples show 
abundant, very fine trellis ilmenite lamellae that are less than 
0.5  in diameter. Some titanomagnetites show exsolution of 
ulvtspinel and pleonaste (Mg-Fe-A1 spinel) in addition to the 
oxidation-exsolution of ilmenite (Figure 8a,8b). After 
oxidation-exsolution of ilmenite from the titanomagnetite 
grains, very fine granular pleonaste exsolved from the 
magnetite along the interface with the ilmenite lamellae. The 
small trellis lamellae subdivide the larger titanomagnetite 
grain (>>100 p) into very small discrete areas of magnetite. 
These small areas of magnetite may be highly anisotropic due 
to the number of sets of lamellae that are oxy-exsolved. At 
high magnifications (1200x) in oil, a very fine clothlike 
texture is observed (Figure 8b). These areas lack abundant 
ilmenite lamellae. This t..'.xture is due to exsolution of 
ulvOspinel from magnetite parallel to the { 100} plane of the 
magnetite. The ulvOspinel was later oxidized to ilmenite,

In the Lebanon Diorite, a small high-temperature

Ilmenite-hematite forms a solid solution above the consolute

Curie and unblocking temperatures in relation 
to mineralogy. Curie temperatures were measured on 
samples from the four intrusions. These were analyzed either 
as rock chips or powders. The samples showed a discrete range 
of Curie temperatures from $40øC to $70øC, indicating a Ti- 
poor titanomagnetite or pure magnetite as the principal 
magnetic mineral. Most samples produced good reversible 
heating and cooling curves indicating little oxidation or 
alteration of the Ti-poor titanomagnetite during the 
thermomagnetic runs. In the thermal stability diagrams 
(Figure 7b), plotted as vector differences, variations in thermal 
blocking temperatures are shown. Some samples, such as 
Tatnic 4-1 and Alfred 2a-3, show one discrete unblocking 
temperature, at $$0øC and $85øC, respectively, while others 
indicate a slight stepped unblocking spectrum. Samples from 
the Lebanon intrusion (LEB 2-4) show stepped unblocking 
temperatures from 500øC to 620øC. Discrete titanomagnetite 
grains (C2) with trellis-type lamellae of ilmenite were 
observed in the Lebanon Diorite which would account for the 
unblocking temperatures up to 580øC and ilrnenite grains with 
{0001 } lamellae of hematite would account for the highest 
temperature portion of the spectrum. 
Grain size and magnetic relaxation. Multidomain 
size grains were observed in all samples and, in fact, are the 
volumetrically dominant size magnetic particles. An 
interesting feature is that most of the stability diagrams from 
the mafic parts of the intrusions display a significant 
component of PSD- and/or SD- type behavior with a MDF 
greater than 30mT (Figure 7). As concluded from Curie and 
thermal un-blocking temperatres, and optical observations, 
this coercive component is carried by titanomagnetite. The 
majority of samples have MDFs above 20mT which is 
considered the maximum coercivity for MD magnetite [Bailey 
and Dunlop, 1983, Dunlop, 1983]. The questions that remain 
are how were the effective magnetic grains formed, exsolved, 
or modified, and when was the remanence blocked? 
Titanomagnetites with [ 111 } oxy-exsolution lamellae of 
ilmenite are the typical magnetic grains in the Tatnic, Alfred, 
and Cape Neddick intrusions. Grain sizes of titanomagnetite 
range from 0.5 nun down to the optical resolution of the 
microscope (about 0.4 Bin). The majority of grains are 
significantly above the grain size limit for PSD grains 
[Moskowitz and Banerjee, 1979]. Optically, on the basis of 
size, the majority of these grains would be classified as 
multidomain and therefore unstable carriers of remanent 
magnetization over the geological timescale of interest. This 
interpretation contradicts the bulk measurements showing that 
the field needed to remove the NRM ranges from 30mT to 
greater than 90mT. The question then arises as to whether 
some of the MD-sized grains (> 81) are behaving as PSD grains 
and are in fact the remanent magnetic carriers. 
It may be that the very fine exsolution features (Figure 8) are 
creating areas of stable pseudo-single-domain grains within 
the multidomain-sized grains. Examples of such a fine-scale 
exsolution are found in the normal gabbro at Cape Neddick 
Complex, and in the Alfred and Tatnic intrusions, where 
exsolution of ulvOspinel and pleonaste (Mg-Fe-A1 spinel) in 
titanomagnetites and oxidation-exsolution of ilmenite (Figure 
8b) are abundant and on a fine scale. The very fine granular 
pleonaste exsolved from the magnetite along the interface 
with the ilmenite lamellae, are possibly producing regions 
that are highly stable magnetically. In the Alfred, Tatnic, and 
Cape Neddick intrusions graphic intergrowths of magnetite 
and titanium-rich biotite and symplectites of very fine to fine- 
grained magnetite and ilmenite with pyroxene have oxidation 
textures in the PSD size range. In addition, some olivines in 
the Cape Neddick sample are oxidized, and contain a very fine 
grained magnetite that would be in the region of PSD and a 
stable carrier of the thermal remanent magnetization (TRM).

Paleomagnetic data for the Alfred, Cape Neddick, Lebanon, 
and Tatnic intrusions are listed in Tables la and lb. The data 
are divided into two sets based on magnetic polarity. The 
normal polarity set consists of 24 sites (149 samples) from 
the Tatnic and Alfred Complexes. The reversed polarity set 
consists of 18 sites from the Cape Neddick Complex and the 
Lebanon Diorite (88 samples). The site mean directions for 
the Alfred intrusions (N = 14 sites) and the Tatnic intrusions (N 
= 10 sites) are shown in Figure !1. In the Alfred and Tatnic 
intrusions there is excellent clustering of the data with no 
evidence of tilting after intrusion, either within or between the 
intrusions. The site mean directions for the Cape Neddick 
intrusions (N = 12 sites) and the Lebanon Diorite (N = 6 sites) 
are shown in Figure 11. These intrusions show good 
clustering of the data and little evidence of tilting within or 
between the intrusions after cooling. 
The Cape Neddick Complex and the Lebanon Diorite pass a 
contact test. In addition to these positive contact tests, recent 
paleomagnetic work on the nearby Triassic Abbott (225 Ma) 
and Agamenticus (228+ 5) plutons by Wu and Van der Voo 
[1988] and Early Jurassic dikes on Seward and Doyle Points 
[McEnroe and Brown, 1992] show little evidence of regional 
overprint, and the results are generally consistent with other 
Late Triassic and Early Jurassic poles. These Triassic and

Jurassic palcomagnetic poles argue against any significant 
post-Cretaceous tilting. 
All sites from the four intrusions are plotted in Figure 11. 
These intrusions show excellent agreement within each 
polarity. After inversion of the mean directions of the 
reversed intrusions through the origin, the confidence limits 
surrounding the mean direction (ot95) of the two polarity 
groups intersect (Figure 12); the mean normal and reversed 
sites are not significantly different at the 95% level [McFadden 
and Lowes, 1981]. The angular dispersion about the site mean 
VGPs (N = 41) is low with an $ = 8.8 ø with upper and lower 
limits at the 95% confidence level of S u = 9.4 ø and $I = 8-3ø 
using the method of Cox [1969]. These values are lower than 
the predicted value (-15) for a calculated palcolatitude of -40 ø 
for the southern Maine intrusions. It appears that palcosecular 
variation has been averaged in the intrusions, and it is 
interesting to note that all other coeval poles, the 
Monteregian Hills [Foster and Syrnons, 1979]; White 
Mountains [Van Fossen and Kent, 1992]; and the Notre Dame 
Bay Newfoundland dikes [LaPointe, 1979], also display lower 
than expected angular dispersion. 
Palcopoles and Comparisons with Other 
Cretaceous Data 
The need for high-precision palcomagnetic reference poles 
has increased as methods and modeling techniques have 
developed. Differences of only a few degrees can be crucial to 
plate motion studies. The cusps present in recent Mesozoic 
apparent pole wander (APW) paths [May and Butler, 1986] are 
the result of new modeling techniques and increased precision 
in palcomagnetic poles. Older techniques [Irving and Irving, 
1982] using the sliding window method averaged out these 
sharp changes in plate motion. Synthetic models [Gordon et 
al., 1984] constrain the path to small circles. High-precision 
data are needed to determine if plates are constrained to small 
circle rotations and, if so, the length of the segment of each 
small circle track. 
The calculated palcopoles are Lebanon Diorite (125 Ma + 3) 
73.2øN, 195.1øE, ot95 =7.5; Tatnic intrusion (122 Ma + 2) at 
65.7øN, 208.4øE, 95 =4.6; Alfred intrusion (120.4 Ma _+ 1.0) 
at 74.0øN, 209.8øE, ot95=3.6; and 74.9øN 175.2øE, ot95 =4.6 
for the Cape Neddick Complex (120.6 Ma + 0.4). A high- 
precision palcopole was calculated from the dual polarity 
intrusions (Table lb.). This 125-120 Ma group palcopole is 
calculated to be 72.3øN, 198.9øE, A95 = 3.3 ø . The pole 
positions of the southern Maine intrusions are shown on 
Figure 13. 
Three earlier studies exist for this time period. The 124+1 
Ma Monteregian Hills, Quebec [Foland et al., 1986), give a 
pole at 73øN, 191øE, ot95 = 2.0 ø [Foster and Syrnons, 1979]. 
The 129 Ma Notre Dame Bay Newfoundland dikes give a pole at 
71øN, 207øE, ot95 = 4.0 ø [LaPointe, 1979]. The White 
Mountains, with an age span of 122.5-112+ 5 Ma, give a mean 
pole of 71.9øN, 187.4øE, A95 = 6.9 ø [Van Fossen and Kent, 
1992]. The coherence of the precisely dated southern Maine 
intrusions and the Monteregian Hills is striking and yields a 
combined pole at 72.6øN, 196.7øE, A95 = 4.4. When the less 
well age-constrained Notre Dame Bay Newfoundland dikes and 
the White Mountains poles are added, this produces a combined 
pole at 71.7øN, 198.4øE, A95 = 4.1 (Figure 13). In addition, 
the coherence in pole positions of the southern Maine 
intrusions, the Monteregian Hills, the Notre Dame Bay 
Newfoundland dikes, and the White Mountains poles argue 
against any significant post-Cretaceous tilting in southern 
Maine. Though these palcopoles are displaced northward from 
May and Butler's [1986] Jurassic-Cretaceous track, their 
positions are lower in latitude than the Late Cretaceous 
palcopoles from Granite Mountain, Arkansas [Globerman and 
Irving, 1988], Elkhorn Mountains, Montana [Diehl, 1991], 
the Adel Mountains, Montana [Gunderson and Sheriff, 1991], 
and Gringo Gulch Volcanics, Arizona [Barnes and Butler, 
1980]. As has been suggested by many authors, there appears 
to have been a decrease in North American plate motion during 
the Early Cretaceous and a virtual standstill until the Middle to 
Late Cretaceous when plate motion increased. This new 
palcopole derived from the southern Maine intrusions would 
support a gradual increase in northwestward plate motion from 
Early to Late Cretaceous. 
The Cretaceous average determined by Mankinen [1978], 
which was used by May and Butler [1986], and the synthetic 
pole calculated by Gordon et al. [1984], which used older data 
with poorer Q factors [Van der Voo, 1993] than recently 
determined poles, should not be used without elimination of 
the poorly determined poles from the averages and the addition 
of recently determined high-precision poles. The importance 
of a reliable Cretaceous reference pole for North America is 
crucial to those reconstructing the paths and rotations of 
displaced terranes of the Western Cordillera of North America. 
The study of microplate tectonics in the Cordillera has been 
seriously hampered by the limited North American 
palcomagnetic database for the Middle Jurassic and Cretaceous. 
The data set presented here should aid in such studies. 
The well-characterized reversed polarity recorded in the 
precisely dated Cape Neddick Complex may represent the best 
date for the magnetic polarity chron M0r. This is the last 
reversal before the onset of the Cretaceous normal superchron. 
In addition, the M0r has been suggested as the Barremian- 
Aptian stage boundary [Gradstein et al., 1994]. 
Summary 
The Early Cretaceous palcopole reported in this account is 
from well-dated (125-120 Ma) intrusions in southern Maine. 
The Alfred and Tatnic Complexes are of normal polarity, 
whereas the Lebanon and Cape Neddick intrusions are of 
reversed polarity. A reversal test is positive at the 95% 
confidence level. High coercivity and high unblocking 
temperature magnetizations are well isolated from 40 of the 41 
sites. The primary nature of the remanence carrier has been 
verified by detailed palcomagnetic and rock magnetic 
experiments, and by optical observations. It is supported by 
the fact that both normal and reversed directions are obtained. 
The dominant remanence carrier is titanomagnetite which 
crystallized from the magma or was produced by deuteric 
oxidation during post-magmatic cooling. The calculated 125- 
120 Ma palcopole at 72.3øN, 198.9øE (A95 = 3.3 ø) plots at 
higher latitude than the predicted pole for North America [May 
and Butler, 1986; Gordon et al., 1984] but is in excellent 
agreement with the coeval and dual polarity Monteregian Hills 
pole of Foster and Syrnons [1979]. The Cape Neddick 
intrusion at 120.6 Ma + 0.4 may represent the best date for the 
reversed magnetic polarity chron M0r.

Several diabase dyke swarms of Paleoproterozoic age form 
a fan-shaped distribution about Lake Superior (Fig. 1). 
Senneterre and Biscotasing dykes are located east of the lake, 
Marathon dykes to the north, and Fort Frances (or 
Kenora- 
Kabetogama) dykes to the west. 
It 
has been suggested that 
one or more of these 
swarms 
is associated with 
Paleopro- 
terozoic rifting and the development of the Animikie Basin, 
which forms part of the Southern Province (Fig. 1) along the 
southern margin of the Superior Province 
(e.g., 
Southwick 
and Day 1983; Fahrig 1987). 
Prior to the present study, the dykes east and west of Lake 
Superior were rather well characterized in 
terns 
of distri- 
bution, age, paleomagnetism, and geochemistry, whereas the 
Marathon dykes were little known. The Biscotasing swarm 
had a well-defined U -Pb age of 2167 f 2 Ma (Buchan 
et al. 1993). The Senneterre swarm was dated at 2214 f 
12 Ma (Buchan et al. 1993), although further analysis has 
yielded a more precise age of 22 
16:: 
Ma 
(J.K. 
Mortensen, 
unpublished data). Both the Biscotasing and Senneterre 
swarms were known to carry primary paleomagnetic 
rema- 
nences (Buchan et al. 
1993), 
and had been studied 
geochemi- 
cally 
(Condie 
et 
ale 
1987). The Fort Frances swarm was 
dated by the 
Wb - Sr technique at 2127 f 67 Ma (Beck and 
Murthy 1982). More precise U -Pb dates of 2076:: and 
2077:; 
Ma are reported in this study and in recent work by 
Wirth et 
a1 . (1 995), respectively. A well-defined primary 
paleomagnetic 
pole (Halls 
1986), 
detailed geochemistry 
(Southwick and Halls 1987; Schmitz et al. 
1995), 
Nd iso- 
topic studies (Wirth and Vervoort 
1995), 
and tectonic setting 
(Southwick and Bay 1983) had also been described 
for 
the 
Fort Frances swarm. 
The age of the Marathon dykes (Fig. 2) was constrained 
only by K-Ar whole-rock dates ranging from 1950 to 
1550 Ma and a K - Ar biotite date of 1705 Ma (Fahrig et al. 
1986). Based on these data, Fahrig et al. (1986) suggested an 
age of intrusion > 2000 Ma. In this paper, we report a U -Pb 
baddeleyite age of 
2121 f +4 Ma for a Marathon dyke. 
Fahrig et al. (1965) reported paleomagnetic results from 
12 samples collected at seven Marathon dyke sites. Each 
sample was demagnetized to peak alternating fields 
(AF's) 
of 
only 13 
mT. 
More detailed measurements were later carried 
out at a single site near Geco mine at Manitouwadge (Fig. 2) 
(Fahrig et al. 1986). Evidence for the primary nature of the 
Marathon reinanence was not obtained in these early studies. 
The impetus for sampling Marathon dykes in the present 
study was twofold: (1') to characterize them in terms of dis- 
tribution, paleomagnetism, U - Pb geochronology , and geo- 
chemistry, and (ii) to clarify their relationship to other 
neighbouring swarms and to rifting along the southern 
margin of the Superior Province. As a U-Pb age was not 
then available for the Fort Frances swarm, material was also 
collected from a Fort Frances dyke for dating and paleomag- 
netism. 
Following the recommendations of Buchan and Halls 
(1990), U - Pb geochronology was conducted at paleomag- 
netic sites, and a rigorous baked contact test was carried out 
to test for the primary nature of the remanence. 
Geological setting 
Paleoproterozoic Marathon diabase dykes trend approximately 
north over an area of at least 30000 km2 north of Lake 
Superior and east of Lake Nipigon (Fig. 2), where they 
intrude 
Archean 
rocks of the Superior Province. The 
extcnt 
of the swarm to the north and east of the area 
shown 
in 
Fig. 2 is unknown, because little work has been done to 
distinguish dykes of different swarms. To the southeast, 
Marathon dykes have not yet been identified beyond the sam- 
pling area, with the possible exception of two dykes located 
east of Lake Superior (sites 28 and 31 of Halls and Shaw 
1988), 
which have paleomagnetic directions similar to those 
of Marathon dykes. To the west of the sampling area, Mara- 
thon dykes are overlain by Mesoyroterozoic rocks of the 
Southern Province in the vicinity of Lake Nipigon. 
Marathon dykes are well exposed in 
roadcuts 
and along 
lakeshores. Elsewhere, they are best traced from 
aeromag- 
netic data. They have subvertical dips, are usually less than 
about 50 m wide, and exhibit chilled margins with sharp 
contacts. 
Dykes of several other swarms are thought to occur 
within 
the sampling area. Keweenawan diabase dykes of approxi- 
mately 1100 Ma age trend east-west in the vicinity 
of 
Lake 
Superior. The 2 167 Ma northeast-trending 
diabase dyke swarm has been studied in detail to the south- 
east and is thought to extend into the sampling area (H.C. 
Halls and K.L. Buchan, unpublished data). Finally, 2473 - 
2446 Ma (Heaman 1995) Matachewan diabase dykes trend 
northwest across the region. 
Sampling and laboratory procedure 
Five to twelve paleomagnetic block samples were oriented 
with sun and magnetic compasses at each of 32 sites (Fig. 2). 
Each sample was drilled in the laboratory to produce speci- 
mens with a diameter of 2.5 cm and a length of 2.2 cm. 
Specimens were measured using either a Schonstedt or modi- 
fied 
BIGICB 
spinner magnetometer, and were subjected to 
stepwise 
AF demagnetization, thermal step heating, or a 
combination of AF demagnetization followed by thermal 
cleaning. 
A baked contact test was carried out at site 29, where a 
north-trending Marathon dyke cuts a northwest-trending 
dyke of the Matachewan swarm. Samples 
were 
collected 
within the Marathon dyke, adjacent to the Marathon dyke in 
the host Matachewan dyke, and farther away in the 
Matache- 
wan dyke. 
A sample for U - Pb geochronology was collected from 
the coarse interior of a - 50 m wide Marathon dyke at paleo- 
magnetic site 22, 
after 
a single baddeleyite fraction was sepa- 
rated from a small hand sample at this site from the earlier 
collection of Fahrig et al. (1965). Likewise, a sample for 
dating was obtained from a >30 m wide Fort Frances 
dyke located on the shore of Kakagi Lake at 
49'14.5'N, 
93O58.5

from the Fahrig et 
al. 
collection that indicated the presence

1986), 
samples were collected for paleomagnetism. They 
yielded results 
similar 
to those of site 24 of 
Halls 
(1986). 
Zircon and baddeleyite were separated from -25 kg

grain size and morphology. Analyses were carried out in the

Discussion 
The 2121 Ma Marathon and 2076 Ma Fort Frances paleo- 
poles (Fig. 11) continue a northwesterly trend in apparent 
polar wander 
for 
the southern Superior Province, 
previously 
established by data for the 2216 Ma Senneterre and 
21617 Ma 
Biscotasing dykes, which were sampled a few hundred 
kilometres to the southeast (Buchan et al. 1993). 
Earlier widely used polar wander paths for North America 
(e.g . , Irving 1979; Hyodo and Dunlop 1989) or the Superior 
Province 
(e.g.. 
Irving et al. 1984; 
Dunsrnore 
and Symons 
1990) young from north to south. These earlier paths were

GEOPHYSICAL RESEARCH LETTERS, VOL. 23, NO. 23, PAGES 3405-3408, NOVEMBER 15, 1996 
Paleomagnetic results from the Upper Silurian of the Shan-Thai-Malay 
block, southwest Yunnan, China 
Haihong Chen, 1 Dalai Zhong, 1 Friedrich Heller, 2 and Jon P. Dobson 3 
Abstract. 77 paleomagnetic samples from the Upper Silurian 
reddish limestone and marlstone of the Shan-Thai-Malay block 
near Baoshan ( 99.1øE, 24.8øN ), western Yunnan, China, reveal 
a pre-folding remnant magnetization, with a mean direction of 
D=49.6 ø, I= -3.2 ø, k=9.7, a95=5.5 ø, corresponding a paleopole at 
207.0øE, 36.8øN. These results, unlike the upper Paleozoic data 
with steeper inclinations published earlier, suggest that the block 
was located at equatorial latitude during late Silurian time, 
probably adjacent to the northern margin of Gondwanaland. 
Introduction 
The Three-River region is a tectonic collage of displaced 
fragments from Gondwana and Cathaysia continents during 
Paleotethys evolution stage( Mitchell, 1981; Stauffer, 1983; 
Zhong, 1995). The Shah-Thai-Malay block, or Baoshan block in 
Chinese part, has long been referred to being a piece of 
continental fragment from Gondwana, indicated by the 
Carboniferous tillite and Gondwana fauna ( Ren et al., 1980; Cao, 
1986 ). While the Simao block and Linchang Arc in the eastern 
vicinity, demarcated by the Changning-Menglian melange Zone 
( Main Paleotethys Suture Zone ), are interpreted to be rifted 
blocks from the Cathaysia continent ( Hsu, 1994 ) in the Late 
Paleozoic. Nevertheless, these blocks are still poorly constrained 
by paeomagnetic data, especially the Lower Paleozoic. The data 
published for the Shan-Thai-Malay block are mainly derived 
from the Upper Devonian, Carboniferous and Lower Permian 
( McElhinny et al., 1974; Fang et al., 1989; Huang and Opdyke, 
1991 ) and these results locate the block at southern hemisphere, 
probably adjacent to Australia during the Late Paleozoic. Several 
recent papers postulated that the majority of the Chinese 
continental blocks were derived from Paleozoic Gondwanaland 
( e.g., Burrett et al., 1990). The early Paleozoic paleomagnetic 
results from Australia suggest that Australia was located at 
northern intermediate to low latitude from the Cambrian to 
Silurian and afterwards moving southward ( Goleby, 1981; Piper, 
1987 ). Till Devonian time, it shifted to southern low latitude. 
The lower Paleozoic paleomagnetic data from the Yangtze and 
North China blocks also show an equatorial inclination ( Lin et 
al., 1985a; Zhao et al., 1993 ). Similarities in Cambrian trilobites, 
early Paleozoic fossil assemblages, phosphorites as well as

Precambrian stratigraphy between South China ( including 
southwest ) and Australia reinforce the explanation by

critical to determine paleolafitude of the block and 
paleogeographic relationships with other Chinese blocks by 
means of paleomagnefism. 
Geology, sampling and measurements 
The Paleozoic and Triassic sequence in the Baoshan Block is 
a continuous marine succession with a total thickness over 
8000m ( Geological Bureau of Yunnan, 1990 ). The folding took 
place in late Triassic to Jurassic time when marine sedimentation 
was ceased and continental reddish clastic rocks started 
accumulation. An unconformity is widely seen between the 
Jurassic and underlain marine strata. The folding was most 
probably caused by the collision event of the Baoshan Block with 
the Lincang arc terrene in the east and Central Burma Block in 
the west. The folded Paleozoic sedimentary cover of the block, as 
a foreland fold and thrust zone of the neighboring orogenic belts, 
is well exposed in the region. The Upper Silurian is composed of 
marine carbonates, and dominated by purple limestone and 
marlstone in the upper part with abundant bioclasts and burrows 
as well as small ripple laminations, which indicate a shallow 
water and oxidized environment. The age of the strata is well 
determined by conodont fossils of Spathognothodus sp., S. 
steinhornensis ? eosteinhornensis, Trichchonodella syminertrica,

Baoshan city ( Fig. 1 ).. The opposite dipping directions of the

for the northern sites ) in the two locations about 20 km away 
from each other make a fold test possible. Lithologies sampled 
are slightly different: sites 1 to 7 come from purple marlstone, 
and sites 8 and 9 were taken from light gray limestone, and sites 
10 to 17 are from reddish limestone. 
Samples from nine sites were processed at the paleomagnetic 
laboratory of ETH at Zurich with a 2G cryogenic magnetometer, 
while another eight sites were measured by a 2G 755-R cryogenic 
magnetometer at the paleomagnetic laboratory of Chinese 
Academy of Sciences at Beijing. The results produced by the two 
laboratories are completely consistent. Stepwise thermal 
demagnetization method was used for all samples. The principal 
component analysis ( PCA ) technique of Kirschvink ( 1980 ) was 
employed for analyzing the demagnetization data. For those 
samples without linearly decaying to the origin but poling to 
remagnetization circles during thermal treatment, great circle 
method was used to evaluate the magnetic directions ( McFadden 
and McElhinny, 1988 ). 
R. esults 
Intensities of natural remnant magnetization ( NRM ) of most 
samples range from 3.5x10 -4 A/m to 1.1x10 -3 A/m. Progressive 
thermal demagnetization revealed that almost all the samples, 
except for those from sites 8 and 9 which are weak and decay 
rapidly in intensities and become unstable above 350øC, show 
double components magnetization ( Fig. 2 ). The low temperature 
component ( LTC ), which generally accounts for less than 20% 
of the initial NRM intensity, and can be defined below 200 øC, is 
a recent viscous overprint acquired during transportation or 
storage with random magnetization directions. The high 
temperature component ( HTC ) in about one third of the samples 
appears above 300 øC and reaches the origin of vector plots at 
around 650 øC. While another two third of the samples either do 
not decay linearly to the origin or become unstable above 600 øC. 
Their vector Changes, however, follow a great circle though with 
relatively small best-fit arc length, giving a possibility for 
evaluating better constrained directions. The site-mean directions 
were determined utilizing set points by PCA and sector- 
constrained great circle intersection ( McFadden & McElhinny, 
1988 ) ( Fig. 3 ). Only a few samples from the northern sites 
show a little fitore complicated magnetization history when 
looking at inclination changes ( Fig. 2e ). The intermediate 
temperature component shown in Fig. 2e is similar in deviated 
declination to the Paleogene direction ( Chen et al., 1995 ) and 
was probably formed by the Tertiary remagnetization. All 
samples from 15 sites are unblocked at temperatures from 625øC 
to 680øC, indicating that hematite is regarded as the prime 
remanence carder, as estimated by reddish color of the rocks. 
Characteristic remnant magnetization ( ChRM ) 
directions are either northeasterly downward ( sites from the 
south ) or upward ( from the northern sites ), both with shallower 
inclinations. They are not completely coincident after tilt- 
correction probably because the overprinted component could not 
be fully cleaned for the southern sites or smaller best-fit arc 
length causing intersections away from the mean. ChRM 
directions of the HT component are mainly northeasterly upward

Discussion and conclusion 
Both overprinted and primary components are revealed in the 
paleomagnetic results from this study. The LT component is 
interpreted to be a secondary magnetization imposed in recent 
overprints. Since the folding in the study area took place mainly 
in the Jurassic, as indicated by the unconformity between the 
Middle Jurassic red beds and underlain marine Paleozoic, the 
prefolding magnetization isolated from the ChRM component 
must have been acquired at least before the Jurassic. The fold test 
for ChRM directions from the two locations shows a maximal 
concentration at about 130% correction. This deviation could 
probably be resulted either from slightly different sedimentation 
periods of the two locations which have not been better 
constrained by fossil records, or the diagenetic chemical 
remanants from the both locations were acquired at slightly 
different times. The pole position calculated from these data is 
well away from both Devonian and Carboniferous poles of the 
same region published earlier ( Fig. 5 ) ( Fang et al., 1989; 
Huang and Opdyke, 1991 ), reinforcing the interpretation of 
primary origin. Widespread remagnetizations during the Meso- 
Cenozoic have been reported from northern Thailand ( Chen and 
Courtillot, 1989; Yang and Besse, 1993 ). Our other Paleozoic 
samples also show a widespread remagnefization during the 
block collisions in the late Mesozoic and early Cenozoic, and 
these results will be presented elsewhere. The Silurian samples 
from this study were indeed suffered a heavy overprint which was 
most probably imposed in the Cenozoic when India and Eurasia 
collided. The reason for survival of primary magnetization from 
this study is probably related to the marly lithology of the 
samples that could more favorable for preventing the thermal 
fluids induced by the nearby orogenesis to reach the rock, and 
this interpretation certainly needs to be further investigated. The 
Upper Silurian pole from this study is far away from the Yangtze 
pole, while closer to the North China pole ( Fig. 5 ), implying 
large post-Silurian relative motions between these blocks. 
It has been a long argument that the Shan-Thai-Malay block 
was rifted from the northern margin of Gondwanaland in late 
Late Paleozoic ( Mitchell, 1981; Stauffer, 1983; Metcalfe, 1988 ). 
This postulation has been supported by a series of similarities in 
Paleozoic fauna, Early Permian cool-water brachiopods and 
foraminifers, and late Paleozoic glacio-marine diamicfites of the 
region with Australia. The Upper Silurian results obtained from 
this study demonstrate a quite shallow inclination, as reported 
from other Chinese blocks such as North China, Yangtze ( Lin et 
al., 19858; Liu et al., 1984; Opdyke et al., 1987; Zhao et al., 
1993 ). The lower Paleozoic paleomagnetic results from Australia 
suggest that Australia was located at northern intermediate to low 
latitude from the Cambrian to Silurian and continuously moving 
southward ( Piper, 1987; Goleby, 1981 ). Till Devonian time, it 
shifted to southern low latitude. The Silurian north pole of 
Australia is very close to the Baoshan Block and other Chinese 
blocks ( see Table 1 ), implying that they might be once closely 
related. The Chinese blocks, along with Australia, may have been 
part of northern Gondwana during early and middle Paleozoic 
time. By the Late Paleozoic, as the main body of Gondwanaland 
was shifting southward and reaching southern high latitude in 
Carbono-Permian time, the major Chinese blocks such as North 
China, Yangtze, Tarim and minor blocks in southeast China must 
have been rifted off and enjoyed equatorial latitudes as suggested 
by paleomagnetic data , fossil records as well as sedimentary 
environments. The Shan-Thai-Malay block had not been rifted 
away from Gondwanaland probably until at least Permian time, 
as indicated by geological, palaeontological and paleomagnetic 
evidences. 
In summary, we interpret the characteristic remnant 
magnetization of the Upper Silurian samples taken from western 
Yunnan to be primary. The paleomagnetic inclinations 
determined from two sampling localities are shallow, suggesting 
a low paleolatitude about 1.6 ø. The Shan-Thai-Malay block, 
together with other Chinese blocks and Australia, may have been 
a part of northern Gondwanaland laying at equatorial latitude 
during late Silurian time, as suggested by both geological and 
paleomagnetic evidences.

Abstract 
The island of Tobago occupies the eastern end of the central (igneous) belt of the Caribbean-South American plate 
boundary zone. Volcaniclastic sediment of the Albian ( - 100 Ma) Tobago Volcanic Group and dikes of similar age within it 
were sampled in two homoclinal sections with different attitudes. The mean of virtual geomagnetic poles for 12 sites 
(25.4”N, 24.l”E, A,, = 4.2”) is well defined, pre-tilting and apparently reliable, yet is far removed from a similar age 
reference pole for South America. Five other paleomagnetic studies of Cretaceous rocks from widely separated localities 
farther west in the plate boundary zone yield pole positions that are remarkably similar to the Tobago pole. Poles obtained 
from the Guajira Peninsula of Colombia, the islands of Aruba and Bonaire, and the Caribbean Mountains of Venezuela are 
among those that agree with the Tobago result. The paleolatitudes for study areas within the plate boundary zone are 
consistent with an origin on or near South America, yet the poles throughout the zone are rotated roughly 90”. Dextral 
relative motion between the Caribbean and South American plates was probably responsible for the rotation. 
Keywords: Tobago; Albian; paleomagnetism; pole positions; Tobago Volcanic Group; Tobago Intrusive Group

2. Region setting and local geology 
The Caribbean plate comprises oceanic litho- 
sphere of the Venezuelan and Colombian Basins; its 
age and place of origin are uncertain. It may be a 
far-travelled piece of the Farailon or some other 
Pacific basin plate (e.g., [4]), or it may be of more 
local origin. Between the Caribbean and South 
American plates is a broad plate boundary zone, 
about 250 km wide, that includes a central belt of 
igneous rocks of Cretaceous age (pillow basalt, is- 
land-arc volcanic and plutonic rocks; Fig. lb), 
flanked by belts of deformed sedimentary rocks. The 
Villa de Cura block, consisting of island-arc 
metavolcanic rocks and intrusions, is apparently an 
outlier of the central belt located within the southern 
flanking sedimentary belt. The central (igneous) belt 
comprises terranes that are exotic to South America 
[5,6]. Occupying the east end of this belt is the 
Tobago terrane [7]. 
The island of Tobago exposes Mesozoic igneous 
rocks in two distinct units ([6,8]; Fig. Ic). One is the 
Tobago Volcanic Group (TVG), consisting of pillow 
lavas, breccia, and volcanogenic turbidites. One lithic 
clast, low in this unit, yielded a 108 + 3 Ma

3. Previous paleomagnetic results 
Paleomagnetic data from the central belt of the 
plate boundary zone imply large clockwise rotations 
of Aruba, Bonaire and at least some parts of the 
Villa de Cura body [ 1,2], and possibly Curacao and 
Los Frailes [ 121 as well. A similar amount of rotation 
was also found in the Mesozoic La Teta lava of the 
Guajira peninsula [ 131. The Santa Ana intrusive com- 
plex of the central belt of Paraguana gave highly 
scattered directions, with an approximately 180” de- 
clination anomaly [ 11. Still other paleomagnetic stud- 
ies [14] have been performed in the southern 
Caribbean region. On Tobago, paleomagnetic direc- 
tions were previously determined from the TIC 
[ 12,151 and the Hawk’s Bill Formation in the western 
part of the island [15,16]. The dacitic flows and 
pyroclastic rocks of the Hawk’s Bill Formation may 
be equivalent in age to the youngest rocks of the 
TVG but have few reliable bedding indicators. Un- 
corrected directions from these studies are extremely 
scattered. They will be reviewed in the discussion, 
along with results for rocks of Mesozoic age that 
satisfy a set of minimal reliability criteria: means 
must have a95 < 20” and be derived from a mini- 
mum of 3 determinations of independent directions 
after a.f. or thermal cleaning [3].

The fold test described above shows that the

Application of reversal and baked contact tests to 
check for remagnetization is hampered by the age of 
the rocks, which is within the mid-Cretaceous inter-

sedimentation and essentially coeval igneous activ-

site #29 can be interpreted as a positive conglomer-

was not remagnetized after deposition. The fission 
track age of 103 Ma on zircons from the TIC [lo] 
shows that wholesale thermal remagnetization after 
that time is unlikely. Furthermore, the low grade of 
metamorphism and lack of cleavage strongly suggest 
that the rocks have always existed at shallow depth 
and low temperature. The weight of this evidence 
suggests the rocks sampled were not significantly 
tilted before magnetization, which was likely original 
or nearly so. Thus, the mean direction after correc- 
tion for tilt should provide a valid estimate of the 
geomagnetic field direction in Tobago during the 
Albian. Note that magnetization during this time of 
normal polarity removes any ambiguity about the 
sense of discordance of Tobago’s pole from refer- 
ence poles.

5. Discussion 
The paleomagnetic test of whether two crustal 
blocks have moved with respect to one another 
consists of comparing coeval paleomagnetic poles. 
To test whether a block has moved with respect to an 
adjacent stable continental craton one normally com- 
pares a pole from tie block with a coeval point on 
the path of apparent polar wander (APW) for the 
continent. We cannot test Tobago’s attachment to the

Caribbean plate because the latter has no reliable 
APW path. We can, however, compare the Tobago 
pole and other poles from the plate boundary zone 
with Cretaceous poles for South America [26-291. 
We chose not to use two of the recent poles from

any of the observed poles in Table 3, and 1291 
because it includes [26] and represents an unspeci- 
fied time range. To obtain the best age matches we 
augmented South American poles with poles from 
North America [30,19] rotated into South American 
coordinates [20]. We then calculated rotation (R) and 
poleward motion (PI [3 I] of the plate boundary zone 
terranes relative to the reference poles. The poles are 
plotted in Fig. 6, and tabulated along with R and P in 
Table 3. Given the large rotations observed, choice 
of reference pole or age of magnetization are not 
critical to the interpretation. 
Six of the nine poles summarized in Table 3 lie in 
a well defined cluster that is displaced about 90” 
from the reference poles. The three outside the clus- 
ter are different. Pole Al comes from the ‘predomi- 
nant’ direction measured in the Aruba batholith; 
Steams et al. [2] speculated that this may represent a 
partial chemical remagnetization acquired much later 
than the nominal age of the intrusion. This interpreta- 
tion is supported by Fig. 6, which shows that pole 
Al lies very near the trajectory defined by rotation 
of the late Cretaceous South American reference 
pole about a point located within the plate boundary 
zone (trajectory approximated by the 30”E meridian). 
Thus, AI may simply have acquired its magnetiza- 
tion during a late stage in *the rotation process. Poles 
Vl and V2 diverge strongly. V2 is derived from only 
two sites, and both Vl and V2 are mainly from 
intrusive rock and their tectonic corrections may be

in doubt. Some of the six ‘cluster’ poles are also 
based on very scanty data, but their close grouping 
and similarly large rotations (Table 3) is suggestive. 
Data from Tobago, Aruba and V4 show no signifi- 
cant poleward motion. In contrast, data from Bl and 
Cl suggest a small amount of northward motion with 
respect to South America. More work is needed to 
determine if their poleward displacement has any 
tectonic significance. Until that is demonstrated, the 
simplest interpretation of the paleomagnetic data is 
that Tobago, and probably the other terranes of the 
central belt, originated near northern South America 
and have been rotated clockwise subsequently by 
dextral shear between the Caribbean and South 
American plates. Perhaps the relatively smaller rota- 
tion of Tobago is related to Tobago’s eastern posi- 
tion in the plate boundary zone.

LATE CENOZOIC PALEOMAGNETISM AND CHRONOLOGY OF ANDEAN BASINS 
 OF BOLIVIA: EVIDENCE FOR POSSIBLE OROCLINAL BENDING' 
 BRUCE J. MACFADDEN2, FEDERICO ANAYA3, HEBERTO PEREZ3, C. W. NAESER4, P. K. ZEITLER5 
 AND K. E. CAMPBELL, JR.6 
 Institute for the Study of Continents (INSTOC), Cornell University, Ithaca, NY 14853 USA 
 ABSTRACT 
 New paleomagnetic and radioisotopic data are reported from two late Tertiary high-elevation, non- 
 marine basins in the eastern Cordillera of Bolivia. (1) Quebrada Honda, located at 22° S lat., consists of a 
 300 m thick section containing abundant Santacrucian or Friasian (middle Miocene) fossil mammals. This 
 locality is constrained by mean 40K/40Ar ages of 12.83 ± 0.11 Ma and 11.96 ± 0.11 Ma, and the local 
 magnetostratigraphy is correlated to chrons C5AA through C5A on the Magnetic Polarity Time Scale 
 (MPTS). The fossil mammals from Quebrada Honda have an extrapolated age of about 13.0 to 12.7 Ma. (2) 
 Micafia, located at 170 S lat., consists of a 205 m thick section containing late Miocene fossil mammals, 
 including a megatheriid sloth and the tiny mesothere Microtypotherium cf. M. choquecotense. This locality 
 is constrained by a fission-track age determination of 6.9 ± 1.1 Ma, and the local magnetostratigraphy is 
 correlated to Chron 7 on the MPTS. The fossil mammals from this section have an extrapolated age of about 
 7.3 to 7.4 Ma. In conjunction with two other published data sets (Ocros, 130 S, and Salla, 170 S), these late 
 Tertiary Andean localities indicate counterclockwise rotation at 130 S, negligible rotation at 170 S, and 
 clockwise rotation at 22° S. These data could represent local small-block rotations on a scale greater than 
 about 6 km2. However, these data are also consistent with a model of late Neogene bending of the Bolivian 
 Orocline. 
 INTRODUCTION 
 The extensive series of high-elevation An- 
 dean basins of Bolivia provide an excellent 
 opportunity for an enhanced understanding 
 of Cenozoic geological history in South 
 America. These non-marine basins are fre- 
 quently highly fossiliferous, and therefore 
 preserve an excellent record of the unique 
 vertebrate fauna that evolved on that conti- 
 nent during the Cenozoic. In addition, these 
 sedimentary basins oftentimes consist of rel- 
 atively thick and generally continuous se- 
 quences, with numerous interbedded vol- 
 canic ash horizons, all of which are necessary 
 prerequisites for combined paleomagnetic

 The purpose of this paper is to present new

 PALEOMAGNETIC PROCEDURES AND ANALYSES 
 The field and laboratory regimes were gen- 
 erally the same at Quebrada Honda, Micafia, 
 and Salla and are therefore described here, 
 rather than repeated below in the sections de- 
 scribing each of these localities. 
 As is standard in magnetostratigraphic 
 studies, three separately oriented hand sam- 
 ples were collected from each field site (hori- 
 zon). The average spacing between sites was 
 about 5 to 6 m and, because of relatively uni- 
 form, fine-grained lithologies, there were no

 mentary sections spanning at least 1 m.y. or 
 more has the advantage of a time averaged 
 view of the ancient geomagnetic field rather 
 than an instantaneous (virtual) geomagnetic 
 pole as is sometimes reported for individual 
 volcanic units. 
 In the laboratory, the paleomagnetic sam- 
 ples were then cut into 2.5 cm cubes and ana- 
 lyzed in a cryogenic magnetometer (Fuller 
 et al. 1985) at the University of Florida. 
 Paleomagnetic specimens analyzed after 1985 
 were kept in a newly built, magnetically 
 shielded room (Scott and Froelich 1985) dur- 
 ing measurement and demagnetization to at- 
 tenuate the effects of the ambient magnetic 
 field. 
 IRM (isothermal remanent magnetization) 
 experiments indicated that a potentially com- 
 plex coercivity spectrum could be encoun- 
 tered from any site (fig. 2C,D). Accordingly, 
 for each site one sample was AF (alternating 
 field) demagnetized and another was ther- 
 mally demagnetized; the third sample was 
 then demagnetized using either AF or ther- 
 mal techniques depending upon the results of 
 the first two samples. In most cases samples 
 were demagnetized in a series of between 
 four to ten steps. In some specimens, addi- 
 tional steps were done to isolate characteris- 
 tic directions of magnetization. 
 All paleomagnetic laboratory results were 
 subjected to the following standard statistical 
 filtering. Linear trajectories, which are inter- 
 preted to represent stable characteristic di- 
 rections, were chosen from segments of 
 orthogonal vector diagrams (fig. 2A,B)

 (Kirschvink 1980) to obtain a least-squares,

 Principal component directions were then

 C) for a third sample was added to the princi- 
 pal component directions so that N = 3, 
 which is the minimum number allowable for 
 Fisher statistics. Site mean directions result- 
 ing from this analysis that had the R statistic 
 below critical values (Watson, in Irving 1964, 
 table 4.4) were rejected for further considera- 
 tion. Only statistically significant (Class I 
 sensu Opdyke et al. 1977) site directions were 
 then combined for overall formational mean 
 directions. Both Class I and Class III sites 
 (usually N-1 samples with concordant direc- 
 tions) were used to interpret magnetostratig- 
 raphy. 
 In the stratigraphic sections studied here 
 the sediments are either flat-lying (Quebrada 
 Honda, Salla) or have very shallow dips (usu- 
 ally -7° at Micafia). It was not possible, 
 therefore, to do a fold-test to determine sta- 
 bility and time of acquisition of magnetiza- 
 tion. However, the results from these sites 
 indicate overlapping normal and reversed 
 populations, suggesting an ancient, stable 
 magnetization (fig. 3). 
 QUEBRADA HONDA 
 Quebrada Honda is located on the physio- 
 graphic boundary between the eastern Cor- 
 dillera and Altiplano in southernmost Bolivia 
 at lat. 21° 57' S, long. 650 25'W at an elevation 
 of about 3500 m (Tojo Sheet, Hoja 6528, 
 1:50,000 topographic series). This locality 
 was originally described (Hoffstetter 1977) 
 because of its interesting middle Miocene 
 fauna consisting of five orders and 11 families 
 of mammals. Subsequent papers on this lo- 
 cality have discussed stratigraphy and addi- 
 tions to the mammalian fauna (MacFadden 
 and Wolff 1981), as well as descriptive papers 
 on Astrapotheria (Frailey 1987), and Eden- 
 tata (Frailey 1988). The age of this fauna is 
 either Santacrucian, or Friasian (see below). 
 During our field work we also discovered 
 another fossiliferous section, Rio Rosario, 
 located some 6 km N of Quebrada Honda. 
 The Rio Rosario section is included here be- 
 cause it contains important fossil mammal 
 horizons and yielded valid paleomagnetic re- 
 sults. McFadden (1989) presented a prelimi- 
 nary discussion of the paleomagnetism of 
 Quebrada Honda and Rio Rosario in a re- 
 gional tectonic context. 
 Preliminary Biostratigraphy.-Faunal lists 
 of mammals from Quebrada Honda have

 been presented elsewhere in the literature 
 (Hoffstetter 1977; MacFadden and Wolff 
 1981), and those from Rio Rosario are cur- 
 rently under study, principally by R. G. Wolff 
 of the University of Florida. Our field work 
 indicates that fossil mammals are not uni- 
 formly dispersed throughout the sections. At 
 Quebrada Honda, fossils occur mostly in a 
 zone between about 25 to 82 m within our 
 composite measured section (fig. 4). At Rio 
 Rosario, fossil mammals occur mostly in the 
 lower 100 m of our measured section (fig. 5). 
 It is unclear, however, whether these fossil 
 localities in the two separate sections repre- 
 sent the same occurrence, i.e., they may or 
 may not be contemporaneous; they do seem 
 to represent the same land-mammal age. 
 Hoffstetter (1977) and MacFadden and 
 Wolff (1981) assign a Friasian age to the fossil 
 mammals from Quebrada Honda, whereas 
 Frailey (1988) suggests Santacrucian affinities 
 based on the biochronology of the edentates.

 This uncertainty about land-mammal age as- 
 signment is not surprising. Current work sug- 
 gests that the Friasian land mammal age else- 
 where in South America is very poorly 
 characterized. Based on new radioisotopic 
 age determinations, Flynn et al. (1989) sug- 
 gest that faunas assigned to these two ages 
 may overlap in time. 
 Lithostratigraphy.-Both the Quebrada 
 Honda and Rio Rosario sections have been 
 mapped as belonging to the Honda Group by 
 GEOBOL (Servicio Geol6gico de Bolivia). 
 These sections consist of about 300 m of prin- 
 cipally fine-grained fluviatile sediments with 
 predominant lithologies reddish brown and 
 yellowish-green silty clays, silts, and fine 
 sands (figs. 4, 5). There are also coarser, len- 
 ticular channel sands and gravels, but these 
 are localized. Several interbedded tuffaceous 
 horizons occur within both the Quebrada 
 Honda and Rio Rosario sections. Unfortu- 
 nately, these distinctive and continuous units 
 cannot be traced laterally within the interven- 
 ing 6 km between Quebrada Honda and Rio 
 Rosario because of lithofacies variations and 
 Quaternary cover. The base of each section 
 consists of about 50 to 100 m of breccia 
 gravels unconformably lying upon Cambro- 
 Ordovician sediments of the Sama and Iscay- 
 achi formations. Unconformably overlying 
 our measured sections, there is a shallow 
 cover (tens of meters or less) of Quaternary 
 fine- to coarse-grained alluvium and fluvio- 
 glacial deposits. 
 Paleomagnetism. -Fifty-nine paleomag- 
 netic sites were collected from our measured 
 sections at Quebrada Honda. In the labora- 
 tory, these were subjected to the demagneti- 
 zation and statistical filtering regimes de- 
 scribed above. As a result of this analysis, 42 
 Class I sites yielded an overall mean 
 paleomagnetic direction of dec. 14.5°, inc. 
 -41.1° (reversed sites inverted, table 1). In 
 addition, five Class III sites were added to 
 this data set to interpret a local magneto- 
 stratigraphy, thereby resulting in usable data 
 from 80% of the originally sampled sites. 
 These data yielded a local magnetostratig- 
 raphy consisting of 12 zones, N1-R6 (fig. 4). 
 Forty-seven paleomagnetic sites were col- 
 lected from the measured section at Rio 
 Rosario. After analysis in the laboratory, 37 
 Class I sites yielded an overall mean 
 paleomagnetic direction of dec. 19.0°, inc. 
 -38.7° (reversed sites inverted, table 1). In 
 addition, four Class III sites were added 
 to interpret a local magnetostratigraphy, 
 thereby resulting in usable data from 87% of 
 the originally sampled sites. These data re- 
 sulted in a local magnetostratigraphy consist- 
 ing of 14 magnetozones, R1-N7 (fig. 5). 
 The local correlation between the Que- 
 brada Honda and Rio Rosario sections, 
 which are separated by about 6 km, is 
 difficult because of several factors including: 
 (1) the lack of demonstrable lateral continuity 
 of persistent units, like the tuffaceous hori- 
 zons; (2) significant facies changes between 
 sections; (3) radiometric calibrations only 
 available for Quebrada Honda; and (4) the 
 fact that the magnetic polarity time scale is 
 very "busy" during the Miocene, thereby re- 
 sulting in numerous small polarity events. 
 Nevertheless, due to the flat-lying nature of 
 the sediments and the presence of generally 
 similar fossil mammals in both sections, it is 
 suggested that Quebrada Honda and Rio 
 Rosario are roughly contemporaneous.

 Geochronology.-Samples for radioiso- 
 topic dating were collected from two tufface- 
 ous horizons interbedded within our mea- 
 sured sections at Quebrada Honda. The 
 lower sample, QH-9, occurs 82 m above 
 the base of our measured section 1 (fig. 4). 
 The upper sample, QH-17, comes from the 
 255 m level within our measured section 2 
 (fig. 4). 
 These samples were analyzed using the 
 40K/40Ar method at the geochronology labora- 
 tory at the Australian National University. 
 After crushing and then washing to remove 
 fine-grained material, these ash samples were 
 processed using standard mineral separation 
 techniques, i.e., a combination of heavy liq- 
 uid and magnetic separation, and seiving. 
 Final separates were thoroughly sonified in 
 acetone to remove any traces of organic sol- 
 vents. 
 Sample QH-9 sanidine contained several 
 percent cloudy grains. The sample was 
 treated in an ultrasonic bath for 3 min, fol- 
 lowed by additional magnetic separation. 
 This entire procedure yielded an essentially 
 pure separate (>99.9%) of clear grains. There 
 remained, however, a few grains containing 
 inclusions. Both biotite samples QH-9 and 
 QH-17 appeared very fresh and consisted of 
 >99.9% pure biotite. 
 The analytical data for these samples are 
 presented in table 2. Samples were split into 
 separate aliquants for K and Ar determina- 
 tions. K concentrations were determined by 
 flame photometry. Ar concentrations were 
 determined by isotope dilution using an 38Ar 
 spike having a concentration known to better 
 than 0.75%. The sanidine was heated to 
 greater than 16000C for 30 min to insure quan- 
 titative extraction of Ar. 
 The interpretation of conventional 4oK/4Ar 
 results obtained from young air-fall volcan- 
 ics, although straightforward in terms of Ar 
 systematics, must take into account several 
 possible sources of geological error. Biotite 
 ages can be incorrect as a result of weath- 
 ering, and both sanidine and biotite ages can 
 be anomalously old due to detrital contamina- 
 tion. The biotite and sanidine analyses for the 
 lower sample, QH-9, yielded mean age deter- 
 minations of, respectively, 15.38 ± 0.10 Ma 
 and 12.83 ± 0.07 Ma (table 2). As it is un- 
 likely for fresh sanidine to lose Ar under 
 near-surface conditions, we interpret the 
 biotite age to reflect detrital contamination. 
 We therefore choose to accept the younger 
 date on sanidine of 12.83 ± 0.07 Ma as the 
 best estimate for the age of the ash sample 
 QH-9. 
 The upper sample, QH-17, within our mea- 
 sured section 2, yielded an age of 11.96 ± 
 0.11 Ma on the biotite separate (table 2). We 
 have no independent radioisotopic check on 
 the age determined for this sample. However, 
 QH-17 lies stratigraphically above QH-9 (fig. 
 4); therefore the younger age for QH-17 rela- 
 tive to QH-9 is internally consistent with the 
 superpositional relationships of the tufface-

 Correlation to the MPTS.-The Quebrada 
 Honda magnetic polarity zonation (figs. 4, 6) 
 is used for correlation to the MPTS because it 
 contains the radioisotopic calibration points. 
 This composite section is dominantly re- 
 versed with several normal polarity zones. 
 Given the 40K/40Ar ages of 12.83 ± 0.07 Ma at 
 the top of R1 and 11.96 ± 0.11 Ma at the 
 bottom of N6, zone N1 is correlated to the 
 top of Chron C5AA, and R1 to R6 to 
 the lower and middle of C5A (fig. 6). There- 
 fore, using the polarity boundaries of the 
 MPTS, the correlated limits of the Quebrada 
 Honda section are between 13.0 and 11.9 Ma. 
 The fossil localities in zones N1 and R1 thus 
 have an extrapolated age of between 13.0 to 
 12.7 Ma. 
 As mentioned above, the correlation of the 
 Rio Rosario section is less secure. Although 
 based on general field relations (i.e., flat-lying 
 and similar elevation) and similar faunas, it is 
 probably contemporaneous with Quebrada 
 Honda. The Rio Rosario section contains 14 
 magnetozones; therefore there is not a one- 
 to-one match with the 12 zones at Quebrada 
 Honda. Like Quebrada Honda, however, Rio 
 Rosario is dominantly of reversed polarity, 
 and it is correlated to the lower and middle 
 parts of Chron C5A of the MPTS. The fossil 
 mammal localities in the middle of the Rio 
 Rosario section are therefore probably be- 
 tween about 13 to 12.5 Ma. 
 These correlations of the local sections to 
 the MPTS are not unique, but the one pre- 
 sented here is consistent with the error limits 
 of the radioisotopic calibration points. Given 
 these correlations, zones N3-N6 at Rio 
 Rosario and N2 and N5 at Quebrada Honda 
 have additional reversed intervals (R4 and R6 
 and R2 and R4, respectively) not recognized 
 on the MPTS. 
 Overall Paleomagnetic Direction.-The 
 paleomagnetic data for all Class I sites from 
 both Quebrada Honda and Rio Rosario (com- 
 bined) yielded a mean paleomagnetic direc- 
 tion of dec. 17.80, inc. - 40.7° (reversed sites 
 inverted, table 3). As will be discussed be- 
 low, these data are of relevance to an under- 
 standing of the late Cenozoic tectonic devel- 
 opment of the central Andes.

 Geochronology.-Samples for fission- 
 track age determination were collected from 
 tuffaceous horizons within our measured sec- 
 tion. Mineral separations were done at Dart- 
 mouth and then sent to the U.S. Geological 
 Survey in Denver for further analysis. The 
 analytical data from these samples (table 4) 
 was determined by the external detector 
 method (Naeser 1979). 
 Zircon grains were mounted in FEP teflon 
 at 3000C, then were polished, and spontane- 
 ous tracks were counted. The zircons were 
 then etched for 34 hr in a eutectic melt of

 covered with an external muscovite detector 
 to record induced fission tracks. These sam- 
 ples were irradiated with NBS glass standard 
 962 in the USGS reactor at Denver. Follow- 
 ing irradiation, the muscovite detector was 
 etched in 48% HF at 20°C for 15 min. The 
 neutron dose was determined by counting the 
 number of tracks in the muscovite detector, 
 which covered the glass standard during ir- 
 radiation. The NBS Cu calibration was used 
 to determine the dose. The error reported in 
 table 4 was determined by Poisson statistics 
 based on the total number of tracks counted.

 SALLA 
 Salla is located in the Cordillera Oriental in 
 central Bolivia about 100 km southeast of La 
 Paz (fig. 1) at lat. 17° 11' S, long. 670 39' W at 
 an elevation of about 3485 to 4085 m. Since 
 its discovery in 1963, this locality has been 
 worked extensively by field crews from the 
 University of La Paz (Bolivia), Mus6e Na- 
 tional de Paris (France), GEOBOL, Kyoto 
 University (Japan), and the University of 
 Florida (USA). In addition to extensive De- 
 seadan mammalian fauna recovered during 
 this field work, Salla has attracted much 
 attention in the literature because the oldest 
 South American platyrrhine primate, 
 Branisella, occurs there. Numerous papers 
 deal with various aspects of this site and are 
 far too numerous to list here; these are refer- 
 enced elsewhere (e.g., MacFadden et al. 
 1985; MacFadden 1990). 
 Of relevance to the tectonic discussion be- 
 low, MacFadden et al. (1985) presented the 
 magnetostratigraphy of the Salla Beds, and 
 additional radioisotopic age determinations 
 are presented by Naeser et al. (1987). Based 
 on results from 10 (of 19 originally collected) 
 paleomagnetic sites, Hayashida et al. (1984) 
 suggested about 250 of counterclockwise ro- 
 tation for the Salla Beds. These results, how- 
 ever, are different from those presented in 
 MacFadden et al. (1985) and below. 
 MacFadden et al. (1985) collected 104 indi- 
 vidual sites from throughout the Salla Beds, 
 and after standard laboratory treatment, 76 of 
 these were used to interpret the local mag- 
 netic polarity stratigraphy. For the present 
 study, only statistically significant sites 
 (Class I, sensu Opdyke et al. 1977) are used, 
 and those with intermediate directions (near 
 90 or 2700) and/or shallow inclinations 
 (< ± 100) were rejected from further tectonic 
 interpretations. As indicated in table 3, the 
 resulting 58 sites (reversed sites inverted) 
 yielded an overall paleomagnetic mean direc- 
 tion of dec. 353.4, inc. -37.4°. 
 TECTONIC INTERPRETATIONS: LOCAL ROTATION 
 OR OROCLINAL BENDING? 
 Our paleomagnetic data for Salla, Micafia, 
 and Quebrada Honda (table 3) are relevant to 
 an understanding of the late Cenozoic tec- 
 tonic history of the Cordillera Oriental of 
 the central Andes. Given the associated 
 confidence intervals, the first two localities 
 are unrotated in any sense, whereas Que- 
 brada Honda has undergone significant clock- 
 wise rotation about a vertical axis. Beck 
 (1989) discusses seven potential geological 
 processes that can result in declination anom- 
 alies. With regard to the sites presented here 
 for Bolivia, there are two possible interpreta- 
 tions for the observed paleomagnetic direc- 
 tions; these data could represent either (1) 
 local (i.e., small-block) structural deforma- 
 tion or (2) oroclinal rotation. 
 1. Local Structural Rotation.-Paleo- 
 magnetic vector rotations, also termed decli- 
 nation anomalies, have been useful in deter- 
 mining rotations of structural blocks in many 
 tectonically active settings. For example, it is 
 known that within the structurally complex 
 Mojave desert of southern California, indi- 
 vidual blocks of some 10 to 100 km2 have 
 undergone independent, late Cenozoic rota- 
 tions (e.g., Luyendyk and Hornafius 1987; 
 Ross et al. 1989; MacFadden et al. 1990). 
 Larger blocks on the order of a few 100 km2 
 are also suggested to have undergone block 
 rotation (Luyendyk 1989). A clear pattern

 2. Oroclinal Rotation.-Carey (1955) pro- 
 posed the concept of an orocline to describe 
 regional tectonic bending of mountain ranges. 
 He coined the term "Bolivian Orocline" 
 (Carey 1958) to describe the flexure of 
 roughly 450 seen in the Andes, with the axis 
 of bending aligned SW-NE along the "Arica 
 deflection." Assuming that this is a valid tec- 
 tonic model, the exact mechanism and age of 
 bending of the Bolivian orocline has re- 
 mained somewhat enigmatic. Carey (1955) 
 suggested that the flexure of 450 ca be ex- 
 plained by bending of the north limb of the 
 orocline above the Arica deflection, whereas 
 some paleomagnetic data suggest rotation of 
 the southern limb (Palmer et al. 1980). On the 
 other hand, Isacks (1988) suggests roughly 
 equal amounts of bending on both limbs of 
 the orocline. Isacks' model is confirmed by 
 relevant paleomagnetic data (summarized in 
 Isacks 1988), most of which are based on 
 Mesozoic rocks and therefore only constrain 
 bending as post-Cretaceous. If the principal

Late Precambrian (850-800 Ma) palaeomagnetic pole for the south 
Indian shield from the Harohalli alkaline dykes: geotectonic 
implications for Gondwana reconstructions 
T. Radhakrishna *, J, Mathew 
Centre for Earth Science Studies, P.O. Box 7250, Akkulam, Trivandrurn 695 031, India 
Received 22 September 1994; accepted 19 January 1996 
Abstract 
Palaeomagnetic results from nine sites of alkaline dykes in the Harohalli area, Dharwar craton, south India, provide the 
best palaeomagnetic pole for the Indian shield during 850-800 Ma. The mean palaeomagnetic direction is D = 7.4°; 1 = 
81.5°; n = 9; K = 46; ot95 = 7.7 °) yielding a pole position at Z = 28°S; ¢ = 260°E (dp/dm = 14/15°), The results for the 
Harohalli dykes, together with earlier results, define a motion of the Indian subcontinent between ~ 1000 and 500 Ma and 
constrain an important geotectonic process between India and Africa during this period. While the 850-800 Ma Indian pole 
differs from the African pole for the same period in the Lotts and Rowley (1990) reconstruction, the Indian and African 
poles for 800-700 Ma and 650-500 Ma demonstrate excellent agreement. Thus, we suggest juxtaposition and collision 
between the African and the Indian continental nucleii along the Mozambique Belt (MB) to have occurred in the latest 
Precambrian (~800-750 Ma). Integration of our results with recent geochronological and petrological investigations in 
the then neighbouring Gondwana segments (India, Sri Lanka, Antarctica and Africa) helps to evaluate recently suggested 
geotectonic correlations between these fragments in the latest Precambrian. The south Indian granulite region extending up 
to the Bhavani shear zone could represent an independent Palaeoproterozoic terrane (SIGT) distinctive from the east coast 
region of India including the Eastern Ghat Mobile Belt (EGMB). The missing seafloor of the 'Mozambique Ocean' seems 
to have been consumed initially during the Late Precambrian ('-~800--750 Ma) by collision between Africa and the south 
Indian shield along the MB. The orogenic activity gradually migrated with time into the Highland/Southwestern Complex 
(HSWC) of Sri Lanka (~600-550 Ma) and then into the Ltitzow-Holm Complex (LHC) of Antarctica (~550-520 Ma) 
giving rise to final amalgamation of the continental blocks to form the Gondwana supercontinent. 
1. Introduction 
The Precambrian basement of the south Indian 
shield is an original Gondwana segment that became 
detached following Mesozoic--Cenozoic drifting. Re- 
constructions of the relative positions of Sri Lanka, 
India, Antarctica and Africa within their pre-drift

into the supercontinent have been the subject of 
interest. Several recent studies have focused on de- 
marcation and correlation of the petrological and age 
provinces within Sri Lanka, south India, Antarctica 
and Africa and have proposed Late Precambrian tec- 
tonic configurations (e.g., Katz, 1989; KrOner, 1991; 
Yoshida et al., 1992; Harris et al., 1994; Shiraishi et 
al., 1994). Palaeomagnetic data from these blocks are

vital for such reconstructions, particularly from India 
because of its centrally located position within the 
reconstructions. However, until recently the Precam- 
brian palaeomagnetic record from the Indian shield 
was scanty. The available data were not regarded of 
sufficient quality in terms of detailed demagnetisa- 
tions, number of sites or lack of isotopic ages to 
enable meaningful comparisons between the conti- 
nents. Our recent palaeomagnetic study on the mafic 
dykes from the granulite region of south India has 
proven important to overcome these defects, and has 
provided a good quality early-Meso- to Mesopro- 
terozoic palaeomagnetic record for India. Here we 
present Neoproterozoic (850-800 Ma) palaeomag- 
netic results from alkaline dykes of the Harohalli 
area in south India. 
The present study of the Harohalli alkaline dykes 
has great significance. Potassium-argon and whole 
rock and mineral isochron ages (Ikramudin and Stue- 
ber, 1976; Anilkumar et al., 1989; cf: Radhakrishna 
and Joseph, 1993) constrain an 850-800 Ma age with 
great certainty. Furthermore, no Late Precambrian 
palaeomagnetic pole has been available so far for the 
south Indian shield. Another simultaneous palaeo- 
magnetic study on the Harohalli alkaline dykes by 
Dawson and Hargraves (1994) produced primary 
vectors for two dykes only, which is not adequate to 
compensate for the paleosecular variation of the geo- 
magnetic field. Therefore, combination of our results 
with the data of Dawson and Hargraves (1994) en- 
ables determination of a high-quality palaeomagnetic 
pole of this age. The data have important tectonic im- 
plications for a Late Precambrian reconstruction of 
Gondwana. 
2. Geological setting, petrography and age 
The alkaline dykes of Harohalli are exposed south 
of Bangalore city between 12038 ' and 12°46'N and 
77023 ' and 77°3YE. See Fig. 1 for a generalised 
geological setting and palaeomagnetic site locations. 
The terrain around Harohalli forms part of the Dhar- 
war craton comprising a granitic complex with sev- 
eral N-S-trending greenstone belts. The local geol- 
ogy of the Harohalli area consists of a basement 
gneissic complex and the elongated body of the 
Closepet Granite, both traversed by various dyke in- 
trusions. Available geochronological data constrain 
the ages of gneissic terrain and granite at >3.0 Ga 
and "-~2.5-2.2 Ga, respectively (Naqvi and Rogers, 
1987; Radhakrishna and Ramakrishnan, 1993). The 
dyke intrusions include metadolerites/norites, un- 
metamorphosed dolerites and alkaline dykes. Ikra- 
muddin and Stueber (1976) have provided field and 
petrographic descriptions and whole-rock K-Ar and 
Rb-Sr dates of these dykes. The unmetamorphosed 
dolerites are olivine dolerite to quartz dolerite in 
composition and are predominantly oriented in NW- 
SE or E-W directions (Fig. 1). Seven whole-rock 
Rb-Sr isotope data yielded a regression line with an 
age of 2420 + 246 Ma. 
The alkaline dykes, whose palaeomagnetism is 
reported here, are classified petrologically as solves- 
bergite, tinguaite and bostonite and chemically as 
trachytes and phonolites (Ikramuddin and Stueber, 
1976). Their trends vary between north (to NE) and 
south (to SW) with variable strike lengths (0.1 to 
8 kin) and widths (<1 to 15 m). At a few places, 
they cross-cut the dolerite dykes. The alkaline dykes 
are either green/grey or reddish brown in colour and 
consist almost entirely of alkali feldspar and alkali 
pyroxenes. The reddish brown dykes were described 
as altered dykes (Dawson and Hargraves, 1994). Dif- 
fusion of hematite staining and alteration of feldspars 
and cores of pyroxene grains is evident. The alter- 
ation is most likely deuteric. Ikramuddin and Stueber 
(1976) reported whole-rock Rb-Sr isotope data on 
eight samples yielding an isochron age of 832 + 40 
Ma and K-Ar whole-rock age of 810 + 25 Ma for 
one of the dykes. Anilkumar et al., 1989 (cf. Rad- 
hakrishna and Mathew, 1993) reported an isochron 
age of 823 :t: 15 Ma based on a combined Rb-Sr 
isotope data of whole-rock and alkali feldspar grains 
of the alkaline dykes. These results strongly attest a 
850-800 Ma age for the alkaline dykes of Harohalli.

using a magnetic compass. All samples were re- 
oriented in the laboratory and 1-inch diameter and 
1-inch long cylindrical specimens were drilled for 
palaeomagnetic measurements. Nine sites (dykes) 
were collected covering the total geographic area of

to eight block samples were taken from each site 
(dyke), thus a total number of 61 block samples were 
used in our palaeomagnetic study. Palaeomagnetic 
measurements were obtained with a MOLSPIN (UK) 
spinner magnetometer interfaced with a portable EP- 
SON computer. The sensitivity of the instrument is 
of the order 0.5 mA/m. Progressive AF demagneti- 
sations were performed on one specimen from each 
of the samples (i.e., total 61 specimens) at 5 naT and

thereafter at 2.5 mT steps until a stable magnetic 
component was isolated or till the intensities of mag- 
netisation had dropped below the sensitivity of the 
instrument. A MOLSPIN AF shielded demagnetiser 
(UK), with a 100 mT peak field was used for AF de- 
magnetisation. Thermal demagnetisations were per- 
formed on one specimen from each of the samples 
(except for site #23 whose samples were magneti- 
cally weaker than the instrument's sensitivity; i.e. in 
total 54 specimens) with progressive heating steps at 
375,420, 450, 480, 510, 530, 550, 560, 570, 580 and 
590°C. Heatings were carried out with a MMTD-1 
Thermal Demagnetiser (UK) capable of heating at a 
peak of 800°C. Demagnetisation data were analysed 
using Zijderveld vector plots, stereographic plots, 
and linear regression tests using principal component 
analysis (based on Kirschvink, 1980, modified by 
Halls, 1986). In the principal component analyses, 
only those linear trajectories of consecutive points 
with an angular uncertainty of < 10 ° were accepted. 
Individual site mean directions were calculated from 
each of the sample vectors and the mean swarm di- 
rection was obtained from the mean site directions 
following Fisher (1953) statistics. 
3.2. Results 
Samples from one of the nine sites (dykes, #23) 
proved almost devoid of magnetic minerals and the 
NRM remanence was too weak to be measured on 
the instrument. Samples of this site therefore were 
not considered for detailed AF or thermal demag- 
netisations. Samples from the remaining eight sites 
generally have low intensities ('-~ 1 A/m to 0.1 A/m) 
except for sites #20D (4 A/m) and #24F (20 A/m). 
Samples of these sites have scattered NRM direc- 
tions with declinations due east or north and either 
positive or negative steep to shallow inclinations. AF 
demagnetisation at a 10--15 mT peak field generally 
proved useful to isolate stable directions in a major- 
ity of the samples (Fig. 2). The directions in many 
samples remained unchanged up to >570°C (Fig. 3). 
Specimens 17B, 19F and 20G showed some change 
upon thermal demagnetisation (Fig. 3) and the di- 
rections between 450 and 550°C closely compare 
with the directions of characteristic magnetisation 
achieved in the other samples of the sites upon 
AF demagnetisation. Although five out of six sam- 
pies in site #18 gave stable directions, these vectors 
are highly scattered and no single consistent vector 
could be isolated. Stable directions from all sam- 
ples of each of the other sites do not show perfect 
within-site clustering; however, the majority of the 
samples (60%) from these sites cluster at steep pos- 
itive inclinations, whereas site #25 shows a reverse 
vector with steep negative inclination (Fig. 4). No 
favourable sampling sites could be located for baked 
contact tests. However, because all sites show good 
between-site grouping with a reverse vector in one 
of the dykes and because the site vectors do not co- 
incide with any other known post-800 Ma direction 
from south India, the mean vector of the Harohalli 
alkali dykes (D = 7.4°; I = +81.5°; Table 1) is con- 
sidered as the direction of primary magnetisation. 
While there is good within-site grouping (Fig. 4), 
there is also a pronounced within-site longitudinal 
spread and some of the samples show a reverse mag- 
netisation (for example 20G, Figs. 2 and 3). This 
indicates different cooling histories for the various 
dykes and we take it that acquisition of remanence 
occurred over a protracted cooling period, thus the 
data would tend to average out the geomagnetic sec- 
ular variation. The study of Dawson and Hargraves 
(1994) also isolated a similar characteristic mag- 
netisation direction in the two sites studied, which 
closely match our results. All samples from their site 
#D21 dyke (different from our sites) were thermally 
demagnetised, and their site #18 samples (from our 
site #18 dyke) were thermally demagnetised up to 
400°C followed by AF demagnetisation between 20 
and 45 mT, Combination of these well agreeing di- 
rections of the two independent studies produces a 
good primary remanence result for the Harohalli al- 
kaline dykes. The results of our palaeomagnetic data 
along with the data of Dawson and Hargraves (1994) 
are compiled in Table 1 and are depicted in Fig. 4 
with ot9s circles.

available isotope ages for these dykes indicate an 
850-800 Ma age for the palaeomagnetic pole. No 
other palaeomagnetic data for this period exist for 
the Indian subcontinent. Thus the pole is potentially 
an important contribution to the south Indian shield 
palaeomagnetic data base. Apart from the Harohalli 
dykes, isotopic age control is available for a palaeo- 
magnetic result for the Malani rhyolites (745 -4- 10 
Ma; Klootwijk, 1975). Hargraves and Bhalla (1983) 
assigned an age of 980 4- 110 Ma to the directions 
of a few dykes, metashale and sandstone in the Cud- 
dapah Basin. The palaeomagnetic directions of these 
rocks are also comparable to the directions of Wa- 
jrakarur Kimberlite (cf. Radhakrishna and Joseph, 
1993); the Kimberlite has been dated at 1090 Ma, 
based on concordant Rb-Sr isotope data of phlo- 
gopite megacrysts from four pipes (Anilkumar et 
al., 1993). Therefore, the combined data of these 
rocks may define an improved Apparent Polar Wan- 
der Path (APWP) for the Indian shield for the latest 
Proterozoic since 1000 Ma. 
The Neoproterozoic--early Palaeozoic Indian pole 
data have been rotated into the African coordinates 
following Lottes and Rowley (1990) reconstruction 
and plotted in comparison with the African pole data 
in Fig. 5. It is evident that the Indian APWP shows a 
large shift for the 1000-500 Ma interval, from high 
latitudes around I000 Ma to equatorial latitudes at 
the time of the Harohalli dyke emplacement, and 
then a significant longitudinal shift up to the early 
Palaeozoic. These displacements correspond to drift 
rates of more than 0.6°/yr. 
The palaeomagnetic record for the Neoprotero- 
zoic to early Phanerozoic of India has important 
implications for the Gondwana configuration, espe- 
cially between the African and the Indian segments. 
McWilliams (1981) proposed a Gondwana recon- 
struction for this period on the basis of palaeomag- 
netic data. In absence of Indian data, other than 
for the ~750 Ma Malani rhyolites, his analysis was 
largely centred on a discussion of apparent polar 
motions between Africa and Australia. According to 
McWilliams (1981), the east and west Gondwana 
segments were, in the Neoproterozoic, quite differ- 
ent and independent crustal blocks and merged in the 
mid-Late Cambrian following collision tectonics in 
the latest Precambrian--early Palaeozoic. Our present 
analysis of pole data (Fig. 5) suggests that India was 
separate from the east African (Congo and Kalhara) 
cratons during the emplacement of the Harohalli 
dykes (850-800 Ma), but appear juxtaposed by 800- 
750 Ma. This deduction supports the broad inference 
of collision between the east and west Gondwana 
segments, but would place the time of collision at
