4.2. Implications for geological correlations and 
reconstructions of Gondwana 
Regional correlations and configurations of 
crustal blocks of the eastern Gondwana have been 
reported recently based on correlations of metamor- 
phic facies and isotopic dating. The present palaeo- 
magnetic results of the Harohalli alkaline dykes per- 
mit us to evaluate and further constrain such re- 
constructions. The review of McWilliams (1981) is 
taken as a starting point for such discussion. He 
proposed that the N-S-trending Mozambique Belt 
(MB) in Africa was the leading edge of the colli- 
sion process and a cryptic suture could be lying in 
western coastal India, Antarctica and/or possibly in 
some of the segmented plateau in the Indian Ocean. 
Cordani and Cooray (1989) and Krrner (1991) iden- 
tified the tectonic events of the MB in the Sri Lankan 
geology based on lithostratigraphic correlations. Sri 
Lanka consists of three lithostratigraphic units: the 
westerly Wani Complex (WC), the central High- 
land/SouthWestem Complex (HSWC) and the east- 
erly Vijayan Complex (VC) (see Fig. 6); the WC 
and HSWC had experienced major structural and 
metamorphic development during 950-550 Ma and 
represent the Sri Lankan extension of the MB. In In- 
dia, the Kerala Khondalite Belt (KKB), to the south 
of the Achankovil shear zone (AC, in Fig. 6) was 
regarded as a possible extension of the MB-WC- 
HSWC belt (e.g. Shiraishi et al., 1994) based on 
a few ages of incipient charnockitisation (Srikan- 
tappa et al., 1985; Hansen et al., 1985; Choudhary 
et al., 1992) and remote sensing data (Drury et al., 
1984). However, Radhakrishna et al. (1990) pointed 
out that the AC does not constitute a major shear 
zone demarcating the boundary between two differ- 
ent crustal blocks because of structural continuity 
across the 'shear' zone. Harris et al. (1994) have 
supported this conclusion because of the absence of 
a distinct crustal history in the Nd TDM ages on either 
side of the AC. 
Harris et al. (1994) proposed that the South In- 
dian Granulite Terrain (SIGT) in India, the WC and 
HSWC in Sri Lanka and the Rayner Complex (RC) 
and the LiJtzow-Holm Complex (LHC) in Antarctica 
constitute a distinct tectonic block that is juxtaposed

Cauvery Shear Zone (PC in Fig. 6) in India. Ac- 
cording to them, their Nd TOM ages from the south 
Indian terrain and those reported from the WC and 
HSWC in Sri Lanka (Milisenda et al., 1988) fall 
between 3.0 and 1.1 Ga in contrast to the TOM ages 
(1.4-1.1 Ga) in the VC. However, the original work 
of Milisenda et al. (1988) documented quite distinct 
Nd TOM ages for the three lithotectonically distinct 
units; the HSWC had TOM ages >2.2 Ga while the 
WC and VC had TOM ages of only 1-2 Ga. Hiroi 
et al. (1994) also revealed contrasting prograde P-T 
evolution for the HSWC and the WC. Shiraishi et 
al. (1994) superposed U-Pb zircon ages and rein- 
forced the Milsenda et al, (1988) distinction of TOM 
ages among the WC, HSWC and VC without excep- 
tion; high-grade metamorphism had occurred during 
610-550 Ma in the HSWC and ~-1100 Ma in the 
WC. Therefore, we suggest that the SIGT with a late 
Archaean-Palaeoproterozoic crustal history (mean 
Nd TOM ages of 2.4 + 0.3 Ga; except for sample 
#19 of their study) might represent an independent 
crustal block. In the absence of convincing evidences 
for crustal welding along the PC, we suggest that 
the SIGT extends beyond the PC to the north, upto 
the Bhavani Shear Zone (BSZ), along which it might 
have been juxtaposed to the Dharwar craton (DC). 
The BSZ exhibits undisputed shear features with 
substantial displacements of crustal blocks. Such a 
process can explain the similarity of TOM ages to 
the south and north of the PC, upto the BSZ. The 
Palaeo- to Mesoproterozoic palaeomagnetic direc- 
tions of the dykes in the SIGT are closely similar to 
the dyke directions reported from the DC (Radhakr- 
ishna and Mathew, 1993). Although good age data 
are presently lacking for the directions from the DC, 
such close similarity, in the absence of recognisable 
younger geological events, has been interpreted to 
indicate that the SIGT and the DC have been to- 
gether as a combined south Indian shield at least 
since the Palaeoproterozoic ('--2000 Ma; ibid). The 
K-Ar and Rb-Sr isotope ages (--2000 Ma) of un- 
sheared/unmetamorphosed dykes (Radhakrishna et 
al., 1995) and Rb-Sr biotite ages in the western 
BSZ (Peucat et al., 1993) also support welding of 
these blocks in the Palaeoproterozoic. Therefore, the 
present palaeomagnetic pole of the Harohalli alka- 
line dykes and its interpretations in the preceding

T. Radhakrishna, J. Mathew / Precambrian Research 80 (1996) 77-87 85 
section would apply to the combined south Indian 
shield. 
Shiraishi et al. (1994) correlated the HSWC of 
Sri Lanka with the LHC of Antarctica. They sug- 
gested that the HSWC and the LHC were continuous 
orogenic belts, intensely deformed and having expe- 
rienced granulite facies metamorphism at "-~610-550 
Ma and 550-520 Ma, respectively. These correla- 
tions, in combination with the correlations between 
the MB in Africa and the HSWC in Sri Lanka, sug- 
gest that the MB orogenic belt developed consequent 
to the ~-800 Ma collision between the south Indian 
shield and African continental nucleii (with meta- 
morphic ages of 750--650 Ma); the orogenic belt 
further extended through the HSWC in Sri Lanka 
into the LHC in Antarctica (Fig. 6). It is interesting 
to find that the ages of orogeny become younger 
from Africa, through Sri Lanka, into Antarctica seg- 
ments. Similar progressively younger orogeny and 
collision events along the Indus suture from west 
to east in the Himalayan region were interpreted to 
reflect collision to have progressed from western to 
eastern regions (for example, Radhakrishna, 1987). 
Applying the same analogy, the orogenic activity 
initiated by the -,~800 Ma collision between Africa 
and India along the MB is proposed to have grad- 
ually migrated with time into Sri Lanka (HSWC) 
and then to Antarctica (LHC) segments leading to 
the final amalgamation of Gondwana segments into 
a supercontinent.

 Remagnetization of the Pyeongan Supergroup in the Yeongwol Area, Korea 
 Seong-Jae DOHI, Dongwoo SUK2, and Yong-Hee PARK' 
 'Department of Earth and Environmental Sciences, Korea University, Seoul, 136-701, Korea 2Department of Earth and Marine Sciences, Hanyang University, Ansan, 425-791, Korea 
 (Received February 10, 1997; Revised July 28, 1997; Accepted July 28, 1997) 
 Paleomagnetic and rock magnetic investigations have been carried out for the late Carboniferous-
 Permian Pyeongan Supergroup, exposed in the Yeongwol area in eastern South Korea. A total of 228 
 independently oriented core samples was drilled from thirteen sites for the study. The mean direction after 
 bedding correction (D/I = 202.7°/-24.6°, k = 2.4, a95 = 36.9°) is more dispersed than the in-situ mean 
 direction (D/I = 175.3°/-58.9°, k = 69.0, a95 = 5.3°), indicating that the fold test is negative at 95% 
 confidence level. In addition, the stepwise unfolding of the characteristic remanent magnetization 
 (ChRM) reveals a maximum value of k at 0% unfolding. Furthermore, authigenic magnetite and hematite 
 grains are identified by the electron microscope observations. These results collectively imply that the 
 ChRM directions were acquired after tilting of the strata by a chemical remanent magnetization when the 
 secondary authigenic magnetic minerals formed. The ChRM directions of the Supergroup, however, pass 
 the reversal test at 95% confidence level suggesting that the remagnetization occurred during the period 
 including both normal and reversed polarity intervals. Because the paleomagnetic pole position (39.4°E, 
 85.6°N, A95 = 8.9°) of the Pyeongan Supergroup calculated from the mean site directions of the ChRMs 
 is close to that of the Tertiary period of the Korean Peninsula, it is interpreted that the remagnetization 
 in this area occurred during the Tertiary. However, it is also plausible that the study area might be rotated 
 about 30° anticlockwise after the remagnetization at the end of the Daebo Orogeny, in the beginning of 
 the Cretaceous period. 
 1. Introduction 
 Many paleomagnetic studies of Eastern Eurasia, a tectonically complicated area due to its many 
constituting cratonic blocks, have identified the relative movements of the blocks during the Mesozoic 
time (Enkin et al., 1992). Although the Korean Peninsula is geographically located in northeastern part 
of Eurasia, its affinities with the blocks to the west are subjected to arguments. Traditionally the Korean 
Peninsula has been considered as part of the North China Block (NCB) in a single Sino-Korean unit. 
However, many recent studies have suggested many other possible interpretations: that the Korean 
Peninsula belongs to the South China Block (SCB) (Lee etal.,1987), that the northern part of the peninsula 
is part of the SCB while the southern part belongs to the NCB (Cruzel and Cadet, 1992), that the 
northeastern part of the Okcheon Belt, whose basement is the Ryongnam Massif, belongs to the NCB (Doh 
and Piper, 1994), and that the Korean Peninsula is an individual terrane (Enkin et al., 1992). 
 Until now the paleomagnetic studies for the Korean Peninsula have been focused on the rocks of the 
Upper Mesozoic to Cenozoic time. In order to identify the tectonic relations of the Korean Peninsula 
within the Eastern Eurasia, the paleomagnetic data of the Lower Mesozoic and earlier times, when 
significant tectonic activities frequently occurred, are necessary. Although several paleomagnetic studies 
of the Upper Carboniferous-Lower Triassic Pyeongan Supergroup in South Korea have been carried out 
previously by many researchers (Shibuya et al., 1985, 1988; Kim and Jeong, 1986; Otofuji et al., 1986, 
1989; Kim, 1989; Doh and Piper, 1994; Lee et al., 1996), it is believed that most of them failed to isolate 
original paleomagnetic components, and/or the number of specimens is insufficient to represent the long 
geologic time interval. Hence much more paleomagnetic data are required to identify the reliable tectonic 
location of the Korean Peninsula for the Paleozoic and Mesozoic era. This study, originally intented to

However, the original division of the Hongjeom and the Sadong Formations is used in this study for the

 The Hongjeom Formation consists of alternating beds of sandstone, shale, and conglomerate of 
bright red and gray in color with an average thickness of about 200 m. Some fusulinids found in the middle 
of the formation indicate that the age of the formation is to be Bashkirian - Early Moscovian (Lee, 1984). 
The Sadong Formation is lying conformably on the Hongjeom Formation with a thickness about 500 m. 
The Sadong Formation consists mainly of gray to dark gray sandstone, shale, and limestone with 4 coal 
beds at the uppermost portion of the formation, which is dated to be Permian by plant fossils (Kawasaki, 
1938). The Moscovian fusulinids are found at the base of this formation (Cheong et al., 1983). 
 3. Field and Laboratory Methods 
 In the field, 2.5 cm diameter cores were drilled with a gasoline-powered portable drill and oriented 
in situ with a magnetic compass. A total of 228 samples from 13 sites was collected: 10 sites from the 
Hongjeom Formation and 3 sites from the Sadong Formation. The locations of sampling sites are shown 
in Fig. 1. 
 Samples were trimmed into 2.2 cm long cylinders in the laboratory. After natural remanent 
magnetization (NRM) and magnetic susceptibility of samples were measured, the samples were de-
magnetized by stepwise alternating field (AF) and thermal demagnetizations. The ASC Scientific thermal 
demagnetizer (model TD-48) and the Molspin AC demagnetizer were used for the thermal and AF 
demagnetizations, respectively. Remanent magnetizations were measured using a Cryogenic magnetom-
eter and a Molspin spinner magnetometer. All the samples were stored in mu-metal boxes to be protected 
from the external magnetic field such as the earth's magnetic field. To avoid acquisition of systematic 
parasitic remagnetization during thermal demagnetization, the samples were turned over at each step. 
 Thermal demagnetization was performed at 100°C, 200°C, 300°C, 350°C, 400°C, 450°C, 500°C, and 
at intervals of 20°C from 520°C to 700°C. To detect any chemical alteration of magnetic carriers on 
heating, magnetic susceptibility was measured at each stage of thermal treatment using a Bartington MS2 
magnetic susceptibility meter. AF demagnetization was performed at the field strength of 5-30 mT with 
5 mT intervals, and 40-90 mT with 10 mT intervals. 
 For representative samples of each site, isothermal remanent magnetization (IRM) acquisition 
experiments and the Lowrie-Fuller test were carried out, and magnetic hysteresis properties were

1220 S.-J. DoH et al. 
measured with a vibrating sample magnetometer (Molspin Ltd., model VSM Nuvo). Electron microscope 
observations were carried out to confirm the characteristic size, shape, paragenesis, and composition of 
magnetic carriers. 
 The paleomagnetic data from all samples were projected on the orthogonal vector diagrams 
(Zijderveld, 1967) and the ChRM direction of each sample was determined using the principal component 
analysis (PCA) with anchored line fit method (Kirschvink, 1980) from at least three or more points. When 
the demagnetization procedures did not isolate stable end-point components and the direction of the 
remanent magnetization changed along a great circle on the equal-area stereonet, the ChRM component 
was determined using the great circle method with sector constraints (McFadden and McElhinny, 1988). 
 4. Paleomagnetic Results 
 The NRM directions (directions before any demagnetization treatments) of the studied sedimentary 
rocks cluster more closely about the mean axial dipole field direction (D/I = 0°/56.5°) than about the 
present-day field direction at the sampling site (353.5°/50°, Fig. 2). It is therefore suggested that the NRMs 
are merely dominated by the secondary NRM components acquired for a fairly long time. The NRM 
intensities vary from 0.07 to 70.03 mA/m. 
 The demagnetization of pilot samples shows that the thermal demagnetization method isolates the 
characteristic component more effectively, while the AF demagnetization, even at the field strength of 90 
mT, can not remove the remanent magnetization successfully. The thermal demagnetization method was 
therefore applied to the remaining samples for this study to isolate ChRMs. During progressive thermal 
treatments, sample Y9-6, a typical dark gray limestone, shows that its magnetic intensity decreases 
continuously toward the origin up to 580°C, the Curie temperature of magnetite, above which the direction 
of remanent magnetization starts to randomize with a very weak intensity (Fig. 3(a)). The red beds reveal 
two distinctive types of thermal demagnetization behaviors. One shows simple decaying of remanence

 5. Rock Magnetic Results 
 The IRM acquisition experiments reveal different acquisition behaviors for the gray limestone and 
red bed (Fig. 6). Samples from the gray limestone (e.g. samples Y9-3 and Y9-6) show a steeply inclining 
IRM intensity to a field of 100 mT and about 80% of saturation is achieved at 300 mT or less. This behavior 
indicates that ferrimagnetic material like magnetite makes an important contribution to the IRM 
acquisition and the influence of canted antiferromagnetic material such as hematite is minor (Lowrie and 
Fuller, 1971; Johnson et al., 1975; Dunlop, 1983; Piper, 1987). Gray sandstone (e.g. sample Y3-5)

 7. Discussion 
 Although it was not successful to obtain the paleomagnetic directional changes from the upper 
Carboniferous to the Permian in this study, it was discovered that the Pyeongan Supergroup in the 
Yeongwol area has been remagnetized. On the contrary to our results, Lee et al. (1996) reported the mean 
direction (D/I = 255°/-2.4°, a95 = 20.8°) obtained from the samples of red shale in the Yeongwol area and 
in the Baekunsan Syncline as the primary remanent magnetization. However, it is doubtful that the results 
by Lee et al. (1996) represent the Permo-Carboniferous Pyeongan Supergroup because only eight samples 
from two sites (sites 605 and 608) were collected from the Yeongwol area. Site 608, very close to sites 
4 and 6 of this study, yielded D/I =186.2°/-68.9° (a95= 6.4°) before tilt correction and D/I = 249.2°/-4.4° 
(095= 6.9°) after tilt correction, being similar to that of this study, while site 605, close to site 10 of this 
study, yielded D/I = 215.6°/88.2° (a95 =11.7°) before tilt correction and D/I = 265.5°/11.9° (a95 = 11.8°) 
after tilt correction which are different from the mean direction of this study (Table 2, Fig. 4). On the basis 
that the mean direction of the ChRM of the Permo-Carboniferous Pyeongan Supergroup from this study 
is interpreted as remagnetized component, it is more likely that the mean direction of site 608 of Lee et 
al. (1996), which is similar to that of this study, must have been acquired after tilting of the strata . 
 The mean ChRM direction before tilt correction is very close to the present axial dipole field, and 
the normal component and the reversed component are not significantly different from antipodal at the 
95% confidence level. These results indicate that the remagnetization occurred during the period 
including both normal and reversed polarity intervals, which is long enough to average out geomagnetic 
secular variations. The periods in which geomagnetic field was characterized by frequent reversals with 
roughly equal duration for the normal and reversed states after the formation of the Pyeongan Supergroup 
are the late Jurassic-early Cretaceous and the late Cretaceous-Quaternary (Harland et al., 1990). 
Therefore, the remagnetized ChRM could be acquired during one of these periods. Compared to the 
paleomagnetic poles from Permian to Quaternary in Korea (Kim and Jeong, 1986; Lee et al., 1987; Kim 
and Kang, 1989; Doh et al., 1994), the paleomagnetic pole position (39.4°E, 85.6°N, A95 = 8.9°) calculated 
from the remagnetized component is close to the Tertiary pole position (Fig. 11). Thus, it can be interpreted 
that the remagnetization occurred during Tertiary. 
 Although this comparison indicates that the remagnetization in the study area could have occurred 
during the Tertiary, any remarkable geologic events, such as orogeny and igneous activity that might cause

Orogeny. If the Cretaceous paleomagnetic direction (D/I = 28.5°/58.4°, a95 =11.7°) at the Yeongwol area 
recalculated using the paleomagnetic pole of the Kyeongsang Basin (205.1°E, 67.4°N, Lee et al., 1987) 
is compared with the mean direction (D/I = 355.3°/58.9°, a95 = 5.3°) before tilt-correction of this study, 
the difference of about 30° in declination between the two paleomagnetic directions is close to the degree 
of rotation of the structural trend of the Yeongwol area from the main Okcheon Belt (see also Fig. 1). The 
structural trends in the Yeongwol area are NS direction, while those in the southeastern region out of the 
Yeongwol area are NE-SW and ENE-WSW (Fig. 1(b), Son et al., 1969). The geologic structures in the 
study area were initiated during the Songnim Orogeny (Triassic) and were subsequently further intensely 
folded and overthrusted during the Daebo Orogeny (Lee, 1987). Moreover, the fact that stepwise 
unfolding test of the Pyeongan Supergroup has maximum k value at 0% unfolding (Fig. 5) also constrains 
the timing of the remagnetization to the end of or after the Daebo Orogeny. Based on these facts, it can 
be postulated that the study area might be rotated about 30° counterclockwise after the remagnetization 
occurred at the end of the Daebo Orogeny (late Jurassic-early Cretaceous). This interpretation is supported 
by the reconstruction of the North Sino-Korean and South Sino-Korean Blocks in a way that the two blocks 
collided during Middle-Late Triassic time and the consequently broken pieces of the North Sino-Korean 
Block, the eastern and western part of the North Sino-Korean Block, suffered clockwise and counter-
clockwise rotations, respectively, until Jurassic time (Lee et al., 1997). The paleomagnetic pole calculated

1230 S.-J. DoH et al. 
from the remagnetized component adjusted for about 30° of clockwise rotation is located at 210.8°E, 
67.8°N (A95 = 8.9°) and this pole is comparable to the Cretaceous pole position (Fig. 11). Nevertheless, 
any concrete evidence of the rotation is not found yet, mainly because there are few structural studies on 
the Yeongwol area until now. The confirmation of the interpretation that the remagnetization followed by 
the counterclockwise rotation occurred at the end of or after the Daebo Orogeny will be made when the 
geologic evidence is found. 
 There are two fundamentally different explanations for remagnetization processes. One invokes the 
realignment of magnetization within pre-existing grains to the ambient field when the pre-existing 
magnetic grains are exposed to the elevated temperature above 250-300°C and below the Curie 
temperature of the magnetic grains for prolonged period of time, known as thermoviscous remanent 
magnetization (TVRM) (Jackson, 1990). The second mechanism involves a chemical remanent magne-
tization (CRM) acquired when new magnetic minerals formed long after the formation of the rocks in the 
direction of the ambient field at low temperature, by the chemical alterations accompanied by the 
tectonically driven fluid migration from active plate margins (McCabe et al., 1983; Oliver, 1986). TVRM 
is most likely to have occurred in rocks when the rocks were buried to depths on the order of kilometers 
for millions of years (Kent, 1985) and when they were under the influence of the regional metamorphism 
or igneous activities. The conodont color index indicates that the paleotemperature in this study area is 
about 300°C (Seo, 1990), which is only high enough to cause the acquisition of TVRM for magnetite of 
MD grains (Jackson, 1990). The major magnetic carriers of gray limestone in this area determined from 
the electron microscope observations and rock-magnetic experiments are in SD - PSD state. Moreover 
any intrusives are not found in and around the study area. Thus remagnetization by TVRM can be denied. 
On the other hand, the electron microscope observations of magnetic carriers in the samples of the 
Pyeongan Supergroup, such as octahedral/cubo-octahedral magnetite crystals in and along the voids and 
microcracks, pyrite partially replaced by magnetite, and pigmentary hematite grains accompanied by 
quartz, feldspars and clay minerals, strongly suggest that the magnetic minerals in the rocks are secondary 
authigenic in origin. Thus the major process that causes the remagnetization in the rocks of the study area 
is the acquisition of CRM due to the formation of the authigenic magnetic minerals under the influence 
of fluids, which might be triggered by the orogeny or igneous activity. 
 8. Conclusions 
 (1) The characteristic remanent magnetization (ChRM) in the Upper Carboniferous-Lower Permian 
Pyeongan Supergroup in the Yeongwol area is carried by both single domain - pseudo-single domain 
magnetite grains and hematite grains. 
 (2) Since the site-mean directions are more dispersed after tilt correction (k2/kl = 0.03), it is con-
cluded that the ChRM was remagnetized after tilting of the strata. 
 (3) The mean direction and the paleomagnetic pole position of the remagnetized component are 
D/I = 175.3°/-58.9° (k = 69.0, a95 = 5.3°) and at 39.4°E, 85.6°N (A95 = 8.9°), respectively, and the pole 
position is comparable to the Tertiary paleomagnetic pole position. Hence, it can be safely concluded that 
the remagnetization occurred during the Tertiary. However, the paleomagnetic pole position, recalculated 
from the remagnetized component adjusted for 30° of clockwise rotation, is at 210.8°E, 67.8°N (A95 = 
8.9°) which is close to that of the Cretaceous of Korean Peninsula. It can be hypothesized that the 
remagnetization followed by the counterclockwise rotation occurred at the end of or after the Daebo 
Orogeny, in the beginning of the Cretaceous period, although this hypothesis should be tested when the 
geologic evidence is available. 
 (4) The remagnetized component in this area is acquired by the chemical remanent magnetization 
due to the formation of authigenic magnetic minerals under the influence of fluid migration.

Abstract 
We sampled nine sites of Jurassic and Cretaceous limestones in the Algarve region, Portugal. Our study yields a 
paleopole for the Portlandian-Valanginian (4 = 256”, A = 58”, A,, = 5”) and a paleopole for the Aptian-Albian (4 = 232”, 
A = 75”, A,, = 8”). These results allow better constraint of the relative rotation of Iberia with respect to Europe: this rotation 
of 22” + 14” is a rather fast event occurring during the Barremian, between 132 and 124 Ma. Confinement of Iberia between 
Africa and Eurasia would explain the rapid rotation of this microplate. The Iberian plate was probably attached to Europe 
until 132 Ma, then detached from Europe and acted as an independent plate during the time of fast rotation preceding the 
oceanic spreading in the Bay of Biscay. 
Keywords: Iberian peninsula; Mesozoic; paleomagnetism; plate rotation 
1. Introduction 
Magnetic anomalies of the Atlantic Ocean con- 
strain the relative motions of Eurasia and Africa with 
respect to North America. These anomalies also 
yield insight into the kinematic relationships between 
the Eurasian, African and Iberian plates and con- 
strain the evolution of the Tethys ocean. For exam- 
ple, rifting between Eurasia, Africa, and North 
America began during the Late Jurassic [ 1,2]. The 
rifting phase was accompanied by the formation of

of the convergent movement of Africa and Eurasia. 
Correlations of the position of the continent-ocean 
margins and the identification of anomaly 34 situated 
in the middle of the Gulf of Biscay help constrain 
the paleogeographic reconstructions of Iberia [3-51. 
However, because a great part of the relative motion 
of Iberia occurred during the Cretaceous quiet mag- 
netic period, its kinematics are poorly constrained, 
which leads to large uncertainties in the initial recon- 
struction.

rotated approximately 35” counterclockwise with re-

Paleogene [6-lo]. Van der Voo [l l] presents a syn- 
thesis of existing paleomagnetic data and lists ex- 
pected paleolatitudes and paleodeclinations as a 
function of time for Madrid if Iberia had remained 
rigidly attached to either Stable Europe or West 
Gondwana. He observes that paleolatitude curves for 
Iberia, Europe and Africa are in very good agree- 
ment. Although the paleodeclination curve of Iberia 
follows that of Africa, it is less well defined. The 
total amount of rotation of Africa is 40” or more 
when compared to Europe, while that of Iberia is 
30-35”. 
Pre-existing paleomagnetic studies in Iberia in- 
clude Oxfordian results from the Iberian range 
[ 12,131, Hauterivian-Barremian and Aptian results 
from the region around Lisbon [14] and Barremian- 
Aptian results from Maestrazgo [15]. These studies 
suggest that: (1) The main phase of rotation of Iberia 
with respect to Europe occurred between 135 and 
120 Ma, while the rotation of Africa with respect to 
Europe continued until the Tertiary. (2) Before the 
Middle-Late Jurassic, there is no paleomagnetic evi- 
dence for significant motion of Iberia with respect to 
Eurasia. (3) After 120 Ma, the main phase of rotation 
was followed by a “translation” motion (rotation 
around a distant Euler pole) during the initial phase 
of the opening of the Bay of Biscay. The translation 
ended during the onset of oceanic anomaly 34 in the 
Late Cretaceous. 
Upper Jurassic and lowermost Cretaceous rocks 
from the region around Lisbon have not yielded 
reliable results because of remagnetization, which is 
probably linked to Early Cretaceous rifting. Simi- 
larly, the Iberian Range was partially remagnetized 
during the Early Cretaceous [ 13,151. In this paper, 
we report Jurassic and Cretaceous paleomagnetic 
data from stratigraphic horizons deposited during the 
opening of the Atlantic and the Gulf of Biscay. We 
selected favourable Late Jurassic-Cretaceous sedi- 
mentary targets, such as small rift basins that contain 
well dated limestones series. Because of the effects 
of Tertiary tectonics, Pyrenean and Betics areas were 
disqualified. The remaining Late Jurassic-Early Cre- 
taceous targets, which were sampled for this study, 
include western Portugal, to the north and south of 
Lisbon, and the Algarve (Fig. 1). 
2. Geological framework of the Algarve 
The sedimentary basin in the Algarve region of 
southern Portugal represents an emerged part of the 
continental margin that formed during the displace- 
ment of Africa with respect to Eurasia and Iberia. 
Mesozoic layers crop out over 150 km in the Al- 
garve basin [ 16,171 from the cape of Sao Vicente, in 
the west, to Tavira, in the east, forming a belt whose 
maximum width is 30 km (Fig. 1). To the north of 
the central part of the Algarve, the sedimentary 
facies are continental. To the west, the Jurassic and 
the lower Cretaceous have continental affinities. The 
Aptian is represented by a thick (300-500 ml marine 
section (sections “Salema” and ‘ ‘Almadena-Porto 
de Mos”). To the east, one finds the thickest lower 
Cretaceous marine series, particularly in sections 
called “Estoi-Pao Branco”, “Monchara-Pocho” 
and ‘ ‘Alfandanga-Marin”. This section is overlain 
by Valanginian sandstones, microconglomerates and 
reefal limestones. After a transgression in the late 
Valanginian, a regressive period commenced. This 
period is marked by sedimentary layers that are 
entirely dolomitised. The lower Aptian is again purely 
marine and relatively thick. The upper Aptian and 
the lower Albian are composed of marly calcareous 
beds, which, in turn, are overlain by another dolomi- 
tised series. In the Tertiary, during convergence be- 
tween Africa and Eurasia, this basin was tilted, 
uplifted and preserved from intense deformation by 
the collision, unlike the Betics chains farther east. 
In the western Algarve, we sampled one site each 
of the Albian and Portlandian. In the eastern Al- 
garve, we sampled two Aptian sites, one Albian site, 
three Valanginian sites and one Portlandian site (Fig. 
1). These latter sites are part of the same series from 
which Galbrun [18] performed a magnetostrati- 
graphic study of the Jurassic/Cretaceous boundary. 
Galbrun found that the rocks had weak magnetic 
intensities and contained large amounts of altered 
magnetic minerals. Despite his findings, because this 
sequence is very complete and continuous from the 
end of the Jurassic to the upper Cretaceous, we 
thought it useful to sample on either side of his

3. Paleomagnetic study 
3.1. Magnetic carriers 
Following the method described by [191, a com- 
posite IRM using magnetic fields of 1.2, 0.4 and 
0.12 T were successively applied to each of the three 
perpendicular axes of a sample prior to thermal 
demagnetization. This method facilitated a more ac- 
curate identification of magnetic carriers (Fig. 2). 
For the Portlandian (sites 37 and 48; Fig. 2a,b), 
Aptian (sites 38 and 46, Fig. 2d,e) and Albian (site 
40, Fig. 2f) the experiment demonstrates the pres- 
ence of two magnetic carriers: one that is not satu- 
rated by fields of 1.2 T and whose unblocking 
temperature occurs at 12O”C, and another that has 
weak coercivities and unblocking temperatures up to 
500°C. The former most likely corresponds to 
goethite, while the latter, which is the main carrier of 
the remanence, probably corresponds to titano-mag- 
netite. A weak fraction of titano-magnetite is also 
found in Valanginian sites 42, 43 and 44 (Fig. 2~). 
For the three Valanginian sites 42, 43 and 44 (Fig. 
2c), and one Aptian site 46 (Fig. 2e) magnetic 
carriers with high coercivity are also found. Their 
magnetization is destroyed only above 625°C. Taken 
together, the experiments suggest hematite resides in 
these samples. Another magnetic carrier is found 
with medium (site 48, Fig. 2b) or hard (site 38, Fig. 
2d) coercivities and unblocking temperatures in the 
range 250-300°C. These characteristics are likely 
attributable to pyrrhotite.

7. Conclusion 
A plate tectonic reconstruction of Africa and Eu- 
rope based on the paleomagnetic data base of [27] 
and oceanic magnetic anomalies and tectonic lin- 
eations [l] is shown in Fig. 9. The APWP attached to 
the Iberian plate is also shown in Fig. 9. In order to 
evaluate the Iberian location at a given time, first the 
corresponding paleomagnetic pole is put on the Earth’ 
axis, and then a rotation about a constant line of 
latitude is made by eye. This approach is limited by 
the use of the present Iberian coastline (instead of 
reconstructed plate boundaries) as well as uncertain- 
ties associated with the reconstruction of the major 
plates. 
At 132 Ma (Fig. 9), Iberia is well located in 
relation to the major plates with its present west 
coast aligned parallel to the Grand Banks and its 
present northern margin parallel to the border of the 
Eurasian shelf. Iberia was still attached to Eurasia, 
while Africa was moving southeastwards with re- 
spect to North America and Eurasia. 
We also show a reconstruction of these plates at 
124 Ma (Fig. 9). It is clear from the comparison of 
the two reconstructions that Iberia accomplished a 
significant rotation between the two times (132 and 
124 Ma), as suggested by our results. Fig. 9 (124 
Ma) suggests that Iberia may have been dragged by 
Africa. At this stage, Iberia follows, but without 
being a real part of, the African plate. In this recon- 
struction, the space between Iberia and Africa ap- 
pears narrower than in the 132 Ma reconstruction. 
Although this apparent difference may result from 
the Iberian boundaries we used or from uncertainties 
in the paleomagnetic and/or kinematic reconstruc- 
tions, a confining of Iberia between Africa and Eura- 
sia would provide suitable conditions for the ob- 
served rapid rotation of this microplate. 
The quick rotation of Iberia during the Early 
Cretaceous was preceded and followed by small 
amplitude rotations with respect to both Eurasia and 
Africa [ 111. This does not exclude the possibility of 
significant relative motions, since paleomagnetic 
measurements poorly constrain “ translatory’ ’ move- 
ments (rotation around a distant Eulerian pole induc- 
ing a very low variation of the declination), espe- 
cially if the variation in latitude is limited. 
Thus, before the Hauterivian, Iberia was attached 
to Eurasia, while Africa separated from America. 
During the Barremian, Iberia underwent a quick 
rotation with respect to Eurasia. This rotation event 
is contemporaneous with other tectonic events occur- 
ring in the western Tethyan realm [28] and is con- 
temporaneous with the beginning of the “hair-pin” 
turn in the APWP curves of Europe and Africa [27], 
possibly suggesting a single cause for the change in 
kinematics. After this episode of rotation, it seems 
that Iberia followed Africa in its eastward motion 
and experienced a moderate rotation with respect to 
Eurasia, while oceanic spreading was under way in 
the Bay of Biscay.

Magnetostratigraphy of Eocene-Oligocene boundary sections 
in Italy: No evidence for short subchrons within chrons 
12R and 13R 
W. Lowrie a L. Lanci b

Received 20 August 1993; accepted 19 July 1994 
Abstract 
The marine magnetic polarity record shows many small-scale anomalies that could be due to short normal 
polarity subchrons within chrons 12R and 13R. New examination of published magnetostratigraphic results from a 
section near Gubbio shows that suspected short chrons in this section are probably not real. The Eocene-Oligocene 
boundary in the stratotype section at Massignano lies just above a tentatively identified normal magnetozone that 
might correlate with a possible short normal subchron within chron 13R. In a new investigation of the weathered 
marlstones in this section, acquisition and thermal demagnetization of IRM reveal a magnetic mineralogy dominated 
by magnetite, with minor amounts of maghemite and hematite. Vector analysis of the natural remanent magnetiza- 
tion discloses a complex structure in some samples: at least two and up to four components were isolated. The 
magnetostratigraphy based on a magnetite component correlates well to the main features of the chron 13N-16N 
polarity sequence. No short polarity subchrons are found, although the resolution is inadequate to exclude the 
possibility that they exist. In particular, we did not find a short normal polarity magnetozone previously located close 
to the Eocene-Oligocene boundary. The results of this study favour the interpretation that low-amplitude magnetic 
anomalies represent geomagnetic intensity fluctuations rather than unresolved short polarity intervals. 
I. Introduction 
The Late Cretaceous and Cenozoic record of 
geomagnetic polarity is lacking in short polarity 
intervals [1]. It is not yet known if the short 
polarity chrons are absent because they never 
occurred or because, lasting less than 20 k.y., they 
are too short to be resolved in the marine mag- 
netic anomaly sequence, which serves as the best 
available record of geomagnetic polarity for the 
past 83 m.y. Magnetostratigraphic investigations 
in continuously deposited sediments have not re-

nation records in cores from DSDP Site 522 
showed no short polarity subchrons within chron 
12R where eight were expected, but three sub- 
chrons were found in chron 13R [2]. 
A thorough revision of the marine magnetic 
database [3], including new evaluation of the rela- 
tive lengths of polarity chrons and subchrons, has 
given a definitive polarity sequence and a new 
magnetic polarity timescale (hereafter referred to 
as CK92). Cande and Kent [4] have addressed the 
origin of small-scale magnetic anomalies ('tiny 
reserved

248 W. Lowrie, L. Lanci / Earth and Planetary Science Letters 126 (1994) 247-258 
wiggles') in this sequence. They concluded that 
the tiny wiggles are more likely due to geomag- 
netic intensity fluctuations than to short polarity 
chrons. A recent magnetostratigraphic study of 
deep-sea sediments from DSDP Site 522 supports 
the intensity-fluctuation hypothesis [5]. The CK92 
timescale indicates the possible existence of many 
short polarity subchrons ('cryptochrons') in the 
early Oligocene. Eight cryptochrons lie in chron 
12R, one in chron 13N and four in chron 13R; 
one of the latter lies very close to the Eocene- 
Oligocene (E/O) boundary. 
The E/O boundary was used as one of the 
time calibration points for the new CK92 
timescale. An interpolated age of 33.7 _+ 0.5 m.y. 
was obtained from K/Ar and Rb/Sr dating of 
biotites from ash layers in magnetostratigraphic 
sections in Umbria, in central Italy [6]. Several 
short magnetozones were reported in these sec- 
tions, which are located in the Contessa gorge, 
near Gubbio in the region of Umbria, and in a 
small quarry at Massignano, near Ancona in the 
region of Marche (Fig. 1). On the basis of its 
lithological and paleontological completeness the 
Massignano section was proposed [7,8] and se- 
lected as the stratotype section for the E/O 
boundary. In this paper we critically evaluate the 
published data from these sections and present 
new magnetostratigraphic results from the 
Massignano section. 
2. Previous results 
In a combined magnetostratigraphic and bios- 
tratigraphic study in an active quarry in the Con- 
tessa gorge the E/O boundary was found to lie in 
the lower part of the Scaglia cinerea formation, 
just above the gradual transition from the under- 
lying Scaglia uariegata formation. The magne- 
tostratigraphy of this section placed the E/O 
boundary within reversed polarity chron 13R [9]. 
This result was confirmed in later magnetostrati- 
graphic investigations elsewhere in the Contessa 
gorge--in a section referred to as Contessa High- 
way lII [10]. Three short normal polarity sub- 
chrons within chron 13R and one in chron 12R 
were reported in this section. However, the pub- 
lished declination and inclination data [10] show 
several aberrations (Fig. 2) and do not agree in 
all points with the interpreted polarity sequence, 
which is based on the computed latitude of the 
virtual geomagnetic pole (VGP) during deposi- 
tion. 
The use of VGP latitude allows the combina- 
tion of declinations and inclinations in a single 
index of polarity. The technique assumes that the 
observed mean direction in a section corresponds 
to a geocentric axial dipole field. This requires 
correcting the observations for possible tectonic 
rotation by referring the declinations to the decli- 
nation of the mean direction. Subsequent plate 
motion is taken into account by using the paleo- 
latitude of the site (calculated from the inclina- 
tion of the mean direction) instead of its present 
latitude. These corrections may have been omit- 
ted in computing the profile of VGP latitude for 
the Contessa Highway III section. A revised plot 
of VGP latitude derived from the published data 
shows no solid evidence for short chrons in 13R 
and 12R (Fig. 2), although it indicates a short 
reversed subchron in chron 13N, which agrees

tion (Fig. 3) a single sample with normal polarity

real, this subchron could constitute a convenient 
marker for the boundary and would have implica- 
tions for the controversial origin of low-amplitude 
marine magnetic anomalies. 
3. Lithology and sampling 
In the quarry in the Contessa gorge, which is 
still being actively exploited, the Scaglia cinerea is 
a dark grey marlstone. In a gradual transition, it 
replaces the Scaglia L, ariegata, which is a vari- 
ously hued, marly limestone containing reddish 
tinted beds. The magnetic properties of the 
Scaglia cinerea in this section are largely due to 
magnetite and are straightforward [9]: alternating 
field and thermal demagnetization readily define 
the characteristic remanent magnetization 
(ChRM). In contrast, the rocks in the small aban- 
doned Massignano quarry have a yellowish hue 
due to weathering. Under this superficial dis- 
colouration the Scaglia cinerea samples were 
greenish brown rather than dark grey. 
The magnetic properties of samples from the 
section have been partially documented. Monta- 
nari and Bice [13] found several types of be- 
haviour during alternating field and thermal de- 
magnetization of the natural remanence. The 
study relied heavily on principal component anal- 
ysis of individual directions and was handicapped 
by weakness and instability of the remanence, 
overprinting and viscous components. The rock 
magnetic properties were not investigated fur- 
ther. 
The bedding in the Massignano quarry dips 
gently and uniformly at 23 ° toward the southwest 
with an azimuth of 227 ° . The rocks are fissile on 
bedding partings, which made sampling difficult. 
The vagaries of the outcrop limited the continuity 
and interval of the sampling. Oriented hand sam- 
ples were taken at somewhat irregular intervals. 
Because it has been proposed as a stratotype 
section for the E/O boundary, the metre levels 
of the measured section in the quarry have been 
marked by metal plaques. This enabled us to 
correlate our sampling with the previous investi- 
gations. Extra samples were taken at and adja- 
cent to the 18 m level where a short normal 
magnetozone had been reported. Cylindrical 
samples were later prepared by drilling 2.54 cm 
diameter cores along the down-dip direction and 
cutting them to the standard height of 2.25 cm. A 
total of 32 levels at an average separation of 70 
cm was sampled in the quarry; sample spacing 
between 17 and 20 m, near the E/O boundary, 
averaged 35 cm. 
4. Rock magnetism

tics [14] were used to investigate the magnetic 
mineralogy of the Massignano samples. The step- 
wise acquisition of isothermal remanent magneti- 
zation (IRM) was observed in progressively in- 
creasing fields up to 1 T. At this stage a second 
IRM in 0.2 T was induced at right angles to the 
first to remagnetize the soft fraction; in a few 
samples three orthogonal IRM components were 
induced in, successively, 1, 0.65 and 0.2 T. The 
composite IRM was then demagnetized thermally

alternating field (AF) demagnetizer; another

thermally. The components of the natural rema-

Some samples showed linear behaviour from 2 to

region of central Italy, which usually show anti- 
clockwise rotations [18]. 
The A- and C-component directions are dis- 
persed along a great circle that passes through 
the B-, D- and ChRM mean directions and the 
present ADF direction. Many of the A-compo- 
nent directions are close to the ADF direction; 
the remainder, together with the C-component 
directions, are streaked along this great circle 
between the ADF direction and the reverse 
ChRM direction (Figs. 7a and c). We conclude 
that the A- and C-components are normal over- 
prints, primarily due to partial remagnetization in 
a recent field, and contaminated by an unre- 
moved element of the B-component. The A-com- 
ponent is probably a simple viscous overprint. 
The C-component is defined in a range of un- 
blocking temperatures above the Curie point of 
maghemite. It was not possible to identify the 
magnetic mineral carrying this component defini- 
tively. Its blocking temperature spectrum was 
narrow, suggesting it may be carried by a limited 
range of grain sizes. The predominance of mag- 
netite in these rocks suggests that it might be a 
secondary phase of magnetite. Examples have 
been reported where secondary magnetite formed 
in carbonate rocks from iron-rich fluids that were 
able to permeate the rocks during tectonic defor- 
mation [19-21]. Thus, the C-component may be 
associated with a secondary magnetite phase that

magnetization process than the post-depositional 
remanence (pDRM) believed to carry primary 
remanence in these rocks, only a small secondary 
phase might be enough to compete with the frac- 
tion of pDRM in the 400-500°C temperature 
range. The direction of the C-component may 
then be a composite of the original pDRM and 
the remagnetized CRM superimposed on it. 
Because of the potential importance of sam- 
ples from the 18 m level at which a short normal 
polarity chron was postulated [12], the AF and 
thermal demagnetization characteristics of this 
level are shown in Fig. 8. Each type of treatment 
resolves two components: an initial component 
magnetized downward to the west-southwest 
(equivalent to the overprinted C-component), and 
a more stable reverse component magnetized up- 
ward to the south. The ChRM of this level has, 
therefore, reverse polarity like the rest of chron 
13R in which it lies. 
6. Discussion 
The stratigraphic plots of declination, inclina- 
tion and VGP latitude (Fig. 9) show a clear 
pattern of magnetozones that can be easily iden- 
tified by comparison with the marine record as 
chrons 13N-16N. The boundary between 13N 
and 13R is not well defined because only one 
sample (at 22 m) could be taken between 21 and 
23.2 m due to the poor condition of the outcrop. 
Unfortunately, this sample had unstable magnetic 
properties that prohibited determination of a sta- 
ble direction. The thickness of chron 13R may be 
as much as 12 m, or as little as 10 m, in the 
Massignano section. This means that the E/O 
boundary at 19 m could fall as much as 30%, or 
as little as 20%, from the top of chron 13R. This 
is a minor uncertainty, with no consequences for 
the calibration of the CK92 timescale (in which 
the boundary was correlated at 14% from the top 
of 13R). 
Our reappraisal of the magnetostratigraphic 
data from the Contessa Highway III section and 
the original and new sets of data from the 
Massignano stratotype section (Fig. 10) generally 
agree well with the polarity sequence in the CK92 
timescale. Our revision of the Contessa Highway 
III magnetostratigraphy of Nocchi et al. [10] shows 
two reversed samples within chron 13N, which 
might correspond to a cryptochron in CK92. 
However, the polarity of these samples is deter- 
mined entirely by their declinations. The inclina- 
tions show no discrepancy; hence misorientation 
of the samples might be suspected. Thus, the 
reality of this 'event' is dubious. We conclude 
that the magnetostratigraphies of the Contessa 
and Massignano sections show no convincing evi- 
dence of short polarity chrons. 
A weakness common to each of these magne- 
tostratigraphic investigations in the Scaglia cinerea 
is the comparatively wide sampling interval. This 
is because sampling of the friable marls was re- 
stricted to beds that did not disintegrate. This 
resulted in an irregular and unfortunately wide 
sampling interval. Closer sampling should be pos- 
sible in the fresher material in a continuous core 
recently drilled through the Scaglia cinerea at 
Massignano [22]. Magnetostratigraphic analysis of 
this core has recently started. 
The durations of the cryptochrons in CK92 
were estimated to be about 8-17 k.y. At Massig- 
nano chron 13R, which according to CK92 lasted 
1.l m.y., is represented by a magnetozone that is 
10-12 m thick. The sedimentation rate of about 1 
cm/k.y, means that a sample spacing of 5-10 cm 
would be needed to detect cryptochrons. In our 
study the mean sampling interval was 70 cm, 
whereas in Bice and Montanari [12] it was 50 cm. 
Except at the 18 and 19 m levels, our samples did 
not come from the same stratigraphic levels as 
those of Bice and Montanari [12]. Combining the 
two data sets gives a mean sampling interval in 
the Massignano quarry of 30 cm, equivalent to 
about 30 k.y. This is still too wide to detect all 
four possible cryptochrons within chron 13R, or 
the eight cryptochrons within 12R. However, if all 
the cryptochrons are real, it is surprising that not 
one of them was detected in these sections. In the 
absence of evidence for the existence of short 
polarity chrons, we favour the interpretation [4,5] 
that the tiny wiggles in the marine magnetic

record are expressions of geomagnetic intensity 
fluctuations.

Palaeomagnetic and chronological study of Miocene welded tufts in 
the northern part of Central Japan: tectonic implications for the latest 
stage of arc formation of Japan 
Yo-ichiro Otofuji a,*, Yasutaka Nishizawa a, Masato Tamai a, Takaaki Matsuda b 
Department of Earth and Planetary Sciences, Faculty of Science, Kobe University, Kobe 657, Japan 
b Department of Geology, Faculty of Science, Himeji Institute of Technology, Himeji 671-22, Japan 
Received 30 January 1996; accepted 12 March 1997 
Abstract 
Kinematical adjustment of tectonic blocks has occurred in the latest stage of arc formation of Japan within central 
Japan. Miocene welded tufts have been sampled for chronological and palaeomagnetic studies from the northern part 
of central Japan. Zircon fission-track dating confirms Middle to Late Miocene ages (13.7-5.0 Ma) for the Yatakezawa, 
Shiobara, Kawaji, Kinugawa, Katashinagawa, Okkai and Ashio Formations. Characteristic directions with high unblocking 
temperature component above 560°C are isolated from 36 sites. Palaeomagnetic directions after tilt correction provide 
a Miocene characteristic palaeomagnetic direction of the northern part of central Japan (36.8°N, 139.3°E): D = 7.3 °, 
1 = 50.3 °, a95 = 6.6 °. Presence of normal and reversed polarities, and a fairly long time average exclude the effect 
of geomagnetic field secular variation. Comparison with the Miocene palaeomagnetic poles of the neighbouring blocks 
indicates that the northern part of central Japan and northeast Japan behaved as a unified block since 15 Ma, whereas the 
Kanto Mountain region moved kinematically as an independent block from the northern block comprised of central Japan 
and northeast Japan at least between 16 Ma and 12 Ma. The boundary between the northern part of central Japan and the 
Kanto Mountain was in a convergent regime with dextral strike slip. A southward force exerted from the northern part of 
central Japan, as well as a northward force by the Izu-Bonin ridge, induced the clockwise rotation of the Kanto Mountain 
region. The northern part of central Japan had welded completely with the Kanto Mountain region by 6 Ma. 
K~words: tectonics; palaeomagnetism; chronology; Japan arc; Miocene 
1. Introduction 
Building of the present arc configuration of the 
Japanese islands has been recognized as a conse- 
quence of differential tectonic rotation of southwest 
and northeast Japan (e.g., Otofuji et al., 1985a; Faure

with the opening of the Japan Sea, a unit block 
of northeast Japan was rifted from the Asian con- 
tinent and rotated counter-clockwise through about 
46 ° since 20 Ma, whereas southwest Japan rotated 
clockwise through more than 45 ° between 20 Ma 
and 14 Ma (Otofuji and Matsuda, 1987; Otofuji et 
al., 1991, 1994; Jolivet et al., 1994). Consequently,

northeastern pan of southwest Japan had met along

The occurrence of a kinematical adjustment ot" 
tectonic blocks in central Japan has been speculated 
during the last decade (Hirooka et al., 1990: Kana- 
ori, 1990; Hayashida, 1994; Fournier et al., 1995). 
Palaeomagnetic studies have identified a large clock- 
wise rotation during a period later than 16 Ma for 
the Kanto Mountain region (Hyodo and Niitsuma, 
1986). The continuation of this clockwise rotation 
later than 12 Ma was suggested with the palaeo- 
magnetic evidence of Miocene volcanic products 
(Takahashi and Watanabe, 1993). Tectonic studies on 
relative rotation of blocks within central Japan have 
provided a clue for depicting an important aspect of 
the detailed arc formation in the latest stage of the 
present Japan Arc. The block rotation emphasizes 
the need to establish the Miocene palaeomagnetic 
directions for blocks within central Japan. 
The Uetsu-Ashio zone occupies a fairly wide 
area in central Japan (Fig. 1), which is located to 
the northeast of the Kanto Mountain region. We 
choose this zone as a tectonic block in central 
Japan to study relative block rotation on the ba- 
sis of palaeomagnetism. This study focuses on the 
Miocene welded tuff formations. We present new 
chronological results by the fission-track method as 
well as a palaeomagnetic study of the Middle to 
Late Miocene welded tuff sequences, because few 
chronological results have been reported from cen- 
tral Japan. 
2. Geological setting and sampling 
Central Japan is the most complicated geological 
segment in the Japanese islands because it is now 
located at the junction of four plates (Pacific, Philip- 
pine, North America, and Eurasia plates) (Demets, 
1992) and was a boundary area in which the north- 
east and southwest Japan arcs had been welded in 
Miocene times (e.g., Taira et al., 1989; Otsuki, 1990) 
(Fig. 1). 
The basement of the northern part of central Japan 
consists of Mesozoic to Palaeozoic rocks compris- 
ing the Joetsu and Abukuma metamorphic belts, 
and the Uetsu-Ashio zone (Editorial Committee of 
Kanto, 1986; Hashimoto, 1991). Since the latter 
zone has preserved Palaeozoic-Mesozoic sequences 
(e.g., the occurrence of Fusulinid-bearing limestone) 
quite similar to the Mino-Tamba terrane in south- 
west Japan (Isozaki et al., 1990), this zone is also 
recognized to be the Jurassic accretionary prism. The 
southern part of central Japan is occupied by Jurassic 
to Miocene basements composed of the Inner zone 
(Ryoke Belt) and the Outer zone (Sambagawa Belt, 
Chichibu-Sanbozan Belt, Shimanto Belt) (Geolog- 
ical Survey of Japan, 1982). The zonally arranged 
terranes of the two zones are an eastward extension 
of the geological structure of southwest Japan, al- 
though a significant change is observed in the trend 
of the lineation of the zonal structure between central 
and southwest Japan. 
Intense felsic igneous activity occurred during 
Cretaceous to Eocene time in the Mesozoic to 
Palaeozoic terranes of central Japan (Fig. 2) (Ed- 
itorial Committee of Kanto, 1986). The Okunikko 
Rhyolites whose ages have been determined at 
56~65 Ma by K-Ar dating (Yanai, 1972) were 
formed during this Palaeogene activity in the Ashio 
zone in the northern part of central Japan. Bi- 
modal volcanism followed in Middle Miocene times 
(Sato, 1994), so that thick piles of volcaniclastics 
were produced from the Ashio to Yonezawa region 
(Table 1): the Osawa Formation in the Yonezawa 
area, and the Yatakezawa, Shiobara, Kawaji, Kinu- 
gawa, Katashinagawa, Okkai and Ashio Formations 
in the Ashio area. Volcanism during Late Miocene

The welded tufts were collected as hand samples

Each palaeomagnetic site typically comprised twelve 
independently oriented samples, distributed over dis- 
tances ranging up to 15 m. The eutaxitic struc- 
ture (lineation of stretched pumice and aligned 
phenocrysts) was identified at each outcrop of the

for post-emplacement tilting. 
3. Age determination 
Fission-track (FI') dating was conducted for zir- 
cons from sixteen welded tuff samples in the seven 
formations. Zircon ages were determined by the 
external detector method using uranium-free mus- 
covite (e.g., Naeser, 1976). Zircons of 60-100 mesh 
size were separated using conventional magnetic 
and heavy-liquid techniques. Zircon separates were 
mounted in PFA Teflon sheets, ground and polished 
to reveal 4 Jr (internal) surfaces. Etching of zircons 
took place in molten KOH and NaOH eutectic at 
either 225°C for times ranging from 15 to 32 h or 
245°C from 6 to 14 h. The etched zircons were irra- 
diated with standard glass covered by the muscovite 
external detectors in either the graphite or DeO fa- 
cility of the Kyoto University Reactor, for which 
Cd-ratios for Au are >2000 and 400, respectively. 
After irradiation, the external detectors were etched 
by 46% HF for 20 min at 20°C. The FT densities 
were measured at a magnification of 925 × under a 
dry 100× objective lens. Ages were calculated using 
the zeta calibration approach. We used a zeta-value 
of 386.3 -t: 23.0 determined dosimeter glass SRM 
612 using the Fish Canyon Tuff, Buluk member tuff 
II and Tardree Rhyolite (Hurford, 1990). Errors were 
calculated using the 'conventional analysis' given 
by Green (1981). Uncertainties in the chronological 
data are quoted at 2 sigma. Results of the FF dating 
are listed in Table 2. 
Only five of the sixteen samples passed the P(X 2) 
test. Since all block samples for the FF dating con- 
tain small amounts of lithic fragments, the analyzed 
zircon grains are expected to be partly contaminated 
by detrital zircon grains. Low P(X 2) are presumably 
ascribable to contamination of the detrital grains. 
The central FT age and age dispersion (Galbraith and 
Lasett, 1993) are calculated for individual samples to 
evaluate the degree of the contamination (Table 2).

4. Palaeomagnetism 
In the laboratory, individual specimens, 25 mm 
in diameter and 23 mm long, were prepared from 
these samples. Natural remanent magnetizations (N- 
RMs) were measured with either a spinner magne- 
tometer (Natsuhara SMM-85) or a ScT cryogenic 
magnetometer according to the intensity of the mag- 
netization. All specimens were subjected to stepwise 
thermal demagnetization up to 620°C. Results for 
each specimen were plotted on orthogonal vector 
diagrams (Zijderveld, 1967) to assess component 
structure as well as on equal-area projections to 
evaluate directional stability. Principal component 
analysis (Kirschvink, 1980) was used to estimate 
the component directions. Palaeomagnetic results are 
listed in Table 3. 
4.1. Demagnetization 
Progressive thermal demagnetization of the sam- 
ples separates the 36 sampling sites into three cate- 
gories (Fig. 3). 
Category A. Sixteen sites exhibit a single mag- 
netic component with unblocking temperatures of 
600-630°C (Fig. 3: 1-3). Little change is observed in 
the direction of remanent magnetization after demag- 
netization at temperatures higher than the Curie tem- 
perature of magnetite. Both magnetite and hematite 
probably carry the stable remanent magnetization 
with almost the same direction. 
Category B. Fifteen sites reveal two distinct mag- 
netization components (Fig. 3: 4-6). The unblock- 
ing temperature of the high-temperature component 
ranges between 590°C and 630°C, indicating that 
both magnetite and hematite carry the stable re- 
manent magnetization. The low-temperature compo- 
nents are removed in the initial stage of demagneti- 
zation by 300°C. 
Category C. Three components have appeared in 
four sites of the Kawaji Formation and in one site of 
the Ashio Formation (Fig. 3:7 and 8). The lowest- 
temperature component is removed by 250°C from 
all sites for both formations. After the middle tem- 
perature component is erased at 350°C for the Kawaji

Y.-i. Otofuji et al./ Tectonophysics 283 (1997) 263-278 271 
Formation and at 500°C for the Ashio Formation, the 
high-temperature component reveals straightforward 
demagnetization behaviour with an unblocking tem- 
perature of about 600°C. Thermomagnetic analysis 
revealed the presence of magnetic minerals with a 
Curie temperature of 350°C in KN725 of the Kawaji 
Formation, suggesting that the middle-temperature 
component is carried by maghemite or pyrrhotite. 
The high-temperature component resides probably 
in titanium-poor magnetite. The highest-temperature 
component direction is recognized as the character- 
istic direction. 
4.2. Palaeomagnetic directions 
Palaeomagnetic directions of the low-temperature 
component magnetization removed by 250°C in the 
categories B and C are dominated in situ by a 
component in the present direction of the Earth's 
magnetic field (Fig. 3). This component is therefore 
ascribable to viscous partial thermoremanent mag- 
netization acquired in recent times (Pullaiah et al., 
1975). 
The high-temperature component directions are 
clustered tightly in each site (Table 3): precision pa- 
rameter ranges from 55.5 to 851.9. Three formations 
(the Osawa, Yatakezawa and Ashio Formations) re- 
vealed normal polarity, and three formations (the 
Kawaji, Kinugawa, and Okkai Formations) reversed 
ones. Both polarities are observed in the Katashina- 
gawa Formation. 
A formation mean direction for the high-tem- 
perature component magnetizations is calculated for 
each formation (Table 4). According to difference 
in lithologic features or the fission-track ages, the 
Yatakezawa and Katashinagawa Formations are di- 
vided into two groups: north and south areas. Palaeo- 
magnetic data of site KK02 with an age of 33.8 Ma 
are not incorporated into the data set of the southern 
part of the Katashinagawa Formation. The seven for- 
mations except for the Kawaji Formation show good 
grouping before and after tilt correction (16<k). Al- 
though the precision parameter decreases after tilt 
correction for the Osawa and Ashio Formations, the 
decrease is insignificant for a negative fold test even 
at 95% level. Increase in the dispersion is possibly 
due to uncertainty in strike measurements (of the or- 
der of ±5 °) for estimating the palaeohorizontal plane 
from the eutaxitic structure in the welded tufts. The 
high-temperature component after tilt correction, ex- 
cept for the Kawaji Formation, is recognized as a 
characteristic palaeomagnetic direction for each site. 
The mean palaeomagnetic direction for the 
high-temperature component magnetizations of the 
Kawaji Formation reveals a significant decrease from 
128 to 10 in the precision parameter after tilt cor- 
rection (Fig. 4). A similar decrease in the preci- 
sion parameter from 119 to 11 is observed for the 
mean palaeomagnetic direction of the low-tempera- 
ture component (Table 4). The ratio of the precision 
parameter before and after tilt correction gives a neg- 
ative fold test at the 99% level (McElhinny, 1964) 
for both the low- and high-temperature components. 
These indicate that the high-temperature component 
is a secondary magnetization acquired after tilting, 
the same as the low temperature one. Occurrence 
of magnetic minerals with a Curie temperature of 
350°C in this formation is presumably evidence of 
origination of secondary magnetization from a rock 
magnetic view point. A fairly large counter-clock- 
wise deflection in declination with reversed polarity 
of the palaeomagnetic direction in situ for the Kawaji 
Formation is also observed in the tilt-corrected di- 
rection of the Shiobara Formation, implying that the 
Kawaji Formation acquired its secondary magnetiza- 
tion when the Shiobara Formation was produced at 
5.0 Ma. The palaeomagnetic directions of the Kawaji 
Formation are, therefore, excluded from further tec- 
tonic investigation.

direction (Fig. 6 and Table 4): Declinations for

occurred between the northern part of central Japan 
and the Kanto Mountain region. The Oligocene- 
Early Miocene rocks from Sado Island and the 
Fukushima area reveal counter-clockwise deflection 
in declination as D = 333 °, and D = 346 °, respec- 
tively (Hirooka et al., 1986). This palaeomagnetic 
evidence implies that the northern part of central 
Japan was subjected to counter-clockwise rotation

Mountain region rotated clockwise as the eastern-

Japan Sea (Hyodo and Niitsuma, 1986). The present 
study shows that the earlier differential rotation of 
the two blocks has continued until at least 12 Ma. 
The northern part of central Japan, however, has 
been united with the Kanto Mountain region at least 
by 6 Ma, because a northerly direction is reported 
(D = 3.5", I = 64") for the 6 Ma palaeomagnetic 
direction of the Chichibu quartz diorite of the Kanto 
Mountain CTakahashi and Nomura, 1989). 
Palaeomagnetic data have established that a maior 
tectonic boundary was located between the northern 
part of central Japan and the Kanto Mountain re- 
gion in Middle Miocene times. The boundary was 
between the sampling area of the Katashinagawa 
Formation with an age of 13 Ma (36°45'N, 139°15'E) 
and that of the Yaekubo Formation with 12 Ma 
(36°15'N, 138°34'E) (Fig. 1). A pronounced low 
gravity anomaly zone with a width of about 30 km 
extends from southeast to northwest, ranging from 
the Kanto Plain, through the area between the north- 
ern part of central Japan and the Kanto Mountain, to 
the Japan Sea (Komazawa et al., 1992: Gravity Re- 
search Group in Southwest Japan, 1994; Shichi and 
Yamamoto, 1994; Komazawa et al., 1994) (Fig. 8). 
Proximity of this anomaly zone and the tectonic 
boundary predicted by the palaeomagnetism sug- 
gest that the block boundary has remained as a low 
Bouguer anomaly zone. Minimum Bouguer anomaly 
in the low zone is less than 0 regal, whereas the max- 
imum at the northern part of central Japan and the 
Kanto Mountain is up to 90 mGal. The fairly large 
low anomaly with the short wavelength is explained 
by crustal thickening of low-density material which 
is formed as a result of compression of lithosphere 
between these two blocks. 
The presence of a structural discontinuity is also 
inferred from geological features between the north- 
ern part of central Japan and the Kanto Mountain 
region. Eastward offsets by 100 km of the vol- 
canic front of Middle Miocene times has been pro- 
voked along the low gravity anomaly zone (Seno 
and Maruyama, 1984; Takeuchi, 1986). The block 
boundary is, therefore, recognized as a fundamen- 
tally transcurrent fault, along which the northern part 
of central Japan has been transported southeastward 
dextrally. Geoscientific studies of palaeomagnetism, 
gravity and geology suggest that the northern part of 
central Japan and the Kanto Mountain were bordered

Formation and evolution of the Masirah ophiolite constrained by 
paleomagnetic study of volcanic rocks 
Edwin Gnos a,*, Mireille Perrin b 
a Laboratoire de Tectonophysique, Universit~ Montpellier If, Place Eugene Bataillon, 34095 Montpellier Cedex 05, France 
b Laboratoire de Gdophysique et Tectonique, CNRS and UniversiM. Montpellier II, Case 060, 34095 Montpellier Cedex 05, France 
Received 13 January 1995; accepted 18 May 1995 
Abstract 
The extrusive rocks of the lower ophiolitic nappe of Masirah Island (Oman) were paleomagnetically studied. Four mean 
directions of magnetization were isolated, one at low temperature, the others at high temperature. The low-temperature 
component, found in most samples, corresponds to a recent viscous and/or chemical remagnetization. The high-temperature 
component, found at three sites in the Centre area, is interpreted as a possible primary magnetization acquired during 
extrusion or, more probably, as an early remagnetization related to subsequent hydrothermal alteration and indicates 
formation of the Masirah ophiolite around a paleolatitude of 40°S, close to the present position of the West Somali basin. A 
second high-temperature component, found in three other sample sites in the Hakl and in the Thumi areas, is probably a 
chemical remagnetization related to the emplacement of the upper ophiolite nappe in late Maastrichtian to Paleocene times. 
Finally a last high-temperature component, found only in the two sites from Naft area, could be a post-tectonic 
remagnetization acquired in Oligocene or Miocene times or represents differential tilting of pillows and sedimentary blocks. 
The high-temperature components are usually fairly scattered due to the very complex tectonic history of the area. 
Nevertheless, the relation between the defined paleopoles and the Indian polar wander is unambiguous and the evolution of 
the Masirah ophiolite from formation up to the emplacement of the second ophiolitic nappe is clearly related to the 
northward movement of the Indian plate. This new paleomagnetic study rules out the possibility of a common or related 
origin for the Masirah and the Semail ophiolites.

Masirah and described the folded Upper Cretaceous 
Fayah Formation from the island. 
Paleomagnetic studies on ophiolites, predomi- 
nantly on the extrusive members and associated sedi- 
ments, are widely used for paleogeographic reloca- 
tion of ancient ocean floor fragments (e.g., Thomas 
et al., 1988; Perrin et al., 1994; Mubroto et al., 
1994). The magnetic mineralogy of lava may un- 
dergo large alterations during seafloor and emplace- 
ment-related metamorphism. However, since sea- 
floor alteration takes place shortly after the extrusion 
of the lava, the first secondary ore mineral formation 
of magnetite or maghemite after Ti-magnetite will 
record the same field period (e.g., Pr~vot et al., 
1979). Although the magnetic intensity is generally 
strongly reduced, the magnetization direction re- 
mains. An off-axis metamorphism in greenschist fa- 
cies may completely reset the magnetic signal to the 
prevailing magnetic field orientation. 
In the present study on lava from the lower 
Masirah ophiolitic nappe, we intend to support evi- 
dence for a complex structural evolution by paleo- 
magnetic methods and to reconstruct the origin of 
the lower Masirah nappe. This study is a contribution 
to the Masirah project led by Prof. Peters, University 
of Bern. 
2. Regional setting 
Recent detailed mapping at a scale of 1:50,000 
has revealed that Masirah is composed of two ophi- 
olitic nappes (Fig. 1; Marquer et al., 1995). A classic 
ophiolite sequence (Penrose, 1972) can easily be 
recognized, although the two nappes are strongly 
affected by pre- and post-nappe faulting. The two 
ophiolite nappes are composed of the following 
lithologic units: the base of the lower ophiolite nappe 
is nowhere exposed and the series starts with layered 
and foliated gabbros containing abundant melano- 
troctolitic to wehrlitic intrusions which bend and 
disturb the gabbro foliation. Small harzburgite out- 
crops are very locally exposed. The sheeted dike 
complex consists of half a meter (to few meters) 
thick dolerite dikes with no or weakly developed 
chilled margins. The dike swarms cut, in most locali- 
ties, the layered gabbros. The sheeted dike complex 
grades upwards into a sheet flow and pillow lava 
sequence which itself is overlain by pre-obduction 
Tithonian to Maastrichtian deep-sea to shallow-water 
sediments with alkaline volcanic or volcanoclastic 
interlayers (Immenhauser, in prep.). The oldest sedi- 
ments of Tithonian age give the age of the tholeiitic 
extrusives. The youngest flysch-type sediments of 
the Fayah Formation (Le M&our et al., 1992) are of 
late Maastrichtian age (Immenhauser, in prep.) which 
gives a maximum age for the thrusting of the upper 
nappe onto the lower (Marquer et al., 1995). The 
Fayah Formation contains boulders derived from 
continental crystalline basement. The sediments at 
the top of the lower nappe are folded and the under- 
lying pillow lavas are imbricated. As a result, the 
pillow lavas and sediments may be steeply dipping. 
The upper nappe was detached around the Moho 
(first occurrence of gabbros) and starts with harzbur- 
gites and few dunites. The sequence grades upwards 
into layered or foliated gabbros containing deformed 
wehrlitic to melanotroctolitic intrusions. The thick- 
ness of the crustal sequence is highly variable and 
the sheeted dike complex commonly intrudes mantle

peridotites. Pillow lavas are only found very locally 
in the upper nappe and represent the highest exposed 
levels. Granitoid intrusions, associated with isotropic 
and pegmatoid gabbros are found in peridotites and 
gabbros. The upper nappe is, in the northern part of 
the island, locally covered by Paleocene to Eocene 
shallow-water carbonates (Le M&our et al., 1992; 
Briner and Stucky, 1994), separated by a lateritic 
horizon from the underlying ophiolite. 
The sheeted dike complex is dominantly ENE 
trending (Moseley and Abbotts, 1979). The so-called 
"melange" of the Masirah fault (Moseley and Ab- 
botts, 1979; Shackleton and Ries, 1990) is the result 
of interference between the subhorizontal thrust 
plane, multiply offset by normal faults, and intersec- 
tion with a flat topography (Marquer et al., 1995). A 
composite profile of the two ophiolite nappes with 
the sandwiched sediments below the thrust contact is 
schematically shown in Fig. 2. 
Important stages in the geological evolution of the 
lower Masirah nappe are: 
(1) formation of tholeiitic extrusives (lower nappe) 
in the Tithonian; 
(2) alkaline volcanism associated with subvol- 
canic trachytes around 123 __+ 2 Ma (N~igler and Frei, 
1994; Immenhauser, in prep.). The volcanic rocks 
are locally deposited on serpentinites or gabbros and 
covered by Cretaceous shallow-water carbonates 
(Immenhauser, in prep.) which indicates important 
tectonic movements and uplift; 
(3) southward directed overthrusting of the upper 
nappe between the Maastrichtian and the Eocene 
causing folding in the sedimentary cover of the 
lower nappe. 
(4) post-Eocene (probably Miocene) NNE-SSW- 
oriented horst and graben formation related to exten- 
sion and followed by N-S- to NNW-SSE-oriented 
normal faulting. These late events are responsible for 
the different levels of Tertiary outcrops and for the

3. Sampling and mineralogy 
Eighty-four volcanic samples (Table 1) were taken 
in the well-exposed sheet flows and pillow and tube 
lavas from the top of the lower nappe with a water- 
cooled drill and oriented using both sun and mag- 
netic compasses. The sample sites are located in Fig. 
1 (sample 72 was lost at the outcrop). The sampled 
lavas are predominantly tholeiitic (Abbotts, 1981), 
aphyric, or contain plagioclase phenocrysts. They 
show a metamorphic overprint in prehnite-pumpel- 
lyite to greenschist facies with alteration of the ma- 
trix to chlorite (actinolite) in green lavas or to zeo- 
lite-smectite-hematite in red iavas (Abbotts, 1981). 
Magnetite-Ti-magnetite-maghemite and ilmenite are 
the dominant magnetic minerals in the rocks. Both 
minerals occur interstitially between plagioclase 
laths. Magnetite shows homogeneous colour under 
reflected light with local oxidation to maghemite- 
hematite. Ilmenite may show exsolution lamellae. 
Ilmenite or Ti-magnetite is commonly replaced by 
fine-grained rutile/anatase. Fine-grained hematite 
and iron-hydroxides are present in red lavas at the 
top of the pillow stack. 
Sedimentary bedding of radiolarian cherts at the 
top of the extrusives was used to define the paleo- 
horizontal. The paleo-horizontal in the Shinzi area 
was defined by well-bedded tuffite layers. The tilt 
corrections listed in Table 1 are the average tilt of 
these overlying deep sea type sediments found clos- 
est to the sample localities. The variable tilt of the 
sediments along the island creates uncertainties for 
the corrections to apply to sample localities which 
are far from any sedimentary outcrop. Moreover, 
sediments in the Naft and Thumi area are commonly 
isoclinally folded with axial fold planes subparallel 
to the strongest dip of the sedimentary bedding and 
also subparallel to sheet flow and lava tube surfaces. 
4. Methods and results 
Standard size specimens were cut from the cores 
in the laboratory and the Normal Remanent Magneti-

CTF cryogenic magnetometer. All samples were

shielded furnace with 50 ° steps. After each heating 
step, the magnetic susceptibility at room temperature 
was monitored using a Bartington bridge. The com- 
ponents of magnetization were defined by principal 
component analysis (Kirschvink, 1980). Site means 
were calculated using Fisher (1953) statistics.

The paleopoles obtained from the Masirah sam- 
ples are listed in Table 4 and presented in Fig. 5 
together with the Master Polar Wander Paths 
(MPWP) for the Indian, African and Eurasian plates 
of Besse and Courtillot (1991). This figure shows 
that several sites have poles on or close to the Indian 
MPWP. If we assume that the determinations for 
these sites are correct, we can estimate the corre- 
sponding time of lava formation and remagnetiza- 
tion. The results for the lower Masirah nappe indi- 
cate an origin at a latitude of 38 ___ 12°S, followed by 
a northward movement together with the Indian plate 
and a metamorphic event at a latitude around 5 _+ 5°S 
sometime between 60 and 50 Ma (Fig. 6). This local 
reset of the paleomagnetic signal in lava of the lower 
nappe seems to be due to the southward directed 
emplacement of the upper Masirah ophiolite nappe
