As long as we have no truly positive fold test, the 
possibility that all measured directions are secondary 
cannot be ruled out completely. This would mean 
that all volcanic rocks were remagnetized during 
folding and imbrication and subsequently affected by 
differential rotations (e.g., ParEs et al., 1994), which 
could explain the dispersion in declination when the 
data are considered in situ. The striking coincidence 
of at least two of the tilt-corrected poles with the 
Indian MPWP makes us prefer the first interpreta- 
tion. 
5. Conclusions 
The two-nappe structure of Masirah island and the 
paleomagnetic indications reported in this study sug- 
gest that Masirah is neither a laterally displaced part 
of the Semail ophiolite nor an in-situ uplift of the 
Indian Ocean floor. The high-temperature directions 
of several sites indicate an origin at latitudes of 
38 _+ 12°S. The evolution, however, between its for- 
mation in the Tithonian (around 145 Ma) and the 
emplacement of the second nappe around the Creta- 
ceous/Tertiary boundary seems to be related to the 
Indian plate. A change in the direction of movement 
of the Indian plate around 125 Ma as a result of the 
initial opening of the Bengali oceanic basin between 
Antarctica and India was proposed by Owen (1983). 
This opening initiated rifting between the Indian 
plate and the Madagascar microplate which is proba- 
bly represented on Masirah by a tectonic phase 
associated with alkaline magmatic activity at 123 _+ 2 
Ma (N~igler and Frei, 1994; Immenhauser, in prep.). 
Comparing different paleogeographic reconstructions 
for the time period 150-120 Ma there is a variation 
in paleo-longitude as large as 60 ° (Savostin et al., 
1986; Scotese et al., 1988; Powell et al., 1988) for 
the position of India. This uncertainity results in a 
highly variable size of the oceanic basin between 
Africa and Madagascar and Madagascar and India. 
The results confirm that between the late Maas- 
trichtian and the pre-Eocene a compressive event 
caused the obduction of the upper onto the lower 
ophiolite nappe. This is probably slightly prior to the 
final obduction of the lower ophiolite nappe onto the 
Arabian continental margin. The youngest Fayah 
sediments of the Batain area (Shackleton et al., 
1990) are of Maastrichtian age similar to Masirah 
island. However, it is not clear if the Fayah forma- 
tion is a special facies of the Aruma Group and 
related to the area of the Oman Mountains and the 
Semail Ophiolite (e.g., Shackleton et al., 1990; 
B6chennec et al., 1992) or if it is of allochthonous 
origin, related to the "Eastern Ophiolite belt". Sup- 
porting indications for a compressive event between 
the Indo-Pakistani and the Afro-Arabian plate at that 
time are found in Pakistan where similar obduction 
ages were obtained for the Muslim Bagh and the 
Bela ophiolites (Allemann, 1979; Mahmood et al., 
1995). This geological evidence may indicate that 
the 95% confidence bar from the paleomagnetic 
measurements shown in Fig. 6 (59.2 Ma) could be 
underestimated or that the Fayah Formation was 
deposited south of its present position (e.g., in the 
area of 5 + 5°S). These conclusions may further 
indicate that the western outline of the Indo-Pakistani 
plate was different in shape to the one generally used

E. Gnos, M. Perrin / Tectonophysics 253 (1996)53-64 63 
in paleogeographic reconstructions, or that the Indo- 
Pakistani plate moved closer to the Afro-Arabian 
plate in the Late Cretaceous. The obduction of the 
Semail ophiolite onto the Arabian continental margin 
seems to have occurred earlier (e.g., Allemann and 
Peters, 1972; Glennie et al., 1974; Tilton et ai., 1981; 
Tippit et al., 1981). This would indicate that where 
the ophiolite belts of the Oman Mountains (Semail 
ophiolite) and the "Eastem Ophiolite belt" overlap 
(e.g., Batain Coast), the Semail ophiolite would rep- 
resent the lower unit. However, the downflexure of 
the Arabian continental crust as a result of the 
obduction of the Semail ophiolite could have facili- 
tated the obduction of the "Eastern Ophiolite belt".

7. Magnetostratigraphic correlations
7.1. Composite polarity scale
The magnetic polarity pattern noted in the particu-
lar Permian±Buntsandstein formations is very simi-
lar. On this basis a composite polarity scale has been
.constructed Fig. 13 . This scale is not equally well
documented since the Lower Rotliegend polarity
scale is only approximate. It was established using
the results from separate outcrops mainly from the
upper part of Autunian. The majority of the second
and third Zechstein cyclothems were not recognized
magnetostratigraphically. The magnetozones were
distinguished using the results of the second or first
category of reliability. If the results were derived
only from one sample, then the polarity columns are
marked by shorter belts.
7.2. Illawarra Re˝ersal
The end of the Kiaman superchron i.e. Illawarra

end of the Kiaman was established in the lowermost

Triassic boundaries
In the Polish part of the CEB the
ZechsteinrBuntsandstein boundary is defined as a

All facts presented above support the theory that
the ZechsteinrBuntsandstein boundary in the Polish

8. Summary
The paleomagnetic studies of Permian±Early Tri-
assic rocks sampled in the outcrops and unoriented
boreholes from the Polish part of the Central Euro-
pean Basin allow creation of a composite magne-
tostratigraphic scale. Magnetostratigraphic correla-
tion with the standard magnetostratigraphic scale
shows that the Illawarra Reversal in the Polish sec-
tions is either located in the lower part of the Upper
Rotliegend or might have not been recorded because
of the stratigraphic gap postulated between the Lower
and Upper Rotliegend formations. The magnetic po-
larity record and biostratigraphical and sedimento-
logical evidence indicate that the Zechstein rBunt-
sandstein boundary marked in the Polish sections is
close to the Permian rTriassic boundary defined as
the bottom of the Griesbachian stage. The Gries-
bachian±Dienerian age of Lower Buntsandstein and
the lower part of Middle Buntsandstein, as well as
the early Anisian age of the whole or the majority of
the Rot Formation seems to be supported and docu-
È
mented by the magnetostratigraphic correlation. Sig-
nificant gaps or stratigraphic condensations near the
Middle BuntsandsteinrRot boundary are very likely.

Late Cretaceous palcomagnetism of the East Ranges island arc 
complex, Kamchatka: Implications for terrane movements 
and kinematics of the northwest Padfie 
Natalia M. Levashova I and Mikhail L. Bazhenov 1 
Geological Institute, Russian Academy of Sciences, Moscow 
Mikhail N. Shapiro 
United Institute of Physics of the Earth, Russian Academy of Sciences, Moscow 
Abstract. A Campanian-lower Paleocene island arc complex was sampled for pa!eomagnetic 
studies at 12 sites in the East Ranges tectonic zone of Kamchatka. After thermal demagnetization, 
a reversed polarity characteristic remanent magnetization (ChRM) was isolated from most 
volcanoclastic and basaltic units as well as from lava debris from intraformational conglomerates. 
The fold and conglomerate tests are positive, and the ChRM in the studied rocks is likely primary. 
The formation-mean inclination of 66.3 ø + 3.7 ø corresponds to a palcolatitude of 48.7 ø _+ 5.0øN 
which is about 20 ø lower than the Late Cretaceous North American reference values. Because 
northward displacement of the studied terrane is indicated by the palcomagnetic data, we examine 
several models of intraoceanic transport with the Pacific and/or Kula plates and coastwise transport 
after terrane accretion, far to the south of the present-day position of Kamchatka. Our preferred 
interpretation is that the studied island arc complex accumulated at about 83-79 Ma; the island arc, 
to which the studied terrane had originally belonged, was active between this time and 65-60 Ma. 
According to geological data, the docking time nearly coincided with cessation of volcanic activity, 
and northward movement of the island arc took place simultaneously with the volcanic activity. 
The absolute motion of a subduction zone should have the same direction as the overriding plate; 
therefore, the subduction zone related to the East Ranges island arc is inferred to have moved 
northward with the Kula plate or with the Kula and Pacific plates, successively, consuming either 
the oceanic periphery of a continental plate or some unknown minor oceanic plate. This process 
went on until 65-55 Ma when the island arc and related subduction zone approached the continental 
margin and became extinct. The proposed models also place additional constraints on kinematics of 
the Kula-Pacific transform plate boundary. 
Introduction 
Since the early 1980s, the tectonic evolution of northeast 
Asia and the entire circum-Pacific orogenic belt has been inter- 
preted according to the concept of tectonostratigraphic terranes 
[Marlow and Cooper, 1983; Debiche et al., 1987; Stavsky et 
al., 1990; $okolov, 1992]. The term \"tectonostratigraphic ter- 
rane\" presumes that a tectonostratigraphic unit, which is differ- 
ent from adjacent units, has been transported over a consider- 
able distance and juxtaposed alongside other units that had dif- 
ferent origins. While identification of a terrane and its bound- 
aries relies mainly on geological data, the original position of 
a terrane and its subsequent kinematics are derived mostly from 
in Kamchatka. Interpretations on the number of independent 
terranes, not to mention their original positions and subse- 
quent horizontal movements, are controversial [Watson and 
Fujita, 1985; Tsukanov, 199!; Geist et al., 1994; Shapiro, 
1995]. Palcomagnetic data can resolve many of these contro- 
versies by providing quantitative estimates of horizontal 
movements to test competing kinematic scenarios. Studies 
have been made in easternmost Kamchatka (East Peninsulas 
zone) [Bazhenov et al., 1992; Pechersky et al., 1997] and fur- 
ther to the north on Karaginsky Island. and Koryakia 
[Kovalenko, 1990, 1992], with most results being based on 
fully demagnetized data with confirmations from field tests. 
The available data from the main part of Kamchatka are of lower

tectonic zones (Figure 1). The West Kamchatka zone comprises

Campanian-Maastrichtian terrigenous rocks that accumulated 
on the continental slope [Shapiro, 1976]. Paleogene to 
Neogene rocks in this zone unconformably overlie Upper 
Cretaceous sediments and are represented by coal-bearing 
molasses, shelf sediments, and minor amounts of subaerial 
volcanics. To the east, the Median Range and East Ranges 
zones consist of Upper Cretaceous-lower Paleocene island arc 
complexes. The Median Range island arc complex is uncon- 
formably overlain by Eocene to Oligocene marine sediments 
and Miocene to Quaternary volcanics. This complex is thrust 
over the West zone along the Lesnov Thrust, which was active 
in the interval from 65-45 Ma. The boundary between the 
Median Range and East Ranges island arc complexes is hidden 
under sedimentary cover of the late Cenozoic Central 
Kamchatka basin. The easternmost (East Peninsulas) zone con- 
sists of Upper Cretaceous and Paleocene-Eocene volcanoclastic 
rocks of island arc affinity [Zinkevich and Tsukanov, 1992] on 
the Kamchatsky Mys, Kronotsky and Shipunsky Peninsulas, 
along the eastern coast of Kamchatka (Figure 1). The latter 
zone is separated from the Kamchatka mainland by a basin that 
is filled with Oligocene to Miocene marine sediments. The 
Kamchatsky Mys Peninsula is also regarded as the westernmost 
part of the Aleutian chain [Markov et al., 1972; Geist and 
Scholl, 1994] or as a separate tectonostratigraphic terrane 
[Watson and Fujita, 1985]. Eocene deformation (ca. 40 Ma) 
affected almost all of Kamchatka, with only minor deformation 
in the Miocene and Pliocene. In contrast, the main folding and 
thrusting events are of Miocene age in the basin that separates 
the East Ranges and East Peninsulas zones. 
Late Cretaceous island arc complexes are known from the 
Median Range and East Ranges zones. A Paleogene-Eocene 
island arc complex is recognized only in the peri-Pacific East 
Peninsulas zone. Oligocene-Miocene island arc volcanism 
occurred inland, partly overlapping the West and Median 
Ranges zones. Finally, in the Pliocene-Quaternary, island arc 
volcanism shifted eastward to its present-day position in east 
Kamchatka (Figure 1). 
The Kumroch Range makes up the northern part of the East 
Ranges zone, ERZ (Figure 1) which comprises strongly 
deformed Campanian-Maastrichtian to Paleocene-lower Eocene 
rocks that are unconformably overlain by weakly deformed 
middle Eocene to Miocene marine sediments and almost flat- 
lying Pliocene to Quaternary volcanics and continental 
deposits. In the west the ERZ is bounded by subvertical faults 
that separate it from the central Kamchatka depression, which 
is filled by Pliocene-Quaternary volcanics and continental 
deposits. Upper Cretaceous-lower Paleogene rocks of the ERZ 
are deformed into tight isoclinal tblds and thrusts with south- 
eastern vergerice. The steeply dipping Vetlov Thrust divides 
this complex into two subparallel bands. The eastern band 
(Vetlov subzone) comprises Paleocene-lower Eocene siliceous- 
tuffaceous clay stones with basalt lenses of oceanic and 
marginal basin affinity (Vetlov Formation). The western band 
comprises thick Upper Cretaceous volcanics of island arc affin- 
ity (Khapitsa Formation and its counterparts) which vary con- 
siderably both along and across strike as well as between thrust 
sheets [Shapiro et al., 1997]. The base of the sequence is never 
exposed; estimates of the age of the volcanic series are based 
on rare radiolaria in siliceous interbeds which indicate a late 
Campanian or Campanian-Maastrichtian, sometimes to 
Maatrichtian-Danian, age [Tsukanov, 1991]. In the south of 
the Kumroch Range, the Khapitsa Formation is overlain, con- 
formably and with gradual transition, by upper Paleocene ter- 
rigenous flysch. Folding and thrusting took place in the middle 
Eocene. 
Geochemically, the Upper Cretaceous-lower Paleocene vol- 
canic sequence of the ERZ is similar to volcanics of intra- 
oceanic island arcs like the Tonga arc [Magakyan et al., 1993].

This sequence resembles contemporaneous volcanics of the 
Median Range zone of Kamchatka and the Olutor zone of 
Koryakia; these three areas are sometimes regarded as a single, 
wide island arc [Zinkevich and Tsukanov, 1992; Shapiro,

Sampling 
We studied the Late Cretaceous Khapitsa Formation in the 
northern and southern parts of the Kumroch Range (Figure 1). 
Several thrust sheets with southeast vergence are recognized in 
the north (Figure 2). Some thrust sheets contain evidence of 
penetrative deformation like cleavage and boudinage, and are 
not suitable for sampling. Using lithological characteristics, 
the thickest thrust sheet can be divided into three members with 
gradual transitions between them. The lower member, which is 
about 1200 m thick, comprises distinctly interbedded greenish 
gray tuffaceous rocks. The beds generally dip to the northwest, 
with variable azimuth and dip. These rocks are fractured but 
have no cleavage, and no systematic grain reorientation was 
observed. Samples were taken from sites 1, 2, 5, and 11 in the 
upper part of this member (Figure 2, Table 1); the exact strati- 
graphic relationships of these sites, however, are unknown. 
The middle member, which is 1500 to 1800 m thick, con- 
sists mainly of conglomerates, agglomerated basalts, and 
andesitic-basaltic tuffs with subordinate interbeds of finer- 
grained tuffs that are cut by thin sills. These sills apparently 
formed almost contemporaneously with host rocks, because 
petrologically similar volcanics are abundant in conglomerates 
both below and above these sills. Samples were taken from the 
three sills and their baked contacts (sites 6, 7, and 10), as well 
as from the fine-grained tuffs (sites 8 and 9). The thin strati- 
graphic intervals studied at each site (Table 1) are separated by 
much thicker layers of coarse-grained rocks. Volcanic debris, 
which is petrograpically similar to that of the sills, was sam- 
pled t¾om a thick conglomerate layer (site 4). 
The upper member, which is about 1000 m thick, consists of 
irregularly interbedded tuffaceous beds of varied grain size. The 
uppermost fine-grained part of the section was either not 
exposed in the studied area or was metamorphozed by Pliocene 
intrusions. As the result, only the lower portion of the upper 
member was sampled (site 12). 
Site 3 was sampled from another, structurally lower, thrust 
sheet (Figure 2) where the division into three members cannot 
be made, and the rocks differ from the upper thrust sheet in 
color and are more zeolitized.

The southern locality (Figure 1; a separate map is not given) 
is characterized by tight N-S trending folds with subvertical 
axial planes. The cores of the anticlines and synclines are 
composed of the Khapitsa Formation and terrigenous flysch, 
respectively. The main folds are cut by numerous small faults, 
with conjugate short-wavelength folds. In general, the Upper 
Cretaceous rocks resemble those of the middle member at the 
northern locality, but zeolitization is stronger, and fewer 
coarse-grained rocks are exposed; in particular, the conglomer- 
ates are absent. Seventy five samples were taken from fine- 
grained tuffs at eight sites. 
The true stratigraphic thickness of the studied outcrops, 
which were treated here as sites, varies from several meters to 
about 200 m (Table 1). One hand block, oriented with a mag- 
netic compass, was taken from each stratigraphic layer, with 
samples being spaced more or less uniformly across the sam- 
pled outcrops. Between one and tour (usually three) cubic spec- 
imens were cut from each block in the laboratory. 
Laboratory Treatment 
One to three cubic specimens from each hand sample were 
thermally demagnetized in 12-16 steps in home-made ovens 
with internal residual fields of about 10 nT. All measurements 
were made on a JR-4 spinner magnetometer with a noise level 
of 0.05 mA/m. The characteristic remanent magnetization 
(ChRM) was determined without anchoring the final linear 
segments to the origin of vector component diagrams 
[Kirschvink, 1980]. ChRMs isolated from sister specimens of 
a hand sample were used to calculate sample means, which, in 
turn, were used to calculate site means. 
Results 
Apart from an unstable remanence removed below 300øC to 
350øC, no consistent directions were isolated from Upper 
Cretaceous rocks from the southern locality, and the entire col- 
lection was discarded. In contrast, similar rocks from the 
northern locality yielded much better data; these data, however, 
are of variable quality. 
Lower Member of the Khapitsa Formation (Sites 1, 2, 5, 
and 11) 
After removal of an unstable remanence at 200øC, the natural 
remanent magnetization (NRM) in most greenish gray tuffa- 
ceous rocks is accounted for by a single ChRM above 250 ø- 
300øC (Figure 3a). The ChRMs generally display a rectilinear 
decay to the origin of the vector component diagram, although 
some are not directed to the origin (Figures 3a and 3b). The 
directions, on average, remain the same irrespective of whether 
the linear segments of the ChRM pass through the origin. 
Complete demagnetization of these rocks, however, was often 
prevented by acquisition of spurious remanence components 
above 500øC. 
In some samples, another remanence component is present 
at low to intermediate temperatures (Figure 3b). Although rep- 
resented by rectilinear segments on demagnetization plots, 
this remanence probably results from partial overlap of 
unblocking temperature spectra of a recent overprint and the 
ChRM. Judging by maximum unblocking temperatures, the 
ChRM appears to reside dominantly in magnetite. After tilt 
correction, the ChRM points upward to the southeast except for 
two samples where this component is of opposite polarity. The

Lava Boulders From an Intraformational 
Conglomerate (Site 4) 
The conglomerate test was performed on 24 lava boulders 
from site 4 (Figure 2). The NRM in the boulders contains a low- 
temperature overprint with a dominant linear component that 
decays to the origin of the diagram (Figures 5a and 5b). In a few 
samples, another component is present at intermediate temper- 
atures (Figure 5c), and the high-temperature component was 
interpreted as the ChRM. ChRM directions are chaotically dis- 
tributed (Figure 5d), and the normalized vector-resultant of 
0.265 is much less than the critical limit of 0.334 for a random 
distribution [Mardia, 1972]. Site 4, where the lava boulders 
were sampled, lies within the middle member of the Khapitsa 
Formation, near sites 1, 2, and 5 in the lower member. On the 
other hand, the rocks from the lower and upper members show 
similar demagnetization characteristics. Thus we interpret the 
positive conglomerate test to be indicative of a primary age for 
the ChRM which we interpret to be valid for the entire upper 
thrust sheet. 
Khapitsa Formation From the Lower Thrust Sheet 
(Site 3) 
After removal of an unstable remanence component at 200 ø- 
300øC, a well-defined ChRM was isolated from most samples 
from site 3, with almost all orthogonal plots decaying to the 
origin (Figures 6a to 6e). The ChRM persists up to 560 ø- 
570øC, which indicates that the ChRM resides in magnetite. 
Site 3 is the only site where the ChRM of many samples has 
normal polarity in stratigraphic coordinates, but ChRM direc- 
tions are scattered (Figure 6f). There is a cluster of northeast 
and downward pointing directions, with several samples 
having southeast declinations and either positive or negative 
inclinations. The streaked distribution of directions hints at a 
possibility of a considerable overprint which remains unre- 
solved despite the apparently good demagnetization data. 
Whatever the origin of this pattern, we did not include these 
data in further analyses. 
Combined Data 
Site means from the lower and upper members of the 
Khapitsa Formation show considerable improvement in group- 
ing after tilt correction. However, a more rigorous comparison 
[McFadden and Jones, 1981] indicates that the mean of site 12 
is statistically different from the other four directions: the cal- 
culated F statistic is 4.45, whereas the corresponding critical 
value is 1.99 (Table 2). Because site 12 is spatially and strati- 
graphically distant from the other sites, and because the differ- 
ence is mainly in declination (Figures 4e and 4t), we attribute 
this divergence to a clockwise rotation or a tilt of the area 
around site 12 relative to the other studied areas. The positive 
fold and conglomerate tests indicate that the ChRM in these 
members of the Khapitsa Formation is probably primary. For 
calculation of the mean inclination for these members, the 
inclination-only statistics [McFadden and Reid, 1982] was ap- 
plied to obtain the value that is used in later analyses (Table 1). 
Poorer consistency of results from the middle member of the 
Khapitsa Formation cannot be attributed to local rotations 
because all of the sites were sampled close to each other (Figure 
2), and site means differ in both declination and inclination 
(Figures 4c and 4d, Table 1). This member consists mainly of 
conglomerates and agglomerated tuffs with rare, thin, fine- 
grained tuffs and sills. This, and scarcity of outcrops, enabled 
us to sample only thin beds at each site (Table 1). Tuffaceous 
rocks can accumulate rapidly, and deposition of a 2-m-thick 
layer could occur (geologically) almost instantaneously. 
Cooling of a few-meter-thick sill and its baked contact to well 
below the Curie temperature also takes a relatively short time. 
We hypothesize that the large scatter of site-means from this 
member is due to poor averaging of secular variation within 
each site; the observed grouping of these five site mean direc- 
tions does not contradict the above explanation. If the above 
explanation is correct, the site means from the middle member

Comparison of Paleolatitude Data From This 
Study With Reference Values 
The positive fold and conglomerate tests suggest a primary 
origin of the ChRM in the rocks from the lower and upper 
members of the nearly 5-km thick Upper Cretaceous-lower 
Paleocene island arc complex. Relatively thick stratigraphic 
intervals were studied at the accepted sites and the tight group- 
ing of tilt-corrected site means (Table 1) imply adequate averag- 
ing of secular variation. We assume that the overall mean 
inclination is an unbiased estimate or; the geomagnetic field at 
the place where this complex accumulated. 
Tilt-corrected mean inclinations for the lower and upper 
members of the Khapitsa Formation are statistically indistin- 
guishable, at 65.9 ø + 3.8 ø and 68.4 ø + 7.6 ø, respectively.

These inclinations correspond to paleolatitudes of 48.2 ø + 
5.0øN and 51.6 ø + 10.8øN, respectively. According to the 
inclination-only analysis, that was applied to the upper and 
lower members of the Khapitsa Formation. The mean inclina- 
tion is 66.3 ø _+ 3.7 ø, which corresponds to a paleolatitude of 
48.7 ø _+ 5.0øN. 
The apparent polar wander paths for Eurasia and North 
America [Besse and Courtillot, 1991] recalculated to the study 
area (56øN, 161øE) predict Late Cretaceous paleolatitudes of 
about 68ø-70øN. The observed value is much lower than 
expected, and northward transportation of the East Range ter- 
fane (ERT) is strongly indicated by the data. We examine two 
end-member models to accommodate such transport: (1) coast- 
wise transport of the island arc terrane alter its accretion far to 
the south of Kamchatka; (2) intraoceanic transport within the 
Pacific and/or Kula plates. All calculations were made in the hot 
spot reference frame. Before making kinematic models, how- 
ever, it is necessary to examine the constraints imposed by 
geophysical and geological data. 
Limits on Tectonic Reconstruction 
Limits Imposed by the Plate Motion History 
The study area is most likely to have been a part of North 
America [Chapman and Solomon, 1976; Cook et al., 1986; 
Riegel et al., 1993], and the tollowing discussion is based on 
this assumption. At 85 Ma the Kula plate formed t¾om the 
ancestral Farallon plate and was separated from the Pacific plate 
by a northwest trending transform fault, the location and sub- 
sequent movement of which are poorly known; it can only be 
presumed that the Kula-Pacific transform boundary had been 
moving westward between 85 and 43 Ma [Engebreison et al., 
1985]. Since 66-61 Ma, this boundary was to the east of the 
East Peninsulas island arc, which probably became active in 
the central-northern Pacific Ocean [Pechersky et al., 1997]. 
After 85 Ma the relative movement of the Kula (Pacific) and 
North American plates was compensated at their convergent 
boundary; the sense of subduction and the position of the plate 
boundary, however, are not clear. This configuration probably 
remained somewhat the same up to 43 Ma, when the Kula- 
Pacific spreading center became extinct. After 43 Ma the 
Pacific plate began to move west-northwest, subnormal to the 
Eurasian margin [Engebretson et al., 1985]. 
Limits on the Age of the Studied Complex 
Paleontological data [Tsukanov, 1991] point to a 
Campanian-Maastrichtian to early Paleocene age for the studied 
formation, but the ages are not well constrained. AS the age of 
the studied formation and its original paleolatitude derived from 
paleomagnetic data are crucial for reconstruction of terrane 
kinematics, the < 20 Myr imprecision in the age of the data 
renders any consequent analysis unconvincing. It would be all 
the more true for terranes that could move with the rapidly mov- 
ing Pacific and/or Kula plates. We tried to further constrain the 
age of our results using the fact that reversed polarity prevails 
in the studied rocks. It is unlikely that normal polarity epochs 
always coincided with hiatuses in sedimentation. Despite the 
imperfect coverage of the Khapitsa Formation by sampling 
sites, the dominance of reversed polarity in the collection indi- 
cates that the accumulation of this formation most probably 
correlates with the longest reversed polarity chron in the Late 
Cretaceous, which are of either early Campanian (83-79 Ma) or 
mid-Maastrichtian (72-70 Ma) age [Cande and Kent, 1992]. It 
is worth noting that mean inclinations for the lower and upper 
members of the studied thrust sheet art very similar (Table l). 
This observation is also in accord with the above assumption 
on relatively rapid accumulation of these rocks. 
Limits on Docking Time 
With major angular unconformiy, marine middle Eocene 
deposits overlie the Upper Cretaceous-lower Paleocene vol- 
canic series, upper Paleogene terfigenous flysch deposits and 
the Paleocene-lower Eocene Vetlov Formation in the southern 
part of the ERZ, thus indicating a middle Eocene age for the 
main deformation event [Bakhteev, 1994]. This indicates a 
middle Eocene upper limit on the docking time of the ERT. 
At about 60 Ma the island arc was not far away from the con- 
tinental shelf, as indicated by the gradual transition from the 
Khapitsa island arc volcanoclastics to the overlying lower 
Paleocene continent-derived turbidites. Volcanic glass and 
pyroxenes systematically decrease through the 15-m transi- 
tion zone. In contrast. quartz, which was absent in the Khapitsa 
Formation, appears in increasing concentrations in this zone. 
Sandstones in the flysch are of varying composition, with 
high quartz content; their accumulation most likely resulted 
from erosion of a large continental landmass [Shapiro et al., 
1992]. The flysch contains thick lenses of coarse-grained 
sandstones with angular or semirounded siltstone debris at the 
base of lenses, which indicate relative proximity to the prove- 
nance area. This flysch, though not a proximal deposit sensu 
stricto, accumulated close to the continental slope, and the 
island arc was unlikely to have been more than a few hundred 
kilometers away from the provenance area. Therefore the sub- 
duction zone that separated the oceanic plate from a continental 
plate to which northeast Asia belonged, should have become 
extinct simultaneously with the cessation of volcanic activity 
in the related island arc, about 60 Ma. Thus the lower limit on 
docking of the ERT to the Eurasian margin is constrained by 
the age of the terrigeneous deposits that overlie the island arc 
complex. 
Cessation of volcanic activity in the ERT island arc nearly 
coincides with two other events. First, activity on the Lesnov 
Thrust, which is the suture between the continental margin 
(West zone) and Upper Cretaceous volcanoclastic complexes 
(Median Range zone), probably occurred at 65 to 45 Ma. 
Second, volcanic activity had started at the Kronotsky island 
arc at the beginning of the Paleocene (66-61 Ma [Pechersky et 
al., 1997]), thus manifesting the formation of a new subduction 
zone between northeast Asia and the oceanic plates. Hence, 
since about 65 Ma, the cotvergence of continental and oceanic 
plates was mainly accommodated by subduction under the 
Kronotsky island arc. 
These three events are probably interrelated. The collision 
of the frontal part of the Cretaceous island arc with the conti- 
nent probably led to cessation of volcanic activity, active 
thrusting along this front and accumulation of continent- 
derived deposits, and the formation of a new subduction zone in 
its rear because of the need to consume the rapidly moving 
oceanic plates. If this scenario is correct, it is most likely that 
at about 65 Ma, the studied terrane was close to the continental 
margin and that collision had already begun. Thus we can 
assume that a docking time of 65-60 Ma for the studied tel'fane 
is probable. 
However, we cannot exclude the possibility that the colli- 
sion led to the main deformation event in the region. In this

24,852 LEVASHOVA ET AL.: CRETACEOUS PALEOMAGNETISM OF KAMCHATKA 
case, collision would have taken place between 55 Ma (the 
upper limit on the age of the rocks that overlie the island arc 
complex) and 45 Ma (the lower limit on the age of the rocks 
that overlie most of the folds and thrusts). Therefore we must 
consider both docking times. After collision, the ERT proba- 
bly moved either much more slowly or not at all with respect to 
northeast Asia. 
Coastwise Translation 
Paleomagnetic data imply that the studied island arc complex 
formed at about 20 ø to the south with respect to its present-day 
position. In principle, northward drift may result from a dis- 
placement within an oceanic plate (or plates) before collision 
with the continental margin, and/or postcollisional movement 
along strike-slip faults, as is well established, for instance, for 
the western margin of North America [Jarrard, 1986; Hagstrum 
et al., 1996]. The main cause of such coast-parallel movement 
is thought to be oblique collision [e.g., Kimura, 1986]. 
The Kula plate always moved subnormal to the Eurasian mar- 
gin, provided that the strike of the margin was more or less 
similar to that at present. Since 43 Ma, the Pacific plate moved 
to the west northwest, subnormal to the Eurasian margin 
[Engebretson et al., 1985]. Hence considerable coastwise 
transport is precluded in these situations (Figure 7). In con- 
trast, convergence of the Pacific plate and northeast Asia was 
more oblique before 43 Ma, and limited coastwise transport 
with the Pacific plate was possible. There are no direct geolog- 
ical observations concerning the presence of large sinistral 
strike-slip faults in Kamchatka; the paucity of outcrops of pre- 
middle Eocene rocks on Kamchatka, however, does not preclude 
their existence. 
At about 65 Ma a subduction zone, related to the East 
Peninsulas island arc, became active, and the relative move-

lntraoceanic Transport 
There are two possible ages of the studied island arc com- 
plex, 83-79 Ma and 72-70 Ma, and two intervals for the dock- 
ing of the ERT, 65-60 Ma and 55-45 Ma. Because the possibil- 
ity of considerable coastwise transport was already excluded, 
we have to assume that the studied terrane was drifting north- 
westward within a rapidly moving oceanic plate. 
Since 65 Ma, the Kula-Pacific transform boundary was to the 
east of the Kronotsky island arc and related subduction zone 
which moved with the Pacific plate [Pechersky et al., 1997]. In 
contrast, between 85 and 65 Ma, the East Ranges island arc 
could have moved either with the Kula or Pacific plates, because 
the location of the Kula-Pacific boundary for this period is 
unclear. It is also possible that the ERT drifted first with the 
Kula plate and then with the Pacific plate. 
As the emplacement could not have taken place before 70 Ma 
or after 45 Ma, the terrane trajectories can be backward modeled 
for docking times of 70, 65, 60, 55, 50, and 45 Ma [Debiche et 
al., 1987]. We calculated trajectories for the both the Eurasian 
and North American plates and found negligible differences. We 
consider four scenarios, based on transpositions of the rocks 
ages and docking times: 
Scenario 1: 72-70 Ma Rocks, Docking at 65-60 
Ma 
Because a terrane of this age could not reach the continental 
margin at about 65-60 Ma with either the Kula or the Pacific 
plate (Figure 8a-b), this scenario is rejected. 
Scenario 2: 72-70 Ma Rocks, Docking at 55-45 
Ma 
Volcanic activity started at the Kronotsky island arc at about 
65 Ma, thus manifesting formation of a new subduction zone 
between northeast Asia and oceanic plates. Theretore since that 
time the convergence of the continental and oceanic plates was 
mainly accommodated by subduction under this island arc. This 
reasoning implies that the ERT was moving within either the 
Kula or the Pacific plate t¾om 72-70 Ma until about 65 Ma; after 
formation of the Kronotsky island arc and the related subduc- 
tion zone, it continued moving with some unknown minor 
oceanic plate, separated from the Pacific plate by the

LEVASHOVA ET AL.: CRETACEOUS PALEOMAGNETISM OF KAMCHATKA 24,853 
Kronotsky island arc. There are, however, no traces of this 
minor plate in Kamchatka. The existence of a minor oceanic 
plate with the extinct Upper Cretaceous island arc within it 
necessarily implies the existence of a Paleocene-Eocene sub- 
duction zone on the continental margin because the minor 
oceanic plate had to be consumed somewhere. Paleocene- 
Eocene volcamsm in Kamchatka west of the Kronotsky island 
arc is scarce and is unlikely be related to a separate subduction 
zone. This scenario cannot be excluded, but it is improbable. 
Scenario 3: 83-79 Ma Rocks, Docking at 65-60 
Ma 
Movement with the Pacific plate predicts docking times at 
about 55 Ma (Figure 8a). We conclude that the studied terrane 
could not have moved permanently with the Pacific plate, and 
at least a part of its motion was accomplished with the Kula 
plate. Movement with the Kula plate for a docking time about 
65 Ma fits with paleomagnetic data and kinematic parameters 
within their uncertainties (Figure 8b). A scenario where the 
studied terrane moved with the Kula plate before ca. 75 Ma and 
then with the Pacific plate until collision with the continent at 
about 65-60 Ma (Figure 8c), also fits well with the available 
data. However, it is not possible to discriminate between the 
two scenarios. Regardless, both scenarios imply that the 
Pacific - Kula boundary was to the west of the ERT before 75 Ma 
and to the east of it after 65 Ma [Pechersky eta!., 1997]. Thus 
this plate boundary had to somehow shift eastward between 75 
and 65 Ma. 
Scenario 4: 83-79 Ma Rocks, Docking at 55-45 
Ma 
If the ERT was moving either with the Kula or with the 
Pacific plate, it had to reach the continental margin long after 
cessation of volcanism in the East Ranges island arc and the 
beginning of activity of the Kronotsky island arc. We can pre- 
sume that when the subduction under the Kronotsky island arc 
started, the ERT was close to the continental margin but had 
not yet collided with it. Kinematically, this scenario is indis- 
tinguishable from the previous one. It remains, however, 
unclear why the ERT became anchored without collision and 
how its final convergence with the Eurasia margin was accom- 
plished. On the basis of the evidence presented above , this 
scenario is not compelling. 
Therefore our preferred interpretation is that the ERT island 
arc complex formed at 83-79 Ma and arrived at the continental 
margin at about 65-60 Ma. 
Tectonic Models 
In addition to the East Ranges island arc, there is also the 
Campanian - lower Paleocene island arc complex in the Median 
Range zone of Kamchatka (Figure 1). The abovementioned two 
complexes are sometimes regarded as parts of one wide island 
arc [Zinkevich and Tsukanov, 1992; Shapiro, 1995]. We can 
also hypothesize the existence of either two coexisting active 
island arcs or just one island arc, which different parts having 
docked onto Kamchatka at different times. Accordingly, three 
models of the tectonic evolution of the northwest Pacific can 
be suggested for the Late Cretaceous. 
The East Ranges island arc was active t¾om 83 -79 Ma until 
about 60 Ma. Because we assume that the docking time of the 
ERT was about 65 - 60 Ma, the northward movement of the 
island arc coincided with its activity. If this movement had 
been continuous, the related subduction zone also had to move 
in the absolute reference frame. The absolute motion of a sub- 
duction zone should have the same sense of motion as the over- 
riding plate [Garfunkel eta!., 1986]. The observed northward 
movement of the Upper Cretaceous island arc indicates that this 
arc did not belong to the slowly southward moving North 
American plate, but rather belonged to a northward moving 
oceanic plate, most probably the Kula plate. This implies that 
the related subduction zone was dipping oceanward and was 
consuming oceanic lithosphere, presumably the oceanic 
periphery of a continental plate or some minor oceanic plate; a 
similar geodynamic situation now exists in the New Hebrides 
trench [Louat and Pe!!etier, 1989]. This process continued until 
the studied island arc became inactive at about 65 - 55 Ma. 
Model I 
We assume that two active island arcs coexisted in the Late 
Cretaceous. In this case, the Median Ranges island arc was near 
the continental margin (Figure 9a), and we presume the exis- 
tence of a minor oceanic plate (which has now completely dis- 
appeared) between the two island arcs. We know nothing about 
the kinematics of this plate and hypothesize that this minor 
plate had been subducting under the East Ranges island arc on 
one side and under the Median Range island arc near the conti- 
nental margin on the other. This process probably stopped by 
about 65 Ma. At that time, the minor plate should have already 
been completely subducted. 
Model 2 
In an alternative model the island arc complexes of the 
Eastern Ranges and the Median Range zones can be treated as 
part of the same northward moving island arc in the Campanian 
- Maastrichtian. As discussed above, the Kula- Pacific trans- 
form boundary had to be to the west of the ERT before 70-75 
Ma and to the east of it after 65 Ma (Figure 9b). This implies 
that an ancient island arc that comprised the island arc com- 
plexes of both the Eastern Ranges.and the Median Range 
zones, was drifting with the Kula plate before 75-70 Ma. At 
about 75-70 Ma, this island arc was divided into two parts by 
the Kula-Pacific transform boundary. The western part of this 
island arc, which is now the Median Range zone, continued 
moving with the Kula plate until it was emplaced. The eastern 
part of the island arc (East Ranges zone) then moved with the 
Pacific plate until its arrival at the continental margin about 65 
- 60 Ma (Figure 9b). 
Model 3 
Finally, the existence of a single wide island arc in the Late 
Cretaceous also fits the paleomagnetic results and kinematic 
data. It also accounts for the formation of the Lesnov Thrust 
simultaneously with cessation of volcanic activity at about 65 
Ma. On the other hand, the present-day width of the Median 
Range and Eastern Ranges zones together is 120 to 150 km, 
and geological data point to its shortening by factor of 2.5-3 
during subsequent folding and thrusting [Shapiro, 1995]. The 
original width of the ancient island arc thus amounts to about 
400 km, which is much wider than the modern intraoceanic 
volcanic zones. 
It is difficult to discriminate between the models described 
above. This situation may become clearer when reliable paleo-

Conclusions 
The prefolding, probably primary, characteristic remanence 
that was isolated from the Late Cretaceous island arc complex 
of the Eastern Ranges zone of Kamchatka suggests that these 
rocks formed at a latitude of 48.7 ø + 5.0øN which is about 20 ø 
south of the latitudes predicted for the Eurasian margin. 
Geological and paleomagnetic data imply that the most likely 
age of the studied rocks is 83-79 Ma. The Eastern Ranges island 
arc probably collided with, or was close to, the Eurasian margin 
at about 60-65 Ma. Kinematic calculations predict that this ter- 
fane was in the middle of the central-northern Pacific Ocean at 
83-79 Ma, and from that time until 65-60 Ma, it was moving 
northwestward either with the Kula plate or with the Kula and 
Pacific plates consecutively. Since approaching the continen- 
tal margin at 65-60 Ma, there were no significant movements 
of this terrane until the time of complete emplacement. 
The suggested tectonic scenario is in accord with geological 
data. Volcanic activity ceased at about 65-55 Ma. The conti- 
nent-derived Paleocene turbidires, which accumulated close to 
the continental slope, overlie the island arc complex with 
gradual transition, thus implying that the island arc became 
extinct when it was close to the continent. The formation of 
the Lesnov Thrust, the suture between the continental margin 
and the Upper Cretaceous arc-related complex, most probably 
occurred at 65-55 Ma. Because the convergence between the 
continental and oceanic plates was mainly accommodated by 
subduction under the Kronotsky island arc since 65 Ma, there is 
no likely mechanism for significant drift of the studied island 
arc after 65 Ma. Theretore, we assume that thrusting in central 
Kamchatka probably resulted from accretion of the Campanian- 
lower Paleocene island arc. 
Eocene deformation (ca 45 Ma) affected the Kumroch Range 
as well as most of Kamchatka. This deformation may have 
resulted from a jump of the subduction zone from its position 
close to the Kronotsky arc in the central-northern Pacific 
Ocean [Pechersky et al., 1997] to a new position along the 
Eurasian continental margin behind the already accreted Upper 
Cretaceous-lower Paleocene arc(s). This new subduction zone, 
which was responsible for Oligocene-Miocene volcanism in 
central Kamchatka, was active until the late Miocene. 
In conclusion, it is evident that paleomagnetic data enable 
the tectonic evolution of Kamchatka to be deciphered and that 
they also help to constrain the kinematics of oceanic plates, as 
is demonstrated for the Kula-Pacific transform boundary. 
Further interpretation is limited not only by the scarcity of 
paleomagnetic data but by poor age constraints on the main 
geological events that formed Kamchatka. Our understanding of 
the accretionary tectonics of northeast Asia and the kinematics 
of oceanic plates will greatly depend on obtaining reliable new 
paleomagnetic data and extensive work that must be directed at 
better dating of geological events.

Timing of the North-South China collision from new 
middle to late Mesozoic paleomagnetic data from the 
North China Block 
Stuart Gilder  and Vincent Courtillot 
Laboratoire de Palomagntisme et Godynamique. Institut de Physique du Globe de Paris, URA 729, Paris 
Abstract. We collected paleomagnetic samples from 43 sites of Middle and Upper Jurassic and 
Cretaceous rocks along a 250 km wide east-west trending belt located north of the suture between 
the North and South China Blocks. In each case, laboratory treatment isolates dual polarity, 
antipodal magnetizations that are demonstrably pre-folding. The paleomagnetic poles show very 
good coherence with coeval poles fi'om other localities from the North China Block (NCB), 
suggesting the apparent polar wander path (APWP) from the NCB is not distorted by post-Middle 
Jurassic local vertical axis block rotations. A comparison of the NCB APWP with that from the 
South China Block suggests that collision continued after the Early Jurassic and ended no later 
than the Late Jurassic. A cusp in the NCB APWP coincides with a marked angular unconformity 
that separates Middle Jurassic fi'om Upper Jurassic and younger sediments. Together, these 
observations indicate that the scissor-like collision and associated deformation ceased at the Middle 
to Late Jurassic boundary (- 159 Ma). The time of rapid (1 ø/Ma) relative angular velocity between 
the two plates (225 to 190 Ma) coincides with a peak in U-Pb and Ar-Ar dates obtained from 
metamorphic rocks in the suture. The combined Late Jurassic and Cretaceous paleomagnetic data 
from both blocks suggest that the united China plate traveled 2000 km north relative to Eurasia 
during the Late Jurassic before docking in the Cretaceous. This younger collision event is also 
marked by a cusp on the Cretaceous part of the Eurasian APWP. 
Introduction 
The eastern half of China contains two major tectonic 
blocks, the North China Block (NCB) and the South China 
Block (SCB), that are separated by the east trending Qinling 
(Dabie) suture (Figure 1). The suture is characterized by high- 
pressure, coesite and diamond bearing eclogites and a complex 
history of arc accretion [e.g., Wang et al., 1989; Xtt et al., 
1992a]. The eastern part of the Qinling belt is truncated by 
the north trending Tancheng-Lujiang (Tan-Lu) fault system 
(TLF on Figure 1). About 500 km north of the Qinling belt, 
another coesite bearing, high-pressure metamorphic complex 
crops out in Shandong and Jiangsu provinces, east of the Tan- 
Lu fault [Hirajima et al., 1990; Enami and Zang, 1990]. 
Similarities of metamorphic mineral assemblages and 
Precambrian stratigraphy suggest both metamorphic 
complexes were once part of the same belt that was later 
displaced by sinistral shear along the Tan-Lu fault [Xu et al., 
1987' Xtt et al., 1992b; Okay and Seng6r, 1992; Xu, 1993' Li, 
1994]. East of the Tan-Lu fault and south of the Shandong- 
Jiangsu (Sulu) metamorphic belt there are places where the 
Paleozoic stratigraphic sequence is typical of the SCB [e.g., 
Zhang eta!., 1984]. 
Early estimates for the age of amalgamation between the 
two blocks vary from Precambrian to Triassic with geologic 
evidence (age of metamorphism, etc.) yielding older ages

tectonic reconstruction of the collision based on 
paleomagnetic data suggests that the SCB and NCB first 
collided near the eastern part of the suture in the Late Permian, 
then progressively scissored together as the SCB rotated 
clockwise with respect to the NCB [Zhao and Coe, 1987, 
1989]. The progressive westward transition from marine to 
continental sedimentation along the suture supports this 
model [Y in and Nie, 1993]. Thus initial contact of the two 
plate margins likely occurred in the eastern part of the suture 
in the latest Paleozoic. 
The U-Pb and Ar-Ar isotopic dates of metamorphic rocks in 
the suture range from the Precambrian to the Cretaceous. 
Interpretation of the dates in recent studies agree that the older 
ones arc related to various tectonic events such as island arc 
collisions, while the younger, especially those between 235 
and 170 Ma, are related to a more extreme collision phase 
between the two major plates [Reischmann et al., 1990; 
Mattauer et al., 1991; Ames et al., 1993, 1996; Eide et al., 
1994; Hacker and Wang, 1995]. 
Age estimates for the end of collision and related 
deformation are ambiguous. Although some Ar-Ar dates of 
metamorphic rocks are early to middle Mesozoic in age, 
equally important are those with Cretaceous ages [e.g., Eide et 
al., 1994]. The younger dates could be related to exhumation 
of the metamorphic terrains or due to argon loss during 
heating from igneous intrusion and volcanism which occurred 
along the length of the suture in the Late Jurassic to Early

In this study we present Middle and Late Jurassic and 
Cretaceous paleomagnetic data from the NCB. These data are 
among the first fi-om the NCB to yield positive told tests. The 
poles are indistinguishable from coeval reference poles from 
the Ordos basin, which further substantiates the reliability of 
the paleomagnetic data from there and supports the notion that 
the NCB behaved as a rigid block. Together with the 
deformation patterns we observed in the field, the 
paleomagnetic data constrain the history of the NCB-SCB 
collision. 
Geology and Sampling 
We sampled middle to upper Mesozoic volcanics and red 
bed, lacustrine, and volcanoclastic sedimentary rocks along a 
250 km east-west trending belt just north of, and parallel to, 
the high-pressure metamorphic rocks that comprise the 
Qinling-Dabie suture in Anhui and Henan provinces (Figure 2). 
Normally, a site represents 8 to 10 samples obtained from a

In Henan Province we collected five sites of Lower 
Cretaceous air fall tuff (Chenpeng Formation) (Figure 2, 
locality d). Four of the Cretaceous sites consist of red air fall 
tuff interlayered with thinly bedded sandstones, the latter of 
which were used to orient the flows. One flow of purple-red air 
fall tuff that overlies the red air fall tuffs was also sampled. 
The Chenpeng Formation contains plant fossils of 
Piceoxrlon manchuricum Sze. and estherias: Eosestheria sp., 
E. elo,gata (Kobayashi et Kusumi), E. aff. middendorffii 
(Jones). and Bairdestheria sp. and unconformably overlies the 
Upper Jurassic Duanji Formation [Henan Bureau of Geology 
and Mineral Resources (HNBGMR), 1989, pp. 250-251]. A 
flow within the 5200 m thick Chenpeng Formation was 
isotopically dated (method unspecified) at 96.5 to 112 Ma 
[HNBGMR, 1989, p. 251]. 
We collected nine sites of Middle Jurassic red medium- to 
fine-grained sandstones and siltstones (Zhuji Formation) at 
two locations in Henan Province: one in Shangcheng county 
and the other in Gushi county (Figure 2, localities b and c). 
The outcrops in both places are considered Middle Jurassic 
because they are (1) thought to correlate with the fossil-rich 
Middle Jurassic Ma'ao Formation and (2) unconformably 
overlain by volcanoclastic sediments (Duanji Formation) 
whose ages are constrained by spore and pollen fossils as 
Upper Jurassic [HNBGMR, 1989, p. 237]. The red beds we 
sampled in Gushi county are intruded by 142 Ma telsic dikes 
[HNBGMR, 1989, p. 243]. At the Shangcheng locality, 
Proterozoic schists overthrust the Zhuji red beds, the latter of 
which contain large schistose clasts near the contact. The 
south dipping beds that we sampled there were mapped as 
overturned by previous workers (Wang Daoxian, field notes, 
1990). 
In Anhui Province (Figure 2, locality a) we collected 10 
sites of Middle Jurassic Zhougongshan Formation red 
siltstones and fine-grained sandstones, 40 km to the 
southwest of Hefei city. These red beds disconformably 
overlie Lower Jurassic Fanghushan Formation white-, yellow-, 
and gray-colored sandstones and siltstones that are locally 
interbedded with coal seams. According to the Anhui Bureau of 
Geology and Mineral Resources (AHBGMR) [1987, p. 151], 
the Zhougongshan sediments are coeval with the nearby 
Middle Jurassic Luoling Formation [AHBGMR, 1987, p. 162]; 
the latter of which contains plant fossils, Radicites sp., 
Elatoclatus sp., and Cladophlebis sp.: gastropods, Amnicola 
c.'fi Zhejiwgenis and Aphanotrhts sp.: ostracods, Darwinela 
impttdica, D. changxinensis, and D. ql'Z oblonga; and bivalves,

Psihmio sp., P. o,alis, P. chaoi, P. giganteus, P. a.l. suni, P.

sichttanensis, P. kweichottensis, P. ninttta, Margarittfera sp., 
Sibireconcha sichttanensis, and Tutuella rotunda [AHBGMR, 
1987, pp. 153-154]. 
In and around Huoshan county, we sampled 10 sites of 
Maotanchang and Heishidu Formation red beds, andesites, and 
volcanoclastic sedimentary rocks. The Upper Jurassic age 
assigned to these formations is constrained by abundant plant, 
bivalve. gastropod, and estheria fossils [AHBGMR, 1987, pp. 
151-152l. Also in and around Huoshan county, we sampled 
two sites of Lower Cretaceous Shibata Formation red beds and 
four sites of Upper Cretaceous Xiafuqiao Formation red beds. 
Remains of plants, bivalves, estherias, and ostracods found 
within the red beds constrain their ages [AHBGMR, 1987, p. 
167]. In Yecheng County we collected three sites of Heishidu 
Formation black shales (Figure 2, locality f). These rocks are 
interesting because we have not observed upper Mesozoic, 
lacustrine, sulfide and organic rich, relatively deep water, 
rhythmically bedded deposits like the Heishidu shales 
elsewhere in south or east China. 
Published stratigraphic sections in Huesban county, where 
some of our samples were collected (Figure 2), show an angular 
unconformity between Middle Jurassic and Upper Cretaceous 
rocks [AHBGMR, 1987, p. 168]. Other sections in nearby 
counties identify angular unconformities between Middle and 
Upper Jurassic strata, and Middle Triassic and Upper Jurassic 
strata, respectively [AHBGMR, 1987, p. 155]; in the Hefei 
basin (Figure 2, locality a) Middle Jurassic strata conformably 
overlie Lowel' Jurassic sediments, elsewhere, Lower Jurassic 
rocks conformably overlie Upper Triassic rocks [AHBGMR, 
1987, p. 153]. Altogether, these sections suggest that an 
angular unconformity separates Middle from Upper Jurassic 
strata. 
Included in Figure 2 are stereonets of the poles to bedding 
and bedding planes of the strata that we sampled for this study. 
The data are separated into two groups: Middle Jurassic and 
Late Jurassic through Cretaceous. The bedding orientations of 
the Middle Jurassic strata define an axial plane that parallels 
the east-west trending Qinling suture (N285 ø 02 ø, o95=9ø), 
whereas the Late Jurassic through Cretaceous strata have a fold 
axis that trends north-south (N354 ø 03 ø, c%5=10ø), orthogonal 
to the rcnd of the Middle Jurassic fold axis. These fold axis 
trends are significantly different at 95% confidence limits. 
Their difference in orientation further indicates that a regional 
tectonic event separates Middle Jurassic from younger 
sediments. Folding of the Middle Jurassic red beds thus likely 
occurred soon after deposition. Upper Jurassic and Cretaceous 
rocks were probably folded in the Cenozoic; beds of these ages 
that we sampled rarely have dips exceeding 30 ø (Table 1). 
Because (1) the axial plane of the Middle Jurassic folds 
parallels the Qinling-Dabie suture and (2) the axial plane 
defined by the folds of the younger sediments is orthogonal to 
the suture, it would seem that north-south directed 
compression acted in the Middle Jurassic and ceased in the Late 
Jurassic. Field and aerial mapping in the Qinling zone 
indicate that south China began extruding east with respect to 
north China in the Cenozoic and continues its eastward course 
relative to the NCB today [Pelt.er et al., 1985; Zhang eta!., 
19951. Thus Cenozoic folding may be linked to the India-Asia 
collision when the Qinling suture was reactivated as a left- 
lateral strike-slip fault in order to accommodate the extrusion 
of the $CB.

Cretaceous Chenpeng, Shibata, and Xiafuqiao 
Formations 
The Cretaceous results come from two rock types: air fall 
tuffs and red beds. Thermal demagnetization of tour sites of 
the red air fall tuff yields easily interpretable Zijderveld 
diagrams (Figures 6a and 6b). Two components are isolated: 
one that trends randomly but is often north and down directed 
(in-situ coordinates) at low temperatures (<300øC), and 
another with reversed polarity that decays toward the origin at 
high temperatures (>300øC). The red color and high 
unblocking temperatures (630ø-680øC) suggests the 
magnetization resides in hematite. The purple-red colored ash 
fall tuff from site C503 yields highly dispersed directions. 
This site was rejected from further analysis. 
The red bed sediments also yield easily interpretable 
demagnetization data. Two components were isolated, both of 
which are north and down directed (Figures 5c and 6d). The 
first component is isolated at low temperatures (<600øC) with 
a precision parameter maxima that occurs at 7+10% unfolding. 
The mcan LTC direction of the red beds at 0% unfolding

postfolding Middle Jurassic LTC direction, and thus both mean

confidence level. The prefolding, antipodal magnetization

Discussion 
The mean tilt-corrected directions from Table I are shown in 
Figure 7. The data indicate a progression in direction from the 
Middle Jurassic to the Cretaceous as inclinations steepen and 
declinations rotate slightly clockwise. Table 2 lists the poles 
from this study together with other Mesozoic to Present poles

difference between the two studies is that the carrier of the

Conclusions 
Pre-l,ate Jurassic poles from the NCB and SCB are 
significantly different at the 95% confidence level. Their Late 
Jurassic poles are indistinguishable, implying that the 
collision of the two plates was over before or during the Late 
Jurassic. Near Middle Jurassic time, the uncertainties of the 
paleomagnetic poles and larger time window of the pole from 
the SCB hampers a more precise answer as to when collision 
terminated. Middle Jurassic fold axes and AMS maximum 
eigenvalue directions are oriented parallel to the suture, and 
some Middle ,lurassic beds are overturned, suggesting that 
compression normal to the suture continued after the Middle 
Jurassic. Upper ,lurassic and Cretaceous fold axes are oriented 
orthogonal to the suture, and the bedding dips of these rocks 
rarely cxccecl 3() ø implyino that compression acting 
pcrpenclicular t() the suture ceased in the Late Jurassic. These 
observations support published stratigraphic sections that 
show an anular unconformity separatino Middle Jurassic from 
younger heels. Taken together, the best estimate for the end of 
collision is near the Middle to Late Jurassic boundary with an 
uncertainty that extends to the means of those series, namely, 
159+1()/-8 Ma [Gradstein et al., 19941. 
For he case of the NCB-SCB collision, palcomagnetic 
studies have successfully identified the timing and kinematics 
of the entire collision process suggestinc, that the two plates 
first contacted in the late Paleozoic and were fully sutured by 
about 160 Ma. Paleontologic data coincide well with the 
paleomagnetic data regarding when the plates came into 
contact. The scissor-like closure was accompanied by a suture- 
parallel change from marine to continental sedimentation, 
with the transition youaging westward. The time of rapid 
relative rotation (lø/Ma) is marked by a peak in U-Pb and Af- 
Ar dates of rocks associated with the collision. The end of 
collision is characterized by a regional angular unconformity, 
a change in the major strain axis orientation from suture- 
normal to suture-parallel, concordance of the paleomagnetic 
poles from both plates, and also a cusp on the NCB APWP. 
Indeed, the identification of cusps in APWPs may be another 
way to date continental collisions. The cusp near the Middle 
to Late Jurassic part of the NCB APWP occurs when the NCB 
and SCB poles converge. This cusp would thus carry the same 
kind of memory of a major collisional event, as do the 130-70 
Ma and 50 Ma features which shape the Eurasian APWP.

ABSTRACT
A magnetic polarity stratigraphy and a
corresponding paleomagnetic pole position
are reported from 113 sampling sites repre-
senting 3000 m of Upper Triassic continental
sedimentary rocks that crop out in the Dan
River–Danville basin of North Carolina and
Virginia. Characteristic magnetizations iso-
lated by thermal demagnetization for either
the hematite-bearing red siltstones or the in-
terbedded magnetite-bearing gray to black
mudstones of the Leakesville Formation are
indistinguishable in mean direction and pass
reversal tests. The magnetic polarity sequence
consists of 11 magnetozones that vary from
»100 m to 800 m in thickness and can be
uniquely correlated within biostratigraphic
constraints to magnetochrons E9n to E14n of
the Newark geomagnetic polarity time scale.
According to this correlation, the sampled
section is the age equivalent of the uppermost
Stockton, the entire Lockatong, and the low-
ermost Passaic formations of the Newark
basin, and represents »7.5 m.y. of deposition.
The late Carnian Dan River–Danville paleo-
pole is located at 55.4°N 100.1°E (A
95 = 1.9°),
which is not significantly different from pale-
opoles reported from essentially coeval rocks
in the Newark basin. Considering that the
Dan River–Danville and Newark basins are
»600 km apart, the close agreement of the co-
eval paleopoles argues strongly for the overall
tectonic coherence of these rift basins with re-
spect to each other and, most probably, with
respect to cratonic North America. Discor-
dant latest Triassic paleopoles from the south-
western United States, which have tended to
be attributed to fast apparent polar wander
for North America in the Late Triassic and
predict anomalously high paleolatitudes for
eastern North America, are best accounted
for by a large net clockwise rotation of the
Colorado Plateau.
INTRODUCTION
An extensive series of rift basins developed in
eastern North America in the Late Triassic and
Early Jurassic during the initial rifting of Pangea
(Fig. 1). These rifts filled with thousands of me-
ters of continental sedimentary and igneous
rocks of the Newark Supergroup (Olsen, 1978;
Froelich and Olsen, 1984). The largest of the ex-
posed basins is the Newark basin, where paleo-
magnetic studies of outcrop sites have outlined a
magnetic polarity stratigraphy (McIntosh et al.,
1985; Witte and Kent, 1989, 1990; Witte et al.,
1991) and have documented an interval of slow
apparent polar wander (Kent and Witte, 1993).
However, the interpretation of paleopoles from
the Newark basin as representative of North
America has been challenged because of appar-
ently conflicting paleomagnetic results from the
southwestern United States (e.g., Molina-Garza
et al., 1995), prompting suggestions that tectonic
rotations may have distorted the paleomagnetic
record in some of the Newark basins (e.g., Ko-
dama et al., 1994a). A detailed reference section
of geomagnetic reversals and Milankovitch
cyclic climate change was obtained for the
Newark basin from study of more than 6500 m
of core recovered under the Newark Basin Cor-
ing Project (Kent et al., 1995; Olsen et al, 1996;
Olsen and Kent, 1996). This complete 30 m.y.
record provides a framework for making specific
comparisons and tests of the stratigraphic and
tectonic development of other Newark Super-
group sequences.
This study focuses on the Dan River–
Danville basin, located 600 km south of the
Newark basin (Fig. 1). Our objectives are to de-
velop a magnetostratigraphy for precise tempo-
ral correlation to the Newark basin, and to use
the corresponding paleomagnetic pole position
for assessing the tectonic coherence of the
Newark rift basins.
GEOLOGIC SETTING AND SAMPLING
Of the 20 or so exposed Newark rift basins,
the Dan River–Danville basin has an exception-
ally large aspect ratio in outcrop, being more
than 165 km long but less than 15 km wide
(Fig. 1, a and b). The basin is bounded on the
northwest by the Chatham fault zone, a south-
east-dipping normal fault system trending about
N30°E. The sedimentary rocks in the basin dip
20° to 50° toward this fault system and generally
rest unconformably over basement along most of
the southeastern margin of the basin. A dual sys-
tem of nomenclature has evolved from the map-
ping by Meyertons (1963) of the Danville basin
in Virginia and by Thayer (1970) of the Dan
River basin in North Carolina. The sedimentary
rocks in the basin are referred to as the Dan
River Group (Thayer, 1970) and have a strati-
graphic thickness of up to more than 4000 m.
The rocks we sampled are partly in Virginia and
partly in North Carolina, and to avoid nomen-
clatural confusion are referred to here as Leakes-
ville Formation (Meyertons, 1963). Late Carnian
pollen, spores, and vertebrates have been found
in the lower and upper Cow Branch Members of
the Leakesville Formation (Robbins and Tra-
verse, 1980; Olsen et al., 1982; Thayer et al.,
1982; Olsen and Gore, 1989).
To assemble a continuous stratigraphic se-
quence, we concentrated paleomagnetic sam-
pling along two overlapping transects of the basin
stratigraphy. The Eden section in North Carolina
was sampled at 28 sites with generally 3 or more
oriented drill-core samples per site in fresh expo-
sures in an unnamed creek bed in the town of
Eden (Fig. 1c). The section begins just above
cyclic gray to carbonaceous black mudstones of
the lower Cow Branch Member and covers
»550 m of reddish to gray siltstones and sand-
stones of the unnamed division of the Leakesville
Formation to just below a covered interval above
which are exposures of the upper Cow Branch
Member. The Cascade section, located »15 km
from the Eden section in North Carolina and Vir-

PALEOMAGNETIC RESULTS
The magnetic properties of the rocks sampled
in the Cascade and Eden sections are similar to
those encountered in the Newark basin sedimen-
tary sequence, especially in the Lockatong For-
mation. Thermal demagnetization of isothermal
remanent magnetization (IRM) suggests that
hematite (high coercivity, maximum unblocking
of 680 °C; Fig. 2, a and b) is the principal carrier
of remanence in the buff to reddish clastic units
(collectively termed “red siltstones” hereafter)
that occur in the unnamed division and the Cas-
cade Station Member of the Leakesville Forma-
tion, whereas magnetite (moderate coercivity,
maximum unblocking at of 580 °C; Fig. 2, a and
c) and/or some f orm of ferromagnetic sulfide
(e.g., greigite or pyrrhotite, with moderate coer-
civity and maximum unblocking to only 350 °C;
Fig. 2, a and d) are the carriers of remanence in
the gray to black mudstones (collectively termed
“gray mudstones” hereafter) that are predomi-
nant in the upper Cow Branch Member.
The gray mudstones of the upper Cow Branch
Member are a generally difficult lithology for pa-
leomagnetic study due to the common presence
of sulfides, which do not seem to preserve an an-
cient magnetization in these rocks. For example,
the success rate of obtaining characteristic mag-
netizations was only 57%, compared to 86% for
hematite-bearing reddish rocks in the New ark
basin study (Kent et al., 1995). In the Cascade
section, we also encountered anomalously high
intensities of na tural remanent magnetization
(NRM) in a number of gray mudstone sites from
the creek beds. Samples collected in the quarries
have NRM intensities that range up to »10 mA/m
(mean, »1 mA/m), whereas some samples from
the corresponding interval sampled in Cascade
Creek have NRM intensities tha t range up to
10 000 mA/m, although the magnetic suscepti-

We attribute the anomalously high NRM intensi-
ties to lightning strikes that preferentially affected
the gray mudstones in the creek beds; these rocks
may be prone to effects of lightning because of
their lower coercivity magnetic minerals and im-
mersion in water, which provides a good path for
electric currents in an area of low topographic re-
lief. A total of 11 Cascade section sites that in-
cluded samples with ratios of NRM intensity to
susceptibility greater than 1 are suspected to have
undergone remagnetization b y lightning and
have been rejected on this basis alone.
Thermal demagnetization was used to resolve
components of NRM. A minimum of 10 demag-
netization steps to 575 °C was scheduled for the
gray to black mudstones, or to 675 °C for the
hematite-bear ing rocks, using techniques and
equipment described by Kent et al. (1995). Vec-
tor end-point diagrams illustrating the range of
NRM demagnetization behavior are shown in
Figure 3.
First removed by » 300 °C in most samples
not affected by lightning is a magnetization
(component A) aligned more or less along the
present-day field (Fig. 3, a–f). Parenthetically,
the gray mudstone samples with anomalously
high NRM intensities tend to have univectorial
magnetizations of various directions as another
signature of lightning effects. More than half
(58) of the remaining 91 sites in gray mudstones
(i.e., exclusive of those obviously affected by
lightning) show evidence for an ancient compo-
nent of magnetization that is revealed from 300
to »560 °C. This characteristic (Cm) component
has a shallow direction that is either southerly
(Fig. 3a) or northerly (Fig. 3b) in different sites.
In many of the other gray mudstone sites, there
is hardly any consistent magnetization remain-
ing above 300 °C (Fig. 3d). Alternating field de-
magnetization was not found to be effective in
resolving the characteristic magnetization in any
of the rocks (e.g., Fig. 3c).
A dual polarity characteristic (Ch) component
can also be resolved in most of the red siltstone
sites over the highest part of the unblocking tem-
perature spectrum, typically from 650 to 675 °C
(Fig. 3,e and f). However, between the unblock-
ing ranges of the A and the Ch components,
many of the red siltstone sites show evidence for
another magnetization; this Bh component has a
northerly and moderately down direction and is
most obvious in but not restricted to sites with a
southerly Ch magnetization (e.g., Fig. 3f).
Least-square line fits were used to determine
the component directions from the c hosen de-
magnetization intervals, typically 100–300 °C for
component A, 300–600 °C for component Bh,
350–575 °C for component Cm, and 650–675 °C
for component Ch. Component estimates with
maximum angular deviations (Kirschvink, 1980)
greater than 15° were rejected as poorly defined
except in a few cases where a great circle trend
was obvious and a stable end point direction was
used. Mean directions were calcula ted using
standard Fisher statistics (Table 1).
Component A was isolated in 142 sites repre-
senting all the principal rock types and has a mean
direction in geographic coordinates of declination
(D) = 351.8°, inclination (I) = 54.3, and a
95 = 1.8°
(Table 1). The A component lies in the vicinity of
the modern field direction (D = 352.5°, I = 66.2°)
and the time-averaged dipole field orientation (D
= 0°,I = 56°), consistent with a relatively recent
origin as a viscous magnetization.
Component Bh was isolated in 57 sites and has
a direction distinctly shallower than component
A in either geographic (D = 8.5°, I = 40.4°, and
a
95 = 2.9°) or bedding coordinates (D = 357.3°, I
= 18.2°, and a95 = 3.2°) (Fig. 4, a and b; Table 1).
The site-mean directions are somewhat but not
statistically significantly better grouped in geo-
graphic than in bedding coordinates. Its uniform
normal polarity, direction, and relatively high un-
blocking temperatures suggest that component
Bh is an overprint of ancient origin carried by
hematite.
Components Cm (60 sites) and Ch (53 sites)
each have a bipolar distribution of directions
(Fig. 4, c and d). There is an insignificant differ-
ence of only 5.1° between the bedding tilt cor-
rected means of the Cm and the Ch sites
(Table 1), suggesting that the magnetite-bearing
and hematite-bearing sites belong to the same
population of characteristic magnetizations. The
mean direction for all 113 sites after inverting to
common polarity is D = 0.3°, I = 3.6°, and a 95
= 2.5° in bedding coordinates. There is only a
slight improvement in grouping with bedding tilt
correction due to the relatively small variation in
structural attitudes; a fold test is therefore incon-
clusive as for the other components (Fig. 4,e and
f; Table 1). Northerly or normal polarity direc-
tions are found in 37 sites (mean D = 0.5°, I
= 6.2°, and a
95 = 4.4°) and southerly or reverse
polarity directions in 76 sites (mean D = 180.1°,

verse directions are within 3.8° of antipodal, pro-
viding a positive reversal test (class B; McFadden
and McElhinny, 1990) and indica ting that the
characteristic directions carried by magnetite or
hematite are not systematically biased by unre-
moved overprints. The Ch and Cm components
thus appear to represent magnetizations acquired

MAGNETOSTRATIGRAPHY
A virtual geomagnetic pole (VGP) was calcu-
lated for each site-mean characteristic component
direction after correction for bedding tilt and was
used to determine an overall mean paleomagnetic
reference pole (Table 2). The latitude of the site
VGP relative to the north axis of the mean refer-
ence pole provides a diagnostic index of polarity
for the delineation of magnetozones, approaching
+90° for normal polarity and –90° for reverse po-
larity. Identification of local magnetozones fol-
lows the nomenclature of Kent et al. (1995), in
this case using the prefix D for the Dan River–
Danville basin, an integer in ascending order from
the base of the sampled section to successive nor-
mal and reverse polarity magnetozone couplets,
and a suffix for the polarity (n for normal, r for re-
verse) of the constituent magnetozones.
The magnetostratigraphy of the Eden section
is based on characteristic magnetizations from
25 sites which delineate 5 magnetozones (D1n to
D3n), whereas data from 88 sites in the longer
Cascade section delineate 9 main magnetozones
(D1r to D5r) (Fig. 5). The Eden section should
overlap with the basal part of the Cascade sec-
tion according to regional stratigraphic relations
(Fig. 1c), and this is supported by the good
match in polarity magnetozones between the
two sections. The lower 1700 m of the Cascade
section is predominantly of reverse polarity, but
is punctuated by three normal magnetozones
that are each »100 m thick, two (D2n, D3n) in
the unnamed member in lower part of the sec-
tion, which are also found in the Eden section,
and another (D4n) that occurs at about the
1250 m level in the upper Cow Branch Member.
All reliable sites in the New, Main, and Old
quarries are from magnetite-bearing rocks and

Correlation of the Dan River–Danville com-

(Kent et al., 1995) can be made on the basis of
biostratigraphic constraints and then optimized
with magnetostratigraph y (Fig. 6). The upper

Lockatong Formation of the Newark basin. This
association allows an excellent match of the
magnetozones in which D1n to D6n of the Dan

E14n of the Newark basin. Within this target in-
terval, only the equivalent of the very thin sub-
