Magnetostratigraphy of Quaternary and late
Tertiary sediments on Banks Island, Canadian
Arctic Archipelago1
R.W. Barendregt, J.-S. Vincent, E. Irving, and J. Baker
Abstract: Sediments approximately 50 m thick from Banks Island (Canadian Arctic Archipelago) contain one of the longest
terrestrial records of Pleistocene climate changes in North America. Samples have been obtained from 126 horizons
distributed among four localitites, of which 116 horizons yielded acceptable paleomagnetic data. In sediments of the
Matuyama Reversed Zone, there are recorded at least two and possibly as many as five full continental glaciations, two
interglacial intervals, and a nonglacial interval at the beginning which is considered preglacial. Subzones attributable to the
Olduvai and Jaramillo are present within the Matuyama Reversed Zone. The Brunhes Normal Zone records three full
continental glaciations and three interglaciations. The Brunhes–Matuyama boundary occurs within interglacial deposits. The
preglacial Worth Point Formation records a climate milder than today, and cooler than that of the late Tertiary. Based on
floral, faunal, stratigraphic, and paleomagnetic constraints, a normal polarity sequence in the Worth Point Formation is
assigned to the Olduvai normal polarity subzone (1.95–1.77 Ma). The earliest direct evidence of glaciation on Banks Island
occurs in sediments that postdate the Worth Point Formation ( <1.77 Ma). Consequently, in the western Canadian Arctic, the
first continental glaciation postdated the first glaciation in the Canadian Cordillera (2.6 Ma) by at least a million years. The
overall mean direction of the Quaternary geomagnetic field in Banks Island does not differ significantly from the geocentric
axial dipole field, and these sediments contain no inclination error.

Introduction
Stratigraphic sections on Banks Island, in the southwestern
Canadian Arctic Archipelago (Fig. 1), provide a record of
multiple continental glaciations and interglaciations. All the
ice sheets originated from distant sources located to the south-
east of Banks Island on the Canadian mainland. The purpose
of this study was to apply paleomagnetism as a tool to define
better the chronology of events, and to relate them to the global
polarity time scale and the oceanic isotope record.
Vincent (1983, 1984, 1989, 1990, 1992) reconstructed a
sequence of nonglacial and glacial events (Table 1). At the
base, he identified a nonglacial interval recorded by the Worth
Point Formation. No glaciogenic sediments occur within or
below the Worth Point Formation, which he therefore consid-
ered to have been deposited prior to the onset of glaciation.
Glaciation began with the extensive continental Banks Glacia-
tion. Then followed a nonglacial interval (Morgan Bluffs
Interglaciation), another glaciation (Thomsen Glaciation), an
interglacial interval (Cape Collinson Interglaciation), and

The record of these events is best preserved at four locali-
ties: Worth Point, Duck Hawk, Nelson River, and Morgan
bluffs (Fig. 1). Paleomagnetic results described previously
from Duck Hawk Bluffs allow the assignment of preglacial
Worth Point Formation, sediments associated with the Banks
Glaciation, and interglacial beds of the overlying Morgan
Bluffs Formation to the Matuyama Reversed Zone (Vincent
et al. 1984; Barendregt and Vincent 1990). The uppermost
beds in the Morgan Bluffs Formation revealed a reversal tran-
sition to the Brunhes Normal Zone. The overlying deposits of
the Thomsen Glaciation, Cape Collinson Interglaciation, and
Amundsen Glaciation were normally magnetized and there-
fore were assigned to the Brunhes Normal Zone. In this paper,
we report new paleomagnetic data from the other three locali-
ties and combine them with earlier data from Duck Hawk
Bluffs to provide a general magnetostratigraphic framework
for the sequence of glacial and nonglacial events on Banks
Island. This framework is given in Table 2, in which, antici-
pating the results described below, the sequence of glacial and
nonglacial events recorded at the four localities is listed.
Paleomagnetic procedures
Although marine wave-cut bluffs provide relatively easy ac-
cess, there are many sampling limitations. Sections are af-
fected by permafrost, are sometimes disturbed by
glaciotectonic processes, and in places are scree covered.
Careful selection and cleaning of outcrops is therefore re-
quired. The common occurrence of very coarse grained depos-
its, particularly in tills, limits any attempt to obtain continuous
vertical sampling. At Worth Point Bluffs and Nelson River
Bluffs, all units occur in a single vertical exposure. At Duck
Hawk Bluffs and Morgan Bluffs, several sections were sam-
pled from which composite records were compiled on the basis
of sedimentological, stratigraphic, and magnetic polarity. Not-
withstanding these limitations, it has been possible to establish
a fairly complete and consistent magnetostratigraphy for the
four localities.
For the present work, samples were collected in 1983, 1988,
and 1992. Sections were, in many instances, cleaned down to
permafrost with jets of water pumped from the sea, left to thaw
for a time, and then trimmed to a vertical face by shovel and
trowel. Plastic holders (cubes in early collections, and cylin-
ders in later collections) were then pressed into the just unfro-
zen sediment and oriented by Brunton compass checked daily
against solar bearings. New data are described from one sec-
tion at Worth Point Bluffs (Fig. 2), one at Nelson River Bluffs
(Fig. 4), and six at Morgan Bluffs (Fig. 5). Previous data from
seven sections at Duck Hawk Bluffs (Fig. 3) are recompiled
herein.
Natural remanent magnetization (NRM) was measured on
automated Schonstedt spinner magnetometers. Twelve read-
ings were obtained from each specimen, yielding four deter-
minations of direction from which within-specimen precision
k
sn was calculated (Irving et al. 1985); ksn is a measure of in-
homogeneity of natural remanent magnetization within speci-
mens ( ks is a measure of inhomogeneity of specimens after
demagnetization). Pilot specimens were selected from each
section and demagnetized at 10 steps up to 100 mT. Based on
results from these, all other specimens were then demagnetized
at selected levels to determine the components present
(Figs. 6–10).
NRM intensities varied through three orders of magnitude.
Intensities at Worth Point and Duck Hawk bluffs ranged from
10
–4 to 10–3 A/m, and at Nelson River and Morgan bluffs from
10–3 to 10–2 A/m. This increase from east to west is compatible
with a source of detritus from Proterozoic mafic dykes and
lavas of Victoria Island and other up-ice igneous rocks to the
southeast. Many specimens have intensities approaching the
limit of detection of the magnetometers (10–4 A/m). Values of
ksn were highly variable, ranging from 2 to 150. Specimens
within which NRM was essentially randomly distributed (ksn <5 )
were rejected. During demagnetization,ks values generally de-
crease, often dramatically, as intensity falls, and when ks fell
below 5 processing was stopped and the specimen rejected.
Altogether 134 specimens, or 15% of the 908 specimens col-
lected, were rejected on the grounds that they contain no dis-
cernible record of the geomagnetic field. Of the samples that
yielded acceptable data, 45% were taken from beds of silts and
clays (including loess and rhythmites), 34% from tills, and
18% from fine sands.
The major objective was to establish a polarity stratigraphy.
A second objective was to obtain mean directions and pa-
leopoles for Quaternary time, for which more precise direc-
tions of magnetization are required. The identification of
polarity was made in this way. If, during demagnetization, the
inclinations remained positive and ≥45°, a specimen was des-
ignated as having normal polarity (N); if, during demagnetiza-
tion, inclination remained or became negative and ≥–45°, a
specimen was designated reversed (R). N and R magnetiza-
tions that have comparatively high internal precisions (k
s ≥ 29,
corresponding to a standard deviation <15°) are designated
N*, R*. N* and R* specimens, which are always silts or clayey
silts, typically have excellent end points and decayed linearly
to the origin on orthogonal diagrams. They are considered to
be good recorders of the geomagnetic field which can be used
to calculate mean directions and paleopoles. N and N*, R and

Worth Point Bluffs
Vincent (1990) identified four units resting on late Tertiary
fluvial coastal plain sediments of the Beaufort Formation
(Fig. 2, Tb). At the base are preglacial colluvial (unit 1) and
paludal (unit 2) sediments of the Worth Point Formation pre-
served as local valley fill. They contain rich in situ paleofauna
and flora, and conditions were sufficiently warm to allow
growth of conifers. These preglacial deposits are in turn over-
lain by a diamicton (unit 3), which Vincent considered to be
derived from the Bernard Till of the Banks Glaciation on the
basis of their similar pebble and matrix lithology. This diamic-
ton has been extensively reworked by periglacial processes
(see below). The sequence is capped by sands and gravels (unit
4) laid down in the Big Sea, a marine transgression which
covered extensive areas of Banks Island at the time of the
Thomsen Glaciation.
Samples from 11 m of colluvial sediments (unit 1) are re-
versed and assigned to the Matuyama Chron (Fig. 2). The
overlying 5 m thick upper paludal member of the Worth Point
Formation (unit 2) exhibits both polarities. At the base, thick
peat mats with silts are normally magnetized, whereas overly-
ing interstratified thinner peat mats and silts are reversed.
The diamicton of unit 3 is normal (Fig. 2). Laterally exten-
sive and overlying Big Sea sands and gravels (unit 4), associ-
ated with the Thomsen Glaciation, are also normal. The
Bernard Till at the nearby Duck Hawk Bluffs locality is re-
versed and of Matuyama age (see below; Barendregt and Vin-
cent 1990). The diamicton at Worth Point Bluffs is normal
(unit 3, Fig. 2), but, as observed in a new exposure in 1992, it
has been severely disrupted by later ground-ice growth. When
this happens, the disrupted body is in part reduced to a slurry,
the original magnetization is destroyed, and a new magnetiza-
tion is acquired as the magnetic grains rotate into the geomag-
netic field (Irving and Major 1964). Hence, the magnetization
of the Worth Point diamicton is probably an overprint resulting
from extensive reworking by periglacial processes.
The colluvial and paludal members of the Worth Point For-
mation lie entirely within the Matuyama Chron. The overlying
diamicton and marine sands and gravels (units 3 and 4) are
assigned to the Brunhes Chron. The organic sediments with
normal polarities within the paludal member could belong to
either the Jaramillo or Olduvai subzones. They are assigned to
the Olduvai subchron (1.95–1.77 Ma; Cande and Kent 1995)
for two reasons. They were laid down in a warm climate, typi-
cal of the latest Pliocene or earliest Pleistocene (Vincent
1990), rather than the cooler conditions of the later early Pleis-
tocene in which the Jaramillo (1.07–0.99 Ma) is located. Sec-
ond, as discussed later, assignment to the Jaramillo would only
allow 80 ka during the Matuyama Chron to accommodate at
least two and possibly as many as five full glaciations, and at
least two interglaciations, all of which are recorded elsewhere
on Banks Island after the deposition of the Worth Point For-
mation. Eighty thousand years is, we believe, insufficient.
Duck Hawk Bluffs
This locality (Figs. 1, 3) contains 11 lithostratigraphic units
(Vincent et al. 1983; Matthews et al. 1986; Vincent 1990). Ae-
olian sediments with associated pond deposits (unit 1), as-
signed to the Worth Point Formation, lie on fluvial late
Tertiary Beaufort coastal plain sands and gravels of the
Beaufort Formation. These are overlain by pre-Banks Sea sedi-
ments (unit 2), Bernard Till (unit 3), and post-Banks Sea sedi-
ments (unit 4), all associated with the Banks Glaciation. Above
these are terrestrial nonglacial sediments, initially assigned to
the Morgan Bluffs Interglaciation (Table 1) (Vincent 1992).

Nelson River Bluffs
At this locality near the southernmost point of Banks Island
(Fig. 1), Vincent (1983, 1990) has described 13 lithostrati-
graphic units (Fig. 4). At the base, there are five tills (units 1,
2, 4, 5, and 6) with variable composition, fabric, and colour. At
least one, but possibly as many as five distinct continental
glaciations are represented, all of which have been assigned
previously to the Banks Glaciation. Contacts between individ-
ual till sheets are well marked. For example, the tills of units 2
and 4 are separated by a continuous boulder pavement (unit 3)
which suggests, but does not prove, that multiple glaciations
occurred. Overlying these till sheets are marine sediments (unit
7) likely associated with a marine transgression (post-Banks
Sea) which followed the glaciation responsible for depositing
the till of unit 6 (Table 1).
The upper half of the section begins with a 9 m thick inter-
glacial sequence of interstratified fine sediments and in situ
peat layers, representing deposition in a perimarine delta (unit
8), and the Kellett Till and the Big Sea rhythmites and deltaic
sands and gravels (units 9 and 10), both deposited during the
Thomsen Glaciation (Nelson River Formation). In situ peats
and shrubs developed on a former tundra surface during the
succeeding Cape Collinson Interglaciation (unit 11). Finally,
pre-Amundsen Sea sediments and Jesse Till (units 12 and 13),
both associated with the Amundsen Glaciation and referred to
the Prince of Wales Formation, were deposited.
Oriented samples were collected from all units, except the
boulder pavement (unit 3) separating the till sheets of units 2
and 4. The distinct till units 1, 2, 4, and 5 have NRMs that are
well grouped, with steep positive inclinations and easterly dec-
linations close to the present Earth’s field. Demagnetization
generally yields scattered but reversed inclinations (Fig. 10; R′
half bars in Fig. 4). Three samples from units 1 and 2 have
clearly defined reversed directions (R full bars in Fig. 4). All
samples have large Brunhes-age overprints, with small under-
lying reversed magnetizations. On this basis, the lower part of
the Nelson River section is assigned to the Matuyama Re-
versed Chron.
Glacial and nonglacial sediments from units 6–13, from the
upper half of the section, have NRM directions tightly clus-
tered almost vertically downward. Magnetizations remain nor-
mal throughout the demagnetization range, and directions
remained little changed up to and often beyond 50 mT (Fig. 6).
No reversed magnetizations were found. The upper part of the
section is therefore assigned to the Brunhes Normal Chron.
The Brunhes–Matuyama boundary lies between the till sheets
of units 5 and 6; therefore, these tills belong to different polar-
ity zones, implying that they are separate lithostratigraphic
units and represent separate glaciations. The results also indi-

Morgan Bluffs
At Morgan Bluffs Vincent (1983, 1990) recognized 13 litho-
stratigraphic units (Figs. 1, 5) distributed among many sec-
tions, of which sections C, D, E, G, H, and L were sampled. As
a result of fieldwork in 1992, minor stratigraphic revisions
have been made and are incorporated herein.
Several units record the first continental ice advance onto
Banks Island and are assigned to the Banks Glaciation: the
pre-Banks Sea sediments (unit 1), Bernard Till and glacioma-
rine sediments (units 2–4), and post-Banks Sea sediments (unit
5) collectively are assigned to the Duck Hawk Bluffs Forma-
tion. These beds are overlain sequentially by interglacial flu-
vial sediments with in situ peat layers (unit 6, Morgan Bluffs
Formation), a suite of marine sediments (unit 7), a till (unit 8),
glaciofluvial gravels (unit 9), and a marine regressive sequence
(unit 10), all associated with an unnamed continental glacia-
tion; pre-Thomsen Sea sediments (unit 11) and Kellett Till
(unit 12) of the Thomsen Glaciation (Nelson River Forma-
tion); and finally by the Jesse Till (unit 13) of the Amundsen
Glaciation (Prince of Wales Formation).
Oriented samples were collected from six sections (C, D,
E, G, H, L). Suitable sediments occurred in all but one of the
units. Sediments associated with the Banks Glaciation (units
1–5), the Morgan Bluffs Interglaciation (unit 6), and an unnamed
glaciation (units 7–10 originally assigned to the Middle Pleis-
tocene Thomsen Glaciation) all exhibited reversed polarity,
and are assigned to the Matuyama Chron. The uppermost units
(11 and 12) associated with the Thomsen Glaciation and unit
13 associated with the Amundsen Glaciation are normal and
are assigned to the Brunhes Chron. The Brunhes–Matuyama
boundary, which lies within the Morgan Bluffs locality, post-
dates the unnamed glaciation (units 7–10) and predates the
Thomsen Glaciation (units 11 and 12).
Fine-grained deposits, which fill fossil ice-wedge casts
(Fig. 11) penetrating the uppermost part of the interglacial
sediments of the reversely magnetized Morgan Bluffs Forma-
tion (unit 6, section C), have normal polarity. These fossil ice
wedges were formed by periglacial processes that affected the
tundra surface at that time. These wedges were buried by re-
versely magnetized sediments of unit 7. Hence, they record an
interval of normal polarity within the Matuyama Chron. They
are assigned to the Jaramillo (1.07–0.99 Ma) rather than to the
Olduvai subzone, because the Morgan Bluffs Interglacial se-
quence, at Morgan Bluffs, is both underlain and overlain by
deposits recording full continental glaciations (units 1–5 and
7–10), indicating that the deposits postdate the warmer Late
Pliocene – Early Pleistocene interval documented by the
Worth Point Formation (Table 2; Figs. 12, 13). The normal
subzone recorded within “warm” preglacial Worth Point sedi-
ments (assigned to the Olduvai) is clearly different from the
normal subzone recorded from “cold” ice-wedge casts within
the Morgan Bluffs Formation (assigned to the Jaramillo).
Correlation of composite sections and
chronostratigraphy
Composite sections showing the lithostratigraphic units and
their polarities are given in Fig. 12. The Brunhes–Matuyama
boundary is shown, as are units recording subchrons within the
Matuyama. From this information, a proposed sequence of
glaciations and interglaciations for Banks Island has been con-
structed (Table 2). The various lithostratigraphic units that
document each event are grouped together. For example, ma-
rine or glaciomarine units unequivocally associated with a spe-
cific glaciation have been combined with the till of that
glaciation. Most events were previously defined (Vincent
1983, 1984, 1989, 1990, 1992), but the paleomagnetic data
now allow new events to be recognized.
Based on the magnetostratigaphic evidence presented for
the four localities on Banks Island, we outline here the modi-
fications to previous correlations of glacial and interglacial
events given in Table 1. The discovery of normally magnetized
paludal deposits (unit 2, section A) within an otherwise
reversely magnetized preglacial Worth Point Formation has

Late Pliocene and Early Pleistocene (Matuyama Chron)
Following deposition of the fluvial coastal plain sediments of
the Beaufort Formation, there was a preglacial interval, docu-
mented by sediments of the Worth Point Formation at Worth
Point and Duck Hawk bluffs. It is assigned to the latest Late
Pliocene or earliest Early Pleistocene based on the preglacial
nature of the deposits, the generally reversed polarity, and the
presence within it of normally magnetized paludal deposits
most probably of Olduvai age.
The first arrival of continental ice, of mainland provenance,
is recorded by the Bernard and other tills referred to the Banks
Glaciation. These tills are present at all localities and are re-
versely magnetized. At Nelson River Bluffs, the tills may re-
cord as many as four distinct continental glaciations. It is not
possible to determine which of the till sheets at Nelson River
Bluffs corresponds to the single till sheet that occurs at Worth
Point and Duck Hawk bluffs. It is interesting to note that on

Banks Island, the first continental glaciation postdated the first
glaciation in the Canadian Cordillera by at least a million
years, the latter occurring sometime within the late Gauss
(3.0–2.6 Ma; Barendregt et al. 1996; Duk-Rodkin and Baren-

An interglaciation of Matuyama age is recognized at Mor-
gan Bluffs, based on the presence of reversely magnetized
fluvial sediments of the interglacial Morgan Bluffs Formation.
Within this formation, there are normally magnetized fine-
grained sediments occurring as fossil ice wedges, which prob-
ably belong to the Jaramillo subzone. These ice wedges were
almost certainly developed on a tundra surface shortly after
deposition of the Morgan Bluffs Formation.
If the assignments of the normally magnetized sediments of
Worth Point Formation to the Olduvai subzone and those of
the Morgan Bluffs Formation to the Jaramillo subzone are cor-
rect, then the Banks Glaciation(s) and the Morgan Bluffs In-
terglaciation date from the Early Pleistocene and their ages
must fall between 1.77 and 1.07 Ma. A further consequence is
that a substantial gap occurs in the Matuyama record at Worth
Point Bluffs (within the upper part of unit 2, above the paludal
member, Figs. 2 and 12).
At Morgan Bluffs, another glaciation of Matuyama age is
recorded by a sequence of reversed glacial sediments postdat-
ing the Morgan Bluffs Interglaciation. This glaciation post-
dates beds we have assigned to the Jaramillo subchron and
therefore probably occurred sometime between 0.99 and
0.78 Ma.
At Duck Hawk Bluffs, an interglaciation, which occurred
at the end of the Matuyama Chron, is recorded in a sequence
of predominantly reversely magnetized nonglacial sediments.
At the top of this sequence, transitional directions and finally
normal polarities are recorded. Hence, the Brunhes–Matuyama
reversal (B–M, 0.78 Ma) occurs within sediments laid down
during this interglaciation (between units 5 and 6, sections A
and H, Figs. 3, 12).
These events are summarized as follows: ( i) a period of
nonglacial (presumably preglacial) sedimentation (<2.58
to <1.77 Ma); (ii) at least one (Banks Glaciation) but possibly
as many as four continental glaciations (<1.77 to >1.07 Ma);
(iii) an interglacial period referred to as the Morgan Bluffs
Interglaciation (<1.77 to >0.99 Ma); ( iv) an unnamed conti-
nental glaciation (<0.99 to >0.78 Ma); and ( v) part of an un-
named interglaciation during which the B–M reversal occurred
(about 0.78 Ma).
Middle Pleistocene (earlier Brunhes Chron)
Following the B–M reversal, a glaciation assigned to the early
Middle Pleistocene is recorded by normally magnetized gla-
cial sediments in the Nelson River Bluffs. Interglacial condi-
tions, documented by terrestrial and perimarine sediments of
normal polarity, are recorded at Duck Hawk and Nelson River
bluffs and are assigned to the earlier part of the Middle Pleis-
tocene. Deposits at these two localities may be correlative or
they may represent two distinct interglaciations. Subsequently,
Banks Island was again glaciated in the latter part of the Mid-
dle Pleistocene (Vincent 1992), as evidenced at all four locali-
ties by normally magnetized deposits of the Thomsen
Glaciation.
These events are summarized as follows: (i) the last part of
the interglaciation that records the B–M boundary (about
0.78 Ma); (ii) an unnamed glaciation (<0.78 Ma); ( iii) one or
more unnamed interglaciations (<0.78 to >0.13 Ma); and
(iv) the Thomsen Glaciation (>0.13 Ma).
Late Pleistocene (later Brunhes Chron)
The Late Pleistocene record begins with interglacial sedi-
ments, which overlie Thomsen Glaciation deposits at the Duck
Hawk and Nelson River localities, and which have been as-
signed to the Sangamon-age Cape Collinson Interglaciation
(Vincent 1992). These are followed by sediments of the
Amundsen Glaciation, and by Holocene sediments of the pre-
sent interglaciation. All are normally magnetized. The Late
Pleistocene is therefore represented by one glacial and two
interglacial intervals, all younger than 0.13 Ma.
Mean direction and paleopole
The material as a whole is not well suited for accurate determi-
nation of geomagnetic field directions, nevertheless an attempt
has been made to do this because of the paucity of Quaternary
records from such high latitudes as Banks Island.
R* and N* magnetizations have been compiled and means
for polarity zones at each locality calculated giving each
specimen unit weight (Table 4). This procedure, although es-
timating mean directions quite well, almost certainly underes-
timates errors. In Table 4, an attempt is made to calculate
means (grand averages) whose errors are more realistic. First,
specimen data from lithologic units set out in Figs. 2, 4, and 5
are averaged, and the means of these averages taken (24 units
at the three localities record N* and R* magnetizations). Sec-
ond, averages are calculated for seven groups of lithologic
units, termed major polarity units, and these are in turn aver-
aged. The major polarity units, which are defined in Table 2,
span approximately 100–200 ka and are considered sufficient
to average out secular variation and provide mean directions
which are not biased through our selective sampling of fine-
grained units and the underrepresentation of coarser units. Sta-
tistically the two procedures give indistinguishable results. We
regard the grouped averages of lithologic units as probably the
best measures. Directional data from Duck Hawk Bluffs (see
Table 4, data from Barendregt and Vincent 1990) are not in-
cluded in the grand averages because the separation of R* and
N* data could not be made from these older observations.
The means of the Brunhes and Matuyama fields fall short
of being antiparallel by 11°, most of which can be accounted
for by statistical errors. The difference is in a sense expected
from the presence of unremoved, very small present field over-
prints. One result is quite clear: the average, irrespective of
sign (in which the effect of residual overprints is removed),
does not differ significantly from the geocentric axial dipole
field (000, 80). Therefore, these sediments contain no inclina-
tion errors. The paleopole calculated from the average of the
lithologic units (n = 24) is 86°N, 300°E (Fisher’s estimate of
precision 6 = 8, and the half angle of the cone of confidence
α
95 = 11°), which is not significantly different from the present
geographic pole.
Summary of paleoclimatic history
Stratigraphic mapping and magnetostratigraphic studies have
established a sequence of polarity zones and subzones and
allowed the allocation of preglacial, glacial, and interglacial
Barendregt et al. 159
© 1998 NRC Canada

events to the global reversal time scale and the classical subdi-
visions of the later Cenozoic (Table 2; Fig. 13). Table 1 gives
the stratigraphic sequences recognized before the present
study. Table 2 is an update of Table 1, based on extensive
additional paleomagnetic sampling, and provides a revision of
the stratigraphic and geological events framework established
for sections on Banks Island. Figure 13 is a composite of all
sections.
During the latest Late Pliocene and earliest Early Pleisto-
cene (2.58 to about 1.77 Ma), nonglacial conditions prevailed.
During this interval, Banks Island was underlain by continuous
permafrost, and fluvial, aeolian, and colluvial processes modi-
fied the landscape. An open larch-dominated forest-tundra
vegetation was present (Matthews et al. 1986; Vincent 1990).
As climate deteriorated, the first of a series of continental
glaciations affected Banks Island. This, the Banks Glaciation,
may have comprised one or up to four glaciations during the
interval 1.77–1.07 Ma. Then followed the Morgan Bluffs
Interglaciation, which contains the Jaramillo subchron and
dates from about 1.0 Ma. Before the Early Pleistocene ended,
an unnamed glaciation reached Banks Island (0.99–0.78 Ma),
and was followed by an interglaciation during which the
Brunhes–Matuyama reversal occurred (0.78 Ma). During the
Middle Pleistocene (0.78–0.13 Ma), an unnamed glaciation,
an unnamed interglaciation, and the Thomsen Glaciation af-
fected the landscape of Banks Island. Finally, during the Late
Pleistocene ( <0.13 Ma to present), the Cape Collinson Inter-
glaciation (Sangamon), the Amundsen Glaciation, and the
present-day interglaciation occurred.
Sediments on Banks Island provide a record of at least two
and possibly as many as five glaciations and two interglacia-
tions (in addition to a preglacial interval) during the Matuyama
Chron. During the Brunhes Chron, three glaciations and three
interglaciations are documented. This is one of the longest and
most complete terrestrial records of climatic fluctuations in
North America during the Quaternary.
The Brunhes–Matuyama reversal on Banks Island occurred
during interglacial conditions. In deep-sea cores, the reversal
occurs at oxygen-isotope stage 19 (De Menocal et al. 1990), a
stage characterized as interglacial. This reversal has also been
located between a reversely magnetized paleosol and a nor-
mally magnetized diamicton at three sections in the Kennedy
Drift of Montana, and at two sections in the Mackenzie Moun-
tains (Cioppa et al. 1995; Barendregt et al. 1991, 1996), sug-
gesting that the field reversed during or after a period of soil
formation (interglacial), but before the arrival of the next ice
sheet (glacial). Therefore, it is very probable indeed that the
reversal took place during interglacial times.

Abstract
We collected 47 sites of Upper Triassic to Middle Jurassic siltstones and sandstones and two sites of Lower Cretaceous
andesites in a large basin located south of the Mongol±Okhotsk suture. The suture separates the Siberian craton to the north
from the Mongolian and Chinese blocks to the south. Laboratory treatment and analyses identify the same post-folding
direction in all rocks. The mean direction (with a corresponding palaeopole at 76.8ëN, 152.2ëE,A95D 4:2ë/ of the overprint
component.ND 49 sites) is signi®cantly different at the 95% con®dence level from the expected time-averaged Brunhes
or present-day ®eld directions. The Lower Cretaceous andesites possess a stable remanent direction at high temperatures
that is distinct at 95% con®dence limits from the overprint direction. The corresponding pole (58.3ëN, 51.0ëE, dp =dm
D 3.8ë=4.6ë), based on only fourteen samples, is signi®cantly rotated 78 :4ë 5:3ë counterclockwise and insigni®cantly
displaced 2:7ë 3:4ë north with respect to the Early Cretaceous reference pole for Siberia. We argue that the rotation is
likely tectonic in nature and not due to a chance reading of the palaeosecular variation of the Earth's magnetic ®eld. Both
the palaeomagnetic data and the folding patterns we observed in the ®eld suggest that deformation associated with the
suture continued after the Early Cretaceous and involved sinistral shear.  1998 Elsevier Science B.V . All rights reserved.

1. Introduction
The Eurasian tectonic mosaic is composed of nu-
merous cratons and fold belts whose histories have
been a topic of active palaeomagnetic research since

Siberian craton to the north from the Mongolian
(Amurian) and Chinese blocks to the south. The
Mongol±Okhotsk suture stretches along the southern
boundary of the Siberian platform from the Sea of
Okhotsk into central Mongolia (Fig. 1). The suture
formed as a result of continental collision between
Siberia and the lithospheric blocks to the south. The
relative position of these blocks during the Palaeo-
zoic and Mesozoic and their accretion or collision
ages are subjects of active research (e.g. [2±6]) and
in some cases the proposed reconstructions, includ-
ing those related to the Mongol±Okhotsk suture, are
hotly debated [7,8].
Misnik and Shevchuk [9] interpreted the rock as-
semblage near the town of Sretensk (118ëE, 52ëN)
in the central part of the Mongol±Okhotsk suture as
an ophiolite. Kuzmin and Fillipova [10] were among
the ®rst to publish on the history of the Mongol±
Okhotsk suture in a plate tectonic framework. Subse-
quently, Parfenov [2] interpreted the geological data
from the eastern segment of the suture consistent
with a subduction model of oceanic crust between
Siberia and the tectonic blocks to its southeast. Near
the ®eld area of this study ophiolites are described
in the Skovorodino region (124.0ëE, 53.8ëN) [11,12].
They contain both mid-oceanic ridge (MORB) and
oceanic island (OIB) basalts, as well as hyperba-
sic rocks, gabbro-tonalites, and plagiogranites [13].
Some of these complexes may be related to volcanic
arc environments. Felsic intrusives parallel to the
suture are thought to young towards the east, going
from Late Carboniferous±Permian in central Mongo-
lia, to Triassic±Early Jurassic in west Transbaikalia,
Late Jurassic in east Transbaikalia, and Cretaceous
in Amur Province, in the far-eastern part of Russia
[13,14]. Palaeontological data also support the exis-
tence of a Palaeozoic to Middle±Late Jurassic ocean
between Siberia and Mongolia [15±17]. Sediments
bearing marine fossils young in the same direction
as the granites (from west to east); there are no open
ocean sediments younger than Permian in central
Mongolia, Early Jurassic in the Transbaikal region,
and Middle±Late Jurassic in Amur Province [15].
Field mapping suggests that some of the ophiolites
overthrust lower Mesozoic rocks, and serpentinite
meÂlanges contain fragments of Jurassic granites [4].
Although few Mesozoic palaeomagnetic data
from Siberia and most of Kazakhstan pass mod-
ern standards of reliability, Besse and Courtillot [18]
constructed a synthetic apparent polar wander path
(APWP) for Eurasia by reconstructing Pangea via
ocean ¯oor magnetic anomalies. Once reconstituted,
the poles from Africa, North America, India, and
Europe were combined into a master APWP. This
master APWP was transferred to each plate, then the
plates (and corresponding APWPs) were restored to
the present reference frame. A comparison of the
combined APWP from the Chinese and Mongolian
blocks with the Eurasian reference path suggests
that they were separated by about 2000 km in the
Late Jurassic, then sutured together in the Cretaceous
[5,6].
2. Geologic overview
Palaeomagnetic samples were collected from 49
sites just north of the Amur River which forms
the political border between Russia and the Peo-
ple's Republic of China (Fig. 1b). Our Franco±
Russian team sampled Upper Triassic to Middle
Jurassic black to grey sandstones and siltstones,
rich in organic material, from three locations: 30
km south of Skovorodino (124.0ëE, 53.8ëN, sites
04±18, 25±36, 43±46), along the Trans-Siberian
railroad between Takhtamygda and Skovorodino
(123.6ëE, 54.1ëN, sites 19±24, 47±50), and 50 km
southwest of Yerofey Pavlovich (121.9ëE, 54.0ëN,
sites 37±42). These sediments were deposited in
a large basin (called the Upper Amur depression
in the Russian literature [15] and the Xinganling
or Ermuerhu basin in the Chinese literature [19]).
From bottom to top, the strata are separated into
formations called: Ogon (Upper Triassic±Carnian
to Norian), Kovali (Lower Jurassic±Pliensbachian±
Toarcian), Skovorodino (Lower to Middle Juras-
sic), Oshurka (Middle Jurassic±Aalenian±Bajocian),
Usmanko (Middle Jurassic±Bajocian±Bathonian),
and Uskali (Middle Jurassic±Bathonian±Callovian).
These formations are dated by abundant plant, pele-
cypod, and belemnite fossils as described in Refs.
[15,20±22]. The average combined thickness of
these formations exceeds 5900 m. In general, sedi-
ment size coarsens upward through the section; how-
ever, the entire sedimentary package is so uniform
in appearance that we could not distinguish among

the various formations in the ®eld. The Mesozoic
lithologies suggest that sedimentation occurred in a
relatively shallow sea. Some workers describe them
as a molasse complex that disconformably overlies
folded early Palaeozoic rocks [15,20,23].
We also sampled two sites (01±02) in two Lower
Cretaceous andesite ¯ows in a quarry near the town
of Taldan (124.5ëE, 53.8ëN). The volcanic rocks at
Taldan overlie both Jurassic sediments and an ancient
metamorphic complex. The base of the Cretaceous
pile has basaltic volcanic breccias and agglomerate
tuffs that contain xenoliths of basement material. The
agglomerate tuffs are covered mostly by porphyritic
andesite ¯ows that attain a thickness of 1000 m.
The upper part of the suite possesses a layer of ter-
rigenous sandstones and tuffaceous conglomerates.
This bed is rich in Lower Cretaceous fresh-water
pelecypods such as Limnocyrena ovalis (Ramm.), L.
wangehinensis (Grab.), L. altiformis (Grab.), Lacus-
trina lepida Ch. Kol., and ¯ora such as Phyllotheca
sibirica (Heer), Coniopteris sp. ex gr. C. nympharum
(Heer), Cladophlebis sp., thus its age is considered
Lower Cretaceous [15,21]. Sedimentary horizons in-
terbedded within the thick volcanic ¯ows enabled us
to obtain bedding orientations.
Fig. 1 contains equal-area stereonets of the bed-
ding attitudes measured in the ®eld. In the ®rst area
(sites 04±18), orientations strike west to southwest
with dips of 30 to 50ë. Bedding is relatively con-
stant over distances of kilometres and it is possible
that the sequence in this area represents a series of
thrust packages that are stacked on southwest-dip-
ping, bedding-parallel thrust faults. The intersection
of the bedding planes de®nes a fold axis oriented
N231ë and dipping 33ë. We note that the bedding
planes of the Cretaceous andesites have attitudes
similar to those from the ®rst area, suggesting that
folding of the Jurassic to Lower Cretaceous units oc-
curred after the Early Cretaceous. This is consistent
with post-Early Cretaceous folding found by Davis
et al. [24] in the Yinshan belt, which they attributed
to the collision of Siberia and Mongolia. In the sec-
ond area (sites 19±24), closer to the suture, the beds
are tightly folded with bedding orientations changing
over distances of tens of metres and with no consis-
tent fold axes. In the third area (sites 37±40), which
is farther from the suture than the second, folding
again occurs on longer wavelengths and the bedding
attitudes de®ne a plunging fold axis (18ë towards
N259ë) similar to that observed in the ®rst area.
3. Sampling, laboratory experiments and
palaeomagnetic results
Samples were collected both as oriented hand
samples and as standard 2.5-cm diameter cores us-
ing a portable drill with core orientation employing
both magnetic and sun compass bearings. Sun com-
pass corrections are particularly important because

de®ne a direction similar to that of the HTC, sug-

low coercivity. The natural remanent magnetization
(NRM) direction after af demagnetization in ®elds
with maximum amplitudes of 0.1 T is southeast and
up, similar to the direction de®ned by the ITC. Total
unblocking of the sample is not achieved by ®elds of
0.1 T. In fact, the magnetization intensity systemati-
cally increases after the sample has been subjected to
applied ®elds of 60 mT. Acquisition of isothermal re-
manent magnetization (IRM) experiments show that
the remanence saturates around applied ®elds of 0.3
T (Fig. 4f). Because the unblocking temperature of
the ITC is higher ( >400ëC) than expected for iron
sulphides (pyrrhotite) and lower than expected for
hematite, and because the bulk coercive force is low
compared to most iron sulphides and hematite [30],
it is doubtful that these minerals contribute to the
magnetic signal.
Because the ITC is anti-parallel to the HTC, the
ITC could be a self-reversed thermal remanent mag-
netization (TRM). Self reversing behaviour is found
in some volcanic rocks of dacitic and andesitic com-
positions [31±33]. Such rocks can contain two ferro-
magnetic minerals, one of which is in the ilmenite±
hematite series (Fe
2/NULyTiyO3) with 0:45 y 0:65.
Curie temperatures corresponding to these composi-
tions lie between 280 and 50ëC, which are the un-
blocking temperatures of most self-reversed TRMs
found in nature. Here, the ITC persists to at least
400ëC. Two alternative explanations for the ITC are:
(1) the rock contains two ferromagnetic minerals that
grew at different times (e.g., primary crystallization
followed by hydrothermal alteration), one during a
period of normal polarity and the other when the
Earth's ®eld was reversed; or (2) site 01 was heated
during a period of reversed polarity and grains with
high bulk coercivities were preferentially thermally
remagnetized during the heating event.
6. Discussion and conclusions
The main conclusion evinced from this palaeo-
magnetic study is that the Upper Triassic to Middle
Jurassic sediments are overprinted. Because the pole
to bedding of the Lower Cretaceous andesites lies
in the same swath as the older sediments (Fig. 1),
we assume that a single deformation event is respon-
sible for the folding of all the rocks; thus the age
of folding (and C1 remanence acquisition) is prob-
ably post-Early Cretaceous. The andesite LTC site
mean direction is indistinguishable at 95% signi®-
cance from the grouping of C1 site mean directions
of the older sediments (Table 1) [34], in agree-
ment with the suggestion that the remagnetization
is a post-Early Cretaceous phenomenon. The com-
bined LTC and C1 in-situ direction is DD 14:7ë,

Because large rotations have only been found
close to the suture zone (Figs. 1 and 5b,c), it is likely
that the counter-clockwise rotation of sites 01 and 02
is local in nature and related to shear associated with
the Mongolia±Siberia collision. The fact that the
Late Jurassic pole corresponding to the locality north
of the suture (Siberian craton, location 24, Fig. 5c)
is concordant (not rotated) with respect to the coeval
poles from the Eurasian reference APWP could be
interpreted to suggest that the edge of the ancient
Siberian craton was less deformed than the relatively
younger Mongolian block to its south. In sum, the
pattern of folding we observed in the ®eld, together
with the pattern of palaeomagnetic rotations, suggest
that deformation related to collision continued after
the Early Cretaceous and included a component of
sinistral shear.

ABSTRACT
Paleomagnetic investigations of Tertiary
dikes and Ordovician carbonate rocks at
Bare Mountain and in the surrounding re-
gion of southwestern Nevada were conducted
to further constrain possible rotations related
to Walker Lane dextral shear and Basin and
Range detachment faulting. Demagnetization
experiments revealed two distinct remanence
components in the Ordovician carbonate
rocks: (1) a dual polarity Permian-Triassic
magnetization carried by magnetite that was
acquired after Paleozoic or Mesozoic folding
but prior to Tertiary tilting; and (2) a dual po-
larity Miocene magnetization carried by
hematite that was acquired after folding and
tilting. The Tertiary dikes also contain a dual
polarity magnetization carried by magnetite
that can be interpreted either as a primary
thermoremanent magnetization or a sec-
ondary chemical remanent magnetization ac-
quired shortly after dike intrusion. Overall,
mean directions for all three magnetizations
roughly coincide with corresponding refer-
ence directions for Nevada. The largest decli-
nation discordance of 16° ± 7° (clockwise)
comes from comparison of the Permian-
Triassic magnetite magnetization to the Late
Permian reference direction for Nevada.
Thus, although structural and geothermal
data, including zircon fission-track ages, indi-
cate that northern Bare Mountain was tilted
20°–40° northeastward about a horizontal
axis during early Tertiary time, we find no ev-
idence for large-scale (i.e., >30°) vertical-axis
rotation. On the basis of these results, we sug-
gest that Bare Mountain forms an autochtho-
nous or parautochthonous footwall within the
Basin and Range and Walker Lane, in a re-
gion where many of the surrounding upper
crustal rocks are detached and significantly
rotated about vertical and steeply inclined
axes. In addition, the nature and timing of
footwall uplift indicated by our paleomag-
netic results do not support tectonic models
that reconstruct Bare Mountain and the
Striped Hills as adjacent segments of a con-
tinuous fold and thrust belt system. Finally,
we suggest that the postfolding Permian–
Triassic magnetization at Bare Mountain
coupled with Paleozoic zircon fission-track
ages indicate that the Meiklejohn Peak thrust
predates Jurassic-Cretaceous (Sevier) defor-
mation and may have instead resulted from a
Permian or earlier contractional event.
INTRODUCTION
Bare Mountain is an exhumed crustal inlier of
folded and faulted Proterozoic and Paleozoic
rocks situated in the southern Great Basin (Fig.
1A, p. 1535) within the central Basin and Range
extensional province of Wernicke (1992). Bare
Mountain is part of the diffuse belt of deforma-
tion known as the Walker Lane that consists of
spatially segregated regions of east-west exten-
sion between northwest-trending zones of dextral
strike-slip or oblique-slip faulting (Stewart, 1988;
Oldow et al., 1994). Deformation within the
Walker Lane and central Basin and Range is
manifested by kilometer-scale translation of up-
per crustal blocks coupled with rotations about
horizontal, steeply inclined, and vertical axes.
Vertical-axis rotations of crustal blocks within
the Walker Lane have been documented and
quantified by paleomagnetic results. For exam-
ple, paleomagnetic directions identified as Ceno-
zoic and Permian-Triassic secondary magnetiza-
tions in Paleozoic carbonate rocks and primary
magnetizations in Cenozoic (mainly Miocene)
clastic rocks and nonmarine limestones show as
much as 100° of clockwise rotation associated
with motion along the Las Vegas Valley shear
(Gillett and Van Alstine, 1982; Nelson and Jones,
1987; Sonder et al., 1994). Significant clockwise
rotations are also observed in the Black Moun-
tains, presumably in response to similar right-lat-
eral shear along the Death Valley–Furnace Creek
fault zone (Holm et al., 1993), and in the Cotton-
wood Mountains, presumably in response to
west-northwest Basin and Range extension
(Snow et al., 1993).
Despite large rotations in many parts of the
Walker Lane, paleomagnetic evidence for sig-
nificant vertical-axis rotations in the region
around Yucca Mountain and at Bare Mountain
is equivocal. Primary magnetization directions
from most of the middle Miocene volcanic
rocks of the southwestern Nevada volcanic field
are not systematically rotated (Hudson, 1992;
Hudson et al., 1994), except within the southern
reaches of Yucca Mountain (Rosenbaum et al.,
1991) and in southwestern Crater Flat, just
south of Bare Mountain (Hudson et al., 1996).
Yet, preliminary paleomagnetic results from
two Miocene dikes at Bare Mountain do not in-
dicate any vertical-axis rotations of the Bare
Mountain block (Zhang et al., 1993).
Structural and sedimentological evidence for
large-magnitude vertical-axis rotations of the
Bare Mountain block is also equivocal. Snow
(1992; 1994), for example, envisioned the Pan-
ama and Meiklejohn Peak thrusts exposed at Bare
Mountain as rotated segments of an Early Per-
mian, pre-Sonoma thrust system that is also ex-
posed in the Cottonwood Range in northern
Death Valley. Reconstruction of the thrust system
predicts large-scale translation along a Cenozoic
regional detachment and a 90° clockwise vertical-
axis rotation of Bare Mountain. Snow and Prave
(1994) argued that paleoflow orientations of
trough cross-bedding axes in the clastic Precam-
brian and Cambrian quartzites at Bare Mountain
are rotated 85° ± 12° clockwise relative to re-
gional paleoflow trends, consistent with their in-
terpretation of ~90° clockwise rotation. In con-
trast, Caskey and Schweickert (1992) and
Schweickert and Lahren (1997) viewed the
Panama and Meiklejohn Peak thrusts as hindward

and forward-verging features of the Mesozoic Se-

Desert fault system, which includes the Bare
Mountain fault, has presumably accumulated
more than 30 km of dextral displacement since
the mid-Miocene with minimal vertical-axis rota-
tion of the Bare Mountain block.
This paper evaluates the possibility of large-
scale vertical axis rotation of Bare Mountain re-
lated to Basin and Range extension and the
Walker Lane transtensional deformation using a
detailed and systematic study of the paleomag-
netism of Bare Mountain, Nevada. Specifically,
paleomagnetic results from 12 Oligocene(?) and
Miocene mafic and silicic porphyry dikes and
20 sites collected in the carbonate rocks of the
Ordovician Antelope Valley Formation at Bare
Mountain are presented. These results are also
examined within the context of the Walker Lane
and Basin and Range tectonics by comparing
them to paleomagnetic directions from 13 addi-
tional sites collected in the lower Paleozoic car-
bonate rocks exposed in nearby ranges of the
Yucca Mountain region, as well as previously
published paleomagnetic results from other
ranges in Nevada and Utah.
GEOLOGIC SETTING AND SAMPLING
Stratigraphy
Bare Mountain exposes nearly 7.5 km of Prot-
erozoic and Paleozoic stratigraphy of the Cor-
dilleran miogeocline. The sequence represents the
proximal (cratonward) facies of the margin con-
sisting of late Precambrian to Cambrian clastic
rocks (mainly quartzites and argillites) and Middle
Cambrian to Devonian shallow-water platform
carbonates overlain by Upper Devonian to Missis-
sippian Antler foredeep deposits (e.g., Trexler 
et al., 1996). The stratigraphic record between
Mississippian sedimentation and Miocene volcan-
ism is not preserved at Bare Mountain; however,
the mountain contains small-volume igneous in-
trusions that yield Cretaceous and Oligocene or
Miocene radiometric ages (U-Pb data from zircon
of 98 ± 27 Ma and K-Ar dates from hornblende of
26.1 ± 1.7 Ma and biotite of 16.6 ± 1.2 Ma as re-
ported in Monsen et al., 1992). If Pennsylvanian
and Permian rocks noted elsewhere in the Basin
and Range and Mojave Desert were also at Bare
Mountain, they have been eroded.
In southern Nevada, Miocene silicic volcan-
ism associated with the southwestern Nevada
volcanic field began about 16 Ma and continued
until about 10 Ma (e.g., Sawyer et al., 1994).
Near Bare Mountain, a nearly 2-km-thick se-
quence of pyroclastic deposits and rhyolitic lavas
was deposited from a complex network of
calderas to the north and northeast. Minor late
Miocene to Holocene basaltic flows and dikes are
also present, including Pliocene and Quaternary
basaltic volcanic rocks of Crater Flat and the
Amargosa Desert. The volcanic sequence is
capped by latest Miocene, Pliocene, and Quater-
nary surficial deposits (Monsen et al., 1992). In
the actively subsiding parts of the basins, the
Pliocene-Quaternary volcanic rocks are partially
or wholly buried by thick accumulations of Qua-
ternary and Holocene alluvium and colluvium
(Stamatakos et al., 1997). Along the eastern flank
of Bare Mountain, a series of vertical, north-
trending, 1–10-m-wide silicic porphyry dikes are
exposed (Cornwall and Kleinhample, 1961; Carr,
1988; Noble et al., 1989). Conventional K/Ar and
40Ar/39Ar dates from dikes in the eastern Bare
Mountain range in age from 14.9 to 13.8 Ma
(Marvin et al., 1989; Noble et al., 1991; Monsen
et al., 1992; Weiss, 1996).
Structure
In its present structural configuration, Bare
Mountain constitutes the footwall of at least two
Neogene extensional-fault systems, the Fluorspar
Canyon detachment and the Bare Mountain fault.

larger Bullfrog Hills detachment system, presum-
ably unroofed Miocene volcanic rocks from
northern Bare Mountain to the present location
north and northwest of the mountain (Maldonado,
1990; Hoisch et al., 1997). The Bare Mountain
fault is a north-south–trending, east-dipping nor-
mal fault with more than 2.5 km of offset that jux-
taposes sedimentary and metasedimentary rocks
against Pleistocene to Holocene deposits of the
adjoining Crater Flat basin (e.g., Ferrill et al.,
1996a; Fridrich, 1998). Because of the possibility
for large-magnitude earthquakes, the Bare Moun-
tain fault is one of the structures that is critical to
safety evaluations and overall performance as-
sessments of the proposed high-level nuclear
waste repository at nearby Yucca Mountain.
In addition to these two Neogene extensional
fault systems, Bare Mountain reveals geologic
evidence of one or more Tertiary (pre-Miocene)
extension events. Structural and geothermomet-
ric results (Stamatakos and Ferrill, 1996) suggest
that Bare Mountain was exhumed and rotated
about a west-northwest horizontal axis between
Eocene and middle Miocene time, prior to exten-
sion along the Fluorspar Canyon detachment.
The cause of this horizontal-axis rotation and ex-
humation is unknown. This tilting event, how-
ever, was itself preceded by down-to-the-south-
east extension along a series of normal faults that
dissect the northwestern corner of the Bare
Mountain block, including the ~2.5 km of dis-
placement currently observed across the Gold
Ace Mine fault (Ferrill et al., 1998).
Bare Mountain also preserves evidence of
Mesozoic or possibly late Paleozoic contrac-
tional deformation. In the northeast corner of
Bare Mountain, the Meiklejohn Peak thrust
places Lower Cambrian through Lower Devo-
nian carbonate rocks and quartzites on Devo-
nian-Mississippian Antler foredeep strata along
a duplex of southeast-verging (in present coor-
dinates) thrust faults (Fig. 1B, p. 1536). In
southern Bare Mountain, the Panama thrust
places Precambrian quartzites northwestward
(in present coordinates) on top of a large foot-
wall syncline of latest Precambrian and Cam-
brian quartzites.
Thermal History
Metamorphic grade and peak geothermal (bur-
ial) temperatures decrease from west and south-
west to the northeast across Bare Mountain. Am-
phibolite facies rocks are exposed west of the
Gold Ace Mine and north of the Conejo Canyon
faults, and subgreenschist and nonmetamorphic
rocks are exposed elsewhere (Monsen et al.,
1992). Peak burial temperatures estimated from
calcite-twin geothermometry (Stamatakos and
Ferrill, 1996), conodont alteration indices (Grow
et al., 1994), and isotopic and fission-track ther-
mochronologies (Hoisch et al., 1997; Ferrill 
et al., 1996b) indicate variations from greater
than 350 °C in the northwest corner of Bare
Mountain to less than 150 °C in the hanging wall
of the Meiklejohn Peak thrust (Fig. 1B, p. 1536).
Geothermometric constraints as well as fold
plunges and fault-bedding intersections show that
Bare Mountain developed this structural plunge
prior to apatite fission-track ages being set in
middle Miocene time (Ferrill et al., 1996b). In
addition, textural features and K-Ar dates from
alunite indicate significant epithermal and hy-
drothermal activity penecontemporaneous with
the later stages of silicic volcanism (ca.
11.0–12.5 Ma), especially in association with al-
tered margins of the silicic porphyry dikes
(Weiss, 1996; Noble et al., 1991).

Sample Collection
At Bare Mountain, samples for paleomagnetic
analyses were collected from 12 sites in the Ter-
tiary silicic porphyry and diorite dikes. These cor-
respond to six dikes mapped by Monsen et al.
(1992) and six dikes not shown on their map (sites
Ti4, Ti6, Ti8, Ti9, Ti11, and Ti12) (Fig. 1B,
p. 1536). At site Ti4, samples were also collected
and analyzed from the altered country rock adja-
cent to the dike walls with the intent of perform-
ing a baked contact test. We sampled 20 sites in
the Ordovician Antelope Valley Formation, seven
sites from the hanging-wall anticline of the Meik-
lejohn Peak thrust, and 13 sites within the foot-
wall rocks of the Meiklejohn Peak thrust (Fig. 1B,
p. 1536). We also collected 13 sites of Ordovician
Pogonip Group carbonate rocks from other local-
ities within the Yucca Mountain region (Fig. 1A,
p. 1535), including 5 sites from the Striped Hills,
2 sites each from the Specter Range, Yucca Flat,
and Pahrump Valley, and 1 site each from imme-
diately north of Mercury, Nevada, and in the
Black Hills between the Nevada Range and the
Las Vegas Range. Paleomagnetic cores were ei-
ther drilled in the field with a gasoline-powered
and water-cooled coring device or collected as
oriented hand samples and cored in the lab. Sam-
ple orientations and bedding attitudes were mea-
sured using a magnetic compass after field checks
verified that magnetizations of the rocks did not
bias compass readings. Between 6 and 16 sam-
ples were collected at each site.
METHODS
Characteristic and secondary magnetizations
were isolated from progressive thermal demagne-
tization of the samples. Standard thermal demag-
netization was supplemented with alternating field
(AF) followed by thermal demagnetization, and
acquisition of anhysteretic remanence and isother-
mal remanence magnetizations to provide addi-
tional information on magnetic mineralogy. Ther-
mal demagnetizations were conducted using a
standard paleomagnetic furnace with a peak tem-
perature of 700 °C and a maximum rest field of 10
nT. An AF demagnetizer with a peak field of 200
mT coupled with an automated internal coil capa-
ble of generating 1G biasing fields were used for
AF demagnetization and anhysteretic remanence
acquisition experiments. An electromagnet capa-
ble of generating static magnetic fields to 1.3 T
was used for isothermal remanence magnetization
acquisition experiments. All magnetic measure-
ments were made using a three-axis cryogenic
magnetometer in the magnetically shielded facility
at the University of Michigan. Peak ambient field
in the shielded room is less than 600 nT.
Magnetic components isolated during demag-
netization experiments were determined from vis-
ual inspection of the linear segments on vector
end-point diagrams. Component directions were
determined from a least square fit of the observed
linear trajectories (e.g., Kirschvink, 1980). Sam-
ple directions were combined to form site means
using simple vector addition, giving unit weight to
each sample direction. Statistical parameters were
calculated from the method of Fisher (1953).
Where possible, fold tests (Graham, 1949) were

Fold-test statistics were based on the McFadden
and Jones (1981) and McElhinny (1964) meth-
ods. In areas where the magnetic declinations sug-
gest significant vertical-axis rotations, an inclina-
tion-only fold test was used (Parés et al., 1994),
following the method of McFadden and Reid
(1982). Calculation of the statistical significance
of tectonic rotations based on paleomagnetic di-
rections was from Demarest (1983).
Two structural corrections were made during
analysis of the paleomagnetic directions, one for
the tilting of the entire Bare Mountain and Striped
Hills blocks related to Tertiary (but pre–middle
Miocene) detachment faulting, and one for fold-
ing of the Paleozoic strata from Mesozoic or late
Paleozoic Cordilleran contractional deformation.
For the plunge correction, site mean directions
were tilted about a horizontal axes. The plunge
axis of the Meiklejohn Peak anticline (trend =
039°, plunge = 33° northeast) was used as the ref-
erence for this correction at Bare Mountain. A
plunge determined from bedding data (trend =
087°, plunge = 30° east) was used as a reference
line for plunge corrections of site means at the
Striped Hills. In the fold tests, magnetization
components from folded Paleozoic carbonates
were rotated about their respective lines of strike
in 5% increments of bedding dip after both mag-
netic directions and bedding orientations were
corrected for respective structural plunges.
A third structural correction, that for footwall
tilting of the Bare Mountain block from Miocene
to recent motion along the Bare Mountain fault,
was too small to be of consequence. Geometric
considerations (i.e., fault dip, width of the foot-
wall block, and cumulative fault displacement) in-
dicate a maximum correction of 7° west about a
roughly north-south axis. Map patterns (Monsen
et al., 1992), however, show that the silicic por-
phyry dikes are essentially vertical, suggesting
that, if the dikes were intruded into Bare Moun-
tain vertically, the actual tilting of Bare Mountain
since the Miocene was less than 5°, and possibly
as small as 2°—an observation consistent with the
1°–3° difference in slope angle of alluvial fans on
the eastern and western flanks of Bare Mountain
(Ferrill et al., 1996a, 1997).
PALEOMAGNETIC RESULTS
Silicic Porphyry and Diorite Dikes
Intensities of the natural remanent magneti-
zations range between 0.1 mA/m and 15 A/m,
although most samples (~95%) yielded natural
remanent magnetization intensities between 1.0
and 100.0 mA/m. The remaining 5% of the
samples with either extremely strong (probably
from lightening strikes) or weak (probably
from extensive hydrothermal or epithermal al-
terations) natural remanent magnetization in-
tensities did not produce coherent and stable
demagnetizations. The demagnetization trajec-

sample intensity and direction. Samples from

Antelope Valley Formation at 
Bare Mountain, Footwall Block
Natural remanent magnetization intensities for
the Antelope Valley carbonates from the footwall
rocks of the Meiklejohn Peak thrust ranged be-
tween 0.1 and 2.0 mA/m. Thermal demagnetiza-
tion of samples revealed either a single or a dual
component magnetization (Fig. 5, A and B). For
samples with two components, the first compo-
nent removed was a present-day field component
(acquired by the samples in the recent geomag-
netic field) with unblocking temperatures to
about 350 °C (Fig. 5A). Because this component
was likely acquired from recent weathering or is
a recent viscous remanent magnetization, it was
not deemed important to the discussion of the
tectonic setting of Bare Mountain.
The characteristic remanent magnetization of
the footwall rocks showed a moderate to steep
north and down or antipodal south and moderate to
steep up directions (in situ coordinates) with un-
blocking temperatures to 630 °C. High coercivities
in excess of 200 mT were observed from AF (Fig.
5C) and combined AF and thermal demagnetiza-
tions. The high coercivity and unblocking temper-
atures above 585 °C suggested that hematite car-
ries the characteristic remanent magnetization in
the footwall samples; thus, in the following dis-
cussions this characteristic remanent magnetiza-
tion is referred to as the H component.
The H component was isolated in samples
from 8 of the 13 footwall sites (Table 2). In three
of the remaining sites (OA V5, OA V10, and
OA V11) remanence intensities were too weak to
isolate the characteristic remanent magnetization
in more than one or two samples. In the other two
remaining sites (OA V3 and OA V9), directions
were obtained from three samples, but the 95%
confidence intervals about the sites means were
excessively large (a
95 > 25°), and thus they were
excluded from further consideration.
For all other samples from these sites, rema-
nence intensities above 300 °C were near the
background level of the cryogenic magnetometer
(~5 · 10
–7 A/m). Although results from the sites
with weak remanence intensity revealed results
consistent with the other sites, only those site
mean directions defined by at least three sample
directions were used to obtain an overall mean di-
rection (Table 2).
Site mean directions from the eight footwall
sites were well clustered about a north and mod-
erate to steep down direction or an antipodal south
and steep up direction (Fig. 6A). The characteris-
tic remanent magnetization directions became
north-northeast and moderately up after correc-
tion for the structural plunge of Bare Mountain
and became progressively more dispersed as bed-
ding was restored to paleohorizontal. The incre-
mental fold test confirms that the H component
magnetization was acquired after folding of these
strata (Fig. 7A). This observation is based on the
assumption that optimal clustering of the direc-
tions during unfolding, defined either by the min-
imum f value or peak kvalue, indicates the posi-
tion of the strata when the rocks acquired their
magnetization (Graham, 1949).

DISCUSSION
Origin of Characteristic Magnetizations 
in the Tertiary Dikes
There are two possible origins for the charac-
teristic magnetization in the silicic porphyry
dikes. The characteristic remanent magnetization
is either a primary thermoremanent magnetization
related to cooling of the dikes at about 14.5 Ma or
a secondary chemical remanent magnetization
carried by hydrothermal and epithermal alter-
ations of the silicic dikes between 11.0 and 12.5
Ma. A third possibility, in which the characteristic
remanent magnetization is a recent viscous rema-
nent magnetization or a partial thermal-viscous
remanent magnetization, acquired in the present
dipole field (PDF), is unlikely. First, the magneti-
zation has both polarity directions, dominated by
reversed polarity directions—a situation uncom-
mon for recently acquired viscous remanent mag-
netizations. Viscous remanent magnetizations
typically have present-day field, normal polarity
directions. Second, the characteristic remanent
magnetization has unblocking temperatures to
580 °C, yet apatite fission track and isotopic dates
show that the dikes remained cool, below about
150 °C, since about 12.5 Ma (Ferrill et al., 1996b;
Weiss, 1996). According to the thermal activation
relationships outlined in Pullaiah et al. (1975), the
acquisition time required for a partial thermal-vis-
cous remanent magnetization in magnetite at 
150 °C is in excess of 10
8 yr.
Because hydrothermal and epithermal alter-
ations occurred soon after intrusion of the dikes in
Miocene time (Weiss, 1996; Noble et al., 1991),
the question of a primary or secondary origin of
the characteristic remanent magnetization cannot
be easily resolved. The contact test did not yield
coherent directions, which is unfortunate because
that test may have constrained the timing of ac-
quisition of dike magnetization. Zhang et al.
(1993) reported that they obtained a positive
baked-contact test and concluded that the dike
remanence is primary, but those results have not
been published. Ultimately, however, resolution
of this ambiguity is not critical to the discussion of
tectonic implications of the characteristic rem-
anent magnetization directions because the differ-
ence in age between dike intrusion and hydrother-
mal or epithermal alterations is only a few million
years and there has been little change in the refer-
ence polar wander path for Nevada during this in-
terval. For this paper, we assumed that the charac-
teristic remanent magnetization is a mid-Miocene
magnetization as young as 11.0 Ma. Precise de-
termination of the origin of the characteristic rem-
anent magnetization awaits more rigorous petro-
graphic and geochemical investigations of the
dikes and the chilled margins.
The remanence in the two Oligocene(?) diorite
dikes in the northwest corner of Bare Mountain
appears to be either a secondary chemical rema-
nent magnetization acquired during hydrother-
mal or epithermal alteration or a secondary
thermoremanent magnetization or partial ther-
mal-viscous remanent magnetization acquired as
the northwestern corner of Bare Mountain was
exhumed and uplifted(?) in middle Miocene
time. Like the silicic porphyry dikes, the diorite
dikes contain a dual polarity magnetizations with
unblocking temperatures near 585 °C and mod-
erate coercivity spectra with a median destructive
field of 20 mT. The difference between the diorite
and silicic porphyry dikes is that the diorite dikes
remained above about 250 °C (Ferrill et al.,
1996b) and perhaps as hot as 450 °C (Hoisch 
et al., 1997) until middle Miocene time, so it is
unlikely they retained a primary thermoremanent
magnetization. For example, the Pullaiah rela-
tionships indicate that rocks heated to 450 °C for
10
6 yr would have an equivalent unblocking tem-
perature in the lab of nearly 530 °C. Therefore,

Origin of the H Component Magnetization
The H component in the footwall rocks (with
respect to the Meiklejohn Peak thrust) at Bare
Mountain and regional sites OP6, OP7, OP11,
and OP12 appears to be a secondary chemical
remanent magnetization acquired in middle
Miocene time. The mean direction of the H
component in in situ coordinates coincides with
the Miocene reference direction and with the
(Cenozoic) intermediate component magnetiza-
tions noted elsewhere in Nevada (e.g., Gillett
and Van Alstine, 1982) (cf. Figs. 6A and 9, A
and B, with the intermediate component shown
in Fig. 11B). The possibility that the magnetiza-
tion is younger, acquired in Pliocene or Quater-
nary time cannot, however, be ruled out. The in-
terpretation that this direction is of Miocene age
is simply based on the presence of both polarity
magnetizations, evidence for significant hy-
drothermal or epithermal alterations during
middle Miocene time (Weiss, 1996), and the
lack of evidence for significant thermochemical
alterations since that time.
Origin of the M Component Magnetization
The M component characteristic remanent
magnetization in the hanging wall of the Meikle-
john Peak thrust and from regional sites OP8,
OP9, OP10, and OP13 is interpreted as a chemi-
cal remanent magnetization related to regional,
late Paleozoic chemical remagnetization, as first
proposed by Gillett and Van Alstine (1982). De-
magnetization characteristics of the M compo-
nent characteristic remanent magnetization are
similar to those observed in other remagnetized
carbonates in Nevada (e.g., Gillett and Geissman,
1993) and to many chemically remagnetized car-
bonates worldwide (e.g., McCabe and Elmore,
1989; Van der V oo et al., 1997). All have peak un-
blocking temperatures in the range 450 to 500 °C
and moderate coercivities with a median destruc-
tive field between 10 and 20 mT. In addition, sat-
uration anhysteretic remanence–isothermal rem-
anence magnetization ratios for samples with this
characteristic remanent magnetization are be-
tween 0.07 and 0.15, slightly lower than values
considered indicative of carbonate rocks with an
authigenic magnetite remanence, but signifi-
cantly larger than values considered representa-
tive of a primary magnetizations in carbonate
rocks (Jackson et al., 1993).
Mean directions of the M component charac-
teristic remanent magnetization are also consist-
ent with a Permian-Triassic magnetization, once
the directions are corrected for tilting related to
Cenozoic Basin and Range extension. For exam-
ple, correction for the northeast structural plunge
of Bare Mountain yields moderate shallow incli-
nations with northwest or antipodal southeast
declinations that fall on the reference Permian-
Triassic path for Nevada (Fig. 11A). The result-
ing directions are also consistent with previously
published results from remagnetized carbonates
in nearby ranges in Utah and Nevada (Table 4,
Fig. 11B). Tilt-corrected directions from OP9,
OP10, and OP13 also yield shallow south-south-
west and up directions that match the reference
Permian-Triassic directions, except that they ap-

tural link between Bare Mountain and the Striped
Hills (Schweickert and Lahren, 1997). In that in-
terpretation, the hanging-wall anticline of the
Panama thrust at Bare Mountain is correlated
across a major right-lateral strike-slip system (the
Amargosa Desert fault) with a panel of vertical to
overturned Paleozoic and Proterozoic rocks ex-
posed in the Striped Hills (presumed to be the
forelimb of an equivalent hanging-wall fold), un-
der the assumption that both folds were once part
of a single continuous structure in the Cordilleran
Sevier fold-thrust belt. If correct, total right-lateral
strike-slip offset of the fold would exceed 30 km.
Yet, to achieve this realignment, the recognized
eastward or northeastward tilts (plunges) of the
Striped Hills and Bare Mountain must also be re-
stored to horizontal. Otherwise, the folds in their
present orientations cannot be restored along a
strike-slip fault to form a single fold as proposed.
This reconstruction would therefore require
restoration of significant vertical offset (up to 7
km accounting for the 28° and 30° plunges and 15
km horizontal separation between Bare Mountain
and the Striped Hills) in addition to the 30 km of
strike-slip displacement. Because the characteris-
tic remanent magnetization in the dikes at Bare
Mountain and the H component in the carbonates
at both Bare Mountain and the Striped Hills are no
younger than about 11 Ma (and were acquired af-
ter tilting) and tilting of Bare Mountain about a
horizontal axis is older than about 14 Ma (prior to
intrusion of the silicic porphyry dikes), this verti-
cal component of offset must be older than 14 Ma.
Strike-slip motion on the proposed Amargosa
Desert fault system is presumed to be younger
than 12.5 Ma, occurring mostly after 11.5 Ma
(Schweickert and Lahren, 1997), and thus it
would postdate the vertical motion. Furthermore,
apatite fission-track thermochronology indicates
that the Tertiary thermal histories of the Striped
Hills and southern Bare Mountain are incompati-
ble (Stamatakos and Ferrill, 1996). Collectively,
these complications, in addition to the ambiguous
structural link between the Panama thrust fold and
the overturned section at the Striped Hills, raise
considerable doubt about the Schweickert and
Lahren (1997) reconstruction.

The observation that the M component charac-
teristic remanent magnetization fails the fold test
at Bare Mountain also shows that folding of the
Meiklejohn Peak thrust anticline occurred prior to
acquisition of this magnetization. The shallow in-
clination of the M component magnetization and
its similarity to other late Paleozoic secondary
magnetizations in the Basin and Range indicate
acquisition in Late Permian or Early Triassic time.
This leads us to conclude that folding of the Meik-
lejohn Peak anticline occurred in late Paleozoic or
early Mesozoic time, prior to Jurassic or Creta-
ceous Sevier deformation. This conclusion is fur-
ther supported by zircon fission-track data, which
yield Pennsylvanian-Permian cooling ages for the
hanging-wall rocks of the Meiklejohn Peak thrust
(Ferrill et al., 1996b). Thus, in spite of differences
in the prediction of large-magnitude vertical-axis
rotations (discussed below), the paleomagnetic re-
sults from this study support Snow’s (1992) hy-
pothesis that this portion of the Basin and Range,
contains pre-Sevier (Permian or older) contrac-
tional structures.
Vertical-Axis Rotations
Comparison of the chemical remanent magne-
tization directions in the dikes to the reference
Miocene direction for Nevada shows no evidence
for large-scale rotations of Bare Mountain. The
data suggest a small, but statistically insignifi-
cant, counterclockwise rotation of –11° ± 13°.
The expected reference direction for this part of
Nevada is D = 357°, I = 55°, DI = 3.0°, DD =
3.7°, based on the Miocene reference pole of
Hagstrum et al. (1987). The amount of counter-
clockwise rotation would be slightly greater
(~2°) if it also included a small correction for the
tilt of Bare Mountain related to post-Miocene
motion along the Bare Mountain fault.
The small counterclockwise rotation is sur-
prising given the prediction that Bare Mountain
rotated clockwise, if at all. The dual polarity
magnetization suggests that the magnetization
was acquired over one or more reversals of the
Earth’s magnetic field and, thus, the counter-
clockwise rotation does not appear to be an arti-
fact of inadequately averaged secular variation of
the Earth’s geomagnetic field. This is especially
true if the dike’s characteristic remanent magne-
tization is a chemical remanent magnetization or
partial thermal-viscous remanent magnetization,
which requires an acquisition time significantly
longer than 5–10 k.y. Given the noted problems
in isolating a single component direction from
the two antipodal components in these rocks,
however, it is possible this apparent counter-
clockwise rotation reflects a slight bias in the
characteristic remanent magnetization directions
due to unremoved components of opposite polar-
ity magnetizations. In addition, the moderate to
steep inclinations (50°–60°) may also obscure ac-
curate quantification of the small-angle rotations
in these rocks.
Comparison of the H component of magneti-
zation with the Miocene reference direction also
reveals negligible rotations. The grand mean di-
rection from Bare Mountain indicates a small
clockwise rotation of 10° ± 6° compared to a sta-
tistically insignificant counterclockwise rotation
of –12° ± 14° for the grand mean direction at the
Striped Hills (Table 3). Although it is possible
that these values represent actual vertical-axis ro-
tations of these blocks, the moderate to steep in-
clinations and small angles make us uneasy about
assigning undue significance to these values.
Comparison of the M component magnetization
at Bare Mountain also indicates only a minor verti-
cal-axis rotation of Bare Mountain, if any. The
plunge-corrected direction for the M component
falls within the Triassic portion of the reference
path for southern Nevada based on the North Amer-
ican apparent polar wander path of Van der Voo
(1993). Because the regional data for Nevada and
Utah suggest that remagnetization is most likely
Late Permian or Early Triassic in age (e.g., Gillett
and Van Alstine, 1982), the Late Permian reference
pole (Van der Voo, 1993) was used to derive the ref-
erence direction of D = 328°, I = 23°, DI = 5.4°, DD
= 4.1°. Comparison of the mean M component
characteristic remanent magnetization at Bare
Mountain with that direction yields a 16° ± 7°
clockwise rotation. Comparison of the M compo-
nent of magnetization to younger Triassic reference
directions yields statistically concordant declina-
tions (Fig. 11A).
Although paleomagnetic results from Bare
Mountain indicate small clockwise and counter-
clockwise rotations, the data clearly do not sup-
port the ~90° clockwise rotation of Bare Moun-
tain suggested by Snow (1992) and Snow and
Prave (1994). In addition, the paleomagnetic re-
sults at Bare Mountain contrast with the post
mid-Miocene 30°–50° clockwise rotations de-
rived from paleomagnetic results of the Miocene
tuffs north, south, and east of the range. Thus,
even though Bare Mountain was tilted about a
horizontal axis during exhumation and uplift, it
appears to have remained relatively fixed about
its vertical axis since at least the late Paleozoic or
early Mesozoic time. We suggest that one way to
accommodate the relatively large rotations ob-
served in the tuffs just south and east of Bare
Mountain is by steep-axis rotations related to ex-
tension along normal faults with the large dis-
placement gradients on the intrabasinal normal
faults in Crater Flat (e.g., Rosenbaum et al, 1991;
Stamatakos and Ferrill, 1998, in press).
Only sites OP9 and OP10 appear to show sig-
nificant vertical-axis rotations in our analysis.
Because of the limited number of sites, it is not
clear how the rotations here relate to overall
Walker Lane transtension and Basin and Range
extension. The presence of what appears to be
Permian-Triassic magnetization preserved in
these rocks, however, makes them ideal candi-
dates for future paleomagnetic investigations in
and around the Pahrump Valley.
CONCLUSIONS
On the basis of the paleomagnetic results
presented in this paper, we reach the following
conclusions.
