and Cheong, 1986; Leeet al., 1987; Kim and Kim, 1991; Kim
et al., 1993; Doh and Kim, 1994; Doh et al., 1994). Only
one paleomagnetic study for the Eumsung basin has been
done by Lee et al. (1992). In that study, results from just 5
samples of 1 site were reported, which can hardly be consid-
ered as representative directions of the strata in the Eumsung
basin. In this study, paleomagnetic results from Cretaceous
rocks in the Eumsung basin are presented by comparing the
results with those from the Gyeongsang basin and other Cre-
taceous basins in order to clarify the magnetic and tectonic
characteristics of the basin.
In terms of the age of granites in the study area, Cheong
et al. (1976) suggested that the granite in the eastern part of
the basin is Jurassic in age, and that of the granite in the west
is Cretaceous. However, Chun et al. (1994) recently argued
that the granite in the west to the basin formed in Jurassic. A
paleomagnetic investigation of the granites in the Eumsung
basin is carried out to constrain the age of the granites utiliz-
ing the timing of the magnetization of the granites.
2. Geologic Setting
The Eumsung basin is a pull-apart basin formed between
left-stepping sinistral “master” strike slip faults, and ﬁlled
with Cretaceous sedimentary rocks which were named as
the Chopyeong Formation (Chun et al., 1994). Precambrian
gneiss and Jurassic granite comprise the basement of the
basin and volcanic rocks are distributed along the eastern
boundary of the basin (Lee and Kim, 1971; Cheong et al.,

1976; Kang et al., 1980; Lee et al., 1989).
The ages of the granites in the eastern and the western parts
of the basin were thought to be Jurassic and Cretaceous, re-
spectively (Cheong et al. , 1976). However, recently Chun
et al. (1994) claimed that the age of the granite in the west-
ern part is Jurassic, because of cataclastic texture at the fault
contact of the granite with sedimentary rocks and presence
of perthite, a feldspar mineral formed in a plutonic rock by
slow cooling of magma, in sandstones collected from central
to western part of the basin. The granite outside the western
boundary, therefore, must be the source rock of the sedimen-
tary rocks in the western part of the basin and predate the
Cretaceous sedimentary rocks.
The Chopyeong Formation consists of various sedimen-
tary rocks, that can be divided into 3 lithofacies; conglomer-
ate facies, greenish mudstone facies, and purplish mudstone
facies (Fig. 1). Conglomerate facies is con ﬁned along the
margin of the basin, and the inner part of the basin is ﬁlled
with greenish and purplish mudstones, containing lenticular
beds of sandstone and clasts-bearing sandstones. Microfos-
sils of Charophytes are found only in greenish mudstone
facies (Choi et al., 1995). This succession is considered to
be formed in a stream dominated alluvial to lacustrine de-
positional environment. Sediments are thought to be mainly
derived from the nearby rocks, such as Precambrian gneiss,
Jurassic granite, and syn-depositional volcanic rocks (Chun
et al., 1994).
After the formation of sedimentary basin, the strata have
been deformed three times (Chun et al., 1994). The ﬁrst de-
formation was caused by the sinistral strike-slip fault which
reactivated the master faults and adjacent faults of the same
attitude in the basin. The second and third deformations were
caused by the NW-SE and the ENE-WSW sinistral strike-slip
fault which cut through the master faults. The folds devel-
oped in the sedimentary rocks were formed by the sinistral
strike-slip faulting and tilting along the master faults and by
the similarly oriented faults. The folds are wide open and
have the NNE to NE trend with low angle of plunging axis in
the central part of the basin and NE-SW trend in the marginal
parts of the master faults.
3. Field and Laboratory Methods
In the ﬁeld, samples were cored with a gasoline-powered
portable drill and oriented with magnetic and sun compasses.
There were no signiﬁcant differences between magnetic and
sun compass azimuths. 765 samples from 41 sites were col-
lected: 31 sites from red bed (purplish mudstone facies and
interlayered siltstone beds in conglomerate facies), 5 sites
from greenish mudstone, and 5 sites from granite (Fig. 1).
In the laboratory, samples were cut into 2.2 cm long cylin-
ders. Remanent magnetization of specimens was measured
using a Molspin spinner magnetometer. To determine suit-
able demagnetization method for the specimens of each site,
pilot samples were demagnetized either by alternating ﬁeld
(AF) demagnetization or by thermal demagnetization. AF
demagnetization was performed at the ﬁeld strength of 5–30
mT with 5 mT interval and 40–90 mT with 10 mT interval us-
ing a Molspin AF demagnetizer. Thermal demagnetization
was performed at 100, 200, 300, 350, 400, 450, 500, and for
temperature range of 520 –700◦C with 20 ◦C intervals using
an ASC Scientiﬁc thermal demagnetizer (model TD-48). To
monitor possible chemical changes of magnetic carriers on
heating, magnetic susceptibility was measured at each step
of thermal demagnetization using a Bartington magnetic sus-
ceptibility meter (model MS2). The samples were stored in
mu-metal boxes to prevent from acquisition of viscous rema-
nence by the external magnetic ﬁeld. The remaining speci-
mens were demagnetized using the suitable method for each
site. The orthogonal vector diagrams (Zijderveld, 1967) for
paleomagnetic data were plotted in order to identify the di-
rections of characteristic remanent magnetization (ChRM)
for each specimen employing the principal component anal-
ysis (PCA) with anchored line ﬁt method (Kirschvink, 1980)
using at least three or more data points presumably follow a
linear segment of a trajectory. Mean directions for individ-
ual sites and formations were calculated using Fisher (1953)
statistics. Specimens showing maximum angular deviation
greater than 15 ◦ and/or revealing directions quite different
from the rest of the specimens within a site were not included
for site mean calculation.
Isothermal remanent magnetization (IRM) acquisition ex-
periments for selected samples were performed using an ASC
Scientiﬁc Impulse Magnetizer (model IM-10). Hysteresis

4. Paleomagnetic Results
4.1 Chopyeong Formation
Among the total of 36 sites from the Chopyeong Forma-
tion, 31 sites are from red bed and 5 sites are from the greenish
mudstone facies. The number of sites in greenish mudstone
is much less because available outcrops are very limited in
the area.
The natural remanent magnetization (NRM) directions of
the Chopyeong Formation are predominantly northerly pos-
itive, clustering more closely about the present- ﬁeld direc-
tion ( D/I = 352.6◦/52.9◦) than the mean axial dipole ﬁeld
(D/I = 0◦/56.3◦), suggesting that the NRMs are merely
dominated by components of viscous origin.
From demagnetization of pilot samples of red bed, ther-
mal demagnetization is turned out to be the most effective
method to isolate the characteristic component from the red
bed because AF demagnetization even at the ﬁeld strength
of 90 mT cannot remove the remanent magnetization suc-
cessfully (Fig. 2(a)). The low temperature component, a
viscous remanent magnetization (VRM) component, can be
removed in the initial demagnetization stage of temperature
at or below 300 ◦C. Above 300 ◦C, a converging component
appears up to 620 –640◦C heating steps, and then the direc-
tion starts to randomize with the increase of susceptibility but
the magnetic intensity decreases continuously until 680 ◦C
(Fig. 2(b)). The ChRM was isolated mainly from 300 ◦Ct o
640◦C. The mean direction of the ChRMs from the red bed
is D/I = 347.0◦/56.8◦ (k = 121.6, α95 = 2.4◦) before tilt
correction and D/I = 1.0◦/62.2◦ (k = 21.4, α95 = 5.7◦)
after tilt correction. The site-mean direction of red bed is
more dispersed after tilt correction.
Both AF and thermal demagnetization methods are effec-
tive to isolate ChRM direction for the greenish mudstone
(Figs. 2(c) and (d)). For the ChRMs isolated using an AF
demagnetization method, the low coercivity component is re-
moved below 15 mT and then the characteristic component
is isolated above 20 mT. The mean direction of the greenish
mudstone is D/I = 353.5◦/60.4◦ (k = 34.8, α95 = 13.1)
before tilt correction and D/I = 358.9◦/58.4◦ (k = 10.7,
α95 = 24.6◦) after tilt correction. Tilt corrected directions are
more dispersed than in-situ directions, indicating greenish
mudstone acquired the remanence after tilting of the strata.
The mean direction of the Chopyeong Formation including
red and greenish beds is D/I = 347.8◦/57.3◦ (k = 92.8,
α95 = 2.5◦) before tilt correction and D/I = 0.7◦/61.7◦
(k = 19.6, α95 = 5.5◦) after tilt correction (Table 1).
4.2 Granite
Granites show two different demagnetization behaviors.
Because samples from the western part of the study area gen-
erally show unstable remanent directions and abrupt changes
in intensity (Fig. 3(a)), it is dif ﬁcult to isolate the ChRMs.
In contrast, samples from the eastern part show stable rema-
nent directions and gradual decrease of intensity (Fig. 3(b)).
In the samples from the western granite, the characteris-
tic components are determined at 5 –15 mT, whereas the
ChRMs for the eastern granite are isolated at 20 –60 mT.
The paleomagnetic mean direction of the two granite bodies
is D/I = 350.5◦/52.8◦ (k = 29.9, α95 = 14.2◦) (Table 2).
The paleomagnetic directions representing the granites in
the east and in the west are, however, separately recalcu-
lated as if they were site-mean directions for the east and
west granites because of the statistically meaningless num-
ber of sites for each granite. The mean direction, calcu-
lated in this way, of the east granite is D/I = 347.0◦/47.7◦
(k = 40.2, α95 = 3.6◦) and that of the west granite is
D/I = 354.6◦/59.5◦ (k = 9.1, α95 = 8.8◦).
5. Rock Magnetic Results
5.1 IRM acquisition experiment
IRM acquisition experiment is employed to distinguish
magnetic carriers whether they are members of magnetite-
ulv¨ospinel series or hematite-ilmenite series. Magnetite is
usually saturated inﬁeld of<150 mT, while theﬁeld required
to saturate hematite ranges from 200 mT for coarse specular
hematite to 2 Tesla or more for ﬁne pigmentary hematite
(Piper, 1987).

5.2 Hysteresis parameters
Hysteresis parameters are measured from the representa-
tive samples of red bed and greenish mudstone. Small cylin-
drical samples of 7 mm in diameter and 10 mm in height were
prepared for hysteresis measurements. Hysteresis loops were
obtained on a Molspin Nuvo vibrating sample magnetometer.
Saturation magnetization ( Ms), saturation remanence ( Mrs),
and coercive force (Hc) were determined after corrections of
the magnetic moment for high ﬁeld paramagnetic and dia-
magnetic slope. Remanent coercivity ( Hcr) was obtained
from stepwise back ﬁeld demagnetization of samples given
IRM. Hysteresis loops from red bed show typical results of
hematite (Fig. 5(a)) and those of greenish mudstone display
typical results of magnetite (Fig. 5(b)).
Hysteresis parameters, such as Ms, Mrs, Hc, and Hcr,o f
samples are listed in Table 3. The values of Hcr are com-
monly used to distinguish magnetic minerals in a way that
minerals of the corundum structure, such as hematite, have
Hcr above 200 mT while minerals of the spinel structure,
such as magnetite, have Hcr below 50 mT (Thompson et al.,
1980). All samples of greenish mudstone and granite have
Hcr less than 50 mT, while all samples of red bed show Hcr
above 300 mT. The grouping on the basis of values of Hcr
is well matched with the grouping based on the IRM ac-
quisition experiments. The ratios of hysteresis parameters,
Hcr/Hc and Mrs/Ms, are used to diagnose the domain state
of magnetic minerals (Day et al. , 1977). All samples from
greenish mudstone of the Chopyeong Formation belong to
pseudo-single domain (PSD) region (Fig. 6). The samples
from granite also reveal that they contain magnetic mineral
in the range of PSD to multidomain (MD) regions. Although
the plot of Mrs/Ms against Hcr/Hc is used to determine the
domain state of magnetite-bearing samples, results from red
bed are also shown in Fig. 6.

6. Electron Microscope Observations
To characterize the shape, size, and paragenesis of mag-
netic carriers, electron microscope observations were carried
out for representative samples from the Chopyeong Forma-
tion and granite. In order to identify iron oxide and adjacent
grains or matrix of magnetic carriers, compositional analy-
sis using energy dispersive spectroscopic (EDS) system for
X-ray analysis were performed.
In samples of the Chopyeong Formation, opaque grains
of submicron to 3 μm in size are abundant, and a few large
irregular grains (10 –20 μm) are also found. As expected
from demagnetization experiments, submicron-size needle
shaped hematite grains in ﬁlling the cleavages of chlorite are
the most frequently observed type of magnetic mineral from
red bed of the Chopyeong Formation (Fig. 7(a)). Hematite
grains shown in Fig. 7(a) suggest that they were formed either
by precipitation from Fe-bearingﬂuids or replacement of pre-
existing phases (Walkeret al., 1981). Large hematite grain of

and sphene is primary in origin.
7. Discussion
7.1 Remagnetization of the Chopyeong Formation
The gently to moderately dipping (10 ◦–40◦) Chopyeong
Formation revealed more dispersed paleomagnetic mean di-
rection after tilt correction (Fig. 9). In this case, it has long
been termed as a negative fold test of McElhinny (1964) using
k2/k1 ratio. McFadden and Jones (1981), however, pointed
out that the fold test is not valid because it is not possible to
test statistically whether the remanence is signiﬁcantly more
clustered after (or before) tilt correction. They proposed a
new hypothesis test to check whether the data are incom-
patible before and after tectonic correction. More recently
Watson and Enkin (1993) argued that the hypothesis test of
McFadden and Jones (1981) has difﬁculties especially when
the remanence is not simply pre- or post-tilting and they sug-
gested that the fold test is rather considered as a parameter
estimation problem to estimate the amount of tectonic tilting
at the time of magnetization than a hypothesis test.
The parameter estimation fold test (Watson and Enkin,
1993) and stepwise unfolding test were performed for the
data of the Chopyeong Formation. The parameter estima-
tion fold test gives the maximum k value for the Chopyeong
Formation at 21.9% untilting, with 95% con ﬁdence interval
of 2% untilting when the number of parametric resampling is
300. Separately computed stepwise unfolding test of the red
bed and greenish mudstone also yielded maximum clustering

with the results of the parameter estimation fold test. The pa-

and greenish beds of the Chopyeong Formation at 20% un-
tilting turns out to be D/I = 350.8◦/57.9◦ (k = 177.9,
α95 = 1.8◦). Incomplete isolation of characteristic compo-
nent, a common cause of a maximum k value not being at
0% or 100%, can be ruled out because the demagnetization
results indicate successful isolation of ChRMs (Fig. 2). The
stepwise unfolding test and the parameter estimation fold
test, showing more tightly clustered mean direction at 20%
untilting, clearly indicate that the ChRM of the Chopyeong
Formation is not a primary component but a remagnetized
one, although it is hard to determine whether the magnetiza-
tion of the Chopyeong Formation was acquired during tilting
or not. This is also supported by the fact that the character-
istic direction is signi ﬁcantly different from the directions
obtained from Cretaceous rocks in the Gyeongsang basin
(Kim and Jeong, 1986; Lee et al., 1987; Doh et al., 1994).
The timing and processes of remagnetization provide im-
portant insights into the orogenic and geochemical process
responsible for the remagnetization (Butler, 1992). There
are several possible mechanisms proposed for remagnetiza-
tion. Chemical remanent magnetization (CRM) acquired by
the formation of authigenic magnetic minerals in associa-
tion with the lateral migration of orogenic or basinal ﬂuids,
introduction of meteoric ﬂuids, as well as migration of hy-
drocarbons has been proposed as the mechanism of remag-
netization (McCabe et al. , 1983; Oliver, 1986; Elmore and
McCabe, 1991). Prolonged exposure to elevated temperature
below the Curie temperature affecting the ability of rocks to
retain a primary NRM has been suggested responsible for the
acquisition of thermoviscous magnetization (TVRM, e.g.,
Kent, 1985). Strain-related remagnetization (e.g., Hudson et
al., 1989) and surface weathering (e.g., Otofuji et al., 1989)
also have been nominated to bring the remagnetization.
Strain-related remagnetization is the most unlike mecha-
nism because the strata are gently tilted without severe de-
formation. Surface weathering should be ruled out because
uniform polarity and the well clustered directions are hard to
be acquired by weathering processes and more importantly
hematite and magnetite observed by electron microscope ob-
servations cannot be produced at the same time by weathering
processes. The intrusion of Cretaceous to Tertiary Bulguksa
granite might cause TVRM. In order to acquire TVRM with
an unblocking temperature of 640 –660◦C for hematite, it
is needed to be heated above 550 ◦C for, at least, 10 My
based on the blocking temperature-relaxation time curves of
Pullaiah et al. (1975). Despite that such temperature con-
dition should have resulted in considerable degree of con-
tact metamorphism in rocks, the strata in the study area do
not show any signs of the metamorphism due to high tem-
perature. Thus, remagnetization by TVRM can be denied.
The electron microscope observations strongly suggest that
the magnetic carriers, hematite and magnetite, are secondary
products formed under the inﬂuence of ﬂuids (Figs. 7 and 8).
Therefore, chemical remagnetization is turned out to be the
major process that causes the acquisition of secondary mag-
netization.
The paleomagnetic pole calculated from the untilted char-
acteristic direction of the Chopyeong Formation is at 53.7◦E,
79.8◦N( K = 49.7, A95 = 3.4◦). This paleomagnetic
pole is close to the Tertiary pole when it is compared with
the paleomagnetic poles of early Cretaceous to Quaternary
in Korea (Fig. 11(a)). Because the sedimentary rocks of

the Y ucheon Group in the Euisung area of the Gyeongsang
basin are compared (Fig. 11(b)). The fact that the paleomag-
netic pole of the Chopyeong Formation is statistically indis-
tinguishable from those of late Cretaceous volcanic rocks
conﬁrms not only that the remanence of the Chopyeong For-

possible rotation of the study area due to the formation of
the sinistral faults should have not further affected the rema-

the western part of the basin, is reported to be 65.98±0.93 Ma
(Lee et al., 1992) coinciding with the timing of remagnetiza-
tion in the study area. Similar aspects of remagnetization are
observed in Y oungdong basin lying in the southern boundary
of the Ogcheon Belt (Cho, 1994). However, in order to un-
derstand more accurate mechanism of the remagnetization
and to constrain the age of the remagnetization, geochemical
studies of the temperature and chemical conditions of ﬂu-
ids and the timing of the fault development in the basin that
might play an important role in the passage of the ﬂuids are
desirable.
7.2 Age of granite
The age of granite in the Eumsung basin is controversial.
The granite in the west to the basin was originally assigned
as Cretaceous in age according to the reported K-Ar age of
112 Ma (Kim, 1971), while the age of the granite in the east
of the basin is assumed to be Jurassic based on an intrusive
relationship to the sedimentary rocks (Cheong et al., 1976).
On the other hand, the same granite near the Jincheon area
yielded an age of 194 Ma by Rb-Sr method (Jooet al., 1979).
However, Chun et al. (1994) recently argued that they found
fault-contacts between the granite and the sedimentary rocks,
thus the granite in the west should be Jurassic in age.
The paleomagnetic mean directions of the granites are
compared to those from previous paleomagnetic studies. It
is revealed that the mean direction of the east granite (D/I =
347.0◦/47.7◦, k = 40.2, α95 = 3.6◦) is similar to the Juras-
sic direction (mean D/I = 334.3◦/51.0◦, α95 = 8.4◦) ob-
tained from granites in the Ogcheon Folded Belt by Kim
and V an der V oo (1990). On the other hand, the paleo-
magnetic direction representing the granite in the west was
compared with the paleomagnetic directions calculated for
the study area (127.61◦E, 36.90◦N) from the published pole
positions of Early Cretaceous to Quaternary. It is found
that the paleomagnetic direction of the granite in the west
(D/I = 354.6◦/59.5◦, k = 9.1, α95 = 8.8◦), is similar to
the Tertiary direction (D/I = 357.3◦/55.0◦) calculated from
the Tertiary pole position of Kim and Kang (1989) (Fig. 12).
Since the mean directions of the east and west granites
are statistically different from each other, it is interpreted
that the two granites were not magnetized at the same time.
As described before, demagnetization features of the gran-
ite in the east are also different from those of the granite in
the west in a way that the samples from the western part of
the study area generally show unstable remanent directions
and abrupt changes in intensity giving rise to dif ﬁculties to
isolate the ChRMs, while the samples from the eastern part
disclose stable remanent directions and gradual decrease of
intensity resulting in better de ﬁned ChRMs (Fig. 3). More-
over it is revealed, based on the IRM acquisition results, that
the major magnetic carrier of the granite in the west (site 35)
is hematite, whereas magnetite is the predominant magnetic
mineral of the granite in the east (Fig. 4(b)). In addition,
electron microscope observations show that hematite is the
dominant authigenic iron oxide mineral resulted from the al-
teration of pre-existing minerals in the granite from the west
(Fig. 8(a)), indicating that the mean direction of the west
granite is suspicious of being a remagnetized component.
Moreover it is also possible that the ChRMs of the granite
in the west of the basin are of VRM origin because lower
coercivity components isolated at 5–15 mT demagnetization
level are included. Thus, it is concluded that the age of the

8. Conclusions
1. It is concluded that the Chopyeong Formation has been
remagnetized based on the fact that the mean direction at 20%
untilting ( D/I = 350.8◦/57.9◦, k = 177.9, α95 = 1.8◦)
is more tightly clustered and the characteristic direction is
signiﬁcantly different from the directions obtained from the
Cretaceous rocks in the Gyeongsang basin, although it is hard
to determine whether the magnetization of the Chopyeong
Formation was acquired during syntilting or not.
2. From the characteristics of remagnetization of the
Chopyeong Formation in the Eumsung basin and electron mi-
croscope observations, it is evident that the strata acquired the
chemical remagnetization due to the formation of secondary
magnetic minerals under the in ﬂuence of ﬂuids presumably
triggered by the igneous activities during late Cretaceous to
early Tertiary.
3. It is revealed that the age of the granite in the east of the
basin is Jurassic because the mean direction of the east granite
(D/I = 347.0◦/47.7◦, k = 40.2, α95 = 3.6◦) is similar to
the Jurassic direction of the Korea Peninsula. Although the
paleomagnetic direction of the granite in the west to the basin
(D/I = 354.6◦/59.5◦, k = 9.1, α95 = 8.8◦) is similar to the
Tertiary direction, the age of the granite is left undetermined
due to the weak intensity and instability of the remanence of
the granite during demagnetization treatments.

Palaeomagnetism of Early Triassic limestones from the Huanan
Block, South China: no evidence for separation between the Huanan
and Yangtze blocks during the Early Mesozoic
Xiaodong Tan,1 Kenneth P. Kodama,1 Pengyan Wang2 and Dajun Fang2
1 Department of Earth and Environmental Sciences, L ehigh University, 31 W illiams Drive, Bethlehem, PA 18015, USA. E-mail: xit2@lehigh.edu
2 Department of Earth Sciences, Zhejiang University, Hangzhou, China
Accepted 2000 March 9. Received 2000 January 7; in original form 1999 January 29
SUMMARY
There has been extensive debate on the timing of the collision between the Huanan
and Yangtze blocks ever since Hsu and co-workers (Hsu et al. 1987, 1988) proposed a
Mesozoic collision model for South China tectonics. We report new rock and palaeo-
magnetic data from an Early Triassic limestone formation from the Huanan Block that
help to constrain its tectonic history. The samples are from two localities [Jiupi (JT),
and Huangben (LT)] in Lianzhou County, northern Guangdong province.
Only thermal demagnetization is eﬀective in decomposing a multicomponent remanent
magnetization. The majority of samples show three components: a low-temperature
component (A), an intermediate-temperature component (B), and a high-temperature
characteristic remanent magnetization (ChRM). The A component has a steep inclination
and is probably drilling-induced. The B component clusters around the present
geomagnetic ﬁeld direction and is a Brunhes-age viscous remanence. Fold test results
suggest that the JT ChRM is pre-tectonic, and that the LT ChRM is a syn- or pre-
folding remagnetization. Samples from the two localities show quite similar acquisition
and thermal demagnetization of the isothermal remanent magnetization (IRM), and
suggest that magnetite carries the ChRM component. However, partial anhysteretic
remanent magnetization (pARM) spectra, anisotropy of anhysteretic remanence (AAR),
rock fabric, and morphology of magnetic extracts are quite diﬀerent for the two localities.
The AAR of JT samples shows low anisotropy (average 2 per cent), and reﬂects a com-
posite compaction and strain fabric. The AAR of LT samples shows a high degree of
anisotropy (average 10 per cent), and is clearly consistent with rock deformation fabrics.
The magnetic extracts of LT samples are dominated by spherical, botryoidal Ti-poor
magnetite, which is probably precipitated from tectonic ﬂuids during deformation, while
the JT magnetic extracts are dominated by rod-shaped Ti-poor magnetite, probably
derived from the erosion of igneous rocks, although minor amounts of botryoidal
magnetite and rod-like magnetite particles can be seen in JT and LT extracts,
respectively.
The rock fabric and magnetic fabric data, and SEM observations of magnetic
extracts corroborate the results of the fold test. The best clustered LT ChRM direction
is D=294°,I=−12°(a95=12°); its pole position is 187 °E, 19°S(dp=6°,dm=12°).
The assumption of a reversed polarity for the JT ChRM direction ( D=198°,I=−20°,
a95=9°) implies that the Huanan Block was in the northern hemisphere during the
Early Triassic, and its pole position, 239 °E, 68°N(dp=5°,dm=10°) is close to Early
Triassic pole positions from the Yangtze Block. A normal polarity for the JT-site
ChRM would require tectonic movements inconsistent with the local geology. Therefore,
the Huanan and Yangtze blocks were not separated in the Early Triassic. The rotation
of the LT locality may have been caused by the collision of the southeast China coastal
terranes and /or subduction of the Paciﬁc plate in the Late Mesozoic.
Key words: Huanan Block, magnetic fabric, palaeomagnetism, SEM, Triassic,
Yangtze Block.

The acquisition of isothermal remanent magnetization
(IRM) and back- ﬁeld demagnetization were conducted on an
ASC IM-10 impulse magnetizer. The acquisition and demag-
netization curves show similar behaviour for the JT and LT
samples (Fig. 9). In most cases, IRM increases rapidly at low
ﬁelds (<0.2 T), and gradually increases until ﬁeld intensities
of 0.9 T are reached. All the samples are close to saturation at
0.9–1.2 T. This behaviour suggests the dominance of low-
coercivity minerals such as magnetite and maghemite, and a
minor amount of high-coercivity minerals, namely haematite,
goethite, and pyrrhotite.

acquired in a ~50 mTD C ﬁeld is also similar for JT and LT
samples (Fig. 9). The ARM unblocking spectra are distributed
between 100 and 550 °C, which is indicative of magnetite.
The IRM decays more rapidly at low temperatures ( <400 °C)
than at high temperatures, and is completely demagnetized
by 500–550 °C. At higher temperatures ( >600 °C), IRM
intensity drops below or to the magnetometer ’s noise level
(1 ×10−11Am 2), and thus haematite is unlikely to be a carrier
of remanence. The unblocking of the IRM component at low
temperatures (<400 °C) may be indicative of goethite, pyrrhotite,
greigite, and/or inversion of maghemite to haematite. Unblocking
of magnetite remanence may also contribute to the IRM decay
at low temperatures. The inversion of maghemite to haematite
might be ruled out by the lack of a signi ﬁcant decrease in
magnetic susceptibility at temperatures above 400 °C (Fig. 7).
Based on the rock-magnetic data, the carriers of the low- and
intermediate-temperature components of magnetization could
be goethite, pyrrhotite, greigite, or magnetite. Since the ChRM
component is isolated between 350 and 500 °C, it is probably
carried solely by magnetite.

The Ti-poor, rod-shaped magnetite is rarely seen in limestone
samples, but it is common in igneous rocks in which magnetite–
ilmenite intergrowths are formed by ilmenite exsolution from
a magnetite–ultrospinel solid solution (e.g. Larson et al. 1969;
Beske-Diehl 1988; Butler 1992; Hodych 1996) or magnetite
crystallizing within the cracks of other mineral crystals, such as
olivine or feldspar (Butler 1992; Zhang & Halls 1995; Warnock
1997). The rod-shaped magnetite is probably derived from the
erosion of igneous rocks.
SEM observations suggest that the magnetic grain size is in
the single-domain or pseudo-single-domain grain size range,
consistent with the results of low-temperature demagnetization.
Liquid nitrogen low-temperature demagnetization can only
remove less than 10 per cent of NRM or IRM intensity,
indicating that single-domain and/or pseudo-single-domain
magnetite is the dominant magnetic carrier of ChRM (e.g. Levi
& Merrill 1978; Dunlop & Argyle 1991; Hodych et al. 1998).
Previous rock-magnetic and petrographic studies suggest that
remagnetized carbonate rocks are dominated by low-coercivity
particles of spherical secondary magnetite (e.g. McCabe et al.

with secondary, botryoidal magnetic particles as carriers of
the remanence. The broad peak in the pARM spectra of the
JT samples reﬂects the contamination of rod-shaped primary
magnetite by botryoidal secondary magnetite as evidenced by
the SEM observations. In addition, the LT intensities of NRM,

Gilder et al. (1996) used Sm –Nd and Rb –Sr isotopic com-
positions to de ﬁne crustal provinces in South China. Their
data suggest a homogeneous Proterozoic crust with no suture
occurring in the Mesozoic. According to Hsu et al.’s (1988)
model, the Yangtze Block subducted under and was accreted
to the Huanan Block during the Late Triassic, with a wide ocean
basin between the two blocks before the collision. However,
there is no geological evidence of volcanic activity or magmatic
intrusions during the Late Palaeozoic and Early Mesozoic in
the middle and eastern Yangtze Block, adjacent to the Huanan
Block. Had the oceanic crust between these two blocks existed,
its subduction beneath the Huanan Block should have left a
signature of that event, including deformation and magmatism.
Geological evidence indicates that magmatic intrusion and
volcanism in the Huanan Block started in the Late Triassic.
Deformation of continental cover rocks was initiated at almost
the same time (Late Triassic) in both the Yangtze and Huanan
blocks. The stratigraphic records and tectonic histories of the
Yangtze and Huanan blocks do not support large-scale relative

The paleomagnetic significance of new U-Pb age data from the Molson dyke swarm, Cauchon Lake area, Manitoba1

Henry C. Halls and Larry M. Heaman

Abstract: U-Pb geochronology, paleomagnetism, and petrography indicate that the Molson dyke swarm, along the western margin of the Superior craton, is a composite of at least two ages of intrusion. The more extensive younger dyke set, the Molson swarm sensu stricto, generally has a 030° trend, is mainly pyroxenitic to noritic with subordinate diabase, and has been related to rifting in a back-arc environment during closure of the Manikewan ocean at about 1920–1800 Ma which culminated in the Trans-Hudson Orogen. A U-Pb zircon age from one of these dykes, located at Cauchon Lake, indicates emplacement at 1877+7, similar to two previous U-Pb age determinations on Molson dykes. Another dyke from Cauchon Lake yields a baddeleyite-zircon U-Pb date of 2091 ± 2 Ma and appears to be part of an older, mainly diabasic suite of east-northeast-trending dykes that may represent a continental rifting episode that preceded the opening of the Manikewan ocean. The new U-Pb age data require a revision to the interpretation of the A, B, and C paleomagnetic poles previously reported from Molson dykes. The A pole (16.1°N, 96.5°W), initially assigned an age of 1883 Ma, is now considered to be younger and derived from a Paleoproterozoic overprint associated with the Trans-Hudson Orogen at about 1700–1800 Ma. Pole B (27.1°N, 140.8°W) from the Molson swarm sensu stricto is now regarded as primary, and dated at 1880 Ma. Pole C can be subdivided into two poles, one virtually the same as B but of opposite polarity (and therefore about 1880 Ma old) and a new pole (53°N, 180°W) derived from a primary remanence and dated at 2091 Ma. The new paleomagnetic interpretations may have important consequences for tectonic models of the Trans-Hudson Orogen and for Paleoproterozoic continental reconstructions.

Résumé : La géochronologie U-Pb, le paléomagnétisme et la pétrographie indiquent que l’essaim de dykes Molson, le long de la bordure ouest du craton du Supérieur, est composé d’au moins deux âges intrusifs. L’ensemble de dykes plus étendu et plus jeune, l’essaim Molson sensu stricto, a généralement une tendance 030°; il a une composition pyroxénitique à noritique et une diabase accessoire. On l’a relié a une zone de fracture dans un environnement d’arrière arc lors de la fermeture de l’océan Manikewan il y a environ 1920–1800 Ma et qui a culminé avec l'Orogène transhudsonien. Une datation U-Pb sur du zircon provenant de l'un de ces dykes localisé au lac Cauchon indique une mise en place il y a 1877±7 Ma, ce qui est semblable à deux déterminations antérieures d’âge sur des dykes Molson. Un autre dyke du lac Cauchon donne une date U-Pb baddeleyite-zircon de 2091 ± 2 Ma et semble faire partie d’un ensemble de dykes où domine le diabase et dont la tendance est ENE; ces dykes pourraient représenter un épisode de distension du continent précédant l’ouverture de l’océan Manikewan. Les nouvelles données d’âges U-Pb exigent une révision de l’interprétation des pôles paléomagnétiques A, B et C antérieurement tirés des dykes Molson. Le pôle A (16,1°N, 96,5°W), pour lequel on a antérieurement déterminé un âge de 1883 Ma, est maintenant considéré comme étant plus jeune et provenant d’une surimpression paléoprotérozoïque associée à l'Orogène trans-hudsonien il y a environ 1700–1800 Ma. Le pôle B (27,1°N, 140,8°W) de l’essaim de dykes Molson sensu stricto est maintenant considéré comme primaire et âgé de 1880 Ma. Le pôle C peut être subdivisé en deux pôles, l’un pratiquement identique à B mais de polarité inverse (et donc vieux d’environ 1880 Ma) et un nouveau pôle (53°N, 180°W) dérivé d’une rémanence primaire et datant d’environ 2091 Ma. Les nouvelles interprétations paléomagnétiques peuvent avoir des conséquences importantes pour les modèles tectoniques de l'Orogène trans-hudsonien et pour la reconstruction continentale au Paléoprotérozoïque.

Introduction

The Molson dyke swarm, located on the western margin of the Superior Province in Manitoba (Fig. 1), has been the subject of several radiometric and paleomagnetic investigations because it has long been considered the remnant of a Paleoproterozoic rift-parallel magmatic event that heralded the opening of the Manikewan ocean (Stauffer 1984). This ocean was formed by rifting of an Archean landmass, and its subsequent closure, first expressed by island-arc magmatism

at 1.92 Ga (Gordon et al. 1990), ultimately formed the \~1800 Ma Trans-Hudson Orogen (THO). A previous U-Pb geochronology project was initiated by Heaman et al. (1986) to establish the emplacement age of the Molson dykes, thereby constraining the timing of the rifting event. Identical high-precision U-Pb zircon ages for two dykes (locations 1 and 2 in Fig. 1) at Cross Lake (1884 ± 2 Ma) and Cuthbert Lake (1883 ± 2 Ma) were interpreted to indicate that most, if not all, of the Molson magmatism was younger than islandarc volcanism occurring within the Manikewan ocean (Heaman et al. 1986), thus demonstrating that the majority of the Molson dykes were not related to the pre-1.92 Ga rifting event.

To resolve this paradox, further research was carried out to determine whether there were indeed multiple ages of dyke emplacement, a suggestion made by Corkery (1985) and supported by crosscutting relationships between mafic dykes observed in the Split Lake block (Fig. 1). Two additional lines of evidence have been put forward that support the field observations of Corkery: (i) a paleomagnetic study of the Molson swarm (Zhai et al. 1994) identified three magnetization directions, designated A, B, and C, all of which were regarded as primary and having distinct ages; and (ii) a U-Pb zircon age of 2072 ± 3 Ma was obtained for a northeast-trending gabbro dyke at Birthday Rapids in the Split Lake block (Heaman and Corkery 1996).

Component A was assigned an age of 1883 Ma by Zhai et al. (1994) on the basis of aeromagnetic anomaly correlation of the dated Cuthbert dyke with A component dykes identified at Landing Lake to the south (Fig. 1). Based on a comparison with well-constrained paleomagnetic pole positions from the Superior Province (e.g., Buchan et al. 1993), Zhai et al. estimated the emplacement age of the B and C dykes to be between 2170 and 2120 Ma.

Here we discuss the paleomagnetic and age implications for the Molson swarm in terms of its origin and relation to the THO in light of new zircon-baddeleyite U-Pb ages obtained for two diabase dykes located along the shore of Cauchon Lake (Fig. 1).

Geological background

The approximately north-northeast-trending Molson dyke swarm occurs within a 100 km wide corridor along the western margin of the Archean Superior Province (Fig. 1). Abundant well-preserved Molson dykes transect the high-grade granulites of the Pikwitonei Domain and are observed to be rotated and metamorphosed within the Thompson belt (Fig. 1) where migmatic gneisses, largely derived from Pikwitonei granulites, were formed through reworking by the THO (Weber 1990). Within the corridor, the Molson dyke swarm covers an area of approximately 26 000 km² and represents a volume of magma of the order of 50 000 km³.

Molson dykes are up to 60 m in width and vary in rock type from gabbro to pyroxenite. Their composition ranges from komatiitic basalt through to more normal tholeiite, the latter in particular exhibiting well-developed chilled margins. A detailed report on the geology and geochemistry of the Molson dykes was published by Scoates and Macek (1978).

U-Pb geochronology

Geology and paleomagnetism of samples

The samples used in this study were collected from pegmatitic pods within two dykes located at Cauchon Lake (Fig. 1) and are from paleomagnetic sites MO91 and MO77 of Zhai et al. (1994). The dyke at site MO91 (location 3 in Fig. 1) has a width of 36 m, trends 060°, and dips 75°NW, approximately conformable with the gneissosity of adjacent host rocks. Petrographically, the dyke is fresh from chilled margin to interior and comprises subophitic diabase with equal proportions of clinopyroxene and plagioclase. Paleomagnetically the site gave a well-defined C magnetization (declination (D) = 120°, inclination (I) = -59°, radius of 95% confidence circle about the direction (α95) = 5.5°, number of oriented cores (Ns) = 7, from both interior and western chilled margin).

Site MO77 (location 4 in Fig. 1) is from an outcrop located in the interior of a fresh dyke composed of plagioclase, clinopyroxene, orthopyroxene, olivine, brown amphibole, and accessory biotite and magnetite. This dyke is coarse grained, contains abundant pegmatite, and is at least 13 m wide with unexposed margins. Faint internal banding suggests a trend of about 070°. Paleomagnetically, the dyke records a well-defined B direction (D = 260°, I = 67°, α95 = 2.7°, Ns = 6).

Analytical techniques

For both samples, approximately 1 kg of drill core was crushed to a fine powder (<300 μm) using a jaw crusher and Bico Disk mill. Baddeleyite-zircon isolation was accomplished using a Wilfley table, combined with standard heavy mineral and magnetic separation techniques. A small amount of both baddeleyite and skeletal zircon shards was recovered from dyke MO91, with zircon tending to form larger (up to 100 μm) and more abundant grains than baddeleyite. Most of the baddeleyite grains were altered, with few pristine crystals present. Sample MO77 contained abundant zircon and pyrite. The zircon varied in colour from colourless to tan, and generally formed irregular fragments. A few broken long prismatic grains were present and typically contained longitudinal inclusion trains. The incipient development of a younger polycrystalline zircon growth was detected on some zircon fragments. Also present were a number of elliptical resorbed zircon grains interpreted to be xenocrystic and not selected for analysis.

Isolation of U and Pb by anion exchange chromatography and determination of their isotopic composition on a VG354 mass spectrometer, operated in single-collector mode, generally followed procedures outlined elsewhere (Heaman and Machado 1992; Heaman and LeCheminant 1993). For sample MO91 two analyses were determined at the University of Alberta, and three at the Jack Satterly Laboratory, Royal Ontario Museum (Table 1). All zircon U-Pb analyses for dyke MO77 were carried out at the Radiogenic Isotope Facility, University of Alberta. At the time of this study (1993–1996), the analytical blanks for U and Pb measured in the two laboratories were 0.5 and 2.0 pg (Royal Ontario Museum) and 1 and 6 pg (University of Alberta), respectively. Age calculations and associated uncertainties were calculated using the program of Davis (1982) and decay constants 1.55125 × 10-0 year-1 for 238U and 9.8485 × 10-10 year−1 for 235U as determined by Jaffey et al. (1971).

U-Pb results

Dyke MO91

The U-Pb results for five fractions (three zircon and two baddeleyite) are presented in Table 1 and on a concordia diagram in Fig. 2a. Two of the zircon fractions (3 and 4) were given an abrasion treatment (Krogh 1982) and plot within error of the concordia curve with 207Pb/206pb model ages of 2091 and 2095 Ma, respectively. The two baddeleyite fractions (2 and 5; solid ellipses in Fig. 2a) are significantly more discordant than the zircon analyses and may have been affected by Pb loss associated with the pervasive alteration of the grains. An interesting feature of these baddeleyite grains is their higher than normal thorium contents (note that the Th/U ratios in Table 1 are much higher than 0.1, a maximum value for typical baddeleyite). Baddeleyite analysis 5 represents the best attempt at isolating the least altered grains. Regression of four of the five multigrain analyses (excluding 2, the most obviously altered baddeleyite grains) yields an upper intercept age of 2091.1±18, interpreted to be the emplacement age of this dyke. This is the oldest emplacement age yet recorded for a “Molson" dyke.

Dyke MO77

The U-Pb results for three multigrain zircon fractions (11-61 grains) are presented in Table 1 and displayed on a concordia diagram in Fig. 2b. Although the three analyses are not collinear, two (1 and 3) have nearly identical 207Pb/206Pb ages of 1875 and 1874 Ma, respectively. The reference line constructed to pass through these two analyses yields an upper intercept age of 1877+7, which we interpret as close to the emplacement age for this dyke. Analysis 2 has a slightly older207Pb/206 Pb age of 1887 Ma and significantly lower uranium content and Th/U ratio (see Table 1). It is possible that a small number of inherited grains were unknowingly included in this fraction.

The C magnetization was originally considered primary because unbaked granulite gneisses collected from the western part of Pikwitonei Lake and in the central one-third of Landing Lake (Fig. 1), where both B and C dykes are found, gave a distinctly different direction D (D = 53.6°, 1 = -64.4°) that was regarded as older (Zhai et al. 1994). Positive baked contact tests indicate that B is primary (Fig. 7 of Zhai et al. 1994) and the new U–Pb data from site

MO77 indicate that it is about 1880 Ma old. Therefore, D and C2 may also date approximately from this time. The C, pole occurs northwest of that for the 2121 Ma Marathon N dykes (42.8°N, 164.4°W), consistent with its assigned age of 2091 Ma.

The antipode of the undated reversed C2 pole position is virtually coincident with that given by B dykes (27.1°N, 140.8°W) which also include both olivine-bearing pyroxenitic-noritic and diabasic types. The two petrographically similar dyke suites will collectively be referred to as the Molson swarm sensu stricto. The occurrence of C2 in the dykes and pervasively, as D, in the granulites suggests that the Molson dyke swarm was intruded during a time interval that included a reversal of the Earth's field direction from C2 to B.

The new age for the B pole is in direct conflict with that reported earlier for the A component (Zhai et al. 1994), which was assigned an age of 1883 Ma on the strength of the Cuthbert dyke U–Pb data (Heaman et al. 1986) and possible correlations of this dyke with those in Landing Lake which carry A. Four lines of evidence suggest that B is indeed about 1880 Ma and, moreover, that A is younger.

First, a dyke, about 100 m wide, follows the Nelson River and is known as the Nelson River dyke. It is the eastern of two megadykes in the Molson swarm that are known to extend for several hundred kilometres (Fig. 1). The dyke is correlated with one in Cross Lake that has given a U-Pb age of 1884 ± 2 Ma (Heaman et al. 1986). The Nelson River dyke has an ultramafic composition and is only exposed at low water levels because it has been preferentially eroded to form the river channel. Site MO89 (location 5 in Fig. 1) of Zhai et al. (1994) is a vertical, 3 m wide diabase dyke, trending 022°, parallel to the river on its western side (Fig. 1). It gives a B magnetization (D = 227°, I = 63°, α95 = 5.8°, Ns = 7). This dyke is unlikely to postdate the Nelson dyke because in the general area of the Molson dykes mafic magmatism younger than 1880 Ma is unknown. Therefore, it is either an apophesis of the Nelson River dyke or, if older, would lie well within the baked zone of the larger dyke and thus would have been magnetically reset by it.

The foregoing evidence suggests that the 1884 Ma Nelson River dyke was intruded at a time when the Earth's magnetic field had a B direction.

Second, the A magnetization was assigned to the 1883 Ma Cuthbert dyke on the basis of a possible correlation with A dykes at the western end of Landing Lake using regional aeromagnetic data. The correlation is uncertain because the linear “dyke" anomalies are not continuous and the dated Cuthbert dyke could pass to the west of Landing Lake (see Fig. 8 of Zhai et al. 1994).

Third, three A dykes at sites MO32, MO51, and MO64 have paleomagnetic results that are consistent with a primary origin for A, because unbaked host rocks in their vicinity give D magnetizations (Zhai et al. 1994). Others, such as those at the western end of Landing Lake, have no host rock data in their vicinity and, therefore, their magnetization could be secondary. The greater abundance of A dykes with increasing proximity to the THO (Fig. 5 of Zhai et al. 1994) supports a secondary origin for A.

Fourth, the secondary nature of A is more strongly suspected for the majority of A dykes found in the Sipiwesk Lake area (Fig. 5 of Zhai et al. 1994), which is closest to the Thompson belt. Here the dykes locally have a foliation parallel to enclosing gneisses and have been recrystallized with the production of secondary amphibole (sites MO14 and MO16). Most of the dykes (all except sites MO21 and MO22) are cut by numerous thin felsic pegmatite veins and frequently have sheared chilled margins. Unfortunately, all granulite gneisses remote from dykes (sites MO18, MO23, and MO24) were paleomagnetically unstable, and thus a negative baked contact test, necessary to prove the secondary origin for A, is lacking. However, the field observations are compelling; dykes showing these secondary features generally do not yield primary magnetizations. For those A dykes (MO32, MO51, and MO64) more remote from the adjacent Thompson belt, where nearby dykes carry B or C, further tests are needed to demonstrate if the A remanence is primary and thus indicative of a still younger magmatic event.

From the foregoing discussion, the age of the A pole is younger than the primary remanence of the 1880 Ma Molson dykes. The dykes have been deformed, presumably in the final collisional-magmatic phases of the THO from about 1720 to 1820 Ma (Machado 1990) and would have acquired their remanence after subsequent cooling. Therefore, without Ar-Ar data, the age of the A pole can only be defined within broad limits of about 1.7–1.8 Ga. The A pole position thus continues the apparent polar wander path, as shown in Fig. 3, on its southeast-directed return journey, although an excursion to higher latitudes, either before or after the A magnetization was formed, is indicated from paleomagnetic studies on units within the orogen which are described in an accompanying paper (Symons and Harris 2000).

Discussion and conclusions

The new U-Pb age data prove conclusively that the Molson dyke swarm sensu lato is a composite of at least two episodes of dyke intrusion separated in time by about 200 Ma. The older, 2091 Ma dykes occur in the northern part of the swarm, are diabasic, and trend generally eastnortheast (Fig. 1). Their age is only slightly younger than the zircon-baddeleyite age of 2111.2 ± 0.6 Ma obtained from a rift-related gabbro in the lower Hurwitz Group of the Hearne Province (Heaman and LeCheminant 1993). The similarity in age and location of these mafic magmatic events, on opposite sides of the THO, suggests that they are related to the opening of the Manikewan ocean (Halls and Heaman 1997). This in turn implies that the Hearne and Superior Provinces (Fig. 1) were once contiguous before they rifted apart.

The younger \1880 Ma dykes, which make up the Molson swarm sensu stricto (Fig. 1), tend to be more ultramafic in composition, generally have north-northeast trends (although north, northwest, and east-northeast dykes are known), and may have originated as a result of rifting in a back-arc setting (Weber 1990).

For the time interval 2230 to \1750 Ma the paleomagnetic apparent polar wander path for the southern Superior Province, based entirely on mafic dykes, is shown in Fig. 3. A similar path, using mafic dykes and associated volcanics, has been obtained from the Minto Block in the extreme northeastern part of the Superior Province (Buchan et al. 1998), although, like the path in Fig. 3, it is poorly dated at its younger end. In this study, a key pole (38.2°N, 186.2°W), from the Minto dykes (U-Pb age on zircon and baddeleyite of 1998 ± 2 Ma), plots in the cluster of poles formed by the Fort Frances, Marathon, and C1 dykes in Fig. 3. Incorporating both data sets in the Superior Province apparent polar wander path suggests that from \2200 to \2100 Ma the pole moved about 1° arc per Ma towards the northwest, and then for the next 100 Ma, from 2100 to 2000 Ma, was more or less stationary. From \2000 to \1750 Ma, the rate of polar wander depends upon the choice of antipodal pole positions for the A and B poles. If the antipode of B is chosen, maximizing the path length with respect to the cluster at 2100– 2000 Ma, the polar wander path (version 1) resumes its fast rate of movement of about 1° arc per Ma, in the same sense as before. If the antipode of A is also plotted, the path reverses its motion to form a hairpin (Irving and Park 1972) at about \ 1900 Ma. If both the A and B poles are plotted as in Fig. 3, the path (version 2) has a hairpin with an apex defined at about 2100-2000 Ma and a rate of polar motion along the return path of only about 0.4° per Ma. Although version 1 of the path violates the minimum path length concept, it yields a hairpin with an apex corresponding closely with the time of ocean closure that culminated in the THO. The meaning of hairpins in terms of changes in the direction of plate motion associated with Wilson cycles and more specifically with orogens was first suggested by Irving and Park (1972). Since the polar wander path of version 2 (Fig. 3) remains within about 30° of arc from the sampling sites throughout the time period 2167 to \1750 Ma, the associated hairpin cannot be readily interpreted in terms of a reversal of plate motion, and the age of its apex (about 2000 2100 Ma) does not correspond with any known orogen.

The apparent polar wander path for the time period 1700– 1900 Ma is extremely uncertain because poles determined from reliably dated remanences are absent. Symons and Harris (2000) suggest that a case can be made for an \1830 Ma hairpin that corresponds to orogenic collision of juvenile terranes of the THO. Their poles are derived from different units within the THO, mainly gneisses, granites, and gabbros, that yield zircon and monazite ages between 1890 and 1770 Ma, which are thought to represent the approximate time of remanence acquisition (Symons et al. 1995; Symons and Harris 2000) The A pole which may also be related to the final phase of the orogen, dated by U-Pb on late pegmatites and gneisses in the adjoining Thompson belt to be from 1720 to 1820 Ma (Machado 1990), appears to be in conflict with most of the THO data, as it plots about 30° of latitude farther south. The problem is that the closure temperatures for Pb in zircon and monazite (>800°C and \725°C, respectively; Heaman and Parrish 1991) are much higher than those temperatures at which a remanence carried by magnetite is acquired (550–580°C), assuming it is entirely a thermal remanence, a difference that is even greater if remanences have a significant chemical component.

A U-Pb study of zircon, monazite, and titanite from the Hearne Province, which forms the westernmost domain of the THO (Fig. 1), documents a high-grade thermotectonic event at about 1810–1830 Ma, with maximum temperatures of \750°C and a cooling rate of \7°C/Ma (Orrell et al. 1999). These authors suggest that this high-temperature regional thermotectonism, which was associated with terminal collision, extended across the Trans-Hudson Orogen to the Thompson Fold Belt in the west. If this conclusion is valid, any thermal remanences formed during subsequent uplift and cooling from within the THO itself could be at least 25 Ma younger than associated U-Pb zircon and monazite ages. Therefore the poles reported from within the orogen (Symons and Harris 2000) have ages that are uncertain with respect to the A pole and have been omitted from Fig. 3.

Despite the uncertainties in the form and interpretation of the Superior Province apparent polar wander path, this work has resulted in a significant change by about 40° of arc in the 1880 Ma pole position. The 2000–1750 Ma segment that includes this data point has been used previously to help fit Laurentia to Baltica at about 1.9 Ga (Buchan et al. 1996b)and to chart the evolution of the THO (Symons et al. 1995), particularly with respect to how the Superior and Hearne margins of the orogen behaved during subduction and in the early stages of continental collision. These interpretations will require modification arising from the repositioning of the key 1880 Ma pole (e.g., Symons and Harris 2000).

ABSTRACT
This article reports the ®rst joint paleomagnetic and U-Pb geochronologic study of Precambrian diabase dikes in the
Anabar Shield and adjacent Riphean cover of Siberia. It was undertaken to allow comparison with similar published
studies in Laurentia and to test Proterozoic reconstructions of Siberia and Laurentia. An east-trending Kuonamka
dike yielded a provisional U-Pb baddeleyite emplacement age of Ma and a virtual geomagnetic pole at 16 7S,1503 5 5
2217E ( , ). A paleomagnetic pole at 6 7N, 2347E ( , ) was obtained from ®ve Kuonamkad m=1 77 d p=1 07 d m=2 87 d p=1 47
dikes. An east-southeast-trending Chieress dike yielded a U-Pb baddeleyite emplacement age of Ma and a1384 5 2
virtual geomagnetic pole at 47N, 2587E ( , ). Kuonamka and Chieress poles are interpreted to be primaryd m=9 7 d p=5 7
but do not average out secular variation. Assuming that the Siberian Plate has remained intact since the Mesopro-
terozoic, except for mid-Paleozoic opening of the Viljuy Rift, then the above results indicate that the Siberian Plate
was in low latitudes at ca. 1503 and 1384 Ma, broadly similar to low latitudes determined for Laurentia from well-
dated paleopoles at 1460±1420, 1320±1290, and 1267 Ma. This would allow Laurentia and Siberia to have been attached
in the Mesoproterozoic, as suggested in several recent studies based on geological criteria. However, because paleo-
magnetic results from the Anabar Shield region do not average out secular variation and the ages of poles from Siberia
and Laurentia are not well matched, it is not yet possible to distinguish between these reconstructions or to rule out
other con®gurations that also maintain the two cratons at low paleolatitudes.
Introduction
Mesoproterozoic to Neoproterozoic continental re-
constructions involving Siberia are a topic of much
debate, often in the context of the postulated su-
percontinent of Rodinia. An early model based on
geological correlations placed the Siberian Plate ad-
jacent to southwestern Laurentia (present coordi-
nates) in the Mesoproterozoic (®g. 1 a; Sears and
Price 1978). More recently, a number of Meso-Neo-
proterozoic reconstructions have located Siberia
next to northern Laurentia (e.g., ®g. 1 b±1e; Hoff-
man 1991; Condie and Rosen 1994; Pelechaty 1996;
Frost et al. 1998; Rainbird et al. 1998). Some are
based on the comparison of Paleoproterozoic or
even Archean geological features between the two

Khudoley 1997; Rainbird and de Freitas 1997; Frost
et al. 1998; Rainbird et al. 1998).
Attempts to use paleomagnetism to determine
the relative location of Laurentia and Siberia in the
late Precambrian have also yielded dramatically di-
vergent results. For example, Poorter (1981) placed
Siberia adjacent to southern Baltica and the British
Isles in the ªLate Precambrian/Cambrianº (®g. 1f).
Piper (1982) located Siberia adjacent to southwest-
ern Laurentia (similar to the reconstruction by
Sears and Price [1978] in ®g. 1 a), using pre-850-Ma
Siberian paleomagnetic data. Scotese and Mc-
Kerrow (1990) proposed that Siberia lay near east-
ern Greenland in the latest Precambrian (®g. 1 g).

Recently, Smethurst et al. (1998) used paleomag-
netic data to place Siberia adjacent to eastern Bal-
tica rather than Laurentia (®g. 1h) or, alternatively,
near East Antarctica in a 750-Ma Rodinia recon-
struction. Unfortunately, Precambrian paleopoles
from Siberia are usually so poorly dated, often with
uncertainties of hundreds of millions of years, that
paleomagnetic reconstructions, like those based on
geology, are suspect.
Recent integrated studies of paleomagnetism and
U-Pb baddeleyite and zircon geochronology on
ma®c dikes and sills (e.g., Buchan et al. 1998) have
demonstrated that it is possible to obtain Precam-
brian paleopoles with high-precision ages. In order
to better constrain the paleolocation of Siberia for
use in paleocontinental reconstructions and to test
published reconstructions involving Siberia, we
have studied the paleomagnetism and U-Pb geo-
chronology of diabase dikes from a river traverse
across the eastern Anabar Shield and adjacent Ri-
phean covered craton of Siberia.
Geological Setting
The Siberian Plate (®g. 2) is underlain mainly by
Archean crust, except in the Paleoproterozoic Ak-
itkan fold belt that may mark the site of Paleopro-
terozoic convergence (Rosen et al. 1994) and in Pa-
leoproterozoic portions of the Aldan Shield (Frost
et al. 1998). Timing of amalgamation of Archean
blocks of the Siberian Plate is controversial. Khra-
mov et al. (1985), on the basis of a comparison of
paleomagnetic apparent polar wander paths, pro-
posed that the Siberian Plate consisted of at least
three blocksÐthe northern, southwestern, and
southeastern portions of the plateÐwhich moved
relative to one another until at least the Cambrian.
Pavlov and Petrov (1997), using paleomagnetism,
argued for the integrity of the Siberian Plate since
at least the Middle Riphean (ca. 1350±1000 Ma).
Zonenshain et al. (1990) suggested that at least ®ve
continental blocksÐªAngara-Anabarº (A and M in
®g. 2), Tungus, Olenek, ªAldanº ( OL, AL, U, and
B in ®g. 2), and StanovoyÐwere separated by ocean
basins of unknown widths in the Paleoproterozoic
but had amalgamated to form a single Siberian
Plate by Early Riphean (ca. 1650±1350 Ma) time.
Rosen et al. (1994) summarized geochronological
evidence for widespread 2000±1800-Ma orogenic
events in the Siberian Plate. They concluded that
the major event or events at 1950±1900 Ma, based
on ages of major fault zones, correspond to its time
of assembly. Hoffman (1991) proposed that the Si-
berian Plate lay adjacent to present-day northern
Laurentia at that time because the events in Siberia
are coeval with similar events that mark the as-
sembly of northern Laurentia.
Most of the Siberian Plate is covered by Riphean
(ca. 1650±650 Ma), Vendian, and Phanerozoic sed-
iments or by the 250-Ma Siberian Traps ¯ood basalt
province. However, Archean basement is exposed
in two large Precambrian shield areas, the Aldan
and Anabar shields, as well as several smaller win-
dows (®g. 2; e.g., Condie and Rosen 1994; Rosen et
al. 1994).
Aulacogens of at least two ages, Riphean and De-
vonian, are present in the Siberian Plate (Zonen-
shain et al. 1990). The younger Viljuy aulacogen
(®g. 2), consisting of the Viljuy (G1) and Ygyatinsky
(G2) grabens, extends westward »600 km into the
Siberian Plate (Zonenshain et al. 1990). Analysis of
paleomagnetic data (Gurevich 1984; Pavlov and Pe-
trov 1996, 1997; Smethurst et al. 1998) suggests a
counterclockwise rotation of the portion of the Si-
berian Plate north of the Viljuy aulacogen relative
to that south of the aulacogen in the mid-Paleozoic
(Wenlock-Esmian: 0.43±0.39 Ga). Smethurst et al.
(1998) estimated a rotation of »207 about a rotation
pole at 607N, 1007E, just west of the basin.
Proterozoic diabase dikes are abundant in the
main areas of exposed basement in the Siberian
Plate and in Riphean and Vendian cover rocks
(Ernst et al. 1996 and references therein). In an ear-
lier study, those in and adjacent to the Anabar
Shield were divided into 10 swarms on the basis of
trend, location, composition, and K-Ar age (®g. 3;
Okrugin et al. 1990). Five of these swarms occur
in the general area of this study. The east-trending
Kuonamka swarm (K-Ar ages of 1600±1200 Ma), the
southeast-trending East Anabar swarm (K-Ar ages
of ca. 1700 Ma), and the east-northeast-trending
Central Anabar swarm (K-Ar ages of 1800±1400 Ma)
intrude highly metamorphosed Archean rocks and,
occasionally, Early Riphean rocks. The Chieress
swarm (K-Ar ages of ca. 1200±900 Ma) and the Ju-
ken swarm (K-Ar ages of 1300±1200 Ma), both of
east-southeast trend, cut Early Riphean cover rocks
immediately to the east of the Anabar Shield.
Sampling and Laboratory Procedure
Eleven diabase dikes were sampled for paleomag-
netism, and of these, eight were also sampled for
U-Pb geochronology, during the course of a rafting
expedition down the Bol'shaya Kuonamka River in
the eastern Anabar Shield region (®g. 3). Each dike
is assigned to one of the swarms described above,
based on an analysis of its trend, petrographic and/
or geochemical characteristics, paleomagnetic di-
rection, and U-Pb or previously published K-Ar age.

Petrography
East-trending Kuonamka dikes at sites 1, 2, 3, 4,
and 14 are diabases consisting dominantly of pla-
gioclase and clinopyroxene, with minor Fe-Ti ox-
ides. In ®ne-grained portions the fabric is inter-
granular, and in medium-grained portions the fabric
is subophitic. The mineralogy at these sites is fresh
except for pervasive sausseritization of plagioclase
at site 14, minor alteration of clinopyroxene at site
3, and deuteric replacement of a trace second fer-
romagnesian mineral at site 1. Myrmekite is ob-
served at site 4 and trace quartz is observed at site
14. Site 3 contains ®ne needles of apatite, and site
14 is cut by a few small aplite (rheomorphic) dikes.
The 75-m-wide east-southeast-trending Chieress
dike at site 17 consists of a marginal phase of gabbro
and a 50-m-wide interior pulse of monzodiorite and
is cut by a late-stage aplite dike. All paleomagnetic
samples were from the monzodiorite phase since
no material of the other phases was found in situ.
The gabbroic phase consists of partially sausseri-
tized plagioclase and weakly uralitized clinopyrox-
ene in an intergranular texture and also opaques
(Fe-Ti oxides) and minor apatite. The clinopyroxene
is partially replaced by pumpellyite, actinolite, and
biotite. The monzodiorite phase contains feldspar
that has been pervasively sausseritized and horn-
blende that has been totally replaced by pumpel-
lyite and actinolite. Minor apatite and quartz are
also present. The aplite dike consists of feldspar
phenocrysts in a ®ne-grained quartz-feldspar ma-
trix. The presence of coexisiting pumpellyite and
actinolite in both the gabbroic and monzodioritic
phases at site 17 implies subgreenschist-grade
metamorphism.
Geochemical studies of Juken dikes with variable
trends at sites 15 and 16 and at the probable con-
tinuation of the east-southeast-trending dike from
site 13 revealed high-K compositions (Okrugin et
al. 1990; A. V. Okrugin, unpub. data). The dike at
site 13 is an altered diabase consisting of highly
sausseritized plagioclase, chlorite after clinopyrox-
ene, Fe-Ti oxides, and minor apatite. Its continu-
ation contains scattered amygdules ®lled with cal-
cite. Sites 15 and 16 are from a dike and a pod (or
neck), respectively, at a single locality and probably
fed an overlying lava ¯ow»10 m above. Texturally,
these intrusions are volcanic breccias containing
amygdules (with chorite and/or calcite), xenoliths
of quartz, lithic fragments, hematized volcanic
glass, and a hematized and/or chloritized ground-
mass. Microprobe analysis (A. V. Okrugin, unpub.
data) indicates that the groundmass consists of po-
tassium feldspar grains (SiO

Paleomagnetic Results
At most paleomagnetic sampling sites a stable rem-
anence was isolated on stepwise AF or thermal de-
magnetization after elimination of a steep down
component, which is probably of viscous origin.
However, in some sites, systematic directional
swings at higher ®elds or temperatures in the de-
magnetization experiments re¯ect the presence of
two stable components. Paleomagnetic directional
data at each site are cataloged in table 1 and plotted
in ®gure 4. Results from each dike swarm are de-
scribed below.
Kuonamka Dikes. East-trending dikes at sites 1,
2, 3, 4, and 14 are assigned to the Kuonamka swarm
(®g. 3). Their mean remanence directions are shal-
low and east to northeast (®g. 4). The large direc-
tional scatter may represent secular variation of a
single swarm, although the presence of more than
one age of dike cannot be ruled out. Sites 2 and 14
exhibit stable northeast remanences with shallow
inclination after elimination of steep viscous com-
ponents (®g. 5a,5 b). In each of these sites the char-
acteristic component was readily isolated using
Kirschvink (1980) analysis. A shallow south-south-
westerly magnetization direction was obtained at
site 3 (®g. 5 c). The remanence at site 3 is approx-
imately reversed to those at sites 2 and 14, although
some samples from site 3 showed evidence of a
normally magnetized component as well. At site 1,
two of the three samples yielded shallow north-
easterly magnetization directions, whereas the
third sample, collected about 200 m away from the
others along the same dike, was magnetized with
the opposite polarity.
At site 4, remanence directions follow long
swings along great circle paths on AF demagneti-
zation (®g. 6). Remagnetization circle analysis (Bai-
ley and Halls 1984) yielded a well-de®ned easterly
intersection, representing the most stable compo-
nent of magnetization. A single sample was ther-
mally demagnetized and also gave a long swing to
the easterly direction.

Age of Magnetization
Buchan and Halls (1990) discussed the importance
of establishing the precise age of magnetization of
diabase dikes and other ma®c intrusions as a pre-
requisite to their use in determining reliable ap-
parent polar wander paths and paleocontinental re-
constructions. U-Pb dating of baddeleyite in this
study establishes the age of emplacement of two
dikes, a -Ma dike (site 17) of the Chieress1384 5 2
swarm and, provisionally, a -Ma dike (site1503 5 5
4) of the Kuonamka swarm. No paleomagnetic ®eld
tests are available to rigorously establish whether
the stable magnetic remanences of either of these
dikes are primary or whether they were acquired
as later overprints. However, there are several rea-
sons for concluding that these dikes and, indeed,
all the sampled sites assigned to the 1503-Ma Kuon-
amka, 1384-Ma Chieress, and ca. 1300±1200-Ma Ju-
ken swarms preserve paleomagnetic directions dat-
ing from the time of intrusion.
First, no major post-1500-Ma metamorphic event
is known to have affected the Anabar Shield region
(e.g., see discussion of Proterozoic orogenic events
in the Siberian Plate in Rosen et al. 1994). Second,
our petrographic observations of the Kuonamka,
Chieress, and Juken dikes indicate low metamor-
phic grades. Kuonamka dikes are fresh or only
slightly altered. The Chieress dike has experienced
only subgreenschist metamorphism. Juken dikes
are more extensively altered, but the alteration is
of a low-temperature type and probably of deuteric
origin. Third, the paleomagnetic directions from
the Kuonamka, Chieress, and Juken dikes are dif-
ferent from those in the country rocks (metamor-
phosed Archean gneisses and schists) in the same
area. Speci®cally, G. G. Kamysheva (in Khramov
1971) obtained remanence directions of , D= 1687

Discussion
The paleolatitude and azimuthal orientation of the
Siberian Plate at 1503 and 1384 Ma, based on the
paleopoles determined in this study from the east-
ern Anabar Shield region (table 1), are illustrated
in ®gure 12 a. For comparison, the early Mesopro-
terozoic positions based on paleomagnetism for
Laurentia are shown in ®gure 12 b. It is assumed
that the Siberian Plate has remained intact since
the Mesoproterozoic, except for the mid-Paleozoic
opening of the Viljuy Rift, although this assump-
tion has yet to be rigorously tested with paleo-
magnetic data from different parts of the Siberian
Plate.
In the drift plots of ®gure 12, paleolongitude is
not constrained by the paleomagnetic data. In ad-
dition, because of ambiguity in magnetic polarity,
a craton can generally be placed in either hemi-
sphere with its orientation differing by 180 7 (e.g.,
compare the two positions of Siberia at 1384 Ma
in ®g. 12a). However, there is no such polarity am-
biguity in the relative positions of a craton at dif-
ferent times if the time intervals between paleo-
magnetic data are too short (
!100 m.yr.) for the
craton to have rotated through 180 7 or to have
drifted over the geographic pole to the opposite side
of the globe.

At both 1503 and 1384 Ma the Siberian Plate is
in low latitudes (®g. 12a). Between 1503 (using the
position based on the mean Kuonamka paleopole)
and 1384 Ma, the craton appears to have rotated
»257 clockwise. However, it should be noted that
this rotation is not statistically signi®cant given
the uncertainties associated with the paleo-orien-
tation of the poles total at least 38 7 (see note to
table 1).
No ca. 1503- or 1384-Ma paleopoles are currently
available for Laurentia, but there are well-dated pa-
leopoles for ca. 1460±1420, 1320±1290, and 1267
Ma (®g. 12 b; see paleomagnetic and U-Pb age tab-
ulation in Buchan et al. 2000). Paleopoles for the
1460±1420-Ma plutons of northeastern and south-
western Laurentia are thought to be primary on the
basis of a positive baked contact test for the ca.
1460-Ma Michikamau anorthosite. The other pa-
leopoles of this group are from the ca. 1450-Ma
Harp Lake Complex, the ca. 1434-Ma Laramie an-
orthosite and Sherman granite, and the ca. 1420-
Ma Mistastin pluton. The 1320±1290-Ma paleopole
is from the Nain anorthosite of northeastern Lau-
rentia. These units are all large plutons that cooled
slowly, so that their primary magnetic remanences
may have been acquired up to several million years
after the U-Pb emplacement ages (e.g., Harlan et al.
1994). The 1267-Ma pole is from the Mackenzie
dike swarm of northern Laurentia.
All the above paleopoles locate Laurentia at low
latitudes with a fairly consistent azimuthal orien-
tation (®g. 12 b). As noted above, the preliminary
paleomagnetic data for Siberia in this study also
places Siberia at low latitudes at ca. 1503 and 1384
Ma. This is consistent with Siberia and Laurentia
moving together in the early Mesoproterozoic.
Thus, a position for Siberia adjacent to the northern
margin of Laurentia (see ®g. 1) is permitted by the
paleomagnetic data. However, other locations for
Siberia adjacent to Laurentia are equally permis-
sible given that the ages of data from the two cra-
tons are not well matched, there are rather large
uncertainties in the paleolatitudes and paleo-ori-
entations of Siberia because of the scatter in the
Kuonamka directions, and the Chieress and Kuon-
amka results do not average out secular variation.
In addition, because of the paleolongitude uncer-
tainty inherent in the paleomagnetic method, the
data would allow the two continents to have been
apart, provided they were both in relatively low
latitudes through the period in question. Additional
well-dated paleomagnetic data are required if the
position of Siberia is to be accurately determined
in the Mesoproterozoic.
The relationship between Siberia and Laurentia
in the Neoproterozoic is also unclear, despite a re-
cent paleomagnetic model of Smethurst et al.
(1998) that locates Siberia either adjacent to Baltica
(®g. 1h) or adjacent to East Antarctica in a ca. 750-
Ma Rodinia reconstruction. This ®t is based on a
comparison of well-dated paleopoles for Laurentia
(summary in Torsvik et al. 1996) at ca. 750 Ma and
the paleopole for gabbro sills that intrude the Sette-
Daban fold belt of southeastern Siberia (Pavlov et
al. 1992; Pavlov 1996). Smethurst et al. (1998) as-
signed an age of 730 Ma to these sills based on K-
Ar dating and geological constraints. However, they
are now known to be much older than previously
thought. Pavlov et al. (1992) gave an Sm-Nd age of
Ma for the sills in their paleomagnetic942 5 18
study. Rainbird et al. (1998) reported minimum em-
placement ages of Ma and Ma974 5 7 1005 5 4
based on U-Pb baddeleyite dating for two sills lo-
cated about 150 km to the north. These ages are
about 250 m.yr. older than the age assigned to the
sills by Smethurst et al. (1998) and invalidate their
paleomagnetic reconstruction (®g. 1 h).
Unfortunately, there are several problems that
prevent the use of the paleopole from the Sette-
Daban sills for reliable reconstructions of Siberia
and Laurentia at ca. 1000 Ma. First, the very small
degree of scatter ( and for eight silla = 2.77 k= 426

be the identi®cation in Siberia of the extensive

of these ages have not been found in Siberia.
However, the 1384-Ma Chieress dike age from
Siberia is almost identical with that of two diabase

(locations in ®g. 12 b). Hart River sills intrude the

which Siberia is located adjacent to northwestern
or western Laurentia. However, Baltica also con-

Such a widespread distribution of ca. 1380 Ma

a single magmatic event at that time.
Conclusions
Diabase dikes that were sampled in the eastern An-
abar Shield region are interpreted to belong to four
Mesoproterozoic and two Paleoproterozoic swarms
on the basis of paleomagnetism, U-Pb or previous
K-Ar geochronology, trend, and petrography. Five
east-trending dikes are assigned to the Kuonamka
swarm, dated herein by the U-Pb method at
Ma. A single dike from the Chieress1503 5 5
swarm yielded a U-Pb age of Ma. Of the1384 5 2
remaining ®ve dikes, three are thought to represent
the ca. 1300±1200-Ma Juken swarm, and the fourth
and ®fth are assigned to the ca. 1800±1400-Ma Cen-
tral Anabar and ca. 1700-Ma Eastern Anabar
swarms.
Paleomagnetic data from the 1503-Ma Kuonam-
ka and 1384-Ma Chieress swarms locate the Anabar
Shield, and perhaps the whole Siberian Plate, at low
latitudes during the early Mesoproterozoic. Well-
constrained paleomagnetic data for Laurentia also
place that craton at low latitudes at 1460±1420,
1320±1290, and 1267 Ma. Thus, these data would
allow Laurentia and Siberia to have drifted together
in the Mesoproterozoic, as proposed by several re-
cent studies using geological criteria. However, the
ages of the paleomagnetic data from the Anabar
Shield and Laurentia are not well matched, the pa-
leomagnetic data from the Anabar Shield do not
average out secular variation, and it remains to be
con®rmed that the Anabar Shield paleomagnetic
data apply to the Siberian Shield as a whole. There-
fore, it is not yet possible to propose a reliable early
Mesoproterozoic reconstruction or to discriminate
between the different reconstruction options for Si-
beria and Laurentia summarized in ®gure 1.
