ABSTRACT
Neogene nonmarine strata in the southern-
most part of the Precordillera thrust belt of
the Andes of Argentina accumulated during
the Miocene and Pliocene in response to east-
ward advance of thrust sheets located to the
west. To link the sequence of deformational
events with the sedimentary record, five strati-
graphic sections in the Mendoza Province
were dated using magnetic polarity stratigra-
phy calibrated with 
40Ar-39Ar dates from in-
terbedded tephras. These data establish age
control on tectonic activity, volcanism, and
deposition.
The existence of a backarc foreland basin
that developed prior to or ca. 16 Ma is
recorded by the oldest strata, the ca. 15.7–12.2
Ma (Baksi time scale) Mariño Formation.
Deposition of this unit is linked to a major
phase of thrust activity in the central part of
the Aconcagua fold-and-thrust belt, in the
Principal Cordillera. Initiation of deposition
coincides with an eastward shift of the sub-
duction-related magmatic foci to the Argen-
tine Principal Cordillera. The overlying ca.
11.7–9.0 Ma La Pilona Formation is thought
to record the initiation of exhumation of the
Frontal Cordillera to the northwest of the
study region. An extensive ash-rich unit, the
8.9 (locally 9.5?) to 8.7 Ma Tobas Angostura
Formation, is correlated with the latest and
probably the largest extrusive episode in the
Principal Cordillera. Chronologic data con-
strain the timing of oil generation in the Cuyo
basin and development of prospective clo-
sures. The new data also require that land
mammalian fossils found in the Río de los Po-
zos Formation are late Miocene, rather than
Pliocene, as previously believed.
Keywords: Andes, Ar/Ar, Argentina, magne-
tostratigraphy, Miocene, Precordillera.
INTRODUCTION
In the late 1950s, it was proposed that the
present-day configuration of the Andes Moun-
tains between lat 33° and 34°S was the result of
several pulses of uplift and deformation of tec-
tonically active belts, the locus of deformation
migrating eastward beginning in the Neogene
(cf. Polanski, 1958, 1963). Incorporating this
hypothesis within a plate tectonic framework,
Ramos (1988) described a tectonic model for
the Neogene evolution of the Andes and linked
the Cenozoic synorogenic deposits that crop out
on the eastern flank of the Andes with the east-
ward migration of the orogenic thrust front dur-
ing the late Tertiary. The chronology of thrust-
ing required testing, however, because of a lack
of crosscutting relationships and geochrono-
logic data. Because magnetostratigraphic stud-
ies of the sedimentary record in other foreland
basins of Argentina (e.g., Johnson et al., 1986;
Bercowski et al., 1986; Jordan et al., 1988, 1990,
1996; Reynolds et al., 1990; Milana, 1991)
proved to be successful in deciphering the time
of motion on thrust faults, a similar approach
was attempted in this study of the Tertiary Men-
doza strata, near lat 33°S (Fig. 1). The most
complete stratigraphic record is exposed in the
south-plunging La Pilona anticline (Fig. 2A)
where most of the sampling was carried out.
Additional sampling was conducted on the east-
ern flank of the Tupungato anticline, located
~25 km farther south (Fig. 2B).
GEOLOGICAL SETTING
The study area (~33°S) is situated above a dip
transition in the subducting Nazca plate. To the
north, the underthrusting plate is nearly horizontal
at depth and, to the south of 33°S, it assumes a dip
of ~30° (e.g., Bevis and Isacks, 1984).Changes in
large-scale tectonic features of the orogen are as-
sociated with this change in the subducting plate
geometry. The flat-subduction segment of Chile
and Argentina (28°–33°S) is characterized by the
lack of an active magmatic arc, the development
of the Precordillera as a thin-skinned thrust belt,
and the basement block uplifts of the Sierras
Pampeanas to the east (Jordan et al., 1983). In
contrast, the Andes to the south of 33°15¢S are
characterized by an active magmatic arc, exten-
sive backarc volcanism, and a narrower zone of
foreland deformation (Jordan et al., 1983; Ramos
and Nullo, 1993; Bermúdez et al., 1993).
At lat 33°S, the Principal and Frontal
Cordilleras and the Precordillera of the Argentine
Andes (Fig. 1) plus the Sierras Pampeanas to the
east represent four north-trending morphotec-
tonic provinces differentiated on the basis of
structural styles, geologic evolution, and mor-
phologic expression. The westernmost of these,
the Principal Cordillera or Main Andes, is com-
posed primarily of a thick sequence of Mesozoic
marine strata that interfingers with a thick accu-
mulation of Upper Jurassic–Lower Cretaceous
volcanic rocks (Yrigoyen, 1979). These strata,
which are overlain by Miocene volcanic and py-
roclastic rocks (Complejo V olcánico Aconcagua;
Ramos et al., 1996), display a thin-skinned
deformation and form the early to late Miocene

Frontal Cordillera mainly exposes an assemblage
of Paleozoic andesitic to silicic magmatic and
sedimentary rocks (Caminos, 1979). During the
Andean orogeny, this morphotectonic unit appar-
ently behaved as a rigid block, disrupted by high-
angle reverse faults, but probably not recording
significant internal shortening at upper crustal
levels (Mpodozis and Ramos, 1990; Allmendinger
et al., 1990). An imbricate structure known as Las
Carreras fault system (see Fig. 1) forms the east-
ern boundary of the Frontal Cordillera. The Pre-
cordillera is a predominantly east-verging fold-
and-thrust belt between 28° and 33°S, with a
thin-skinned structure that has been developed on
early to late Paleozoic sedimentary rocks (Baldis
and Chebli, 1969). Deformation of the Pre-
cordillera to the north of the study area (~31°S)
started ca. 20 Ma and continued to the present
(Jordan et al., 1993a, 1993b).
The study area is located at the southernmost
portion of the Precordillera, where the thrust
belt is expressed at the surface by deformed Ter-
tiary strata (Fig. 1). The oldest rocks in the re-
gion are of Ordovician age (Varela et al., 1993;
Fig. 2A). Middle to Upper Triassic nonmarine
strata and subordinate volcanic rocks overlie
volcanic rocks of the Choiyoi Group. Hydrocar-
bon reserves generated in the Mendoza Triassic
rocks are concentrated in several oil fields and are
largely controlled by structural traps, such as the
La Pilona and Tupungato anticlines, the two study
localities (Dellapé and Hegedus, 1993). About
3500 m of deformed Paleogene to Pliocene-
Pleistocene(?) nonmarine clastic strata discon-
formably overlie the Triassic rocks (Rolleri and
Fernández Garrasino, 1979). The Cenozoic suc-

STRATIGRAPHY OF THE TERTIARY

locally 35 m thick in the Tosca de Mariño sec-

bers: a basal member of sandstones with gyp-

Mancilla (1989) interpreted this formation as an
ancient continental sabkha. The stratigraphic
age of this formation is constrained by verte-
brate fossils from the upper member and may
range from upper Eocene to lower Miocene
(e.g., Milana et al., 1993, and references
therein).
Mariño Formation
The Mariño Formation, which unconformably
overlies the Divisadero Largo Formation
(Yrigoyen, 1993a), is subdivided into three
members. The lower member attains a thick-
ness of ~50 m in the Tosca de Mariño section
(section I; Fig. 2A) and consists of purplish and
greenish conglomerate and sandstone beds al-
ternating with red mudstone and a few ben-
tonite horizons. The intermediate member mainly
comprises a distinctive 180-m-thick pile of
cross-bedded sandstones rich in glass shards.
The upper member is ~800 m thick and consists
of sandstones and gray conglomerates interbed-
ded with red mudstones. The contacts between
the members mark recognized changes of dep-
ositional facies. The lower and upper members
are interpreted to record fluvial-alluvial deposi-
tion in an arid to semiarid setting dominated by
ephemeral-stream processes; strata of the inter-
mediate section are of eolian origin (Irigoyen,
1997).
The age of the Mariño Formation was previ-
ously poorly constrained, ranging from early
Oligocene to middle Miocene (e.g., Yrigoyen,
1993a; Jordan and Ortiz, 1987). A reworked tuff
horizon collected from the uppermost part of this
unit in the Arroyo del Agua Blanca section (sec-
tion II; Fig. 2A) was dated as 12.03 ± 0.45 Ma
(sample Md-12, Table 1) (Irigoyen, 1997; Irigoyen
et al., 1999).
La Pilona Formation
The La Pilona Formation is as much as ~800
m thick in the La Pilona area. Its basal portion in-
cludes strata previously termed Tobas Grises In-
feriores (Lower gray tuffs; Truempy and Lhez,
1937). Field mapping in this study did not find
any basis for distinguishing a separate basal unit.
This formation unconformably overlies the Mar-
iño Formation (Yrigoyen, 1993a), although the
unconformity is not obvious in the study sec-
tions. The lowest third of the La Pilona Forma-
tion consists mainly of gray sandstones and con-
glomerates. It is overlain by a tuffaceous finer
grained succession containing a few ash-fall hori-
zons, one of which is known as Horizonte de
Ceniza Blanca (White ash horizon; Truempy and
Lhez, 1937). The ~200-m-thick uppermost part
of this unit mostly comprises conglomerates. La
Pilona Formation is interpreted to record fluvial
and clay-playa deposition (Irigoyen, 1997).
Based on radiometric data, Yrigoyen (1993a,
1993b) assigned the La Pilona Formation to the
late Miocene (ca. 11.1–9.8 Ma). Irigoyen (1997)
and Irigoyen et al. (1999) dated two samples col-
lected near the middle of the formation (Md-6,
White ash horizon, and Md-13 of Table 1). For
sample Md-6, Irigoyen et al. (1999) have taken
10.53 ± 0.16 Ma as the best age estimate, which
is a weighted average of 10.42 ± 0.20 Ma from
laser step-heating analysis on hornblende and
10.75 ± 0.29 Ma from total fusion analysis on bi-
otite. Sample Md-13 hornblende yielded an age
of 9.63 ± 0.22 Ma (Table 1).
Tobas Angostura Formation
The extensive ash-rich Tobas Angostura Forma-
tion attains a thickness of 100–120 m in the
Tupungato area and overlies the La Pilona Forma-
tion with apparent unconformity (Yrigoyen,
1993a). These volcanogenic deposits include
coarse- and fine-grained tuffs, reworked tuffs,
sandstones, and conglomerates with varying
amounts of pyroclastic material, agglomerates,
lapilli layers, and air-fall horizons. This formation
is interpreted to record the response of a semiarid
fluvial system to the pyroclastic volcanism, where
deposition occurred in broad extensive areas
(Irigoyen, 1997).
Based on radiometric data, Yrigoyen (1993a,
1993b) assigned this formation to the late
Miocene (ca. 9.8 Ma). Three samples (Md-5,
Md-10, Md-15; Table 1) collected from air-fall
ash beds in three different locations of the study
area provided age constraints on this unit.
Irigoyen (1997) and Irigoyen et al. (1999) re-
ported evidence of loss of radiogenic 
40Ar from
sample Md-15 biotite in laser step-heating exper-
iments. Therefore, they interpreted the horn-
blende ages of 8.64 ± 0.17, 9.30 ± 0.68, and 9.54
± 0.13 Ma from samples Md-5, Md-10, and Md-
15, respectively, as the best age estimates.
Río de los Pozos Formation
The Río de los Pozos Formation is grada-
tional from the Tobas Angostura Formation
(Yrigoyen, 1993a). In the Tupungato area, this
formation exhibits a variable thickness up to
400 m, due to the unconformity with the over-
lying Mogotes Formation (Yrigoyen, 1993a).
The Río de los Pozos Formation comprises
mudstones, yellowish tuffaceous mudstones
and sandstones, and gray conglomerates. These
strata are interpreted to record deposition from
unconfined and channelized flows in a semiarid
setting (Irigoyen, 1997). Abundant remains of
land mammal fossils were collected from this
unit in the Tupungato area (cf. Yrigoyen,
1993b). The magnetostratigraphic study proved
to be helpful in calibrating the ages of these
fossils.
Mogotes Formation
The Mogotes Formation, which was not sam-
pled for magnetostratigraphy, consists of boulder
conglomerates interbedded with red mudstones
and sandstones and a few tuffaceous horizons.
These deposits probably represent proximal allu-
vial-fan facies, although a possible glacial origin
has been suggested (Cortés, in Ramos, 1990).
MAGNETOSTRATIGRAPHY
Sampling Procedure
Five profiles (I–V , Figs. 3, 4, locations in Fig. 2)
were studied to establish the magnetic polarity
stratigraphy of the Neogene units, except for the
Mogotes Formation. Sampling followed the pro-
cedures established by Johnson et al. (1975). We
collected a minimum of three oriented hand sam-
ples at each sampling site. Where possible, they
were spaced ~1.5 m apart within the same sedi-
mentary bed. We sampled a total of 111 paleo-
magnetic sites separated by an average of 25 m
through the stratigraphy. The preferred lithologies
for paleomagnetic sampling were clay and silt, al-
though fine-grained sandstones were collected
when finer grained rocks were not available (i.e.,
in the eolian member of the Mariño Formation)
and/or when they were too fissile to be easily sam-
pled. In some instances, the stratigraphic separa-
tion between sites was larger than the average due
either to lack of exposure (middle part of the La
Higuerita section) or to the occurrence of thick
conglomerate sequences. Stratigraphic thicknesses
were measured with a tape and/or a Jacob staff us-
ing a Brunton compass and bench marks. Paleo-
magnetic laboratory and analytical procedures are
described in the Appendix.
Results
The stratigraphy of the five sampling profiles,
locations of the paleomagnetic sites, and a sum-
mary of the paleomagnetic data are shown in Fig-
ures 3 and 4. Most samples are stably magnetized.
Typical examples of thermal demagnetization are
shown in Figure 5. The natural remanent magne-
tization (NRM) of most of the samples includes
two components of magnetization. The character-
istic component has either a north and up or south
and down direction and blocking temperatures
that are typically above 250 °C. It is interpreted as
a detrital remanent magnetization (DRM) carried
by titanomagnetite and/or titanohematite. The

The mean characteristic directions after tilt
correction for normal and reversed class I sites
from each paleomagnetic section are listed in
Table 2. The magnetization directions from the
Tosca de Mariño, Arroyo del Agua Blanca, and
La Higuerita sections of the western limb of the
La Pilona anticline are rotated clockwise
~13°–30° from the present axial dipole field,
which has a zero declination. However, the mag-
netization direction of the El Molino section on
the eastern limb of the anticline is rotated slightly
counterclockwise from the present axial dipole
field. The observed difference in declination be-
tween the two limbs may be related to internal
strains in the system that were not accounted for
by correcting for tilt about a horizontal axis, or to
block rotations about a vertical axis.
Chronology of the Neogene Units
The local magnetic polarity stratigraphies ob-
tained in this study can be correlated with the ge-
omagnetic polarity time scale (GPTS), which in
turn is based on marine magnetic anomalies
(e.g., Opdyke and Channell, 1996). Several time
scales for the Neogene are available. Among the
most recent are those of Baksi (1993), Cande
and Kent (1995), and Berggren et al. (1995). The
GPTS proposed by Baksi (1993) is shown for
comparison with the local magnetostratigraphy
in Figure 8 and is used throughout the following
discussion, because the long normal chron C5n,
which has been identified in the studied sections,
is precisely dated by the 
40Ar-39Ar technique (cf.
Baksi et al., 1993). The GPTS of Cande and
Kent (1995) and that of Berggren et al. (1995) do
not differ from that of Baksi (1993) by more than
0.3 m.y. between 12 and 8 Ma, the interval that
includes all the dated tephra beds of this magne-
tostratigraphic study. However, the Cande and
Kent (1995) and Berggren et al. (1995) GPTSs
become increasingly discordant with respect to
the Baksi (1993) scale for ages greater than 12.0
Ma. Baksi (1993) placed the base of C5ADn at
15.66 Ma, whereas Cande and Kent (1995) and
Berggren et al. (1995) located it at 14.61 Ma.
This discrepancy stems in part from the choice
of different tie points in the middle Miocene.
Tosca de Mariño Section
The Tosca de Mariño section includes strata of
the Divisadero Largo (3 sampling sites) and Mar-
iño formations (36 sites) and consists of two sep-
arate segments (IA and IB, Fig. 2) located
~1.5 km apart. They share a sandstone unit that is
physically continuous from one segment to the
other. At the top of the section is a fault that sug-
gests that at least a portion of the Mariño Forma-
tion is missing. There are 22 sites from the Mar-
iño Formation that are class I; 9 sites from the
Mariño Formation and all 3 sites from the Di-
visadero Largo Formation are class II. The
stratigraphy, location of paleomagnetic sites, and
virtual geomagnetic pole (VGP) latitudes used to
calculate the magnetic polarity zonation are sum-
marized in Figure 3-I. Examples of stable nor-
mally and reversely magnetized specimens from
the Mariño Formation are shown in Figure 5A.
The magnetostratigraphy of this section is no-
table for the long dominantly normal polarity

Formation and for the large number of reversals
encountered. At least 15 geomagnetic reversals
spanning a 772 m stratigraphic section are
recorded by the Mariño Formation at the sam-
pling locality. Many of the polarity intervals
stratigraphically above site 19 are based on data
from single sites and their lengths cannot be ac-
curately determined. Nevertheless, a series of
short polarity zones is recorded.
The magnetic polarity stratigraphy of the Tosca
de Mariño section is rather difficult to interpret
above site 23 because of the short polarity inter-
vals that are recorded. The section can perhaps
most easily be matched with the Baksi (1993)
GPTS between 15.8 and ca. 12.0 Ma (Fig. 8),
with the dominantly normal interval between
about 15.7 and 14.5 Ma in the marine record
(C5ADn-C5ACn) corresponding to the long
dominantly normal interval near the base of the
sampled section. The series of short polarity inter-
vals in the top two-thirds of the section corre-
spond with the series of short polarities above
C5ACn in the GPTS, although a correlation of
specific polarity zones is difficult to achieve. A
tentative correlation is shown in Figure 8, with the
upper normal interval of the section equivalent to
C5An.2 or C5An.1. Support for this correlation
comes from the isotopic age of 12.03 ± 0.45 Ma
(Irigoyen, 1997; Irigoyen et al., 1999) near the top
of the Mariño Formation in the nearby Arroyo del
Agua Blanca section, which is thought to be litho-
logically equivalent to the upper portion of the
Mariño Formation of the Tosca de Mariño sec-
tion. In addition, the long normal interval of the
sampled section (15.7–14.5 Ma) corresponds ap-
proximately to a prominent eolian unit (middle
member) that has been regionally correlated with
the ca. 20 Ma and 15–14 Ma eolian sandstones
that occur north of the study area (Milana et al.,
1993; Jordan et al., 1993a).

The magnetic polarity zonation log derived
from the VGP latitudes shows that the ~70 m
thick faulted block of the Mariño Formation
strata at the bottom of the profile records a nor-
mal magnetozone followed by a reversed magne-
tozone. Above the faulted block, the Mariño

The Arroyo del Agua Blanca section is no-
table for two reasons: (1) it captures a long nor-
mal polarity magnetozone at the base of the La
Pilona Formation, and (2) it contains two iso-
topically dated ash horizons. The ash horizon in
the La Pilona Formation yields an age of 9.63 ±
0.22 Ma (Md-13), whereas the ash horizon at
the top of the Mariño Formation is dated as
12.03 ± 0.45 Ma (Md-12) (Irigoyen, 1997;
Irigoyen et al., 1999). Based on these age con-
straints and the configuration of the local mag-
netostratigraphy, the long normal polarity zone
is readily correlated with the long normal chron
C5n (anomaly 5) of the GPTS, between 11.08
and 9.67 Ma (Fig. 8).
The Md-13 horizon, dated at 9.63 ± 0.22 Ma,
falls within a normally magnetized interval that
is stratigraphically above the long normal mag-
netozone. It may be correlated with either
chron C4Ar.2n, between 9.57 and 9.50 Ma, or
chron C5n.1n, between 9.83 and 9.67 Ma
(Baksi, 1993). If correlated with chron C4Ar.2n,
then the tiny reversed polarity zone (C5n.1r)
near the top of the long normal chron C5n of
the GPTS was not sampled in the local section.
The short section of the Mariño Formation at
the base of the Arroyo del Agua Blanca profile is
interpreted to be bracketed by the interval ca.
12.7–12.0 Ma. Near the top of the section, sample
Md-12 yielded an age of 12.03 ± 0.45 Ma. This
suggests that the two normal polarity magneto-
zones between fault F
2 and the dated ash horizon
correspond to C5An.2 and C5An.1 of the GPTS.
As noted earlier, this correlation and the litholog-
ical similarity between the Mariño Formation of
the Arroyo del Agua Blanca section and the upper
portion of the Mariño Formation in the Tosca de
Mariño section suggest that the top of the Mariño
Formation in the Tosca de Mariño section is also
ca. 12.0 Ma.
If the long normal interval at the bottom of
the La Pilona Formation in the Arroyo del Agua
Blanca section is correlated with C5n of the
GPTS, and if Md-12 is accepted, then there is a
gap of at least 1 m.y. in the Arroyo del Agua
Blanca section. Based on this interpretation,
this study locates the unconformity at the first
appearance of a conglomerate bed having char-
acteristics typical of those of the La Pilona
Formation.
La Higuerita Section
The La Higuerita section (section III, Fig. 2)
includes three formational units, the upper part of
the Mariño Formation (4 sampling sites), the La
Pilona Formation (34 sites), and the Tobas An-
gostura Formation (5 sites). The precise locations
of the unconformities that separate these three
units (cf. Yrigoyen, 1993a) are not obvious in the
study section. Because of poor exposure, the lo-
cation of the contact between the Mariño and the
La Pilona Formations was placed arbitrarily at
the first appearance of a gray conglomerate with
sandstone layers, which is typical of this unit. For
the upper unconformity, this study assumed that
the base of the Tobas Angostura unit is marked by
a tuffaceous greenish mudstone interval with ash-
rich sandstone lenses and scattered lapilli. The
upper 10 m of this section represents the gradual
transition between the Tobas Angostura and Río
de los Pozos Formations. Twenty-seven sites in
the section are class I sites and 12 sites are class
II. The stratigraphy, location of the paleomag-
netic sites, and paleomagnetic data from the La
Higuerita section are summarized in Figure 4-III.
Examples of paleomagnetic results for individual
specimens of the La Pilona Formation are shown
in Figure 5C.
No information on magnetic polarity of the
Mariño Formation was obtained in the lowest 67
m, as the first two sites are class III. Above these
sites, the Mariño Formation records a reversed and
a normal magnetozone. The La Pilona Formation
records a thick normal magnetozone that extends
from 264 to 500 m. The remainder of the forma-
tion is reversely polarized except for a short nor-
mal magnetozone between 653 and 715 m. The
~120-m-thick Tobas Angostura Formation records
consistent normal polarity.
Stepwise thermal demagnetization demon-
strates that in most La Pilona samples the T
b spec-
trum of the characteristic component is close to
the Curie temperature of hematite. However, sam-
ples from the lower part of the La Pilona Forma-
tion (sites 63–67) and a few from higher strati-
graphic levels (sites 80 and 82) have T
bs no higher
than 580–600 °C, suggesting that magnetite may
be the major carrier of the stable remanence (e.g.,
Fig. 5C).
The La Higuerita section is notable for (1) a
long normal polarity magnetozone in the La Pi-
lona Formation, and (2) two isotopically dated ash
horizons. The Md-6 ash horizon of the La Pilona
Formation yields a weighted average age of 10.53
± 0.16 Ma, and the Md-10 tuff horizon of the To-
bas Angostura unit yields an age of 9.30 ± 0.68 Ma
(Irigoyen, 1997; Irigoyen et al., 1999). The long
normal polarity magnetozone in the La Pilona
Formation is assigned to chron C5n (11.08–9.67
Ma) based on its distinctive length and the con-
straints provided by the isotopic ages. However, al-
though the isotopic ages clearly indicate that the
long normal interval is equivalent to chron C5n,
the Md-6 isotopic age of 10.53 ± 0.16 Ma at the
top of the interval is significantly older than the age
assigned to the younger boundary of chron C5n,
using either the Baksi (1993) or Berggren et al.
(1995) time scale. The younger limit of chron C5n
in the Baksi (1993) GPTS is 9.67 ± 0.22 Ma (2s)
based on 
40Ar-39Ar plateau ages from three lava
flows in the transition zone (Baksi et al., 1993;
Baksi, 1993). The age discrepancy could reflect an
unidentified erosional unconformity in the study
section ca. 9.7 Ma, perhaps within the fine-grained
interval of the section, where it would not be read-
ily recognized. If so, the upper portion of the long
normal magnetozone would not be recorded and
the 10.53 ± 0.16 Ma age could accurately record
the age of the ash horizon.
The remainder of the La Pilona Formation
above the long normal interval is assigned to re-
versed chron C4Ar. The age of the normal magne-
tozone within the long reversed interval near the
top of the La Pilona Formation is ambiguous and
represents either chron C4Ar.1n or C4Ar.2n. There
are no isotopic ages to constrain the age of the
Mariño strata below the unconformity that sepa-
rates this unit from La Pi
lona Formation. Tenta-
tively, the normal polarity magnetozone recorded
in these strata is correlated with chron C5An.1
(12.30–12.48 Ma), based on lithostratigraphic cor-
relation of this part of the section with the expo-
sures in the Arroyo del Agua Blanca section.
The normal polarity magnetozone located
above the unconformity that separates the Tobas
Angostura and La Pilona Formations is assigned
to chron C4An (8.59–8.92 Ma). This correlation
is based on (1) the isotopic age of sample Md-10
(Irigoyen, 1997; Irigoyen et al., 1999) and (2) the
fact that chron C4An is the first relatively long
normal interval above the long reversed chron
C4Ar in the GPTS.

cludes the Tobas Angostura and the Río de los
Pozos Formations. The latter unit could not be

The Quebrada de la Angostura section (V ,

The El Molino and Quebrada de la Angostura
sections include strata of the same units, the Tobas
Angostura Formation and the lower part of the
Río de los Pozos Formation. The normal polarity
magnetozone in both sections is assigned to chron
C4An, and the reversed polarity zone in the Que-
brada de la Angostura section is correlated with
chron C4r. The grounds for this interpretation are
(1) the 
40Ar-39Ar isotopic ages from both sections,
(2) the isotopic age obtained at an equivalent

In the El Molino section, the isotopically dated

the GPTS. The beginning of this chron is placed

1993). The normal polarity zone in the Quebrada
de la Angostura section located ~25 km south of

Angostura section record somewhat older strati-

with the boundary between the Tobas Angostura
and Río de los Pozos formations occurring at
about 9.3 Ma.
Summary
This magnetostratigraphic study of Neogene
nonmarine strata of the Mendoza Precordillera
suggests the following. (1) Deposition of the
Mariño Formation started ca. 15.7 Ma (GPTS of
Baksi, 1993) if the proposed correlation between
the long normal interval at the base of the Tosca
de Mariño section and polarity chron C5ADn-
C5ACn is correct. Deposition continued to ca.
12.0 Ma, the age of an ash-fall horizon from the
uppermost part of the unit. (2) Deposition of the
La Pilona Formation in the La Higuerita section
started ca. 11.7 Ma, assuming a constant sedi-
mentation rate for the lower part of this unit, and
continued to ca. 9.0 Ma. However, in the Arroyo
del Agua Blanca section, deposition of the La Pi-
lona Formation started no earlier than ca. 11.1
Ma, assuming that the unconformity between the
Mariño and La Pilona Formations is marked by
the first appearance of conglomerate beds typical
of the La Pilona Formation. (3) In the La Pilona
area, deposition of the Tobas Angostura Forma-
tion occurred between ca. 8.9 and 8.7 Ma, and
was followed immediately by deposition of the
Río de los Pozos Formation. (4) Farther south, in
the Tupungato area, isotopic dating suggests that
deposition of the Tobas Angostura Formation
may have commenced ca. 9.5 Ma, earlier than in
the La Pilona area. (5) The stratigraphy of the
Neogene succession exhibits regional unconfor-
mities that mark hiatuses of ~100 k.y. to ~4 m.y.
The unconformity between the Mariño and La
Pilona Formations likely represents an interval of
~1.0 m.y. in the Arroyo del Agua Blanca section,
but may span a shorter interval in the La
Higuerita section. The unconformity between the
La Pilona and Tobas Angostura Formations
recorded in the La Higuerita section probably
represents a short interval of 10–100 k.y.
Yrigoyen (1993a) and Irigoyen (1997) suggested
that a hiatus of ~3–4 m.y. separates the Río de los
Pozos and Mogotes Formations.
TECTONIC IMPLICATIONS
The magnetostratigraphy reported in this pa-
per, in conjunction with 
40Ar-39Ar data (Irigoyen,
1997; Irigoyen et al., 1999), establishes age con-
straints for the syntectonic strata of the Mendoza
Precordillera. In addition, this study also estab-
lishes a correlation between the sedimentary
record and episodes of deformation and/or vol-
canic activity in the western thrust belts (i.e., the
Principal and Frontal Cordilleras) and constrain
the timing of deformation of the Neogene suc-
cession.
The oldest Mariño strata record the existence
of a foreland basin that developed prior to or ca.
16 Ma (GPTS of Baksi, 1993) as a result of a tec-
tonically induced subsidence. The commence-
ment of Neogene sediment accumulation in the
study area is coeval with a major phase of thrust-
ing in the Aconcagua fold-and-thrust belt (cf.
Ramos, 1996; Cegarra and Ramos, 1996). The
correlation between thrusting in the Principal
Cordillera and sedimentation in the adjacent fore-
land is confirmed by a provenance study carried
out on rocks of the Mariño Formation and paleo-
current data (Irigoyen, 1997), which will be re-
ported in detail in another paper.
The beginning of deposition of Neogene strata
in the study area ca. 16 Ma is also temporally co-
incident with the eastward shifting of the subduc-
tion-related magmatic foci to the Argentine Prin-
cipal Cordillera. The volcanic and pyroclastic
rocks cropping out in the Aconcagua fold-and-
thrust belt (Complejo V olcánico Aconcagua;
Ramos et al., 1996) are 15.8–8.5 Ma, whereas in
the adjacent Chilean region to the west, the vol-
canic rocks of the Farellones Formation record an
important period of magmatic activity between
ca. 20.4 and 16.6 Ma (Rivano et al., 1990; Ramos
et al., 1991, 1996). Furthermore, geochemical
data from the volcanic rocks in this region sug-
gest that the subduction zone of the Nazca plate
began to flatten by ca. 16 Ma, long before mag-
matism ceased, and that thickening of the conti-
nental crust related to the tectonic stacking of the
Andean Cordillera evolved since about that time
(Kay et al., 1991, and references therein; Ramos
et al., 1991).
This study demonstrates that the initiation of
foreland-basin subsidence and deposition at the
study site are similar in age to the development of
thin-skinned tectonics in the central part of the
Aconcagua fold-and-thrust belt (e.g., Ramos,
1988, 1996; Cegarra and Ramos, 1996) and,
hence, are genetically linked. The initiation of an
important phase of thrusting in the Principal
Cordillera and the eastward migration of the calc-
alkaline volcanic axis may be linked with the flat-
tening of the descending plate ca. 16 Ma (cf.
Ramos et al., 1991; Ramos, 1996).
Episodes of volcanic activity occurring in the
Cordilleran region were sometimes recorded in the
study area, as inferred from the age of the air-fall
tephras interbedded in the nonmarine deposits
(Irigoyen, 1997; Irigoyen et al., 1999). For exam-
ple, the earliest 15.8–8.5 Ma volcanic activity in
the Aconcagua region is recorded by bentonite
horizons of the ca. 15.7 Ma lower member of the
Mariño Formation and by the highly tuffaceous
nature of the middle member, which contains

abundant glass shards. In addition, the extensive
ash-rich unit, the ca. 8.9–8.7 Ma Tobas Angostura
Formation, is correlated with the latest extrusive
episode in the Principal Cordillera ca. 8.5 Ma.
This latter correlation is supported by the lateral
variations in thickness of the Tobas Angostura
unit, which tapers to the east-southeast (cf.
Yrigoyen et al., 1954), suggesting that the eruptive
vents were located to the west-northwest of the
study area in the direction of the Aconcagua peak.
In addition, the facies assemblage of the Tobas An-
gostura Formation (cf. Irigoyen, 1997) accounts
for a volcanic episode that included a voluminous
pyroclastic eruption, which was responsible for
providing abundant volcanic detritus (lapilli,
ashes) that overwhelmed the basin. This interpre-
tation is consistent with the occurrence of a thick
sequence of dominantly proximal pyroclastic-flow
deposits, tuffs, and lavas, and with the presence of
gas-escape structures in the uppermost part of the
Aconcagua mountain (cf. Ramos et al., 1996), and
suggests that the latest eruptive episode was likely
the largest in the region.
Exhumation and displacement of the Frontal
Cordillera overlapped in time with deformation
in the Principal Cordillera (Irigoyen, 1997). The
latest phase of deformation in the Aconcagua
fold-and-thrust belt is thought to have occurred at
9–8 Ma (cf. Ramos, 1996; Cegarra and Ramos,
1996). A multiple data set that includes timing of
facies changes, paleocurrent data, accumulation
rates, and provenance allows a temporal correla-
tion to be made between deposition of the ca.
11.7–9.0 Ma La Pilona Formation and exhuma-
tion of the Frontal Cordillera to the northwest of
the study site (Irigoyen, 1997). Immediately east
of the Las Carreras fault system, on the eastern
flank of the Cordón del Plata (Fig. 1), the
youngest Mogotes Formation includes conglom-
erates with very large boulders of Paleozoic mag-
matic and sedimentary rocks that were almost
certainly derived from the Frontal Cordillera im-
mediately to the west. Therefore, the basal un-
conformity of the Mogotes Formation is likely
the result of exhumation and deformation in the
flanking thrust belt and probably developed as a
result of diachronous pulses of deformation
along the Cordón del Plata (Irigoyen, 1997).
Deformation of Neogene strata occurred in
the late Pliocene–early Pleistocene(?), as dis-
cussed in the following. The present location of
the orogenic front at lat 33°S, in the eastern
foothills of the Precordillera (e.g., Figueroa and
Ferraris, 1989), clearly indicates that deforma-
tion has progressed eastward since deposition of
the Mogotes Formation. Deformation is still ac-
tive, as inferred from earthquake focal mecha-
nisms (Triep, 1987; Ramos, 1990), intense com-
pressive deformation, and evidence of neotectonic
activity in the study area (Irigoyen, 1997) and
farther east, in the foothills of the Mendoza Pre-
cordillera (Bastías et al., 1993).
Combined paleomagnetic and tephra chron-
ologies on the continental deposits are particu-
larly useful in providing temporal constraints for
the timing of oil generation and development of
prospective closures. The study area encom-
passes a region of active oil production known as
the Cuyo basin, an elongate northwest-striking
basin that includes Middle to Upper Triassic non-
marine strata and subordinate volcanic rocks, in-
terpreted to be the sedimentary fill of a conti-
nental rift basin (Kokogian et al., 1993, and
references therein). Hydrocarbon reserves gener-
ated mainly from the Late Triassic Cacheuta For-
mation are concentrated in several oil fields; one,
the Cacheuta-Tupungato depocenter (Kokogian
et al., 1993), includes the La Pilona and Tupun-
gato anticlines. The structure of the region based
on subsurface data has been published in simpli-
fied form (e.g., Sarewitz, 1988; Kozlowski et al.,
1993). According to Jordan and Ortiz (1987), the
thickness of sedimentary cover above the
Cacheuta Formation at the end of deposition of
the youngest Mariño strata is about 2500 and
3000 m in the Cacheuta and Potrerillos areas, re-
spectively, sufficient for the beginning of oil gen-
eration. This study indicates that these conditions
were not achieved before ca. 12 Ma, the age of
the youngest Mariño strata, and were enhanced
after deposition of the overlying ~1000-m-thick
La Pilona Formation, the youngest strata of
which are dated as ca. 9 Ma.
Structural traps developed during regional
east-west contraction in the late Pliocene–early
Pleistocene(?), and most of the closures relate to
folds and reverse faults genetically linked with
the reverse reactivation of Triassic major normal
faults (Dellapé and Hegedus, 1993, and refer-
ences therein). Motion on the La Pilona and
Tupungato structures started after the beginning
of deposition of the Mogotes Formation ca. 3.0
Ma (Yrigoyen, 1993a); and ceased prior to ca.
0.4–0.3 Ma, the ages of the air-fall horizons in-
terbedded with Quaternary gravels in the La Pi-
lona and Tupungato areas (Irigoyen, 1997;
Irigoyen et al., 1999). The occurrence of growth
geometries in strata of the Mogotes Formation
cropping out ~35 km farther east, in the Barran-
cas anticline (Chiaramonte, 1996), suggests that
deformation may have been also partially syn-
chronous with deposition of this unit in the study
area. Fracturing of potential reservoir rocks
(Potrerillos, Río Blanco, Barrancas, and Papa-
gayo Formations of Triassic-Paleocene age; Del-
lapé and Hegedus, 1993) may have occurred dur-
ing development of closures, improving their
permeability and providing conduits for oil under
pressure to migrate along fracture planes into
previously sealed reservoir-quality rocks.
Magnetostratigraphy also allows calibration
of the ages of land mammalian fossils collected
in the Neogene units of the study area, enhanc-
ing the precision of biostratigraphic ages. In par-
ticular, the Río de los Pozos Formation provided
abundant fossil remains that were collected in
the eastern flank of the Tupungato anticline, <2
km to the northeast of the Quebrada de la An-
gostura section (see Fig. 1 in Yrigoyen, 1993b).
Previous studies assigned the Río de los Pozos
Formation to the Pliocene (e.g., Pascual and
Odreman Rivas, 1973) or to the latest Mio-
cene–early Pliocene (e.g., Yrigoyen, 1993a),
based on the fauna described in the following.
As summarized by Yrigoyen (1993b) and listed
in Pascual and De la Fuente (1993), the faunal
assemblage includes the Hydrochoeridae Kiyu-
therium aff. K. orientalis Francis and Mones of
the order Rodentia, the Mesotheriidae Typotheri-
opsis silverai Cabrera and the Hegetotheriidae
Hemihegetotherium achathaleptum Rovereto,
both of the order Notoungulata, and a cranium of
a capybara-type animal of the subfamily Car-
diatheriinae (Procardiotherium sp.?). This as-
semblage was collected near the ca. 9.3 Ma con-
tact between the Río de los Pozos Formation and
the underlying Tobas Angostura unit. Therefore,
the mammal-bearing strata are late Miocene
(Tortonian) rather than Pliocene and hence con-
tain Huayquerian fauna instead of a Pliocene
Montehermosan fauna according to land-mam-
mal age boundaries defined by Pascual and De la
Fuente (1993). Indeed, the Huayquerian land
mammal age (Simpson, 1940) is named for the
Huayquerías Formation that crops out in the area
~100 km south of the city of Mendoza, in which
vertebrate remains of late Miocene age occur
(Marshall et al., 1986).

APPENDIX
40Ar-39Ar Geochronologic Laboratory Procedures
of Irigoyen et al. (1999)
Pure mineral separates of hornblende and biotite
were prepared using standard heavy liquid and magnetic
methods followed by handpicking. Mineral irradiation
was performed in the research reactor at McMaster Uni-
versity, Hamilton, Ontario. Mineral separates were ana-
lyzed at the Massachusetts Institute of Technology using
resistance furnace step-heating and laser total fusion
techniques, and at the Geological Survey of Canada us-
ing the laser 
40Ar-39Ar step-heating method. Procedures
and instruments are similar to those explained in
Hodges et al. (1994) and Villeneuve and MacIntyre
(1997), respectively. Ages for Massachusetts Institute of
Technology and Geological Survey of Canada analyses
are referenced to Fish Canyon Tuff biotite (FCT-3) and
Fish Canyon Tuff sanidine (FCT-Kf), respectively. In
both cases, apparent ages are assumed to be 28.03 ± 0.1
Ma (Renne et al., 1994). More details were given in
Irigoyen (1997) and Irigoyen et al. (1999).
Paleomagnetic Laboratory and Analytical 
Procedures
In the laboratory, hand samples were cut and ground
into 2.5 cm cubes. Measurements were carried out in a
magnetically shielded room (magnetic field <3000 nT)
at the Geological Survey of Canada in Ottawa. Speci-
men remanence was measured with a DSM-1 digital
spinner magnetometer. Demagnetization experiments
on 10 pilot specimens were conducted to determine
whether thermal or alternating magnetic field (AF) de-
magnetization provided the most effective method of
isolating the stable component of magnetization. Spec-
imens were AF demagnetized in 15 to 20 steps to a
peak field of 100 mT using a Schonstedt single axis de-
magnetizer, model GSD-1. AF demagnetization had lit-
tle effect on the magnetization on some of the pilot
specimens.
Following the pilot study, systematic stepwise ther-
mal demagnetization experiments were carried out on
the rest of the collection. For most sites, at least one
specimen was demagnetized in 16 steps to peak tem-
peratures of 100, 200, 250, 300, 350, 400, 450, 500,
530, 560, 580, 600, 620, 640, 660, and 680 °C using a
Schonstedt thermal demagnetizer, model TSD-1, mod-
ified to maintain temperatures within ±3 °C. If the first
specimen that was measured from a given site revealed
a stable component of magnetization, the second spec-
imen was subjected to fewer heating steps, usually 250,
350, 450, 500, 530, 550, and 630 °C. Additional steps
were included when appropriate. If the first specimen
displayed a complex pattern of demagnetization, the 16
step heating procedure was also used for the second
specimen. The third specimen of stable sites was de-
magnetized in two or three steps, generally 500, 550,
and 600 °C. Occasionally, more steps were included.
For most sites, magnetization directions for individual
specimens were established using the least-squares fit
method of Kirschvink (1980). In a few specimens, the
magnetization directions of the characteristic component
were too scattered to employ this method, and an end
point was calculated as the mean of the semistable di-
rections using Fisher statistics (Fisher, 1953). Mean
directions for each site, before and after correction for
tilting about a horizontal axis, were calculated using
Fisher statistics. The corresponding virtual geomag-
netic poles (VGPs) were calculated and divided into
three classes. Class I sites have a mean magnetic di-
rection based on three samples and satisfy Watson’s
(1956) criterion for nonrandomness at the 95% confi-
dence level (R ‡2.62). Class II sites are those with N = 2
and those with N = 3 and R < 2.62. For class II sites the
polarity is not in doubt. The length of magnetic polarity
zones based on single class II sites is poorly constrained.
Class III designates those sites where the three speci-
mens have widely divergent directions. Class III sites are
not used to define polarity zones. They are often located
between sites of opposite polarity and may, in some
cases, represent transitions between the two polarities.
The boundary between zones of different polarity is
placed midway between consecutive normal and re-
versed data points.

Age and palaeomagnetism of the Mundine Well dyke swarm,
Western Australia: implications for an Australia–Laurentia
connection at 755 Ma
Michael T.D. Wingate a,*, John W. Giddings b
a Tectonics Special Research Centre, Department of Geology and Geophysics, The University of Western Australia,
Nedlands, W A 6907, Australia
b Australian Geological Survey Organisation, Canberra, ACT 2601, Australia
Abstract
Integrated U–Pb geochronology and palaeomagnetic studies of the Mundine Well dyke swarm (MDS) of the
Pilbara Craton, Western Australia, are employed to test the hypothesis that Australia and Laurentia were joined as
part of the Rodinia supercontinent. Ion microprobe U–Pb dating of zircon and baddeleyite indicates that the MDS
was emplaced at 755± 3M a( 9 5% conﬁdence interval ) and palaeomagnetic results conﬁrm that the swarm is equivalent
in age to dykes of the Northampton Inlier. A positive contact test between an MDS dyke and an older dolerite sill
indicates that the MDS magnetisation dates from the time of dyke emplacement and cooling at 755 Ma. Combining
new palaeomagnetic data for eight MDS dykes with previous results for six Northampton dykes yields a palaeopole
for Australia at 135 ° E, 46° N( A95=4° ). The MDS palaeopole lies 30 ° away from the 780 to 740 Ma APW path
segment for Laurentia, indicating that, if the Rodinia reconstruction is correct, breakup between Australia and
Laurentia occurred prior to 755 Ma. It has been suggested elsewhere that the Sturtian glaciation in Australia preceded
or accompanied breakup. If so, the Sturtian rocks should be older than 755 Ma and hence may not be coeval with
glaciogenic rocks of the post-755 Ma Rapitan Group in Laurentia. Crown copyright © 2000 Published by Elsevier

New palaeomagnetic results from the ‘cap dolomite’ of the
Neoproterozoic Walsh Tillite, northwestern Australia
Z.X. Li *
Tectonics Special Research Centre, Department of Geology and Geophysics, The University of Western Australia,
Nedlands, W A 6907, Australia
Abstract
An interpreted primary magnetic remanence that passed a fold test has been revealed from six sampling sites in
the pink ‘cap dolomite’ of the Neoproterozoic Walsh Tillite, southern Kimberley, northwestern Australia. A
palaeomagnetic pole ( WTC ) at (21.5 ° S, 282.4° E) with dp =12.2° and dm=15.4° , based on results of the ﬁve best
sites, gives a palaeolatitude of 45 ± 12° for the sampling region, and ca 25 ± 12° for the Adelaide Fold Belt where two
Neoproterozoic glaciations occur. This palaeopole falls 58° away from the Marinoan glaciation (the Elatina Formation)
pole, and the palaeolatitude for the region studied is around 30 ° higher than that predicted by the Marinoan and
younger Neoproterozoic poles from Australia. If the WTC pole is accepted as a palaeopole at the end of the Walsh
glaciation, the Walsh Tillite is thus likely to be of Sturtian (ca 770–750 Ma) rather than Marinoan age. A comparison
of the revised late Mesoproterozoic to Neoproterozoic apparent polar wander path (APWP) for East Gondwana with
that of Laurentia suggests that supercontinent Rodinia broke apart by about 750 Ma, after the Sturtian glaciation.
The new data do not discriminate between the snowball Earth model and the high-obliquity Earth model for the
Neoproterozoic time. The revised APWP suggests a ‘stop-and-go’ fashion of movement for East Gondwana during
the Neoproterozoic. Published by Elsevier Science B.V.
Keywords: Australia; Cap dolomite; Neoproterozoic; Palaeomagnetism; Rodinia; Walsh Tillite

JOURNAL OF GEOPHYSICAL RESEARCH, VOL. 105, NO. B2, PAGES 2805-2815, FEBRUARY 10, 2000 
New constraints on the Upper Permian and Lower Triassic 
geomagnetic polarity timescale from 
the A badeh section (central Iran) 
Yves Gallet, 1 Leopold Krystyn, 2 Jean Besse, 
and Luc-Emmanuel Ricou 1 
1 Abdolah Saidi, 3 
Abstract. We present the magnetostratigraphy of the Abadeh section (central Iran). Thermal 
demagnetization shows two magnetic components: one at low unblocking temperatures, 
which corresponds to a present day-field direction, and another at high temperatures. This 
second component, which contains both polarities, is interpreted as a primary magnetization 
acquired during sediment deposition at a paleolatitude of about 7.7øS. A sequence of 14 
magnetic polarity zones is obtained in the intervals during the Upper Dzhulfian-Lower 
Changhsingian (Upper Permian) and during the Griesbachian (Lower Triassic). Combining 
data from south China, Canada, Pakistan, and Iran, we propose a composite (but still 
uncomplete) Upper Permian and Lower Triassic geomagnetic polarity timescale. 
1. Introduction 
The construction of a reliable geomagnetic polarity 
timescale (GPTS) during the Upper Permian and the Lower 
Triassic is of particular interest in order to correlate the 
successive events of the Permo-Triassic mass extinction, often 
considered as the most severe over the entire Phanerozoic [e.g., 
Sepkoski, 1990; Erwin, 1994]. Magnetostratigraphic studies of 
biostratigraphically well-dated marine sections from South 
China and Pakistan presently document the chronology of the 
geomagnetic reversals during the Upper Permian [Heller et at, 
1988, 1995; Steiner et at, 1989; Haag and Heller, 1991]. More 
than 10 magnetic polarity intervals follow the Kiaman 
superchron, and the end of Kiaman would occur during the 
Wordian [Heller et at, 1988, 1995; Steiner et at, 1989; Haag 
and Heller, 1991] (see also Thdveniaut et at [1994], Ernbleton et 
aL [1996], and Gialanella et at [1997] for continental 
sediments). 
However, several problems still plague the construction of 
the Upper Permian GPTS. The Chinese sections display rather 
different magnetic polarity patterns and cannot be easily 
correlated with each other [Heller et at, 1995]. The correlations 
between the Nammal Gorge section from Pakistan studied by 
Haag and Heller [1991] and the Chinese sections are also 
problematic: Heller et at [1995] suggested a correlation 
between the Dzhulfian-Dorashamian age Chhidru formation 
from Nammal Gorge and the Changhsing formation from China, 
but it is now widely considered from biostratigraphic data that 
the Upper Changhsing time period is not present in Pakistan 
[e.g., Iranian-Japanese Research Group (IJRG), 1981; Shen et at, 
1984; Sweet, 1992; Wardlaw and Pogue, 1995; Baud et at, 
1996]. We felt that additional results were required to better

2. The Abadeh Section 
The so-called Abadeh section (latitude 30ø54'N and 
longitude 53ø13'E; Figure 1) is located in the province of Fars, 
about 260 km south of Esfahan and 60 km southeast of the city 
of Abadeh. The sequence crops out in the Hambast Range at an 
altitude of -2000 m. The Uppermost Permian consists of the 
Hambast Formation, which has a thickness of 34 m in our 
section (Figure 2). The lower part of the Hambast Formation 
comprises a 17-m-thick alternating sequence of tens of 
centimeter thick greyish to black limestone beds and shales 
(unit 6 [IJRG, 1981]), while the upper part consists of reddish 
nodular and thin bedded limestones of ammonitico rosso type 
(unit 7 [IJRG, 1981]). After a distinct lithologic change, 
sedimentation resumed during the Lower Triassic first with a 
short shaly interval (30 cm of so-called Transition beds) 
followed by the thin bedded \"en plaquettes\" pale greyish 
limestones and shales of the Elikah Formation. This latter 
formation is very thick (several hundred meters) and forms cliffs 
in the landscape. The thin interval of stromatolites (algal 
biolithites) at the base of the Elikah Formation is interpreted as 
regressive shallow water deposits by IJRG [1981]. The studied 
section is monoclinal, dipping 40øto 60 ø toward the west- 
southwest. 
In the Tethys area, serious stratigraphic problems result from 
the different and competing Upper Permian chronostratigraphic 
scales established in China and Iran (Transcaucasia). The 
ammonoid faunas are unfortunately significantly different and 
cannot be unequivocally correlated [e.g., Zhao et at, 1978; 
Ruzhencev and Sarycheva, 1965] (see Tozer [1994] for a 
discussion). As a consequence, we consider the correlations 
based on conodonts far more reliable, and we use the zonation 
suggested by Kozur [1990, 1995] for the Permian and the one 
recently proposed by Orchard and Krystyn [1998] for the

Triassic (Figures 3a and 3b). The location of the Permo-Triassic 
boundary that we consider for the Abadeh section follows 
Tozer's [1967] definition and accords with the so-called 
\"eventostratigraphic boundary\" of Meishan [Wang, 1995] 
between beds 24 and 25 (in the sense of Yin et o2 [1996a,b]). It 
reflects the major faunal turnover from Permian to Triassic 
neogondolellid conodonts and allows well-constrained 
biostratigraphic correlations between many Chinese sections 
[Yinet o2, 1996a,b], as well as between China, Iran (Abadeh), 
and Canada. 
The biostratigraphy of the Abadeh section was first described 
by Taraz [1969, 1971, 1974], and the conodonts were 
subsequently examined by Kozur [1975] and Kozur et o2 [1975]. 
The most recent and most comprehensive study has been 
carried out by a joint Iranian-Japanese research group in 1981. 
We have rechecked the Permian part of the section. The main 
reason for that was the correlation by IJRG [1981] of the 
Neogondolella orientalis conodont zone (otherwise Dzhulfian) 
with the Dorashamian Shevyrevites and Shevyrevites- 
Paratirolites zones, although the Dzhulfian guide ammonite 
Araxoceras latum was found in the top of the Orientalis zone 
(Figures 2 and 3b). The detailed lithologic description of the 
section provided by IJRG [1981] allowed us to integrate easily 
our new samples into the previous conodont data framework. 
Altogether, these data form the basis for the adopted conodont 
zonation of the section (Figure 2). 
All samples from unit 7 of the Permian Hambast Formation 
are rich in diagnostic platform conodonts. The 
magnetostratigraphic sampling starts right above the last 
appearance datum (LAD) of Neogondolella leveni and of 
neogondolellids close to N. guangyuanensis (in the sense of Mei 
eta/. [1994]; see also Kozur [ 1995]). The Upper Dzhulfian is 
documented within the first 7 m by the occurrence of both N. 
transcaucasica and N. orientalis. A certain differentiation of this 
interval is only indicated by the greater abundance of N. 
transcaucasica in the lower part. The first appearance datum 
(FAD) of N. subcarinata is above 7 m, the conodont zonal 
guide of the Dorashamian, which occurs up to the top of the 
Hambast Formation. The Upper Changhsingian (equivalent to 
the Changxingensis zone)is clearly missing in Abadeh and lies 
within a submarine hiatus at the Permo-Triassic boundary in this 
region. In the Shahreza section located about 100 km north of 
the Abadeh section [Besse et O2, 1998], we only found above the 
Paratirolites beds a 30-cm-thin nodular limestone level with 
Upper Changhsingian conodonts (N. postwangi, 
N. cf. changxingensis), similar to that of the Dorashamian type 
region in Transcaucasia [Kotlyar et al., 1984]. All over Iran (and 
Transcaucasia), the topmost Permian (i.e., Upper 
Changhsingian) strata are therefore very thin, either condensed 
or removed by lowermost Triassic submarine erosion. The 
paraconformity at the Permo-Triassic boundary in Abadeh 
claimed by Taraz [1974] and also by the Iranian-Japanese 
Research Group [1981] is thus a fact though it has later been 
rejected by Kozur [1989] and by Sweet [1992].

The Lower Triassic magnetic polarity sequence from Abadeh 
is concordant with the one obtained from the well-dated 
Griesbach Creek section from Canada (Figures 3b and 7 [Ogg 
and Steiner, 1991]). In particular, they show the presence of a 
normal interval during the uppermost part of the Griesbachian 
and the Griesbachian/Dienerian boundary, which is not found in 
the Chinese sections [Steiner et 02, 1989, 1993]. Ogg and Steiner 
[1991] proposed the occurrence of an additional short normal 
polarity interval during the Upper Griesbachian (called GN2) 
that we do not observe in Abadeh. This event is based on the 
stratigraphic correlation between the poorly dated Creek of 
Embry and the Griesbach Creek sections. Note that Hounslow e t 
02 [1996] also suggested the occurrence of other very short 
polarity intervals during the Griesbachian from Central Svalbard 
(Barents Sea region) sections, which remain unconfirmed and 
not well described since no paleomagnetic analysis is provided.

Remagnetization of Lower Cretaceous limestones 
from the southern Pyrenees and relation to 
the Iberian plate geodynamic evolution 
Jaume Dinars-Turelll 
Paleomagnetic Laboratory, Fort Hoofddijk, Utrecht, Netherlands 
Jesfis Garcfa-Senz 
Departament de Geodin/tmica i Geoffsica, Universitat de Barcelona, Barcelona, Spain 
Abstract. Paleomagnetic study (34 sites) of thick Cretaceous -5000 rn marine carbonate strata 
from the Organyt Basin (OB) in the southern Pyrenees reveals a uniformly normal polarity charac- 
teristic remanence with varying declination (D) (Berriasian-Barremian, D = 295ø; Aptian-Albian, 
D = 348 ø, upper Cretaceous, D = 354 ø) that resides in magnetite and predates Late Creta- 
ceous/Tertiary folding. The lack of reverse polarity magnetizations in the Berriasian-Barremian 
series, together with their distinct hysteresis properties that are typical of remagnetized carbonates 
elsewhere, are taken as evidence for a secondary overprint in the lower part of the succession. A 
hypothesized age of remagnetization near the Barremian/Aptian boundary fits with a major tecto- 
sedimentary event in the basin that changed deposition from platform to basinal conditions and 
increased subsidence during the Aptian. The angular difference (-53 ø) between declination from 
the remagnetized strata and the mean for Aptian-Albian strata indicates that a counterclockwise 
rotation occurred between the two acquisition times. Part of this rotation is interpreted to be local 
and due to slip variation along strike of a normal fault that bounded the basin and tilted the pre 
Aptian series. This Cretaceous extensive phase is framed in the rift evolution of the northern mar- 
gin of the Iberian plate. The inferred remagnetization age within the OB falls within the range of 
previously inferred widespread Cretaceous remagnetization events affecting the Iberian plate. In 
the OB, remagnetization is speculated to have taken place through chemical (burial diagenetic) 
origin rather than simple thermoviscous resetting. 
1. Introduction 
It has always been critical in paleomagnetic research to accu- 
rately assign ages to the different magnetization components 
identified in progressive demagnetization. This aspect has ac- 
quired paramount importance since it has become clear in the last 
20 years that many rocks can acquire geologically stable, secon- 
dary yet ancient, magnetizations that post-date the absolute or 
biostratigraphic age of the rock [e.g., Kent, 1979, 1985; Scotese et 
al., 1982; McCabe et al., 1983]. A prominent example has been 
the recognition that sedimentary rocks over a large part of North 
America (and Europe) were remagnetized during the Pennsylva- 
nian and Permian periods (the well-known late Paleozoic remag- 
netization \"event\" in the Appalachian orogen) (see McCabe and 
Elmore [1989] for a review). 
Many paleomagnetic studies of different rock units from the 
Iberian Peninsula are suggestive of remagnetization processes, 
although the ages and inferred mechanisms appear to be different 
[Schott, 1985; Schott and Peres, 1987; Galdeano et al., 1989; 
Moreau et al., 1992; Villalain et al., 1994; Judrez et al., 1994, 
1996, 1998; Pards and Roca, 1996]. Most studies report the exis- 
tence of a Cretaceous remagnetization, dated either by the bio- 
stratigraphic age of the rocks studied [Galdeano et al., 1989;

Moreau et al., 1992], or inferred by comparison with the Iberian 
apparent polar wander path (APWP) [Judrez et al., 1994, 1996, 
1998]. The Cretaceous APWP for Iberia, however, is only poorly 
determined, and well-defined paleomagnetic data are required to 
quantify the Mesozoic counterclockwise rotation of the Iberian 
Peninsula, which is related to the opening of the North Atlantic 
and the Bay of Biscay. This major geodynamic feature is docu- 
mented through paleomagnetic studies [e.g., Van der Voo, 1967, 
1969] and oceanic magnetic anomalies [e.g., Srivastava et al., 
1990]. It is essential, however, that paleomagnetic directions are 
obtained from tectonically stable areas of Iberia and that good 
magnetic age control is available (especially for secondary rema- 
nences). It is worth pointing out that data from contractional belts 
(i.e., thrusted units within the alpine orogens) might still be useful 
if relative vertical axis rotations of the different stratigraphic units 
from a given homogeneous tectonic block are documented. The 
relative angular variations of declination are independent of 
younger emplacement-related rotations and may be extrapo- 
lated/compared with data from the \"stable\" areas. 
The present study reports on the paleomagnetic and rock- 
magnetic signature of a thick (-5000 m) Cretaceous series that 
crops out in the B6ixols thrust sheet from the southern Pyrenees. 
The study is a follow-up of an extensive magnetotectonic re- 
search project carried out in the south Pyrenean Upper Thrust 
Sheets that provided directional information for the Aptian- 
Albian (16 sites) and Upper Cretaceous (4 sites) series from the 
B6ixols unit [Dinarbs-Turell, 1992; Dinarbs-Turell et al., 1991 ]. 
The study has now been extended to the Berriasian-Barremian

series (14 sites), and we have completed rock-magnetic investiga- 
tions for the entire Cretaceous series in order to tackle the prob- 
lems outlined above. We document both the existence of an Early 
Cretaceous remagnetization that affected part of the series, and 
subsequent counterclockwise rotation, which has implications for 
the Iberian Mesozoic geodynamic scenario. 
2. Geologic Setting 
The Organyh Basin (OB) is a west-east trending graben over 
80 km long and up to 15 km wide, filled with 4500 m of Lower 
Cretaceous sedimentary rocks. It forms part of a system of Meso- 
zoic basins linked to the evolution of the North Atlantic margin. 
The OB was formed upon a substratum of Hercynian basement 
with a cover of Stefanian, Permian, Triassic and Jurassic sedi- 
ments. During the Alpine orogeny, part of the sedimentary cover 
was detached and involved into the South Pyrenean Upper Thrust 
Sheets [Muoz, 1991]. The southern margin of the graben is in- 
verted in the frontal part of the B6ixols thrust sheet as a footwall 
short cut and related hangingwall folds [Bond and McClay, 
1995]. The northern exposures coincide with a passive-roof back- 
thrust located in the contact with the Axial zone antiformal stack 
(Figure 1). To the east the B6ixols thrust is cut by the Segre 
oblique thrust, which was active during the Early Oligocene as an 
out-of-sequence thrust [Verges, 1993]. 
Chronostratigraphy for the Lower Cretaceous series is based 
on ammonites, planktonic and benthic (chiefly orbitolinids) fo- 
raminifera together with calpionellids and indicates an Early 
Tithonian-Late Berriasian age for the lower part of the section 
(Nla unit, Figure 2) up to the middle Albian for the Coll d'Abella 
limestones (Figure 2) [Peyberns, 1976; Caus et al., 1990; 
Martinez, 1982; Schwenke, 1993; Bernaus, 1995; Garcœa-Senz et 
al., 1995]. The chronostratigraphy of the Upper Cretaceous strata 
is based primarily on planktonic foraminifera [G6mez-Garrido, 
1987] and ammonite biostratigraphy [Martt'nez, 1982]. The de- 
velopment and subsequent inversion of the Organyh Basin can be 
summarized in four phases. 
2.1. Extensional Basin (Berriasian-Middle Albian) 
The graben formed in the hangingwall of a major south bound- 
ing fault oriented E-W. In transversal section the basin margin 
was monoclinally flexed at the fault tip, as proved by the onlap 
and tilting toward the basin of the Aptian sequences. The dis- 
placement of the fault dies-out westward along strike, linking to 
an oblique NW-SE transfer zone located near La Pobla de Segur. 
Four distinct infilling phases are recorded. 
2.1.1. Berriasian-Valanginian sequence. The onset of rifting 
is marked by a major unconformity close to the Tithonian- 
Berriasian boundary. The Jurassic platform became emergent and 
was deeply eroded in the footwalls of the basin-forming faults. 
Initial breccias shed from fault scarps are overlain by open ma- 
rine carbonates and shales, with a shallowing-up evolution (Hos- 
tal Nou I sequence) (Figure 2). Valanginian deposition is charac- 
terized by condensed parasequences in restricted marine nviron- 
ments (Hostal Nou II sequence). This phase of \"early extension\" 
ended with an important unconformity extending from the Late 
Valanginian to the Hauterivian. 
2.1.2. Barremian-lower Aptian sequence. The Barremian 
stratigraphy is overall characterized by shallow carbonates with a 
transgressive-regressive evolution (Prada I and Prada II se- 
quences) (Figure 2). 
2.1.3. Bedoulian-Gargasian sequence. A fundamental 
change in deposition occurred close to the Barremian/Aptian 
boundary. The area occupied by the Barremian platform became 
basinal in a facies sense, with accumulation of hemipelagic marls 
and black shales that indicate an increase in bathymetry (Cab6 
and Senyfis Formations). This transgressive cycle is related to the 
acceleration in slip along the major southern boundary fault. 
After the tilting maxima the basin was progressively filled at sea 
level, with no signs of active faulting, ending the sequence with a 
widespread regression. 
2.1.4. Clansayesian-Middle Albian sequence. Black shales 
and hemipelagic marls make up most of the succession (Font 
Bordonera and Lluh Formations). The top of the sequence is 
eroded under the Cenomanian unconformity (Figure 2). 
2.2. Cenomanian Inversion 
Up to 3000 m of Lower Cretaceous strata were removed be- 
fore the mid to Late Cenomanian as consequence of contraction 
oblique to the graben boundaries that gently folded the synrift 
package. 
2.3. Stable platform (Mid-Late Cenomanian-Early Santonian) 
Following inversion, subaerial erosion reduced the Lower Cre- 
taceous strata to a nearly smooth plain. Overlying the erosion 
surface, relatively uniform sedimentation prevailed from Ceno- 
manian through Early Santonian time (Santa Fe, Reguard, and 
Anserola Formations). 
2.4. Pyrenean Orogeny (Late Santonian-Maastrichtian) 
Compressive tectonics led to basin inversion with the devel- 
opment of folds and shortcut thrusts. Detailed investigations of 
the syninversion deposits indicates that the B6ixols thrust, along 
with the Sant Corneli anticline and the Santa Fe syncline (Figure 
1), grew during the Campanian and the Maastrichtian [Sirn6, 
1986, Bond and McClay, 1995] and was later reactivated with 
lesser amount of displacement during the late Eocene and early 
Oligocene. 
3. Sampling and Laboratory Procedures 
A total of 34 sites spanning the Cretaceous series from the 
B6ixols thrust sheet has been studied (Table 1). In general, the 
rock types are dark gray colored limestones (mudstones to wack- 
stones), marly limestones, and marls (Table 1). Massive platform 
limestones predominate in the pre-Aptian sequences and well- 
bedded hemipelagic marls and marly limestones constitute the 
main lithology for the Aptian-Albian sequences (see point 2). 
Samples were cored (2.54 cm in diameter) with a portable gaso- 
line-powered drill. A site typically consists of 5 to 8 samples 
distributed along 5 to 10 m of stratigraphic section. In some sites, 
however, more than 10 m were covered (Table 1) and/or a major 
number of samples were taken. Cores were split in the laboratory 
into standard specimens (2.2 cm in length) for paleomagnetic 
measurements. The natural remanent magnetization (NRM) and 
its response to stepwise thermal or alternating field demagnetiza- 
tion were measured in a GM400 two-axis cryogenic magnetome- 
ter at the University of Oxford (Aptian-Albian and Upper Creta- 
ceous sites), and in a 2G Enterprises cryogenic magnetometer at 
the University of Utrecht (Berriasian-Barremian sites). Character- 
istic remanent magnetizations (ChRM) were computed by least 
squares fitting [Kirschvink, 1980] on the orthogonal demagnetiza- 
tion plots [Zijderveld, 1967]. The initial susceptibility and its 
variations upon thermal cleaning were measured on a Kap- 
pabridge (KLY-2) instrument. Stepwise acquisition of a uniaxial

4.3. Demagnetization of the NRM 
All Aptian-Albian and Upper Cretaceous strata (sites 1 to 20; 
Table 1 and Figure 6a) show similar behavior during NRM de- 
magnetization. Thermal and alternating field treatment yield 
similar directions but thermal demagnetization was preferably 
used. Two remanent magnetization components can be identified, 
in addition to a third component, which is removed below 100 ø- 
100 150øC and seems to be related to a drilling or storage viscous 
acquisition (i.e., is parallel to the specimen long axis). A low- 
temperature, low-coercivity component (L) with unblocking tem- 
peratures of less than 300øC or a coercivity of about 20-25 mT is 
then removed (Figure 6a). This component conforms to the pre- 
sent geomagnetic field direction and therefore is regarded as a 
secondary recent overprint. Finally, a high-temperature compo- 
nent (H) with unblocking temperatures distributed from about 
250øC to 450ø-500øC is observed. The high-temperature compo- 
nents decay toward the origin in their orthogonal vector plots. 
Above those temperatures, growth of new magnetite is identified 
by an increase in susceptibility and erratic behavior in demag- 
netization. The paleomagnetic site mean directions of the H com- 
ponent for the Aptian-Albian sites (sites 5 to 20; Table 2 and

properties are also different in those sites (i.e., they match the

5. Discussion 
The polarity of the H component for all sites in Aptian-Albian 
and Upper Cretaceous strata (sites 1 to 20) is normal. This is in 
agreement with the biostratigraphic age of the rocks (i.e., it corre- 
sponds to the normal chron C34n or Cretaceous Quite Zone, 
Figure 2). Moreover, the positive fold tests as well as hysteresis 
properties collectively argue in favor of a primary magnetization 
(i.e., acquired during or soon after deposition). The mean Aptian- 
Albian direction from the OB (Table 2 and Figure 6b) is statisti- 
cally coincident with the expected Aptian reference direction for 
Iberia derived from strata near Lisbon [Galdeano et al., 1989] 
(D/I = 349.1ø/51.8 ø, a95 = 7.0). Reference directions are calcu- 
lated for a common location at Tremp (42.2øN/løE, Figure 1). 
Seemingly, the Upper Cretaceous mean direction (Table 2) does 
not differ significantly from the Upper Cretaceous calculated 
reference direction obtained from the Lisbon basalts [Van der 
Voo and Zijderveld, 1971] (D/I = 354.90/43.9 ø, a95 = 3.0). These 
observations have been previously used to support lack of vertical 
axis rotation during Alpine deformation and emplacement of the 
B6ixols thrust sheet [Dinarbs-Turell, 1992; Dinarbs-Turell et al., 
1991]. 
Normal polarities for the H component were also observed for 
all our Berriasian-Barremian sites (sites 21 to 34). In this case, 
however, the inferred biostratigraphic age places them within an 
interval with numerous reversals (Berriasian-Barremian, Figure 
2). Even considering that the Hauterivian is missing and that 
paleomagnetic sampling is not continuous, the absence of reverse 
oolaritv H maenetizations in those sites makes them suspicious of 
remagnetization. As an example, sites 30 and 31, which span 10 
and 40 m, respectively, along the entire N3 Valanginian unit 
(sampling resolution of-2 m) (Table 1 and Figure 2), do not 
show any reverse polarity magnetizations. As outlined above, the 
hysteresis properties for the Berriasian-Hauterivian and older 
Barremian sites (24-34) indeed indicate that those sites are re- 
magnetized. As mentioned above, strata at the three younger 
Barremian sites (Prada II sequence, sites 21-23), which might be 
Aptian in age given the biostratigraphic information, have hys- 
teresis properties that classify them as unremagnetized and there- 
fore they have been considered separately. The aspects related to 
the paleomagnetic directional data from the Berriasian-Barremian 
sites are discussed below.

Mesozoic strata have been described in more external structures 
in the southern Pyrenees [Dinars-Turell and McClellan& 1991; 
Dinars-Turell, 1992, 1994]. They were related to weathering 
along aerial exposure associated to Tertiary thrust-sheet em-

magnetizations seem to be unrelated to the observed secondary 
magnetization in the Organyh Basin. 
Next we analyze the alternative possibility of remagnetization 
prior to Late Cretaceous folding and the potential mechanisms for 
such remagnetization. One possibility is that the remagnetization 
took place around the Barremian/Aptian boundary. This is based 
on the following observations: (1) the boundary between remag- 
netized and non remagnetized rocks, as defined by the hysteresis 
properties, occurs around the Barremian/Aptian boundary; (2) 
this boundary coincides with a significant change in declination 
toward more north directed directions in younger non remagnet- 
ized strata. If this interpretation is correct, the mean remanence 
declinations in the Organyh Basin define a rotational path from 
west directed declinations for the remagnetized Berriasian- 
Barremian sites to north directed declinations for younger strata 
with primary magnetizations (Table 2 and Fig. 8). The directional 
implications of this interpretation are discussed below. 
One of two mechanisms, including chemical remagnetization 
related to one or more diagenetic events [e.g., McCabe et al., 
1983; McCabe and Elmore, 1989] and thermoviscous resetting 
[Kent, 1985], is usually invoked for remagnetized carbonate 
rocks. Generally, however, the ultimate process responsible for 
the remagnetization is often poorly understood and open to de- 
bate. Migration of fluids [e.g., Ge and Garven, 1992] expelled or 
derived from orogenic belts is regarded as a possible mechanism 
of remagnetization because the circumstantial spatial and tempo- 
ral association with secondary magnetizations, although often no 
direct geochemical characterization of the fluid can be made. A 
burial diagenetic origin for a secondary magnetization has re- 
cently been described for some North American Pennsylvanian 
carbonate rocks [Banerjee et al., 1997] and is supported by oxy- 
gen isotope ratios in their authigenic magnetites [Ripperdan et 
al., 1998]. A widespread remagnetization of Mesozoic carbonates 
of the Vocontian trough, southeast France, has also been inter- 
preted as a consequence of burial diagenesis during basin matura- 
tion [Katz et al., 1998]. A transition from high to low NRM and 
anhysteretic remanent magnetization intensifies was found to 
correlate with presence/absence of smectite, with both features 
occurring at different biostratigraphic positions along the basin 
[Katz et al., 1998]. Moreover, strontium isotope data are not 
consistent with alteration by orogenic-type fluids, which rein- 
forces the burial diagenetic remagnetization hypothesis for those 
rocks. 
We have shown in the OB how saturation remanence (Ms) and 
NRM intensity both vary from high values in the oldest 
remagnetized strata to lower values in the younger non 
remagnetized strata. Unfortunately, the clay mineralogy and their 
burial diagenetic trends in the Cretaceous of the OB have not 
been studied to allow direct comparison with the paleomagnetic 
results. Also, data on the organic matter maturation throughout 
the basin are not available to independently test the burial 
diagenetic mechanism as the cause for the secondary authigenesis 
of magnetite. Nevertheless, this mechanism remains a testable 
hypothesis in the OB. Moreover, there is a good agreement 
between the postulated timing of this remagnetization and the 
subsidence history derived for the OB. The hypothesized age near 
the Barremian/Aptian boundary for the remagnetization event 
coincides with an increase of subsidence that changed the 
depositional trend to basinal conditions with a high sedimentation 
rate (Figure 2). The possibility of a thermoviscous resetting 
related to a thermal event remains more unlikely. This is basically 
because there is no apparent coincidence between the timing of 
remagnetization in the OB, as outlined in this study, and other

5.2. Implications for the Iberian Cretaceous Evolution 
If the ChRM of the Berriasian-Barremian limestones truly 
represents a secondary magnetization acquired at about the Bar- 
remian/Aptian boundary time, then the implications of the pa- 
leomagnetic data from the OB can be further analyzed. As the 
respective Aptian-Albian and Late Cretaceous data from the OB 
match the corresponding reference directions for lberia, we have 
no reason to invoke significant rotation related to thrust sheet 
emplacement. The angular difference between the Aptian-Albian 
mean direction and the direction of the Barremian/Aptian secon- 
dary magnetization is -53 ø, whereas the site mean direction for 
the oldest non remagnetized sites (21-23, Upper Barremian- 
Lower Aptian strata) is at an intermediate position (Figures 8 and 
9). Given that the rotation of the Iberian peninsula estimated from 
paleomagnetic data amounts to less than 40 ø [Van der Voo, 1967; 
Galdeano et al., 1989; Van der Voo, 1993], the internal relative 
rotation observed along the stratigraphic package of the OB must 
represent, at least partially, a Cretaceous age local rotation of the 
basin or of a larger \"Pyrenean\" domain. The rotation of the Ibe- 
rian peninsula (Figure 9) can be partitioned as two phases consid- 
ering all the available paleomagnetic data. A fast Barremian age 
counterclockwise rotation of-26 ø is likely, although data for this 
age and hence the rate of rotation is largely defined by a single 
study on sedimentary rocks near Lisbon [Galdeano et al., 1989] 
(point 6 in Figure 9). An additional counterclockwise rotation of 
-13 ø occurred between the Albian and the Maastrichtian. The 
data from the OB are consistent with a very fast counterclockwise 
rotation of pre-Albian age and a subsequent minor rotation. How- 
ever, the exact age and magnitude do not coincide with the Ibe- 
rian data set. In the OB the main rotational phase appears to have 
taken place between Late Barremian and the Early Aptian and is 
about 53 ø. Furthermore, the hypothesized Barremian/Aptian age 
for the remagnetization in the OB is similar to the range of the 
inferred age for the secondary magnetization acquisition in Juras- 
sic rocks from the Iberian Range deduced by comparison with the 
Iberian reference dataset [Judrez et al., 1998] (Figure 9). Yet, the 
total amount of Mesozoic rotation in the Iberian Range (-33 o), as 
defined by the primary Jurassic direction, is less than the inferred 
Cretaceous rotation in the OB. Therefore, and independently of 
whether the remagnetization events are coeval, the data from the 
OB indicates that this domain has likely behaved individually at 
least during its pre-Albian evolution. We believe that most of the 
counterclockwise rotation observed in the OB represents a Creta- 
ceous local rotation. This is consistent with a westward slip de- 
crease of the E-W normal fault that bounded the basin at the time 
(now frontal thrust as consequence of the Pyrenean inversion) as 
inferred by tectosedimentary evidences [Vergds and Garcœa-Senz, 
2000].
