A prefolding magnetization of normal polarity residing in 
magnetite (H component) has been recovered in all Lower and 
Upper Cretaceous strata from sites in the Organyh Basin at the 
B6ixols thrust sheet. Despite the similar behavior of samples 
from all parts of the section during NRM demagnetization, we 
believe that the H component does not date to the age of the rocks 
in oldest Berriasian-Barremian sites and hence represents a re- 
magnetization. One argument supporting this is that all sites dis- 
play normal polarity magnetization, although the biostratigraphic 
age of the rocks places them in an age interval with numerous 
reversals. Additionally, the hysteresis properties are consistent 
with previously recognized properties of other limestones that 
have been remagnetized. A primary nature of the H component is 
likely for younger sites in Aptian-Albian and Upper Cretaceous 
strata, based on both their polafity-biostratigraphic placement and 
their rock magnetic properties. 
The paleomagnetic direction of the H component implies 
about 53 ø counterclockwise relative rotation between the time of 
acquisition of the secondary magnetization in the Berriasian- 
Barremian sites and that in the Aptian-Albian sites, which have a 
primary magnetization. Assuming the hypothesis of remagnetiza- 
tion at about the Barremian/Aptian boundary (i.e., the magnetiza- 
tion of the Berriasian-Barremian sites has this age) the amount of 
rotation is well above the accepted maximum amount of Meso- 
zoic rotation for Iberia (-35 ø-40ø). Consequently, we invoke that 
at least part of the inferred rotation is local and probably linked to 
faulting along basin bounding structures. Furthermore, rocks 
were remagnetized during a stage preceding the subsidence 
maxima in the basin and the rotation itself. Burial diagenesis is 
regarded as a plausible mechanism of remagnetization. Independ- 
ent studies on the clay mineralogy and organic matter evolution 
remain to be done in the OB. In any case, the use of hysteresis

Patagonia: a key to constrain the timing of rotations during
the breakup of southwestern Gondwana?

Abstract
A paleomagnetic study in Jurassic and Cretaceous rocks from the Can ‹ado¤n Asfalto basin, central Patagonia,
indicates the occurrence of about 25^30‡ clockwise rotation in Upper Jurassic^lowermost Cretaceous rocks, whereas the
overlying mid-Cretaceous rocks do not show evidence of rotation. This constrains the tectonic rotation to be related to
a major regional unconformity in Patagonia, which in turn seems to be close in time with the early opening of the South
Atlantic Ocean. The sense and probably the timing of this rotation are similar to those of other paleomagnetically
detected rotations in different areas of southwestern Gondwana, suggesting a possible relationship between these and
major tectonic processes related with fragmentation of the supercontinent. On the other hand, the mid-Cretaceous rocks
in the region yield a paleopole located at Lat. 87‡ South, Long. 159‡ East, A95 = 3.8‡. This pole position is consistent
with coeval high-quality paleopoles of other plates when transferred to South American coordinates, implying it is an
accurate determination of the Aptian (circa 116 Ma) geomagnetic field in South America. ß 2000 Elsevier Science
B.V. All rights reserved.
Keywords: paleomagnetism; Patagonia; tectonics; Mesozoic; Gondwana
1. Introduction
Patagonia was the locus of pervasive extension-
al tectonics during the early stages of Gondwana
breakup [1^4]. Early to Middle Jurassic crustal
stretching was mainly taken up by the develop-
ment of NW^SE trending fault-bound basins
(Fig. 1). This led to a regional basin and range
depositional setting associated with widespread
bimodal volcanism. By the Late Jurassic the areas
a¡ected by normal faulting enlarged and became
interconnected at the time that the volcanic activ-
ity diminished. Most normal faulting ceased by
the time that oceanic crust began to form in the
southern South Atlantic (i.e. earliest Cretaceous).

A regional unconformity between the Upper Ju-
rassic^Neocomian and the mid-Cretaceous is a
conspicuous feature throughout the region. Later,
Cenozoic tectonic inversion locally a¡ected rocks
as young as Lower Tertiary.
Despite its history of crustal instability, paleo-
magnetic results from Jurassic and Cretaceous
rocks in Patagonia have been used to construct
apparent polar wander paths (APWP) for South
America [5^7] without taking into account the
possibility of vertical-axis rotations. In order to
explore the e¡ects of the Jurassic and younger
tectonics on the paleomagnetic record, we per-
formed paleomagnetic sampling in four areas in
the Can‹ado¤n Asfalto basin, central Patagonia.
This region is particularly pertinent for our pur-
poses because its stratigraphy and structure have
been recently re¢ned by ¢eldwork carried out for
oil exploration. Paleomagnetic results from Upper
Jurassic^lower Neocomian rocks in one area in-
dicate the occurrence of a clockwise tectonic ro-
tation in a tens of kilometers-sized crustal block
during the Early Cretaceous, whereas data from
coeval rocks in other areas are inconclusive for
tectonic analysis. This rotation is related to a ma-
jor regional unconformity in Patagonia, and
seems to be close in time with the early opening
of the South Atlantic Ocean. Possible implications
of these results in the framework of western
Gondwana breakup are discussed.
2. Jurassic^Cretaceous evolution of the Can ‹ado¤n
Asfalto basin
The Can‹ado¤n Asfalto basin is located in the
southern part of the North Patagonian Massif
(Fig. 1). When describing its evolution, Figari et
al. [8,9] divided the Mesozoic column into four
major units or megasequences, each representing
di¡erent stages in the development of the rift ba-
sin (Fig. 2). We used this megasequence classi¢-
cation as the stratigraphic guide to carry out the
paleomagnetic work.
The evolution of the Can ‹ado¤n Asfalto basin
started during the Late Triassic^Early Jurassic
with the development of NW^SE-oriented half-
grabens with their depocenters to the SW. The
early depositional record comprises conglomer-
ates and sandstones grouped into the Megase-
quence 0 (MS0). During the Middle Jurassic to
early Late Jurassic, the halfgrabens were ¢lled
by a thick volcaniclastic unit (Lonco Trapial
Formation), followed by black shales and calca-
reous lake deposits with interbedded basaltic
£ows (Lower Can ‹ado¤n Asfalto Formation).
Both these unit are grouped into the Megase-
quence 1 (MS1).
Fault reactivation during latest Jurassic created
room for two depositional cycles which consti-
tute the Upper Jurassic to Neocomian Upper

3. Paleomagnetism
3.1. Sampling
Two hundred thirty six oriented core and block
samples of volcanic and sedimentary rocks were
taken from ten localities, representing four areas
sparsely distributed over a region of more than
5000 km
2 (Fig. 2). Sampled areas were selected
in order to obtain information about the regional
unconformity that separates MS1^MS2 from
MS3. Thus, paleomagnetic data from at least
one locality corresponding to either MS1 or
MS2, and another locality representing MS3,
are available for each area. All sections in sedi-
mentary rocks involved stratigraphic packages
from about 40 to 600 m thick, from which several
¢ne-grained beds were sampled. Typically one
to ¢ve samples were taken from each bed, and
at least 15 samples from each section. This pro-
cedure was followed in order to average out
the paleosecular variation (PSV) within the local-
ity. A similar procedure was followed by sampling
several £ows in volcanic localities. Additional
data of the region that we used in this study
are those reported by Somoza [6] for rocks of
MS3.
Most Jurassic^Neocomian rocks (MS1 and
MS2) are variably tilted throughout the region.
In contrast, most sampled mid-Cretaceous rocks
(MS3) are subhorizontal, being tilted only where
Cenozoic tectonic inversion occurred.
3.1.1. Area 1: Sierra de Pichin ‹anes (Fig. 2b)
All samples of this area belong to basaltic £ows
of the Lower Can‹ado¤n Asfalto Formation (MS1).
The outcrops are continuous on both sides of the
Chubut River (Fig. 2c), dipping 25‡ towards the
southwest. A 200 m thick section was sampled in
two locations (CA and BA sections, 54 samples)
along the west side of the river. Samples in the
northern location (BA) were obtained above and
below a 10 m thick limestone bed which is inter-
calated in the middle part of the basaltic section.
Only the lower levels of the section were sampled
in the southern location (CA). An additional lo-
cation (PCH section, 10 samples) was sampled in
a 30 m thick section located on the eastern side of
the river. The MS3 is represented by the LP local-
ities from Los Adobes and Cerro Barcino Forma-
tions whose results have been previously reported
by Somoza [6]. These mid-Cretaceous rocks crop
out in the eastern side of the Sierra de Lonco
Trapial (Fig. 2), being variably tilted during Ce-
nozoic tectonic inversion. Farther to the east they
are subhorizontal, overlying the basaltic outcrops
in the western margin of the Chubut River (Fig.
2a).
3.1.2. Area 2: Gorro Frigio depocenter (Fig. 2b)
Outcrops of the Upper Can ‹ado¤n Asfalto For-
mation (MS2) are particularly widespread in this
area (Fig. 2a). We took samples (CX location, 48
samples) in a thick section of this unit, where
strata dip about 25‡ to the northwest. Thirty-
nine mudstones to ¢ne-grained sandstones sam-
ples correspond to the upper sedimentary cycle,
whereas the remaining nine samples are mud-
stones of the lower cycle. Farther to the northwest
we took 28 samples (K location, Fig. 2a) in an-
other section of the upper sedimentary cycle
where strata dip 7‡ towards the northeast. A
few kilometers eastward of the CX section, we
sampled the MS3 (LC section, 18 samples) where
Los Adobes and Cerro Barcino Formations lie
subhorizontal.

3.2. Methods
At least two standard specimens of each sample
were subjected to stepwise demagnetization. Re-
manence measurements were done with either a
three-axis 2G Enterprises cryogenic magnetometer
or a modi¢ed DIGICO spinner magnetometer.
Alternating ¢eld demagnetization used either a
2G600 or a prototype tumbling demagnetizer.
Thermal demagnetization was carried out employ-
ing a Schonstedt TSD-1 furnace. Bulk magnetic
susceptibility was measured after each thermal
step in order to monitor possible magnetic miner-
al changes. Isothermal remanent magnetization
(IRM) was applied to identify the minerals that
carry the magnetization.
Paleomagnetic components observed in the
specimens were determined using principal com-
ponent analysis [10]. A magnetic component was
accepted only if the maximum angular deviation
(MAD) was less than 10‡. A mean direction for
each stratigraphic level was obtained by averaging
magnetic components from specimens of each
sedimentary bed or volcanic £ow. In some cases
this procedure was performed by combining mag-
netic components with demagnetization circles
[11]. The obtained single-stratigraphic-level direc-
tions within each section were averaged using
standard Fisher [12] statistics to obtain section-
mean directions.
Time-averaged virtual geomagnetic poles
(VGP) derived from section-mean directions
were compared with reference paleopoles for sta-
ble South America. As most Mesozoic South
American APWP available in the literature con-
tain paleopoles from Patagonia, we constructed
an alternative set of reference poles by combining
paleomagnetic data of South America (excluding
Patagonia) and other plates. The criteria followed
for paleopole selection as well as the reconstruc-
tion parameters used to transfer the data to South
American coordinates are described in the Appen-
dix.
3.3. Description and interpretation of the results
In this part we describe the paleomagnetic be-
havior of the samples and discuss the origin of the
observed paleomagnetic directions. First we
present and discuss the data from the MS3 in
the entire region. Then, data of the MS2 and
MS1 from each particular area are presented.

3.3.6. Summary
Several of our results are not suitable for tec-
tonic analysis. Paleomagnetic data from several
£ows in a more than 200 thick basaltic section
of MS1 at area 1 failed in averaging out PSV.
Paleomagnetic directions obtained from MS2 at
area 3 suggest the occurrence of a remagnetiza-
tion associated with mid-Cretaceous weathering.
Results from the area 4 have either poor resolu-
tion (MS2 in FSJ section) or evidences of remag-
netization (MS3 in FSK section).
In contrast, the results from MS3 in areas 1, 2,
and 3 suggest that the studied region has acted as
a coherent structural block with respect to verti-
cal-axis deformation since Aptian times. More-
over, the time-averaged paleomagnetic pole from
these rocks of MS3 is concordant with coeval pa-
leopoles of other plates transferred to South
American coordinates, suggesting structural integ-
rity of the region with respect to cratonic South
America since mid-Cretaceous (Fig. 3c).
On the other hand, results from Upper Juras-
sic^Neocomian rocks at area 2 indicate that an
area of nearly 1000 km
2 underwent a clockwise
tectonic rotation of about 25‡ (Fig. 4d). Results
from MS3 in this area constrain the age of this
tectonic rotation to be Early Cretaceous.
4. Discussion
During latest Jurassic to earliest Cretaceous,
Patagonia was a piece of Gondwana subjected
to widespread extension bordered by the evolving
Southern Atlantic rift system to the east, and a
zone of active convergence to the west (Fig. 1).
Our results indicate that Upper Jurassic to lower-
most Cretaceous rocks of the Can ‹ado¤n Asfalto
basin underwent clockwise vertical-axis rotation
prior to deposition of overlying Upper Barre-
mian? to Aptian rocks. This rotation seems to
be related to extensional deformation in central
Patagonia. Although available data do not permit
an estimate of the extent of the zone a¡ected by
rotational deformation, several lines of evidence
suggest it could be greater than the area sampled
in this study.
An important tectonic feature in central Pata-
gonia is the poorly understood Gastre Fault Sys-
tem which was originally described as a NW^SE
left lateral strike^slip system throughout the
studied region [17] (Fig. 1). On the other hand,
Rapela and Pankhurst [18] proposed that this
fault system acted as a dextral shear zone during
the Early to Middle Jurassic. The rotation we
document could be kinematically consistent with
this last proposal, but its timing is di¡erent. At a
greater regional scale, recent interpretations sug-
gest that this fault system is part of a major Ju-
rassic to Early Cretaceous intracontinental dex-
tral-shear zone that also involved the Agulhas^
Falklands Fault zone in the southernmost Atlan-
tic (Fig. 1) [18^21]. However, both the large
amounts of strike^slip motion attributed to the
Gastre Fault System in some of these models as
well as its proposed eastward continuation across
the Argentine continental shelf are di⁄cult to rec-
oncile with the regional geology of Patagonia (e.g.
[22]). Despite uncertainties about the regional ex-
tent and timing of displacement on the Gastre
Fault System, it could have been an important
structure to accommodate extension (or transten-
sion) and associated rotations in a wide region of
Patagonia during the early stages of western
Gondwana breakup.
In recent years, the important role of rotations
(from small crustal blocks to microplates) in ac-
commodating deformation during the breakup of
southwestern Gondwana has been recognized
[21,23^28], although di¡erences in tectonic inter-
pretations indicate a complex history of deforma-
tion. For instance, paleomagnetic results from Ju-
rassic dolerite dykes in the western Falkland
(Malvinas) Islands (Fig. 1) suggest the occurrence
of a large clockwise rotation. Both the mechanism
and the timing of this rotation are disputed (e.g.
[21,25,28]). In particular, Thomson [28] argues for
a Valanginian age of rotation, which implies sim-
ilarity in time with rotation of the Can ‹ado¤nA s -

taceous clockwise rotations older than 110 Ma
also have been found in several microplates of
Western Antarctica [24,26,29].
Although the consistency in sense and timing of
these tectonic rotations is suggestive, we accept
that any possible relationship remains speculative.

Nevertheless, our results suggest that further pa-
leomagnetic work on Jurassic and Cretaceous
rocks in Patagonia could help to better under-
stand the kinematics and timing of deformations
during the early stages of western Gondwana
breakup. On the other hand, our paleomagnetic
results suggest that rotational deformation in cen-
tral Patagonia ceased by the time sea £oor spread-
ing started in the Southern Atlantic. As a conse-
quence, paleomagnetic studies on mid-Cretaceous
and younger rocks from Patagonia could yield a
suitable record of the ancient South American
geomagnetic ¢eld, whereas data from older rocks
should be treated with caution for APWP pur-
poses.
5. Conclusions
Our paleomagnetic results in central Patagonia
provide evidence for about 25^30‡ clockwise rota-
tion in a tens of kilometers sized crustal block
during the Early Cretaceous. Although we can
not resolve unambiguously the relationship with
tectonic rotations detected in other regions of
southwestern Gondwanaland, the available paleo-
magnetic data seem to suggest that clockwise ro-
tations occurred in widely separated areas during
the Early Cretaceous. This encourages to perform
further systematic paleomagnetic and isotopic
studies of Jurassic and Cretaceous rocks in Pata-
gonia. Potential results could provide a better
understanding of deformation during the breakup
of Gondwana.
On the other hand, our paleomagnetic data in-
dicate that mid-Cretaceous and younger rocks
from Patagonia are useful for determination of
the APWP of South America. We obtained an
updated Aptian (circa 116 Ma) paleopole located
at Lat. 87‡ South, Long. 159‡ East, A95 = 3.8‡.

Appendix
Late Jurassic^mid-Cretaceous reference poles for
South America
Although the ages of the sampled rocks in this
study span from Middle Jurassic to mid-Creta-
ceous, the older ones (MS1) did not give suitable
information for tectonic analysis (see 3.3.5). Thus,
for our purposes we determined only reference
poles spanning from Late Jurassic to mid-Creta-
ceous. To do this, we compiled paleomagnetic
data from di¡erent continents and determined
three reference poles with mean-ages at 145 þ 5,
130 þ 5, and 115 þ 5 Ma. The two older paleopoles
are useful for their comparison with data from
MS2, whereas the younger paleopole is appropri-
ate for analyzing MS3 results. The time-scale used
is that of Gradstein et al. [30].
Methods and results
Requisites for paleopole selection and accep-
tance were: (1) well de¢ned magnetizations and
evidence supporting successful averaging of the
PSV; (2) the age of the magnetization to be ac-
ceptably constrained; (3) no unresolved structural
complications and reasonable structural coher-
ence of sampled region with the craton. Rather
than a large data set including paleopoles of lesser
quality, we preferred working with a small num-
ber of high quality poles derived from multiple
plates, whenever possible. This procedure was
useful to diminish any possible bias produced
by a particular plate-reconstruction, although it
could not be applied for all the time-intervals
in this study. Table 3 lists the selected paleo-
poles.
Many ¢nite rotation parameters between plates
have been re¢ned in recent years by better satel-
lite-derived gravity ¢eld and additional magnetic
data. We used some of these updated reconstruc-

transferred. Some additional considerations about

low. We consider that the obtained reference
poles (Table 5) satisfactorily represent the ancient
magnetic ¢eld in South America.

ABSTRACT
 
We report paleomagnetic and geochronologic results
from two Late Proterozoic mafic dikes exposed in Archean-
cored uplifts from northwestern Wyoming and 
 
40
 
Ar/
 
39
 
Ar re-
sults from a gabbro sill that intrudes lower sedimentary strata
of the Belt Supergroup in western Montana. The gabbro sill
yields a 
 
40
 
Ar/
 
39
 
Ar plateau date of 776 Ma that records the
age of sill emplacement during Late Proterozoic time. Paleo-
magnetic results from the mafic dike at Mount Moran, Teton
Range, and the Christmas Lake dike, Beartooth Mountains,
indicate magnetizations with similar directions and virtual
geomagnetic poles (VGP’s), which we interpret to be prima-
ry thermoremanent magnetizations acquired during dike em-
placement and cooling. A hornblende from the Christmas
Lake dike yields a 
 
40
 
Ar/
 
39
 
Ar plateau date of 774 Ma, which
is statistically identical to that of the gabbro sill from western
Montana. The similarity of the dike site-mean directions and
VGP’s suggest that their magnetizations are of similar age.
 
40
 
Ar/
 
39
 
Ar results from a hornblende-pyroxene concentrate
from the Mount Moran dike are discordant and contain ex-
cess 
 
40
 
Ar; a precise estimate of the age of this sample is not
possible given our data, but the paleomagnetic and geochro-
nologic results suggest that it is of Late Proterozoic age, and
not Middle Proterozoic as previously argued. The VGP’s
from the Mount Moran and Christmas Lake dikes are similar
to those of identical age from southwestern Montana and
northern and western Canada. These mafic dikes and sills are
part of a regional magmatic event that affected the western
part of the Laurentian craton at about 780 Ma.

INTRODUCTION
 
Swarms of Proterozoic mafic sheets are a common fea-
ture of many uplifts of Wyoming and western Montana. In the
basement-cored uplifts of the Archean Wyoming province,
they are represented by dikes of diverse trend, composition,
and apparent age. Reported dike ages from the basement up-
lifts range from about 2.6 Ga to 0.75 Ga, with apparent age
maxima at 2.56 Ga, 2.2–2.0 Ga, 1.45 Ga, 1.3(?) Ga, 1.2 Ga,
and 0.75 Ga (Snyder and others, 1989; Baadsgaard and Muel-
ler, 1973; Wooden and others, 1978). In western Montana,
mafic intrusions are generally found as sills that intrude sed-
imentary strata of the Middle Proterozoic Belt Supergroup
and have apparent ages of 1.45–1.38 Ga and 0.75 Ga. Despite
their wide occurrence and the recognition that mafic dike and
sill swarms may be sensitive recorders of fundamental geo-
logic and geodynamic processes (Halls, 1982), correlation of
dike and sills of similar age and geochemical compositions
between uplifts of western Montana and Wyoming has been
limited in scope and is problematic. Although dikes in some
individual uplifts have been extensively studied, at present
there is little detailed information regarding the regional dis-
tribution of sheets of particular age groups or their geochem-
ical characteristics. Hence, the tectonic and geodynamic
significance of many swarms is poorly understood.
It has long been recognized that the natural remanent
magnetization (NRM) acquired by mafic dikes during cool-
ing can be a reliable recorder of the geomagnetic field and can
be geologically stable throughout billions of years. These
properties make paleomagnetism an extremely powerful tool
for correlating dikes of individual swarms over wide areas
(Buchan and Halls, 1990). Recent advances in geochrono-
logic dating methods, including the recognition that mafic
dikes can sometimes be dated with great precision by the
U-Pb technique and, in some cases, by the

TETON RANGE
 
The Teton Range of northwestern Wyoming (fig. 1) is a

Cretaceous–early Tertiary) structural block that has been
modified by Pliocene-Recent movement along a zone of ma-

2). Approximately 170 km

is exposed, including complexly deformed gneisses and am-

K-Ar dates from the Mount Moran dike were reported
by Reed and Zartman (1973) and gave apparent ages of 775
Ma for a whole-rock sample from a chilled margin and 583
Ma and 396 Ma for plagioclase from near the dike center.
Due to the discordance between the dates and the recognition
that K-Ar dates may be spurious due to the loss or gain of
 
40
 
Ar, Reed and Zartman (1973) dated hornblende and biotite
from several basement rocks collected in a traverse perpen-
dicular to the dike contact. Their objective was to date dike
emplacement by partial to complete resetting of the host
rocks adjacent to the dike contact. They found that horn-
blendes, regardless of proximity to the dike contact, gave
dates of 2,800 to 2,650 Ma, which closely approximates the
inferred age of regional metamorphism of the basement
rocks. Biotite dates from three samples gave apparent ages of

dike. Reed and Zartman (1973) argued that the closest bi-
otite, located 1.5 m from the 30-m-thick dike, should have
been elevated to temperatures sufficient to cause partial to
complete resetting of its K-Ar age. They concluded that the
minimum age for the Moran dike was 1,450 Ma and that
younger dates were unreliable.
Paleomagnetic samples for this study were collected
from a shoulder east of the main face of Mount Moran at an
elevation of about 2,750 m (fig. 2).
 
BEARTOOTH MOUNTAINS
 
The Archean crystalline basement of the Beartooth
Mountains of south-central Montana and northwestern Wy-
oming (fig. 1) hosts an extensive array of mafic dikes that
trend generally northwest; some north- and northeast-trend-
ing dikes are also present (Prinz, 1964) (fig. 3). Using
geochemical criteria, Mueller and Rogers (1973) identified
at least four geochemical groups, based primarily on varia-
tions in TiO
 
2

BELT SUPERGROUP
 
Mafic sills are common in lower sedimentary strata of
the Middle Proterozoic Belt Supergroup, a thick (> 15,000
m) sedimentary prism composed of clastic and carbonate
rocks deposited along the western margin of North America.
They have been called the Purcell sills in the United States
and Moyie sills in Canada, with these terms applied to a wide
range of rocks including diabase, diorite, quartz diorite, gab-
bro, metadiorite and metagabbro (Snyder and others, 1989).
Sills range in thickness from 1 to 500 m, and in some areas,
sills have inflated the Belt stratigraphic section by as much as
30 to 35 percent (Höy, 1989). Typically, sills that intrude the
Belt Supergroup are coarse grained and consist primarily of
plagioclase and clinopyroxene, although some contain sig-
nificant hornblende, biotite, and granophyre. Most are exten-
sively altered due to hydrothermal conditions following
emplacement (i.e., deuteric alteration) or possibly due to sub-
sequent low-grade regional metamorphism and deformation.
Use of the terms “Purcell” or “Moyie” when describ-
ing the sills of the Belt Basin is confusing because no single
identifying physical or geochemical characteristic distin-
guishes a “Purcell” or “Moyie” sill from any other sill and
because these terms have been applied to sills that may
have been emplaced during more than one intrusive event.
Also, the term is sometimes confused with the Middle Prot-
erozoic Purcell lavas (Höy, 1989), which may not be extru-
sive equivalents of any mafic sills. At least two episodes of
sill emplacement (about 1,450–1,420 Ma and 800–780 Ma)
in the Belt Basin have been recognized (Zartman and oth-
ers, 1982; Höy, 1989; Ross and others, 1992), and there
may be others (Ross and others, 1992). For these reasons,
we suggest that use of “Purcell” should be avoided when re-
ferring to any of the numerous mafic sills that intrude sedi-
mentary rocks of the Belt Supergroup.
The gabbro sample dated in this study was collected
from a poorly exposed sill along Wolf Creek, approximately
6 km northwest of Wolf Creek, Mont. (fig. 4). The sill is ap-
proximately 40 m thick and intrudes undivided sedimentary
strata of the Empire and Spokane Formations of the lower
part of the Belt Supergroup (Schmidt, 1978). The sill consists
primarily of fine- to medium-grained plagioclase and cli-
nopyroxene, with minor biotite, hornblende, and granophyre.
Locally, the gabbro is coarse and consists of a highly differ-
entiated granophyre that contains abundant, randomly orient-
ed, dark-brown to black hornblende needles as much as 7 mm
long from which a hornblende concentrate was extracted.
Samples for paleomagnetic analysis were not collected from
this sill because it is located near the frontal margin of the
fold and thrust belt, and paleomagnetic analysis of nearby
Cretaceous volcanic and sedimentary strata have demonstrat-
ed that these rocks have been subjected to local vertical-axis
rotations during Late Cretaceous–early Tertiarycontractional
deformation (Jolly and Sheriff, 1991).

ANALYTICAL METHODS
 
At Mount Moran, we collected seven blocks of the dike,
which were oriented using a Brunton compass. In the labora-
tory, individual samples were obtained from these blocks us-
ing a water-cooled diamond drill bit fitted to a drill press. Ten
samples from the Christmas Lake dike were obtained with a
portable drill; individual samples were oriented using mag-
netic and solar compasses and a clinometer. An additional
five samples were collected at or near the contact of the
Christmas Lake dike in order to conduct a baked contact test
(Everitt and Clegg, 1962) to determine whether the observed
dike remanence was primary, or acquired at some time after
dike emplacement.
The natural remanent magnetization (NRM) of each
sample was measured using either cryogenic or spinner mag-
netometers. Detailed alternating field (AF) demagnetization
was conducted on all specimens and proved effective in iso-
lating the sample characteristic remanent magnetization
(ChRM). Duplicate specimens from a few samples were also
thermally demagnetized using a low-magnetic induction fur-
nace. Demagnetization results were examined using vector
diagrams, stereographic projections, and normalized intensi-
ty decay diagrams. Sample ChRM directions, defined by
three or more colinear points on vector diagrams, were cal-
culated using principal components analysis (PCA) (Kirsch-
vink, 1980); all ChRM directions used in this study had
maximum angular deviation values less than 7
 
°
 
. Site-mean
directions were calculated using statistics from Fisher (1953).

DISCUSSION
Both the Mount Moran dike from the Teton Range and
the Christmas Lake dike from Beartooth Mountains give
similar paleomagnetic directions and VGP’s that plot at low
latitudes in the western Pacific Ocean (fig. 9). The concor-
dance of 
40Ar/39Ar and U-Pb dates from the Christmas Lake
dike indicates that it is Late Proterozoic in age and that its
geochronologic systems have not been disturbed by subse-
quent thermal events. The baked contact test from the Christ-
mas Lake dike, although not conclusive, strongly suggests
that the observed magnetization is a TRM acquired during
cooling following dike emplacement. Because closure tem-
peratures to 
40Ar diffusion for hornblende (i.e., 480 °C to
540°C) overlap unblocking temperatures for magnetite, we
suggest that the 776-Ma age from the hornblende from the
Christmas Lake dike probably closely approximates the age
of remanence acquisition in the dike. Assuming that the
ChRM in the Mount Moran dike is also a TRM acquired dur-
ing dike emplacement and cooling, the similarity in paleo-
magnetic directions and VGP’s from the Mount Moran and
Beartooth dikes strongly suggest that both were emplaced at
about the same time.

southern Tobacco Root Mountains, Harlan (1993) found pa-
leomagnetic and geochronologic evidence for two distinct
episodes of dike emplacement in Middle and Late Protero-
zoic time. Paleomagnetic results from geochemical group-B
dikes (Wooden and others, 1978) gave magnetizations of
northwest declination and shallow negative inclination,
similar to those observed in the Mount Moran and Christ-
mas Lake dikes.

these dikes give apparent ages of 769±7 Ma (2 s), and bi-
otite from host gneiss immediately adjacent to the contact
of a group B dike gave an apparent age of 780 Ma (S.S.
Harlan, unpub. data). Preliminary U-Pb data from zircon
and baddeleyite from these dikes give similar

dates of 782±8 Ma and 785± 8 Ma (S.S. Harlan and W. Pre-
mo, unpub. data). VGP’s from the Mount Moran, Christmas
Lake, and southern Tobacco Root Mountains dikes are
similar to those reported from (1) mafic dikes and sills that
intrude Late Proterozoic strata in the Mackenzie Mountains
of the northern Cordillera in Canada and (2) mafic sills
(Hottah sheets) from the northwestern Canadian shield near
Great Bear Lake (table 2; fig. 9). Both the dikes and sills
from the Mackenzie Mountains and the Hottah sheets of the
northwestern Canadian shield give relatively precise U-Pb
baddeleyite dates of 779 Ma (LeCheminant and Heaman,
1994) that are essentially identical to the 780- to 770-Ma
dates from the Christmas Lake dike, Tobacco Root Moun-
tains dikes, and the gabbro sill exposed near Wolf Creek,
Mont. The similarity of the Mount Moran VGP to VGP’s
from 780- to 770-Ma dikes from elsewhere in Montana and
western North America, and the 
40Ar/39Ar results presented
here, suggests that the age of the Mount Moran dike is Late
Proterozoic in age, and not Middle Proterozoic as argued by
Reed and Zartman (1973). Further isotopic determinations,
possibly using U-Pb technique, are needed to more precise-
ly identify the age of dike emplacement.
On a regional scale, the consistency of VGP’s and iso-
topic dates from dikes and sills from northwestern Wyo-
ming to northern Canada demonstrates the coherence of the
western margin of the North American craton since Late
Proterozoic time and suggests that all the observed

13CONCLUSIONS
magnetizations are primary in origin (Park and others,
1995b). Mafic magmatism at 780–770 Ma appears approxi-
mately synchronous over a broad expanse of western North
America that extends from the Canadian Arctic to north-
western Wyoming, a distance greater than 2,400 km. Using
high-precision U-Pb dates on baddeleyite from mafic dikes
and sills in northern Canada and the Christmas Lake dike in
the Beartooth Mountains, Wyoming, A.N. LeCheminant
(oral commun., 1994) established a composite age of
781+6/–3 Ma for this event and has tentatively termed it
the “gunbarrel igneous event.” Emplacement of a quartz di-
orite plug dated as 778 Ma (U-Pb, zircon) (Jefferson and
Parrish, 1989) and eruption of the coeval Little Dal basalts
in the Mackenzie Mountains (Dud´ as and Lustwerk, 1997)
and mafic volcanic rocks of the Windermere Group of
northeastern Washington (762±44 Ma, Sm-Nd mineral iso-
chron) (Devlin and others, 1988) may be manifestations of
this same event. Identification of 780- to 760-Ma 
40Ar/39Ar
and K-Ar dates on sills from the lower parts of the Belt Su-
pergroup, including the Wolf Creek sill from this study,
suggests that they may be more common than previously
thought, but detailed geochemical and high-precision geo-
chronologic data are necessary to better understand their
distribution. Numerous studies (Link and others, 1993;
Harper and Link, 1986; Elston and McKee, 1982; Christie-
Blick and Levy, 1989; Stewart, 1972) report the presence
of Late Proterozoic mafic intrusive and volcanic rocks to
the south, but whether they are part of this event is unclear
given the paucity of reliable isotopic dates from this region.
The cause of widespread mafic magmatism at 780 to
770 Ma remains enigmatic. LeCheminant and Heaman
(1994) suggest that mafic magmatism was a response to ma-
jor extension accompanying development of a rift margin
along the western margin of the North American craton dur-
ing Late Proterozoic time. Park and others (1995b) argue that
trends from dike subswarms in northwestern Canada and
Wyoming define part of a crudely radial pattern that was
associated with an ancient mantle plume that produced a gi-
ant radiating dike swarm, similar to those of the 1.27-Ga
Mackenzie (LeCheminant and Heaman, 1989) and 0.73-Ga
Franklin (Heaman and others, 1992) magmatic events. The
two hypotheses may not be exclusive, as thermal effects as-
sociated with the mantle plume may have been a precursor
to, or caused, Late Proterozoic rifting. The proposed location
of the plume center is off the present coast of western North
America, and Park and others (1995b) argue that the plume
center and other parts of the radial swarm were severed from
the craton by Late Proterozoic and early Paleozoic rifting
and development of a passive continental margin. The rifted
continental mass(es) that contain the remnants of the radial
dike swarm are unknown but may include parts of east Ant-
arctica and Australia, if parts of these continents lay adjacent
to the western margin of the Laurentian craton at about 800
Ma to form part of the supercontinent Rodinia (Dalziel,
1991; Moores, 1991; Hoffman, 1991; Brookfield, 1993;
Borg and De Paolo, 1994; Powell and others, 1993). Recent-
ly, Park and others (1995b) suggested that the approximately
800-Ma Gairdner dike swarm of western Australia may be
part of the radial dike swarm formed at 780–770 Ma. If cor-
rect, this interpretation and the hypothesis that western Aus-
tralia lay adjacent to the North America continent can be
tested by comparing high-quality paleomagnetic and geo-
chronologic data from this and other studies of Late Protero-
zoic dikes and sheets from western North America with
those from the Gairdner dike swarm.
CONCLUSIONS
40Ar/39Ar isotopic dates from two mafic dikes and a
gabbro sill from northwestern Wyoming and western Mon-
tana yield similar Late Proterozoic dates of about 770 Ma.
The Mount Moran dike from the Teton Range and the Christ-
mas Lake dike from the Beartooth Mountains yield similar

VGP’s that are essentially identical to those from rocks of
similar age elsewhere in Montana and Canada. Together, the
paleomagnetic and geochronologic data from this and other
studies provide evidence for a regional mafic magmatic
event at 780–770 Ma that affected a large area of western
North America. Mafic magmatism may have been a response
to a mafic plume that preceded rifting and breakup of the
North American continent during Late Proterozoic and early
Paleozoic time. The paleomagnetic and geochronologic data
from this and other studies may be useful in testing the valid-
ity of Late Proterozoic continental reconstructions.

Abstract
Bhandari et al. [Bhandari et al., Geophys. Res. Lett. 22 (1995) 433^436; Bhandari et al., Geol. Soc. Am. Spec. Paper
307 (1996) 417^424] reported the discovery of iridium-bearing sediments sandwiched between basalt flows in the Anjar
area (Kutch province, India). They concluded that the signature of the K/T impact had been recorded and that onset of
volcanism in the Deccan traps preceded the K/T boundary, excluding the possibility of a causal connection. This paper
reports complementary analyses of Anjar outcrops by a joint Indo^French team, where we focused on cosmic markers
(iridium and spinels) in the intertrappean sediments and
40Ar/39Ar dating and paleomagnetism of the lava flows.
Anomalous Ir concentrations (up to 0.4 ng/g) are confirmed, with up to three thin and patchy enriched layers which
cannot be traced throughout the exposed sections. Despite careful search, no Ni-rich spinels were found. Eight basalt
samples provided
40Ar/39Ar results, four on plagioclase bulk samples, four on whole rocks. Spectra for whole rocks all
indicate some amount of disturbance, and ages based on plagioclase bulk samples seem to be consistently more reliable
[Hofmann et al., Earth Planet. Sci. Lett. 180 (2000) 13^28]. The three flows underlying the Ir-bearing sediments are
dated at V66.5 Ma, and two overlying flows at V65 Ma. Magnetic analyses (both thermal and by alternating fields)
uncovered clear reversed primary components in the upper flows, and more disturbed normal components in the lower
flows, with evidence for an additional reversed component. There are reports [Bajpai, Geol. Soc. India Mem. 37 (1996)
313^319; Bajpai, J. Geol. Soc. London 157 (2000) 257^260] that the intertrappean sediments contain uppermost
Maastrichtian dinosaur and ostracod remains above the uppermost Ir-bearing level, and may not be mechanically
disturbed. We propose the following scenario to interpret these multiple field and analytical observations. Deccan trap
volcanism started within uppermost Maastrichtian normal chron C30N at V66.5^67 Ma in the Anjar area. Volcanism
then stopped at least locally, and lacustrine sediments were deposited over a period that could be in the order of 1^2
Ma. The K/T bolide impact was recorded as a deposit of Ir, and possibly (though not necessarily) spinels. Volcanism

1. Introduction
In the two decades following the discovery of
an iridium layer in sedimentary sections contain-
ing the Cretaceous^Tertiary boundary [9], two
main scenarios, one involving an asteroid or com-
etary impact, the other a massive volcanic erup-
tion, have been suggested as the cause of the mass
extinction. Work on both the Deccan traps of
India and the Chicxulub impact crater in Mexico
has con¢rmed that both ‘catastrophic’ events ac-
tually occurred at the same time, though on di¡er-
ent time scales, and must be taken into account in
any quantitative model of the evolutionary turn-
over (for overviews see, for example, [6,10]).
A major step in establishing the occurrence and
relative timings of impact and volcanism has been
the identi¢cation by Bhandari et al. [1,2] of an
iridium-enriched layer in intertrappean sediments
within the thin series of Deccan £ows in the Anjar
area (Kutch province, western India). Bhandari et
al. [1] measured concentrations of Ir and Os 15
times higher than in adjacent sediments and two
orders of magnitude higher than the underlying
basalts. Based on chemical and stratigraphic cri-
teria, they concluded that a limonite layer did
correspond to the fallout ejecta of the KTB bolide
impact. They also concluded that volcanism was
already active when the impact occurred and
therefore could not have been triggered by it.
These results were deemed most important and
a joint Indo^French team of geochemists and geo-
physicists returned to the Anjar region in April
1995 for complementary sampling.
40Ar/39Ar dat-

3. Cosmic markers
The purpose of this part of the study was to
identify Ni-rich spinel, a mineral derived from the
oxidation of meteoritic material layer [15] which is
usually found in the K/T boundary clay layer [16^
19]. The multiple Ir-rich levels identi¢ed in Anjar
[1] raise questions about the conditions of sedi-
mentation and/or about the possible occurrence
of multiple impacts at the end of the Cretaceous.
The identi¢cation of Ni-rich spinel crystals in one
or several of the Anjar Ir levels would help to
understand the formation conditions of this un-
usual section. We selected those samples most en-
riched in Ir. All samples with concentrations high-
er than 0.1 ng g
31 were then analysed for Ni-rich
spinel.

3.1. Iridium
Iridium concentrations were measured by in-
strumental neutron activation analysis of whole
rock samples. Samples, about 100 mg each,
housed and sealed in pure silica vials, were irra-
diated for 3^4 h in the 10
14 nc m 32 s31 neutron
beam of the Osiris reactor (Pierre Su«e Laboratory,
Saclay). Ir was counted for a few hours with a
coincidence spectrometer (see [20,21] for a de-
scription of the method) detecting the coincidence
of 316^468 keV Q-ray lines resulting from the ra-
dioactive decay of
192Ir. Two Ir standards were
used: fragments ( V0.050 mg) of the Negrillo
iron meteorite (a very homogeneous meteorite
calibrated in the Orsay-Gif laboratory) and small
pieces ( w0.2 mg) of an Ir^Al alloy with 5.2 ppm
of Ir. The detection limit is around 25 pg g 31.
Two basalt samples from £ows F3 and F4 were
analysed with slightly improved sensitivity.
Data from Anjar 1a are plotted on Fig. 2a. One
can ¢rst note that the background value is high,
around 50^100 pg g 31. Three small maxima are
observed in chocolate-coloured limonitic layers 1,
2 bis and 3. It is worth noting that the highest
concentrations are found in the samples provided
by N.B. In Anjar Ib (Fig. 2b), we ¢nd a ¢rst
maximum 10 cm below the base of the chert
bed, possibly the horizontal equivalent of the ¢rst
chocolate-coloured layer of Anjar Ia (but here the
colour is light grey). The rust-coloured layer (35
cm below the base of the chert bed) also shows a
very small overconcentration. The correspondence
with layers 2, 2 bis or 3 is uncertain. In Anjar II
(Fig. 2c), two samples have low but signi¢cant Ir
concentrations. In the basalt samples of £ows F3
and F4, Ir concentrations are lower than 25 pg
g
31.
Our data con¢rm the existence of several Ir-
enriched levels in the intertrappean layers [1].
We note however that these levels cannot be re-
garded as continuous horizons: they are not well
de¢ned and locally display some splitting. Such
small scale heterogeneities are likely to explain
the di¡erences between the concentrations found
in our samples (LSCE samples) and in those pre-
viously collected by N. Bhandari (PRL samples).
PRL samples were especially selected for their
dark chocolate colour. In contrast, LSCE samples
were neither selected in the ¢eld nor in the labo-
ratory. They are bulk samples representing some
horizontal average of the so-called chocolate
layers. In addition they might have been contami-
nated by the material from adjacent layers. The
di¡erences between concentrations in PRL sam-
ples analyzed at PRL, on one hand, and at
LSCE, on the other, are probably due to a similar
reason. PRL samples analyzed at LSCE were col-
lected by PRL but ground and homogenized at
LSCE without preselection for their dark colour.
Under such conditions it is not surprising that the
measured Ir concentrations in PRL samples ana-
lyzed at LSCE (for instance: 0.9 ng/g in the sec-
ond chocolate layer) are higher than in LSCE
samples (0.4 ng/g in the same layer), and that
the Ir concentrations in PRL samples appear still
higher when prepared and analyzed at PRL (1.2^
1.6 ng/g). The multiple Ir-enriched levels together
with the strong horizontal di¡erences between
Anjar 1a and Anjar 1b, separated by only a few
meters, suggest that sediments were severely re-
worked.
3.2. Ni-rich spinel
Ni-rich spinel is a strongly magnetic mineral,
which can be easily extracted from a liquid phase
with an electro-magnet. Each sample was selected
from well-ground and homogenised sediment. The
sample weights were in the range 500^1000 mg.
After dissolution of the carbonate fraction, using
10% hydrochloric acid, the residue was circulated
in a closed-loop funnel, activated by a peristaltic
pump. Magnetic particles were collected in a glass
tube placed in the gap of a magnetic separator.
The separator was run for 20^30 min to ensure
that all magnetic particles would be collected. The
funnel was then rinsed with water. The magnetic
separator was switched o¡ and the particles ar-
rested in the magnet gap were washed out with
alcohol and recovered on a 0.4 Wm Nucleopore
¢lter. The collection e⁄ciency of the system for
magnetic particles such as Ni-rich spinel was high-
er then 95%. Crystals larger than 1 Wm were
counted and sorted according to size and compo-
sition, using a JEOL 840 scanning electron micro-

scope coupled to a PGT X-ray energy dispersive
spectrometer. An automatic routine selects par-

cording to speci¢c chemical composition criteria
(NiO concentration must be higher than 1% and
TiO

Among thousands of terrestrial spinel crystals,
we did not ¢nd any crystal bearing the character-

The most likely explanation for the high iridi-
um concentrations observed in the Anjar inter-
trappean sediments is that they are in some way

That these sediments do correspond to the bound-
ary and are in place [1,2] would seem to be in
agreement with earlier reports that the last dino-
saur remains occur below the sediments. The local
existence of multiple Ir-rich levels is an important
observation which does not necessarily imply that
multiple collisional events occurred at the K/T
boundary: the observed multiplicity could indeed
have resulted from redeposition e¡ects.
Bajpai [4] uncovered fossiliferous sediments
from fresh excavations near the original iridium
site, yielding ‘abundant dinosaur (ornithoid) egg-
shells identical to those found between the middle
and upper iridium levels’, yet above the upper-
most iridium level. However, correlation between
his section and our section has not been estab-
lished. More recently, Bajpai and Prasad [5]
have described the occurrence of theropod egg-
shell fragments together with late Cretaceous os-
tracods above the upper iridium level. Moreover,
they note the absence of any exclusively Paleocene
taxa, and believe that there was only minor later
mechanical reworking. This would place all of the
Ir-bearing sediments within the uppermost Maas-
trichtian, prior to but not at K/T time.
The absence of Ni-rich spinel suggests that the
lowermost K/T clay layer is not present at Anjar.
This is not necessarily surprising in view of the
lines of evidence which indicate that this section
may be disturbed and probably incomplete (viz.
the multiple and relatively low Ir anomalies, as far
as K/T anomalies go, strong horizontal variations
in the stratigraphical extent of the geological
units, and possibly the paleontological observa-
tions of [4,5]). The absence of spinels at Stevns
Klint (Denmark), a section where a hiatus might
exist at the top of the Cretaceous [24,25], has been
noted. We must keep in mind that K/T spinel
crystals, unlike Ir, are not uniformly distributed
at a global scale. In several continuous K/T sites,
Ni-rich spinel crystals are rare (for instance at
Mimbral in Mexico [26]). Finding this mineral in
the Anjar intertrap would have ¢rmly established
a causal link between the Ir anomalies and the K/
T event but the absence of this mineral leaves the
question open.
The Ir data do suggest that the Anjar intertrap
contains some imprint of the K/T boundary
event, since such anomalous concentrations with-
in uppermost Maastrichtian to K/T sediments are
unlikely to be due to terrestrial processes and are
believed to provide evidence for the impact. Be-
cause the observations of Bajpai and Prasad [5]
argue against signi¢cant mechanical reworking, a
likely explanation is that the observed lacustrine
sediments were indeed entirely emplaced within
the uppermost Maastrichtian, prior to K/T time,
that the impact signatures were deposited on top
of those, and that further chemical and £uid alter-
ation, most likely following emplacement of the
F4 £ow, led to downward redistribution of the
iridium, which became enriched at several distinct
levels and locations in a heterogeneous, nonuni-
form fashion. This interpretation is consistent

The interpretation of the paleomagnetic data
that we obtain from the Kutch region is di⁄cult
for two reasons. One is due to the lack of good
stratigraphic constraints in the area. As a conse-
quence, the chronology of basaltic £ows proposed
by Ghevariya [14] could, as already pointed out,
in part be erroneous (see in particular the di¡erent

two very distinct types of paleomagnetic behav-

to distinguish two groups of sites, which could
have erupted at di¡erent times: these two groups
indeed constitute, respectively, the lower and
upper parts of the sequence, separated by the iri-
dium-bearing sediments. The second di⁄culty is
due to the paleomagnetic behaviour observed in
several sites. Whereas those sites from the upper
part of the sequence are clearly of reversed mag-
netic polarity (assuming of course that the mag-
netisation was acquired during trap emplacement,
which is supported by magnetic analyses), the
sites from the lower part of the sequence yield
two components with opposite polarities. The ¢rst
has normal polarity and is isolated by AF demag-
netisation; it is likely carried by magnetite. The
second component with reversed polarity has a
high blocking temperature range above 560‡C
and could be carried by magnetite, maghemite
or possibly hematite. If the component with re-
versed polarity is carried by maghemite or hema-
tite, we propose that it was acquired due to alter-
ation, probably linked with emplacement of the
overlying reversed £ows, after the original compo-
nent with normal polarity carried by magnetite.
Following this scheme, the lower part of the se-
quence would have a ‘primary’ normal polarity
and the upper part of the sequence a ‘primary’
reversed polarity. The change in polarity would
then coincide with the intertrappean sediments,
between £ows F3 and F4, containing the Ir-en-
riched layers. Site AJ12, located in these sedi-
ments below the Ir layer, apparently has a normal
polarity, which may agree with the polarity of the
underlying lava £ows, but then cannot be of K/T
age (in agreement with the paleontological obser-
vations of [4,5]). Site AJ13 unfortunately does not
provide any reliable paleomagnetic results, which
could have better constrained the link between the
Ir layers and the K/T boundary. But, again, we

7. Conclusion
In conclusion, pending further detailed geolog-
ical ¢eldwork, most notably on the validity of the
Kutch stratigraphy [12,14], we believe that the
following scenario, though certainly non-unique,
is the simplest one ¢tting available observations,
including the most recent described in the present
paper.
An early phase of Deccan trap volcanism oc-
curred near 66.5^67 Ma (F1, F2, F3), most likely
within magnetic normal chron C30N [27] in the
Kutch area. This is on the early side compared to
ages found in the main part of the province, no-
tably along the thick Mahabaleshwar section
[3,7,8], though it is consistent with the idea that
volcanism did not start prior to C30N. Note that
this may have involved only a very small volume
of lava. Volcanism would have stopped locally in
Kutch for 1 to 2 Ma, when uppermost Maas-
trichtian lacustrine sediments were deposited.
These sediments, which have apparently not
been signi¢cantly reworked mechanically [4,5],
bear witness to the K/T impact (within C29R) in
the form of anomalous but redistributed iridium
concentrations, but with no other cosmic marker
such as Ni-rich spinels. Shortly following this, and
still within chron C29R, volcanism resumed in
Kutch as witnessed by a series of reversed £ows

near 65 Ma in age (F4, F6, F8). At that time, the
underlying normal £ows su¡ered some amount of
reversed remagnetisation and the sediments were
altered: most notably, the iridium from the
topmost sediments was redistributed, probably
through £uid £ow, in the layers below. Evidence
for minor later volcanism is attested by a normal
crosscutting dyke (F5); the last £ow (F9) at
61 þ 1.6 Ma has a very perturbed spectrum and
a large uncertainty and is of little value [11].
This scenario does not contradict the occurrence
of Deccan trap volcanism within a series of three
chrons (C30N, C29R and C29N [3,6^8]), with
most of the volume erupted within a period of
less than 1 Ma (much of this in reversed chron
C29R which contains the K/T boundary). The
Kutch sequence provides evidence for minor (?)
volumes at an early time (up to 67 Ma). But the
image of regular long lasting volcanism is not
supported (see [3]). The main ¢nding of Bhandari
et al. [1] that Deccan volcanism and K/T bolide
impact were both recorded in India, and could be
shown to have occurred at the same general time
(though not the same time scales), without any
causal connection, is basically vindicated. In clos-
ing, we should recall the di⁄culties encountered
in obtaining accurate mapping, stratigraphic
placement, reliable age determinations or identi¢-
cation of primary paleomagnetic components in
several £ows. There is therefore ample room for
further work on these fascinating outcrops.

sequences studied are all well dated biostratigraphically and have undergone only very minor 
deformation, mainly during the late Carboniferous, and extremely low grades of 
metamorphism (anchizone or less). After stepwise thermal demagnetisation of samples and 
principal component analysis of the data, up to two paleomagnetic directions can be clearly 
identified after removal of a present-day magnetic overprint. The first component (labeled 
B) is identified only in samples from the CCR with intermediate unblocking temperature 
spectra (300ø-400øC). An overall mean direction of 1870/-03 ø, semi angle of cone of 95% 
confidence a9s=9.0 ø, and precision parameter k =- 43.1 in situ, and 195ø/03 ø a95=24.4 ø, and 
k =- 7.1 (51 samples at seven sites) after bedding correction is obtained for B. The exact age 
of this secondary component is uncertain, but when compared to published paleomagnetic 
data, a late Carboniferous to Early Triassic age could be inferred. A stable endpoint direction 
(labeled C) can be identified between 400 ø and 600øC in samples from both regions. For the 
CCR it is southwesterly directed with intermediate inclination values in situ, and yields a 
mean direction of 2080/48 ø, a9 = 12.8 ø and k=-28.4 (six sites) after bedding correction. It 
passes the fold test, is considered to be primary in origin, and is thus indicative of the Siluro- 
Devonian paleofield direction in the CCR. In the Pyrenean samples the C direction is 
northwesterly directed in situ, with a mean direction of 240ø/51 o, a9=6.5 o and k=-86.5 
(seven sites) after bedding correction. Although there is a clear improvement in grouping of 
these site mean directions, this is not significant at the 95% level of confidence. Combining 
the site mean directions obtained for component C from both regions yields an overall mean 
direction of 224ø/51 ø, a9=8.5 ø and k=-24.6 (13 sites) after bedding correction. The 
improvement in grouping is significant at the 99% level of confidence at 90% unfolding, 
reinforcing the interpretation that this is a primary magnetisation. Adopting the reversed 
polarity option, the inclination value obtained translates into paleolatitudes of 30øS, placing 
NE Spain in the same latitudinal belt as the Armorican Massif and the Barrandian terrane of 
the Bohemian Massif (i.e., the Armorican Terrane Assemblage) in latest Silurian/earliest 
Devonian times. 
1. Introduction 
Pre-Mesozoic geology of the Iberian Peninsula is very 
complex, and a number of different tectonostratigraphic zones 
have been defined (Figure 1), namely, the Cantabrian Zone, 
West-Asturian-Leonese Zone, Central Iberian Zone, and the 
Ossa Morena and South Portuguese Zones. The South 
Portuguese Zone is clearly an exotic terrane which accreted 
onto Iberia in early Carboniferous times [Silva et al., 1990; 
Quesada et al., 1991 ]. Tectonic affinities of the Ossa Morena 
Zone, southern Spain, are more equivocal. On the basis of

To date, most paleomagnetic studies of the Iberian Terrane 
have concentrated on the Cantabrian Arc of northern Spain. 
Although no primary magnetisations have yet been recogni- 
zed in these sequences, both geological and paleomagnetic 
evidence suggest that oroclinal bending of this arc occurred 
during the closing stages of the Variscan orogeny, possibly 
even into the Triassic [Franke, 1989; Matte, 1991; Quesada 
et al., 1991; Hirt et al., 1992; Ries and Shackleton, 1976; 
Ziegler, 1990; Pars et al., 1996]. Paleomagnetic results 
available from elsewhere in the Iberian Massif are from Early 
Ordovician age sequences from northern Spain (Cabo de 
Perias [Perroud, 1983]) and central Portugal (Bu9aco red beds 
[Perroud and Bonhomrnet, 1981 ]). Although neither of these 
results are of particularly high quality (both have poor age 
constrains, and the demagnetisation and analytical techni- 
ques are not up to modem standards), they indicate high 
southerly paleolatitudes, as would be expected from the 
geological record. Perroud et al. [1991] published paleo- 
magnetic results from Siluro-Devonian age sequences from 
the Almaden in central Spain. These data, however, have 
subsequently been shown to represent remagnetisation 
directions [Pars and Van der Voo, 1992]. The only other 
results available are those of Perroud and Bonhomrnet [ 1984] 
from Late Silurian age rocks of the San Pedro region. These 
data indicate fairly shallow paleolatitudes (-20øS); the age of 
magnetisation, however, is only rather loosely controlled and, 
as stated by the original authors, could have been acquired 
any time between Late Silurian and mid-Carboniferous times. 
Detailed stratigraphic correlation between many of the 
Paleozoic terranes now incorporated within the Alpine fold 
belt and along the southern margin of Europe is particularly 
difficult due to the often high degree of deformation and 
metamorphism. Paleozoic sequences in the eastern Pyrenees 
and Catalan Coastal Ranges (CCR) are further complicated ,

there are many faunal similarities between the various 
Paleozoic terranes now located along the southern margin of 
Europe, i.e., the Montagne Noire, Massif de Mouthoumet, the 
Northern Greywacke Zone (northern Alps), and the Carnic 
Alps. Facies studies suggest that from Ordovician until at 
least mid-Devonian times, deposition in these regions took 
place in a passive margin environment, with a stable hinter- 
land to the south and a deepening basin located to the north 
[Echtler, 1990; Feist et al., 1994; Julivert et al., 1987; Matte, 
1991; Heinisch et al., 1987; Quesada et al., 1991]. Fur- 
thermore, the Devonian pelagic nodular limestone facies 
(Griotte facies) which are typical for the Pyrenees and the 
Montagne Noire are in marked contrast to the general shallow 
water shelly carbonates found in the Iberian and Armorican 
Massifs [Julivert et al., 1987]. These differences are strong 
enough to suggest a separate facies province. Faunal 
assemblages from the Cantabrian region, Catalunya, and the 
Pyrenees are also appreciably different from other regions of 
the Ibero-Armorican Arc; thus the Paleozoic sequences in 
northeastern Spain and southern France may have been 
independent of the Iberian terrane, possibly forming part of 
an indentor block which caused bending of the Ibero-Armori- 
can Arc in late Variscan times [Riding, 1974; Robardet and 
Guiterrez-Marco, 1990]. Paleogeographic affinities, however, 
are difficult to deduce from the geological record alone, and 
it remains unclear if the Catalan Coastal Ranges and the Axial 
Zone of the Pyrenees (here collectively termed the Catalan 
Terrane) were part of the Iberian Massif in the early Paleozoic, 
if they formed an independent microplate, if they formed part 
of the Armorican Terrane Assemblage, or if they remained 
adjacent to the northern margin of Gondwana. In addressing 
these questions, a detailed paleomagnetic study of Siluro- 
Devonian boundary rocks from the Catalan terrane has been 
carried out. 
2. Local Geology and Paleomagnetic Sampling 
The oldest exposed sediments of the CCR and the eastern 
Pyrenees, NE Spain, are generally classed together as 
Cambro-Ordovician in age (Figure 1), and comprise a monoto- 
nous sequence of greywackes, sandstones, and phyllites 
with minor limestone horizons. The Silurian is represented by 
sequences of black graptolite shales, ubiquitous throughout 
Europe, which often acted as major d6collement horizons due 
to ductility contrast during Variscan deformation in the 
Pyrenees. These sediments are in turn overlain by a continu- 
ous sequence of Devonian through to early Carboniferous 
limestones and calcareous shales. The main phase of 
deformation in both regions was in the late Carboniferous, 
and the folded Paleozoic sequences are unconformably 
overlain by Westphalian to Stephanian age volcanic and 
sedimentary rocks. In general, the Variscan structures in 
these regions show little evidence for pervasive Alpine 
deformation. 
Although Paleozoic rocks are fairly extensively exposed in 
the CCR (Figure 1), they tend to be rather highly deformed 
and metamorphosed such that Cambrian to Lower Silurian 
rocks are too highly metamorphosed and deformed to be 
suitable for paleomagnetic research. Upper Silurian to mid- 
Carboniferous sediments, although poorly exposed, have 
undergone, at most, anchizone metamorphism and were only 
very gently folded during the mid Upper Carboniferous 
(Westphalian) deformation. Upper Silurian and Lower 
Devonian sequences are exposed in a working quarry at 
Santa Creu d'Olorda, near Barcelona, where two formations 
can be recognized. The lower formation, dated as Upper 
Ludlovian to Lower Lochkovian (conodont stratigraphy), 
comprises massive nodular limestones, whilst the upper 
formation (Lochkovian to Emsian graptolite zones) consists 
of alternating marls and limestones with pelagic and 
hemipelagic faunas [Garcia-L6pez et al., 1990]. Samples were 
collected from seven sites in the Santa Creu d'Olorda quarry, 
covering a stratigraphic interval from the lower Pridolian 
carbonate sequences through to the Lockhovian marly 
limestones with a stratigraphic thickness of some 200 m. 
In the eastern Pyrenees, Paleozoic sediments and basement 
rocks, which were uplifted during the Tertiary, are now 
exposed extensively in the Axial Zone. Although one of the 
most pronounced characteristics of these sequences are their 
high-temperature/low-pressure metamorphism, in the 
southern border of the Axial Zone metamorphic grades are 
much lower, in places reaching, at most, only 
anchimetamorphism [Zwart, 1986]. Furthermore, the higher 
stratigraphic levels in general have undergone much less 
deformation and lower grades of metamorphism, and the 
Devonian to Carboniferous sediments have not undergone 
any significant tectonic burial. The Silurian is again 
represented by graptolite shales, overlain by a complete 
sequence of Devonian through to early Carboniferous 
carbonates. There is no evidence for any deformation event 
prior to the late Carboniferous, and Westphalian D to 
Stephanian age sediments unconformably overlie the older 
folded sequences. In general, Tertiary deformation and 
metamorphic overprinting of the basement is only very weak 
and confined to major fault zones [Wickham and Oxburgh, 
1986]. Devonian age sediments are very well preserved in the 
Axial Zone, and a number of faunal studies, in particular 
conodont biostratigraphy, provide rather precise relative age 
constraints. Earliest Devonian outcrops are extremely limited, 
and sampling was concentrated near the village of Ba6n, 
southwest of La Seu d'Urgell (Figure 1). These rocks 
comprise dark grey, medium bedded limestones and shales of 
the Gedinnian (Lochkovian) age Rueda Formation (Sierra 
Negra subfacies). Samples were collected from nine sites (72 
samples) over a stratigraphic thickness of some 150 m and 
were subjected to detailed thermal demagnetisation 
experiments. 
All samples were collected using a portable petrol-driven 
drill and oriented in the field using Sun and/or magnetic 
compasses. Samples were then stepwise thermally de- 
magnetised, and magnetisations were measured using a 2G 
cryogenic magnetometer. Results were analyzed using 
principal component analysis with orthogonal [Zijderveld, 
1967] and stereographic projection of the data. Fisher [ 1953] 
statistics were used in all cases. Although none of the 
samples have undergone any apparent penetrative deforma- 
tion, the anisotropy of magnetic susceptibility was measured 
on a number of samples using a KLY-2 Kappabridge. The 
results show that only very low degrees of magnetic align- 
ment (-1%) are present, indicating that despite their complex

3. Paleomagnetic Results 
During thermal demagnetisation experiments of samples 
from the eastern Pyrenees, two directions of magnetisation 
can be clearly identified in samples from seven out of nine 
sites. The first has fairly low unblocking temperatures 
(generally removed below 300øC) and is termed the A 
magnetisation direction. In most cases this component is 
northward directed with fairly steep positive inclination 
values in situ and is interpreted to reflect a present-day 
overprint direction. In a very small number of samples a 
northeasterly component of magnetisation can be identified, 
again with fairly steep inclination values. This may reflect an 
overprint direction related to deformation during the Alpine 
orogeny, but it is not possible to clearly isolate this from the 
present-day overprint direction. Both directions are carried 
by minerals with similar magnetic properties, and the extent to 
which the present-day component overlaps the northeasterly 
direction cannot be determined. Thus, no geodynamic 
interpretation of the north easterly direction can be made in 
terms of tectonic rotations related to younger deformation 
events.

Natural remanent magnetisation intensities are fairly low

4. Interpretation and Comparison of Results 
In the earliest Devonian samples from the Pyrenees the C 
direction of magnetisation can be identified in a total of 36 
samples from seven sites. It yields an in situ mean direction 
of 3070/58 ø, k=44.2 and %5=9.2, and 240ø/51 ø, k=-86.5 and 
a9s=6.5 after bedding correction (Figure 6). Although there is 
a clear improvement in the statistical grouping of site mean 
directions, this is not significant using the fold test of 
McElhinny [ 1964], with maximum k ratios of 2.06 (N=7) at 90% 
unfolding. It should be noted, however, that within two sites, 
there is a slight variation of structural attitude, and in both 
cases the fold test is positive within site. Also, when the fold 
test is applied at the sample, rather than site level, it is 
positive with 99% confidence at 93% unfolding [McElhinny, 
1964]. An alternative interpretation is that the in situ overall 
mean direction of 307ø/58 ø is a more recent overprint direction 
of Cretaceous or younger age. Whilst this is possible, it is 
not the favored interpretation, given the improvement in 
statistical parameters after bedding correction both within 
and between sites. 
The southerly and shallow B direction of magnetisation 
can be identified in seven sites from the CCR and yields an 
overall site mean direction (7 sites) of 1870/-03 ø, k=-43.1 and 
tt0s=9.0 ø in situ, and 195ø/02 ø, k--7.1,005=24.4 ø after bedding 
correction (Figure 5 and Table 1). It fails the fold test of 
McFadden [ 1990], demonstrating that acquisition ofmagneti- 
sation postdates deformation and is of secondary origin. 
Taking the B direction of magnetisation at face value, it is in 
good agreement with the late Carboniferous direction 
expected from the apparent polar wander (APW) path for 
stable Europe. However, it would reasonably be presumed 
that in post-Paleozoic times, this region was part of the 
Iberian plate and thus should reflect counterclockwise 
rotations of some 35 ø related to opening of the Bay of Biscay 
in the late Mesozoic. One possible interpretation, therefore, 
is that these data indicate that the Catalan terrane was not a 
stable part of Iberia in post-Variscan times and has undergo- 
ne a relative, post-Mesozoic clockwise rotation [see e.g., 
Pards et al., 1988]. Alternatively, the secondary directions 
identified in this study are similar to Lower Triassic results 
obtained from central Spain [Pards andDinares-Turell, 1994; 
Van der Voo, 1967; Osete et al., 1997], although as a whole, 
most Permo-Triassic paleomagnetic data from Iberia show a 
clear counterclockwise rotation. Such rotations are not 
apparent in the overprint direction identified in this study. 
However, whether this is due to thrust sheet rotation, block 
rotations in relation to Alpine deformation, or simply that this 
region was not part of the Iberian plate remains equivocal. In 
summary, before an age and the tectonic implications of the 
B direction can be described with any confidence, more 
reliable paleomagnetic data are required from younger 
sequences in this region, as well as data from the Iberian 
Peninsula as a whole in order to remove ambiguities within 
the current paleomagnetic data set for this region in Permo- 
Triassic times.

The C magnetisation direction from the CCR is identified 
with single polarity, in 34 samples from six sites, yielding an 
overall site mean direction of 2180/44 ø, k=6.2 and a95=29.1 ø in 
situ, and 2080/48 ø, k=-28.4 and a95=12.8 ø after bedding 
correction (Figure 6 and Table 2). The improvement in 
statistical parameters is significant at the 95% level of 
confidence using the test of both McFadden [1990] and 
McElhinny [ 1964]. This is taken as a good indication that the 
high-temperature C component ofmagnetisation is prefolding 
in origin. The apparent streaking of the data obtained from 
these samples (Figure 5) could be taken as indication that in 
some samples the B component has not been completely 
isolated from the high-temperature component. It is also 
possible that there has been small-scale intraformational 
rotation in this thrusted sequence. This could explain the 
apparent smearing of the bedding corrected CCR5 and CCR6 
data along a small circle. These two sites were collected from 
the upper part of the sequence. However, taking into account 
the great circle analysis (see above), the significance of the 
fold test at site level, and that the C component is in most 
cases identified at higher temperatures as a stable endpoint 
direction after the removal at intermediate temperatures of 
component B, we feel confident that the overall mean 
direction obtained for C does approximate to the primary 
direction of magnetisation. 
The two sampling regions in this study are situated in 
rather different tectonic settings, and differential rotations of 
the sampled units may be expected. While we are aware that, 
strictly speaking, it may not be correct to combine the data 
from the two regions which may have undergone different 
deformational histories, given that both sets of data yield 
positive fold tests, it was decided to combine the data at the 
site level in order to carry out a regional fold test. This 
results in an overall in situ mean of 262ø/61 ø, k=5.5 and 
0[95 = 19.5 ø for component C, and 224ø/51 o, k=_24.6 and 0[95=8.5 o 
(13 sites) after bedding correction (Figure 7). The 
improvement in statistical parameters is positive at the 99% 
level of confidence using the fold tests of both McElhinny 
[1964] and McFadden [ 1990] and at 90% unfolding. This is 
quite compelling evidence that component C from both 
regions is the primary direction ofmagnetisation. Component 
C, therefore, translates into paleolatitudes of- 30øS for the 
Catalan Coastal Ranges and eastern Pyrenees in Siluro- 
Devonian times.

The declination values indicate a small amount of differen- 
tial rotation between the two regions. This may be related to 
differential rotation of the two regions during either Variscan 
or Alpine deformation. No further interpretation of the 
declination values can be attributed to the results, however, 
due to problems already mentioned with regards to the post- 
Paleozoic tectonic development in this part of the Iberian 
Peninsular. First, it is not clear if this part of the eastern 
Pyrenees was part of the Iberian plate in Mesozoic times or if 
it was coherent with stable Europe. Furthermore, rotation of 
Catalunya in post-Eocene times has been suggested. The 
lack of well-defined overprint directions and the lack of 
control on the tectonic coherence of the regions does not 
allow a valid interpretation of the declination values obtained. 
5. Conclusions 
A high-temperature paleomagnetic direction is identified in 
a total of 13 sites (75 samples) from Siluro-Devonian 
boundary sediments in the Catalan Coastal Ranges and Axial 
Zone of the eastern Pyrenees of NE Spain. Combining the 
site mean directions from both regions yields a direction of 
224ø/51 ø, k=-24.5 and 0195-\"8.5ø after bedding correction. The 
directions pass the fold test with 99% confidence, indicating 
the primary nature of this component of magnetisation. The 
declination value is difficult to accurately interpret, given the 
possibility of younger, but as yet not clearly quantified, 
rotations of the area. The inclination value, however, 
demonstrates that both regions were at paleolatitudes of 
some 30øS in latest Silurian to Early Devonian times (Figure 
8). This is similar to paleomagnetic results obtained from Late 
Silurian rocks from the Tepla-Barrandian of the Bohemian 
Massif [Tait et al., 1994] and from Early Devonian rocks of 
the Armorican Massif [Tait, 1999]. These two massifs 
formed part of the Armorican Terrane Assemblage (ATA), 
i.e., the Paleozoic Gondwana-derived terranes which today 
constitute part of the Variscan fold belt of Europe, south of 
the Rhenohercynian Zone. These terranes were previously 
considered to have formed part of a coherent microplate (the 
Armorican microplate), but from paleomagnetic and 
geological evidence it is now clear that the concept of a 
coherent Armorican microplate is no longer valid and the 
various blocks were separated by minor oceanic basins [Tait 
et al., 1997; Franke et al., 1995]. Although there are no 
reliable paleomagnetic data for the Siluro-Devonian of the 
Iberian Massif, on faunal and lithological grounds it is fairly 
clear that the Iberian and Armorican Massifs were closely 
related throughout the Paleozoic [Robardet and Guiterrez- 
Marco, 1990; Quesada et al., 1991]. Thus the different units 
of the ATA all appear to have had similar northward drift 
histories during the Paleozoic and in Late Silurian times were 
all situated between paleolatitudes of 25 ø and 30øS (Figure 8). 
The results presented here from northeastern Spain 
demonstrate that this region was adjacent to the southern 
margin of the Armorican Terrane Assemblage and have 
important implications for the geodynamic evolution of this 
region in Paleozoic times, although the tectonic relationship 
between this region and the Iberian Massif remains equivocal 
due to the lack ofpaleomagnetic data from Spain and Portugal 
during the Paleozoic.

Laurentia are all well constrained for the Paleozoic as a whole
