Figure 8. Palaeogeographic reconstruction for Siluro- 
Devonian boundary times based on data from the present 
study, Torsvik et al. [ 1992] for Baltica, Charmell et al. [ 1992] 
for Avalonia, Bachtadse et al. [2000] for Siberia, Tait [ 1999] 
for the Armorican Massif, and Tait et al. [1994] for the 
Barrandian Zone of the Bohemian Massif. Two different 
options for the position of Gondwana are indicated. The 
dotted outline indicates the palaeoposition according to the 
more complex APW path based on the paleomagnetic data of 
Schmidt et al. [1990]. The solid outline indicates the 
preferred position using the more conservative APW path of 
Bachtadse and Briden [1991]. A, Iberian Massif; B, 
Catalunya and Eastern Pyrenees; C, Armorican Massif and 
French Massif Central; D, Saxothuringia; E, Barrandia. 
(see review papers by MacNiocall and Smethurst [1994]; 
Torsvik et al., [1992, 1996] and Smethurst et al., [1998]), 
paleogeographic reconstructions for mid-Paleozoic times 
remain contentious with regards to Gondwana [Van der Voo 
[1993],' Bachtadse et al., 1995]. Basically, there are two 
different options from the existing paleomagnetic data set. A 
more complicated APW path for Gondwana can be adopted 
(path Y after Morel and Irving [1978], and subsequently 
modified by Schmidt et al., [ 1990]), in which case the northern 
margin of Gondwana would have been in an equatorial 
position in Siluro-Devonian boundary times (see dotted 
outline in Figure 8). The alternative APW path (path X of 
Morel andIrving [ 1978], more recently redefined by Bachtad- 
se and Briden [ 1991 ]) involves gradual northward movement 
of Gondwana throughout the Palaeozoic and places the 
northern margin of Gondwana at approximately 65øS at the 
Siluro-Devonian boundary (see solid outline in Figure 8). 
Whichever of these two models is adopted, it is clear from the 
new palaeomagnetic data that the ATA, including the Catalan 
terrane, did not remain adjacent to the north African margin 
of Gondwana. Alternative paleogeographies based on 
biogeographic and climatic evidence place the North African 
margin of Gondwana between- 50 ø and 30øS in the Siluro- 
Devonian [Scotese et al., 1999, Scotese and McKerrow; 1991 
and references therein, McKerrow et al., 2000]. None of 
these biogeographic models are in apparent direct conflict 
with the new palaeomagnetic data presented here from NE 
Spain.

ABSTRACT
Magnetostratigraphy, isotopic dating,
and sandstone petrography establish age
limits on the depositional history of ;2100
m of foreland basin strata in the Neogene
Meta Ân Subgroup of northwest Argentina.
The strata were deposited between ca. 15.1
and 9.7 Ma in the eastern Sistema de Santa
Ba Ârbara. The region is positioned above the
Cretaceous Salta rift basin, in the Transi-
tion Zone between modern relatively steep
and ¯at subducting segments of the Nazca
plate.
Formations within the subgroup are
shown to be diachronous over a 60 km dis-
tance; the younger ages are in the east.
Changes in paleocurrent ¯ow directions
and the lithic clast component of sandstones
collected from the Arroyo Gonza Âlez section
suggest that basal ¯uvial strata were de-
rived from the craton to the east beginning
in middle Miocene time, just prior to 15.1
Ma. By ca. 14.5 Ma, the paleocurrent
¯owed from a source in the west and sedi-
ment accumulation rates increased dramat-

apparently began by 13.7 Ma and thrusting

Sandstones from Rõ Âo Yacones suggest

ued for several million years longer be-

INTRODUCTION
The Central Andes are frequently cited as a
type example for mountain ranges generated
from the subduction of oceanic lithosphere be-
neath a continent (e.g., Moores and Twiss,

The work reports the chronologic develop-
ment of middle Miocene sedimentation in the
Sistema de Santa Ba Ârbara portion (Fig. 1) of
the Transition Zone at the southern end of the
Subandean zone. Using dating from magnetic
polarity stratigraphy aided by a ®ssion-track
age and chronologic information from other
areas in the Transition Zone, crosscutting re-
lations, and changes in the lithic content of the
sandstones, we interpret the middle Miocene
tectonic development of the region.
Nazca plate subduction is characterized by
signi®cant along-strike subduction angle
changes beneath the western margin of South
America (Jordan et al., 1983). Foreland struc-
tural provinces of northwest Argentina devel-
oped in three tectonic domains characterized
by differences in the subduction angle and the
orientation of preexisting structural fabrics.
An area of inclined subduction where the Naz-
ca plate descends at an angle of about 30 8 to
the east is between 18 8 and 248S. Farther to
the south, between 28 8 and 338S, is an area of
subhorizontal ( ;58) subduction (Barazangi
and Isacks, 1976). The Transition Zone is sit-
uated between these subduction domains
(248±288S).
TRANSITION ZONE PROVINCES
Our work focuses on the middle Miocene
tectonic history of the northern part of the
Transition Zone (248±268S). Structural aspects
of the Neogene foreland provinces to the north
of the Transition Zone continue along strike
through the Transition Zone but undergo
marked changes before terminating at the
southern margin (Barazangi and Isacks, 1976;
Jordan et al., 1983; Allmendinger et al., 1983).
Bevis and Isacks (1984) proposed that the
subducting plate is deformed by a broad gen-
tle ¯exure through the Transition Zone.
Salta Rift Basin
Grier et al. (1991) demonstrated that the ge-
ometries of Andean tectonism in the Transi-
tion Zone are consistent with the inversion of
the Cretaceous Salta rift basin and with Neo-
gene shortening by thrust reactivation of Cre-
taceous listric normal faults. Westward ver-
gence in the western Cordillera Oriental
portion of the Transition Zone (Fig. 2) is lo-
calized near the western boundary of the Salta
rift basin, where the Puna and the western
Cordillera Oriental meet (Grier et al., 1991).
The eastern part of the Sistema de Santa Ba Âr-
bara (discussed in the following) is located
above the eastern boundary of the rift. The
northern limit of the Sierras Pampeanas is lo-
cated roughly along the southern rift margin.
The rift is partitioned into six named sub-
basins: the Lomas de Olmedo, Tres Cruces,
Sey, Alemanõ Âa, El Rey, and Meta Ân (Fig. 3).
The subbasins are grouped around the central
Salta-Jujuy structural high (Fig. 3; Marquillas
and Sal®ty, 1988; Mon and Sal®ty, 1995) and
are ®lled with Salta Group strata (Table 1).
Compressional regional stresses were initi-
ated by Neogene time. Continental clastic
strata of the Ora Ân Group buried the rift during
the Quechua phase of the Andean orogeny as
a foreland basin developed eastward across
the area (Comõ Ânguez and Ramos, 1995).
Puna
The Puna Plateau is situated along the Ar-
gentina-Chile border between the main range
of the Andes and the Cordillera Oriental. It
represents the southern extension of the broad-
er Altiplano that is to the north in Bolivia and
Peru. The Puna-Altiplano is characteristic of
the inclined subduction region. It continues
through the Transition Zone, tapering to its

Cordillera Oriental
The Cordillera Oriental is a predominantly
eastward-verging fold-thrust belt bounding the
eastern edge of the Puna (Fig. 1) in the in-
clined subduction region. Vergence in the
Transition Zone varies from predominantly
westward verging in the west to eastward
verging in the east (Fig. 2), resulting from re-
activation of the rift-bounding faults (Grier et
al., 1991). The Cordillera Oriental is wider in
the Transition Zone than it is in the inclined
subduction area (Fig. 1). Grier and Dallmeyer
(1990) suggested that eastward progression of
deformation in the Cordillera Oriental at these
latitudes was faster than that in the Sierras
Pampeanas immediately to the south.
Many peaks rise above 5000 m along steep-
ly dipping fault planes. Rapid Neogene uplift
caused signi®cant unroo®ng of these ranges.
In many ranges, greenish phyllites are ex-
posed along with the Phanerozoic strata. Like
the Puna, the Cordillera Oriental and Suban-
dean zone also terminate along the irregular
southern boundary of the Transition Zone
(Jordan et al., 1983). Uplift of the Cordillera
Oriental began in the late Oligocene in Bolivia
(Horton, 1998) but appears to have started in
the middle Miocene in northern Argentina
(Reynolds et al., 1996; Herna Ândez et al., 1996,
1999).
In the southern Transition Zone, two ranges
of the Sierras Pampeanas are wedged between
the Puna and Cordillera Oriental, extending to
the north of 26 8S. The Sierras Pampeanas are
Laramide-style basement uplifts found in the
eastern foreland region of the ¯at subduction
domain (Jordan and Allmendinger, 1986).
Sistema de Santa Ba Ârbara
The Subandean zone in the Transition Zone
is de®ned by the Sistema de Santa Ba Ârbara,
the only structural province con®ned exclu-
sively to the Transition Zone (Fig. 1). The re-
gion is densely vegetated and humid, subtrop-
ical conditions cause deep weathering pro®les.
Exposure is limited to arroyos incised into the
¯anks of Neogene mountains, where rapid
downcutting provides fresh, relatively contin-
uous exposures along select streams.
Structures in this province exhibit af®nities
with the basement block uplifts of the Sierras
Pampeanas immediately to their south. The
basement cores of the Sistema de Santa Ba Âr-
bara ranges have not been unroofed due to a
thick sedimentary cover provided by in®lling
of the Salta rift basin thrusting (Allmendinger
et al., 1983). Like the Sierras Pampeanas, the
Sistema de Santa Ba Ârbara is characterized by
predominantly broad, low-amplitude folds
generated by predominantly westward-vergent
thrusting (Allmendinger et al., 1983).
Gebhard et al. (1974) summarized the Ter-
tiary lithostratigraphic units and published a
good regional geologic map. Other strati-
graphic contributions by Russo and Serraiotto
(1978) and Mingramm and Russo (1972) con-
stitute the basis of the stratigraphic work in
the region. Jordan and Alonso (1987) included
the province in their regional analysis of the
Subandean zone.
To the north of the Transition Zone, the
Subandean zone on the east side of the Cor-
dillera Oriental is occupied by the Sierras Sub-
andinas. The Sierras Subandinas arose along
predominantly eastward-verging thrust faults,
beginning in the late Miocene (Herna Ândez et
al., 1996, 1999; Reynolds et al., 1993, 1996).
Nearly all of the rocks exposed in this region
are Neogene foreland basin-®lling strata.
These rocks were uplifted and exposed as
eastward-migrating thrusting progressed
through western parts of the Subandean basin.
Older strata are exposed in Bolivia. The re-
gion has recently received much attention
from the petroleum industry (Belotti et al.,
1995; Herna Ândez et al., 1996, 1999; Moretti
et al., 1996; Giraudo et al, 1999), but is still
relatively unknown in the geologic literature.

Implications for Petroleum Exploration
Diachroneity of uplift caused an eastward
progression of burial of organic-rich horizons
in the Salta Group across the Neogene fore-
land basin in the Transition Zone. An expected
result would be the eastward younging of hy-
drocarbon maturation ages in the source rocks
of the basin. Thrust-related structural traps de-
veloped during the Neogene are also diach-
ronous across the region. Limits to the ages
of these structures, seen on seismic lines, can
be established where they crosscut the dated
Neogene strata. Comparison of local matura-
tion ages with the age of the structural traps
should allow evaluation of target structures
with relatively tight temporal precision.
CONCLUSION
We present evidence suggesting that uplift
of the Sierra de Santa Ba Ârbara, in the western
Cordillera Oriental, began ca. 13 Ma. Eleva-
tion of this range is apparently related to the
rise of the Cumbres Calchaquõ Âes and the Si-
erra de Quilmes, the northernmost ranges of
the Sierras Pampeanas. The Sierra de Quilmes
began to rise 13±12 Ma along the southwest-
ern margin of the Salta rift basin. These are
the earliest ages reported for tectonic activity
in the Cordillera Oriental of Argentina and the
Sierras Pampeanas. Malizia et al. (1995) re-
ported a ca. 12.7 Ma age for the initiation of
the Sierra de Velasco uplift in the central Si-
erras Pampeanas ;300 km to the south-south-
west in the ¯at subduction area. Regional
drainage patterns prevented us from establish-
ing uplift ages for the Sierra de Candelaria
(Figs. 3B and 11 F), the easternmost Pampean
range at these latitudes.
Uplift of the Transition Zone ranges appears
in our model to progress in a northeasterly di-
rection (Fig. 11). It began in the west along
westward-verging thrust faults. The faults are
reactivated listric normal faults formed during
the Cretaceous opening of the Salta rift (Grier
et al., 1991). After mountain building com-
menced along the western margin of the rift,
it migrated eastward across the Salta basin,
vergence direction being dependent upon the
orientation of preexisting extensional struc-
tures. By ca. 10 Ma, uplift was active across
the width of the Cordillera Oriental between
258 and 268S, but between 24 8 and 258S east-
ward migration lagged. Faulting is not evident
at Rõ Âo Yacones until after ca. 6.4 Ma (Vira-
monte et al., 1994).
The Sistema de Santa Ba Ârbara, in the Su-
bandean zone of the foreland region, was not
elevated until after 9 Ma. Uplift in the Suban-

APPENDIX 1. PALEOMAGNETIC
COLLECTIONS, METHODS, AND
ANALYSIS
Oriented samples were collected from 77 stations,
initially at ;30 m stratigraphic intervals, in 1990.
A minimum of three, ®st-sized samples was col-
lected at each station. An additional 21 stations
were collected in 1992 and 1995 to support single-
site polarity zones and to clarify problem areas.
Sandstones were also collected in 1995 for petro-
graphic analysis. Measurement of the section with
a Jacob's Staff and Abney Level proceeded as the
1990 samples were collected. Sites were located
with respect to an existing measured section pro-
vided by Yacimientos Petrolõ Âferos Fisicales (Fig. 5).
Samples were generally collected from reddish
siltstones or mudstones with the hope that the mag-
netic minerals would be suf®ciently ®ne grained to
retain a reliable magnetic signal. Some samples in
the Anta Formation were very ®ne grained sand-
stones. All 1990 samples were milled into 2.5 cm
cubes at Universidad Nacional de Salta. Samples
collected in 1992 and 1995 were taken with a Pom-
eroy Drill using standard coring techniques.
The natural remanent magnetizations (NRM) of
the 1990 samples were measured on the three-axis
vertical ScT cryogenic magnetometer at the Hawaii
Institute of Geophysics. The 1992 and 1995 samples
were measured with the three-component 2G Su-
perconducting Rock Magnetometer (SRM) at the
University of Pittsburgh. NRM magnetic dipole mo-
ment per unit volume (M, amperes per meter) val-
ues varied between 9.1 3 10
23A/m and 1.3 3
1021A/m. M values approximate an even distribu-
tion between the two extremes.
We subjected 12 samples to stepwise alternating
®eld demagnetization experiments to determine the
magnetic properties of the strata. This treatment was
successful with some samples but with others failed
to separate the components of the NRM. All other
samples were subjected to stepwise thermal demag-
netization (Fig. A1). Samples collected in 1990
were treated less rigorously that the 1992 and 1995
samples. They were demagnetized until they pro-
duced a consistent orientation, but were not com-
pletely demagnetized. The 1992 and 1995 samples
were treated to total demagnetization. Results from
the demagnetization experiments suggest that the
principal carrier of remanent magnetization is he-
matite in the Rõ Âo Seco and Anta Formations and
both magnetite and hematite in the Jesu Âs Marõ Âa
Formation.
A statistical mean direction of the paleomagnetic
vector was determined for each site using the meth-
od described by Fisher (1953). Statistically signi®-
cant results, using the R statistic (Watson, 1956),
suggested that the stable component of magnetiza-
tion had been isolated. As used here, class I sites
are those whose mean direction satis®es Watson's
criteria. When the number, N, of samples 5 3, an
R . 2.62 is considered to be statistically signi®cant
(Watson, 1956). Class II sites designate stratigraphic
levels for which only two samples from the site sur-
vived to be analyzed.
Of the 98 paleomagnetic sites, 8 were collected
in the Lumbrera Formation and are not included in
our data set. Of the Neogene sites, 79 are shown in
the magnetic polarity column (Fig. 8). Of the sites,
67 provided class I data and 12 are class II. Six
sites failed to ®t into a class I or II category. Sam-
ples from ®ve very friable horizons were destroyed
during transport to the lab or during analysis. All of
the sites that were destroyed and all of the indeter-
minate sites were collected in 1990 and were resam-
pled during subsequent visits.
Figure A1 illustrates the thermal demagnetization
behavior of one sample from the Rõ Âo Seco Forma-
tion, two from the Anta Formation, and one from
the Jesu Âs Marõ Âa Formation. All exhibit a present-
day viscous component that was removed by the
®rst several thermal treatments, after which rela-

from a red siltstone in the middle of the Rõ Âo Seco

Accuracy of the paleomagnetic results was ex-

providing a positive reversal test (class C; Mc-

Large clockwise rotations in an extensional allochthon, Alboran Domain
(southern Spain)
E. PLATZMAN 1, J. P. PLATT 1, S. P. KELLEY 2 & S. ALLERTON 3
1Department of Geological Sciences, University College London, Gower Street, London WC1E 6BT, UK
(e-mail: e.platzman@ulc.ac.uk)
2Department of Earth Sciences, Open University, Milton Keynes MK7 6AA, UK
3Robertson Research International, Llanrhos, Llandudno LL30 1SA, UK
Abstract: Palaeomagnetic, structural and geochronological analysis of a suite of Oligocene maﬁc dykes
intruded into the Malaguide allochthon in the Internal Zone of the Betic Cordillera demonstrate that at
least 134 /p8clockwise vertical-axis rotation of a large region occurred, probably during early Miocene
thrusting onto the External Zones. Initial results from Ar/Ar whole rock analysis suggests that the dykes
were probably intruded over a period of time between 23 Ma and 30 Ma. Results of demagnetization
experiments demonstrate that the remanence in many of the dykes is composed of one to three
components. The lowest temperature component is poorly deﬁned. The intermediate temperature (IT)
component, carried by pyrrhotite, has reversed polarity, a declination of 314 /p8and an inclination of /p148/p8.
This component was probably acquired during cooling after greenschist-facies metamorphism. The high
temperature (HT) component is carried by magnetite and was probably acquired at or shortly after
intrusion. This component has both reversed and normal polarity, with an average declination of 320/p8and
an inclination of /p113/p8. Rotation of approximately 35 /p8about a horizontal NNE-trending axis, in
present-day coordinates, brings the inclination of the HT component into statistical agreement with both
the IT component and the expected inclination for the Oligocene. This rotation leaves the dykes in a
near-vertical orientation but brings the foliation in the surrounding schists to approximately horizontal.
We suggest that the original regional foliation may have been sub-horizontal and related to the ductile
phase of late-orogenic extension in the Betic Cordillera. The dykes were intruded sub-vertically into the
schists with an original NW–SE trend. The region was then tilted and rotated clockwise by 23/p8/p515 before
acquiring the IT component after which it underwent 134/p8/p510/p8of clockwise rotation about a vertical axis.
Keywords: Betic Cordillera, Oligocene, palaeomagnetism, dykes, absolute age.
The Internal Zone of the Betic Cordillera of southern Spain
(Fig. 1) forms part of an Alpine collisional orogen, known as
the Alboran Domain, that underwent late orogenic extensional
collapse in the Miocene to form the present-day Alboran
Sea in the Western Mediterranean (Platt & Vissers 1989;
Garcı´a-Duen˜as et al . 1992). The deformational history
involved (1) large-scale thrusting of Palaeozoic to Early Terti-
ary rocks, accompanied by high P/T ratio metamorphism,
during Late Cretaceous? to Early Tertiary time, (2) ductile
extension, accompanied in places by medium to low P/T ratio
metamorphism during Late Oligocene to Early Miocene time
(Vissers et al. 1995; Platt et al. 1998; Argles et al. 1999; Platt &
Whitehouse 1999) and (3) brittle extension leading to the
formation of marine sedimentary basins during the Miocene
(Comas et al . 1999). The Alboran Domain is surrounded to
north, west, and south by the External Betic–Rif arc, a
Miocene thin-skinned fold and thrust belt that accommodated
both the extension of the Alboran Domain and the continuing
convergence of Africa and Iberia (Platt & Vissers 1989;
Garcı´a-Duen˜as et al . 1992; Platzman 1992). Thrusting in the
External Betic–Rif arc and in unmetamorphosed rocks of the
Dorsale Complex along the margin of the Alboran Domain
was accompanied by large clockwise vertical-axis rotations
(Osete et al. 1988; Platzman 1992; Platzman & Lowrie 1992;
Allerton et al . 1993; Platzman et al. 1993; Platt et al. 1995),
which contributed to the development of the structural
geometry at scales ranging from that of individual thrust sheets
to that of the arcuate orogen as a whole (e.g., Kirker & Platt
1998).
Relatively little palaeomagnetic work has been carried out in
the Internal Zone, mainly because of the widespread metamor-
phism, structural complexity, and the scarcity of rocks with
well-developed magnetic remanences in this region. Results
from the peridotite massifs in Spain (Fig. 1) and in Morocco,
however, suggest that these rocks may have undergone about
45/p8and 74 /p8of clockwise and anticlockwise rotations respect-
ively (Saddiqi et al. 1995; Feinberg et al. 1996) although it was
not possible to correct these results for the possible e ﬀects of
later tilting. The sense and amount of these rotations are
comparable to those found in the External Betic–Rif arc.
Work on unmetamorphosed Mesozoic and Tertiary sediments
much further east, in the Sierra Espun ˜a (Fig. 1), suggest
progressive clockwise rotation of about 180 /p8during the late
Oligocene to early Miocene (Allerton et al. 1993). Data from
middle to late Miocene volcanic rocks in the Cabo de Gata
region (Fig. 1) show evidence of both clockwise and anticlock-
wise rotation (Calvo et al. 1997), possibly associated with late
Miocene to recent strike-slip faults in the area. It seems likely
that vertical-axis rotations have played at least as important a
role in the tectonic evolution of the Internal Betic–Rif arc as in
the External arc. The purpose of this paper is to present an
integrated palaeomagnetic, structural and geochronological
study of part of a suite of Tertiary dykes within the Internal
Zones of the Betic Cordillera, which sheds some light on the

timing of vertical-axis rotations and their role in the tectonic
evolution of the region.
Geological setting
The main body of the Internal Zone of the Betic Cordillera is
traditionally divided into three major tectonic complexes: in
descending order the Malaguide, Alpujarride, and Nevado –
Filabride Complexes. These were originally regarded as nappe
complexes derived from di ﬀering palaeogeographical domains
(e.g., Egeler & Simon 1969), but the boundaries between them
are now thought to be major low-angle normal sense faults or
shear zones that have reactivated or cut earlier thrust contacts
(Platt 1986; Platt & Vissers 1989; Garc ı´a-Duen˜as et al. 1992;
Jabaloy et al. 1993; Lonergan & Platt 1995). The timing of
events in the Internal Zone is currently debated (compare Platt
1998 and Balanya´ et al. 1997, for example), but radiometric
data strongly suggest a period of rapid exhumation and
cooling in early Miocene time, associated with the extensional
phase of tectonics that created the Alboran Sea and related
extensional basins onshore (Zeck et al. 1992; Monie´ et al.,
1994; Platt et al. 1998; Platt & Whitehouse 1999). The periph-
eral regions of the extended Internal Zone were emplaced
onto the African and Iberian continental margins during the
Miocene, to form the presently emergent Internal Zones of the
Betic and Rif orogens. Extensional tectonics in the Internal
Zone and thrusting in the External Betic –Rif arc appear to
have overlapped in time.
The area we have studied lies within a region of approxi-
mately 50 km by 30 km to the north of the city of Malaga that
has been assigned to the Malaguide Complex (Fig. 1). Three
broadly deﬁned geological units can be distinguished (Fig. 2).
The lowest unit consists of low-grade phyllites and psammites
of probable Early Palaeozoic age, locally carrying biotite and
andalusite; this is overlain by a sequence of Late Palaeozoic
carbonate and clastic rocks showing very low-grade metamor-
phism; and these are overlain in turn by apparently unmeta-
morphosed Permo-Triassic to Cretaceous clastic and
carbonate rocks (IGME 1978, 1979; Tubia et al . 1993). This
sequence is generally regarded as being stratigraphic in nature,
and the contacts are regionally sub-horizontal. The contact
between the middle and upper units is likely to be an uncon-
formity of post-Variscan age. The nature of the contact
between the lower and middle units is unclear, but in view of
the contrast in metamorphic grade across it, it may be a late
Alpine extensional fault. The lowest and middle units both
show regionally developed tectonic fabrics, and are cut by
numerous brittle normal faults. The structural geometry and
history of the lower unit is discussed in more detail below.
The Malaguide rocks are cut by a suite of altered ma ﬁc
dykes. These show relict magmatic textures, with primary
zoned plagioclase, clinopyroxene and/or hornblende, and
ilmenite. The primary grain size varies from 0.2 mm to 1 mm,
and some dykes contain 5 mm plagioclase phenocrysts, now
heavily altered. Plagioclase is altered to varying degrees to
white mica and epidote minerals, and the ma ﬁc phases are
largely altered to ﬁne grained feathery aggregates of pale green
clino-amphibole. Ilmenite is now largely preserved as skeletal
crystals in which exsolved magnetite lamellae have been al-
tered, and the ilmenite itself partly altered to sphene. Second-
ary titanite, chlorite, white mica and pyrrhotite are abundant,
and some samples contain metamorphic biotite. There is no
textural evidence for ductile deformation. Most of the dykes

are found in the lowest (Early Palaeozoic) unit, but some also
occur in the middle (Late Palaeozoic) unit: the latter show
signiﬁcantly less alteration. None have been reported from the
upper unit. The dykes invariably cut the ductile deformational
fabrics, but are cut by the normal faults. In the area we have
studied, they are for the most part sub-vertical and trend
east–west. One K –Ar whole rock age of 22 Ma has been
previously obtained (Torres-Roldan et al. 1986). The rocks
have a MORB-type geochemistry, and have been attributed to
shallow melting of asthenospheric mantle, following removal
and thinning of lithospheric mantle beneath the collisional
orogen in late Oligocene time (Turner et al. 1999).
Structure
The rocks of the lowest (Early Palaeozoic) unit in the
Malaga region consist of interlayered graphitic phyllites and
psammites with a strong foliation sub-parallel to lithological
layering. This foliation is a ﬁnely spaced di ﬀerentiated
crenulation cleavage, and in thin-section an earlier slaty-type
cleavage can be seen in the crenulation arcs. Both the
crenulation cleavage and the earlier fabric are de ﬁned by
ﬁne-grained (10 –50 µm) white mica and chlorite. In the
transect that we have studied the main foliation has a moder-
ate to steep westerly dip, with a mean value of 34/p8towards 295/p8
(Fig. 3a). We found no evidence of macroscopic folding related
to this foliation, but it is locally deformed by mesoscopic open
folds, particularly associated with brittle normal faults.
One or more lineations lie in the foliation plane. The
commonest is a ﬁne crenulation lineation developed in the
phyllites, which is likely to be the intersection of the main
crenulation cleavage and the older fabric. Psammites com-
monly show a lineation de ﬁned by elongate deformed clastic
particles and detrital mica, and by elongate pressure shadows
around these particles: this is likely to be an elongation
lineation, representing the ﬁnite extension direction during the
deformation that produced the main fabric. The two lineations
are not readily distinguishable in the ﬁeld, and appear to be
sub-parallel: we have therefore grouped the data together. The
mean orientation of the aggregated lineation data plunges 22 /p8
towards 351/p8(Fig. 3b). This indicates a north –south direction
of ﬁnite extension in the present-day reference frame.

The age of the deformational fabrics is not known with
certainty. Because of the lack of ductile deformation in the
Mesozoic rocks of the Malaguide Complex, cleavage and
lineation in the underlying Palaeozoic rocks are commonly
assumed to be of Variscan age (e.g., Balanya´ & Garcia-Duen˜as
1987). For reasons discussed later in this paper, however, we
suggest that the crenulation cleavage and the dominant
lineation in the lowest unit in the Malaga region may be of
Alpine age, and their absence in the Mesozoic unit may re ﬂect
the presence of a signi ﬁcant late extensional fault separating
the lowest unit from the rocks above.
The foliation in the lowest unit is locally overgrown by
porphyroblasts of andalusite (now commonly altered to ﬁne-
grained phyllosilicates) and by biotite. Biotite is also associated
with microscale fractures roughly normal to the main fabric,
which probably served to allow ingress of ﬂuids.
The dykes crosscut the main foliation in the lowest and
middle units, and are for the most part undeformed, with a
mean orientation of 80 /p8towards 185/p8From a structural point
of view they constitute a set of extensional fractures related to
north–south extension in the present-day reference frame. The
density of dykes varies: on average they have produced less
than 5% extension, but locally, over north –south distances of
several hundreds of metres, they have produced as much as
30% extension. Within the north –south traverse that we have
studied in detail (Fig. 2) the density of dykes decreases
northwards.
Ductile deformational fabrics and dykes are all cut by
normal faults with widely varying trends. Most faults carry
wear grooves or quartz-ﬁbre lineations indicating the direction
of motion. Displacements are for the most part not deter-
minable, although some faults displace dykes by distances of
up to 20 m. In places where the dykes are strongly disrupted by
the faulting, they can be rotated into gently dipping orienta-
tions adjacent to the faults. The most common set of faults dip
SW, with a mean orientation of 32 /p8towards 212/p8, and a mean
slip vector of 36 /p8towards 214 /p8(Fig. 3c and d). Subordinate
east- and west-dipping faults may constitute a later con-
jugate set (Fig. 3c). These data suggest approximately NE –SW
extension in the present-day reference frame.
Thermochronological analysis
Ar/Ar methods and data
Whole rock fragments were hand picked from crushed and 250 –
500 µm sieved samples. Samples were then cleaned ultrasonically in
methanol and wrapped in aluminium foil prior to irradiation. They
were irradiated at the RISOπ reactor, Copenhagen. After irradiation,
the samples were loaded into ﬂat bottomed holes, 2 mm in diameter,
2 mm deep in an aluminium platten, each containing 20–30 such holes.
Several grains of whole rock were loaded into each hole allowing
suﬃcient space for individual grains to be fused. The plattens were
loaded into an ultra-high-vacuum laser mini-chamber and placed
under a heat lamp overnight to reduce atmospheric blank levels.
Argon was extracted by slowly increasing the power of a focused laser
until total fusion of a target grain. The laser source was a Spectron
SL902TQ CW Nd/YAG laser, maximum power 17W in TEMoo
mode. The beam was directed into a customized Leica Metallux
3 microscope and focused at the sample surface via the objective lens.
Laser power was time-controlled via a computer-controlled external
shutter. The sample was observed using a CCD camera, coaxial with
the laser beam. Gases were released by laser step-heating, sequentially
increasing the laser power. Sample gas was gettered using Zr/Al alloy
getters and after 5 minutes, equilibrated via automated valves into a
MAP 215-50 noble-gas mass spectrometer. Peaks between 35 and 41
were scanned 10 times and amounts extrapolated back to the inlet
time. Blanks were analysed before and after each sample analysis and
the mean of the two blanks was used to correct the sample analysis for
most of the measured isotopes. Overall mean blank levels for
40Ar,
39Ar and 36Ar are (130, 50 and 6) /p210/p114 cm/p13. The resulting
analyses were corrected for mass spectrometer discrimination, 37Ar
decay and neutron-induced interferences. The corrections used were
(
39Ar/37Ar)Ca=0.00065, ( 36Ar/37Ar)Ca=0.00026, based upon a mean
from salts analysed from several irradiations and ( 40Ar/39Ar)K=0.045
measured in this irradiation. GA1550 biotite standard (Age=98.8 Ma,
Renne et al. 1998) was used to monitor the neutron ﬂux during
irradiation. The samples were packed closely in a single evacuated tube
and the adjacent standards yielded similar J values close to 0.00639.
Nine of the least altered dykes were analysed. Six of these
nine, however, did not produce reproducible ages. Results
from dyke M7A (30.2/p52.8 Ma) and M7B (18.5/p50.5 Ma) have
been published in Turner et al . (1999). Although both these
samples exhibit somewhat noisy plateaux they do show signi ﬁ-
cantly di ﬀerent release pro ﬁles suggesting di ﬀerent phases
dominate the release. M7A shows a saddle shaped release
proﬁle with a plateau of around 80% release in the central
portion. Petrographic analysis reveals that very little, if any,
original hornblende or biotite remains in M7A and therefore
the 30.2 Ma date is most likely to be coming from the
unaltered plagioclase. In dyke M7B the ﬁrst 70% of argon
release de ﬁnes the plateau age of 18.5 Ma and is associated
with low Ca/K ratio ( c. 4). Given the state of alteration of
these rocks, this younger age is likely to be re ﬂecting ﬂuid
ingress and growth of new minerals, including the ﬁne grained
white mica observed in thin section, during metamorphism.
As diabase clasts occur in sediments of Burdigalian age
(Alonso-Chaves & Rodriguez-Vidal 1998), however, this date
may represent the ﬁnal stages of cooling after metamorphism.
Dyke M17, intruded into the middle (late Palaeozoic) geo-
logical unit proved to be the best site for both magnetic and
geochronological analysis (Fig. 4, Table 1). Samples from this
dyke show the least degree of alteration. Three steps yielded a
reproducible age over 39% of the
39Ar release with a weighted
mean age of 23.0/p50.4 Ma (2/afii9846errors). Unlike the more altered
samples this sample shows very little indication of Ca/K
changes through the heating schedule. Ca/K ratios are gener-
ally around 24 (though as high as 31), fall to 14 in the
mid-release but rise again to 20 –24 in the late release suggest-
ing that this date comes from unaltered plagioclase. The three
reproducible ages span the full variation of Ca/K, but do not
meet the criteria for a true plateau age (see McDougall &
Harrison 1999) and we have thus considered an isochron of all
points which yields an age of 23.0/p52.6 Ma. Removing the ﬁrst
point changes the age by less than the errors and we consider
this the best estimate for the ﬁnal age. The ‘crankshaft’ style
release pattern may result from a recoil artefact causing
apparent age variations in the ﬁner grained portions of this
whole rock sample.
Crucially, none of these samples shows any indication of
ages older than Oligocene. They do indicate, however, the
dykes are likely to have been intruded over a period of time
during the late Oligocene.
Palaeomagnetic analysis
Magnetic methods
Samples for magnetic analysis were obtained from 17 sites (28 dykes),
16 of which are located in the lower geological unit exposed in the
1190 E. PLATZMAN ET AL .

gorge of the river Guadalmedina, which cuts through the entire body
of Malaguide rocks from the Internal/External Zone Boundary to
Malaga, near the coast (Fig. 2). One site (M17) comes from the middle
unit, a few kilometres NE of Malaga. At each site one to ﬁve dykes
were sampled. This sampling scheme was designed to try to minimize
the eﬀects of secular variation.
Samples were obtained either with a portable petrol-powered rock
drill or as oriented block samples which were taken back to the
laboratory to be drilled. When cores were taken on site, ﬁve to eight
cores were obtained from each dyke to allow for statistical analysis.
The cores were oriented using a Brunton compass and an orienting
platform which includes a sun compass for magnetically strong
samples. Standard cylindrical cores of 2.5 cm diameter and 10 cm
length were later cut into 2.25 cm length samples.
In the laboratory the samples were analysed to isolate the stable
characteristic component of remanent magnetization (ChRM). Step-
wise thermal and alternating ﬁeld (AF) demagnetization procedures
were used. During the thermal demagnetization procedure each sample
was demagnetized with a minimum of ten steps based on a scheme
designed after a detailed pilot demagnetization study. Natural rem-
anent magnetization (NRM) measurements were made on either a
two-axis cryogenic magnetometer or a Jr5A spinner magnetometer.
Data obtained from the demagnetization experiments were plotted on
Zijderveld vector diagrams. ChRM directions were then obtained from
these plots using linear regression techniques.
On a set of representative samples, bulk susceptibility was measured
between each thermal demagnetization step to monitor possible
changes in magnetic mineralogy that can occur as a result of heating
and dehydration.
Isothermal remanent magnetization (IRM) acquisition experiments
were conducted on representative samples to peak ﬁelds between 1 and
2 T on a ASC pulse magnetizer. After saturation, smaller ﬁelds of
0.2 T and 0.05 T were imparted to orthogonal axes. The rocks were
then thermally demagnetized with an ASC thermal demagnetizer.
Natural remanent magnetization
Results of thermal and AF demagnetization demonstrate that
the remanence in many of the dykes is composed of one to
three components (Table 2). In some dykes, however, the
remanence is completely unstable and does not respond to
either thermal or AF demagnetization techniques. Samples
from sites M1, 7, 8, 9, 13, 14 and 16 did not carry a stable
remanence.
In general, results show that the lowest temperature com-
ponent usually unblocks at less than 200 /p8C and appears to be
in the direction of the present-day magnetic ﬁeld. This com-
ponent may also be present at the lowest coercivities (<20 mT).
It is commonly unstable and poorly deﬁned, however, and was
therefore not investigated further. The intermediate tempera-
ture component unblocks between 200 /p8C and 450/p8C. It has an
average declination of 314 /p8and an average inclination /p148/p8
(/afii9825

age, but the declination implies a very large 134 /p8clockwise

component of magnetization with the highest unblocking

Dykes at site M2 were found to be unstable during thermal
demagnetization, and hence were generally demagnetized using
AF techniques, which isolated one or two components of
remanence. The higher coercivity component has a inclination
that is steeper than expected and a NW declination. In the

some indication that the ChRM is, in fact, an intermediate

temperatures above 450 /p8C, appears to be oriented SE and

The remainder of the sites that produced interpretable data,
including sites, M6, M12 and M15 (Fig. 5f), have two com-
ponents of remanent magnetization. The low temperature
component either shows no clear direction or present-day
directions. The high temperature ChRM isolated above 400 /p8C
is oriented NW and up with an inclination that is signi ﬁcantly
shallower than the expected values.
Isothermal remanent magnetization
Thermal demagnetization of the three axis IRM was used to
characterize the magnetic minerals in these dyke rocks. IRM
acquisition experiments as shown in (Fig. 6) gave curves
highly suggestive of a ferromagnetic carrier. Complete satu-
ration at ﬁelds <0.5 T e ﬀectively rules out antiferromagnetic
carriers such as goethite and hematite, which saturate in
much higher ﬁelds. In detail, however, there is a suggestion
of an initial saturation between 0.1 –0.12 mT before the ﬁnal
saturation at 0.3 T suggesting the presence of two low
coercivity phases.
Thermal demagnetization of multicomponent IRM (Lowrie
1990) gives a much clearer indication of the magnetic minerals
present in the samples. Results show that most of the magnet-
ization resides in the intermediate (between 0.05 T and 0.2 T)
and low coercivity fractions (<0.05 T) (Fig. 6a). This suggests
that there is unlikely to be a signi ﬁcant amounts of high
coercivity magnetic minerals such as goethite or haematite in
these rocks. This result was corroborated by the thermal
demagnetization experiments (Fig. 6b). Instead, the most likely
remanence carriers are a mixture of both coarse and ﬁne
grained sulphide and magnetite with Curie temperature
between 300/p8C and 350/p8C and above 500/p8C respectively. It was
often noted, however, that in the thermal demagnetization
experiments (NRM) the intermediate temperature component
was not completely demagnetized at temperatures as high as

Discussion
The relationship between these data sets and an explanation in
terms of a history of deformation is not straightforward. The
main di ﬃculty is to explain the shallow inclination of the
high-temperature component of magnetization. This com-
ponent is most likely to be carried by magnetite with a
remanence acquired at the time of initial emplacement of the
dykes. Possible explanations for its orientation include: (a) that
the region lay at low latitudes, where the magnetic ﬁeld is
gently inclined, at the time this magnetic component was
acquired; (b) that a gently-dipping magnetic fabric was
imposed on the dykes during deformation; (c) that the dykes
have been tilted subsequent to magnetization.
During the late Oligocene, southern Iberia lay close to its
present latitude and therefore the dykes would be expected to
have an inclination of approximately 50 /p8(Westphal et al.
1986). This e ﬀectively rules out the ﬁrst possibility.
The second possibility is that a magnetic fabric resulting
from penetrative deformation associated with the formation of
the fabric in the surrounding schists may have caused the
inclination in the dykes to be shallower than expected. To
explore this possibility both the anisotropy of susceptibility
(AMS) and the anisotropy of magnetic remanence of the dykes
were measured. AMS measures the anisotropy of all magnetic
minerals in the rock. These include the remanence-carrying
minerals but also other paramagnetic minerals such as micas
and amphiboles. Results of this work yielded an aniso-
tropy factor of less then 1% implying that there is no preferred
orientation of the magnetic minerals in the dyke rocks. In
contrast to AMS, anisotropy of magnetic remanence (Jackson
1991) examines the preferred orientation of the remanence-
carrying minerals only. Results of this work show that there is
as much as 22% anisotropy in the orientation of the remanence
carrying minerals. The shape and orientation of the anisotropy
ellipise indicate that this fabric, is primarily a planar fabric
(foliation, 19.6%) oriented sub-parallel to the dyke. The direc-
tion of the maximum anisotropy is steeply dipping oriented
sub-parallel to the dip of the dyke (80 /p8to 174) and the
minimum anisotropy is sub-horizontal ( /p110/p8). This fabric is
therefore unlikely to be associated with either the gently
dipping fabric in the surrounding schists or the de ﬂection of
the remanence vector into the horizontal. The simplest inter-
pretion of the observed preferred orientation is that it is a ﬂow
fabric imposed at high temperatures as the dykes were intruded
into the country rock.
The third possible explanation for the shallow inclination of
the high temperature component of magnetization is that the
dykes were rotated about horizontal axes after magnetization.

explain the shallow inclination by simple tilting of the dykes
about an east–west axis parallel to their trend would require a
tilt towards the north of about 70 /p8(assuming an original 50 /p8
plunge for the remanence, appropriate for a Oligocene age for
the dykes). This would imply that the dykes, now essentially
vertical, were intruded with a regionally consistent dip of 10/p8N,
which is geologically unlikely. A tilt of this magnitude should
also produce a detectable di ﬀerence in the grade of metamor-
phism of the country rocks: over a north –south distance of
20 km a 70 /p8tilt would produce a di ﬀerence in the depth of
burial at the present surface of 19 km, which would correspond
to a pressure di ﬀerence of about 5 kbar, and a likely tempera-
ture di ﬀerence of 500 /p8C or more. No such di ﬀerence in the
pressure or temperature of metamorphism in the country
rock is detectable. Domino-style rotation on closely spaced
faults could produce tilting without such large di ﬀerences in
metamorphic grade. The only set of structures we have found
that could produce such an e ﬀect is the SW-dipping set of
normal faults. The mean dip of these structures (32 /p8) suggests
that they have not experienced more than 30 /p8of tilt, and the
slip vector on these faults (36 /p8to 214) is nearly normal to the
sub-horizontal remanence, so that slip and rotation on
these faults could not explain the present attitude of the
remanence.
Tilting about a NNE–SSW horizontal axis could provide an
acceptable solution to the problem, as it would produce little
change in the orientation of the dykes, but would alter the
orientation of the high-temperature component of remanence.
We have somewhat arbitrarily chosen a rotation axis trending
025/p8(parallel to the strike of the regional foliation) to illustrate
this, but we emphasize that any approximately NNE-trending
rotation axis would work as well. Correction for a tilt to the
WNW of 34/p8about an axis trending 025 /p8gives a tilt-corrected
magnetization of /p143/p8/329/p8, /afii9825
95=10/p8(reversed polarity) for
the high-temperature component, which is statistically indis-
tinguishable at the 95% con ﬁdence level from the intermediate
temperature component ( /p148/p8/314/p8, /afii9825
95=10/p8). The tilt-
corrected orientation for the dykes is 87 /p8/003/p8. This solution
also produces less of a problem in terms of variations in the
exposure level: an overall tilt in the Malaguide Complex to the
WNW is reasonable in view of the exposure of unmetamor-
phosed Mesozoic rocks and Tertiary ﬂysch to the west, and
of the underlying metamorphosed rocks of the Alpujarride
Complex to the east (Fig. 1).
An interesting consequence of the proposed tilt-correction is
that it suggests that the main foliation in the rocks was
subhorizontal before tilting, with a tilt-corrected stretching
lineation trending 346 /p8. The age and tectonic signi ﬁcance of
these fabrics is uncertain, but if the foliation was originally
subhorizontal it may be Alpine in age, and re ﬂect the ductile
phase of late-orogenic extension. The ﬁnite extension direction
indicated by the lineation is consistent with the extension
direction indicated by the dykes.
Turning this argument around and assuming that the
original foliation was horizontal it is possible to correct the
magnetic remanences by rotating them about a local horizon-
tal axis de ﬁned by the local strike of the foliation (tectonic
correction). In the area sampled, there is considerable vari-
ation in the orientation of the schistosity (Table 3) and
consequently the amount of rotation will vary from site to
site. Results of this exercise show that the mean orientation
of the high temperature remanence ( /p146/p8to 337 /p8)i sn o t
signiﬁcantly changed from the direction obtained by the bulk
rotation. However, the /afii9825
95 and the precision parameter
(/afii982595=5, /afii9837=87.1) are signi ﬁcantly improved even using the
most stringent conditions (McElhinny 1964). The angular
dispersion (10 /p8) is, in fact, somewhat less then might be
predicted from models of secular variation (15 /p8) (McFadden
et al . 1991). It is therefore possible that because a relatively
low proportion of the dykes gave useful results, we have not
adequately averaged out secular variation. Given that we
have sampled at least one reversal, however, it is equally
possible that Oligocene secular variation is somewhat smaller
then expected.
A reversal test (McFadden & McElhinny 1990) on the HT
component before tectonic correction yields an angle of 26 /p8
between the mean directions of the normal and reverse obser-
vations and is therefore negative. After tectonic correction,
however, this angle becomes 10 /p8, well within the /afii9825
95 level of
conﬁdence to give a positive Class C reversal test. The positive
fold test and reversal test imply that the magnetization is more
likely to have been acquired when the foliation was horizontal
than in its present orientation. It is interesting to note that if
we correct the data in this way the declination of the HT
component after correction becomes signi ﬁcantly di ﬀerent
from the IT component. This implies that there was 23 /p8/p515/p8
clockwise rotation of this unit between the acquisition of the
HT component at 30 Ma and the IT component at 18 Ma. This
rotation would therefore have occurred during the extensional
phase of tectonics in the Alboran domain.
Vertical axis rotation of about 134 /p8clockwise took place
after the acquisition of the intermediate temperature rema-
nence. This is carried by pyrrhotite, and could either be a
thermal remanence associated with the peak metamorphic
temperatures, or it could be a chemical remanence acquired as
the pyrrhotite grew above a critical size during the alteration.
The fairly uniform alteration of the dykes is consistent with
metamorphism under greenschist-facies conditions, and is
most plausibly explained in terms of emplacment into the
country rock phyllites before or during the regional meta-
morphism. The lack of ductile deformation in the dykes, and
the fact that they cut the main foliation, however, suggests
that they were emplaced late in the metamorphic history,
after the ductile deformation, but possibly before the thermal
peak, which produced the late andalusite and biotite porphy-
roblasts. This therefore leaves open the possibility that the
magmatic event caused or was associated with the thermal
peak.
The orientations discussed above for the foliation,
lineation, dykes, and the tilt axis must all be corrected for
the vertical axis rotation, giving the following values:
foliation— subhorizontal; lineation trend — 188/p8; dykes 87 /p8/
206/p8; tilt axis — 228/p8.
Brittle normal faulting postdates the dykes and the meta-
morphic event, and therefore probably postdates acquisition of
the secondary remanence. We cannot establish the relative
timing of brittle faulting and vertical-axis rotation. However,
in view of the coincidence between the uncorrected extension
direction indicated by the normal faults (034/p8) and the partially
corrected (Fig. 6c) extension direction indicated by both the
dykes (049/p8) and the stretching lineation (031/p8), it is tempting to
suggest that the rotation occurred between the ductile
and brittle phases of extension. Given the existence of large
clockwise vertical-axis rotations in the immediately adjacent
External Zones, however, we suggest that the most plausible

explanation for the post-IT vertical-axis rotation is that they
were acquired during the thrust emplacement of the periphery
of the Alboran Domain onto the Iberian margin, and therefore
post-date the main period of extensional tectonics within the
Alboran Domain. If this suggestion is correct, the direction of
extension implied by the brittle faults must be corrected for
134/p8of vertical-axis rotation, giving an original orientation of
078/p8.
Conclusions
We suggest the following sequence of events to explain the
present structural geometry and palaeomagnetic data in the
Malaguide Complex around Malaga (Fig. 7).
Following Alpine contractional tectonics at an uncertain
time in the Late Cretaceous to early Oligocene interval, the
main foliation formed in a subhorizontal orientation in
response to the start of late orogenic extension, while the lower
unit was still at su ﬃcient depth, and hence temperature, to
deform by ductile processes. This conclusion must be regarded
as speculative.
Intrusion of vertical NW –SE-trending dykes took place
over a period of time between 23 Ma and 30 Ma (Oligocene),
at which time they acquired the high-temperature magnetic
remanence upon cooling through the blocking temperature
of magnetite. The dating of dyke intrusion is subject to
considerable uncertainty, but the original orientation of the
dykes is reasonably well constrained by the data. The exten-
sion direction during dyke emplacement was 206 /p8, sub-
parallel to the ﬁnite extension direction of 188 /p8during the
ductile deformation.
After intrusion of the dykes, but before they acquired the
intermediate-temperature remanence, the region was rotated
23/p515/p8about a vertical axis and tilted to the south by
approximately 35 /p8about a horizontal axis trending about
251/p8.
The peak temperature of greenschist-facies metamorphism is
likely to have occurred after dyke emplacement, producing
post-tectonic andalusite and biotite in the country rocks, and
the greenschist-facies assemblages in the dykes.
Acquisition of the intermediate-temperature remanence
in the dykes occurred during the greenschist-facies meta-
morphism, or during cooling at the end of the period of
metamorphism and alteration.
Brittle normal faulting took place after the greenschist-facies
metamorphism, probably during the early Miocene. This ﬁnal
phase of extension may be re ﬂected by the cooling age of
18 Ma. The extension direction during this phase was probably
east–west (079/p8).
Vertical-axis rotation through a clockwise angle of 134/p8took
place after the greenschist-facies metamorphism, and probably
after the end of brittle normal faulting. This may have been

Paleomagnetism and geochronology of the Late Cretaceous- 
Paleogene island arc complex of the Kronotsky Peninsula, 
Kamchatka, Russia' Kinematic implications 
Natalia M. Levashova 
Geological Institute, Russian Academy of Sciences, Moscow 
Mikhail N. Shapiro 
United Institute of Physics of the Earth, Russian Academy of Sciences, Moscow 
Vladimir N. Beniamovsky, and Mikhail L. Bazhenov 
Geological Institute, Russian Academy of Sciences, Moscow' 
Abstract. The remnants of ancient island arcs are exposed in the 
Achayvayam-Valagina and East Peninsulas tectonic zones of the 
Olutor-Kamchatka region, northeast Russia. Geochemically, Late 
Cretaceous to Paleogene island arc complexes of the East Penin- 
sulas zone are similar to intraoceanic island arcs, and the East 
Peninsulas zone is regarded as the extinct Kronotsky island arc. 
Paleomagnetic and biostratigraphic studies of Late Cretaceous and 
Paleogene island arc rocks were carried out at 21 sites in the east- 
ern part of the Kronotsky Peninsula, which belongs to the East 
Peninsulas zone. Characteristic remanent magnetizations of both 
polarities isolated from most sites pass reversal and fold tests; the 
Cretaceous result is also supported by a positive conglomerate test 
on lava boulders from an intraformational conglomerate. Mean 
inclinations of Late Cretaceous, Ypresian and Bartonian rocks 
correspond to paleolatitudes of 44.8 ø + 8.0øN, 38.6 ø + 3.5øN, and 
45.1 ø + 7.0øN, respectively. I'hese values are-20 ø lower than the 
corresponding reference values for the North American plate tbr 
the Cretaceous and Ypresian and -14 ø lower for the Bartonian. 
Therefore northward transport of the Kronotsky island arc is indi- 
cated. Kinematic evolution of the Kronotsky island arc in the Late 
Cretaceous-Paleogene was reconstructed using published kine- 
matic parameters. In addition, we incorporated into analysis the 
geological and published paleomagnetic data for the Late Creta- 
ceous and Tertiary island arc complexes of the Cape Kamchatka 
Peninsula from the East Peninsulas zone and the Late Cretaceous 
island-arc complexes of the Achayvayam-Valagina zone. As a re- 
sult, two alternative scenarios of kinematic evolution for the Kro- 
notsky island arc are proposed. According to both of them, the 
Kronotsky island arc was moving with the continental plate in 
Late Cretaceous time and with the Pacific plate from the begin- 
ning of the Paleocene until docking with the Eurasian margin in 
Miocene-Pliocene time. 
1. Introduction 
The territory between the Siberian platform and Pacific Ocean 
comprises numerous tectonic units of various origins and ages

(Figure la). Currently, popular tectonic models ascribe the growth 
of the northwest Pacific continental margin to accretion and colli- 
sion of allochthonous crustal fragments (tectonostratigraphic ter- 
ranes). The Olutor-Kamchatka region in particular is thought to be 
composed of a number of such terranes [Watson and Fujita, 1985; 
Zmkevich and Tsukanov, 1992]. Most of these terranes include 
Late Cretaceous to Paleogene volcanic rocks of island arc affinity 
and are regarded as accreted remnants of island arcs. However, 
the number of the island arcs and their original positions and sub- 
sequent kinematics are uncertain and therefore.controversial [Ko- 
nonov, 1989; Zonenshain et al., 1990; Geist et al., 1994]. 
Combined geological and paleomagnetic studies make it possi- 
ble to reconstruct the configuration of convergent boundaries for 
various periods of time and hence to test the alternative paleo- 
geographic and kinematic scenarios. This seems to be a topic of 
major importance as the uncertainties in plate boundary locations 
may result in discrepancies between the observed geological data 
and plate motion models. Therefore new information on the tec- 
tonic evolution of northeast Asia may affect the views on plate 
kinematics of the entire Pacific. 
The remnants of the ancient intraoceanic island arcs are found 
in the Achayvayam-Valagina and East Peninsulas tectonic zones 
of the Olutor-Kamchatka region (Figures lb and l c). In order to 
reconstruct the kinematics of these ancient island arcs one should 
know the interval of volcanic activity of each arc, the ages of is- 
land arc collision with the continental margin, and the paleolati- 
tudes of each paleoarc at various times. The latter can be derived 
only from paleomagnetic data. Such data for the island arc com- 
plexes of the Achayvayam-Valagina zone, summarized by Le- 
vashova et al. [1998], indicate that these complexes had originally 
belonged to a single island arc which was >2000 km south from 
the continental margin, reaching its present position in early Terti- 
ary time. Paleocene and Eocene paleomagnetic data for the island 
arc complex from Cape Kamchatka, which belongs to the East 
Peninsulas zone, indicate intraoceanic transport of an active island 
arc over the distance of >2000 km [Pechersky et al., 1997]. These 
earlier publications, however, treated each tectonic zone sepa- 
rately and hence did not result in a consistent tectonic scenario for 
the entire Olutor-Kamchatka region.

Thrusts are regional faults, which divide the Olutor-Kamchatka 
region into four main tectonic zones of the northeastern strike. 
These are, from the west to the east, the West Kamchatka-Uke- 
layat zone, the Achayvayam-Valagina zone (AVZ), the Vetlov 
zone and the East Peninsulas zone (EPZ) (Figures lb and lc). 
The West Kamchatka-Ukelayat zone comprises strongly de- 
formed sediments that accumulated on the continental slope [Sha- 
piro, 1976]. These sediments are of Campanian-Maastrichtian and 
Late Cretaceous to early Eocene age in Kamchatka and the Olutor 
zone, respectively [Chekhovich et al., 1990]. Late Cretaceous 
rocks in Kamchatka are unconformably overlain by Paleogene to 
Neogene coal-bearing molass and shelf sediments with minor 
amounts of subaerial volcanic rocks. Terrigenous formations of 
the West Kamchatka-Ukelayat zone are separated from Cam- 
panian-Maastrichtian volcanosedimentary rocks of the AVZ by 
the gentle to moderately steep Lesnov Thrust having western ver- 
gence (Figure l c). The age of motions along this thrust becomes 
younger from south to north, occurring between the end of the 
Cretaceous to the beginning of the Paleogene in the southern part 
of the Median Range [Flerov and Koloskov, 1976] and to the Pa- 
leocene-middle Eocene on the Kamchatka Isthmus [Shantzer et 
al., 1985]. In the Olutor zone, movement along the thrust had 
stopped only by middle Miocene time [Chekhovich et al., 1990]. 
In the Achayvayam-Valagina zone to the east and southeast 
from the Lesnov thrust, most of the Late Cretaceous complexes 
are strongly deformed and cut by numerous faults. In the Olutor 
zone these complexes comprise Albian-Campanian mid-ocean 
ridge basalt and chert and Campanian-Maastrichtian tuffs and lava 
of island arc affinity [Kazimirov et al., 1987]. The Campanian- 
Maastrichtian rocks are thought to be an island arc, while the A1- 
bian-Campanian series constitutes the oceanic basement of this 
arc [Chekhovich et al., 1990]. In Kamchatka most of the Late 
Cretaceous volcanoclastic complexes are exposed in the Median 
Range, Eastern Ranges, and on Karaginsky Island (Figure lb). 
The Median Range and Eastern Ranges are separated by the sedi- 
ment-filled late Cenozoic Central Kamchatka basin. The island 
arc complexes are unconformably overlain by Eocene to Oligo- 
cene marine sediments and Miocene to Quaternary volcanic rocks. 
In the Eastern Ranges, however, the island arc rocks are overlain 
conformably and with a gradual transition by middle-upper Paleo- 
cene terrigenous flysch. A continent-derived material is absent 
altogether in volcanic rocks; in contrast, volcanic material of is- 
land arc affinity is very scarce in the flysch [Bakhteev et al., 
1994]. Geochemically, the Late Cretaceous volcanoclastic com- 
plexes of the entire AVZ are similar to volcanic rocks of intraoce- 
anic island arcs such as the Tonga arc [Zinkevich et al., 1993]. 
These complexes were assumed to originally belong to the single 
Achayvayam-Valagina island arc (AVIA) [Zinkevich and Tzuka- 
nov, 1992]. This hypothesis was confirmed by paleomagnetic data 
on the island arc complexes of the entire AVZ [Levashova et al., 
1998]. 
The steep Vetlov Thrust separates the AVZ and Vetlov zone, 
which consists of Paleocene to Eocene siliceous and terrigenous 
sediments with some lenses of MORB-type basalts, pelagic cherts 
and limestones; at least a part of these lenses belongs to chaotic 
complexes [Tsukanov, 1991; Bakhteev et al., 1994]. Some cherts 
contain Late Cretaceous radiolaria. The Vetlov zone is strongly 
deformed and cut by numerous steep thrusts of eastern vergence. 
This zone is regarded as an accretionary prism [Zinkevich and 
Tstkanov, 1992] which was formed after the AVIA had docked 
with the continental margin and the Oligocene-Miocene subduc- 
tion-related volcanic activity had commenced in central Kam- 
chatka (Figure lb).

Cretaceous basalts and tuffs of island arc affinity are found in a 
limited part of the Kronotsky Peninsula (Figure 2). Paleogene ba- 
salts are widespread on the Kronotsky Peninsula and very similar 
to those from Cape Kamchatka [Khubunaya, 1987]. All basalts 
are of island arc affinity; MORB-type and intraplate basalts are 
unknown here. Irrespective of their age, high-alumnium pla- 
giotholeiites from the EPZ resemble plagioclase-porphyric 
tholelites from the Tonga, Kermadec, and other island intraoce- 
anic arcs [Khubunaya, 1987; Puzankov, 1994]. Paleogene rocks of 
the EPZ are significantly different from contemporaneous rocks of 
the other tectonic units of Kamchatka, where lower Eocene rocks 
are mainly siliceous and middle to upper Eocene rocks are terri- 
genous. On the whole, the EPZ is regarded as the extinct Kronot- 
sky island arc [Zinkevich and Tsukanov, 1992]. Although Late 
Cretaceous and Paleogene island arc complex is deformed every- 
where in the EPZ, the age of deformation is poorly constrained 
owing to a lack of overlying well-dated rocks. In particular, fold- 
ing on the Kronotsky Peninsula is older than Pliocene. 
The EPZ is separated from the Kamchatka mainland by the 
Tushev basin filled with upper Eocene to Miocene terrigenous 
sediments that are best exposed to the south of the Kronotsky 
Peninsula. The steep Grechishkin Thrust of eastern vergence

1997]. This thrust and conjugate folds in the Tushev basin are

Middle Eocene deformation affected almost all of Kamchatka, 
with only minor deformation occurring in the Miocene and Plio-

age in the Tushev basin. Paleocene-Eocene island arc volcanics 
are abundant in the EPZ, but very scarce inland. Widespread Oli-

AVZ, and similar Pliocene-Quaternary volcanism is mainly lim- 
ited to east Kamchatka (Figure lb). 
3. Geological Setting and Sampling 
Paleogene volcanic rocks on the Kronotsky Peninsula are 
weakly deformed, constituting a regional westward dipping ho- 
mocline cut by numerous faults with small conjugate folds. Late 
Cretaceous rocks are limited to the northeastern part of the Penin- 
sula and are more deformed; for instance, these strata form an an- 
ticline with the partly overturned northern limb at locality M (Fig- 
ure 2). Everywhere, Late Cretaceous and Paleogene rocks are 
separated by melange zones and/or faults with intense conjugated 
fblds. On the other hand, Late Cretaceous and Paleogene forma- 
tions are visibly very similar, and their subdivision is based on 
scarce fauna, thus making unclear the exact relationship between 
Late Cretaceous and Paleogene rocks. 
The oldest part of the Late Cretaceous section (lower member 
of the Cape Kamenisty Formation [Raznitsyn et al., 1985]) is 
composed of basalt flows up to several tens of meters thick inter- 
calated with layered coarse- to fine-grained tuffs and conglomer- 
ates with abundant lava boulders indicating shallow water accu- 
mulation for these rocks. Fine-grained varieties are finely strati- 
fied, without traces of slumping. All contacts of this member with 
other formations are faulted. These rocks form an anticline and 
are locally intruded by small diabase bodies of unknown age. At 
the limbs of this fold (locality M; Figure 2), 105 oriented hand 
samples were collected from volcanoclastic rocks (seven sites) 
and pillow lava (five sites). In addition, 18 lava boulders from an 
intraformational conglomerate were collected for the conglomer- 
ate test. According to radiolaria found at the section base (Or- 
biculiforma quadrata, Orbiculiforma cf vacaensis, Archaeospon- 
goprunum sp. (sp 1, sp 2, sp 3), Prunobrachiurn ex gr. sibericum, 
Lithocampe aff eligantissima, Dictyocephalus sp., and Archae- 
dictyomitra sp.), these rocks are of Coniacian-early Campanian 
age [Tsukanov, 1991]. Later, new radiolaria found in the tuf- 
fhceous rocks of the same section (Porodiscus cretaceous Clark et 
Campbell, Amphibrachium sibericum Gorbovetst, Prunobrachium 
sibericun (Lipman), P. cf crassum (Lipman), Spongurus sp., Sty- 
losphaerrs cf pussilla (Campbell et Clark), Staurodictya fresno- 
ensts Foreman. Prtoxiphotractus sp., Archaeodictyomitra regina 
(Campbell et Clark), Dictyomitra striata Lipman, D. multicostata 
Zittel gr., and Amphipyndax cf alamedaensis (Campbell et Clark) 
(M. Boyarinova, unpublished data, 1997) and Orbiculiforma 
renillaeformis Pessagno, Amphibrachiurn cf rnucronaturn Lip- 
main, Spongrurus sp., Prunopyle sp., Prunobrachium incisum 
Koslova, P cf longurn Pessagno, Dictyomitra lamellicostata 
Foreman, Strictomitra manifesta Foreman, and Amphipyndax 
stocki (Campbell et Clark) (V. Vishnevskaya, unpublished data, 
1996)) indicate a Campanian-Maastrichtian age for the section. 
The upper member of the Cape Kamenisty Formation [Raznit- 
syn et al., 1985], exposed at locality N (Figure 2), is cut by nu- 
merous fhults. Twenty-five samples were collected from the 200 
m thick section of pillow lava (site N 1) and tuffs (site N2). Poorly 
preserved radiolaria (Orbiculiforrna renillaeforurnis, Arnphibra- 
chium cf mucronatum, Prunobrachium? incisum, Spongurus sp., 
and Prunopyle sp.) indicate a Maastrichtian-Paleocene age for the 
tuffaceous rocks [Tsukanov, 1991]. However, an Ar/Ar determi- 
nation on a single sample of pillow lava (P. Renne, unpublished 
data, 1996) indicates an age of-80 Ma (early Campanian). On the 
whole, the age of the rocks studied at localities M and N is most 
likely Campan ian-Maastrichtian. 
Eocene volcanoclastic rocks underlain by basal conglomerates 
and pillow lava form a gentle syncline at locality O (Figure 2). 
The upper part of this section was studied by Bazhenov et al. 
[1992]; for this study, twenty-nine oriented hand samples were 
collected from pillow lava at four sites. Planktonic foraminifera 
(Subbotina aequiensis, S. aff contorta, S. cf nana, S. aff incisa, 
and S. ex gr. achtschacujmensis) at the base of the sedimentary 
section at locality O (Figure 2) can be correlated with the early 
Ypresian (early Eocene) zone Morozovella wilcoxensi which has 
been recognized in other sections of the West Pacific [Beniamov- 
skT et al., 1992; Volobueva et al., 1994]. A few meters above, an- 
other complex of planktonic foraminifera (Subbotina inaeq- 
uispira, S. pseudoeocaena pseudoeocaena, S. cf eocaenica, and 
Globanimalina (Pseudohastigerina) wilcoxensis) is similar to the 
Globanomalina (Pseudohastegerina) wilcoxensis zone in upper 
lower Ypresian to lower Lutetian (middle Eocene) rocks of the 
western North Pacific [Beniamovsky et al., 1992; Beniamovsky 
and Gladenkov, 1996]. Still a few meters higher, a rich complex 
of foraminifera (Subbotina inaequispira, S. pseudoeocaena pseu- 
doeocaena, Pseudohastigerina wilcoxensis, Subbotina boweri, S. 
linaperta, S. peudoeocaena compacta, S. posttriloculinoides, S. 
eocaenica irregularis, Pseudohastigerina micra, Acarinina cf 
bullbrooki, and A. broedermanni) belongs to the Subbotina boweri 
zone and indicates a middle Lutetian age for this horizon. The 
three zones mentioned above comprise the lower 10-13 m of the 
section. According to the foraminifera (Subbotina praebulloides, 
S ncretacea, S. galavasi ,S. tripartita, Catapsidrax dissimilis, 
and Acarinma rugosoaculeata), the upper part of the section be- 
longs to the Subbotina praebulloides zone of Bartonian (late Eo- 
cene) age that is well known in east Kamchatka [Beniamovsky et 
al., 1992; Beniamovsky and Gladenkov, 1996]. 
Thus the sediments at locality O cover the interval from the 
early Ypresian to Bartonian, which is in agreement with the avail- 
able nannoplankton data [Shcherbinina, 1997]. The first three 
zones, however, comprise <15 m of the section, whereas the Bar- 
tonian part is several tens of meters thick. Therefore the main part 
of the collection of Bazhenov et al. [1992], who mainly sampled 
the middle and upper parts of the sedimentary sequence at this lo- 
cality, is of Bartonian age (ca. 40 + 2 Ma), whereas the section 
base and underlying basalts are older. Thus the basalts are proba- 
bly not younger than 56-53 Ma. In sharp contrast to these data is 
the Ar/Ar determination on a single basalt sample of-40 Ma (P. 
Renne, unpublished data, 1996).

4. Paleolnagnetic Study 
4.1. Methods 
The thicknesses of the outcrops (sites) studied vary from sev- 
eral meters to several tens of meters (Tables 1 and 2), and samples 
were distributed more or less uniformly across the outcrop. One 
hand sample oriented with a magnetic compass was taken at each 
stratigraphic level. One to two cubic specimens from each hand 
sample were subjected to progressive thermal demagnetization in 
12-18 steps up to 610øC. One specimen was thermally demagnet- 
ized in a homemade oven with internal residual fields of-10 nT 
and rneasured with a JR-4 spinner magnetometer having a noise 
level of 0.05 mA/m in the Paleomagnetic Laboratory of the Geo- 
logical Institute in Moscow. Some duplicate specimens were 
thermally demagnetized in a multishield furnace and measured 
with a cryogenic magnetometer in a nonmagnetic room in the Pa- 
leomagnetic Laboratory of the Institut de Physique du Globe in 
Paris. Duplicate specimens from some basalt samples were sub- 
,jected to alternating field demagnetization with a 2G cryogenic 
magnetometer in the Paris Laboratory. Anisotropy of magnetic 
susceptibility (AMS) was measured with the aid of a kappa-bridge 
KLY-2. Demagnetization results were plotted on orthogonal vec- 
tor diagrams [Zijderveld, 1967], and linear trajectories were used 
to determine directions of magnetic components by a least squares 
fit comprising three measurements or more [Kirschvink, 1980]. 
The characteristic remanent magnetization (ChRM) was deter- 
mined without anchoring the final linear segments to the origin of 
the vector diagrams. Components isolated from the sister speci- 
mens of a hand sample were used to calculate the sample means, 
which were in turn used to calculate site means. 
4.2. Results 
4.2.1. Late Cretaceous rocks. Pillow basalt and tuffaceous 
rocks at locality M are strongly magnetized, with intensities of 
natural remanent magnetization (NRM) ranging from 1.63 to 71.9 
A/m in the basalts and from 0.11 to 11.4 A/m in the sediments. A 
single ChRM was isolated from most lava samples above 200 ø 
(Figure 3a); in just a few samples, a low-temperature overprint 
persisted up to 400 ø (Figure 3b). Some tuff samples also had a 
single ChRM above 2000-300 ø (Figure 3c), whereas another 
component is present at low to intermediate temperatures in many 
samples (Figures 3d and 3e). This intermediate-temperature 
component has a direction statistically indistinguishable from the 
ChRM direction in stratigraphic coordinates but is much more 
scattered. Although represented by linear segments on 
demagnetization plots, this component is likely to result from 
partial overlap of unblocking spectra of a recent overprint and the 
ChRM. Some samples, after a sharp initial drop in NRM intensity, 
showed erratic behavior above 350ø-400øC and were rejected. 
Unblocking temperatures for most samples between 550 ø and 
580 ø indicate that magnetite is the main remanence carrier (Figure 
3). Magnetizations of both polarities were found, and an up- 
section R-N-R-N succession of polarity zones was identified (R 
indicates reversed, and N indicates normal).

The NRM in the basalt boulders is mainly accounted for by a 
single component showing linear decay to the origin, similar to

ChRM directions are randomly distributed (Figure 4c), yielding

the 95% critical limit of 0.377 [Mardia, 1972]. 
Thus the ChRM in Late Cretaceous rocks passes the fold test, 
and its normal and reversed directions are nearly antipodal. The 
conglomerate test is also positive for the rocks from locality M. 
Relatively thick stratigraphic intervals studied at the accepted 
sites, the tight grouping of tilt-corrected site means (Figure 4b, 
and Table 1), and the presence of several polarity zones testify to 
adequate averaging of geomagnetic secular variation. Close 
agreement of ChRM directions in the lava flows and sediments 
indicates that no inclination error is present. At some sites we 
sampled well-stratified fine-grained tuffaceous rocks which most 
likely would not accumulate on a tilted surface. Therefore the 
ChRM in the Late Cretaceous rocks is most probably primary and 
a reliable record of the ancient geomagnetic field.

5. Summary of Paleomagnetic and Rock 
Ages Data 
In most samples, radiolaria indicate a Campanian-Maastrich- 
tian age tbr the rocks at locality M. However, some of the samples 
were dated as Coniacian-early Campanian. Paleomagnetic study 
revealed an R-N-R-N polarity sequence (from bottom to top) at 
locality M; thus at least two zones of normal and two of reversed 
polarity are present here. The upper boundary of the Cretaceous 
normal superchron at ca. 83 Ma coincides with the Santonian- 
Campanian boundary [Cande and Kent, 1992], and the pre-Cam- 
panian age of the studied section can be excluded. Moreover, 
there are only one reversed and one normal polarity chrons in 
Campanian time [Cande and Kent, 1992], and it is unlikely that 
the 200 m thick studied section of intercalated lava flows, con- 
glomerates, and tuffs encompasses the two oldest long R and N 
polarity zones in the Campanian (ca. 8 Ma). We think that the ob- 
served R-N-R-N polarity sequence is probably not older than 
early Maastrichtian (anomaly 32, 72-74 Ma) when shorter polarity 
zones occurred. Therefore we infer the age of the section to be 
late Campanian-Maastrichtian or even Maastrichtian. 
Poorly preserved radiolaria imply a Maastrichtian-Paleocene 
age for the rocks at locality N. An Ar/Ar age for basalt from the 
lower part of the section is -80 Ma. However, all ChRM direc-
