In the reversed polarity samples (fig. 7B) progressive alternating field demagnetization also indicated the presence of two or three components of magnetization. A variety of low coercivity normal components with a west or northeast and down direction were easily removed at low fields up to 20 mT. The stable higher coercivity compónent was usually well isolated above 20 mT. The majority of these samples revealed a characteristic remanent magnetization of dominantly south to southwest and shallow up directions, though with slightly steeper inclinations than the normal polarity samples. The variations in coercivities as shown by the stability diagrams (fig. 8, 5-1-2 and 7-2-2) indicate variations in grain size and textures of the magnetic carriers, titanomagnetite, titanomaghemite, and fine-grained skeletal magnetites. The titanomaghemite and the fine-grained skeletal magnetites produced by the olivine probably contribute to the high-coercivity component.

These unblocking temperatures are consistent with a magnetite component of Usp2o-o. As shown on the stability diagrams (fig. 10) a small remanence persisted above 585°C, the unblocking temperature of pure magnetite. This component is less than 4 percent of the original magnetization and may be due to titanomaghemite and hematite lamellae in the ilmenites present in some samples. The remanent magnetization directions obtained from thermal demagnetization studies are consistent with those from the alternating field decay procedures.

Magnetic site directions.—Table 2 contains a summary of the mean magnetic directions and statistical parameters determined for the eleven sites. Fisher statistics (Fisher, 1953) were applied to the data to obtain site mean directions at the 95 percent confidence level. The normal and reversed directions are not êxactly antipodal (see below) and are distinguishable at the 95 percent confidence level. The mean directions of the normal and reversed polarity sites are D = 7.0°, I = 9.2°, a95 = 2.7°, and D = 203.7°, I = −15.0°, a95 = 3.5°, respectively. The overall mean directions for the normal and reversed dikes would not change appreciably even if the excluded samples were used in the mean calculation. After inverting the reversed data a combined direction was calculated of D = 13.4°, I = 11.5°, a95 = 5.4°. The mean study paleoinclination yielded a paleolatitude of 5.8°. It should be noted that the normal and reversed data form two well clustered groups having small ag5's for both within and between sites calculations. The smaller agg's for the separate normal and reversed data sets as compared to the overall mean may indicate that paleosecular variation was not completely averaged out.

The in-situ remanent magnetic directions determined for the samples from the eleven sites are plotted on an equal-area diagram in figure 11. The within-site dispersion is minor, and the between-site scatter is low in each polarity group. The reversed and normal directions are not antipodal at the 95 percent confidence level (McFadden'and Lowes, 1981) as graphically shown in figure 12. The lack of complete antipodality might be explained in three ways:

1. The most plausible explanation is that dikes were intruded at two significantly different times. Éach group could have intruded and cooled quickly representing a short sampling of the geomagnetic field with paleosecular variation not completely averaged out, as indicated by the low between-site scatter. The time between the intrusions of the normal and reversed dikes could have been short, on the scale of 104 or 10⁵ yrs. The slightly different geochemistry and petrography of the normal and reversed díkes also support different intrusive events.

2. The lack of antipodality might be due to an unremoved contaminating component, either of viscous or chemical origin. Such a component should lie somewhere along the great circle joining the two directions. The trend and plunge of this great circle is N6°W, 30°NE, so that the contaminating component would have had a maximum plunge of 30°. Such a shallow plunge could not have been produced by a viscous remanence from a present-ield overprint. Alternatively, the dikes could have originally been antipodal and suffered a post-intrusion remagnetization of chemical nature (CRM). Because there is slightly more dispersion in the data from the reversed dikes than the normal dikes, it appears that they might have been more affected by a CRM. In some of the polished cores from the reversed dikes a small percent of titanomaghemite was observed. If, at a later time, some titanomagnetite in the reversed dikes was altered to titanomaghemite, producing a new chemical remanent magnetization, then a highly coercive component would be produced, which would not be removed either by a strong alternating field or by thermal demagnetization prior to the removal of the original thermal remanent magnetization carried by titanomagnetite. Because approx 96 percent of the magnetization is carried by titanomagnetite or magnetite, such a proposed alteration component could not be solely responsible for the lack of antipodality of the paleomagnetic directions, though the final direction would still be a mixture of the two components. In this case the normal and reversed dikes could be temporally associated but fail the reversal test due to a later CRM alteration in the reversed dikes. The alteration to titanomaghemite in the reversed dikes does appear to be deuteric in nature. If this had occurred at a time when the geomagnetic field contained a standing nonaxial component, then other late Triassic coeval paleomagnetic studies should show a similar lack of antipodality. There is evidence for lack of antipodality in the Newark red beds in New Jersey (Witte and Kent, 1990).

3. The possibility of a stable remanent magnetic direction obtained through self-reversal of an ilmenite has been discussed by Nord and Lawson (1992). It is highly unlikely in this case due to the composition of these ilmenites (McEnroe, ms) and the fact that the mechanism of self-reversal requires a very rapid'chill from high temperature.

Pole position.—The virtual geomagnetic poles (VGP) obtained from this study are given in table 2. The mean pole position for the dikes of normal polarity is 52.7°N, 97.1°E (dp = 1.4, dm = 2.7), similar to the Carnian-Norian paleopole for the Newark sediments, 53.6°N, 101.6°E, a95 = 4.8° (Witte and Kent, 1990). The Rhode Island normal paleopole with its 95 percent confidence circle overlaps the May and Butler (1986) Apparent Polar Wander Path for North America (fig. 13) and is similar to the Carnian synthetic reference pole (54.6°N, 102.3°E) calculated by Gordon, Cox, and O'Hare (1984). The reversed dikes produce a paleopole at 50.2°N, 70.2°E (dp = 1.8, dm = 3.6). This is displaced in a southwesterly direction from the Late Triassic-Early Jurassic segment of the Apparent Polar Wander Path. This westward displacement of the reversed paleopole could be a result of secular variation of a longstanding nonaxial dipole component in the late Triassic field. If this displacement is a result of secular variation then it should be seen in other coeval studies. Other similar paleopoles are the Late Triassic (?)-Early Jurassic diabases from North Carolina with a paleopole 52.6°N, 60.2°E, a95 = 7.8° (Smith, 1987) which is statistically indistinguishable from the middle Norian Owl Rock Member of the Chinle Formation, 56.9°N, 73.6°E, a95 = 2.6° (Bazard and Butler, 1991). However, there does not seem to be enough evidence to attribute this displacement conclusively to secular variation.

The Rhode Island pole calculated using both the normal and reversed dikes is 52.6°N, 88.4°E (dp = 3.7°, dm = 7.3°) and is plotted on figure 13. This pole falls slightly southward of expected Late Triassic directions. However, at the 95 percent confidence level, it is statistically indistinguishable from other Late Triassic paleopoles, including Newark basin Hettangian red beds (RBH) at 55.5°N, 94.6°E (Witte and Kent, 1990), the Lower Fundy Group (LF) at 45.3°N, 97.1°E (Symons, Bormann, and Jans, 1989), the Abbott pluton (Ab) at 48.3°N, 92.3°E (Wu and Van der Voo, 1988) which is dated at 221 ± 2 (Foland and Faul, 1977), the Pogo Agie Formation (P) at 56°N, 96°E (Van der Voo and Grubbs, 1977), and the Upper Shale Member of the Chinle Formation (C) at 57.4°N, 87.8°E (Bazard and Butler, 1991). It also plots distinctly earlier than the pole obtained from detrital remanence in the earliest Jurassic red beds of the Deerfield Mesozoic basin (DRB, McEnroe and Brown, 1992), the Early Jurassic Holden\diabases in Massachusetts (H) (McEnroe, 1989), and the Seaward Point dike in Maine (SP) (S. A. McEnroe, unpublished data).

CONCLUSIONS

The Rhode Island dikes were intruded after the Permian Alleghanian orogeny but prior to the breakup of Pangaea. The Rhode Island dikes exhibit a primary magnetization àcquired in the Late Triassic. The majority of the magnetization in the Rhode Island diabases was acquired as a thermal remanent magnetization during the cooling of the dikes. Alternating field demagnetization was successful in removing secondary overprints in most samples and isolating the primary directions. Thermal demagnetization and reflected liġht-microscopy were used to interpret thermal unblocking temperature and stability. The majority of the magnetization is unblocked below the Curie temperature for magnetite. A very small component of the remánent magnetization obtained from the reversed polarity dikes may have been acquired as a later CRM by the formation of titanomaghemite, though this could as likely have occurred during deuteric alteration of the dikes. The combined normal and reversed pole calculated from the high unblocking temperature magnetization yields a paleopole of 52.6°N, 88.4°E and paleolatitude of 5.8°N, consistent, at the 95 percent confidence level, with other recently determined late Triassic poles.

The Rhode Island dikes differ in their geochemical signatures and petrology from the Jurassic Eastern North America diabases. The Late Triassic paleomagnetic age is in good agreement with the more alkalic within-plate chemical signatures obtained from these dikes. These even differ from the oldest members of the early Jurassic ENA diabases which are also characterized as within-plate tholeiites, and the paleomagnetic poles show that both groups were intruded prior to the breakup. of Pangaea. A progression toward more MORB-like tholeitiic signatures of the ÉNA diabases as shown on discriminant diagrams is observed for the two geochemically distinct Pelham-Loudville and Ware and correlative groups. These have paleopoles that plot at higher latitudes and after the J1 cusp, which may well represent the onset of spreading in the modern Atlantic.

Introduction
The geotectonic position of Iran with respect to the
Scytho-Turanian plate (Eurasia) in the north and the
Arabian plate (Gondwana) in the south is controver-
sial. Stöcklin (1974, 1977) concluded that during the
Palaeozoic Iran was an extension of the Arabian plat-
form, and thus a part of Gondwana, possibly bordered
by a Palaeo-Tethys in the north. These connections
were reversed in the Mesozoic, when Central Iran be-
came attached to the northern continent, but detached
from the Gondwana mother continent by the Neo-Te-
thys. Brunn (1976), however, believes that Iran has al-
ways been an integral part of Eurasia, whereas Takin
(1972) considers Central Iran to have been a microcon-
tinent which drifted between Gondwana and Eurasia.
New geological evidence (Davoudzadeh and
Schmidt 1982; Davoudzadeh and Weber-Diefenbach
1987) indicates that the North Iran suture which sepa-
rates the North Alborz range from the South Alborz
(Fig. l) is the major suture of the Palaeozoic Tethys,
separating the southern carbonate shelf from the Scy-
tho-Turanian active margin. The area north of the
North Iran suture was part of the Scytho-Turanian

294
plate during most of the Palaeozoic. The closing of the
Palaeo-Tethys was followed by the Hercynian orogeny
and was completed by the Early Cimmerian move-
ments in the Middle Triassic. In SW Iran the Zagros
belt is a major marginal basin of the Arabian plate. It is
limited to the NE by the Main Zagros Thrust (Neo-Te-
thyan suture).
Previous palaeomagnetic investigations in Iran
(Becker et al. 1973; Soffel et al. 1975, 1980, 1989, 1992;
Davoudzadeh et al. 1981; Soffel and Förster 1983, 1984;
Schmidt and Soffel 1983, 1984) were focussed on the
construction of the Apparent Polar Wander Path
(APWP) of the Central-East-Iran Microplate (CEIM).
Wensink (Wensink 1979, 1982, 1983; Wensink and Var-
ekamp 1980) also contributed to the palaeomagnetic
database for Iran. The most recent review on this sub-
ject has been published by Soffel et al. (1992), and all
previously published pole positions for the CEIM and
the Turan Plate are listed in Table 4. All data in con-
junction with the new results presented in this study
have been used for the reconstruction of the drift histo-
ry and rotations of the CEIM with respect to the neigh-
bouring tectonic units (e.g. the Turan Plate in the north
and Arabia in the south). The large differences be-
tween the APWP’s of the CEIM, Gondwana and the
Turan Plate were interpreted in terms of differences in
palaeo-latitudes and relative rotations between the
blocks. The possible phases of continental collisions
(Kimmerian and Alpidic phases) could be demon-
strated. The geological consequences of our palaeo-
magnetic studies have been discussed by Davoudzadeh
et al. (1981) and Schmidt and Soffel (1984).
With the logistical support of the Geological Survey
of Iran (GSI) it was possible to carry out additional pal-
aeomagnetic sampling in 1986 and 1991–1992 on rocks
dating from the Precambrian to the Tertiary. Part of
these samples served for test measurements on
oriented hand samples in new areas of interest to inves-
tigate the suitability of various rock types for later stud-
ies. Reliable new palaeomagnetic data could be ob-
tained from Cretaceous and Triassic rocks. For details
and other results we refer to Rolf (1991) and Schmidt
(1992).
Major structural units of Iran
Fundamental differences in crustal character and in age
of basement consolidation allow three major structural
units to be distinguished in Iran, separated from each
other by ophiolite bearing sutures. The three major
units and their main constituents are as follows:
1. The southern unit with a crystalline basement which
consolidated in Late Precambrian times, and a plat-
form-type Palaeozoic development with continuous
sedimentation from Triassic to Plio-Pleistocene
times. This unit comprises the Zagros folded belt,
which was folded in a late alpine tectonic phase
(Pliocene).
2. The central unit is interpreted as an assemblage of
marginal Gondwana fragments that were united with
the mother continent and separated from the north-
ern continent (Eurasia) in the Palaeozoic, but de-
tached from Gondwana and attached to Eurasia in
the Early Mesozoic, and were finally rejoined by
Gondwanic Afro-Arabia in the Late Cretaceous–
Early Tertiary. It comprises Central Iran and the Al-
borz. This unit went through all different alpine tec-
tonic phases (Stöcklin 1977).
3. The northern unit is sharply separated from the cen-
tral unit by the North Iran suture (Davoudzadeh and
Schmidt 1982). It is characterized by continental
crust including remnants of more or less cratonized
former (Palaeozoic) oceanic crust which are thought
to represent relics of the Palaeo-Tethys. The north-
ern unit represents a marginal strip of the Hercynian
realm of Central Asia, broadly overlapped by the
Alpine realm. It was deformed and largely consoli-
dated by strong early Kimmerian folding and a Late
Alpine folding. The northern unit comprises the Tal-
esh Range (NW of Rasht), northern Alborz, the
South Caspian depression and the Kopet Dagh
Range.
Other criteria, such as structural style, age and inten-
sity of deformation, as well as age and nature of mag-
matism, are used to subdivide these major zones into
smaller structural–stratigraphic blocks.
Geology and structural history of the
Central-East-Iran microplate
Central Iran, in a broad sense, comprises the whole
area between the North and South Iranian range. With-
in the Iran Plate the Central-East-Iran microplate is
bordered by the Great Kavir fault in the north, by the
Nain-Baft fault in the west and southwest, and by the
Harirud fault in the east (Fig. 1). It is surrounded by
the Upper Cretaceous to Lower Eocene ophiolite and
ophiolitic mélange. The microplate itself consists of dif-
ferent structural components: the Lut Block, the Ker-
man-Tabas Block, the Yazd Block and the Anarak-
Khur Block. All these blocks are separated from each
other by major faults and have different lithostratigrap-
hic records. The major stratigraphic, tectonic and mag-
matic characteristics of the different blocks are as fol-
lows:
The Lut Block was consolidated in Upper Protero-
zoic. Its younger sedimentary cover is generally flat ly-
ing, and large areas are covered by Cainozoic volcanics
and Quaternary sand dunes and playas.
The Kerman–Tabas Block is characterized by strong
lateral variations in thickness of the Palaeozoic forma-
tions (up to 7000 m in the Tabas–Shirgesht area and
only 1000 m in the Kalmard area NW of Tabas) and by
well-developed Mesozoic sedimentary strata. Cenozoic
volcanics, widely distributed in the Lut Block, are al-
most totally absent in the Kerman–Tabas Block.

evaporite facies. Middle and Upper Jurassic formations
which are well developed in the Tabas–Kerman Block,
are missing or only poorly developed in the Yazd
Block. Mesozoic magmatism is common (Shir-Kuh
Granite 50 km SW of Yazd, Zarin Granite 80 km NNE
of Yazd).
The Anarak–Khur Block is characterized by a thick
(5000–8000 m) Palaeozoic metamorphic series consist-
ing mainly of detrital sediments and volcanic rocks. The
marine Triassic sequence of Nakhlak (up to 2500 m
thick) is significantly different from the carbonate plat-
form facies of Central Iran. Cretaceous formations are
well developed (Lower Cretaceous is up to 3000 m
thick). The Saghand–Bafq Block belongs to this Block;
it was dislocated later tectonically towards the south
(Davoudzadeh and Weber-Diefenbach 1987).
Sampling areas and measurement procedures
The sampling areas are indicated in Fig. 1. Area no. 1 is
situated in the Anarak–Khur Block near Nakhlak and
is part of the CEIM. Area no. 2 is located near Saghand
and lies between the Yazd Block and the Kerman–Ta-
bas Block, both of which belong to the CEIM. Area
no. 3 to the north of Sirjan is situated at the southern
rim of the CEIM. Clearly outside the CEIM is area
no. 4 in the region of Natanz. Table 1 shows the sites,
geographic coordinates, lithologies, rock ages, number
of sites and number of samples. The tectonic setting of
the sites was also determined for tectonic correction to
the palaeohorizontal position and for a fold test.
Drill cores were taken from the in situ rock forma-
tion or from oriented hand samples, from which stand-
ard cylindrical specimens (2.5 cm in diameter, 2.2 cm in
length) were obtained. The measurement and the anal-
ysis of the natural remanent magnetization (NRM) was
done mostly with a superconducting (cryogenic) mag-
netometer of type LETI (Grenoble, France). The NRM
of the rocks was tested with respect to its stability and
origin using alternating field (AF) and/or thermal (TH)
demagnetization, depending on the predominant ferro-
magnetic ores (magnetite, titanomagnetite, hematite,
goethite) of the rocks. The decay of the NRM during
the demagnetization treatment in field-free space was
analysed using multicomponent analysis for the deter-
mination of the characteristic remanent magnetization
(ChRM) as decribed in standard textbooks on palaeo-
magnetism (e.g. Van der Voo 1993). Both orthogonal
vector plots (Zijderveld diagrams) and equal area ste-
reonets were used for the presentation of the analysis
of the NRM. Additional rock magnetic measurements

Palaeomagnetic results
Nakhlak (area no. 1)
The Nakhlak area (part of the Anarak–Khur Block) is
situated approximately 30 km northeast of the small
town of Anarak in the southern part of the Great Kavir
(Fig. 1). The Triassic Nakhlak group, described by Da-
voudzadeh and Seyed-Emami (1972), comprises ap-
proximately 2540 m of limestone, sandstone, shale and
conglomerate . Much of the rock is tuffaceous. The
rocks of the Nakhlak group range in age from Upper
Scythian to Ladinian (Early and Middle Triassic). The
base of the Nakhlak group is not exposed; dune depos-
its cover the lowest exposures. The sequence is overlain
unconformably by limestones and sandstones of Creta-
ceous age. The marine Triassic sequence of Nakhlak is
significantly different from the carbonate platform fa-
cies of Central Iran. In Iran this facies type is exposed
only in a few localities north of the North Iran suture
(e.g. Aghdarband in eastern Kopet Dagh). The Nakh-
lak group was displaced from its original position (west
of Herat on the Turan plate) by the rotation of the
Central-East-Iran microplate (Davoudzadeh et al.
1981).
In this area we collected hand samples from Triassic
limestones at three sites and tuffites at four sites from
which 92 specimens were obtained. The mean initial in
situ NRM direction of the limestones is: D p221.67,
Ip86.77, N p42, k p9.8, 
a95p7.47 and for the tuffites:
Dp340.67, Ip66.47, Np50, kp8.3, a95p7.47. They dif-
fer significantly from the present local geomagnetic
field direction in Iran (D p57, Ip557). The AF demag-
netization was not successful for the complete destruc-
tion of the NRM. Only few specimens showed a consis-
tent grouping of directions during thermal demagneti-
zation (see Fig. 2a, b) in the blocking temperature
range above 300 7C after bedding correction. The mean
ChRM direction of 12 specimens from four sites is:

Saghand (area no. 2)
The Saghand area is situated on the eastern margin of
the Yazd Block in the centre of Central Iran (Fig. 1)
and forms part of the Central-East-Iran microplate. In
this area several sequences of Palaeozoic metamorphic
rocks are exposed. The rocks vary from high-grade me-
tamorphic to slightly and even nonmetamorphosed va-
rieties. All are associated with volcanics and/or volca-
no-detritics. The Saghand area is dominated strongly
by N-S trending basin and range extensional tectonics,
forming a mosaic structure of mainly N-S elongated
zones. The faults between them have been reactivated
at various times.
The Cretaceous limestones are slightly metamorp-
hic. A number of 112 samples (cores) were collected
within the same more or less subhorizontal formation
mainly at four sites along a profile of 30 km. The in situ
NRM groups around a mean direction of D p346.57,
Ip35.47, N p112, k p9.8, 
a95p4.57. Only few samples
gave reliable results after the minor bedding correc-
tions. With AF demagnetization a consistent
ChRM(AF) component could be isolated between
10 mT and 100 mT on 16 samples with a mean direction
of D p345.27, I p28.57, N p16, k p74.0, 
a95p4.37. By

298
thermal demagnetization a ChRM(TH) component
with D p338.57, I p25.27, N p17, k p47.0, a95p5.27
could be isolated in the blocking temperature range be-
tween 300 and 590 7C. The corresponding Zijderveld di-
agrams are shown in Fig. 2c and d. Both ChRM direc-
tions are regarded as primary. The combined mean re-
manence direction obtained from alternating field and
thermal demagnetization (D p340.77, I p26.37, N p33,
kp44.3, 
a95p3.87) and its virtual geomagnetic pole
(pole no. 2) are listed in Table 2. The VGP is also plot-
ted in Fig. 4.
Sirjan (area no. 3)
The Sanandaj–Sirjan metamorphic belt, which runs pa-
rallel to the Zagros from SE to NW Iran, joins the Tau-
rus orogenic belt in Turkey (Fig. 1). This belt is sepa-
rated from the Zagros by a narrow zone of deep thrust
and reverse faults (the Zagros Thrust Zone).
In the Sirjan area, at the western side of the Nain–
Baft fault, the Palaeozoic metamorphic sequence is
more than 5000 m thick. It consists of carbonates, pelit-
ic and psammitic rocks as well as basic volcanics and
ultrabasic rocks. K/Ar radiometric dating of the Ghouri
area (west of Sirjan) revealed ages of 404 B8 Ma to
362B7 Ma (Adib 1978). Devonian pollen and spores,
some Crinoids and other fossil fragments are reported
as well.
The Triassic basalts in the Sirjan area are only slight-
ly metamorphic. The initial NRM directions of the 89
samples (cores) from two sites are very scattered. After
AF demagnetization two groups of stable directions
could be found. One of them, called ChRM(AF1) has a
mean in situ direction (before tectonic correction) of
Dp3.37, I p47.97, N p27, k p51.3, 
a95p3.97 which
points more or less in the direction of the present local
geomagnetic field in Iran (D p57, Ip557). Although 5
of the 22 directions are reversed (passing a positive re-
versal test), we think that this component is secondary
because of its coincidence with typical Tertiary rema-
nence directions in Iran. Its VGP (153.2 7E, 87.1 7N)
is close to the present geographic pole and agrees with
Late Tertiary pole postions of the CEIM. The other
group of directions after AF demagnetization in the
range between 10 and 100 mT has a mean direction aft-
er bedding correction of D p113.77, I p34.87, N p25,
kp34.5, 
a95p5.07 and is called ChRM(AF2). The
ChRM(AF2) direction was also confirmed by thermal
demagnetization of a second set of samples in the
blocking temperature range from 400 to 590 7C yielding
a ChRM(TH) with Dp115.57, Ip35.47, Np19, kp76.0,
a95p3.97. Figure 2e and f show the corresponding Zij-
derveld diagrams. Two of the 19 directions are reversed
passing a positive reversal test. A combination of the
ChRM(AF2) and the ChRM(TH) directions yields a
mean ChRM direction of D p114.57, I p35.17, N p44,
kp45.9, 
a95p3.27. The corresponding VGP (pole no. 3)
is shown in Fig. 4. It is situated close to other Late Pal-

aeozoic/Early Mesozoic VGP positions of the CEIM.
We regard the combined ChRM(AF2)/ChRM(TH) di-
rections as a primary Triassic remanence component.
All data are listed in Table 2.
Natanz (area no. 4)
The Natanz–Soh area is situated between Esfahan and
Kashan (Fig. 1). It forms part of the western Central
Iran, but is situated outside of the CEIM (almost
150 km to the west). The geology of this area has been
described by Zahedi (1973).
The area contains no evidence of Carboniferous and
Early Permian beds. This important gap displays no an-
gular unconformity. Permian deposits are conformably
overlying the last beds of the Devonian Bahram Forma-
tion. The Triassic beds begin with 50 m of red conglom-
erates, sandstones and siltstones (Abyaneh Formation)
which is attributed to the Lower Triassic (Upper Scy-
thian). On top of this detritic sequence follow 1000 m
of dolomites and limestones corresponding to the Mid-
dle Triassic Shotori Formation.
There is a very rapid change in the nature of the se-
dimentation from Middle Triassic dolomites and limes-
tone to the very thick, sandy argillaceous deposits with
some limestones of the Upper Triassic (Nayband For-
mation, 1400 m) and Liassic (Shemshak Formation,
1000 m). This is regarded as evidence for a change in
the palaeogeographic conditions during the Triassic.
No evidence of the Dogger, Malm and Neocomian
stages could be found in the Natanz–Soh area. The Ap-
tian and Albian limestones and marls (1000 m) uncon-
formably overly folded beds of the Liassic and Upper
Triassic.
A number of 44 drill cores were collected at five
sites yielding 161 specimens of red sandstones and silt-
stones of the Abyaneh Formation, dolomites of the Sho-
tori Formation (Lower-Middle Triassic) and limestones
of the Nayband Formation (Upper Triassic). Only ther-
mal demagnetization was successful for the analysis of
the NRM. A Zijderveld diagram for thermal demagne-
tization is shown in Fig. 2g. From all five sites well-de-

fined ChRM directions could be determined from a suf-
ficient and comparable number of specimens. The
mean ChRM directions of each site are also plotted in
Fig. 3 before and after tectonic correction. At most sites
two polarities of remanence could be observed, and in
all cases the reversal test of McFadden and McElhinny
(1990) is seen to be positive. Before tectonic correction
the five sites have the following mean ChRM direction
of Dp44.67, Ip37.57, Np5, kp10.5, 
a95p24.87. After
tectonic correction, there is only a small directional
shift of the mean (D p33.37, I p25.17, N p5, k p69.0,
a95p9.37), but the scatter is reduced considerably. The
precision parameter k is improved after the tectonic
correction by a factor of 6.6, which means that the fold
test is positive with a probability of 99% using the fold
test of McElhinny (1964). Therefore, we regard this
ChRM direction as a primary Triassic direction. The
mean remanence direction of the five sites and the vir-
tual geomagnetic pole position are listed in Table 2.
The corresponding VGP (pole no. 4) is plotted in
Fig. 4. It is situated close to the mean Triassic pole of
the Turan Plate.
Interpretation of pole positions
Figure 4 shows the Apparent Polar Wander Paths
(APWP; north poles) of the CEIM (diamonds) and the
Turan Plate (circles) using the data listed in Table 4 to-
gether with the new pole positions of this paper
(squares). Their numbers refer to the pole numbers giv-
en in Table 2. The mean location of the CEIM (58 7E;
327N) is indicated by the triangle.
The Triassic pole (no. 1) from the Nakhlak area is,
within the error limits, in reasonable agreement with
the previously published Triassic pole of Soffel et al.
(1984); see also Table 3. It confirms in principle the
large counterclockwise rotation of the CEIM since the
Triassic (Davoudzadeh et al. 1981; Schmidt and Soffel
1983). The Cretaceous pole (no. 2) from the Saghand
area is regarded as reliable from the demagnetization
behaviour of the rocks and several rock magnetic char-
acteristics indicating a primary carrier of remanence. It
is close to other Cretaceous poles of the CEIM and
confirms this section of its APWP. In the Sirjan area on
the southern rim of the CEIM the Triassic pole (no. 3)
is situated in the vicinity of other Late Palaeozoic–Ear-
ly Mesozoic poles of the CEIM and is far apart from
the Triassic pole position for the Turan Plate. From this
we conclude that the Sirjan area may be regarded as
part of the CEIM. The area to the north of Sirjan must
also have carried out a considerable counterclockwise
rotation (ca. 1207) with respect to the Turan Plate since
the Triassic.

The new more reliable Triassic pole for the CEIM
based on poles from four different areas in the CEIM
has the following data: 317.5 7E, 12.7 7N, N p4 areas,
Kp14.1, 
a95p25.37. It is plotted in Fig. 4 as a diamond
(TR*) and has been connected by dashed lines with the
APWP of the CEIM as an alternative path for the
Triassic. The extended sampling of Triassic rocks in the
Natanz area (pole no. 4) gave reliable data according to
the standard criteria in palaeomagnetism (sufficient
number of samples, positive reversal test and fold test).
The close agreement of this Triassic VGP with the
APWP of the Turan Plate (see Fig. 4) indicates that the
Natanz region, and possibly also the entire area to the
west of the CEIM (between the Alborz in the north
and the Zagros in the south), must be regarded as being
situated close to the southern extension of the Turan
Plate during the Triassic. The presently available Trias-
sic poles for the CEIM and for the area of Natanz out-
side the CEIM have been compiled in Table 3.
Conclusions and geodynamical interpretation
The new palaeomagnetic investigations in Iran were ex-
tended also to some areas outside the Central-East-
Iran microplate and can be summarized as follows: The
APWP of the CEIM from the Triassic through the Ter-
tiary is generally confirmed by new data from areas
within or close to the CEIM. Triassic poles from vol-
canic rocks of the area north of Sirjan indicate that this
area must also have been rotated together with the
CEIM. The new mean Triassic pole for the CEIM, de-
rived from the results of Soffel et al. (1992), Wensink
(1983) and this paper (see Table 3) is at: 317.5 7E,
12.77N, N p4 areas, K p14.1, 
a95p25.37. It has been
named TR * in Fig. 4 and has been connected with the
APWP of the CEIM with dashed lines. Because the
four Triassic poles from the CEIM originate from areas
close to major fault systems, we think that their scatter
is due to small local tectonic movements.
The Triassic pole (no. 4) from the Natanz area out-
side the CEIM (167.2 7E, 53.77N, Np5 sites, dmp10.07,
dpp5.4) is in good agreement with the mean Triassic
pole of the Turan plate (149 7E; 497N) showing that the
area to the west of the CEIM was close to the Turan
Plate during the Triassic.
Previously existing palaeomagnetic data for the
CEIM (Soffel et al. 1992; listed in Table 4) and the data
of this paper were used to reconstruct the palaeoconti-
nental configuration of the region for the Triassic using
published data from Gondwana (Van der Voo 1993),
the Turan Plate (Khramov and Rodionov 1980) and the
new results for the Triassic of this paper (see Table 3).
The reconstruction is shown in Fig. 5.
The present configuration of the plates and micro-
plates in the vicinity of Iran are shown in Fig. 5a. The
CEIM has been marked with a north-pointing arrow
for a better illustration of its rotation since the Triassic.
Figure 5b represents the situation in the Triassic
(220 Ma). During the Triassic the Iran Plate (without
the CEIM, which is regarded as a separate unit) is situ-
ated close to the rims of the southern extension of the
Turan Plate, whereas the CEIM is in a more southeas-
terly position. Its progressive westward motion was
combined by a large (120–130 7) counterclockwise rota-
tion.

The CEIM performed an anticlockwise rotation of
nearly 65 7 from the Late Triassic to Middle Jurassic.
During the Upper Jurassic and the Cretaceous, the
CEIM carried out a further anticlockwise rotation of
357. The rift zones were closed in Early Tertiary by con-
vergence of the CEIM and Iran plate. This collision was
accompanied by additional anticlockwise rotation of
the CEIM of 35 7. Thus, the total amount of anticlock-
wise rotation of the CEIM since the Triassic with re-
spect to Eurasia is approximately 135 7. Ophiolite and
ophiolitic mélange surrounding the Central-East-Iran
microplate are the remnants of this rift zone.

also gratefully acknowledged. Dr. V. Bachtadse helped to make

the GMAP software by Dr. T. Torsvik. We are also grateful for

J. Tait, in the reviewing process.

INTRODUCTION
Palaeomagnetic studies are generally carried out on intru-
sive igneous rocks (such as mafic dykes) and low-grade sedi-
mentary rocks. High-grade metamorphic rocks, however ,
may also be carriers of palaeomagnetic information that
corresponds to the time of exhumation and cooling (Dunlop
& Ozdemir 1997). This study was aimed at determining
whether meaningful palaeomagnetic results could be
obtained from high-grade rocks from the Mesoproterozoic
Albany Mobile Belt in southern Western Australia (Figure
1). The Bremer Bay region of the Albany Mobile Belt was
chosen as its deformation history is well constrained by
U/Pb SHRIMP and Rb/Sr geochronology (Black et al. 1992).
The consistency of palaeomagnetic results of Early
Cambrian dolerite dykes throughout the Albany Mobile
Belt (Harris & Li 1995) has shown that there has been 
negligible tilting during breakup between Western
Australia and Antarctica.
This study sought to determine a palaeomagnetic 
pole for these high-grade rocks and late dykes for com-
parison to the Australian apparent polar wander path. The
Australian apparent polar wander path for the Mesopro-
terozoic (Idnurm & Giddings 1988) is presently constrained
by a small number of studies, the majority of which have
concerned northern and central Australia. Magnetic
anisotropy was also measured in order to determine 
how magnetic fabric relates to regional strain and thus to 
indirectly establish the timing for acquisition of the 
magnetic fabrics.
GEOLOGY AND SAMPLING
In the Albany Mobile Belt along the southern and 
southeastern margins of the Archaean Yilgarn Craton
(Figure 1), Archaean and Palaeoproterozoic granitoid,
gneiss, metasediment and mafic dykes have been reworked
within a dextral transpressional regime at approximately
1.2 Ga (Black et al. 1992). A Central Domain of granulite
facies gneiss has been obliquely thrust onto amphibolite
facies gneiss of the Northern Domain (Beeson et al. 1988).
There is a transitional contact with the Southern Domain,
which is comprised of dominantly amphibolite facies
gneiss and syn- to post-tectonic granitoids. Granulite facies
assemblages are locally preserved in the Southern Domain,
especially in cores of regional anticlines. In recon-
structions of the Rodinia supercontinent, the Albany
Mobile Belt separates the Yilgarn Craton from the East

Granulite facies tonalitic gneiss, mafic granulite and late metadolerite dykes from Bremer Bay in the
Mesoproterozoic Albany Mobile Belt yield palaeomagnetic remanence that were acquired between
ca 1.2 Ga and 1.1 Ga. A well-constrained pole (66.6°N, 303.7°E) fits the ca 1.2 Ga part of the
Precambrian Australian apparent polar wander path. This pole is in agreement with the high-
latitude position of Australia at ca 1.2–1.1 Ga shown on some Rodinia reconstructions. More data are
required before any significance can be attributed to a second, poorly defined pole (41.8°S, 243.7°E)
that falls at some distance from the ca 0.8 Ga part of the Australian apparent polar wander path.
Magnetic anisotropy measurements from all samples except late granite dykes indicate northeast–
southwest elongation (i.e. parallel to the local trend of the orogenic belt) and northwest–southeast
contraction. This is in agreement with the orientation of principal strain axes deduced from structures
formed during late stages of ductile deformation. The mean magnetic fabric lineation (long axis of
the strain ellipsoid) is subparallel to a mineral elongation lineation and the axes of late upright to
inclined folds. Short axes of the strain ellipsoid determined from magnetic fabric measurements are
in a similar orientation to poles to the axial surfaces of these folds and to the associated cleavage.
This mean shortening axis bisects late conjugate ductile shear zones that overprint the folds. This study
has shown that structurally complex high-grade gneisses and intrusive rocks with variable timing 
relationships may yield meaningful palaeomagnetic results for late stages of metamorphism. Magnetic
anisotropy analysis is also seen to be a valuable tool in providing principal strain directions for late
ductile deformation.
KEY WORDS: Albany Mobile Belt, gneiss, magnetic anisotropy, Mesoproterozoic, palaeomagnetism.

the basement gneiss complex in Meghalaya in north-
eastern India, from where it is thought to continue across
India along the Central Indian Tectonic Zone (Harris 1993).
Granulite facies tonalitic and mafic gneiss of the
Central Domain are best exposed in the Bremer Bay region
(Figures 1, 2) in the eastern part of the belt where it trends
northeast. The presence of 3.1 Ga zircon cores with 1.2 Ga
zircon overgrowths and Sm–Nd model ages of ca 2.1 Ga
(Black et al.1992) in tonalitic gneiss indicates Archaean and
Palaeoproterozoic precursors. High-grade metamorphism
in the Central Domain granulites and intrusion of late- to
post-tectonic granitoids occurred at ca 1.2 Ga based on U/Pb
SHRIMP geochronology . The Rb/Sr system has closed at ca
1.1 Ga. (Black et al. 1992). There is a southwards progres-
sive overprinting of Proterozoic fabrics and an increase in
metamorphic grade across the Northern Domain (Beeson
et al. 1988). Mafic horizons that are generally concordant
with the regional gneissosity in the Northern Domain 
represent metamorphosed equivalents of dolerite dykes of
unknown age in the southern Yilgarn Craton (Beeson et al.
1988). Isoclinally folded mafic granulite layers in the
Central Domain (Figure 3a) may represent a higher grade
equivalent of these dykes. The presence of a major tectonic
contact between the Central and Northern Domains does
not, however , allow for a direct correlation between dykes
in the Yilgarn Craton and mafic granulites and no
geochronology and geochemistry are available to confirm
this hypothesis.
A complex deformation history during high-grade meta-
morphism is recorded in the Bremer Bay area. Northwest-
verging folds and thrusts, along with southeast-verging
‘back-thrusts’, indicate northwest–southeast contraction
during convergence between East Antarctica and the
Yilgarn Craton. Northeast-striking normal shear zones 
and widespread boudinage (especially of mafic layers) 
indicate subsequent subhorizontal northwest–southeast
extension. Quartz, plagioclase, K-feldspar , orthopyroxene
and clinopyroxene ± magnetite ± biotite pegmatites, which
intrude boudin necks and normal shear zones (Figure 3c)

LABORATORY METHODS AND MAGNETIC
PROPERTIES
Thirty-three block-orientated samples were collected from
mafic and tonalitic granulite, metadolerite and granitic
dykes, using a sun compass for sample orientation. Eighty-
eight cylindrical specimens (25 mm diameter) were drilled
from the sampled blocks. The palaeomagnetic and magnetic
anisotropy study has been carried out in the palaeo-
magnetic laboratory of the Tectonics Special Research
Centre at the University of Western Australia. Magnetic
remanence was measured using a 2G755R cryogenic mag-
netometer . At least one specimen from each block was sub-
jected to stepwise thermal demagnetisation using MMTD2
furnaces manufactured by Magnetic Measurements (~10 nT
residual field). Also at least one specimen from each block
was subjected to stepwise alternating field (AF) demag-
netisation using a 2G600 automated degaussing system. The
results obtained from the pilot collection were used for
determining the demagnetisation intervals and for the
number of steps to be used for the remaining specimens.
Magnetic susceptibility was measured after each heating
step with a MS2 susceptibility meter . Isothermal remanent
magnetisation (IRM) experiments were carried out using
a MMPM9 pulse magnetiser .

Figure 11 shows some examples of the comparison of
AF demagnetisation curves for NRM and SIRM. This is the
version (Dunlop & Ozdemir 1997) of the Lowrie–Fuller test
(Lowrie & Fuller 1971). This test is often used to determine
grainsizes and domain states present in rocks. Although the
test is not as definitive as would be liked, particularly on
synthetic materials, it is appealing because it is simple,
and combined with other evidence further constrains
interpretation. The Lowrie–Fuller test predicts that for fine
(SD/PSD) particles, a low-field TRM (i.e. an NRM if
acquired in the Earth’s field during cooling) is more stable
than a high-field TRM, approximated here by using an
SIRM. For coarse (MD) particles this relationship is
reversed. Therefore, a simple comparison of the demag-
netisation of NRM followed by repeat demagnetisation of
SIRM, indicates the predominant domain state of the 
magnetic particles in a sample. In most cases for our study
it gave a zero result (Figure 11c). Figure 11a (tonalitic
gneiss) and Figure 11b (mafic granulite) show two excep-
tions that indicate the SD behaviour . The typical MD result
for granite is shown on Figure 11d.
All these analyses indicate that the studied meta-
dolerites, mafic granulites and tonalitic gneisses are 
suitable for palaeomagnetic analysis as they contain a 
sufficient amount of magnetite not only with MD, but 
also with PSD and SD structure, and therefore may carry
a stable ancient remanence. Further demagnetisations also
indicated the presence of hematite in at least some of these
rocks. It appears unlikely that the granites studied contain
some stable remanence.

Not a single sample contains both of these components.

CR] of these
samples and mafic granulites with BB1 direction have been
found. BB2 component is rather scattered (Figure 6b) 
and absent in tonalitic gneiss, dolerite and granite. Mean
directions, statistics and pole positions for BB1 and BB2
components are given in Table 1.
DISCUSSION AND CONCLUSIONS
Figure 15 shows the palaeomagnetic poles for BB1 and BB2
components together with the 1200–600 Ma fragment of the
Australian apparent polar wander path (Idnurm &
Giddings 1988; Idnurm et al. 1995) and fragments of the
Phanerozoic Australian apparent polar wander path
(Harris & Li 1995). The BB1 pole (66.6°N, 303.7°E) fits the ca
1.2 Ga part of Precambrian Australian apparent polar
wander path. However , this particular part is poorly deter-
mined as some of the earlier poles it is based on have 
been revised (Tanakah & Idnurm 1994) and other poles have
poor age constraints. The closeness of this part of the
Australian apparent polar wander path to the Late Palaeo-
zoic Australian apparent polar wander path must also be
considered. No Late Palaeozoic thermal or chemical event
that could cause the magnetic overprint, however , is known
for the Bremer Bay area. Although there has been local 
dextral strike-slip reactivation of probable Early Cambrian
age (Harris & Li 1995) in areas of steeply dipping, north-
east-striking gneissic foliations, formation of cataclastic
fabrics in this event suggests deformation occurred at a
shallow level in the crust. The temperature in this late 
brittle event would therefore be expected to have then been
lower than the Curie temperature, so that resetting would
not occur . However , no late penetrative cataclastic fabrics
were developed in the areas sampled due to the shallower
dip of the original gneissosity . Dolerite dykes that intruded
in some other parts of the Albany Mobile Belt in an Early
Cambrian event (Harris & Li 1995) are also absent in the
Bremer Bay region. Magnetic anisotropy measurements
are also in agreement with the Mesoproterozoic defor-
mation, but are inconsistent with the deformation regime
interpreted for the Early Cambrian event (east-south-
east–west-northwest shortening, north-northeast–south-
southwest extension: Harris & Li 1995). All these factors
lead us to conclude that the palaeomagnetic pole records
the ca 1.2–1.1 Ga metamorphic event. Given its Precambrian
origin, the steep inclination of the BB1 component 
also supports the high-latitude position of Australia 
at approximately 1200–1100 Ma shown on some Rodinia
reconstructions (Gose et al. 1997).
The BB2 pole (41.8°S, 243.7°E) falls at some distance from
the ca 0.8 Ga part of the Australian apparent polar wander
path (Figure 15). However , this palaeomagnetic direction
has poor statistics (Figure 6b, Table 1) and is based on seven
samples only , so an additional study is necessary to confirm
(or reject) it before any tectonic interpretations can be
made.
The consistency of the palaeomagnetic BB1 pole from
the Albany Mobile Belt with the Australian apparent polar
wander path illustrates that high-grade rocks from within
an orogenic belt with a complex deformation and intrusive
history may yield meaningful palaeomagnetic results. The
magnetic anisotropy is also in close agreement with 
structural data. This study thus opens the way for more
research in the Albany Mobile Belt and in similar orogenic
belts (where palaeomagnetic work has not been previously
attempted) on palaeomagnetic determinations and the use
of magnetic fabric for structural analysis.

Paleomagnetically defined rotations from the Precordillera 
of northern Chile' Evidence of localized in situ 
fault-controlled rotations 
Darren E. Randall

Andrew J. Tomlinson

Abstract. A paleomagnetic study of Paleocene, Cretaceous, 
and Jurassic units in the ?recordillera of northern Chile (26øS 
to 27øS) demonstrate a complex pattern of crustal rotations. 
The region was selected to investigate the pattern of 
deformation associated with the Sierra Castillo-Agua Amarga 
Fault and its associated structural subdomains, which form 
part of the Domeyko 'Fault System, the fault system that 
controls much of the structure of the Chilean Precordillera. 
Paleocene lavas from the center of the study area pass a fold 
test, indicating the primary nature of the remanence in these 
rocks. A second group of lavas from the south has a similar 
formation mean inclination after tilt correction for a uniform 
dip, which coupled with the presence of reversals, suggests 
that these lavas also carry a primary remanence. The data 
indicate clockwise rotations of-35 ø and 42 ø respectively, for 
the two sampling localities. Three geographically separate 
areas of Lower Cretaceous red beds also reveal primary 
remanences based on the presence of sites with reversed 
polarity at two of the localities and an inclination-only fold 
test of the three locality mean directions for this formation. 
These sampling areas yield remanence directions that reveal 
30 ø of counterclockwise and 31 ø of clockwise rotation as well 
as an area without statistically significant rotation. These data 
include the first well-constrained counterclockwise rotation to 
be recovered from rocks in the southern central Andes, 
although mapping suggests the block involved is of limited 
geographic extent. Jurassic strata failed to yield any reliable 
results. Overall, the data indicate a greater variability in the 
rotation pattern than has previously been observed in most 
comparable areas south of the Arica Deflection. The variation 
cannot be explained by large-scale rotation mechanisms, such 
as oroclinal bending or domino-style block rotation by widely

magnitude with the Eocene transpressional deformation

tectonics in controlling rotations in this part of the south 
central Andes and the importance of understanding the local 
structure of regions sampled for paleomagnetic study. 
1. Introduction 
Paleomagnetic investigations carried out in the central 
Andes have identified a fairly consistent pattern of clockwise 
rotations to the south of the Arica Deflection (Figure l a) and 
counterclockwise rotations to the north [e.g., Beck, 1988, 
1998; Roperch and Carlief, 1992; Somoza et ai., 1996; 
Randall, 1998]. Individual rotations and the large-scale 
pattern observed have been attributed to various tectonic 
models and mechanisms. At the center of controversy in the 
differing models is the role of large-scale versus local 
processes in the generation of the overall rotation pattern. 
Large-scale mechanisms include forearc wide rotations due to 
oroclinal bending produced by differential shortening [Isacks, 
1988; Roperch and Carlief, 1992; Butler et al., 1995; 
MacFadden et al., 1995] and large-scale domino-style block 
rotation by widely separated transandean basement faults 
[Abels and Bischoff, 1999]. Local processes include rotations 
of smaller-scale crustal blocks in response to oblique 
subduction [Beck, 1988; Hartley et al., 1988; Forsythe and 
Chisholm, 1994; Randall et al., 1996; Somoza et al., 1996; 
Taylor et al., 1998] and rotation of detached or partially 
detached thrust sheets [Hartley et al., 1992a, Butler et al., 
1995]. 
This paper presents results from a paleomagnetic study in 
the Andean Precordillera of northern Chile. The study area 
lies between 26 ø and 27øS and 69015 ' and 69ø40'W, in the 
region of the major mining districts of El Salvador and 
Potrerillos (Figure 1). Jurassic to Paleocene volcanic rocks 
and Cretaceous sedimentary units were sampled for

investigation was designed to assess the magnitude and 
distribution of rotations within an area that has faults with

Combining paleomagnetic and structural data allows the 
relationships between deformation and block rotation to be 
identified and in the current study indicates that localized in 
situ fault-controlled rotations dominate the pattern of rotations 
in the Precordillera of northern Chile between 26øS and 27øS. 
2. Regional Geology

consequence of four distinct tectonomagmatic episodes in the 
evolution of the Chilean margin which young successively 
and episodically eastward. During the Late Triassic to Early 
Cretaceous the magmatic arc lay in th Coastal Cordillera, and 
the Precordillera formed part of an extensive back arc to intra- 
arc basin system [Mpodozis and Ramos, 1989; Scheuber and 
Reutter, 1992; Ardill et al., 1998]. During the mid- 
Cretaceous the magmatic arc migrated eastward to occupy the 
present-day Central Depression [Scheuber and Reutter, 1992;

The major structural feature of the studied area is the north- 
south trending fault system comprising the Sierra Castillo and 
Agua Amarga Faults (SC-AA) (Figure 1), which together with 
the La Ternera Fault System, to the south, and the Sierra de 
Varas and West Fissure Fault Systems, to the north, comprise 
the Domeyko Fault System [Maksaev and Zentilli, 1988; 
Tomlinson et al., 1993; Mpodozis et al., 1993]. The SC-AA 
Fault separates two areas with contrasting Mesozoic histories, 
indicating activity of the SC-AA Fault since the Jurassic 
[Cornejo et al., 1993; 1997]. 
The Mesozoic geology west of the SC-AA Fault comprises 
a Jurassic-Cretaceous succession of predominantly volcanic 
rocks intercalated with marine limestones, terrigenous 
sandstones, volcaniclastic sandstones, and breccias (Figure 2).

Cornejo et al., 1993]. These are superseded by the Upper 
Jurassic Quebrada Vicufiita sequence [Cornejo et al., 1993, 
1998], a series of basaltic-andesitic lavas intercalated with 
thin marine sedimentary horizons, and the Upper Jurassic- 
Lower Cretaceous Pedernales Formation, comprising marine 
limestone and volcaniclastic sandstones [Harrington, 1961 ]. 
Subsequently, a regional marine regression lArdill et al., 
1998] led to the accumulation of fluvial and aeolian facies 
arkosic sandstone and coastal sabkha facies evaporites, which 
together form the Quebrhda Monardes Formation [Surez and 
Bell, 1985; Bell, 1991] and its correlative, the Agua Helada 
Formation [Garcia, 1967]. 
The Late Cretaceous and Paleogene magmatic arc is 
represented by three major phases of activity, occurring in the 
Late Cretaceous, Paleocene, and Eocene-Oligocene [Cornejo 
et al., 1997]. One of the most widely exposed units from this 
arc is the Paleocene (63-55 Ma) Cerro Valiente sequence, a 
highly variable sequence of flows with lesser amounts of 
ignimbrites and breccias [Cornejo et al., 1993, 1998]. This 
unit lies unconformably to paraconformably on the Lower 
Cretaceous sedimentary rocks and Upper Cretaceous volcanic 
rocks. The Eocene-Oligocene saw the emplacement of 
numerous, widely distributed intrusions, including shallow- 
level bodies associated with the economically important 
porphyry copper deposits. The Eocene intrusions are coeval 
with the last major deformational event in the Precordillera, 
the Incaic orogenic phase, which generated most of the 
important structures in the studied area [Tomlinson et al., 
1993; Mpodozis et al., 1994; Cornejo et al., 1997]. Since 
abandonment of this arc and subsequent eastward relocation 
of magmatism in the Oligo-Miocene, the Precordillera region 
has undergone a period of uplift. 
3. Structural Geology 
Although having an earlier history as a Mesozoic 
extensional fault, the main phase of motion on the SC-AA 
Fault was during the Eocene contractional deformation of the 
magmatic arc [Tomlinson et al., 1993; Cornejo et al., 1997]. 
At this time, the Sierra Castillo fault was reactivated as a near- 
vertical sinistral strike-slip fault with a component of up on 
the east slip [Tomlinson et al., 1993; Niemeyer, 1999]. In 
contrast, the southern fault segment, the Agua Amarga thrust, 
is a westside up oblique reverse fault. Despite the opposite 
senses of vertical movements on these two fault segments, 
Tomlinson et al. [ 1993] argued that they are contemporary and 
form a single master fault for a sinistral transpressive system 
kinematically linked to the broad zone of deformation east of 
the SC-AA Fault. 
To the east of the SC-AA Fault are three distinct but 
kinematically related structural domains of subsidiary faults 
(Figure 1) [Tomlinson et al., 1993]. (1) The Northern domain 
consists of a fold-and-thrust belt which can be subdivided iro 
two subdomains based on structural style: an eastern 
subdomain characterized by thin-skinned, ramp flat style 
folding and thrusting and a western subdomain displaying 
thick-skinned, fault propagation fold style deformation 
involving the Paleozoic basement (Figure 2). Bedding,

reverse faults, and folds in the domain have strikes and trends 
of-10-25 ø (Figure 3a). (2)The Central domain is located at 
the southernmost end of the fold-and-thrust belt and is a 
complex region of thrusting and folding associated with 
numerous dextral E-W strike-slip faults. In this domain, the 
lower, easterly positioned thrust faults have decreasing 
displacements along strike to the southwest and die into tip 
line folds or terminate in the eastern ends of dextral E-W 
strike-slip faults which transfer the thrust displacement to the 
next higher and westerly positioned thrust. Other thrust faults 
unite directly with higher thrusts. As a consequence, the 
shortening on lower thrusts is progressively replaced to the 
southwest by added movement on higher thrusts. In this 
manner, the domain is interpreted to be a displacement 
transfer zone in which shortening across a broad zone in the 
northern domain is transferred to a few higher thrusts, 
particularly the Agua Amarga thrust. Over much of the 
central domain the regional structural features have 
orientations of 0300-045 ø (Figure 3b). In the southwest sector 
of the domain, where the higher reverse faults dominate the 
shortening, the structural trends shift to a N-S orientation 
(Figure 3c), except in a-2 x 2 km area near Mina Vieja where 
the structures trend 350-40 ø counterclockwise with respect to 
those in the surrounding area (Figures 3d, 3e, and 4). This 
observation led Cornejo et al. [1993] to predict that this small 
block had experienced counterclockwise rotations. (3) The 
Southern domain is characterized by sinistral strike-slip faults 
with a NW orientation. The NW trending faults with greatest 
continuity and displacement occur in the Quebrada Cinaga 
area (Figure 2) and connect the southern end of reverse faults 
in the central domain to NNE oriented high-angle reverse 
faults in the La Coipa area (Figure 1). They are interpreted to 
represent another transfer zone [Cornejo et al., 1993]. 
Outside this transfer zone the faulting is minor, and instead, 
deformation is dominated by shortening related to the Agua 
Amarga thrust. 
Syntectonic and post-tectonic intrusions associated with the 
faults indicate that regional deformation was initiated by 42 
Ma, continued until at least 36 Ma, and ended by 32 Ma 
[Tomlinson et al., 1993; Mpodozis et al., 1994; Cornejo et al., 
1997]. The SC-AA Fault and associated domains define a 
wide deformation zone with structure orientations and 
kinematics consistent with development in response to 
sinistral transpression where the SC-AA acted as the master 
fault to the structural system. In most types of transpression, 
clockwise and counterclockwise rotation of passive markers 
of different orientations are expected [Fossen and Tikoff, 
1998]. Folds formed at an angle to the master fault rotate 
toward it with progressive transpression [Sanderson and 
Marchini, 1984; damison, 1991]; therefore counterclockwise 
rotations may be anticipated in the fold-and-thrust belt of the 
northern domain. In the southern domain, if slip on the NW 
faults accommodates rotation, these faults and the intervening 
blocks might rotate either clockwise or counterclockwise 
depending on the relative importance of the pure and simple 
shearing components in the deformation history, with system- 
perpendicular pure shearing (contraction) producing sinistral 
slip on the NW faults and clockwise rotations and system- 
parallel sinistral simple shearing generating dextral slip on the 
NW faults and counterclockwise rotations. Considering the 
evident importance of shortening in the system and the 
sinistral slip sense of the NW faults, a clockwise rotation is 
expected. The central domain is more complex in that it is 
part of the fold-and-thrust belt and so could have 
counterclockwise rotations but also has a component of 
dextral E-W simple shearing related to displacement transfer 
in the locus of shortening and so could have clockwise 
rotations. 
4. Paleomagnetic Sampling and Analytical 
Procedures 
Samples from 66 sites were collected and analyzed from 
the central and southern structural domains east of the SC-AA 
Fault and from a small area above the Agua Amarga thrust, 
west of the main trace of the SC-AA Fault (Figure 2). 
Samples were collected from the Cerro Valiente (Paleocene) 
and Quebrada Vicufiita (Upper Jurassic) sequences and from 
the Quebrada Monardes (Lower Cretaceous) and Sierra Fraga 
(Jurassic) Formations. The Cerro Valiente and Quebrada 
Vicufiita sequences were sampled from the southern and 
central domains. The Quebrada Monardes Formation was 
sampled in the southern domain and at Mina Vieja in the 
central domain, where the structures trend counterclockwise 
with respect to the equivalent structures in the surrounding 
area. The northern domain was not sampled because of its 
inaccessibility, and only the Sierra Fraga Formation could be 
sampled from west of the SC-AA Fault (Figure 2). 
Natural reinanent magnetizations (NRM) were measured 
mainly using a Molspin MS2 or Geofyzika JR4 spinner 
magnetometer. A CCL cryogenic magnetometer was also 
used for some of the Quebrada Monardes Formation samples. 
Specimens were stepwise demagnetized by thermal or two- 
axis tumbling alternating field (AF) methods through at least 
12 steps until they became unstable, or to 700øC or 100 mT, 
respectively. During thermal demagnetization, bulk 
susceptibility was measured after each thermal 
demagnetization step to detect heat-induced mineral changes. 
Remanence directions were determined using principal 
component analysis [Kirschvink, 1980]. Components were 
defined by a minimum of three points on vector endpoint 
diagrams and were considered stable when they had a 
maximum angular deviation (MAD) not exceeding 15 ø , 
although in most cases the observed MAD were < 10 ø In 
some cases, multiple magnetic components with overlapping 
blocking or coercivity spectra required the use of 
remagnetization circles combined with endpoints [McFadden 
and McElhinny, 1988] to isolate the characteristic remanent 
magnetization (ChRM). Mean directions for each geological 
unit and sampling locality were calculated by combining site 
mean directions [Fisher, 1953]. 
5. Paleomagnetic Results 
5.1 Cerro Valiente Sequence (Paleocene)

collected and demagnetized from the Cerro Valiente

Of the 10 sites from the central domain, seven carry a 
consistent tilt-corrected direction, taken to be the ChRM, 
directed to the NE with moderate inclination or its antipode 
(Table 1 and Figure 6). Three sites excluded from the 
formation mean all have remanence directions that lie > 2cs 
away from the ChRM after tilt correction. The grouping of 
the seven sites is significantly better after tilt correction and 
passes a fold test at the 99% confidence level [McElhinny, 
1964]. All nine sites from the southern domain carry a 
ChRM, again directed to the NE with moderate upward 
inclination or, in two sites, its antipode (Table 1 and Figure 
6). The uniformity of the bedding corrections means that a 
meaningful fold test cannot be performed on this data. 
Application of a reversal test [McFadden and McElhinny, 
1990] yields an indeterminate result for both study areas at the 
95% confidence level, probably a consequence of the uneven 
distribution of normal and reverse polarity sites at each 
sampling locality. In both cases the angle between the 
polarity groups is smaller in tilt-corrected than in situ 
coordinates. 
5.2 Quebrada Monardes Formation (Lower Cretaceous) 
Twenty-four sites were collected from the Quebrada 
Monardes Formation (Figure 2) as oriented hand samples and 
field-drilled cores. Sites QM1 to QM8 were collected from a 
gently SW plunging, open anticline in the south of the study 
area near Quebrada Cerros Bravos. Sites QM15 to QM24 
were collected farther north, from a NW trending anticline in 
Quebrada Cignaga. Both of these sampling localities lie 
within the southern domain of NW trending strike-slip faults. 
Sites QM9 to QM14 come from a 20 m plus thick section 
with approximately constant dip near Mina Vieja (Figure 4) in 
an area having anomalous structural trends in the southwest 
sector of the central domain, as previously described. 
The total NRM intensities for these red bed samples range 
between 0.5 and 187 mAm -, with the majority < 50 mAm - 
Demagnetization behavior in the samples is variable and 
typically multicomponent (Figures 7a- 7d). In some cases the 
components have overlapping blocking spectra (Figure 7d), 
and the ChRM is only recovered as a linear segment in two or 
three samples from the site, while others only define 
remagnetization circles. When clearly isolated, low 
unblocking temperature components tend to be either present- 
day field directions, interpreted as long-term VRM, or are 
dispersed, representing laboratory-induced VRM. Despite the

Sites from the Quebrada Cerros Bravos region yielded a 
consistent ChRM, directed upward in the NE quadrant or, in 
two sites, its antipode (Table 2 and Figure 8a). Where stable 
endpoints were recovered, it was through thermal treatment 
above 580øC. All but one of the 10 sites analyzed from the 
Quebrada Ci6naga locality carried both normal and reversed 
polarity components (Table 3 and Figure 8b), with the 
reversed polarity component only isolated by demagnetization 
above 580øC (Figure 7d). The mean directions of the two 
polarity groups are antipodal at the 95% confidence level, 
both in situ and tilt corrected, passing the reversal test with a 
C classification in both cases [McFadden and McElhinny, 
1990]. Thermal demagnetization to temperatures > 580øC 
isolated a consistent normal polarity remanence direction, 
directed upward in the NW quadrant from all six sites 
collected from near Mina Vieja (Table 2 and Figure 8c). One 
site (QM12) has a relatively poorly defined site mean 
direction (0[95 > 20ø), but it is broadly consistent with the other 
sites and hence is included in the overall group mean. 
The positive reversal test demonstrates that the directional 
difference between the two polarities groups at the Quebrada 
Ci6naga locality is small, so either group mean could be used 
for the tectonic analysis. However, the direction recovered 
from the hematite component has an inclination closer to that 
expected at this sampling latitude. Furthermore, the 
remanence recovered from the Quebrada Monardes Formation 
at Quebrada Cerros Bravos and Mina Vieja was isolated 
above 580øC, suggesting it is carried by hematite. Therefore, 
to ensure that we are comparing similar age magnetizations 
across the formation, the hematite component of the Quebrada 
Cidnaga rocks is preferred as the ChRM for the remainder of 
the discussion.

of the shallow dips and relatively consistent strike azimuths at 
each locality. Statistical comparison of the formation mean 
directions from the three localities does, however, pass an 
inclination-only fold test. In this test the fact that the angle 
between the paleomagnetic remanence direction and the 
bedding plane must remain constant during any rigid-body 
rotation can be used as a tilt test on a regional scale, even 
where the localities have different rotation histories 
[McFadden and Reid, 1982]. Thus comparison of in situ and 
tilt-corrected paleomagnetic inclinations can be made from 
our three different areas that appear to have different rotation 
histories as indicated by their declinations. The effect of 
progressive untilting on the precision parameter k of the three 
formation mean inclinations, following the statistical method 
of McFadden and Reid [1982], is shown in Figure 9. The 
increase in k after correction exceeds the 99% confidence 
level for an F test distribution and thus constitutes a 
statistically significant improvement and hence a positive test. 
We therefore interpret this magnetization as a prefolding 
remanance and not a postfolding remagnetization. 
5.3 Jurassic Formations 
The majority of samples from the Jurassic formations 
failed to yield stable directions or geologically interpretable 
primary remanence directions (Table 4). For the most part, 
samples showed two types of behavior: in situ northerly 
directions with moderate upward inclinations, consistent with 
a viscous remanence acquired in the present field direction; or 
directions that are inconsistent with either the present field 
direction or the ChRM identified from other units when 
considered either in in situ or tilt-corrected coordinates. 
Samples without obvious present-day components typically 
had high total NRM intensities that decayed rapidly when 
subjected to AF demagnetization, reminiscent of the effects of 
lightning strike-induced isothermal remanent magnetizations. 
Tilt-corrected site mean directions in some of the Quebrada 
Vicufiita sequence sites have a tendency toward NE directed 
declinations with moderate upward inclinations or, in one 
case (site QV7), its antipode, consistent with some of the data 
recorded in the younger units. The in situ directions of these 
sites, however, fall close to the Earth's present field direction, 
and the site mean directions overall have increased scattering 
on tilt correction, undermining our confidence in the 
directions having any geological significance. Only four sites 
from the Sierra Fraga Formation group sufficiently well after 
tilt correction to pass a fold test [McElhinny, 1964]. The 
confidence limits on both the individual site mean directions 
and the resultant formation mean coupled with the shallow 
inclination of the tilt-corrected formation mean, which implies 
major north-south displacement, make us skeptical of the 
significance of these data. 
5.4 Identification of Magnetic Carriers 
The nature of the magnetic carriers in all units was 
investigated using acquisition of isothermal remanent 
magnetization (IRM) and subsequent thermal demagnetization 
of three component IRM with along-axis fields of 800, 300, 
and 50 mT [Lowtie, 1990]. Additionally, high-temperature 
susceptibility behavior was also examined for some samples: 
IRM experiments on the Cerro Valiente sequence 
demonstrate behavior consistent with a mixture of low- and 
high-coercivity carriers in varying proportions. This is 
consistent with the demagnetization behavior of the NRM and 
suggests that magnetite and hematite are carriers of natural

6. Discussion and Interpretation 
6.1 Interpretation of the Mean Directions 
In the Cerro Valiente sequence, seven of 10 sites in the 
central and all nine sites from the southern domain carry a 
ChRM. The demagnetization behavior from this unit is 
relatively simple, and the within-site variation is much less 
than that observed in the other formations. Site directions 
from the central domain pass a fold test, indicating a 
prefolding remanence. Uniformity of the structural 
corrections in the southern domain prohibits a meaningful 
fold test. The inclination of the formation mean direction 
from the south is, however, much closer to that from the

central region when both directions are considered in tilt- 
corrected coordinates. This, combined with the presence of 
sites with opposing magnetic polarities, suggests that the 
Cerro Valiente rocks in the southern domain also carry a 
prefolding remanence and not a postfolding remagnetization. 
The reason for the failure of three sites in the central 
domain to record the ChRM is uncertain. Some samples 
carried very high NRM intensities (up to 2400 mAm 'l) and 
had low median destructive fields (typically, below 15 mT), 
suggestive of possibly having been remagnetized by lightning 
strikes. It is noteworthy, however, that the three site mean 
directions group better before application of a tilt correction 
(Figure 6) and therefore may be recording a later, postfolding 
remagnetization. The origin of this remagnetization may be 
related to hydrothermal activity associated with emplacement 
of the Eocene porphyry copper-related intrusions. If the 
remanence recovered is a postfolding remagnetization, the 
consistency of its directions with the prefolding remanence 
recovered from the other sites (Figure 6) suggests that both 
were acquired prior to any tectonic rotation of the central 
domain. 
The demagnetization behavior of samples from the 
Quebrada Monardes Formation is variable and complex, but a 
ChRM was recovered from sites at all three sampling 
localities. The positive result from the inclination-only tilt 
test coupled with normal and reversed polarity site mean 
directions at two of the three sampling localities provides 
strong evidence that the remanence direction recovered from 
the Quebrada Monardes Formation is prefolding in origin. 
The presence of both polarity components in nine of the 10 
sites from Quebrada Cidnaga is tentatively interpreted as 
being a combination of a detrital magnetization carried by 
magnetite and an early diagenetic magnetization carried by 
hematite.

Some sites in the Quebrada Vicufiita sequence and Sierra 
Fraga Formation show the influence of lightning strikes. The 
reason for the failure of other sites to yield reliable 
paleomagnetic directions in these Jurassic units is less certain. 
Thin section analysis did, however, reveal pervasive alteration 
of these rocks with a mineral assemblage consistent with the 
effects of hydrothermal fluids. 
6.2 Comparison with Paleomagnetic Reference Directions 
The apparent polar wander path for South America remains 
the subject of much debate owing to the poor constraints on 
many of the available poles [e.g., Beck, 1988, 1998; Randall, 
1998]. As the remanences recovered in this study predate the 
Eocene folding and are regarded as primary, the Cerro 
Valiente sequence and Quebrada Monardes Formation mean 
directions need to be compared with Paleocene and Early 
Cretaceous poles, respectively. 
Comparison of the formation mean directions with 
directions calculated from appropriate reference poles 
[Randall, 1998] clearly demonstrates significant and variable 
amounts of rotation with, in most cases, insignificant 
latitudinal displacement (Table 5). Both formation mean 
directions from the Cerro Valiente sequence indicate 
statistically significant southward latitudinal transport, 
contrary to the insignificant shift suggested by the Quebrada 
Monardes Formation data and the regional geologic and 
paleomagnetic data sets, which indicate margin-parallel 
transport in the central Andes is negligible [e.g., Beck et al., 
1994; Randall, 1998]. This apparent inconsistency with the 
Paleocene data may result from a problem with the Paleogene 
reference pole determination [Randall, 1998]. When 
compared with other proposed reference poles for the 
Paleogene or Paleocene [e.g., Beck, 1988; Butler et al., 1991; 
Roperch and Carlief, 1992], the amount of latitudinal 
displacement is variable and sometimes statistically 
significant, suggesting that the available Paleocene reference 
poles may not be well determined yet. 
The results from both localities in the Cerro Valiente 
sequence reveal statistically significant clockwise rotations.

7. Tectonic Implications 
The variation in the magnitudes and senses of rotation 
observed in this study cannot be explained by a single large- 
scale mechanism, such as oroclinal bending or domino-style 
block rotation by widely separated transandean faults, and 
instead indicate that local tectonics dominate the pattern of 
rotations. The greater clockwise rotations in the Cerro 
Valiente sequence could be interpreted to indicate a 
multistage history of rotations with an earlier 
counterclockwise rotation of the Quebrada Monardes 
Formation. However, the spatial consistency of the rotations 
with the regional structures suggests the pattern can be best 
explained in terms of a single post-Paleocene tectonic event 
where the rotation is localized and due to deformation related 
to the SC-AA Fault System and its subsidiary fault domains. 
It is impossible to discount a contribution from a large-scale 
process which would add a uniform rotation to the different
