localities, but the variation in the amounts of rotation can only 
be explained by local controls. Furthermore, the magnitudes 
of the clockwise rotations greatly exceed those predicted by 
current oroclinal bending models. The driving force for the 
rotations was apparently the major regional sinistral 
transpressive phase associated with deformation of the arc at 
-42-32 Ma [Tomlinson et al., 1993; Mpodozis et al., 1994; 
Cornejo et al., 1997]. 
Within the southern domain the amount of rotation 
recorded by the Cerro Valiente, Quebrada Cerros Bravos, and 
Quebrada Ci6naga sampling localities increases toward the 
SC-AA Fault (Figure 11). This implies a gradient in the 
deformation across the southern domain, at least with respect 
to vertical axis rotations, wherein deformation increases 
toward the master fault. Similar deformation and 
paleomagnetic rotation gradients have been observed in the 
borderlands of other transcurrent fault systems and have been 
modeled analytically and numerically [Nelson and dones, 
1987; Sonder et al., 1986]. Following such models, the 
rotation gradient in the southern domain indicates the 
rotations are related to activity of the SC-AA system, but 
furthermore, given the sinistral sense of the simple shearing 
component of the master fault, the clockwise sense of the 
rotations suggests the rotations are a result of the pure-shear 
shortening component of the deformation. Although the 
above cited numerical models treat only the classic 
(nontranspressive) wrench-type fault systems, in theory the 
same gradients can occur for the shortening component in 
transpressive systens [Dewey et al., 1998]. 
The lack of a paleomagnetically determined rotation in the 
Quebrada Ci6naga area, despite being located where the NW 
trending strike-slip faults have the greatest displacements, 
suggests that these faults did not produce significant rotation. 
The lack of rotation may be related to a number of factors, 
including the faults are widely spaced (2-4 km), their slips are 
small (hundreds of metres to 1-2 km), and they appear to act 
as a transfer zone between two belts of shortening, suggesting 
the shear zone boundaries may be parallel to the faults 
themselves, in which case there would be no domino-style 
rotation associated with them. The NW trending faults 
maintain a more or less constant strike across the southern 
domain, despite the variation in paleomagnetic rotations, 
suggesting those faults in the Quebrada Cerros Bravos and 
Cerro Valiente localities developed late in the deformation 
history. 
One alternative hypothesis is that the southern domain 
suffered a more or less homogeneous clockwise rotation and 
that sinistral shear on the NW trending faults in the Quebrada 
Ci6naga area overprinted a counterclockwise rotation. The 
hypothesis cannot be excluded, but it seems less probable in 
that it requires the fortuity that the overprinting 
counterclockwise rotation be of similar magnitude as the 
clockwise rotation. 
Abels and Bischoff [1999] recently proposed a model 
wherein widely spaced NW trending basement faults transect 
the entire Eocene forearc and produce clockwise declination 
anomalies by a domino-style rotation of large crustal blocks. 
As their model is largely based on the geology of the southern 
domain, the data contained herein pertain directly to their 
model. In their model, one of their NW trending transandean 
faults corresponds to the set of NW trending faults in the 
Quebrada Cinaga area. The mapping of Cornejo et al. 
[1993, 1998] indicates, however, that the faults in Quebrada 
Ci6naga do not cut the SC-AA Fault, nor do they cut stratified 
units located in the hanging walls of the reverse faults which 
the NW trending faults terminate into; instead the stratified 
units strike across the ends of the NW trending faults (Figure 
2). We do not dispute Abels and Bischoffs [1999] suggestion 
that the Eocene NW trending faults may have had an origin in 
the reactivation of older basement structures that have a 
greater continuity, but we do dispute that these basement 
faults were reactivated across the entire width of the forearc 
as Eocene transandean faults. Instead, the mapping indicates 
that the Eocene activity of the NW trending faults is localized 
and that they are secondary to the main N-S trending 
structures in the area. Furthermore, although the basic form

In the central domain the clockwise rotation obtained from 
the Cerro Valiente sequence is interpreted as the result of the 
kinematics of the displacement transfer that characterizes the 
area (Figure 12). In the kinematic model, differential 
movement on lower thrusts, related to the progressive 
replacement of their displacement by movement on higher, 
westerly positioned thrusts, causes clockwise rigid-body 
rotations and E-W dextral shear manifested by numerous E-W 
dextral strike-slip faults. The model is consistent with the 
notably more NE trend of structures in the domain compared 
to those in the northern fold-and-thrust belt and in the 
southwestern sector of the central domain (Figure 3). In fact, 
if the NE trending structures are rotated back to undo the 
declination anomaly indicated by the paleomagnetic data, the 
structures become N-S trending, parallel to the structural grain 
in the southwest sector (Figure 12a). 
The counterclockwise rotation at the Mina Vieja sampling 
locality is consistent with the structural trends in the 
immediate area (Figures 3 and 4) and the prediction of 
Cornejo et al. [1993]. If the structural trends are restored by 
the rotation amount (-30 ø clockwise), the map-scale fault 
bend anticline becomes N-S trending, and the dextral strike- 
slip faults become E-W striking, parallel to the correlative 
structures in the surrounding area. This suggests the N-S 
structural grain in the surrounding area is a primary 
orientation with no significant paleomagnetic rotation. 
Crosscutting relations indicate that the counterclockwise 
rotation of the Mina Vieja region occurred during the Eocene 
deformation. Since the rotation affected the trend of the fault 
bend anticline and dextral strike-slip faults, it must postdate 
the generation of these Eocene structures. Late in the 
deformation history, the-36 Ma Potrerillos Cobre porphyry 
intrusion [Marsh et al., 1997] was emplaced in the core of the 
anticline and contains in its contact aureole a metamorphic 
foliation having an orientation consistent with the regional 
shortening direction [Tomlinson, 1994]. The orientation of 
the cleavage is the same both east of the intrusion, where 
bedding strikes N-S, and northwest of the intrusion, where the 
cleavage transects the counterclockwise-rotated fault bend 
anticline (Figure 4). Maintenance of the cleavage orientation 
across the area suggests the counterclockwise rotation 
precedes the cleavage formation at-36 Ma. 
The mechanism by which the counterclockwise rotation 
was accomplished is less clear as it is inconsistent with the 
kinematics of the central domain described above. 
Furthermore, since the rotation is highly localized it is 
unlikely to be a result of the SC-AA system-parallel sinistral 
simple shearing. Cornejo et al. [1993], in addition to 
describing the E-W trending dextral faults, reported several E- 
W trending sinistral faults. They interpreted the sinistral 
movements to represent reactivation of the dextral faults 
during a second, probably unrelated, event. We propose the

to be recorded in the southern central Andes. Hartley et al. 
[1992b] report data from the Mejillones Peninsula which 
likewise suggest counterclockwise rotations. However, many 
of the site mean directions are poorly determined statistically, 
and the range of rotations among sites is so large that they did 
not calculate a mean for the formation or area. They 
attributed the rotations to small-scale fault block rotations, 
with each site representing an independent record of rotation. 
The Mina Vieja rotation is apparently highly localized, and so 
no inferences can be drawn from this data about the large- 
scale tectonics of the studied area or the tectonic history of the 
Andean margin, but it does serve to demonstrate the 
importance of local tectonics for rotations in the south central 
Andes. 
This is now one of several studies in the Andean margin 
where detailed paleomagnetic sampling over small structurally 
well-constrained areas has revealed complex patterns of 
rotation. Other examples from the Argentine Puna [Aubry et 
al., 1996] and the Bolivian Altiplano [Butler et al., 1995] 
have also shown temporal and spatial variability of rotations. 
Together these integrated studies highlight the importance of 
local tectonic influences on the observed rotation patterns and 
demonstrate that an understanding of local structure is crucial 
to the interpretation of rotation data. Furthermore, care 
should be taken when using paleomagnetic data to interpret 
the large-scale tectonic evolution of the Andes and other 
tectonically active margins. 
8. Conclusions 
The presence of dual magnetic polarities at four of the five 
sampling localities, a positive inclination-only fold test in the 
Quebrada Monardes Formation, and a positive fold test in the 
Cerro Valiente sequence indicates that all units carry a 
predeformational and probably primary remanence. 
Comparison with appropriate reference poles indicates 
varying amounts of rotation in the region east of the SC-AA 
Fault. The pattern is too complex to be explained by large- 
scale tectonic rotation mechanisms alone, whether it be 
oroclinal bending or large-scale domino-style block rotation. 
The model proposed to explain the interpreted rotations is 
therefore one of discrete, localized, in situ rotations resulting 
from an Eocene sinistral transpressive event wherein response 
to the transpressional deformation is varied and forms several 
distinct domains of differing tectonic style, rotation amounts, 
and rotation senses. 
Results from the southern domain of sinistral strike-slip 
faults demonstrate a decrease in clockwise rotation with 
increasing eastward distance from the master fault trace, 
irrespective of the age of the sampled unit. This is consistent 
with the rotations being related to activity of the SC-AA Fault. 
Furthermore, the clockwise sense of the rotations is consistent 
with the structural style that indicates a dominance of 
shortening over margin-parallel shear in the transpressive 
system. Since units as young as Paleocene are affected, the 
rotations must be post-Paleocene in age. The result from the 
central domain likewise records a post-Paleocene clockwise 
rotation and is interpreted in terms of rotation due to 
differential motion on thrust sheets in a displacement transfer 
zone between the fold-and-thrust belt to the north and the N-S 
trending reverse faults, including the Agua Amarga thrust, to 
the south. Sites collected from the Quebrada Monardes 
Formation in the Mina Vieja area record a counterclockwise 
rotation that is highly localized and interpreted as a result of 
E-W sinistral shear developed during differential movement 
of the underlying thrust; the differential movement possibly 
being imposed by along-strike mechanical heterogeneities in 
the block through which the thrust propagated. The 
counterclockwise rotation affects Eocene structures but not a 
cross-cutting cleavage developed late in the deformation 
history and associated with the 36 Ma Potrerillos Cobre 
porphyry intrusion. These relations therefore bracket the 
timing of rotation to the Eocene. 
Overall, the data highlight the importance of localized 
tectonics in controlling rotations, even where the rotations are 
the consequence of a single deformational event. 
Furthermore, it underscores the significance of relating 
rotations interpreted from paleomagnetic data in terms of the 
structure and tectonic history of the sampling locality.

Paleomagnetic research in Chile is supported by NERC grant

(SERNAGEOMIN-Chile). We would like to thank Paula Comejo 
and Antonio Diaz for their assistance in the field. Paleomagnetic 
analysis was carried out using Randy Enkin's software. Constructive 
reviews by R. Butler, J. Kley, and P. Roperch have helped improve 
the manuscript.

Paleomagnetic study of Upper Jurassic rocks from the
Sichuan basin: tectonic aspects for the collision between the
Yangtze Block and the North China Block
Masahiko Yokoyama a;*, Yuyan Liu b, Nadir Halim a, Yo-ichiro Otofuji a
a Department of Earth and Planetary Sciences, Faculty of Science, Kobe University, Kobe 657-8501, Japan
b China University of Geosciences, Wuhan 430074, China
Received 26 March 2001; received in revised form 17 August 2001; accepted 4 September 2001
Abstract
A paleomagnetic study has been carried out on Late Jurassic redbeds in the Sichuan basin, at the northern part of the
Yangtze Block. Upper Jurassic brownish-red sandstones and brownish-red siltstones were collected in the Penglaizhen
Formation at 26 sampling sites around Jiangyang city (30.4‡N, 104.5‡E). Thermal demagnetization isolated a high
temperature magnetization component with a maximum unblocking temperature of about 690‡C. The primary nature
of magnetization acquisition is ascertained through a 95% confidence level positive fold test, as well as a positive
reversal test. The tilt-corrected overall mean direction of 24 sites is D = 25.9‡, I = 26.7‡ (
K95 = 4.7‡), leading to a
paleomagnetic pole situated at 61.3‡N/222.7‡E (A95 = 4.2‡). This pole position agrees with two other Late Jurassic poles
from the Sichuan basin, indicating that this basin has behaved as a rigid block since Late Jurassic. These three poles
from the Sichuan basin therefore provide a characteristic Late Jurassic pole for the stable part of the Yangtze Block
(64.3‡N, 231.2‡E, A
95 = 6.7‡). Comparison of the Late Jurassic pole of the Yangtze Block with the contemporaneous
pole for the North China Block (NCB) identifies a significant difference, implying that the relative movement between
the Yangtze Block and the NCB continued during, and probably after, the Late Jurassic. Paleomagnetic and geological
evidence reveals that the Yangtze Block collided first with the NCB during the Early Permian, and continued to
penetrate into it while undergoing a clockwise rotation until the Early Cretaceous. ß 2001 Elsevier Science B.V. All
rights reserved.
Keywords: paleomagnetism; tectonics; Upper Jurassic; Yangtze Platform; plate collision
1. Introduction
The Asian continent is a mosaic of tectonic
blocks (Fig. 1a). One of the most prominent tec-
tonic events that a¡ected these blocks during the
Mesozoic is the collision between the Yangtze
Block and the NCB. This collision occurred along
the east-trending Qinling^Dabieshan suture zone.
According to paleomagnetic studies [1,2], the two
blocks ¢rst collided during the Permian near their
eastern parts, and then progressively scissored to-
gether as the Yangtze Block rotated clockwise
with respect to the NCB. This scissor-like colli-

sion model is supported by the progressive west-
ward transition from marine to continental sedi-
mentation along the Qinling^Dabieshan suture
zone [3].
The age assignment for the cessation of colli-
sion is controversial, although a scissor-like mo-
tion of the collision is con¢rmed by both geolog-
ical and paleomagnetic evidence. The geological
estimate leads to an age older than that estimated
paleomagnetically. Stratigraphic correlations and
sedimentary features within the Qinling^Dabie-
shan suture zone suggest a Late Triassic cessation
of the collision [4,5], whereas preliminary paleo-
magnetic studies claim that the collision contin-
ued until the Middle Jurassic [6] or even the Mid-
dle Jurassic^Late Jurassic boundary [7^9]. This
discrepancy on the age assignment is due to di¡er-
ent de¢nitions for the cessation of the collision.
Indeed, the geological evidence reveals the timing
of closure of a proto-ocean between the Yangtze
Block and the NCB, whereas the paleomagnetic
data provide an age for the cessation of the rela-
tive motion some time after the ocean that existed
between them had vanished. In order to decipher
the relative motion between these two blocks at
the latest stages of collision after the closure of
the Qinling^Dabieshan suture zone, detailed post-
Late Triassic paleomagnetic studies are required
for the Yangtze Block as well as for the NCB.
Post-Late Triassic paleomagnetic poles have
been computed for areas spread over the Yangtze
Block [2,7^9]. The northwestern and southwestern
parts of this block were subjected to Cenozoic
intra-cratonic deformation [10^12], and paleo-
magnetic poles from these areas can not be re-
garded as representative of the stable block. It is
therefore necessary to establish a characteristic
paleomagnetic pole from a tectonically stable
part of the Yangtze Block, in order to understand
its relationship to the NCB.
We have focused in this study on Late Jurassic
formations from the Sichuan basin that is consid-
ered to be a stable part of the Yangtze Block.
Indeed, this basin is widely covered by Jurassic
and Cretaceous strata in which no faults are ob-
served. On the basis of Late Jurassic paleomag-
netic data from this area, a characteristic Late
Jurassic pole for the Sichuan basin is established,
and compared to a pole for the NCB in order to
examine relative motions between the two blocks.
2. Geological setting and sampling
The Sichuan basin extends for 1000 km E^W
and 500 km N^S, and is mainly ¢lled with Mes-
ozoic continental redbeds (Fig. 1b). According to
the Bureau of Geology and Mineral Resources of
Sichuan Province [13], Upper Jurassic strata in
the Sichuan basin are subdivided into the Suining
and the Penglaizhen Formations, ascendingly.
The Penglaizhen Formation consists of sand-
stones and mudstones. It underlies the Lower Cre-
taceous Chengqiannyan Group disconformably.
The Penglaizhen Formation is assigned to the
Late Jurassic on the basis of abundant ostracods
such as Darwinula oblonga and Darwinula legumi-
nella [14].
Paleomagnetic sampling was carried out around
Jiangyang city in the northwestern part of the
Sichuan basin, and focused on the Upper Jurassic
Penglaizhen Formation. In the northwestern part
of this basin, Upper Jurassic and Lower Creta-
ceous redbeds are gently folded along northeast-
trending axis. As early Neogene Formations un-
conformably overly Jurassic to Paleogene strata in
the northwestern margin of the basin [15], the
folding is considered as having occurred at the
early Neogene.
The Penglaizhen Formation widely crops out as
a monoclinal sequence with dip shallower than
10‡ south of Jiangyang city, whereas northwest
of the city this formation is folded into a north-
east-trending anticline (Fig. 2). Twenty-six sites
were sampled, eight of which were collected
from both limbs of the anticline (three sites
from the northern limb and ¢ve sites from the
southern limb). The remaining 18 sites were col-
lected from the monoclinal sequence. Only one
sedimentary layer was sampled at each site. These
sedimentary layers consist of brownish-red-col-
ored rocks (siltstones, silt-sandstones and ¢ne-
grained sandstones), except for three red silt-sand-
stone layers (JY16, JY17 and JY18). Five to ten
hand samples were collected at each site. The
present declination value at the sampling site is

3. Paleomagnetic results
Samples were cut into 23-mm long and 25-mm
diameter specimens. Remanent magnetization was
measured using a 2G cryogenic magnetometer.
Stepwise thermal demagnetization up to 690‡C
was conducted with a Natsuhara TDS-1 thermal
demagnetizer. Acquisition of isothermal remanent
magnetization (IRM) and back-¢eld demagnetiza-
tion were performed on a 2G pulse magnetizer up
to maximum ¢elds of 2.7 T. Magnetic compo-
nents were resolved using principal component
analysis [17].
For the brownish-red-colored specimens, the
larger grain sizes possess the weaker natural re-
manent magnetization (NRM) intensities
[3.3 þ 2.6(10
33 A/m) for siltstones, 2.2 þ 1.5(10 33
A/m) for silt-sandstones, and 1.6 þ 0.8(10 33 A/m)
for ¢ne-grained sandstones]. Thermal demagneti-
zation revealed two magnetic components. The
low temperature component (LTC) was erased
by 150‡C. The high temperature component
(HTC), with an unblocking temperature of
690‡C, appeared above 450‡C for the siltstones
(Fig. 3a,b), whereas the silt-sandstones and ¢ne-
grained sandstones revealed distinct HTC in the
temperature range between 650 and 690‡C (Fig.
3c,d). No HTC was isolated from the ¢ne-grained
sandstones in one site (JY06).
Specimens from the red silt-sandstones have a
stronger magnetization than those from the
brownish-red silt-sandstones [the mean NRM in-
tensity is 6.5 þ 5.0(10
33 A/m)]. These specimens
yielded two magnetic components during thermal
demagnetization (Fig. 3e). After cleaning the LTC
in the ¢rst stages of demagnetization (by 300‡C),

4. Reliability of paleomagnetic directions
Because the paleomagnetic directions for eight
sites come from both limbs of an anticline, fold
tests can be applied. The mean direction from the
eight sites is D = 20.1‡, I = 28.8‡ ( k = 36.4,
K95 = 9.3‡) in in situ coordinates, and D = 23.1‡,
I = 26.8‡ (k = 67.0 K95 = 6.8‡) in stratigraphic coor-
dinates. The precision parameter ( k) increases
from 36.4 to 67.0 after tilt correction, although
the fold test of McElhinny [18] is inconclusive at
the 95% con¢dence level. A rigorous fold test
proposed by McFadden and Jones [19] is positive
at the 95% con¢dence level; the statistic P is
0.677 in in situ and 0.086 in stratigraphic coordi-
nates, while the critical value is 0.648 at the
95% con¢dence level. The tilt-corrected mean di-
rection is thus considered to be of pre-folding
origin.

5. The characteristic Late Jurassic pole for the
stable part of the Yangtze Block
The Late Jurassic paleomagnetic pole for the
Jiangyang area lies at 61.3‡N/222.7‡E
(A
95 = 4.2‡) (Table 2). This pole is compared to
other coeval poles for the Sichuan basin in Table
2 and Fig. 6a. Late Jurassic poles based on reli-
able paleomagnetic data sets with a positive fold
test are reported from Bazhong [12] and Wang-
chang [21], and lie respectively at 64.7‡N, 236.0‡E
(A
95 = 7.0‡) and 66.6‡N, 236.4‡E ( A95 = 7.6‡).
While the Jiangyang pole is computed for the
southern area of the northwestern part of the Si-
chuan basin, those of Bazhong and Wangchang
counties are for its northern area. However, the
pole for Jiangyang is indistinguishable from the
poles of Bazhong and Wangchang at the 95%
con¢dence level (6.9‡ þ 8.2‡ and 8.0‡ þ 8.7‡, re-
spectively). This indicates that no signi¢cant rela-
tive motion has occurred between the northern
and southern areas of the northwestern part of
the Sichuan basin since the Late Jurassic.
The pole for Jiangyang is compared with the
coeval pole for Ya’an (29.9‡N, 102.9‡E) in the
northwestern peripheral part of the Sichuan basin
[10]. The pole for Jiangyang is signi¢cantly di¡er-
ent from the pole for Ya’an at the 95% con¢dence
level (19.5‡ þ 14.2‡). This di¡erence can be de-
scribed as a signi¢cant counter-clockwise rotation
(19.7‡ þ 15.1‡) and a non-signi¢cant southward
displacement (5.3‡ þ 11.4‡) of the Ya’an area.
This indicates that Ya’an area su¡ered relative
rotation with respect to Jiangyang area, and to
the other area of the Sichuan basin in general.

For this reason, we decide not to include the
Ya’an pole in the computation of the Late Juras-
sic characteristic pole for the Sichuan basin.
A mean Late Jurassic pole for the Sichuan ba-
sin has thus been calculated using poles from the
Bazhong, Jiangyang and Wangchang localities
that cover a large area of the northwestern part
of the basin; this pole lies at 64.3‡N/231.2‡E
(A
95 = 6.7‡). In the central part of this basin,
Upper Jurassic strata widely crop out as £at-lying
sequences, indicating that the central part of the
basin has experienced little tectonic deformation
since the Late Jurassic. The Bureau of Geology
and Mineral Resources of Sichuan Province [13]
report that no large faults a¡ect the Upper Juras-
sic strata between the northwestern and central
parts of the basin. Based on this stable aspect,
pointed out by geological evidence as well as by
similar pole positions from the three areas, the
Sichuan basin is assumed in the following as a
tectonically stable area. Therefore, we consider
that the pole we have computed represents a char-
acteristic Late Jurassic pole for the tectonically
stable part of the Yangtze Block.

As the Ya’an area is situated within the Long-
menshan thrust belt that separates the Sichuan
basin from the Songpan^Ganzi fold belt, we sug-
gest that this relative motion is due to local scale

The mean pole we have computed is signi¢-
cantly di¡erent from the pole of Huili [7,8] de-
rived from the southwestern part of the Yangtze
Block (Fig. 6b). The discrepancy between these
pole positions suggests a southward movement
of the Huili area with respect to the rigid Yangtze
Block. Yokoyama et al. [12] attribute this move-
ment to a large southward displacement of the
southwestern part of the Yangtze Block as an in-
dependent tectonic block, referred to as the
‘Kungdian High’ [22]. The amount of southward
displacement evaluated from the present study is
16.0‡ þ 8.2‡, which corresponds to 1800 þ 900 km.
The pole from the southwestern part of the Yang-
tze Block has therefore been an excluded from
calculation of the characteristic pole for the stable
part of this block.
6. Tectonic aspects of the collision between the
Yangtze Block and the NCB
In order to discuss tectonic aspects of the colli-
sion between the Yangtze Block and the NCB, the
paleomagnetic poles of these two blocks are com-
pared during the interval between the Late Per-
mian and Early Cretaceous (Table 2, Fig. 7).
Since the Sichuan basin is now identi¢ed as a
tectonically stable part of the Yangtze Block, new
characteristic Late Permian and Early Triassic
poles for the Yangtze Block are recalculated
from paleomagnetic poles reported from the Si-
chuan basin. The Early Cretaceous pole is recal-
culated from paleomagnetic directions of four
sites at Guanyin (29.1‡N, 104.6‡E) and four sites
at Xinjin (30.4‡N, 103.8‡E) [10]. No Middle Tri-
assic to Middle Jurassic poles are computed be-
cause of the lack of paleomagnetic data from the
Sichuan basin for that time window.
Late Permian to Early Cretaceous poles for the
NCB are based on reviews by Enkin et al. [2] and
Gilder and Courtillot [9]. Permo^Triassic magne-
tostratigraphic data recently reported [23] are ac-
cepted as reliable, and listed in Table 2. The char-
acteristic Late Jurassic pole is computed using

The poles of the Yangtze Block are located
apart from those of the NCB at the Late Permian
and the Early Triassic (Fig. 7a,b). The angular
distances are larger than 55‡. The pole positions
for the NCB from the Middle Triassic to the Mid-
dle Jurassic successively approach the Late Juras-
sic pole position of the Yangtze Block (Fig. 7c).
By the Late Jurassic, the pole position of the
Yangtze Block is still signi¢cantly di¡erent from
that of the NCB at the 95% con¢dence level
(11.7‡ þ 9.2‡) (Fig. 7d). The paleomagnetic poles
from the two blocks, however, occupy the same
position by the Early Cretaceous (Fig. 7e). We
suggest on the basis of these results that the rela-
tive motion between the Yangtze Block and the
NCB was still taking place during the Late Juras-
sic. The scissor-like collision phenomena which
occurred later than the Early Permian [1] has
most likely been taking place until the Early Cre-
taceous.
The relative motion of the Yangtze Block with
respect to the NCB, between the Late Jurassic
and the Early Cretaceous, is described in terms
of clockwise rotation (6.8‡ þ 9.8‡) and northward
displacement (9.8‡ þ 7.4‡) of the Yangtze Block
(Fig. 8). The Euler pole, which superimposes the
poles of the Yangtze Block and NCB, lies at ap-
proximately 20.0‡N/150.0‡E. As the solution for a
Euler pole is not unique, we have chosen the one
situated east of the Yangtze Block to enable both
the clockwise rotation and northward displace-
ment of the Yangtze Block to take place. The
displacement about this Euler pole predicts a
left-lateral motion along the Tan^Lu Fault system
that represents the eastern boundary between the
Yangtze Block and the NCB. According to Xu et
al. [25], a left-lateral displacement of 1000^1500
km took place along this fault system during the
Mesozoic. The highest peak of this left-lateral dis-
placement occurred in the last part of the Late
Jurassic or the earlier part of the Early Creta-
ceous between 140 Ma and 130 Ma (the average
rate of this left-lateral displacement is up to 5^10
cm/yr). The sense and timing of the movements
on the Tan^Lu Fault system, determined by ¢eld
observation, is consistent with those expected
from paleomagnetism. The clockwise rotation
and northward displacement of the Yangtze
Block is in our opinion a realistic Late Jurassic
tectonic scenario for the collision.
Since geological investigation of the Qinling^
Dabieshan suture zone indicates that ocean clo-
sure was complete by the Late Triassic [3^4], the
Late Jurassic relative motion between these blocks
is attributable to penetration of the Yangtze
Block into the NCB. Okay and Sengor [26] pro-
posed that exhumation of the ultra-high-pressure
rocks within the Qinling^Dabieshan suture zone is
mainly caused by intracontinental thrusting and
concomitant with erosion and back thrusting of
this suture zone. They proposed that this phe-
nomenon is similar to that in the Himalayas
that resulted from the indentation of India. The
intracontinental thrusting would have given rise
to a Late Jurassic to Early Cretaceous heat
source, which is suggested by U^Pb ages
(132 þ 10 Ma and 152 þ 13 Ma) on granites in
the Qinling^Dabieshan suture zone and in the
Shandong area [27]. We conclude that penetration
of the Yangtze Block is a Late Jurassic tectonic
aspect of the collision between the Yangtze Block
and the NCB.

Paleomagnetism and 40Ar/39Ar-dating of Late Mesozoic Volcanic 
Pipes of Minusinsk Depression (Russia) 
V.Yu. Bragin, V.N. Reutsky, K.D. Litasov, V.G. Mal’kovets, A.V. Travin, and D.V. Mitrokhin 
United Institute of Geology, Geophysics and Mineralogy SB RAS, Koptyuga ave.3, Novosibirsk, 630090, 
Russia 
Received 25 April 1997; accepted 21 October 1997 
Abstract. Volcanic pipes with K-Ar ages 65-49 Ma 
(Zubkov et.al., 1989) are widespread in the Minusinsk 
depression. We present the results of the first 
paleomagnetic investigation on four volcanic pipes (42 
samples). accompanied by “Ari”Ar dating. All four pipes 
yield a high temperature ChRM component of reversed 
polarity with mean direction D=l78.8, I=-62, n=33, 
k=160.7. a95=7.3. However, some samples from the Bele 
pipe demonstrate another direction (D=244.3, I=-58.2, n=4, 
k=407.4. a95=4.6). 40Ar/‘9Ar method gave plateau ages of 
pipes ranging from 74 to 81 Ma. These results cast some 
doubt on previous K-Ar dating. The paleomagnetic poles 
corresponding to both directions of magnetization are 
statistically different from the APWP of Eurasia given by 
Besse and Courtillot (1991). Paleomagnetic poles from 
basaltic rocks of the near-Baikal region (Khramov, 1984) 
are consistent with the first direction identified from 
Minusinsk depression, but again are different from the 
APWP of Eurasia. These data, therefore, call into question 
the validity of the Eurasian APWP to Northern Asia. 
0 1999 Elsevier Science Ltd. All rights reserved 
1 Introduction 
The Apparent Polar Wander Path (APWP) for Eurasia 
(Besse and Courtillot, 199 1) is usually employed as a basic 
reference curve for Late-Mesozoic - Cenozoic 
paleomagnetic constrains of Asia (Thomas, et al, 1996, 
Kravchinsky et al, 1996, Zhao et al. 1996). Nevertheless, 
the majority of paleomagnetic data from volcanic rocks of 
Siberia (Khramov, 1984) are in a rather poor agreement 
with the Eurasian APWP. The question now arises of 
whether it is possible to extend the Eurasian APWP to 
Siberia. The only way to solve the problem is to perform 
Correspondence to: V.Yu.Bragin, United Institute of 
Geology, Geophysics & Mineralogy SB RAS, Koptyuga 
ave.3, Novosibirsk, 630090, Russia. 
E-mail: kaz@uiggm.nsc.ru 
paleomagnetic and 40Ar/39Ar investigations on volcanic 
rocks from within the Siberian Craton, which has been a 
stable tectonic regime since the Late Mesozoic. One of the 
most suitable areas for such investigations is the Minusinsk 
Depression, where volcanic pipes of Late Mesozoic - Early 
Cenozoic age intrude into slightly deformed Devonian and 
Carboniferous strata. In this paper we present the first 
paleomagnetic and radiometric results on four of these. 
2 Geological setting and sampling 
2. I Geology 
The Minusinsk Depression is located within the Caledonian 
fold belt of Northern Asia (Fig. 1). This depression is of 
complicated tectonic origin, and its formation was 
accompanied by intensive alkaline-subalkaline Devonian 
volcanism. Brief reviews and some geodynamic 
interpretation of the development of this region are given 
by Zubkov et al. (1989) and Ashchepkov et al. (1995). 
A ring of Mesozoic - Cenozoic alkaline-basalt volcanism 
has been found at the northern margin Minusinsk 
Depression. The volcanic pipes and dikes arc grouped over 
the margins of Kopievo dome-shaped uplift and located 
near flexures and main faults (Fig.1). These volcanic bodies 
represent the root system of volcanic eruptions, forming 
volcanic pipes of complex structure, lava necks and 
numerous dikes. Pipes mostly are multiphase structures 
composed of eruptive breccias with altered groundmass 
containing abundant debris of basalts and hypabyssal 
basanites. No cover facies have been identified. Despite 
textural variety of the basalts, their chemical composition 
remains constant, and they are all classed as basanites. The 
volcanic rocks have been intruded into Devonian- 
Carboniferous age terrigenous deposits. 
The K-Ar isotopic ages (Zubkov et al., 1989) for these 
four volcanic pipes are found within the range of 71-45 Ma.

Samples were measured using a JR-4 spinner-

4 Results 
4.1 Paleomagnetism 
Two directions of magnetization can be resolved by 
thermal demagnetization (Fig.2). The first direction is of 
normal polarity, and is usually removed bellow 400°C. It 
has a large scatter and most likely represents viscous 
magnetization or its remains. The high temperature 
component of magnetization, defined by univectoral decay 
towards the origin, is isolated generally between 450°C and 
600°C. This direction is termed the ChRM and is identified 
only with reversed polarity. The sample ChRh4 directions 
group tightly into compact clusters with mean-pipe 
directions in close agreement. Only four samples from the 
Bele pipe show anomalous directions (Bele-2) different 
from the other pipes. The overall mean characteristic 
direction (excluding Bele-2 directions) were computed 
from four mean directions for different pipes (Fig.2 and 
Tab. 1)

5 Discussion 
Disparity between 40Ar/‘9Ar and K-Ar data arc probably 
caused by samples character. The inner structure of 
explosive pipe is sufficiently heterogeneous to carry out 
whole rock measurements. However, minerals here are 
vulnerable to surface factors and secondary thermal 
processes. Using step heating in Ar-Ar measurements it is 
possible divide gas fractions from secondary changed and 
fresh minerals. In this case the Ar-Ar plateau age seems to 
be more closely to the rock origin time than K-Ar age. The 
K-Ar dating based on the consideration of all sample gas 
quantity the apparent K-Ar age may be lowered.

Reversed polarity of ChRM directions for all pipes well 
correlate with obtained 4oAr/39Ar ages (taking into account 
confidence limits) and probably represents the end of 33R 
reversed polarity chron of the Magnetic Polarity Time 
Scale (Harland et al., 1989) whereas variations in K-Ar 
ages imply the presence both normal and reversed polarity 
for pipes with different ages. 
Distinctions between paleomagnetic poles obtained and 
poles of Eurasian APWP (Besse and Courtillot, 1991) are 
statistically significant as their confidence limits do not 
overlap (Fig. 2). Furthermore most of the Cretaceous and 
Cenozoic paleomagnetic directions obtained from the 
neighbor Baikal region (Khramov, 1984) and Gomy Altai 
(Thomas et al., 1996) also exhibit counterclockwise 
rotation relative to ((stable Asia)). The similar trend in 
discordance suggests that it is not random and may reflect 
real motions of Siberian blocks. 
6 Conclusions 
AriAr dates from volcanic pipes from Minusinsk 
depression yield apparent ages of about 80 Ma, which we 
consider to be the best estimation for investigated pipes. 
Paleomagnetic data from the pipes yield well-defined 
reversed polarity magnetization with a virtual geomagnetic 
pole at 78.3’N, 271’E (A95=9.9”). Our 40Ar/‘9Ar dates 
indicates that the magnetization was probably acquired at 
the end of chron 33R (Harland et al., 1989). The virtual 
geomagnetic pole obtained in this study statistically differs 
from the reference APWP for Eurasia of Besse and 
Courtillot (1991) and thus calls into the question the 
implementation of Eurasian APWP to Northern Asia.

Paleomagnetic reconnaissance of early Mesozoic
carbonates from Williston Lake, northeastern
British Columbia, Canada: evidence for late
Mesozoic remagnetization
1
Giovanni Muttoni, Dennis V. Kent, and Mike Orchard
Abstract: Three classic sections of Middle and Late Triassic fossiliferous limestones cropping out around Williston
Lake in British Columbia, Canada, were sampled for paleomagnetic study. The objective was to test the suitability of
these units for detailed magnetobiostratigraphic study with the aim of improving the reference Triassic geomagnetic
polarity time scale. The Williston Lake characteristic magnetizations differ, however, from any Triassic North America
cratonic reference directions. A satisfactory agreement is found instead with Cretaceous – early Cenozoic North America
cratonic reference directions. The exclusive occurrence of normal polarity suggests that remagnetization likely occurred
during the Cretaceous long normal superchron. Remagnetizations may have been triggered by connate brines, which
moved along aquifers of porous sandstones and carbonates in the early stages of Laramide folding.
Résumé : Trois sections fossilifères classiques de calcaires (Trias moyen et tardif), affleurant autour du lac Williston
en Colombie Britannique, ont été échantillonnées pour une étude paléomagnétique. L’objectif était de s’assurer de la
pertinence de ces unités pour une étude magnéto-bio-stratigraphique détaillée visant à améliorer l’échelle référentielle
de temps de la polarité géomagnétique au Trias. Les magnétisations caractéristiques du lac Williston diffèrent toutefois
de toute direction cratonique référentielle au Trias en Amérique du Nord. Toutefois, une corrélation satisfaisante est
établie avec les directions cratoniques référentielles du Crétacé–Cénozoïque précoce en Amérique du Nord.
L’occurrence exclusive d’une polarité normale suggère qu’il y eut probablement une remagnétisation au cours du long
superchron normal du Crétacé. Les remagnétisations peuvent avoir été déclenchées par des saumures connées qui se
sont déplacées le long d’aquifères de grès et de carbonates poreux dans les premières phases du plissement Laramide.

Introduction
The magnetostratigraphy and biostratigraphy of several
marine and continental sedimentary sequences of Early,
Middle, and Late Triassic age have been studied in recent
years with the aim to construct a reference Triassic geomagnetic
polarity time scale (GPTS; e.g., Ogg and Steiner 1991; Kent
et al. 1995; Gallet et al. 1996, 1998; Muttoni et al. 1997).
The most complete sequence of Late Triassic to earliest Jurassic
magnetic polarity reversals comes from the Newark conti -
nental rift basin succession of eastern North America (Kent
et al. 1995), which led to the construction of the first reliable
GPTS for 30 Ma of the Late Triassic (Kent and Olsen 1999).
Triassic stage boundaries are, however, historically based
on marine biostratigraphy, essentially from ammonoids and
conodonts. We performed a paleomagnetic reconnaissance at
three classic sections of Middle and Late Triassic marine
fossiliferous limestones around Williston Lake in northeastern
British Columbia. These sections have provided an integrated
conodont–ammonoid biostratigraphic scale for the North
America Triassic marine realm (Orchard and Tozer 1997).
This study is aimed at testing the suitability of these sections
for more detailed magnetostratigraphic study to correlate the
marine biostratigraphic zonation to the nonmarine Newark
reference GPTS.

Triassic succession was deposited within a major cratonic
embayment along the passive margin of the North American

that characterizes the Triassic system of the Foothills and
Front Ranges of the Western Canada Sedimentary Basin.
Williston Lake was created in 1967 for the generation of
hydroelectric power on Peace River. As a result, many of the
long-known Triassic outcrops studied since the 1920s by
F.H. McLearn and later by E.T. Tozer of the Geological Survey
of Canada were submerged and thus removed from further
study. However, with the creation of Williston Lake, several
new and unweathered Triassic rock localities became accessible
along the shoreline. At these localities, Tozer (1982, 1994)
collected new important Middle and Late Triassic ammonoid
assemblages, and Orchard and Tozer (1997) developed an
integrated conodont–ammonoid biostratigraphic scale.

Sampling localities
We focused our attention on three localities located along
Peace Reach on the northern shore of Williston Lake. From
west to east, these localities are Black Bear Ridge, Brown
Hill, and Beattie Ledge (also known as Beattie Hill; Fig. 1).
(1)The Black Bear Ridge section (56°05 ¢N, 236°58 ¢E) is
about 200 m thick and consists of the uppermost part of the

the entire Norian Pardonet Formation, which is capped with

Hettangian Fernie Formation. According to conodont
biostratigraphy, the Triassic section ranges from the upper
Carnian Nodosus Zone to the upper Norian Bidentata Zone.

located within the Monotis beds of late Norian age, 30 m
below the Triassic–Jurassic boundary (see note to Table 1 for

(2) The Brown Hill section (56°06 ¢N, 237°07¢E) consists

(Ladinian) to the Pardonet Formation of upper Norian age.

Rock magnetic properties
The intensity of the natural remanent magnetization
(NRM) at Black Bear Ridge, Brown Hill, and Beattie Ledge
is 6.0, 3.0, and 1.9 mA/m, respectively. The magnetic
mineralogy of selected samples was determined with acquisi-
tion curves of isothermal remanent magnetization (IRM) and
thermal decay of a composite IRM imparted at 2.5, 0.6, and
0.2 T fields along sample orthogonal axes according to the
method described by Lowrie (1990). IRM acquisition curves
reveal that the Pardonet Formation at Black Bear Ridge is
dominated by a soft coercivity component that saturates at
fields of about 0.4 T (Fig. 3, sample BB12.2B). The thermal
unblocking characteristics of orthogonal-axes IRM show that
this dominant low-coercivity magnetic phase has maximum
unblocking temperatures of 500–575°C (Fig. 4 a), suggesting
magnetite as the main carrier of the magnetic remanence.
IRM acquisition curves of representative samples from the
Ludington Formation at Black Bear Ridge (BB1.1B) and the
Liard Formation at Brown Hill (BH8B) and Beattie Ledge
(BL1.2B) reveal the presence of a soft coercivity phase,
again consistent with magnetite, which variably coexists
with a higher coercivity phase that does not saturate at 2.5 T
fields (Fig. 3). Thermal decay of orthogonal IRM shows that
this higher coercivity phase, mainly carried by the 2.5 T
field curve, persists to 675°C, and is, therefore, attributed to
hematite (e.g., Figs. 4 b–4d).

master apparent polar wander path (APWP) in North America
coordinates of Besse and Courtillot (1991) and selected Tri -
assic reference paleopoles from North America (Kent and
Witte 1993; Kent and Olsen 1997; Fig. 8).
The Williston paleopole at any degree of unfolding is far
removed from Triassic North American reference paleopoles
from either on or off the Colorado Plateau (Fig. 8). Asoutherly
motion of about 3000 km would be required to reconcile
Williston with North America Triassic cratonic paleopoles.
There is no geologic or paleomagnetic evidence, however,
that the Foothills and Front Ranges have ever moved
northward or southward by any substantial amount, only
that they have been thrust faulted east-northeast by a few
tens of kilometres during Laramide deformation pulses
(D.T.A. Symons, personal communication, 2000). Up to
4000 km of tectonic displacement in a northerly direction
during the Cretaceous–Eocene has been proposed for
allochthonous accreted and parautochthonous terrains of the
northern Cordillera located to the west of the Foothills and
Front Ranges (Irving et al. 1996 and references therein). The
exclusive occurrence of normal polarity remanence directions,
when the Middle and Late Triassic are characterized by two
or more reversals per million years (Muttoni et al. 1997;
Kent and Olsen 1999), is an additional argument against a
primary origin for the Williston remanence.
The full range of statistically significant Williston
paleopoles between 72 and 100% unfolding is compatible in
colatitude with the Cretaceous–Cenozoic portion of the stable
North America APWP. At 72% unfolding, the Williston
paleopole is rotated by 10 ± 12° clockwise with respect to
the Early Cretaceous North America reference paleopole
(124–88 Ma) of Van Fossen and Kent (1992; latitude
71.2°N, longitude 194.1°E), whereas at 100% unfolding the
Williston paleopole is rotated by 19 ± 10° counterclockwise
from this reference pole. At 87% unfolding, where directional
grouping is best, the angular distance between the Williston
and Cretaceous reference paleopoles is 7.5 ± 9°, whereas at
80% unfolding the paleopoles are also statistically indistin -
guishable (Fig. 8).
We suggest that Triassic rocks at Williston Lake were
remagnetized during the initial stages of the Cretaceous–
Cenozoic Laramide orogenic phase between 72 and 100%
unfolding. The exclusive occurrence of normal polarity
directions can then be reconciled with remanence acquisition
during either the Cretaceous long normal superchron, a
period of the Earth’s magnetic field from about 118 to 84
Ma characterized by stable normal polarity, or perhaps one
of the somewhat shorter, but still appreciable in length, normal
polarity chrons in the Late Cretaceous (e.g., C33n). Large-scale
dextral strike-slip faults associated with the Cretaceous–Eocene
northern Cordillera tectonics in the parautochthonous-accreted
terrains region to the west of the North America craton (e.g.,

Cretaceous remagnetizations in North
America
In the North America continent, remagnetizations of
Cretaceous age have been reported along the Rocky
Mountains from Mexico (Fig. 9, locality 1) to the northern
Canadian Cordillera (locality 22), up to the Northwest Territories

Gromme 1983). Remagnetizations are frequently of
thermoviscous or thermochemical origin (Kent 1985; Miller
and Kent 1988) associated with the emplacement of
batholiths or volcanic activity (localities 2–4, 10–12, 16, 18,

orogenic events (localities 1, 7, 8, 13, 14, 19). In the Foothills
of the Rocky Mountains and in the adjacent foreland domains,
remagnetizations of Cretaceous age have been specifically
associated with tectonically induced migration of mineralizing
fluids (localities 9, 15, 21, 24). The emplacement of thrust
sheets in zones of convergence causes the expulsion of
chemically active, hot fluids from the margin sediments toward
the craton (Oliver 1986, 1992). These fluids are thought to
play key roles in geologic phenomena, such as the distribution
of hydrocarbons and ores, the variation in the rank of coals,
and the growth of authigenic minerals, and were considered
responsible for widespread thermochemical remagnetizations
in the Appalachians during the Carboniferous – Early Permian
(Miller and Kent 1988 and references therein) (Fig 9, solid
circles). A similar mechanism involving fluid-flow events
associated with the Laramide orogeny has been recently
proposed to explain Cretaceous remagnetizations and other
geological phenomena in the Western Canada Sedimentary
Basin and adjacent Foothills regions (Enkin et al. 1997,
2000; Symons et al. 1998 b, 1999; Gillen et al. 1999; Cioppa
et al. 2000; Fig. 9, locality 15). In the Peace River Arch
area, large-scale fluid flows of Late Cretaceous – early
Cenozoic age moved from elevated recharge zones in the
west toward the eastern flank of the Western Canada
Sedimentary Basin, overprinting Precambrian–Devonian
fission-track data (Issler et al. 1990). It is, therefore, possible
that Triassic rocks at Williston Lake in the Peace River Arch
area were also remagnetized by fluid events of the type
described by Issler et al. (1990).
Conclusions
This study was aimed at obtaining magnetostratigraphic
data to establish a well-dated magnetic reversal sequence in
the Middle and Late Triassic classic fossiliferous localities at
Williston Lake in the Peace River Arch area of northwestern
British Columbia. However, all sites have been remagnetized
and cannot be used for their intended purpose. Sedimentary
rocks at Williston Lake bear only normal polarity magneti -
zation when the Middle and Late Triassic have been proved
to have frequent reversals (Muttoni et al. 1997; Kent et al.
1995). Williston magnetization components differ from any
Triassic North America cratonic (or Colorado Plateau) reference
direction, and a large-scale southerly motion would be
required if they were in fact Triassic, at odds with the
geological history of the northern Cordillera (Irving et al.
1996). Good agreement is found instead with Cretaceous – early
Cenozoic North America cratonic directions, and the exclusive
occurrence of normal polarity suggests that remagnetization
may have occurred during the Cretaceous long normal
superchron. Remagnetizations may have been triggered by
connate brines moving eastward along aquifers of porous
sandstones and carbonates (Bachu 1995) prior to or in the
early stages of folding in the Rocky Mountains thrust–fold
belt toward the North American craton during Laramide
orogeny in the Cretaceous, as suggested also for localities
elsewhere in the Western Canada Sedimentary Basin (e.g.,
Gillen et al. 1999). This study provides additional evidence
that the North America continent was affected by large-scale
remagnetizations associated with Cretaceous – early Cenozoic
orogenetic events such as the Sevier and (or) Laramide in
the west coast domains, complementary to the Paleozoic
Alleghany orogeny in the east coast domains. The virtual
absence of plate motion and, therefore, polar wander in the
North America continent during the Cretaceous (the so-called
“North America paleopole standstill,” Fig. 8) limits the use
of paleomagnetism to discriminate between remagnetizations
related to the Cretaceous (e.g., Sevier) or those of the
Cretaceous – early Cenozoic Laramide orogeny. On the
basis of pole position analysis on ancient remagnetized
rocks, however, we tend to exclude the occurrence of older
remagnetizations like those possibly associated with the Antler
or Sonoman orogeny of Late Devonian – Carboniferous and
Permian–Triassic age, respectively. The Sevier–Laramide
tectonic episode seems, therefore, to have overprinted any
previous one, like in the Appalachians, the Alleghany orog -
eny has commonly overprinted Taconic or Acadian
remagnetizations.

A palaeomagnetic study and age determinations of Tertiary rocks
in Nicaragua, Central America
S.-A. Elming,1 P. Layer2 and K. Ubieta 3
1 Department of Applied Geophysics, Lulea University of Technology, 97187 Lulea, Sweden. E-mail: sten-ake.elming@sb.luth.se
2 Geophysical Institute, University of Alaska, Fairbanks, Alaska, USA
3 Centro de Investigaciones Geoscientiﬁcas (CIGEO), the Autonomous University of Nicaragua (UNAN), Managua, Nicaragua
Accepted 2001 May 31. Received 2001 May 30; in original form 2000 February 4
SUMMARY
Palaeomagnetic, K–Ar and Ar 40 /Ar39 measurements have been made to elucidate
Nicaragua’s plate tectonic history. These show that the Nicaraguan Highland rotated
90u counterclockwise between 30 and 18 Myr ago, but the Paciﬁc Coastal Plain has not
rotated.
A lack of data has prevented a direct comparison with the tectonic history of adjacent
areas, in particular, the Chortis Block, which is the part of the Caribbean Plate that
is geologically most closely related to the Nicaraguan Highland. However, our data
suggest that the Caribbean Plate in this part of Central America was not consolidated
until c. 15 Ma.
Key words: Nicaragua, palaeomagnetism, radiometric ages, tectonic reconstructions,
Tertiary rocks.
INTRODUCTION
Nicaragua forms part of the Caribbean Plate (Fig. 1), which
is built up of a number of allochthonous terranes (Case et al.
1984) and has a complex geological history resulting from the
interaction between the North and South American, Farallon,
Cocos and Nazca plates. The present boundaries of the
Caribbean Plate are deﬁned by the distribution of seismic activity
(Molnar & Sykes 1969). Former plate boundaries evolved from
the relative positions of North and South America following the
Late Triassic–Jurassic break-up of Pangaea. In most Pangaea
reconstructions the area presently occupied by the Caribbean
Plate was overlapped by North and South America (Bullard
et al. 1965; Van der Voo et al. 1976; Pindell 1985), and the
Caribbean Plate is regarded as allochthonous to its neighbour-
ing plates. This means that North and South America are not
the rifted margins of the present-day Caribbean basin.
Duncan & Hargraves (1984) presented a model for the
evolution of the Caribbean in which the core of the plate was
formed from the lava that was poured out onto the Farallon
Plate when it moved eastwards over the Galapagos hotspot.
When the space between the Americas was big enough the
Caribbean entered the gap. Atc. 80 Ma the migration of South
America away from North America was more or less com-
pleted (Pindell 1985) and this may have been the time that the
Caribbean Plate entered.
Caribbean Plate boundaries have been predominantly either
strike-slip or convergent. Pindell & Dewey (1982) and Sykes
et al. (1982) suggest two distinct stages for the development of
the northern Caribbean Plate boundary. The ﬁrst is charac-
terized by a Late Cretaceous–Palaeocene northward conver-
gence, resulting in collision and suturing of the Antillean arc
with the Bahamas platform. This stage ended during the latest
Early Eocene–earliest Middle Eocene. The Caribbean Plate
then started to move eastwards relative to the North and South
American plates. The western part of this strike-slip boundary
evolved as a large pull-apart basin, the Cayman Trough. The
time of opening of the Cayman Trough has been estimated
at 45–50 Ma (Rosencrantz et al. 1988), and, from magnetic
anomalies produced by sea-ﬂoor spreading in the trough, the
rate of eastward movement has been estimated (Rosencrantz
et al . 1988). The trough opened at a rate of 20–30 mm yr
x1
from c. 50 to 30 Ma, when there was shift in the spreading ridges
and a slow-down of opening to less than 15 mm yr x1. This
probably reﬂects a reorganization of relative motion between
the North America and Caribbean plates.
As the Caribbean Plate is composed of various blocks and
microplates, a tectonic reconstruction of these is a basis for
the understanding of the formation of the Caribbean. Central
America can be divided into four major regions (Dengo 1969,
1985; Escalante 1990), the Maya, Chortis, Chorotega and Choco
Blocks (Fig. 1). The Chortis Block is deﬁned to encompass
southern Guatemala, Honduras, northern Nicaragua and
the western Nicaraguan Rise. This block has a pre-Mesozoic
continental-type crust, unlike the oceanic Chorotega Block in
the south. Central Nicaragua has been related to neither the
Chortis Block nor the Chorotega Block, while southwestern
Nicaragua may form part of the Chorotega Block (Di Marco
et al. 1995). The Chorotega Block constitutes most of the
southern Middle American landbridge and it has been suggested
that it formed the western edge of the Caribbean Plate during
the Late Cretaceous–Palaeocene (Di Marco et al. 1995). In an

GEOLOGY OF NICARAGUA
Nicaragua can be divided into at least two different tectonic
regimes separated by the SE–NW-trending Nicaraguan
Depression (Fig. 2), which has been deﬁned as a half-graben
(McBirney & Williams 1965). The Cocos Plate subducts below
the Caribbean Plate with northeastward motion, and an
associated chain of volcanoes is located in the western edge of
the depression parallel to the trench.
East of the depression, Nicaragua is dominated by Tertiary
volcanic rocks of the Central American Highlands, which
extend SE–NW through the country. In northern Nicaragua
these volcanic rocks are superimposed on metamorphosed
Palaeozoic and Mesozoic rock formations. The volcanic rocks
can be divided into the Matagalpa and Coyol groups. The
Oligocene–Palaeocene Matagalpa Group volcanics are thought
to be deposited on an ignimbrite plateau (Ehrenborg 1996).
The Pliocene–Miocene Coyol Group, which consists mainly of
lavas, breccias, lahars and locally of pyroclastic rocks, has been
divided into upper and lower subgroups (Parsons Corporation
Report 1972), characterized by basaltic rocks overlain by inter-
mediate to acid volcanic rocks. Ehrenborg (1996) has explained
the repeated stratigraphic sequence using a facies model, relating
various volcanic centres to each other and superseding the
older subdivision of the Coyol Group.
To the west of the depression, in the Paciﬁc Coastal Plain,
the rocks are predominantly of sedimentary origin and are
assumed to have been deposited on a Nicoya Complex type of
basement (Parsons Corporation Report 1972). The sediments,
tuffaceous shale, siltstone, greywacke, sandstone and lime-
stone, range in age from Cretaceous to Miocene (Rivas, Brito,
Masachapa and El Fraile formations) and are overlain by
sediments of similar composition to the El Salto Formation
and the pyroclastic deposits of the La Sierra Group (McBirney
& Williams 1965; Parsons Corporation Report 1972).
Seyfried et al. (1987) regard the Upper Cretaceous Rivas and
the Eocene Brito formations as parts of a continuous succession.
The Masachapa Formation is Oligocene in age (Auer 1942,
unpublished paper; Zoppis Bracci & Del Guidice 1958) and
the boundary between the Brito and Masachapa formations
has been interpreted as conformable (McBirney & Williams
1965). Also, the contact between the Masachapa Formation
and the overlying Miocene El Fraile Formation is regarded
as conformable (McBirney & Williams 1965; Kuang 1971) and
the El Fraile Formation interﬁngers with part of the volcanic
Tamarindo Formation.
The rocks of the Nicaraguan Highland are generally affected
by low-grade metamorphism of zeolite facies (Levi et al. 1987),

PALAEOMAGNETIC SAMPLING
Samples for the present study were collected from the
Nicaraguan Highland and from the Paciﬁc Coastal Plain.
The study includes some 245 samples from 30 sites (Fig. 3),
collected as block samples or with a portable drill, and oriented
with sun or magnetic compasses. Generally, each sampling site
represents a 10–20 m
2-scale outcrop. In the Highland, pre-
dominantly volcanic rocks from the Miocene Lower Coyol
Group and from assumed Oligocene–Palaeocene rocks of the
Matagalpa Group were sampled. As the tectonic control was
often poor, our ambition has been to collect samples of rocks of
similar age but geographically well-separated in order to detect
later local tectonic movements.
To the west of the Nicaraguan Depression we collected
sedimentary and intrusive rocks of the Rivas Formation, sedi-
mentary rocks of the Brito Formation and volcanic rocks of the
Tamarindo Formation. The ages of these formations are Upper
Cretaceous, Eocene and Miocene–Pliocene, respectively.
MINERALOGICAL STUDIES
Petrographic and X-ray diffraction studies (Nystro ¨m & Levi
1985; Elming 1985) have been carried out on specimens of
andesite, basalt and sedimentary rocks from a number of sites.
Most of the Tertiary rocks of this study are only incipiently
altered. As weathering is a particular problem in tropical
areas, martitization, the alteration of magnetite to haematite,
is a more or less common phenomenon. Martitization is here
developed preferentially on the grain surfaces and in the
crystals along lamella structures and in cracks. The degree of
martitization varies in the samples but is better developed in
rocks from some sites (e.g. sites 1, 3 and 6). Although the
remanent magnetization of haematite is usually more resistant
to demagnetization than magnetite, no signiﬁcant relation
between degree of martitization and directional variations of
the characteristic magnetizations was found. Magnetite is

K–Ar AND 40 Ar / 39 Ar RADIOMETRIC AGE
DETERMINATIONS
In order to constrain the ages of magnetizations in this study,
we have dated samples from selected palaeomagnetic sites by
the K–Ar and
40Ar /39Ar methods. Previous Rb–Sr and K–Ar
dating of whole-rock and mineral phases (Zoppis Bracci 1961;
Barr & Escalante 1969; McBirney & Williams 1965) from both
the Highland and the Paciﬁc Coastal Plain were of poor
resolution and indicate that many of the units may have been
emplaced over a long duration. Dating the same samples and
ﬂows for which we have stable magnetic directions allows us to
avoid assigning ‘incorrect’ or estimated ages to the magnetization.
The K–Ar age determinations were made by R. M. Macintyre
at the Scottish Universities Research and Reactor Centre
(Table 1). One–four palaeomagnetic samples from each of the
11 sites 2, 3, 6, 8, 9, 10, 11, 12, 13, 16 and 17 were analysed,
including andesite and basalt from the Lower Coyol and
Matagalpa groups and a diabase dyke (Table 1). Basalts from
sites 12 and 14 and the basic dyke at site 10 are not identiﬁed
in the ﬁeld as being part of any speciﬁc group; however, based
on evidence presented here, we have assigned these sites to the
Matagalpa and Lower Coyol groups, respectively. From the
Paciﬁc Coastal Plain, ignimbrite and basalt were dated. One of
the dated basalts was associated with palaeomagnetic site 25.
X-ray diffraction analyses and observations from thin-
sections (Nystro¨m & Levi 1985) show that most of the samples
are relatively well preserved. However, these relatively unaltered
rocks do contain up to 10 per cent montmorillonite and zeolite,
minerals known to pose problems for K–Ar whole-rock dating.
This potential for disturbance can be seen in some of the age
scatter in sites where more than one age determination was
made. For example, samples from sites 9 and 10 (Table 1) show
signiﬁcantly different ages of samples from the same ﬂow.
Although K–Ar ages from the Lower Coyol Group tend to be
younger than those from the Matagalpa Group, the ages from
the two groups show large ranges and overlap. Thus it is
possible that either some ﬂows have been misassigned in the
ﬁeld or that the K–Ar dating systematics have been disturbed in
some samples due to alteration.
In order to assess the extent of alteration in the samples and
the reliability of the K–Ar ages better, selected whole-rock
samples were dated by the

Paciﬁc Coastal Plain
One K–Ar age from a palaeomagnetic site of the Tamarindo
Group has an age of 12.3t 1.7 Myr for a basalt (site 25;
Table 1). Three additional samples from other locations of the
Tamarindo Group not associated with palaeomagnetic sites
have ages of 18.4t4.9 Myr (rhyolite ignimbrite), 15.4t0.5 Myr
(acid ignimbrite) and 13.7 t0.8 Myr (basalt) (Elming 1999).
The weighted average age for these samples is 14.8 t0.5 Myr.
Nicaraguan Highland
Eight of the 12 K–Ar age analyses of Lower Coyol rocks
are from basalt ﬂows and cluster about a single mode with a
weighted average age of 16.9t0.4 Myr. Of the remaining four
analyses, two (a 13 Myr age from site 11 and a 40 Myr age
from site 10) are not consistent with other more reliable samples
within the site and probably reﬂect argon loss or gain due to
alteration. Two samples from site 3 are from andesite rather
than basalt and they have an average age of 24.9 t0.8 Myr.
These ages are signiﬁcantly different from the average of the
basalt ages. It is not known if this difference reﬂects two stages
of volcanism in the Coyol Group or if the andesite samples have
incorporated excess argon and hence the ages are anomalous.
The spectrum of a single
40Ar /39Ar measurement from site
10 (Fig. 4) shows evidence of argon loss and the sample has an
integrated age of 17.5 t0.3 Myr. The integrated age of this
sample is similar to the average K–Ar age, which implies that
many of the Coyol samples may either have experienced some
argon loss or have been emplaced over a period of c. 2 Myr.
The plateau age of this sample is 18.5t 0.4 Myr and we
interpret this age to reﬂect more closely the true age of this
rock. In the absence of further geochronological information to
constrain the age of the Lower Coyol Group, we assign it an
age of c. 18 Myr.
The 13 K–Ar ages from the Matagalpa Group range from
about 18 to about 31 Myr (Table 1). 10 of the 13 ages form a
poorly constrained mode with an average age of 25.9t1.1 Myr.
It is probable that the samples of the Matagalpa Group reﬂect
multiple events (e.g. Ehrenborg 1996; Hodgson 1999) and an
average age of all sites is not geologically signiﬁcant.
Within the Matagalpa Group, the La Batea Formation
appears to be the youngest unit. Samples from sites 16 (basalt)
and 17 (andesite) of this formation have K–Ar ages of 25.8 and
17.8 Myr. Three samples were dated by the
40Ar /39Ar method.
Two of the samples show evidence of excess argon, probably
from a later alteration event. The average age for the basalt
unit (site 16) is about 23 Myr, while the age of the andesite
(site 17) is 19.6 Myr, signiﬁcantly younger.
Based on the palaeomagnetic evidence (presented below), the
remaining Matagalpa samples can be divided into two groups,
sites 8, 9 and 12, and sites 13 and 14. 11 K–Ar ages from the
ﬁrst group show a ‘bimodal’ distribution with two ages of
c. 18 Myr and nine ages scattering between 23 and 32 Myr,
with a mean K–Ar age of 26.5 t0.9 Myr. An
40Ar /39Ar age
of 23.80t 0.14 Mr is seen for a single sample from site 8,
consistent with the group of older ages. A sample from site 12
has an
40Ar /39Ar age of 17.61t 0.24 Myr, consistent with the
younger age group. These young ages are similar to ages seen
in ﬂows mapped as Lower Coyol, and it is possible that the
younger ages seen at these sites represent a second pulse of
magmatic activity.

Samples from sites 13 and 14 form the second palaeomagnetic
group. The mean K–Ar age from site 13 (two samples) is
27 Myr, while an 40Ar /39Ar plateau age of 32.1 t0.2 Myr is
seen from site 14 (Fig. 4). Although it is impossible to assess the
amount of argon loss from samples of site 13, it is possible that
these samples are signiﬁcantly older than those from other
Matagalpa sites and have an age of c. 30 Myr.
Age summary
Based on our new geochronological evidence, most of the
samples dated by the
40Ar /39Ar method show either signiﬁcant
argon loss or signiﬁcant argon gain. If these signs of alteration
are prevalent throughout the sample suite, then interpretation
of the K–Ar ages is difﬁcult. Nevertheless, we can infer that the
age of the Tamarindo Group of the Paciﬁc Coastal Plain is
c. 15 Myr, samples correlative with the Lower Coyol Group are
c. 18 Myr, the La Batea member of the Matagalpa Formation
is c. 20 Myr, Matagalpa sites 8, 9 and 12 are c. 24 Myr and
sites 13 and 14 are c. 30 Myr.
PALAEOMAGNETIC RESULTS
The specimens were demagnetized by conventional alternating
ﬁeld (AF) and thermal demagnetization techniques and remanent
magnetizations measured with spinner and cryogenic magneto-
meters. The different components of remanence were deﬁned
by principal component analyses (Kirschvink 1980), and vectors
deﬁned with mean angular deviations larger than 7u have been
rejected. The site mean directions and formation means were
calculated using Fisher (1953) statistics.
It was possible to isolate well-deﬁned high-stability mag-
netizations in 26 of the 30 sites that were sampled. The results
from some sites were discarded due to very poor within-site
groupings of directions. Usually there were no more than two
components of remanent magnetization (Fig. 5), one of which
was of low coercivity with a direction similar to that of the
present Earth ﬁeld (PEF; D=0u, I=43u).
The Nicaraguan Highland
Rocks assumed to be of the Coyol Group or of similar age have
been sampled at seven sites (2, 3, 4, 7, 10, 11 and 18; Fig. 3).
The coercivity of the remanence varies but the soft portion is
generally erased at c. 20 mT (Figs 5a and b). Although the
number of samples in each site is often small, the directions
of the highest-stability component, referred to as the charac-
teristic magnetization (Butler 1992), usually form well-deﬁned
means (Table 2; Fig. 6a) and they are of predominantly
reversed polarity when compared to the PEF. It seems possible
to distinguish two groups of directions. One (sites 2, 3, 4 and 7)
is characterized by negative inclinations and the other (sites 10,
11 and 18) by shallow and positive inclinations. However,
the gradual change from positive to negative directions may
reﬂect a trend of changing magnetization ages, rather than two
distinctly different times of magnetization. Therefore, these sites
are treated together here (mean of sites: D=180.2u, I=x2.8u,
a
95=11.9u; Table 3), representing one magnetization age. On
the basis of the age data presented here, the age of magnetization
is estimated at c. 18 Myr.
The rest of the rocks sampled in the Nicaraguan Highland
are assumed to be of Matagalpa age, i.e. older than c. 20 Myr.
The characteristic magnetizations are of dual polarity; however,
reversed polarities dominate. The inclinations are generally
rather shallow, i.e. less than c.t30u, and on changing the mag-
netizations to reversed polarity the declinations vary from
c. 90u to 150uE.
The basalt and andesite of the La Batea Formation (sites 5,
15, 16 and 17) are all sampled from the central southern part
of the Highland. The characteristic magnetization is generally of
high coercivity and the blocking temperatures indicate the
carrier to be magnetite–titanomagnetite (Fig. 5d). At site 17 the
remanence is of lower coercivity, but the direction is still stable
up to 65 mT. Only at this site is the magnetization of normal
polarity. When changing the polarity of the site mean directions
to reversed, the declinations of the site means are quite similar,
while the inclinations are different. The fairly big differences
in inclinations may indicate local tectonic disturbances. As the
inclinations are shallow, declinations would be little affected
by tilting; however, we have no evidence of tilting from ﬁeld
observations. The site mean directions form a mean for the
La Batea Formation ( D=148.8u, I=5.9u, a
95=16.1u; Table 3)
signiﬁcantly different from that of the Coyol Group (Fig. 6c). The
whole-rock K–Ar and
40Ar /39Ar data suggest a magnetization
age for this formation of c. 20 Myr.
Matagalpa rocks were also sampled in the central parts of
the Highland (sites 8, 9, 12, 13 and 14; Fig. 3). These rocks yield
directions of magnetization (Fig. 6a) of reversed and dual
polarities, signiﬁcantly different from those of the La Batea
Formation. The declinations vary from c. 90u to 140uE and the
inclinations are predominantly negative and lower than c. 30u.
It is possible to distinguish two groups of directions with
signiﬁcantly different declinations of c. 130uE (sites 8, 9 and 12)
and 90uE (sites 13 and 14), respectively. The rocks of the two
groups are sampled from geographically well-separated areas
(Fig. 3).
The coercivity of remanence of the ﬁrst group varies but the
directions are fairly stable after being demagnetized in 10 mT
AF. The rock at site 8 carries characteristic magnetizations of
dual polarity, which may indicate that the rock at this site has
not been remagnetized. As for the La Batea Formation the
mean directions of the sites (Table 2) show that the inclinations
are different while the declinations are quite similar. The
direction of magnetization at one of the sites (site 12) of this
grand mean is also anomalous with respect to its
40Ar /39Ar age.
The mean direction for this group of sites is also very poorly
deﬁned ( a
95=40.2u; Table 3) and cannot be used to represent
any speciﬁc age of magnetization.
The coercivity of the characteristic magnetization of the
second group is usually high and in some samples the mag-
netization is of dual polarity (Fig. 5c), possibly indicating
a primary origin of magnetization. The two site means are
not signiﬁcantly different from each other and the directions
probably belong to a single population. The mean of the sites
(D=93.0u, I=x22.0u) is also very close to the mean of the
samples (D=92.9u, I=x17.9u, a
95=4.0u; Table 3). The age data
suggest magnetization ages for this second group of 30 Myr.
Basalt of only a few million years in age (site 6) has been
sampled off the Caribbean coast of Nicaragua (Fig. 3). This
rock carries a stable remanent magnetization with a direction
(D=346u, I=22u) similar to that of the theoretical dipole ﬁeld
(Fig. 6a; Table 2).

The virtual geomagnetic pole (VGP) positions (Fig. 7)
calculated from the site means and the grand means of the
Highland show the same trend of distribution as poles calculated
from Cretaceous rocks in Honduras (Gose 1985; Gose & Finch
1992). The centres of the polar arcs coincide with the sampling
region, which means that the distribution of poles may have
its origin in local structural rotations as well as plate tectonic
rotations (MacDonald 1978, 1990).
The Paciﬁc Coastal Plain
From the Paciﬁc Coastal Plains, basalt (site 25) and andesite
(site 26) of the Tamarindo Group have been sampled. The site
mean directions are of both reversed ( D=186u, I=x23u, site
25; Fig. 6b; Table 3) and normal ( D=356u, I=19u, site 26)
polarities and on inverting the polarity of one they are not
signiﬁcantly different. After removing a soft component of
remanence with a direction similar to that of the PEF, the
magnetization of the basalt is of high coercivity and the
directions are stable up to 100 mT AF (Fig. 5e). The portion of
soft remanence is much smaller in the andesite and a stable
magnetization is isolated after treatment in c. 25 mT AF. The
mean direction of the two sites ( D=0.9u, I=21.1u) is not
signiﬁcantly different from the mean of the samples ( D=2.0u,
I=21.6u, a
95=3.2u; Table 3). The Tamarindo Group is regarded
as equivalent to the Coyol Group of the Highland and an age of
c. 15 Myr is estimated for the magnetization on the basis of the
age data presented here.

ORIGIN OF MAGNETIZATION
The pole positions calculated from the characteristic mag-
netizations of the rocks in the Highland and the Paciﬁc Coastal
Plain sometimes fall close to the geographical pole, which may
imply that the rocks have been remagnetized.
Mineralogical studies of rocks from the Highland indicate
only low-temperature ( j120 uC) burial metamorphism and
predominantly unaltered magnetite as the magnetic mineral.
Also, the palaeomagnetic study shows that magnetite is the
dominant carrier of remanence. Usually there are only two
components of magnetization even though the coercivity and
blocking-temperature spectra are often rather wide (e.g. Fig. 5d).
The soft components often have directions similar to that of the
PEF, indicating this magnetization to be a viscous remanence.
In the Highland there are remanent magnetizations of both
polarities and at some sites there are magnetizations of mixed
polarity. Although reversals are no guarantee of a primary mag-
netization, they support an interpretation of a primary origin
of the characteristic magnetizations (Van der Voo 1990). The
burial metamorphism seems not to have affected the primary,
high-blocking-temperature magnetization of the rocks, although
it is probably the reason for the disturbed K–Ar system
resulting in the wide scatter of the measured K–Ar ages.
Also in the Paciﬁc Coastal Plain, the rocks have been
affected by burial metamorphism, but the temperatures did
not exceed c. 120 uC. Due to probably slow erosion and uplift
this relatively low temperature may have affected grains with
laboratory unblocking temperatures of some 250 uC (Pullaiah
et al. 1975). Both Rivas and Brito sediments are volcanogenic,
which means that magnetite may be expected as a carrier of a
detrital remanence. This is also supported by the unblocking
temperatures of the Brito sandstone and shale. A large portion
of the remanence is erased at temperatures below 250 uC
and the characteristic magnetization is deﬁned in the temper-
ature range 300–580 uC. This means that the characteristic
magnetization is probably a detrital magnetization not affected
by burial metamorphism. The Brito sedimentary rocks carry
magnetizations of dual polarity and Gose (1983) reported a
magnetostratigraphic zonation of normal and reversed polarities
in the Brito Formation, which most probably rules out the
possibility of remagnetization. When structural correction is
performed the precision of the mean direction for the Brito
Formation increases, as indicated by the ratio of the precision
parameters after ( k
