Kississing Lake on the southern flank of the Kisseynew domain had very large viscous remanent magnetization components and, although the individual specimens had well-defined ChRM components, their directions were poorly clustered for most sites. Further, the site mean ChRM directions, while clearly post-folding and metamorphic in origin, did not form a cluster from which to derive a useful pole position (Symons and Harris, 1998).

A paleomagnetic study on the Wapisu gneiss dome in the northern part of the Kisseynew domain proved successful (Figure 1) (Symons and Harris, 1999). This dome is nearly circular and \6 km in diameter. It is composed of amphibolitic gneisses derived from turbiditic sediments and sill-like leucogranitic intrusions (Baldwin et al., 1979). Based on data from 17 sites around the perimeter in the steeply-dipping flanks, a stable post-folding ChRM direction was isolated that gives a pole position at 119.5° W, 75.8° N (dp = 9.5°, dm = 10.0°) (Figure 8). Based on radiometric ages for metamorphic and post-metamorphic rocks in the area, the Wapisu gneiss dome's ChRM was interpreted to record post-peak metamorphic cooling at \1810 ± 10 Ma. Assuming that exhumation occurred without tilt, it was speculated that the pole position marked an \90° hairpin in the APWP from the juvenile terrains of the THO, marking the collisional impact of the Archean Sask craton and/or Hearne craton against the Paleoproterozoic Kisseynew domain and driving it into the Archean Superior craton.

A positive paleomagnetic result was obtained from the Deschambault Post and "Tower Island" granite plutons in the Glennie domain that are intruded by the Deschambault pegmatites of this study (Figures 1 and 3) (Symons et al., 1999). These small circular to ovate late syntectonic to post-tectonic intrusions are composed of massive leucocratic granodiorite-granite and quartz monzonite and outcrop over \4.3 and\5.8 km2, respectively (Padgham,

Geologists mapping in the Glennie domain note that the only period of granodiorite-granite magmatism in the domain occurred between \1830 and 1840 Ma, and that these plutons appear similar to ones found \25 km to the west in the Brownell Lake area that contain D2 and D3 fabrics that imply an age of \1830 Ma (McNicoll et al., 1992; G. Delaney, pers. comm., 1999). Symons et al. (1999) suggested an emplacement age of \1795 ± 15 Ma based on: (a) the lack of reported fabric by Padgham (1968), implying an age of <1822 ± 6 Ma; (b) the undistorted circular shape of the Deschambault Post pluton that is incompatible with the steeply-plunging D3 syncline in the Oskikebuk Lake schists and gneisses into which it is intruded; (c) peak metamorphic U-Pb monazite ages of 1808 ± 3 Ma and 1804 +5/-4 Ma in the Hanson Lake area about 25 km to the southeast; (d) cross-cutting 1766 ± 5 Ma pegmatites of this study that provide a minimum age; and, (e) the fact that the pole positions for the plutons, if corrected for the plunge of the D3 syncline found in the host rocks, would be radically different from all other THO poles. The combined pole position determined from 14 sites in the Deschambault Post pluton and 6 sites in the "Tower Island" pluton is located at 102.4° W, 76.7° N (d = 5.9°, dm = 6.2°). Symons et al. (1999) noted that the pole fits reasonably well on the extrapolated extensions of the apparent polar wander path segments for the Lynn Lake – La Ronge domain and for the Hanson Lake block, which bound the Glennie domain. Thus they suggested that the pole may be indicating a substantial slowdown in the rate of apparent polar wander or drift rate that is a common feature found for continent-continent collisions.

The pole position derived from the Deschambault pegmatites (DP) is located at 84.0° W, 67.5° N (d = 7.6°, dm = 7.8°) (Figure 8). On calculation this pole is significantly different at the 95% confidence level from the pole for the intruded \1795 ± 15 Ma Deschambault Post and “Tower Island" granite plutons (DG) using the McFadden and Lowes (1981) discrimination test. This difference implies a very few degrees of either polar wander or terrane tilt between \1795 and \1766 Ma, and it provides a paleomagnetic contact test (Everitt and Clegg, 1962) that implies that the ChRMs of the pegmatites are primary. The presence of specimens with a reversed polarity and the high unblocking temperatures in both magnetite and hematite similarly support the retention of a primary remanence despite the pole's closeness to the present Earth's dipole field (Figure 8). Note also that these unblocking temperatures are close to the closure temperature for the U-Pb monazite radiometric system of about 695° ± 45°C (Kingsbury et al., 1993) so that the 1766 ± 5 Ma age is closely matched by the ChRM.

Further, both the DP and DG poles lie on the extensions of the APWP segments for the Lynn Lake – La Ronge belt and the Hanson Lake block, and they are the two terranes that bound the Glennie domain on its west and east sides, respectively (Figure 1). This geometry implies a swing of \40°counterclockwise in the direction of apparent polar wander and thus in terrane drift direction. This result is entirely consistent with the \90° counterclockwise swing or hairpin recorded by the pole for the \1810 ± 10 Ma Wapisu gneiss dome pole from the Kisseynew domain in relation to the APWP segments for the bounding Superior craton and Flin Flon belt. The fact that substantial counterclockwise changes in the APWP direction are evidenced for the Glennie and Kisseynew domains, indicates a major change in direction of plate motion between\1830 to 1775 Ma relative to the previous 60 Ma period. As Irving and Park (1973) noted, such a hairpin is an expected result from an orogenic collision. The North American APWP, for example, records hairpins of \90° during the \370 Ma Acadian, \325 Ma Alleghanian and \100 Ma Laramide orogenies (Besse and Courtillot, 1991; Van der Voo, 1993).

The third aspect shown by the DP pole is that it marks a prolonged 60 Ma period of very slow apparent polar wander. The average rate of wander for the four defined APWP segments prior to 1830 Ma is about 14 ± 4 cm/a. This is a moderately rapid rate but certainly within the range that has been well defined for large plates over several tens of millions of years during the Phanerozoic that have given values up to \20 cm/a (Meert et al., 1993). In contrast, the three poles for the THO that postdate \1830 Ma do not show a coherent age progression and indicate a much slower rate of no more than 5 ± 4 cm/à with the Deschambault pegmatites' pole giving a very slow rate of \1 cm/a. Thus the post \1830 Ma paleomagnetic results for the THO define a stillstand or period of slow apparent polar wander, which is a common feature for colliding continents because their drift tends to stall or slow dramatically upon collision with respect to the time-averaged magnetic or rotational pole (Irving and Park, 1973).

The Archean cratons involved in the collision are still uncertain. Given the 1815 ± 15 Ma ages for regional metamorphism in the Kisseynew and Glennie domains, it is clear that both the Sask and Superior cratons are involved. It could be that they collided with each other with the Hearne craton not yet involved or, alternatively, that the Sask and Superior cratons were adjacent to each other and that the Hearne craton impacted against them at \1815 ± 15 Ma. Needed to help resolve the problem is reliable paleomagnetic data for the 1830 to 1770 Ma period for the Superior and Hearne cratons and/or their bounding Thompson and Wollaston fold belts, respectively, with the \1770 Ma pegmatites (Table 1) being an obvious target.

6 Conclusions

The 1766 ± 5 Ma pegmatites at Deschambault Lake retain a primary ChRM that resides principally in magnetite and hematite but also in pyrrhotite in a few specimens. The ChRM is predominantly of normal polarity, is considered to be a thermoremanent magnetization, forms a coherent population of site mean directions, and gives a pole position of 84.0° W, 67.5° N (d = 7.6°, dm = 7.8°). This result, in concert with previously published poles from the \1810 ± 10 Ma Wapisu gneiss dome and \1795 ± 15 Ma Deschambault Post and "Tower Island" plutons, defines a stillstand and hairpin in the APWP for the THO terranes following assembly and accretion at \1830 Ma through to \1760 Ma. This pattern of paleomagnetic poles is typically found in a plate during the several tens of millions of years following a collisional orogeny.

1. Introduction
It is widely believed that the Cenozoic tectonics
of East Asia was in£uenced to a large extent by
the India^Asia collision [1]. However, the late
Mesozoic tectonic evolution of East Asia, after
the amalgamation of major tectonic blocks in
East China in the Jurassic [2,3], remains uncer-
tain. Based on paleomagnetism [2] and global
plate reconstructions [4], some authors claim
that the Eurasian continent has remained stable
through the Cretaceous, while others propose that
active tectonism, including collision, accretion and
vertical-axis rotation of various-sized terranes oc-
curred for the entire Mesozoic in the periphery of
East Asia [5,6].
The aim of this study is to present paleomag-
netic data from amongst the mid-Cretaceous sedi-
mentary basins in southwest Japan. These Creta-
ceous sedimentary basins are regarded as pull-
apart basins, which were once formed in close
relation to strike-slip faults along the Asian con-
tinental margin [7]. As the motion of these strike-
slip faults is ultimately related to plate interac-
tions and associated intra-continental deforma-
tion, determining the paleoposition of these pull-
apart basins is expected to be critical for clarifying
the tectonic evolution of East Asia during the
Cretaceous.
An increasing number of paleomagnetic and
geochronological studies of the Tertiary rocks in
the Japanese arc [8^10] have clearly documented
that the arc experienced rapid clockwise (south-
west Japan) and counter-clockwise (northeast Ja-
pan), vertical-axis rotations in the Middle Mio-
cene. However, the paucity of paleomagnetic
studies of the pre-Tertiary rocks makes it di⁄cult
to delineate the origin and development of the
proto-Japanese arc prior to the back-arc basin
opening. The available Cretaceous data are de-
rived mainly from igneous rocks [9], and those
from sedimentary strata, which pass the fold test
under well-de¢ned structural and chronostrati-
graphic control, are scarce. This situation is
mainly due to the limited occurrence of suitable
outcrops and partly to the early Tertiary remag-
netization [11]. A few successful results were ob-
tained from the Late Cretaceous deposits along
the Median Tectonic Line (MTL) of southwest
Japan [12], from which several Late Cretaceous
polarity chrons, as well as their mean geomagnetic
pole, were determined. In the quest for a more
reliable, pre-Tertiary apparent polar wander
path (APWP) of the Japanese arc, we aimed at
the Cretaceous deposits distributed along the
western extension of the MTL in central Kyushu
Island (Fig. 1). We provide the paleomagnetic re-
sults from the Goshonoura Island in the Amaku-
sa district of west-central Kyushu, where we could
examine Cretaceous, red bed-bearing, marine suc-
cessions that rarely occur along the Asian conti-
nental margin.
2. Geological setting
On Kyushu Island, pre-Cenozoic geologic units
trend ENE^WSW and represent part of a Creta-
ceous to Paleogene accretionary complex [13].
Along the north side of the MTL several Creta-
ceous sedimentary basins occur as E^W elongated
depressions ¢lled with thickclastic deposits of
shallow- to deep-sea, partly paralic, facies [7].
They tend to be younger to the east, with the
Goshonoura basin of western Kyushu being
mid-Cretaceous, while on Shikoku Island the east-
ernmost Izumi basin is latest Cretaceous. The
structural and lithological characteristics suggest
that they are pull-apart basins caused by Creta-
ceous strike-slip displacement of the proto-MTL
[14]. These marine successions are unique when
compared with the coeval deposits on the Asian
continent that are mainly terrestrial [15]. Creta-
ceous red beds of terrestrial origin occur in north-
ern Kyushu and westernmost Honshu Island as
well as on the Korean Peninsula. However,
many of them are remagnetized [16] and the few
pre-folding magnetizations reported so far are
from limited localities in the southeastern Korean
Peninsula [6,17] and eastern China [2]. This is why
we have chosen the Goshonoura Group as a suit-
able target for a comparative study on the origin
and development of Cretaceous basins on the
Asian continent and its eastern margins.
The mid-Cretaceous Goshonoura Group crops
out in the Goshonoura Island and nearby islets of

there are a few cases in which component B can-
not clearly be isolated due to overlap of demag-
netization spectra (Fig. 3c). We then applied the
method of Ho¡man and Day [26], but it turned
out that the number of those indirect data was
too small (only three) to a¡ect the overall statis-
tics. It is notable that component B from any
single site exhibits neither consistent directional
grouping nor geomagnetic polarity. Their direc-
tions, when plotted on an equal-area net, show
large azimuthal scatter lying along a great circle,
whose pole is oriented almost vertical in geo-
graphic coordinates and inclines moderately in
stratigraphic coordinates (Fig. 4). Angular devia-
tion from the best-¢t great circle [23] for the latter
is 21‡, which is slightly greater than for the former
(16‡). These directional behaviors suggest that
component B is unlikely to be remagnetization
acquired by a single, uniform thermal event, but
rather seems to be related to magnetic mineralog-
ical alteration caused by long-term, diagenetic
processes. Though it might be appropriate to
call the unusual component B an ‘intermediate
stability overprint’, we will hereafter use ‘compo-
nent B’ for the sake of simplicity.
Component C initially appears around temper-
ature steps of 440^480‡C, above which it shows
almost linear decay toward the origin. Numbers
of components B and C for each site are summa-
rized in Table 1. The unblocking temperature
spectrum of component C is unique in that there
appear in many cases to be two peaks: one over
560^590‡C heating intervals and the other over
650^680‡C, suggesting that component C resides
not only in hematite. Discussion on the possible
carriers of component C, as well as component B,
will be given below in association with rockmag-
netic analyses. The in situ, overall mean direction
of the 18 red bed sites (Dec=90‡, Inc=33‡,
K95 =9‡, U=17) is signi¢cantly di¡erent from the
geocentric dipole ¢eld and, after bedding-tilt cor-
rections, shifts more easterly and downwards,
with much less directional dispersion, that is

to be statistically signi¢cant using a conservative
fold test of McElhinny [27], resulting in the ratio
of

17=2.41, which is greater than the 95% con¢-
dence limit of 1.77. The positive fold test suggests
that only component C is pre-folding.

repeatedly observed around 550‡C. The curve in
vacuum (Fig. 6b) is also irreversible between

These curves suggest that red beds generally
contain at least three intrinsic magnetic minerals,
such as maghemite, hematite and a small amount

200‡C may be indicative of oxidation of iron hy-

4.2. IRM acquisition and demagnetization
A stepwise IRM acquisition experiment was
carried out for those red bed samples which
hold all three components (Fig. 7b,c) and, for
comparison, that for which component B could
not be isolated (Fig. 7a). They appear to be di¡er-
ent in acquisition rate for the early steps, with
Fig. 7a showing a steep rise at ¢rst whereas Fig.
7b,c display a moderate build-up. In excess of
0.3^0.5 T, however, all the IRMs keep increasing
with no saturation even at 2 T. The acquisition
curves, coupled with corresponding coercivity
spectra, suggest the presence of hematite and low-
er coercivity minerals such as magnetite or ma-
ghemite.
Features in accord with the IRM acquisition
curves are demonstrated in a di¡erent fashion
by composite IRM acquisition and thermal de-
magnetizations (Fig. 8), which were made for
each of the three daughter specimens in Fig. 7.
It is obvious that the hard (2.0 T) and medium
(0.4 T) fractions remain up to 680‡C, while the
soft fraction (0.4 T) is removed, though not com-
pletely, by 580‡C. An in£ection at around 180^
200‡C, commonly recognized for the soft fraction
and only slightly for the medium fraction, seems
to correspond to that observed for the thermo-
magnetic curves, suggesting dehydration of some
iron hydroxides, or presence of small amount of
Ti-rich titanomagnetite. We thus consider that
this soft IRM fraction corresponds to component
A of NRM, which most likely resides in titano-
magnetite and/or iron hydroxides. Also, a small
in£ection of the soft fraction in the 320^400‡C
range would imply a minor contribution of pyr-
rhotite.
4.3. Origin of ChRM
Results of the thermal demagnetizations and
rockmagnetic studies above demonstrate that
the major magnetic minerals responsible for
ChRMs include not only ¢ne-grained hematite
but some others with lower coercivity and un-
blocking temperature. Direct evidence for this
conclusion is provided by the common observa-
tion of coarse-grained martite (Fig. 9), which is
hematite as a pseudomorph of magnetite. Pigmen-
tary hematite surrounding martite grains is obvi-
ously a major carrier of component C, but martite

is thought to be another potential carrier. Careful
observation of the martite grains does not neces-
sarily show homogeneous, complete hematization
of magnetite, but rather suggests that there re-
main small portions consisting of maghemite as
a precursor to hematite. The intergrown, ¢ne-
grained maghemite could hold a fraction of com-
ponent C, presumably that with relatively lower
unblocking temperature of 400^480‡C to 580‡C.
There is one observation in the ¢eld that seems
critical to distinguish the origin of ChRMs of red
beds. That is a mixed interface between one red
bed and an overlying grayish sandstone layer,
which provides evidence of considerable bioturba-
tion (Fig. 10). Commonly, gray burrows penetrate
the red bed, yielding a clear contrast in color and
lithofacies. These syndepositional features suggest
that hematite is one of the primary constituents of
red beds. This ¢eld observation itself does not
preclude the possibility of magnetic overprint fol-
lowed by the acquisition of components A and B.
However, coupled with the lithological and min-
eralogical contrast between red beds and the over-
lying gray layers, we view component C as a de-
positional, or post-depositional, remanent
magnetization (DRM, or pDRM). Iron hydrox-
ides, such as goethite, which generally are weath-
ering products in soils, were probably deposited
and acquired DRM. We assume that detrital mag-
netite, which presumably coexisted as a parent of
martite at the time of deposition, also gave rise to
DRM. Post-depositional maghemitization of the
detrital magnetite may have produced chemical
remanent magnetization (CRM), which could be
responsible for lower unblocking temperature
fractions of component C and most of component
B as well.
The anomalous, azimuthal scatter of compo-
nent B as in Fig. 4 emerges in a more intriguing
manner upon converting to virtual geomagnetic
pole (VGP). Namely, VGPs determined for all
the in situ directions of component B also lie
along a great circle (Fig. 11). Assuming that com-
ponent B is CRM of daughter maghemite, then
the best-¢t great circle, on which a mean VGP of
component C lies as well, would help us to assess
when maghemitization tookplace. This is because
experiments [29] show that there are CRMs with
intermediate directions between the applied ¢eld
and the parent remanence direction, and they tend
to de£ect away from the parent remanence as ox-
idation proceeds. Accordingly, we postulate that
the large azimuthal scatter of component B is at-
tributable to inhomogeneous maghemitization
and grain size of parent magnetite, and hence
the VGPs corresponding to various degrees of
maghemitization come to lie on the great circle.
Considering that component C has one single
normal polarity, the great circle distribution of
VGPs of component B may further suggest that
the maghemitization occurred over a time interval
containing at least one polarity transition, because
the vector combination of the remagnetized direc-

5. Discussion
In Fig. 12a we show the overall mean geomag-
netic pole of component C from Table 1, together
with Cretaceous to Tertiary poles from southwest
Japan [30], a mean Cretaceous pole from the sta-
ble part of China [2], and that from eastern China
[31]. When compiling the poles, we omit data
from northeast Japan [32], which suggest a post-
Cretaceous, large tectonic rotation quite di¡erent
from elsewhere. We also exclude results from Ko-
rea [6,17] because they are indistinguishable from
the mean pole of China. It is apparent in Fig. 12a
that paleomagnetic poles from southwest Japan
exhibit a unique APWP consisting of two, Creta-
ceous and Tertiary, paths with di¡erent orienta-
tions. The two paths appear to intersect forming a
cusp between the latest Cretaceous and the Paleo-
gene. Greater deviation of the Tertiary poles with
age away from the North pole is attributed to a
rapid, clockwise rotation of southwest Japan with
respect to Eurasia [10], but the Cretaceous path
based on results from sedimentary rocks is drawn
for the ¢rst time by this study.
Since the amalgamation between the North
China Block(NCB) and the South China Block
(SCB) in the Jurassic [2,3], there appears to have
been no large internal deformation in the eastern
Asian continent. It is claimed that collision of the

for most of the Cretaceous [2], we infer that
southwest Japan underwent a southward migra-
tion relative to Eurasia, with displacement of
18($^Bx8‡ in paleolatitude for the mid- to Late Cre-
taceous. In other words, a comparison of the pa-
leolatitude of the Goshonoura Group, which is
45($^Bx7‡N, with the present position referred to
west-central Kyushu (32‡N), leads to the conclu-
sion that proto-southwest Japan was located fur-
ther to the north in excess of 10‡ in the mid-Cre-
taceous.
Finally, we interpret the southward migration
of southwest Japan in terms of regional tectonics
in the periphery of northeastern Asia to the east
of the Siberian craton. Although the tectonic evo-
lution of this entire area is still controversial,
some authors regard this area as a collage of ter-
ranes or microplates of various ages and origins
[36^38]. Paleomagnetic data are scarce, but a few
studies by Russian workers [39^41] suggest that
Mesozoic fragments of island-arc a⁄nity origi-
nated far south from the present continental mar-
gin. We assume that these allochthonous com-
plexes drifted northward, in association with the
other exotic terranes like the Okhotsk Sea micro-
plate, and they collided and accreted in succession
with northeast Asia in the late Mesozoic. Accord-
ingly, we postulate that proto-southwest Japan,
after its amalgamation with northeast Asia, was
transported southward along the continental mar-
gin to accommodate the penetration of such
exotic blocks as the Okhotsk Sea microplate.
We thus propose a possible tectonic model
(Fig. 13), which is similar to those proposed for
the India^Asia collision in that large-scale trans-
port of intra-continental terranes occurs in the
vicinity of a colliding landmass.
In our model, the Cretaceous pull-apart basins
in East Asia including the Goshonoura basin lie
along strike-slip faults, which were presumably
reactivated by the collision of the Okhotsk Sea
microplate. Previous geodynamic models of East
Asia based on the Mesozoic plate reconstruction
[5] suggest that sinistral displacement was domi-
nant for the strike-slip fault systems in this region,
in which exotic terranes underwent signi¢cant
coast-parallel translation. However, we emphasize
that the collision of the Okhotsk Sea microplate
gave rise to a change in motion of the fault sys-
tem, whereby pull-apart basins in the proto-Japa-
nese arc migrated to the south. We propose that
the deformation of the eastern margin of Asia
would have been a¡ected by suspected collision
of allochthonous terranes over the mid- to Late
Cretaceous time.

Abstract
New paleomagnetic investigations on the Ethiopian trap series have been undertaken at the Abbay and Kessem
gorges in an attempt to better constrain the 30 Ma paleomagnetic pole of Africa. We sampled six thick massive
basaltic lava flows, totaling 230 m, from Abbay Gorge and 10 lava flows, 180 m in thickness, from Kessem Gorge.

curves, many of which are irreversible, may indicate chemical remagnetization, notably low temperature
maghemitization. Only one flow (KS04) with a clear 580‡C Curie temperature was apparently unaffected by
chemical remagnetization. The ChRM direction of this flow is identical to that in other flows, which suggeststhat if

new insights for early Cenozoic clockwise rotation
Koji Uno
Department of Environmental Sciences, Faculty of Integrated Human Studies, Kyoto University, Sakyo-ku, Kyoto606-8501, Japan.
E-mail: unokoji@gaia.h.kyoto-u.ac.jp

SUMMARY
Palaeomagnetic samples in the Upper Cretaceous Arima Group have been collected from two
areas in the middle of Southwest Japan. Tuffaceous sediments were sampled at eleven sites
in the Arima area and welded tuffs were sampled at four sites in the Ikuno area. Thermal
demagnetization isolated characteristic remanent magnetization components with unblocking
temperatures of 500–580
◦C from all the sites. After tilt correction, the characteristic directions
provide Late Cretaceous mean directions for the Arima area (D = 46.6◦, I = 53.7◦, α95 = 3.7◦)
and the Ikuno area ( D = 78.4◦, I = 44.7◦, α95 = 9.5◦). I interpret these data to show that
the palaeomagnetic pole from the Arima area has been rotated counter-clockwise relative
to those from the central part of Southwest Japan, while the pole from the Ikuno area is in
good agreement with palaeomagnetic poles from the central part of Southwest Japan. The
pole for the Ikuno area together with previously reported ones give a new Late Cretaceous
pole representative of the central part of Southwest Japan. This pole is rotated 64.6
◦ ± 15.5◦
clockwise with respect to the coeval one for the North China Block. In my model, the tectonic
history of Southwest Japan includes Early Tertiary clockwise rotation of about 23
◦ and Middle
Miocene clockwise rotation of about 42 ◦, resulting in a total rotation of Southwest Japan
by 65◦. The Early Tertiary clockwise rotation occurred in an area incorporating the Korean
Peninsula and Southwest Japan, and the Middle Miocene clockwise rotation was associated
with the opening of the Japan Sea.
Key words: Cretaceous, palaeomagnetism, Southwest Japan.
1 INTRODUCTION
The Japanese Islands are located in the easternmost part of the Asian
continent facing oceanic plates to the east (Fig. 1a). The Japanese
Islands have been recognized as continental slivers rifted from the
Asian continent, associated with the opening of the Japan Sea
(Otofuji et al. 1985). As a consequence of the rifting, Southwest
and Northeast Japan experienced clockwise and counter-clockwise
rotations respectively (Otofuji & Matsuda 1987; Otofujiet al. 1991,
1994; Jolivet et al. 1994). The amount of rotation in the eastern and
western parts of Southwest Japan (Fig. 1a) is reduced relative to that
in the central part of Southwest Japan (Faure & Lalev´ ee 1987; Itoh
1988; Ishikawa 1997).
The clockwise rotation of Southwest Japan in response to the
opening of the Japan Sea occurred during the Middle Miocene.
Otofuji & Matsuda (1987) suggested that more than 80 per cent of
the net rotation occurred later than 16.1 Ma and ceased by 14.2 Ma.
At about 15 Ma Southwest Japan was at the peak of rotational motion
(Hayashida 1986; Otofuji et al. 1991). This timing of rotation from
palaeomagnetism is concordant with those from geochronological
data, marine magnetic anomaly patterns and ODP Leg 127 drilling
results (Seama & Isezaki 1990; Kaneoka et al. 1990; Shipboard
Scientiﬁc Party Leg 127 and Leg 128 1990).
Early Miocene palaeomagnetic directions from Southwest Japan
show consistent declinations of about 40–50
◦ (Hayashida & Ito
1984; Hayashida 1986; Hayashida et al. 1991; Otofuji et al. 1991;
Kojima et al. 2001). On the other hand, Late Cretaceous palaeo-
magnetic directions from Southwest Japan have larger declination
values of about 70
◦ (Otofuji & Matsuda 1987). There has been an
issue that the Middle Miocene tectonic event does not account for
the discrepancy in declinations between Late Cretaceous and Early
Miocene times. T wo factors are relevant to this discrepancy. One
is that the Cretaceous palaeomagnetic pole for the Asian continent
(North China Block) (Gilder & Courtillot 1997) gives an easterly-
deﬂected expected declination at the reference point of Southwest
Japan. Another is the clockwise rotation of the Korean Peninsula
with respect to the North China Block in Early Tertiary time (Ma
et al. 1993; Uchimura et al. 1996; Uno 2000). Because Southwest
Japan is considered to have been ﬂanked on the eastern side of
the Korean Peninsula at this time (Otofuji & Matsuda 1983), this
clockwise rotation may be superimposed on Cretaceous palaeomag-
netic declinations from Southwest Japan. If the amount of rotation

At present, a Late Cretaceous pole from one locality (the San’in

study of Cretaceous rocks in Southwest Japan (Otofuji & Matsuda

to establishing the representative pole for Southwest Japan. More
sampling is required to improve the Late Cretaceous pole position
for Southwest Japan with which to make a comparison with those
from the North China Block and the Korean Peninsula.
This paper focuses on the Arima and Ikuno areas in the middle
of Southwest Japan because this region lacks palaeomagnetic data
(Fig. 1a). The stratigraphic sampling target for this palaeomagnetic
study is the Late Cretaceous Arima Group, which is distributed in
both Arima and Ikuno areas. I present new palaeomagnetic data
from the two areas and a Late Cretaceous palaeomagnetic pole for
the central part of Southwest Japan. This is the ﬁrst report dealing
with Japanese Mesozoic data in the light of tectonics of the East
Asian continent. The Arima and Ikuno areas are 60 km apart from
each other.
2 GEOLOGICAL SETTING
AND SAMPLING
The Late Cretaceous Arima Group unconformably overlies the
Jurassic–Early Cretaceous Tamba Group and the Early Cretaceous
Sasayama Group, and is unconformably overlain by the Eocene –
Oligocene Kobe Group. The Arima Group is well exposed in the
Arima (34.8
◦N, 135.3◦E) and Ikuno (35.2◦N, 134.7◦E) areas to the
north of Kobe (Fig. 1b). It is made up mainly of rhyolitic lavas
and pyroclastic rocks, and is divided into three parts (lower, middle
and upper formations) (Kasama & Y oshida 1976; Nakazawa et al.
1987). The upper formation of the Arima Group is K –Ar dated
at 72.1 ± 3.6 Ma (Y oshida & Kawada 1987). Tilting of the Arima
Group occurred prior to the Eocene.
In the Arima area, all the three formations are composed mainly
of welded tuffs. Welded tuffs in the middle and upper forma-
tions of the Arima area are rich in lithic fragments, whereas those
in the lower formation rarely contain lithic fragments (Kasama
& Y oshida 1976; Nakazawa et al. 1987). Eutaxitic structures in
welded tuffs are not observable in this area. The three formations
are demarcated by two tuffaceous lake deposits of about 200 m in
thickness: the Sogawa sedimentary rocks demarcate the lower and
middle formations, and the Gen ’noike sedimentary rocks demar-
cate the middle and upper formations. They dip 12 –22
◦ northward

In the Ikuno area, the lower and middle formations are com-
posed mainly of volcanic breccias and lavas (Nakazawaet al. 1987).
Welded tuffs are found in the upper formation. Eutaxitic structures
are observed at some outcrops in this formation. The tilt of eutaxitic
structure is gentle for all the sites ( <20
◦), with dip directions of
110◦ and 310–330◦.
Tuffaceous mudstones and sandstones in the Sogawa (sites AG1–
6 and AG12) and Gen ’noike (sites AG8 –11) sedimentary rocks
were collected at eleven sites in the Arima area, and welded tuffs in
the upper formation (sites IG1–4) were collected at four sites in the
Ikuno area (Fig. 1b). In each site, six to eight hand samples were
distributed over distances ranging up to 10 m and were oriented by
magnetic compass.
3 P ALAEOMAGNETISM
In the laboratory, cores of 25 mm in diameter and 22 mm long
were prepared from each hand sample. Natural remanent magneti-
zations (NRMs) were measured with a 2-G Superconducting Rock
Magnetometer (SRM). All samples were subjected to progressive
thermal demagnetization treatment with a Natsuhara TDS-1 ther-
mal demagnetizer. Results for each sample were plotted on orthog-
onal vector diagrams (Zijderveld 1967) to evaluate the demagnetiza-
tion behaviours (Fig. 2). Principal component analysis (Kirschvink
1980) was used to estimate directions of the magnetic components
(Table 1).
Samples from the Arima area have initial NRM intensities ranging
from 2×10
−3 to 3×10−4 Am−1. Thermal demagnetization revealed
a stable remanent magnetization component following removal of
a component at around 260
◦C (Figs 2a –e). The high-temperature
component is well-deﬁned and generally resolved by demagnetiza-
tion steps above 260 ◦C, where more than half of the initial NRM
persists. For each sample, the high-temperature component with an
unblocking temperature of 500
◦C is regarded as a characteristic re-
manent magnetization component, which is identi ﬁed from all the
sites.
The site-mean directions of the characteristic component clus-
ter well at each site: the precision parameter (k-value) ranges from
74.0 to 461.4. These directions are of east declination and relatively
steep inclination before tilt correction, and of northeast declination
and intermediate positive inclination after tilt correction (Fig. 3).
Mean directions of the 11 sites before and after tilt correction are
D = 69.6
◦, I = 57.8◦ with α95 = 2.9◦ and D = 46.6◦, I = 53.7◦ with
α95 = 3.7◦, respectively. The timing of remanence acquisition could
not be established by the fold test alone, because the bedding atti-
tudes are essentially monoclinal. Although the precision parameter
decreases from 253.8 to 151.1 after tilt correction, the decrease is
not quite demonstrably signi ﬁcant for a negative fold test at the
95 per cent conﬁdence level (McElhinny 1964).
The characteristic component of the Arima Group is not at-
tributed to a secondary origin because of the following points.
(1) The clear demarcation between the characteristic component and
lower-temperature component in orthogonal vector diagram sug-
gests little overlap of unblocking temperature spectra between these
components. (2) The 11 site-mean directions before tilt correction
are signiﬁcantly removed from the present Earth ’s ﬁeld direction
(D = 352.9
◦, I = 49.0◦) and axial dipoleﬁeld direction (D = 0.0◦,
I = 54.3◦). (3) A thermal perturbation in the Arima area is restricted
to a small area in its southeastern periphery, as evidenced by distri-
bution of biotite hornfels (Kasama & Y oshida 1976).
Samples from the Ikuno area have initial NRM intensities ranging
from 5 Am
−1 to 4×10−2 Am−1. With the exception of a component
removed in the ﬁrst three or four steps of treatment (260 –320◦C),
thermal demagnetization isolated a stable remanent magnetization
component with an unblocking temperature of 580
◦C, suggesting
that it resides in magnetite. The high-temperature component de-
cays univectorially to the origin and is regarded as a characteristic
remanent magnetization component, which is identiﬁed from all the
sites.
The site-mean directions of the characteristic component have
the precision parameter ranging from 32.9 to 155.0. The four site-
mean directions before tilt correction, with a mean of D = 264.3
◦,
I =− 44.2◦ with α95 = 16.4◦, show westerly declinations and vari-
able inclinations between −25◦ and −56◦, while these directions
after tilt correction, with a mean of D = 258.4◦, I =− 44.7◦ with
α95 = 9.5◦, have westerly declinations with intermediate negative
inclinations (Fig. 4). Tilt correction increases the precision parame-
ter of the mean direction from 32.6 to 93.9. The precision parameter
after tilt correction is 2.9 times greater than before tilt correction.
Although the fold test is not signiﬁcant at the 95 per cent conﬁdence
level (McElhinny 1964), the improvement of the clustering suggests
that the characteristic component is likely primary magnetization.
The tilt-corrected mean direction of the Ikuno area, presumably
of primary origin, is compared with the mean directions of the
Arima area before and after tilt correction. An inclination contrast
between the two areas may be calculated to test whether or not the
Arima area has been remagnetized. With respect to the tilt-corrected
mean direction of the Ikuno area, the in situ mean direction of the
Arima area shows an inclination difference of 13.6
◦ ±9.9◦, while the
tilt-corrected one shows an inclination difference of 9 .0◦ ± 10.2◦.
Because the difference in inclination becomes insigni ﬁcant af-
ter tilt correction, I interpreted this observation to show that the
characteristic component of the Arima area is not of secondary
magnetization.
An alternative explanation of the characteristic direction of the
Arima area is remagnetization. The in situ direction of the Arima
area is closer to the tilt-corrected direction of the San’in area (Otofuji
& Matsuda 1987) than the tilt-corrected Arima direction: the
in situ Arima direction differs by 14 .2
◦ ± 10.4◦ from the coeval
San’in direction, while the tilt-corrected Arima direction differs by
20.5◦ ± 10.7◦ from the San’in direction. It may be possible that the
Arima area suffered complete remagnetization after tilting (Late
Cretaceous–Eocene) and prior to the opening of the Japan Sea
(∼15 Ma).
4 DISCUSSION
Palaeomagnetic poles for the Arima and Ikuno areas are calculated
on the basis of the tilt-corrected characteristic directions from each
area. They are located at 52.2
◦N, 211.8◦E, A95 = 3.8◦ and 24.1◦N,
210.0◦E, A95 = 8.5◦, respectively (Table 2). Previously reported Late
Cretaceous poles for Southwest Japan are available from the Nohi
area (eastern part of Southwest Japan, Otofujiet al.1999), Koto area
(central part of Southwest Japan, Fukuma & Torii 1990), Izumi area
(central part of Southwest Japan, Kodama 1990), San’in area (cen-
tral part of Southwest Japan, Otofuji & Matsuda 1987) and North
Kyushu area (western part of Southwest Japan, Ishikawa 1997)
(Fig. 1a). A Cretaceous reference pole for the North China Block lies
at 78.6
◦N, 202.6◦E with A95 = 6.2◦ (Gilder & Courtillot 1997), and
a Cretaceous pole for the Korean Peninsula falls at 61.2◦N, 199.5◦E
with A95 = 6.6◦ (Zhao et al. 1999).

Early Tertiary clockwise rotation of about 23 ◦ observed in data
from the Korean Peninsula is also recorded in Late Cretaceous data
from the central part of Southwest Japan. Rotation of an area incor-
porating the Korean Peninsula and Southwest Japan is anticipated
for the reconstructions between the Korean Peninsula and Southwest
Japan in Early Tertiary times: many authors claimed that Southwest
Japan wasﬂanked on the eastern side of the Korean Peninsula in this
period (Otofuji & Matsuda 1983; Hayashida et al. 1991; Smith &
Y amauchi 1994; Leeet al. 1999). If Southwest Japan, together with
the Korean Peninsula, was subjected to Early Tertiary clockwise ro-
tation by about 23
◦, a clockwise rotation of about 42 ◦ is expected
to have occurred during the Middle Miocene opening of the Japan
Sea because Southwest Japan records a total clockwise rotation of
65
◦ (Table 2). According to Otofuji (1996), the amount of clockwise
rotation associated with the Middle Miocene opening of the Japan
Sea is determined to be 42
◦. There is good agreement between the
expected and observed values of rotation. It is therefore concluded
that Southwest Japan underwent Early Tertiary clockwise rotation
by 23
◦ and Middle Miocene clockwise rotation by 42◦, resulting in
a total rotation of Southwest Japan by 65◦.

Mountains igneous province, Missouri

[1] A paleomagnetic investigation of the St. Francois Mountains
igneous province in southeastern Missouri provides a key 1476 ±
16 Ma paleomagnetic pole for Laurentia. The pole (13.2  S,
219.0 E; dp = 4.7  ,d m=8 . 0  ) is considered primary on the basis
of positive conglomerate, inverse baked contact, and fold tests. An
analysis of 1470 – 1430 Ma poles from Laurentia highlights key
differences between poles obtained from the Belt Supergroup,
Electra Lake gabbro, and cratonic North America. Paleolatitudes
based on the Lower Belt Supergroup poles are enigmatic, as two
previous studies yielded a difference of 10  . Our new pole,
combined with an analysis of previous results, favors the higher
latitude interpretation for the Lower Belt Supergroup.
Paleolatitudes from the younger Belt rocks indicate lower
latitudes than coeval rocks from elsewhere in Laurentia for
which there has been no adequate explanation. A comparison of
the St. Francois Mountain pole with similar-age poles from Baltica,
Siberia and Australia allow first-order tests of proposed continental
configurations. Paleomagnetic data from Australia are compatible
with proposed Rodinia reconstructions, whereas paleomagnetic
data from Baltica are not. We are unable to rigorously test the
alternative suggestion that places Siberia against the western
margin of Laurentia due in part to large errors associated with
Siberian paleomagnetic data. I

1. Introduction
[2] Mesoproterozoic continental configurations between Sibe-
ria, the elements of East Gondwana, and Laurentia are controver-
sial. The controversy arises, at least in part, because of a paucity of
high-quality paleomagnetic data from these continents as well as
discordance of the extant results [see Harlan and Geissman , 1998].
On the one hand, Sears and Price [2000] argue for a northeastern
Siberian conjugate margin with present-day western Laurentia,
whereas others [ Hoffman, 1991; Condie and Rosen , 1994; Frost
et al., 1998, and references therein] link Siberia to the present-day
northern margin of Laurentia with some variation in orientation.
The placement of Siberia against the northern margin follows from
suggestions that position Australia and Antarctica against the
western margin of Laurentia in either the southwest United
States-East Antarctica (SWEA T) or Australia-western United
States (AUSWUS) configuration [ Dalziel, 1997; Karlstrom et al. ,
2000; Burrett and Berry , 2000]. Interestingly, none of these
configurations has strong paleomagnetic support [ Meert, 1999;
Torsvik et al. , 2001; Meert and Powell , 2001], although ideally,
paleomagnetism could distinguish among the various models if
there are high-quality poles from the various cratonic elements in
question [Ernst et al. , 2000; Torsvik et al., 1996]. A recent attempt
to test possible linkages between Siberia and Laurentia by Ernst et
al. [2000] used a new 1503 ± 5 Ma paleomagnetic pole from the
eastern Anabar shield region of the Siberian craton. The major
limitation to their analysis was a lack of coeval paleomagnetic
poles from Laurentia and the large error associated with their
Siberian pole (see section 4.2). Furthermore, if one is to test
alternative reconstructions for Siberia during this interval of
Mesoproterozoic time, it would require coeval data from Australia
and Antarctica since these landmasses are also argued to occupy
the region adjacent to present-day western Laurentia [e.g., Dalziel,
1997; Karlstrom et al. , 2000].
[
3] The St. Francois Mountains (SFM) region of Missouri is a
1476 ± 16 Ma igneous province in central Laurentia (Figure 1;
mean age compiled from V an Schmus et al. [1993] excluding
Munger granite porphyry). Previous paleomagnetic studies [ Hsu
et al. , 1966; Hays and Scharon , 1966] were inconclusive in
demonstrating a primary magnetization from these rocks,
although directional comparisons between similar-aged units
(Michikamau intrusion and Harp Lake Complex of the Canadian
shield) suggested that a primary magnetization might be pre-
served. Nevertheless, the magnetization age of both the Michi-
kamau and Harp Lake intrusive units may postdate their 1450 –
1460 Ma U-Pb age thereby negating a direct comparison with the
SFM poles (see discussion in section 4.1). Harlan and Geissman
[1998] compared paleomagnetic data from the Belt Supergroup
(1400 – 1470 Ma), the Electra Lake gabbro (1433 Ma) and
midcontinent poles from North America (including the early
SFM studies) and argued that possible rotations of the Belt
Supergroup, Electra Lake gabbro (1433 Ma), or both could
explain the discrepancy in paleomagnetic poles from those units.
In an effort to test some of these continental configurations and

establish the tectonic relationships between paleomagnetic poles
from Laurentia, we resampled the 1476 Ma SFM province in

1.1. Geologic Setting and Age
[4] The St. Francois Mountains (SFM) of southeastern Missouri
(Figures 1, 2a and 2b) consist of nearly 40,000 km 2 of acidic
volcanic and plutonic rocks [ Berry, 1976; Kisvarsanyi, 1980] of
which  00 km 2 are exposed at the surface. The SFM form the
uplifted core of the Ozark Dome and are overlain by flat lying or
gently dipping lower Paleozoic rocks. The lowermost Paleozoic
rocks overlying the SFM consist of either a boulder conglomerate
of presumed Cambrian age or the Upper Cambrian Lamotte sand-
stone (  00 Ma). There are also rare occurrences of paleosol
between the SFM rocks and the overlying Lamotte sandstone.
[
5] The SFM represent the exposed northeastern terminus of a
much larger, and mostly subsurface, Mesoproterozoic granite-
rhyolite province in North America that flanks the southern and
eastern margins of the 1.8 – 1.6 Ga Great Plains Orogen and the
eastern margin of the Colorado Province. It extends in the subsur-
face from the Texas panhandle to southeastern lower Michigan
[V an Schmus et al. , 1987, Figure 1].
[
6] The geologic history of the SFM begins with the main
caldera-forming eruptions, caldera collapse, and intrusion of
shallow magmas into their own ejecta at 1476 ± 16 Ma
[Kisvarsanyi, 1980]. A second cycle of alkaline intrusion and
magmatism occurred around 1.38 Ga [ Kisvarsanyi and Kisvarsa-
nyi, 1989; Lowell and Darnell , 1996], followed by a volumetri-
cally smaller episode of primarily mafic magmatism (gabbroic
intrusions, dike swarms, and minor flows) at  .33 Ga [ Lowell
and Young , 1999; Ramo et al. , 1994; R. Tucker, personal
communication, 2000]. The rocks show minor postemplacement
metamorphism except in regions where (1) the volcanic rocks are
intruded by their parent magmas following caldera collapse; (2)
the rocks are intruded by a suite of younger granitic intrusions at
1.38 Ga or by mafic bodies at 1.33 Ga, and (3) there is
mineralization and faulting associated with these younger mag-
matic episodes or subsequent reactivation [ Clendenin et al. , 1989;
Lowell, 1991; Kisvarsanyi and Kisvarsanyi , 1989]. The dominant

structural features in the SFM are a series of caldera collapse
structures that caused quasi-radial tilting of the volcanic rocks
and, in some cases, intrusion of the collapsed volcanic rocks by
their parental magmas [ Kisvarsanyi, 1980; Sides et al. , 1981;

Butler Hill caldera (Figure 2a) [ Lowell, 1991] and the Taum Sauk
caldera (Figure 2b) [ Anderson et al. , 1969]. There are also a
number of Neoproterozoic faults related to the opening of the
Reelfoot rift (Figure 1) that were reactivated during Paleozoic and
younger times [ Clendenin et al. , 1989; Kisvarsanyi, 1980].
1.2. Previous Work
[7] Paleomagnetic studies in the SFM have a long history and
appear to be one of the earliest paleomagnetic studies conducted in
the United States (see Ph.D. thesis by Hays [1961] and M.A. thesis
by Hsu [1962]). The results were eventually published by Hays
and Scharon [1966], who calculated a paleopole at 5  N, 210  E
(a
95 =1 0  ). Although Hays and Scharon [1966] sampled almost
exclusively in the volcanic units, they did not provide detailed site
descriptions or apply any tilt correction to their data. Later that
year, Hsu et al. [1966] published additional results from the SFM
that agreed with the results of Hays and Scharon [1966] with a
resultant paleopole at 0.9  S, 219 E( a95 =5 . 0 ). Hsu et al. [1966]
did report a tilt-corrected direction for their samples, but they
argued that the structures reflected primary flow features on the
basis of increased scatter upon tilt correction. Their tilt-corrected
paleomagnetic pole falls at 5  S, 214.4 E( a
95 =6 . 2 ). Both studies
applied blanket alternating field demagnetization to the samples
between 50 – 80 mT, but as we show in section 2, these fields may
not adequately resolve primary directions in all samples, whereas
thermal demagnetization was more effective in separating compo-
nents of magnetization in our study. As both previous studies were

analysis and orthogonal vector plots, details of demagnetization
trajectories were not included. Subsequent geologic and structural
studies showed that the tilting of the volcanic units occurred
during collapse of the calderas, and therefore a tilt correction of
the data might help determine the primary or secondary nature of
the magnetization [ Kisvarsanyi, 1980; Lowell, 1991, and referen-
ces therein]. Given that the SFM province contains a number of
mafic dikes, a boulder conglomerate, and tilting related to the
collapse of the primary volcanic centers, we saw an opportunity to
apply a number of stability tests to these rocks in order to ascertain
the age of the magnetization in the rocks.
2. Methods
[8] A total of 154 samples from 22 sites within the St. Francois
Mountains igneous province were collected with a water-cooled
portable drill. Sites were distributed among both volcanic and
intrusive rocks including samples from a younger (circa 1330 Ma)
suite of mafic dikes and their host rocks. In addition, clasts of SFM
volcanic and intrusive material were drilled from the Cambrian-
age boulder conglomerate. All samples were oriented using both
solar and magnetic compass in the field. Structural orientations
were determined on the volcanic sequence of rocks for use in the
fold test. The samples were then cut into individual cylindrical
specimens, and the bulk susceptibility of each sample was meas-
ured using a Sapphire Instruments susceptibility bridge. A pilot
selection of samples was chosen for stepwise thermal and alter-
nating field demagnetization. In nearly every case, stepwise
thermal demagnetization was able to more clearly define the
individual vector components in the samples, and the remaining
samples were treated using thermal methods. In an effort to
determine the magnetic carriers within the samples, both isother-
mal remanence acquisition studies (IRM) and three-axis thermal
demagnetization of IRM [ Lowrie, 1990] tests were conducted.
Samples were stored and measured in the shielded magnetic room
at Indiana State University. Thermal and alternating field demag-
netizations were carried out on an either an ASC-Scientific TD-48

3. Results
[9] A total of 18 of 22 sites yielded consistent directional data.
Samples from two of the granitic sites behaved erratically during
thermal and alternating field demagnetization and yielded no
consistent directions. Site 15 yielded directions that appeared to
be approximately reverse (tilt corrected) to the characteristic
direction as given in Table 1 (Figures 3a – 3c). Because this was
the only site that showed a reverse magnetization in the SFM and
the relatively large a
95 (21 ), we did not include this site in our
mean calculation. Nevertheless, it does suggest that the magnet-
ization of these rocks spanned an interval that included at least one
field reversal.
[
10] Samples from the remaining 18 sites showed stable
magnetic behavior during both thermal and alternating field
demagnetization; however, alternating field demagnetization
was unable to fully demagnetize most samples, and the majority
were treated using stepwise thermal treatment. Typical demag-
netization behaviors are shown in Figures 4 and 5. In general,
removal of either a present-day field or randomly directed
overprint was followed by nearly linear decay of the character-
istic component of magnetization. In situ directions were largely
confined to the west-southwest quadrant and downwardly direc-
ted with considerable scatter (Table 1). The mean in situ
direction is D = 232.8  , I = +48.5  (Table 1; k =7 . 8 a
95 =
13.2 ] and compares favorably to the directional data observed
in the previous studies of the SFM by Hsu et al. [1966] and
Hays and Scharon [1966]. Tilt correction of the data results in a
considerable improvement in grouping and is discussed in
section 3.3. along with other tests that help constrain the age
of magnetization in the SFM rocks.

several locations and contains clasts of both granitic and volcanic

Middle to Late Cambrian on the basis of stratigraphic relationships
with the overlying Late Cambrian-aged Lamotte sandstone [ Kis-
varsanyi et al. , 1981]. We sampled 13 boulders from this con-
glomerate. Individual clasts exhibited low-temperature unblocking
directions consistent with a viscous overprint of recent origin and

3.2. Baked Contact Test
[12] Both the granitic and volcanic rocks of the St. Francois
Mountains are intruded by mafic dikes of variable width. These
dikes are believed to represent the last igneous pulse in the St.
Francois region and have been dated to  330 Ma [ Lowell and
Young, 1999; Ramo et al. , 1994; R. Tucker, personal communica-
tion, 2000]. We sampled a detailed profile through one of the dikes
and sampled several of the smaller dikes and the contact rocks at
another site. The results of the baked contact test are somewhat
ambiguous (Figure 7a – 7f). Figure 7f shows a stereoplot of mean
results from dikes and baked contacts at site 4 where the Grassy
Mountain ignimbrite (GMI) is intruded by a 1.2 m wide dike
(Figure 8a). Results from the GMI distant from the dike show
directions consistent with the prefolding magnetization discussed
in section 3.3 (D = 259  , I = +44  ; Figures 7a and 7f ). Samples
from the dike at site 4 yield a mean direction that is different from
the volcanics/granites (D = 325  , I = +59  ; Figures 7b and 7f). In
contrast, the baked country rock near the dike at site 4 exhibited
stable behavior during demagnetization, and the directions are
consistent out to one-half dike width distance (D = 76  ,I=
+45 ; Figures 7c and 7f ). At face value, these results suggest a
negative baked contact test for site 4.
[
13] Dike samples from a small dike swarm at site 3 (intrud-
ing the Slabtown granite), show similar directions to the baked
country rocks at site 4 (Figures 7e and 8b). Samples taken from
the host granites at site 3 show a weak overprint consistent with
both the baked contact directions at site 4 and directions from
the intruding dike swarm (Figures 7d and 7f ). The mean
direction from the smaller dikes and baked contacts at both
sites 3 and 4 is D = 60.8  , I = +48.6  (2 sites, 17 samples). Our
preferred interpretation is that these NE down directions are
related to the timing of dike emplacement (circa 1330 Ma) and
provide a positive baked contact test for the 1330 Ma rocks and
a positive inverse baked contact test for the country rock. An

provides evidence that the host rocks have retained their magnet-

[14] We have no definitive explanation for the NW down
directions observed in the larger dike; perhaps it is related to the
presence of larger magnetic domain sizes that tend to be more
unstable. We also note that the large dike is heavily fractured and
mineralized and may have been the site of channeled fluid flow
along its margin during a younger time. Many of the dike samples
do not reach a stable endpoint (Figure 7b), but a few trend (at
higher temperatures) toward the E-NE direction observed in the
country rocks. In contrast, the dikes at site 3 have sharp and fresh
contacts with their host rocks.
[
15] A positive inverse baked contact test for the host rocks
constrains the age of magnetization to older than 1330 Ma. There
are few similar-age poles from North America at 1330 Ga. A
virtual geomagnetic pole (VGP) obtained from seven samples in
Kansas drill core [ Kodama, 1984] yielded a similar inclination to
our study; however, the declination was nearly 180  different. The
declination in the Kodama [1984] study was based on the premise
that the overprint was acquired in the present-Earth’s field, and the
older component is primary. Thomas and Piper [1992] reported
paleomagnetic data from the supposed circa 1300 Ma Ericksfjo ¨rd
lavas of Greenland that are clearly different from the directions we
observe in our dikes; however, Paslick et al. [1993] suggested the
age of the Ericksfjo¨rd lavas was closer to 1.2 Ga, and therefore a
direct comparison to our VGP is not reasonable. In addition,
Thomas and Piper [1992] noted reversal asymmetry of nearly
30 in these rocks and a number of intermediate directions
attributed to nondipole components of the Earth’s field. The closest
reliable pole to our dike VGP is derived from the 1267 ± 2 Ma
MacKenzie dike swarm [ Buchan and Halls , 1990]. This pole falls
some 40  from our dike VGP , but the difference can be accounted
for by normal plate motion during the time interval between the
two poles. We have just completed a second field season to the area
to sample additional sites in the younger magmatic suites to better
constrain this magnetization.

site 9) and several of the units were nearly flat lying. We are
unable to uniquely determine the amount of tilting in the granitic
bodies but point out that the tilting of the volcanic units was likely
synchronous with caldera collapse, and the intruding granites
would have suffered only minor postemplacement tilting in
regions of reactivated faults. Lowell [1991] argues on the basis
of data provided by Clendenin et al. [1989] that the entire Butler
Hill caldera (Figure 2a) was tilted a maximum of 10  to the
southwest by Late Proterozoic or Phanerozoic faulting along the
Simms Mountain Fault (Figure 2a). Sides [1980] also concluded
on the basis of field and petrologic data that the Butler Hill
batholith was tilted to the SW between 9  –1 1 , although the exact
timing of the tilting was not discussed. Lower Paleozoic strata
overlying the Butler Hill batholith are nearly flat lying at, and
between, our sites 1 – 6, and dikes intruding the granites at site 3
are near vertical, as is the dike at site 4. We therefore have applied
a regional tilt correction to sites 1 – 6 where we see no obvious
bedding with a strike of 150  and a dip of 10  in accordance with
the estimates of Sides [1980] and Bickford et al. [1981]. We
applied the tilt test using data from 18 of 22 sites, and the results
are shown in Figure 9a – 9c. The in situ grouping improves
significantly during stepwise unfolding of the rocks and reaches
a maximum at 100% unfolding (see Figure 9c). The tilt-corrected
direction in the SFM rocks is D = 233.4  , I = +36.9  (k = 27.0;
a
95 =6 . 8  ). Comparison of k values (unfolded/folded) in the
classic McElhinny [1964] fold test yields a k2/k1 value of 3.46
(critical value is 1.78), indicating that the magnetization was
acquired prior to folding of the rocks. The fold test was also
applied using the McFadden [1990] test. The critical value of x
(n = 18 sites) is 6.919 (99%). The McFadden [1990] fold test
assigns a probability to the null hypothesis that a particular
magnetization was acquired prior to, synchronous with, or post-
folding of the rocks. The SFM study yielded an SCOS value of
7.894 (in situ). Our result signifies that a postfolding magnet-
ization can be rejected above the 99% confidence level. The
combined result of these fold tests indicates that the magnet-
ization in the SFM rocks was acquired prior to the event(s) that
formed the folding in the rocks. Since the folding of these rocks
was broadly synchronous with the formation of the caldera
collapse features documented by Kisvarsanyi [1980], the positive
fold test in the SFM provides very powerful evidence that these
rocks carry a primary magnetization dating to their emplacement
age.
3.4. Rock Magnetism and Magnetic Mineralogy
[17] The opaque mineralogy of the SFM rocks has been
discussed in detail by a number of authors [see, e.g., Hsu et al. ,
1966; Sides, 1976; Blades and Bickford , 1976; Kisvarsanyi et al. ,
1981; Lowell, 1991]. The primary opaque iron oxide minerals in
the volcanic rocks are hematite and magnetite. The granitic rocks
are dominated by magnetite. The magnetic minerals are thought to
be primary igneous minerals, although some formed during late-
stage eruption hydrothermal alteration [ Hsu et al. , 1966; Sides,
1976; Blades and Bickford , 1976; Lowell, 1991]. For example, the
Grassy Mountain ignimbrite (sites 4, 5, and 10) contains an
abundance of aligned hematite specks that have imparted a fabric
to the rock as a result of rheoignimbritic flow [ Sides, 1976].
Hematite has also been noted in the middle zone of the Lake
Killarney unit (sites 8 and 9) and in a number of ash flow tuffs near
our sites 16 and 18 [ Sides, 1976; Blades and Bickford , 1976;
Kisvarsanyi et al. , 1981]. Lowell [1991] describes magnetite as an
accessory mineral in the Silvermine granite (site 7) and the Butler
Hill/Breadtray granite (site 1). Additional opaque mineralogy
descriptions are given by Kisvarsanyi et al. [1981] and Hsu et
al. [1966].
[
18] Thermal demagnetization decay curves indicate that the
stable remanence in the SFM rocks is carried by either magnet-
ite or hematite (Figures 3 – 6 and Figure 10a). Isothermal
remanence acquisition curves (IRM, Figure 10b) also show clear
indications of both hematite and magnetite. Thermal demagnet-
ization of three-axis IRM [ Lowrie, 1990] confirms the presence
of both intermediate and high-coercivity fractions dominated by
hematite (Figures 10d, 10e, and 10g) or magnetite (Figure 10f
and 10h). A few samples exhibit a broad range of coercivity
fractions carried by hematite (Figure 10c). Collectively,
the petrographic examinations cited earlier in section 3.4
and the rock magnetic behavior described in this study suggest
that the primary remanence in our samples is carried by both
hematite and magnetite.
4. Discussion
[19] New paleomagnetic data from the St. Francois Mountains
igneous province in Missouri provide a key paleopole for
Laurentia at 1476 ± 16 Ma. We consider the paleomagnetic pole
primary on the basis of the unmetamorphosed nature of the rocks,
a positive conglomerate test (magnetization age > 500 Ma),
positive inverse baked contact test (magnetization age > 1330
Ma), and a positive fold test (magnetization age > deformation  
caldera collapse). We also note a reversed direction at one site in
the Taum Sauk rhyolite; however, in the absence of confirmation
from other sites in the SFM, we did not use this site in our mean
calculation (Table 1).

4.1. Comparison to Laurentian Paleomagnetic Poles
[20] Discrepancies in paleomagnetic data from Laurentia for
the time period from 1400 – 1475 Ma were recently highlighted
by Harlan and Geissman [1998] in their discussion of the Electra
Lake gabbro (1433 Ma) pole. Harlan and Geissman [1998] noted
that selected paleomagnetic data from igneous intrusions from
eastern North America (including the previous SFM results;
Figure 11a) yielded a mean direction of 0.5  S, 214.7  E( a
95 =
6.2 ) and was statistically different than the results from the
Electra Lake gabbro (21.1  S, 221.1  E, a95 =3 . 4 ) and a mean
pole from the Belt Supergroup (18.8  S, 207.2  E, a95 =5 . 6  ).
New paleomagnetic data from the Belt Supergroup (R. Enkin,
personal communication, 2001) do not statistically change the
older results of Elston and Bressler [1980], although there is an
indication of a slight eastward migration of the poles from the
uppermost Belt rocks. The age of the Belt Supergroup is better
constrained by new U-Pb ages on the interlayered volcanics and
intrusions [ Evans et al. , 2000; Anderson and Davis , 1995]. Ages
of the lower Belt sediments are constrained by U-Pb data from
the Moyie sills. Anderson and Davis [1995] concluded that these
sills were emplaced shortly after deposition of Aldridge/Pritchard
Formations at 1468 ± 2 Ma. Age constraints for the Upper Belt
rocks are provided by the Logan Pass bentonite (in the Helena
Formation) with a U-Pb zircon age of 1454 ± 9 Ma, a rhyolite in
the uppermost Purcell Lavas with a U-Pb age of 1443 ± 7 Ma
and a U-Pb age of 1401 ± 6 Ma for a thin tuff between the
Bonner quartzite and Libby Formation in the Upper Belt rocks
[Evans et al. , 2000].
[
21] Paleomagnetic directions from the Lower Belt Supergroup
rocks are enigmatic [ Vitorello and V an der V oo, 1977; Elston and
Bressler, 1980] (Table 2 and Figure 11a). Although both studies
yield approximately the same declination, the inclinations of
Vitorello and V an der V oo [1977] were some 20  steeper than
the results of Elston and Bressler [1980]. Elston and Bressler
[1980] commented that the difference in inclinations had no
readily apparent explanation but noted that they appeared to be
restricted to the northeastern part of the Belt Basin. Upon close
inspection of their results, we note that Elston and Bressler
[1980] calculated a mean direction on the basis of directional
data at 550  C, whereas Vitorello and V an der V oo [1977]
calculated their mean direction on the basis of high-temperature
components (> 630  C) using orthogonal vector plots. The pale-
olatitude obtained by Vitorello and V an der V oo [1977] of
22.8
+3.9/ .5 is identical (within error) to that predicted by our
new SFM results (Figure 11b).
[22] U-Pb crystallization ages of the Michikamau and Harp
Lake intrusions are 1460 ± 5 Ma and 1450 ± 5 Ma,
respectively. The predicted paleolatitude for the Belt Super-
group based on a combined Michikamau/Harp Lake (HL) pole
is also systematically higher than the observed paleolatitude in
the upper Belt rocks (  3 to 20  ). There is also a difference
between the observed Electra Lake gabbro (ELG) paleolatitude
and that predicted by the Michikamau/HL (24  versus 37  );
however, the Laramie anorthosite/Sherman granite pole [ Harlan
et al. , 1994] is similar to the Michikamau/Harp Lake pole
(Figure 11a).
[
23] Collectively, the data from the SFM and Michikamau/HL
rocks suggest that the paleolatitudes observed in the Belt rocks are
lower than would be expected for their present-day location at the

edge of the North American craton (see Figure 11c). There are a
number of possible explanations for these observed differences.
The first is that the SFM/HL/Michikamau poles do not accurately
reflect the position of Laurentia because of possible tilting of the
intrusions. Alternatively, we could argue for possible inclination
shallowing in the Belt Supergroup rocks, but we have no way to
accurately assess this possibility, and it remains an ad hoc explan-
ation for the observed differences. R. Enkin (personal communi-
cation, 2001) has compiled new data from the Upper belt rocks that
show a small eastward motion in the Belt apparent polar wander
path (APWP) such that the cited differences in this paper may be
somewhat less for the younger segment of the path (Figure 11c).
Harlan and Geissman [1998] propose a number of rotation and
tilting possibilities to explain the differences in paleomagnetic
poles from the central craton poles and those from the marginal
ELG and Belt rocks. It is possible that undetected rotations of any,
or all, of these poles can account for the observed differences, or
that the timing of magnetization assigned to the intrusive bodies
based on their U-Pb ages overestimates the true age of magnet-
ization. More data from similar-age units may help distinguish
among the possible explanations.
4.2. Comparison With Other Continents
[24] Accepting the SFM pole as representative for Laurentia
at 1476 ± 16 Ma allows us to test proposed continental
configurations for the Mesoproterozoic. Although the Rodinia
hypothesis is considered valid from  100 Ma to  50 Ma, the
links between Australia-Antarctica, Siberia, and Baltica are
considered valid for Mesoproterozoic and earlier time [ Gower
et al. , 1990; Ross et al. , 1992; Dalziel, 1997; Sears and Price ,
2000]. The identities of the continents adjacent to the present-
day western coast of Laurentia are controversial. For example,
Ross et al. [1992] have argued for an Australian source for the
Belt Supergroup on the basis of detrital zircon data, while Sears
and Price [2000] argue that Siberia was the source continent for
these zircons. Gower et al. [1990] have argued for a Mesopro-
terozoic linkage between Baltica and Laurentia (Nena). Ideally,

paleomagnetic data can test these proposed configurations pro-
vided key poles are available for similar time periods from these
continents. Paleomagnetic tests of continental coherence are
more robust when closely spaced poles are available to define
apparent polar wander paths (APWPs). Table 2 lists selected
paleomagnetic poles available from Laurentia, Siberia, Australia,
and Baltica for the interval from 1500 Ma to 1430 Ma. The
data are limited in their power to distinguish among the
various models as no APWPs can be constructed for this
interval of time. Therefore the following analysis should be
viewed with caution as we have assumed polarity choices for
the models and attempted a ‘‘closest fit’’ approach to the
reconstructions.
[
25] Paleomagnetic data from Australia are derived from the
mafic intrusions and host rocks of the Mt. Isa inlier [ Tanaka and
Idnurm, 1994] and the Gawler Range V olcanics [ Chamalaun and
Dempsey, 1978]. The Mt. Isa pole is assigned an age of 1525 ±
25 Ma [ Tanaka and Idnurm , 1994]. There is some controversy
about the age of magnetization recorded by the Gawler Range
V olcanics (GRV). The emplacement age of the GRV is 1592 ± 2
Ma [ Fanning et al. , 1988]; however, recent work [ Daly et al. ,
1998] suggests that the region underwent deformation and meta-
morphism during the 1540 – 1565 Ma interval. Tanaka and
Idnurm [1994] and Idnurm [2000] noted the similarity between
the GRV pole and the Mt. Isa pole and suggested that a
purported postfolding magnetization in the GRV might be as
young as 1525 Ma.
[
26] New paleomagnetic data from the Anabar shield region of
Siberia [ Ernst et al. , 2000] are derived from the 1503 ± 5 Ma
Kuonamka dikes. Five of these dikes yield a paleomagnetic pole at
6 N, 234  E (dp = 14  ,d m=2 8  ) that the authors considered
primary on the basis of the extremely low metamorphic grade of
the rocks and the fact that directional data from the host rocks are
significantly different from the dikes.
[
27] There are a number of paleomagnetic studies from the
Baltic shield with ages between 1455 – 1530 Ma [ Piper, 1980;
Bylund, 1985]. These poles yield a grand mean at 27.9  S, 3.8  E
(a95 = 18.8  ). Our best estimate for the age of this mean pole is
1520 ± 7 Ma.
[28] Figure 11d shows these paleomagnetic poles rotated to
the Rodinia configuration of Dalziel [1997]. Both the Gawler
Range V olcanics (GRV) and the Kuonamka dike pole (KD) fall
close to coeval poles from Laurentia; however, the Baltica
mean pole (BMP , including the individual poles used to derive
BMP) and Mt. Isa pole (MI) fall well away from the Lau-
rentian poles. Testing possible cratonic coherence or specific
reconstructions with individual poles can be misleading since
slight rotations or large errors can lead to misinterpretations
about the validity of a particular reconstruction. A better,
though nonunique, test is to rotate the continents to their
correct paleolatitudes by assuming a polarity that will minimize
the distance between cratons. Once the continents are placed at
this paleolatitude and orientation, they can be moved longitudi-
nally to a closest approach. Figure 11e shows the continents
rotated to one possible closest approach fit using the SFM pole
for Laurentia, for the KD pole, the Baltica mean pole, and the
Gawler Range volcanic poles (using a South Pole option for
the poles listed in Table 2). Figure 11f uses the same polarity
choice for the Laurentian and Baltica poles, but uses the Mt.
Isa pole from Australia (South Pole) and a North Pole option
for the Siberian pole. The fit in Figure 11e approximates the
Rodinia configuration of Dalziel [1997] for Siberia and Aus-
tralia, whereas Figure 11f is close to the AUSWUS config-
uration of Karlstrom et al. [2000]. In fact, one cannot reject
either the SWEA T or AUSWUS configurations on the basis of
the extant paleomagnetic database for this time period. Never-
theless, it should be reemphasized that the age range of these
poles may span over 50 Ma. Sears and Price [2000] have
argued that Siberia was adjacent to the western margin of
Laurentia rather than Australia-Antarctica on the basis of geo-
logical correlations between the two continents. At first glance,
Figure 11e would appear to negate this possibility, but the
paleomagnetic pole for Siberia has a large error (28  ). It is
therefore possible to position Siberia farther south in Figure 11e
against the western margin of Laurentia. A choice of opposite
polarity for the Siberia pole also brings Siberia closer to the
western margin of Laurentia; however, the orientation precludes
matching of geologic features critical to the arguments of Sears
and Price [2000].
5. Conclusions
[29] The SFM igneous province in southeastern Missouri has
provided a key 1476 ± 16 Ma paleomagnetic pole for Laurentia.
The pole is considered primary on the basis of a positive con-
glomerate test (pole age > 500 Ma), a positive inverse baked
contact test (pole age >1330 Ma) and a positive fold test (pole age
> deformation  caldera collapse  476 Ma). An analysis of
similar-aged poles from Laurentia highlights key differences

between the Belt Supergroup poles, the Electra Lake gabbro pole,
and poles from cratonic North America. We note that the SFM pole
is consistent with the paleolatitude suggested by the Lower belt
rocks obtained by Vitorello and V an der V oo[1977]. An, as of yet,
unexplained paleolatitudinal offset exists between data obtained
from the Upper belt rocks and igneous intrusions from cratonic
Laurentia.
[
30] The debate regarding the Mesoproterozoic position of
Siberia cannot be settled using the existing paleomagnetic data.
Sears and Price [2000] have argued for a western Laurentia
connection and described possible source rocks for the Belt
Supergroup in Siberia. A strict interpretation of the new pale-
omagnetic data from Siberia [ Ernst et al. , 2000] tends to favor
the Dalziel [1997] position, but because of the large error
associated with the paleomagnetic pole, Siberia can also be
placed in the approximate position favored by Sears and Price
[2000]. Finally, we caution that these paleogeographic conclu-
sions are based on a comparison of broadly coeval poles and a
‘‘closest approach’’ technique that may err significantly in the
relative longitudinal position and orientation of the continents
depending on the choice of polarity. It is perhaps an understate-
ment to suggest that additional high-quality paleomagnetic data
are needed to provide a robust test of Mesoproterozoic paleo-
geographies.

Post-Middle Oligocene origin of paleomagnetic rotations in
Upper Permian to Lower Jurassic rocks from
northern and southern Peru
Stuart Gildera;/C3, Sonia Roussea, Daniel Farberb, Brendan McNultyc,
Thierry Sempered, Victor Torrese, Oscar Palaciose

Received 5 November 2002; received in revised form 24 February 2003; accepted 27 February 2003
Abstract
Wereportpaleomagneticdatafrom28sitesofUpperPermiantoLowerJurassicstratafromnorthernandsouthern
Peru.InnorthernPeru(6‡S),astablemagneticcomponentfromsixPermo-Triassicsitespassesfoldandreversaltests.
The overall mean pole agrees well with Late Permian to Triassic poles from cratonal South America, suggesting this
part of Peru has experienced neither significant rotation nor latitudinal transport since the Permo-Triassic. In
southern Peru (13 to 16‡S), thermal demagnetization isolates stable magnetic components in 16 of 22 Upper Permian
to LowerJurassicsites collectedalongthetransitionbetween theAltiplanoandtheEastern Cordillera. These16 sites
arerotated14to147‡counterclockwiseandpassaninclinations-onlyfoldtest.Withinthesamestructuralzone,three
other Permo-Triassicsitesas wellas 10Paleocenesites alsoshowimportantcounterclockwiserotations[Roperchand
Carlier,J.Geophys.Res.97(1992)17233^17249; Butleretal.,Geology23(1995)799^802].Thelargemagnitudeand
exclusively counterclockwise sense of rotation suggest that the tectonic regime included an important sinistral shear
component. Nocorrelation exists between rotation amount and rock age, suggesting the rotationsare post-Paleocene
in age. Because the rotations occur along the fringe of the Eastern Cordillera, they were likely produced during its
structural formation, hence from the Late Oligocene to Present. Sinistral shear acting in the northern part of the
Bolivian Orocline appears much more pronounced than that north of the Abancay Deflection, which likely arises
from differences in convergence obliquity.

1. Geologic setting and previous paleomagnetic
work
The Andes, one of the world’s longest and

(Fig. 1, inset). While their present morphology
arises mainly from Late Cenozoic geodynamic
processes [3], the geology recorded within the
range infers a protracted history of deformation.
The Peruvian segment of the Andes contains evi-
dence of spatially variable Paleozoic and older

those from the north (6‡S) are not rotated. SFUACC is the left-lateral fault system running from Cuzco-Pisac through Lake Titi-
