6. Discussion
6.1. Age of magnetization
The Fourth of July Batholith is considered to be a
post-tectonic intrusion because it shows only minor
brittle deformation, has primary flow structures
around the margins, and has only minor petrographic
alteration (Aitken, 1959; Mihalynuk et al., 1992) .
Further, most local deformation of the host rocks is
thought to have ended by the Early to Middle Jurassic
with the imbrication and obduction of the Cache
Creek Terrane over the Stikine Terrane (Monger,
1977; Cordey et al., 1991; Mihalynuk et al., 1992) .
The similarity of the U – Pb and hornblende
40Ar/39Ar ages from the main granodiorite phase at
f 173 Ma points to relatively rapid initial cooling of
the batholith upon intrusion. The equivalence at
f 165 Ma between the biotite 40Ar/39Ar ages from
the granodiorite (FJ21) and the eastern lamprophyre
dike (FJ01) suggests either: (1) the dike intruded the
granodiorite when it was at an elevated temperature
and both then cooled through the closure temperature
of biotite at ca. 280 jC; or (2) the dike reheated the
surrounding granodiorite to >280 jC upon intrusion,
thereby resetting the granodiorite biotite systematics
to the dike’s age and negating any possibility of
reconstructing the thermal closure history of the
granodiorite. The slightly younger argon age of
f 162 Ma for the western lamprophyre dike (FJ07)
suggests that the dike swarm is slightly younger than
the granodiorite or had multiple intrusive events.
Further, the thermal effect of these small dike intru-
sions on the large granodiorite batholith is limited:
therefore, scenario (1) above is preferred.
Overall, there is no evidence that a high temper-
ature alteration event has affected the Ar systematics
(f 280 jC), the magnetic properties (>300 jC), or the
hornblende chemistry (>500 jC). Therefore, the
reported ages, measured pressures, temperatures and
ChRM directions are considered primary with the
magnetization being acquired at f 173 Ma.
6.2. Geobarometric summary
Minor topographic corrections have been made to
the geobarometric data. The most eastern sites, i.e.,
sites FJ24-27, are at the highest elevations, and there-
fore no correction will be made to them. The sites
along the road, just east of Atlin Lake are, on average,
760 m below the most eastern sites. Therefore, 21
MPa will be added to the pressures at sites FJ02, FJ03,
FJ29 and FJ31, i.e., 760 m  .028 MPa/m = 21 MPa.
Sites FJ09 and FJ12 are about 855 m below the most
eastern sites, and therefore, 24 MPa will be added to
their pressures (Fig. 5) .
There is a significant difference in pressures and
the resulting crystallization depths in the batholith
between the sites on the western shore of Atlin Lake
that average 3.6 km and those to the east of the lake
that average 9.1 F 2.2 km. These data suggest differ-
ential uplift of f 6 km across the lake. Minor fractur-
ing and alteration of granitic outcrops along the shores
led Aitken (1959) to first suggest the presence of a
fault zone along the lake. Although the apatite fission-
track dates are imprecise, they also suggest the pres-
ence of a fault, giving similar uplift ages of f 65 Ma
on the east side of Atlin Lake and an earlier 93 Ma on

the west side ( Fig. 2 , Table 1 ) and implying differ-

With more concrete geobarometric evidence of sub-
stantial differential uplift across Atlin Lake in hand, it
is proposed herein to formally name the fault the
‘‘Atlin Lake Fault Zone’’.
The crystallization depths for the two sites on the
western shore of Atlin Lake are not significantly
different at the 95% confidence level and thus provide
no evidence for tilt, i.e., F 60 MPa = F 2.2 km ( Table
3, Fig. 5 ). East of the lake, the batholith does show a
systematic decrease in pressure from the north to the
south, implying differential uplift. The differential
uplift could record the vertical motion of discrete fault
blocks, without tilting of the batholith, however, there
are no obvious east – west faults through the batholith
to support this hypothesis. Conversely, the batholith
may have been tilted as a single entity. If true, then the
crystallization depths yield a south – southwest-side
down tilt of f 9j. This possible tilting event is
probably not syn-intrusion because the ChRM direc-
tions would likely then be ‘‘streaked’’ in an elongated
pattern (e.g., Symons et al., 2000a ). Therefore, the
tilting event is likely post-magnetization and the
paleomagnetic directions will require tectonic correc-
tions. Assuming vertical emplacement of the mafic
dikes, their present average dip of f 75j from hori-
zontal to the north – northeast also implies f 15j of
south – southwest-side down tilt of the batholith after
dike emplacement to support the geobarometric data.
6.3. Tectonic summary
6.3.1. Cache Creek Terrane
The similarity of biotite
40Ar/39Ar ages between
the lamprophyre dikes and the granodiorite, plus the
petrologic similarities, suggest that intrusion of the
batholith and the dikes was nearly coeval and, there-
fore, both likely retain similar ChRM directions. In
fact, their cones of 95% confidence overlap both mean
directions, which proves that they are statistically the
same. The combined in situ unit mean ChRM direc-
tion is at D = 49.5j, I =7 0 . 5j, a
95 = 3.0j, and k =7 3
(N = 31 sites; Table 4), which yields a 173-Ma paleo-
pole at 54.9 jW, 63.4jN( dp = 4.5j, dm =5 . 2j). Com-
pared to the 173-Ma reference pole of 249 jW, 67.5jN
(a95 =3 . 5j) that is interpolated from the apparent
polar wander path (APWP) of Besse and Courtillot
(1991), the unit paleopole is near-sided, suggesting
that the batholith and hosting Cache Creek Terrane
have been translated away from the reference pole or
‘‘southward’’ by 9.0 F 3.7j (1000 F 410 km) and
rotated clockwise by 79 F 6j (Fig. 11) . Correcting
for the 9 j south – southwest-side down tilt towards
f 190 j yields a unit mean ChRM direction of
D =0 7 7j, I =7 5j, a
95 =3 . 0j,a n d k =7 3 (Table 4)
and an associated paleopole of 81.2 jW, 54.6 jN
(dp = 5.0j, dm = 5.5j). Comparison of this paleopole
with the 173-Ma reference pole suggests that the
batholith and hosting Cache Creek Terrane have been
significantly translated away from the reference pole
or ‘‘southward’’ by 16.1F 3.7j (1790 F 410 km) and
rotated clockwise by 107 F 7j (Fig. 11) .
Three other Jurassic reference poles for the North
American craton (e.g., Gordon et al., 1984; May and
Butler, 1986; V an der V oo, 1993) have been compared
with the tectonic-corrected pole from the Fourth of July
Batholith (Fig. 11). Use of one of these other reference
poles would increase the southward translation esti-
mate by 3 j to 4j and the rotation estimate by F 4j.
The tectonically corrected tectonic motion estimate
of the Fourth of July Batholith is dissimilar to that
previously published for the Atlin area supracrustal
rocks. Cole et al. (1992) suggested that the host rocks
for the Fourth of July Batholith showed no translation
and only minor counter-clockwise rotation assuming
Early Jurassic remagnetization. However, their results
are considered with caution because there is no age
control on either the remagnetization or deformation
events. Further, their two sampling areas are small and
may not average out secular variation, particularly if
the ChRM is a remagnetization component as sug-
gested by the fact that all of their samples retain a
normal polarity despite being supposedly acquired
during a time period with many polarity changes
(e.g., Cox, 1982; Opdyke and Channell, 1996 ), as is
found for the Fourth of July Batholith and associated
dikes. Also, their two sampling sites are located on
either side of the then unrecognized Atlin Lake Fault
Zone, so that the tilt on the eastern side of the lake was
not in consideration, which could affect the data of
their southern sampling site.
6.3.2. Stikine Terrane
The 206 – 190-Ma Hazelton – Takla volcanic rocks
that are exposed in the Stikine Terrane in central

British Columbia (Fig. 1) also show dissimilar esti-
mates of translation but large rotations. Monger and
Irving (1980) obtained an estimate of f 1300 km of
northward translation and clockwise rotations of
about  3j to 14 j for three small sampling areas.
Using two different reference poles, Gordon et al.
(1984) and May and Butler (1986) suggested that
there was no translation. V andall and Palmer (1990)
obtained a translation estimate of 0 F 10j and clock-
wise rotation estimates of 14 j,7 9j and 117j for three
different areas of these volcanic rocks. The variability
in the rotation values is not surprising because the
sampled units dip steeply and thus likely incorporate
plunge estimate errors, and because their primary
remanence is carried by both magnetite and hematite
and thus likely incorporates errors from the incom-
plete demagnetization of the specimens (e.g., Monger
and Irving, 1980 ). However, the mean clockwise
rotation found for the Hazelton – Takla Group of
58 F 47j is similar to clockwise rotation estimates
found for Cretaceous rock units in the Intermontane
Belt, supporting the validity of the Hazelton – Takla
Group tectonic estimates.
Paleomagnetic results for the f 177-Ma Teslin
Crossing Stock in the Stikine terrane of the southern
Y ukon yielded a southward translation estimate of
21.1 F 7.4j and a clockwise rotation of 33 F 18j,
thus having translation values that are similar to the
results for the Fourth of July Batholith (Table 5) .
There is no evidence for tilt of the Teslin Crossing
Stock; biotite geothermometry does not statistically
support a tilt, nor do the horizontal host rocks (Harris
et al., 1999a) .
6.3.3. Quesnel Terrane
Two studies in southern British Columbia provide
Jurassic tectonic estimates for the Quesnel Terrane.
The f 198 Ma Guichon Batholith yielded a revised
geobarometrically corrected paleomagnetic result that
implies a 13.8 F 6.6j northward translation and
43 F 7j clockwise rotation for Quesnellia (Harris,
1998; Harris et al., 1998) . These values correct for
the measured 6.0 j tilt down to the northeast, but they
are not statistically significantly different from the
original values (Symons, 1971, 1983) . The f 203-Ma
Copper Mountain Intrusions could not be tested geo-

6.3.4. Yukon-Tanana Terrane
The f 190 Ma Big Creek Batholith lies within the
Y ukon-Tanana Terrane in central Y ukon (Fig. 1) .
Using the 190-Ma reference pole, the geobarometri-
cally corrected paleomagnetic results suggest that this
terrane is 9.3 F 6.1j near-sided and rotated counter-
clockwise by 32 F 11j. Although the translation esti-
mate is relatively similar to the Fourth of July estimate,
the counter-clockwise rotation is opposite in sense to
that found in Stikine and Cache Creek rock units, but
has recently been found elsewhere in the Y ukon-
Tanana Terrane (e.g., McCausland et al., 1998;
Symons et al., 2000b ). Thus, the Y ukon-Tanana Ter-
rane appears to have been a parautochthon to the North
American craton since the Early Jurassic, and to have
had a very different tectonic history than the Stikine
and Cache Creek terranes (Symons et al., 2000b) .
6.3.5. Intermontane assembly
These southern translation estimates from Jurassic
rocks in the Cache Creek and Stikine terranes contrast
with the northward estimates from Cretaceous and
Paleocene units in these same terranes (Table 5). This
implies a dramatic change in the tectonic evolution of
the Intermontane Belt terranes during the Late Juras-
sic. Specifically, the translation and rotation estimates
for the Fourth of July Batholith indicate that the Cache
Creek Terrane was located at a latitude north of the
North American craton during the Early Jurassic, and
likely outboard of the North American Craton within

7. Conclusions
Argon geochronology results on hornblende sepa-
rates indicate that the Fourth of July Batholith is
f 173 Ma old, in agreement with U – Pb zircon
analyses. Further, dates for biotite separates indicate
that the batholith and associated mafic dikes cooled
through f 280 jCa t f 165 Ma. Geobarometric
analyses indicate the presence of a north – south fault
running along the length of Atlin Lake with the east
side having been uplifted by f 6 km more relative to
the west side. Further, the Fourth of July Batholith
appears to have been tilted uniformly down by f 9j
towards the south – southwest at f 190j. Tilt-cor-
rected paleomagnetic analyses suggest that the Cache
Creek Terrane has been significantly translated
16 F 4j southward and rotated 107 F 7j clockwise
since the Middle Jurassic. This result is in agreement
with the Jurassic Teslin Crossing Stock translation
estimate from the Stikine Terrane, but not with other
estimates from the terranes underlying the Intermon-
tane Belt. Further, the proposed tectonic model sug-
gests that the Stikine and Cache Creek terranes were at
a similar paleolatitude north of the North American
craton at f 175 Ma and far off the margin, before
moving southeasterly towards the craton to amalga-
mate with Quesnellia by the mid to Late Jurassic. This

Differences in paleomagnetic interpretations due to the choice
of statistical, demagnetization and correction techniques:
Kapuskasing Structural Zone, northern Ontario, Canada
Graham J. Borradaile a,*, Tomasz Werner b, France Lagroix c
a Department of Geology, Lakehead University, 955 Oliver Road, Thunder Bay, Ontario, Canada P7B 5E1
b Institute of Geophysics, Polish Academy of Sciences, ul Ksie ˛cia Janusza 64, 01452 Warsaw, Poland
c Institute for Rock Magnetism, University of Minnesota, Minneapolis, MN 55455, USA
Received 7 May 2002; accepted 22 November 2002
Abstract
The Kapuskasing Structural Zone (KSZ) reveals a section through the Archean lower crustal granoblastic gneisses. Our new
paleomagnetic data largely agree with previous work but we show that interpretations vary according to the choices of statistical,
demagnetization and field-correction techniques. First, where the orientation distribution of characteristic remanence directions
on the sphere is not symmetrically circular, the commonly used statistical model is invalid [Fisher, R.A., Proc. R. Soc. A217
(1953) 295]. Any tendency to form an elliptical distribution indicates that the sample is drawn from a Bingham-type population
[Bingham, C., 1964. Distributions on the sphere and on the projective plane. PhD thesis, Yale University]. Fisher and Bingham
statistics produce different confidence estimates from the same data and the traditionally defined mean vector may differ from the
maximum eigenvector of an orthorhombic Bingham distribution. It seems prudent to apply both models wherever a non-Fisher
population is suspected and that may be appropriate in any tectonized rocks. Non-Fisher populations require larger sample sizes
so that focussing on individual sites may not be the most effective policy in tectonized rocks. More dispersed sampling across
tectonic structures may be more productive. Second, from the same specimens, mean vectors isolated by thermal and alternating
field (AF) demagnetization differ. Which treatment gives more meaningful results is difficult to decipher, especially in
metamorphic rocks where the history of the magnetic minerals is not easily related to the ages of tectonic and petrological events.
In this study, thermal demagnetization gave lower inclinations for paleomagnetic vectors and thus more distant paleopoles. Third,
of more parochial significance, tilt corrections may be unnecessary in the KSZ because magnetic fabrics and thrust ramp are
constant in orientation to the depth at which they level off, at approximately 15-km depth. With Archean geothermal gradients,
primary remanences were blocked after the foliation was tilted to rise on the thrust ramp. Therefore, the rocks were probably
magnetized in their present orientation; tilting largely or entirely predates magnetization.

1. Introduction
The Kapuskasing Structural Zone (KSZ) of north-
ern Ontario is a well-documented example of upthrust
lower crust, for which most contemporary research is
documented by Percival (1994) and Percival and West
(1994) (Fig. 1) . The zone thrust up Archean lower
crustal granoblastic gneisses, dated at 2750 – 2500 Ma,
that rose on a ramp from a subhorizontal decollement,
now at a depth of f 15 km (Geis et al., 1990; Percival
and Card, 1983) . Intracratonic uplift and cooling
occurred at f 1900 Ma, exposing a dextrally sheared
lower-crust section >15 km thick. KSZ shows strong
positive gravity and magnetic anomalies which,
together with recent seismic surveying, indicate that
lower crustal rocks were thrust up from the west over
the Archean Abitibi Greenstones, which crop out to the
east of the Kapuskasing Structural Zone (Atekwana et
al., 1994) .
On the east, KSZ is bounded by the Ivanhoe Lake
Fault Zone. Interpretations of seismic profiles suggest
that it dips f 45j to the northwest, which is steeper
than the thrust (Fig. 1b) . The seismic profile docu-
ments reflectors to a depth of approximately 15 km,
emphasizing contributions from gently inclined reflec-
tors. They appear to show that the lower crustal slice
maintains constant orientations of its internal fabrics
and of its internal seismic reflectors to depths z 10
km. The thrust surface and seismic reflectors within
the lower crustal granulites are subparallel to the
magnetic foliations (Borradaile et al., 1999) and dip
f 20j, more gently than the Ivanhoe Lake Fault
(Shaw and Percival, 1990; Leclair et al., 1994) . Pres-
sure estimates from petrogeneses and radiometric ages
constrain the pre-thrusting uplift rate to approximately
0.03 km/Ma following late Archean tectonism at 2670
Ma (Percival, 1994; Percival and West, 1994) . This is
quite modest by comparison with modern tectonic
environments and is similar to contemporary continen-
tal denudation rates. A wealth of recent geochrono-
logical, geobarometric and geothermal data permit
some reasonable constraints on uplift rates (Hanes et
al., 1994; Krogh and Moser, 1994; Ma¨der et al., 1994;
Percival and Peterman, 1994; Percival et al., 1994;
Williams et al., 1992) . During thrusting of the Kapus-
kasing granulites to the surface at f 1900 Ma, the
uplift rate was four times higher, f 0.12 km/Ma, but
still less than Phanerozoic orogenic uplift rates. Con-
servative geothermal gradients were previously used
(30 jC/km), although values closer to 50 jC/km may
be possible based on our knowledge of metamorphic
studies. Such imprecision makes it difficult to estimate
the depth of the Curie isotherm or any blocking
temperature isotherm with sufficient precision to fix
the age of any paleomagnetic signal. Comparison of
paleopole locations with the tentative apparent polar
wander paths (APWPs) is a more optimistic strategy.
The granoblastic rocks of the Kapuskasing Struc-
tural Zone (KSZ) lack anisotropic features that can be
used in structural mapping to determine finite strain
directions and infer kinematics. However, magnetic
fabrics reveal subtle tectonic microfabrics precisely
and reproducibly (Borradaile, 1988; Borradaile and
Henry, 1997; Hrouda, 1982) . Recently, we applied the
techniques of measuring anisotropy of magnetic sus-
ceptibility (AMS) and anisotropy of anhysteretic rema-
nence (AARM) in the KSZ (Borradaile et al., 1999) .
The AMS method determines the anisotropy of mean
susceptibility tensor for all grains, but primarily that of
the aligned paramagnetic mafic crystals that dominate
>95% of the induced magnetic response to a low
applied field. This low-field technique was applied to
263 specimens before any demagnetization experi-
ments that could disturb the AMS. It is known that
high-field exposure may change magnetite’s AMS
(Potter and Stephenson, 1990) , and that oxidation
during thermal demagnetization may change AMS
even more significantly by the alteration or creation
of oxides (Borradaile and Lagroix, 2000) . Our AMS
results mostly define the orientation distributions of
the silicate matrix. AARM isolated the orientation
distribution for the assemblage of remanence-bearing
grains, a technique explained by Jackson (1991) . Our
previous work on magnetic mineralogy, hysteresis and
Curie temperatures confirms that the remanence-bear-
ing phase is almost exclusively magnetite, further
confirmed by the upper limit of the blocking-temper-
ature spectra. Borradaile et al. (1999) confirmed this
from Curie-temperature determinations, although
minor remanence components were attributed to local-
ized hematite alteration, and a mineral with a Curie
temperature f 260 jC, which may be a titaniferous
iron oxide (Dunlop and O¨ zdemir, 1997; McEnroe et
al., 2001) . AARM defines the principal directions for
the orientation distribution of magnetite’s grain shapes.
The technique is more restrictive on the suitability of

The use of the mean-tensor plot requires some consid-
eration (Borradaile, 2001) .I n Fig. 2c and f , the mean
tensors for AMS and for AARM are shown for speci-
mens, without standardization. Standardization or nor-
malization is a procedure that weighs the orientations
of individual specimens according to their mean sus-
ceptibility. Consequently, the mean tensor axial ori-
entations and their 95% confidence cones are influ-
enced more by high-susceptibility specimens. In the
case of AARM, the mean-tensor orientations corre-
spond well with the density plots of the maximum and
minimum principal AARM axes (cf. Fig. 2f, d and e ).
This is because only the magnetite subfabric contrib-
utes to AARM; that subfabric is reasonably homoge-
neous and each specimen has approximately similar
anhysteretic susceptibility. In contrast, the AMS mean
tensor (Fig. 2c) does not correspond quite as closely to
density plots of its principal axes (Fig. 2a and b) . This
is due to the contribution of a high-susceptibility,
oblique magnetite subfabric that in some specimens
deflects the net AMS fabric away from the orientation
of the silicate matrix.
Petrographic and structural observations show that
the magnetite subfabric is younger than the silicate
fabric and that the two fabrics developed successively
in a noncoaxial strain history. The silicates grew first,
defining a very feeble metamorphic foliation due to the
low shape anisotropy of grains in the granulite facies.
Subsequently, magnetite developed in part by exsolu-
tion from mafic silicates. Magnetic anisotropy isolates
the orientation of the plane of flattening at a different
part of the kinematic history; AMS detects the orien-
tation distribution of the silicates but it with contribu-
tions from the accessory oxides. AARM isolates the
younger orientation distribution of magnetite. This has
been recognized along transpressed Archean terrain
boundaries in adjacent regions (Borradaile and Dehls,
1993; Werner and Borradaile, 1996; Borradaile et al.,
1999). AMS maxima define the mean extension axis
which corresponds to the minimum compressive stress
during crystallization of the silicate fabric (Fig. 2b and
c). AARM maxima indicate mean extension during
crystallization of the magnetite subfabric (Fig. 2e and
f). The AMS and AARM mean foliations are separated
by a dihedral angle < 15 j (Fig. 2) . The silicate fabric
mainly responded to EW extension on a north-dipping
foliation whereas the subsequent magnetite fabric
developed during W-plunging extension on a WNW-
dipping foliation (cf. Fig. 2c and f ).
It is important to know how deep the fabrics persist
without change in orientation because this will influ-
ence the decision concerning a paleomagnetic tilt
correction. In this region, estimates of the required tilt
corrections have decreased with the advancement of
structural and seismic knowledge from 30 j to 15 j
(Constanzo-Alvarez and Dunlop, 1988) to < 10 j
(Symons et al., 1994) . Fortunately, the Lithoprobe
project provided an ENE – WNW seismic profile
(Fig. 1b) which revealed diffuse pervasive seismic
reflectors throughout the KSZ granulites to z 15-km
depth. Their true dip is unknown as they have only
been recorded in the profile plane, and the contribution
of shallow reflectors is recorded at the expense of
others. Nevertheless, in the profile, their mean orien-
tation is parallel to that of the average AMS and
AARM foliations projected from the surface. Thus,
we propose that seismic reflectors are an expression of
the metamorphic fabric defined by AMS and AARM.
The orientation of all three fabrics may therefore be
similar to depths z 10 km, following the orientation of
the seismic reflectors ( z 15 km), and at a similar or
slightly lower inclination than the thrust ramp (Per-
cival and West, 1994) . Thus, the KSZ ramp geometry
may have been exhumed without significant tilting.
Blocking-temperature isotherms ( f 450 – 550 jC)
would have been achieved at original depths z 10
km using conservative estimates of Archean geother-
mal metamorphic gradients ( f 2600 Ma). This would
mean that the granulites were magnetized in their
present orientation, and any significant tilt correction
may be unnecessary. However, Constanzo-Alvarez
and Dunlop (1988) recognized a spatial distribution
of unblocking temperatures and a combination of
heterogeneous tilt corrections across the strike of the
KSZ that permitted a model involving late tilting of
preserved A-component remanences.
2. Choices in the treatment of paleomagnetic data
Paleomagnetism was studied extensively in the
KSZ, accompanying the Canadian Lithoprobe program
of seismic reflection studies. Results were chiefly
obtained by Bates and Halls (1990, 1991a,b) , Buchan
et al. (1993) , Constanzo-Alvarez and Dunlop (1988) ,
G.J. Borradaile et al. / Tectonophysics 363 (2003) 103–125 107

Constanzo-Alvarez et al. (1993) , Ernst and Buchan
(1993), Ernst and Halls (1984) , Halls et al. (1994) ,
V andall and Symons (1990) and Symons and V andall
(1990). Symons et al. (1994) summarized the findings
in a comprehensive synthesis. Our resampling in-
creases the existing database by approximately 8%,
which is sufficient to validate our results by compar-
ison with others. Since the sample size is adequate and
the main results are corroborated by earlier work, it
permitted us to experiment with different paleomag-
netic procedures. Our contribution is not to bring
different data but to show that different procedures
may lead to different interpretations of KSZ tectonics
and of the global movements of the KSZ rocks by
comparison with the tentative apparent polar wander
paths (APWPs) for the late Archean and with the more
confident paths for the Early Proterozoic rocks
(Buchan et al., 1990, 1993, 1996, 2000, 2001; Dunlop,
1983; Constanzo-Alvarez and Dunlop, 1988, Con-
stanzo-Alvarez et al., 1993; Irving and McGlynn,
1981; Symons and V andall, 1990; Symons et al.,
1994; V andall and Symons, 1990).
The variations in procedure with which we have
experimented involve the following items. First, the
results of alternating field (AF) and thermal demagnet-
ization define slightly different paleopole locations.
Second, characteristic remanence vectors (ChRM)
yield slightly different confidence cones and central
orientations if the sample is considered to have been
drawn from a Bingham population (Bingham, 1964) ,
rather than from the commonly assumed Fisher pop-
ulation (Fisher, 1953) . Third, a tilt correction may be
unnecessary due to the apparent correspondence of
uniformly dipping metamorphic and magnetic folia-
tions in the KSZ with similarly oriented seismic re-
flectors which persist at constant orientation to depths
z 10 km.
Our results are compared against the backdrop
provided by the apparent polar wander paths (APWP)
available from the literature. It is appreciated that the
APWPs are tentative in nature but we caution the
reader that they are probably just as reliable as APWPs
from some tectonized Cenozoic sequences. This is
because magnetization mostly postdates strain during
post-tectonic exhumation. Thus, contentious correc-
tions for tilt, folding and strain are unnecessary. It is
acknowledged that the precision of ages is generally
poor, with the exception of recent findings by Buchan
et al. (1993, 1996, 2000, 2001) and some of the earlier
data tabulated by V andall and Symons (1990) . The
APWPs are based on the results of the above cited
w o r k e r sp l u st h er e s u l t so fDunlop (1979, 1983,
1984a,b, 1985) from adjacent areas and are summar-
ized in Fig. 7a . The reader is cautioned to note the
stretching of longitude at high latitudes in Gall’s World
map projection.
Previous paleomagnetic studies included 235 sites
and 1652 specimens reported from all preceding pub-
lications available to us. This almost certainly implies
some site duplication because the area is poorly
exposed. The interpretation of these data by Symons
et al. (1994) reveals a consensus of opinion, with the
exception of minor debates concerning polarity
switches, the amount of tilting and of vertical-axis
rotation due to local tectonics. The principal con-
clusions obtained almost exclusively by thermal de-
magnetization appear to be as follows. The oldest
geologically significant signal reported is a normal
A-component magnetization dated at f 2550 Ma
(37% of data). The youngest significant paleomagnetic
event is a reversed B-overprint (77% of data), timed
variously between approximately 1100 and 1800 Ma.
The latter is attributed to remagnetization during
Proterozoic exhumation of the KSZ.
For our study, alternating field (AF) demagnetiza-
tion was performed in a Sapphire Instruments demag-
netizer with triple-layer, mumetal shielding ( < 1 nT
residual field) and peak AF between 80 and 200 mT,
depending on the coercivity in question, incremented
in steps as small as 0.1 mT. At least 20 increments of
AF demagnetization were used per specimen. Internal
circuitry corrects for spurious ARM and our software
automatically alerts the user to spurious gyrorema-
nence contributions (Stephenson, 1983) .T h e r m a l
demagnetization was performed in a triple-layer,
shielded, non-inductively wound, ceramic furnace with
a residual field < 1 nT. This apparatus was manufac-
tured in our laboratory. A few later demagnetization
experiments used a recently acquired MMTD80 ther-
mal demagnetizer. At least 10 steps of demagnetization
were performed on each specimen from 80 to >600 jC.
Rotatable, three-dimensional vector plots were viewed
interactively during demagnetisation, as were conven-
tional, two-dimensional vector graphs (Zijderveld,
1967). This permitted simultaneous determination of
the direction of significant vector components by a

Our independent survey of 41 sites and 114 speci-

By tradition in paleomagnetism, the representation
of distributions with both up and down vectors may
use the combined projection of the upper and lower
hemispheres simultaneously, differentiating points on
the upper hemisphere with open symbols, from those
on the lower hemisphere with solid symbols (Fig. 3a).
Alternatively, for small numbers of points and ease of
comparison with structural orientations, all data may
be plotted on the lower hemisphere, representing up-
vectors by their antipodal projection onto the lower
hemisphere (Fig. 3b) . Either of these traditional
approaches may present difficulties in visualization
where there are large numbers of data or where the
paleomagnetic vectors must be compared with large
numbers of structural axes (e.g. normals to foliation,
mineral lineation or magnetic fabric axes as in Fig. 2).
Like structural axes, large numbers of vectors benefit
from the evaluation using density contours that objec-
tively characterise an orientation distribution. Density
contours can be useful in the evaluation of paleomag-
netic data but it may be that presentation difficulties
have limited their use since their introduction in this
context (e.g. Stupavsky and Symons, 1982 ). This is
unfortunate; density contours are particularly valuable
in data reconnaissance since they are independent of
any preconceived statistical model, unlike confidence
regions around mean directions. Density contours may
be especially useful in paleomagnetic studies of
deformed rocks in which remanence vectors may be
dispersed due to the effects of magnetic anisotropy,
stress-remagnetization or finite strain effects (Borra-
daile, 1997; Werner and Borradaile, 1996) .
Fisher et al. (1987) introduced a split-stereogram
projection that permits inspection of vector orienta-
tions and their density distributions on both upper and
lower hemispheres, simultaneously. The downward-
seeking vectors are plotted with their density contours
on the lower hemisphere in a conventional manner.
On an adjacent circular diagram, the upper hemi-
sphere is plotted. Our use of the split stereogram is
slightly different from Fisher et al. (1987) and is
shown in Fig. 3c (inset). Whereas Fisher et al. unhinge
the hemispheres about the north mark, we unhinged
about the east mark, flipping the upper hemisphere
up-and-over eastwards. This may be visually more
intuitive to geologists ( Fig. 4a , inset) as north is
retained at the top of each diagram in our usage.
Structured patterns in density contours may be readily
traced from upper to lower hemisphere using the split
projection. It is also sometimes easier to identify
clusters and outliers from those concentrations (Fig.
4b), although in the other orientation distributions of
vectors, we were unable to justify exclusion of any
stereogram points.

By tradition, and with good reason, most samples of
paleomagnetic vectors are considered to be drawn
from a population of points on the sphere that has
circular symmetry about the mean vector. The mean
vector is determined without assuming any statistical
model for the population by vector summation. How-
ever, for paleomagnetic purposes including determi-
nation of paleopole locations and APWPs, it is
essential to establish the confidence limits about the
mean vector, usually at the 95% level. Formal hypoth-
esis testing is rarely pursued, most workers using
visual comparison of confidence regions to ascertain
similarity or difference between mean vectors. How-
ever, hypothesis testing of orientation distributions is
discussed by Fisher et al. (1987) .
The assumption that the population has circular
symmetry about the mean vector is central to the
statistical treatment introduced by Fisher (1953) and
is almost universally used and almost universally ap-
propriate in paleomagnetism. This simple model has
sound theoretical and experiential support in the case
of stable paleomagnetic vectors. First, when an iso-
tropic material is instantaneously magnetized, a dipole
geomagnetic field can only produce an axial – circu-
lar – symmetric distribution of remanence vectors. Sec-
ond, the anisotropy of most rocks is so low that
remanence dispersal due to the internal fabric is rare
(Fuller, 1963, 1970; Hrouda, 1982; Rochette et al.,
1992; Stephenson et al., 1986) . Since orientation
distributions have a finite angular range, variance is
a difficult concept of restricted use. However, the in-
verse concept of a precision parameter ( j) for n orien-
tations is readily approximated by a concentration
parameter k=(n  )/(n /C0R), where R is the resultant
(e.g. Butler, 1992 ). For the case of a symmetrically
circular distribution of vector endpoints on the sphere,
the Fisher model permits the easy calculation of the
95% confidence limit about the vector mean by the
approximation a
95 = 140j/(kn). This expression appro-
ximately defines a95 in degrees as the apical angle of a
confidence cone that is circular in cross-section and
coaxial with the mean vector. Its projection on an
equal-area stereogram is non-circular, except when
the mean vector is precisely vertical. In spite of this,
the equal-area stereogram is obviously retained be-
cause the areal distortion of the equal-angle stereogram
causes far greater visual bias in interpreting orientation
distributions. In this paper, all projections are equal in
area, and most are in the lower hemisphere except
where designated upper hemispheres appear on the
right-hand side of the hinged-net device (Figs. 4 – 6).
The circular distribution of vector termini on the
sphere is a good model in most paleomagnetic studies.
However, increasingly more paleomagnetic work is
being performed on tectonized rocks. Whether the
remanences were acquired before or during tectonic
deformation, circular distributions of vectors on the
stereogram are less likely. The most common alter-
native vector distribution lies along some part of a
great circle forming an ellipse. A statistical model for
their elliptical distribution on the sphere was estab-
lished by Bingham (1964) with practical applications
rendered easier by Mardia and Zemroch (1977) . Many
other distributions can be investigated (Fisher et al.,
1987; Mardia and Jupp, 2000) and although small
circle distributions may arise during folding of older
remanences, there are good geological and theoretical
reasons for expecting almost all single event, homo-
geneous and macroscopic structural processes to pro-
duce great circle dispersions. Most paleomagnetic
vector distributions follow either the Fisher distribu-
tion or the Bingham distribution, which give rise to
the circular – symmetrical and the elliptical – ortho-
rhombic patterns, respectively. An elliptical distribu-
tion on the sphere may be modelled with simpler
mathematics than the Bingham model using the
bivariate normal distribution on the sphere (Le Goff
et al., 1992) . The more simply calculated confidence

There are four possible causes of great-circle dis-
persion in this study, and their presence is readily
detected using density plots on the split-stereogram
projection (Figs. 4a and 5a). The first possibility is that
magnetic anisotropy due to a metamorphic foliations
may have deflected the paleofield. AMS was first
developed to alert paleomagnetists to this possibility
(e.g. Fuller, 1963, 1970 ). In metamorphic rocks, par-
ticularly high-grade granulites without platy minerals,
a linear rather than planar fabric is more common.
Nevertheless, a linear anisotropy may deflect paleo-
field toward the lineation, also causing an elliptical
dispersion along a great circle.
Second, preexisting remanences may be dispersed
by the effects of finite strain, where the finite strain
ellipsoid has semi-axes X z Y z Z (Borradaile, 1991,
1993, 1997; Werner and Borradaile, 1996; Cogne ´ and
Perroud, 1987; Hirt et al., 1986; Kodama, 1988; Low-
rie et al., 1986) . The concept is that, in some way, re-
manence vectors spin like passive line markers towards
the maximum extension direction, as with conven-
tional strain markers, e.g. acicular mineral grains. This
simple model may be accepted where the remanence in
a mineral grain is parallel to the grain’s long axis,
where the grains are large enough to rotate compatibly
with a homogeneously straining rock mass and where
stress does not disturb remanence preservation within
the grain. This stretches credulity since we understand
that the ChRM is a vector sum of spin moments
distributed through magnetic domains in stress-sensi-
tive grains and in subgrains that cannot strain homo-
geneously with the rock matrix at the macroscopic
level. Nevertheless, some case studies from the field
and laboratory confirm patterns of disturbed ChRMs
that are compatible with the finite strain ellipsoid
orientation in (op. cit. and Borradaile, 1997). Whether
or not such simple ‘‘homogeneously strained remanen-
ces’’ actually owe their origin to that mechanism, they
reveal that some component of the remanence, usually
the hardest component (ChRM), is deflected towards
the maximum extension X and away from the max-
imum shortening axis Z. However, following well-
known concepts of progressive strain, line markers do
not rotate from Z towards X by the shortest route,
unless the finite strain ellipsoid is perfectly oblate
(X = Y). Instead, the locus of the vectors is drawn
towards the intermediate extension direction ( Y)o n
its path towards X. Thus, according to small variations
in strain and in initial orientations, the vectors may be
scattered to lie on some arc someway between Z and X.
In reality, the dispersion does not follow a great circle
but, in practice, the pattern may be approximated by
part of a great circle because the range of orientations is
usually small.
Third, under stress, domain walls may be mobilized
to accept a new remanence. Such stress-induced rema-
nences are occasionally detected in field studies but
they are also demonstrated in laboratory experiments
(Borradaile, 1992a,b, 1994) . The latter show that
remagnetization adds vector components along a great
circle connecting the field direction with the original
remanence, regardless of the symmetry or orientation
of the stress tensor. Experiments show that the softer
remanence components are most easily replaced in
multi-domain magnetite, although hard remanence
components may be more amenable to stress demag-
netization in hematite (Borradaile, 1992a,b, 1994;
Borradaile and Mothersill, 1989) .
Fourth, rocks from different sites within a region
may acquire their remanences at different times for
several reasons, including mineralization, changes in
thermal or chemical conditions and localized mechan-
ical events that may impose stress or strain remagne-
tization. The duration of these events may be similar to
the intervals separating successive locations of the
terrain during tectonic plate motion. Thus, paleomag-
netic vectors from a single site may be smeared along
the APWP . V ector components smeared in this way
will mostly follow a great circle, which will be better
defined, and more convincing, if reversals are detected.
Our samples of significant vectors isolated by
thermal ( n = 35) or by AF demagnetization ( n = 79)
are small in comparison to the sample size required in
many other branches of science. For example, in
structural geology, such small numbers of directions
or axes would be considered inadequate to discrim-
inate between unimodal and multimodal distributions,
and between circular symmetry and partial-girdle dis-
tributions. However, in paleomagnetism, distributions
are mostly more homogeneous, more concentrated and
magnetic vectors have intrinsic constraints on the
range of possible and reasonable orientation distribu-
tions, as discussed above. If the distribution is indeed
homogeneous and coherent, the only reasonable pos-

The mean direction of the vectors is obtained
simply by vector summation, and this is adequate for
the Fisher distribution. However, in the case of a
Bingham distribution, the eigenvectors provide a more
meaningful estimate of the principal concentrations.
The minimum eigenvector is normal to the dispersal
plane and the maximum eigenvector is parallel to the
peak concentration. The Bingham 95% confidence
limit is then centred about the maximum eigenvalue
as an elliptical cone with its major axis ( a
1) parallel to
the dispersal plane. The aspect ratio ( a1/a2)o ft h e
elliptical confidence cone reflects the degree to which
the distribution is dispersed away from the maximum

a
95, even if the sample of vectors was not drawn from a

In this study, ChRMs isolated by AF and thermal
demagnetization appear to be dispersed along a great
circle (Figs. 4a and 5a). Two modes appear in the lower
hemisphere contours but it is difficult to determine
their importance when so few vectors are included.
Given the dispersed nature of the distribution and the
expectations of a Bingham-population in such rocks, it
would seem imprudent to use a Fisher model. This
raises the issue of sampling and interpretation of
orientation distributions. Paleomagnetic vectors from
tectonized rocks may be reasonably expected to follow
a Bingham distribution. The greater geometrical com-
plexity of the elliptical distribution requires a larger
sample of specimens. This may require a different
sampling strategy from traditional paleomagnetic stud-
ies. For homogeneous Fisher distributions in sediments
or volcanic rocks, multiple specimens from a few
carefully selected individual sites provide the best
statistical characterization. However, the dispersion
of vectors in tectonized rocks, whether due to stress,
strain or paleofield-refraction, is better represented by
the widest possible spatial distribution of specimens
within an approximately homogeneously strained
domain. Thus, many sites should be sampled, prefera-
bly distributed according to some structurally deter-
mined sampling plan. This is implicit in earlier studies
of the KSZ where sampling traverses are reported, in
part corresponding to the seismic reflection profiles
(e.g. Constanzo-Alvarez and Dunlop, 1988; Symons
and V andall, 1990 ). In our study, we used 40 sites
determined by outcrop availability and structural posi-
tion (Borradaile et al., 1999) . Of course, pragmatism
reduces the number of specimens per outcrop. For the
40 sites, we determined a total of 127 normal (down)
ChRMs and 33 reversed (up) ChRMs which we term
the A- and B-components, respectively. We also deter-
mined secondary vectors that are not further reported
here as they are ‘‘soft’’ components corresponding
fairly obvious to viscous remagnetization in Bruhnes’
epoch geomagnetic fields.

3. Our interpretation
Thermal and AF demagnetization yields different
distributions of primary A-component vectors, and in
each case, the orientation distributions of A-compo-
nents have either multiples modes or some structured
distribution that does not conform to the ideal sym-
metrically circular cluster of points on the sphere. In
these circumstances, replotting the orientations, center-
ing them on their mean direction (Fisher et al., 1987) or
on some important structural axis may be easily
accomplished in computer software such as we use
(Spheristat by Pangaea Scientific). However, our data
are conveniently distributed with concentrations of
paleomagnetic vectors that are steep, either up or
down, so that we may retain the geographic frame of
reference and simply use Fisher et al.’s split hemi-
sphere technique to flip over the usual upper hemi-
sphere. Of course, this will not be possible in general;
in other studies, especially where concentrations have
low inclinations, data should be centred before adopt-
ing the split-hemisphere presentation.
The ChRMs isolated by thermal demagnetization
(Tables 1 and 2) are illustrated in Fig. 4 . The inter-
pretation of the density distribution of vectors on a
Fisher-split net (Fig. 4a) reveals that the reversed (right
net) and normal remanences (left net), although they
are not an anti-parallel pair, could lie on the same great
circle. This is difficult to recognize from conventional
stereographic projections using a single net. The Fisher
mean, with its large confidence cone centred on 055/
25, is meaningless, and the presence of two modes
(upper and lower hemispheres) would have alerted us
to this anyway. However, the Bingham statistical
model might satisfy the distribution of all data, both
normal and reversed, with a tight confidence ellipse.
The separate treatment of the two modes (Normal and
Reversed polarities) is shown in Fig. 4b .I tw a s
possible in this study to separate the data according
to its distribution on the upper and lower hemispheres.
In the general case where modes are not steeply
inclined, it would be necessary to centre the data and
then split the sphere about some plane that was not
originally horizontal.
The lower hemisphere projection (left) appears to
be best explained by a Bingham model because the
data disperse along a great circle with the confidence
ellipse symmetrically located in the density distribu-
tion. However, the reversed directions shown in the
inverted upper hemisphere (right) are more agreeably
modelled by a Fisher distribution, there being no
indication of dispersion along a plane. Therefore, the
Bingham model is preferred for the normal remanences
but the Fisher model is satisfactory for the reversed
vectors. This makes some difference to which mean
direction we accept, and as we shall show, to the
position of the KSZ on the APWP .
The results for characteristic vectors isolated by AF
demagnetization are shown in Fig. 5 . In all cases,
confidence cones are smaller due to the larger sample
size and homogeneous nature of the density distribu-
tion of vectors. In Fig. 5a, all data including the normal
and reversed modes are treated as one sample. The
Fisher model produces a sensibly located mean vector
with a modest a
95. However, the distribution clearly
follows a great-circle girdle that suggests that the
population is Bingham in nature. Bingham statistics
define a symmetry plane that passes symmetrically not
only through the lower hemisphere data (left net) but
also through the reversed mode on the upper hemi-
sphere (right net). The elliptical confidence cone is
agreeably small. When we split the data according to
the two main modes, one normal the other reversed as
in Fig. 5b, the Bingham model is very satisfactory for
the lower hemisphere (normal vectors), but the Fisher
model is preferred for the upper hemisphere (reversed
vectors).
In conclusion, the normal remanences seem to
follow a Bingham model due to dispersion along a
north-dipping plane. However, the plane strikes NW –
SE for thermally isolated vectors and NE – SW for
vectors isolated by AF demagnetization. These are
the ‘‘A ’’ or older Archean signals of other authors. In
contrast, the reversed remanences, the younger, late
Archean or Proterozoic ‘‘B’’ chemical overprint of
other researchers appear to be drawn from a Fisher
population, there is no tendency for the vectors to
smear along a great circle.
For the moment, we shall not debate the merits of
thermal versus AF demagnetization, which is a well-
discussed aspect of rock magnetism that must be
decided with a knowledge of the history of magnetic
mineralogy (Butler, 1992; Dunlop and O ¨ zdemir,
1997). It does not attempt to undo the natural magnet-
ization process but rather sets the artificial goal of
separating distinct vector components according to

their relative age. Different laboratory techniques
including the familiar thermal and alternating field
demagnetization methods, as well as less popular
chemical and low temperature methods, all may isolate
differently oriented vector components. In this study,
there are differences between mean directions isolated
by AF and thermal demagnetization, particularly for
the A-component (normal remanences, Figs. 4b and
5b). Furthermore, we are concerned that the differ-
ences due to different statistical treatments of the same
data are almost as great as the differences due to
demagnetization techniques. This may be observed
by comparing the Fisher and Bingham confidence
regions on the same stereograms (Figs. 4b and 5b) .
This is summarized in Fig. 6 where the relative
confidence cones about the mean vector are shown for
each treatment in different shades of grey; lighter gray
for Fisher confidence region and darker gray for
Bingham region. For reference, AMS and AARM
foliations and the mean orientation of seismic reflec-
tors are shown. We believe that the magnetic fabrics
are an expression of the metamorphic foliation, which
is otherwise difficult to observe in granoblastic rocks,
in the field, due to the absence of platy minerals. The
similar orientations of the three planar structures are
encouraging, not withstanding the inaccuracies in
determining the true dip and strike of the mean seismic
reflection surfaces from two-dimensional profiles and
depths inferred from two-way travel times.
There appears to be no simple angular relationship
between the normal polarity (‘‘A ’’) hard remanences on
the lower hemispheres ( Fig. 6a and b , left sides). That
is, Fisher or Bingham confidence cones do not corre-
spond to any principal anisotropy axis (AARM, AMS
or seismic reflection plane). Moreover, the Bingham
dispersal plane is unrelated to the foliations or principal
axes of either magnetic anisotropy (AMS or AARM).
This is encouraging for paleomagnetism as one may
deduce that there is little anisotropy deflection of
remanence during its acquisition. However, the distri-
butions are different for vectors isolated by thermal and
AF techniques. Furthermore, one could deduce that
there is little possibility of post-acquisition deflection
of remanence by tectonic strain (or stress). Similarly,
the B-components (reverse remanences, right stereo-
grams, Fig. 6a and b ) appear uninfluenced by aniso-
tropy, but the Bingham mean directions differ for
thermal and AF-treatments.
The most compelling manner in which to evaluate
paleomagnetic results is to inspect the paleopole posi-
tions on a world map and compare them with the
available apparent polar wander paths. Two cautionary
notes are in order. First, any map projection will
compromise comparisons. Where paleopoles lie on
one hemisphere, spherical projections of the globe
suffice. Here, the paleopoles are so widely distributed
that a plane map projection is preferred, with the
disadvantage that there is enormous distortion of
longitudinal differences at high latitudes. Furthermore,
APWPs for the late Archean and early Proterozoic for
the Superior Province (Fig. 7) are extremely tentative
by comparison with APWPs for Phanerozoic time, and
there have been some considerable revisions over the
last 30 years in the light of refined geochronology (Fig.
8). The difficulty of performing stability tests (even
reversal-tests), the long metamorphic and thermal
history and the difficulty of applying tilt where the
tilt-axis is poorly known, all constrain APWPs very
loosely by comparison with those of Phanerozoic time.
Nevertheless, the APWPs provide a useful frame of
reference based on a consensus of published results.
Fortunately, almost all studies have sensibly avoided
and excluded remanences that may have been affected
by penetrative deformation, the finite strain of struc-
tural geology. Finally, it is only since the mid-1980s
that reliable high-precision U – Pb geochronology has
been able to determine the age of magnetization-
events. Even so, considerable are apparent; largely
before high precision U – Pb geochronology, an
Archean APWP was documented that traversed from
the south Atlantic through Africa and Asia between
2700 and f 2000 Ma (Irving, 1979; Dunlop, 1983,
1984a,b, 1985 , Fig. 8a ). Refinements in light of more
precise geochronology and new paleomagnetic data
revised the Archean APWP for 2700 – 2400 Ma to curl
over Siberia and Scandinavia (Symons et al., 1994;
V andall and Symons, 1990 , Fig. 8a ). These paths are
shown because they are still valid loci for contempo-
rary paleopole determinations for post-metamorphic
cooling remanences ( z 2700 Ma) of highly deformed
metamorphic rocks in northern Ontario.
More reliable paleopole estimates come from late-
orogenic and cratonic dikes and other minor intru-
sions, for which tilt corrections are negligible or
unnecessary. Reliable, high precision geochronology
is now available for some of these rocks. Conse-

Next, consider the A-components which have nor-
mal polarity. These generally have higher unblocking
temperatures and lower coercivities than the B-com-
ponents and, in previous studies, were attributed to the
early acquisition as the Kapuskasing gneisses un-

isotherm that is related to the experimental blocking
temperature. Clearly, the mean paleopole locations and
their 95% confidence regions do not lie on any part of
the published APWPs (Fig. 7a and b) . Tectonic and
paleomagnetic literature on the KSZ has offered vary-
ing tilt corrections for these early vectors, e.g. 15 –

and f 10jNW by Symons and V andall (1990) .I fa
tilt-correction is required for the A-component, we
find little structural information to discriminate
between those suggestions; neither value significantly
affects paleopole locations. Initially, a tilt-correction
seemed mandatory. The upthrust lower crustal
gneisses are tilted on a NW-dipping ramp structure
(Fig. 1 and Atekwana et al., 1994 ). However, the
magnitude of the ramp was not at first understood,
and since the magnetic fabrics and seismic reflectors
are subparallel, we suggest that all the microfabrics,
visible, AMS and AARM, extend to similar depths
(Fig. 1) . This makes it most unlikely that the entire
KSZ ramp was steepened to its present orientation by
tilting that post-dated metamorphism and the block-
ing-in of the A-components. Based on the common
maximum blocking temperatures for the early rema-
nence (>400 jC, Table 1), a conservative geothermal
gradient of 30 jC/km predicts blocking temperature
isotherms at a depth of f 13 km. The orientations of
the microfabrics persist to these depths, even now.
Prior to denudation, their orientation would have been
retained even deeper into the crust. Therefore, we
suggest that a tilt correction may be unnecessary. Even
if a tilt-correction was applied, it would deflect the A-
component vectors so that their paleopoles would lie
still further westward, not eastward, and the disagree-

less (Fig. 7a). At present, we can offer no explanation
for the discrepancy between our early paleopole
locations situated in the North Atlantic region and
the closest part of the APWP (2600 – 2500 Ma) in
Siberia (note the large longitudinal dilation of loca-
tions at high latitudes in the map projections). Most
seriously, mean paleopoles determined by thermal
demagnetization differ from those fixed by AF demag-
netization, significantly in the case of the A-compo-
nents (Fig. 7a) .
4. Conclusions
First, the seismic profile shows that the thrust ramp
and its associated magnetic – petrofabric foliation has
constant inclination to depths that probably exceeded
the blocking-in isotherm depths for the A-component.
This means that the uplifted granulites were magne-
tized in their present orientation and a tilt-correction
for their A-component is probably unnecessary. More-
over, correction for any WNW tilt on the ramp would
increase the discrepancies between our A-component
paleopole locations and the tentative Archean APWP
(Fig. 7a) .
Second, despite well-defined AMS and AARM
fabrics, there is no obvious anisotropy-deflection or
tectonic-deflection of either the A-component or B-
component remanences. The A-component TRM and
B-component chemical overprint may be regarded as
reliable indicators of paleopole locations.
Third, although we used the same specimens for
different treatments, thermal demagnetization produ-
ces differences from AF demagnetization that gives
some concern. The merits and disadvantages of those
treatments and others, such as low-temperature
demagnetization and chemical demagnetization, are
discussed in the literature (Butler, 1992; Dunlop and
O¨ zdemir, 1997; McElhinny and McFadden, 2000;
V an der V oo, 1993) . The choice is even more
difficult in metamorphic rocks where magnetite
grain-size is not necessarily a strong clue to the
age of the mineral or its remanence. For example,
hard remanences may be carried by fine grains that
grew late in the metamorphic history and the effects
of stress may ‘‘magnetically harden’’ grains. On its
own, differential stress may remagnetize grains.
Thus, a coercive or refractory remanence may not
necessarily be ancient where metamorphic and tec-
tonic processes have been active. The differences

between paleopole locations are small for the B-
component (Fig. 7b and c) , but the overlap of the
a95 confidence regions for the A-component is unsat-
isfactory (Fig. 7a) . However, the sense of discrep-
ancies between paleopole locations defined by
thermal demagnetization from those defined by AF
demagnetization is consistent. Thermally defined
paleopoles lie further from the site than those defined
by AF demagnetization; they correspond to shallower
inclinations. Inspection of the paleopoles in relation
to the lines of co-latitude about the Kapuskasing site
clarifies this (Fig. 7a) .
Finally, using the same data, the determined
paleopole locations and confidence regions differ
according to statistical treatment. Since statistical
treatments are non-destructive experiments, it seems
prudent to inspect all paleomagnetic data from
strained rocks, routinely, for any tendency to form
a partial girdle that would suggest the sample was
drawn from a Bingham population. For the B-com-
ponents, the mean paleopole locations lie in the NE
Pacific and their a
95 confidence regions coincide
when two outliers are excluded (Fig. 7b and c) . They
appear to correspond to the Proterozoic APWP at
magnetization ages of 1400 – 1200 Ma (Fig. 7b) .
Earlier published opinions ranged from 1050 (cf.
Fig. 7c ) to 1860 Ma (Table 2) . However, whichever
statistical procedure is applied to the A-component
remanences, their mean location and confidence
regions are influenced significantly by the choice
of demagnetization treatment (Fig. 7a) . A-component
paleopole locations lie far from the tentative and
poorly constrained APWP , for which the best match-
ing age is f 2500 Ma.

Paleomagnetism of Paleozoic and Mesozoic sediments
from the southern margin of Mongol-Okhotsk ocean,
far eastern Russia
V adim A. Kravchinsky1
Physics Department, University of Alberta, Edmonton, Canada
Andrey A. Sorokin
Division of the Regional Geology and Hydrogeology, Far East Branch of Russian Academy of Science,
Blagoveshchensk, Russia
Vincent Courtillot
Laboratoire de Pale´omagne´tisme, Institut de Physique du Globe de Paris, Paris, France
Received 15 June 2001; revised 1 March 2002; accepted 6 March 2002; published 24 October 2002.
[1] This paper presents new data from paleomagnetic investigations of Middle Paleozoic
(Early-Middle-Late Devonian, Early Carboniferous) and Middle Jurassic geological
units from the Amuria block south of the Mongol-Okhotsk suture zone. With fold tests
for all localities, and two polarities for the Devonian, our new results constrain the
evolution of the Mongol-Okhotsk ocean from the Devonian to the Middle Jurassic. The
corresponding paleopoles lie at 21.6  N, 6.3  E( dp/dm =5 . 3 /10.6 ) for Early Devonian,
26.3 N, 345.3  E( dp/dm =6 . 4 /12.8 ) for Early-Middle Devonian, 24.6  N, 12.9  E( dp/
dm =8 . 7 /16.9 ) for Middle-Late Devonian, 40.5  N, 352.4 E( dp/dm =9  /16.7 ) for Late
Devonian, 39.8  N, 31.6  E( dp/dm =1 0  /15.5 ) for Early Carboniferous, and 46  N,
37.9 E( dp/dm =9 . 4 /13.4 ) for Middle Jurassic. The poles confirm that the large
Paleozoic Mongol-Okhotsk ocean closed during the Jurassic, ending up in the late
Jurassic or early Cretaceous at the eastern end of the suture zone, as originally proposed
on geological grounds. The new paleomagnetic results exhibit large tectonic rotations
about local vertical axes, which we interpret as probably arising from both the collision
process and left-lateral shear movement along the suture zone, related to incipient
extrusion of Amuria due to indentation of India into Asia.

1. Introduction
[2] The eastern part of Eurasia is a complex collage
consisting of both large and small continental blocks
separated by Paleozoic and Mesozoic fold belts formed in
the locations of former paleo-ocean basins. One of the
largest structures is the Mongol-Okhotsk fold belt in the
far eastern part of Russia. This belt is a complex system,
comprising fragments of E-W trending Paleozoic and Early
Mesozoic structures, between the southern margin of the
Siberian craton to the north and the Amurian composite
microcontinent to the south (Figure 1). According to recent
geodynamic reconstructions, the belt is regarded as consist-
ing of relics of a vast ocean, now preserved as a complex set
of terranes, squeezed between the above mentioned con-
tinental masses [ Zonenshain et al. , 1990; Natal’in and
Borukaev, 1991; Parfenov et al. , 1999].
[
3] At present, the issue concerning the width of the
Mongol-Okhotsk paleo-ocean as well as the timing and
kinematics of its closure remain unresolved. According to
commonly accepted models, the vast Mongol-Okhotsk
ocean existed from the Riphean up to the Early [ Sengor
and Natal’in , 1996] or Late [ Zonenshain et al. , 1990]
Jurassic, and closed in a scissors manner [ Zonenshain et
al., 1990; Zhao et al , 1990], or may have formed as the
result of sliding of the Amurian microcontinent along the
southern margin of the Siberian craton [ Parfenov et al. ,
1999].

[4] Paleomagnetic data published in the geological liter-
ature which should define the paleoposition of the Siberian
and north China cratons, show significant discrepancies in
paleolatitudes up to Early Cretaceous time [ Zhao et al. ,
1996; Enkin et al. ,1 9 9 2 ; Gilder and Courtillot ,1 9 9 7 ;
Kravchinsky, 1995, 2002a; Smethurst et al. , 1998]. Also,
there are not enough reliable paleomagnetic data from many
of the blocks, which comprise the Amurian microcontinent.
We have studied Paleozoic and Mesozoic sedimentary
deposits located south of the Mongol-Okhotsk suture
(Upper Amur region), which represent the largest part of
the Amurian microcontinent. This allows us to estimate the
width of the Mongol-Okhotsk ocean as a function of time
and to constrain kinematic models of its closure.
2. Brief Geological Review
[5] Paleo-oceanic structures within the Mongol-Okhotsk
fold belt comprise ophiolite fragments, metabasaltic chert,
and also turbidites and terrigenous-carbonaceous deposits
[Sorokin et al. , 1996]. Paleontological observations allow
one to identify Devonian and Carboniferous sediments, and
within the eastern segment, Lower and Upper Permian,
Triassic and Lower Jurassic ones [ Kozlovsky, 1988; Parfe-
nov et al. , 1999]. Along the southern rim of the Mongol-
Okhotsk fold belt, a system of paleobasins filled with
Paleozoic and Mesozoic sediments is found. These are
interpreted as passive continental margins [ Zonenshain et
al., 1990; Parfenov et al. , 1999], i.e., fragments of the
southern (in modern coordinates) margin of the paleo-
ocean. Paleozoic terrigenous and terrigenous-carbonaceous
deposits compose sublatitudinal linear folds with limbs
  – 10 km along northwestern border of the Amuria block.
The folds usually have asymmetric form. North limbs
(toward closed Mongol-Okhotsk ocean) are steep (65 –
75 ), south limbs have lesser slopes (25 – 45  ). These folds
contain folds of smaller scale with width down to 50 m.
Faults are typical in the region (mainly as strike slip and
thrust faults), and they cut many folds. As a result, in some
areas Paleozoic sediments cover Middle-Late Jurassic com-
plexes. Sediments are changed to muscovite- and quartz-
bearing schists near major tectonic zones.
[
6] The Paleozoic shelf deposits of the Mongol-Okhotsk
paleo-ocean were studied in the Upper Amur region, where
they fill the Oldoy and Gaga-Sagayan paleobasins. These
extend over more than 600 km, along the northern margin of
the Amurian microcontinent and are characterized by sim-
ilar conditions of sedimentation. The most complete
sequence is recorded within the Oldoy paleobasin, and
comprises the following six formations [ Turbin, 1994]: (1)
Omutnaya formation, silurian quartz sandstones, quartzite,
siltstone, grit stone and conglomerates with a thickness of
600 – 1000 m; (2) Bolshoy Neaver formation, lower Devon-
ian sandstone and siltstone with a thickness in excess of
1300 m; (3) Imachi formation, lower-Middle Devonian
siltstone and limestone with a thickness exceeding 500 m;
(4) Oldoy formation: Middle-Upper Devonian clay shales,
siltstone, tuffites and rhyolite tuffs; thickness is over

symmetrical, extending in NE and east directions. Angles
of dip are 30 – 60  .
[

Average sampling coordinates are 127.0  E, 53.6  N. Paleo-

[10] The Mesozoic sedimentary deposits have been inves-
tigated within the Upper Amur and Zeya-Dep paleobasins.
The former is filled with Upper Triassic, Lower and Middle
Jurassic marine, and Middle Jurassic paralic deposits.
Descriptions of these deposits and paleomagnetic measure-
ments have been published earlier [ Halim et al. , 1998a].
The sampling area is shown in Figure 1 (area D). This
paleobasin is filled with Upper Triassic and Middle-Upper
Jurassic deposits; in general the sequence comprises over
3000 m of Upper Triassic sandstone with siltstone bands,
overlain by the following five formations: Usmanka for-
mation: Middle Jurassic sandstones with siltstone bands
(over 1100 m); Uskali formation: Middle Jurassic sand-
stones and siltstones with volcanics and tuff-breccia bands
(over 1400 m); Ayak formation: Middle Jurassic sandstones,
siltstones, lenses of conglomerates, grit stone, tuffites and
tuffs (over 1500 m); Dep formation: Middle-Upper Jurassic
sandstone, siltstones, argillites and carbonaceous argillites
(over 1000 m); and Lower Molchan formation: Upper-
Jurassic sandstones with siltstone, argillites, tuffs and coals
(over 1500 m).
[
11] The Mesozoic sediments of the Zeya-Dep paleobasin
are deposited upon strongly deformed Paleozoic rocks. The
Upper Triassic, Uskali and Usmanka formations are char-

Molchan formations are characterized by plant remains

[

[17] About 80% of the studied samples were measured
with a cryogenic magnetometer (2G Superconducting Rock
Magnetometer) in Paris. In order to compare results, 10% of
the samples from the same blocks were demagnetized in
both Paris and Irkutsk. The two sets of laboratory results are
virtually identical. Thermal demagnetizations were made
with Schonstedt oven, installed in the magnetically shielded
room at IPGP (total field in cooling region is about 5nT).
Demagnetization by AF turned out to be ineffective for
these sediments, which is why most samples were thermally
demagnetized. Changes in magnetic mineralogy during
thermal demagnetization were monitored by measurements
of magnetic susceptibility after each heating step.
[
18] Changes in the intensity and direction of remanent
magnetization vectors during demagnetization experiments
were analyzed using orthogonal vector end-point projec-
tions [ Zijderveld, 1967]. Magnetic component directions
were identified using principal component analysis (PCA)
[Kirschvink, 1980], or remagnetization great circles method
[Halls, 1976] with sector constraints [ McFadden and McEl-
hinny, 1988]. Site-mean directions were determined using
Fisher’s [1953] statistics or, in the case of combined direc-
tional data and remagnetization circles, using McFadden
and McElhinny ’s [1988] statistics. Data were processed
using the paleomagnetic data treatment softwares of Enkin
[1990] and J.-P . Cogne´ (free software Paleo Mac) and the
Opal software [ Vinarsky et al. , 1987].
4. Paleomagnetic Results
4.1. Early Devonian Bolshoy Neaver Formation
(417 – 395 Ma) of the Oldoy Paleobasin
[19] The isothermal remanent magnetization (IRM)
acquisition curves (Figure 4) show that magnetite is the
most likely carrier of remanence in all studied localities.
During thermal demagnetization of the samples, we sepa-
rated two different components of NRM (Figure 5). A low-
temperature component (LTC) is removed after heating up
to 250 – 300 C. The Fisher [1953] average of this compo-
nent in geographic coordinates is D
g = 14.5  , Ig = 75.2

postcollisional rotations during final stages of closing of the
Mongol-Okhotsk ocean. There is no paleolatitude difference
with either the NCB ( /C1l =3 . 8 ±5  ), or Eurasia ( /C1l =
1.3 ±3 . 3 ). Upper Amuria was therefore probably rotated
by some 75  counterclockwise with respect to Eurasia and
China during post-Cretaceous collisional processes.

Devonian to the Present

between Siberia to the north (in present-day coordinates),
and Amuria/north China to the south was closed between
the Early Permian in eastern Mongolia and the Jurassic in
Trans-Baikalia, and the Cretaceous in the Pacific part of
Russia [ Kuzmin and Fillipova , 1979; Parfenov, 1984;
Kravchinsky, 1990; Zonenshain et al. , 1990; Zhao et al. ,

Reconstruction of the North China platform relies on data
by Zhao et al. [1996] and Gilder and Courtillot [1997];
paleopositions of the Amuria block for the Mesozoic and
Cenozoic follow Pruner [1992], Halim et al. [1998a] and
Kravchinsky et al. [2002a]; and paleopositions of the Tarim
block follow Bai et al. [1987], McFadden et al. [1988],
Fang et al. [1990], Li et al. [1990], and Gilder et al.
[1996].
[
39] In order to constrain the paleoposition of the Siberian
platform, we used the APWP of Siberia from Smethurst et
al. [1998] at 435 Ma, the poles of Kravchinsky et al.
[2002b] at  60 Ma and  50 Ma and the APWP of
Eurasia from 240 Ma to the Present [ Besse and Courtillot ,
1991; Va n d e r Vo o, 1993]. The new Paleozoic part of the
APWP of Siberia is shown by a dashed line in Figure 12 on
the basis of the 360 Ma pole from Kravchinsky et al.
[2002b].
[
40] Between 435 and 360 Ma, the Russian platform
(with Baltica and a large part of western Europe) became
part of Laurussia (Laurentia and Russia) [ Smethurst et al. ,
1998]. Unfortunately, there are no reliable paleomagnetic
data for Siberia between 360 and 250 Ma. Northward
motion of Siberia to high northern latitudes was associated
with  0 clockwise rotation between 360 (Figure 14) and
250 (Figure 14) Ma [ Kravchinsky et al. , 2002b].
[
41] Zhao et al. [1996] [see also Va n d e r Vo o, 1993; Li et
al., 1988] showed that north China was at the equator in the
Middle Devonian (Figure 14). Based on the Middle-Late

Devonian pole for NCB of Huang et al. [2000], the NCB
was at the same latitude as the Amuria microcontinent
(Figure 14, left), but more rotated relative to Siberia
(/C1D = 166.1  ± 15.3  ). At this time Tarim was subequato-
rial, and moving northward [ Bai et al. , 1987; Fang et al. ,
1990; Li et al. , 1988]. The position of the Russian platform
(with Baltica) is reconstructed after Torsvik et al. [1992,
1996]. Kazakhstan is positioned according to Pechersky and
Didenko [1995]. The absolute dating of Montero et al.
[2000] indicates that the closure of the Uralian paleo-ocean
started in the south and migrated progressively northwards,
between 320 (Figure 14) and 250 (Figure 14) Ma. During the
Paleozoic, the Amurian blocks were always situated between
north China and Siberia in equatorial to tropical latitudes,
moving gradually to the North, from about 0  in Early-
Middle Devonian to about 15  in Late Devonian, 20  in
Early Carboniferous, and 30 in the late Permian (Figure 14).
[
42] At 250 Ma, Siberia continued its clockwise rotation
at high northern latitudes. The last stage of formation of
northern Eurasia involved final accretion of Russia and
Siberia along the Uralian belt. North Eurasia was incorpo-
rated into Pangea at this time [ V an der V oo, 1993; Torsvik et
al., 1996; Smethurst et al. , 1998]. This could appear to
somewhat contradict the estimates of Zonenshain et al.
[1990] on the age of the collision between Amuria and
Siberia. In effect, on the basis of the age of metamorphism
and intraplate magmatism from the Mongolian Khingayn
Mountains, these authors date the collision as Late Carbon-
iferous – Early Permian for the western part of Amuria. This
is related to the ‘‘scissors-like’’ closure of the Mongol-
