New palaeomagnetic results from the Whin Sill complex: evidence for a multiple
intrusion event and revised virtual geomagnetic poles for the late Carboniferous
for the British Isles
D .L I S S ,W .H .O W E N S&D .H .W .H U T T O N
Department of Earth Sciences, University of Birmingham, Birmingham B15 2TT, UK
(e-mail: dirk_liss@yahoo.co.uk)
Abstract: A large-scale palaeomagnetic study (125 specimens from 88 sampling localities) has been carried
out on the Whin Sill complex and its associated dykes in northern England. The dominant carrier of remanent
magnetization of the doleritic rocks is relatively pure magnetite of pseudo-single domain size, and the
characteristic remanent magnetizations are typically well deﬁned and unidirectional. Regionally consistent
palaeomagnetic directions are obtained from three geographically distinct parts of the Whin Sill complex, here
named as the Holy Island Sill (Declination/Inclination ( D=I) ¼ 189:5= /C0 2:8, Æ
95 ¼ 6:3), the Alnwick Sill
(D=I ¼ 194:6= /C0 25:6, Æ95 ¼ 8:1) and the Hadrian’ s Wall–Pennines Sill ( D=I ¼ 189:2=3:3, Æ95 ¼ 3:5).
Although the Holy Island Sill and the Hadrian’ s Wall–Pennines Sill are of similar age ( c. 296 Ma) and
indistinguishable on palaeomagnetic grounds, the difference in palaeomagnetic directions between them and
the Alnwick Sill demonstrates the multi-component nature of the complex; magma-ﬂow indicators suggest
that the Holy Island Sill and the Hadrian’ s Wall–Pennines Sill may also represent separate intrusion events.
Dykes local to the three sills have remanence directions corresponding to their respective sills and can
tentatively be identiﬁed as their feeder dykes. Virtual geomagnetic poles for the three palaeomagnetic sites
are: Holy Island Sill and Holy Island Dyke, 346.8E, 35.4S; Alnwick Sill, High Green Dyke and St. Oswald’ s
Chapel Dyke, 337.1E, 47.1S; Hadrian’ s Wall–Pennines Sill and Hett Dyke, 347.1E, 32.9S.
Keywords: sills, dykes, palaeomagnetism, emplacement, dolerite.
The late Carboniferous doleritic Whin Sill complex of northern
England represents the archetype for sheet-like concordant
intrusions; from it, indeed, geology acquired the term ‘sill’ (e.g.
Dunham & Strasser-King 1982; Johnson & Dunham 2001).
There is widespread evidence of igneous activity in NW Europe
in the late Carboniferous and early Permian; for example, in the
Midland Valley of Scotland (Dunham & Strasser-King 1982),
the Oslo Rift (Neumann 1994; Sundvoll & Larsen 1994) and
southern Sweden (Obst 1999). The suggestion of Ernst &
Buchan (1997, 2001) that all these occurrences are related and
are manifestations of a plume-related ‘Jutland event’, has
refocused interest on igneous activity in the region. Although
the Whin Sill complex has been studied for more than a
century (references given by Dunham & Strasser-King 1982;
Randall 1995; Johnson & Dunham 2001; and a Presidential
Address by Francis (1982) to the Society), problems regarding
its mode of emplacement and the location of feeder dykes still
remain.
As the dolerites of the Whin Sill complex carry a stable
characteristic remanent magnetization, palaeomagnetic results
from the complex have provided an important datum. A study by
Storetvedt & Gidskehaug (1969), following pioneering work by
Creer et al. (1959), has provided a magnetization direction that is
accepted as deﬁning a key virtual geomagnetic pole (VGP) for
the late Carboniferous, contributing to the apparent polar wander
path of the British Isles (Torsvik et al. 1989; Piper et al. 1991).
This paper reports on an extensive palaeomagnetic study
carried out on the Whin Sill complex and its associated dykes.
The results of the study provide new information on both the
intrusion history of the Whin Sill complex and its accepted VGP ,
revealing previously unresolved detail in both.
Geological setting and sampling
The Whin Sill complex is a large tholeiitic quartz dolerite
intrusion in northern England (Fig. 1). On land its outcrop
extends for c. 120 km in a north–south direction and c.8 0k mi n
an east–west direction but, as the sill complex generally dips
underneath the North Sea, its true extent is unknown. The
complex has a maximum observed thickness of c. 80 m and its
average thickness is of the order of 30 m. The stratigraphical
horizons into which it is emplaced range from Dinantian to
Westphalian and the overburden thickness at the time of
emplacement has been estimated as between 0.5 and 1 km
(Francis 1982).
Four major ENE–WSW-trending doleritic dykes are associated
with the Whin Sill complex (Fig. 1); from north to south these
are the Holy Island Dyke, the High Green Dyke, the St. Oswald’ s
Chapel Dyke and the Hett Dyke. The thickest of these dykes is
the High Green Dyke, which reaches a width of up to c.6 5 m .
The close geographical relationship and the petrological afﬁnity
between the dykes and the sill complex have led several workers
to propose that the four dykes formed the feeders to the complex
(Holmes & Harwood 1928; Anderson 1951; Francis 1982;
Goulty et al . 2000). Additional geochemical data seem to
conﬁrm this ﬁnding (Thorpe & MacDonald 1985). Nevertheless,
no direct relationship between the dykes and the Whin Sill
complex can be demonstrated anywhere in the ﬁeld, and there is
some dispute in the literature as to whether the dykes acted as
feeders (Smythe 1930; Johnson & Dunham 2001).
The Little Whin Sill, another dolerite intrusion, also occurs in
the study area (Fig. 1). The Little Whin Sill forms a thin leaf
above the main sill and is, in contrast to the main Whin Sill
dolerite, olivine bearing (Dunham & Kaye 1965; Harrison 1968).

The magma that fed the Little Whin Sill was less evolved and is
believed to represent an early differentiate of the normal Whin
Sill magma (Wadge et al. 1972; Johnson & Dunham 2001).
The age of the Whin Sill complex and the associated dykes
can be narrowed down to Late Carboniferous to Early Permian
by stratigraphical evidence. They intrude Upper Carboniferous
host rocks (Westphalian B–C), but do not penetrate the Permian
units (Dunham & Strasser-King 1982). However, clasts of Whin
Sill dolerite are reported from breccias of Early Permian age
from the Vale of Eden (Holmes & Harwood 1928; Dunham
1932). The age of the intrusion is also well constrained by
several radiometric analyses. K–Ar analyses on 21 specimens
suggest a mean age of 295 /C6 6 Ma for the Whin Sill complex
and the associated dykes (Fitch & Miller 1967) and a recent Ar/
Ar study yielded an age of 294 /C6 2 Ma for the Holy Island Dyke
(Timmerman, pers. comm.). In addition, a provisional but precise
U–Pb baddeleyite age of 297 Ma has been determined (Hamilton
& Pearson, pers. comm.) from the southernmost part of the
intrusion, in the area of Middleton (Fig. 1).
For this palaeomagnetic study, dolerite block samples from the
Whin Sill complex and the four related dykes were collected
from 88 localities (Fig. 1). The number of dyke outcrops sampled
is relatively small as it is very difﬁcult to ﬁnd dyke exposures
from which fresh, oriented specimens can be taken. The block
samples were oriented in the ﬁeld by magnetic compass; this
procedure was checked and found adequate as no deﬂection of
the compass needle, caused by the potentially high magnetization
of the dolerite, could be observed.
Palaeodirectional analyses
The oriented dolerite block samples were drilled in the laboratory
(Owens 1994). In total, 125 cylindrical samples of standard size
(diameter 2.5 cm, length 2.2 cm) were analysed for their char-
acteristic remanent magnetization (ChRM). The samples were
stepwise thermally demagnetized in an MMTD1 furnace and
their remanence was measured using an AGICO JR5a spinner
magnetometer. Both furnace and magnetometer were constantly
shielded against any external magnetic laboratory ﬁeld.
In a pilot demagnetization study 24 samples were measured in
steps of 50 8C from room temperature to 700 8C with two
additional measurements at 525 and 575 8C. These analyses
showed that most samples have a discrete unblocking tempera-
ture interval between 450 and 550 8C and that all samples are
fully demagnetized at c. 575 8C. For routine demagnetization,
measurements were therefore made at room temperature, fol-
lowed by 50 8C intervals from 250 8C to a maximum temperature
of 600 8C, with an additional measurement taken at 575 8C.
The ChRM of the individual samples was analysed using
Zijderveld diagrams (Zijderveld 1967), and plots of normalized
magnetic intensity ( J/J
0) v. temperature were used to identify the
related blocking temperature spectra. All samples revealed
shallow southerly directed ChRM vectors that are generally very
well deﬁned (Fig. 2). Figure 3 shows four representative Zijder-
veld and intensity plots. All samples have a very strong remanent
magnetization at room temperature (average J0 ¼ 2566 mA m/C0 1)
and were fully demagnetized at c. 575 8C, which coincides with
the Curie temperature of pure magnetite (e.g. Dunlop & O¨ zdemir
2001). However, whereas the ChRM vectors for all samples are
relatively consistent, the intensity v. temperature plots show
distinctively different patterns and can be divided into four
groups (Fig. 3). Most of the samples fall into group 1 (70%,
Fig. 3a) and are characterized by a discrete blocking temperature
interval of typically 50–150 8C with unblocking generally start-

samples is relatively homogeneous. Samples of group 2 (17%,
Fig. 3b) show a distributed blocking temperature interval and the
specimens typically lose their magnetization gradually until they
are completely demagnetized at c. 575 8C. This demagnetization
behaviour points either towards a heterogeneous magnetic grain-

all their magnetization within a discrete unblocking interval. The
initial increase in the total magnetization indicates that these
samples incorporate magnetic vectors of relatively opposing
directions. Stepwise thermal demagnetization gradually removes

magnetization carried by the magnetically harder constituents
becomes dominant. No common ChRM direction could be
isolated for any softer component. The temperature intervals at
which the unblocking of the individual components occur
indicate that the harder magnetic directions are carried by
magnetite and/or Ti-poor TM whereas the softer magnetic
directions are probably carried by Ti-rich TM, or possibly by
monoclinic pyrrhotite.
Magnetic mineralogy and domain state
The reliability of palaeodirectional results is largely determined
by the composition and domain state of the remanence carriers.
In general, it is harder to overprint the direction of magnetization
in single domain (SD) and pseudo-single domain (PSD) grains
than it is in the larger multidomain (MD) grains. The former are
therefore responsible for most of the stable remanence analysed
in palaeomagnetic studies. To determine the composition and the
magnetic grain size of the remanence carriers of the Whin Sill
complex, the magnetic mineralogy has been studied microscopi-
cally and standard rock magnetic techniques have been applied
to a representative subgroup of samples.
Reﬂection microscopy
Microscopic analyses reveal that the oxide mineralogy of the
dolerites is dominated by magnetite and ilmenite. The two
minerals typically occur as coarse-grained intergrowths and
mostly comprise ilmenite as oxidation–exsolution lamellae in
magnetite. The two minerals can also be present in a sandwich
texture. Ilmenite is generally unaltered whereas magnetite shows
varying degrees of alteration ranging from fairly fresh to heavily
altered with a strongly pitted texture. Apart from the oxide
phases smaller amounts of sulphides are present. Pyrrhotite is the
most commonly occurring sulphide, sometimes being altered to
hematite and magnetite along its basal cleavage; this suggests
that the mineral occurs in its hexagonal variety, as monoclinic
pyrrhotite does not possess this basal cleavage. Microprobe
analyses on pyrrhotites in the dolerites of the Whin Sill complex
have also suggested that the mineral is present in its hexagonal
variety (Dunham & Strasser-King 1981). Whereas monoclinic
pyrrhotite is ferrimagnetic, the hexagonal variety is antiferro-
magnetic (Dunlop & O¨ zdemir 2001). This explains why, during
stepwise demagnetization, signiﬁcant magnetization loss was
rarely recorded at the Curie temperature of pyrrhotite (group 3
behaviour; Fig. 3c), even though the mineral is present in
virtually every sample.
Samples from within the ﬁrst 10 cm from the sill contact are
generally atypical in their opaque mineralogy. These specimens
comprise ilmenite in a very ﬁne skeletal texture and no magnetite
is apparent.

were performed under an argon atmosphere to prevent oxidation
of the specimen’ s mineralogy by atmospheric oxygen during
heating.
For the individual samples the maximum unblocking tempera-
tures were determined graphically from the k–T heating curves.

Only one sample (Fig. 4a) shows nearly reversible behaviour
during heating and cooling, indicating that the specimen did not
suffer signiﬁcant chemical changes during the analysis. For most of
the other samples the susceptibilities measured during cooling are
signiﬁcantly lower than those measured during heating (Fig. 4b).
For these specimens it is proposed that at least some of the magnetite
oxidized to maghemite and the lower susceptibility hematite.
All samples show the Hopkinson effect (Hopkinson, 1889), in
which the susceptibility initially increases with rise in tempera-
ture. Thermal enhancement of the susceptibility occurs because,
above the blocking temperature but below the Curie temperature,
a magnetic grain behaves superparamagnetically (Clark &
Schmidt 1982). The width of the Hopkinson peak, which
determines over what temperature range there is signiﬁcant
enhancement of the susceptibility, is controlled by the width of
the blocking temperature spectrum (Dunlop 1974). The height
and the width of the Hopkinson peak can therefore provide a
rough indicator of the magnetic grain size. The gentle increase in
susceptibility with rise in temperature observed for specimen WS
195Ar (Fig. 4a) might reﬂect the presence of larger MD magne-
tite grains. In contrast, sample WS 113 (Fig. 4b) shows a
relatively narrow Hopkinson peak, probably indicating the
presence of PSD or small MD magnetite grains.
Hysteresis and saturation isothermal remanent
magnetization (SIRM) properties
Hysteresis loop shape has been widely used to characterize
magnetic properties. Day et al . (1977), by cross-plotting para-
meterized measures of loop shape, have devised a plot in which
grains of different size and magnetic character fall in different
ﬁelds. They plotted M
rs/Ms (the ratio of saturation remanence to
saturation magnetization) against Hcr/Hc (the ratio of the coerciv-
ity of remanence to the coercive force). Coercivity of remanence,
the back-ﬁeld required to reduce a saturation remanence to zero,
cannot readily be determined from hysteresis loop measurements
and requires separate back-ﬁeld measurements. However, a
related property, the coercivity of remanent hysteresis, H
rh, which
is determinable from the hysteresis loop, has been shown to be
an adequate estimator of the coercivity of remanence (Fabian &
von Dobeneck 1997; Karloukovski 2000).
In this study a limited number (18) of back-ﬁeld experiments
have been carried out to conﬁrm the relationship between H
cr and
Hrh (Fig. 5a). On this basis, by estimating Hcr from Hrh, a Day plot
has been made for all 41 samples for which hysteresis curves were
measured. All measurements were carried out on a Molspin Nuovo
vibrating sample magnetometer and the results were analysed
using the software package Hystear (von Dobeneck 1996).
The 18 specimens for which back-ﬁeld measurements were
made have values of Hcr between 10 and 63 mT. As previous
workers have found, values of Hrh slightly overestimate Hcr
(Fabian & von Dobeneck 1997; Karloukovski 2000). In estimat-
ing Hcr* (the asterisk is introduced to denote an estimated
quantity) from Hrh the relationship Hcr/C3 ¼ 0:9 Hrh has been used
(Fig. 5a); the scatter observable in Figure 5a is too small to affect
conclusions drawn from the Day plot (Fig. 5b). From the Day plot
it is clear that most samples plot within a narrow area in the PSD
ﬁeld. Only two samples, WS 51 and WS 74, plot in the MD ﬁeld.
Summary of the rock magnetic properties
Optical and magnetic analyses have shown that the dominant
carrier of remanent magnetization of the dolerite of the Whin
Sill complex is relatively pure magnetite, probably resulting from
deuteric oxidation of original TM. The magnetite typically has
an overall magnetic grain size in the PSD state; this might reﬂect
a spread of grain sizes from SD, through PSD, to ﬁne MD. A
previous study on the magnetic mineralogy of the Whin Sill
complex (Thomas et al . 1995) came to a similar conclusion. In
addition, pyrrhotite is present in most samples but mainly in its
hexagonal, aniferromagnetic variety. Only 7% of the analysed

specimens contain monoclinic pyrrhotite, which can contribute to
the total remanent magnetization of the rocks.
Hysteresis measurements showed that the two samples WS 51
and WS 74 are signiﬁcantly softer magnetically than the typical
samples. It is likely that at least some of the magnetite in these
specimens has grown hydrothermally. That these samples also
have the highest bulk susceptibilities (sus 0 .100 3 10/C0 3, Appen-
dix 1) as expected for MD magnetite adds to this suggestion.
The two samples were therefore omitted from the statistical
palaeodirectional analyses.
The two specimens WS 8-211 and WS 8-233 were also
rejected from further analysis as these specimens came from the
contact zone ( ,10 cm) of the sill. Microscopy studies revealed
that the opaque mineralogy of these samples is atypical; no
magnetite was observed and skeletal ilmenite represents the
dominant oxide phase. Further, the two specimens have suscept-
ibilities of c. 0.85 3 10
/C0 3, compared with an average value of
32.5 3 10/C0 3 obtained from all specimens.
Palaeodirectional results
The remanence measurements show that the samples of the Whin
Sill complex have a strong room-temperature magnetization (aver-
age 2566 mA m
/C0 1, Appendix 1). In general, thermal demagnetiza-
tion yielded only a single remanence component in a specimen (e.g.
Fig. 3a). Only occasionally could a second, softer palaeomagnetic
component be isolated. These softer components are removed at
temperatures of 250 8C and are randomly oriented. The ChRM of
all specimens analysed is southerly directed, of reversed polarity
and well deﬁned (Appendix 1). Block and site averages are listed in
Appendix 2, together with statistical parameters.
It is not immediately clear whether a tilt correction should be
applied to the dataset. In the study area the host rock bedding is
typically gently dipping and dips rarely exceed 158. There is
evidence that the host rock stratigraphy was tilted at least to some
degree, prior to the intrusion of the Whin Sill complex. In the
northernmost part of the study area the complex is emplaced as a
ﬂat sheet into the Holburn anticline, cutting through the eastern
fold limb into the core of the anticline (e.g. Robson 1977). This
relationship clearly demonstrates that the area was deformed prior
to the intrusion event. On this basis, it will be assumed here that
no signiﬁcant tilting of the Whin Sill complex occurred after the
intrusive body acquired its magnetization; palaeodirectional
results are quoted without any tilt correction applied.
Discussion
By plotting the palaeodirectional data for the individual regions
of the Whin Sill complex and the associated dykes it becomes
apparent that there are two distinctively different signatures
(Fig. 6). For most of the Whin Sill complex the data are
southerly directed with small positive or negative inclinations. A
different pattern is observed for the Whin Sill complex in the
Alnwick area, for the High Green Dyke and for the St. Oswald’ s
Chapel Dyke. The data for these three regions are more steeply
inclined and only of negative inclination. The mean palaeomag-
netic directions for the individual intrusions are summarized in
Table 1 and the detailed results for individual specimens and
block averages are given in Appendix 1 and 2.
Field observations do not support signiﬁcant post-emplace-
ment tilting of the Whin Sill complex. The two different
signatures are therefore unlikely to be due to tectonic block
tilting or block rotation. Thus, the different palaeomagnetic
patterns must reﬂect at least two igneous events during which
local ﬁeld inclination was distinctively different. This in turn
means that, today, we are dealing with at least four geographi-
cally separated sill bodies (Fig. 6). Three of these are named,
from north to south, as the Holy Island Sill (Fig. 6, 1), the
Alnwick Sill (Fig. 6, 2), and the Hadrian’ s Wall–Pennines Sill
(Fig. 6, 3). The Little Whin Sill (Fig. 6, 4) cannot be differen-
tiated on the basis of the palaeomagnetic results from the
Hadrian’ s Wall–Pennines Sill but differences in its petrology
(Dunham & Kaye 1965; Harrison 1968) show that this smaller
sill was emplaced prior to the other intrusions (Wadge et al .
1972; Johnson & Dunham 2001). Further discussion will focus
only on the three larger sills.
The regionally plotted data also suggest relationships between
the dykes and the individual sills. The Holy Island Dyke has a
very similar palaeomagnetic signature to the Holy Island Sill
(Fig. 6), which suggests that this dyke formed the feeder to the
Holy Island Sill. The palaeomagnetic directions for the St.
Oswald’ s Chapel Dyke and the High Green Dyke are within the
error limits of the more steeply inclined direction of the Alnwick
Sill, indicating that the two dykes and the sill might have been
emplaced contemporaneously. The closer geographical location of
the High Green Dyke to the Alnwick Sill suggests that this dyke
may have fed the sill in the Alnwick area. In the southern part of
the study area the Hett Dyke is the only dyke that has a similar
palaeomagnetic signature to the Hadrian’ s Wall–Pennines Sill. It
is therefore likely that the Hett Dyke formed the feeder to this sill.
Dyke data are sparse and relationships between the individual
dykes and sills cannot be unequivocally proven. Nevertheless, the
combined evidence of related palaeomagnetic directions and of
proximity argue for the proposed feeder relationships.
Further evidence that the Whin Sill complex today consists of
three larger geographically separate sill bodies comes from the
shaded relief aeromagnetic anomaly map (Fig. 7). The outcrops of
the Whin Sill complex and the related dykes are plotted onto this
map and the Permo-Carboniferous dykes match with strong linear
magnetic anomalies. In particular, the Holy Island Dyke can be
traced further to the east, well offshore. In addition, the aero-
magnetic map suggests that the High Green Dyke steps to the
north, being in direct connection to the southernmost part of the
Alnwick Sill. This further supports the proposal that the High
Green Dyke might have formed the feeder to the Alnwick Sill.
Even though some of the details of the aeromagnetic anomaly
map are lost in conversion into black-and-white reproduction, it is
apparent that Whin Sill outcrops bound regions that have the
short-wavelength and high-amplitude textures characteristic of a
strong and shallow-sourced magnetic anomaly (Fig. 7, location 1).
This anomaly is therefore most likely to be the expression of the
subsurface continuation of the Whin Sill complex. Onshore the
Whin Sill complex is surrounded by relatively smooth magnetic
anomalies (Fig. 7, location 2), indicating that these areas are not
underlain by the doleritic intrusion. Smooth anomalies also occur
between the Holy Island Sill and the Alnwick Sill (Fig. 7, location
3) and arguably between the Alnwick Sill and the Hadrian’ s Wall–
Pennines Sill (Fig. 7, location 4), suggesting that the present-day
Whin Sill complex consists of three geographically distinct sill
bodies, which are not connected in the subsurface. It is not
possible to identify the offshore extension of the three sill areas on
the basis of the aeromagnetic anomaly map. The anomaly caused
by the dolerite is generally less well deﬁned in the North Sea than
it is onshore for two reasons: (1) the ﬂight line separation is
greater over the North Sea (3 km compared with 2 km onshore);
(2) the thickness of the Permian strata increases rapidly into the
North Sea, which smooths the magnetic anomaly signal.
The Holy Island Sill and the Hadrian’ s Wall–Pennines Sill

cannot be separated on the basis of their palaeomagnetic
directions, and, as discussed above, both appear to be of similar
age. Evidence that the two bodies do represent separate intru-
sions derives from a study of magma-ﬂow indicators. Macro-
scopic ﬂow indicators and measurements of anisotropy of
magnetic susceptibility (AMS) show that the magma ﬂow in the
Holy Island Sill was southward directed and away from its
proposed feeder dyke, the Holy Island Dyke (Liss et al . 2002).
For the Hadrian’ s Wall–Pennines Sill, in contrast, the magma
ﬂow was predominantly northward (Liss 2003), consistent with
the Hett Dyke acting as a feeder.

studied previously, notably by Creer et al . (1959), Storetvedt &

Creer et al . worked on 36 localities spread along the Whin Sill
outcrop (in present terms, Holy Island Sill, seven localities;
Alnwick Sill, eight localities; Hadrian’ s Wall–Pennines Sill, 18
localities (one rejected); Little Whin Sill, three localities (one
rejected)). No systematic cleaning was applied; natural remanent
magnetization (NRM) directions were scattered in an oval pattern
very similar to that of Figure 2. Although Creer et al . (1959)
calculated a single, tilt-corrected, mean palaeomagnetic direction
(declination/inclination ( D/I) 187.8/ /C0 4.9) it is now possible to
see the non-Fisherian scatter of directions as arising from the
mixing of two distinct populations. Near-horizontal ﬁeld inclina-
tions from the Holy Island Sill and the Hadrian’ s Wall–Pennines
Sill (25 localities) bias the mean, which compares favourably
with that found here for these sills (Table 1).
Storetvedt & Gidskehaug (1969) worked on eight localities
(Holy Island Sill, two localities; Alnwick Sill, ﬁve localities (one
unstable); Hadrian’ s Wall–Pennines Sill, one locality). They
applied routine alternating ﬁeld demagnetization and distin-
guished two groups of magnetization directions corresponding
closely to those recognized here. On the basis of limited thermal
demagnetization, however, they rejected all near-horizontal mag-
netizations as contaminated with a secondary overprint and
reported a mean direction of ( D/I 193.8//C0 21.7), based on ﬁve
localities, four of which are from the Alnwick Sill (see Table 1).
Thomas et al. (1995), in a study directed towards palaeointensity
determination, reported results from ﬁve localities, all in the
Hadrian’ s Wall–Pennines Sill, and supported by extensive rock-
magnetic investigation. ChRM directions were isolated by ther-
mal demagnetization; the tilt-corrected mean direction found was
(D/I 180.0//C0 4.4). Overall, the results from these earlier studies,
when placed in their regional contexts, are in agreement with
those of the present study.
Virtual geomagnetic poles (VGPs) have been calculated
separately for the three areas of the Whin Sill complex and their
associated dykes (Table 1) by treating VGPs from individual
localities as Fisher distributed. The plot of the mean VGPs and
their conﬁdence limits (Fig. 8a) demonstrates the similarity of
the pole positions of the Hadrian’ s Wall–Pennines Sill and the
Holy Island Sill. By contrast, there is an angular separation of
about 17 8 between these and the VGP of the Alnwick Sill, a
difference that, in terms of the calculated conﬁdence limits, is
signiﬁcant. Figure 8a also shows that the VGPs of Creer et al .
(1959) and Thomas et al . (1995) are close to those of the
Hadrian’ s Wall–Pennines Sill and the Holy Island Sill, whereas
the VGP of Storetvedt & Gidskehaug (1969) is close to the
position of that for the Alnwick Sill.
A VGP is calculated on the assumption of a geocentric dipole
model for the Earth’ s magnetic ﬁeld, for an instant reading of the
palaeoﬁeld direction; non-dipole components of the ﬁeld are
reﬂected in the scatter of time-equivalent VGP directions. A
palaeomagnetic pole, by contrast, is an average, calculated from
VGPs (or remanence directions), over a period of time (of the order
of 10
5 a) long enough to account for secular variation (see
McElhinny & McFadden 2000, p. 22). In palaeomagnetic terms, an
igneous intrusion event lasts until all the remanence is blocked in,
thus the remanence in a thick sill or dyke may reﬂect some secular

variation of the geomagnetic ﬁeld. However, even for a sill of 80 m
thickness (the maximum for the Whin Sill complex in outcrop),
cooling times are only of the order of 10 2 a and, relatively,
instantaneous. On this basis the averaged remanence directions for
the three intrusion events identiﬁed here are analysed as VGPs.
McElhinny & McFadden (2000, p. 79) stated that ‘a typical
paleomagnetic site should represent, as near as possible, a single
point in time relative to the time frame over which the paleomag-
netic ﬁeld changed’. In accordance with this usage, the localities
sampled in this study contribute to three palaeomagnetic sites,
identiﬁed as the three separate sill bodies. There has been a
looseness of usage of the term ‘site’ in the palaeomagnetic
literature, resulting in potentially misleading entries to the Global
Paleomagnetic Database (see McElhinny & McFadden 2000, p.
230); for example, Storetvedt & Gidskehaug (1969) are reported as
measuring 24 samples from ﬁve sites. For this reason this paper,
following McElhinny & McFadden (2000), distinguishes clearly
between the terms (sampling) locality and (palaeomagnetic) site.
In palaeomagnetic terms it makes a signiﬁcant difference
whether the intrusion of the Whin Sill complex is regarded as a
single intrusion event (see Storetvedt & Gidskehaug 1969),
leading to a single VGP , or, as seen here, as the product of three
separate events, characterized by separate VGPs.
The straightforward interpretation of the present data is that
the three VGPs represent instances of the palaeoﬁeld, with the
scatter between them arising from secular variation. In terms of
recent behaviour of the geomagnetic ﬁeld, an angular difference
of VGPs of 178 is large but not implausible.
Other interpretations are possible. The present data fall within
the Kiaman Reversed superchron ( c. 311–262 Ma, Opdyke
1995). It has been argued that secular variation is suppressed
during superchrons (Courtillot & Besse 1987; McFadden &
Merrill 1995), in which case a 17 8 shift would be highly unusual
(and would support the rival view (Kruiver et al . 2000, 2002) of
non-suppressed secular variation). On the former argument,
however, VGPs might be interpreted as pole positions and be
compared directly with a relevant apparent polar wander path. In
Figure 8b the VGPs from this study are plotted against represen-
tative pole positions and VGPs (data in Table 2) from the British
Isles, for the Carboniferous–Permian period spanning the time of
intrusion of the Whin Sill complex. It is notable that the current
results follow this path, whereas secular variation might be
expected to cause movement in any direction. The VGPs for the
Holy Island Sill and the Hadrian’ s Wall–Pennines Sill might then
be compared with the late Carboniferous–early Permian data
(Fig. 8b, 6-8); the radiometric ages reported above, of c. 296 Ma,
would support this. The VGP for the Alnwick Sill might be
compared with the Permian data (Fig. 8b, 9–11), suggesting that
the Alnwick Sill represented a later, possibly Permian, intrusion
event and a resurrection of activity of the igneous centre. Four of
the 21 K–Ar analyses performed by Fitch & Miller (1967) are
from the Alnwick Sill but their ages range from 269 /C6 18 Ma to

Whatever the merits of these arguments, the key contribution
of this study is the demonstration, palaeomagnetically, of signiﬁ-
cant differences within the Whin Sill complex, and the consequent
geological implication that the sill is a multi-component body.
Conclusions
The palaeomagnetic analyses of this study have revealed that the
dominant carrier of remanent magnetization of the Whin Sill
dolerite is relatively pure magnetite in the pseudo-single domain
size range. The characteristic remanent magnetization of speci-
mens is typically well deﬁned and unidirectional. The regional
palaeodirectional results show distinctive palaeomagnetic signa-
tures. These data in conjunction with an interpretation of the
aeromagnetic anomaly map and a combined study on magma-
ﬂow indicators and AMS (Liss et al . 2002; Liss 2003) allow
subdivision of the Whin Sill complex into three larger geographi-
cally separate sill bodies. These are named (from north to south)
the Holy Island Sill, the Alnwick Sill and the Hadrian’ s Wall–
Pennines Sill. The Little Whin Sill has been identiﬁed previously
as a fourth, separate sill on the basis of petrological evidence,
although palaeomagnetism cannot distinguish it from the sur-
rounding Hadrian’ s Wall–Pennines Sill. On the basis of the
palaeodirectional results it is also possible to suggest possible
relationships between the exposed contemporaneous dykes and
the individual intrusions. It is proposed that the Holy Island
Dyke formed the feeder to the Holy Island Sill, that the High
Green Dyke and St. Oswald’ s Chapel Dyke are contemporaneous
with the intrusion of the Alnwick Sill, with the High Green Dyke
being a possible feeder to this sill, and that the Hett Dyke
probably fed the Hadrian’ s Wall–Pennines Sill. The study thus
demonstrates the potential of palaeomagnetism, in favourable
circumstances, to yield hitherto unresolved detail of the develop-
ment of an igneous intrusion.
Virtual geomagnetic pole positions have been calculated for
the three major components of the Whin Sill complex, without
application of a tilt correction, which, it is argued, is unneces-
sary. These are: Holy Island Sill and Holy Island Dyke, 346.8E,
35.4S; Alnwick Sill, High Green Dyke and St. Oswald’ s Chapel
Dyke, 337.1E, 47.1S; Hadrian’ s Wall–Pennines Sill and Hett
Dyke, 347.1E, 32.9S. Although the VGPs for the Holy Island Sill
and the Hadrian’ s Wall–Pennines Sill are very similar, indepen-
dent evidence indicates that all three VGPs represent distinct
igneous events. On this basis the VGP of Storetvedt & Gidske-
haug (1969), widely used for the late Carboniferous of the
British Isles, should be amended.

Absolute paleointensities and paleodirections of miocene and
pliocene lavas from Fernando de Noronha, Brazil
R. Leonhardt a,∗, J. Matzka a, E.A. Menor b
a Department for Earth and Environmental Sciences, Geophysics Section, Ludwig-Maximilians-Universität, München, Germany
b Engenharia de Minas, Universidade Federal de Pernambuco, Recife, Pernambuco, Brazil
Received 22 June 2003; received in revised form 8 September 2003; accepted 9 September 2003
Abstract
Forty-four volcanic units were sampled on the Equatorial Atlantic Island of Fernando de Noronha, Brazil. Twenty-seven
sites are from the 1.8–3.3 Myr old Quixaba formation, and the others are from the approximately 8–12 Myr old Remedios
formation. Analyses of paleodirections yielded normal and reverse polarities in both formations with virtual geomagnetic
poles (VGPs) and VGP dispersion (S
f )o fV G Plat: 86.9◦,V G Plong: 136.3◦, Sf : 11.2◦ for the Quixaba formation and VGPlat:
86.8◦,V G Plong: 196.7◦, Sf : 15.5◦ for the Remedios formation. Successful paleointensity determinations were obtained for
9 of the 27 sampled units in the Quixaba formation. A modiﬁed Thellier method was used that includes checks to monitor
alterations and repetition of demagnetization steps to detect multidomain tails of partial thermoremanent magnetizations
(pTRM) and magnetization stabilization processes. Furthermore, the additivity of pTRMs was monitored during this mod-
iﬁed technique of the Thellier experiment. These additivity checks provide a quality test for correcting the paleointensity
determination for magnetomineralogical changes which occur during laboratory treatment. Such correction methods were
used for analyzing approximately 50% of the determinations and lead to a reduction of the within-site scatter. The mean
paleointensity result of 29.3
/H9262T, corresponding to a virtual axial dipole moment (V ADM) of 7 .5 × 1022 Am 2, yields ap-
proximately the present day ﬁeld strength. Mean values of the paleodirections for volcanic units of reversed and normal
polarity are closer to a dipolar ﬁeld conﬁguration than previously observed. Today’s geomagnetic ﬁeld in the Equatorial
Atlantic shows a signiﬁcant dipole anomaly. Our results indicate that this anomaly was far less pronounced in the geological
past.

1. Introduction
Paleomagnetic results of Tertiary lava ﬂows are
important aspects in the study of long-term average
features of the Earth’s magnetic ﬁeld. One of the basic
assumptions of paleomagnetism is that the geomag-

fax: +49-89-2394-4205.
E-mail address: leon@geophysik.uni-muenchen.de (R. Leonhardt).
netic ﬁeld is on average an axial dipole, parallel to
the Earth’s axis of rotation. However, paleomagnetic
data of the past million years show persistent and sys-
tematic departures from this simple model ( Gubbins
and Kelly, 1993). McElhinny et al. (1996) found that
a purely zonal ﬁeld geometry of an axial dipole and
an axial quadrupole is sufﬁcient to ﬁt all available
paleomagnetic data for the past 5 Myr from lava ﬂows
and sediments. Johnson and Constable (1995, 1997) ,
however, require non-zonal terms in the spherical

doi:10.1016/j.pepi.2003.09.008

286 R. Leonhardt et al. / Physics of the Earth and Planetary Interiors 139 (2003) 285–303
harmonic description of the time-averaged paleomag-
netic ﬁeld using lava ﬂow data. In particular Johnson
and Constable (1995) describe a persistent hemi-
spheric asymmetry and an asymmetry between the
normal and the reversed geomagnetic ﬁeld in their
model, which later was attributed to be an artifact due
to poor distribution of and unrecognized errors within
the data ( Johnson and Constable, 1997; Carlut and
Courtillot, 1998 ). Paleointensity data has been used
for modeling (e.g. Kono and Hiroi, 1996 ), but the
paleointensity data set is, as yet, insufﬁcient to obtain
detailed models of time-averaged paleomagnetic ﬁeld
(e.g. Hatakeyama and Kono, 2002). Furthermore, ab-
solute paleointensity data for the last 5 Myr is charac-
terized by large ﬂuctuations and uncertainties ( Juarez
and Tauxe, 2000).
A pronounced feature of the Johnson and Constable
(1995) time-averaged ﬁeld model for the last 5 Myr
is an inclination anomaly during reversed states of
the geomagnetic ﬁeld in the Equatorial and South
Atlantic Ocean, which is accompanied by a declina-
tion anomaly. The anomaly in the model of Johnson
and Constable (1995) heavily relies on ﬁve reversely
magnetized sampling sites located on Fernando de
Noronha (Richardson and Watkins, 1967 ). A distinct
inclination anomaly over Fernando de Noronha is also
found in the present day ﬁeld geomagnetic ﬁeld (e.g.
IGRF 2000).
It is the purpose of this work to extend the exist-
ing paleomagnetic data from Fernando de Noronha
(Richardson and Watkins, 1967; Mazoires et al., 1971;
Schult et al., 1986 ) in terms of paleodirections and
absolute paleointensities. Samples from 44 volcanic
units were obtained and analyzed for rock magnetic
and paleomagnetic characteristics. Directional results
are compared to previously published data and we
scrutinize normal versus reverse ﬁeld asymmetry, as
well as persistent long-term anomalies of the geo-
magnetic ﬁeld for Fernando de Noronha. Absolute
paleointensity determinations were conducted using a
modiﬁed Thellier-type technique, which allow for the
recognition of possible biases by multidomain (MD)
remanence. This methodology provides a quality
check regarding correction methods for magnetomin-
eralogical changes which occur during laboratory
treatment. Finally, our paleointensity results are com-
pared to published intensity values of the same time
range.
2. Geology and sampling strategy
Fernando de Noronha island is about 365 km north-
east of Natal, Rio Grande do Norte, Brazil on 3.85
◦
south and 32.4◦ west. The island constitutes the east-
ern end of a chain of volcanic sea-mounts which are
thought to be of hotspot origin (e.g. Rivalenti et al.,
2000). Basically, two main volcanic formations are
deﬁned on the island ( Fig. 1). The main rocks of the
Quixaba formation (3.3–1.8 Myr) are ankaratritic lavas
of similar composition indicating a common mantle
source ( Ulbrich et al., 1994 ). The Remedios forma-
tion with an average age of 9 .5 ± 1.1 Myr consists
of phonolites, nephelinites, alkali trachytes, and al-
kali basalts. Age determinations were conducted by
Cordani (1970) using the K/Ar technique. Samples
from 44 sites of both formations were obtained pre-
dominantly from coastal outcrops where successions
of lava ﬂows are exposed ( Fig. 1 ). From the Quix-
aba formation 27 volcanic units were sampled, 25
ankaratritic lava ﬂows, one dyke (site FN-Q16) and
a nepheline basanite from Illa Cuscus (site FN-Q1).
Seventeen volcanic units were sampled in the Reme-
dios formation. Sites FN-R6, FN-R7, FN-R9, FN-R5
(8.8 Ma), FN-R3 and FN-R8 are phonolitic units. The
alkali trachyte of site FN-R13 has an age of 10.8 Ma.
Four lava ﬂows (FN-R14 to Fn-R17) were sampled
in approximately 12.3 Myr old alkali basalts. In ad-
dition, samples from one glenmuirite site (FN-R4),
two dykes (FN-R1, FN-R2) and essexites (FN-R10 to
FN-R12, 9.4 Myr) were taken in the Remedios forma-
tion. From each site at least ﬁve separately oriented
drill cores were taken, oriented with a magnetic and a
sun compass. Whenever possible, the individual sam-
ples of one unit were taken with horizontal spacings of
several meters and different vertical positions. There
are no indications for major tectonic movements like
rotations, faulting and unconformities in the sampled
volcanic units on Fernando de Noronha, wherefore no
tectonic corrections are applied.

In order to quantify whether the sampled lavas
recorded independent states of the geomagnetic ﬁeld,
comparison of directions using the F-distribution test
(e.g. Butler, 1992), were conducted. The probability
to which successive ﬂows are independent was cal-
culated and for values less than 95% between ﬂows,
the lavas are assumed to have recorded the same ge-
omagnetic ﬁeld. Calculation started from the lowest
and, therefore, oldest ﬂow. F-distribution statistics for
the Capim Açu section support the presence of ﬁve
different directional records of the past geomagnetic
ﬁeld, whereas only two were isolated for the Leão
Beach section. Non-independent sites were combined
to directional groups ( Table 1 ). This purely direc-
tional approach to serial correlation is supported by
paleointensity determinations of samples from the
Leão Beach section, where ﬂow FN-Q18 and FN-Q19
show almost identical paleointensity values.

6. Paleointensity determination
6.1. Selection criteria
Only samples yielding consistent within-site ChRM
directions were used for paleointensity determina-
tions. Suitable samples for Thellier-type paleointen-
sity determinations were selected based upon the
results of rock magnetic examinations and ore mi-
croscopy observations. Samples showing a single
high Curie temperature, indicative of high tempera-
ture oxidation during ﬂow emplacement, were used as
they are considered to be insensitive to further oxida-
tion under laboratory conditions. As thermomagnetic

curves were not measured from every sample of one
site and since standard and continuous demagnetiza-
tion experiments showed that within-site differences
are common, additional pre-selection methods were
applied. Low-ﬁeld susceptibility measurements after
each thermal demagnetization step allow the estima-
tion of the thermal stability of the samples. Samples
with only slight variations are termed to be suitable.
Twenty-nine specimens were subjected to AF demag-
netization of an anhysteretic remanent magnetization
ARM (150 mT AC, 50 /H9262T DC) before and after heat-
ing to 200, 400 and 550
◦C, respectively. These mea-
surements, which are similar to the alteration analysis
of Shaw (1974) , provide a accurate quantiﬁcation
of possible alteration mechanisms. Two examples of
these experiments are shown in Fig. 5 wherein AF
demagnetization of an ARM at room temperature is
plotted versus the AF demagnetization of an ARM
after several heating steps. If the ARM demagnetiza-
tions following subsequent heating steps are linearly
related with a slope of one, then no alteration oc-
curred (Fig. 5a). Irreversible changes of the magnetic
information due to alteration at moderate tempera-
tures ( Kosterov and Prévot, 1998 ) as well as high
temperature alteration can be detected. Alteration at
low temperatures (e.g. stress release in titanomag-
netites), which could lead to spurious paleointensity
estimates, are normally not detected using standard
checks during the Thellier experiment, as only a small
percentage of the NRM is lost below 300
◦C. Fig. 5b
shows a gradual alteration of a sample during labora-
tory treatment at temperatures above 200
◦C. The low
coercivity fraction increases during heating, whereas
the high coercivity fraction decreases. Such samples
are not suitable for paleointensity determinations.
Only samples from 12 sites of the Quixaba forma-
tion passed the selection criteria for paleointensity de-
termination.

6.3. Paleointensity determinations
Specimens from 12 of the 44 sampled volcanic units
were selected and subjected to paleointensity determi-
nations. Altogether, 42 successful determinations were
obtained from 49 specimens indicative of an accurate
pre-selection procedure. Representative examples of
Thellier-type paleointensity determinations are shown
in Fig. 6 . Analysis of paleointensity determinations
was performed using standard NRM/pTRM plots. For
identiﬁcation of linear segments within NRM/pTRM
diagrams only successive points were used.
6.4. Corrections for magnetomineralogical changes
If alteration checks are continuously performed
over the entire experimental temperature range and
assuming that alteration happens predominantly be-
low the temperature of the respective check, a method
proposed by Valet et al. (1996) can be used to correct
for magnetomineralogical changes during laboratory
treatment. A fundamental requisite for this correc-
tion method is the absence of MD remanence. As
shown above, the additivity checks are similar to the
standard pTRM checks, with an added sensitivity to
T
ub <T b. Therefore, one can use the method of Valet
et al. (1996) to correct the paleointensity determi-
nation using the pTRM checks. For this technique,
the cumulative sum of the individual differences be-
tween checks and associated pTRM values up to
heating step i − 1 is subtracted from the measured
pTRM value at step i. After applying the alteration
correction, the additivity checks should fall on the
corrected pTRM values for cases of SD remanence.
If this is not the case, a signiﬁcant bias from MD
remanence or continuous alteration during repeated
heating steps is present. Two examples of alteration
corrected results are shown in Fig. 7. Fig. 7a shows
a slightly downward curved NRM/pTRM plot. Nei-
ther the repeated demagnetization steps nor the ACs
show a signiﬁcant inﬂuence of MD remanence. After
check correction, the fraction of the NRM covered
by the linear segment is well above 50%. A similar
paleointensity result is obtained for the non-corrected
analysis. In Fig. 7b an example is shown for which it
is not possible to analyze the non-corrected determi-
nation. After check correction, the ACs coincide with
the pTRM values and a linear segment covering most
of the blocking temperature spectrum is obtained.
Twenty specimens of the collection were analyzed
using check correction. For seven of these, analysis
without check correction would have failed.

7. Discussion
7.1. Directional aspects
The distribution of normal and reverse directions
from the Quixaba formation show two distinct areas.
Reversely magnetized units were found only on the
western side of Fernando de Noronha. K/Ar age deter-
minations (Cordani, 1970)yield ages of about 2.5 Myr
for these volcanic units, emphasizing that this part of
the island formed during the early Matuyama polarity
chron. All other Quixaba samples from the main is-
land show normal magnetizations with associated ages
of about 3.0 Myr and were extruded during the Gauss
polarity chron. Two sites (FN-Q2 and FN-Q3) on Ilha
Rata, northeast of Fernando de Noronha, also show
normal directions. According to Cordani (1970) the

7.2. Paleointensity determination and alteration
correction
Global coverage of absolute paleointensity data,
when compared to that of paleodirectional results,
is markedly deﬁcient in data quantity and quality.
Absolute paleointensities are difﬁcult to obtain and
require lengthy experimental procedures. Further-
more, the success rate of these experiments is gen-
erally poor, well below 50%. Rigorous pre-selection
methods greatly enhance the success rate in case of
our samples from Fernando de Noronha. The success
rate commonly describes the ratio of obtained results
versus attempted determinations, and not the ratio
of obtained paleointensity versus obtained paleodi-
rection of individual volcanic units. For our data the
later ratio results in 25% and is comparable to other
paleointensity studies. In addition to the rock mag-
netic pre-selection experiments, the correction for
magnetomineralogical changes additionally increased
the success rate. McClelland and Briden (1996) and
Valet et al. (1996) investigated such correction meth-
ods and came to the same basic conclusion: alteration
correction is valid, if all of the following conditions
are fulﬁlled and can adequately demonstrated during
laboratory treatment:
• The pTRM check, which is used for correcting the
paleointensity determination, is sensible for alter-
ation below the temperature at which the check is
performed. Therefore, the alteration product, which
formed during thermal demagnetization, must only
affect unblocking temperatures below the subse-
quent alteration check.
• MD remanences and MD tails must not be present.
The remaining NRM should not be affected during
pTRM acquisition.
• There should be no ongoing alteration during re-
peated heating/cooling cycles to the same or lower
temperatures.
• Checks must be performed successively and should
cover the whole temperature spectrum of the exper-
iment.
The modiﬁed paleointensity experiment, performed
on the samples of Fernando de Noronha, satisﬁes most
of these requirements. Alteration checks were per-
formed continuously from 100
◦C up to the maximum
temperature after every second heating step. Additiv-
ity checks and repeated demagnetization steps are sen-
sitive for MD remanence. Since two heating/cooling
cycles are conducted between the pTRM check and
the associated additivity check, ongoing alterations are
also monitored by the additivity check. In addition to

R. Leonhardt et al. / Physics of the Earth and Planetary Interiors 139 (2003) 285–303 301
MD tails, repeated demagnetization steps may be af-
fected by destruction of remanence with blocking tem-
peratures above the actual heating step. Formation of
new remanence above the actual heating step is mon-
itored, if it happens during a ﬁeld-on step.
Alteration affecting higher blocking temperatures
than the heating step of the alteration check and lower
temperatures than the previous demagnetization step,
however, cannot be monitored with any of the de-
scribed checks during the experiment. This can cause
an unrecognized failure to the paleointensity determi-
nation. The inﬂuence of this effect is reduced, how-
ever, if the temperature interval between check and
demagnetization steps is small during the experiment.
For all paleointensity experiments, where check cor-
rection is applied (Table 2), the maximum temperature
difference was ≤60
◦C at heating steps above 380 ◦C.
The heating step dependent ARM AF demagnetiza-
tion experiments (see Fig. 5), show no signiﬁcant al-
teration at temperatures below 400
◦C and only slight
alteration above 400 ◦C for samples where the check
correction was applied. This test is sensitive to all al-
terations during laboratory thermal treatment. How-
ever, due to the different grain size dependence of
ARM and TRM (e.g. Yu et al., 2003 ), the ARM test
can only be a ﬁrst order approximation of alteration
occurring during Thellier-type experiments. For seven
specimens from the collection, a paleointensity deter-
mination would have not been possible without check
correction (e.g. Fig. 7 b). The majority of the other
specimens, where check correction is applied, show
results similar to those obtained when non-corrected,
within a smaller fraction of the NRM ( Fig. 7a). Us-
ing only non-corrected determinations would result in
very similar mean paleointensity values for most sites,
albeit with higher within-site scatter. This ﬁnding is a
further indication that alteration correction improves
the results. When comparing non-corrected and cor-
rected paleointensity determinations in one site, sim-
ilar results for most lavas, except sites FN-Q16 and
FN-Q15, are found. None of the specimens of site
FN-Q16 could be analyzed without check correction,
but all of the applied checks during the determination
and thermal dependent ARM demagnetizations on sis-
ter samples point to a suitability for analysis, result-
ing in similar values for the individual specimens. Site
FN-Q15 shows high within-site scatter, whether or not
applying check correction.
In addition to the directional differences from an
axial dipolar ﬁeld, the virtual axial dipole moments
were calculated from the mean paleointensity values of
normal and reverse geomagnetic ﬁeld states (Table 4).
The values are similar for the reverse and normal state
of the ﬁeld and the overall mean value of(7.5±2.6)×
10
22 Am 2 is only slightly lower than the present day
magnetic moment. This observation is in agreement
with the ﬁndings of Heller et al. (2002)whose paleoin-
tensity database analysis points to a Pliocene dipole
moment close to 8×10
22 Am 2. These authors suggest
that submarine basaltic glass (SBG) samples, which
are included in the paleointensity database analysis of
Juarez and Tauxe (2000) , are biased by chemical al-
teration processes, leading to an underestimation of
the paleointensity. Smirnov and Tarduno (2003) came
to a similar conclusion, suggesting systematically too
low paleointensities for SBG older than 0.5 Ma.Juarez
and Tauxe (2000) obtained an average value of 5 .5 ×
10
22 Am 2 for the last 5 Myr, signiﬁcantly lower than
the mean value obtained for Fernando de Noronha.
Hence, our study phenomenologically supports the ar-
gumentation of Heller et al. (2002) and Smirnov and
Tarduno (2003).
8. Conclusions
(1) Pre-selection of samples using a combination of
rock magnetic experiments, ore microscopy, and
ARM demagnetizations after different heating
steps, greatly enhanced the success rate of pale-
ointensity measurements for our samples from
Fernando de Noronha.
(2) Additivity checks monitor the inﬂuence of MD
remanence during Thellier-type experiments and
ongoing alteration during repeated heating steps.
Furthermore, these checks provide a measure for
the quality of corrections for magnetomineralogi-
cal changes. The application of alteration correc-
tion further enhanced the success rate and leaded
to a reduction of the within-site scatter of paleoin-
tensity determination indicating an improvement
of the results.
(3) The mean paleomagnetic poles for the Quixaba
and Remedios formation are similar to those
expected from an axial dipolar ﬁeld. Analyses
of paleomagnetic mean values show that the

302 R. Leonhardt et al. / Physics of the Earth and Planetary Interiors 139 (2003) 285–303
geomagnetic dipole anomaly during the pliocene
is far smaller in this region than previously found
in paleomagnetic data and that observed for the
present day ﬁeld.
(4) Similar V ADMs are observed for normal and re-
verse ﬁeld states during the Pliocene on Fernando
de Noronha. The obtained values are similar to
the present day magnetic moment.

Abstract
Petrographic, geochemical and paleomagnetic analyses of the Mississippian Turner Valley Formation provide constraints on
diagenesis and ﬂuid ﬂow events in the Western Canada Sedimentary Basin. Paleomagnetic plugs and companion geochemical
samples were taken from two drillcores, with Fullbore MicroImage log orientations. Dolomite from both wells yielded two
magnetization directions. The low-temperature, low-coercivity direction is a drilling-induced remanence rather than a viscous
remanent magnetization. The high-temperature, high-coercivity remanence direction is Cretaceous, and there is no sign of a
primary Mississippian direction. Geochemical analyses of matrix dolomite yield
d 18O values ranging from 0.65 to 23.34‰
(VPDB standard) and d 13C values ranging from 1.77 to 3.05‰ VPDB. The least depleted samples have stable isotope values
consistent with, or only slightly depleted from, postulated Mississippian dolomite values. The remaining sample values exhibit
a negative covariant trend consistent with either mixing with another diagenetic ﬂuid or recrystallization during burial.
Petrographic analysis reveals the presence of a recrystallization event that caused zoning and a gradual increase size of the
dolomite crystals. This event is thought to have caused both the Cretaceous paleomagnetic remanence and the altered
geochemical values. The minor enrichment in Sr radiogenic isotopes, relative to coeval seawater values, suggests that both
an extrabasinal source for any ﬂuid and large-scale ﬂuid ﬂow are unlikely. The results also indicate that magnetic remanences
are very sensitive to visually minor changes in carbonate recrystallization from heat or pressure, so that great care must be taken
in correlating paleomagnetic and geochemical data. q 2000 Elsevier Science B.V. All rights reserved.
Keywords: paleomagnetism; stable isotope geochemistry; carbonates; diagenesis; Western Canada Sedimentary Basin; Mississippian
1. Introduction
Previous work has suggested close links between
orogenically derived ﬂuid ﬂow and magnetization
ages observed in the associated foreland. For
example, many Mississippi Valley type lead–zinc
deposits show a close correlation between their paleo-
magnetically determined age and major tectonic
events (see Symons et al., 1996, for discussion). A
second example is the Permian ‘Kiaman overprint’.
This widespread secondary magnetization is found in

most Paleozoic carbonate and clastic formations in
eastern North America, and its timing correlates
with that of the Alleghanian and Ouachita orogenies
(Oliver, 1986, 1992; McCabe and Elmore, 1989;
Bethke and Marshak, 1990). Precipitation of magnetic
minerals from large-scale ﬂuid migration driven by
sediment compaction, tectonic ‘squeezing’ or gravity,
is usually invoked as the causal mechanism for the
magnetization (Jackson and Beales, 1967; Cathles
and Smith, 1983; Garven, 1985; Bethke, 1986).
Thus, paleomagnetism can be used to date ﬂuid
migration, provided the ﬂuid is capable of forming
remanence-carrying minerals. An extension of this
hypothesis suggests that, if an area has undergone
two ﬂuid ﬂow events, it could then be possible to
date both events (Lewchuk and Symons, 1996). For
calcareous sedimentary rocks, the observed para-
genetic sequence sets out the relative timing of
diagenetic events, and paleomagnetic techniques can
date events when magnetic minerals are precipitated
or recrystallized.
The ﬁrst purpose of this study is an investiga-
tion of drill core orientation using paleomagnetic
techniques. Modern techniques, such as Fullbore
MicroImage logging, enable one to correlate
major structures in the wall rocks to structures
within the core, and thereby to orient the core.
However, such logs are unavailable for most
older wells, in which case paleomagnetism often
provides an alternative method of orientation. In
many core samples, low coercivity/low tempera-
ture or viscous remanent magnetization (VRM) is
present that is aligned to either the present Earth’s
magnetic ﬁeld (PEMF) or the dipole-averaged
Earth’s magnetic ﬁeld (DEMF) (Kodama, 1984;
Rolph et al., 1995; Lewchuk et al., 1998). By
measuring the orientation of its VRM, drillcore
can be absolutely oriented in 3-D space so that
directional properties such as fracture orientations
can be obtained for reservoir analysis. The second
purpose of this study is to use paleomagnetic,
geochemical and petrographic techniques in
combination to study a Mississippian carbonate
gas reservoir in the Western Canada Sedimentary
Basin (WCSB) (Fig. 1). Correlation of the magne-
tization components to the paragenetic sequence,
determined through petrographic and geochemical
techniques, allows us to date major diagenetic
events such as dolomitization-inducing and/or
hydrocarbon-bearing ﬂuid migration. This is
important in the WCSB where the timing of
both reservoir-creating dolomitization and of
hydrocarbon-bearing ﬂuid migration has been the
subject of debate for a number of years (Nesbitt
and Muehlenbachs, 1994; Qing and Mountjoy,
1994).
2. Regional geologic setting and stratigraphy
Eastward or cratonic-verging thrusting occurred
throughout eastern British Columbia and western
Alberta during the Jurassic/Cretaceous Columbian
and Laramide orogenies, creating the thrusts and
folds of the Foreland Belt of the Canadian
Cordillera. Moose Mountain formed in a series of
overlapping thrust sheets that are underlain by low-
angle sole faults (Fig. 2). The surface sheet is folded
into an anticlinal structure because its sole fault
steps up from the Cambrian to Devonian strata. At
the surface this anticlinal structure forms Moose
Mountain, an elongated dome with its long axis
oriented northwest–southeast (Ower, 1975). The
dome is bounded to the east by the Moose Mountain
sole fault and to the west by the Prairie Mountain
and Forgetmenot thrust faults. Mississippian strata
of the Banff Formation are exposed at the center
of the dome.
The Mississippian Turner Valley Formation lies
within the platform carbonates of the Rundle
assemblage in the Foothills of southern Alberta
(Fig. 1). In the Moose Mountain area, 80 km
southwest of Calgary, the Turner Valley Forma-
tion is overlain by the Mount Head Formation
and underlain by the Shunda and Pekisko forma-
tions (Fig. 2). At the surface, the Turner Valley
Formation consists of enchinoderm-rich limestones
and dolomites (Macqueen and Bamber, 1967). In
the subsurface, the formation consists of three
informal members: the ‘lower porous’, ‘middle
dense’, and ‘upper porous’ members. The lower
and upper members consist of echinoderm and
echinoderm-bryozoan grainstones and packstones,
whereas the middle member consists of mostly
dolomitized wackestones and mudstones (Al-
Aasm and Lu, 1994).

3. Methodology
Core from wells 10–14–23–7W5 or Well 14 and
2–23–23–7W5 or Well 23 in the Mississippian
Turner Valley Formation of the Moose Field was
sampled for analysis at the Alberta Energy Utilities
Board core facility in Calgary.

3.2. Paleomagnetism
Each core was re-assembled into segments that
were as long as possible on which an arbitrary master
orientation line (MOL) was drawn to provide a refer-
ence position for the paleomagnetic plugs. The 2.5 cm
diameter plugs were drilled perpendicular to the core
axis, and their azimuths were measured relative to the
MOL. Each plug was sliced into one to three paleo-
magnetic specimens of ,2.2 cm length. The potential
for introducing spurious magnetizations during well
drilling has been recognized (Pinto and McWilliams,
1990) and therefore, the plugs were taken as far from
the outer edges of the core as possible. Fullbore
MicroImage logs were used to determine the fracture
and bedding orientations of segments relative to both
their MOL and the surrounding bedrock, so that the
true orientation of their MOL was determined.
Rotation of magnetization directions along with
rotation of the MOL to its true orientation, including
correction for the borehole deviation from vertical,
resulted in the orientation of the specimens in 3-D
space, so that their true paleomagnetic directions
could be determined.
Prior to analysis, the specimens were stored for
three months in a magnetically shielded room with a
ﬁeld intensity of ! 1% of the Earth’s magnetic ﬁeld
in order to allow the least-stable laboratory magneti-
zation components to decay. All subsequent testing on
the specimens was done in the shielded room, mini-
mizing the possibility of the acquisition of a spurious
magnetization. The natural remanence magnetization
(NRM) of each specimen was measured using a Cana-
dian Thin Films CTF-420 cryogenic magnetometer
which can detect a magnetization intensity down to
about 5 £ 10
26 A=m for a standard paleomagnetic
specimen. If two specimens were obtained from a
plug, one was subjected to alternating ﬁeld (AF)
demagnetization in about 25 steps from 2 to 140 mT
using a Sapphire Instruments SI-4 AF demagnetizer
and the other was thermally demagnetized in about 30
steps from 80 to 580 8C using a Magnetic Measure-
ments MMTD-1 thermal demagnetizer. If only a
single specimen was obtained, it was thermally
demagnetized, and for plugs with three specimens,
two were thermally and one was AF demagnetized.
Thermal demagnetization was used preferentially
because previous work in the WCSB had suggested
that it was more effective for isolating the magnetic
components (Lewchuck et al., 1998).
The individual remanence vector components from
the specimens were obtained using the principal
component method of Kirshvinck (1980). Most com-
ponents were deﬁned over at least three demagnetiza-
tion steps and all had maximum angular deviation
angles of ,138. Component mean directions for
groups of specimens were calculated using Fisher
(1953) statistics.
Rock magnetic experiments were done to deter-
mine the mineralogy and grain size of the main
magnetic minerals. Isothermal remanent magnetiza-
tion (IRM) acquisition paths were measured by
progressively magnetizing the specimen in 15 steps
with an increasing direct current (DC) ﬁeld up to a
maximum of 900 mT using a Sapphire Instruments
SI-6 pulse magnetizer to reach the saturation iso-
thermal remanent magnetization (SIRM) and then
AF demagnetizing the SIRM in 10 steps up to
100 mT.
4. Results
4.1. Petrography and geochemistry
The diagenetic history of the Moose ﬁeld includes
episodes of early siliciﬁcation, matrix-destructive
dolomite formation, brecciation, anhydritization,
compaction, and late ﬂuorite and calcite vein-ﬁlling
(Fig. 3). The paragenetic sequence is based on
petrographic observations and corroborated with geo-
chemical evidence. The most signiﬁcant and relevant
diagenetic events are discussed below.
4.1.1. Dolomitization
Four types of dolomite are present in the Turner
Valley Formation. From oldest to youngest they are:
pervasive matrix microdolomite, pseudomorphic
dolomite, mesodolomite, and vug-rimming coarse
dolomite.
The pervasive microdolomite is a fabric-destruc-
tive, non-ferroan, subhedral dolomite that replaces
the matrix and allochems (Figs. 4a and 5a). The
crystals are typically 5–30 mm in size and non-
stoichiometric (mean CaCO
3 56.1 mol%; Table 1).
In some samples, this dolomite also occurs in

Mesodolomite crystals range from 40–100 mm
(Fig. 5c) and show a gradual increase in size from
the microdolomite range to the largest mesodolomite
crystal size. Mesodolomite is anhedral to subhedral,
non-ferroan, non-stoichiometric (mean CaCO
3
56.1 mol%; Table 1) and sometimes shows concentric
zoning with dark cores and bright rims under UV
illumination, although the contact between the core
and the rim is irregular. The mesodolomite apparently
postdates microdolomite as suggested by its larger
crystal size. It shows a covariant trend in its isotopic
composition, unlike that of microdolomite (Fig. 6)
with its
d 18O values ranging from 23.74 to
27.51‰ VPDB, while its d 13C values range from
10.65 to 12.54‰ VPDB (Table 2), and the correla-
tion coefﬁcient ( R2) for the six samples is 0.79.
However, the mesodolomite’s 87Sr/86Sr values are
slightly more radiogenic than the Mississippian
seawater composition (Fig. 7).
Pseudomorphic dolomite (e.g. Sibley, 1982) forms
as a single, non-ferroan, inclusion-rich crystal of dolo-
mite that mimics the morphology of crinoid ossicles.
Based on its relationship with mesodolomite, it
appears that the formation of this dolomite overlaps
with the mesodolomite or formed slightly earlier.
Vug-rimming coarse dolomite cement occurs in
some samples, postdating the earlier dolomites. It is
euhedral, 100 mm in size, non-ferroan and non-
stoichiometric (mean CaCO
3 55.3 mol%; Table 1).
Under UV illumination, this dolomite is occasionally
zoned. Bitumen is often found lining the coarse dolo-
mite in the vugs, suggesting that bitumen formation
postdates the dolomite.

4.1.2. Calcite cementation
Calcite cementation is a very minor process in the
diagenetic history of the Turner Valley Formation in
the Moose Field. Early-precipitated equant calcite
cement occupies pore spaces in crinoidal grainstones
and coated grains. It has a low-Mg concentration
(mean MgCO
3 0.08 mol%), undetectable Mn and Fe,
and a high Sr concentration (mean  988 ppm;
Table 1). Later vein-ﬁll blocky calcite crosscuts the
dolomite phases (Fig. 4c). The carbon and oxygen
isotopic signatures from one sample of the early
calcite cement indicate partial preservation of primary
marine isotopic signatures when compared to
Mississippian carbonates (Fig. 6), whereas the later
calcite cement inﬁlling veins show more depleted
oxygen and carbon isotope values. The
87Sr/86Sr
analysis value from one sample of blocky calcite is
more radiogenic than Mississippian seawater (Fig. 7).
4.1.3. Anhydritization
Early, nodular anhydrite is observed in some facies
associated with algal ﬁlaments and the dolomitized
matrix (Fig. 4b). The nodules are subrounded, and
usually less than 1 cm in diameter. This anhydrite
resembles anhydrite formed in a sabhka environment
(e.g. McKenzie, 1981; Butler et al., 1982), but it is a
volumetrically minor component of the cores.
Secondary anhydrite is found in some fractures and
is associated with late ﬂuorite, quartz, magnesite,
minor sulﬁdes, and calcite.
4.1.4. Siliciﬁcation
Silica is a minor rock-forming component. It has a
restricted distribution, appearing as coexisting micro-
crystalline chert, chalcedony and coarser crystalline
quartz (Fig. 5b). The silica replaces the original lime-
stone, preserving some primary features (Fig. 5b). In

dolomite crystals ﬂoating in the chert. From these
cross-cutting relationships, it appears that silica
replaced the fossil during the shallow burial stage
and overlapped dolomitization. In contrast, quartz
cement inﬁlling some veins is a late diagenetic event.
4.1.5. Late diagenetic phases
Veinlets of ﬂuorite, quartz and ferroan calcite cross-
cut all former stages, and must represent late events.
These veins are generally ,1 mm wide and occur
throughout most of the sampled core length (Fig.
4c) except for a larger ﬂuorite vein that is associated
with the late quartz. Minor pyrite mineralization
occurred after the formation of late anhydrite and
appears to have replaced chert and dolomite. It is
worthwhile to note here that the sulﬁdes are volume-
trically very minor, have very limited distribution, and
have a large grain size. Magnesite was also noticed in
some samples, where it is associated with the ﬂuorite,
quartz and ferroan calcite. Finally, bitumen occurs
as a coating on the vug-ﬁlling coarse dolomite and
other mineral phases and occupying the core of
mesodolomite (Fig. 5c).

4.2.2. Remanence directions
The NRM intensities are between 1 :0 £ 1023 and
1:0 £ 1025 A=m with the dolomite specimens in the
upper portion and the anhydrite specimens in the
lower portion of the range. Almost all of the
specimens have very steep, normal-polarity NRM
directions (Fig. 10). Upon demagnetization, they
tend to exhibit two magnetization components: a
low temperature, low coercivity component removed
below 2408C or 25 mT, and a high temperature, high
coercivity component that is typically removed
between 240 and 400 8C or 25 and 100 mT. These
directions can be seen by examination of Fig. 11,
where the horizontal and vertical components of the
magnetization are shown separately. In thermally
demagnetized specimens, no coherent signal was
apparent above 400–450 8C because their intensities
either fell below the magnetometer noise level or
increased sharply from the growth of new magnetic
minerals (Fig. 11).

5. Discussion
5.1. Dolomitization
The paragenetic sequence (Fig. 3), determined
through petrologic and geochemical analysis, allows
constraints to be placed on the timing and origin of
dolomitization events. Petrographic evidence
suggests that matrix microdolomite formed early in
the diagenetic history of the Turner Valley Formation
in a marine-dominated system. Its crystal size, non-
stoichiometric nature, association with algal ﬁlaments
and nodular anhydrite, as well as the presence of detri-
tal quartz, suggest formation in a near-shore, peritidal
environment (McKenzie, 1981; Patterson and
Kinsman, 1982; Muller et al., 1990), whereas grain-
stone and wackestone facies were deposited in shoals
further offshore. This dolomite appears to have
formed prior to any appreciable compaction because
all stylolites crosscut it. However, most of its isotopic
signatures are inconsistent with those of a

syndepositional and/or very shallow burial origin,
which may indicate modiﬁcations during successive
stages of diagenesis (Malone et al., 1994; Machel,
1997).
d 18O isotope values of the matrix dolomite
show a negative shift in the magnitude of ,4‰,
but the narrow range of d 13C values suggests low
water–rock interaction in a rock-buffered system
(Fig. 6). The isotopic values of this dolomite also
fall very close to those of pervasive dolomite in the
Turner Valley Formation from the nearby Quirk
Creek Field (Fig. 6b; Al-Aasm and Lu, 1994).
87Sr/86Sr ratios of the microdolomite (Fig. 7) fall
very closely to the Mississippian seawater value
which suggests an unmodiﬁed, or only slightly modi-
ﬁed, seawater signature. Similar values have been also
found for the Quirk Creek microdolomite (Al-Aasm
and Lu, 1994).
Recrystallization of microdolomite to meso-
dolomite (Fig. 5) is supported by petrographic and
geochemical evidence. The evidence includes: (1) a
gradual increase in dolomite crystal size; (2) the
presence of concentric zoning in some dolomite crys-
tals, with irregular boundaries between the core and
the rim; (3) a negative shift in oxygen isotopes; and (4)
the partial enrichment of radiogenic Sr (Figs. 5–7).
Recrystallization of early-formed dolomite often
occurs and is thought to take place in shallow, low-
temperature and/or deep, high-temperature environ-
ments (e.g. Mazzulo, 1992; Smith and Dorobek,
1993; Al-Aasm and Lu, 1994; Kupecz and Land,
1994; Neilsen et al., 1994; Yoo and Lee, 1998). It
could alter isotopic and geochemical signatures within
the dolomites (Malone et al., 1994; Durocher and
Al-Aasm, 1997). In the present study, microdolomite
is believed to have recrystallized to mesodolomite
during the shallow to intermediate burial stage, post
late calcite and silica cementation. The isotopic vari-
ations of mesodolomite show a covariant trend
between oxygen and carbon isotopes (Fig. 6a). A simi-
lar trend in isotopic values has been observed in the
Mississippian carbonates from the Pekisko Formation
in the Sylvan Lake Field in Alberta (Fig. 6b; Al-Aasm
et al., 1996). Al-Aasm and Lu (1994) suggested that
the pervasive dolomitization at Quirk Creek Field
occurred as the result of mixing of phreatic fresh
waters with marine waters or brines, possibly during
the Pennsylvanian. The covariant trend can be attrib-
uted to evolving poreﬂuids with depth and/or mixing
of two types of ﬂuids (cf. Frank and Lohmann, 1995).
Petrographic, burial history and isotope data can be
used to interpret changes in the oxygen isotope
composition of the diagenetic ﬂuids responsible for
