around 850 Ma reported from the Sveconorwegian of SW Sweden,
so it is not clear what could cause the resetting of magnetite- and
haematite-based remanence in rocks of Eastern Segment and Pro-
togine Zone (Bylund 1992; Pisarevsky & Bylund 1998). We may
guess that some kind of low temperature chemical remagnetization
took place, as it happened in the Appalachians (e.g. McCabe &
Elmore 1989), but much more interdisciplinary studies are neces-
sary to approach this problem.
6.2 The Sveconorwegian Loop
New palaeomagnetic data presented in this paper, combined with
new geochronological data that constrain the ages of previous, re-
liable palaeomagnetic results, have signiﬁcant implications for the
Fennoscandian APWP and the Sveconorwegian Loop.
The palaeopoles from Swedish maﬁc intrusions (Table 2) with
ages from 965 to 916 Ma are similar (Fig. 5), implying that Baltica
was located at ∼30
◦ latitude, and underwent minimal drift during
this interval. We realize that the 966 Ma Nilstorp result is from
a single dyke and thus is unlikely to have averaged PSV . Other
poles provide better averaging of PSV , however, more well-dated
palaeomagnetic data are highly desirable.
In view of the suggestion of the<900 Ma major remagnetization
event in SW Sweden and SW Norway, we can subdivide palaeopoles
into three distinct clusters at 1100 to 1040 Ma, 965 to 915 Ma, and
<900 Ma (Fig. 5), suggesting that the Baltica APWP indeed forms a
loop. The 965 to 915 Ma group is located at∼30
◦ east of the∼1100
to 1040 Ma group, implying a clockwise age progression within this
loop. The age of the ‘younger’ end of the loop (i.e. the time when
Baltica returned from polar to moderate latitudes) is unclear.
There is general agreement that Laurentia and Baltica were part
of the Late Mesoproterozoic to Early Neoproterozoic superconti-
nent Rodinia (e.g. Hoffman 1991; Dalziel 1997; Weil et al. 1998;
Pisarevsky et al. 2003). The presence of nearly coeval loops for the
Laurentian and Baltican APWPs is evidence in support of their in-
corporation in a single supercontinent. However, the present palaeo-
magnetic database for ∼1000 to 800 Ma is insufﬁcient to delineate
the exact shapes of these loops and to provide, for direct compari-
son, precisely dated coeval poles from both continents. As a result,
several different Laurentia-Baltica reconstructions can be accom-
modated (Fig. 6). Geological constraints for these reconstructions
and their implications is discussed by Cawood & Pisarevsky (2006).
Our new results, together with our re-assessment of previous reli-
able results, in light of new geochronological data, provide several
potential key poles for Baltica.
The shape and age progression of the Laurentian APWP for
∼1000 to 800 Ma (the ‘Grenville Loop’) is also debated (Hyodo &
Dunlop 1993; Weilet al.1998; Alvarez & Dunlop 1998; McElhinny
& McFadden 2000; Pisarevskyet al. 2003; Meert & Torsvik 2003).
Most Laurentian poles for this time interval are either from meta-
morphic rocks with ambiguous ages of magnetization (e.g. Buchan
& Dunlop 1976; Warnocket al.2000), or from sedimentary rocks of
imprecisely known age (e.g. Weilet al. 2003). New palaeomagnetic
data from well-dated∼970 to 900 Ma Laurentian rocks are required
to verify the Laurentia-Baltica reconstruction within Rodinia.

Paleomagnetism of the Baiyisi volcanic rocks (ca. 740 Ma)
of Tarim, Northwest China: A continental fragment of
Neoproterozoic Western Australia?
Baochun Huang a,∗, Bei Xu b, Chunxia Zhang a, Yong’an Lic, Rixiang Zhu a
a Paleomagnetism and Geochronology Laboratory (SKL-LE), Institute of Geology and Geophysics, Chinese Academy of Sciences,
Beijing 100029, China
b The Key Laboratory of Orogenic Belts and Crustal Evolution, Peking University, Ministry of Education, Beijing 100871, China
c Institute of Geology and Mineral Resources, Bureau of Geology and Mineral Resources of Xinjiang, Urumqi 830000, China
Received 19 January 2005; received in revised form 15 June 2005; accepted 13 September 2005
Abstract
We report a paleomagnetic pole from the SHRIMP U-Pb zircon dated Baiyisi volcanic rocks in the Xishankou area at the northern
edge of the Tarim Block, Northwest China. Rock magnetic and microscopic observations indicate that the characteristic remanent
magnetization (ChRM) isolated by both thermal and alternating-ﬁeld demagnetization is preserved in original single domain (SD)
or pseudo-single domain (PSD) low-titanium titanomagnetite grains. The new paleomagnetic pole (Q = 5) indicates that the Tarim
Block was located in equatorial paleolatitudes at ca. 740 Ma and was most likely situated against Western Australia during the most
of Neoproterozoic and the early Paleozoic. We suggest that the Tarim Block could be a continental fragment rifted from Western
Australia during the break-up event of the Rodinia supercontinent at ca. 820–750 Ma.

1. Introduction
Following Hoffman’s (1991)earlier Neoproterozoic
reconstruction of the Rodinia supercontinent proposing a
connection between the East and Southeast Asian blocks
and Northern Australia, cumulative studies have shown
that most Eastern Asian blocks were not juxtaposed to
Northern Australia during the Neoproterozoic (e.g. Li
et al., 1995, 1996, 2004; Li and Powell, 2001; Piper and

Yang et al., 2004). For the Tarim Block of central Asia
(Fig. 1a), the connection of Tarim to Northern Australia
has remained unchanged in Neoproterozoic reconstruc-
tions for more than a decade (e.g. Hoffman, 1991; Li
et al., 1996, 2003b; Powell and Pisarevsky, 2002; Chen
et al., 2004). Notwithstanding this, the paleoposition of
the Tarim Block is uncertain for most of the Neoprotero-
zoic. The putative paleogeographic position of Tarim in
Neoproterozoic reconstructions is generally based on (1)
biostratigraphic and tectonostratigraphic correlation of
Neoproterozoic successions between the Tarim Block
and Australia (e.g. Brookﬁeld, 1994; Li et al., 1996 )
and (2) a close early Paleozoic biogeographic and lithos-
tratigraphic association of Tarim with the South China

Block (SCB) and Australia (e.g.Burrett and Richardson,
1980; Burrett et al., 1990; Nie and Rowley, 1991; Shu
and Chen, 1991 ). Although the Tarim Block is known
to incorporate a complete mid- and late-Neoproterozoic
succession, including several horizons of rift volcanics
and three glaciations (e.g. Gao and Qian, 1985; Gao
et al., 1985; Brookﬁeld, 1994; Xiao et al., 2004; Xu et al.,
2005), and some new geochronologic and geochemical
data provide constraints on the ages of the glaciations
and the correlation with glaciations elsewhere (Xu et al.,
2003, 2005; Xiao et al., 2004 ), few reliable paleomag-
netic data have been reported to help for constrain the
geodynamics of the Tarim Block during the Neoprotero-
zoic.
Recently, Chen et al. (2004) reported a paleomag-
netic pole from the 807 ± 12 Ma Aksu dyke swarm
(ADS) in the Aksu area in the northwestern Tarim
Block, and proposed that Tarim might have been jux-
taposed to the north of Australia with the Aksu dykes
being the northward continuation of lamprophyre dykes
and kimberlite pipes in northeast Kimberley district of
Western Australia. This ca. 800 Ma paleomagnetic pole
provided ﬁrsthand evidence for the Kimberley–Tarim
connection (Li et al., 1996 ); however, the small angu-
lar differences between the in situ site-mean direction
for the ADS ( Chen et al., 2004 ) and both the present
earth ﬁeld and geomagnetic dipolar ﬁeld leaves some
doubt about its reliability as a primary paleomagnetic
pole. A variant of the revised Kimberley–Tarim con-
nection ( Chen et al., 2004 ) places the present north-
ern edge of the Tarim Block offshore rather than fac-
ing Australia. Since the thickest and most complete
mid- and late-Neoproterozoic successions were devel-
oped in the Quruktagh region at the northern edge of the
Tarim Block (Fig. 1a and b; Gao and Qian, 1985; Gao
et al., 1985 ) and successive rifting is necessary to pre-
serve such complete successions (Brookﬁeld, 1994), the
revised Kimberley–Tarim connection (Chen et al., 2004)
could have been a short-lived connection and may have
been disaggregated in the break-up of the early Neo-
proterozoic supercontinent at ca. 820–750 Ma (Li et al.,
2003b).
In this paper, we present a paleomagnetic result from
the SHRIMP U-Pb zircon dated Neoproterozoic Baiyisi
volcanic rocks in the Xishankou area at the northern edge
of the Tarim Block, which aims to help us understand
the paleogeography of the mid- and late-Neoproterozoic
glaciations of the Tarim Block, and permit a paleomag-

zoic continental reconstructions.
2. Geology and paleomagnetic sampling
The northern edge of the Tarim Block is well-
known for a thick and almost complete mid- and
late-Neoproterozoic succession characterized by several
horizons of glacial deposits and rift volcanic rocks sep-
arated by thick deposits predominantly of shales, sand-
stones and limestones (Fig. 1b; Gao and Qian, 1985; Gao
et al., 1985; Brookﬁeld, 1994; Xiao et al., 2004; Xu et al.,
2003, 2005). According to the correlation based mainly
on lithology, the Neoproterozoic succession is divided
into lower and upper parts and includes eight formations
(Gao and Zhu, 1984; Gao and Qian, 1985), possibly with
an unconformity between the lower and upper series (e.g.
Wang, 1986). The lower part unconformably overlies
the Mesoproterozoic Pargangtag Group and includes, in
ascending order, the Baiyisi, Zhaobishan, Altungal and
Tereeken formations, whereas the upper part is uncon-
formably overlain by lower Cambrian siliceous rocks
(the Xishanbulak Formation) and is divisible into the
Zhamokti, Yukengol, Shuiquan and Hangelchaok for-
mations (Fig. 1c).
We have sampled the Baiyisi volcanic rocks from
the Xishankou section (41.60
◦N, 86.54◦E) at the west-
ern end of the Quruktagh area, northern Tarim ( Fig. 1a
and b), where three Neoproterozoic formations, Baiy-
isi, Zhaobishan and Altungal could be identiﬁed. The
Baiyisi Formation in Xishankou has a thickness of about
640 m and consists mainly of ﬁve layers (Fig. 1d) com-
prising about 13 m of interbedded layer of sandstones
and mudstones at the base then about 177 m of diamic-
tites followed by ∼23 m of volcanic rocks, ∼23 m of
shales and ∼404 m of volcanic rocks at the top. The
SHRIMP U-Pb age analysis gives a weighted mean age
of 755 ± 15 Ma for sample (Xb006) collected near the
base of the Baiyisi volcanic rocks in the southeast of the
Xinger area ( Xu et al., 2005 ) and indicates the oldest
eruption age of the Baiyisi volcanic rocks. The Baiy-
isi volcanic rocks in Xishankou that appear above the
Baiyisi diamictite unit (Fig. 1d; Xiao et al., 2004)h a v e
also been geochronologically studied and a SHRIMP
U-Pb zircon age of 727 ± 10 Ma has been assigned to
the top horizon of volcanic rocks in the Baiyisi Forma-
tion (Li Z.X., personal communication). Geochemical
studies suggest that the Baiyisi volcanic rocks in the
Xishankou, Saimashan and Xinger areas of Quruktagh
are made up of a bimodal volcanic suite comprising
basalt and dacite-rhyolite, and resembling the tholei-
itic basalts in continental rift ( Gao et al., 1985; Jiang
et al., 2001; Xu et al., 2003, 2005 ). Altogether seven
sites were sampled in basalts using a portable gasoline-
powered drill and oriented by sun compass. For each
site, between 8 and 10 cores were generally collected
from discrete basalt ﬂows, however, because the portable
drill broke down in the ﬁeld, only 4 cores were collected
for the site kz53. The bedding attitude of the Baiyisi
volcanic rocks (Strike/Dip = 305
◦/37◦, α95 = 9.5◦)w a s
determined from eight individual measurements from

lous and perhaps questionable measurement from the
underlying shales (Strike/Dip = 20
◦/45◦), which shows
ca. 90◦ difference in azimuth of strike with the other

3. Results
Following sample preparation one pilot 2.2-cm long
cylindrical specimen from each site was subjected
to acquisition and back-demagnetization of isother-
mal remanent magnetization (IRM) using JR-5A spin-
ner magnetometer and 2G660 pulse magnetizer. These
experiments show saturation to occur by 0.3–0.5 T
with remanence coercivity (Hcr) deduced from back-
demagnetization of the saturation IRM to be less than
50 mT (Fig. 2 ). These results indicate low-coercivity
magnetite or low-titanium titanomagnetite as the pre-
dominant carrier of remanence in the Baiyisi volcanic
rocks.
A total of 51 specimens were subsequently subjected
to either progressive thermal or alternating ﬁeld (AF)
demagnetization. Progressive thermal demagnetization
up to 550–590
◦C was carried out in 17–18 steps in a
MMTD60 thermal demagnetizer with a residual mag-
netic ﬁeld of less than 10 nanotesla (nT) in the cen-
ter of the oven. Progressive AF demagnetization up to
80–90 mT was conducted in 12–13 steps using an AF

4. Discussion
4.1. Origin of the characteristic remanence
Both thermal and alternating-ﬁeld demagnetization
were able to isolate a characteristic remanent mag-
netization up to peak demagnetization temperatures
510–570
◦C in the former case or peak alternating ﬁelds
of 70–90 mT in the latter case. Together with the mag-
netic behavior of acquisition and back-ﬁeld demagne-
tization of the saturation IRM, this implies that the
ChRM component is most likely to be carried by low-

4.2. Neoproterozoic paleogeography of Tarim
There is remarkable similarity in the stratigraphic
sequence, the ages of the Neoproterozoic thermo-
tectonic events, and in the ages of cratonization between
Tarim and South China ( Lu et al., 2003 and references
therein). Hence, it is likely that the Tarim Block might
have been juxtaposed against the SCB during the most
of Neoproterozoic times. The debate regarding the South
China paleoposition within the Neoproterozoic super-

The new ca. 740 Ma paleomagnetic pole indicates that
the Tarim Block was located in equatorial paleolatitudes
supportive of low latitudes for the Sturtian glaciations
(e.g. Evans, 2000 ) and for the hypothesis of a snow-
ball earth (e.g. Hoffman et al., 1998) at ca. 750–720 Ma.
Because of uncertainty of polarity of this new Precam-
brian paleopole, Tarim may have been located adjacent to
Southwestern Australia (positions 1 and 2 inFig. 7) with
either slight counterclockwise or large clockwise rota-

the early Neoproterozoic (position 0 in Fig. 7, dashed
line). However, we prefer to place the Tarim Block in
the vicinity of the Southwestern Australia during ca.
740 Ma with the now north-facing Neoproterozoic to
Devonian passive margin facing the Australia and Maw-
son continents (position 1 in Fig. 7). According to this
conﬁguration, the Tarim Block was subjected to a south-
ward drift with a slight counterclockwise rotation with
respect to its conjectural early Neoproterozoic conﬁgu-
ration after the occurrence of a break-up event in Rodinia
around 820–750 Ma (Li et al., 2003b). A comparison of
paleolatitudes at reference points in Tarim, South China
and Australia shows that the three blocks occupied the
equatorial tropical latitudes during around 750 Ma to the
early Paleozoic (Fig. 8), suggesting that the Tarim Block
could have remained in close proximity to Western Aus-
tralia during the late Neoproterozoic and the early Pale-

and Western Australia between ca. 750 Ma and the early
Paleozoic is coincident with their close Neoproterozoic
tectonostratigraphic records (e.g. Wang, 1986; Li et al.,
1996; Preiss, 2000; Wang and Li, 2003; Xiao et al., 2004;
Xu et al., 2005) and close early Paleozoic trilobite afﬁni-
ties (e.g. Burrett and Richardson, 1980 ). Nevertheless,
detailed relationships between Tarim, South China and
Australia during the late Neoproterozoic and early Pale-
ozoic can be further constructed until more precisely
dated and high-quality paleomagnetic data are available;
at present these are particularly sparse for the Neopro-
terozoic and early Paleozoic of Tarim.

Geological observations provide additional informa-
tion supporting the view that the Tarim Block was
most likely situated against Western Australia during
most of the Neoproterozoic. There is a consensus that
the 807–785 Ma maﬁc dyke swarm in the northwestern
Tarim Block ( Chen et al., 2004 ; Zhang L.F., personal
communication) and the 783 ± 10 Ma bimodal intru-
sive complex in the southwestern Tarim Block ( Zhang
et al., in revision) are signiﬁcant evidence that the Tarim
Block was involved in mantle plume activity beneath
west Rodinia possibly resulting in the break-up of the
supercontinent (Li et al., 2003b ). Meanwhile SHRIMP
U-Pb zircon age and geochemical features of the Baiyisi
volcanic rocks suggest that the Baiyisi glaciation could
correlate with the Chang’an glaciation in the SCB and
the Sturtain-Rapitan glaciation in other Rodinia blocks,
and also suggesting that the Baiyisi bimodal volcan-
ism was part of second global magmatism during the
break-up of Rodinia (Xu et al., 2005). These observations
indicate that the Tarim Block may be a candidate for a
continental fragment that rifted from Western Australia
during plate reorganization associated with the break-
up of Rodinia at ca. 820–750 Ma ( Li et al., 2003b ). A
preliminary mean paleopole obtained from the mid- and
late-Neoproterozoic rocks in Wushi at the northwestern
margin of the Tarim Block that unconformably overlies
the early Neoproterozoic Aksu Group (Gao et al., 1985;

5. Conclusions
A new paleomagnetic pole has been obtained from
the SHRIMP U-Pb zircon dated Baiyisi volcanic rocks
in the Xishankou area of the northeastern edge of the
Tarim Block. Rock magnetic and microscopic observa-
tions indicate that the ChRM preserved in SD or PSD
low-titanium titanomagnetite grains could be primary
remanence. The new ca. 740 Ma paleomagnetic pole
indicates that the Tarim Block was located in equato-
rial paleolatitudes supportive of low latitudes for the
Sturtian glaciations and for the hypothesis of a snowball
earth at ca. 750–720 Ma. Geological information and a
comparison of ca. 750 Ma to early Paleozoic paleolati-
tudes in Tarim, South China and Australia suggest that
the Tarim Block could be a continental fragment rifted
from Western Australia during continental break-up. We
argue that the Tarim Block was most likely situated close
to South China and Western Australia in the early Neo-
proterozoic supercontinent and then drifted to equatorial
paleolatitudes after the putative break-up event at ca.
820–750 Ma. However, further high-quality paleomag-
netic data and geochronologic constraints are essential
to perfect and reﬁne the Neoproterozoic geodynamics of
the Tarim Block.

Abstract
A U–Pb baddeleyite age of 2367± 1 Ma from a diabase dyke together with previously published age data, suggests that a major
early Proterozoic dyke swarm cuts across the structural grain of the Archean Dharwar craton in India. Paleomagnetic data suggest
the swarm is at least 300 km wide and 300 km long and has a fan angle of at least 30
◦ with convergence to the west. It was originally
emplaced at high latitudes, and together with the Widgiemooltha dykes of the Yilgarn block of Australia, may have been a segment
of a larger radiating swarm related to a long-lived plume event that was active for about 50 My from 2418 to 2367 Ma. A regional
change in the intensity of brown feldspar clouding in the dykes suggests that the Dharwar craton was tilted northwards, in harmony
with previous observations on the structure and metamorphism of the Archean rocks. Towards the south the brown feldspar clouding
becomes more intense and locally assumes a blacker, more “sooty” appearance. The black clouding, whose precise origins remain
unknown, is accompanied by a remagnetization and appears to coincide closely with a region of carbonatite magmatism at∼800 Ma,
and with a shear zone and change in structural trend related to Pan-African deformation at∼550 Ma. Paleomagnetic studies suggest
that (i) the high coercivity part of the remanent magnetization is carried by magnetite exsolved within either brown or black clouded
feldspars and (ii) as a more general observation, diabase with brown clouded feldspar can carry a primary magnetization but not if
the clouding is black.

In this paper we present new paleomagnetic and U–Pb
age data that provide a key early Proterozoic paleomag-
netic pole for the Indian subcontinent, and which bear
upon the reality or otherwise of the postulated fan-shaped
swarm from the Dharwar craton.
2. General geology
The Dharwar craton of India is formed of four major
units: the Peninsular gneisses forming a typical Archean
TTG gneiss terrain, greenstone belts, metasedimentary
rocks, and late potassic granites, such as the Closepet
granite (Fig. 1), dated at ∼2.5 Ga (Friend and Nutman,
1991), that form the ﬁnal Archean magmatic event. The
craton can broadly be divided into older western (West-
ern Dharwar Craton: 3.3–2.7 Ga) and younger eastern
(Eastern Dharwar craton: 3.0–2.5 Ga) blocks ( Swami
Nath and Ramakrishnan, 1981; Naqvi and Rogers, 1987;
Chadwick et al., 2000). The regional metamorphic grade
changes gradually southwards across the craton as a
whole from greenschist facies in the north to gran-
ulite facies in charnockitic terrains in the south (Fig. 1).
Rb–Sr whole rocks ages from granites and gneisses in
the eastern Dharwar craton range from about 2545 to
2128 Ma (Table 1 of Pandey et al., 1997 ), suggesting
that Archean ages have been variably reset by a regional
event at ∼2.1 Ga. Paleoproterozoic sedimentary rocks
overlie the Archean basement and include the Cuddapah
basin which is crescent-shaped with gentle easterly dips
in the map area (Fig. 1). Within the Cuddapah basin, vol-
canics occur about 2 km above the base of the sequence
and associated sills give a Rb–Sr whole rock–mineral

in the western Cuddapah basin shows that the curvature
in the units of the Dharwar craton is at least older than
∼2 Ga and was probably established by the end of the
Archean.
The southern boundary of the Dharwar craton is
marked by a major shear zone in amphibolite facies,
that appears to have been active during Pan African
orogenic activity at ∼550 Ma and which separates the
craton from high grade, charnockitic Pan-African ter-
ranes to the south ( Meissner et al., 2002; Santosh et
al., 2003 ). Across this shear zone which occurs close
to many of our sampling sites ( Fig. 1 ), the dominant
NNW-trending structural grain of the Dharwar craton
changes to one with an E to NE trend. At the eastern end
of this shear zone in the vicinity of Harur a number of
carbonatite and associated syenite intrusions occur. The
age of this igneous activity is close to 800 Ma ( Kumar
et al., 1998 , mica and whole rock Rb–Sr isochrons of
770 Ma; Schleicher et al., 1998, whole rock Pb–Pb age
of 801 ± 11 Ma).
3. Proterozoic dyke swarms of the Eastern
Dharwar craton
A basic problem that has hindered until recently the
emergence of a coherent picture of dyke swarm emplace-
ment across the Dharwar craton is that the majority
of radiometric ages have been obtained by the K–Ar
method or its variant, Ar–Ar step heating, and are there-
fore susceptible to error either by inherited argon or by
argon loss. From cross-cutting ﬁeld relations, together
with whole rock K–Ar and paleomagnetic data, at least
four ages of dykes swarms have been proposed in dif-
ferent areas of the craton ( Anjannappa, 1975; Gokhale
and Waghamare, 1989; Radhakrishna and Joseph, 1996;
Poornachandra Rao, 2005 ). On a more regional scale,
from aerial photo, aeromagnetic and ﬁeld studies, as
many as ﬁve different episodes of dyke intrusion have
been proposed around the Cuddapah basin ( Murty et
al., 1987). Most of the dykes are quartz tholeiites and
have trends that are typically E–W, NE and N, but more
alkaline dykes, sometimes with olivine, have N and NW
trends (Murty et al., 1987, their Table 1).
Published paleomagnetic data from the Dharwar cra-
ton up to 1980 was reviewed by Hargraves and Bhalla
(1983) who demonstrated that the various studies of dyke
swarms gave widely scattered and sometimes conﬂicting
data. The relatively low reliability of both the paleo-
magnetic and K–Ar radiometric data as judged by their
associated error estimates may explain the lack of agree-
ment between data from different parts of the craton, with
the result that no convincing pattern of dyke swarm intru-
sion, either spatially or temporally, has emerged. The
range in K–Ar or Ar–Ar ages on dykes has been taken to
mean that the craton has been subjected to many dyking
episodes between 650 and 2400 Ma (e.g. Radhakrishna
and Joseph, 1996; Poornachandra Rao, 2005). However,
a key observation from both Landsat images and ﬁeld
studies is that of the hundreds of dykes having several
trends in the vicinity of the Cuddapah basin ( Murty et
al., 1987), only one has been observed to cut the basal
sedimentary units (see Anand et al., 2003 ), which sug-
gests that the vast majority of the dykes intruded before
∼1.9 Ga.
Radiometric dating using the Sm–Nd, Rb–Sr and
U–Pb methods is beginning to conﬁrm that the dykes
are mainly Paleoproterozoic in age and comprise two
major magmatic episodes centred at ∼2.1 and ∼2.4 Ga.
An E–W trending dyke at location A in Fig. 1 yielded a
Rb–Sr age of 2370 ± 230 Ma (Ikramuddin and Stueber,
1976) and another dyke of the same trend at location
Bi n Fig. 1 has given a Sm–Nd age of 2454 ± 100 Ma
from a 7-point whole rock–mineral isochron (Zachariah
et al., 1995). Sm–Nd data from three NW-trending maﬁc
dykes in a region centred on 16.7
◦N 77.7◦E, NW of
the Cuddapah basin in Fig. 1 , yield an isochron age
of 2173 ± 64 Ma (Pandey et al., 1997 ). More recently,
the Paleoproterozoic ages have been conﬁrmed by U–Pb
age data on baddeleyite and zircon from 11 dykes across
the Dharwar craton showing that the igneous activity
is bracketed between 2.4 and 2.0 Ga, and includes a
U–Pb baddeleyite age of 2365.5± 1.1 Ma from the dyke
at location A ( French et al., 2004 ). The disturbed iso-
topic systems in Archean rocks summarised in Table 1
of Pandey et al. (1997) may in part reﬂect these Paleo-
proterozoic magmatic events.
Paleomagnetic studies on dykes from the Dharwar
craton have proven challenging because surface outcrops
are frequently lightning-struck, and quarries and road
cuts containing fresh exposures are relatively rare. It
has been demonstrated (e.g. Halls, 1991) that the most
stable, highest coercivity and unblocking temperature
remanences in Canadian Paleoproterozoic dykes come
from chilled margins, where magnetite grain sizes are
small. In India the preservation of fresh chilled margins
is relatively rare, so that many paleomagnetic stud-
ies, particularly those prior to ∼1980 have not stressed
chilled margins in sampling strategies, with the result
that interior samples have yielded generally low coer-

civity remanences. These magnetizations show a large
within-site directional dispersion because of the difﬁ-
culty in separating them from more dominant lightning
and recent weathering components.
A key paleomagnetic study was that by Dawson and
Hargraves (1994) who obtained a stable characteristic
remanence with a steep negative inclination from three
E–W trending dykes at location A (including the one
dated by the U–Pb dated method), southwest of the Cud-
dapah basin. In the same area a steep down direction
characterised N–S trending alkaline dykes one of which
yielded a Rb–Sr age of 810 ± 25 Ma (Ikramuddin and
Stueber, 1976). A second key paper was that by Kumar
and Bhalla (1983) who reported an easterly dyke (loca-
tion C in Fig. 1), also with a steep negative inclination
(D =7 0
◦ I = −73◦), that yielded a positive baked contact
test where it was observed to cut another dyke with NE
trend from which three sites remote from the intersection
gave a consistent magnetization direction that averaged
D = 64, I = −7
◦. This result suggests that the steep neg-
ative direction as found in easterly trending dykes is
a primary one. No paleomagnetic work has been done
on the dyke at location B in Fig. 1. A summary of the
most reliable published paleomagnetic results that show
a steep negative inclination indicates that nearly all of
them are from WNW to ENE trending dykes (Table 1and
Fig. 2). A notable exception occurs in the granulite ter-
ranes of the southern Dharwar where NE trending dykes
also show the steep negative component (Radhakrishna
and Joseph, 1996).
In a seminal paper Pichamuthu (1959) showed that
the maﬁc dykes of the Dharwar craton show increased
cloudiness of their groundmass feldspars towards the
south. A similar observation occurs in the 2445 Ma Mat-
achewan dyke swarm of Canada where it was shown
that the clouding is the result of the exsolution of mag-
netite and other minerals, possibly including amphibole,
from the feldspar lattice as a result of slow cooling at
large crustal depths (Halls and Zhang, 1995, 2003). The
intensity of the clouding was shown to increase with
the depth of exhumation in the Matachewan swarm, so
that it gives a crude measure of the crustal depth at
which the exposed part of the dyke originally resided.
In the Dharwar craton, granite and volcano-sedimentary
belts at greenschist facies metamorphism pass south-
wards to higher grade charnockitic terranes in granulite
facies. This, together with the increased clouding of the
groundmass feldspars and the analogous properties of
Matachewan dykes ( Halls and Zhang, 1995 ), suggests
that the craton has been tilted northwards following the
emplacement of the dykes. This conclusion is in harmony
with previous observations of NNW-plunging folds in
the Archean (Pichamuthu, 1953) and petrological studies
of the Closepet granite that show a northward decrease in
crustal depth from about 26 to 14 km in 300 km (Moyen
et al., 2003).
In Canada the Matachewan dykes that exhibit feldspar
clouding, have been uplifted at approximately 2.0 Ga,
some 20 km along a major crustal uplift known as the
Kapuskasing Zone, yet still retain a paleomagnetic direc-
tion that is similar to dykes from shallower crustal levels
outside the uplifted area. It was shown that the clouding
causes a stable, high coercivity remanence that resides
in the ﬁne-grained magnetite exsolved in the feldspars,
and that this remanence dated from the general time of
Matachewan igneous activity rather than being a product
of a later geological event (Halls and Zhang, 2003).
4. Field and experimental methods
4.1. Geochemistry and petrography
To help identify dykes that are geochemically dis-
tinct from others and which may therefore belong to
different magmatic episodes, 20 samples of chilled mar-
gins, representing 12 different dykes, were analysed for
major, minor and trace elements. Lower detection lim-
its are ± 0.01 % for major elements and approximately
2 ppm for Rb, Sr, and Y , 3 ppm for Zr, 5 ppm for Cr and
20 ppm for Ba. Petrographic thin sections were obtained
for all dyke interiors, with particular attention paid to
clouding intensity of the feldspars as originally reported
by Pichamuthu (1959). Polished thin sections were also
obtained for reﬂected light examination and for use on
the scanning electron microscope in the Geology Depart-
ment, University of Toronto, in order to study the nature
of the feldspar clouding.
4.2. U–Pb geochronology
All U–Pb analytical work was carried out in the Jack
Satterly Geochronology Laboratory (JSGL) at the Uni-
versity of Toronto. Samples for geochronology were
collected from quarries in the central, coarse-grained
portion of a 20–30 m thick diabase dyke, striking 290
◦,
at paleomagnetic site 2, near Yeragumballi (WSW of
Henur, Fig. 1). A small quantity (approximately 0.25 kg)
of fresh drill core material was crushed and ﬁnely
ground using standard jaw crusher and disc mill tech-
niques, and then decanted in water of its suspended ﬁnes.
The residue was treated with conventional heavy liquid
methods and Frantz
TM isodynamic magnetic separation
techniques in order to isolate the least magnetic grains
within the dense mineral fractions. Roughly 20 grains

4.3. Paleomagnetism
A total of 24 paleomagnetic sites were obtained from
ENE – to ESE – trending dykes (Fig. 1), comprising on
average about six block samples oriented by both sun
and magnetic compass. Many sites lacked chilled mar-
gins, a few were in quarries but most were from natural
outcrops. After the blocks were cored, the cores were
cut into cylindrical specimens 2.45 cm in length and in
diameter. At least one specimen per sample was subject
to detailed stepwise alternating ﬁeld (AF) demagnetiza-
tion, using a Schonstedt TD-1 instrument, to a maximum
ﬁeld of 100 mT, in order to separate components by their
coercivity. Thermal demagnetization using a Schonst-
edt TSD-1 was also carried out on selected specimens
and sometimes on those that had previously been AF
demagnetized. After each incremental demagnetization
step, the natural remanent magnetization (NRM) was
measured at the Erindale paleomagnetic laboratory on
a modiﬁed DIGICO magnetometer with reproducibil-
ity down to 10
−3 Am−1. This instrument is equipped
with a software routine designed to average out vari-
ations in magnetization directions that are a function
of the last demagnetization axis in single axis demag-
netizers and which become more apparent once the
NRM intensity falls below about 20% of its initial value.
This averaging routine was particularly important in the
Indian samples because the characteristic component
was often only isolated below 5% of the NRM intensity.
The directional data were then analysed using Principal
Component Analysis (Kirschvink, 1980) in combination
with stereoplots and vector diagrams, following nor-
mal paleomagnetic procedures. Acceptance criteria for
linear segments on vector diagrams were: number of con-
secutive demagnetization points ≥3 and the maximum
angle of deviation ( Kirschvink, 1980) ≤10
◦. The vari-
ation of susceptibility as a function of temperature to
700
◦C, using a Sapphire Instruments SI3 meter, was
also obtained on selected samples in order to identify
remanence carriers.
5. Results
5.1. Petrography
5.1.1. Primary mineralogy and texture
Representative photomicrographs of all dykes are
characterised by approximately equal proportions of
clinopyroxene and plagioclase constituting about 90% of
the rock (Fig. 3). The clinopyroxene is subhedral, occa-
sionally anhedral, and the overall texture is equigranular,
rarely sub-ophitic. Accessory minerals form the remain-
ing 10% and approximately in order of abundance are:
(1) a strongly pleochroic (yellow green to blue green)
amphibole which rims the clinopyroxene and also occurs
as isolated grains; (2) myrmekite, often with larger areas
of quartz; (3) biotite and magnetite, often intergrown;
(4) orthopyroxene in corroded grains lying with clinopy-
roxene and (5) apatite needles, abundant in areas of
myrmekite. In the lower metamorphic grade areas of
the Dharwar craton, chlorite and uralite become more
conspicuous. Baddeleyite and/or zircon may be respon-
sible for pleochroic haloes seen in amphibole, biotite and
chlorite grains but due to the paucity of these minerals in
most of the dykes, only sites 2, 10 and 25 were identiﬁed
as possible candidates for U–Pb dating. Olivine, titanite
and epidote were not positively identiﬁed in any of the
thin sections. All the dykes are extremely similar in their
primary mineralogy and texture and differ only in degree
of alteration.

In the more northern sites, pyroxene is more altered to
a ﬁbrous amphibole (probably uralite) and dirty aggre-
gates, and plagioclase is more saussuritised. However in

probability of ﬁt). This result is interpreted to represent a

5.4. Geochemistry
Major and minor element geochemical results from
fresh chilled margins show ( Fig. 11) that the dykes are
iron-rich tholeiites, with MgO typically about 5 wt.%,
TiO
2 about 1.5 wt.% and Fe 2O3 at about 14–17 wt.%
(Table A1). They show that all the dykes, whether from
black-clouded feldspar dykes like sites 6 and 14, or from
brown-clouded ones like 3, 10 and 19, have extremely
similar compositions consistent with their being from the
same swarm. However,Table A2shows that dyke 25 with
a trend of 265
◦ has distinctly higher Ba and lower Y/Zr
values, suggesting it may not share the same petrogenesis
as the other dykes. Preliminary U–Pb results from two
fractions of baddeleyite from this dyke suggest a primary
crystallization age of approximately 1894 Ma, indicating
that dyke 25 could be a feeder to the Cuddapah sills,
and therefore is distinct from the older 2367 Ma diabase
swarm that is the focus of this study.
6. Discussion
The direction of the B component (Fig. 7) is close to
that of the Present Earth’s ﬁeld (D = 358
◦, I = +10◦)s oi t
could be ascribed to relatively recent tropical weather-
ing. However, in many southern sites (e.g. 3, 5 and 16)
that show B in addition to A, samples were taken from
deep quarries, where recent weathering extends 2–3 m
below the surface. Also in these sites and others (6, 7, 9,
13, 14 and 15) where only B is found, the dykes do not
show any evidence of hydrous alteration; the feldspars
and pyroxene are as fresh as in other southern sites. The
only difference in thin section appears to be in the nature
of the feldspar inclusions whereby those samples show-
ing component A have feldspars that show the brown
tea-colour clouding, and those that show B have cloudy
areas that are completely or partially converted to the
sooty appearance. Therefore some metamorphic event
under dry crustal conditions may be responsible. What-
ever the nature of the event it occurs over a distance
of about 300 km being recorded in two areas of dykes
(sites 13–15 and 5–9) and also from dykes in between
which also carry the B remanence (seeFig. 2and Table 2
of Radhakrishna and Joseph, 1996). A curious property
of the alteration is that it occurs locally often within
a few kilometres of dykes with brown feldspar cloud-
ing that display only the A remanence. The area of B
remanence closely coincides with the major Pan African
shear zone (Drury and Holt, 1980; Meissner et al., 2002),
which lies less than 30 km south of our most southerly
sites in the Henur area, but appears to pass through the
region where sites 13–15 are located ( Figs. 2 and 5 ).
The lack of secondary hydrous minerals in the dykes
carrying sooty feldspars suggests that the conversion
from brown to sooty clouding has involved an alter-
native ﬂuid such as CO
2. A B-like component, found
in Archean host rocks, is more common in the SE part
of Fig. 1 (Piper et al., 2003) where carbonatite igneous
activity at ∼800 Ma is most common. About 5 km east
of Salem, SW of the Harur sites ( Fig. 1) plagioclase in
charnockites has developed clouding close to carbonatite
veins (R. Srinivasan, unpublished data) and fenitization
of the host rocks in the vicinity of the carbonatites has
been reported (Borodin et al., 1971). These observations
suggest that CO
2-charged magmatic ﬂuids associated
with carbonatite emplacement are capable of causing
the sooty clouding. Charnockite formation during the
∼550 Ma Pan- African orogenic cycle has been reported
from south of the shear zone (Santosh et al., 2003) so that
CO
2 ﬂushing associated with this event (e.g.Piper et al.,
2003) may also be responsible for the sooty clouding
and hence the B component. In terms of their petrogra-
phy, geochemistry, and the occasional survival of the A
component, as in site 5, dykes exhibiting sooty feldspar
clouding are similar to the dykes with brown clouding.
Their trend is also similar except in the extreme southeast
where dykes at sites 13–15 have a more NW trend. How-
ever, these dykes show more signs of shearing, appear to
lie within the shear zone, and therefore may have been
rotated. One important point is that if the B component
is caused by ∼550 Ma charnockite formation and/or by
800 Ma carbonatite activity, its direction is very different
from the steep direction recorded in the∼800 Ma Haro-
halli alkaline dykes by Dawson and Hargraves (1994) ,
although the highly altered nature of these dykes ren-
ders the primary nature of their pole uncertain. The B
pole lies close to the Indian apparent polar wander path,
about 30
◦ from that of the 760 Ma Malani rhyolite in
NW India (Torsvik et al., 2001) on the younger side of
the Indian apparent polar wander path, so we surmise that
the Neoproterozoic was characterised by shallow rather
than by steep inclinations in southern India.
Important conclusions from our observations are that
a primary component (A) resides in dykes with brown
feldspar clouding and that a secondary (B) magnetization
is preserved in those dyke with black feldspar clouding.
The precise mechanism by which the sooty clouding has
formed is unknown, but we may speculate that CO

produced during the ∼800 Ma carbonatite event and/or
by later charnockite formation associated with the Pan-
African orogen, combined with Fe in the feldspar to
produce magnetite and carbon. We would envisage that
this process would be pervasive at deep crustal levels,
but could also occur at shallower depths where CO
2
could move along dyke chilled margins (such as at
site 3) and other potential zones of fracture. Scanning
electron microscopy shows that micron to sub-micron
grains include magnetite, and that many smaller ones, as
opposed to few larger ones, seem to respectively char-
acterize the sooty and brown clouding types, but further
work is required to examine the feldspars for carbon.
Regardless of the exact mechanism by which the sooty
clouding is produced, our empirical observations sug-
gest that petrographically fresh diabase dykes exhibiting
plagioclase feldspars with a black, rather than brown
clouding, have been remagnetized.
Component C is found as the characteristic compo-
nent in one dyke (No. 26, Table 2) and therefore may
signify a different magmatic episode. The same direc-
tion occurs along with A and B at site 5 and has been
reported from NNW trending dykes in northern Kerala
by Radhakrishna et al. (1986) and also as a signiﬁcant
component in the Archean host rocks (Piper et al., 2003,
their Fig. 17).
The mean pole position for the A component incor-
porating the present data and with the site acceptance
criteria of N ≥ 4 and α
95 ≤ 15◦ gives a pole position of
Plat = 13.6◦N, Plong = 59.6◦E, N = 7 andA95 = 13.9◦ or its
antipode (Fig. 12A). Our pole results agree at the 95%
conﬁdence level with the mean pole position calculated
from all published data satisfying the same acceptance
criteria ( Fig. 12 B, Table 5). The combined pole posi-
tion using all the data is: P
lat = 15.7◦N, Plong = 56.9◦E,
N = 25 and A95 = 5.6◦ (Fig. 12C). One important obser-
vation, seen in both independent data sets ( Fig. 12 A
and B) is a bimodal separation of basically equatorial
paleopoles versus others of higher paleolatitude. Expla-
nations for the bimodal behaviour are either that two
dyke populations of different age are represented, or that
the lower paleolatitudes are the result of contamination
of component A by B or B-like components. All sam-
ples contributing directional estimates to Fig. 12A were
examined for the presence of component B. It was found
that 44 samples yielding A remanence declinations in
the SE quadrant and thus the higher latitude paleopoles,
whether from dyke or host rock, were 100% free of com-
ponent B. However, of 31 samples with A declinations
in the NE quadrant and thus yielding the lower latitude
paleopoles, two thirds contained the B component. On
average the former group more frequently gave stable
end-points whereas the latter one gave linear segments
that did not pass through the origin or were less well-
determined while still passing the acceptability criteria
for linearity. The conclusion is that below about 5% of
NRM intensity where many A segments were deﬁned,
B-like components may still contaminate the data. How-
ever, the lack of streaking and the formation of a cluster
of poles that become less Fisherian after removal of the
low latitude poles, suggests that the combined mean of all
the data is probably the best estimate of the pole position,
as given in Table 5.
A search of the IAGA Global Paleomagnetic data
base (http://dragon.ngu.no) and the compilation byErnst
and Buchan (2001) does not reveal any other dykes
with well-determined primary paleomagnetic poles and
an age similar to 2367 Ma. The closest age is that
for the Widgiemooltha dykes in western Australia
(2410–2418 Ma, Doehler and Heaman, 1998; Nemchin
and Pidgeon, 1998), which also cut orthogonally across
the structural grain of granite-greenstone belts in the
Archean Yilgarn block. A continental reconstruction
(Fig. 13) shows that India and Australia are both at high
paleolatitudes, and that the dyke trends (and greenstone
belts) can be made similar at the closest approach of the
two cratons when they are only about 2000 km apart.
Since paleolongitude is not constrained by the paleo-
magnetic data, either continent is free to move around its
paleolatitude. InFig. 13two positions of India are shown
to illustrate that the two sets of dykes may represent
segments of a giant radiating swarm, centred approx-
imately at the pole, that are either close together or
far apart. The 50 My age difference between the Indian
and Widgiemooltha dykes does not necessarily mitigate
against them being the product of a single plume. In
the Lake Superior Region a large radiating swarm, with

about 50 My long if gabbro–anorthosite bodies of the
2490–2475 Ma East Bull Lake intrusive suite ( James
et al., 2002 ), found in the focal region of the swarm,
are related. Both radiating swarms suggest a long-lived
and episodic plume that was virtually stationary during
each magmatic “event”. It is therefore speculated that
the Dharwar and Widgiemooltha dykes also represent
part of a long-lived plume from which the dykes radiate.
The Widgiemooltha swarm has, like the Indian dykes,
an overall tholeiitic composition ( Hallberg, 1987)b u t
contains more olivine-bearing, more MgO-rich, dykes
towards the centre of the Yilgarn block ( Fig. 11 A).
However a Ti–Zr–Y plot (Pearce and Cann, 1973) can-
not distinguish between the two dyke sets ( Fig. 11B).
Detailed incompatible trace element investigations that
may be able to demonstrate a genetic connection have
yet to be carried out on either swarm.
7. Conclusions
U–Pb geochronological and paleomagnetic data sug-
gest that a major radiating dyke swarm, at least 300 km
wide and with an age of 2367± 1 Ma, crosses the Dhar-
war craton of India. The associated paleomagnetic pole,
derived from a primary remanence, suggests that India
was at high latitudes at this time. Despite the uncertainty
in paleolongitude, a position for the Dharwar craton
can be found that is only about 2000 km away from
the Yilgarn craton in Australia as given by 2415 Ma
Widgeimooltha dykes, and is such that the dyke trends
are similar. Given the observation that some Paleopro-
terozoic radiating swarms have durations of the order of
50 My, it is possible that the Widgiemooltha and Dharwar
dyke suites have issued from a common plume centre.
A comparison of the paleomagnetic response from
Dharwar dykes differing only in the character of their
feldspar clouding, suggests that black feldspar clouding
is a carrier of secondary magnetization, in this case prob-
ably associated with Neoproterozoic carbonatite activity
at 800 Ma and/or with Pan-African charnockite forma-
tion at ∼550 Ma, whereas diabase with brown clouding
yields a magnetization that is more likely to be primary
or temporally close to primary. This is an important
observation given that the characteristic component in
many dykes is deﬁned only at the highest coercivities,
where magnetite inclusions in feldspar are likely to form
a signiﬁcant fraction of the magnetic carriers.

The McKinnons gold mine, *35 km southwest of Cobar in New South Wales is a non-operational
opencut mine with extensive regolith proﬁle development down to a depth of *80 m. Twenty-three
oriented paleomagnetic samples, from saprolite at different levels through the proﬁle, yielded two well-
deﬁned paleomagnetic poles, one of Paleocene age (60 + 10 Ma), and the other of Miocene age
(15 + 4 Ma). These reﬂect two periods of remagnetisation associated with deep, intense, oxidative
weathering under humid conditions. They provide important time constraints for the history of climate
change, weathering and landscape evolution of the Cobar region.
KEY WORDS: Cobar, McKinnons mine, New South Wales, paleomagnetic poles, regolith, weathering.
INTRODUCTION
Time constraints are critical for a proper understanding
of landscape evolution. Speciﬁc weathering and land-
scape evolution events are generally difﬁcult to constrain,
and an age range provided by stratigraphy may be the
only temporal constraint that can be obtained (Pillans
2005). Generally speaking, regolith-dating methods, such
as radiocarbon, luminescence, U-series and cosmogenic
nuclides, are restricted to dating events less than ca 5M a
(Pillans 1998). More ancient weathering events in regolith
materials can be dated by methods such as argon dating
(K–Ar and
40Ar/39Ar) (Vasconcelos et al . 1992; Dammer
et al. 1996), paleomagnetism (Idnurm & Senior 1978;
O’Sullivanet al.2 0 0 0 ) ,d18O of clays (Bird & Chivas 1989)
and (U–Th)/He (Pidgeon et al. 2004; Heim et al. 2006).
Different geochronological techniques date different
weathering and landscape-forming events. For example,
paleomagnetism dates the terminal, dehydration stages
of intense, chemical weathering or increased seasonal-
ity (Idnurm & Schmidt 1986), while d
18O clay dating
records periods of mineral formation under more
generally humid conditions (Bird 1988). Thus, different
methods may be combined to give a range of different
ages for different materials and processes from the same
proﬁle.
Thick regolith proﬁles are developed in the Cobar
region and have altered the surface expressions of ore
bodies at the Elura, CSA, Peak, New Cobar and
McKinnons mines. However, apart from the recent
study by McQueen et al . (2007), little is known about
the age of the regolith in the Cobar region. Here we
report the results of a paleomagnetic dating study of the
weathering proﬁle at the McKinnons gold mine, 35 km
southwest of Cobar.
PALEOMAGNETIC DATING OF REGOLITH
IN AUSTRALIA
Principles
The most important mineral for paleomagnetic dating of
ferruginous weathered proﬁles in Australia is hematite,
which is chemically stable within the regolith (Idnurm
& Schmidt 1986). The characteristic remanence carried
by hematite is a chemical remanent magnetisation
(CRM), acquired during weathering of regolith materi-
als under oxidising conditions (Butler 1992). An
important characteristic of such CRMs is that they are
acquired over sufﬁciently long periods of time ( 410 ka)
to average out secular variation of the Earth’s magnetic
ﬁeld. They can thus be used to determine paleomagnetic
pole positions. Furthermore, extended or intense weath-
ering generally results in the destruction of any prior
remanent magnetisation. Thus, paleomagnetic ages

from regolith materials are related to weathering
events, rather than the time of rock formation.
In our experience, the preservation of a stable
magnetic remanence in regolith is favoured when
hematite is formed in intensely weathered saprolite,
below the zone of modern soil formation, and below any
transported cover. In their review of paleomagnetic
studies of regolith proﬁles, Idnurm & Schmidt (1986)
postulated that two key environmental conditions for
the formation of deep, chemically weathered proﬁles are
a humid climate, favourable to chemical weathering,
and a low-relief topography. Idnurm & Schmidt (1986)
also outlined the necessary factors for the development
of stable remanence, and concluded that these factors
preclude continuous magnetisation. Rather, they appear
to be best met in dehydration reactions during the
terminal stages of intense weathering, or shortly after
the intense weathering has ceased. Thus, while mag-
netic minerals may be precipitated, altered, dissolved
and re-precipitated during the formation of a weathered
proﬁle, the age of acquisition is likely to correspond to
the latter stages of active weathering.
Paleomagnetic weathering ages are calculated by
comparing weathering poles with the Australian
Apparent Polar Wander Path (AAPWP). In this study
we use the AAPWP of Schmidt & Clark (2000) as our
reference path, which includes the revised Late Meso-
zoic to Cenozoic poles of Idnurm (1985, 1994).
Previous work
One of the ﬁrst studies to use the AAPWP for dating
weathering events in Australia was by Schmidt &
Embleton (1976), who reported paleomagnetic results
from Late Paleozoic and Mesozoic rocks in the Perth
Basin and adjacent areas of Western Australia. They
identiﬁed a stable high-temperature magnetisation,
which was similar in direction for all rocks, regardless
of age, and which they interpreted as a blanket
remagnetisation resulting from a period of regional
lateritisation. The age of the weathering-induced re-
magnetisation was estimated to be Late Oligocene to
Early Miocene by comparison with the AAPWP of
McElhinny & Embleton (1974). More recent revisions
of the AAPWP (Idnurm 1985, 1994) indicate a Late
Miocene or Pliocene age (6 + 4 Ma). Schmidt et al .
(1976) studied two sites in South Australia—a sub-
basaltic weathering proﬁle on Kangaroo Island and red
clays in the Springﬁeld Basin, near the Flinders
Ranges—and found similar paleomagnetic poles to those
from the Perth Basin, with similarity to a secondary
(overprint) pole from the Montejinni Limestone in the
Northern Territory (Luck 1970). They concluded that the
poles may reﬂect a synchronous weathering event that
affected a large area of Australia.
Several studies have yielded ages ranging from latest
Cretaceous through to Neogene at various sites across
the continent (Pillans 1977; Idnurm & Senior 1978; Bishop
et al. 1982; Schmidt et al. 1982; Schmidt & Ollier 1988; Nott
et al. 1991; Acton & Kettles 1996). Idnurm & Senior (1978)
determined a mid-Paleocene paleomagnetic age for
the widespread, ferruginous Morney weathering proﬁle
in the Eromanga and Surat Basins in Queensland.
Subsequent work by Pillans (2002, 2005) at a number of
sites has yielded similar mid-Paleocene ages suggesting
that these represent another continent-wide episode of
intense, deep oxidative weathering in Australia.
Other studies have reported pre-Late Cretaceous
paleomagnetic weathering ages (summarised in Pillans
2005). In the Cobar region, at the New Cobar mine, 3 km
southeast of Cobar, a Jurassic age has been obtained by
Pillans ( in McQueen et al. 2007). At the Northparkes
copper–gold mine, near Parkes in central New South
Wales Pillans et al . (1999) reported mid-Carboniferous
weathering ages. When combined with apatite ﬁssion-
track data (O’Sullivan et al . 2000), the paleomagnetic
data showed that the landscape at Northparkes had
undergone multiple phases of stability and weathering
as well as kilometre-scale burial and erosion.
REGIONAL GEOLOGY
The Early Devonian Cobar Basin (Figure 1) located in
central western New South Wales, forms part of the
Central Subprovince of the Lachlan Orogen. The basin
formed in a backarc, intracratonic basin setting, with
coeval deep-water troughs and ﬂanking shallow-water
shelves (Glen 1987; Glen et al. 1996). It was inverted and
structurally deformed in the Middle Devonian to
Carboniferous. The basin ﬁll (Nurri Group and
Amphitheatre Group) consists of sedimentary rocks,
mainly of siliciclastic facies. Trough sediments depos-
ited during initial basin rifting included turbidites, very
minor volcanic rocks and, nearby, minor limestones
(Nurri Group, lower Amphitheatre Group and Bidda-
birra Formation). Later inﬁlling deposits were mainly
deep-water turbidites of the Biddabirra Formation and
upper Amphitheatre Group (Glen et al . 1985; Byrnes
1993). Older, Paleozoic rocks are dominantly metasedi-
mentary sequences, including the Girilambone and
Wagga Groups, and intruding Silurian granites. The
Lower Devonian Cobar Supergroup is partly overlain by
Lower to Upper Devonian ﬂuvial sediments of the Mulga
Downs Group (Byrnes 1993; Glen et al. 1996).
Sediments of the Mesozoic Eromanga and Surat
Basins overlie the Paleozoic rocks north of the Cobar
region, and the Cenozoic Murray Basin onlaps to the
southwest (Figure 1). The Eromanga Basin contains
major transgressive–regressive sequences spanning the
Jurassic to mid-Cretaceous. The last marine incursion
into the Eromanga–Surat Basin ended in the Albian
(ca 110 Ma), and since that time the region is inferred to
have been subaerially exposed (Frakes et al . 1987). The
Murray Basin consists of mostly non-marine sands, silts
and clays with some poorly lithiﬁed marine sedimen-
tary rocks in the south. These are overlain by Quatern-
ary duneﬁelds and ﬂuvio-lacustrine sediments (Brown
& Stephenson 1991), the character of which generally
reﬂects the change to a more arid climate and related
landscape processes.
Rocks in the Cobar Basin are deeply and intensely
weathered with leached outcrops, residual soils, and
alluvial and colluvial cover of varying thickness
(McQueen et al. 2007). The region has generally low
relief, with more resistant, locally siliciﬁed lithologies

MCKINNONS MINE
The McKinnons mine is located near the southwestern
margin of the Cobar Basin (Figure 1) near the axial trace
of the Nullawarra Anticline, a major northwest (F
1)-
trending fold hinge (Glen 1987). It is hosted by low-grade
metasedimentary rocks of the lower Amphitheatre
Group (Early Devonian), which includes turbiditic
siltstones and sandstones and limestone lenses. The
McKinnons deposit is in an erosional setting of subdued
relief with undulating low rises ( 520 m). Progressive
erosional stripping and downward development of the
weathering proﬁle resulted from gentle northward
tilting of this part of the Cobar Basin during the Early
Cenozoic (Duk-Rodkin et al. 2004). This is also evidenced
by apparently decreasing depths of erosion to the north.
Weathering at the McKinnons mine extends to more
than 80 m depth (Figure 2), with the economic miner-
alisation only found in the saprolite (Marshall & Scott
1999; McQueen et al . 2005). A detailed study of the
geology and structure of the McKinnons deposit can be
found in Elliott et al. (1998). Representative paleomag-
netic samples were taken from several areas of the
McKinnons openpit (Figure 3), with most from highly
ferruginous saprolite which is known to yield more
reliable paleomagnetic results.
Samples
At the base of the pit, the oxidation (weathering) front is
irregular and largely controlled by joints, shear zones
and other fractures. Samples taken from this area of the
pit are characterised by grey to greenish and dark-red to
orange mottles, a subhorizontal bedding fabric with iron
staining and vertical quartz-veins-ﬁlling cleavage, up to
1 m from the faults (samples MCK21–MCK23: Figure 2).

The main (unmined) sulﬁde lens is also partly
weathered, with a green to yellow clay-rich coating, up
to 1 mm thick on the exposed surfaces. The smaller,
subsidiary sulﬁde lenses are dark-grey to black, in ﬁne-
grained, massive sandstone with a siliciﬁed, blocky
outcrop pattern. This material is orthogonally jointed
with inﬁlling iron oxides. The rims of the lenses are
characterised by more intensively oxidised material
than the immediately adjacent parts of the proﬁle.
Around the sulﬁde lenses, iron oxidation and other
weathering is still strongly controlled by shear zones,
and has resulted in pinkish coloration of the surround-
ing saprock.
The bleached saprolite zone is the most prominent
part of the regolith proﬁle at the McKinnons mine
(Figure 2). As with all other parts of the proﬁle it is
heavily siliciﬁed, with a major clay component. Macro-
scopic features such as jointing have been preserved,
but bedding and other primary sedimentary structures
have been largely destroyed where mineralisation is

present. The bleached saprolite is generally friable or
clay-rich, and unsuitable for paleomagnetic work. How-
ever, there are oxidised patches with concentric bands
of pink, purple, yellow and red material, similar in
appearance to liesegang banding, from which blocks
were taken. Samples were also taken from the top of the
bleached saprolite zone (samples MCK01–MCK04,
MCK19–MCK20: Figure 2). These came from parts of
the proﬁle with concentric iron banding, which appears
more intensely ferruginised than oxidised patches
deeper in the bleached saprolite.
An intensely weathered and oxidised zone lies
between the bleached zone and overlying mottled zone,
from about 15 to 30 m depth (Figure 2). There is a major
north–south shear associated with this heavily oxidised,
bright red, yellow and orange material. It is generally
blocky, and heavily jointed. In the southwestern corner
of the McKinnons mine, there is a small pit, which
exposes the transition from the bleached saprolite zone
to the more ferruginous, upper zones. Material here
consists of red, siliciﬁed and strongly fractured rock
associated with a shear zone. There is iron oxide zoning,
generally with a red core, orange transition zone and
yellow-brown margin concentrated along and parallel to
fractures. Eight samples were collected from this area
(samples MCK05–MCK07, MCK13–MCK18: Figure 2).
The mottled zone at the McKinnons pit (Figure 2)
contains two types of mottling. The upper part has
mottles (10–100 cm in width) with both nodular and
apparently bedding-parallel iron oxide concentrations.
The latter include thin, resistant iron oxide material
alternating with slightly thicker, less resistant iron
oxides, which appear to pick out compositional banding
in the parent rock. An area of mega-mottling immedi-
ately underlies this mottling. The mega-mottles consist
of large (1–3 m wide), irregular patches of iron oxide-
rich material separated by varying thicknesses of
bleached white or orange, clay-rich material. Samples
were collected from both the mottles and mega-mottles
(samples MCK08–MCK11: Figure 2).
A veneer of red soil, up to 70 cm thick, overlies the
mottled zone (Figure 2). In some places a thin stone-line
is developed at the interface of the soil and saprolite. In
the northeast corner and east wall of the pit there is a
*65 m-wide oblique section through a channel-ﬁll
deposit, which contains rounded and poorly sorted
debris of generally coarse, mixed lithologies (quartz,
siltstones and sandstones). The channel boundary is
characterised a thick, calcareous layer. Mottling is
strongly developed in the channel sediments.

compass or a Brunton compass, as described in Butler
(1992). Several standard paleomagnetic cubes ( *8c m

RESULTS
NRM directions from the McKinnons samples are
distributed around the modern pole position. Demagne-
tisation curves were multicomponent, with usually only
one easily deﬁnable component (Figure 3), which
displayed both normal and reversed directions, and
were stable to high temperatures. A stereoplot of the
characteristic remanent magnetisation (ChRM) direc-
tions highlights the two different populations (Figure 4).
Thermal demagnetisation results for specimens from
one block (MCK23) were not analysed, because a large
increase in susceptibility indicated formation of a
heating-induced magnetisation. No other specimens
displayed this behaviour.

IMPLICATIONS FOR REGIONAL REGOLITH
DEVELOPMENT AND LANDSCAPE EVOLUTION
Traditional models of landscape evolution for central
and western New South Wales have emphasised pene-
planation or pediplanation concepts of classical geomor-
phology (King 1950; Langford-Smith and Dury 1965;
Dury 1966; Ongley 1970). Some of these models also
implied that duricrust layers (silcretes and indurated
ferruginous zones) could be used as continuous
morphostratigraphic markers. However, more recent
studies have focused on the signiﬁcance of drainage
evolution and changes in base-level in the surrounding
Mesozoic and Cenozoic sedimentary basins (Spry 1999,
2003; Gibson & Chan 1999). These later studies have
found evidence for a variety of differently aged features
and similar regolith materials preserved in various parts
and levels of the landscape. This is consistent with a
landscape evolution model incorporating continuous and
concomitant weathering, erosion and deposition, primar-
ily controlled by bedrock lithology and structure, climate
and, to a lesser degree, tectonics. Ferruginised and
siliciﬁed regolith materials, which are resistant to
further chemical weathering and erosion, have also
exerted a signiﬁcant lithological control on landscape
development. Parts of the Cobar region were inundated
by the Albian marine transgression into the Eromanga
Basin (Exon & Senior 1976; Frakes et al. 1987; Spry 1999;
Gibson & Chan 1999). Since that time the region is
thought to have been subaerially exposed. Incised

The results of the present study clearly demonstrate

the McKinnons area during the Cenozoic by demon-

(ca 15 Ma). This is also consistent with broadly similar
ages for intense ferruginisation at other sites in the
Cobar region (McQueen et al . 2007). These episodes of
strong ferruginisation reﬂect signiﬁcant changes in
weathering, hydrological and chemical conditions
developed during ongoing weathering through the
Cenozoic. There is good stratigraphic control on the
later episode of strong ferruginisation at a site near
Wilga Tank, northeast of Cobar, where Miocene leucitite

WEATHERING AGES AND LONG-TERM CLIMATE
CHANGE
The most important proxy for climate information
spanning the entire Cenozoic is arguably the oxygen
isotope ( d18O) record from deep-sea sediments (Kennett
& Stott 1991; Bralower et al. 1995; Zachos et al. 1997). The
d18O composition of marine benthic foraminifera is a
ﬁrst-order measure of global ice volume, from which it
can be deduced that the general trend in global climate
during the Cenozoic is towards cooler temperatures,
driven largely by growth of the Antarctic ice sheet
(Figure 6).
From d
18O records and other evidence (e.g. paleobo-
tanical evidence), it is clear that the southern hemi-
sphere experienced a warmer, wetter climate
throughout much of the Paleocene and Early Eocene
than at present. Two major events are recognised within
this interval, the ﬁrst being a very warm period at the
Paleocene/Eocene boundary (the Late Paleocene Ther-
mal Maximum) and the second being the Early Eocene
Climate Optimum. This so-called ‘Greenhouse World’ in
the Early Cenozoic was brought to an end by initiation
of the Antarctic ice sheet and rapid cooling of the
Southern Ocean by *58C at around the Oligocene/
Eocene boundary (Kennett et al . 1974; Kennett &
Shackleton 1976; Savin 1977; Zachos et al . 2001), leading
into the icehouse world of the Late Cenozoic.
Whereas today much of Australia is arid to semiarid,
with low rainfall across much of the rest of the
continent, Early Cenozoic Australia experienced less
seasonal, warmer, wetter climates than today. As the
Cenozoic progressed, the climate became more seasonal
and temperate, with the onset of major aridity around 5–
4 Ma (Bowler 1976), but intensifying from 3 to 2 Ma
(Fujioka et al. 2005). Evidence from the Australian arid
zone indicates that throughout much of the Cenozoic it
experienced a much more humid climate than that
prevailing since the start of the Quaternary. Evidence
from the large internal drainage basins that enclose
Lakes Eyre and Frome in central Australia indicates
extensive lacustrine environments during the Miocene,
with macrofossil evidence conﬁrming the prevalence of
subtropical conditions at the time (Alley 1998).
Martin (1998) examined the Cenozoic climate history
of southeastern Australia, including southern New
South Wales and Victoria, in the context of increasing
aridity. From paleobotanical evidence, it was concluded
that precipitation was 41500 mm during the Paleogene,
declining from the Middle–Late Miocene to the Late
Pliocene. There was a further decrease to 500–800 mm in
the Plio-Pleistocene. Throughout the Cenozoic, grass-
land became more dominant, developing ﬁrst in the
northwest of Australia, and later in the southeast.
Aridity in the central part of the continent, and
seasonality closer to the coast, became predominant
climate trends from the Miocene, and both have
intensiﬁed since the Late Pleistocene. A generalised
precipitation curve from Martin (1998) is shown in
Figure 6, compared with a global sea-surface tempera-
ture curve derived from d
18O records from deep-sea
cores (Zachos et al. 2001).
Paleomagnetic ages obtained from the McKinnons
mine equate well with the climatic record. Periods of
drying out of the proﬁle, associated with a lowering of
the water-table, are marked by intense oxidation and
hematite ﬁxation, yielding a strong paleomagnetic signal.
This appears to have occurred in the Paleocene resulting
in a preserved magnetic age. The marked seasonality
during the Miocene, shown in both the paleoprecipitation
and paleotemperature records, was again favourable to
the formation of ferruginous weathering proﬁles, as
recorded by the Miocene age in the McKinnons proﬁle.
The lack of paleomagnetic ages between the Paleocene
and the Miocene may be explained by limited changes in
oxidation or hydrologic conditions, or may possibly
reﬂect periods of greater landscape instability. Unstable,
eroding land surfaces are not conducive to the preserva-
tion of paleomagnetic signals. While climate may be the
main driver, regional tectonism and base-level change
associated with transgressions and regressions in the
Murray Basin will have had an added effect on the
preservation of weathering proﬁles.
CONCLUSIONS
Paleomagnetic dating shows that during the Cenozoic,
there were two major periods of secondary hematite
formation at the McKinnons mine, in the Cobar region.
The ﬁrst of these reached its terminal stages in the
Paleocene, and the second in the Middle Miocene,
broadly consistent with other paleomagnetic data,
which indicate continent-wide weathering regimes con-
ducive to the formation of secondary hematite during
these time periods (Pillans 2002). It appears that the
Miocene weathering extended deeper than, or comple-
tely overprinted, the Paleocene weathering. A more
favourable climate, more stable landscape, or both,
conducive to this weathering regime, existed for a
longer period in the Miocene than in the Paleocene.
Erosion has resulted in the truncation of the Paleocene
weathering proﬁle. Reduced erosion, and a deepening
weathering front, by the Early to Middle Miocene
allowed preservation of part of the older proﬁle and
deeper weathering to produce the 15 Ma proﬁle.
Results from this study indicate that the landscape
evolution and weathering history of the region dates
back at least to the Cretaceous–Paleocene boundary.
This implies that the area was subaerially exposed for
periods of *10 Ma during the Paleocene–Eocene and the
Miocene. The long-term landscape stability necessary
for such deep oxidative weathering proﬁles to develop
indicates that the Cobar region probably separated
marine sedimentation in the Murray Basin from the
Eromanga and Surat Basins. The ages provide further
evidence for episodic deep, intense chemical weathering
under favourable climatic conditions across the region,
and substantiate other paleomagnetic ages, which

These weathering ages can be compared with recon-

published work, which show a cooling trend over the
last 40 Ma, following an extended period of high mean
annual temperatures in the Paleocene and Eocene.
In conjunction with this cooling, total precipitation
decreased, and rainfall became more seasonal. The
weathering ages relate to the onset of seasonal climate
and the initiation of aridity in the Late Miocene.
Recognition of two major periods of weathering-
related hematite ﬁxation, reﬂecting signiﬁcant changes
in paleoclimate through the Cenozoic, has important
implications for geochemical dispersion in the regolith
of the Cobar region. Iron oxides/oxyhydroxides, includ-
ing hematite, are important hosts for elements released
and dispersed from weathering ore deposits. Periods of
humid, deep weathering would have dispersed some
elements but ﬁxed others in the iron oxides and
oxyhydroxides. Subsequent weathering under drier or
arid conditions would have imposed a chemically and
physically different weathering regime with different
dispersion processes, predominantly mechanical. These
processes are discussed by other workers, and are
reﬂected in the development of extensive sheetwash
and surface lag (Scott et al . 1991; Cohen et al. 1996 and
references therein).

abstract
The existence of a pre-Rodinia Precambrian supercontinent, variously called Nuna or Columbia, has
been widely speculated in the past decade, but the precise timing of its existence and its conﬁguration
have been uncertain due to the lack of unequivocal paleomagnetic and geological constraints. Here we
report high-quality paleomagnetic results from the well dated   1780 Ma Xiong’er Group in southern
North China Block (NCB). A total of 110 paleomagnetic samples from 14 sites were collected and
subjected to stepwise thermal demagnetization. After removing a low temperature component (CL) of
viscous magnetic remanence acquired in recent geomagnetic ﬁeld, a high temperature component (CH),
carried by hematite and magnetite in redbeds and volcanic samples, has been isolated. It gives a mean
direction of ( D¼ 18.41, I¼/C0 3.71,
a95 ¼7.61, N ¼14) after bedding correction, and a corresponding
paleomagnetic pole at 50.2 1N, 263.01E( A95 ¼ 4.51). The CH passed a reversal test and was interpreted as
a primary remanence. This new pole plus three other high-quality poles from the NCB that have been
more precisely dated at 1769 7 3 Ma, 1560–1440 Ma and 1437 721 Ma deﬁne a 1780–1440 Ma
apparent polar wander path (APWP) for the NCB. This, together with an update of global high quality
paleomagnetic dataset, allows us to demonstrate that the pre-Rodinia supercontinent Nuna likely
existed at least between   1780 Ma and   1400 Ma. Our paleomagnetism-based global reconstruction,
for the ﬁrst time, quantitatively assembles all major cratons together; it encompasses previously
proposed regional links including the SAMBA connection between Baltica, Amazonia and Western
Africa (Johansson, 2009), connections between Laurentia, Baltica and Siberia at the core of Nuna ( Evans
and Mitchell, 2011 ), the proto-SWEAT connection between Laurentia, East Antarctica and Australian
blocks ( Payne et al., 2009 ), and the NCB–India connection ( Zhao et al., 2011 ).

1. Introduction
Although it has long been speculated that the Earth’s evolution
may have been dominated by cycles of supercontinent assembly
and breakup (e.g., Nance et al., 1988 ), our understanding of past
supercontinents has mainly been limited to the last 1000 Ma, with
more conﬁdence being placed on the history of the ca. 320–180 Ma
supercontinent Pangea ( Veevers, 2004) than the ca. 900–700 Ma
supercontinent Rodinia (Li et al., 2008a). Our knowledge of an even
older supercontinent, possibly formed by global ca. 1800 Ma oro-
genic events and variably named Nuna (Hoffman, 1997)o rC o l u m b i a
(Rogers and Santosh, 2002; Zhao et al., 2002 ; Zhao G. et al., 2004 ),
has been more tenuous, and early papers were mostly based on
intercontinental geological correlations that are intrinsically non-
unique. Early attempts of paleomagnetically examining Nuna-
related continental reconstructions (e.g. Idnurm and Giddings,
1995; Payne et al., 2009 ; Wu et al., 2005 ) were hampered by the
lack of high-quality paleomagnetic results, or merely regional rather
than global considerations. Evans and Mitchell (2011) provided a
recent update on the assembly and breakup of the centre of Nuna,
between Laurentia, Baltica and Siberia. Here we use new paleomag-
netic results from North China, as well as recent results from
Australia, India, and Amazonia, to examine the positions of these
continental blocks in Nuna. Together with the proposed Laurentia–
Baltica–Siberia connection (Evans and Mitchell, 2011), we are now
able to present a geologically and paleomagnetically viable conﬁg-
uration for the bulk of Nuna.
2. New paleomagnetic results from North China
2.1. Geological background

metamorphic basement, covered by post-1.85 Ga, little-deformed

Our new paleomagnetic investigation was carried out on the
well-dated Xiong’er Group, which unconformably overlies the
