found in southern Shanxi Province and western Henan Province,
with an outcropping area of   60,000 km2 (Fig. 1 ). It consists
mainly of andesites and basaltic andesites, with minor dacites,
rhyolites and red mudstones ( He et al., 2009 ). Volcanic strata of
the Xiong’er Group are traditionally classiﬁed into three parts: the
Xushan Fomation at the bottom, the Jidanping Formation in the
middle, and the Majiahe Formation at the top. However, this
subdivision was mainly based on petrological compositions and
has been challenged by recent geochronological work ( He et al.,
2009). The Xushan Formation and the Majiahe Formation have
similar petrological compositions. They both are dominated by
basaltic andesites and andesites, but the Majiahe Formation
contains more sedimentary red-beds. Zircon U–Pb ages of the
volcanic rocks from these two formations are both   1780 Ma,
indistinguishable within uncertainties ( Fig. 1 b). They may repre-
sent rapid magmatic activity in the south margin of the NCB in
late Paleoproterozoic, slightly older than the Taihang dyke swarm
in the interior of this craton (ca. 1770 Ma, Halls et al., 2000 ; Wang
et al., 2004 ).
Age constraints for the Jidanping Formation are more complex.
The Jidanping Formation contains fewer basaltic rocks but more
dacites and rhyolites and subvolcanic rocks than the Xushan and
Majiahe formations. Some volcanic rocks of the Jidanping Forma-
tion gave the same ages within errors as the Xushan and Majiahe
formations, but others gave ages as young as 1450 Ma ( He et al.,
2009), suggesting that the lithostratigraphically deﬁned Jidanping
Formation has a wide range of ages.
Our paleomagnetic sampling was carried out for the Xushan and
Majiahe formations in the Waifang Mountain region (   33157
0N,
  1121270E, Fig. 1b), because these formations not only have tight
age constraints of ca. 1780 Ma, they are also better outcropped and
more fresh in that area. Outcrops without clear geological contact
and concrete paleo-horizontal markers, such as those in the
Jidanping Formation, were not considered in this study. A total of
110 oriented core samples were obtained from 13 sites in dark-gray
or purple-gray basaltic andesites or andesites, and one site in purple
mudstones of the Majiahe Formation. They were oriented using a
magnetic compass, combined with a sun compass when possible.
Orientation differences between the two devices are within 711 in
most cases, and the differences are less than 731 for all samples.
The strata tilt is gentle; most sites have dips of 5–20 1 toward the
southwest.
2.2. Experimental condition
All samples were cut into 22-mm-long specimens and subjected
to stepwise thermal demagnetization. Remanence measurements
were made with an AGICO JR-6A spinner magnetometer and
demagnetization was made using an ASC TD-48 furnace in
5–20 1C steps up to 685 1C, or until the remanence became too
weak to measure. The instruments in the paleomagnetism labora-
tory of China University of Geosciences (Beijing) are housed in
room-size Helmholtz coils with a low magnetic ﬁeld of   200 nT in
the sample loading region. The internal residual ﬁeld in the furnace
is lower than 10 nT. During the experiments, samples were further
protected from magnetic contamination by m-metal shielding.
Magnetic hysteresis parameters (i.e., saturation magnetization,
Ms, saturation remanence, Mrs, coercive force, Hc, and coercivity
of remanence, Hcr) were measured for representative samples
using an alternating gradient magnetometer (MicroMag 2900).
The magnetic ﬁeld was cycled between 71.8 T for each sample.
Ms, Mrs, and Hc were determined after correction for the para-
magnetic contribution. Hcr was obtained when each sample was

2.3. Paleomagnetic results
The natural remanent magnetization (NRM) intensities of the
volcanic samples are in the range of 30–800 mA/m, while those of
the sedimentary samples (red-beds) range from 10 to 20 mA/m.
After the removal of a stray viscous magnetization, two magnetic
components were identiﬁed in most samples ( Fig. 2 ). A lower-
temperature component CL was often found at the temperature
range of 200–500 1C. Its in situ mean direction is close to that of
the present local geomagnetic ﬁeld ( Fig. 3 a and c), suggesting
an origin of viscous magnetization acquired in recent times.
A higher-temperature component CH is well deﬁned, generally
above 540 1C. The high unblocking temperatures of component
CH strongly suggest that the main magnetic carriers are magne-
tite and hematite in the volcanic rocks, and hematite in the

3. Reconstructing Nuna using paleomagnetic data
In the following discussion, we use the paleomagnetic method
to determine the relative positions of continents by matching
their APWPs (or fragments of APWPs), but at the same time
consider geological arguments for possible past connections.
Paleomagnetic data were selected using Van der Voo’s (1990)
7-point criteria system and they are listed in Table 2 , including
each pole’s age information, position and error parameters, most
important ﬁeld stability tests performed, and the original refer-
ences. This data table includes new results from the NCB, and
other newly published results for other continents. There is good
data coverage for Laurentia, Baltica and the NCB for the interval
of   1.78–1.40 Ga. Australia has good data coverage for the
1.80–1.60 Ga interval. However, for the remaining cratons, the
data are spread more sparsely.
Using the available high-quality paleomagnetic data ( Table 2 ),
we present in Fig. 6 a reconstruction of Nuna that includes all the
world’s major cratons. The tight Laurentia–Siberia–Baltica ﬁt
proposed by Evans and Mitchell (2011) can be conjoined to the
SAMBA ﬁt of Baltica with Amazon and West Africa ( Johansson,
2009), with an additional constraint provided by the new 1.42-Ga
paleomagnetic pole from Amazon ( Bispo-Santos et al., 2012 ). On
the other side of Nuna, the Australia–Mawsonland–Laurentia
connection of Payne et al. (2009) is modiﬁed to include additional
intracontinental deformation following that of Li and Evans
(2011), in a ‘‘proto-SWEAT’’ connection similar to that shown in
outline form by Evans and Mitchell (2011) , except that we now
have ca. 1.8–1.6 Ga paleomagnetic data supporting such a con-
nection ( Fig. 6 a and b, and discussions below).
Herein we add two other cratons to a quantiﬁed Nuna
reconstruction: India is placed according to a ca. 1.8-Ga pole from
its Bundelkhand massif ( Pradhan et al., 2010 ), and the NCB is
positioned by superimposing its four selected poles between
1.78 Ga and   1.44 Ga atop coeval poles from the combined
cratonic assemblage as described above ( Fig. 6 ). Our paleomag-
netic interpretation supports the geological idea that the present
south margin of the NCB represented an active continental
margin in Nuna and likely faced an open ocean, whilst its north
margin was connected to a large landmass ( Zhao et al., 2011 ).
Zhao et al. (2002 , 2011) and Zhao G. et al. (2004) placed the NCB
adjacent to India on the basis of similarities between their
Archean to Paleoproterozoic basement terranes, and our paleo-
magnetic reconstruction supports such a connection for Nuna
time, but pre-1.8 Ga paleomagnetic data from both cratons are
still lacking. Recent geochronological work has dated maﬁc sills in

1.80 Ga poles from India, Australia, Baltica, Siberia and the Slave
block of Laurentia broadly deﬁne a convergent swath through
that interval ( Fig. 6a). This indicates that these blocks might have
commenced to connect to each other earlier, as a single plate
representing the accretionary core of the nascent supercontinent.
The Superior craton joined the assembly at ca. 1.81 Ga ( St-Onge
et al., 2009 ), and Wyoming craton accreted even later,
at ca. 1.75 Ga ( Dahl et al., 1999 ). The 1.79-Ga pole from Amazonia
also does not support this conﬁguration ( Fig. 6 b) and suggests
that Amazonia might have joined Nuna later, also, perhaps as part
of a single plate with Volgo–Sarmatia that docked against Fen-
noscandia at ca. 1.75 Ga ( Bogdanova et al., 2008 ; Elming et al.,
2001).
The 1770-Ma poles from Baltica and North China, as recon-
structed, imply a small APWP oscillation in geon 17, which we did
not illustrate for the sake of simplicity ( Fig. 6 b). The 1645 Ma ED
pole from northern Australia is shown atop younger poles from
Baltica, but it lies at the apex of a prominent oscillation in the
McArthur Basin APWP for Australia ( Idnurm, 2000 ). If northern
Australia was part of Nuna, and if that oscillation is real, then it
merely has not been sampled yet by other cratons, which
generally have a poor geon-16 paleomagnetic record. The paleo-
pole from the   1590 Ma Gawler Range Volcanics has recently
been suggested to be a late Paleozoic remagnetization ( Schmidt
and Clark, 2011 ), and has therefore been removed from the data
table here. The considerable scatter in the geon-14 poles from
Laurentia is independent of our reconstruction.
Despite these anomalies, with our reconstruction that encom-
passes almost all major continents, all selected high-quality poles for
the time interval of 1.8–1.4 Ga fall on a common APWP (Fig. 6ba n d
c), whereas poles of 41.8 Ga from different continents or cratons
diverge with increasing ages (Fig. 6a). These data suggest that Nuna

geological grounds ( Hoffman, 1997 ; Rogers and Santosh, 2002 ;
Zhao et al., 2002 ; Zhao G. et al., 2004 ). In addition, we place the
Cathaysia block of south China as an extension of western Laurentia,
as proposed by Li and co-workers (Li Z.X. et al., 1995; Li et al., 2008b).
West Africa is devoid of Mesoproterozoic paleomagnetic data, but we
follow Johansson (2009)in proposing a long-lived connection of that
block to Baltica and Amazon. The only large cratons missing from our
model are Congo–S~ao Francisco and Kalahari, which lack reliable data
from the interval 1.8–1.3 Ga, the Yangtze craton of south China, and
Tarim, both of which lack extensive pre-Neoproterozoic exposures
and may themselves be collages of much smaller earlier continental
fragments.
Widespread 1.6–1.2 Ga large igneous events across the super-
continent ( Fig. 7 a) may signify early extension related to the
breakup of Nuna. However, as discussed earlier in this paper,
paleomagnetic data appear to support a coherent Nuna until ca.
1.40 Ga. Paleomagnetic poles younger than ca. 1.3-1.2 Ga ( Table
2), when rotated into the coordinates of our reconstructed Nuna
conﬁguration, diverge from each other; this implies Nuna’s
breakup at that time, coincident with emplacement of numerous
late Mesoproterozoic large igneous provinces (cf. Ernst et al.,
2008; Evans and Mitchell, 2011 ). At the moment, paleomagnetic
poles are lacking for many continents for the time interval of 1.4–
1.2 Ga ( Table 2 ), and we are therefore yet unable to determine
more precisely exactly when did Nuna broke apart. However, if
the widespread 1.28–1.26 Ga large igneous events are linked to
the supercontinent disaggregation ( Evans and Mitchell, 2011 ),
then the prolonged 1.6–1.2 Ga LIP events in the lead-up of Nuna
fragmentation is not dissimilar to the protracted breakup process
of Rodinia, which lasted over 200 Myr from ca. 850 Ma initial
rifting ( Li et al., 2008a ; Li et al., 2011 ), to 720–650 Ma major
fragmentation (Li and Evans, 2011 ) and ca. 600 Ma ﬁnal dispersal
(Cawood and Pisarevsky, 2006 ).
4. Conclusions
We report here new paleomagnetic results from the
  1780 Ma Xiong’er Group in NCB, which have yielded a high
quality paleomagnetic pole at 50.2 1N, 263.0 1E( N¼14, A95 ¼4.51).
Together with three other high quality paleomagnetic poles from
the NCB, with ages of   1769 Ma,   1500 Ma and   1437 Ma, they
deﬁne a ca. 1780–1400 Ma APWP for the NCB, depicting Equatorial
to low-latitudinal paleogeographic positions that are in good agree-
ment with the climate indicators in the strata.
A review of all available global paleomagnetic data enabled us
to reconstruct, for the ﬁrst time, a near-complete global-scale
supercontinent Nuna (also known as Columbia) that formed by
ca. 1.75 Ga, and lasted till at least ca. 1.4 Ga ( Figs. 6 and 7 ). Our
paleomagnetism-based global reconstruction is in agreement
with previously proposed, geologically based models, including
the SAMBA connection between Baltica, Amazonia and Western
Africa ( Johansson, 2009 ), the Nuna core connection between
Laurentia, Baltica and Siberia ( Evans and Mitchell, 2011 ), the
proto-SWEAT connection between Laurentia, Mawson block and
Australian blocks ( Goodge et al., 2008 ; Payne et al., 2009 ) and the
NCB–India connection ( Zhao et al., 2011 ). In addition, our recon-
struction for the ﬁrst time, quantitatively merges them into a
single and coherent supercontinent.
Our Nuna reconstruction, constrained by both our new results
and an updated global paleomagnetic dataset, is also consistent
with key geological features including the ca. 1.8 Ga orogenic belts
leading to the assembly of Nuna ( Fig. 7 b) and Mesoproterozoic
global intraplate extensional basins and large igneous province
(LIP) record possibly related to the breakup of Nuna ( Fig. 7a).
The breakup of Nuna may have commenced after ca. 1.4 Ga,
but available paleomagnetic data are not yet complete enough to
allow a more precise depiction of Nuna’s fragmentation.

Paleomagnetic study of the late Neoproterozoic
Bull Arm and Crown Hill formations
(Musgravetown Group) of eastern Newfoundland:
implications for Avalonia and West Gondwana
paleogeography
1
Sergei A. Pisarevsky, Phil J.A. McCausland, Joseph P. Hodych, Sean J. O ’Brien,
Jennifer A. Tait, and J. Brendan Murphy
Abstract: A paleomagnetic study of subaerial volcanic rocks and associated siltstones of the Ediacaran Bull Arm Formation
in the Avalon Zone of Newfoundland revealed a stable bipolar, hematite-borne primary remanence supported by positive
conglomerate, contact, and fold tests. Mean remanence directions in two distal areas (Bonavista and Argentia) are similar,
indicating a low paleolatitude position of Avalonia at ∼570 Ma. Redbeds of the overlying ∼550 Ma Crown Hill Formation
also carry a primary bipolar hematite-borne remanence with moderate inclination, indicating that Avalonia remained at low
to medium paleolatitudes through the end of the Ediacaran. Combining our results with previously published paleomagnetic
data of Avalonia suggests moderate-scale drift of Avalonia through low southern paleolatitudes through the latter half of the
Ediacaran, providing a paleogeographic context for the development of the first complex metazoan life.
Résumé : Une étude paléomagnétique de roches volcaniques subaériennes et de siltstones associés de la Formation de Bull
Arm (Édiacarien) de la zone Avalon de Terre-Neuve révèle une bipolarité stable, une rémanence primaire dans l ’hématite,
laquelle est supportée par un conglomérat positif, un contact et des études sur les plis. Les directions moyennes de la réma-
nence dans deux secteurs distaux (Bonavista et Argentia) sont semblables, indiquant une basse position paléolatitude d ’Ava-
lonia vers ∼570 Ma. Les lits rouges de la Formation de Crown Hill ( ∼550 Ma) sus-jacente conservent aussi une rémanence
primaire bipolaire dans l ’hématite avec une inclinaison modérée, indiquant qu ’Avalonia est demeuré à des paléolatitudes bas-
ses à moyennes jusqu ’à la fin de l ’Édiacarien. Nos résultats combinés à des données publiées antérieurement sur Avalonia
suggèrent un déplacement à échelle moyenne d ’Avalonia à travers de basses paléolatitudes sud durant la deuxième moitié de
l’Édiacarien, fournissant un contexte paléogéographique pour le développement de la première vie complexe des métazoai-
res.

Introduction
The late Neoproterozoic was a time of dramatic paleogeo-
graphic changes. One supercontinent (Rodinia) finally broke
up and another one (Gondwana) began to assemble. Several
oceans (Mozambique, Adamastor, Brazilliano) closed during
the formation of Gondwana as others (Iapetus, Paleo-Asian,
Tornquist) began opening between Laurentia, Baltica, Sibe-
ria, Gondwana and other cratonic blocks. However, the pale-
ogeographic reconstructions for this time remain
controversial (e.g., Dalziel 1997; Cordani et al. 2003; Meert
and Torsvik 2003; Tohver et al. 2006; McCausland et al.
2007, 2011; Li et al. 2008; Pisarevsky et al. 2008).
The main reason for this controversy is the sparsely popu-
lated Neoproterozoic paleomagnetic database (McElhinny

and Lock 1996; Pisarevsky 2005). Very few reliable and
well-dated paleopoles are available for the major cratons
through the late Neoproterozoic (see reviews of Collins and
Pisarevsky 2005; McCausland et al. 2007; Pisarevsky et al.
2008). Consequently, these data do not allow unequivocal
global paleogeographic reconstructions for the time interval
between ∼620 and 540 Ma (the Ediacaran Period; Knoll et
al. 2004). There is still a paucity of reliable Ediacaran paleo-
magnetic data from many major cratons, such as West Africa,
Congo, Kalahari, Siberia, Amazonia, and others. There is
also controversy regarding interpretation of Ediacaran paleo-
magnetic data from Laurentia and Baltica (McCausland and
Hodych 1998; Pisarevsky et al. 2000, 2001; Meert and Van
der Voo 2001; Cawood and Pisarevsky 2006; McCausland et
al. 2007, 2011).
Paleomagnetic poles from smaller terranes are rarely used
for global paleogeographic reconstructions. Block rotations,
oroclinal bending, and other regional and local processes oc-
cur during the accretion of small terranes to large continents
and their subsequent transport along plate boundaries (e.g.,
Coney et al. 1980; Abrajevitch et al. 2008). The exact orien-
tations of small blocks at different times during these proc-
esses are, therefore, hard to reconstruct. Consequently, only
the paleolatitudes obtained from paleomagnetic studies of
small terranes are usually applicable as constraints for the pa-
leopositions of paleocontinents.
Although faunal endemism indicates temporary separation
of Avalonia (parts of Newfoundland, Nova Scotia, New Eng-
land, southern UK, and Belgium) from Gondwana in the late
Ediacaran and Early Cambrian (Landing 2005), Avalonia is
usually considered to have been located among the Peri-
Gondwanan terranes that were distributed near the northern
(present coordinates) margin of Gondwana, adjacent to Ama-
zonia and (or) West Africa at ∼600–540 Ma (e.g., Kroner
and Hegner 1998; Friedl et al. 2000; McNamara et al. 2001;
Murphy et al. 2004; Thompson et al. 2007; Nance et al.
2008, 2010; Pisarevsky et al. 2008 and references therein).
Avalonia’s paleogeographic position is particularly important
because regional tectonic studies indicate that it faced an
open ocean from the late Neoproterozoic to the early Paleo-
zoic (Murphy and Nance 1989).
The first paleomagnetic data from West Avalonia were
published more that 50 years ago (Nairn et al. 1959). How-
ever, most published results cannot be considered reliable be-
cause of a lack of convincing evidence for a primary
remanence and (or) poor geochronological control. Only a
few paleomagnetic results pass these modern criteria, as will
be discussed later in the text. In this work, we present a new
paleomagnetic study of mid to late Ediacaran volcanic rocks
and redbeds of the Bonavista and Avalon peninsulas, New-
foundland, and discuss their implications for understanding
the paleogeographic history of Avalonia with respect to
Gondwana at the end of the Neoproterozoic.
Geology and sampling
The Bonavista and Avalon peninsulas (Figs. 1, 2) are parts
of the Avalonian tectonostratigraphic zone of Newfoundland
(Williams 1979), which represents the core portion of West
Avalonia (O ’Brien et al. 1996). Paleomagnetic sampling was
conducted during the summer of 2007 in two localities: (1) in
the northern portion of the Bonavista peninsula in the vicin-
ity of Plate Cove West, Red Cliff and King ’s Cove, and (2)
on the western shore of the Avalon peninsula, near Argentia.
The latter sampling supplements a pilot study conducted by
Jordan (1999), the results of which are also included herein.
Bonavista locality: Bull Arm and Crown Hill formations
Neoproterozoic rocks in the eastern part of the Bonavista
peninsula belong to two Neoproterozoic sedimentary basins:
(1) the eastern St. John ’s basin (Figs. 1D, 2), which includes
the Conception, St John ’s, and Signal Hill (Gibbett Hill For-
mation) groups; and (2) the western Bonavista basin
(Figs. 1A; 2), which includes the Connecting Point and Mus-
gravetown groups (O ’Brien and King 2002; Normore 2010).
The basins are separated by the Spillars Cove – English Har-
bour fault (Fig. 2; Normore 2010). All these strata were
folded and faulted in the Siluro-Devonian during collision of
Avalonia with Laurentia (Dallmeyer et al. 1983; O ’Brien et
al. 1996, O ’Brien and King 2002). Oriented paleomagnetic
samples were collected from two units of the Musgravetown
group: bimodal subaerial volcanic rocks of the Bull Arm For-
mation and younger redbeds of the Crown Hill Formation
(Figs. 1, 2).
The Bull Arm Formation consists mainly of dark vesicular
basalt of volcanic-arc affinity with synvolcanic epidote and
hematite alteration, intercalated with reddish massive rhyo-
lites and subordinate clastic sedimentary rocks (O ’Brien and
King 2002; Normore 2010). The subaerial to marine, typi-
cally bimodal succession can be traced southwards from the
Plate Cove area of the Bonavista peninsula through the type
locality at Bull Arm to the Placentia Bay coast of the Avalon
peninsula (Fig. 1); it also crops out on the western coast of
Bonavista Bay (O ’Brien and Knight 1988; O ’Brien and King
2002). The Bull Arm Formation overlies red conglomerate
(Cannings Cove Formation, Fig. 1A) of the basal Mugrave-
town Group, which in turn lies with pronounced angular dis-
cordance on the 620 –610 Ma turbidites of the Connecting
Point Group (Jenness 1963; Dec et al. 1992; O ’Brien 1993;
Fig. 1). The Bull Arm Formation passes upward into the
Rocky Harbour Formation (Fig. 1A) — a widespread shal-
low-marine clastic succession. In the western part of Bona-
vista Bay, the Bull Arm Formation at its contact with the
overlying Rocky Harbour Formation has been dated at

The main sampling locality for the Bull Arm Formation
lies along highway roadcuts and adjacent quarries between
Summerville and Plate Cove West, with one other quarry lo-

well exposed, dipping moderately to steeply eastwards. In
these sites, we were able to establish a stratigraphic order
within which to interpret the paleomagnetic results. Paleohor-
izontal for some sites was not easy to determine, given the
massive appearance of some flows and only occasional oc-
currence of stratified siltstone. We have applied tilt correction

Separate cooling units were sampled by recognizing litholog-
ical breaks across siltstone units, alternation between mafic
and felsic flows or the occurrence of ferruginous oxidized
flow tops. In all, 11 separate flows from the Bull Arm For-
mation were sampled in the Bonavista locality.
The overlying Rocky Harbour Formation contains con-
glomerates with mafic and felsic cobbles derived from the
Bull Arm Formation. A large (2 m × 2 m × 1 m) boulder of
conglomerate was sampled next to the Bull Arm sample sites
in the Plate Cove area, to perform a paleomagnetic conglom-
erate test (Graham 1949) of the underlying Bull Arm Forma-
tion.
The Crown Hill redbeds conformably and gradationally
overlie the Rocky Harbour Formation (Fig. 1A) and outcrop
in the northern part of the western horn of the Bonavista
peninsula (Fig. 2). We collected red siltstones to mudstones
from gently northeast-dipping beds at shoreline exposures in
the Duntara area and in three roadcut outcrops along the
Duntara – King’s Cove Highway (sites C15 –C19; Fig. 2).
Red conglomerate of the Crown Hill Formation exposed
near Red Cliff contains mafic and felsic volcanic pebbles of
the Bull Arm Formation (Fig. 2); these were sampled for a
second, regional conglomerate test (site BA13). The Crown
Hill redbeds are disconformably overlain by Lower Cambrian
red and green shales and minor limestones of the Bonavista
Formation, exposed in the core of an open syncline at Keels
that plunges gently to the north (Fig. 2). Penetrative deforma-
tion is pervasive in the core of the syncline, but it is repre-
sented only by widely spaced, subvertical cleavage planes in
the Crown Hill Formation redbeds at Duntara, east of the
Duntara fault. Sites C15 –C19 in the Crown Hill redbeds be-
tween Duntara and King ’s Cove do not appear to require
plunge correction as they lie within a structure that is sepa-
rate from the Keels syncline.
The youngest detrital zircons in the Crown Hill Formation
are ∼557 Ma (Pollock et al. 2009). Hence, the age of the
studied redbeds is bracketed between 557 and 542 Ma, the
age of the base of the lower Cambrian. The Crown Hill For-
mation has been correlated with similar latest Neoproterozic
redbeds of the Rencontre Formation (Long Harbour Group),
exposed in the southwestern Avalon Zone (O ’Brien et al.
1990, 1995; O ’Brien and King 2002). These redbeds overlie
rhyolites dated at 551 ± 6 Ma (O ’Brien et al. 1995; Tucker
and McKerrow 1995). This regional correlation is consistent
with the detrital zircon results and makes the depositional age
constraints for Crown Hill slightly tighter: 551 –542 Ma.
Argentia locality: Bull Arm Formation
For regional comparison the Bull Arm Formation volcanic
rocks were also sampled in the Argentia area of the south-
western Avalon peninsula (Fig. 1, 3), which follows up on
the pilot study by Jordan (1999). Here, the age constrains
are less certain — the Bull Arm Formation in Argentia is
thought to be correlative with the Bonavista exposures (e.g.,
ca. 570 Ma), although no geochronological data exist from
this area. Regional tectonism of the western Avalon Zone of
Newfoundland, which includes both Argentia and Bonavista
areas, has been correlated with that of the adjoining Gander
Zone and is the result of the juxtaposition of the zones dur-
ing regional sinistral transpression along the Dover Fault
shear zone (Fig. 1). Deformation and synkinematic magma-
tism along this crustal boundary is coeval with orogen-scale
tectonism and is dated as mid- to late Silurian (Dunning et
al. 1990, Holdsworth 1991, Schofield and D ’Lemos 2000;
O’Brien et al. 1996; van Staal et al. 1998, 2009; Murphy
and Nance 2002).
Ten paleomagnetic sites were collected by oriented block
sampling (Jordan 1999) and with a portable drill (in this
study), from gently west- and east-dipping flows and interca-
lated siltstones on both limbs of an open anticline exposed in
roadcuts along Highway 100 west of Dunville (Fig. 3; King
1988). Paleohorizontal was readily obtained from the interca-
lated siltstones. From regional mapping, the sample sites in
the east limb are approximately at the same stratigraphic level
as those of the west limb (King 1988), allowing for a simple
paleomagnetic fold test (Graham 1949).
Analytical methods
Remanence behaviour was determined by detailed stepwise
thermal demagnetisation ( ≤20 steps, to 600 °C), using a
Magnetic Measurements MMTD1 furnace and the 2G cryo-
genic magnetometer in the University of Edinburgh (Edin-
burgh, Scotland). Stepwise alternating field (AF)
demagnetisation ( ≤20 steps, up to 100 mT) was also applied,
using an AGICO LDA-3A tumbling demagnetiser. Magnetic
mineralogy was investigated from demagnetisation character-
istics and, in selected samples, from measuring the variation
of susceptibility versus temperature (20 –700 °C) using the
AGICO Kappabridge MFK-FA with the CS3 apparatus. Parts
of the collection were studied in the paleomagnetic laborato-
ries of Oxford University (Oxford, UK), Utrecht University
(Utrecht, The Netherlands), The University of Western Aus-
tralia (Perth, Australia), and University of Windsor (Windsor,
Ontario, Canada). The Argentia locality pilot study (Jordan
1999) was undertaken at Memorial University (St. John ’s,
Newfoundland, Canada), with experimental procedures simi-

Paleomagnetic analysis
Bull Arm Formation, Bonavista locality
Petrographic analysis indicates that the mafic flows of the
Bull Arm Formation are variable in grain size and texture.
The finer grained samples contain rare microphenocrysts of
plagioclase and pseudomorphs of clinopyroxene set in a
fine-grained matrix dominated by chlorite and microlites of
plagioclase that display eutaxitic flow textures. Both the phe-
nocrysts and the microlites are extensively saussuritized and
are primarily altered to epidote, chlorite, and minor calcite.
Opaque minerals occur as ( i) abundant, fine ragged grains
homogenously distributed throughout the matrix, ( ii) inhomo-
genously distributed clusters that surround clinopyroxene
pseudomorphs, ( iii) fine needles within altered plagioclase,
and ( iv) in localized fractures that occur at variable angles to
the flow fabric. For each occurrence of opaques, magnetite
exhibits partial to extensive alteration to hematite.
The coarser grained rocks are less altered and contain mi-
crophenocrysts of augite and plagioclase (now albite). The
augite is partially pseudomorphed by chlorite and epidote.
Plagioclase is variably saussuritized. Opaques are dominated
by magnetite, which is partially to extensively altered to hem-
atite. The freshest flows are relatively coarse grained and
contain olivine that, although variably altered, preserves
some relatively fresh grains. Even in these samples, however,
the opaque minerals are predominantly ragged grains that are
homogenously distributed throughout the matrix and are
moderately to extensively altered to hematite.
Magnetic susceptibility vs. temperature experiments on
specimens from the Bull Arm volcanic rocks indicate a pres-
ence of both magnetite and hematite as potential remanence
carriers (Fig. 4). AF demagnetisation was not effective for
the studied rocks — the maximum field of 100 mT was not
enough for proper isolation and removal of the characteristic
remanent magnetization (ChRM), indicating that the rema-
nence contribution from hematite is dominant. Thermal de-
magnetisation of mafic rocks revealed two stable remanence
components with unblocking temperatures of 500 –580
and >630 °C (Fig. 5). The medium temperature component,
carried by magnetite, is rather scattered, with the varying of
site mean a
95 between 16° and 52° (Table 1). In situ site
mean directions weakly cluster with a south, shallow down
direction, best represented by sites BA3 through BA7. The
overall mean direction for the mid temperature component is
characterized by a Fisher ’s precision parameter k < 3, and is
too poorly described to warrant further statistical analysis.
Demagnetisation of rhyolites associated with some sites was
not successful — the isolated remanence component direc-
tions were random and excluded from further analysis.
The high-temperature hematite-borne component in the
mafic rocks is significantly less scattered than the low-tem-
perature component, and it is bipolar (Table 2; Fig. 6). If the
sites from the main sampling locality north of Summerville
are placed in stratigraphic order, then, from the bottom to
the top we have a “normal” (SW downward) interval (sites
BA5 to BA1), then an “inverse” (NE upward) interval (sites
BA8, BA11, and BA10) and again a “normal” interval on the
top (site BA12). This apparently regular magnetostratigraphic
pattern favours a primary nature of the high-temperature
component. The stratigraphic position of the geographically
isolated site BA6 ( “inverse”) with respect to the main section
is not clear.
Most sites exhibit a Fisherian distribution of specimen di-
rections (Fisher 1953). One exception is site BA7, which pro-
duced an elongated distribution and was excluded from
further interpretation (Fig. 7). The mid-temperature and
high-temperature mean directions of site BA2 are consistently
∼90° clockwise rotated with respect to those of adjacent sites
BA1 and BA3 (Tables 1, 2), suggesting that this site has ex-
perienced an unrecognized local block rotation with respect
to the stratigraphy. It is noteworthy that site BA2 was
sampled from a blocky, massive flow that outcropped in a
vertical fissure through a high road cut and has no paleohor-
izontal control.
The nine site-mean directions form two roughly antipodal
groups (Fig. 6 a), but the reversal test of McFadden and
McElhinny (1990) is negative. However, if site BA5 is ex-
cluded because of its 37° difference from the mean direction,
the test becomes positive (Rc, D = 18.2°, D
c = 19.5°;
Fig. 6 b). As this exclusion might be considered as somewhat
biased, we include site BA5 in the overall mean calculation.
In our view, the reason for the reversal test uncertainty is the
paucity of bedding constraints in the Bonavista section. The
stratified sediments associated with the flows are sparingly
exposed, so we were forced to extrapolate their bedding;
note that the flows and bedding dip moderately to steeply to-
wards the northeast in this section, so uncertainty in paleo-
horizontal will be manifested as inclination errors in the
high-temperature mean directions, causing poor statistics and
uncertainty in the reversal test.
Given these circumstances, we interpret the overall tilt-cor-
rected mean direction of declination ( D) = 209.8°, inclination
(I) = 34.7° ( a
95 = 16.8°), based on five “normal” and four
“reversed” site mean directions, to adequately represent the
ancient hematite-borne magnetization in the Bull Arm For-
mation at the Bonavista locality.

Conglomerate tests
Three outcrops were used for conglomerate tests (Graham
1949) of the Bull Arm volcanic rocks. We collected pebbles
and cobbles of both mafic and felsic rocks. However, as the
paleomagnetic study of rhyolite flows typically revealed scat-
tered directions, we used only mafic cobbles for the con-
glomerate tests.
The first outcrop (site BA9) is a 2 m × 2 m × 1 m boulder
of conglomerate from the overlying Rocky Harbour Forma-
tion (Fig. 1). Cobbles of up to 15 –20 cm size are represented
by mafic and felsic rocks of the Bull Arm Formation. The
high-temperature hematite-borne component (Fig. 8 a) in the
mafic cobbles produced a random distribution, but with con-
sistency within cobbles (Fig. 9 a). The Rayleigh statistics r =
R/n = 0.312 compared with r
c = 0.7 for five cobbles at 95%
confidence level (Mardia 1972), so this test is positive.
The second outcrop (site BA13) represents pebble con-
glomerates of the even younger Crown Hill Formation near
Red Cliff (Fig. 2), which contain pebbles of the Bull Arm
volcanic rocks in a red siltstone matrix. This is a regional
conglomerate test, applicable to both the Bull Arm volcanic
rocks and the host Crown Hill Formation. The high-temper-
ature component (Fig. 8 b,8 c) in mafic pebbles shows a pro-
pensity for northerly, upwards directions, but nevertheless is
also positive (Fig. 9 b) with r = 0.44 compared with rc =
0.56 for eight pebbles. We note that the conglomeratic red
beds at Red Cliff are strongly cleaved along planes that dip
steeply to the southeast, parallel to the regional fold axial
planes (Fig. 2); it is possible that some pebble mean direc-
tions with slightly lower (ca. 630 °C) unblocking temperature
carry the signal of a partial overprint that is directed in a
north and shallow upwards direction (Fig. 8 c), acquired dur-
ing folding and penetrative deformation. This apparent north,
shallow up overprint direction is antipodal to the in situ mag-
netite-borne south, shallow down direction found in sites
from the Bonavista Bull Arm volcanic rocks (Table 1). How-
ever, most of the pebbles carry a hematite-borne remanence
(Fig. 8 b) apparently without any overprint.
A third test has been carried out with four mafic clasts in a
2 m thick rhyolite flow and associated red mudstone overly-
ing the site BA6 amygdaloidal basalt flow; this test may be
considered to be an intraformational “pseudo-conglomerate”
test, with the clasts having been drawn from the underlying
basalt flow. The distribution of these clast mean high-temper-
ature hematite-borne component (Fig. 8 d) directions appears
to be random between clasts and consistent within clasts
(Fig. 9 c), although four clasts are too few to carry out a stat-
istically significant test. However, the r = 0.302 is rather
small even compared with r
c = 0.7 for n = 5 (Mardia 1972),
so we consider this test as tentatively positive.
Contact test
A 10 m thick basalt flow at site BA5 is underlain by finely
laminated purple siltstone, which we sampled at 15 cm, 2 m,
and 4 m stratigraphic distances below the flow. Figure 9 d
shows the ChRM directions of the BA5 basalt flow and the
siltstones below the contact. The ChRM direction of the
baked sediment at 15 cm is similar to that of the overlying
basalt flow. The direction of the sample taken 2 m below the
flow is only slightly different and possibly also baked by the
flow. The sample taken 4 m below the flow is magnetized
inversely, so the contact test is positive if we assume that
geomagnetic reversal occurred after the deposition of silt-
stone, but before the cooling of the lava flow. However, we
cannot exclude an alternative possibility that the reversal oc-
curred during the deposition of the sediment located from 4
to 2 m from the contact.

Crown Hill Formation, Bonavista peninsula
We collected red siltstone and mudstone samples from the
upper part of the Crown Hill Formation in a coastal outcrop
east of Duntara and in three outcrops along the Duntara –
King’s Cove road, which represent stratigraphically lower
levels (Fig. 2). All strata dip gently to the north-northeast.
Thermal demagnetisation of the Crown Hill red beds show
dominance of hematite (Fig. 12). The bipolar ChRM is quite
stable and consistent (Fig. 13; Table 3). The reversal test of
McFadden and McElhinny (1990) is positive (Rc, D = 3.5°,
Dc = 15.3°). Importantly, the stratigraphically higher sites
(C15a, C15b, C17) and the topmost sample of the strati-
graphically lower site C18 have an exclusively “normal”
(northwest, downward) polarity. The samples in the lower
part of the section (the rest of site C18 and sites C19a and
C19b) have “inverse” (southeast, upward) remanence direc-
tions, except for one sample in site C19a. This magnetostrati-
graphic pattern, supported by the positive reversal test, and
the positive regional conglomerate test sampled in the Crown
Hill Formation at Red Cliff (Fig. 9 b), suggests that the
ChRM carried by the Crown Hill Formation is primary. The
tilt-corrected mean direction from six sites in the Crown Hill
red beds is D = 333.8°, I = 42.4° ( a
95 = 14.6°), including
two “inverted” sites (Table 3).
Discussion
Mid-Ediacaran Bull Arm Formation
In this study, we have found that mafic volcanic flows and
associated siltstones of the Bull Arm Formation carry a pri-
mary hematite-borne ChRM, which is indicated by a positive
(Late Silurian – Early Devonian) fold test for the Argentia lo-
cality and by three positive conglomerate tests in the Bona-
vista locality. The Bull Arm Formation at both localities
features reversals that are stratigraphically controlled. We
consider it likely that the ChRM was acquired soon after the
extrusion of these sub-aerial lavas, probably during oxidation
associated with their cooling.
The Bull Arm result obtained from the Bonavista locality
is from flows that are correlated with Bull Arm volcanic
rocks dated at 570

a more uncertain age, being only constrained to be pre-fold-

respect to the dated Bull Arm volcanic rocks. The mean re-

are similar and their circles of confidence overlap (Fig. 14),

Late Ediacaran Crown Hill Formation
The result from the ca. 550 Ma Crown Hill Formation in-
dicates that West Avalonia lay at 24.2°S ± 5.3°S at the close
of the Ediacaran (Table 4). Notably, the mean direction from
the Crown Hill Formation is rotated over 90° clockwise from
the mean directions of both Bonavista and Argentia ca. 570
Ma Bull Arm results, despite the overall similarity of the
NNE–SSW structural trends in Bonavista and western Ava-
lon peninsulas (Fig. 1), implying tectonic rotation of the
whole terrane, or possibly a 570 to 550 Ma large true polar
wander (TPW) event (McCausland et al. 2007), with Avalo-
nia lying near the TPW axis of rotation. The Crown Hill
mean direction is also, however, strikingly dissimilar to any
from the subsequent Paleozoic records in Avalonia (Hodych
and Buchan 1998), except for the ca. 442 Ma Midland Minor
intrusive suite of East Avalonia, which is similarly anoma-
lous and interpreted to possibly represent a rotated block (Vi-
zan et al. 2003).
Paleogeographic implications for Avalonia in the
Ediacaran
Our new data from Bull Arm and Crown Hill Formations
indicate low to medium paleolatitudes for West Avalonia at
∼570 and ∼550 Ma. Based on the results from this study
alone, West Avalonia appears to have resided at low to me-
dium paleolatitudes during the latter part of the Ediacaran,
placing the ca. 565 Ma Ediacaran fauna-bearing strata at Mis-
taken Point and on the Bonavista peninsula (Narbonne and
Gehling 2003; O ’Brien et al. 2006) at <32°S during their
deposition.
We reviewed other published 620 –540 Ma paleomag-
netic results from both East and West Avalonian terranes
in view of more recent geochronological research on rocks
that had been studied paleomagnetically (Tucker and Phar-
aoh 1991; Compston et al. 2002; Schofield et al. 2010).
After filtering out Phanerozoic overprints and data without
proper demagnetization schemes there are six (including
three new results of this study) West Avalonian and five
East Avalonian paleomagnetic results (Table 4; Fig. 15).
Because of the poor Cambrian paleomagnetic database, the
sign of paleomagnetic polarity for Precambrian Avalonia
results is unclear, but we will assume a southern hemi-
sphere polarity, as suggested by most published Ediacaran
paleogeographic reconstructions (e.g., Dalziel 1997; Cor-
dani et al. 2003; Meert and Torsvik 2003; Murphy et al.
2004; Tohver et al. 2006; McCausland et al. 2007; Li et
al. 2008; Pisarevsky et al. 2008).

The paleomagnetic results for West and East Avalonia to
first order agree with one another, producing similar paleola-
titude estimates where ca. 600 and ca. 570 Ma comparisons
can be made (Fig. 15). This comparison supports the idea
that West and East Avalonia were together throughout the
Ediacaran, as expected from geological considerations (e.g.,
Cocks and Fortey 1982; McKerrow et al. 1992; Murphy et
al. 2004; Nance et al. 2008 and references therein).
The ages are not uniformly distributed, with only one rela-
tively high paleolatitude of 55° ± 8° from the Roxbury For-
mation, New England (Fang et al. 1986) for the time interval
between 593 and 570 Ma. Its imprecise age is constrained by
the 593 Ma youngest detrital zircon in the lower part of the
formation (Thompson et al. 2007) and by the youngest of a
range of zircon dates of the ash bed in the overlying Cam-
bridge Argillite, which is 570 Ma (Thompson and Bowring
2000). The Roxbury result was characterized by Thompson
et al. (2010) as a possible overprint, but it is apparently sup-
ported by a positive conglomerate test for primary remanence,
though without details (Fang et al. 1986). We retain the Rox-
bury result in Table 4 and in Fig. 15 and leave the judgement
to the reader and future studies of the Roxbury Formation.
All other Avalonia paleolatitudes in Table 4 are below 40°.
We should also note that three results from Uriconian
rocks in East Avalonia with ages between 568 and 564 Ma
(entries 8 –10 in Table 4) all indicate low paleolatitude, but
none of these studies provide convincing evidence for pri-
mary or near primary remanence. However, the correspond-
ing paleopoles lie apart from the Phanerozoic European
Apparent Polar Wander Path (McElhinny and McFadden
2000), so a younger overprint seems to be unlikely.
The paleolatitude drift history of Avalonia can be inter-
preted in two ways: if the solitary higher paleolatitude result
from the Roxbury Formation is primary, then Avalonia would
appear to have moved from paleolatitudes of ∼30°S at
∼600 Ma to ∼55°S during the deposition of the Roxbury
Formation, and then back to ∼35°S or lower paleolatitudes
by 570 Ma. Interestingly, the postulated residence of Avalo-
nia at >45°S at some time between 593 and 565 Ma corre-
sponds with the occurrence of glaciogenic sedimentation in
Avalonia, in the Boston area (ca. 590 Ma; Thompson et al.
2007) and at Gaskiers, Newfoundland (584 –582 Ma; Bowr-
ing et al. 2003; Hoffman and Li 2009).

if the New England portion of Avalonia was not strictly

Geodynamic implications from Avalonian paleomagnetic
results
Application of the Avalonian paleomagnetic results to Ed-
iacaran global paleogeography depends on the proximity of
Avalonia to major continents. Most workers agree that the
Avalonian blocks were Peri-Gondwanan terranes and at 600 –
550 Ma were attached or situated close to the (present) north-
ern margin of Amazonia and (or) West Africa (McNamara et
al. 2001; Murphy et al. 2004; Thompson et al. 2007; Nance
et al. 2008, 2010 and references therein). These two major
continents were probably juxtaposed to each other in a Gond-
wanan configuration (Trompette 1994, 1997). Unfortunately,
Ediacaran paleomagnetic data from Amazonia and West
Africa are scarce and controversial, so their paleolatitudes at
∼600–550 Ma are unknown (Tohver et al. 2006). In this sit-
uation, paleomagnetic data from peri-Gondwanan terranes
may provide paleolatitudinal constraints for these West
Gondwanan cratons. We shall follow this hypothesis of the
West African – Amazonian affinity of Avalonia.
Published global paleogeographic reconstructions for 600 –
550 Ma vary considerably (e.g., Grunow et al. 1996; Dalziel
1997; Cordani et al. 2003; Pisarevsky et al. 2008 and referen-
ces therein). The main reason is the Laurentian paleomag-
netic database, which contains two sets of equally reliable
paleopoles indicating either high- or low-latitude position of
Laurentia correspondingly (see a summary of Pisarevsky et
al. 2008 and references therein). If all of the Ediacaran paleo-
poles for Laurentia are primary, an unusually high rate of
plate movement or some contribution of TPW is required
(McCausland et al. 2007; 2011). Consequently, two alterna-
tive sets of reconstructions have been proposed (Murphy et
al. 2004; McCausland et al. 2007; 2011; Pisarevsky et al.
2008).
Another possibility involves the dominant contribution
from a rapid interchange event in the Earth ’s moment of in-
ertia tensor (inertial interchange true polar wander (IITPW);
Kirschvink et al. 1997). The idea has been further developed
(Evans 1998, 2003) and criticized (Meert 1999; Tsai and Ste-
venson 2007). If the IITPW hypothesis is correct, evidence of
similar rapid apparent polar wander (APW) should be present
coevally in the rock records of all continents. Schmidt and
Williams (2010) demonstrated that there is no large shift in
paleolatitude for Australia, although their compilation does
show a relatively large APW for that continent during the Ed-
iacaran.

Recently, Abrajevitch and Van der Voo (2010) suggested
that the controversy of Laurentia and Baltica Ediacaran pa-
leopoles could be explained by an alternation of the geomag-
netic dipole axis between a geocentric coaxial and an
equatorial alignment. This is an interesting idea, but it is in
need of further testing. In particular, as for the IITPW, the
geocentric equatorial dipole hypothesis requires similar be-
haviour of paleopoles from other continents.
In general, the low to moderate southerly paleolatitudes of
Avalonia through the Ediacaran (Fig. 15) imply that the adja-
cent Amazonia – West Africa margin of West Gondwana
similarly did not experience much change in paleolatitude,
thus potentially placing a constraint on global geodynamic
models. The result from the Roxbury Formation (Thompson
et al. 2007) is the only relatively high paleolatitude for Edia-
caran Avalonia (Table 4; Fig. 15) and, consequently, for the
“northern” West Gondwana (northern parts of Amazonia and
West Africa in present coordinates). Excluding the Roxbury
Formation result, the Avalonia paleolatitude distribution sup-
ports a “low-latitude” Laurentia model for the global late
Neoproterozoic paleogeography (Pisarevsky et al. 2008), be-
cause the “high-latitude” Laurentia model requires near-polar
position of this area in mid-Ediacaran time, assuming that
Laurentia and West Gondwana were closely associated
throughout the Ediacaran.

The shift in West Avalonia ’s cratonic affinity along the
West Africa stems mainly from the apparent southwards shift
of West Gondwana between 570 and 550 Ma. The relative
motion between Avalonia and the Amazonia – West Africa
margin is represented schematically in Fig. 16 b as a dextral
transcurrent motion of about 1000 km along the margin.
These results are broadly consistent with models in which
Avalonian magmatism is terminated between 600 and 540
Ma by the generation of a San Andreas-style transform fault
(Murphy et al. 2000) and with detrital zircon data from Edia-
caran aged clastic rocks which indicate a shift from Amazo-
nian to West African provenance in the Ediacaran (Gutiérrez-
Alonso et al. 2005).
Conclusions
1. Paleomagnetic study of the ∼570 Ma Bull Arm volcanics
in Bonavista and Argentia localities of the Avalon Zone,
Newfoundland reveal a consistent bipolar ChRM, carried
by hematite, that is likely primary, as shown by several
positive field tests and by apparent magnetostratigraphic
pattern in the studied section. Paleomagnetic directions
are slightly different in Bonavista and Argentia, which
may because of to slight structural differences between
the two localities, or possibly age difference between the
studied rocks. A less stable magnetite-borne component
in the Argentia locality postdates Silurian folding.
2. The paleomagnetic study of the ∼550 Ma Crown Hill red
beds in the northern part of the Bonavista peninsula re-
veal a stable bipolar hematite borne ChRM supported by
positive reversal test and by a magnetostratigraphic pat-
tern in the studied section.
3. These results suggest a low-latitude position of Avalonia
in the mid- to late Ediacaran, during the period when
complex Ediacaran fauna became established in West
Avalonia.
4. Ediacaran paleolatitudes of Avalonia indicate only moder-
ate-scale drift of this terrane and suggest that the Amazo-
nia – West Africa portion of Gondwana underwent little
drift during this time, assuming Avalonia maintained a re-
latively fixed relationship with those cratons.
5. Alternatively, a ∼1000 km dextral motion of Avalonia
with respect to Amazonia – West Africa can be inferred
from the comparison of Avalonia paleolatitudes with the
position of West Gondwana at ∼570 and ∼550 Ma, as-
suming West Gondwana was assembled prior to 570 Ma.

Amazon craton: Evidence for Grenvillian emplacement of exotic

Abstract
We apply a new diagenetic dating technique to determine the age of magnetization for Precambrian sedimentary rocks in the SW Amazon
craton. Two new paleomagnetic poles are reported from the rocks of the Aguapeí Gp.: red beds of the Fortuna Fm. (P lat = 59.8°N, Plon = 155.9°E,
A95 = 9.5, K = 14, 18 sites, N/n 128/115, Q = 5) and the reverse-polarity mudstones of the overlying V ale da Promissão Formation (P lat = 49.5°N,
Plon = 89.3°E, A95 = 12.5, K = 30, 6 sites, N/n = 94/80, Q = 4). The Fortuna Fm. magnetization is hosted by massive, interstitial hematite cement and
constitutes a post-depositional remanence. The age of diagenesis of the red beds is well-constrained by the 1149 ± 7 Ma U –Pb age of authigenic
xenotime rims on detrital zircons determined by SHRIMP analysis. The magnetite-hosted remanence of the V ale da Promissão Fm. may be detrital
in origin, but the age of deposition is poorly constrained. The reliable and precisely-dated Fortuna Fm. paleomagnetic pole fixes the
paleogeographic position of the Amazon craton near the SE Appalachians portion of North America at 1.15 Ga. These data demonstrate a mobile
Grenvillian link between these two cratons, and support the recent identification of Amazon crust in the Blue Ridge province region of North
America.

1. Introduction
Reliable paleomagnetic data provide a quantitative, global
reference frame for shifting tectonic plates. For Pre-Jurassic
times, this reference frame is indispensable due to the destruc-
tion of geological evidence such as marine magnetic anomalies
or the non-unique aspects of faunal correlations or paleoclimate
indicators. The “reliability” is established by linking two
observations: reconstruction of the time-averaged field from
an isolated magnetic remanence and the determination of the
age of the magnetization. Improvements in instrumentation and
magnetic cleaning techniques now allow for routine measure-
ment of a wide range of magnetic remanences (10
− 3–102 A/m)
from diverse rocks. In contrast, the age of magnetization is
established by relative dating methods or is assumed to date
from the time of rock formation, which is especially problematic
for barren Precambrian sedimentary rocks where the rock age is
not easily determined. A survey of the global database shows
that sedimentary rocks constitute more than one-third of

with an average uncertainty N 10% of the rock age. To put this
in perspective, a widely adopted criterion rejects magnetizations
with N 4% age uncertainty ( V an der V oo, 1990 ), elimi-
nating N80% of extant results from Precambrian sedimentary
rocks. A new technique for the dating of diagenesis holds great
potential for providing precise age constraints hitherto lacking
in paleomagnetic investigations of Precambrian sediments.
A key issue in Precambrian geology revolves around the
supercontinent Rodinia ( Torsvik, 2003 ), the configuration
and position of which are considered to have had a major role
in the onset of Neoproterozoic global glaciations ( Donnadieu
et al., 2004 ). The link between the Amazon craton and eastern
Laurentia across the Grenvillian collision zone (1.2 –1.0 Ga) is a
key feature of the Rodinia supercontinent, the rupture of which
marks the opening of the Iapetus Ocean at the beginning of the
Phanerozoic era. The configuration of the two continents in the
Precambrian supercontinent varies in the original reconstruc-
tions following the match of either collision zone metamorph-
ism ( Hoffman, 1991 ) or post-rift thermal subsidence and
stratigraphy ( Bond et al., 1984; Dalziel, 1992 ). Data from the
Amazon craton itself suggest a different configuration begin-
ning with a southerly collision site ( Tohver et al., 2002 ) fol-
lowed by strike-slip migration of the Amazon towards a
more central location near the Grenville Province of Ontario –
New York ( Tohver et al., 2005a ).
The recent identification of exotic Amazonian crust lodged
within the basement of the southeastern Appalachians ( Carrigan
et al., 2003; Loewy et al., 2003; Tohver et al., 2004a ) appears to
corroborate this strike-slip passage, but only well-dated
paleomagnetic data can provide the necessary spatial reference
frame to confirm this scenario [e.g., Hanson et al. (2004) ].
In this paper we present new paleomagnetic and geochro-
nological data from late Mesoproterozoic sediments of the
Aguapeí Group, western Brazil. These sediments were depos-
ited in the southwestern margin of the Amazon craton, over the
Paragua shield. Barren sedimentary rocks from the Precambrian
era are difficult to date, especially so for clastic rocks.
Paleomagnetic studies of these rocks are further complicated
by the uncertain origin of the magnetization as either a depo-
sitional remanence (DRM) or post-depositional remanence
formed by the growth of an authigenic phase (CRM) ( V erosub,
1977). We overcome these problems by using a novel technique
to date diagenesis, U –Pb analysis of authigenic xenotime rims
on detrital zircon. Together, these new data provide a high
quality, well-dated paleomagnetic pole that constrains the

1.1. SW Amazon Regional Geology
The Amazon Craton (Fig. 1) is bisected by the E–W trending
Paleozoic basin (Solimões- Amazonas) that underlies the
Amazon River. A late Archean nucleus in the NE portion of
the craton is bordered by accretionary belts that are progres-
sively younger to the SW ( Santos et al., 2000; Tassinari et al.,
2000), although the general lack of outcrop and geophysical
data has led to debate over the position and significance of the
various geochronological provinces that comprise the craton
(Pinho et al., 2003 ). The youngest addition to the Amazon
craton is the Paragua block, a subcontinental shield in eastern
Bolivia (Fig. 1) that has been interpreted as either separate from,
or as a subprovince of the Amazon craton before 1.1 Ga ( Boger
et al., 2005 ). A minimum age for a joint Amazon –Paragua
history derives from the 1.1 Ga high-grade metamorphism of
the suturing Nova Brasilândia Metasedimentary Belt ( Santos
et al., 2000; Rizzotto, 1999 ). Collision must have taken place
before metamorphism, given the clockwise pressure –tempera-
ture path of continental collisions; e.g., the 50 –55 Ma collision
between India and Eurasia caused Himalayan regional meta-
morphism 20 –40 Ma later ( Hodges, 2000 ). Because rates of
orthogonal convergence and burial are related ( Thompson et al.,
1997), we infer a 50 Ma lag time for the transpressive Nova
Brasilândia belt ( Rizzotto, 1999) and a common geography for
the Paragua –Amazon craton by 1.15 Ga.
Rocks of the correlated Sunsás and Aguapeí Gps. overlie the
1.7–1.4 Ga Paragua basement rocks of Bolivia and Brazil
(Fig. 1 ), respectively. In Bolivia, the deposition of ca. 6 km
Sunsás Gp. psammites and pelites is ascribed to a deltaic-fluvial
environment (Litherland et al., 1989 ). Deformation and granite
intrusion during the eponymous orogeny at ≥ 1076 Ma ( Boger
et al., 2005 ) were marked by prominent NW –SE trending
mylonite belts with sinistral displacement ( Litherland et al.,
1989). In Brazil, the 1 –2 km thick Aguapeí Gp. comprises
basal conglomerates and red sandstones (Fortuna Fm.), overlain
by pelitic rocks and fine lithic, sub-arkosic rocks (V ale da
Promissão Fm.), topped by quartz sandstones of the Morro
Cristalina Fm. (Souza and Hildred, 1980; Saes and Leite, 1993 ).

2. Sampling and methods
Paleomagnetic sampling consisted of 123 oriented cores and
7 hand samples collected from 25 sedimentary levels of the
Fortuna Formation and V ale da Promissão Formation of the
Aguapeí Group (Fig. 1b). Cylindrical cores were drilled using a
portable, gasoline-powered rock drill, and whenever possible,
both magnetic and solar compasses were used for sample
orientation. Details of site locations are included in Table 1.A
total of seventeen sites were taken from steep bluffs of the
reddish Fortuna Formation near the town of Vila Bela on the
Brazil–Bolivia border. This flank is located outside the core of
the Aguapeí Belt, with deformation restricted to gentle, open
folds (Fig. 1b). The first 15 sites were taken from a continuous,
~ 22 m thick stratigraphic section, with sites 16 and 17 collected
from exposures of uncertain stratigraphic position relative to the
first sites. Seven sites (sites 19 –25) were collected from the
eastern flank of the Aguapeí belt, close to the towns of Rio
Branco and Salto do Céu ( Fig. 1 b). The grey sediments from
these sites are from the V ale da Promissão Formation that
overlies the Fortuna Formation. The sediments from site 19
(road outcrop) are cross-cut by a sill which appears locally as
small blocks of drift. Unfortunately, it was not possible to
collect samples from sediments far from the sill for a baked
contact test. This, and other basic sills were also collected for
paleomagnetic analysis and their results have been presented by
Elming et al. (submitted). One of the sills was selected for dating,
and the
40Ar/39Ar analysis on biotite yielded a well defined
plateau age of 980.6 ± 1.7 Ma. Only one site (site 18 in Table 1)
was collected from the internal, more deformed portion of the
Aguapeí belt just to the south of the town of Pontes e Lacerda (Fig.
1b), although the beds at this site were flat-lying.
Samples were cut into 2.2 × 2.5 cm cylindrical specimens
and submitted to step-wise thermal and alternating field
(AF) demagnetization in the paleomagnetic laboratories at the
Universidade de São Paulo (USP), Brazil, and the University of
Luleå, Sweden. Polished thin sections were made from repre-
sentative samples, with reflected light microscopy and scanning
electron microscopy in conjunction with energy dispersive
spectroscopy used to examine the opaque mineralogy. A total
of 236 specimens from 25 sedimentary layers were analyzed
after magnetic cleaning. Magnetic remanence was measured
using a 2 G cryogenic magnetometer after step-wise treatment
by alternating fields (AF) or thermal demagnetization. AF
demagnetization was carried out using an automated three-axis
AF-demagnetizer (upper limit of 170 mT) and thermal
demagnetization was carried out in a Magnetic Measurements
(MMTD60) oven or a Schonsted oven, with peak temperatures
within ± 2 °C and a heating time of 1 h. In São Paulo these
instruments are housed in a magnetically shielded room with
ambient field b 1000 nT. Magnetic components for each
specimen were identified in orthogonal plots, and calculated
using least-squares fits ( Kirschvink, 1980 ). Fisherian statistics
(Fisher, 1953) were used to calculate vector mean directions and
paleomagnetic poles. Additional magnetic measurements were
performed in a Moslpin vibrating sample magnetometer for
hysteresis curves, and a Magnetic Measurements pulse mag-
netizer was used for isothermal remanence acquisition.
Zircons were separated from a sample of the Fortuna
Formation (JO2), the basal member of the Aguapeí Group,
using standard techniques: crushing, sieving, milling, separa-
tion by Frantz magnetic separator, and concentration on heavy
liquids. Approximately 2500 grains were mounted in epoxy,
polished, and carbon coated for scattered electron microscopy
(SEM). Grains were examined using backscattered electron
imagery for the presence of authigenic xenotime overgrowths
wide enough for SHRIMP analysis ( ≥ 10 μm). SHRIMP
analysis was carried out at the Curtin University of Technology,
Western Australia, using an analytical spot of about 10 μm and
six scans. All data are corrected for matrix effect using the MG1
standard (490 Ma; ( Fletcher et al., 2004 )), and are quoted at 2 σ
level. Presented ages are
207Pb/206Pb ages corrected for
common lead using the 204Pb content.

3. Results and observations
3.1. Magnetic components
The natural remanent magnetization (NRM) intensities vary
from 0.224 × 10− 3 A/m up to values as high as 17.4 A/m. AF
demagnetization on the red sediments of the Fortuna Formation
eliminates a soft component (7.5 –30 mT) that persists during
thermal demagnetization to temperatures up to 560 °C –580 °C
(Fig. 2 a, b). This overprint having been removed, we observe
a northerly, upward direction that persists to temperatures be-
tween 600 °C and 660 °C ( Fig. 2 a to b). As for the grey
sandstones and pelites of the V ale da Promissão Formation,
most samples record a soft, randomly-oriented magnetic
component with coercivities from 0 to 20 –30 mT ( Fig. 2 c)
and unblocking temperatures up to 400 –450 °C ( Fig. 2 d).
Removal of this overprint reveals a south/southwestern, rela-
tively steep downward inclination direction with higher coer-
civities and unblocking temperatures that range from 450° to
580 °C ( Fig. 2 c to d).
The occurrence of normal, upward paleomagnetic directions
appears to be confined to the basal Fortuna Formation, with
reversed, downward directions found solely in the overlying
V ale da Promissão Formation. The one exception to this pattern
is site 19 ( Fig. 2e to f), where samples of the V ale da Promissão
Formation are normally magnetized close to a ca. 980 Ma mafic
sill. Magnetic directions of sediments and sills in this site
are similar suggesting a thermal resetting of the sediments. In
consequence, site 19 was not considered in determining the
mean direction of V ale da Promissão Formation. In order to test
if the V ale da Promissão and Fortuna directions shared
equivalent antipodal means, we have applied the McFadden
and Lowes (1981) statistical test. The normal and reversed
directions (Fig. 3) did not pass the reversal test suggesting that a

3.2. Rock magnetism and textures of magnetic carriers
The higher coercivity, highe r temperature component
isolated from the Fortuna red beds is carried by hematite,
whereas the low coercivity, random overprint observed in these
rocks seems to be carried by magnetite. Hysteresis loops of
Fortuna Formation rocks have a wasp-waisted form, reflecting
the mixture of these high and low coercivity fractions ( Fig. 4a).
This bi-modal signal is also revealed by isothermal remanence
(IRM) acquisition curves ( Fig. 4c). They show a sharp increase
in the first 200 mT, probably as a result of the tiny magnetite
fraction in the samples. Then, the curves show a smooth
increase in remanence, due to the hematite fraction, getting
close to saturation at 3 T, the higher field produced in our pulse
magnetizer.
In addition to the rock magnetic characteristics, the
ubiquitous presence of hematite in Fortuna Formation samples
is evident from the red color of the rocks in hand sample. In thin
section, hematite occurs as massive cement in the interstitial
spaces between grains, which are in clear contact with one
another. This grain-supported texture suggests that the grains
were not coated in iron oxides prior to deposition ( Fig. 5a), but
that the hematite cement filled available pore spaces during later
diagenesis. This is also suggested by the intergrowth of hematite
cement and “hairy” illite, a clear diagenetic feature (Fig. 5b). The
phosphatic cements that overgrow detrital minerals such as
monazite and zircon are also interpreted as diagenetic in origin
(Fig. 5c).
Samples from the V ale da Promissão Formation show
contrasting magnetic characteristics when compared to the
Fortuna Formation red beds. Hysteresis loops show tight waists
and fast saturation at fields below 300 mT ( Fig. 4 b). Samples
show coercivity values between 1.1 and 24.6 mT, typical of
magnetite grains. IRM-acquisition curves for some samples
show a fast increase in remanence, attaining saturation at
inducing fields below 300 mT ( Fig. 4 c). Other samples,
however, show much slower increase in remanence suggesting
a high coercivity fraction in addition to magnetite in these rocks
(Fig. 4 c). Hence, hematite may also be present in the V ale da
Promissão sediments, but no consistent paleomagnetic direction
is observed in these rocks above 580 °C. Reflected light
microscopy of opaque, detrital minerals in polished thin
sections reveals the presence of trellis-type textures that result
from high temperature alteration of magmatic titanomagnetite
by oxyexsolution ( Haggerty, 1976).
3.3. Paleomagnetic poles
Based on the magnetic characteristics and petrographic
observations, we argue that the characteristic remanent magne-
tizations are primary in both Fortuna and V ale da Promissão
Formations. The general lack of tectonic activity in the region
and the distinctiveness of these remanent directions from known
Phanerozoic paleomagnetic directions support this inference.
The mean directions determined from the characteristic
remanences of the Fortuna Formation (normal) and the V ale
da Promissão Formation (reversed) are different (Table 1), as are
the magnetic mineralogies, and the ages of magnetic acquisi-
tion. We calculate two separate paleomagnetic poles for the

3.4. Geochronology
Of the ~ 2500 grains examined, eighteen are marked by the
presence of xenotime overgrowths ( Fig. 6 a) with a total of
twelve grains with sufficiently thick rims to be analyzed by
SHRIMP ( ≥ 10 μm). Xenotime is a rare earth-rich yttrium
phosphate (YPO4) that grows as a chemical precipitate rim
during diagenesis by scavenging of dissolved phosphorus from
seawater or P-bearing shales ( Rasmussen et al., 1998;
Rasmussen et al., 2005 ). The SHRIMP analyses are shown in
the plot of
206Pb/238Pb versus 207Pb/235U( Fig. 6 b). Of the
eleven analyses obtained, nine align in a regression line at 1149 ±
7M a( Table 2). One age is a discordant outlier and other is a
younger concordant age of 960 ± 46 Ma. The younger and
concordant age of 960 Ma is comparable to some Ar –Ar ages
and may reflect a younger event, perhaps hydrothermal activity.
The U and Th contents of the analyzed xenotime grains are high:
821–5531 ppm and 3602 –37068 ppm, respectively. The age of
1149 ± 7 Ma calculated from the nine remaining analyses is
interpreted as the age of diagenesis and serves as a minimum age
for the deposition of the Fortuna Fm., the basal member of the
Aguapeí Group. Detrital zircons from other sample of Fortuna
Formation (MT1) collected at São Vicente gold mine in Mato
Grosso, was dated by Santos et al. (2005) where the youngest
grain (d.9-1) is 1165 ± 27 Ma old. Combining the detrital zircons
information and the diagenetic xenotime data we conclude that
deposition of Fortuna Formation of Aguapeí Group is
constrained between 1165 ± 27 Ma and 1149 ± 7 Ma.

4. Discussion
4.1. Age of magnetization in Fortuna and V ale da Promissão
Formations
The origin of the magnetization in sedimentary rocks is a
long-standing question in paleomagnetic studies ( V erosub,
1977; Larson et al., 1982; Tauxe and Kent, 1984; Beck et al.,
2003). The problem lies in reconciling the scale-independent
magnetic properties of the bulk rock with petrographic obser-
vations that range in scale from optically-observed minerals and
textures to the submicroscopic magnetic minerals or domains
inferred from scanning electron or transmission electron
microscopy. The origin and age of the V ale da Promissão
Formation magnetization is typical of this problem. Although
the presence of detrital magnetite grains is suggestive, petro-
graphic observations alone cannot confirm that these grains host
a primary, depositional remanence. Additional indication of the
primary nature of magnetization in these rocks is given by an
incomplete baked contact test for this unit, given by the results
of site 19, sampled close to a mafic sill, compared to the other
sites of the collection. Samples from sediments and the mafic
intrusion collected in site 19 show concordant directions,
whereas sediments collected far from any intrusion have a
different direction. But even in the case where the magnetization
is primary, we still face loose age constraints with the age of
magnetization bracketed between the age of detrital zircons in
the underlying Fortuna Formation (dated at N1165 Ma) and the
age of later episode of mafic dykes intrusion (dated at 980 Ma).
Although there are no significant hiatuses presently recognized
in the Aguapeí Group depositional history, the difference in
paleomagnetic direction and polarity between the Fortuna
Formation and the overlying V ale da Promissão Formation
suggests a substantial period of time elapsed between the
acquisition of magnetization in these formations. The inter-
pretation of the magnetization for the basal Fortuna Formation is
simpler since the most likely carrier of the high temperature,
high coercivity, characteristic remanence (ChRM) in the under-
lying Fortuna Formation is the abundant hematite cement. If this
is correct, then the Fortuna Formation ChRM is post-deposi-
tional, since the interstitial hematite cement formed during
diagenesis and lithification of these sediments. Based on the
diagenetic age of 1149 ± 7 Ma established by the U –Pb analysis
of authigenic xenotime, we assign an age of magnetization for
the post-depositional remanence.
4.2. Implications for Rodinia
Proposed permutations of the Rodinia supercontinent began
to arise soon after the original geometries of Hoffman (1991)
and Dalziel (1992) were advanced. The later, derivative models
mostly adhere to the key assumption of a Laurentia-centered
supercontinent that was assembled via Grenvillian collisions on
the (present-day) eastern margin of proto-North America and
later disassembled during Neoproterozoic rifting. The paleo-
geography of the intervening ~ 500 Ma initially attracted little
comment, other than some debate as to when rifting along the
(present-day) western margin of Laurentia began ( Prave, 1999).
This apparent consensus has been undermined by the recent
work of both geologists [e.g., ( Hanson et al., 2004; Kroner and
Cordani, 2003; Cordani et al., 2003 )] and paleomagnetists
[e.g., ( Wingate et al., 2002; Pisarevsky and Natapov, 2003;
Meert and Torsvik, 2003; Tohver et al., 2006 )] questioning the
monolithic nature of the Rodinia supercontinent, in particular
the assertion that all of the continents were arrayed near or
alongside Laurentia. For example, the elegant simplicity of the
original match in Grenvillian-aged metamorphic provinces
has been clouded by the recognition that cooling ages are
preserved throughout the Laurentian belt, whereas the south-
western Amazon retains a mixture of cooling and deformation
ages (Tohver et al., 2005a,b ). In the last few years an evolving
Laurentia–Amazon connection has been proposed to explain
structural, isotopic and geophysical data on the southwestern
Amazon and eastern Laurentia ( Tohver et al., 2004a,b, 2005b ).
The new paleomagnetic data that we present here do support a
direct, tectonic link between Laurentia and Amazonia at
1.15 Ga, but they suggest a dynamic Rodinia that contrasts
with the stasis of the original models.
The Fortuna Formation provides a well-dated, well-char-
acterized paleomagnetic pole based on a direction that is distinct
from any known overprinting directions. Using the quality
criteria of V an der V oo (1990), the pole is assigned a Q-factor of
5. Given the uncertainties outlined above regarding the V ale da
Promissão Formation ChRM, we restrict the following discus-
sion of paleogeography to the 1.15 Ga position established for
the Amazon craton by the Fortuna Formation. Considering the
new pole presented here and the Nova Floresta pole (NF)
presented by Tohver et al. (2002) a segment of apparent polar
wander path (APWP) for Amazonia can be traced between 1200
and 1149 Ma. In case there was no relative motion between
Amazonia and Laurentia, this APWP can be compared to that of
Laurentia. As a first approximation we consider the Laurentian
path defined by paleomagnetic poles from Upper Bylot (UB,
1204 ± 22 Ma, 8°N, 205°E, A
95 = 4) and Abitiby dikes (AD,
1141 ± 1 Ma, 43°N, 208°E, A95 = 14). A rotation of 41.9° around
an Euler pole at 60.35°N and 310.7°E would account for the
match of the two APWP segments defined above. But when
applied to the continents, this rotation places the western margin
of Amazonia more than 5000 km far from the eastern margin of
Laurentia (Fig. 7). Given the abundant evidence for collision in
both cratons in this time interval this paleogeographic configu-
ration would require a significant intervening block between
Laurentia and Amazonia by this time. Moreover, isotopic evi-
dence for Amazonian heritage in blocks of the present-day
eastern margin of Laurentia and vice-versa argue strongly on the
connection between these two cratons.
We prefer instead to compare pole by pole the Amazonia and
Laurentia database. According to this approach, the relative
position of the Amazon craton determined from the Nova
Floresta and Fortuna Formation poles is depicted in Fig. 7 .I n
these reconstructions, the Amazon craton has shifted along-
strike from the original 1.2 Ga collision site farther southeast
(present-day), typified by the Llano Uplift region, toward the
(present-day) SE Appalachians. Geological evidence for this

motion is found in the presence of large-scale, sinistral strike-
slip shear zones active throughout the 1.2 –1.0 Ga interval in
SW Amazonia ( Tohver et al., 2005b; Litherland et al., 1989 ).
The 1.15 Ga position of the Amazon craton opposite the present-
day SE Appalachians has left other telltale signs, notably the
rocks of the western Blue Ridge/Mars Hills (BRMH) terrane
which are exotic to Laurentia. A non-Laurentian mantle
reservoir for the BRMH rocks was identified using Pb and Nd
isotopic signatures ( Loewy et al., 2003; Tohver et al., 2004a ),
and rock samples from this terrane contain relict zircons with
ages characteristic of SW Amazonia (Carrigan et al., 2003 ). The
age of the high-grade deformation in the SE Appalachians that
attended the docking of these rocks onto the Grenvillian margin
of Laurentia is constrained to the 1145 –1075 Ma interval
(Aleinikoff et al., 2000 ). Isotopic evidence points to docking
during the earlier portion of this 70 Ma interval, since the ε
Nd
values of rocks much younger than 1.15 Ga are positive,
reflecting a Laurentian mantle source ( Tohver et al., 2004a). We
also note that the NE –SW directed compressional event
discerned by Aleinikoff et al. (2000) for this deformation is
parallel to the (present-day) strike of Grenvillian rocks, echoing
the earlier findings of Mosher (1998) that the colliding continent
approached from the (present-day) SW. Thus, the NE directed
compression parallel to the Llano and Grenville tectonic fronts is
compatible with a strike-slip scenario, observations that are
comfortably accounted for by the ongoing strike-slip motion of
Amazonia.
This dynamic scenario involves a net sinistral strike-slip
motion of the Amazon craton across Laurentia's margin
between 1.2 and 1.0 Ga, initiating with the collision along the
southernmost Laurentia (Llano region, Texas), reaching the SE
Appalachians by 1.15 Ga. This motion is described by a 15°
rotation about Euler pole located at 75°N, 155.5°E ( Fig. 7), with
the general NE –SW trend of the Grenvillian margin approx-
imating a small circle to this Euler pole. Continued motion
along this small circle within an overall transpressive setting
would result in net strike-slip motion and contribute to the long
span of Grenvillian orogenesis (1.2 –1.0 Ga).
