Brichta swarms have a length of ∼500 km and a width of
∼200 km.
Reconstruction of Beechey dyke swarm across Bathurst
fault
In the current configuration (Fig. 2 a), undated NNW-
trending Beechey dykes occur both southwest and northeast
of the Bathurst fault. Southwest of the fault they are found
mainly southeast of the Kilohigok basin between latitude 65°
and 65.8°N, but have been reported to intrude the base of the
Goulburn Group in the southeastern portion of the basin
(Frith 1981). Northeast of the fault they are found between
∼65.7°N and the Arctic coast. If the Beechey dykes were
emplaced before movement occurred on the Bathurst fault,
then the reconstruction of Fig. 2 b eliminates most of the ap-
parent offset between the main portions of the swarm on ei-
ther side of the fault, and indicates that the swarm originally
had a length of at least 200 km and a width of at least 120 km.
Age-correlative magmatic events on other cratonic blocks
Several dyke swarms and sill or volcanic provinces on
other Archean cratons have U –Pb ages within 20 million
years of the age of the Malley swarm. The 2235 ± 2 Ma Kik-
kertavak dykes of the Nain Province of the North Atlantic
craton (Cadman et al. 1993) and ca. 2240 Ma dykes of the
Vestfold Hills in Antarctica (Lanyon et al. 1993) are slightly
older than the Malley swarm. On the other hand, ca. 2218 –
2216 Ma Nipissing sills and Senneterre dykes of the Superior
craton (Andrews et al. 1986; Noble and Lightfoot 1992; Bu-
chan et al. 1993), ca. 2220 –2206 Ma Koli sills of Karelia
(summary in Vuollo et al. 1995), ca. 2220 –2209 Ma Kandla-
madugu and Somala dykes of the Dharwar craton of India
(French and Heaman 2010), 2214 ± 10 Ma BN-1 dykes of
the North Atlantic craton in Greenland (Nutman et al. 1995),
and ca. 2209 ± 15 Ma Cheela Springs Basalts of the Ha-
mersley basin of the Pilbara craton of Australia (Martin et
al. 1998) are a little younger. Of these units, only the Nipiss-
ing sills and Senneterre dykes of the Superior craton have a
key paleopole (Buchan et al. 1993). A comparison between
the Slave and Superior paleomagnetic results are discussed
later in the text.
In addition, a primary paleopole has been reported for On-
geluk lavas of the Kaapvaal craton (Evans et al. 1997), which
may be roughly coeval with the Malley dykes, based on a
Pb–Pb age of 2222 ± 13 Ma (Cornell et al. 1996). However,
other authors (e.g., Bau et al. 1999) questioned this age based
on an older Pb –Pb age of 2394 ± 26 Ma from overlying
Mooidraai dolomite. Therefore, a precise U –Pb age is re-
quired to test an Ongeluk –Malley age correlation.
Age of Malley dyke remanence
A field test is not available to demonstrate that the Malley
remanence is primary. Nevertheless, it is substantially older
than 2.03 Ga, based on the positive baked contact test at the
Lac de Gras – Malley intersection. In addition, evidence sug-
gests that it significantly predates 2.12 Ga and likely predates
2.19 Ga, as discussed later in the text.
As described earlier, NE-trending Malley dykes carry a
consistent up SE remanence, whereas the E- to ESE-trending
MD1 “Dogrib” dyke at sites 40 and 41 is magnetized down
WNW (Fig. 6), similar to 2.19 Ga Dogrib dykes near Yel-
lowknife. There are two possible intepretation of these re-
sults. Most likely, the difference between the remanences in
the Malley and Dogrib dykes indicates that there has been
no previous overprinting of the dykes in the study area at or
before 2.19 Ga. If this is the case, the “Dogrib” remanence at
sites 40 and 41 is primary, and the Malley remanence was
acquired significantly before 2.19 Ga, either at the time of or
shortly after dyke emplacement at 2.23 Ga.
In the alternative, and less likely interpretation, the agree-
ment of the MD1 “Dogrib” dyke remanence and its polarity
with that of Dogrib dykes near Yellowknife and the differ-
ence with the remanence direction of Malley dykes are sim-

In this case, it could only be concluded that the Malley (and

based on the conclusion reached earlier that the remanence of
Dogrib dykes in the Yellowknife area is older than the ca.
2.12 Ga emplacement age of Indin dykes. However, there is
no evidence of a regional post 2.19 Ga metamorphic event in
the study area or near Yellowknife that could have com-
pletely reset high unblocking temperature remanences of the
Malley and Dogrib dykes. Therefore, we conclude that this
scenario is unlikely, and the Malley remanence was acquired
at the time of or shortly after dyke emplacement.
Implications for paleocontinental reconstructions
Assuming that the paleopole for the 2.23 Ga Malley
swarm is primary or acquired shortly after dyke emplace-
ment, as seems likely, it is useful to compare it with the pri-
mary pole for the crosscutting 2.03 Ma Lac de Gras dykes
and with the sequence of key poles that define an APWP for
the Superior craton, especially the pole for the 2.22 Ga Ni-
pissing sills and Senneterre dykes, which were intruded
shortly after the Malley dykes (Fig. 10). The virtual geomag-
netic pole from the well-dated 2.19 Ga Dogrib dykes is also
shown for comparison, although it must be used with caution
because it is based on only two dykes, does not average out
secular variation, and, hence, its ellipse of confidence may
greatly underestimate its uncertainty.
It should be noted that relative polarity of the Superior
poles is known because the time intervals ( ≤50 million years)
between poles are too short to allow the use of antipoles in
the APWP. Similarly, the relative polarity between the Malley
and Dogrib poles is known. However, the polarity of Malley
and Dogrib poles relative to the Lac de Gras pole is unclear
because of the long time gap ( ∼160 million years) between
the Dogrib and Lac de Gras poles. Malley and Dogrib poles
are located in Fig. 10 a using the polarity that minimizes their
distance from the Lac de Gras pole, and in Fig. 10 b using the
opposite relative polarity option. It should also be noted that
the relative polarity of Superior and Slave poles is unknown,
so that the Slave craton poles could be located on the oppo-
site side of the globe to their position in Fig. 10. The Slave
and Superior poles are plotted on the same side of the globe
in Fig. 10 simply for convenience.

(Fig. 10), consistent with the relatively short time interval
(∼40 million years) between the emplacement of the two
swarms. The Malley and Dogrib poles are far from that of
the 2.03 Ga Lac de Gras dykes, indicating that substantial
drift of the Slave craton occurred between 2.19 and 2.03 Ga,
and, hence, that plate tectonic processes were operating dur-
ing this interval.
Malley dykes are only slightly older than 2.22 Ga Nipiss-
ing sills and Senneterre dykes of the Superior craton, which
have been shown to carry a primary remanence (e.g., Buchan
1991). The Malley and Nipissing poles are distinct (Fig. 10),
indicating that the two cratons were not in their present rela-
tive positions at 2.23 –2.22 Ga. This is consistent with an ear-
lier conclusion that the two cratons were not in their present
relative positions at ca. 2.03 Ga based on a comparison of
the Lac de Gras paleopole and 2.07 –2.00 Ga poles from the
Superior craton (Buchan et al. 2009).
In utilizing paleomagnetic data from two cratons to establish
their relative locations, it is best to compare detailed APWPs
for the two blocks. Paths with similar shapes indicate the two
blocks were drifting in unison on the same tectonic plate; dif-
fering shapes indicate that they were on separate plates. How-
ever, as yet there is no APWP for the Slave craton. An
alternative approach (Buchan et al. 2000), when APWPs are
not available, is to compare individual paleopoles of identical
age from the two cratons. This is rather difficult in the case of
the Slave and Superior data because of the mismatch in age be-
tween Dogrib and Lac de Gras poles and poles from the Supe-
rior craton. Nevertheless, a preliminary analysis is warranted.
In Fig. 11, the latitudinal positions and azimuthal orienta-
tions of the Slave craton at 2.23, 2.19, and 2.03 Ga are com-
pared with the latitude and orientation of the Superior craton
as it drifted through the 2.22 –2.00 Ga interval. It is important
to note that paleolongitude is unconstrained by the paleomag-
netic data, so that the relative longitudinal position of Slave
and Superior cratons in Fig. 11 is arbitrary. Because relative
polarity of the Slave and Superior paleopoles is not known,
two polarity options are possible. The Superior craton is arbi-
trarily placed in one hemisphere, whereas the Slave craton is
shown in both hemispheres, with either position permitted by
the paleomagnetic data.
It should also be noted that paleomagnetic data indicate
that the western portion of the Superior craton (Fig. 1) ro-
tated counterclockwise ∼15° relative to the eastern Superior
sometime after 2.07 Ga (Halls and Davis 2004; Buchan et
al. 2007 a; Evans and Halls 2010). Therefore, to simplify the
analysis which follows, the Slave craton data are only com-
pared with results from the eastern Superior.
If one chooses the polarity options in Fig. 11 that place the
Slave and Superior cratons in opposite hemispheres, then the
two cratons are at quite different latitudes and could not have
been near neighbours throughout the 2.23 –2.03 Ga period. If
one chooses polarity options with Slave and Superior cratons
in the same hemisphere, then Slave craton paleolatitudes at
ca. 2.23, 2.19, and 2.03 Ga are roughly similar to those of
the Superior craton through the 2.22 –2.00 Ga period. How-
ever, the relative azimuthal orientation of the two cratons dif-
fers significantly. For example, the relative orientation at
2.23–2.22 and 2.07 –2.00 Ga differs by ∼70°–90° (depending
on whether the Lac de Gras orientation is compared with that
for the somewhat younger Minto or older Lac Esprit dykes).
This suggests that, if the two cratons were in close proximity
to one another, they were not moving together on the same
tectonic plate throughout this period. This interpretation is in
agreement with geological evidence that the two cratons were
not near neighbours during the early Paleoproterozoic
(Bleeker 2003), including their distinct records of mafic mag-
matic events in this period. Further Slave craton paleopoles
are required to test whether the two cratons moved together
during some portion of the 2.23 –2.22 Ga period.
Because longitude is unconstrained in Fig. 11, it is not im-
mediately obvious whether the Slave and Superior cratons
may have drifted during this period at a large distance from
one another, but on the same plate, perhaps as distant parts
of a single supercontinent. This possibility can be examined
by comparing the great-circle distance between pairs of poles
from the two cratons that have identical age ranges (Evans
and Pisarevsky 2008). Significantly different great-circle dis-
tances would indicate that the cratons were on separate
plates. Similar great-circle distances are a necessary, but not
sufficient, condition for determining that the cratons were on
the same plate. In the case of the Slave and Superior data of
Fig. 10, such a comparison is not strictly possible because
there are no pairs of identical-aged poles from the two cra-
tons. Nevertheless, the following two examples illustrate the
method and the uncertainties of the present data set.
In Fig. 10 b, the great-circle distance between the 2.23 Ma
Malley pole (or the nearby 2.19 Ga Dogrib virtual geomag-
netic pole) and the 2.03 Ga Lac de Gras pole of the Slave
craton is similar to the great-circle distance between the
2.22 Ga Nipissing pole and either the 2.07 Ga Lac Esprit or
2.00 Ga Minto pole of the Superior craton, which might sug-
gest that the two cratons could have been on the same plate
at great distance from one another during this ∼200 million
years period. However, the pole ages for the two cratons are
not matched, and there are no Slave poles within this long
interval, so that further data are required before a definitive
interpretation is possible. On the other hand, the great-circle
distance between the Superior 2.22 Ga Nipissing and 2.17 Ga
Biscotasing poles of Fig. 10 a
is substantially longer that the
great-circle distance between the 2.23 Ga Malley and
2.19 Ga Dogrib poles, which might suggest that the two cra-
tons were not on the same plate during this ∼50 million years
interval. However, once again, the time intervals for the two
cratons are not matched, so that if the Superior polar wander
occurred mostly in the latter half of the 2.22 –2.17 Ga inter-
val, it would go unrecorded in the older Slave data. In addi-
tion, the Dogrib virtual geomagnetic pole, based on only two
dykes, is very poorly defined. Once again, further data are
required to reach a definite conclusion.

Conclusions
The main conclusions of this paper are as follows:
1. Northeast-trending Malley dykes of the east-central Slave
craton were emplaced at 2231 ± 2 Ma based on U –Pb
baddeleyite dating.
2. The Malley dyke swarm may continue northeast across the
Bathurst fault as the Brichta swarm, for a total swarm
length of ∼500 km, based on a recontruction of the
eastern Slave craton, which restores 115 km of left-lateral
offset along the fault (Tirrul and Grotzinger 1990), as
well as strong geochemical similarities between Malley
and Brichta dykes.
3. Malley dykes, including the dated dyke, carry a stable high
unblocking temperature characteristic remanence, with a
mean direction of D = 138.3°, I = –53.8° ( a
95 = 5.8°,
k = 81), and a corresponding paleopole is at 50.8°S,
50.0°W (dm = 8.1°, dp = 5.6°).
4. The Malley remanence was acquired before 2.03 Ga, and
likely before 2.19 Ga. However, a field test is required to
establish if the remanence is primary.
5. The paleopoles from well-dated units in the Slave craton
suggest that plate tectonic processes were operating
within the 2.23 –2.03 Ga period.
6. If the Malley paleopole is primary, a comparison between
Slave craton paleopoles for the 2.23 Ga Malley dykes and
2.03 Ga Lac de Gras dykes with poles on the Superior
craton APWP between 2.22 and 2.00 Ga indicates the
following:
a. The two cratons were not in their current relative
position during this period.
b. The two cratons likely did not drift in close proximity to
one another as part of a single (super)continent through-
out the period, in agreement with geological evidence.
c. Further studies are needed to test whether they drifted
together for part of this period or whether they may
have drifted at a distance from one another on the
same tectonic plate.

A palaeomagnetic and 40Ar/39Ar study of mafic dykes in southern
Sweden: A new Early Neoproterozoic key-pole for the Baltic Shield
and implications for Sveconorwegian and Grenville loops

We present the results of palaeomagnetic and40Ar/39Ar studies of the Proterozoic mafic dykes in the
Norrköping and Falun areas of the southern Sweden. The primary remanence of two 939 ± 3 Ma dykes is
supported by the rigorous baked contact test. The remanence direction of two other dykes, one of which
was previously U–Pb dated at 946 ± 1 Ma is close to the reverse direction of 939 Ma dykes. Using these
results together with previously published 935 ± 5 Ma palaeomagnetic data from the Göteborg-Slussen
mafic dykes and some dykes from the Falun area we calculated the mean 946–935 Ma palaeopole for
Baltica (0.9◦S, 240.7◦E, A95= 6.7), which can be qualified as the key pole. Using this pole together with
other date we conclude that the Grenville and Sveconorwegian loops of Laurentian and Baltican Apparent
Polar Wander Paths are temporary displaced by 100–150 m.y. We propose new palaeogeographic recons-
tructions of Baltica and Laurentia at ca. 940 Ma and ca. 850 Ma. We also present two new Mesoproterozoic
non-key poles from 1410 Ma and 1595 Ma dykes.

1. Introduction
Assembly of continents into a late Precambrian superconti-
nent, Rodinia, has been suggested in a number of studies (e.g.
McMenamin and McMenamin, 1990; Dalziel, 1991, 1997; Hoffman,
1991). Models of Rodinia are mostly based on ca. 1350–1000 Ma
orogenic belts, tectonic links between mobile belts across the cra-
tonic margins, global analyses of the balance of Neoproterozoic
and Early Palaeozoic continental margins and some palaeomag-
netic data. Early Neoproterozoic tectonic reconstructions suggest
a connection between Baltica and Laurentia (e.g. Hoffman, 1991;
Dalziel, 1991, 1997; Weil et al., 1998; Dalziel et al., 2000; Pisarevsky
et al., 2003; Li et al., 2008) in Rodinia. Since palaeomagnetism
is the only tool for reconstructing the latitudinal position and
orientation of cratons it plays an important role for these recons-
tructions. However, reliable palaeomagnetic data are sparse (e.g.
Buchan et al., 2001) and more “key” palaeomagnetic poles, i.e. well
dated poles that fulfill criteria for original magnetization, etc. (Van

Voo, 1990; Buchan et al., 2000) are needed for testing the
palaeogeographic reconstructions. Due to the often high contents
of magnetite, fast cooling and thereby small magnetic grain sizes
and stable remanent magnetizations, mafic dykes are often excel-
lent recorders of the Earth magnetic field. Palaeomagnetic data
from mafic dykes forms a significant part in the palaeomagnetic
databases (e.g. McElhinny and Lock, 1996; Pesonen et al., 2003;
Pisarevsky, 2005).
In southern Sweden Early Neoproterozoic dyke swarms are
widespread and have been the target for a large number of
palaeomagnetic studies (e.g. Poorter, 1975; Patchett and Bylund,
1977; Bylund, 1985, 1992; Bylund and Elming, 1992; Bylund and
Pisarevsky, 2002; Pisarevsky and Bylund, 1998, 2006). Most of these
studies are from dolerite dykes in the Protogine Zone (PZ; Fig. 1)
that defines a metamorphic boundary that separates the Southwest
Scandinavian province in the west from the Transscandinavian
Igneous Belt (TIB; Patchett et al., 1987) and the Southern Sve-
cofennian subprovince (SSv) in the east (e.g. Gaál and Gorbatschev,
1987). The TIB and the Southwest Scandinavian province formed
by crystal growth of the Baltic Shield with a westward younging
during the TIB (ca. 1850–1670; Gorbatschev, 2004) and the Goth-
ian period (1700–1550 Ma) (e.g. Åhäll and Larson, 2000; Andersen

Fig. 1. The geology of the south-western part of the Fennoscandian Shield (a). The inlet in figure (a) marks the area where this study was concentrated on.
et al., 2004, Högdahl et al., 2004). From the late Palaeoproterozoic
time the continental margin of a suggested continuous Laurentia-
Baltica was the location of long lived subduction and terranes’
accretion (e.g. Åhäll et al., 2000; Karlström et al., 2001; Andersen
et al., 2004; Bingen et al., 2008; Pisarevsky and Bylund, 2010).
The Sveconorwegian (in Laurentia Grenvillian; ca. 1150–900 Ma)
continent-continent collision resulted in deformation and meta-
morphism of the Gothian orogen in Southwestern Sweden (e.g.
Åhäll and Gower, 1997). The event resulted in a major deformation
zone, the Mylonite Zone (Fig. 1; e.g. Gorbatschev, 1980), a zone that
has been active during both Sveconorwegian thrusting and subse-
quent phases of exhumation (e.g. Stephens et al., 1996; Berglund,
1997).40Ar/39Ar hornblende ages from the Mylonite Zone indicate
deformations as late as ca. 915 Ma ago (Page et al., 1996), while ca.
40–70 km away from the Mylonite Zone two Sveconorwegian ages
were identified, at 934–931 Ma and 1007–960 Ma, the younger ages
suggested to be related to orogenic uplift. Deformation up to 40 km
east of the Protogine Zone has been demonstrated from structural
mapping (Wahlgren et al., 1994). Palaeomagnetic data older than
ca. 900 Ma from southwestern Sweden should therefore be used
with caution, since they may have been subjects to metamorphic
overprints or tectonically disturbed and therefore not necessarily
representing the Baltic Shield as a whole.
Palaeomagnetic results from 935 ± 3 Ma mafic dykes (Göteborg-
Slussen dykes; Fig. 1) in the Southwestern Scandinavian province,
west of the Mylonite Zone, were presented by Pisarevsky and
Bylund (2006). The data are of good quality, however, no full field
test demonstrating an original magnetization was presented. Here
we will present a new ca. 935 Ma-highly reliable pole for the Baltic
Shield. This is based on new palaeomagnetic data fulfilling field
test of primary magnetization and 40Ar/39Ar age determinations
from mafic dykes in the eastern part of the Southern Svecofen-
nian subprovince. This pole is compared and combined with the
palaeomagnetic data from the 935 Ma dykes in the Southwest
Scandinavian province and 946 Ma dykes from Dalarna. The
combined
new
palaeomagnetic pole forms an important input to the
discussion of the shape and timing of the Sveconorwegian Appar-
ent Polar Wander Path (APWP) loop (e.g. Patchett and Bylund, 1977;
Elming et al., 1993), which is similar in shape to the Grenville Loop
in the Laurentia APWP (e.g. Hyodo and Dunlop, 1993; Weil et al.,
1998) and has been a basis for palaeogeographic reconstruction of
Baltica vs. Laurentia at 935 Ma.
2. Geology, sampling and laboratory technique
Mafic dykes in the southeastern part of the Southern Svecofen-
nian subprovince (Figs. 1 and 2) comprise several dyke swarms,

Sampling localities for this study are marked by filled circles.

predominantly trending in E–W directions, however, NW–SE, N–S
and a few NE–SW trending dykes are also observed (Risku-Norja,
1992). The dykes intrude gneissic and granitic rocks that were
formed during the Svecofennian orogeny at 1.9–1.8 Ga ago. In the
gneisses there are often amphibolite layers that have been inter-
preted as intrusive sills from a late stage of the orogeny (Wikström,
1975). There are two major groups of 1.9–1.8 Ga intrusive rocks, a
synorogenic suite of granitic to ultrabasic composition and a sero-
rogenic suite with mainly migmatite gneisses. The rocks have been
deformed and sometimes fractured.
The dykes are of tholeiitic to alkaline composition (Risku-Norja,
1992) and they were intruded after the cratonization following the
Svecofennian orogeny, thus distinctly different from intraorogenic
Svecofennian dykes also found in the region. Importantly the stud-
ied dykes are located relatively far from (>100 km), and to the east
of the Protogine Zone and it is unlikely that they were influenced
by late Sveconorwegian overprint. Trace elements data suggest that
the dykes originate from a mantle source (Risku-Norja, 1992). E–W
trending dykes, the Breven-Hällefors dykes (Bylund, 1985), have
been dated at ca. 1595 ± 3 Ma (U–Pb, baddeleyite; Söderlund et al.,
2005; Rejmyre, Fig. 2) and the N–S trending dykes probably belong
to the subparallel Blekinge Dalarna Dolerites (BDD), which
been
have
dated in the range 978–946 Ma (U–Pb baddeleyite; Söderlund
et al., 2005). Apart from the Breven-Hällefors dykes no ages have
been reported for dykes in the area of this study (Fig. 2).
In this study 97 samples were collected from 8 mafic dykes
(Figs. 1 and 2; localities 1–5) in the southeastern part of the South-
ern Svecofennian subprovince and from one dyke (Falun, locality
6; Fig. 1) north of this area. In one locality (locality 1; Fig. 3)
samples were collected from two NE (N38◦E) trending dykes (Y1
and Y2) that cut two NW (N53◦W) trending dykes (O1 and O2),
which formed an excellent opportunity for baked contact tests. The
younger Y1 and Y2 dykes are subvertical, while the O1 and O2 dip
ca. 48◦to the SW. Chilled margins are observed in both generations
of dykes in the contact to the gneiss and in for the younger dykes
also in contact to the older dyke. The samples were collected from
various parts of the dykes and for the baked contact tests in the
older dykes at increasing distances from the younger dykes.
Two other dykes, trending NW (localities 2 and 3, N50–60◦W),
were sampled to the west of locality 1, at a distance of 14 km
and 2 km, respectively (Fig. 2). Both dykes are ca. 1 m wide and
subvertical. The dykes at sites 4 (Rejmyre) and 5 (Hällefors) are
E–W trending and belong to the Breven-Hällefors dyke system. The
Rejmyre dyke is ca. 15 m wide and located ca. 40 km northwest of

the locality 1. The rock at locality 5 forms a part the ca. 1 km wide
Hällefors dolerite dyke and it is located ca. 60 km north–north–east
of locality 1. Both dykes were sampled from their central parts.
The last dyke included in this study (Falun, locality 6, Fig. 1) is
situated north of the area described by Risku-Norja (1992). This
dyke belongs to the 978–946 Ma old Blekinge Dalarna dolerite
(BDD) dyke swarm (Solymon et al., 1992; Söderlund et al., 2005). In
Dalarna different dykes in this swarm has previously been sampled
for palaeomagnetic studies by Patchett and Bylund (1977), Bylund
(1985) and Bylund and Elming (1992). Patchett and Bylund (1977)
collected 10 samples at different locations along the same dyke as
in locality 6 and here we collected 9 samples in a locality where that
dyke has been dated at 945.7 ± 1.2 Ma (–-Pb baddeleyite; Söderlund
et al., 2005).
A portable rock coring drill was used for the sampling and the
samples were oriented with sun and magnetic compasses.
The intensity and direction of remanent magnetization was
measured with a SQUID (2G-DC) magnetometer and the speci-
mens were AF-demagnetized in steps of 5 mT up to 30 mT and in
10 mT steps up to 120 mT. Thermal demagnetizations were per-
formed using a Schonstedt (TDS1) oven at intervals of 50◦C up to
500◦C and 10–30◦C for higher temperatures. The remanence vec-
tors were defined by least square fit of vectors in 3-D space (Torsvik,
1986; Torsvik et al., 1996) and by principle component analyses
(Kirschvink, 1980). The magnetic susceptibility was measured on
crushed specimens during heating and cooling using a  appabridge
(KLY-3 and CS-3, AGICO).
Specimens from the palaeomagnetic samples were also sub-
mitted for 40Ar/39Ar whole rock dating at the Geochronology
laboratory at the University of Alaska, Fairbanks. The cores were
crushed, washed and sieved to obtain small (∼0.5 mm) whole-
rock chips for dating. The monitor mineral MMhb-1 (Samson and
Alexander, 1987) with an age of 513.9 Ma (Lanphere and Dalrymple,
2000) was used to monitor neutron flux (and calculate the irradi-
ation parameter, J). The samples and standards were wrapped in
aluminum foil and loaded into aluminum cans of 2.5 cm diame-
ter and 6 cm height. The samples were irradiated in position 5c of
the uranium enriched research reactor of McMaster University in
Hamilton, Ontario, Canada for 20 MW-h.
Upon their return from the reactor, the sample and monitors
were loaded into 2 mm diameter holes in a copper tray that was
then loaded in a ultra-high vacuum extraction line. The monitors
were fused, and samples heated in a step-wise manner, using a 6-
W argon-ion laser following the technique described in York et
(1981),
al.
Layer et al. (1987) and Layer (2000). Argon purification was
achieved using a liquid nitrogen cold trap and a SAES Zr–Al getter at
400◦C. The samples were analyzed in a VG-3600 mass spectrom-
eter at the Geophysical Institute, University of Alaska Fairbanks.
The argon isotopes measured were corrected for system blank and
mass discrimination, as well as calcium, potassium and chlorine
interference reactions following procedures outlined in McDougall
and Harrison (1999). System blanks generally were 2 × 10−16mol
40Ar and 2 × 10−18mol36Ar, which are 10–50 times smaller than
fraction volumes. Mass discrimination was monitored by running
both calibrated air shots and a zero-age glass sample. These mea-
surements were made on a weekly to monthly basis to check for
changes in mass discrimination. Plateau ages (P in Table 1) were
based on the criteria of three or more contiguous fractions (with
a roughly constant Ca/K ratio) accounting for more than 50% gas
release, having a Mean Square Weighted Deviation (MSWD) less
than 2.5. For samples that show “plateau-like” segments, but not
meet the criteria, a weighted average age of the plateau-like steps
is calculated (W in Table 1). Some samples were run twice to check
for reproducibility. A summary of all the40Ar/39Ar results is given
in Table 1, with all ages quoted to the ±1 sigma level and calcu-
lated using the constants of Steiger and Jaeger (1977). Integrated
and plateau ages include error in the irradiation parameter (0.5%).
3. 40Ar/39Ar age determinations
Two samples from the “young” dyke Y1 (samples 96, 99; Fig. 3),
three samples from the “old” dyke O2 (samples 158, 160, 162) and
three samples from the contact (sample 93) and hybrid zone in dyke
O2 (samples 88 and 89) were dated.
The age spectra from the samples collected in the dyke Y1 (96
and 99; Fig. 4) exhibit a slight amount of excess argon (anomalous
old ages for the first steps) and do not meet the criteria for plateaus,
but weighed mean ages for more than 45% of gas release are iden-
tical with an average age of 939 ± 3 Ma (Table 1). For sample 99,
7 fractions comprising 64% of gas release form a well-constrained
isochron age of 941 ± 3 Ma (Fig. 4), confirming the weighted mean
age 941 ± 6 Ma.
The samples from the O2 dyke, which were collected at ca.
15 m from the contact to younger dykes, show evidence of excess
argon, especially in the high Ca/K steps. The average age from the
three samples, two plateau ages and one weighted average age, is
1411 ± 9 Ma.

Some samples are run twice to check for reproducibility. For dyke Y1 an isochron age (A) was defined, with fraction included in the calculation shown by the small arrows.
This age supports the weighted average age of the dyke (C). Ages from the dyke O1 are determined for samples ca. 15 m away from the young dykes (B) and for samples in
the contact to the dyke Y1, and at 0.95 m and 1.4 m from the contact to Y1(D).
Sample 93 is collected from the baked contact in dyke O1 (Fig. 3)
as part of a transect of samples collected at increasing distances
from the contact to the young dyke Y1. Two runs of this sample
give reproducible results with age spectra that are saddle-shaped,
i.e. older at high and low 39Ar release due to excess argon. The
youngest weighted average age in each saddle is ca. 1173 Ma, which
means the sample was not totally reset by the intrusion of the dyke
Y1, but still retains some of its older argon. The spectra steps up
to an age of ca. 1800 Ma, but a correct age for the dyke is difficult
to estimate from these data. The samples collected at 0.95 m (89)
and 1.4 m (88) from the contact were run twice and with repro-
ducible results. The first part of the spectrum from the sample at
0.95 m is characterized by argon loss and very anomalous high Ca/K
ratios, perhaps due to plagioclase microinclusions. The second part
of the spectrum has low Ca/K ratios, reflecting the groundmass of
the dyke, and an average age of 1378 ± 12 Ma. This age is about
30 Ma younger than the age of the O2 dyke as determined on sam-
ples outside the hybrid zone. That age difference could reflect either
a different event or a small amount of argon loss due to the young
dyke intrusion. The third part of the spectrum steps up to ages of ca.
1700 Ma and probably reflects excess argon. The spectrum from the
sample 88 is more or less identical to that of 89 and the weighted
average age from two runs is 1399 ± 20 Ma, i.e. similar to the age
of the sample 89. The amount of excess argon in the high temper-
ature release is much lower than that from the samples collected
in the contact to the cutting dyke and at 0.95 m from the contact,
suggesting a relationship between excess argon and distance from
the dyke

4.2. Locality 2
The Borg dyke carries a NRM (Fig. 6a; S2010.02) with a median
destructive field (MDF, Dunlop and Özdemir, 1997) of ca. 15 mT.
Three different components could be isolated, one erased in very
low alternating field intensities (<20 mT) with a direction close to
that of the present Earth field (PEF), a second of intermediate to
high coercivity (decl. = 4.7◦, incl. = 16.2◦) and a third isolated after AF
treatment in field higher than the previous components (>65 mT).
The second component may be an artifact resulting from overlap-
ping coercivity spectra expressed by the gradual change in direction
along a great circle from the low to the highest coercivity direction.

5. Origin of magnetization and anisotropy of magnetic
susceptibility
The magnetization in the “young” dykes (Y1 and Y2) at local-
ity 1 is carried by low-titanium titanomagnetite as indicated
from unblocking temperatures (>ca. 530◦C) and susceptibility vs. temperature ( –T) measurements (Curie temperature ca. 550◦C;
Fig. 5a and 8a). This is true also for the baked contact of the “old”

dyke O1 at the same locality, however, the Curie temperature
indicates a somewhat higher titanium content (Fig. 8b). The pres-
ence of small, but noticeable, Hopkinson peaks in the  –T curves
indicate that the remanence is carried in part by highly stable
single-domain particles. Since single-domain particles carry stable
remanent magnetizations, this gives an additional evidence for a
primary magnetization.
The measurements of anisotropy of magnetic susceptibility
(AMS) show a degree of anisotropy of 5–10% for the O1 and O2
dykes, 3–7% for the Y1 and Y2 dykes and less than 10% for the Falun
dyke, which is the usual for igneous rocks with a primary mag-
netic fabric (Hrouda, 1982). The shape of the anisotropy ellipsoid
is expressed by the shape parameter T (Jelinek, 1981), for which
0 < T < 1 express oblate shaped ellipsoid and −1 < T < 0 express a pro-
late ellipsoid. T values are here positive (T = 0.09–0.88), indicating
that the magnetic fabric for the dykes is oblate, i.e. the dykes are
magnetically foliated. We interpret the AMS data as a primary flow
indicator (Knight and Walker, 1988; Tauxe et al., 1998). The AMS
data reveal orientations of the foliation planes of the young dyke
Y1 (strike 29◦E, dip 83◦) that are parallel to the dyke plane. Also for
the O1 and O2 dykes the magnetic foliation planes (strike 217◦E,
dip 46◦) are parallel to the dyke planes, which are thus not ver-
tical but dip ca. 45◦to the southwest. This may suggest that these
older dykes were initially inclined or that they have been tilted after
intrusion.
The Falun dyke is also magnetically foliated, with a subver-
tical foliation plane (dip = 84◦NE) trending 332◦E, i.e. parallel to
the trend of the dyke determined by geological mapping

Discussion
6.1. New 945–932 Ma high quality pole for Baltica
The new 939 ± 3 Ma palaeomagnetic data from dykes Y1 and
Y2 presented here is supported by rigorous baked contact test.
There are several previously published ca. 970–910 Ma Baltican
palaeopoles, some of them are precisely dated, but there were not
a single one with proven primary ChRM (Table 3). However, the
mean pole from just two dykes should be qualified as represent-
ing a near instantaneous recording of the Earth’s magnetic field,
and is not likely to have averaged palaeo-secular variation (PSV).
To obtain a really valuable ‘key’ pole other palaeomagnetic results
of similar age are needed.
Pisarevsky and Bylund (2006) published a palaeomagnetic study
of the four 935 ± 3 Ma (U–Pb baddeleyite; Hellström et al., 2004)
Göteborg and Slussen dykes carrying bipolar ChRM directions very
similar to that of Y1 and Y2 dykes.
The 946 ± 1 Ma (U–Pb baddeleyite; Söderlund et al., 2005)
Falun dyke carries almost the same ChRM direction (Locality 6;
Plat = −1.7◦, Plon = 242.3◦, A =
95
2.6◦) as reversed Y1 and Y2 direc-
tions. It is also similar to the previous study of the same Falun
dyke by Patchett and Bylund (1977; Plat. = −6.1◦, Plon. = 237.6◦,
A =
95
5.7◦), however somewhat better defined. Considering that
the remanence directions of Patchett and Bylund (1977) were not
defined using vector analysis and the mean direction was calculated
from least scatter in magnetic directions during demagnetization,
which was the best approach at the time, we use the new pole pre-
sented here to represent the Falun dyke (locality 6, Table 2). Bylund
and Elming (1992) and Bylund (1985) studied three dykes (Ander-
sbro, Gällsjön and Ejen) located nearby and trending in the same
direction as the Falun dyke. The ChRM directions are coherent and
also very close to that of the Falun dyke Table 3; Fig. 7), which may
argue for them being part of the same generation of dykes. The
age difference between the Y1/Y2 dykes and BDD Falun dykes is
relatively small (939 ± 3 and 946 ± 1 Ma).
Importantly, the Y1/Y2 dykes in Norrköping area and Falun
dykes are located ca. 90–100 km east of the Protogine zone, i.e.
much further to the east than has been suggested for the limit
of crystal reworking during the Svecororwegian (Wahlgren et al.,
1994). K–Ar ages of biotite from southeast Sweden (Åberg, 1978)
indicate that the K–Ar system started to close at ca. 1.55 Ma and was
completed at ca. 1.40 Ma, i.e. the rocks were not reheated above
ca. 300 ± 50◦C, the closure temperature for K–Ar in biotite. Fis-
sion track studies (Tullborg et al., 1996) of subsidence and uplift
from an area some 150 km south of the present study area, reveal
temperatures of the present surface at 250 ± 50◦C at 820 ± 88 Ma.
This resetting of the fission-track ages was interpreted related to
sedimentary burial and uplift. This means that any tectonic disturb-
ance or palaeomagnetic overprint related to the Sveconorwegian
orogeny is unlikely.
As will be shown later, the drift velocity of Baltica at that
time was apparently low, which makes it reasonable to combine
the Y1/Y2, Göteborg-Slussen and Falun area data and here we
present a mean 946–935 Ma pole, based on 10 different dykes:

6.2. New palaeopoles for 1595 ± 3 and 1411 ± 9 Ma
The Hällefors A (entry 37, Table 4; Piper, 1980) and locality 5
(Hällefors) poles most probably are from the same giant dyke. This
dyke has a similar trend as the 1595 ± 3 Ma Rejmyre dyke (local-
ity 4). ChRMs of two dykes are nearly antipodal (Table 2; Fig. 7b)
and the palaeopoles are not significantly different from poles of the
ca. 1570 Ma Kumlinge-Brändö and Föglö Sottunga dykes in Finland
(Fig. 9; Table 4, entries 39–40). Hence we suggest that the Hälle-
fors dyke belongs to the same magmatic event as the ca. 1595 Ma
Rejmyre dyke. These two new VGPs are included to the Table 4
(entries 36 and 38).
Field observations and orientation of magnetic foliation plane
indicate that the O1 and O2 dykes in site 1 are not vertical but
dip ca. 45◦ to the southwest. Since there are no geological evi-
dence for a post- 1411 ± 9 Ma and pre- 939 ± 3 Ma tilting, an initial
inclined emplacement of the dyke is likely. The calculated pole
positions (O1a: Plat. = 19.2◦, Plon. = 204.0◦ and O2a: Plat. = 21.0◦,
Plon. = 203.9◦, Table 2) are not significantly different from the pole
calculated from the dyke at locality 2 (Borg) and a mean ca. 1411 Ma
pole (entry 23 in Table 2; Fig. 9) is calculated from the O1a, O2a
dykes and the Borg dyke (locality 2) poles. This mean pole plots
not so far from the ca. 1450–1470 Ma reference poles (Fig. 9;
Table 4, entries 24–33), and the 10–15◦difference can be explained
by 40–60 m.y. difference in age. Although only three dykes are
included in the mean and secular variations are most probably not
averaged out, this pole adds new data to the gap in reliable Baltica
poles between ca. 1450 and 1270
6.3.

Sveconorwegian and Grenville loops and palaeogeographic
implications
There is a strong geological evidence for the close position
of Baltica and Laurentia during almost the whole Neoproterozoic
(e.g. Winchester, 1988; Gee et al., 1994; Fairchild and Hambrey,
1995; Higgins et al., 2001). The match between the two conti-
nents was in part based on the apparent similarity between the
so-called Grenville and Sveconorwegian APWP (Apparent Polar
Wander Path) loops. There were debates about the exact shapes
and the direction of younging of the poles (clockwise vs. anti-
clockwise loops; Fig. 10; e.g. Weil et al., 1998; Hyodo and Dunlop,
1993; Elming et al., 1993; Pisarevsky and Bylund, 1998), but there
was a general agreement about two important features. First,
the “bottoms” of both loops were marked with palaeopoles of
ca. 980–930 Ma (the poles with highest southern latitudes). Sec-
ond, the near-equatorial parts of both loops are populated by ca.
1000–1020 Ma poles and ca. 900–800 Ma poles.
The southern-most part of the Laurentian (Grenville) loop was
constrained by palaeopole from the Haliburton Intrusion A (Buchan
and Dunlop, 1976), with age estimated by authors at 980 ± 10 Ma.

The southernmost part of the Baltica (Sveconorwegian) loop was
constrained by several studies of the ca. 930 Ma Rogaland Igneous
Complex (RIC) and related rocks (e.g. Table 4, entries 10–12). These
poles are in an apparent contradiction with the new key pole,
which is presented in this study, and all of them revealed steep
upwards ChRM directions. Brown and McEnroe (2004) suggested
a significant difference between the time of intrusion and the
age of ChRM, suggesting the latter to be ca. 900 Ma. Walderhaug
et al. (1999) presented a well-dated 848 Ma primary pole from
the Hunnedalen dykes, which was very close to the poles from
the Rogaland complex. Lately Walderhaug et al. (2007) obtained a
869 ± 14 Ma40Ar/39Ar biotite age from a noritic dyke related to RIC
and argued that it represents an uplift/cooling age, which better
represents the age of the remanence in SW Norway. Palaeomag-
netic studies of mostly undated >60 mafic dykes in the Protogine
Zone in southern Sweden revealed that ChRM of all dykes south of
the Ljungby – Alvesta road, i.e. south of the 57◦N latitude, is upward
steep, like the RIC ChRM. Most of dykes north of this line are mag-
netized with more shallow inclinations, similar to the BDD

the Falun area. Pisarevsky and Bylund (1998) also found RIC-like
remanence direction in the ca. 950–930 Ma metamorphic rocks in
southern Sweden west of the Protogine Zone. Such geographically
bound distribution of ChRM directions suggests a regional remag-
netization event. The timing of this remagnetization is probably
constrained by the ca. 870–850 Ma poles of Walderhaug et al. (1998,
2007), but the mechanism is unclear. Page et al. (1996) reported a

younger than 915 Ma. Hence the ca. 870–850 Ma remagnetization
event in southern Sweden, if occurred, should have been of a low-
temperature nature. New studies are necessary.
We agree with Walderhaug et al. (1998, 2007) and suggest that
the real age of the southernmost palaeopoles constraining the Sve-
conorwegian loop is likely to be ca. 870–850 Ma. If so, the Grenville
and Sveconorwegian loops are not coeval – their age difference is
ca. 150 Ma (Fig. 11). However, most poles used for the Grenville
loop were from poorly dated metamorphic rocks with uncertain
age of their remanence. Using only well-dated Laurentian poles,
only the older, “downward” part of the Grenville loop is palaeo-
magnetically constrained and there are no reliable Laurentian poles
between 1000 and 790 Ma (Fig. 11; Table 5). On the other hand, Sve-

In spite of this incompatibility of the two APWP loops, we still
suggest the integrity of Laurentia and Baltica in the Neoprotero-
zoic as it is shown in Fig. 12. First, there is a geological evidence for
this reconstruction after ca. 1000 Ma (e.g. Li et al., 2008; Pisarevsky
et al., 2008; Cawood et al., 2010 and references therein). In partic-
ular, it is consistent with the existence of the long-lived Meso- to
Neoproterozoic passive continental margin along the eastern and
northeastern edge of Baltica. The eastern Greenland was also a pas-
sive continental margin during most of Neoproterozoic (Li et al.,
2008 and references therein), which is consistent with the recon-
struction in Fig. 12. On the contrary, outcrops of Neoproterozoic
sediments in western Scandinavia are fragmented and generally
interpreted to represent non-marine environments in the middle
of Laurentia-Baltica continent (Fig. 12; e.g. Winchester, 1988). Sec-
ond, the coeval ca. 615 Ma poles from Laurentia and Baltica (Murthy
et al., 1992; Kamo and Gower, 1994; Walderhaug et al., 2007) sup-
port this reconstruction for the Early Ediacaran time and match the
suggested model of the Late Ediacaran opening of the Iapetus ocean
(e.g. Pisarevsky et al., 2008).
Fig. 12 shows the palaeomagnetically permissive reconstruction
of Laurentia and Baltica (the central part of Rodinia) at 940 and
870 Ma. The closeness of ca. 960–920 Ma poles (Table 4; Fig. 10)

7. Conclusions
We obtained the first age determinations for mafic dykes in the
southeastern part of the southern Svecofennian Subprovince.

S.-Å. Elming et al. / Precambrian Research 244 (2014) 192–206 205
The palaeomagnetic and geochronological study of the
939 ± 3 Ma mafic dykes near Norrköping, Sweden revealed a pri-
mary remanence supported by a rigorous contact test.
Averaging this and previously published palaeomagnetic results
on coeval mafic dykes in other areas provide a new 946–935 Ma key
pole for Baltica. This primary pole is significantly different from the
palaeopole of the ca. 930 Ma Rogaland Igneous Complex (RIC) and
some coeval mafic and metamorphic rocks in southern Sweden. We
support the previous suggestion of Walderhaug et al. (2007), that
the remanence of RIC-related rocks in southern Norway is signifi-
cantly younger than the time of the igneous event. We also suggest a
low-temperature remagnetization event in southern Sweden after
ca. 900 Ma.
The new 946–935 Ma pole indicates that the distribution of
poles in the “Sveconorwegian loop” was clockwise as has also been
suggested for the Grenville loop of Laurentia.
Palaeogeographic reconstructions demonstrate a slow low lati-
tudinal drift of joint Laurentia – Baltica continents between ca. 960
and 920 Ma and a quick movement towards the polar area by ca.
870–850 Ma.
The two new palaeopoles of ca. 1411 Ma and ca. 1595 Ma added
to the palaeomagnetic database give new constrains to the appar-
ent polar wander of Baltica.

Abstract
A combined paleomagnetic and 40Ar /39Ar study was carried out along eight stratigraphically overlapping sections in the
Oligocene Afro-Arabian flood volcanic province in Yemen (73 sites). The composite section covers the entire volcanic
stratigraphy in the sampling region and represents five polarity zones that are correlated to the geomagnetic polarity time
scale based on
40Ar /39Ar ages from this and previous studies. The resulting magnetostratigraphy is similar to that of the
conjugate margin in Ethiopia. The earliest basaltic volcanism took place in a reverse polarity chron that appears to correspond to
C11r, while the massive rhyolitic ignimbrite eruptions correlated to ash layers in Oligocene Indian Ocean sediment 2700 km
away from the Afro-Arabian traps, appear to have taken place during magnetochron C11n. The youngest ignimbrite was
emplaced during magnetochron C9n. Both
40Ar /39Ar and paleomagnetic data suggest rapid b 1 Ma eruption of the basal basalt
units and punctuated eruption of the upper silicic units over a duration potentially as long as 3 Ma with interspersed eruptive
hiatuses. Eruption of the basal basalts may have preceded the Oi2 cooling event.
The paleomagnetic pole k = 74.28N, u = 249.18E (A95 = 3.68; N = 48) is supported by a positive reversal test. Paleosecular
variation, estimated as the angular standard deviation of the VGP distribution 14.2 8 + 2.38 /  .78, is close to expected,
suggesting that the paleomagnetic pole represents a time-averaged field. The pole is in excellent accord with the

1. Introduction
Large igneous provinces (LIPs) represent major
geodynamic events associated with regional-scale up-
lift, massive volcanism, and in some cases continental
rifting and breakup [1]. Geochronology and magne-
tostratigraphy studies have played an important role in
our understanding of LIPs, particularly in document-
ing the very rapid emplacement in only a few Ma for
most LIPs (e.g., [1,2]), indicating that LIP occurrences
may be related to different and more dynamic mantle
convection processes than those driving the Earth’s
normal-state plate tectonics. Geochronology and mag-
netostratigraphy data have also documented synchro-
ny between many LIP occurrences and major global
environmental changes including biotic mass extinc-
tions, suggesting that LIP eruptions may be capable of
causing global environmental and climatic effects
[2,3].
This study presents new paleomagnetic, magnetos-
tratigraphic and

2. Geology, stratigraphy and sampling
The Oligocene Afro-Arabian traps ( Fig. 1 A) rep-
resent one of the youngest and best preserved LIPs
on Earth, with an original volume estimated to have
been at least 1.2  
6 km2 [4]. Magnetostratigraphy
and geochronology data from the Ethiopian part of
the province have suggested that major basaltic
flood volcanism in Ethiopia began about 31 Ma
ago with the bulk of emplacement occurring over
a period of 1–2 Ma [4–7]. This rapid emplacement
is most easily explained by the plume-head or
plume-impact model [8], in which widespread ba-
saltic flood eruptions occur as the inflated head of a
rising new mantle plume approaches the base of the
lithosphere. A plume-impact origin is also supported
by geochemical observations [9], the regional dome-
shaped uplift between ~35 and ~30 Ma [10], and
the anomalously low seismic shear velocity in the
present-day Afro-Arabian upper mantle [11].
The Yemeni margin of the LIP ( Fig. 1 B) contains
roughly 10% of the entire volume of erupted Oligo-
cene Afro-Arabian flood volcanism [12]. Geochro-
nology data suggest that volcanism in Yemen took
place from 30.9 to 27.1 Ma ( [13]; this paper ). The
earliest volcanic activity is composed entirely of
basaltic lava flows, while more silicic volcanic pro-
ducts such as rhyolitic ignimbrites and tuffs domi-
nate the middle part of the stratigraphy, followed by
an upper bimodal sequence [14] (Fig. 2 ). Our sam-
pling region around the capital city Sana’a ( Fig. 1 C)
lies along the northern outskirts of the Afro-Arabian
LIP where the volcanic sequence remains relatively
untectonized and therefore more attractive for paleo-
magnetic studies compared to the extensively faulted
and much thicker lava sequences in central parts of
the province. The relatively simple geological setting
also makes volcanostratigraphic correlation of sam-
pling profiles possible through direct field observa-
tions. The eight stratigraphically overlapping sections
that sampled for the present study cover the entire
volcanic stratigraphy in the sampling region ( Fig. 2 ),
and their stratigraphic correlation has been confirmed
by subsequent petrographic studies and geochemical
correlations [14].

3. Analytical methods
3.1. Paleomagnetic demagnetization experiments
One specimen from each core was subjected to
detailed demagnetization experiments at the paleo-
magnetic laboratories at Lund University and Univer-
sity of California, Santa Cruz. The majority of
samples (~90%) were subjected to alternating field
(AF) demagnetization using an automatic 3-axis AF
demagnetizer, and the remaining ~10% were sub-
jected to thermal cleaning using a laboratory-built
furnace. Susceptibility versus temperature experi-
ments indicate that the magnetic mineralogy is dom-
inated by variably oxidized titanomagnetite for both
basaltic and rhyolitic units, consistent with median
destructive fields being lower than 40 mT and maxi-
mum unblocking temperatures ranging between 200
and 580 8C. For roughly 10% of the samples it was
not possible to isolate the characteristic remanent
magnetization (ChRM) due to strong lightning in-
duced overprints indicated by stronger than average
natural remanent magnetization (NRM) intensities and
highly scattered within-site NRM directions. For two
sites (JS5 and JK11) it was not possible to define a
site–mean ChRM. For the remaining samples the
direction of the ChRM was defined using standard
principal component analysis [15] and we accept
ChRM directions that could be defined with maxi-
mum angle of deviation less than 3 8 and the number
of demagnetization points larger than 5. Typical
examples of accepted samples are shown in Fig. 3 .
The site–mean directions are given in Table 1 and
shown in geographic and stratigraphic coordinates in
Fig. 4 .
3.2.
40Ar /39Ar geochronology
A total of 15 sites best representing the eruptive
stratigraphy was selected for 40Ar /39Ar geochronol-
ogy. The samples were crushed and sieved into two
or three fractions (generally 160–315, 315–500 Am,
and as applicable, N500 Am). Matrix, mafic pheno-
crysts and feldpsar with inclusions were removed by
use of a magnetic separator. Plagioclase separates
were washed in purified water and alkali feldspar
were bathed briefly in dilute ( b1%) HF and then
washed in purified water. Then ~20–30 mg of trans-
parent feldspar was hand picked under a binocular
microscope and loaded into a total of four aluminum
disks. Two fine-grained basaltic samples (YJB99.38
and YJB99.41) contained only very tiny plagioclase
(V 63 Am), and were crushed, instead, for whole
rock analysis. For these two samples 350–500 Am
size fractions of cleaned whole rock matrix were
washed in purified water. One whole rock sample
(YJB99.41) was additionally prepared using a brief
(~5 min) 5% HF acid leaching, and then washed.
The three whole rock matrix samples (~50 mg of
each) were then loaded into an additional aluminum
disk.
Samples in each of the 5 aluminum disks, were
bracketed with the monitor mineral Fish Canyon sani-

reactor at Oregon State University. After irradiation,
~10 mg of feldspar was degassed in 6–26 steps depend-
ing on sample behavior, using a defocused CO
2 laser
(Synrad) and integrator lens, and analyzed with a MAP
215C mass spectrometer at the Berkeley Geochronol-
ogy Center (BGC). Nucleogenic production ratios

4.3. Tectonic correction
Precise in-field estimates of the structural attitude
are often difficult to obtain due to limitations in
exposure, and the lack of the third dimension into
the exposed rock surface. Since incorrect tectonic
corrections may bias a paleomagnetic pole without
affecting its statistical confidence limits it is impor-
tant to recognize uncertainties related to tectonic
correction. This is particularly true for apparently
well-defined poles, such as the one obtained in
present study, used for fine-scale paleogeographic
and paleogeodynamo studies with the assumption
that the A95 value represents the actual uncertainty.
Comparison of in-field dip/strike measurements with
highly precise multi-model stereo photogrammetry
data in geological settings similar to Yemen of
exposed and slightly dipping lavas has found that
in-field dip/strike readings typically are 2–5 8 wrong
[18]. It is therefore fair to assume similar uncertain-
ties in our in-field dip/strike readings. Since several
units were sampled along different profiles with
variable structural attitude (e.g., Fig. 2 and Table
1), we may, in fact, test the in-field dip/strike
estimates by comparing site mean direction prior
to and after tectonic correction, i.e., by performing
a fold test. Analyzing the entire dataset we observe
a better grouping of data after tectonic correction
(Fig. 4 B) and also obtain a positive fold test [24]
with the maximum untilting at 115% as demonstrat-
ed on Fig. 8 . On the other hand, if we analyze only
the SAM and Escarpment ignimbrites, the two units
sampled at the greatest number of distinct locations
(five), we find that the maximum in the precision
parameters occurs at 80% (Sam ignimbrite) and
45% (Escarpment ignimbrite) untilting. This sug-
gests that dip values may have been slightly under-
estimated ( Fig. 8 ), or alternatively that there is some
noise in the paleomagnetic recording (e.g., [25]). In
either case, the analysis underlines that the actual
uncertainty of the site–mean directions are larger
than suggested by their a
95-values. Given that the
structural attitudes are different for different profiles
(Table 1 a) the uncertainties related to in-field strike/
dip estimates will tend to average out, but never-
theless the 3.6 8 A95-value is an underestimate of
the actual uncertainty.

6. Discussion
6.1. Paleomagnetic poles and paleogeography of the
Afro-Arabian traps
The Ethiopian part of the Afro-Arabian traps has
been extensively studied, and all available paleomag-
netic data were recently analyzed by Kidane et al.
[27]. They suggest that only data based on detailed
demagnetization and principal component analysis
should be considered. Combining all reliable paleo-
magnetic data they obtain a well-defined pole for the
Ethiopian part of the province based on 76 indepen-
dent paleomagnetic units (see Table 3).
P . Riisager et al. / Earth and Planetary Science Letters 237 (2005) 647–672 665

The Arabian part of the Afro-Arabian traps has
been less studied and only one paleomagnetic pole
exists, from the As Sarat volcanic field in southwest-
ern Saudi Arabia [28]. The failed reversal test for the
As Sarat pole was originally taken to support a dis-
placed dipole source of the Oligocene Earth’s mag-
netic field [28] but this hypothesis is not supported by
our data nor by the Ethiopian data [27] and it is
possible that the failed reversal test is related to the
crude demagnetization technique, which did not re-
move secondary overprints. The As Sarat paleomag-
netic pole lies 4.6 8 away from the pole obtained in the
present study and is statistically distinct at the 95%
confidence level. Therefore we exclude the As Sarat
paleomagnetic data [28] from the following analysis.
6.2. Oligocene Afro-Arabian paleogeography
Seafloor magnetic anomalies and geochronology
of dredged basaltic rocks indicate that sea-floor
spreading has been taking place only since 5–6 Ma
in the Red Sea [29]), while significant pre-drift exten-
sion is believed to have taken place since ~25 Ma
[10]. The amount of pre-drift extension is difficult to
quantify, however, and it varies between different
plate kinematic models that aim to restore the Afro-
Arabian paleogeography prior to rifting (e.g., [29–
35]). Based on our Yemen paleomagnetic pole and
that of Ethiopia [27] we may attempt to test the
various plate kinematic models in a manner similar
to analyses of pre-drift extension at Atlantic bordering
continents [36,37]. Although the A95 values of ~3 8
for the Ethiopian and Yemen paleomagnetic poles are
too large to differentiate between all the kinematic
models with statistical significance, we note that the
plate kinematic model of Joffe and Garfunkel [33]
best brings the poles in agreement ( Table 3 and Fig.
9). This plate kinematic finite rotation pole assumes a
pre-drift extension of ~200 km in the Red Sea prior to
the initiation of centralized sea floor spreading, slight-
ly more than other models.
6.3. Geometry of the Oligocene time-averaged paleo-
magnetic field
A fundamental concept in paleomagnetism is the
so-called geocentric axial dipole (GAD) hypothesis,
which states that the Earth’s magnetic field is, on the
average, a GAD. Assuming the GAD hypothesis is
correct, paleomagnetic poles yield quantitative esti-
mates of both rotations around vertical axes and lat-
itudinal tectonic transport. The GAD hypothesis is
therefore very important for paleomagnetic paleogeo-
graphic reconstructions. For the last 5 million years,
where plate tectonic motion can be ignored and tests
of the GAD hypothesis are relatively simple, it
appears that the time-averaged field configuration
largely matches that of a GAD, although a small
~5% quadrupole contribution cannot be excluded
[38,39]. For older intervals in the Earth Ts history,
paleomagnetic data are scarce and plate tectonic
reconstructions are less certain. It is therefore more
difficult to test the GAD hypothesis, which may ex-
plain why some authors have argued for significant
long term non-dipole fields [4,36,40] while other
studies suggest a GAD field [41,42].

40Ar /39Ar geochronology. A means to circumvent
radioisotopic age uncertainties is given by the study of
Ukstins Peate et al. [56] that, based on Pb and Nd
isotope ratios and rare earth element compositions,
demonstrated that the Jabal Kura’a and SAM ignim-
brites (both part of the N1 normal, see Fig. 2 ) are the
source of ash layers identified in ocean drilling pro-
gram (ODP) drill cores at site 711. Since these ash
layers are correlated to magnetochron C11n based on
biostratigraphy data [57] it appears that central
Yemeni N1–R2–N2 polarity sequence corresponds
to magnetochrons C11n.2n–C11n.1r–C11n.1n, which
is, in fact, in good accordance with the
40Ar /39Ar and
the CK95 time scale (e.g., Fig. 6). The underlying R1
polarity zone therefore should correspond to C11r,
which is also supported by six 40Ar /39Ar age data
(this study) giving a mean age of 30.19 F 0.20 Ma that
correlates well with the CK95 age of C11r but less
well with the HA97 time scale. An onset of volcanism
in C11r in Yemen is similar to Ethiopian magnetos-
tratigraphy [4,5], and, thus supports the hypothesis of
a coeval onset Oligocene flood volcanism throughout
the Afro-Arabian LIP .
The R3 reversed polarity section is constrained by
two ages on silicic units of 28.35 F 0.14 and 27.92 F
0.10 Ma (JB228II and JB232, respectively, [13]), and
has an estimated duration of ~0.5 F 0.1 Ma. The N3
normal polarity zone is represented by a single unit,
the Bayt Mawjan ignimbrite with an age of 27.67 F
0.12 Ma. Thus the transition from R3 to N3 is esti-
mated to have occurred at ~27.8 F 0.2 Ma. While it
is difficult to uniquely correlate the R3 polarity
zone to the GPTS, the overlying and youngest
polarity zone, N3, appears to share good correspon-
dence with C9n.
The onset of the N2 normal polarity period is well
constrained by the age of the Iftar Alkalb flow
(29.48 F 0.13 Ma), but this may be succeeded by an
eruptive hiatus. None of the subsequent overlying
units in the N2 period are constrained by accepted
age data, and thus the period of time represented by
N2 could be as long as 1 Ma. The R2 polarity zone,
which, based on strong outside constraints [56,57],
corresponds to the brief C11n.1r Subchron, has a well-
constrained age of ~29.5 F 0.1 Ma (based on the ages
29.47 F 0.14 Ma age of the underlying SAM ignim-
brite and 29.48 F 0.13 Ma for the overlying BB7
unit), potentially providing a new tie-point for cali-
bration of the GPTS. However, an ~29.5 F 0.1 Ma age
for C11n.1r is only in marginal agreement with pre-
vious determinations. Coulie et al. [7] define the onset
of C11n.1r to have taken place at 29.75 F 0.10 Ma.
Unfortunately, these reported
40Ar /39Ar ages [7] are
based on a standard (HD-B1) whose intercalibration
with our standard is not well established, and an
P . Riisager et al. / Earth and Planetary Science Letters 237 (2005) 647–672668

accurate comparison of ages between this study and
that of Coulie et al. [7] cannot be made at this time.
Additional studies provide 40Ar /39Ar and magnetic
data from the Ethiopian part of the Afro-Arabian traps
[4,5,57] assigning an age of 30.1 F 0.1 Ma to the
underlying C11n.2n, in good agreement with our
data, but a slightly older age of 29.7 F 0.1 Ma to the
end of C11n.1r. The reason for the discrepancy in the
age of the brief C11n.1r Subchron remains unclear at
this time. One possible explanation is that the R2
reverse polarity zone is an excursion within C11n,
and that the actual C11n.1r is not recorded in our
sampled sequences.
Underlying the brief R2 reversal is a set of normal
polarity lavas and pyroclastic units within the N1
zone. The reverse to normal transition is bracketed
by ages of the upper basalts (at the top of R1) as just
discussed and the overlying Akraban Trachyandesite
(near the base of N1) at 29.61 F 0.08 Ma. We thus
estimate the age of this reversal at 29.8 F 0.2 Ma. The
lower basaltic flows span 30.51 F 0.36 to
29.94 F 0.24 Ma, a statistically unresolvable interval
of time contained within the reversed R1 zone.
6.5. Environmental impact of Afro-Arabian flood
volcanism
Several papers have discussed the temporal coin-
cidence between LIP volcanism and global environ-
mental changes [2,3]. The Afro-Arabian LIP has been
suggested to have a causal relationship with the Eo-
cene–Oligocene biotic extinctions [58]. Extensive
geochronologic and magnetostratigraphic studies in
Ethiopia demonstrate that the Afro-Arabian LIP
post-date the Eocene–Oligocene boundary, however,
and a potential temporal link to the global Oi2 cooling
event at about 30 Ma has instead been suggested [4,5].
According to the chronology of Pekar and Miller [59]
the Oi2 cooling event takes place at the base of Chron
C11r and therefore is synchronous with the onset of
Afro-Arabian basaltic volcanism. Since the bulk of
Afro-Arabian basaltic volcanism seems to have been
rapidly erupted, a causal link to the Oi2 event cannot
be ruled out. From other LIPs there is preponderance
of evidence that basaltic LIP volcanism relates to
global climate perturbations through volatile emis-
sions [3]. The massive silicic Afro-Arabian volcanism
is also a likely candidate to drive global cooling
through massive airborne particulate ejection i.e., the
bvolcanic winter Q mechanism as some of the ignim-
brite units are found in Indian Ocean sediments, 2700
km away from the Afro-Arabian traps, implying that
these units were emplaced on a near-global scale and
that individual eruptive volumes may have been larger
than 3000 km
3 dense rock equivalent [14]. However,
these silicic units were erupted episodically over a
period of ~3 Ma allowing potential climate recovery
between eruptive episodes, and the main silicic Afro-
Arabian volcanism occur in C11n and therefore post-
date the Oi2 cooling event.
7. Conclusions
In this paper, we have documented that
(i) The paleomagnetic pole of this study k = 74.28N,
u = 249.18E (A95 = 3.68; N = 48) is in excellent
accord with the paleomagnetic pole obtained
from the Ethiopian part of the Afro-Arabian
province, after closure of the Red Sea.
(ii) Analysis of this new paleomagnetic pole in con-
junction with contemporaneous paleomagnetic
poles available from different latitudes suggest
that Oligocene paleomagnetic field was domi-
nated by the axial dipole with only insignificant
non-dipole field contributions.
(iii) The massive rhyolitic ignimbrite eruptions, cor-
related to ash layers in Oligocene Indian Ocean
sediment 2700 km away from the Afro-Arabian
traps [56], took place during magnetochron
C11n.
(iv) Silicic and bi-modal volcanism preserved on the
Arabian Peninsula was episodic over ~3 Ma and
seems to post-date the Oi2 global cooling event.
(v) The bulk of basal basaltic volcanism in Yemen
took place in b 1 Ma during a reverse polarity
chron that appears to correspond to C11r and
cannot be ruled out as having a causal role in the
Oi2 global cooling event.

A paleomagnetic test for northward tectonic
transport of the eastern Selwyn Basin, northern
Canadian Cordillera: data from the mid-Cretaceous
Ragged Pluton
D.T.A. Symons, K. Kawasaki, C.J.R. Hart, and M.J. Harris
Abstract: Ragged Pluton is a member of the Tungsten Plutonic Suite in the eastern Selwyn Basin. This circular massive
97 Ma granitic pluton is *5 km in diameter. It intrudes deformed and metamorphosed clastic strata of the Neoproterozoic
to Lower Cambrian Vampire Formation. Thermal and alternating field step demagnetization data for 216 specimens from
21 plutonic sites isolated a stable characteristic remanent magnetization (ChRM) direction at 20 sites of declination D =
325.98, inclination I = 80.48 (a
95 = 2.78, k = 142). Thermal demagnetization and saturation remanence analysis show that
the ChRM is carried by both single-domain pyrrhotite and magnetite. Ragged Pluton’s paleopole at 73.9 8N latitude,
191.48E longitude (dp = 5.0 8, dm = 5.2 8) is concordant with its co-eval 97 Ma North American reference paleopole, show-
ing at 95% confidence that the pluton has not been significantly rotated or translated relative to North America. This
paleomagnetic result favours tectonic models in which the eastern Selwyn Basin is autochthonous, or nearly so, since the
mid Cretaceous.

Introduction
The inboard portions of the northern Cordillera consist of
the carbonate-dominated, Mesoproterozoic to Paleozoic
Mackenzie Platform and the clastic-dominated Neoprotero-
zoic to Paleozoic Selwyn Basin that were variably deformed
in the Mesozoic into the Mackenzie and Selwyn fold and
thrust belts, respectively. Much of the Selwyn Basin was in-
truded later by suites of Cretaceous plutons with related
metamorphic activity. Despite their apparently stable posi-
tion as miogeoclinal cover on the North American cratonic
edge, previous paleomagnetic studies have led to four dis-
tinct tectonic scenarios being suggested for the Selwyn Ba-
sin since the mid-Cretaceous (Fig. 1).
From the analysis of >40 reliable Mesozoic and Cenozoic
paleopoles from the Intermontane Belt (IMB) and Yukon–
Tanana (Y–T) terranes, Symons et al. (2005) calculated that
the northern IMB terranes were rotated clockwise by 35 8 ±
148 between 102 ± 14 and 54 Ma and by a further 16 8 ±6 8
since 54 Ma. From this rotation, they estimated an ENE–
WSW shortening of 305 ± 125 km across the Selwyn Basin
and Mackenzie Mountains between the IMB and ancestral
North America in southeastern Yukon and southwestern
Northwest Territories. Two alternatives could accommodate
this shortening. One option assumes thick-skin tectonics
caused the Selwyn Basin to be deformed as it was driven
east-northeastward, perhaps contributing to the arcuate trend

of the Mackenzie Mountains. Alternatively, assuming thin-
skin tectonics, the IMB terranes could have slid over the
Selwyn Basin and since been eroded without significantly
deforming its strata. Both options should give paleomagnetic
paleopoles showing the Selwyn Basin to be autochthonous
or para-autochthonous, except that the thick-skin option
should also show a clockwise rotation.
Based on paleomagnetic results from the *70 Ma Car-
macks Group volcanics, Enkin et al. (2006) suggested that
the Selwyn Basin strata originated *1950 ± 600 km further
south relative to ancestral North America. The Carmacks
volcanics appear to rest on rocks of the IMB and Y–T ter-
ranes (Fig. 1), leading Enkin et al. (2006) to infer that the
Selwyn Basin’s strata were allochthonous to North America
and part of the far-traveled Baja British Columbia micro-
plate (Irving et al. 1996). If true, then mid-Cretaceous rocks
in the basin should have significantly shallower characteris-
tic remanent magnetic (ChRM) inclinations than those of
North America.
In southeastern British Columbia, Irving and Archibald
(1990) analysed paleomagnetic data from the massive *97
Ma Skelly Creek Batholith in a similar geologic setting on
the North American margin (Fig. 1) (Gabrielse et al. 1991).
They concluded that the batholith is close to its present loca-
tion relative to ancestral North America, thereby supporting
the traditional geologic viewpoint that the batholith is an
autochthonous, or at least para-autochthonous, part of North
America since *97 Ma (Gabrielse 1967; Gordey and
Anderson 1993).
Here we report paleomagnetic results from the *97 Ma
Ragged Pluton, the first such results from the easternmost
Selwyn Basin (Fig. 1). Our objective was to provide an ini-
tial test of the proposed tectonic models for the basin.
Geology
The stratigraphic sequence in southeastern Yukon and
southwestern Northwest Territories comprises a westward-
thickening wedge of mid-Proterozoic to mid-Jurassic
miogeoclinal sedimentary rocks that are similar to those de-
posited elsewhere along the western Cordilleran margin of
North America (Gordey and Anderson 1993). Although
characterized as a passive margin assemblage, this sequence
records a number of uplift, erosional, and rifting events. In
the mid-Jurassic, an island-arc terrane from the southwest
collided against the miogeocline that caused imbrication
and folding of the sedimentary succession through the Early
Cretaceous, forming two distinct fold belts (Gordey and
Anderson 1993). On the northeastern side, the competent
carbonate-dominated shallow-water platformal strata de-
formed to create the Mackenzie Fold Belt (Fig. 1). On the
southwestern side, in contrast, the incompetent shale-
dominated deeper water basinal sediments were intensely
folded with slaty cleavage to form the Selwyn Fold Belt. In
the mid-Cretaceous, five plutonic suites were emplaced into
the Selwyn Fold Belt, i.e., 109–95 Ma Anvil, 96–93 Ma
Mayo, and 92–90 Ma Tombstone suites in the northern and
western Selwyn Basin and the 106–96 Ma Hyland and 98–94
Ma Tungsten suites in the southern and eastern basin (Hart et
al. 2004). The intrusion of the plutonic suites has been attrib-
uted to crustal thickening from deformation and thrust sheet
stacking in the basin (Gordey and Anderson 1993; Mair et al.
2006).
Ragged Pluton, a member of the Tungsten Plutonic Suite
and remote from older Hyland plutons, is composed of
massive 98 to 94 Ma aluminous granitic intrusions that out-
crop in an *50 km wide belt for *300 km along the
Yukon – Northwest Territories border in the easternmost

resolution ion microprobe (SHRIMP) U–Pb age (C.J.R.
Hart, personal communication, 2007). The Tungsten suite
plutons are predominantly reduced, peraluminous musco-
vite–biotite monzogranites (Gordey and Anderson 1993;
Hart et al. 2005) with low Fe
2O3/Fe ratios of *0.1–0.3,
high ilmenite content, moderate to low magnetic susceptibil-
ities, and low aeromagnetic expression (Hart et al. 2004).
Typically, these plutons have homogeneous compositions,
massive undeformed textures, steep sides, and flat tops, and
were likely emplaced at depths of *5 to 7 km.
Ragged Pluton is circular in plan with a diameter of
*5 km (Fig. 2). It intrudes the Neoproterozoic to Lower
Cambrian Vampire Formation, which undergoes a lateral fa-
cies transition to the Hyland Group (Gordey and Anderson
1993; Gordey and Makepeace 2003). The Vampire Forma-
tion is composed of brown to greenish-grey siltstones with
minor fine-grained quartz sandstones and shales that have
been metamorphosed locally to orthoquartzite, phyllite,
slate, and argillite. Near Ragged Pluton, the Vampire For-
mation is conformably overlain by carbonates of the Lower
to Middle Cambrian Sekwi Formation and by Upper Cam-
brian to Lower Ordovician limestone formations, which are
conformably overlain in turn by undifferentiated strata of
the Paleozoic Road River Group.
Structurally, Ragged Pluton was emplaced into the crest
of an open anticline with contacts that crosscut bedding.
Although there are numerous small-offset north- and north-
east-trending normal faults in the region, the only potentially
significant post-mid-Cretaceous displacements are west-side-
