mary, the age of remanences in the Ghost-Indin lakes region are
difﬁcult to assess without further study. Although it is possible
that the remanences are primary, they may represent overprin-
ting or partial overprinting associated with the Calderian orogeny
that affected Wopmay orogen (Hildebrand et al., 2010) and the
Indin Lake area (Frith, 1993), or overprinting of post-Hudsonian
age (Irving et al., 2004).
8.3. APW paths and implications for continental reconstructions
The primary paleopoles determined in this study for the Indin
and Ghost dykes of the Yellowknife region are plotted in Fig. 12
for comparison with paleopoles from other precisely dated dyke
swarms in the Slave craton and with paleopoles that deﬁne the
APW path for the Superior craton (see Table 4). On the ﬁgure, we
have included the Ghost dyke poles calculated independently for
reversed (labelled R) and normal (N) dykes because they do not pass
the reversal test. R is considered more reliable because it is based
on 17 dykes, whereas N is derived from only six dykes. R is also
better dated because the Ghost U-Pb age was determined from a
reversed dyke. Paleomagnetic data from Superior craton units that
are 2.07 Ga or older record a relative rotation of 10–20◦ between
the eastern and western portions of the craton (Halls and Davis,
2004; Buchan et al., 2007; Evans and Halls, 2010). Therefore these
data sets are distinguished in Fig. 12.
For simplicity, Slave paleopoles are plotted on the same side
of the globe as the Superior poles in Fig. 12, although the relative
polarity of Slave and Superior poles is uncertain. The relative polar-
ity of paleopoles is well established along the early portion of the
Superior APW path where the ages of adjacent paleopoles differ by
only10–50 Myr, time intervals that are too short to permit the use
of antipoles. Relative polarity is less secure for the younger portion
of the track, especially in the case of the 120 Myr gap between
the Minto and Molson poles. The Slave craton paleopoles outline a
rudimentary APW path, although relative polarity is often less cer-
tain than in the case of the Superior track, because of the longer
time intervals between adjacent poles (especially the 100 Myr gap
between the Indin and Lac de Gras poles and the 140 Myr gap
between Lac de Gras and Ghost poles). For simplicity, in Fig. 12,
the relative polarities that are used for the Slave APWP and for
the youngest portion of the Superior path are chosen to minimize
the distance between the poles. However, Fig. 13, which illustrates
the latitudinal drift and rotation of the Slave and Superior cratons,
includes both polarity options.
The data of Fig. 12 can be used to examine (a) whether plate
tectonic processes were active during the 2.23–1.88 Ga period, (b)
whether the Slave and Superior cratons were in their current rela-
tive positions prior to 1.88 Ga and (c) whether they drifted relative
to one another between 2.23 and 1.88 Ga.
Like the Superior paleopoles, Slave paleopoles in Fig. 12 are not
stable with time, but are distributed along a track. Thus both cra-
tons were drifting through the 2.23–1.88 Ga interval, indicating
that plate tectonic processes were operating at that time and con-
ﬁrming previous interpretations based on more limited data from
the Slave craton (e.g., Buchan et al., 2012; Mitchell et al., 2014).
Older Slave craton paleopoles from 2.23 Ga Malley (Buchan et al.,
2012) and 2.19 Ga Dogrib dykes (Mitchell et al., 2014) are located
only ∼20◦ apart (Fig. 12), as might be expected given the relatively
small (∼40 Myr) difference in emplacement ages. However, Dogrib
and 2.13–2.11 Ga Indin poles are located ∼70◦ apart, suggesting that
relatively rapid drift occurred in the interval between 2.19 and 2.11
Ga, as the Slave craton drifted from latitude 20◦ in one hemisphere
to latitude 50◦ in the opposite hemisphere (Fig. 13). Alternatively,
because of the magnetic polarity ambiguity, the craton may have
drifted from 20 to 50◦ latitude in one hemisphere while rotating
through ∼170◦ (Fig. 13).
Paleopoles from 2.13 to 2.11 Ga Indin, 2.025 Ga Lac de Gras
and 1.885 Ga Ghost dykes correspond to an equatorward drift of
the Slave craton from 50◦ to 25◦ paleolatitude along with a small
counterclockwise rotation (Fig. 13). However, because the time
intervals between these poles are relatively long (∼100 Myr and
140 Myr), a more complex path may emerge as data are acquired
within these intervals and as relative magnetic polarity is clari-
ﬁed. Indeed, highly scattered paleopoles from ca. 1.96 to 1.87 Ga
units on the margins of the Slave craton (Fig. 1) have been variously
interpreted as recording (a) a long “Coronation Loop” in the APW
path (e.g., Irving and McGlynn, 1979), (b) “large variable rotations
[of local sampling areas] about local vertical axes” during indenta-
tion of the Slave craton into the Rae craton (Irving et al., 2004), (c)
rapid rotations of the Slave, Rae and Hearne cratons as the latter
encountered the Superior continental margin during closure of the
Manikewan ocean (Halls, 2014), or (d) multiple episodes of true
polar wander (the rotation of the solid Earth relative to the Earth’s
spin axis) superimposed on a systematic counterclockwise rotation
of 12◦ for units near the McDonald fault (Fig. 1) and clockwise rota-
tion of 12◦ for units near the Bathurst fault during indentation of
the Slave craton into the Rae Province (Mitchell et al., 2010). More
paleomagnetic and geochronological studies are needed to evaluate
these models for several reasons: rotations appear likely (although
Mitchell et al. (2010) argue that they are relatively minor), multiple
remanence components are common, most remanences have yet
to be demonstrated primary and most rock units are not precisely
dated. We restrict further discussion to data from the stable portion

The rudimentary Slave APW path of Fig. 12 from precisely dated

2.13–2.11 Ga before swinging at right angles towards the south-
west and crossing Central America into the eastern Paciﬁc Ocean.
In contrast, the Superior craton APW path for the same time interval
begins off the central east coast of South America and runs parallel
to the western coast of the Americas to the northern Paciﬁc Ocean
by 2.07 Ga before making a counterclockwise loop and re-crossing
itself at 1.885 Ga (Fig. 12). The fact that the Slave and Superior
paleopoles do not lie on a single APW path demonstrates that the
two cratons were not in their present relative positions during the
2.23–1.885 period, supporting the conclusion of previous studies
based on more limited data sets (Buchan et al., 2009, 2012; Mitchell
et al., 2014). This conclusion is bolstered by the distinct difference
between the paleopoles for the coeval (2.13–2.11 Ga) Indin and
Marathon dykes of Slave and Superior cratons respectively, and the
difference between the paleopoles for the coeval (1.885 Ga) Ghost
and Molson dykes. The difference between the 1.885 Ga paleopoles
for Slave and Superior cratons is consistent with geological evi-
dence for ﬁnal collision between the Superior craton and the rest
of Laurentia (aggregate of Hearne, Rae, Slave, Wyoming, and North
Atlantic cratons) at ca. 1.83–1.80 Ga (Hoffman, 1989; Corrigan et al.,
2009; St Onge et al., 2009).
Not only are the APW paths for the Slave and Superior cratons
distinct, but they have different shapes with the Superior track
looping back to cross itself at ca. 1.885 Ga, whereas the Slave track
does not (Fig. 12). This demonstrates that the two cratons were
not drifting on the same tectonic plate–either together, or at a
distance–throughout the 2.23–1.885 Ga interval. However, it does
not preclude their moving in unison during some portion of this
interval. For example, between 2.22 and 2.12 Ga the Superior cra-
ton poles fall roughly on a >90◦ great-circle arc. The 2.23 and 2.12
Ga Slave craton poles are separated by ∼90◦ and could also repre-
sent endpoints of a great-circle arc, although intervening data are
sparse. Coeval great-circle arcs of similar length for the two cratons
could reﬂect motion of the two cratons on a single tectonic plate
with a large distance between them (cf. calculation of Mitchell et al.,
2014). Alternatively, it could reﬂect true polar wander at a moder-
ate rate (e.g., Tsai and Stevenson, 2007) as discussed by Mitchell
et al. (2014), although substantial drift associated with plate tec-
tonic processes would also likely have occurred given the extended
length of time (>100 Myr) involved. Further key paleopoles are
required to better address these possibilities.
Proterozoic APW paths based exclusively on key paleopoles are
not yet available from any Archean cratons other than the Slave
and Superior. Indeed, individual key paleopoles that are coeval with
key poles from the Slave (or Superior) craton are sparse, making it
difﬁcult to attempt robust reconstructions. There are no key poles
whose ages match those of the 2.23 Ga Malley, 2.13–2.11 Ga Indin,
or 2.025 Ga Lac de Gras poles. A paleopole has been reported (Fahrig
et al., 1984) for the 2.19 Ga (LeCheminant et al., 1997) Tulemalu
dyke swarm of the Rae craton, which is coeval with the Dogrib
dyke swarm of the Slave craton. However, the Tulemalu pole has
not been demonstrated to be primary, so that the relative loca-
tion of the two cratons remains speculative (LeCheminant et al.,
1997).
Except for the Superior craton, only the Siberian craton and the
Kaapvaal craton of southern Africa have key paleopoles that are
approximately coeval with the 1.885 Ga Slave craton pole. Didenko
et al. (2009) reported a primary pole for 1878 ±4 Ma Lower Akitkan
redbeds of the Lake Baikal region of southern Siberia based on a
positive intra-formational conglomerate test. Inclination shallow-
ing of the magnetic remanence, which can occur in sedimentary
rocks during deposition or later compaction (e.g., Kodama, 2012), is
likely minimal in these redbeds because the inclination is very low
(see discussion in Buchan, 2014). The Lower Akitkan pole indicates
that Siberia was straddling the equator, and hence may have been
off the northern Slave craton margin (positions D or J in Fig. 14),

Matching magmatic “barcodes” (Bleeker et al., 2000) of the two
cratons suggests a number of shared events (e.g., Ernst et al., 2014)
and thus a certain degree of proximity (on the scale of a typical
magmatic event, i.e., 1000–2000 km). For instance, several units
that are coeval with the ca. 0.72 Ga Franklin magmatic event of
northern Laurentia have been identiﬁed in southern Siberia (Ernst
et al., 2014). On the other hand, a robust counterpart of the large
1.27 Ga Mackenzie igneous event of northern Laurentia remains
to be identiﬁed in southern Siberia, although a single maﬁc dyke
which is only slightly younger (1.26 Ga) has been reported (Ernst
et al., 2014).
In addition, numerous difﬁculties remain with correlating
northern Laurentian cratons and orogenic belts into southern
Siberia, as exempliﬁed by essentially all different permutations of
a close Laurentia-Siberia ﬁt having been proposed in the past (e.g.,
Hoffman, 1991; Condie and Rosen, 1994; Pelechaty, 1996; Frost
et al., 1998; Rainbird et al., 1998; Evans and Mitchell, 2011). Critical
to this problem is the fact that the Slave craton is very well charac-
terized and distinct (e.g., Bleeker and Davis, 1999; Bleeker, 2003;
Bleeker and Hall, 2007), as is Wopmay orogen (e.g., Hildebrand
et al., 2010), whereas conclusive counterparts have yet to be iden-
tiﬁed from southern Siberia. Recent work also calls into question
correlation of the Akitkan fold belt (Donskaya et al., 2008) with
the Thelon belt. Finally, post-collisional 1.88–1.85 Ga granitoids
around the Irkutsk promontory of southern Siberia (Poller et al.,
2005; Donskaya et al., 2009), suggest a possible suture which would
need to be accounted for in any detailed correlation. All these difﬁ-
culties related to a close ﬁt of southern Siberia to northern Laurentia
(see further discussion in Pisarevsky et al., 2008) would be relaxed
by a more distant ﬁt as suggested by position J in Fig. 14 or by the
reconstructions of Pisarevsky et al. (2014).
Sears and Price (2003) argue on geological and geophysical
grounds that Siberia was located adjacent to western Laurentia
from the Paleoproterozoic to the Neoproterozoic. However, the key
paleopole reconstruction of Fig. 14 is not compatible with such a ﬁt
at ca. 1.88 Ga.
The only other craton for which a ca. 1.88 Ga key paleopole has
been reported is the Kaapvaal craton, where Lubnina et al. (2010)
determined a primary pole of approximately this age for the Black
Hills dykes. It indicates that the Kaapvaal craton was at a paleolat-
itude of ∼40◦, similar to the 1.88 Ga paleolatitude for the Superior
craton (see Fig. 4 of Buchan, 2014) and only slightly higher than the
1.885 Ga paleolatitude of ∼30◦ for the Slave craton. These data per-
mit the Kaapvaal craton to have been close to either the Superior or
Slave at ca.1.88 Ga. However, further key paleopoles are required
from the Kaapvaal craton to reach any deﬁnite conclusion about
whether it was attached to, or moving in unison with, either of
these cratons.
Halls (2014) proposed a model of ∼3000 ± 1000 km of Paleopro-
terozoic crustal shortening between the Slave and Superior cratons
associated most likely with the Trans-Hudson orogen and based on
analysis of key paleomagnetic poles that were then available from
the Superior craton and poor quality poles for the Slave craton and
in a few instances from the Rae and Hearne cratons. He argued that
the 2.23–1.80 Ga poles for the Superior craton fall along a SE-NW
trending APW path at right angles to the trend of the Trans-Hudson
orogen and that similar-aged Slave craton poles, although of poorer
quality, also fall on a distinct but similar-trending path (Halls, 2014,
p. 45). As a result, he described a model in which the Slave, Rae,
Hearne and Superior cratons maintained their present-day rela-
tive orientation with respect to one another as oceans opened and
closed between them during the 2.23–1.80 Ga period (Fig. 4 of Halls,
2014). In particular, changes in the distance separating coeval poles
from the Slave and Superior cratons were interpreted in terms of
opening and closing oceans and crustal shortening. However, the
new primary poles for the Slave craton determined in this study
and other recent publications and plotted in Fig. 12 do not fall on a
single SE-NW trending path, but rather show a right angle bend at
ca 2.12 Ga. Hence, the 1.885 Ga Slave pole lies far from the 2.23–2.12
portion of the Slave track, in contrast to the 1.88 Ga Superior pole,
which falls on the earlier portion of the Superior track. The model
of crustal shortening will need to be reevaluated in light of these
new key pole data.
9. Conclusions
Study of the paleomagnetism of precisely dated 2.13–2.11 Ga
Indin and 1.885 Ga Ghost dykes of the Yellowknife region, and
comparison with paleomagnetism of Paleoproterozoic dykes from
elsewhere in the Slave and Superior cratons leads to the following
conclusions:
1. Northwest- to north-northwest-trending Indin and northeast-
to north-northeast-trending Ghost dykes of the southwestern
Slave craton carry distinct paleomagnetic remanences in the Yel-
lowknife region, with corresponding paleomagnetic poles at 36◦
N, 76◦ W (A95 = 7◦) and 2◦ N, 106◦ W (A95 = 6◦), respectively.
2. Indin and Ghost remanences in the Yellowknife region are pri-
mary based on baked contact or baked contact proﬁle tests
reported herein and by Schwarz et al. (1985), as well as the dis-
tinct remanence directions observed in Ghost, Indin and older
Dogrib dykes of the area.
3. The rudimentary APW path for the Slave craton between 2.23
and 1.885 Ga, based on paleomagnetic poles from ﬁve precisely
dated dyke swarms, indicates that the craton drifted through-
out the period and suggests that plate tectonic process were
operating.
4. A comparison of the Slave track with the coeval segment of the
well-established APW path for the Superior craton suggests that:
(a) Superior and Slave cratons were not in their present relative
locations in the 2.23–1.885 Ga period, in agreement with
geological evidence that the ﬁnal collision of the Superior
craton with the aggregate of Hearne, Rae, Slave, Wyoming
and North Atlantic cratons to form Laurentia occurred later,
at ca. 1.83–1.80 Ga (Hoffman, 1989; Corrigan et al., 2009; St
Onge et al., 2009).
(b) The two cratons drifted relative to one another on separate
tectonic plates during at least part of the 2.23–1.885 Ga inter-
val, but could have been located on the same plate, albeit at a
great distance from one another, during the early 2.23–2.12
Ga portion of the interval.
5. A comparison of the Ghost pole with a coeval key pole for the
Siberian craton permits a 1.88 Ga reconstruction in which south-
ern Siberia faces the northern Slave/Laurentia margin, similar to
ﬁts that have been proposed as late as 1.38 Ga in some earlier
studies, although the distance between the two cratons is poorly
constrained.

Electron microscopy of iron oxides and implications for the 
origin of magnetizations and rock magnetic properties of 
Banded Series rocks of the Stillwater Complex, Montana 
Weixin Xu' 
Department of Geological Sciences, University of Michigan, Ann Arbor 
John W. Geissman 
Department of Earth and Planetary Sciences, University of New Mexico, Albuquerque 
Rob Van der Voo and Donald R. Peacor 
Department of Geological Sciences, University of Michigan, Ann Arbor 
Abstract. The origins of multiple magnetizations of the Archean Stillwater Complex have 
been investigated through scanning electron microscopy and seamting transmission electron 
microscopy observations of mineralogieal relations, using representative samples from nine 
sites in mafic Banded series rocks. On the basis of directional grouping and demagnetization 
behavior, three magnetizations (here labeled A, B, and C) have been recognized. The natural 
reinanent magnetizaton (NRM) is typically dominated by only one of these magnetizations and 
multicomponent behavior in individual specimens is rare. The A remanenee resides in 
magnetic grains of high median destructive fields and high, discrete laboratory unblocking 
temperatures and is inferred to be a primary thermoremanent magnetization, of circa 2.71 Ga 
age. The B and C magnetizations, of lower median destructive fields and more distributed 
unblocking temperatures, are inferred to be secondary and related to alteration, including 
serpentinization, involving limited, moderate to low-temperature fluid interaction, perhaps in 
response to thermotectonic events (e.g., matic dike emplacement). Samples with NPdVI 
dominated by the A magnetization contain titanium-free magnetite needles (width < 1 m and 
maximum dimension between about 2 and 50 Im) with preferred orientations in cumulus 
plagioclase crystals; these oxides are interpreted to have formed during initial crystallization of 
cumulus phases. In samples containing only B or C magnetizations, such needles are absent in 
cumulus plagioclase, whereas secondary Fe-bearing silicates, particularly zoisite and chlorite, 
are conspicuous. The samples dominated by the B or C magnetizations contain anhedral !ow- 
chromian magnetite (FeCr2-xFex04, 1.5 < x < 2.0) along fractures in both cumulus plagioclase 
and pyroxene and in zones of more pervasive alteration of pyroxenes. The paragenesis of these 
oxides is consistent with an origin related to hydrothermal alteration. Hysteresis data show that 
p!agio½lase crystals containing magnetite needles have higher reinanent coercivities (/-/cr = 60 
to 100 roT), whereas plagio½lase crystals with anhedral c!u:omian magnetite have remanent 
coercivities less than 60 roT, consistent with their alternating field response. Because oxygen 
isotope data show no indication of appreciable alteration of host plagioclase, we infer that the 
absence of magnetite needles and their associated A magnetization are caused by selective 
alteration of the magnetite needles to nonmagnetic phases in the remagnetized gabbros. In this 
case, rock magnetic and paleomagnetic data appear to be higher resolution indicators of 
fluid/rock interaction than the stable isotope data. Anhedral chromian magnetite precipitated 
during hydrothermal alteration and therefore carries secondary magnetizations.

Palcomagnetic Results 
The palcomagnetism of the Stillwater Complex was first 
studied by Bergh [1968, 1970]. Based on limited yet careful 
(for the time) demagnetization work, Bergh reported a well- 
defined, well-grouped magnetization in relatively fresh 
Banded Series rocks from nine sites at two localities. The 
magnetization reported was only of one polarity and yielded a 
mean direction having a declination of about 160 ø and an 
inclination of about -40 ø after correction for restoration o1 
igneous layering to the horizontal. He interpreted this 
magnetization to have been acquired during the initial 
crystallization of the complex, the age of which was then 
poorly known. He also obtained well-grouped data (after 
correction: declination/inclination of about 16 ø/+26 o ) from a diabase dike that cuts Banded Series rocks. 
More extensive palcomagnetic sampling, initial results ot  
which are reported by Geissrnan and Mogk [1986], has 
demonstrated the presence of at least three geologically significant magnetizations, referred to here as A, B, and C, in 
Banded Series rocks of the Stillwater Complex, based on the 
demagnetization behavior of the NRM and directions of the 
magnetizations that were isolated. The B and C 
magnetizations, furthermore, have also been identified in 
Proterozoic marie dikes that intrude the complex. At the site 
level, for the samples examined in this study, magnetizations 
are acceptably grouped (Table 1). Examples of both AF and 
thermal demagnetization behavior (Figures 3 and 4), revealed 
that each of the magnetizations has unique characteristics. 
The A magnetization is of dual polarity, with an in situ 
direction that is east to northeast (or west to southwest) with a 
generally moderate to steep (30 ø to 60 ø ) negative (or positive) 
inclination (Figure 3). Of the sites yielding this 
magnetization, the east and negative inclination remanence 
predominates (Table 1). For the sake of possible comparison 
with palcomagnetic data of comparable age, after restoration 
of magmatie layering to the horizontal, using present strike 
axes [Geissrnan and Mogk, 1986], the east and negative magnetization becomes south directed with a moderate to 
shallow negative inclination, as originally reported by Bergh 
[1968, 1970]. The A magnetization is characterized by high 
( > 550øC) and discrete laboratory unbloeking temperatures 
(Figure 3) and high ( > 50 roT) median destructive fields 
(Figure 3) and, presumably, coereivities, suggesting that it is 
carried by free single-domain (SD) and pseudo-single-domain 
(PSD) magnetite. 
The B magnetization is considerably more dispersed than 
the other two magnetizations and usually has an in situ 
direction with a north (or south) declination and moderate to 
steep positive (or negative) inclination (J.W. Geissman, 
unpublished data, 1996). Corrected for the orientation of the 
magmatie layering in the Stillwater Complex, this component 
has a north-northeast (or south-southwest) declination and 
positive (or negative) shallow inclination (Table 1). One of 
the samples (B42C) revealing the B magnetization (note in 
this case the magnetization is of north-northwest declination 
and moderate negative inclination) was obtained from rocks in 
contact with a Proterozoic marie dike. In comparison to the A 
magnetization, this magnetization usually has mow 
distributed laboratory unblocking temperatures and median 
destructive fields generally less than 30 roT.

The NRM of over 95% of the Banded Series rocks studied

Oxide Mineralogy- Microscopic Observations 
In comparison to the many detailed and systematic studies 
of silicate mineralogy, relatively little comprehensive work 
has been carried out on Fe-Ti oxides in Banded Series rocks of 
the Stillwater Complex. Maze and Carlson [1982] reported 
petrographie observations and electron microprobe data for 
oxides in Banded Series rocks from the lower Noritc and from 
the upper Banded Zone (Figure 2). Of the distinct types of 
oxide occurrences described, only one probably has relevance 
to the palcomagnetism of these rocks because of the overall 
grain size of the oxides. Maze and Carlson observed 1 to 10 
grn low-Ti magnetite and ilmenite grains in what they 
interpreted to be occasional magmatie glass inclusions in 
cumulus plagioelase. The composition of the glass inclusions 
was reported to be similar to cumulus orthopyroxenes in the 
same samples. The abundance of this type of oxide 
occurrence appears to be small relative to finer-grained oxides 
identified in STEM observations, as described below. 
Geissrnan et al. [1988], in a discussion of paleomagnetic 
microanalytical techniques, reported limited STEM 
observations on a single sample of plagioclase f¾om an 
amphibole/plagioclase pegmatite dike cutting upper Banded 
Series rocks. Submicron magnetite grains were found in 
unaltered plagioclase areas. An association between these 
grains and the remanence isolated from separated plagioclase 
grains was suggested. 
Petrography 
All samples studied are coarse-grained marie rocks mainly 
composed of cumulus plagioclase and pyroxene. Based on 
optical microscopy, plagioclase, mainly as a cumulus phase, 
composes more than 60% (60 to 95%) by volume in all the 
studied samples (Table 2). Pyroxenes exhibit a range of 
compositions and textures. Pyroxene minerals can be divided 
into clinopyroxene and low calcium pyroxene (LCP), 
including orthopyroxene and pigeonitc. Clinopyroxene (cpx) 
concentration ranges from 5 to 25% (Table 2), and this phase 
occurs as both cumulus and intercumulus material. 
Intercumulus clinopyroxene sometimes contains exsolution 
lamellae of orthopyroxene. LCP concentrations range from 0 
to 30% (Table 2). Low calcium pyroxene also occurs as both 
euhedral cumulus and postcumulus phases. Pyroxene 
exsolution and inversion features in Banded Series rocks have

Optical Microscope and SEM Observations of Iron 
Oxides 
Because conventional EDS analysis does not permit clear 
distinction among magnetite, hematite, and goethite and 
because they all have similar fine grain sizes, they cannot be 
definitely identified using optical microscopy and SEM. We 
therefore refer to them using the general term \"iron oxide.\" 
Four iron oxide grain types/associations have been 
observed: (1) equant euhedral iron oxide, (2) needle-shaped 
iron oxide, (3) anhedral frae-grained iron oxide, and (4) mixed 
iron oxide/iron sulfide assemblages. In addition, ilmenite is 
found as inclusions in plagioclase and pyroxene grains, as 
both elongated plates and irregularly shaped plates. 
Titanomagnetite, as reported by Maze and Carlson [ 1982], 
was found to be extremely rare in the samples studied. 
Indeed, only one sample, which does not carry a stable NRM, 
was found to contain fitanomagnetite, implying no obvious 
correlation between NRM and the presence of titanomagnetite 
grains.

Discussion and Conclusions 
Correlation Between Characteristic Magnetic Mineral 
Assemblages and ?aleomagnetism 
Based on demagnetization characteristics, the samples 
examined can be divided into three groups' (1) Samples with 
only high coercivity and high unblocking temperature A 
magnetizations (sample: B14C), (2) samples carrying 
component A as well as a minor low-intensity, superimposed 
magnetization (samples B40I, B32H, B35A, B67D, and

comparison of the observed iron oxides and the 
magnetizations isolated in these samples (Table 5) suggests 
several correlations between magnetic mineral genesis and 
remanenee properties. 
Chromium-bearing magnetite is not a common magnetic 
phase in geologic materials and relatively little is known of its 
magnetic properties and their variations with composition. 
Robbins et al. [1971] demonstrated synthetic Cr spinels to be 
characterized by the molecular formula FeCr2_xFexO 4 (0 < x 
_< 2). The magnetic properties of this system (FeCr2-xFex04) 
vary among three compositional ranges: 0 < x < 0.68' 0,68 _< 
x _< 1.38; and 1.38 < x < 2.0. The compositions of low- 
chromian magnetite observed in the Stillwater gabbros lie 
mostly in the third region, where the Curie temperature 
decreases linearly with increasing Cr 3+ substitution from 
about 580øC (pure magnetite) to 380øC for clu'omian 
magnetite (x = 1.38)[Robbins et al., 1971, Figure lb]. The 
magnetic moment also decreases with increasing Cr 3+ from 4 
Bohr magnetons (pb) for pure magnetite to 3 pb for chromian 
magnetite (x = 1.38) [Robbins et al., 1971, Figure lc]. The 
magnetic properties of the ehromian magnetite observed in the 
Banded Series gabbros are comparable to low-Ti 
titanomagnetites, which have moderately reduced Curie 
temperatures and magnetic moments in comparison to pure 
magnetite.

Ages of Identified Magnetizations 
Direct observation of the characteristics of magnetic phases 
in samples with geologically stable (either primary or 
secondaT) NRM can provide information about the geologic 
h/story of the rock and facilitate correlation of magnetizations 
with specific geologic processes. By definition, primary NRM 
in igneous rocks must be carried by magnetic minerals formed 
during crystallization, or early alteration, at temperatures 
above the maximum blocking temperature and is acquired 
during temperature decrease over the blocking temperature 
range. Secondary NRM, of CRM origin, is often carried by 
phases whose magnetization was stabilized principally by 
grain growth, not by a decrease in thermal energy, below the 
maximum blocking temperature in a later geologic event. 
Bergh's [1968, 1970] \"primary\" magnetization is what we 
label the A magnetization and current work indicates that it is 
of dual polarity (J.W. Geissman, unpublished data, 1996). 
Rock magnetic studies show that plagioclases from samples 
with A magnetizations have Her > 65 mT (some Her > 100 
roT) and Mr/M s > 0.2, suggesting that the volumetrically 
dominant magnetite grains are in the pseudo-single-domain 
grain size range [Day et al., 1977]. However, the boundaries 
of the domain type fields on the Day's plot are also dependent 
on grain shape [Borradaile et al., 1993]. Magnetite needles 
observed in unaltered plagioclase areas have high two- 
dimensional aspect ratios indicating that they are single- 
domain grains [Evans and McElhinny, 1969]. The magnetite 
needles are generally either parallel or perpendicular to the 
(010) plane and inclusions grown in these two orientations 
have minimum interface energy [Fleet, !982]. The 
morphology (needle-shaped single crystal), chemical 
composition (pure iron oxide), and distinct orientations of 
these magnetite grains all are consistent with a high 
?rnperature subsolidus origin [McConnell, 1974]. The 
gneous origin and single domain nature of these magnetite 
needles are consistent with the interpretation that component A magnetizations are carried by magnetite needles and are 
pmary magnetizations acquired during initial cooling of the Stillwater complex at circa 2.710 Ga. Banded Series rocks 
whose NRM consists solely of the A magnetization have 
provided an internally consistent palcointensity determination for the late Archean, using the double Thellier thermal method 
(J.W. Geissman and C.J. Hale, manuscript in preparation, 
1996). 
The dominant carriers of the B and C magnetizations are 
anhedral Cr-magnetite grains introduced during hydrothermal 
alteration and local serpentinization of Banded Series rocks. 
These magnetizations are interpreted to be secondary and, in 
the absence of direct geochronologic data bearing on the age 
of these magnetizations, likely ages can only be proposed in 
the context of extant Precambrian paleomagnetic data from the 
Precambrian eraton of North America (i.e., Laurentia). The 
reliability of the comparison is severely hindered, because the 
oldest high-quality palcomagnetic data from the Wyoming 
Province, outside of, possibly, the A magnetization from the 
Stillwater complex, are from the circa 1.42 Ga Laramie 
Anorthosite/Sherman Granite [Harlan et al., 1994] emplaced 
in Archcan rocks of the Wyoming Province and 
Paleoproterozoic rocks stabilized along its southeast margin. 
The palcomagnetic record for the Wyoming Province prior to 
circa 1.42 Ga is nonexistent. The general agreement between 
the circa 1.42 Ga data from the Laramie Anorthosite/Sherman 
Granite and intrusions of similar age in the Superior and other 
provinces suggests that by this time the Wyoming Province 
was clearly stabilized with respect to other provinces of 
similar or older age. The Superior Province has yielded the 
majority of older Precambrian data for Laurentia. Although 
several workers argue that stabilization of the Wyoming 
relative to the Superior Province occurred earlier, in the 
Paleoproterozoic, there are no palcomagnetic data available to 
confn-m this. With these limitations in mind, we briefly 
review possible ages for the B and C magnetizations in the 
Stillwater Complex gabbros. 
We assume that both of these secondary magnetizations 
must be corrected for deformation related to Late Cretaceous 
to early Tertiary (Laramide) uplift of the Beartooth Mountains. 
Positive inclination B magnetizations, after correcting for 
moderate (50 ø to 70 ø ) north-northeast side down tilt are of 
shallow positive inclination and north declination. This 
direction is comparable to results from the well-studied circa 
2.45 Ga Matachewan dike swarm in the Superior Province 
[e.g., Halls, 1991] but too shallow in inclination compared to 
younger Paleoproterozoic results from the Superior Province 
[Buchan et al., 1994]. A possible interpreted age for 
acquisition of the B magnetization is the early 
Paleoproterozoic (2.3 to 2.5 Ga)and limited geochronologic 
data suggest that at least some of the numerous marie dikes 
that cut the Stillwater Complex were emplaced during this 
time period [Page, 1977]. 
The C magnetization, of southeast (or northwest) 
declination and shallow inclination, is corrected to a shallow 
negative to, more commonly, a moderate positive inclination 
and southeast declination (or antipode). Its palcomagnetic 
pole lies along either the descending (circa 1.85 Ga) or 
ascending (circa 1.70 Ga) ann of the Coronation loop in the 
Proterozoic apparent polar wander path for Laurentia [Irving, 
1979], derming Hudsonian events affecting Archean and 
Proterozoic rocks. We again emphasize that none of the data 
defining this loop were obtained from Wyoming Province 
rocks, so our correlation is subject to considerable uncertainty. 
Nonetheless, we note that limited geochronologic data also 
suggest that the time period between about 1.8 and 1.6 Ga 
was marked by marie dike emplacement in the Beartooth

Mountains [Page, 1977]. Elsewhere in southwest Montana, 
there is evidence for a tectonic event that led to local 
penetrative metamorphism and resetting of K-Ar and Rb-Sr 
mineral systems at circa 1.8 Ga [Gilletti, 1966; O'Neill et al., 
1988; Erslev and Sutter, 1990; Harlan et al., 1996]. We 
favor the reasonable interpretation that acquisition of the C 
magnetization was in response to marie dike emplacement 
and attending fluid mobilization. 
Correlation Between Magnetization Events 
Affecting the Stillwater Complex 
We propose distinct associations between (1) an interpreted 
primary magnetization in the Stillwater complex and Ti-free 
needle-shaped magnetite in unaltered plagioclase areas and 
(2) secondary magnetizations and anhedral Cr-magnetite as 
well as the absence of abundant Ti-free magnetite needles in 
cumulus plagioclase. The associations prompt important 
considerations concerning the retention of primary 
magnetizations in Banded Series rocks and the destruction of 
early formed magnetic phases in rocks with introduced 
secondary magnetic phases. In this context, any predictive 
measures of how to discriminate between marie intrusive 
rocks carrying exclusively primary magnetizations and those 
that have been remagnetized in one form or another would be 
useful for paleomagnetic studies of such rocks. 
The source for the chromium in secondary, anhedraI 
magnetite is most likely the peridotitc member of the 
Ultramarie Series, where essentially all of the cumulus 
chromite occurs [Jackson, 1961, 1963]. Beenson and 
Jackson [ 1969] noted that chromite in the peridotitc member 
has been pervasively altered, with a major alteration product 
low-chromian magnetite (Fe.*Mg0.J [ Vea.,Cr0.2, Alo.04 J O 4 
identical in composition to the Cr-magnetite observed in 
remagnetized Banded Series marie rocks (Table 3). Iron and 
chromium were likely transported by hydrothermal fluids from 
the Ultramarie Series rocks during serpentinization. 
Regardless of the source of the chromium in secondary 
magnetite in Banded Series rocks, our observations show an 
abundance of' fractures along which fluids penetrated the 
remagnetized rocks containing secondary oxides (Figures 5e, 
5f, and 7g). 
Concerning the presence of magnetite needles, recognized 
in unaltered parts of cumulus plagioe!ase, we speculate that 
their absence requires a process by which they were destroyed 
in samples now characterized by secondary magnetizations. 
This argmnent, again, assumes that magnetite needles in 
cumulus plagioelase were acquired early in the crystallization 
history of Banded Series rocks. The timing of magnetite 
growth in plagioelases in emulate and other marie rocks, in 
relationship to remanenee properties, has been the subject of 
some investigation [e.g.,Halls and œalmer, 1990; Zhang and 
Halls, 1995]. In marie dikes of the Kapuskasing area, north 
central Ontario, Halls and ]>abner [1990] noted a correlation 
between elouding of plagioclase and depth of emplacement. 
Although the likely phases responsible for darkening of 
plagioclase were never investigated at high resolution, Halls 
and Palmer [1990] attributed the clouding to \"minute 
inclusions of spinel, magnetite, or other minerals\" and argued 
that the degree of ½1ouding was related to the depth of 
emplacement of the dikes and attending alteration at deep, 
upper amphibolite to granu!ite grade, crustal levels. The 
Stillwater Complex was emplaced at a relatively shallow 
crustal depth. A 2 to 3 kbar total pressure estimate for pelitic 
hornfels rocks at the base of the complex, as summarized by Geissrnan and Mogk [1986] is consistent with magmatie 
fractionation patterns suggesting a shallow level of 
emplacement [McCallurn et al., 1980]. Banded Series rocks 
were probably no deeper than 10 km at the time of 
crystallization, and thus there is no compelling reason to 
correlate growth of fine magnetite needles in cumulus 
plagioclase with subsequent alteration at moderate to deep crustal levels. The relatively minor fluid interaction in 
Banded Series rocks led to alteration of presumably early 
formed oxides to chlorite and zoisite (Figures 7a and 7b). 
Destruction of early formed magnetite needles was a relatively 
subtle process in terms of fluid/rock interactions, because 
cumulus plagioclase grains in remagnetized rocks are largely 
unaltered and there does not appear to be any correlation 
between the presence of secondary magnetizations and 
significant modification to the oxygen isotope systematics 0f 
cumulus plagioclase grains. Parts of cumulus plagio½lase 
grains located in areas with few fractures escaped 
hydrothermal alteration and thus preserve the primary 
magnetization carried by magnetite needles. However, we 
cannot rule out the possibility that primary magnetite needles 
were absent when the plagioclase crystallized in some rocks.

The Amazonian Craton represents an important piece in the Paleoproterozoic paleogeography of the
Earth. This study presents paleomagnetic data obtained on well-dated (U–Pb) 1790 Ma mafic sills from
the Avanavero magmatism in northern Amazonian Craton (Guiana Shield). AF and thermal treatments
revealed southeastern, low downward/upward inclination, remanent magnetization directions that are
carried by moderate to high-Hcand high-TBTi-poor titanomagnetite. The site mean directions cluster
around the mean Dm= 138.2◦, Im= −3.4◦(N = 13, ˛ 95= 13.0◦), which yields a robust paleomagnetic pole
(AV pole) at 27.9◦E, 48.4◦S (A95= 9.6◦) with a Q-value of 5. The characteristic component disclosed for the
Avanavero sill matches that obtained for sediments collected along the baked contact and are distinct from
those away from the sill. The Avanavero directions are also significantly different from those obtained for
younger units, with ages spanning from 1420 to 520 Ma, suggesting the sills carry a primary remanence.
The Avanavero pole helps in constraining the paleogeography of the central pieces of Columbia. It is
compatible with the Baltica and Amazonian Cratons SAMBA link in the Columbia Supercontinent at about
1780 Ma, but other configurations are also possible. When compared to other Paleo- to Mesoproterozoic
paleomagnetic poles from the southern Amazonian Craton (Central Brazil Shield), our new paleomagnetic
pole suggests intracratonic motions within the southern area of the Craton, probably after 1420 Ma ago.
We tentatively suggest that these movements are related to the collision of the Paraguá Block with the
proto-Amazonian Craton at about 1350–1320 Ma ago.

1. Introduction
The paleogeography of Proterozoic supercontinents is still con-
troversial because of the difficulties and uncertainties that arise
when someone compares the geological and geophysical record
of continental fragments that once have come together to form
them (Pesonen et al., 2003). Nevertheless, it is believed that at least
twice in the Proterozoic continents assembled to form superconti-
nents (Hossain et al., 2007): at ca. 1850 Ma ago with the Columbia
Supercontinent (e.g., Rogers, 1996; Rogers and Santosh, 2002; Zhao
et al., 2004, 2006, 2008; Meert, 2012; Kusky et al., 2007; Johansson,
2009; Yakubchuk, 2010), and at ca. 1100–1000 Ma with the Rodinia
supercontinent (e.g., Hoffman, 1991; Dalziel, 1997; Weil et al.,
1998; D’Agrella-Filho et al., 1998; Pesonen et al., 2003; Li et al.,
2008; Evans, 2009).

Geological setting
The Amazonian Craton (Fig. 1a) is one of the largest stable
cratonic areas in the world (430,000 km2). It is exposed in two
large areas separated by the Phanerozoic Amazonian sedimentary
basin comprising the northern Guiana Shield and the south-
ern Central-Brazil or Guaporé Shield (Lacerda-Filho et al., 2004;
Schobbenhaus et al., 1984; Santos et al., 2000). Its northeastern
part consists of two Archean nuclei (>2600 Ma – Central Amazo-
nian Province in Fig. 1a) encircled by a predominantly accretionary
Paleoproterozoic belt (2250–2050 Ma) which form the Maroni-
Itacaiúnas Province (Tassinari and Macambira, 1999; Tassinari
et al., 2000). The southwestern part of this Archean nucleus
was accreted by subduction-related juvenile magmatic arcs form-
ing the 1980–1810 Ma Ventuari-Tapajós, and the 1780–1600 Ma
Rio Negro-Juruena Provinces (Tassinari et al., 2000; Pinho et al.,
2003; Schobbenhaus and Brito-Neves, 2003; Cordani and Teixeira,
2007). In the Mesoproterozoic, subduction-related magmatic arcs
of the 1600–1300 Ma Jauru Terrane in the Central-Brazil Shield
(Rondonian-San Ignacio Province) developed until the final colli-
sion of the Paraguá Terrane at ca. 1320 Ma (Bettencourt et al., 2010).
This collisional model was recently extended to the northwest
with the recognition of the Trincheira ophiolite by Rizzotto and
Hartmann (2012). These authors interpret these rocks as a record
of oceanic crust relics associated with the collision of the Paraguá
Block with the proto-Amazonian Craton along the Alto Guaporé
Belt at the Middle Mesoproterozoic (Fig. 1b). In this geotectonic

scenario the E-W 1100–1000 Ma Nova Brasilândia belt (NBB)
located between the proto-Amazonian Craton and the Paraguá
block, and once interpreted as a suture zone between these two
cratonic blocks (Tohver et al., 2004), most probably represents
intracratonic reactivations occurred during the development of the
Greenvile-type 1200–950 Ma Sunsás-Aguapeí Belt (e.g., Teixeira
et al., 2010). Similar 1420 Ma paleomagnetic poles obtained for
the Nova Guarita dykes and the Indiavaí intrusive, whose areas are
located on opposite sides of the NBB, corroborate this intracratonic
interpretation (D’Agrella-Filho et al., 2012).
The study area is located in the Central Amazonian Province
(CAP; Fig. 1a), which is composed of Archaean continental crust
(>2600 Ma) affected by significant Paleoproterozoic magmatic
events. The study area is part of a CAP domain known as Roraima
Block. This block is completely covered by the 1980–1960 Ma
Surumu acid volcanic rocks and the overlying ca. 1870 Ma sedi-
mentary sequences of the Roraima Supergroup, that includes the
basal Arai Formation, the Suapi Group and the Uaimapué Formation
at the top (Fig. 1c) (Teixeira et al., 1989; Tassinari and Macambira,
1999; Santos et al., 2003). The Roraima basin is possibly related to
a N-S extensional event, responsible for the development of nor-
mal E-W faults and transference faults. It has been interpreted as
an intracontinental type basin with regional rhombohedral geom-
etry controlled by NW-SE system faults. Later, during the K’Mudku
Episode around 1.2 Ga the basin experienced a weak positive inver-
sion involving the reactivation of normal upthrow faults, where
the transfer faults worked as lateral ramps. At the southern border
of the basin along the Brazilian side, in the proximity of the E-W
faults, the Roraima Supergroup was affected by en echelon folds.
Towards the center of the basin, no deformation was recorded in
these rock units, suggesting their primary stratigraphic relation-
ships were preserved (Reis et al., 2012).
Mafic sills and dykes of the Avanavero magmatic event intruded
into the volcanic and sedimentary formations of the Surumu Group
and the Roraima Supergroup (Brito Neves, 2011; Reis et al., 2010,
2013). The Avanavero magmatism extends to the surrounding
countries of Venezuela, Guyana and Suriname, and forms a large
igneous province (LIP). The sills follow the original structures of the
Roraima sedimentary rocks, i.e., their bedding planes. In the study
area these structural planes have northwest-southeast strikes and
dip to northeast between 5◦ and 20◦ (Fig. 1c). Groeneweg and
Bosma (1969) were the first to use the name Avanavero to des-
ignate dolerite dykes and large irregular sheet-shaped bodies in
the Avanavero area and other locations in Suriname. In Brazil, this
Proterozoic basic magmatism comprises four levels of sills that are
informally called Cotingo, Camararém, Paiuá and Pedra Preta sills
(Pinheiro et al., 1990). The Cotingo sill intrudes the Surumu volcanic
rocks. It is about 140 km long and 40 m thick and strikes WNW-
ESE. A small sill near the contact between the Surumu volcanics
and the Arai sandstones is known as Camararém sill. It extends
northwards to the Guyanas where it is known as Tumatumari sill.
Sill Camararém is 30 meters thick and follows the orientation of
the host sedimentary rocks dipping 20◦ to northeast (see Fig. 1c).
Paiuá sill is 20 m thick. It cuts quartz sandstones at the first 200
meters of the Arai Formation and dips ca. 15◦to the northeast (see
Fig. 1c). Finally, the Pedra Preta sill cuts across the Suapi Group,
where siltstones near the contact with the mafic rock were horn-
felsed (Pinheiro et al., 1990). A thickness of about 250 meters is
estimated for this sill that shows a gentle dip of around 12◦to the
northeast (Fig. 1c). Basic dykes associated with major faults (NE
and NW trends) in the Roraima Supergroup are interpreted as the
feeders of the poorly differentiated Avanavero dolerite sills. Meso-
zoic basic dykes associated with major mainly NE faults cut all the
Proterozoic rocks (Reis et al., 2004).
The Avanavero rocks comprise dark-gray medium to coarse
grained dolerites and gabbros, and subordinately by
and

micro-quartz diorites (Reis et al., 2013). Under the micro-
scope they are composed of plagioclase, pyroxene and amphibole,
with magnetite and ilmenite as accessory minerals. Late hydro-
thermal processes are common, such as alteration of plagioclase
to clay minerals and/or albite (Pinheiro et al., 1990). Dolerite dykes
show generally subophitic texture, and are composed of plagio-
clase (labradorite), pyroxene (augite and occasionally pigeonite),
hornblende and chlorite. Sericite and epidote appear as accessory
minerals (Reis et al., 2013).
U–Pb ages in baddeleyite were obtained for several dolerite
dykes and sills of the Avanavero magmatic suite. These comprise
ages of 1794 ± 4 Ma for a dolerite intrusive into the Omai gold
deposit in Guyana (Norcross et al., 2000), a 1787 ± 14 Ma age for the
Cipó dolerite and a 1782 ± 3 Ma age for the Cotingo dolerite (Santos
et al., 2003). Similar ages were also obtained for correlative mafic
intrusions in Pará and Amazonas Brazilian States, located several
hundreds of kilometers south of the studied area. They comprise a
1780 ± 7 Ma age for the Crepori sill in southwest Pará State, and a
1780 ± 3 Ma age for the Quarenta Ilhas sill in northeast Amazonas
State (Santos et al., 2002). Recently, Reis et al. (2013) presented two
new U–Pb baddeleyite ages for Avanavero rocks: a 1795 ± 2 Ma age
for the Pedra Preta sill, and a 1793 ± 2 Ma age for a dolerite sill cross-
cutting the Urupi Formation (Central-Brazil Shield), whose rocks
have been correlated with those from the Roraima Supergroup. A
mean age of 1788.5 ± 2.5 Ma was calculated from all U–Pb ages and
is assumed to be the best age estimate for the Avanavero magmatic
event. Besides,40Ar–39Ar analysis on biotite of a dolerite located
in Guyana yielded an integrated age of 1798 ± 2 Ma (Onstott et al.,
1984) that is in agreement with the U–Pb ages dataset. This age and
the fact that the Arai Group show only anchimetamorphic mineral
assemblages are strong evidence that the region was not submitted
to temperatures higher than 300◦C after the emplacement of the
Avanavero sills.
3. Sampling and methods
Paleomagnetic sampling was performed around the small vil-
lage of Uiramutã at the northern Roraima State (Brazil) where 118
standard oriented cylindrical cores were taken from 19 sites of four
well-exposed sills (Cotingo, Camararém, Paiuá and Pedra Preta)
from the Avanavero suite (Fig. 1, Table 1). From the Pedra Preta
sill, estimated to be 250 m thick, we sampled 7 sites (#1 to #5,
#18, #19 in Table 1 and Fig. 1) at different levels of the sill. Three
sites (#6, #7 and #8) were sampled from the Paiuá sill, estimated
to be 20 m thick. Four sites were sampled from the Camararém sill,
estimated to be 30 m thick, and five sites (#13 to #17) from the ca.
40 m thick Cotingo sill. Samples were oriented using both sun and
magnetic compasses. A baked contact test was attempted at site
#6 at the border of the Paiuá sill with host sandstones (Fig. 2). At
this point, the Paiuá sill is covered by six meters of sandstones dip-
ping 15◦to the northeast. In addition to the 8 cylinders collected in
the sill, we have sampled six oriented cores from the sediments at
the following distances from the contact: 300 cm (FR11-I), 326 cm
(FR11-J), 366 cm (FR11-K), and 516 cm (FR11-L, FR11-M, FR11-N)
(Fig. 2).
At the laboratory, cylindrical cores were cut into 2.2 cm height
specimens. Step-wise alternating magnetic field (AF) and thermal
demagnetization techniques were employed to separate the char-
acteristic remanent magnetization (ChRM) component carried by
the samples. Steps of 2.5 mT (up to 15 mT) and 5 mT (15–100 mT)
were employed for AF demagnetization using a 2-axis tumbler Mol-
spin AF demagnetizer. Thermal demagnetization was performed
using a Magnetic Measurements TD-60 furnace in steps of 50◦C
(from 150◦C up to 500◦C) and 20◦C (from 500◦C up to 600◦C).

5. Magnetic mineralogy
Under alternating magnetic field (AF) treatment all samples pre-
sented mean destructive fields of less than 20 mT, but two distinct
coercivity distributions can be observed: (i) for some samples the
intensity of magnetization falls to less than 5% of the NRM before
20 mT demagnetization (samples FR11-C2 and FR145-A4 in Fig. 5a),
whereas (ii) other samples preserve more than ∼10% of the total
intensity at fields as high as 100 mT (samples FR4-F2 and FR1-D3 in
Fig. 5a). The low-coercivity magnetic grains are usually associated
with secondary components, while moderate and high coercivity
magnetic grains represent the ChRM isolated in the samples. Ther-
mal demagnetization showed two types of unblocking temperature
spectra: (i) a more common discrete spectrum, where unblock-
ing temperatures are limited to the range between 500–550◦C and
600◦C (samples FR2-B5, FR3-D2 and FR88-E1 in Fig. 5b) and (ii) a
distributed spectrum, where it is possible to distinguish two wide
ranges of unblocking temperatures between 0◦C and 450–500◦C
and between 500◦C and 600◦C (sample FR85-C4 in Fig. 5b). The
characteristic remanent magnetization (ChRM) is normally associ-
ated with the highest unblocking temperatures, whose magnetic
carriers are represented by Ti-poor titanomagnetite, as shown by
the decay intensity curves.
Isothermal remanent magnetization (IRM) acquisition curves
for all samples are very similar, giving saturation fields of less than
300–400 mT (Fig. 5c). These coercivities are typical of magnetite or
titanomagnetite minerals. Narrow-waisted hysteresis curves were
obtained for samples from all sites, giving coercivities between
4.3 mT and 24.9 mT, also typical of (titano)magnetite grains. In the
Day’s plot (Day et al., 1977, modified after Dunlop, 2002) most
samples fall into the pseudo-single domain (PSD) field, or along
a trend parallel to the theoretical SD/MD mixing curves of Dunlop
(2002) (Fig. 5d). This is consistent with the stable ChRM directions
disclosed by thermal and AF treatment.
Both reversible and irreversible high-temperature (20–700◦C)
thermomagnetic curves were obtained, most of them with a pro-
nounced Hopkinson peak and a strong decay in susceptibility at
around ∼580◦C (Fig. 5e and f). Low-temperature thermomagnetic
curves show a susceptibility peak at around −150◦C denoting
the Verwey transition. These characteristics are typical of low-
Ti titanomagnetite grains (Dunlop and Ozdemir, 1997), which
are the main magnetic carriers of ChRM direction in the studied
rocks.
6. Petrography
Petrographic analyses were performed in samples with consis-
tent ChRM directions and also in samples showing unstable
inconsistent

directions. Mineralogical compositions and textures
observed in thin and polished sections for samples with differ-
ent magnetic behavior typically show differences that may explain
their contrasting paleomagnetic results.
Samples with stable magnetization show subophitic textures,
consisting predominantly of plagioclase (ca. 50–55%), augite
(35–40%), biotite (2–5%), opaque minerals (2–5%), hornblende (<
1%) and epidote (< 1%). Some samples (FR4-F1, FR5-G1, FR85-B1,
FR144-C3, and FR145-A1) show hornblende rims replacing augite,
and occasionally myrmekite (samples FR1-B1 and FR4-F1). In pol-
ished section, the preserved euhedral magnetite crystals (Fig. 6A
and B) are interpreted as the carriers of the ChRM. Minor quantities
of hematite and martite (Fig. 6C) are present and probably result
from late magmatic oxidation, but do not contribute significantly
as remanence carriers of the ChRM. Occasionally, anhedral crystals
of magnetite or hematite are observed as intergranular growths.
Locally, magnetite grains present fine ilmenite lamellae, diagnos-
tic of high-temperature oxidation-exsolution processes (Fig. 6B).
Magnetite is rarely observed in thin-sections of samples FR143-A1,
FR144-C3, and FR145-A1, although it is the main magnetic carrier
of the ChRM direction.
Samples with unstable magnetization consist predominantly
of plagioclase (ca. 50–55%), hornblende (10–20%), augite (0–20%),
quartz (0–10%), biotite (5–10%), and opaque minerals (5–10%). Thin
and polished sections indicate features typical of hydrothermal
processes, such as hornblende appearing as alteration rims in augite
crystals or in opaque minerals such as hematite (Fig. 6D). More-
over, a higher percentage of myrmekitic textures is observed in
these samples. Opaque mineral are predominantly hematite, mar-
tite, and locally preserved magnetite (Fig. 6E). Corrosion features
(Fig. 6D) are frequent in these samples, which could be the result
of dissolution of (or substitution by) new minerals (hornblende
or biotite). Martite crystals present patches or venules of thick
ilmenite (Fig. 6F).
In addition to the mafic intrusions, we have also examined thin-
sections from the host sandstones close and away of the baked
contact in site #6. Close to the contact the sandstones show mag-
netite crystals with skeleton forms (Fig. 7A), sometimes partially
replaced by martite (Fig. 7B). Away from the contact, martite replac-
ing magnetite grains and hematite as cement are more frequent
(Fig. 7C and D).

8. Discussion
8.1. The Avanavero paleomagnetic pole
Stable southeastern directions with low downward and upward
inclinations (AV component) were disclosed in samples from the
Avanavero sills. Magnetic experiments indicate that pseudo-single
domain magnetite grains with moderate to high coercivities and

mochronology described above together with the fact that the
Avanavero pole does not match younger poles for the region, sug-

Since only four sills were sampled a question arises if sec-
ular variation was eliminated. The angular dispersion (s = 18.2◦)
obtained in the Avanavero collection is compatible with an ade-
quate sampling of geomagnetic secular variation. However, this
dispersion may be related to later tilting that affected the sills.
The intracratonic ca. 1200 Ma K’Mudku tectonic event affected the
area to the SE of the Avanavero event (Cordani et al., 2010). It
is considered to have been developed under low (to moderate)
temperature conditions, and follows pre-existing E-W to NE-SW
structural features that affected the country rocks at Paleoprotero-
zoic times (Fraga et al., 2009). In spite of its regional importance
in central Amazonia, this event did not affect the studied sills.

the only possible way that site mean directions express the record
of secular variation is to assume relatively slow cooling rates for
the sills. The cooling rate of magmatic rocks depends of various

the temperature contrast to the host rock. Simple thermal conduc-
tion models provide crude estimations on the time of cooling of
igneous intrusions (Jaeger, 1968). It depends on the square of the
half-tickness of the intrusion. For the Avanavero sills, the complete
cooling of the intrusions considering their thickness would be of
∼100 years for Paiuá, Camararém and Cotingo, and 5000 years for
Pedra Preta. It is worth noting that each sill has intruded at different
depths into the sedimentary succession, along more than 900 m of
stratigraphic thickness implying different cooling rates and in con-
sequence different remanence blocking times. From the 13 sites
included in the Avanavero mean direction, seven are from the Pedra
Preta sill, four are from the Cotingo sill, one is from the Camararem
sill and one is from the Paiuá sill. The Pedra Preta sill, which con-
centrates most of the sampling sites, is the uppermost sill in the
stratigraphy (see schematic profile in Fig. 1). Such a large intrusive
rock would take at least thousands of years to cool. This is coherent
with the medium to coarse grain sizes of the Avanavero rocks (dia-
bases up to gabbros) as described above. Although the other sills
are thinner they intruded different levels in the stratigraphy and
likely record the field at different times. In this way, we believe site
mean directions shown in Fig. 4 represent records of paleosecular
variation which was averaged out in the general mean.
The Avanavero pole (AV: 27.9◦E, 48.4◦S, N = 13, A = 95 9.6◦,
K = 19.6) satisfies 5 out of the 7 quality criteria proposed by Van
der Voo (1990) as follows: (1) U–Pb dating on dolerites from sev-
eral sills and dykes yielded well-defined and concordant ages, with
a mean of 1788.5 ± 2.5 Ma, which likely represent the age of magne-
tization acquisition; (2) the AV pole was derived from a set of 153
specimens (13 sites) and has adequate Fisher’s statistical param-
eters (A = 95 9.6◦, K = 19.8); (3) remanence vectors were isolated by
least-squares fit from orthogonal diagrams (Kirschvink, 1980) after
stepwise AF and thermal demagnetization; (5) the Avanavero rocks
in the investigated area are situated in the Archean Amazonia-
Central Province, which remained stable during the
of

the Ventuari-Tapajós (1980–1810 Ma) and Rio Negro-Juruena
(1780–1550 Ma) provinces, and the ca. 1200 Ma K’Mudku event
seemed to have only slightly affected the Avanavero rocks at its
southern border; (7) similar directions are not found in young units
from the same region or cratonic block. Two criteria were not sat-
isfied: (4) the baked contact test is not complete since we cannot
prove that the direction found in the host rock far from the con-
tact is primary or older than that of the intrusion; and (6) only a
single polarity was found for these rocks. In sum, the Avanavero
pole (AV) may be regarded as a robust pole (Q = 5), and as such it
can be used to constrain the paleogeographic position of the proto-
Amazonian Craton at ∼1789 Ma and test the paleogeography of the
proto-Amazonian Craton in the Columbia Supercontinent.
8.2. SAMBA connection and Laurentia in Columbia
A paleomagnetic based reconstruction of the Columbia Super-
continent at ∼1780 Ma was presented by Bispo-Santos et al.
(2008). In their reconstruction Laurentia, Baltica, North China and
Amazonian Craton were laterally disposed along a Paleo- to Meso-
proterozoic subduction-related mobile belt at the western side
of the supercontinent (Fig. 10a). The position of the Amazonian
Craton in that reconstruction was constrained by the 1780 Ma
Colíder Group paleomagnetic pole. Recently, D’Agrella-Filho et al.
(2012), interpreting new paleomagnetic data from the 1416 Ma
Indiavaí mafic intrusive, proposed a very similar configuration
(Fig. 10b), but which incorporated rotations within Baltica. In
their model, Sarmatia (together with Amazonia and West Africa)
were rotated 43◦ counterclockwise about an Euler pole at 48◦N,
42.2◦E relative to the Fennoscandia/Volgo-Uralia block following
Bogdanova et al. (2008) and Elming et al. (2010). In their interpre-
tation, D’Agrella-Filho et al. (2012) placed the North China block
between Fennoscandia and Amazonian Craton, but suggested a
triple junction between Fennoscandia/Sarmatia, North China and

of SAMBA after Johansson (2009), in a paleogeography of Columbia
where Laurentia, Baltica, Amazonia and West Africa Cratons formed
a great continental mass, which remained together for 500 Ma,

Four paleomagnetic poles are presently available for Baltica
in the time interval between 1790 Ma and 1750 Ma (Table 2):
the Ropruchey sill (Fedotova et al., 1999), the Shoksha Formation
(Pisarevsky and Sokolov, 2001), the Hoting Gabbro (Elming et al.,
2009) and the Småland Intrusive (Pisarevsky and Bylund, 2010). A
U–Pb zircon age of 1786 ± 10 Ma is attributed to the Hoting Gabbro
but younger 1650–1610 Ma 40Ar–39Ar biotite ages for the same
rocks bring some uncertainties concerning the age of the Hoting
pole. Until recently the Ropruchey sill’s pole was constrained by
a U–Pb zircon age of 1770 ± 12 Ma (Fedotova et al., 1999) but a
precise baddeleyite age of 1751 ± 3 Ma recently obtained for these
rocks suggests a younger age for it (Lubnina et al., 2012). This is
consistent with the fact that this pole differs by some degrees
from the 1784–1769 Ma Småland Intrusions pole (Pisarevsky and
Bylund, 2010). The age of the Shoksha pole is constrained between
1800 Ma using a glauconite K–Ar age for the underlying Petroza-
vodsk Formation and the 1751 ± 3 Ma age of the Ropruchey sill that
cuts the Shoksha Formation. The agreement between the Shoksha
(BA-3) and Hoting (BA-4) poles with the well-dated Ropruchey sill
pole (BA-2) (Fig. 11, Table 2) strongly suggests these three poles
represent the Baltica position at about 1750 Ma ago. These poles
also agree (within error) with the Laurentian 1750 Ma pole, a mean
of nineteen post-Hudsonian poles with ages between 1760 and
1740 Ma calculated by Irving and colleagues (2004) (LA-1 in Fig. 11
and Table 2). In the Baltica/Amazonian Craton reconstruction pro-
posed here, the older 1784–1769 Ma Småland Intrusions pole (BA-1
in Fig. 11) matches within error the ca. 1790 Ma Avanavero pole
(AC-1) corroborating the SAMBA connection of Johansson (2009).
A similar Laurentia/Baltica/Amazonia configuration was also
recently proposed by Mertanen and Pesonen (2012) based on
1530 Ma paleomagnetic poles from Laurentia, Baltica and Ama-
zonian cratons. Although paleomagnetic data for West Africa
for this time interval is actually absent, geological evidence and
older 2100–1970 Ma paleomagnetic data corroborate the Amazo-
nia/West Africa link shown in Fig. 11 (Onstott et al., 1984; Nomade
et al., 2003; Evans and Mitchell, 2011; Bispo-Santos et al., 2014).
This great continental mass was probably the core of the Columbia
Supercontinent (Salminen and Pesonen, 2007). Its western margin,
formed by the contiguous Laurentia, Baltica and proto-Amazonian
craton, was the scenario of coeval Andine-type, subduction-related
accretionary mobile belts during Paleo- to Mesoproterozoic, which
formed the Yavapai-Mazatzal-Labradorian (1800–1400 Ma) in

8.3. Avanavero pole versus Colíder Group pole
The Baltica/Amazonia link in the Columbia Supercontinent pro-

were only partially affected by the ca. 1200 Ma K’Mudku event
at its southern part (Cordani et al., 2010). As stressed above, the

Avanavero ChRM direction is likely a primary thermo-remanent
component. Meanwhile the 1790 Ma Colíder Group pole was
obtained for felsic rocks from southern Amazonian Craton, where
NW-SE magmatic arcs (forming the Jauru Terrane) were in progress
up to 1.32 Ga, with the final collision of the Paraguá Terrane
(Bettencourt et al., 2010). No field tests were performed for the
Colíder Group because of poor outcropping conditions. An easy
interpretation is that the Colíder magnetization represents a sec-
ondary component, and it cannot constrain the position of the
Amazonian Craton at 1790 Ma ago. In this case the SAMBA model
of Johansson (2009) could have prevailed at 1790–1780 Ma as indi-
cated by the Avanavero pole.
Alternatively, the Colíder Group pole could also represent
a primary magnetization. Its stable, high-coercivity and high-
unblocking temperature ChRM component seems to be carried
by primary magnetite and/or hematite (Bispo-Santos et al., 2008).
If both Avanavero and Colíder Group poles represent primary
magnetizations acquired at about 1790 Ma, then relative tectonic
movements must have occurred between the northern Avanavero
area and the southern Colíder area after 1790 Ma. Fig. 12a shows the
Avanavero and Colíder Group poles and the Amazonian Craton in
its present position. The Colíder Group pole is located to the west of
the Avanavero pole, and a rotation of 47.7◦of the Colíder Group pole
about an Euler pole at 23.8◦N, 327.6◦E (Fig. 12a), brings both poles
together. Approximately NW dextral strike-slip motions between
the northern Avanavero area relative to the southern Colíder area
could explain the different positions of these poles (Fig. 12b).
The Mesoproterozoic (ca. 1420 Ma) Nova Guarita (Bispo-Santos
et al., 2012) and Indiavaí (D’Agrella-Filho et al., 2012) poles from
southern Amazonian Craton are also plotted to the west of the
1460–1420 Ma poles from Baltica and Laurentia in the SAMBA
model (Johansson, 2009) (Table 3, Fig. 12c). This suggests that most
of these movements, if they occurred, must have happened after
1420 Ma ago.
The recent recognition of the Trincheira ophiolite (see topic 2) at
the southwestern edge of the Amazonian block suggests the dock-
ing of the Paraguá block to the proto-Amazonian craton along the
Alto Guaporé Belt to have occurred at the Middle Mesoproterozoic,
between ∼1470 and 1320 Ma (Bettencourt et al., 2010; Rizzotto
and Hartmann, 2012). NW-SE lineaments (the Buiuc¸ u shear zone)
are observed to the east of the Trincheira ophiolite, their
rocks
mylonitic
being dated at 1466.5 ± 1.4 Ma (Ar–Ar in muscovite) and
1467.8 ± 0.8 Ma (Ar–Ar in sericite). These shear zones are inter-
preted as a result of the Rondonian-San Ignacio Orogeny (Almeida
et al., 2012), which culminated with the Paraguá block collision.
We speculate that if both paleomagnetic poles result from pri-
mary directions, reactivations of these faults can be, at least in
part, responsible for the NW-SE dextral movements implied by the
available paleomagnetic data.
9. Conclusions
This study presents paleomagnetic data performed on mafic
sills from Avanavero magmatism, northern Roraima State (north-
ern Amazonian Craton), with a mean age of 1788.5 ± 2.5 Ma (U–Pb,
zircon). AF and thermal treatments revealed southeastern direc-
tions with downward/upward inclinations, carried by moderate
to high-Hc and high-unblocking temperatures Ti-poor titanomag-
netite/magnetite. Directions obtained from the host rocks close
to the intrusion match the ones disclosed for the sills. Directions
obtained in sandstones far from the intrusions are different. But
we cannot claim for a positive baked contact test because the
directions of the host sedimentary rocks away from the contact
can result from a much younger remagnetization. The calculated mean direction (Dm= 138.2◦; Im= −3.4◦; N = 13, ˛ =
95
13.0◦) for the
Avanavero sills, yielded the paleomagnetic pole (AV pole) at 27.9◦E,
48.4◦S (A =
95
9.6◦), which can be classified with a reliable factor
Q = 5. The presently available Paleoproterozoic paleomagnetic poles
corroborate the SAMBA model of Johansson (2009), with a nearly
equatorial Columbia Supercontinent being formed by Laurentia,
Baltica, proto-Amazonian Craton and West Africa, although other
configurations are also possible (e.g., Pisarevsky et al., 2014).

A new paleomagnetic study was carried out on 15 sites of the Sierra de las Ánimas complex, exposed in
SE
 Uruguay. A paleomagnetic remanence was isolated at six sites, and this direction is likely to be pre-
tectonic
 and primary. Mean directions from ﬁve of these sites are consistent with the SA2 paleomagnetic
pole,
 which is based on a previous paleomagnetic study of the complex. A new paleomagnetic pole
was
 computed for compiled results from the Sierra de las Ánimas complex (SAn, 12.2◦ S, 258.9◦ E, A95:
14.9◦). A geochronological study based on U/Pb (SHRIMP) dating of magmatic zircons was also carried
out
 on three samples of the Sierra de las Animas Complex, yielding a grand mean age of 578 ± 4 Ma.
The

1. Introduction
The late Proterozoic chronology of the fragmentation of Rodinia
and the assembly of Gondwana is poorly constrained (e.g. Li et al.,
2008; Murphy et al., 2013). Reliable paleomagnetic data on accu-
rately dated rocks are essential to reconstruct the paleogeographic

evolution of the different cratonic blocks. The relevant time period
should encompass the entire period over which Rodinia disinte-
grated and Gondwana formed, from around 800 up to 500 Ma. The
Río de la Plata craton (RP, Fig. 1) is a relatively small crustal block
with Paleoproterozoic (and very minor Archean) basement, that
forms the southernmost cratonic unit of South America (Dalla Salda
et al., 1988; Cingolani and Dalla Salda, 2000; Cordani et al., 2000;
Rapela et al., 2007, 2011; Bossi and Cingolani, 2009). The paleogeo-
graphic position of the Rio de la Plata craton over the 800–500 Ma
interval is poorly known. Some workers favor a close proximity of

the Rio de la Plata craton to Amazonia, and therefore to Eastern Lau-
rentia (e.g. Weil et al., 1998; Meert, 2001; Collins and Pisarevsky,
2005; Li et al., 2008; Gaucher et al., 2011), though no conclusive
geologic evidence supports that reconstruction. In contrast, several
geological studies (e.g. Campos Neto, 2000; Tohver et al., 2012) have
shown that the Rio de la Plata was surrounded by several Neopro-
terozoic oceanic domains that were closed by the end of that era,
and might have never been part of Rodinia (Kröner and Cordani,
2003; Tohver et al., 2006; Rapela et al., 2007).
A review of the available Neoproterozoic paleomagnetic data
from the Rio de la Plata craton suggests that this block was not con-
nected to Eastern Laurentia in the Ediacaran (Rapalini et al., 2013).
These authors deﬁned an apparent polar wander path (APWP) for
the Río de la Plata craton from around 600 to 500 Ma based on
eleven paleomagnetic poles. This APWP is marred by known uncer-
tainties: some of these poles should be regarded as mean virtual
geomagnetic poles due to low number of sites or samples, and some
of the poles are based on remagnetizations, the age of which is
inferred from the pole position, while other poles show poor conﬁ-
dence ovals and/or age uncertainties. Despite the progress made in
the last decade, a more robust APWP for the Rio de la Plata craton
is clearly needed.
The Sierra de las Ánimas Magmatic Complex, exposed in SE
Uruguay, provided the ﬁrst late Neoproterozoic to early Paleo-
zoic paleomagnetic results for the Río de La Plata craton (Sánchez
Bettucci and Rapalini, 2002). Two paleomagnetic poles (SA1 and
SA2) were calculated from this complex with assigned ages to
these poles of ca. 520 and 550 Ma, respectively. This interpreta-
tion indicates either long-lived magmatism (over 30 Ma) or two
discrete magmatic events, one in the Ediacaran (SA2) and one in
the Cambrian (SA1). However, in the absence of precise geochrono-
logical determinations for these rocks, these age assignments are
weakly constrained and inferential. More recently, Oyhantc¸ abal
et al. (2007) reported a well-behaved, 40Ar/39Ar plateau age of
579 ± 2 Ma for hornblende from the Pan de Azúcar syenite, which
would imply a signiﬁcant revision to the age of the SA2 pole, assum-
ing that the hornblende does not record protracted cooling of the
body. This geochronological uncertainty aside, it must be stated
that both the SA1 and SA2 poles are based on a relatively small num-
ber of sites and consequently show large uncertainties in their posi-
tions. A third mean virtual geomagnetic pole reported by Sánchez
Bettucci and Rapalini (2002) derived from study of the glaciogenic
sedimentary rocks of the Playa Hermosa Formation. This pole, com-
puted from only 6 samples, was interpreted as primary in origin and
dating from the inferred ca. 600 Ma age of sedimentation.
In order to construct a more robust apparent polar wander
path for the Río de la Plata craton, we conducted a new pale-
omagnetic study on the Sierra de las Animas complex and the
Playa Hermosa Formation. This paleomagnetic study was com-
plemented by geochronologic determinations by U–Pb (SHRIMP)
