2. Geology and sampling
The Sierra de Las Ánimas complex is an association of intrusive,
volcanic, and sedimentary rocks generated during an extensional
stage within the evolution of the Neoproterozoic Brasiliano-Pan
African orogeny (Sánchez Bettucci and Rapalini, 2002). The stud-
ied area is situated in southeastern Uruguay (Fig. 1), and presents
a complex stratigraphic sequence. The Sierra de las Ánimas com-
plex is a bimodal igneous suite of both shallow intrusive bodies
and volcanic, pyroclastic deposits. Trachytes are the most abun-
dant and geographically widespread. Extrusive units comprise
pyroclastic rhyolites and minor basalts. According to Oyhantc¸ abal
et al. (2007), shallow intrusive bodies like the Pan de Azúcar
syenite and associated microsyenitic dykes comprise the shal-
low magmatic plumbing of the complex. These same workers
reported an 40Ar/39Ar cooling age of 579 ± 2 Ma for the Pan de
Azúcar syenite, considered as part of the Sierra de Las Animas
Complex.
The Playa Hermosa Formation (Masquelin and Sánchez Bettucci,
1993) is a volcano-sedimentary succession exposed mainly along
the coastline close to the town of Piriápolis (Fig. 2). It has been
interpreted as a glacially inﬂuenced clastic sequence, at least in its
lower part, that makes up the inﬁlling of the Playa Verde basin (see
Pazos et al., 2011 and references therein, for a detailed descrip-
tion of this formation). The upper part of this succession shows
a large number of volcanic intercalations, either as synsedimen-
tary lavas or sills or as dykes. This volcanism has been ascribed
to the Sierra de las Ánimas complex. A preliminary paleomag-
netic study on the basal levels of the Playa Hermosa Formation
was reported by Sánchez Bettucci and Rapalini (2002). Based on
only six sample directions, these authors obtained a mean virtual
geomagnetic pole that falls close to the 595 Ma Campo Alegre pole
(D’Agrella-Filho and Pacca, 1988), which was interpreted as a likely
age of deposition of ca. 600 Ma for the basal levels of the Playa
Hermosa Formation. The position of this preliminary paleomag-
netic pole suggested that the glacial event associated to the lower
levels of this formation may have occurred at low to intermediate
latitudes.
We collected one hundred and ﬁfteen oriented samples with
a portable drill at ﬁfteen sites distributed in different magmatic
lithologies as basalt, trachyte and micro-syenite of the Sierra de
las Ánimas complex. This new sampling was done with the aim
of improving the statistical parameters of poles SA1 and SA2 pub-
lished by Sánchez Bettucci and Rapalini (2002). Samples were also
collected for geochronologic studies at three sites that yielded pos-
itive paleomagnetic results in the original study. They were the
Pan de Azucar syenite (sites SA-1, SA-2, SA-3 and SA-8, see also
Oyhantc¸ abal et al., 2007) and a micro-syenite (SA-20), both con-
tributing to pole SA2 (interpreted as of ca 550 Ma) and the El Tambo
Rhyolite (SA-12) contributing to pole SA1 (interpreted as of ca.
520 Ma).
Sixteen new paleomagnetic samples were collected at the basal
levels of the Playa Hermosa Formation. They were approximately
distributed into four sites, although no proper sites were deﬁned
since all samples were collected over c.4.5 m of stratigraphy. One
sample was also collected from these levels for U–Pb (SHRIMP) dat-
ing on detrital zircons in order to determine source and maximum
depositional ages for the Playa Hermosa Formation.
3. Laboratory procedures
Paleomagnetic samples were submitted to standard stepwise
demagnetization techniques. Alternating ﬁeld (AF) demagnetiza-
tion proved to be more efﬁcient in those sites that presented
well-deﬁned magnetic components. Specimens were submitted to
steps of 3, 6, 9, 12, 15, 20, 25, 30, 40, 50 and 60 mT in most cases,
with demagnetization steps of up to 100 mT used for some sam-
ples. Remanence directions were measured in a fully automated 2G
DC cryogenic magnetometer. AF demagnetization was performed
in a static three-axis degausser attached to the magnetometer.
Thermal demagnetization was accomplished in a dual-camera ASC
non-magnetic oven, with internal magnetic ﬁelds under 10 nT.
Bulk susceptibility was monitored with a Bartington MS-2 suscep-
tometer and anisotropy of magnetic susceptibility with a MFK-1A
kappabridge (AGICO). All laboratory procedures were done at the
Daniel A. Valencio paleomagnetic laboratory (IGEBA, Universidad
de Buenos Aires). Magnetic components were deﬁned by means
of principal component analysis (Kirschvink, 1980) after visual
inspection of demagnetization diagrams (Zijderveld plots) for each
specimen. Maximum angular deviations up to 15◦ were accepted,
although over 85% of all determined components showed MAD
<10◦. Mean directions for each site were computed following
standard Fisherian statistics (Fisher, 1953). In just one site combina-
tion of isolated vectorial components and remagnetization circles
(McFadden and McElhinny, 1988) was employed. In the case of the
Playa Hermosa Formation no mean site directions were computed
as each sample corresponded to a slightly different stratigraphic
level.
Zircon crystals were separated by crushing and sieving of sam-
ples, followed by Wilﬂey table and heavy liquid separation. Grains
were then handpicked using a binocular microscope, and then
mounted in epoxy resin for polishing prior to scanning electron
microscope and cathodoluminescence imaging (Fig. 3). The epoxy
mounts were cleaned and gold-coated to have a uniform electrical
conductivity for SHRIMP analysis. The zircon standard used was
BR266 zircon (559 Ma, 903 ppm U). The isotopic composition of the
minerals was determined using the SHRIMP II housed at Curtin Uni-
versity. Prior to spot analysis, rastering of the ion beam was carried
out for 120–150 s to remove the gold coating and reduce the com-
mon Pb contaminant within the gold coating. A primary ion beam of
2.5–3 nA with a diameter of ∼25 /H9262m was focused onto the polished
surface. The common Pb correction was carried out using the mea-
sured amount of 204Pb. Isotope data were reduced using the SQUID2
software (Ludwig, 2009). Data were plotted on concordia diagrams
using the Isoplot 3 software (Ludwig, 2008), with 2/ESC error ellipses
on the concordia plots and all ages reported at the 2/ESC conﬁdence
level in the text.
4. Geochronologic results
4.1. The Sierra de las Animas Complex
Three samples were collected from the sites studied by Sánchez
Bettucci and Rapalini (2002) in order to constrain the age of the
rocks and the observed paleomagnetic remanences. Samples SdAn1
and SdAn3 are from sites (site SA-20 and sites SA-1, SA-2, and SA-3,
respectively) representing the older SA2 direction, originally con-
sidered to be ca. 550 Ma. Sample SdAn1 is a microsyenitic dyke
intruding the upper levels of the Playa Hermosa Formation along
the beach near Piriápolis. All ages discussed here are 238U–206Pb
ages; U–Pb analytical data and location details for all samples are
provided in Supplementary Table S1. Zircons from sample SdAn1
are characterized by Th/U ratios >0.5 and as high as 2, consistent
with a magmatic origin for these grains. SHRIMP spot analyses
from cores and rims failed to distinguish age zoning, consistent

4.2. The Playa Hermosa Formation
Forty-one detrital zircons from a sample collected at the basal
levels of this formation were analyzed by U–Pb SHRIMP. Consid-
ering only concordant analyses with common Pb contamination
of <1.5%, the ages of these grains deﬁne a bimodal population
(Fig. 5), with ca. 60% of zircons with ages of 2050–2200 Ma, typ-
ical of the Paleoproterozoic basement of the Río de la Plata craton
(Rapela et al., 2007). The second, younger group represents 40%
of the population, and the median age of this younger popula-
tion is ca. 615 Ma (+6/−10 Ma, 96.5% conﬁdence level). Using the
“youngest detrital zircon” function of Isoplot, the youngest Monte
Carlo result is 593 (+11/−18) (Fig. 5b, inset), in close agreement with
the youngest single analytical result from a zircon with a 206Pb/238U
age of 594 ± 16 Ma (2/ESC). The source for this younger population is
likely to be the products of extensional magmatism in the adjacent
Dom Feliciano Belt. Noting that the Sierra de las Ánimas is intru-
sive into the Playa Hermosa Formation, the age of deposition is
constrained to a period between ca. 594 Ma and the 578.0 ± 4.3 Ma
intrusion, consistent with the 590–600 Ma age imputed to these
basal deposits by Sánchez Bettucci and Rapalini (2002).
5. Paleomagnetic results
5.1. The Sierra de las Animas Complex
Only six out of sixteen sites from this complex provided
reliable and consistent paleomagnetic results after detailed demag-
netization. The remaining ten sites generally showed unstable
magnetic behavior during demagnetization or very poor directional
consistency of remanence. In all cases alternating ﬁeld (AF) demag-
netization proved more efﬁcient than thermal cleaning to isolate
and determine the magnetic components. Fig. 6 illustrates some
examples of samples with positive demagnetization behavior. In
all cases a well-deﬁned magnetic component is erased by ﬁelds
between 15 and
 60 mT. In some cases (Fig. 6a and b) some 10–20%
of the original remanence may remain after 60 mT. In all cases a
linear trend
 towards the origin is observed. This was interpreted
as the characteristic remanence of these rocks. Five out of these
six sites (AN-1, 3, 7, 8 and 13) presented mean directions consis-
tent with those corresponding to the six sites from which pole SA2
(Sánchez Bettucci and Rapalini, 2002) was originally calculated.
These eleven sites’ mean directions are shown in Table 1 and plot-
ted in Fig. 6d. Site AN-12 presented a well-deﬁned mean direction
that is not consistent with the remaining sites and was ruled out.
The Sierra de las Ánimas Complex outcrops are not affected by sig-
niﬁcant deformation, only minor tilting has affected some areas.
Therefore, just two sites have been corrected for tilting (Table 1).
Fig. 6d and e shows a better clustering of mean site characteristic
directions after bedding correction, suggesting a pre-tilting mag-
netization. Application of the McElhinny (1964) statistical fold test
is inconclusive (Fisherian statistical parameter k jumps from 12 to
20), but the direction–correction test of Enkin (2003) produces a
positive result with best grouping at 98.6% of bedding correction.
These results strongly suggest in favor of a pre-tilting magnetiza-
tion.
A virtual geomagnetic pole was computed from the average
characteristic remanence of each site (Table 1). These were aver-
aged with those mean site directions presented by Sánchez Bettucci
and Rapalini (2002). The overall mean is the new paleomagnetic
pole for the Sierra de las Ánimas complex (SAn: 12.2◦ S, 258.9◦ E,
A95: 14.9◦). Considering the ages obtained from paleomagnetic
sites for this pole, in particular SA20, an age of 578 Ma can be applied
conﬁdently to such paleomagnetic pole.
Surprisingly not a single site yielded a remanence direction
compatible with the group of directions determined by Sánchez
Bettucci and Rapalini (2002) from which paleomagnetic pole SA1
was computed.
5.2. The Playa Hermosa Formation
Sixteen oriented cores were collected at the basal levels of the
Playa Hermosa Formation on siltstones to ﬁne-grain sandstones
of glacially related origin. These samples can be roughly grouped
into four sites and were aimed at improving the original results
published by Sánchez Bettucci and Rapalini (2002).
The anisotropy of magnetic susceptibility (AMS) was measured
for all samples (23 specimens) prior to demagnetization, and the
data were analyzed using the standard statistical approach of
Jelinek (1978, 1981). Results are presented in Fig. 7. The bulk sus-
ceptibility of these rocks was homogeneous with a mean value
of 3 × 10−4 SI, suggesting that the paramagnetic fraction is likely
dominant (Tarling and Hrouda, 1993). Fig. 7c and d shows that

(Fig. 7b) produces a peculiar distribution of AMS axes, in which
there seems to be no relation between the bedding and the foliation
planes. Although no remanence anisotropy has been investigated in
these samples, the bulk susceptibility values suggest that the mag-
netic fabric is probably due to phyllosilicates population, which are
the modally dominant Fe-bearing minerals.
The geometrical disposition of the AMS axes resembles that
found in several clastic sedimentary rocks and unconsolidated
sediments and attributed to macroscopically imperceptible defor-
mation due to tectonic processes during or immediately after
deposition (e.g. Sagnotti and Meloni, 1993; Mattei et al., 1997; Parés
et al., 1999; Soto et al., 2009; Fazzito et al., 2011). This magnetic
“cryptofabric” has more frequently been determined in compres-
sional settings. However, Cifelli et al. (2005) have described similar
magnetofabrics in extensional basins. In all cases the orientation
of AMS axes (in particular kmax) is governed by the orientation of
the regional or local strain ellipsoid. This phenomenon has been
generally described in Neogene sediments or sedimentary rocks.
A possible explanation for the magnetic fabrics found in the Playa
Hermosa Formation is that these rocks record a tectonic “cryptofab-
ric” coeval with their deposition or early diagenesis. Unfortunately,
no unambiguous ﬁeld evidence on the age of the folding/tilting of
the Playa Hermosa sediments is available. One favored hypothesis
suggests that it is related to extensional tectonic disturbance asso-
ciated to the emplacement of the Sierra de las Ánimas magmatism.
If so, the age of its magnetic fabric might postdate deposition no
more than 10–20 Ma, consistent with the interpretation presented
above.
According to the results published by Sánchez Bettucci and
Rapalini (2002), samples from the Playa Hermosa Formation pre-
sented more coherent demagnetization behavior when submitted
to AF rather than thermal cleaning. Maximum applied alternating
ﬁelds reached 120 mT. Although several samples showed unstable
magnetic behavior, a characteristic magnetic component could be
isolated in 7 samples from two sites (Fig. 8a and b), in ﬁelds between
12 and 60–80 mT. These samples generally showed a low-coercivity
(viscous?) large overprint with random direction that could be eas-
ily erased at ﬁelds under 12 mT. As previously found by Sánchez
Bettucci and Rapalini (2002) a small high coercivity component
(>60 mT) was also found in some samples (Fig. 8b), although with
low directional consistency. The characteristic remanence points
down and southwards (Table 2). Fig. 8c and d shows the newly
determined sample directions together with those previously pub-
lished by Sánchez Bettucci and Rapalini (2002). Bedding attitudes
of the sampled strata shows slight differences between sites. How-
ever, the homoclinal nature of the exposed succession renders any
tilt test as indeterminate. Response to isothermal remanence acqui-
sition tests (Sánchez Bettucci and Rapalini, 2002) and petrographic
observations suggest that the remanence in the sediments of the
Playa Hermosa Formation is carried by detrital titanomagnetite.

6. Discussion
6.1. Implications for the Rio de la Plata APWP and Gondwana
assembly
Originally, Sánchez Bettucci and Rapalini (2002) proposed that
the Sierra de las Animas magmatism extended for at least 30 Ma
between ca. 550 and 520 Ma. The paleomagnetic basis for this
interpretation lies with the two signiﬁcantly different charac-
teristic remanence directions observed at different sites in the
complex: a moderately inclined, northeast and downward direc-
tion (SA1), and a dual polarity East and down (or West and up)
with moderate to high inclinations (SA2). Lithological correla-
tions using antiquated geochronological data were consistent with
two magmatic episodes at ca. 550 Ma for SA2 and ca. 520 Ma for
SA1, whose corresponding paleomagnetic poles presented large
conﬁdence ovals (Sánchez Bettucci and Rapalini, 2002). These
workers also reported a small number of paleomagnetic results for
the Playa Hermosa Formation, which was assigned a ca. 600 Ma
age.
Our new results allow us to revise these results substantially,
notably by rejecting the primary nature of the SA1 pole, and signif-
icantly constraining the age of the primary SAn pole (new results
compiled with the SA2 pole and recalculated) from the Sierra de
las Ánimas complex and the PH pole from the Playa Hermosa For-
mation (PH). With regard to the ﬁrst point, we found no samples
preserving the remanent direction underpinning the SA1 pole posi-
tion. Furthermore, new geochronological data from the El Tambo
Rhyolite indicate a ca. 578 Ma age for these rocks in conﬂict with the
interpreted Cambrian (ca. 520 Ma) age for the magnetization. The
newly obtained age strongly suggests that the Sierra de Las Ánimas
Magmatic Complex formed during a relatively short time during
the Early Ediacaran, and that pole SA1 is a likely remagnetization
of Cambrian age.

The age discrepancies between these different poles prevent
us from ruling out small magnitude movement between these
cratons after ca. 578 Ma. However, the clustering of these poles,
or possibly, their arrangement along a single APW path strongly
argues in favor of a coherent “Central Gondwana” by that time
sensu Sánchez Bettucci and Rapalini (2002) and Tohver et al.
(2006). Reﬁning the magnitude of possible displacements with
respect to the assembly of the Congo-São Francisco and Río de
La Plata cratons will need further paleomagnetic data from both
cratons.

the controversy over the Clymene Ocean (Trindade et al., 2006;

cratonic blocks of South America by either 600 Ma (Cordani et al.,
2013) or not until the middle Cambrian (Tohver et al., 2012). A
simple comparison of the position of the ca. 600 Ma Adma dior-

Separation of Amazonia–West Africa from Laurentia is very
loosely controlled by paleomagnetic data between around 615
and 525 Ma. Major geological evidence indicates that ﬁnal opening
of the eastern passive margin of Laurentia occurred in the latest
Ediacaran (565–550 Ma, Cawood et al., 2001). Traditionally, this
has been interpreted as ﬁnal break-up of Rodinia by drifting apart
of Amazonia–West Africa from Laurentia (e.g. Li et al., 2008). In
this scenario, the existence of a large Clymene ocean as depicted
in Fig. 10 is unavoidable. An alternative possibility as proposed
by McCausland et al. (2011), suggests an older age for separation
of Amazonia (perhaps around 600 Ma) while generation of the
eastern passive margin of Laurentia (ca. 550 Ma) is attributed to
rifting of peri-Amazonian blocks (i.e. Arequipa-Antofalla and other
Proterozoic Andean terranes). However, the Campo Alegre pole

and the Playa Hermosa and Villa Mónica mean virtual geomagnetic
poles indicate a large paleolatitudinal gap between Amazonia and
Rio de la Plata cratons by ca. 600 Ma. Only if the latter three poles
are ruled out and the older age for separation of Amazonia from
Laurentia (ca. 600 Ma) is assumed, a large Clymene ocean can be
avoided. Reliable paleomagnetic data from the Amazonia and West
Africa cratons for the 550–600 Ma lapse is necessary for a deﬁnitive
answer.
6.2. Implications for Gaskiers-aged glaciation
The position of the new paleomagnetic pole for the Playa Her-
mosa Formation is not signiﬁcantly different from the original
virtual geomagnetic pole albeit with new constraints of ca. 594–ca.
578 Ma for its age. Although no ﬁeld test is available for the origin
of the characteristic remanence of these sedimentary rocks, a pri-
mary remanence is consistent with the pole position close to the
595 Ma Campo Alegre lavas paleomagnetic pole (D’Agrella-Filho
and Pacca, 1988). However, the validity of the latter as represen-
tative of the Rio de la Plata craton for the Ediacaran has been
questioned (Font et al., 2011). Nevertheless, similar positions with
the Villa Mónica Fm mean virtual geomagnetic pole (SBf, Rapalini
et al., 2013) reinforces the likelihood of a primary origin. The Playa
Hermosa pole positions, computed both in situ and after bedding
correction of the remanence directions, does not coincide with any
reference paleomagnetic pole for South America since the Late
Carboniferous (Besse and Courtillot, 2002; Torsvik et al., 2008)
suggesting that a remagnetization in the last 320 Ma is unlikely.
Magnetic fabric results point to lack of signiﬁcant inclination shal-
lowing in the Playa Hermosa sediments, which suggest that the
13.0◦ + 9.5◦/−5.5◦ paleolatitude for deposition of the glacially inﬂu-
enced sediments (inferred from its paleomagnetic pole) favors low
latitude glaciation at the Rio de la Plata craton during the Early
Ediacaran. However, a ﬁeld test on the primary nature of this mag-
netization is needed before more robust conclusions are extracted
from these data.
The ca. 594–ca. 578 Ma interval of possible deposition of the
Playa Hermosa Formation was contemporaneous with the well-
dated accumulation of the Camaquã Supergroup in Brazil (Janikian
et al., 2008, 2012). The glacial characteristics observed in the
Playa Hermosa Formation contrasts with the absence of glacial
characteristics in that basin (Janikian et al., 2008) Taken together
with the low latitude of these deposits, these results provide evi-
dence for a low-latitude Gaskiers-aged glaciation in the Rio de la
Plata craton in contradiction of the conclusions of Janikian et al.
(2008).
6.3. Implications for the Ediacaran geomagnetic ﬁeld
A long lasting debate has taken place in the last two decades
regarding the Ediacaran paleomagnetic database of Laurentia
(Symons and Chiasson, 1991; Meert et al., 1994; Pisarevsky et al.,
2001; McCausland et al., 2007, and many others). The controversy
revolves around highly disparate, high and low inclination mag-
netic remanences preserved in cratonic rocks of similar age. For
example, reliable paleomagnetic poles suggest that Laurentia was
located at a low paleolatitude at around 615 Ma (Long Range dykes,
Murthy et al., 1992) and again sometime after ca. 560 Ma (e.g., Sept
Iles intrusion, Tanczyk et al., 1987; Buckingham ﬂows, Dankers
and Lapointe, 1981; Skinner Cove Formation poles, McCausland
and Hodych, 1998). However, for a relatively brief period between
590 and 570 Ma, Laurentia appears to have occupied high, nearly
polar, latitudes (e.g., Callander Complex, Symons and Chiasson,
1991; Catoctin volcanics, Meert et al., 1994; see also McCausland
et al., 2007, and references therein and Table 3). Furthermore,
some of these units (Sept-Iles, Catoctin) seem to carry both high
and low inclination directions as apparent primary magnetizations.
Recent paleomagnetic results from the Baies de Moutons syenite
in Eastern Laurentia (McCausland et al., 2011) of ca. 585 Ma, have
conﬁrmed the presence of a high latitude component (A) with a
second, unrelated, component (B) from slightly younger intrusions
of the same complex yielding low paleolatitudes for Laurentia.
Abrajevitch and Van der Voo (2010) point out a similar paradox
in the Baltica paleomagnetic database, in which the ca. 583 Ma Fen
Carbonatite Complex (Meert et al., 1998) and one component of the
584 Ma Alno Carbonatite Complex (Meert et al., 2007) show steep
inclinations that would indicate high paleolatitudes for Baltica.
Low inclination results from the Alno Carbonatite and the ca.
580 Ma Ukranian traps directions (Elming et al., 2007) suggest low
paleolatitudes.
Different explanations have been proposed for this high/low
inclination paradox. They range from very fast plate tectonic
displacements (Meert et al., 1993, 1994; McCausland et al.,
2007), paleomagnetic artifacts due to unreliable data (Pisarevsky
et al., 2001, 2008), inertial interchange true polar wander (Evans,
2003; Kirschvink et al., 2005) or unusual geomagnetic geometries
(Abrajevitch and Van der Voo, 2010). These last authors ruled out
plate tectonic displacements or true polar wander on the basis of
non-actualistic or impossibly fast plate motions or pan-lithospheric
shifts. Instead, Abrajevitch and Van der Voo (2010) speculate that
the middle Ediacaran Earth Magnetic Field had two apparently
stable conﬁgurations, a geocentric axial dipole (GAD) and a geo-
centric equatorial dipole (GED). There is no evidence for such
non-uniformitarian behavior of the geomagnetic ﬁeld in Phanero-
zoic times, and the mechanisms underlying the GED/GAD duality
are obscure. However, we can test whether the SAn pole, from
rocks now dated at ca. 578 Ma, is consistent with a primary mag-
netization obtained during this putative GED/GAD behavior of the
geomagnetic ﬁeld.
Like the “high” and “low” latitude poles of similar age from
Laurentia and Baltica, the angular distance between SAn and SA1
poles is over 70◦. A geomagnetic ﬁeld changing between a GAD and
a GED geometry allows for paleolongitudinal constraints in pale-
ogeographic reconstructions, provided either a single GED state
prevailed with a preferred geographical position, as proposed by
Abrajevitch and Van der Voo (2010). Fig. 11 shows a paleomag-
netically controlled paleogeographic reconstruction of Laurentia,
Baltica and Rio de la Plata–Congo-São Francisco cratons for the
middle to late Ediacaran (ca. 585–555 Ma). Laurentia and Baltica
have been reconstructed assuming the low-latitude option, using
the Sept-Iles pole (ca. 564 Ma) and the mean Baltica poles (ca.
555 Ma, Meert et al., 2007), respectively. Rio de la Plata and Congo-
São Francisco are considered as already attached or very close
to each other and are positioned according to SAn (ca. 578 Ma)
obtained in this study. In this reconstruction, the Catoctin vol-
canic and Callander Complex poles from Laurentia as well as
the Fen Complex and the Anlo Carbonatite poles from Baltica
fall relatively close to each other, and near the equator, illus-
trating the hypothesis of the GED conﬁguration. However, the
SA1 pole falls quite far from the other group. The relative longi-
tudinal position of the Rio de la Plata–Congo-São Francisco has
been selected following Rapalini et al. (2013). There is a clear
mismatch between the SA1 pole and the remaining equatorial
poles. Overlapping them is not possible since this would require
overlapping the continental crusts of Río de la Plata–Congo-São
Francisco with that of Baltica. On the other hand, choosing the
antipodal location of SA1 and therefore the Rio de la Plata–Congo-
São Francisco land masses would place these cratons on an
opposite hemisphere to Laurentia, turning highly unlikely the
550–525 Ma accretion of Amazonia and other blocks to form Gond-
wana (Trindade et al., 2006; Tohver et al., 2012). In summary,
our analysis conﬁrms that the SA1 pole is likely a Cambrian

7. Conclusions
A new paleomagnetic and geochronologic study on the Sierra de
las Ánimas complex and the Playa Hermosa Formation exposed in
southern Uruguay yielded signiﬁcant results. U/Pb (SHRIMP) dat-
ing on magmatic zircons allow us to determine that the complex
was erupted around 578 Ma and did not extend into the Cambrian.
Similar dating on detrital zircons from the Playa Hermosa sedi-
ments constrain their deposition to the 595–578 Ma interval, which
suggest that they are related to the Gaskiers glaciation. Paleomag-
netic analysis permitted to deﬁne a more robust and well dated
paleomagnetic pole at 578 Ma for the Río de la Plata craton. This
new pole (SAn) supersedes the SA2 pole of Sánchez Bettucci and
Rapalini (2002). No remanence directions compatible with the SA1
pole determined by these authors, and considered of Cambrian
age, were found in the new study. The new geochronologic con-
straints indicate that rocks from which SA1 was computed are also
of middle Ediacaran time. Paleogeographic reconstructions for the
middle Ediacaran (ca. 575 Ma) support the existence of a wide Cly-
mene Ocean between the Río de la Plata and Congo-São Francisco
cratons on one side and Amazonia and West Africa on the other.
New paleomagnetic results on the Playa Hermosa sediments sug-
gest that these glacially related sediments were deposited at low
latitudes, although more robust paleomagnetic data is needed. The
hypothetical co-existence of two stable conﬁgurations of the Earth
Magnetic Field, with geomagnetic poles situated either at the geo-
graphic poles or at the equator in the middle Ediacaran, cannot
explain SA1 pole located near 90◦ from SAn. A Cambrian remagne-
tization affecting some units of the Sierra de las Ánimas complex is
the simplest explanation for SA1.

a b s t r a c t
The middle to late Neoproterozoic records the transition from the dispersal of supercontinent Rodinia
to
 the subsequent assembly of supercontinent Gondwana. Determining paleogeographic positions of the
major
 cratons during this transition is crucial to understand the displacement histories of these blocks.
However,
 high-quality paleomagnetic results from well-dated rocks during this period remain sparse for
the
 cratons. In this paper, we have carried out a paleomagnetic study of the succession of the Cryogenian
Qiaoenbrak
 formation (Fm) in the Aksu area, NW China, which contains diamictites that are of probable
glacial
 origin. The age of the studied section is constrained at around 730 Ma based on the stratigraphy and
recent
 zircon U–Pb chronologic data. Stepwise alternating ﬁeld (AF) and thermal demagnetizations gen-
erally
 reveal two-component magnetizations. The low temperature (coercivity) component was removed
by
 ∼300 ◦C (∼30 mT) and the high temperature (coercivity) component decayed toward the origin, deﬁn-
ing
 the characteristic remanent magnetization (ChRM). Rock magnetic data indicate that magnetite is the
major
 remanence carrier. A negative fold test for an isoclinal soft-sediment fold, the presence of both
normal
 and reversed polarities, and positive conglomerate tests in conjunction with the presence of pris-
tine
 sedimentary features by microscopic inspections of thin sections suggest that the remanence was
acquired
 shortly after the deposition, i.e. post-depositional remanent magnetization (pDRM), which is
very
 close to the magnetic ﬁeld at the time of deposition. Fourteen out of 17 sites yield stable ChRMs with
a
 mean direction of Ds = 246.1◦ , Is = 30.4◦ , ks = 14.1, ˛95 = 11.0◦ in stratigraphic coordinates, corresponding
to
 a paleopole (Q = 6) at /NAK = 6.3◦ S, ϕ = 17.5◦E, A95 = 9.1◦ . Together with geologic constraints, the new paleo-
magnetic results place the Tarim Block at 16.3 ± 5.6◦ N adjacent to either the west or east of Australia (WOA
or
 EOA) at around 730 Ma, but the WOA position is preferred based on the overall relatively favorable
evidence.
 In addition, since the studied diamictites of the Qiaoenbrak Fm that are of probable glaciogenic
origin
 yield a low paleolatitude, this study may lend support to the “Snowball Earth” hypothesis during
the
 Neoproterozoic times.

1. Introduction
The Neoproterozoic era saw the dispersal of the supercontinent
Rodinia, the subsequent re-amalgamation giving birth to another
large landmass Gondwana, and the accompanying large-scale
glaciations on the fragmentary landmasses (Hoffman et al., 1998;
Schrag and Hoffman, 2001; Hoffman and Schrag, 2002; Torsvik,
2003; Condon et al., 2005; Deynoux et al., 2006; Trindade and
Macouin, 2007; Li et al., 2008; Meert and Lieberman, 2008;
Rino et al., 2008; Macdonald et al., 2010; Bradley, 2011). Precise
reconstruction of the major cratons during this interval is crucial

to establish the displacement histories of these cratons and to
further understand the associated geodynamic processes within
a supercontinent cycle. As one of the important cratons in the
supercontinent Rodinia and one of three major blocks in China,
the Tarim Block contains a complete Mesoproterozoic to Neopro-
terozoic succession (Gao et al., 1985; XBGMR, 1993; Xiao et al.,
2004; Xu et al., 2005, 2009; Turner, 2010; Zhu et al., 2011), which
documented the assembly and breakup of the supercontinent
Rodinia, and the major glaciations in the Neoproterozoic (e.g. Xiao
et al., 2004; Xu et al., 2005, 2009; Lu et al., 2008). However, the
paleogeographic positions of the Tarim Block during this interval
remain poorly constrained.
The Tarim Block has been qualitatively positioned adjacent to
the northwestern Australia at a high latitude based on the simi-
lar tectonostratigraphies of both blocks (Hoffman, 1991; Li et al.,

1996, 2008; Li and Powell, 2001) or the southeastern Australia at
a low latitude based on proposed radiating dyke swarms (Lu et al.,
2008). Paleomagnetic studies of the Neoproterozoic rocks provide
crucial quantitative constraints on the paleopositions of the Tarim
Block (Chen et al., 2004; Huang et al., 2005; Zhan et al., 2007). Chen
et al. (2004) obtained a paleopole from the Aksu dyke swarms and
placed the Tarim Block to the north of Australia at an intermediate
latitude of 43 ± 6◦N at ∼800 Ma. Huang et al. (2005) conducted a
paleomagnetic study of the Baiyisi volcanic rocks in the Quruqtagh
area and obtained an equatorial paleolatitude for the Tarim Block
at ∼740 Ma. However, it is not possible that both paleopoles from
these two studies can ﬁt the apparent polar wander path (APWP)
of Rodinia in one single reconstruction (Evans, 2009). One has to
ﬁt one paleopole with the Rodinian APWP and invoke a tectonic
or overprinting event to explain the departure of the other pole
from the Rodinian APWP (Evans, 2009). The difﬁculty in reconcil-
ing these two poles partly arises from the large age uncertainties of
studied rocks. For instance, the Aksu dyke swarms were previously
assigned an age of 807 ± 12 Ma (Chen et al., 2004), and was later
revised to 785 ± 31 Ma (Zhan et al., 2007). More recently, zircon
U–Pb chronologic studies show that the Aksu dyke swarms likely
emplaced at ∼760 Ma (Zhang et al., 2009a) or even younger than
∼730 Ma (Zhu et al., 2011).
The difﬁculties in reconciling the available paleomagnetic poles
emphasize an urgent need to obtain more reliable paleomagnetic
data from well-dated strata in the Tarim Block. In this study, we
have carried out a detailed paleomagnetic investigation of a succes-
sion of the Qiaoenbrak Fm in the Aksu area (Fig. 1a) that contains
the Neoproterozoic diamictites, which are of probable glaciogenic
origin (Gao et al., 1981, 1985; XBGMR, 1993; Carroll et al., 2001;
Gao and Chen, 2003; Zhu and Wang, 2011). The age of the studied
section can be fairly well constrained with the new U–Pb zircon
ages from the Aksu area and its equivalent stratigraphic interval
in the Quruqtagh area of the northeastern Tarim Block (Fig. 1a).
This study contributes to constrain the paleogeographic position of
the Tarim Block in the Neoproterozoic and could further test the
snowball earth hypothesis.
2. Geological setting and sampling
The pre-Cambrian rocks of the Tarim Block mainly crop out
along its northern margin and consist of the Neoarchean to
Mesoproterozoic metamorphic basement and the Neoproterozoic-
Cambrian unmetamorphosed sedimentary cover (Lu et al., 2008;
Long et al., 2010; Cao et al., 2011; Shu et al., 2011; Ge et al., 2012;
He et al., 2012; Long et al., 2012; Ma et al., 2012; Zhang et al., 2012;
Zhao and Guo, 2012; Zhao and Cawood, 2012). In the Aksu area
(Fig. 1a), the well-exposed pre-Cambrian successions are composed
of, from the bottom to the top, the Proterozoic Aksu Group, the
lower Sinian Qiaoenbrak Fm and the Yuermeinak Fm, and the upper
Sinian Sugetbrak Fm and the Chigebrak Fm (Fig. 1b). The lower and
upper Sinian successions in the Tarim Block correspond to the Cryo-
genian (Nanhua) and Ediacaran strata, respectively (Fig. 1b) (the
Stratigraphy Committee of China, 2001; Gradstein et al., 2004). The
Aksu Group consists of metasedimentary rocks, greenschists, and
blueschists, and was intruded by a series of NW-trending maﬁc
dykes. The Qiaoenbrak Fm and the Yuermeinak Fm are mainly com-
posed of feldspathic arenite, siltstone, lithic feldspar sandstone,
and conglomerates. These two formations also contain diamic-
tites, within which ﬂat-iron stones, striated clasts, and drop stones
occur, suggesting that the diamictites were probably of glacio-
genic origin (Gao et al., 1981, 1985; XBGMR, 1993). The Sugetbrak
Fm is 400–450 m thick and comprises the red conglomerates, ﬂu-
vial sandstones interbedded with three layers of 15–20 m thick
basalt, and the gray lacustrine mudstones. The overlying Chigebrak
Fm
 is composed mainly of thickly bedded, pale gray stromatolitic
dolomite which was deposited in an extensive lake or a marine
transgressional environment (Gao et al., 1985; Turner, 2010).
We conducted a detailed paleomagnetic investigation of a sec-
tion in the Qiaoenbrak Fm that contains diamictites in the Aksu
area (Fig. 1a and c). The diamictites are represented by two con-
glomerate beds that are separated by a ∼30 m thick sedimentary
sequence, which is composed of thinly bedded, greenish siltstones
and mudstones and contains a soft-sediment fold (Fig. 1c). Both
the lower and the upper conglomerate beds consist of subangular
to subrounded, poorly sorted clasts of various lithologic compo-
sitions. The lower conglomerate bed is about 20 m thick and is
dominated by gray sandstone and red granitic pebbles/cobbles. The
upper conglomerate bed is ∼50 m thick and contains three 1–2 m
thick ﬁne- to coarse-grained sandstone layers that are intercalated
within the upper segment of this conglomerate bed. The num-
ber of pebbles/cobbles in the uppermost of the conglomerate bed
decreases gradually upsection. Below and above the diamictite unit
are thin- to medium-bedded red or yellowish sandstones (Fig. 1c).
We collected eight sites from the ∼80 m thick red sandstone
sequence below the diamictite unit and six sites from the ∼90 m
thick red sandstone sequence above the diamictite unit. Two sites
from the interbedded sandstones within the upper conglomer-
ate bed and one site from the greenish siltstone sequence that
separates the two conglomerate beds were collected. Since these
beds show little variations in attitudes and generally dip toward
240–250◦ at about 50–60◦, we collected samples from the two
conglomerate beds and the soft-sediment fold to perform conglom-
erate tests and a fold test to constrain the age of remanence (Fig. 1c).
Two sites were collected from the two conglomerate beds (sites
AK9 and AK18) and about 10 pebbles/cobbles of different litholo-
gies were sampled at each site. For the soft-sediment fold, samples
were collected from both limbs and the hinge of the fold (site AK16).
All samples were collected with a portable gasoline-powered rock
drill and generally 8–12 cores were drilled at each site. The orienta-
tion of each core was measured with a magnetic compass mounted
on a Pomery orientation device.
3. Laboratory techniques
In the laboratory, cores were cut into standard cylindrical spec-
imens of 2.5 cm in diameter and 2.2 cm in length. To characterize
magnetic mineralogy, representative specimens were chosen for
several rock magnetic experiments. The isothermal remanent mag-
netization (IRM) acquisition was measured with an ASC IM-10-30
impulse magnetizer and a JR-6A spinner magnetometer. Spectral
analyses of IRM acquisition curves are performed to identify differ-
ent coercivity components (Kruiver et al., 2001). Thermo-magnetic
properties were determined using a KLY-3S kappabridge suscep-
tibility meter coupled with a CS-3 furnace. To further constrain
the magnetic mineralogy, representative samples were magne-
tized sequentially along Z-, Y-, and X-axis at ﬁelds of 2.4 T, 0.4 T,
and 0.12 T, respectively, and then were subjected to stepwise ther-
mal demagnetization (Lowrie, 1990). The anisotropy of magnetic
susceptibility (AMS) was measured using the KLY-3S kappabridge.
Both thermal and alternating ﬁled (AF) demagnetizations
were used to isolate the characteristic remanent magnetization
(ChRM). Progressive thermal demagnetization was carried out in
16–22 steps at a 50 ◦C increment for low temperatures (<300 ◦C)
and a 20 or 30 ◦C increment for high temperatures (>300 ◦C)
up to 600–680◦C. AF demagnetization was conducted in about
18 steps up to 90–100 mT. Since pilot experiments show that
thermal demagnetization is more effective in isolating ChRMs
than AF demagnetization, the majority of specimens were then
subjected to thermal demagnetization. Remanence of specimens

The

to

4.2.
 Paleomagnetic results
The intensities of the natural remanent magnetization (NRM)
of the majority of samples vary from 2.93 × 10−4 A/m to
8.70 × 10−3 A/m. About one third of specimens yield erratic
directions upon demagnetization and are excluded from further
analysis. Most of the remaining specimens exhibit two-component
magnetizations (Fig. 5a–f) and granitic pebbles/cobbles from the
conglomerate beds often show one-component magnetization,
with an unblocking temperature at ∼580 ◦C (Fig. 5g). For the two-
component magnetizations, the low temperature component (LTC)
is typically removed by ∼300 ◦C or ∼30 mT, and the high temper-
ature component (HTC) is generally isolated from about 300 ◦C up
to 570–600◦C or from 30 mT to 90–100 mT. The LTC directions
are well concentrated in geographic coordinates with a site-mean
of Dg = 355.8◦, Ig = 62.6◦, ˛95 = 3.0◦, which is similar to the present
Earth’s ﬁeld (PEF) and is interpreted as the present-day overprint.
The HTCs decay toward the origin (Fig. 5a–f) and represent the
ChRMs of specimens. All ChRMs show normal polarities except sites
AK12 and AK13 that contain ChRMs of reversed polarities. The site
mean directions are summarized in Table 1.
4.3.
 Petrographic results
Examination of polished thin sections with a microscope reveals
that the studied sandstones are composed of ∼35–55% quartz
(100–800 /H9262m), ∼30–50% feldspar (100–1500 /H9262m), ∼13–15% lithic
fragments (100–1300 /H9262m), and rare heavy minerals such as epi-
dote, sphene, biotite, muscovite, zircon and opaque minerals
(Fig. 6a–d). The greenish siltstones are dominated by ﬁne-grained
monocrystalline quartz and plagioclase (Fig. 6d). Boundaries of
grains and lithic fragments, particularly opaque phases probably
including magnetite in both sandstones and siltstones, are sharply
deﬁned and show no signs of mineralogic alterations. These fea-
tures suggest that the studied rocks are pristine.

5. Discussion
5.1. Timing of the remanence acquisition
5.1.1. Field stability tests
The age of the ChRMs is constrained by a fold test and two con-
glomerate tests. Nine out of 10 samples from both limbs and the
hinge of the isoclinal, soft-sediment fold within the greenish silt-
stones (AK16, Fig. 1c) yield stable ChRMs (Table 2). The ChRMs
are moderately grouped in geographic coordinates (Fig. 7a), and
become dispersed (Fig. 7b) after the tilt correction with the kg/ks
ratio of 24.1/1.4. A fold test indicates that the maximum grouping
occurs
 at 4.64 ± 6.36% untilting (Fig. 7c), suggesting a negative fold
test (Enkin, 2003). Consequently, the remanence was acquired after
the soft-sediment folding.
The randomness test (Watson, 1956) was applied to the two
conglomerate beds that are separated by the greenish siltstone
sequence. Eight out of 11 samples from the lower conglomerate
bed yield ChRMs (Fig. 8a) and the resultant vector of the ChRMs is
R = 4.12, which is less than the critical value of R0 = 4.48 for N = 8
at 95% conﬁdence level (Watson, 1956), indicating a passage of the
conglomerate test. For the upper conglomerate bed, six out of 8
samples yield stable remanent magnetizations (Fig. 8b) and the
resultant vector R = 3.76, which is less than 3.85, the critical value

Since soft-sediment folding occurs in the early stage of depo-
sition when water content is modest such that sediments are
cohesive enough to retain the shape of a layer and yet soft enough to
easily deform. Therefore, the negative soft-sediment fold test and
the positive conglomerate tests suggest that the ChRMs likely rep-
resent the post-depositional remanent magnetizations (pDRMs),
i.e. remanence acquired shortly after deposition (Butler, 1992;
Tauxe, 2010). Indeed, pDRM is believed common in many sedimen-
tary environments and is often considered an accurate recorder of
the geomagnetic ﬁeld at or very close to the time of deposition
(Butler, 1992).
5.1.2. Age of the diamictite in the Qiaoenbrak Fm
The Qiaoenbrak Fm was considered to be the Mid-
Neoproterozoic in age based on the presence of micro-paleobotanic
fossils (Gao et al., 1985). The age of the Qiaoenbrak Fm can be fur-
ther constrained by the radiometric ages obtained from rocks below
and above the Qiaoenbrak Fm (Fig. 1b). The Aksu Group, which
underlays the Qiaoenbrak Fm, comprises metasedimentary rocks
and maﬁc schists, and was intruded by a series of NW-trending
unmetamorphosed maﬁc dykes. LA-ICP-MS U–Pb dating of detrital
zircons from the metasedimentary rocks of the Aksu Group yields a
maximum deposition age of 727 ± 12 Ma (Zhu et al., 2011). SHRIMP
U–Pb zircon dating of the unmetamorphosed maﬁc dykes gives an
emplacement age of 759 ± 7 Ma (Zhang et al., 2009a). Consequently,
a maximum age of ca. 730–760 Ma is inferred for the Qiaoenbrak
Fm from these age data. Overlying the Qiaoenbrak Fm is the Yuer-
meinak Fm, which is covered by the Sugetbrak Fm (Fig. 1b). LA-ICP-
MS U–Pb dating of detrital zircons from the uppermost Qiaoenbrak
Fm and the lowermost Yuermeinak Fm yields maximum deposi-
tion ages of 727 ± 8 Ma and 719 ± 9 Ma, respectively (Ding, H.F.,
personal communication), which are compatible with the age of
∼600 Ma for the Sugertbrak Fm (Zhan et al., 2007; Zhu et al., 2011)
that overlays the Yuermeinak Fm (Fig. 1b). These ages allow a mini-
mum age for the Qiaoenbrak Fm to be placed at ∼720 Ma. Therefore,
the age of the Qiaoenbrak Fm can be bracketed between ∼720 and
∼760 Ma based on the U–Pb zircon age data from the Aksu area.
The age of the Qiaoenbrak Fm, particularly the diamictites, can
be further constrained by the ages of its equivalent Neoproterozoic
strata from other parts of the Tarim Block. It is well known that
the Neoproterozoic strata in the Aksu area can be correlated with
those in the Quruqtagh area at the northeastern margin of the Tarim
Block (Fig. 1a). In particular, the diamictites in the Qiaoenbrak Fm
in the Aksu area is considered coeval with the diamictites in the
Baiyisi Fm in the Quruqtagh area (Fig. 1a; Gao et al., 1981, 1985;
XBGMR, 1993). The diamictites in the Baiyisi Fm are sandwiched
into two basalt layers. SHRIMP zircon U–Pb dating of the volcanic
rocks above the diamictites yields an age of 725 ± 10 Ma (Xu et al.,
2009) and the volcanic bed below the diamictites gives two ages of
755 ± 15 Ma (Xu et al., 2005) and 740 ± 7 Ma (Xu et al., 2009). There-
fore, the age of diamictites in the Baiyisi Fm is bracketed between
∼725 Ma and ∼740 Ma. This age interval is compatible with the age
of ∼720–760 Ma for the Qiaoenbrak Fm, supporting the correlation
of diamictites in the Qiaoenbrak Fm and the Bayisi Fm. Therefore,
the studied diamictite section in the Aksu area was likely deposited
at around 730 Ma.

5.1.3. The paleopole of the diamictite in the Qiaoenbrak Fm
Among the 15 sites that yield stable ChRMs and site-means
(Table 1), site AK12 shows an ˛95 greater than 20◦ and is excluded
from further analysis. The mean of site-means of the remaining
14 sites is calculated at Dg = 256.6◦, Ig = 85.6◦, kg = 13.5, ˛95 = 11.3◦
in geographic coordinates, and Ds = 246.1◦, Is = 30.4◦, ks = 14.1,
˛95 = 11.0◦ in stratigraphic coordinates (Fig. 9a and b), which cor-
responds to a paleopole at /NAK = 6.3◦S, ϕ = 17.5◦E, A95 = 9.1◦ with a
paleolatitude of 16.3 ± 5.6◦. This paleopole is signiﬁcantly differ-
ent from the previously published younger paleopoles of the Tarim
Block (Fig. 10) (Li, 1990; Zhan et al., 2007; Zhao et al., 2008; Gilder
et al., 2008; Huang et al., 2005; Sun and Huang, 2009), further
attesting the primary origin of the remanence of the studied section.
To test the robustness of this new paleopole, we perform the
following analysis. Because sites AK2, AK13, and AK19 has only
one stable ChRM at each site and the site mean for sites AK2, AK13
and AK19 is based on only one ChRM at each site (Table 1). These
three sites are thus excluded to obtain a new site-mean direction
of Dg = 304.2◦, Ig = 84.5◦, kg = 19.0, ˛95 = 10.7◦ in geographic coordi-
nates and Ds = 251.6◦, Is = 32.4◦, ks = 19.8, ˛95 = 10.5◦ in stratigraphic
coordinates (Fig. 9c and d), which corresponds to a new paleopole
at /NAK = 1.7◦S, ϕ = 14.7◦E, A95 = 8.9◦, with a paleolatitude of 17.6 ± 5.3◦
(Table 1). Obviously, the two paleopoles and paleolatitudes are
essentially same, demonstrating that the paleopole (/NAK = 6.3◦S,
ϕ = 17.5◦E, A95 = 9.1◦, N = 14) with a quality factor Q = 6 (Van der
Voo, 1990) obtained from the studied section is robust.
5.2.
 Implications for the late Neoproterozoic paleogeography of
the Tarim Block
In paleogeographic reconstructions, similar tectonostrati-
graphic records serve as the ﬁrst-order evidence for the close
proximity of different blocks. While it is long known that Tarim and
Australia have highly comparable Neoproterozoic tectonostratigra-
phy (Hoffman, 1991; Li et al., 1996, 2008; Zhao and Cawood, 1999;
Li and Powell, 2001; Zhao et al., 2004; Lu et al., 2008; Rino et al.,
2008; Turner, 2010), the similarity in the Neoproterozoic history
between Tarim and South China is relatively recently recognized
and is increasingly appreciated (Lu et al., 2003, 2008). The ca. 1.0 Ga
Tarimian Orogeny (Zhang et al., 2003) is similar to the Jinningian
(or Sibao) Orogeny of South China in character and timing, and both
likely corresponded to the Grenville Orogeny during the assembly
of Rodinia (Lu et al., 2008). Also, maﬁc intrusions of similar ages
(ca. 820–750 Ma) occur in both Tarim and South China (Table 3),
indicating coeval rifting events that were likely associated with
the breakup of Rodinia (Li et al., 1999, 2003). In addition, the sub-
sequent Cryogenian (Nanhua) and Edicaran (Sinian) sedimentary
sequences, particularly the intervals of glacial deposits in Nanhua
System, in Tarim are highly comparable with the Neoproterozoic
successions in South China (Lu et al., 2003). The striking similarity
in the Neoproterozoic stratigraphy and tectonic history between
Tarim and South China strongly suggests that these two blocks were
contiguous to each other in Rodinia (Lu et al., 2003, 2008).

In addition to matching similar tectonostratigraphy, well-
dated, reliable paleomagnetic data can provide further quantitative
constraints on the positions and orientations of blocks in
paleogeographic reconstructions. Rigorous analyses of available
paleomagnetic data from various major continents allowed a
reconstruction of the ∼750 Ma Rodinia (Meert, 2003; Torsvik,
2003), within which Tarim Block is absent probably due to the
lack of adequate constraints by high-quality paleomagnetic data.
Our reconstruction of the paleogeographic position of Tarim Block
at 730 Ma is based mainly on the basic framework of the 750 Ma
Rodinia conﬁguration of Torsvik (2003). The approximate pos-
itions of major blocks such as Australia and South China at 730 Ma
are reconstructed according to their interpolated paleolatitudes
using their ∼750 Ma paleopoles and the next available good-
quality younger paleopoles (Fig. 11). For example, Australia at
∼730 Ma is positioned at the interpolated paleolatitude of ∼15◦N
using the ∼755 Ma paleopole (Wingate and Giddings, 2000) and
the ∼600 Ma paleopole (Sohl et al., 1999). Similarly, South China
Block is placed at 31◦N using the ∼748 Ma paleopole (Evans et al.,
2000) and the ∼630 Ma paleopole (Macouin et al., 2004). Laurentia,
India,
 and other continents are included in Fig. 11 for refer-
ence.
Our new paleomagnetic data from the Qiaoenbrak diamictites
indicate that Tarim block underwent ∼250◦ clockwise rotations and
was located at a low paleolatitude of 16.3 ± 5.6◦ at around 730 Ma.
The paleogeographic position of Tarim at ∼730 Ma can then be
reconstructed as follows. First, Tarim block is rotated ∼250◦ in a
counterclockwise sense to restore its original orientation. Second,
geological constraints are utilized to overcome the polarity ambi-
guities. Since Tarim was likely adjacent to Australia during most of
the Neoproterozoic times as evidenced by the marked similarity in
tectonostratigraphy between Tarim and Australia (Hoffman, 1991;
Li et al., 1996, 2008; Li and Powell, 2001; Lu et al., 2008; Rino et al.,
2008; Turner, 2010), and Australia remained in the northerly inter-
mediate to low latitudes throughout the Neoproterozoic time (Sohl
et al., 1999; Wingate and Giddings, 2000), Tarim Block is placed at
16.3 ± 5.6◦N, rather than 16.3 ± 5.6◦S. Third, as paleomagnetic data
cannot constrain the paleolongitude, Tarim Block can be juxtaposed
to either the west (model #1) or east (model #2) of Australia at
16.3 ± 5.6◦N at ca. 730 Ma (Fig. 11). In light of the marked similarity

paired reconstruction for model #1 would place South China close
to the northwestern margin of Australia (Fig. 11). This position for
South China is plausible because it can satisfy the similar tectonos-
tratigraphic records with Australia and India (e.g. Li et al., 2003;
Jiang et al., 2003) and its subsequent tectonic evolution is compat-
ible with that of Australia (e.g. Yang et al., 2004).
It is also possible that the “east of Australia” (EOA; model #2)
was linked to the Tarim Block. Besides the similar Neoproterozoic
stratigraphy and the glacial intervals between Tarim and Australia,
the Grenville Orogen in the Tarim Block may be the eastward
continuation of the ∼1300–1100 Ma Albany-Fraser-Musgravian
Orogen in the central Australia (Myers, 1993; Myers et al., 1996;
Cawood and Korsch, 2008; Kirkland et al., 2011). In addition, the ca.
820–720 Ma magmatism in the Tarim Block can be correlated with
that in the southeastern Australia (Wingate et al., 1998; Li et al.,
2008; Lu et al., 2008; Wang et al., 2010) (Table 3). Furthermore, the
rifting event that produced the ∼750 Ma (Neoproterozoic) bimodal
volcanic rocks in Tarim (Xu et al., 2005, 2009) may correspond to
the Franklin event in Laurentia. Together with the similar-aged rift-
ing event in the adjacent South China Block (model #2, Fig. 11)
these events could result from a common cause – a mantle plume
activity (Heaman et al., 1992; Denyszyn et al., 2009), because the
maﬁc dykes in Tarim, South China, Australia and Laurentia that
manifest these rifting events in different continents constitute a
giant radiating dyke swarm (Fig. 11), which implies a mantle plume
activity. Indeed, similar approach has been employed in recogniz-
ing plume activities in not only supercontinent Rodinia (Li et al.,
2003), but also other supercontinents such as Columbia (Zhao et al.,
2004; Hou et al., 2008a,b). Despite this, model #2 requires a com-
plicated displacement history for the South China Block. The South
China Block broke off from the northeastern margin of Australia in

Neoproterozoic. It then had to move from the northeastern mar-
gin to the western margin of Australia to account for its physical
connection with western Australia in early Paleozoic based on the
biogeographic data (e.g. Burrett et al., 1990). However, a driving
mechanism for such a required complicated displacement history
is lacking.
Overall, the available evidence weighs more toward the WOA
position than the EOA position. The WOA position is different from
the previous reconstructions that placed the Tarim Block to either
the northern Australia (Chen et al., 2004; Zhan et al., 2007) or the
southwestern Australia (Huang et al., 2005). The northern Australia
position (Chen et al., 2004; Zhan et al., 2007) is mainly based on a
proposition that the Aksu dyke swarms in the Tarim Block, which
were estimated to be ca. 807 Ma (Chen et al., 2004), represent the
northward continuation of the ca. 820–800 Ma lamprophyre dykes
and kimberlite pipes (Pidgeon et al., 1989; Li et al., 2003) in the
northern Australia. However, recent radiometric data show that
the Aksu dyke swarms likely emplaced at 759 ± 7 Ma (SHRIMP U–Pb
age; Zhang et al., 2009a) or even younger than ca.730 Ma (Zhu et al.,
2011). The disparate ages of Aksu dyke swarms in the Tarim Block
and the lamprophyre dykes and kimberlite pipes in the northern
Australia may cast doubt on the validity of the early proposition.
The WOA position of the Tarim Block appears to be more compat-
ible with the southwestern Australia reconstruction (Huang et al.,
2005). Huang et al. (2005) obtained an equatorial paleolatitude
for the Tarim Block from the Baiyisi volcanic rocks that were esti-
mated to be ca. 740 Ma. Recent SHRIMP zircon U–Pb geochronologic
data from the volcanic rocks overlying and underlying the Baiyisi
diamictites show an age of 725 ± 10 Ma and 740 ± 7 Ma, respec-
tively (Xu et al., 2009). Since Huang et al.’s (2005) paleomagnetic
data were collected from the volcanic rocks overlying the Baiyisi
diamictites, the age of the Baiyisi paleopole would likely be 725 Ma
or younger. The WOA position at ∼730 Ma would imply that the
Tarim Block drifted southward subsequently and reached the equa-
torial region by ∼720 Ma.
Our new paleomagnetic results and previous paleomagnetic
data from Tarim Block permit an improved understanding of the
kinematics of Tarim Block during the late Neoproterozoic to early
Paleozoic interval. In this study, we have obtained a ∼730 Ma
paleopole at /NAK = 6.3◦S, ϕ = 17.5◦E, A95 = 9.1◦, N = 14 for Tarim Block.
Together with the available late Neoproterozoic to early Paleozoic
paleopoles (Chen et al., 2004; Huang et al., 2005; Zhan et al., 2007;
Sun and Huang, 2009), a preliminary apparent polar wander path
(APWP) for Tarim is reconstructed (Fig. 12a). The overall similar
tracks of the APWPs of both blocks suggest the close proximity of
Tarim and Australia during the late Neoproterozoic. Tarim Block
underwent southward displacement from ∼750 Ma to ∼720 Ma
and remained in the equatorial area from ∼720 Ma to 650 Ma. The
displacement history of Tarim Block is by and large similar to those
of Australia and South China during the interval from ∼750 Ma to
∼650 Ma (Fig. 12b), suggesting that there were no signiﬁcant rel-
ative latitudinal displacements among these blocks. Tarim Block
subsequently moved northward prior to drifting southwardly to
reach the intermediate latitudes in the southern hemisphere in
the early Paleozoic (Zhao et al., 2008), while both Australia and
South China drifted slightly southward and remained in the equa-
torial region from ∼650 Ma to ∼600 Ma (Fig. 12b). This indicates
that Tarim Block separated from Australia and South China and
experienced a different displacement history after ∼650 Ma. Addi-
tional data are needed to decipher the driving mechanism for the
northward displacement of Tarim Block from ∼650 Ma to ∼600 Ma.
Alternatively, Tarim Block may remain close to Australia during
the Neoproterozoic–Paleozoic transition because the age of the
∼600 Ma paleopole of Tarim Block is not tightly constrained. The
age of ∼600 Ma of the studied Sugetbrak Fm was estimated by cor-
relating its carbon isotope curve with that of South China (Zhan
et
 al., 2007). The LA-ICP-MS U–Pb dating of detrital zircons from
the basal Sugetbrak Fm provided a maximum depositional age of
602 ± 13 Ma for the Sugetbrak Fm (Zhu et al., 2011). Thus, the pale-
omagnetically studied section of the Sugetbrak Fm (Zhan et al.,
2007) is likely younger than 600 Ma. If the age of the studied Suget-
brak section is revised to 560–570 Ma, the latitudinal displacement
pattern of Tarim Block would mimic that of Australia during the
Neoproterozoic-early Paleozoic transition (Fig. 12b).

Nevertheless, since the paleomagnetic data of this study were
obtained directly from the Qiaoenbrak diamictites, which are of
probable glaciogenic origin and equivalent to the Baiyisi diamic-
tites (Gao et al., 1981, 1985; XBGMR, 1993; Zhu and Wang, 2011),
this study potentially provides the ﬁrst direct constraint on the
paleolatitude of the glacial deposits in the Tarim Block. Our newly
determined low paleolatitude of 16.3 ± 5.6◦N joins the paleomag-
netic data from other cratons (e.g. Embleton and Williams, 1986;
Schmidt and Williams, 1995; Sohl et al., 1999; Schmidt et al., 2009)
in supporting the snowball earth hypothesis (Kirschvink, 1992;
Hoffman et al., 1998; Hoffman and Schrag, 2002) that argues for
low-latitude glaciations during the Neoproterozoic.
6. Conclusions
We have presented a detailed paleomagnetic and rock mag-
netic study of the Neoproterozoic diamictites of the Qiaoernbrak
Fm in the Aksu area, NW China to quantitatively constrain the
paleogeographic positions of the Tarim Block during the transition
from Rodinia breakup to Gondwana assembly in the middle to
late Neoproterozoic. The age of the studied section is constrained
at ∼730 Ma based on the stratigraphy and recent zircon U–Pb
chronologic data. Progressive alternating ﬁeld (AF) and thermal
demagnetization isolated ChRMs that mainly reside in magnetite
and are interpreted as pDRMs on the basis of the negative fold
test of a soft-sediment fold, the presence of both normal and
reversed polarities, positive conglomerate tests, and the pristine
sedimentary features of the studied rocks. Fourteen out of 17 sites
yielded stable ChRMs that correspond to a paleopole of /NAK = 6.3◦S,
ϕ = 17.5◦E, A95 = 9.1◦, N = 14 with a paleolatitude of 16.3 ± 5.6◦.
The new paleomagnetic results in conjunction with geologic
constraints place the Tarim Block alongside to either west or east
of Australia (WOA or EOA) at 16.3 ± 5.6◦N and the WOA position
is considered more likely based on the collectively favorable
evidence. Since the paleomagnetic data are obtained directly from
the ∼730 Ma diamictites that are probably glaciogenic in origin,
the newly determined low paleolatitude provides supportive
evidence for the Neoproterozoic snowball earth hypothesis.

The Modipe Gabbro is a Precambrian intrusive unit hosted by the Kaapvaal craton of South Africa and pro-
vides
 one of the oldest records of geomagnetic ﬁeld behavior in the late Archean. Earlier paleomagnetic
research
 into the Modipe Gabbro provided valuable insight into its magnetic properties and mineral-
ogy,
 but predate the development of paleomagnetic tools that are important in unraveling potentially
complex
 histories of Precambrian rocks. Further, a lack of information about the precise age of the
intrusion
 prevented this earlier paleomagnetic study from being used to evaluate the tectonic history
of
 the Kaapvaal craton. Here we present a comprehensive paleomagnetic and geochronologic study of
the
 Modipe Gabbro that complements and builds upon the existing work. The emplacement age of the
gabbro
 (2784.0 ± 1.0 Ma), established using the U–Pb ID-TIMS method on baddeleyite, links the intrusion
to
 nearby igneous bodies in the Kaapvaal craton, establishing one of the oldest fully differentiated mag-
matic
 events in the geologic record. The precise age of the Modipe Gabbro and ﬁeld observations about its
strike
 allow us to perform a tilt correction using the both the attitude and paleomagnetism of the nearby
Derdepoort
 basalts. The tilt-corrected data allow a comparison of Kaapvaal craton’s paleolatitude with
that
 of the Pilbara craton at 2.78 Ga, with implications for the existence of the supercraton Vaalbara.

1. Introduction
The transition from the Archean to the Paleoproterozoic
(3.0–2.5 Ga) is a key period in Earth’s geophysical and geochem-
ical evolution. In particular, this period encompasses an episode of
substantial continental crustal growth and preservation, thought to
be related to periodic mantle overturn events and extensive plume
volcanism (Condie, 2001). This reconstitution of the upper mantle
by deeper hotter mantle was followed by, or was synchronous with,
the assembly and breakup of some of the planet’s earliest supercon-
tinents or supercratons (Nance et al., 1986; Williams et al., 1991;
Young et al., 2001; Cheney, 1996; Aspler and Chiarenzelli, 1998;
Condie, 2001; Barley et al., 2005), and the development of oxy-
genated conditions in the atmosphere. Establishing links between
these major environmental changes and the suspected mantle-
plume tectonic regime that characterized the late Archean is an
ongoing research focus that is often hampered by the absence of
reliable paleomagnetic and geochronologic constraints.

One of the earliest and most inﬂuential paleomagnetic stud-
ies on Archean rocks was that of Evans and McElhinny (1966),
who examined the Modipe Gabbro in the Kaapvaal craton. This
intrusive unit outcrops as a chain of low rising hills, or inselbergs,
approximately 15 km long extending from southern Botswana into
northern South Africa (Fig. 1). The Modipe Gabbro was emplaced
as a sub-horizontal, sill-like body and the low-lying areas between
the gabbro inselbergs consist of soils derived from the Gaborone
Granite (McElhinny, 1966). Although exposures between the gab-
bro and the granite are exceedingly rare, Evans and McElhinny
(1966) reported a sheared contact between the two lithologies that
suggested that the gabbro was intruded by the granite. Importantly,
they reported a positive baked contact test between the two litholo-
gies. They also noted exceptionally stable magnetizations in the
gabbro with high coercivities (≥180 mT) and high unblocking tem-
peratures (>500 ◦C) and identiﬁed elongate magnetite inclusions
exsolved within clinopyroxene as the main carrier of remanence
(Evans et al., 1968). Subsequent work on similar occurrences of
magnetite exsolved from clinopyroxenes has shown that they are
robust recorders of the geomagnetic ﬁeld (e.g., Renne et al., 2002;
Feinberg et al., 2005; Muxworthy et al., 2013). However, these
exsolved magnetite crystals are not ubiquitous throughout the
Modipe Gabbro, and identical, stable remanences are found in those

fore, at least one other primary magnetic phase present, and we
have identiﬁed it as part of this study. There are no clear paleo-
horizontal indicators within the Modipe Gabbro, which precludes
evaluating whether a tilt-correction to paleomagnetic directions is
needed. Evans and McElhinny (1966) established a paleolatitude of
80◦ for the Modipe Gabbro without using any form of tilt correction,
and the corresponding virtual geomagnetic pole (VGP) calculated
from the mean of their sampling sites (33.3◦ S and 31.1◦ E) is still
used when discussing the tectonic history of the Kaapvaal craton.
The exact position of the Kaapvaal craton relative to that of the
Pilbara craton is especially important when considering the con-
ﬁgurational history of the supercontinent Vaalbara.
Two years after their paleomagnetic analysis of the Modipe Gab-
bro, McElhinny and Evans (1968) estimated the strength of the
Earth’s ancient geomagnetic ﬁeld, or paleointensity, at the time the
unit was emplaced. The Earth’s magnetic ﬁeld is generated by con-
vection of the liquid iron outer core and recordings of the strength
of the ﬁeld through time have been highly sought after to address
questions about the stand-off distance of the solar wind (Tarduno
et al., 2010) and the timing of the nucleation of solid inner core
(Smirnov et al., 2003). This study has been updated by the recent
work of Muxworthy et al. (2013) to indicate that magnetic ﬁeld
strength at the time of emplacement was approximately 80% of the
modern ﬁeld. However, the usefulness of this paleointensity esti-
mate has been blunted due to ambiguity surrounding the Modipe
Gabbro’s precise paleolatitude and age.
Until now, the age of the Modipe Gabbro has been roughly con-
strained by Rb–Sr and K–Ar ages determined by McElhinny (1966).
Rb–Sr total rock measurements yielded an age of 2630 ± 470 Ma.
K–Ar measurements of pyroxene separates from three sites
yielded ages ranging from ∼2600 to ∼3000 Ma with uncertain-
ties of ±100 Ma. The average of these pyroxene K–Ar dates is
2758 ± 126 Ma when recalculated with the calibration of Renne
et al. (2011) (Supplemental Data File). K–Ar measurements
on plagioclase separates yielded anomalously young ages of
1983–1934 Ma, which were interpreted to possibly reﬂect ther-
mal resetting by the nearby Bushveld Complex. The average K–Ar
plagioclase age of McElhinny (1966), recalculated per Renne et al.
(2011), is 1961 ± 52 Ma, which overlaps with integrated 40Ar/39Ar
cooling ages for plagioclase from a Bushveld gabbro reported by
Cassata et al. (2009). Thus, while portions of the paleomagnetic
analysis of the Modipe Gabbro have long been known to be of high
quality, it has been difﬁcult to make use of these analyses owing to
the poor geochronologic constraints on the unit.
Here we report the results of a new paleomagnetic and
geochronologic study of the Modipe Gabbro. We make use of
modern paleomagnetic protocols, including least-squares ﬁtting
and great circle analyses, to examine and reﬁne the earlier pale-
omagnetic work of Evans and McElhinny (1966). Rock magnetic
techniques are used to better characterize the extent of mineralogic
alteration experienced by the magnetic oxides within the gabbro
since their formation in the late Archean. The precise emplacement
age of Modipe Gabbro is determined using U–Pb TIMS geochrono-
logical methods using baddeleyite as a geochronometer. These
improved paleomagnetic and geochronologic data allow us to bet-
ter constrain the precise position of the Kaapvaal craton at the time
of the Modipe Gabbro’s emplacement and to use the data from the
Modipe Gabbro in reconstructions and evaluations of the super-
continent Vaalbara.

2. Petrography of the Modipe Gabbro
The Modipe Gabbro consists primarily of medium-grained
labradoritic plagioclase and clinopyroxene, both of which exhibit
progressively increasing levels of alteration toward the southeast.
This spatial trend in degree of alteration, combined with the K–Ar
plagioclase ages, is consistent with thermal effects of the Bushveld
Complex, which outcrops 20 km to the south of the Modipe Com-
plex. In more heavily altered samples, the clinopyroxene is replaced
by actinolite and chlorite with minor amounts of secondary mag-
netite, while plagioclase is altered to sericite (Fig. 2). Plagioclase
grains also exhibit low-level deformation features including bent
twin planes, growth steps in twin boundaries, and deformation
twins nucleating at high stress sites at grain boundaries (Fig. 2 and
Supplemental Data File). This low-level alteration is similar to that
observed in maﬁc dykes and sills that have undergone alteration
by metasomatic ﬂuids during and immediately after emplacement
(e.g., France et al., 2009). The textures observed in the Modipe

alteration likely occurred either during original emplacement of
the Modipe Gabbro or during the subsequent emplacement of the
Bushveld Complex toward the south. Despite this minimal alter-
ation, the Modipe is exceptionally well preserved and the more
northerly inselbergs show no petrographic evidence of regional
metamorphism.
Fe-oxides observed in thin section include large (>300 /H9262m)
grains of primary magnetite decorating the edges of plagioclase
laths, and secondary magnetite associated with the alteration of
Fe–Mg silicate minerals such as pyroxene and olivine. No Fe-
sulﬁdes were observed. Thorough examination of thin sections
from all four collection sites revealed no evidence of exsolved
magnetite inclusions in pyroxene. Evans and McElhinny (1966)
reported such inclusions in samples from just one site (BO), which is
located on the Botswana side of the Modipe Gabbro. The samples in
the present study were collected solely from the South African side
of the Modipe Gabbro, suggesting that conditions in this portion of
the Modipe were either (1) not suitable for the exsolution of mag-
netite from pyroxene, or (2) that the inclusions were sufﬁciently
disturbed during alteration of the pyroxene that they have become
obscured or destroyed.
3. U-Pb Geochronology
A description of the U–Pb isotopic methodology and results
for sample MO-3 are given in the Supplemental Data File and
the Concordia diagram of Fig. 3. Ten single baddeleyite crystals
yield a 207Pb/206Pb age of 2784.0 ± 1.0 Ma (2/ESC), with an MSWD
of 1.7. The uncertainty given does not include decay-constant
errors; including them produces an uncertainty of ±7.0 Ma. Using
the updated 235U decay constant and uncertainty of Mattinson
(2010), the 207Pb/206Pb age is 2779.9 ± 1.0 Ma without including
decay-constant uncertainties, and ±2.7 Ma when they are included.
For the purposes of consistency with previously published U–Pb
ages discussed here, we report the age and uncertainty using
only the decay constants of Jaffey et al. (1971) and ignoring the
decay-constant errors. These errors must be considered however,
in comparing our results with those from any other radioisotopic
system. Th/U ratios are between 0.02 and 0.05, typical values for
baddeleyite. Uranium concentrations are between 323 ppm and
770 ppm. The data are concordant or slightly discordant (up to
2.6% discordant, sample #10) (Fig. 3, Supplementary Table 2), but
give consistently overlapping 207Pb/206Pb ages. The discordance is
attributed to minor Pb loss, and the lower intercept of a regression
line through all data goes through the origin, making any event
that would disturb the U–Pb systematics of the baddeleyite grains
unlikely.
In the context of establishing a precise and accurate age for
the larger magmatic event using the most up-to-date radioisotopic
parameters as of the time of this writing, the age of 2779.9 ± 1.0
[2.7] Ma must be the preferred age of emplacement. However, the
geological interpretations of our data require direct comparison
with previous work, which has not been re-calibrated using the
new 235U decay constant. Therefore, for our purposes the average
207Pb/206Pb age of 2784.0 ± 1.0 Ma reported here is considered the
age of emplacement of the Modipe Gabbro.
4. Rock magnetism
Expanded descriptions of the rock magnetic and paleomagnetic
methodologies are included in the supplemental information ﬁle.
4.1. Room temperature measurements
Mass normalized, in-phase susceptibility values range from
1.1 × 10−7 to 2.1 × 10−6 m3 kg−1, with a median value of
2.5 × 10−7 m3 kg−1. Susceptibilities from samples collected at the
southernmost site, MO3, are three times greater than those of
the other sites (Supplemental Data File). Other room-temperature
magnetic properties from MO3 stand out when comparing results
between sites. The median coercivity (Hc) at MO3 (8 mT) is sig-
niﬁcantly lower than that of MO1 (13 mT), MO2 (17 mT), or MO4
(15 mT). Similarly, the median “squareness” ratio, Mr/Ms, at MO3
(0.09) is notably lower than that of MO1 (0.13), MO2 (0.19), or MO4
(0.21).
4.2. Magnetic properties as a function of temperature
To determine the composition of the magnetic minerals in
the Modipe Gabbro a subset of samples were selected for
high-temperature susceptibility and strong-ﬁeld thermomagnetic
measurements. Measurements of susceptibility as a function of
temperature revealed a mean Curie temperature of 579 ± 11 ◦C
(N = 11), and the heating portion of the /US(T) experiments are shown
in Fig. 4. Cooling curves are generally reversible and are not shown
here in order to allow the reader to better evaluate changes in
susceptibility during heating. The /US(T) experiments show that mag-
netic mineral concentrations vary across the Modipe Gabbro, and
in some cases, ferromagnetic minerals are sufﬁciently rare that
their signal in the /US(T) data is nearly obscured by the paramagnetic
behavior of the silicate matrix minerals (e.g., amphibole, pyroxene,
and olivine). Regardless of the concentration of magnetic material,
the Curie temperature estimates are well clustered near 580 ◦C, the
temperature expected for stoichiometric magnetite.
Strong-ﬁeld thermomagnetic measurements produced a mean
Curie temperature of 582 ± 6 ◦C (Fig. 4), in good agreement with the
susceptibility data. These results are slightly lower than the 600 ◦C
unblocking temperature reported in Evans and McElhinny (1966)
and Evans et al. (1968), but are still within acceptable agreement,
as these older estimates were determined using relatively coarse
6–8 step thermal demagnetization protocols.
