Abstract—Detailed paleomagnetic studies have shown that the effusive Permian–Triassic traps in the Kotui
River valley were formed as the result of volcanic activity , which occurred in the form of volcanic pulses and
individual eruptions with net duration of at most 7000–8000 years, excluding the periods of volcanic quies-
cence. According to the analysis of the paleomagnetic data earlier obtained by Heunemann and his coauthors
[2004b] on the Abagalakh and Listvyanka sections in the Norilsk region, those geological units were formed
during 25 volcanic pulses and separate eruptions, whic h all lasted up to 8000 years altogether, whereas the
total time of formation (including the periods of volcanic quiescence) exceeded 10000–100000 years for the
Norilsk section and was probably a bit shorter for the Ko tui section. Comparison of the positions of virtual
geomagnetic poles calculated for the Norilsk and the Kotui sections provides no grounds to suggest that these
sections were formed at different geological times.The scatter in the positions of the virtual geomagnetic poles
(VGP) for the directional groups and individual directions (58 altogether) jointly for the two sections (more
than 160 lava flows) indicates that the secular geomagnetic variations at the Permian–Triassic boundary had
similar amplitudes to those that occurred in the past 5 Ma.

nation accuracy of the mean paleomagnetic direction
being 4°–6°, this means that the volcanic flows that
were outpoured with a gap exceeding 300–400 years
will normally have statistically different mean paleo-
magnetic directions. In contrast, the flows that were
formed within such a time interval will be character-
ized by statistically undistinguishable directions.
Hence, if the average directions of the neighboring
flows are statistically indiscernible (e.g., at the 95%
confidence level), these flows can be organized in
directional groups, each corresponding to a given indi-
vidual volcanic pulse. Hereinafter, volcanic pulses will
be understood as the short bursts of volcanic activity
(and corresponding series of flows) separated by rela-
tively longer quiet periods.
The number of directional groups and individual
directions (the latter correspond to the individual
flows that statistically differ in their average directions
from the neighboring flows) in this case will be equal to
the number of volcanic bursts during which the geo-
logical section of interest was formed. Here, it is
assumed that each volcanic pulse lasted at most 300–
400 years, while each individual flow corresponded to
a time interval of at most 10–100 years [Thordarson
and Self, 2003; Chenet et al., 2009].
The statistical procedure that we applied to identify
the directional groups and individual directions is
described in [Chenet et al., 2009].
We note that the geomagnetic variations are not
unidirectional and thus the D–I (declination–incli-
nation) diagram may contain overlaps (see, e.g., [Gal-
let et al., 2002]). However, in our opinion, such over-
laps are unlikely for the neighboring pulses. If such a
situation still occurs, this event will be recognized as a
single pulse instead of being identified as two separate
pulses, which will result in an insignificant underesti-
mation of the number of pulses in the section.
Another paleomagnetic constraint, which we used
while studying the lava flows, is based on the hypothe-
sis of geocentric axial dipole [Khramo v et al., 1982],
widely adopted in the paleomagnetic community .
According to this hypothesis, the geomagnetic field,
which is time-averaged over rather long interval, coin-
cides with the field of the magnetic dipole placed in
the center of the Earth an d aligned with the Earth’s
rotational axis. The length of the interval of time aver-
aging should be sufficiently large to annihilate the geo-
magnetic variations; to date, this interval is commonly
assumed by most researchers [Tauxe, 2010] to be 
104–
105 years. If this hypothesis is valid (which is indeed
supported by numerous investigations, see, e.g.,
[McElhinny , 2004]), the mean paleomagnetic direc-
tion, determined for the stratigraphic interval formed
within 
104–105 years and longer, will correspond to the
dipole’s pole that coincides with the pole of the
Earth’s rotation. (Evidently , here, the considered time
interval should be sufficiently short to allow one to dis-
regard the plate motion, which must be taken into

pole, which averages the secular variations, is referred
to as the paleomagnetic pole.
Correspondingly , if the pole calculated for some
stratigraphic interval with an unknown duration statis-
tically significantly differs from the known paleomag-
netic pole (for the given time and given tectonic
block), we should suspect that the secular variations in
this interval have not been completely averaged. This,
in turn, suggests that the formation of the considered
stratigraphic unit took less than 10
5 years. As a result,
we obtain the second paleomagnetic constraint, which
can be used for estimating the duration of the forma-
tion of trap volcanic sequences.
The third and the fourth paleomagnetic constraints
are applicable if the section under study contains
intervals corresponding to the geomagnetic reversals
or geomagnetic excursions. Since, according to the
current estimates [Merrill et al., 1996], the duration of
the reversals and the excursions does not usually
exceed 10000 years and 2000–3000 years, respectively ,
we may conclude that the duration of the formation of
the corresponding intervals of the geological section
also does not exceed these values.
It is worth noting that caution should be exercised
when applying each of the mentioned paleomagnetic
constraints, since all of them are based on certain
assumptions. On the other hand, it should also be rec-
ognized that these assumptions are often very well sub-
stantiated and they rely on generally used paleomag-
netic research practice.
THE OBJECT OF THE STUDY
The field works of 2008–2009 were focused on the
magnetostratigraphic study of the lower part of the
volcanic trap section of the Maimecha–Kotui region
(Fig. 1). During these expeditions, we have described
and sampled several exposures outcropping along the
Kotui River valley in the region of the Medvezhya
River mouth and 10 km downstream of the Kayak vil-
lage (Fig. 1). Stratigraphically , the studied segment of
the section corresponds to the Arydzhang suite and to
a considerable portion of the Onkuchak suite of the
Kogotok series. Following [Fedorenko et al., 2000], it
is assumed in the present work that the youngest flows
and tuffs, which are underlain by the terrigenous
sequences of the Tungusskaya series (
C2-P 2) and
regarded by several authors as members of the Kharda-
khskaya or Potokoiskaya suite [Y egorov , 1995], refer to
the bottom of the Arydzhang suite.
The Arydzhang suite is predominantly composed
of the volcanic flows of alkaline ultramafic and mafic
rocks (melanephilinites, melilites, limburgites, and
picrites) with separate thin tuff interbeds. The overall

PALEOMAGNETIZM
From each flow , 8 to 20 samples were taken, whose
orientation was determined using the magnetic com-
pass. No effect of the ro cks on the compass readings
was noticed, which agrees with the information from
our German colleagues who worked earlier on these
exposures and used solar and magnetic compasses in
their work [Heunemann, 2004a]. The laboratory tests
were carried out in the Schmidt Institute of Physics of
the Earth, Russian Academy of Sciences (RAS) in
Moscow; in the Laboratory of Rock Magnetism at the
Faculty of Geology , Moscow State University; and in
the Institut de Physique du Globe de Paris. The tests
were conducted according to the standard technique
[Zijderveld, 1967; Khramov et al., 1982; Shipunov ,
1999; Collinson, 1980; Kirschvink, 1980; McFadden,
1988; McFadden and McElhinny , 1990; Enkin, 1994;
T orsvik et al., 1990].
All specimens were subjected to detailed thermal
cleaning with heating up to 
580–680°С. The number
of progressive thermal demagnetization steps was nor-
mally at least 15; in some cases, the number of steps
was greater. The thermal demagnetization of the spec-
imens was carried out using thermal demagnetizers
(including TD-80 furnaces designed by Magnetic
Measurements Ltd., UK), providing values of the
uncompensated field as low as at most 5–10 nT . The
remanent magnetization of the specimens was mea-
sured using the SQUID magnetometer designed by
2-G Enterprices and using the JR-6 spinner magne-
tometer. During the measurements of the magnetiza-
tion, the specimens were shielded from the external
magnetic field. The measurement data were processed
using the Enkin [1994] computer program package,
where the PCA (Principal Component Analysis)
method [Kirschvink, 1980] is applied for the identifi-
cation of the components of magnetization. The
parameters of secular variations were calculated using
the program package developed by Tauxe [2010].
The quality of the paleomagnetic record in differ-
ent flows is different. The paleomagnetic signal is most
distinctly identified in the samples of the Onkuchak-
skaya suite. In most of the samples of this suite, two
components of magnetization are reliably revealed.
The relatively less stable component of magnetiza-
tion, which has an orientation close to the direction of
the present geomagnetic field, is removed at tempera-
tures of 
200–250°С. After the removal of this compo-
nent, the specimen preserves one (characteristic)
component of magnetization, which is destroyed in
the temperature interval 
200–600°С (Fig. 2a and 2b).
The paleomagnetic record in six flows from the lower
part of the suite (flow6–flow11) was strongly noised,
which prevented us from identifying the characteristic
magnetization in these samples.
The overall Arydzhangskaya suite exhibits a poor
paleomagnetic record, which is inferior to that of the
Onkuchakskaya suite. Nevertheless, by taking a
greater number of samples and by targeting those seg-
ments of flows that are the most promising for signal
retention, we managed to obtain the average paleomag-
netic directions for practically all sampled stratigraphic
units. Unfortunately , for some flows (see Table 1) we
were not able to achieve the desired accuracy of deter-
mination of the average direction (characterized by
the value of the radius of the circle of confidence,
alfa95). The magnetization of rocks of the Arydzhang-
skaya suite has the same component content as the
rocks of the Onkuchakskaya suite (Figs. 2a and 2b):
there are two components, the less stable one, being
directed close to the present geomagnetic direction,
and the more stable ancient characteristic component.
The less stable component is removed by heating up to
200–250°С, while the range of unblocking tempera-
tures for the characteristic component of magnetiza-
tion spans 550–600°С and sometimes higher.
The distributions of the flow-mean geomagnetic
directions of the characteristic component for both
suites are presented in Figs. 2c and 2d. As seen from
this figure and Table 1, the specimens have both the
normal and the reversed polarity of magnetization.
The mean directions of the normal and the reversed
polarity are almost antipodal; nevertheless, the rever-
sal test [McFadden and McElhinny , 1990] is negative
for the whole set of vectors and for the Arydzhangskaya
suite alone. The probable reasons for this are the insuf-
ficient averaging of secular geomagnetic variations or
the presence of some relatively small contribution of
the present geomagnetic field component, which has

The detailed magnetomineralogical studies of the
Onkuchakskaya rock series showed that the main mag-

The presence of magnetic minerals that have been
formed at the early stages of the geological history of
rocks, the positive conglomerate test, the occurrence
of almost antiparallel directions of the normal and the
reversed polarity , and the closeness of the calculated
geomagnetic directions to the trap directions esti-

characteristic magnetization is the primary (or close to
the primary) magnetization. That the magnetization is
the primary magnetization is also supported by the
presence of the directional groups in the sections that

DISSCUSSION OF THE RESUL TS
Directional Groups and Individual Directions 
Overall, we have studied 80 flows of the Arydzhang-
skaya and Onkuchakskaya suites. The mean paleo-
magnetic directions were determined for 75 flows
(Table 1). According to the analysis based on the tech-
nique described in [Chenet et al., 2008], there are 16
directional groups and 17 individual directions in the
rocks of the Kotui section. The number of flows for
which the directional groups were determined was 2 to
10 (Fig. 3b). The largest volcanic pulses (which we
determine from the directional groups) are the P12
(5 flows), P8 (3 flows) and P10 (10 flows) pulses,
which have thicknesses of 57, 50, and 49 m, respec-
tively .
We applied the same method to analyze the data
obtained by Heunemann and his coauthors [2004b]
for the Norilsk section, which they have studied on the
Abagalakh and Listvyanka exposures. The analysis
showed that there are 16 directional groups and 9 indi-
vidual directions in this section (Table 2, Fig. 3a). The
P1 (12 flows) and P16 (8 flows) are the largest pulses
here, each corresponding to a stratigraphic interval
with a thickness noticeably in excess of 100 m.
The Virtual Geomagnetic Poles
of the Kotui and the Norilsk Sections 
Many authors (see the discussion in [Gurevitch et al.,
2004]) correlate the stratigraphic intervals of the Kotui
and the Norilsk sections, which have the normal geo-
magnetic polarity (Figs. 4a and 4e). In this connec-
tion, it is instructive to compare the succession of the
positions of the virtual geomagnetic poles (VGP)
obtained in the present work for the Kotui section with
a similar succession for the Norilsk section [Heune-
mann, 2004b] for the mentioned and the adjacent
stratigraphic intervals. In the lowermost part of the
Norilsk sequence, Heunemann with his coauthors
recognizes the flows corresponding to the geomag-
netic reversal followed by the geomagnetic excursion
that occurred soon after the reversal (see Table 2). This
part of the section together with several subjacent
reversely magnetized flows of the Ivakinskaya suite will
be further conventionally referred to as the transitional
interval (TR). The transition interval is followed by the
interval of normal polarity (N), which corresponds to
the normal field.
In the Kotui section, soon after the reversed polar-
ity changes into the normal polarity , we observe three
consecutive flows with the anomalous paleomagnetic
directions (flow-3–flow1). Following Heunemann
and his coauthors [2004b], we supposedly correlate
these directions with the geomagnetic excursion. Cor-
respondingly , for the convenience of comparison, here
we also define the transitional interval (the hard1–
flow1 flows) and the normal (the flow13–fl42 flows)
intervals (TR and N).
The succession of the transitional VGP of the Kotui
section, unlike the corresponding Norilsk succession,
does not contain any record of the reversal; however,
as in the Norilsk succession, it includes anomalous
poles (poles 8, 9, and 10 in Fig. 4g supposedly corre-
sponding to the excursion) preceded by the normal
northern virtual poles (poles 4, 5, 6, and 7 in Fig. 4g).
Since the number of the latter is small and their clus-
tering is relatively weak, one cannot make any sound
inferences regarding their statistical coincidence or
difference from the corresponding poles of the Norilsk
section (poles 5, 6, 7 in Fig. 4c) because the parameter
γc for them [McFadden and McElhinny , 1990] is
greater than 25 °. It may only be noted that they are

no reasonable grounds to believe that the geomagnetic
field during the excursions is a dipole field, the differ-
ence in the positions of the corresponding poles for the
considered regions, which are spaced apart by more
than 500 km, cannot be regarded as a sure indication
of different geomagnetic excursions.
Therefore, the attempt to verify the identity of R–N
transitions of the Kotui and the Norilsk sections by
comparing the virtual geomagnetic poles of their tran-
sitional intervals proved to be a failure.
The comparison of the average poles of the normal
intervals of the Kotui and the Norilsk sections
(Figs. 4d, 4h, Tables 1, 2, poles N2, K2) shows that
they are statistically undistinguishable (
γ/γc =
8.0°/10.9°). The same holds true also for the poles
obtained from all directional groups and the individual
directions, except for the anomalous poles (poles N1
and K1, γ/γc = 6.9°/7.6°). Poles N1 and K1 are also very
close to the Triassic paleomagnetic poles NSP2 and
NSP4 of the Siberian platform [Pavlov et al., 2004].
The geological data and the isotopic datings
[Fedorenko et al., 2000; Kamo et al., 2003] unambig-
uously indicate that the both sections were formed
within a relatively short geological time of at most a
few Ma. This means that if the secular geomagnetic
variations in both sections relating to the same rigid
plate are completely removed by averaging, the corre-
sponding paleomagnetic poles should coincide, just as
we actually observe in our studies.
Thus, the statistical indiscernibility of the Norilsk
and the Kotui mean poles can be regarded as an indi-
cation of the secular variations having been com-
pletely averaged in the discussed sections; the sections
themselves were formed (see the second paleomag-
netic constraint discussed above) within a time interval
that is in excess of 
104–105 years.

CONCLUSIONS
Let us summarize the above discussion. According
to [Heunemann et al., 2004b], the lower part of the
Norilsk section bears the re cords of the reversed geo-
magnetic field and the field at the time of the geomag-
netic excursion, while in other parts of the section the
secular geomagnetic variations are rather well aver-
aged. Thus, based on these data, we may assert that,
although the individual members of the section were
formed within a rather short time (flows vs1–gd1 in
less than 10 000 years, flows tk3–nd6 in less than
2000–3000 years), the overall duration of the forma-
tion of the Norilsk section was more than 10000–
100000 years.
In the course of the formation of this section, the
eruptive activity occurred in the form of either volca-
nic pulses or single eruptions. Overall, 25 pulses and
single eruptions took place during the geological his-
tory of the Norilsk section, whose net duration
(excluding periods of quiescence) did not exceed
7000–8000 years (see the discussion of the first paleo-
magnetic constraint in the section The Method).
The number of pulses and single eruptions (16 and
17, respectively) established for the Arydzhangskaya
and Onkuchakskaya suites shows that the net eruptive
activity during the deposition of the Kotui section
(excluding the quiescence periods) also lasted about
7000–8000 years. The total time of the Kotui section’s

Palaeomagnetism and the age of the Cracow volcanic rocks

SUMMARY
Permian rhyodacites, melaphyres and tuffs from the Cracow area (South Poland) were sampled
for the palaeomagnetic and isotope studies. Single-grain U-Pb dating of most zircon grains
separated from the rhyodacites gave mean age of magma emplacement of 294.2 ± 2.1 Ma.
Some zircons, however, displayed younger ages (268.7 ± 3.4 Ma), probably related to the
metasomatic alterations of these rocks. T wo Permian components of magnetizations related
to these processes were isolated and together with previously deﬁned Late Carboniferous–
Permian palaeomagnetic poles from South Poland were used for construction of the regional
apparent polar wander path (APWP). The Early Permian segment of this APWP shows a
certain departure from the coeval part of the Fennoscandian APWP due to anticlockwise
rotations of studied rocks most probably caused by mid-Permian sinistral tectonic movements
along reactivated prominent Variscan faults of Central Europe. This sense of tectonic mobility
does not support the hypothesis about transformation from Pangea ‘B’ to Pangea ‘A’ along an
intra-Pangea dextral megashear during the Permian. Older than previously assumed ages of the
post-Variscan igneous rocks of Central Europe reduce overlap of Gondwana’ s and Laurussia’ s
parts of the Early Permian Pangea ‘A’.
Key words: Palaeomagnetism applied to tectonics; Continental tectonics: strike-slip and
transform; Europe.
1 INTRODUCTION
The Late Palaeozoic conﬁguration and history of Pangea is still de-
bated. Most of palaeomagnetic data indictate a substantial amount
of overlap of continental crust in the Early Permian between Gond-
wana and Laurussia if reconstructed in Pangea ‘A’ conﬁguration
(Wegener 1924; Irving 1977, 2004; Muttoniet al. 1996). The intro-
duction of the Pangea ‘B’ model (Irving 1977) seemed to eliminate
this problem. Since Pangea ‘A’ is well deﬁned in the Early Jurassic
just prior to opening of the North Atlantic the scenario of transfor-
mation from the model ‘B’ to ‘A’ had to be presented. According to
Muttoni et al. (2003) the transformation from Pangea ‘B’ to Pangea
‘A’ took place during the Permian because Late Permian palaeo-
magnetic data allow a Pangea ‘A’ conﬁguration. They cited also
geological factors supportive of an intra-Permian age for the transi-
tion. This transformation along an intra-Pangea dextral megashear
system of about 3500 km occurred after the cooling of the Variscan
mega-suture (see Arthaud & Matte 1977, Matte 1991) and lasted
ca. 20 Myr. It should be stressed that in the model of Muttoniet al.
(2003) the main SE–NW trending faults of Central Europe being a
part of the Late Palaeozoic strike-slip system of Arthaud and Matte
(1977) acted also as dextral ones.
Torcq et al. (1997) postulate Triassic age of the intra-Pangean
translation. In their model the Early Triassic global transgression
was a consequence of the development of new ocean ridges re-
sulting from the rupture of Pangea B and the opening westward of
NeoTethys.
New Permian palaeomagnetic data from Gondwana seem to
support a Pangea ‘B’ palaeogeography in Early Permian times
(Rakotosolofo et al. 2006). However, detailed selection of Per-
mian palaeomagnetic poles from Laurussia performed by Van der
V oo and Torsvik (2004) signiﬁcantly decreases the overlap be-
tween both parts of Pangea ‘A’ model. Moreover, new isotope
study of Permian igneous rock from Scandinavia (Van der V oo
& Torsvik 2004) may indicate that the mean age of the Autu-
nian volcanites from post-Variscan Europe can be older than pre-
viously assumed. If so, then overlap of Gondwana’ s and Laurus-
sia’ s parts of the Early Permian Pangea ‘A’ could be additionally
reduced.
The palaeomagnetic data from the Sudetes (Nawrocki 1998) and
some geological observations performed in the southern part of
Germany (Mattern 2001) indicate that during the Permian the NW–
SE trending faults recorded rather a sinistral sense of the tectonic
transport. Anticlockwise rotations of the Late Carboniferous to
Early Permian palaeomagnetic poles with respect to the coeval poles
from the Fennoscandia were reported from the Sudetes and because
of this, a local Sudetian apparent polar wander path has been pro-
posed (Nawrocki 1998; Jele´nska et al. 2003).

The preliminary aim of this paper is to deﬁne an age of the Cracow
volcanic rocks and to yield palaeomagnetic poles from these rocks.
New palaeomagnetic studies should answer the questions if older
palaeomagnetic data from Europe used for the construction of the
Permian Pangea are properly time constrained. We are also going
to check if anticlockwise rotations deducted from palaeomagnetic
data from the Sudetes were a local phenomenon or took place in the
zone of another main fault of central Europe—Cracow-Hamburg as
well.
2 STUDY AREA AND PREVIOUS
P ALAEOMAGNETIC RESULTS
The border zone of the Brunosilesia and Ma /suppresslopolska terranes is
deﬁned by a narrow fault zone ‘Cracow-Lubliniec’ that probably
represents a segment of much larger, transcontinental tectonic line
‘Cracow-Hamburg’ (Fig. 1a;˙Zaba 1999). This zone has Proterezoic
foundations, and was active from earliest Palaeozoic through to
Cenozoic times. The effects of polyphase activity of this fault control
the structural features of the whole zone including areas with igneous
rocks of the Krzeszowice region, where vertical faulting, related to
the tectonic activity of the deep substratum, led to the formation of
numerous fault macroblocks (op. cit.).
The Late Palaeozoic volcanic rocks of the Krzeszowice region are
exposed over an area of approximately 200 km
2 about 20 km west of
Cracow in Southern Poland (Fig. 1b). Composition of the volcanic
rocks ranges from basaltic trachyandesites to rhyodacites with mi-
nor andesites and lamprophyres (Czerny & Muszy´nski 1997, 2000).
Basaltic trachyandesites form several lava ﬂows intercalated with
pyroclastics and erupted along SE–NW trending faults bordering
Nieporaz-Brod/suppressla graben (Fig. 1b). Sporadically basaltic rocks form
small intrusions, for example, a sill in Nied´zwiedzia G´ora. Rhyo-
dacites intruded at shallow levels forming predominantly laccoliths
and have been encountered in Zalas-Orlej, Mikinia and Dubie vicin-
ity. Felsic tuffs outcrop in the area of Filipowice. All volcanic rocks
have high (or very high—e.g. Filipowice tuff) potassium contents.
The potassium enrichment is attributed to postmagmatic processes,
for example, adularyzation and seladonization (S /suppresslaby 1987, 1990;
Parchoniak & Weiser 1992; Czerny & Muszynski 1997). Apart from
the beds deformed in the contact zones developed near the igneous
bodies the Permian and younger sedimentary rocks of the Krzes-
zowice region dips very gently (ca.3
◦) to the east.
The ﬁrst age determinations of volcanic rocks in the Krzeszow-
ice region were based on the Filipowice rhyodacitic tuffs superpo-
sition relatively to travertines. The tuffs are contemporaneous with
the travertines palaeontologically dated as being Early Permian in
age (Lipiarski 1971). In turn, isotopic dates obtained for the Fil-
ipowice tuffs have been interpreted as timing of the late potassium
remobilization. The K-Ar whole rock method yields 193 ± 0.7 Ma
somewhat different from that of the biotite 230± 11 Ma (Borucki &
Oberc 1964). Autigenic illite separated from the same rock showed
199.3 ± 0.7 Ma (Michalik et al. 2004). Dating of the Zalas rhy-
odacite with track’ s method indicate 295 Ma (Skowro´nski 1974).
Basaltic trachyandesites have not been dated so far.
The exposures of the volcanic rocks of the Zalas-Orlej area are
concordant with the gravimetric anomaly of a diameter of 4–6 km
2
(Kurbiel 1978). The study on the tectonics of the porphyritic intru-
sion proved that all the outcrops belong to a single magmatic stock (a
laccolith), resulting from magma injection into the Lower Carbonif-
erous mudstones (D˙zu/suppressly´nski 1955). These are porphyritic rocks with
plagioclase, biotite and altered hornblende phenocrysts and red or
grey matrix composed predominantly of quartz, K-feldspar and ap-
atite. The rocks were classiﬁed as rhyodacites (Czerny & Muszy´nski
1997; Lewandowska & Rospondek 2003; Musia/suppressl 1996; Muszy´nski
1995). The variation of the rock colour is ascribed to late or post-
magmatic rock alterations (Musia /suppressl 1996; S /suppresslaby 1987). Similar in
size and chemistry Mikinia rhyodacite do not show macroscopic
diversity but the top of the volcanic body displays high potassium
enrichment (e.g. Bolewski 1939; S/suppresslaby 1990). The phenocrysts as-
semblage additionally to that described from Zalas contains quartz.
On the basis of geological (Parachoniak & Weiser 1992) and geo-
chemical (Czerny & Muszy´nski 2000) observations, genetically as-
sociated with the Mikinia rhyodacite volcano are tuffs from Filipow-
ice. These felsic tuffs are classiﬁed as trachytes (op. cit.) probably
due to potassium enrichment (Michalik et al. 2004). Maﬁc rocks
cropping out in the vicinity of Regulice have in part ﬂuidal textures
and miarolitic cavities. The pyroclastic material terminates each lava
ﬂow. Fine grained plagioclase (form labrador-andesine-oligoclase
group) and pyroxene (from diopside-augite group) groundmass with
few olivine (hypershen often altered to iddingsite) phenocrysts is a
signiﬁcant feature of the massive variety of these rocks (Czerny &
Muszy´nski 1997). They are classiﬁed as basaltic trachyandesites
(op. cit.).
The volcanics from the Krzeszowice region were palaeomagnet-
icaly studied by Birkenmajer and Nairn (1964). Result of this study
is not helpful for stratigraphic correlation of these rocks because
it was based on limited number of samples only and the statisctics
parameters are very poor. Moreover, the authors did not perform the
palaeomagnetic contact tests. An attempt of the age estimation for
the Zalas laccolith using the palaeomagnetic method was done by
Nawrocki et al. (2005). For this purpose samples were taken from
the rhyodacites and neighbouring Visean sediments cropping out
in three localities. T wo components of magnetization were isolated
in the volcanic rocks and Visean sediments. The ‘A’ component,
common for the greenish rhyodacites and Visean sediments (posi-
tive contact test), was carried by magnetite and was regarded to be
primary (Nawrocki et al. 2005). The comparison of the mean incli-
nation of this component with the expected (reference) stable Eu-
ropean inclinations lead to conclusions that the Zalas laccolith was
emplaced about 280 Ma ago. The second component ‘B’, character-
istic for reddish rhyodacites, was carried by hematite and according
to the authors (op. cit.) was recorded during the Late Permian ( ca.
260 Ma) metasomatic alterations of these rocks. The palaeomag-
netic poles calculated for the ‘A’ component is not in agreement with
the corresponding Permian segment of the Baltic APWP . Nawrocki
et al. (2005) draw a preliminary interpretation, suggesting that the
disagreement was due to anticlockwise block rotations of the stud-
ied rocks, most probably connected with the Early Permian sinistral
transtensional tectonic regime in the area of Central Europe. Up to
this time poor age constrains for the Permian segment of the Baltic
APWP and limited number of studied outcrops and samples pointed
out the necessity of further palaeomagnetic and isotope studies of
the volcanics from the Krzeszowice region.

4 ISOTOPE AGES
A total of 23 analyses were done on single zircon grains (Table 1).
Most of zircons from the Zalas quarry and all zircons from the Orlej
quarry are concordant forming one cluster with an age of 294.2 ±
2.1 Ma (Figs 2b–d). The mean age calculated for the zircon grains
from the Zalas quarry only is a bit older (295.1 ± 2.6 Ma). Sur-
prisingly four zircon grains from the Zalas quarry assemble in the
second cluster revealing the presence of another mean isotope age
of 268.7 ± 3.4 Ma (Figs 2b and c). Analyses 16.1 (Table 1) is
strongly discordant (Fig. 2b). In summary, the data from the Zalas
rhyodacite provides strong evidences of the Early Permian (Sakmar-
ian/Asselian) zircons, and clearly suggest also the presence of zircon
grains of middle Permian age (Wordian-Kungurian). This age corre-
sponds to the age of metasomatic alterations of these rocks inferred
from preliminary palaeomagnetic data (Nawrocki et al. 2005).

emplacement. Because of this the component ‘A’ was recordedca.
294 Ma ago. The second component, ‘B’, characteristic for the red-
dish rhyodacites and melaphyres that underwent metasomatic alter-
ations, is carried by hematite and was recorded most probably thanks
to metasomatose. There is no direct evidence that the younger zir-
con age (Fig. 2b, Table 1) is coeval with metasomatic alterations.
It should be stressed, however, that there is no other processes that
could reset or annex zircon grains in the Cracow volcanites. Because
of this the most likely age of the metasomatose and the component
‘B’ is of about 270 Ma (Fig. 2c).
The mean palaeomagnetic poles calculated for the Cracow vol-
canites have been compared with the apparent polar wander path
(APWP) characteristic for the Fennoscandian part of the East Euro-
pean Craton. The APWP characteristic for the whole of pre-Alpine
Europe should be treated rather as to big simpliﬁcation since many
Late Carboniferous to Early Permian poles from Variscan Europe
depart distinctly from the coeval Baltic poles (Cogn´e et al. 1993;
Nawrocki 1998; Henry et al. 1999; Jele´nska et al. 2003). It should
be stressed that these poles display the same, anticlockwise course
of rotations. The departure of the poles deﬁned in the Permian St
Affrique and Largentiere basins is explained as resulting from re-
gional syn-extensional tectonics (Cogn´e et al. 1993; Henry et al.
1999). Anticlockwise rotations of palaeopoles isolated from the
Late Carboniferous to Early Permian sedimentary and volcanic
rocks of Sudetes is regarded as consequence of regional transten-
sion and activity of sinistral faults (Nawrocki 1998) or as effect
of block rotation of the whole Variscan Europe (Jele´ nska et al.
2003).

Up till now an age of the Autunian volcanites from the Sudetes
have not been constrained by any modern isotope study. In order to
deﬁne their palaeomagnetic age, the palaeoinclinations deﬁned for
some Sudetian volcanic rocks (Nawrocki 1997, 1998), after recal-
culation to geographic coordinates of Cracow, have been compared
with the reference curve of palaeoinclination characteristic for Late
Carboniferous–Late Permian of southern Poland. It is clearly visible
that inclination of direction ‘A’ characteristic for the Cracow vol-
canites and inclinations characteristic for the Autunian rhyodacites
and melaphyres studied in the Sudetes form one cluster (Fig. 8).
Therefore, it is likely that Autunian volcanic activity in both places
of southern Poland took place ca. 294 Ma ago and was constrained
to a relatively short geological event.
The inﬂuence of the Early Permian magmatism on the palaeo-
magnetic record in remagnetized carbonates of western and cen-
tral Europe still has not been proven. Permian remagnetizations of
Palaeozoic carbonates were documented in several places of pre-
Alpine Europe (e.g. Nawrocki 1993; Zegers et al. 2003; Zwing
et al. 2005; Grabowski et al. 2006). A comparison of reference
curve of palaeoinclination with the inclinations characteristic for
remagnetized Devonian carbonates from Upper Silesia and Holy
Cross Mountains (Nawrocki 1993; Grabowski et al. 2006) leads to
the conclusion that two events of Permian remagnetization of these
carbonates were coeval with the magma emplacement and with the
metasomatose of volcanic rocks from the Cracow region (Fig. 8).
It means that remagnetizing brines were most probably initiated by
the same processes. The paths for regional migration of brines and
thermochemical or chemical remagnetizations were opened thanks
to two Permian tectonic events. A limited time of Autunian magma-
tism in both regions of southern Poland and observed rotations of
Early Permian palaeomagnetic poles could indicate that the magma
emplacement and its later metasomatose were accompanied by a
short periods of transtensional tectonic activity.
The eastern departures of northern palaeomagnetic poles isolated
from the Autunian rocks of southern Poland may indicate anticlock-
wise rotations of the studied rocks of magnitude up to 45
◦ (pole OC1,
Nawrocki et al. 2005). The youngest pole deviated in such a way
from the Fennoscandian reference path was isolated from the upper
Autunian sediments covering the Early Permian igneous rocks in the
North Sudetic Basin (Nawrocki 1998). On the other hand the palaeo-
magnetic pole ‘B’ and pole isolated from the Zechstein sediments
of Sudetes (Nawrocki 1997) overlap the Fennoscandian APWP . Be-
cause of this, the onset of anticlockwise tectonic rotations predates
Zechstein and metasomatic alterations of Cracow volcanics.
The mid-Permian anticlockwise rotations of the studied rocks
were inducted by wrenching tectonics, most probably associated
with a regional sinistral strike slip activity of the Cracow-Hamburg
prominent fault zone that separates two Cadomian terranes—
Brunosilesia and Ma/suppresslopolska. The same process was proposed for
tectonic rotations of the same age and direction detected in the
Sudetes (Nawrocki 1998) where sinistral tectonic activity revealed
at that time the Intra-Sudetic Fault. Some structural studies ( ˙Zaba
1999; Aleksandrowski et al. 1997) support our hypothesis about
Permian sinistral tectonic activity of main fault zones in southern
Poland. Another solution assuming regional tectonic anticlockwise
rotation of the whole Variscan belt in Poland (Jele´nska et al. 2003)
cannot be inferred from palaeomagnetic data because the magnitude
of rotations is different being usually less in the igneous rocks than
in their sedimentary cover. Moreover, this process involved also the
Cracow area that was outside of the Variscan orogen. The Early
Permian left-lateral motion between Baltica and Western Europe
recorded by major NW-trending faults of the Bohemian Massif is
postulated by Mattern (2001) who interpreted a strike-slip origin of
some Early Permian basins.

The sinistral tectonic activity of major NW-trending faults of
Central Europe dos not support the model of Muttonii et al. (2003)
in which these faults are presented as dextral ones (Fig. 9b; see also
Matte 1991). Palaeomagnetic data from the Cracow area and the
Sudetes indicate at that time the opposite, that is, sinistral sense of
tectonic activity. On the other hand it cannot be deﬁnitely excluded
that the NW-trending faults of Central Europe were not engaged in
dextral megashear of pre-Alpine Europe proposed by Muttoniet al.
(2003).
A substantial amount of overlap of continental crust in the
Early Permian between Gondwana and Laurussia if reconstructed in
Pangea ‘A’ conﬁguration can be signiﬁcantly reduced after detailed
selection of Permian palaeomagnetic poles from Laurussia (Van der
V oo & Torsvik 2004). This reduction can be also due to older ages of
the Autunian volcanites from post-Variscan Europe than previously
assumed. The mean ages of palaeomagnetic poles isolated from the
Autunian igneous rocks of western margin of the Bohemian Massif
(Soffel & Harzer 1991) and the Sudetes (Nawrocki 1997) is deﬁned
in the Global Palaeomagnetic Databaseon 278 and 285 Ma, respec-
tively. Isotope data and the results of comparison of palaeomagnetic
inclinations presented here may indicate that at least for the Sudetes
and the Cracow area the real age is older than previously assumed.
The location of Laurusia at 280 Ma presented in Fig. 9(c) was esti-
mated by interpolation between palaeopole ‘A’ and ‘B’. The overlap
of Gondwana’ s and Laurussia’ s parts of the Early Permian Pangea
‘A’ is in this reconstruction unseeable. It should be stressed, how-
ever, that Permian palaeomagnetic data for Gondwana are scarce.
Gondwana’ s position is based on the running mean pole of Torsvik
and Van der V oo (2002). It does not differ signiﬁcantly from the
location proposed by Rakotosolofo et al. (2006) on the basis of the
Early Permian palaeomagnetic pole from Peru.
8 CONCLUSIONS
The following conclusions can be drawn from this study.
1. The single-grain U-Pb dating of Cracow igneous rocks indi-
cate the mean age of 294.2 ± 2.1 Ma for the rhyodacite magma
emplacement and could indicate younger age (268.7 ± 3.4 Ma) for
the metasomatic alterations of these rocks.
2. T wo Permian components of magnetizations related to these
processes were isolated. The regional APWP characteristic for S
Poland constructed on the basis of palaeomagnetic poles deﬁned in
the Cracow region and the Sudetes shows a certain departure from
the coeval part of the Fennoscandian APWP due to anticlockwise
rotations of studied rocks.
3. Detected rotations were caused by the middle Permian sinistral
tectonic movements along reactivated prominent Variscan fault of
Central Europe.
4. Older than previously assumed ages of the post-Variscan ig-
neous rocks of Central Europe reduce overlap of Gondwana’ s and
Laurussia’ s parts of the Early Permian Pangea ‘A’.
5. Early Permian volcanism and mid-Permian metasomatic ac-
tivity were coeval with two events of remagnetizations of Devonian
carbonates in Poland.

Magnetic characteristics of the Hiltaba Suite Granitoids
and Volcanics: Late Devonian overprinting and related
thermal history of the Gawler Craton
P. W. SCHMIDT 1* AND D. A. CLARK 2
1CSIRO Earth Science & Resource Engineering, PO Box 136, North Ryde, NSW 1670, Australia.
2CSIRO Materials Science and Engineering, PO Box 218, Lindﬁeld, NSW 2070, Australia.
The *1590 Ma Gawler Range Volcanics (GRV) and 1595–1575 Ma Hiltaba Suite Granitoids (HSG), from
the central Gawler Craton of South Australia, can be divided into an oxidised Roxby Downs-type
containing hematite and magnetite, and a less oxidised Kokatha-type that commonly contains
ilmenite and titanomagnetite. In both types the predominant magnetic phase is pure end-member
magnetite, except for a minor amount of titanomagnetite present in the Kokatha-type Black Yardea
Dacite. The characteristic remanence observed in the GRV is directed upward to the northeast. A fold
test is strongly negative, indicating that this characteristic remanence is a post-folding overprint
although the age of folding is uncertain. Rock magnetic properties identify magnetically unstable
multidomain magnetite particles. The magnetisation has been blocked as the crust cooled from above
multidomain (MD) unblocking temperatures probably during a mid-phase of the Alice Springs Orogeny
(ASO). The in situ mean direction, not corrected for tilt, from 69 samples is declination ¼ 22.68,
inclination ¼ 744.98, a
95 ¼ 6.98 and the corresponding pole position is latitude lp ¼ 69.58S, longitude
jp ¼ 36.18E, dp ¼ 5.58,d m ¼ 8.78. No directions of opposite polarity were found and no consistent
remanence was found in either type of the HSG. The pole position from GRV is consistent with other
Australian paleopoles from rocks of about 360–370 Ma. Apatite ﬁssion track ages (AFTA) for the Gawler
Craton have yielded a mean age of 331 + 30 Ma. It is likely that the remanence and ﬁssion tracks have
been reset during exhumation/cooling after the ASO. The younger AFTA of *330 Ma are consistent with
the track retention temperature (100 + 208C) being attained after the higher remanence blocking
temperature of *42008C. The apatite ages are consistent with thermal modelling of 40Ar/39Ar data
from K-feldspars from the nearby Mount Painter Province.
KEY WORDS: South Australia, Gawler Range Volcanics, Hiltaba Suite Granitoids, Alice Springs Orogeny,
paleomagnetism, ﬁssion track dating
INTRODUCTION
The *1590 Ma Gawler Range Volcanics (GRV) and the
1595–1575 Ma Hiltaba Suite Granitoids (HSG) outcrop in
the central Gawler Craton of South Australia. They
produce characteristic, although quite distinctive, mag-
netic anomalies and can be easily mapped beneath
cover. The volcanics typically produce very active
magnetic patterns, while the patterns above granitoids
range from subdued to remarkably ﬂat and smooth. The
HSG and GRV can be subdivided into two types, each
correlated with a distinctive mineral association. The
more oxidised members are of the Roxby Downs-type
and are associated with Fe-oxide-Cu–Au mineralisation,
while the less oxidised Kokatha-types are associated
with vein Au ( +Sn+Ag) mineralisation (Budd et al .
1998). Here we report magnetic properties of the Hiltaba
Suite Granitoids and the Gawler Range Volcanics.
Magnetic remanences and susceptibilities of samples
were measured to characterise the different assem-
blages and assist mineral exploration and geological
interpretation of magnetic surveys over the Gawler
Craton. In addition, standard paleomagnetic methods
were applied to determine the characteristic stable
remanences present to place constraints on geological
events that have affected the Gawler craton.
GEOLOGICAL SETTING
The evolution of the Gawler craton began in the late
Archean ( 42500 Ma) with formations represented by
meta-sediments interlayered with banded iron forma-
tions, carbonate and siliceous rocks, and felsic and
maﬁc–ultramaﬁc volcanics including komatiites (Hand
et al . 2007). The volcanics have been interpreted (Swain
et al . 2005) to have formed in an active subduction
environment. The dominant U–Pb detrital zircon ages
for the metasediments range between ca 2850 and 2510
Ma with minor older zircons ranging between ca 3150

Australian Journal of Earth Sciences (2011) 58, (361–374)
ISSN 0812-0099 print/ISSN 1440-0952 online  2011 Geological Society of Australia
DOI: 10.1080/08120099.2010.549239

and 2950 Ma (Swain et al . 2005). Felsic to intermediate
intrusions followed at ca 2520 to 2500 Ma, and the
sequence was subsequently deformed and metamor-
phosed in the early Paleoproterozoic Sleafordian oro-
geny (2480–2420 Ma).
The Proterozoic development is divided into two
intervals from 2000 to 1690 Ma and from 1690 to 1500 Ma
by Hand et al. (2007). The older interval is dominated by
rift-basin development, sedimentation and emplacement
of the Donington granitic batholith at ca 1850 Ma in the
eastern Gawler Craton. This interval was terminated
by the 1730 to 1690 Ma Kimban orogeny. The younger
interval was dominated by igneous and volcanic activ-
ity. Fanning et al. (1988) provide U–Pb dates for
deformed volcanics of 1790 and 1740 Ma, and show that
the voluminous Gawler Range Volcanics (GRV) and
correlatives were erupted over a short interval at
1592 + 2 Ma, and later intruded by anorogenic granites
of the Hiltaba Suite Granitoids (HSG) at *1575 Ma.
Outcrop is most abundant in the central Gawler
Craton particularly on the western and south-western
margins of the GRV. The HSG and GRV are thought to
be derived from partial digestion of the crust by mantle
plumes (Neumann et al . 2000). The GRV and HSG are
regarded as comagmatic having compositions similar
to A-type magmas (Giles 1988; Creaser & White 1991;
Creaser 1996). Recently Budd (2006) and Skirrow et al .
(2006, 2007) have demonstrated that the Hiltaba Suite
and Gawler Range Volcanics include both I- and A-type
compositions. In the eastern and central Gawler Craton
there is a predominance of A-type granites and volca-
nics, whereas I- types are largely restricted to the
central and western parts of the craton.
Although the GRV and HSG have been generally
described as ‘anorogenic’ (Giles 1988; Drexel et al . 1993),
this notion has been more recently challenged by the
increasing recognition of syntectonic features of the
HSG (Creaser 1996; Ferris et al . 2002; McLean & Betts
2003; Lyons et al . 2005; Hand et al . 2007). Nevertheless,
the granitoids are typically circular in outcrop.
The GRV and HGS are closely related to widespread
mineralisation within the Gawler Craton (Johnson &
Cross 1995), such as the world-class Olympic Dam Cu–U–
Au–Ag ore deposit (Haynes et al. 1995) and Pb–Zn–Ag
mineralisation at Menninnie Dam (Roache 1996).
Wyborn et al . (1998) distinguishes between mineral
associations corresponding to the Roxby Downs-type
and the Kokatha-type. The Roxby Downs-type granitoids
are strongly oxidised, fractionated and are character-
istically pink due to hematite dusting of the feldspar
crystals. This type is associated with Fe-oxide–Cu–Au
deposits (Budd et al . 1998). The Kokatha-type granitoids
are more reduced than the Roxby Downs-type and
may contain pyrite. This type is associated with vein-
hosted Au ( +Sn+Ag) and displays a subdued magnetic
expression.
The GRV form a large dominantly felsic, bimodal
volcanic province that can be subdivided into an upper
and a lower group. The lower group corresponds to
the more oxidised (Roxby Downs-type) and is of
varied lithologies, gently to steeply tilted and contains
dacite-rhyodacite-rhyolite lava domes and ﬂows and
some ignimbrites with thick, intercalated sequences of
basaltic lavas. These rocks typically carry magnetite.
The upper group comprises thick, subhorizontal, por-
phyritic dacite sheets, predominantely ignimbritic in
origin, and is ilmenite and titanomagnetite-bearing
(Stewart 1993; Allen et al. 2008) belonging to Budd et al .
(1998)’s Kokatha-type.
Of the rocks sampled for this study the Charleston
Granite, Cunyarie Rocks Granite, Bittali Rhyolite,
Eucarro Dacite, Yannabie Rhyodacite and Paney Rhyo-
lite represent the Roxby Downs-type, while the Kokatha-
type is represented by the Buckleboo Granite, the
Yardea Dacite, the Black Yardea Dacite, rhyolites and
porphyritic rhyolites.
PREVIOUS PALEOMAGNETIC STUDIES
Chamalaun & Dempsey (1978) reported paleomagnetic
results for the Gawler Range Volcanics. Alternating
ﬁeld (AF) demagnetisation isolated magnetisation
moderately upward-directed to the northeast. Thermal
demagnetisation was performed on a few selected
specimens representing different lithologies which
showed a single magnetic carrier with a Curie tempera-
ture below 600 8C, consistent with that carrier being
magnetite. The thermal results gave directions similar
to those from the AF demagnetisation but no mean
directions were reported. Chamalaun & Dempsey (1978)
reported that no consistent magnetisation directions
were observed after heating to 600 8C. They carried out
XRD studies on representative lithologies and reported
that only diffraction lines from magnetite were ob-
served. The XRD data are thus consistent with the
thermal demagnetisation results in that there is no
evidence of hematite making a contribution to the
remanence which Chamalaun & Dempsey (1978 p. 259)
found ‘a little surprising as the acid volcanics are often
red . . . and hence could contain a signiﬁcant amount
of hematite.’ Any hematite present is apparently too
ﬁnely divided to show up on XRD or to retain a stable
remanent magnetisation.
From AF demagnetisation, the mean direction that
Chamalaun & Dempsey (1978) determined from 52
magnetically stable samples (from 62 samples collected
at 22 sites) was declination D ¼ 34.38, inclination
I ¼ 748.18, k ¼ 15.1, a
95 ¼ 5.28 and corresponding pole
position at latitude lp ¼ 60.48S, longitude jp ¼ 50.08E,
dp ¼ 4.48, dm ¼ 6.88. They also calculated a mean direc-
tion based on ﬁve lithological groups. Interestingly, the
mean direction from each group is not signiﬁcantly
different from the means of other groups (this detail is
returned to below). No directions of opposite polarity
were found and no ﬁeld tests were performed to
constrain the age of the magnetisation.
Schmidt & Clark (1992, 2000) revisited the Gawler
Range Volcanics and after stepwise thermal demagneti-
sation of 26 samples found a declination ¼ 32.38, in-
clination ¼ 743.28, k ¼ 20.0, a
95 ¼ 6.58. The results herein
include these 1992/2000 results as a sub-set and add
results from a further 43 GRV samples for a total of 69
samples.
362 P. W. Schmidt and D. A. Clark

NEW ROCK MAGNETIC AND PALEOMAGNETIC
DATA
The Gawler Peninsula ﬁeld excursion handbook pub-
lished by the Geological Society of Australia’s Struc-
tural Geology and Tectonics Specialist Group (Parker
et al . 1988) proved to be a very useful guide to the
geology of the Gawler Range Volcacnics and the
Hiltaba Suite Granitoids. We also used a Magellan
GPS navigation instrument and an Elliot susceptibility
meter for guidance in sampling. A schematic geological
map for the Gawler Craton with sampling localities is
shown in Figure 1. Sample localities are also listed in
Table 1.
A total of 69 oriented cores/blocks from 14 units of
the Hiltaba Suite Granitoids and Gawler Range Volca-
nics were collected using a magnetic and sun compass
apparatus. A portable rock drill was used to take
2.5 cm diameter cores except where rocks were extre-
mely hard, in which case block samples were collected.
Between three and nine specimens, 2.2 cm high 6
2.5 cm in diameter were machined from the block
samples and at least two from each core sample. Two
specimens per block and one per drill core were
subjected to detailed paleomagnetic and rock magnetic
experiments.
Laboratory techniques
Routine paleomagnetic laboratory methods (Collinson
1983; Butler 1992) were employed. Remanent magnetisa-
tion was measured using a CTF three-axis cryogenic
magnetometer at CSIRO North Ryde, NSW. Hysteresis
parameters and thermomagnetic curves were measured
using a Munich Variable-Field Translation Balance
(VFTB: URL: 5http://www.vftb.com/gallery.shtml4).
The demagnetisers used include a Schoenstedt AF
demagnetiser and an in-house carousel furnace housed
in a 10-coil Helmholtz set that provides feedback
controlled ‘ﬁeld-free’ space to about +5 nT. All speci-
mens were subjected to stepwise thermal demagnetisa-
tion of between 10 and 15 steps. An in-house
susceptibility bridge was used to measure low ﬁeld
magnetic susceptibility and k–T curves (Ridley & Brown
1980). Anisotropy of magnetic susceptibility was mea-
sured using a DIGICO anisotropy spinner interfaced to
a PC.
Rock Magnetism
Hysteresis properties of rocks are useful in inferring
the average domain structure of magnetic particles
in rocks. Such domain structures are important when
Figure 1 Map showing paleomagnetic sampling site in Hiltaba Suite Granitoids and Gawler Range Volcanics. Base map is
from PIRSA. Site details are given in Table 1.
Magnetic characteristics of the Hiltaba Suite Granitoids and Volcanics 363

considering the stability of remanent magnetisation
and the likelihood that the magnetic remanence of a
rock is original, or at least could withstand geological
events such as burial subsequent to its formation. Day
et al . (1977) used two ratios to infer domain structure.
These are the ratios of the coercivity of remanence to
the bulk coercivity ( H
cr/Hc) and the saturation rema-
nent magnetisation to the saturation magnetisation
(Mrs/Ms). The bulk coercivity, Hc, saturation remanent
magnetisation, Mrs, and saturation magnetisation, Ms,
are derived from a hysteresis loop where the magneti-
sation is measured in a high ﬁeld of up to 1 T. The
paramagnetic response, which is linear to very high
ﬁelds, and has been ﬁtted and removed. Hcr, being a
remanence related parameter, is measured in zero ﬁeld
after applying incrementally higher magnetic ﬁelds
opposed to a (previously) saturated remanent magneti-
sation (see Figure 2a, b). The squarer the hysteresis
loop, the more magnetically hard is a material. In
terms of the above ratios this translates into high
values ( 40.05) of ( M
rs/Ms) and low values ( 54) of
Hcr/Hc. Such values indicate grains with only a few
domains, known as the pseudo-single domains (PSD),
which, like single domains (SD), cannot be completely
demagnetised. Acicular SD magnetite theoretically can
possess M
rs/Ms values of 0.5. Alternatively, low values
(50.05) of ( Mrs/Ms) and high values ( 44) of Hcr/Hc
suggest a high multiplicity of domains whose magne-
tisations to a large extent mutually cancel each other.
This state is known as multidomain (MD), implying the
existence of many walls within grains. Such walls can
easily be moved through stress changes and thermal
ﬂuctuations at elevated temperatures. Rocks carrying
MD magnetite grains are easily remagnetised by
natural events.
A Day plot determined for samples of HSG and GRV
is shown in Figure 2c. The majority of samples fall
above the H
cr/Hc ¼ 4 cutoff, identifying them as MD. The
HSG samples in particular fall well into the MD region
with one sample (Charleston Granite) having an ex-
treme H
cr/Hc ratio of almost 20 indicating its remanence
is very soft.
One sample (from site BYD1 in the Black Yardea
Dacite) just falls in the PSD region, suggesting its
remanence is reasonably stable. Nevertheless the char-
acteristic direction of this unit is indistinguishable from
those of MD units. While other GRV lithologies,
especially the Kokatha-types, show M
rs/Ms values some-
what higher than the usual MD-PSD cutoff ratios of 0.05,
remagnetised limestones from North America and
Europe often exhibit elevated H
cr/Hc values, probably
attributable to minor amounts of ultraﬁne superpara-
magnetic (SPM) grains (Dunlop & O ¨ zdemir 1997, p.323)
and we assume that the presence of SPM or ultra-soft
grains may be the case with the GRV. The boundaries
separating SD to PSD, and PSD to MD are imprecise.
Susceptibility versus temperature ( k–T) curves
(Figure 3a, b), and saturation magnetisation versus
temperature ( M
s–T) curves (Figure 3c, d), show that the
only signiﬁcant magnetic mineral present in both Roxby
Downs and Kokatha types is almost pure end-member
magnetite. The inﬂection near 350 8C (Figure 3d) for the
Black Yardea Dacite, is the only hint of a titaniferous
phase. However, it is very minor. The irreversibility of
the thermomagnetic curve, which indicates that this
extra magnetic phase breaks down above *4008C, is also
consistent with the presence of some maghemite in the
sample, which is commonly associated with incipient
weathering of magnetite-bearing rocks.
The HSG and GRV display a range of properties
from moderately to weakly magnetic (Table 1). The
most intensely magnetic unit was the Kokatha-type
Black Yardea Dacite (BYD2) with a natural remanent
magnetisation (NRM) of 3.2 Am
–1 and susceptibility of
about 0.0036 SI. The least intensely magnetic unit was
the Roxby Downs-type Bittali Rhyolite (BR1) with an
NRM of only 37 mAm
–1 and a susceptibility of only
0.00015 SI.
Roxby Downs-type Hiltaba Suite Granitoids, the
Charleston Granite (HS1) and Cunyarie Rocks (HS2)
are both quite magnetic, although the former possesses
a moderate susceptibility but only a weak remanence,
while the latter has a moderate remanence of 2.4 Am
–1
but a low susceptibility of about 0.0075 SI. No consistent

direction of NRM was observed in the Cunyarie Rocks
unit despite the moderately strong remanence. The
Kokatha-type Buckleboo Granite (HS3) is weakly mag-
netic with a remanence of only 357 mAm –1 and a
susceptibility of about 0.0015 SI. Thus, while the Roxby
Downs-type HSG are magnetically stronger than the
Kokatha-type Buckleboo Granite, the Kokatha-type GRV
are magnetically stronger than the Roxby Downs-type
GRV. Remembering that it was the Kokatha-type GRV
that show the higher M
rs/Ms ratios suggests that of all
the rocks sampled these would seem the most likely to
retain any vestige of original thermoremanent magne-
tisation (TRM).
Overall magnetic properties are not diagnostic in
distinguishing between Roxby Downs or Kokatha-type
rocks. The MD nature of these carriers and, except for a
minor titanomagnetite component in the Kokatha-type
Black Yardea Dacite, their apparently uniform composi-
tion of pure end-member magnetite prevent the use of
hysteresis or thermal techniques from differentiating
their magmatic parentages.
Anisotropy of magnetic susceptibility (AMS) has also
been investigated and results from all sites are listed in
Table 2 (HSG) and Table 3 (GRV). The AMS is generally
about 2% in the volcanics and about 4% in the
granitoids. It is known that the DIGICO AMS delineator

parameters determined from B-H experiment (after paramagnetic correction), and (c) Day-plot correlating Mrs/Ms and
Hcr/Hc to identify magnetic domain structure.
Magnetic characteristics of the Hiltaba Suite Granitoids and Volcanics 365

Figure 3 Susceptibility versus temperature ( k–T) curves
(a, b), in low ﬁeld ( *1 mT), and (c, d) saturation magnetisa-

can produce a lineation bias towards (cylindrical)
specimen axes (Heller & Schultz-Krutisch 1988; Aubourg
et al . 2004) but this is for weak fabrics and at the time
this was the only instrument at our disposal. There is a
mixture of prolate and oblate ellipsoids in both sets. The
t factor in Tables 2 and 3 is positive for oblate ellipsoid
and negative for a prolate ellipsoid. There do not seem to
be any well-developed axes that are consistent between
sites. The AMS of the GRV is low and a much larger
study would be required to discern any patterns present
(see McPhie et al. 2008 below). While the AMS of the HSG
is somewhat higher than that of the GRV, there do not
seem to be any consistent axes. A much higher number
of sites may disclose some regional trends but there
do not appear to be any trends present for the three
granitoid sites in this study.
McPhie et al . (2008) studied the AMS of the Eucarro
Rhyolite to locate source vents. They found foliations
strike NW and dip steeply SW or NE respectively,
depending whether near the base or top of the ﬂow.
They successfully identiﬁed two ‘lobes’ of the rhyo-
lite, one west-central that ﬂowed from the SW and the
other to the east that ﬂowed from the N. The only
Eucarro Rhyolite site collected here (ED1: Table 3)
has a 3% foliation dipping steeply to the north. This
single result compares well with McPhie et al . (2008)’s
site EF15 (their table 1 and ﬁgure 5a). Both their site
EF15 and our site ED1 were from the west-central
lobe.
Characteristic magnetisations
Samples were subjected to thermal demagnetisation,
sometimes with alternating ﬁeld (AF) pre-treatment
for high intensities (see Figure 4a). This treatment
was successful in removing very intense components
that may have been the result of lightning. After
applying principal-component analysis (PCA) to de-
magnetisation data from the GRV, a consistent high
temperature remanence directed up to the north to
north east was found (Table 4). This component
showed a spread of unblocking temperatures from as
low as 200 8C upward, and was not fully demagnetised
until 580 8C which is consistent with the Curie point of
magnetite. This is typical of pure end-member magne-
tite and especially typical of MD magnetite, which can
have a tail of unblocking temperatures up to the Curie
point even for partial TRMs acquired at much lower
temperatures (Dunlop & O ¨ zdemir 1997 p. 248). Direc-
tions from HSG samples after PCA analysis resulted
in scattered directions around the present or dipole
ﬁeld and no geological signiﬁcance is attributed to
them.
Orthogonal projections of the demagnetisation vec-
tors for representative GRV samples are shown in
Figure 4. Sample YD01c1 (Figure 4a) exhibits a large
soft component that is removed by two AF steps of
30 mT and 60 mT before complete thermal demagnetisa-
tion is achieved after 580 8C. In this sample the soft
AF component has the same direction as the high
temperature component, suggesting that the high in-
tensity is not the result of lightning but is genuinely
chacteristic of this unit. Other samples (Figure 4b–f)

DISCUSSION
The paleomagnetic pole position from the GRV is plotted
on Australia’s Mid to Late Paleozoic apparent polar
wander path (APWP) in Figure 7 following Clark &
Lackie (2003). The poles that comprise the APWP are
listed in Table 5. Since the GRV magnetisation is shown
here to be an overprint, it is appropriate to estimate the
age of the overprint from its position on the APWP using
the nearest well-dated pole positions. As pointed out by
Clark & Lackie (2003), the GRV poles calculated by
Chamalaun & Dempsey (1978) and Schmidt & Clark
(1992, 2000) lie close to the poles from the Hervey Group
(375–359 Ma) and Silver Hills Volcanics (345–330 Ma).
The GRV pole calculated here ( N ¼ 69) supersedes that of
Schmidt & Clark (1992, 2000 N ¼ 26) and falls a little to
the south closer to the Worange Point Formation pole
(375–359 Ma) in African coordinates. This difference is
trivial and by either estimation (Schmidt & Clark 1992,
2000 or herein) the GRV magnetisations appear to be
Late Devonian in age. Statistical tests described above
indicate no signiﬁcant difference between this new
result and the previous results from the GRV. The
‘key-pole’ status afforded the GRV pole (Idnurm &
Giddings 1988) must be abandoned.
It has long been recognised that many rock units
throughout central and southern Australia have been
remagnetised during the Late Paleozoic. This has often
been attributed to the waning phase of the Alice Springs
Orogeny (ASO), which seems to have lasted for a
considerable time. McLaren et al. (2002) present thermo-
chronological evidence from the Mount Painter area
for denudation events probably associated with the ASO
at 430, 400 and about 330 Ma. These events would also

have affected the Gawler Craton. Schmidt & Embleton
(1987) have synthesised the ASO magnetic overprints,
showing them to be variously pre-, syn- and post-folding
in age. Many of the pole positions are apparently mid- to
late Carboniferous in age, suggesting that they coin-
cided with the waning phase of the ASO ( 5330 Ma).
On the basis of apatite ﬁssion-track ages (AFTA),
Spikings et al. (2006) extend the effects of the ASO to the
Mt Isa and Murphy Inliers of northeast Australia. There
is increasing evidence that the ASO affected cratonic
areas for thousands of kilometres from central Austra-
lia. Ferguson (1981) reported a mean of 331 + 30 Ma for
13 AFTA for the Gawler Craton and AFTA for shattered
Yardea Dacite from the Acraman impact site yield an
age of 319 + 19 Ma (data pers. comm . G. E. Williams 2000
courtesy of I. R. Duddy, Geotrack International, Mel-
bourne). These early Carboniferous ages indicate when
the Gawler craton cooled below the apatite ﬁssion track
retention temperature (100 + 208C). The unimodal, nega-
tively skewed distribution of track lengths reﬂects a
slow, steady cooling history with the ﬁssion tracks
marking the time *1008C was reached, some tens of
millions of years after attainment of the temperatures
that are associated with the overprint magnetisations
carried by the GRV. This is in agreement with Kohn
et al. (2002) who concluded on the basis of AFTA that the
denudation chronology for the Gawler Craton ‘shows a
fairly uniform rate of ca 10 m per million years over the
last 300 million years’ (p. 710). If linear, this implies that
the Gawler Craton has undergone ca 3 km of erosion
since 300 Ma; however, there is a reasonable likelihood
that some periods saw higher denudation rates than
others, especially the period immediately following
uplift associated with the ASO.
The denudation model of Kohn et al. (2002) is based
partly on the paleogeothermal gradient assumed. If this
were elevated compared with those of the present day,
then the calculated thickness of crustal erosion would
be less. Nevertheless, assuming a higher paleogeother-
mal gradient for the Gawler Craton in the Late Paleozoic
(Williams & Wallace 2003) suggests 2 km of erosion is
not unreasonable.
CONCLUSIONS
The measured magnetic properties of the Hiltaba Suite
Granitoids explain their highly variable airborne mag-
netic signatures. Cunyarie Rocks (HS2) displays a
prominent anomaly, while the magnetic signature of
the Buckleboo Granite (HS3) is ﬂat. This is usually
attributed to the Hiltaba Suite Granitoid subdivision of
oxidised hematite/magnetite bearing Roxby Downs-type
(Cunyarie Rocks granite) and ilmenite/titanomagnetite
bearing Kokatha-type (Buckleboo Granite). However,
rock magnetic tests here have identiﬁed magnetite as
the overwhelming magnetic mineral, in both types of
rocks, except for a minor phase of titanomagnetite in the
Kokatha-type Black Yardea Dacite. As expected from
their airborne magnetic signatures, the Buckelboo
Granite is very much less magnetic than the Cunyarie
Rocks granite, so while no rock magnetic evidence for
titanomagnetite was found in the Buckelboo Granite,
the amount is extremely small. Since ilmenite is not
ferromagnetic, the tests applied here are not able to
quantify the amount of ilmenite that may be present in
the Kokatha-types.
No simple picture emerges from comparing Roxby
Downs and Kokatha-type GRV, although the Yardea
Dacite and Black Yardea Dacite (Kokatha-types) appear
to be more magnetic than most Roxby Downs-types.
However, one of these latter types, the Eucarro Dacite, is
also quite magnetic.
The Gawler Range Volcanics at Uno are dipping
almost vertically to the north but possess remanence
directions similar to those found in almost ﬂat lying
volcanics to the west, and also to those reported by
Chamalaun & Dempsey (1978). Clearly, the Gawler
Range Volcanics have been magnetised after tilting.
Comparison of the GRV pole position with Australia’s
mid to late Paleozoic apparent polar wander path
suggests that the overprint magnetisations date from
the late Devonian (375–360 Ma).
Apatite ﬁssion track ages indicate that (the present
surface of) the Gawler Craton cooled through the
*1008C isotherm in the Late Carboniferous, some tens
of millions of years after attainment of the peak
temperatures and after the magnetic overprint of the
Gawler Range Volcanics became blocked. The magnetic
overprints and AFTA therefore each represent an
isotherm records, albeit of different temperatures, of
the cooling of the Gawler Craton after the widespread
Alice Springs Orogeny.

Abstract A collection was made in January 2009 of 10 oriented samples from each of 54 sites in lavas on
Sao Tome Island (nominal location 0.3  N, 6.5 E). Some sites were affected by lightning leaving a total of 42
sites for analysis of paleosecular variation. Overall magnetic properties were excellent (highly stable magnet-
izations carried by pseudosingle domain magnetite). After principal component analysis of progressive alter-
nating ﬁeld demagnetization data for the samples, 22 sites had normal polarity magnetizations (D5 0. 6
 ,
I 52 8.3 , a95 5 4.3 , j 5 53.1) and 20 had reverse magnetizations (D 5 176.0 ,I 5 4.2 , a95 5 7.3 , j 5 20.8);
the directions are within 58 of antiparallel, yielding a positive reversal test. The combined data set of 42 site
mean virtual geomagnetic poles converted to common (normal) polarity yields a pole position at 86.08N,
211.5 E, A9553.1 . Ar/Ar and K/Ar dating reveals that these rocks are Miocene in age ( –11 Ma), old enough
to allow northerly plate motion to help explain the slightly far-sided pole position. The between-site disper-
sion in virtual geomagnetic poles was estimated as the angular standard deviation, S
b, and equaled 11.48 with
95% conﬁdence interval between 9.98 and 13.48.
1. Introduction
The time-averaged ﬁeld initiative (TAFI) program [ Johnson et al., 2008] ended without new data being gener-
ated from within 15 8 of the Equator [ Lawrence et al., 2006], which is a critical region for understanding paleo-
secular variation of the geomagnetic ﬁeld. Consequently, we undertook studies of the paleomagnetism of
lava ﬂows from equatorial regions in Ecuador (  .68S) [Opdyke et al., 2006], Kenya (  8,2 . 68N) [Opdyke et al.,
2010], and the Galapagos ( 8S) [Kent et al., 2010]. The present study is an extension of these efforts.
Following sampling at Mt. Kenya and the reconnaissance collection from the Loiyangalani region [ Opdyke
et al., 2010], we had planned to return to Loiyangalani the next year to collect more samples. However, pub-
lic disorder in Kenya at the time prevented us from doing this, therefore we chose to sample lavas on Sao
Tome in the Gulf of Guinea as an alternative site virtually on the Equator (Figure 1).
A paleomagnetic study of volcanics on Sao Tome was previously published by Piper and Richardson [1972];
they reported results from 49 sites using a least-scatter criterion on 2–5 samples per site that were subjected
to progressive alternating ﬁeld demagnetization. Other recent studies on volcanics in the region have been
reported by Ubangoh et al . [1998] on mainland Cameroon and by Herrero-Bervera et al. [2004] on Mt. Came-
roon, a study that is technically excellent but has only 10 sites reported. We therefore decided to resample
and reanalyze the lavas on Sao Tome, which were thought to be Plio-Pleistocene ( –5 Ma) in age.
2. Geology
Sao Tome Island is part of the Cameroon Volcanic Line. Pagalu is the last volcanic island in this chain and
lies to the southwest of Sao Tome, which was constructed on oceanic crust [ Fitton and Dunlop , 1985]
(Figure 1). The volcanic rocks on the continent at the northeast end of the Cameroon trend are older and
mainly Miocene and Oligocene in age. Mt. Cameroon, which is one of Africa’s largest active volcanoes, is
dominantly of Brunhes (middle and late Pleistocene) age and sits on continental crust near the current
coastline [ Fitton and Dunlop , 1985]. The origin of the volcanic rocks is a matter of debate and may be

The result of our Ar/Ar dating (described below) indicates that most of the lavas currently exposed at sea level
are Miocene in age ( –11 Ma) even though younger lavas havebeen reported at higher elevations.
Lavas are exposed along the shoreline of Sao Tome along a beautiful paved road with fresh outcrops where
blasting was used in road construction. Seaside exposures are abundant where the lavas are being actively
eroded and not too badly weathered. Tracks branch off the highway to the coast or to plantations in the
northern part of the Island. Jungle covers large areas of the central part of the island, which as a result is rel-
atively inaccessible. Sampling was carried out mainly on roadside and beachfront outcrops using a hand-
held gasoline-powered coring device with diamond bits which drilled cores 2.5 cm in diameter to a depth
of 3 to 6 cm. Ten cores were drilled from each of 54 sites (outcrops). The cores were oriented using a Brun-
ton compass and checked with a sun compass when possible. The sampling was carried out over several
meters of outcrop to make certain that inadvertent sampling of a rolled boulder or outcrop struck by an iso-
lated lightning strike would not wipe out the site. It was not possible in most cases to discern the strati-
graphic relationship between sites (lavas) and in at least two cases in our study adjacent sites evidently
sampled the same lava based on the coincidence of the directions.
3. Laboratory Studies
The samples were returned to the U.S. and processed in the Paleomagnetic Laboratory at the University of
Florida. The samples were sliced into samples about 1cm thick. The natural remanent magnetization (NRM)
of each sample was measured on a 2G cryogenic magnetometer and demagnetized using a commercially
available alternating ﬁeld (AF) demagnetizer. We have found that the most serious secondary overprint is
caused by lightning strikes; therefore, progressive AF demagnetization was routinely employed because
this hard overprint cannot be removed as effectively by thermal demagnetization.
Magnetic hysteresis curves to 1 Tesla were obtained from representative samples from all sites on a Micro-
mag AGFM (Figure 2). The resulting plot of hysteresis parameter ratios (Figure 3) showed that the samples
from Sao Tome fell predominately in the usual pseudosingle domain region with only one site in the single
domain region and another near the multidomain region [ Day et al ., 1977].
The results of progressive AF demagnetization were analyzed using principal component line ﬁtting [ Kirsch-
vink, 1980]. Three or more points were employed to determine the direction. If the line did not trend toward
the origin, the sample was not included in the analysis. Demagnetization results for samples from four rep-
resentative sites are shown in Figure 4. Three of the sample results (Figures 4a, 4c, 4d) are straightforward
with linear demagnetization trajectories to the origin and shallow inclinations yielding both reverse polarity
(southerly) and normal polarity (northerly) directions. Site aj (Figure 4b), however, exhibits scattered direc-
tions to the south and a separate cluster with steep negative inclinations. We interpret this to be an inter-
mediate (transitional) direction. This is not surprising since both polarities are present in our data set. The
paleomagnetic data from the near-multidomain site did not yield useable results.
Site-mean directions were calculated [ Fisher, 1953] and are given in Table 1 and plotted in Figure 5. There
are 22 normal polarity sites and 20 reverse polarity sites, for a total of 42 out of 54 sites that yield acceptable
data. The normal sites are well grouped (D 5 0.68,I 52 8.38, a
95 5 4.38, j 5 53.1) whereas the reverse sites
are somewhat more dispersed (D 5 1758,I 5 4.28, a95 5 7.38, j 5 20.8). The directions can be combined
since the data pass a reversal test at a high conﬁdence level (category A of McFadden and McElhinny
[1990]). The overall statistics for 42 sites after inverting the reverse polarity site directions are D 5358.48,
I 52 6.38, a95 5 4.18, j 5 30.0.
Virtual geomagnetic poles (VGPs) were calculated from the site-mean directions and are plotted in Figure 6.
The mean VGP after inverting reverse polarity site directions is located at 86.0 8N, 211.58E, (A95 5 3.18), which
is just signiﬁcantly different (far-sided) from the geographic axis. VGP dispersion was calculated using the
method of Cox [1969] and yields an angular standard deviation, S b of 11.4 8 with 95% conﬁdence interval
between 9.98 and 13.48.
We can compare the results of this study to that of Piper and Richardson [1972]. It is rather amazing that the
mean direction of our results (D 5 358.48,I 52 6.38) is within an insigniﬁcant 1 8 of their study (D 5 359.2 ,
I 52 7.0 ). This shows clearly that older studies should not berejected out of hand, especially for younger lavas.

The angular dispersion of VGPs, estimated as the between-site angular standard deviation (Sb) [ McElhinny
and Merrill, 1975], from the database studies (Table 3) is plotted against collection latitude in Figure 8a. Lati-

paleomagnetic data and described by various models [ Cox, 1970; McElhinny and Merrill , 1975]. We have
shown earlier [ Opdyke et al ., 2010] that VGP dispersion is indeed low at the equator whereas data from Ant-
arctica in high southern latitudes as well as from Iceland and Nunivak Island in high northern latitudes have
higher dispersion. High-quality results from low latitudes have become more abundant in recent years and
are an extension of the TAFI project. These studies include those based on samples that were collected in

actual geomagnetic dispersion. Both studies are set in actively deforming regions and along a convergent
plate boundary and therefore prone to tilting. In the early stages of studies of paleosecular variation, oce-
anic islands were the preferred collecting localities [e.g., Cox, 1971; Doell and Cox , 1971; Watkins et al ., 1972].
To make more progress in the future, restudy of many of these islands should be attempted and areas of
active tectonism (e.g., arc volcanoes) should be avoided.
