ment; it is typically eliminated by ~20 mT or ~400°C. In samples from
Grants Intrusive, component B decays to the origin between 400 and
560°C, or by ~80 mT. Two (of 16) samples from this site behaved errat-
ically at high temperature and were excluded from further analysis.
Samples from the Chamberlain Diatreme became unstable above
400°C, yielding erratic directions due to thermal alteration, so compo-
nent B is only de ﬁned by AF demagnetization; it is observed to decay
by ~60 mT. In samples from the Hart Creek Diatreme, component A is
removed more rapidly during the initial demagnetization steps, and
holds a greater proportion of the total remanence, relative to the corre-
sponding component from the other intrusive breccias. Component B is
largely unblocked between 450 and 560°C, but in some samples a rem-
anence remains above 600°C, and the segment de ﬁning component B
does not trend to the origin (Fig. 2c). In these samples, a higher labora-
tory unblocking temperature component (C) can be de ﬁned, and it is
sub-parallel to component A. This C-component is also observed to
persist above 200 mT in some samples that were AF-demagnetized. In
two (of 10) samples, only components A and C were identi ﬁed.
Samples from the Willow Lake Dike and Downeys Bluff Sill yield two
components of magnetization that are highly-similar to those identiﬁed
in the intrusive breccias, and we assign them the same labels (compo-
nents A and B) (Fig. 2d,e). In the Willow Lake Dike, component A can rep-
resent up to 50% of the natural remanent magnetization (NRM) and is
removed by ~20 mT or ~ 300°C, after which component B decays univec-
torially to the origin. Unblocking of component B is often distributed be-
tween 300 and 560°C during thermal demagnetization and is complete
by 50 mT during AF demagnetization. Demagnetization of Downeys
Bluff Sill samples is complete by 60 mT or 570°C, and cleaning of the
lower stability component (A) is complete by ~ 10 mT or ~ 300°C.
Unblocking of the B-component is typical ly distributed between 300
and 570°C, but, in a few samples, unblocking at an intermediate temper-
ature (250 –450 °C) appears to be distinct from higher temperature
decay (500 –570 °C), suggesting the presence of a distinct phase.
Directional differences between the intermediate and high-temperature
vector segments are less than 5°. AF demagnetization spectra do not
reveal any correlative distinction in coercivity during removal of the
B-component.
Samples of the Downeys Bluff Limestone taken from the baked
contact zone adjacent to the ~ 0.2 –0.5 m sill typically preserve only
one component of magnetization, sub-parallel to the B-component
identiﬁed in the sill ( Fig. 2f). Unblocking of this magnetization occurs
primarily between 260 and 330°C, but a minor fraction of the rema-
nence can persist to 550°C. AF demagnetization is only partly effec-
tive; ~ 30% of the remanence remains after application of a 200 mT
peak ﬁeld. Component A is apparent in a few samples, but it represents
a very minor fraction of the NRM and is removed during the initial de-
magnetization steps. By contrast, unbaked samples of the Downeys
Bluff Limestone preserve only the A-component, which decays uni-
vectorially to the origin ( Fig. 2 g). The remanence of the unbaked
samples is distinctly less stable, as ~ 90% of the NRM is removed by
application of 100 mT or 300°C.
Considering its relative stability and directional consistency, we
assign the B-component the characteristic remanent magnetization
(ChRM) of these rocks. We have calculated site-mean directions of
this ChRM from 6 of the 7 sites sampled (the unbaked Downeys Bluff
Limestone does not exhibit component B) ( Fig. 3 ; Table 1 ). Within
these 6 sites, 87% of the samples (n = 68/78) were retained for the
ChRM site-mean calculations. 13% of the samples were rejected due to
thermal alteration, erratic behavior, or anomalous directions. The com-
bined site means give the following paleomagnetic pole: 54.1°S, 300.7°E
A95 = 4.8°, N = 6. If tilt-corrections are applied, the pole (hereafter“IL”)
is located at 56.3°S, 302.9°E (A 95 = 3.8°). Our results are in excellent
agreement with the earlier ﬁndings of Reynolds et al. (1997) ;s i t e -
mean directions common to both studies (from Grants Intrusive and
Downeys Bluff Sill/Limestone) differ by ≤2.2°.
5. Magnetic mineralogy
Hysteresis measurements reveal that the Chamberlain Diatreme,
Grants Intrusive, Downeys Bluff Sill, and the Willow Lake Dike are dom-
inated by a low-coercivity magnetic phase ( Fig. 4 a,b). In conjunction
with the thermal demagnetization observations (wherein the ChRM
was typically removed by 560° –570°C), and known mineralogy of
these igneous bodies, we interpret the ChRM of these rocks to be carried
by low-Ti titanomagnetite.Reynolds et al. (1997) reported evidence of
low-Ti titanomagnetite in Grants Intrusive and Downeys Bluff Sill from
thermomagnetic analysis. There are no strong indications of a second
magnetic component in the hysteresis behavior of samples of these
rocks, suggesting that the low-temperature/coercivity A-component is
held by a less-stable sub-population of titanomagnetite, perhaps distinct
in composition or size. Specimens from the contact metamorphosed
Downeys Bluff Limestone show both low- and high-coercivity compo-
nents in variable proportions, indicating that some magnetic phases
may be heterogeneously distributed relative to the chip-size used in
the experiments. The low-coercivity phase is again consistent with
low-Ti titanomagnetite, according to the thermal demagnetization ob-
servations. The high-coercivity phase may be the principal ChRM
carrier, observed to unblock between 260 and 330°C. Reynolds
et al. (1997) interpreted this phase as pyrrhotite, which has a high-
coercivity and a Curie point of ~ 325°C ( Rochette et al., 1990 ).
The hysteresis behavior of a specimen from the Hart Creek Dia-
treme is controlled by a high-coercivity phase; demagnetization
of a sister-specimen (from the same sample) shows the NRM of
this sample is dominated by the C-component. The persistence of
the C-component above 600°C and its association with the observed
high-coercivity behavior suggests it may be carried by hematite. The
lower temperature components (A and B) are again attributed to
titanomagnetite, although the low-coercivity phase in the measured
specimen — evident by the “goose-necked ” shape of the loop ( Tauxe
et al., 1996 ) — is minor.
Low-temperature remanence data from a specimen of the baked
Downeys Bluff Limestone supports the interpretation that its rema-
nence is carried by pyrrhotite. The specimen was imparted with an
isothermal remanent magnetization at room-temperature and cycled
down to 10 K and back, during which time regular measurements of
remanence were made. Notable changes in remanence occurred at
~ 120 K and ~ 32 K, which correspond to known magnetic transition
temperatures in magnetite and pyrrhotite, respectively ( Fig. 4c).
6. VGP distribution analysis
It is commonly assumed that the distribution of VGPs is approxi-
mately circularly symmetric at all latitudes (but with increasing scatter
pole-ward, due to the relative intensity of non-dipoleﬁelds) (Harrison,
2009; Tauxe and Kent, 2004 ). Due to the non-linear relationship be-
tween VGPs and magnetic ﬁeld directions, the corollary of this latitude-
independent circular symmetry of VGPs is the expectation of non-circu-
lar and latitude-dependent distributions of directions (except at high-lat-
itudes) (Creer et al., 1959; Tanaka, 1999). Tauxe and Kent (2004)used a
statistical model of the ﬁeld to deﬁne this theoretical distribution of di-
rections as a function of latitude and insightfully proposed that it could
be used to identify departures from the expected distribution of a set of
directions generated by a geocentric axial dipole (GAD) at any given lat-
itude. In practice, this is achieved by comparing the observed “
elonga-
tion” of a directional data-set with the expected elongation from the
theoretical function at a speciﬁcl a t i t u d ed eﬁned by the mean inclination
of the data-set. Elongation is deﬁned by Tauxe (1998)as the ratio of the
intermediate and minimum eigenvalues (τ2/τ3) of the orientation matrix
of the magnetization directions. This so-called elongation –inclination
(E/I) technique has led to an increasing recognition of inclination
shallowing in sedimentary rocks ( Kent and Tauxe, 2005; Krijgsman
and Tauxe, 2006; Yan et al., 2005 ) and to discussions regarding the
42 M. Domeier et al. / Tectonophysics 511 (2011) 38 –52

structure of the geomagnetic ﬁeld through time ( Tauxe, 2005; Tauxe
and Kodama, 2009 ).
The principal drawback of the E/I technique is that a large amount
of data (≥100–150 site-level directions) are required to conduct a mean-
ingful analysis, because the method assumes that the data-set fully
captures the directional variance due to secular variation (Tauxe et al.,
2008). Small data-sets, therefore, may exhibit apparent elongations
reﬂecting an under-sampling of the short-term ﬁeld variance, rather
than a true departure from GAD expectations. Unfortunately, paleomag-
netic studies with 100+ independent site-mean directions are currently
rare; there are none within the paleomagnetic records we are considering
here (Table 2). Thus, none of the individual studies present a sufﬁciently
large data-set for a rigorous directional distribution analysis. Yet, collec-
tively, these studies constitute an ample data-set that likely represents
a full characterization of secular variation. Because several of these studies
were conducted on the same formations (e.g. Moenkopi Fm., Chugwater
Fm., Cutler Fm.), and many more are derived from lithologically similar
continental redbeds,we postulate that it is reasonable, although admit-
tedly not ideal, to combine and collectively analyze these data-sets for
common/widespread departures from GAD expectations, as they may
be similarly biased. The latitude-dependence of the expected distribution
of magnetization directions prevents us from combining data-sets with

7. Discussion
7.1. Interpretation of paleomagnetic results
We interpret the ChRM of the intrusive rocks and contact metamor-
phosed limestone to be a primary, Middle Permian (~270 Ma) magne-
tization. The exclusively reversed polarity of this remanence is
consistent with magnetization acquisition during the Kiaman Reversed
Superchron, which extended from ~318 –265 Ma ( Gradstein et al.,
2004; Opdyke et al., 2000 ). The Middle Permian K –Ar and 40Ar–39Ar
age determinations on the Grants Intrusive and Downeys Bluff Sill dis-
count the possibility of a signi ﬁcant ( N300°C) thermal event after
~270 Ma, which rules out a secondary magnetization of thermal origin.
A secondary chemical remanent magnetization (CRM) is similarly
unlikely due to the identi ﬁcation of titanomagnetite as the principal
remanence carrier.Reynolds et al. (1997)observed magnetite–ilmenite
intergrowths and TiO2-rich high-temperature alteration products - both
indicative of an igneous origin - in Grants Intrusive and Downeys Bluff
Sill. Furthermore, we note that the position of the paleomagnetic
pole resembles other Middle Permian poles from Laurentia, but not
younger ones (Kent and Irving, 2010). We interpret the low-tempera-
ture/coercivity component (A) to be an overprint of recent origin. The
paleomagnetic pole determined from this component (79.7°N, 349.7°E
A95 = 18.4°; in situ coordinates) resembles that of the present day
ﬁeld. The C-component observed in the Hart Creek Diatreme and inter-
preted to reside in hematite, is also interpreted as a recent overprint,
perhaps developed by surface oxidation of primary titanomagnetite.
We observe a minor reduction in the estimated α95 of the mean
paleomagnetic direction after tilt-correction (applied to data from
the Chamberlain Diatreme and Grants Intrusive), but note that this
is not statistically signi ﬁcant at the 95% con ﬁdence level, and does
not constitute a positive tilt-test. Furthermore, the nature and timing
of the tilting is not well-established. Host strata for the Willow Lake
Dike and the Downeys Bluff Sill exhibit no signi ﬁcant structural dip
(b5°). Strata near the Hart Creek Diatreme exposure exhibit a minor
dip to the NW, but the cross-bedded nature of this poorly exposed
sandstone precludes any con ﬁdent structural restoration. Exposures
of strata near Grants Intrusive and the Chamberlain Diatreme exhibit
clear bedding contacts with a signi ﬁcant dip. The Chamberlain Dia-
treme occurs along the Herod Fault Zone, a NE-trending structure
which was likely active after emplacement of the Diatreme, and
may be responsible for this locally observed dip. Grants Intrusive is
exposed on the southwest ﬂank of Hicks Dome, which is assumed to
have developed contemporaneously with the regional magmatism;
thus, the structure may pre- or post-date the intrusion. We prefer
the tilt-corrected result, due to the minor improvement in site-
mean clustering.
7.2. Interpretation of VGP distribution analysis
It is evident from the example VGP distributions ( Fig. 5c) that the
shallowing of magnetic ﬁeld directions results in an elongation of the

the sampling site. In the model, the site longitude was set to 0°, so
the ﬂattening of directions has expectedly resulted in an elongation
of the VGP distribution along the 90° –270° meridians. Because all of
the Laurentian data-sets have been rotated into the same reference
frame (sampling site longitude = 0°), the incidence of inclination
shallowing in these records should be re ﬂected in an elongation of
the VGP distribution in the same sense. Fig. 6 illustrates a clear 90°
(= 270°) preference in the elongation direction of these data-sets,
in support of the hypothesis that inclination shallowing has affected
the paleomagnetic records from these redbeds. The grouped results
in Fig. 7 b,c similarly exhibit a clear 90° –270° elongation of the VGP
distribution. In both grouped analyses, the calculated value of elonga-
tion is statistically distinct (95% conf.) from a circular distribution
(elongation = 1), indicating that signiﬁcant shallowing of the inclina-
tions has occurred. This conclusion is reinforced by the analysis of the
Yemeni volcanic rocks, which yield a very low VGP elongation, in
agreement with the expectation that unshallowed directions (from
a GAD) should produce a circularly symmetric VGP distribution
(Fig. 7 d). Our exercises in sub-sampling and centering synthetic
data have resulted in elongation estimates that are reasonably close
to (and statistically indistinguishable from) the elongations derived
from the original data and the model expectations, thereby implying
that our sample sizes and centering procedure are not introducing
any systematic bias ( Fig. 7e).
Beck et al. (2003) conducted a similar VGP distribution analysis of
paleomagnetic data from Triassic and Jurassic redbeds from the Colora-
do Plateau, but concluded that the observed elongations were due to a
protracted magnetization acquisition. Cederquist et al. (1997) ,e x a m -
ining the elongation of Carboniferous –Early Jurassic magnetization
directions from Laurentia, also concluded that the observed elongate
distribution was due to the inclusion of apparent polar wander in the
data as a consequence of protracted magnetization acquisition. This al-
ternative interpretation is predicated on the assumption that the ChRM

of these redbeds is dominantly chemical in nature, and was acquired
over a prolonged period by the slow growth of authigenic (pigmentary)
hematite in the form of a grain-coating/cement. However, a review of
the original studies shows that the contribution of pigmentary hematite
to the ChRM is often minor (if existent), relative to the contribution by
specular hematite, of detrital origin. Such a depositional remanent mag-
netization (DRM) is supported by the lateral continuity of polarity inter-
vals across hundreds of kilometers and across lithologic boundaries
(Purucker et al., 1980; Steiner et al., 1993), sequential changes in mag-
netization through thin sedimentary units (Shive et al., 1984), positive
intraformational conglomerate and soft-sediment fold tests ( Elston
and Purucker, 1979; Magnus and Opdyke, 1991; Molina-Garza et al.,
1991; Symons, 1990; Symons et al., 1989), co-linear magnetization di-
rections with detrital magnetite (Steiner, 1988), characteristic specular-
ite demagnetization behavior ( Collinson, 1974; Gose and Helsley,
1972), and by petrographic observations ( Elston and Purucker, 1979).
More broadly, recent work on Carboniferous and Late Triassic–Early Ju-
rassic redbeds from North America has demonstrated a common shal-
low inclination bias, implying that the ChRM of these redbeds is
predominantly a DRM ( Bilardello and Kodama, 2010; Kent and Irving,
2010; Kent and Tauxe, 2005). Following our review of the original stud-
ies, we have labeled the records that present evidence consistent with a
DRM as the ChRM ( Table 2). We have also labeled the results that the
primary authors explicitly associated with a CRM, although we stress
that these determinations are not conclusive. If most of the paleomag-
netic records are derived from DRMs, as we argue the evidence sug-
gests, then the agreement between VGP distribution elongation and
Laurentian APW, as observed by Cederquist et al. (1997) and Beck et
al. (2003), is merely coincidental. Indeed, the late Paleozoic–early Me-
sozoic APWP of Laurentia is roughly orthogonal to its central meridian,
so that most sampling sites with a shallow inclination bias could be
expected to yield a VGP distribution with an elongation apparently co-
incident with the APWP. We consider most of the redbed paleomagnet-
ic records to be depositional in nature, and interpret the elongate VGP
distributions to be a consequence of inclination shallowing.
7.3. Magnitude of shallow inclination bias
The obvious reduction in VGP scatter between panels b and c inFig. 7
is an indication of the presence of unremoved magnetization overprints
in the data-sets of McMahon and Strangway (1968). As such, we regard
the result in panel c to be the most representative of the primary records,
although the change in the elongation estimate between the panels is
negligible. The elongation determined from the data in panel c is 4.71;
the bootstrap conﬁdence limits extend from 3.51 to 6.45. Numerical exer-
cises conducted on the VGP sets generated by TK03.GAD have demon-
strated that the 95% bootstrap con ﬁdence limits on the estimated
elongation of any given data-set have a 95% probability of overlapping
with the “true” mean VGP elongation (from Fig. 5a), provided that the
data-set is sufﬁciently large (N ≥100–150) (Fig. 7a ) .T h i si sa ne x p e c t e d
outcome where both the“true” mean VGP elongation is well-determined
and the individual sample-sets fully characterize the short-term direc-
tional variance in the ﬁeld (model). Because our combined Laurentian
data-set is sufﬁciently large, we may exclude all theoretical shallowing
factors (f) that do not produce mean VGP distribution elongations that
overlap with the bootstrap conﬁdence bounds on the elongation estimate
from the Laurentian data. If we use the uncorrectedmean inclination of
the data-set to calculate the sampling site latitude, our elongation esti-
mate (with error) suggests that shallowing by a factor of f =0 . 5 2 t o
f = 0.37 has affected the data-set (circle,Fig. 7c ) .H o w e v e r ,t h i sa p p r o a c h
is not strictly correct, as the theoretical curves are estimates of VGP distri-
bution elongation for various f v a l u e sa tt h et r u es a m p l i n gs i t el a t i t u d e
(i.e., determined from the corrected mean inclination, which is typically
unknown). Instead, a recursive correction –calculation process can be
employed, wherein the maximum and minimum allowable inclination
corrections can be determined according to those f values that would
still lie within the con ﬁdence bounds of the elongation estimate after
the inclination correction is performed. The highest sampling site latitude
allowed by the data (by the maximum inclination correction consistent
with the elongation estimate) is depicted by a diamond inFig. 7b,c. The
shallow nature of the theoretical curves at low-latitudes and the low-
mean inclination (5.3°) of the grouped data-sets precludes any dramatic
shift in the range of potentialf values; applying the recursive inclination
corrections changes the potential range to: f =0 . 5 4 t of = 0.39, with a
mean of f = 0.46. For reference,Bilardello and Kodama (2010)compiled

More speciﬁcally, Kent and Tauxe (2005) determined eight f values
from Late Triassic redbeds from North America, which ranged from
f=0 . 6 6 t of = 0.4, with a mean value off = 0.56.
7.4. Implications for APWP of Laurentia
Although the IL pole resembles other Middle Permian poles from
Laurentia, it does exhibit a signiﬁcantly higher paleolatitude, as evident
by its position relative to the Middle Permian segment of the Laurentian
APWP of Torsvik et al. (2008) (Fig. 8a). Due to the prevalence of paleo-
magnetic records from continental redbeds in the compilation byTorsvik
et al. (2008), we argue that this discrepancy is due to a widespread shal-
low inclination bias in the poles derived from sedimentary rocks. Our
VGP distribution analysis supports this argument, in that the compiled
data exhibit an elongation that is statistically distinct (95% conf.) from
the expectations of a VGP distribution generated by a GAD. Our conserva-
tive estimate of elongation suggests that an average shallow inclination
bias equivalent to shallowing byf = 0.54 is present in the paleomagnetic
records of these continental redbeds.
To consider the effect that an inclination correction will have on the
Laurentian APWP, we have ﬁrst updated the 300 –235 Ma compilation
of Torsvik et al. (2008) , according to the 2009 geologic timescale
(Table 2). Of the ﬁve igneous results that were reported in the original
compilation, only one result (#37) remains after updating the ages;
and this result is derived from a single intrusion (i.e. single cooling
unit), highlighting the importance of the new IL result. We have also
added an Early Triassic result from a diatreme in British Columbia
(#36), but this result is also based on a single cooling unit. In Fig. 8b
we plot the updated APWP after correcting the inclination of all redbed
records with an f value of 0.54. There is an obvious improvement in the
agreement between the IL result and the Middle Permian segment of
the APWP after these corrections. In Fig. 8c we correct the redbed re-
cords according to f = 0.46, which corresponds to the mean estimated
shallowing factor determined from our VGP distribution analysis. This
correction does not appreciably improve the agreement between the
IL pole and the APWP relative to the more conservative correction of
f = 0.54. We note the increasing A95 of the mean poles with increasing
inclination correction (decreasingf), and attribute this to our simplistic
“average” correction. Although we have argued that the redbeds are all
likely affected by a shallow inclination bias, it is unlikely that they all
share a bias of exactly the same magnitude. We contend that our
analysis is a valuable demonstration of the widespread presence of
too-shallow inclinations in these records, and that our correction offers
a better approximation of the true Laurentian APWP, but future detailed
work will be necessary to more precisely correct the results for each re-
cord. Due to the correlation between mean pole A95 and f and the lack of
signiﬁcant improvement between the corrections of f = 0.54 and
f = 0.46, we prefer the conservative correction.
Regardless of the improvement between the IL pole and the
Laurentian APWP, the shift in the APWP after inclination correction brings
it into better agreement with the APWP of Gondwana. After updating the
ages of the poles used in the Laurentian compilation, the APWP also ex-
hibits a sharp bend in the latest Paleozoic, as previously observed in
Gondwana's APWP (Domeier et al., 2011). The discrepancy remaining be-
tween the APWPs in Fig. 8 b may be ascribed to a similar shallow

inclination bias— among other data-pathologies— in the paleomagnetic
records from Gondwana. InFig. 8d we compare the f = 0.54 inclination
corrected APWP of Laurentia with aﬁltered Permian and Triassic paleo-
magnetic data-set from South America (Domeier et al., 2011). Although
this ﬁltered data-set is not explicitly corrected for inclination shallowing,
it includes more poles based on data from igneous rocks than the larger
Torsvik et al. (2008) compilation, and the included records have been
subjected to more stringent selection criteria. The separation between
the Late Permian pole from the ﬁltered South American data-set and
the Late Permian poles of the inclination corrected APWP of Laurentia in
Fig. 8di sg r e a t l yr e d u c e dr e l a t i v et oFig. 8a, supporting the contention
that the long-standing discrepan cy between the APWPs of Laurussia
and Gondwana may simply be a manifestation of systemic bias.
8. Conclusions
Our investigation of shallow intrusive rocks and a contact metamor-
phosed limestone in southern Illinois (cratonic Laurentia) yields a new
Middle Permian (~270 Ma) paleomagnetic pole with a paleolatitude
that is distinctly higher than that of the Middle Permian segment of
the reference APWP of Laurentia. We argue that this discrepancy is
due to a widespread, shallow inclination bias in the Laurentian paleo-
magnetic data, following the observation that the reference APWP
is dominated by data derived from continental redbeds. A comparison
between theoretical VGP distributions and published VGP sets from
the Laurentian redbeds reveals the latter to have a distribution that is
incompatible with the expectations of TK03.GAD. The commonly elon-
gate VGP distributions observed in the Laurentian redbed paleomagnet-
ic records are instead consistent with a pervasive shallow inclination
bias, suggesting that a “ﬂattening” on the order of f = 0.54 to f = 0.39
(mean of f = 0.46) has affected the inclinations. Using the conservative
estimate of shallowing ( f = 0.54), we correct the inclinations of the
redbed paleomagnetic records and demonstrate that the modiﬁed Lau-
rentian APWP agrees more closely with both our new igneous rock-
based paleomagnetic pole and the APWP of Gondwana. We contend
that such a shallow inclination bias is also likely to be widespread in
the sedimentary rock-based paleomagnetic records from Gondwana,
and that this data-pathology may be the principal cause of the long-
standing disparity between the APWPs. Finally, we note that the ap-
proach adopted here is simplistic in its assumption that all the redbeds

This paper presents the results of a paleomagnetic study undertaken on samples from Lower Triassic and Lower
Cretaceous sediments within the northeastern Sichuan Basin, China, in an area close to the Daba Mountains. Step-
wise thermal demagnetization was used to isolate the characteristic higher temperature component (HTC) for
these samples. These HTC (T1: D = 53.7°, I = 21.6°, α
95 = 6.5°; K1: D = 28.9°, I = 25.7°, α95 = 6.6°) passed
both fold and reversal tests, and indicate that these sediments have undergone sequential clockwise rotations rel-
ative to the Sichuan basin. These detected tectonic rotations were probably caused by the obstruction of the
Hannan massif during Mesozoic thrusting within the southern Daba Mountains. The northeastern Sichuan Basin
and the central Yangtze Fold Belt formed part of a continuous belt of basins (the northern Yangtze Basin), and
acted as a coherent tectonic domain during the Early–Middle Jurassic. The Daba Mountains and the central Yangtze
Fold Belt subsequently underwent rapid uplift and cooling around the Late Jurassic and Early Cretaceous. This sug-
gests that tectonic rotations within both the central Yangtze Fold Belt and the Daba Mountains were very probably
caused by intra-continental deformation over a long period of time rather than a single tectonic event.

1. Introduction
The collision between the North China Block (NCB) and South China
Block (SCB) is one of the most important geological events during the
Mesozoic formation of East Asia. This process is thought to haveﬁnished
by the Early–Middle Jurassic (Yang et al., 1992; Yang and Besse, 2001),
and subsequent compressional deformation of the Yangtze Block during
the Late Jurassic and Cretaceous was associated with the development
of a Mesozoic thrust system that extended from the Xuefeng and
Wuling mountains in the southeast, to the Sichuan Basin in the north-
west (Yan et al., 2003). This area is far from any present-day continental
margins, and the majority of the post-Late Triassic deformation oc-
curred in an intracontinental setting ( Liu et al., 2012 ). These observa-
tions suggest that deformation in the Yangtze block after the NCB–SCB
collision was not limited to the margins.
Recent studies of the Middle Yangtze Fold Belt have identiﬁed clear
clockwise rotations, as indentiﬁed using paleomagnetic data obtained
from Triassic strata ( Huang and Opdyke, 1996, 1997; Su et al., 2005;
Tan et al., 2007 ). However, the processes that caused this rotation are
unclear. For example, Huang and Opdyke (1996, 1997) determined
that the Middle Triassic paleomagnetic declination from the central
Yangtze Fold Belt is roughly paralleled to E –W trending fold axes, al-
though samples taken closer to the Qinling suture yielded northerly pa-
leomagnetic declinations. Thus, Huang and Opdyke (1997) suggested
that these rotations were not related to the NCB–SCB collision. In addi-
tion, Yang and Besse (2001) tested the oroclinal –rotation hypothesis
within the Yangtze Fold Belt by comparing paleomagnetic declinations
and strike directions for the Mesozoic fold axes in latest Permian to Mid-
dle Triassic sediments, concluding that this hypothesis was negative. Fur-
thermore,Tan et al. (2007) compared paleomagnetic rotations with fold
axis trends within the Yangtze Fold Belt and suggested that the general
clockwise rotation was in fact related to the NCB–SCB collision, although
the timing of the clockwise rotation is not well constrained, and further
studies are needed to determine whether the central Yangtze Fold Belt
is in fact an orocline. This question cannot be answered until data are
obtained from younger sediments in this area. However, analysis of
Jurassic sediments within the Zigui area did not yield primary paleo-
magnetic directions (Tan et al., 2007 ) Therefore, we tried to ﬁnd new
evidences from other areas near the northwestern margin of the SCB.
The Daba Mountains form a curved tectonic belt within the southern
Qinling Orogen; the southward bend in these mountains contrasts sharp-
ly with the rest of this orogenic. In the Daba fold belt, the Chengkou –
Zhongbao fault has been a key boundary between the Northern and
Southern Daba Mountains (Fig. 1). Many geological studies were carried
out in this area ( Dong et al., 2006; S. Dong et al., 2008; Y. Dong et al.,
2008; Guo et al., 1996; He et al., 1997, 1999; Hu et al., 2012; Liu et al.,

that intense Late Jurassic–Early Cretaceous intracontinental tectonism oc-
curred within the southern Qinling Orogen and the Northern Daba Moun-
tains. This deformations affected Mesozoic sedimentary cover sequences
in this area, and thrusting and foldingoccurred throughout almost the en-
tirety of the southern Daba Mountains. However, this southwestward-
directed thrusting was obstructed by the rigid Hannan and Huangling–
Shennongjia massifs to the west and east, respectively, resulting in the
formation of an arcuate structure in this area (G u o e ta l . ,1 9 9 6 ;L i ue ta l . ,
2006; Zhang et al., 2010).
Previous study of the Early–Middle Jurassic sediments in the Southern
Daba Mountains (Wang and Zhang, 2010) provided evidence of a Late
Jurassic–Early Cretaceous clockwise rotation (26.5 ± 9°). The curved tec-
tonic belts within the Daba Mountains and the central Yangtze Fold Belt
have a number of similarities, including: (1) a close relationship to the
NCB–SCB collision, (2) evidence of late Mesozoic tectonic rotations,
(3) location within the margins of the Yangtze block, and (4) both
areas contain Late Triassic and Early Jurassic sediments. Given these
similarities, here we present a new model for tectonic rotations within
the central Yangtze Fold Belt. This model is based on data obtained
from Mesozoic sediments near the Daba Mountains, and provides in-
sights into the tectonic evolution of the Qinling Orogen and the post-
collisional processes that affected both the North and South China
plates.
2. Geological setting and sampling
Paleomagnetic samples were obtained using a portable drill and
were collected from the Lower Triassic Feixianguan and Lower Creta-
ceous Cangxi formations along roads between Zhenba County in Shaan-
xi Province and Tongjiang city in Sichuan province. The Feixianguan
Formation consists of aubergine-colored marlite that contains Early Tri-
assic Claraia aurita, Claraia stachei,a n d Eumorphotis mulliformis fossils,
whereas the Cangxi Formation consists of brick red and aubergine-
colored mudstones and siltstones (BGMRS, 1991).
A total of 24 sites were drilled (13 sites within the Feixianguan for-
mation and 11 sites within the Cangxi formation), all of which were ori-
ented with a magnetic compass (Fig. 1). Samples were cut into 2.2-cm-
long specimens at the Paleomagnetic Laboratory of Nanjing University,
China, and present-day geomagnetic declinations were determined
(−2.6°at Zhenba County) using the International Geomagnetic Refer-
ence Field (Mandea and MacMillan, 2000).

4. Discussion
Using these primary remanent magnetizations, the corresponding
Lower Triassic and Lower Cretaceous poles were calculated (T1: 36.5/
208.3°, A 95 = 5.9°; K1: 57.7/225.8°, A 95 = 6.0°). These results were
then compared with coeval poles from areas around the Sichuan basin
(Table 3 ; Fig. 8 ). The Lower Triassic and Lower Cretaceous poles
obtained from this studies showed distinct clockwise rotations relative
to the Sichuan basin (T1, 9.3 ± 5.3°; K1, 8.8 ± 8.3°). Considering an-
other clockwise rotation (26.5 ± 9°) detected by our previous work
(Wang and Zhang, 2010) carried out on the early–middle Jurassic strata,
the Mesozoic strata in our research area showed a series of clockwise
rotations.

to the west, and the subduction of oceanic crust of the Paciﬁc Plate to the
east (Dong et al., 2011; Ratschbacher et al., 2003). Data of ESR (Electron
Spin Resonance) on quartz of the conjugate joint and ﬁssion track (Liu
et al., 2006; Shen et al., 2007 ) indicated that the majority of folding
within the South-Daba Mountains mainly occurred during the Early
Cretaceous. This suggested that the tectonic rotation detected in this re-
search might have resulted from long-term tectonic events that peaked
in the Early Cretaceous, sometime after the deposition of the Cangxi For-
mation. However, it was not possible to determine the timing of the end
of this long-term process, as the study area does not contain exposed
Late Cretaceous and younger sediments.
The amalgamation between the NCB and SCB is thought to have
ceased around the Early –Middle Jurassic (Yang et al., 1992; Yang and
Besse, 2001), although subsequent intracontinental tectonic process oc-
curred within the NCB and SCB until the Early Cretaceous. This suggests
that the rotations detected by our results may have been associated
with the initial stages of this tectonic developing process, and further re-
search in different areas of the Daba Mountains is needed to test the
oroclinal–rotation hypothesis.
Paleomagnetic data from Triassic units indicated that the central
Yangtze Fold Belt also underwent a similar clockwise rotation relative
to the Sichuan basin ( Huang and Opdyke, 1996, 1997; Steiner et al.,
1989; Su et al., 2005; Tan et al., 2007 ). Tan et al. (2007) argued that
this rotation was probably related to the collision between the NCB
and SCB. However, the timing of this clockwise rotation is still unknown,
and the limited number of Jurassic and Cretaceous paleopoles for this
area means that a detailed rotation model cannot be constructed.
However, stratigraphy and thermochronology can be used to provide
alternative evidence for the rotation of this area. Liu et al. (2005) sug-
gested that a continuous belt of basins, termed the northern Yangtze
Basin developed along the southern front of the Qinling–Dabieshan dur-
ing the Early –Middle Jurassic with the northeastern Sichuan, Zigui
and Dangyang Basins also ﬁlled by the same depositional system.
Southward-directed thrusting of the northern Yangtze fold thrust
belt (NYFB) and northwestward-directed thrusting of the Jiangnan fold
thrust belt (JNFB) caused Later Jurassic to the Early Cretaceous uplift of
the Zigui Basin uplifted, resulting in the migration of the depocenter to
the northern Sichuan Basin. In addition, apatite ﬁssion-track dating
indicates that the Tongbai–Dabie region, Huangling and the Daba Moun-
tains areas underwent rapid uplifting and cooling event during the Later
Jurassic to Early Cretaceous (Hu et al., 2006; Shen et al., 2007, 2009). This
was followed by a period of relative thermal stability before accelerated
uplifting in the Cenozoic. This suggests that the tectonic rotations within
both the Middle Yangtze Fold Belt and the Daba Mountains were the re-
sult of similar processes, with bo th being affected by late Mesozoic
intracontinental deformation associated with long-term tectonism rath-
er than a single tectonic event.

Abstract To better understand the India-Asia collisional process and intracontinental deformation within Asia,
a paleomagnetic study has been conducted on the Qushenla Formation lavaﬂows dated at ~132– 120 Ma from
the Yanhu area in the western Lhasa terrane. Stepwise thermal demagnetization isolates stable characteristic
remanent magnetizations, which include dual polarity and pass fold tests at a 99% conﬁdence level, indicating
primary magnetizations. The tilt-corrected site-mean direction for 51 sites is D = 28.2°, I =3 4 . 5 ° , a n dk = 74.3°
with α95 = 2.3°, corresponding to a paleopole at 61.4°N, 192.9°E (A95 = 2.1°). Our new paleomagnetic data,
combined with previous Cretaceous volcanic paleomagnetic data from the Lhasa terrane, show that the
precollisional southern margin of Asia was at ~16.8°N with a relatively E-W alignment and that the Lhasa terrane
did not experience signiﬁcantly discrepant north-south movement although local vertical axis rotations did
take place after the Cretaceous. Comparison with the apparent polar wander paths (APWPs) of India and the
Cretaceous-Paleocene paleopoles of the Tethyan Himalaya shows that the India-Asia collision was at ~54.3 Ma
and the Greater India during the Paleocene had a large northern extent of ~2000 km (~18.1°) beyond its present
northern margin. Comparison with the Cretaceous Eurasian APWP indicates that a latitudinal convergence
of ~1000 km has taken place between the Lhasa terrane and Eurasia since the India-Asia collision. The
amount of north-south shortening deduced from Cretaceous paleomagnetic data is consistent with that
accommodated by the Cenozoic fold and thrust belts between the Lhasa terrane and the Hexi corridor.
1. Introduction
The ongoing collision between India and Asia has created the Himalayan-Tibetan Orogen, which is the
youngest and most spectacular continent-continent collisional belt on Earth [e.g.,Yin and Harrison, 2000]. In the
last four decades, many geologic and geophysical investigations have been carried out in the Himalayan-
Tibetan Orogen and its neighboring regions to manifest the India-Asia collisional process and associated
intracontinental deformation within Asia [e.g., Molnar and Tapponnier,1 9 7 5 ;Patriat and Achache,1 9 8 4 ;Otofuji
et al.,1 9 8 9 ;Yang and Besse,1 9 9 3 ;Meyer et al.,1 9 9 8 ;Yang et al., 2002; Huang et al., 2006; Lippert et al., 2011;
Li et al., 2013a]. However, disputes still exist concerning the magnitude of postcollisional convergence between
the Lhasa terrane and stable Asia from more than 1500 km [Achache et al., 1984; Lin and Watts,1 9 8 8 ;Chen et al.,
1993; Sun et al., 2008, 2010, 2012] to only a few hundred kilometers [ Tan et al., 2010], the age of the India-Asia
collision from the Late Cretaceous (~70– 65 Ma) [e.g., Cai et al.,2 0 1 1 ;Mo et al., 2003, 2008; Tong et al., 2008; Yin
and Harrison, 2000] to the Eocene/Oligocene boundary (~34 Ma) [eg.,Aitchison et al., 2007], and the width of the
Neo-Tethyan Ocean during the Late Jurassic– Early Cretaceous from only 1300 km [Xiao and Wang, 1998] to
more than 6000 km [e.g., Van Der Voo et al. , 1999; Chen et al., 2012].
Paleomagnetism is the only technique that can quantify the plate paleolatitude as a way to constrain
kinematic processes of plate movement. Therefore, many Cretaceous paleomagnetic studies from the Lhasa
terrane [Pozzi et al. , 1982; Westphal et al. , 1983; Achache et al. , 1984; Lin and Watts , 1988; Chen et al. , 1993;
Sun et al. , 2008, 2012; Tan et al., 2010; Chen et al. , 2012; Tang et al., 2013], which was located along the

precollisional paleolatitude and thereby constrain the age of the India-Asia collision, the postcollisional
convergence within Asia and even the width of the Neo-Tethyan Ocean. Noticeably, the reported Cretaceous

[Tauxe, 1993] or from rock in which bedding is dif ﬁcult to identify, which makes it almost impossible to
recover its original level. Furthermore, some paleomagnetic data lack robust ﬁeld tests; positive ﬁeld tests
such as fold and reversal tests are vital for enhancing the reliability of a paleomagnetic result [ Van der Voo ,
1990]. In addition, the Lhasa terrane is long and narrow, with a width of only 100 to 300 km from south to
north but a length of ~2000 km from east to west (Figure 1). Previous Cretaceous paleomagnetic
investigations, with the exception of the western one reported by Chen et al. [1993] and the two central ones
reported by Chen et al. [2012] and Tang et al. [2013], mainly focus on the eastern part of the Lhasa terrane
(Figure 1). To better constrain the paleolatitude and shape of the southern margin of Asia prior to the
Cenozoic India-Asia collision, more reliable Cretaceous paleomagnetic data from the western part of the
Lhasa terrane are needed.
In this paper, we present a combined paleomagnetic and geochronological data set from Lower Cretaceous
lava ﬂows near the town of Yanhu, in the western part of the Lhasa terrane. Our new paleomagnetic data
overcome many of the de ﬁciencies mentioned above in previous Cretaceous paleomagnetic studies.
2. Geology and Sampling
The Tibetan Plateau is principally an agglomeration of ﬁve terranes; from north to south these are the Kunlun-
Qaidam, Songpan-Ganzi-Hoh Xil, Qiangtang, Lhasa, and Himalayan terranes (Figure 1). The Lhasa terrane is
located between the Tethyan Himalaya on the south and the Qiangtang terrane on the north. Previous
geological observations showed that it was located at the southern margin of Asia prior to its collision
with India in the Cenozoic and that it accreted onto the Qiangtang terrane of the growing Asian continent
during the latest Jurassic to earliest Cretaceous [Chen et al., 1993; Matte et al., 1996; Metcalfe, 2006; Halim et al.,

Fifty-four sampling sites were selected on two sections separated by ~20 km (Figure 2). Thirty-eight of these
sites, incorporating 426 core samples, were collected from section A (32°20.3 ′N, 82°33.9′E) located ~20 km
southeast of the town of Yanhu, where the bedding dips steeply toward the east at 63 –82° (Figure 3a).
Another 16 sites, incorporating 173 core samples, were drilled from section B (32°24.8 ′N, 82°45.2′E). This
section lies ~30 km southeast of Yanhu, where the dip is about 27° toward the south (Figure 3b). The bedding
attitudes in both sampling sections are obvious due to the discrepant weathering of different volcanic rocks,
and can be readily determined at boundaries between two different lavas or other volcanic rocks (Figure 3).
Generally, each site contains at least 10 core samples and spans several meters in stratigraphic thickness — or
at least one lava ﬂow (Figures 3d and 3e). All the core samples, which were cut into 2.2 cm long specimens
in the laboratory, were collected using a portable gasoline-powered drill and were oriented by both a
magnetic compass and a Sun compass. Comparing these two oriented results revealed a declination
difference less than 2°, indicating that the local magnetic disturbance in both sections can be neglected.

3. U-Pb Zircon Geochronology
Zircons were ﬁrst separated from protoliths for each sample, following the methods introduced by Xiu et al.
[2001], and then were hand-picked under a binocular microscope, mounted in epoxy resin, and polished to
expose the internal structure of each grain. The morphology and internal structures of the zircons were

The U-Pb isotopic analysis was carried out using laser ablation sampling and multiple collector inductively

and are free of inclusions and cracks. U-Th-Pb concentrations were calibrated using NIST612 as an
external standard. Fractionation correction of the U-Pb isotope was conducted using GJ-1 as an

The zircon grains are euhedral to subhedral and show prismatic shapes (50 to 150 μm in length) with an
aspect ratio of ~2 (Figure 4). These characteristics, combined with the clear oscillatory zoning in CL images,
suggest that they are magmatic in origin.
Zircon U-Pb analyses for all samples yield multiple age groups, suggesting different sources for the zircons.
The weighted mean 206Pb/238U ages of the youngest age groups are interpreted as the timing of
emplacement of the studied volcanics, and those of other older age groups may be from inherited zircons,
representing the timing of earlier magmatic activity in the region.
The youngest Zircon U-Pb ages are shown in Figure 5. The lowermost and uppermost samples of section A
yield weighted mean 206Pb/238U ages of 132.0 ± 2.0 Ma (Figure 5a) and 126.4 ± 1.1 Ma (Figure 5b),
respectively. Zircons from sites YH39 and YH54 give weight mean 206Pb/238U ages of 120.0 ± 1.0 Ma and
120.8 ± 0.9 Ma, respectively (Figures 5c and 5d). These ages indicate that the two volcanic rock sequences
erupted during the Early Cretaceous, and they have not overturned during folding.

123.1 ± 0.9 Ma (Figure 5e), which is consistent with Zenong Gp volcanism from ~130 to ~110 Ma [Zhu et al., 2008].

Backscattered electron (BSE) images and EDS analyses show that the studied volcanic specimens contain

5. Paleomagnetic Results
All thermal demagnetization and remanence measurement were performed at the PEML of CUGB where
magnetometers and ovens are located in a shielded room with a residual ﬁeld of less than 300 nT. Remanent
magnetization was measured using a JR-6A spinner magnetometer, and thermal demagnetization over 16 to 21
steps was carried out in an ASC-TD 48 furnace with an internal residualﬁeld of less than 10 nT. Demagnetization
temperature intervals are generally 100– 50°C in the low-temperature part and shift to 20 – 5°C in higher
temperatures. Characteristic remanent magnetization (ChRM) directions of 459 specimens from 53 sites
(YH1– YH53) were determined using principal component analysis [Kirschvink, 1980], and ChRM directions of 10
specimens from the site YH54 were obtainedusing remagnetization great circle planeﬁtting techniques [McFadden
and McElhinny, 1988]. Site-mean directions were calculated using Fisherian statistics [Fisher, 1953]. Paleomagnetic
data were analyzed using the computer program packages developed by Enkin [1990] and Cogné [2003].
With the exception of the specimens from site YH54 that cannot obtain a reliable high temperature
component (HTC) using principal component analysis, those from other sites generally have the same
demagnetization characteristics and a reliable HTC can be determined. Typical orthogonal diagrams shown
in Figure 9 reveal that most specimens do not have a stable low-temperature component close to the present
geomagnetic ﬁeld direction, but rather a reliable HTC, which decays toward the origin, can be isolated
between 400°C and 620 – 680°C. Furthermore, the HTCs isolated from three specimens (one specimen from
the site YH28 and the other two from YH32) show reverse polarity directions which are almost antipodal to
the normal HTC directions (Figures 9f and 9g). An unblocking temperature as high as 620 – 680°C and a rapid
decay of remanence intensity between 500 and 580 °C, together with the above mentioned rock magnetic
results, show that both magnetite and hematite are abundant in the studied specimens (Figures 6 and 7) and
suggest that the HTC is carried by magnetite and hematite.
Each site-mean direction of HTCs is listed in Table 1. Except for sites YH40 and YH41, for which the site-mean
directions are proved to be outliers according to the Jackknife test [ Cogné, 2003] and might have been
magnetized during a geomagnetic excursion, all other sites have similar site-mean directions after tectonic
corrections. However, considering that ChRM directions from site YH54 were obtained using the
remagnetization great circle plane ﬁtting techniques, we also exclude this site from further discussion.
Noticeably, although the ChRM directions of the remaining 51 sites are fully intersectional within the 95%
conﬁdence limit (Figure 10), section A yields a tilt-corrected site-mean direction of Ds = 26.5°, Is = 31.8°,
ks = 89.5 and α95 = 2.5°, which is a bit different from section B that provides a tilt-corrected site-mean

6. Averaging Out Paleosecular Variation
Volcanic rocks acquire thermal remanence during cooling in the presence of a magneticﬁeld and thus are the
most accurate records of the geomagnetic ﬁeld [Tauxe, 1993]. However, paleomagnetic records from volcanic
rocks provide only spot readings of geomagnetic ﬁeld behavior. To obtain accurate paleolatitudes, we have
to not only make exact structural corrections but also average out paleosecular variation. Noticeably,
although it is controversial whether the VGP scatter ( S value) is a suitable parameter for quantifying
paleosecular variation [ Linder and Gilder, 2011, 2012], a widely accepted approach is to compare the VGP
scatter with those expected by McFadden et al. [1991]. Considering that more than 99% of specimens yield
normal polarities and their U-Pb zircon ages range from 132.0 ± 2.0 Ma to 120.0 ± 1.0 Ma, we compared the
VGP scatter of the Early Cretaceous Qushenla Fm volcanic rocks with the expected value of the CNPS. Our
new paleomagnetic results show that the ChRM directions of 51 sites have a VGP scatter of 8.4, which
falls into the expected VGP scatter interval (7.0 – 11.3) at 95% con ﬁdence limits and is reasonably consistent
with the expected value of 8.7 [McFadden et al., 1991]. This, together with the sampling of lava ﬂows spanning
a long time from 132.0 ± 2.0 Ma to 120.0 ± 1.0 Ma as determined by U-Pb zircon ages (Figure 5), a large
number of paleomagnetic sites sampled from different lava ﬂows (Figure 3 and Table 1), and the HTC

In addition to the above mentioned volcanic paleomagnetic data, seven sedimentary paleomagetic results
from the eastern Lhasa terrane have been reported from red beds of the Shexing Fm, which has been
previously referred as the Takena Fm (Table 2). These seven red bed results yield paleolatitudes ranging from

et al. [1984]; (2) two available Cretaceous paleomagetic investigations on basalt ﬂows intercalated with red
beds showed that the two site-mean directions for the interbedded red beds and basalt ﬂows are quite

unresolved problem for the validity of paleomagnetic data from red beds [Tan et al., 2010; Najman et al., 2010;

the 95% conﬁdence level is also comparable with those from red beds (Table 2), we also ignore this limestone
paleopole in further discussion because it is from only 22 specimens, with a large error bar and without a
robust ﬁeld test.

7.2. The Age of the India-Asia Collision
Because the widely accepted geological boundary between India and Asia is located at the present-day
Indus-Tsangpo suture zone that separates the Tethyan Himalaya in the south from the Lhasa terrane in the
north [e.g., Yin and Harrison , 2000; Yin, 2010], the age of the India-Asia collision can be determined by the
paleolatitudinal intersection of the northern margin of the Tethyan Himalaya and the southern margin of
the Lhasa terrane (Asia) [e.g., Dupont-Nivet et al. , 2010; Chen et al. , 2010; Meng et al. , 2012]. For the Lhasa
terrane, the Cretaceous volcanic paleomagnetic results from the middle western Lhasa terrane show that its
southern margin before the India-Asia collision was located at ~16.8°N for the reference point (29.8°N, 84.0°E)
at the present-day middle western Indus-Tsangpo suture. For the Tethyan Himalaya which is generally
accepted to represent the northern extent of Greater India [e.g., Yin and Harrison , 2000; Ali and Aitchison ,
2005; Yi et al. , 2011; Meng et al. , 2012], paleomagnetic results from the Zongpu, Zhepure Shan, and Youxia
Formations in the Dingri area have suffered from serious remagnetization [ Tong et al. , 2008; Liebke et al. ,
2013]. However, Patzelt et al. [1996] obtained two paleopoles in the Gamba and Duela areas at 65.4°N,
277.6°E with d p/dm = 3.8°/7.6° (ZP1) for the Zongpu Fm (59 ± 4 Ma) and 55.8°N, 261.4°E with d p/dm =
4.4°/8.6° (ZS) for the Zongshan Fm (68 ± 3 Ma), corresponding to paleolatitudes of 5.8° ± 3.8°N and 4.4° ± 4.4°S
for the reference point at 29.8°N, 84.0°E (Table 3).Dupont-Nivet et al.[2010] applied the E/I correction method to
these paleomagnetic data from Himalayan limestone and suggested that they have not been affected by

A paleolatitude of 11.9° ± 2.5°N for the northern margin of the Tethyan Himalaya at 57.5 ± 1.5 Ma is much
farther south than 16.8° ± 1.5°N for the precollisional southern margin of the Lhasa terrane, showing that
the collision between the Tethyan Himalaya (India) and the Lhasa terrane (Asia) could not have occurred at
57.5 ± 1.5 Ma. The paleolatitude difference suggests that the northern margin of the Tethyan Himalaya
must have moved ~4.9° farther north before reaching the southern margin of the Lhasa terrane. The drift
rate of the Tethyan Himalaya is well determined by the expected paleolatitude calculated from the
apparent polar wander paths (APWPs) assuming that no signi ﬁcant relative displacement to the Indian
plate occurred in the period between the age of the Zongpu Fm and the initial collision. Previous
paleomagnetic results reported by Patzelt et al. [1996] and Yi et al. [2011] indicated that the northern
margin of the Tethyan Himalayan lay at 4.4° ± 4.4°S at 68 ± 3 Ma, 7.1° ± 3.5°N at 60.5 ± 1.5 Ma, and 11.9° ± 2.5°N
at 57.5 ± 1.5 Ma for the above mentioned reference point (Table 3), indicating that the Tethyan Himalayan
moved northward at a velocity of ~16.9 cm/yr for the time interval of 68.0 – 60.5 Ma and ~17.6 cm/yr for the
time interval of 60.5 – 57.5 Ma, respectively. These velocities for the Tethyan Himalaya between 68.0 and
57.5 Ma are in good agreement with the expected drift rate of ~16.8 cm/yr during ~70 – 55 Ma derived from
the Besse and Courtillot [2002] Indian APWP. We extrapolated a constant velocity of 17.1 cm/yr, which
is deduced from the time interval of 68.0 – 57.5 Ma, to yield a time span of ~3.2 Myr after ~57.5 Ma for
the northern margin of the Tethyan Himalaya (Greater India) to intersect with the southern margin of the
Lhasa terrane at ~16.8°N. This provides the most lik ely age for the collision of the Lhasa terrane and the
Tethyan Himalaya at ~54.3 Ma, which is consistent with (1) the remarkable slowdown of convergence
velocity between India and Asia occurred at 55 – 50 Ma [Torsvik et al. , 2008; Molnar and Stock , 2009; Copley
et al. ,2 0 1 0 ;van Hinsbergen et al. , 2011a], (2) the age of the last marine sediments recorded and the
ﬁrst occurrence of ophiolitic detritus and the Asian detritus on the Tethyan Himalaya dated at 55 – 50 Ma
[Zhu et al., 2005; Green et al., 2008; Najman et al. , 2010], and (3) the subduction-related ultrahigh-pressure
rocks in the Himalaya dated at early Eocene [ Guillot et al. , 2008].
Notably, when the northern margin of the Tethyan Himalaya collided with the southern margin of the
Lhasa terrane at ~16.8°N and ~54.3 Ma (Figure 11), the Indian craton was at ~1.3°S for the same reference
point (29.8°N, 84.0°E) based on the APWP of India [ Besse and Courtillot , 2002, 2003] and interpolating a
constant northward drift velocity between 60 Ma (7.8° ± 4.0°S) and 50 Ma (3.6° ± 4.1°N). This indicates that a
paleolatitudinal difference of ~18.1° (~2000 km) still exists between the Tethyan Himalaya and the Indian
craton (Figure 12). Such a paleolatitudinal difference can be explained by that either an oceanic basin
that existed between the Tethyan Himalaya and the Indian craton during the Cretaceous and Paleocene
[Van der Voo et al. , 1999; Ali and Aitchison , 2008; van Hinsbergen et al. , 2012; Metcalfe, 2013] or a Greater
India during the Paleocene that had a large northern extent of ~2000 km (~18.1°) beyond its present
northern margin [e.g., Yi et al. , 2011; Meng et al. , 2012]. However, considering that no suture zone has been
identiﬁed between the Tethyan Himalaya and the Indian craton, as well as new Triassic paleomagnetic
results suggested a ~1300 km northward extension of Greater India since the Triassic [ Ran et al. , 2012], the
paleolatitudinal difference of ~18.1° (~2000 km) most probably represents a contiguous northward extent
of the Greater India that has been accommodated by crustal shortening within the Himalaya and the
subduction of the Indian lithosphere beneath the Himalaya and Asia [e.g., DeCelles et al., 2002; Kind et al. ,
2002; Yi et al. , 2011; Meng et al. , 2012].
7.3. Quanti ﬁcation of Intracontinental Shortening Within Asia
The APWP for Eurasia and India have been reconstructed by Besse and Courtillot [1991, 2002] and Torsvik et al.
[2008, 2012]. The Besse and Courtillot [1991] Eurasian APWP , reappraised byBesse and Courtillot [2002], is most
widely used as a reference curve for late Meso-Cenozoic paleomagnetic studies in Asia. Notably,
paleomagnetic poles constructed for the Eurasian APWP are based mainly on data from northwestern
Europe, with few from Siberia or eastern Asia. However, recent geological and geophysical evidence has
shown that relative tectonic movements between the western (European) and eastern (Siberian) parts of the
Eurasian Plate were still in existence during the Cenozoic [e.g., Yegorova and Starostenko, 1999; Trifonov, 2004;
Bergerat et al. , 2007]. Cogné et al. [2013] proposed that the Besse and Courtillot [2002] Eurasian APWP is not

applicable to Siberia and East Asia and that its misapplication may cause the observed paleolatitude of
Siberia and East Asia regions to be ~10° lower than that expected from the Besse and Courtillot [2002]
Eurasian APWP in the Cenozoic. Furthermore, Cogné et al. [2013] also constructed a new reference APWP for
eastern Asia using paleomagnetic data from the Siberian craton, Amuria, the North and South China Blocks,
and the Korean Peninsula. However, the Cretaceous reference poles (~70 – 130 Ma) from Besse and Courtillot
[2002] are basically consistent with those from Cogné et al. [2013], indicating that the most widely used APWP
is still suitable to constrain Asian Cretaceous paleomagnetic data.
Comparing the paleolatitude (~16.8°N) observed from Cretaceous volcanic data with that (~26.1°N) expected
from the Eurasian average pole ( λ = 80.1°N, φ = 193.7°E with A95 = 2.1°) between 70 and 130 Ma shows a
signiﬁcant paleolatitude difference of 9.3° ± 2.6° for the reference point, corresponding to a north-south
directional convergence of 1000 ± 300 km. Notably, the anomalously low paleolatitudes have also been
observed in many Cretaceous and Tertiary paleomagnetic studies over central Asia and Tibet. These
anomalously low paleolatitudes have been attributed to several possible hypotheses, such as compaction-
induced inclination shallowing [e.g., Gilder et al. , 2001; Dupont-Nivet et al. , 2002; Tan et al., 2003, 2007; Tauxe
and Kent, 2004; Tauxe, 2005], a poorly constrained Eurasian APWP or nonrigidity of the Eurasian plate [ Cogné
et al., 1999, 2013], a long-lasting nondipolar geomagnetic ﬁeld [e.g., Westphal, 1993; Chauvin et al., 1996;
Si and Van der Voo , 2001], and tectonic shortening [e.g., Besse et al., 1984; Frost et al., 1995; Halim et al., 1998;
Chen et al. , 2002; Sun et al. , 2012]. Because compaction-induced inclination shallowing exists only in
sedimentary rocks, such an explanation is not applicable to the present case from volcanic rocks. Due to the
anomalously low paleolatitudes observed in this study that are obtained using the valid Cretaceous part of
the Eurasian APWP , the observations cannot be attributed to a poorly constrained Eurasian APWP or
nonrigidity of the Eurasian plate, either.
Westphal [1993] and Chauvin et al. [1996] ﬁrst proposed that a long-lasting nondipolar anomaly of the
geomagnetic ﬁeld during the Tertiary was a possible cause of the anomalously low paleolatitudes observed
in central Asia. However, many previous studies have shown that the main departure from an axial dipole is
an axial quadrupole and/or an octupole which amounts to no more than 3 – 5% of the total magnetic ﬁeld
[e.g., Coupland and Van der Voo , 1980; Besse and Courtillot , 1991; Carlut and Courtillot , 1998; Johnson et al. ,
2008]. Furthermore, Gilder et al. [2003] presented paleomagnetic data from Early Cretaceous volcanic rocks,
with an age that corresponds to those of the Zenong Gp and Qushenla Fm volcanic rocks, of the Tarim Basin.
Their paleomagnetic data yielded a paleolatitude which is consistent with the one calculated from the Besse
and Courtillot [2002] Eurasian reference APWP. Gilder et al. [2003] thereby rejected a long-standing
nondipolar geomagnetic ﬁeld for the region during that time. Therefore, there is no clear evidence that
attributes the observed low paleolatitudes in the Cretaceous volcanic rocks to a long-lasting nondipolar
geomagnetic ﬁeld.
The paleolatitude difference of ~9.3° between that observed in the Lhasa terrane and that expected from the
Eurasian APWP can be attributed to north-south intracontinental shortening between the Lhasa terrane
and Eurasia due to the Cenozoic collision of India and Asia and ongoing convergence. It is worth emphasizing
that the 1000 ± 300 km of north-south shortening deduced from these Cretaceous volcanic paleomagnetic
data is consistent with the 600 – 1000 km that is accommodated by Cenozoic fold and thrust belts between
the Lhasa terrane and the Hexi corridor (Figure 1) [ Yin and Harrison , 2000; Spurlin et al. , 2005; Yin et al. ,
2007; van Hinsbergen et al. , 2011b]. These belts include the Nan Shan thrust belt (NST) (~360 km), the Qimen
Tagh-North Kunlun thrust system (QTNK) (70– 270 km), the Fenghuo Shan-Nangqian fold and thrust belt (FSN)
(70– 110 km), and the Shiquanhe-Gaize-Amdo thrust system (SGA) (120 – 250 km).
8. Conclusions
We have presented new geochronologic and paleomagnetic results from 54 sites in the Lower Cretaceous
lava ﬂows of the Yanhu area in the western Lhasa terrane. These new paleomagnetic data not only satisfy the
secular variation model but fulﬁll all the seven quality criteria proposed by Van der Voo [1990] to appraise the
reliability of paleomagnetic data. Based on the new paleomagnetic data from lava ﬂows, and earlier
Cretaceous and Paleocene paleomagnetic data from the Lhasa terrane and the Tethyan Himalaya, several
main conclusions can be summarized, as follows:

1. The Lhasa terrane experienced no signi ﬁcantly discrepant north-south movement after the Cretaceous,
but local vertical axis rotations have taken place.
2. The precollisional southern margin of Asia was aligned relatively E-W.
3. The India-Asia collision in the middle western sutural zone was at ~16.8°N and ~54.3 Ma.
4. The Greater India during the Paleocene might have a large northern extent of ~2000 km (~18.1°) beyond
its present northern margin.
5. A north-south shortening amount of ~1000 km has taken place between the Lhasa terrane and Eurasia
(the Hexi corridor) since the India-Asia collision.

A paleomagnetic and rock magnetic study of the Manicouagan
impact structure: Implications for crater formation
and geodynamo effects
Michael Eitel1, Stuart A. Gilder 1, John Spray 2, Lucy Thompson 2, and Jean Pohl 1
1Department of Earth and Environmental Sciences, Ludwig Maximilians University, Munich, Germany, 2Planetary and Space
Science Centre, University of New Brunswick, Fredericton, New Brunswick, Canada
Abstract We report rock magnetic and paleomagnetic data from the ~214 Ma Manicouagan (Canada)
impact crater based on 25 widely distributed sites of impact melt and basement rocks collected at the
surface as well as from boreholes drilled to depths ≤1.5 km. Titanomagnetite and titanohematite carry the
magnetic remanence in impact melts above 320 m elevation and in most basement rocks. Impact melts
below 320 m contain solely titanomagnetite. Magnetic susceptibility and saturation magnetization, proxies
for titanomagnetite concentration, increase more tha n tenfold toward the base of the thickest impact melt
that underwent fractional crystallization. The titano magnetite-enriched zone partially contributes to a
2000 nT magnetic anomaly in the crater ’s center. Stepwise demagnetization reveals a single, normal
polarity magnetization component in all samples re gardless of the magnetic phases present. Coeval
lock-in remanence times for titanomagnetite and tita nohematite indicate that the titanohematite formed
>570°C during oxi-exsolution. The average paleomag netic direction and intensity coincide well with
214 Ma reference values. We ﬁnd no evidence for an aberration of the geomagnetic ﬁeld over the several
thousands of years it took to cool a 481 m thick po rtion of the impact melt body. Hence, the energy
released by the Manicouagan impact that created one of the 10 largest known craters on Earth provoked
no measurable disturbance of the geodynamo. Magn etic anisotropy of clast-free impact melts de ﬁne
magnetic lineation directions that are, in places, radially oriented with respect to the crater ’s center.
Centrifugal ﬂow of the melt within the evolving transient crater probably generated the fabric.
1. Introduction
Meteorite impact craters are common morphologic features in the solar system. The energy released during
impact events can exceed that of the largest terrestrial earthquakes by several orders of magnitude. Some of
this kinetic energy penetrates deep within the planet, potentially in ﬂuencing the magnetohydrodynamic
regime in the core, which could in turn perturb the dynamo generation process (see Eitel et al . [2014] for a
more detailed discussion). Evidence linking meteorite impacts to anomalous magnetic ﬁeld behavior arises
from correlating tektite layers with the paleomagnetic records in marine sediments [ Glass and Heezen ,
1967; Durrani and Khan , 1971; Glass and Zwart , 1979; Hartl and Tauxe , 1996]; however, the correlations are
highly debated [ Burns, 1990; deMenocal et al ., 1990; Schneider and Kent , 1990; Glass et al ., 1991; Schneider
et al., 1992].
To test the link between dynamo perturbation and hi gh-energy shock events, we initiated a paleomag-
netic study of rocks within meteorite craters whose ferromagnetic minerals cooled through their Curie
temperatures after impact. The objective is to samp le impact lithologies as a function of cooling time,
e.g., from the margins toward the interior of impact me lt sheets, to identify potential changes in magnetic
ﬁeld direction and/or intensity. To date we have carried out such work in the Ries (Germany [ Koch et al .,
2012]), Rochechouart (France [ Eitel et al ., 2014]), and Mistastin (Labrador, Canada [ Hervé et al ., 2015])
craters. Anomalous ﬁeld behavior has not been observed in any of them —possibly because the energy
released from these impact events was insuf ﬁcient to have an in ﬂu e n c eo rb e c a u s et h er o c k sc o o l e dt o o
fast after impact and “missed” the event. The amount of time captured by the magnetic record in these
craters did not exceed 400 years.
We now focus on the Manicouagan crater (Québec, Canada; Figure 1), whose rim-to-rim diameter of 85 km
ranks it as one of the ten largest impact craters on Earth [ Earth Impact Database , 2015]—2 to 3 times larger
in diameter than the craters we previously studied. Estimates of the energy released from this event range

2. Geological Setting and Sampling
The Manicouagan structure in Québec (Canada, 51.4°N, 68.7°W; Figure 1) formed when a 4 –6 km diameter
projectile impacted Proterozoic crystalline bedrock at hypervelocity. Several isotopic methods de ﬁne a
Late Triassic age for the impact. The K-Ar method applied to the impact melt yielded 210 ± 8 (2 σ)M a
[Wolfe, 1971], which was recalculated at 214 ± 8 Ma using revised decay constants [ Steiger and Jäger , 1978;
Grieve, 2006]. Jahn et al . [1978] obtained an Rb-Sr isochron age of 214 ± 5 Ma, while U-Pb dating on zircons
deﬁned a concordant age of 214 ± 1 Ma [ Hodych and Dunning , 1992]. An initial strontium 87Sr/86Sr value of
0.7099 supports the interpretation that the impact melts were derived from the Proterozoic basement
[Jahn et al ., 1978; O’Connell-Cooper et al ., 2012]. Zircons extracted from the melt sheet yielded 213.2
± 5.4 Ma based on (U-Th)/He [van Soest et al ., 2011]; (U-Th)/He applied to titanite separated from anorthosite
in the central uplift yielded 208.9 ± 4.1 Ma [ Biren et al ., 2014]. Diaplectic glass from basement rocks lying
10–12 km from the crater ’s center is suggestive of shock pressures ~35 GPa [ Grieve and Head , 1983], while
stishovite and maskelynite in the central uplift connote peak shock pressures from 12 to 30 GPa [ Biren and
Spray, 2011].
The Manicouagan structure is one of the best preserved and well-exposed impact craters on Earth [ Spray
et al ., 2010]. Impact melt sheet occurrences are restricted to the central 55 km diameter island (Île René
Levasseur), with rim collapse features occurring on the mainland at ~65 km diameter and beyond. The central
island is separated from the mainland by the Manicouagan reservoir, which is part of a hydroelectric program
initiated in the 1960s. From 1994 through to 2006, a number of drilling operations took place on the island to
appraise the structure as a potential analogue for the Sudbury impact structure of Ontario —a crater
renowned for its world-class Cu-Ni sul ﬁde and platinum group element deposits. While no signi ﬁcant eco-
nomic indicators have been found to date, the drilling programs furnished ~18 km of core, 10 km of which
is now held by the Planetary and Space Science Centre at the University of New Brunswick. Moreover, four
holes exceed 1.5 km in depth, thus providing an unprecedented window into the deeper structure of the
crater stratigraphy [Spray and Thompson, 2008]. Speciﬁcally, the 1.5 km deep M0608 drill hole, situated close
to the geometric center of the structure, penetrated >1 km of clast-free, differentiated impact melt and a
further 400 m of clast-laden impact melt before encountering footwall basement rocks. Thicker (~500 m)
sections of clast-free impact melt were also present in two other holes, drilled to the north and south of
M0608. Other centrally located drill holes to the east and west, with only a thin layer of impact melt, or none
at all, aid in delineating a probable fault controlled N-S trough of impact melt and demonstrate a locally
castellated structure to the crater ﬂoor at Manicouagan [ Spray and Thompson , 2008]. Previous estimates,
based on surface mapping and sampling, placed the melt sheet thickness at 200 –300 m [Floran et al ., 1978].
In August 2010, we drilled and oriented 198 cores at 25 sites in impact melts and basement rocks throughout
the crater; most basement rocks come from near the central uplift (Figure 1b). Cores were oriented either
manually with a magnetic compass or with an automated system [ Wack, 2012]. The average declination
anomaly from 78 Sun compass readings is  .8° ± 2.5°, which coincides well with that expected from the
international geomagnetic reference ﬁeld ( .2°). We also studied the impact melts from three drill holes
(M0302, M0603, and M0608; Figure 1b) that penetrated 702 m, 322 m, and 1529 m below the surface, respec-
tively. These deep cores stem from a commercially driven drilling program by three mining companies at 38
locations in the crater. The text below reports depths relative to sea level. Further details surrounding these
cores are reported in Spray and Thompson [2008], Spray et al . [2010], and O’Connell-Cooper and Spray [2011].
3. Experimental Results
3.1. Curie Temperature
We measured the temperature dependence of the magnetization with a Petersen Instruments variable ﬁeld
translation balance in an applied ﬁeld of 30 mT (surface cores) or 37 mT (deep drill cores) (Figure 2). Most
impact melt and melt-bearing breccia samples collected near the surface exhibit one or two de ﬂections in
the temperature ranges between 530 and 570°C and/or between 600 and 650°C, which are indicative of
relatively Ti-poor titanomagnetite and titanohematite, respectively (Figures 2a –2d). Anorthosite basement
rocks have Curie temperatures similar to the impact melts, lying generally in the range from 526 to 565°C
and around 610°C (Figure 2e). Gneissose diorite from site 25 has Curie temperatures either close to that of
stoichiometric magnetite (575°C) or higher ( >600°C) (Figure 2f). One observes a high degree of reversibility

Figure 4e shows a Day plot of the basement rocks (including basement clasts entrained in melt-bearing breccia
or in impact melt at the base of the impact melt sheet) for samples that only have a dominant Curie temperature
below 580°C. Titanomagnetite-bearing, deep-seated plutonic rocks like anorthosite and diorite would typically
plot in the multidomain ﬁeld on this graph, yet the samples from Manicouagan lie well within the pseudo
single-domainﬁeld. There are three potential explanations. One unlikely scenario is that titanohematite, clearly
present in many surface samples, is not expressed in the Curie temperature measurements but inﬂuences the
remanence and coercivity ratios. Although minor amounts of titanohematite could alter the coercivity ratio, it
should not raise the remanence ratio. Second is that high-temperature oxidation reduced the grain size fraction,
displacing preimpact titanomagnetite grains that would originally lie in the multidomain ﬁeld toward the
single-domainﬁeld on the Day plot. Such an effect was observed at the Mistastin crater, where baked anortho-
site within 1 m of the contact with impact melt has higher coercivity than nonbaked anorthosite lying farther
away from the contact [ Hervé et al ., 2015, Figure 6]. Third, pressure cycling of slightly oxidized multidomain
magnetite makes it more single-domain-like [ Gattacceca et al ., 2007; Carporzen and Gilder , 2010]. Figure 4e
superimposes the pressure-cycled data on the Day plot, which shows the evolution that multidomain magnetite
undergoes when pressurized up to 5.8 GPa. As the pressures involved at Manicouagan exceed 30 GPa, it is not
surprising that some samples plot well above the experimental result at 5.8 GPa. Moreover, Hervé et al. [2015]
found that the anorthosite basement rocks at Mistastin trend from multidomain to single domain when
approaching the center of the crater where pressures were greater. In sum, we interpret that the higher than
expected remanence ratios and lower than expected coercivity ratios of the titanomagnetite-bearing basement
rocks at Manicouagan reﬂ
ect both pressure and temperature effects related to the impact.

Demagnetization characteristics of the impact melts (Figures 5a –5l) are similar to those of the basement
rocks (Figures 5m –5p). Both thermal and alternating ﬁeld demagnetization unblock magnetization compo-
nents that decay univectorially to the origin after the ﬁrst few demagnetization steps. Despite the presence
of a single magnetization direction, normalized thermal demagnetization decay plots usually identify
multiple inﬂections at temperatures consistent with the in- ﬁeld thermoremanent data (Figure 2), e.g., indica-
tive of titanomagnetite and titanohematite. Alternating ﬁeld demagnetization to 75 mT removes nearly all of
the original moment in some samples (Figure 5k), while for others it is less effective (30% in Figure 5i, 70% in
Figure 5e). Magnetization directions for the latter case still trend toward the origin, which shows that the
higher coercivity component possesses the same direction as that with lower coercivity.
An important aspect of the demagnetization data is that a single magnetization direction of normal polarity
was recorded by all magnetic phases in each sample, meaning that the blocking of the remanence was
coeval for all magnetic recorders in a given rock. This observation holds true even when accounting for
directional differences among samples throughout the crater, which vary enough to be visible (if present)
on the orthogonal plots. The fact that we observe no such difference implies that the creation of titanohema-
tite (oxidation) occurred above titanomagnetite Curie temperatures and that no subsequent alteration by
weathering or hydrothermal activity inﬂuenced the ferrimagnets. Hence, the titanohematite likely originated
from high-temperature oxidation that occurred during degassing and not from convection or diffusion that
brought oxygen down into the melt from the surface.

3.5. Paleointensity
Absolute paleointensity experiments were performed according to the multispecimen, parallel differential, par-
tial thermal remanent magnetization (pTRM) protocol of Dekkers and Böhnel [2006] on 186, 5 mm diameter
cylindrical specimens taken from outcrops and from core M0603 that escaped drill-induced overprinting. The
multispecimen method was selected in preference to the classic Thellier-Thellier-type experiments given the
complex magnetic mineralogies and propensity of multidomain-sized grains in the Manicouagan samples.
Moreover, the magnetization of the samples rarely alters when heating in air at high ( >500°C) temperatures
(Figure 2). We only used specimens if the angle between their inclination measured at room temperature
deviated less than 60° from the core ’s z axis, which was the applied ﬁeld direction in the laboratory. Sample
magnetizations were measured after demagnetizing in two steps at 100°C and 500°C in a null ﬁeld. After null
ﬁeld heating to 500°C, we again heated them to 500°C and cooled them down to room temperature in the
presence of a magneticﬁeld (pTRM step), after which the samples were thermally cycled to 100°C in a nullﬁeld
before their magnetizations were measured. A heating threshold of 500°C was chosen because it was low
enough to avoid alteration and at least 20% of the natural remanent magnetization decayed by 500°C in step-
wise thermally demagnetized samples (Figure 5). The pTRM step was made in six discreteﬁelds from 10 to 60μT
for the surface samples and in eight discrete ﬁelds from 10 to 45 μT for the drill core samples.

exhibits a well-developed, ductile ﬂow fabric whose lineation trends radially from the crater ’s center
