in Supporting Information  S1). To better constrain the eruption age of our sampling lavas, we collected a 
dacitic andesite sample (MD43) for zircon U-Pb dating.
3. Methods
We applied heavy liquid and magnetic separation techniques to filter out zircon separation in sample MD43 
and purified them by handpicking use a binocular microscope, then we captured Cathodoluminescence 
(CL) images using a JSM-6510 Scanning Electron Microscope to display the internal structures of zircon 
grains. Zircon U-Pb isotopes were analyzed at the Department of Geological Sciences, University of Florida 
using a “Nu-Plasma HR” laser ablation multi-collector inductively coupled plasma mass spectrometer (LA-
MC-ICP-MS) equipped with 213 nm tandem Applied Spectra laser. Each acquisition incorporated 20 s back-
ground and followed a 30 s ablation (30 μm spot size) on zircon grains using Argon and Helium as carrier 
gas. FC-1 (1099.0 ± 0.7 Ma) zircons were used as external standards for calibration (Black et al., 2003). Raw 
data reduction was processed with a spreadsheet CALAMARI and diagrams were generated using Isoplot 
(Ludwig, 2003). Analytical data are summarized in Table S1 in Supporting Information S1.
We cut all oriented core specimens into 2.2 × 2.5 cm standard size and selected pilot samples from each 
sampling section for rock magnetic analysis. Hysteresis loops, Isothermal Remanent Magnetization (IRM) 
acquisitions and back-field demagnetization of saturated IRM (SIRM) were analyzed using a Micromag 
3900 Vibrating Sample Magnetometer at University of Florida. The andesite sample MD42-8 was subjected 
to a magnetization-temperature dependence experiment using a variable field translation balance at the 
Institute of Geology and Geophysics of the Chinese Academy of Sciences (IGGCAS). We then carried out 
stepwise thermal and/or alternating field demagnetization (>15 steps) on all core specimens to isolate char-
acteristic remanent magnetizations (ChRMs) at IGGCAS (sites MD35-43) and the Magnetotectonics Lab 
of Peking University (sites MD144–149). Both labs are magnetically shielded rooms with residual field less 
than 300 nT. For each demagnetization step, cores were heated in an ASC TD48-SC oven (internal field less 
than 10 nT), then measured using a 2G-755 superconducting rock magnetometer. Remanence components 
were isolated using principal component analysis (Kirschvink,  1980). Fisherian statistics were calculat -
ed using PMGSC (Enkin et al.,  2003), Pmagpy (Tauxe et al.,  2016) and/or paleomagnetism.org (Koymans 
et al., 2020) for crosscheck.
4. Results
4.1. Zircon U-Pb Dating
CL images display well-developed oscillatory zonation for most zircon grains of dacitic andesite sample 
(MD43), which are euhedral crystals with lengths range from 50 to 150 μm and length/width ratios of 3:2 to 
3:1 (Figure 3a). Zircon grains with discordant values (>5%) were excluded from mean calculation. A total of 
29 concordant analysis of zircon separations generated 206Pb/238U ages of 288–300 Ma and yielded a weight-
ed mean age of 291.8 ± 2.1 Ma (MSWD = 0.4, n = 29; Figure 3b).
4.2. Rock Magnetism
Magnetic signals of the sandstones from the Linxi (ML28-5) and Zhesi (MZ33-8) formations are relatively 
weak (Figures  4a–4f). Hysteresis loops are nearly reversible and fully saturated before 0.4 T (Figures  4a 
and 4d). The Bc and Bcr values are very low and SIRM values are less than 3 × 10−8 Am2/kg (Figures 4a, 4b, 
4d and 4e). Values of Mrs/Ms and Bcr/Bc are 0.04–0.09 and 3.06–4.67 respectively, indicating magnetite sizes 
near pseudo-single domain (PSD) to multi-domain (MD) (Dunlop,  2002). Component analysis of IRM ac -
quisition (Kruiver et al., 2001) yielded inconclusive results due to the noisy signal (Figures 4c and 4f). These 
indicate that the dominant magnetic carrier in the sandstones is low coercivity magnetite.
Magnetization-temperature dependence curve for the andesite sample (MD42-8) from the Dashizhai For -
mation is not fully reversible for the heating and cooling curves before ∼530 °C. In the heating process, 
the magnetization slightly decreases before ∼530  °C, followed by a rapid decrease up to ∼585  °C (Fig-
ure 4h). The hysteresis loop is narrow and essentially saturated at 0.4 T (Figure 4g). The SIRM values reach-
es 6 × 10 −6 Am2/kg. Values of Mrs/Ms and Bcr/Bc are 0.12 and 4.11 respectively, suggesting a PSD state of

magnetite (Figures  4g and  4i; Dunlop,  2002). Component analysis isolated three end-members including 
the low coercivity component (39.8 mT), intermediate coercivity component (107.2 mT) and high coercivity 
component (708.0 mT) (Figure 4j; Kruiver et al., 2001). The above analyses indicate magnetite is the domi-
nant magnetic carrier of the lavas in the Dashizhai Formation. A minor high coercivity component can be 
attributed to hematite formed by deuteric oxidation during lava cooling.
4.3. Paleomagnetism
The low temperature components (LTCs) of sandstones from the Linxi Formation were typically removed 
before 530°C (Figures 5a and 5b). Remanences are unstable after removal of LTCs (Figure 5b) and no stable 
ChRMs were isolated from these samples. Demagnetization of sandstones from the Zhesi Formation isolat-
ed single component, which were typically eliminated before 350°C and pointed to the origin (Figure  5c). 
The LTCs from both formations are close to the present geomagnetic field and indicative of a possibly recent 
overprint. Results from the Linxi and Zhesi formations are discarded for further analysis.
We identified two components in most lava samples of the Dashizhai Formation (Figures 5e–5n). The 
low stability components are scattered and typically removed by 250–450°C and 10 mT. Well-determined 
ChRMs were typically isolated between 500–560°C and 15–100 mT from at least four steps. We accepted the 
best resolved ChRMs with maximum angular deviation less than 15° then converted them to specimen-level 
VGPs (Table S2 in Supporting Information S1). Two types of cutoffs were applied to the VGPs, namely the 
fixed −45° and Vandamme cutoffs (Vandamme, 1994), and generated almost identical screening results. We 
chose the fixed −45° cutoff to filter out the most reliable data for further statistics (Figures  6a–6c; Table S2 
in Supporting Information  S1). Specimen-level mean ChRMs is calculated from the Fisher mean of VGPs 
and evaluated for paleosecular variation (PSV) of geomagnetic field using the N-dependent A95-envelope 
test (Deenen et al.,  2011). The mean ChRMs calculated from 116 out of 154 specimen-level VGPs is Dg/
Ig = 60.7°/−77.7°, kg = 5.0, α95 = 6.6° before and Ds/Is = 20.3°/−45.9°, ks = 31.1, α95 = 2.4° after tilt correc-
tion (Figures 6b and 6c). The A95 value falls into the N-dependent envelope (A95min = 1.8° <  A95 = 2.4°< 
A95max = 4.1°, N = 116, K = 30.4; Figure 6a; Table S2 in Supporting Information S1), indicating an averaged 
PSV in our data set. Data with negative inclinations were inverted and compared with the positive group. 
Both groups share a common true mean from 1000 bootstrapped Cartesian coordinates at 95% confidence 
(Figure 7; Tauxe, 2010), indicative of a positive reversal test. We also calculated the site-mean direction of 
ChRMs with Dg/Ig = 70.6°/−77.5°, kg = 4.8, α95 = 21.2° before and Ds/Is = 20.6°/-46.6°, ks = 55.7, α95 = 5.4° 
after tilt correction (N = 13 sites; Figures  6d and 6f; Table 1). Overall clustering improves after tilt correc -
tion with ks/kg = 11.66 > F (13, 13) = 1.98, suggesting a positive fold test at 95% confidence limit (Table  1; 
Figure 3. (a) Cathodoluminescence images of representative zircon grains from the dacitic andesites (MD43) of the Dashizhai Formation, showing 206Pb/238U 
ages of each analyzed spot; (b) U-Pb concordia diagram and weighted mean age plot.

294 ± 2 Ma (Zhang, 2013) and 313 ± 2 Ma (Zeng et al., 2011). Our zircon U-Pb dating for the dacitic andesite 
(MD43) yielded an age of 291.8 ± 2.8 Ma. Our sampling therefore spans an interval between 292–313 Ma

by combined rock magnetic analysis; (R4) positive fold tests; (R6) positive reversal tests and (R7) no re -
semblance to younger poles. However, our sampling location is rotated with respect to the eastern part of 
the Songliao block due to the Triassic left lateral motion along the Nenjiang-Balihan Fault (Figure  1a; Liu 
et al., 2017), so that these data fail the fifth R-criteria (R5) of Meert et al. (2020). Above all, we consider the 
new pole is reliable for paleolatitudinal reconstructions.
A summary of Permo-Carboniferous paleomagnetic data from North China, Siberia and blocks in the east-
ern CAOB are given in Table 2. The Apparent Polar Wander Path (APWP) for Siberia is adopted from Tors-
vik et al. (2012) and not corrected for inclination shallowing as all data are from igneous rocks. It is notewor-
thy there are only two reliable poles (360 Ma and 250 Ma) and the remainder of the APWP is interpolated. 
Another APWP of Siberia (Alternative A; Cocks & Torsvik,  2007) adopted the 275 Ma result of Pisarevsky 
et al. ( 2006), which yields much higher paleolatitudes for Siberia and indicates a separation from Baltica 
until 250 Ma. Here we choose not to use this APWP as the 275 Ma pole is similar to younger Triassic poles 
and amalgamation between Siberia and Baltica much likely occurred before the Early Permian (Cocks & 
Torsvik, 2007; Domeier & Torsvik, 2014; Han et al., 2011). The APWP of North China is adopted from Zhang 
et al. (2021), which corrected all clastic poles (data corrected by the original authors are excluded) using a 
flattening factor (f) of 0.7 to achieve consistency between coeval clastic and igneous results. Compared to 
redbeds, inclination shallowing is less significant in non-redbeds clastic rocks (Bilardello & Kodama, 2010), 
which characterized the data set of the CAOB. As a flattening factor of 0.6 has been advocated for the Low-
er Triassic redbeds in North China using anisotropy of remanence (Xue et al.,  2021) and E/I corrections 
(Zhou, Huang, et al., 2018), here we choose to apply f = 0.7 to correct the non-redbeds clastic data. In this 
way, we can achieve a consistent correction in the CAOB and adjacent blocks (see more details in Zhang 
et al., 2021). Paleolatitudinal comparison for the different blocks are calculated to a common reference site 
at 43°N, 114°E.
Zhao et al. ( 2020) reported a 283 Ma result from volcanic rocks in the Erguna block and advocated for a 
unified North China-Amuria block no later than the Early Permian. These data were obtained from 54 
specimens that yielded negative results in PSV tests. They argued that because of similarities to coeval 
rocks in Mongolia (Chen et al.,  1997; Li et al.,  2012; Pruner, 1992; Xu et al.,  1997) and the Xilinhot block 
(Zhao et al., 2013), PSV was properly averaged. A closer look at those data reveals the following issues. The 
22.8° ± 5.7°N expected paleolatitude of Zhao et al. ( 2020) is much higher than that of Pruner ( 1992) at 
5.1° ± 11.6°N. This inconsistency suggests the results do not average PSV. The results of Chen et al. (1997) 
did not fully remove Mesozoic overprints and PSV is unlikely averaged from the limited data set of 25 spec-
imens (Zhang et al., 2021); The results of Li et al. (2012) lack field tests and most demagnetizations display 
single component. Besides, they are significantly different from the recent results (Zhang et al.,  2021) ob-
tained from the same strata (290 Ma), which have positive fold tests and averaged PSV. The Xilinhot result 
(Zhao et al., 2013) spans most of the Permian period (300–252 Ma) and therefore are not strictly coeval with 
Figure 7. Reversal test of specimen-level characteristic remanent magnetizations (Tauxe, 2010). Data with downward directions are compared with upward

the 283 Ma result from the Erguna block. Lastly, the results of Xu et al. ( 1997) were assigned speculative 
remagnetization ages and the paleolatitudinal estimates show large uncertainties (5.1°N–19.9°N–34.7°N 
before and 12.2°N–27.0°N–41.8°N after inclination flattening correction; Table 2). If we compare the more 
robust 290 Ma results (Zhang et al., 2021) with that of Zhao et al. (2020), a 20.8° ± 6.7° difference in paleo-
latitudinal estimates is observed. Thus, we argue that more samples maybe needed to fully average out PSV 
for the data set of Zhao et al. (2020) before use in paleogeographic reconstructions.
5.1. A Unified Amuria Block at the Permo-Carboniferous Boundary
The ∼303 Ma paleopole in this study displays large discrepancy in declination with respect to the 308 Ma 
pole from the SMXB of Mongolia block (Figure  8; Zhang et al.,  2021), due to vertical-axis rotations of the 
sampling localities, as illustrated by the extensive Mesozoic aged strike-slip faulting in the eastern CAOB 
(Figures 1a and 1b; Zhao et al., 2015). The above two poles fall along a small circle band (Figure 8), indicat-
ing similar paleolatitudes of ∼34°N for the Songliao-Jiamusi (33.2° ± 5.4°N) and Mongolia (34.0° ± 3.8°N; 
Zhang et al., 2021) blocks at the Permo-Carboniferous boundary (Figure 9; Table 2).
From a geological perspective, the timing of the NHS is controversial with estimates ranging from the Early 
Devonian to Early Triassic. Based on stratigraphic analysis and consistent 460–420 Ma magmatic age pop -
ulations from both sides of the NHS, Xu et al. ( 2015) argued for an Early Devonian aggregation between 
the Songliao block and the SMXB. However, this model is challenged by a discovery of the Late Devonian 
to Early Carboniferous arc northwest of the NHS (Liu et al.,  2019; Feng et al.,  2015; Zhao et al.,  2010). To 
the southeast of the NHS, Carboniferous subduction of the Nenjiang Ocean beneath the Songliao-Jiamusi

block was recognized along the northwestern margin of the Songliao basin (Ma et al.,  2020). The existence 
of a Carboniferous subduction system precludes a pre-Carboniferous closure of the Nenjiang Ocean. Miao 
et  al.  (2004) argued for a Triassic closure based on the geochemistry of the Xinkailing-Kele complex in 
the northeastern segment of the NHS. Crystallization ages of the protolith rocks were dated to between 
340–292 Ma with metamorphic ages of 216 Ma. The protolith ages were argued to reflect the development 
of island arcs and the metamorphic ages to collisional events between the Songliao-Jiamusi and SMXB. 
Limited Permo-Triassic subduction records from the NHS provide weak support for the existence of a Nen-
jiang Ocean during this interval. In more recent studies, several lines of evidence from the NHS region 
support closure of the Nenjiang Ocean by the Late Carboniferous. These include (a) sedimentary facies 
transition from marine strata in the Early Carboniferous to continental facies in the Late Carboniferous (Liu 
et al., 2017); (b) the 320 Ma syn-tectonic S-type granites in the Moguqi area (Ma et al., 2020) which imply a 
syn-collision tectonic setting; (c) evidence for extension throughout the studied region during the Early Per-
mian and extensive coeval post-orogenic A-type granites (Feng et al., 2015; Liu et al., 2017; Shi et al., 2015; 
Wu et al., 2002) and rift-related bimodal volcanic rocks (Zeng et al., 2011).
The western continuation of the Nenjiang suture is represented by the Hegenshan Ophiolites. The Hegen -
shan Ocean was traditionally regarded as a back-arc ocean basin that separated the SMXB from the Xilinhot 
block (Eizenhöfer & Zhao, 2018; Liu et al., 2017, 2019; Miao et al., 2008; Xiao et al., 2018; Zhou et al., 2015). 
Alternatively, it has been interpreted as a continuation of the Nenjiang Ocean, which separated the Songliao 
block rather than the Xilinhot block from the SMXB (Figures  1a and 10). Emplacement of the Hegenshan 
ophiolite is older than 280  Ma, most likely sometime between 300–335  Ma, based on the unconformity 
between the Hegenshan ophiolite and overlying sandstones of the Middle Permian Zhesi Formation (Fig -
ure 1a; Zhou et al., 2015). Thus, the Hegenshan Ocean most likely closed in conjunction with the Nenjiang 
Ocean before the Early Permian.

5.2. Equatorial Paleopostions of the Xilinhot and North China Blocks
The suture zone between the Songliao and Xilinhot blocks is cryptic due to the irregular and sporadic occur-
rences of the ophiolites at the periphery of the Xilinhot block (Figure 1a; Zhou et al., 2015; Liu et al., 2019). 
Paleontological and paleomagnetic evidence do show differences between the two blocks. The Upper Car -
boniferous limestones in the Xilinhot block developed tropical Tethyan phylloid algal-bearing reefs (Yan 
et al.,  2019) that are similar to North China but distinct from the Boreal-realm characterizing the Mon -
golia and Songliao-Jiamusi blocks (Niu et al.,  2021; Shen et al.,  2006; Tian et al.,  2016; Ueno, 2006; Wang 
et al., 2013). The Xilinhot and North China blocks were located at low equatorial latitudes that are signifi -
cantly different from the Songliao-Jiamusi blocks that were located in the horse latitudes ( ∼33.2° ± 5.4°N; 
Figures 9 and 10; Table 2). The distinct paleolatitudes and distribution of Permo-Carboniferous flora and 
fauna of the Xilinhot and Songliao blocks negate the assumption of a unified Songliao-Xilinhot block dur -
ing the Late Carboniferous to Early Permian.

5.3. Paleogeographic Reconstruction of the CAOB
Incorporating the available geological evidence, we propose a paleogeographic reconstruction model for 
the CAOB in a paleomagnetic reference frame (at 300 Ma; Figure 10). The North China and Xilinhot blocks 
were situated at equatorial paleolatitudes. The unified Amuria block was separated from Siberia by the 
northeasterly facing MOO and from North China and Xilinhot blocks by the trumpet-shaped PAO. The PAO 
opened to the east during the Permian and gradually closed at ∼250 Ma, when the Xilinhot block finally 
amalgamated with North China and Amuria (Figure 9).
In the western part of the CAOB, multiple arc-continent and continent-continent collision events occurred 
in the Late Carboniferous to Early Permian, including (a) collision of Kazakhstan and Baltica that resulted 
in the closure of the Ural Ocean (Torsvik et al., 2012); (b) arc-continent collision of the East Junggar arc and 
Altai block that closed the Ob-Zaisan Ocean (Han & Zhao, 2018 and references therein); (c) continental col-
lision of the Tarim and Kazakhstan-Central Tianshan-Yili blocks that closed out the South Tianshan Ocean 
(B. F. Han et al., 2011; Y. G. Han et al., 2019). The East Junggar arc and Altai block bridged the gap between 
Amuria and Siberia, located at the hinge of the Mesozoic Mongol-Okhotsk Orocline. The bridge negates a 
cut-through seaway that connected the MOO and PAO during Permo-Triassic times and reconciles paleo -
magnetism and geological data as Mesozoic oceanic strata are absent in this area (Bazhenov et al.,  2016). 
The trapped Junggar oceanic crust was progressively destroyed in the Permian accompanied by intra-conti-
nental deformation (Yi et al., 2015).
6. Conclusions
We carried out the first integrated paleomagnetic and geochronologic study on Upper Carboniferous to 
Upper Permian volcanic-sedimentary sequences from the western margin of the Songliao block. Rock mag-
netic analyses revealed that low coercivity PSD to MD magnetite is the dominant magnetic carriers of the 
Permian sandstones and PSD magnetite for the 313–292 Ma volcanic rocks from the Dashizhai Formation. 
Well-isolated ChRMs are exclusively obtained from the volcanic rocks (116 specimens from 13 sites), and 
the mean direction is Dg/Ig = 70.6°/−77.5°, kg = 4.8, α95 = 21.2° before and Ds/Is = 20.6°/−46.6°, ks = 55.7,

The ChRMs passed fold and reversal tests and are likely primary records of geomagnetic field in ∼303 Ma. 
The corresponding pole locates at Plat = 12.8°S, Plong = 102.4°E (A95 = 5.4°, N = 13 sites) and meets six out of 
seven R-criteria proposed by Meert et al. (2020) and are reliable for paleogeographic reconstruction.
Along with previously published paleomagnetism data and geological evidence, we propose a reconstruc -
tion model for the CAOB at the Permo-Carboniferous boundary. Closure of the Nenjiang Ocean led to the 
final amalgamation of the Songliao-Jiamusi and Mongolia blocks, forming a unified Amuria block that was 
situated at ∼34°N in ∼300 Ma. The mid-latitudinal Amuria block was separated from the equatorial North 
China and Xilinhot blocks by the Paleo-Asian Ocean until its final closure at ∼250 Ma.

and also a reset 40Ar/39Ar age of ~800 Ma obtained on a glauconite. Our results, combined with existing
paleomagnetic data indicate that the Narji Limestone and Sequence III carbonates of the other Southern Purana
basins share a similar primary paleomagnetic signature. The paleomagnetic poles of these carbonates plot
consistently, and are used to calculate a mean pole (36.3◦N, 070.8◦E, A95 =10.7◦) that compares well with a
~1.19 Ga Indian pole. Our results contradict the view that Sequence III carbonates of the individual Southern
Purana basins were deposited at different times as previously inferred from geochronological data. Instead, we
suggest that these carbonates represent interconnected successions deposited in middle to late Mesoproterozoic
times during an extensive marine flooding event on the Southern India craton. Our results support the suggestion
that the existing Neoproterozoic ages for Sequence III may reflect post-depositional events.

The uplift and evolution of the Tibetan Plateau (TP), and the underlying controlling processes, are of
majorinterestingeology.TheTPiscomposedofseveralterranes(Figure1)andwasformedbythecolli-
sion and combination of these terranes since the early Paleozoic (Metcalfe, 2013; Wang et al., 2014; Xu
et al., 2011; Yin & Harrison, 2000; Zhu et al., 2013, 2016). The Qiangtang terrane originated from
GondwanainthePaleozoic(Metcalfe,2013;Yin&Harrison,2000)andbecameattachedtothesouthern
edge of the Asian continent in the early Mesozoic (Ding et al., 2013; Mo & Pan, 2006; Peng et al., 2015;
Song et al., 2015). The Qiangtang‐Lhasa collision commenced following the closure of the
Bangong‐Nujiang Ocean (BNO), resulting in considerable crustal shortening which has exerted a major
influenceontheevolutionoftheTP(Murphyetal.,1997).Hence,theevolutionoftheBNOandthepro-
cesses involved in the Qiangtang‐Lhasa collision are crucial in understanding the early evolution of the
central TP.

geochronologicalevidence.Meanwhile, severalstudiessuggestthattheBNOwasopenedfromtheEarlyto
MiddleJurassic,asindicatedbyophiolites(Wang,Aitchison,etal.,2008;Quetal.,2010).Furthermore,several

Keywords: The Permian remagnetization belt that affects the southwestern margin of Gondwana has an important
Guachos formation geographic extension reaching several South American cratons and terranes. A paleomagnetic pole for the Early
Remagnetization Cambrian Guachos Formation in the Eastern Cordillera of Argentina was computed (LG: Lat: 58.1◦S, Long:
Paleomagnetism 20.2◦E, A95: 6.4◦, n: 30), that likely corresponds to a Permian remagnetization and suggests that such belt might
extend further north than previously envisaged. We performed several rock-magnetic studies on this succession
of laminated fine grain sandstones and siltstones in order to determine the magnetic phases that carry the
remanence. Thermomagnetic (k vs. T) curves, field and frequency dependence of bulk susceptibility, hysteresis
loops, isothermal remanent magnetization acquisition and back-field curves, three-axis IRM thermal demagne-
tization, among others, permitted to establish magnetite as the main mineral carrying the remanence. Micro-
scopic observations confirmed a secondary chemical origin for magnetite. Magnetic fabric studies indicate a
tectonic fabric, consistent with cleavage developed on these rocks together with low-grade metamorphism.
However, a Permian remagnetization, as suggested by the paleomagnetic pole position, cannot be related to
Cambrian deformation and metamorphism and might be related to hydrothermal processes.

the Sierra de Mojotoro shows no important deflection at the sampling
locality, so that a large tectonic rotation due to Andean orogeny seems
unlikely. This suggests an Early Permian remagnetization for the Gua-
chos Formation. Our rock magnetic data and petrographic analyses plus
the magnetic fabrics results clearly indicate that secondary magnetite
due to chemical precipitation carries this remanence and suggest a
Permian age for such an event. No previous reports of Late Paleozoic
remagnetization are known from the Eastern Cordillera on NW
Argentina. The unique reverse polarity found in the studied samples also
is consistent with the Late Carboniferous-Early Permian Kiaman Reverse
Polarity Superchron (Gradstein et al., 2012), and therefore with the
inferred age of remagnetization.
Magnetite is confirmed by different rock-magnetic experiments as
the main carrier of magnetic remanence in the Guachos Formation.

with the development of tectonic fabric and cleavage in these rocks is
not easily reconciled with a Permian age as suggested from the paleo-
magnetic pole position. Low grade metamorphism in Guachos Forma-
tion occurred in Early Cambrian times, linked to the final stages of the
Tilcaric orogenic phase (Moya, 1998). The simplest explanation for the
tectonic overprint is to assign it an age older than the ca. 500 Ma
unmetamorphosed Meson Group that overlies it. Although no major

inferred from the Guachos Formation mean characteristic remanence.

Keywords: Mangkang area was located at a paleolatitude of 20.5 ± 0.9 ◦ N during the late Eocene. A comparison
Eastern Himalayan Syntaxis of paleolatitudes of the Qiangtang block with those inferred from the apparent polar wander paths
Paleomagnetism (APWP) of India and Eurasia suggests that the Eastern Himalayan Syntaxis was formed after 35 Ma
late Eocene when Eurasia was penetrated by ∼600 km by northward-moving India. This is consistent with geologic
southeastern Tibetan Plateau evidence of intra-continental shortening in the foreland of the Eastern Himalayan syntaxis. The northward
counterclockwise penetration of the corner of India also resulted in the large right-lateral strike-slip
system of the Sagaing fault (SGF), with ∼400-600 km of displacement between the EHS and the Shan-
Thai block. Thus, the northward wedging of the EHS indicates minimal southward displacement of
the Shan-Thai block. Our results link the tectonic activity of the EHS to the lateral extrusion of the
southeastern margin of the Tibetan Plateau, providing a new perspective on the evolution of this region
since the late Eocene.

Paleomagnetism of the Oatka Creek Member of the Marcellus Formation

Paleomagnetism of the Oatka Creek Member of the Marcellus Formation: 
A Devonian paleopole for North America
D. Minguez1,†, K.P. Kodama1, and T. Engelder2
1Department of Earth and Environmental Science, Lehigh University, 1 W. Packer Avenue, Bethlehem, Pennsylvania 18015, USA
2Department of Geosciences, The Pennsylvania State University, University Park, Pennsylvania 16802, USA
ABSTRACT
This study presents paleomagnetic results 
from the Oatka Creek Member of the Mar -
cellus Formation. Paleomagnetic specimens 
were subsampled from a 50.8-mm-diameter 
subsurface drill core obtained from the 
Valley and Ridge physiographic province 
of Pennsylvania. Alternating field (AF) de-
magnetization techniques demonstrate that 
the Oatka Creek specimens retain multiple 
components of magnetization. The lowest-
coercivity component, component A, was 
isolated by peak fields up to 20 mT and has 
characteristics of a drilling-induced rema-
nence. Component B was isolated over a 
range of peak AF fields between 20 and 50 
mT in the upper 100 m of the core, and points 
south with intermediate downward inclina-
tions in geographic coordinates. Scanning 
electron microscopy, energy dispersive spec-
troscopy, and rock magnetic experiments 
yield evidence that suggests component B is 
a detrital remanent magnetization in mag-
netite. We corrected these directions for bed-
ding tilt and inclination shallowing and cal-
culated a paleopole at lat. 29.4°, long. 116.9°, 
A
95 = 1.3°, with an age of 388–389 Ma con-
strained by biostratigraphy and radiometric 
dating. This paleomagnetic pole could help 
fill a data gap in the paleomagnetic record 
for North America that spans the Middle 
Devonian to Early Mississippian Periods. 
Component C was isolated throughout the 
core using AF fields between 50 and 100 mT 
and points south with shallow downward in-
clinations in geographic coordinates. Com-
ponent C directions agree with a chemical 
remanence in pyrrhotite from a previous 
paleomagnetic study of the Marcellus For -
mation. Component C is likely also a chemi-
cal remanent magnetization in pyrrhotite 
acquired during maximum burial tempera-
tures achieved in the Permian, which may 
have catalyzed pyrrhotite formation. Com-
ponent D was isolated in specimens from the 
lower 20 m of the core, using peak AF fields 
between 20 and 100 mT, and it points north 
with shallow downward inclinations in geo-
graphic coordinates. The lower 20 m of the 
core shows evidence of significant hydrother-
mal alteration. The component D directions 
yield a paleopole in good agreement with the 
Jurassic reference pole, and a pulse of hydro-
thermal alteration in the lower portion of the 
Oatka Creek Member is consistent with other 
thermal events in the region ca. 180 Ma. Our 
results indicate that subsurface cores from 
the Appalachian foreland may provide an 
opportunity to greatly improve the Paleozoic 
paleomagnetic record for North America.
INTRODUCTION
Over the last several decades, paleomagnetic 
research has shown that sedimentary rocks 
from the Appalachian foreland basin, especially 
carbonates, commonly contain a late Paleo-
zoic secondary magnetization. This secondary 
magnetization is often attributed to basinwide 
fluid migration and magnetite authigenesis in 
the Permian (Irving and Strong, 1985; McCabe 
and Elmore, 1989; McCabe et al., 1989), and it 
has been useful in constraining the spatio-tem-
poral pattern of Alleghanian deformation (e.g., 
Stamatakos et al., 1996). It is less common that 
paleomagnetists find primary magnetizations 
preserved in the Appalachian foreland. This 
is particularly true for the Devonian system, 
with the exception of the heavily relied upon 
results from the Catskill Formation (Miller and 
Kent, 1986). As a result, workers determin-
ing the apparent polar wander (APW) path for 
North America have either interpolated the path 
between Early Devonian and Early Mississip-
pian reference poles (Cocks and Torsvik, 2011; 
Torsvik et al., 2012), or they have used results 
with broad uncertainties in the age of the mag-
netizations for the Devonian portion of the path 
(Van der V oo, 1990). Thus, a robust Devonian 
paleopole would be a valuable contribution to 
the North American paleomagnetic record.
Recently, Manning and Elmore (2012) have 
shown that the Union Springs Member of the 
Middle Devonian Marcellus Formation contains 
the typical Permian secondary magnetization 
found in Appalachian foreland rocks. Samples 
in their study were obtained from outcrops in 
the Valley and Ridge physiographic province of 
Pennsylvania, on the south limb of the Pennsyl-
vania salient. Thermal demagnetization of speci-
mens reveals two components of magnetiza-
tion: an intermediate component that unblocks 
between 310 °C and 350 °C, and a characteristic 
component that unblocks between temperatures 
of 350 °C and 480 °C. The two components 
have very subtle differences in direction, both 
yielding Late Permian paleomagnetic poles. 
Their samples demonstrate the Verwey and 
Besnus transitions, indicating magnetite and 
pyrrhotite are the remanence carriers. No Devo-
nian age magnetizations were recovered. These 
observations suggest that pyrrhotite formed and 
acquired a chemical remanence during late sul-
fate diagenesis nearly contemporaneously, if not 
contemporaneous, with magnetite authigenesis 
in the Permian in the Union Springs Member.
In our study, we show that the overlying 
Oatka Creek Member of the Marcellus Forma-
tion, sampled in the subsurface by drill core on 
the north limb of the Pennsylvania salient in 
the Valley and Ridge Province, retains multiple 
components of magnetization, isolated using 
alternating field (AF) demagnetization. Multiple 
lines of evidence suggest that one of these com-
ponents is detrital in nature, and therefore has a 
Middle Devonian age. This magnetization may 
better define the middle Paleozoic APW path 
for North America. The other remanence com-
ponents indicate multiple phases of iron-sulfide 
authigenesis and characterize a drilling-induced 
remanence in these Paleozoic rocks. Our results 
indicate that subsurface cores from the Appala-
chian foreland may provide an opportunity to 
improve the Paleozoic paleomagnetic record for 
North America.

GEOLOGIC SETTING
The Valley and Ridge Province of Pennsyl-
vania is composed of lithified sediments shed 
off the ancient Appalachian Mountains as they 
formed in a series of orogenies spanning the 
Late Ordovician to Early Permian. During the 
Acadian orogeny, the Oatka Creek Member of 
the Marcellus Formation was deposited as the 
basinal shale equivalent of the Catskill Delta 
complex under anoxic-sulfidic conditions 
(Werne et al., 2002; Lash and Engelder, 2011, 
and references therein). Anoxic-sulfidic condi-
tions promote the formation and preservation of 
iron-sulfide remanence carriers like pyrrhotite 
(Fe
1–xS) and greigite (Fe 3S4) at the expense of 
iron oxides like magnetite (Fe 3O4; Horng and 
Roberts, 2006; Rowan et al., 2009). Radiometri-
cally calibrated biostratigraphy gives an age of 
388–389 Ma for the Oatka Creek Member in 
the northwest Appalachian foreland (Brett et al., 
2011; Kaufmann, 2006).
Deformation of the Appalachian foreland 
took place during the Alleghany orogeny. 
Stamatakos et al. (1996) demonstrated that 
remagnetization of Appalachian basin rocks 
occurred relatively quickly, in the latter part of 
the Permian, compared to the propagation 
of folds through the basin. Permian paleomag-
netic directions appear to postdate folding near 
the hinterland margin, be synfolding in the cen-
tral part of the Valley and Ridge, and predate 
folding toward the Appalachian Plateau. The 
rocks collected for this study were recovered 
from an area that closely neighbors rocks with 
synfolding Permian magnetizations to the east 
and prefolding Permian magnetizations to the 
west (Fig. 1; fig. 5 in Stamatakos et al., 1996). 
The bend in the Appalachians known as the 
Pennsylvania salient predates the episode of 
Permian remagnetization, as paleomagnetic 
directions of Permian age are statistically indis-
tinguishable on the north and south limbs of 
the salient (Stamatakos and Hirt, 1994). This 
tectonic event appears to have mostly affected 
the magnetizations of Cambrian–Ordovician 
rocks (Cederquist et al., 2006). Therefore, we 
do not expect rotation of our results from the 
Marcellus Formation on the north limb of the 
salient relative to those from the Marcellus For-
mation on the south limb from Manning and 
Elmore (2012).
METHODS
To sample the Marcellus Formation in the 
subsurface, an AX 50.8-mm-diameter vertical 
drill core was extracted near Sunbury, Penn-
sylvania (Fig. 1A). Orientation was achieved 
by aligning bedding observed in the core paral-
lel to bedding observed in the surface outcrop 
(dip angle = 30°, and dip direction = 167°). 
The core was sawed lengthwise in half along 
dip direction (Figs. 1B and 1C), and 25-mm-
diameter paleomagnetic samples were drilled 
from the core perpendicular to dip direction 
(drill azimuth in geographic coordinates = 257°, 
0°). After correction for bedding dip, the core 
spanned 120.2 m of stratigraphic section from 
the top of the Purcell carbonate unit to the top of 
the Oatka Creek Member.
Samples for preliminary paleomagnetic mea-
surements were split into two batches. The first 
batch was stepwise thermally demagnetized 
in an ASC thermal demagnetizer (25 °C steps 
from 100 °C to 300 °C and then 20 °C steps 
to 580 °C). The second batch was stepwise 
demagnetized with AF (5–10 mT steps from 0 
to 110 mT). Measurements of remanence and 
AF demagnetization were performed using a 
2G Enterprises 755 superconducting rock mag-
netometer. The AF procedure isolated compo-
nents of magnetization more consistently than 
the thermal demagnetization procedure, which 
often resulted in acquisition of strong magne-
tizations that obscured demagnetization of the 
natural remanent magnetization (NRM; likely 
due to oxidation of iron sulfides). The remaining 
specimens were demagnetized following the AF 
procedure (N = 461). Components of remanent 
magnetization were obtained by principal com-
ponent analysis of vector end-point diagrams 
(Kirschvink, 1980). Noncurved portions of 
demagnetization paths defined by three or more 
points, and maximum angular deviation (MAD) 
values less than 15° were fit. Coercivity analysis

was performed using the results of acquisition 
of isothermal remanent magnetization (IRM) 
using an ASC impulse magnetizer, following 
the routine of Kruiver et al. (2001).
To identify the magnetic minerals pres-
ent in our samples, scanning electron micro-
scope (SEM) and energy dispersive spectros-
copy (EDS) analyses of microprobe polished 
thin sections were performed using a Hitachi 
TM-1000 tabletop SEM. Results from this 
instrument do not include estimates of oxygen 
abundance and are semiquantitative. However, 
iron and sulfur abundances were available, and 
known specimens of pyrrhotite and pyrite were 
easily distinguishable using EDS. To determine 
the unblocking temperatures associated with 
components of magnetization isolated over sep-
arate coercivity ranges, orthogonal IRMs were 
imparted to a subset of samples (1000 mT along 
the z axis, 200 mT along the x axis, 45 mT along 
the y axis) and stepwise thermally demagnetized 
(Lowrie, 1990).
To determine if the natural remanence carried 
by iron sulfides and iron oxides was separable, a 
subset of samples was partially thermally demag-
netized to 100 °C, and 150 °C, and in 20 °C 
steps from 200 °C to 320 °C. This regime should 
demagnetize pyrrhotite and nearly completely 
remove any remanence carried by greigite if 
present (maximum unblocking temperatures are 
near 320 °C and ~322 °C, respectively; Dekkers, 
1989; Roberts, 1995) while minimizing speci-
men alteration and the resulting large increases 
in magnetization, which we typically observed 
in samples at temperatures above 300 °C. The 
magnetization remaining after thermal treatment 
to 320 °C, ideally dominated by iron oxides, was 
removed following the AF demagnetization pro-
cedure already described.
To test the hypothesis that paleomagnetic 
directions were contaminated with a drilling-
induced remanence, natural and laboratory rema-
nences were compared between subsamples near 
the exterior and interior of the drill string follow-
ing Audunsson and Levi (1989). Audunsson and 
Levi (1989) showed that the drilling remanence 
in their drill core was strongest in samples 
toward the exterior of the core, pointed radi-
ally inward toward the core center, and had 
similar stability to AF demagnetization as a 
10 mT IRM. Paleomagnetic specimens in this 
study were subsampled by cutting the speci-
men in half, with one half toward the exterior 
of the drill core (toward the cutting surface) and 
the other toward the interior (12.5 mm width; 
Fig. 1C). NRM directions and intensities were 
compared to determine if the exterior samples 
matched the expected pattern of higher intensity 
and a radially inward direction (west and steep 
in geographic coordinates is radially “in” for 
our samples) predicted by the observations of 
Audunsson and Levi (1989). We also imparted 
the subsamples, and a subset of complete speci-
mens, with 5, 15, and 25 mT IRMs, which were 
subsequently demagnetized in alternating fields 
in 5 mT steps, to compare the decay of the IRM 
with the decay of natural remanence following 
the same treatment.

AF Demagnetization
AF demagnetization of samples from the 
upper 100 m of the core typically isolated three 
components of magnetization (Table 1; Figs. 3 
and 4). The lowest-coercivity component (com-
ponent A) was isolated by peak fields up to 20 
mT and points west and steeply down in geo-
graphic coordinates (Figs. 3 and 4). The inter -
mediate-coercivity component (component B) 
was isolated between fields of 20 and up to 50 
mT and points south and intermediate down in 
geographic coordinates. The highest-coercivity 
component (component C) is isolated between 
fields of 50 and 100 mT and points south and 
shallow in geographic coordinates. The iso-
lation of component C from component B is 
clearly demonstrated in geographic projections 
of the demagnetization results (Fig. 4), which 
show a distinct noncurved transition between 
the two components.
AF demagnetization of samples from the 
lower 20 m of the core yielded one of two pos-
sible combinations of magnetization compo-
nents. The first combination is component A, 
described already, which was removed by AF 
fields up to 20 mT, and then component C, as 
described already, except that it was isolated 
between 25 and 100 mT, trended into the ori-
gin, and was often not fully removed by fields 
up to 110 mT (Fig. 5A). The second combina-
tion is of component A, isolated by peak fields 
up to 20 mT, and then the north and down 
direction observed in thermal demagnetization 
of samples from the lower portion of the core 
(component D), isolated with fields between 
20 and 110 mT, and trending into the origin 
(Figs. 5B and 6D).

Drilling Remanence Experiment
NRM intensities of exterior subspecimens 
were roughly twice as high as those taken from 
the interior of the core (Fig. 8). Both subsam-
ples yielded a west and steeply down direction 
in geographic coordinates over AF demagneti-
zation steps up to 20 mT (Fig. 9). The exterior 
samples did this much more consistently, and 
the directions cluster well (Fig. 10A). Com-
ponents isolated between 20 and 50 mT from 
interior and exterior subsamples point south and 
intermediate down in geographic coordinates 
and are indistinguishable from each other (Fig. 
9B). Components isolated between 50 and 100 
mT point south in both cases, but samples from 
the exterior of the core tend to be steeper (Fig. 
9C); however, only three specimens of nine ana-
lyzed yielded this high-coercivity component.
Exterior subsamples showed NRM demag-
netization behavior that closely resembled 
the response of a 25 mT IRM over AF fields 
between 15 and 20 mT (Fig. 9C). The demag-
netization of NRM for interior subsamples was 
not similar to any of the demagnetization behav-
iors for any of the IRM fields used (Fig. 9D). 
Whole paleomagnetic specimens had an NRM 
response to AF demagnetization that resembled 
the exterior subsamples, with normalized inten-
sities for NRMs and IRMs decaying equally up 
to fields between 15 and 20 mT, at which point 
the decay paths diverged (Figs. 3C and 3D).
Thermal Demagnetization of Orthogonal 
IRMs (Lowrie Test)

Coercivity Analysis
Forward modeling of IRM acquisition curves 
demonstrates that samples from the upper 
100 m can be accounted for by two populations 
of magnetic minerals with mean coercivities of 
52.5 and 177.8 mT (Fig. 12; Table 2). The coer-
civity spectra of these modeled populations par-
tially overlap, and the lower-coercivity mineral 
dominates the IRM acquisition.
SEM and EDS
Basic petrographic observations of polished 
thin sections revealed opaque, euhedral miner-
als crosscutting calcite-rich microfossils. SEM 
observations showed that these grains are iron 
sulfides, with elemental abundances similar to 
pyrrhotite (Figs. 13A and 13B). Framboid struc-
tures were commonly observed with iron and 
sulfur weight percent values between stoichio-
metric pyrite and greigite (Figs. 13B and 13C). 
Non-sulfur-bearing iron grains (iron oxides) are 
common within sedimentary structures resem-
bling clay floccules (edge-face contacts of clay 
particles). The grains themselves are on the 
order of 2 mm in diameter and are not euhedral 
(Figs. 13D, 13E, and 13F).
DISCUSSION
Carriers of Magnetic Remanence
Lowrie (1990) tests from the upper 100 and 
lower 20 m of the core clearly demonstrated 
two distinct mixtures of magnetic minerals. 
The upper part of the core contained a rela-
tively high-coercivity mineral (≥ 200 mT) that 
was resistant to thermal demagnetization up to 
260 °C, and then rapidly decayed up to 320 °C. 
Subsequent thermal demagnetization to 500 °C 
resulted in an increase in the specimen’s mag-
netization. This behavior is consistent with 
thermal decay of rocks containing natural pyr-
rhotite (Torii et al., 1996), which oxidizes at 
high temperatures, resulting in an increase in 
magnetization. Pyrrhotite is also the only rema-
nence-carrying iron sulfide with potentially very 
high coercivities (up to 1 T; Lowrie 1990), and 
so we conclude that pyrrhotite is an important 
low-temperature, but relatively high-coercivity 
remanence carrier in this part of the core. The 
lower-coercivity components from the upper 
part of the core gradually decayed until 450 °C, 
and then remained constant through 560 °C, at 
which point the demagnetization behavior was 
obscured by the aforementioned, continuing 
increase in magnetization intensity of the speci-
men. Magnetite is likely the remanence carrier 
of the lower-coercivity, higher-unblocking-tem-
perature magnetization. Although the SEM and 
EDS data give only qualitative results, it is evi-
dent that there are abundant iron sulfides (Figs. 
13A–13C) and occasional iron oxides (Figs. 
13D–13F). The crosscutting textural relations 
of the iron sulfides suggest they are secondary 
in nature, whereas the sharp contacts between

Laboratory remanences imparted to speci-

completely demagnetized by 450 °C, with 
stability in the high-coercivity component up 
to 260 °C and rapid decay until 320 °C. The 
lower-coercivity components gradually decayed 
over this range, although the 45 mT component 
decayed little between 200 °C and 320 °C, and 
then rapidly decayed. It is clear that the lower 
portion of the core is dominated by iron sulfides, 
with no remanence stable at high temperatures, 
indicating an absence of magnetite. This behav-
ior is consistent with samples taken from the 
horizon dominated by the component D direc-
tion (425–430 m) and the horizon below domi-
nated by component C directions (435–450 m). 
We conclude that pyrrhotite is likely the high-
coercivity remanence carrier, as in the upper 
part of the core. The lower-coercivity rema-
nence carrier could be greigite or a low-coerciv-
ity fraction of pyrrhotite.
Origins of Magnetic Components
Drilling-Induced Remanence
Regardless of clear changes in mineralogi-
cal composition between the upper and lower 
portions of the drill core, the overwhelming 
majority of samples from both sections yielded 
a low-coercivity remanence with west and inter-
mediate to steep directions (component A; Figs. 
3, 4, and 6). The direction and resistance to AF 
treatment of component A are consistent with 
drilling-induced remanences observed in basalt 
drill cores from Audunsson and Levi (1989). 
Those authors observed radially inward mag-
netic directions with stability to AF demagneti-
zation similar to a ~10 mT IRM, and decreas-
ing intensity toward the center of the drill core. 
Our component A direction matches all of these 
characteristics, except that the decay of the natu-
ral remanence is consistent with a stronger mag-
netic field of the drill string than that observed 
in Audunsson and Levi’s core. Otherwise, the 
component A direction points toward the cen-
ter of the core (in geographic coordinates, west 
and steeply down for specimens taken from the 
east portion of the core), and NRM intensity is 
unequivocally higher in specimens closer to the 
cutting surface (Fig. 8).

drilling remanence (Fig. 10A). The excellent 
agreement of component B directions from 
interior and exterior samples (Fig. 10B) sug-
gests that AF fields were successful in isolating 
the intermediate-coercivity component from 
the component imparted by the drill string. The 
higher-coercivity component C does seem to be 
steeper in exterior samples compared to interior 
samples, but only a low number of specimens 
yielded the directions necessary to make this 
comparison. If the high-coercivity component 
from exterior samples is systematically steeper, 
it could indicate there is also a shock-induced 
component to the drilling remanence, similar to 
what was observed in sulfide-bearing sediments 
by Shi and Tarling (1999). These authors stated 
that new pyrrhotite was formed from other iron 
sulfides due to mechanical shocking, with a 
remanence parallel to the field of the drill string, 
which resisted both AF and thermal treatment. 
This shock-induced remanence affected sam-
ples from the exterior of their drill core, but not 
the interior. It also did not affect samples that 
had only iron-oxide remanence carriers, imply-
ing that only the iron-sulfide fraction should be 
affected by shocking of the core. In general, AF 
fields of 100 mT were able to completely or 
nearly completely demagnetize specimens from 
our core, except for those specimens removed 
from the lower portion of the core, which sug-
gests that shock-induced drilling remanence, if 
present, was much less important than the mag-
netization induced by the magnetic field of the 
drill string.
The presence of a strong drilling-induced 
remanence may explain the absence of a vis-
cous modern-day overprint. Weaver et al. (2002) 
observed a low-coercivity modern-day overprint 
in a magnetite- and pyrrhotite-bearing mudstone 
from Sakhalin, Russia, that is reasonably analo-
gous in terms of magnetic mineralogy to the 
Marcellus Formation. If the Oatka Creek Mem-
ber were contaminated by a modern-day over -
print, we would expect it to behave similarly 
to the rocks studied by Weaver et al. (2002). 
However, the geographic direction of compo-
nent A is not parallel with a modern-day field 
direction. It seems likely that if a modern-day 
overprint existed, it was erased and replaced by 
the magnetic field direction of the drill string. 
None of the other components of magnetiza-
tion had modern-day field directions or curved 
demagnetization paths that would suggest 
higher-coercivity components are contaminated 
by a modern-day direction.

straight paths with occasional deviations up to 
300 °C (Figs. 2 and 7), but the directions were 
inconsistent, pointing west and intermedi-
ate down, south and steep down, or south and 
intermediate down. Further heating to 320 °C, 
340 °C, and 360 °C would be necessary to com-

heating at these steps caused large increases in 
magnetization, obscuring the decay of natural 
remanence. Without being able to completely 
thermally demagnetize the iron sulfides, all of 
the observed components of magnetization (A, 
B, and C) persisted in post-thermal AF demag-
netization (Fig. 7).
The stratigraphic pattern of AF results yields 
some insight into the magnetic carriers of each 
component (Fig. 14). Component C was con-
sistently isolated over relatively high AF fields 
and was ubiquitous throughout the core. Given 
the persistence of a high-coercivity population 
of pyrrhotite throughout the core indicated by 
the Lowrie tests, and the secondary nature of 
the pyrrhotite indicated by SEM observations, 
it is likely that the component C magnetiza-
tion is a chemical remanence acquired during 
pyrrhotite authigenesis. Manning and Elmore 
(2012) observed a chemical remanent magne-
tization in pyrrhotite in the underlying Union 
Springs Member that yielded a paleopole near 
the Permian reference pole (Fig. 15). The deep-
est burial (and highest temperatures ~200 °C) 
for the Marcellus Formation at this location 
was achieved during the Permian (Evans et al., 
2014), which yields the temperature conditions 
under which pyrrhotite formation is more likely 
to be catalyzed (Schoonen and Barnes, 1991). 
Thus, we expect a Permian direction carried by 
secondary pyrrhotite in our samples that agrees 
with the study by Manning and Elmore (2012). 
We calculated a paleopole from the component 
C directions by averaging individual sample 
virtual geomagnetic poles. In geographic coor-
dinates, the pole lies far west of the APW path 
for North America; in stratigraphic coordinates, 
the pole lies near the Middle Triassic reference 
pole (Fig. 14). Neither of these pole locations 
is consistent with the existing geochemical 
or paleomagnetic results. There may be some 
error in our approach to orientation of the drill 
core used in this study. A simple 11.7° coun-
terclockwise vertical-axis rotation of the drill 
core aligns our component C paleopole (from 
tilt-corrected directions) with the Permian ref-
erence pole and the results of Manning and 
Elmore (2012). A prefolding origin of this 
remanence is reasonable given the temporal 
pattern of folding discussed by Stamatakos 
et al. (1996). We suggest that orientation of the 
core in this manner is an improvement on our 
original orientation, and we corrected all the 
other components with an 11.7° counterclock-
wise vertical-axis rotation.
The possibility that component B results 
from overlap between components A and C can 
also be addressed by the stratigraphic pattern 
of AF results (Fig. 14). Component B is only 
observed in the upper 100 m of the core, where 
Lowrie tests and SEM observations yielded 
evidence of detrital magnetite. Component B 
is not observed in the lower 20 m of the core, 
despite the persistence of components A and C, 
and where Lowrie tests indicated only iron-sul-
fide remanence carriers are present. Thus, the 
results show that simple overprinting of com-
ponent C with component A does not produce 
component B, and that component B is only 
observed where magnetite is present. Based 
on these observations, we reject the hypothesis 
that components A and C overlapped to produce 
component B. Instead, we suggest that com-
ponent B is a detrital remanence in magnetite, 
which is isolated from the drilling remanence 
and the chemical remanence in pyrrhotite. 
Given our primary interpretation of component 
B, it is necessary to apply a tilt correction and 
inclination shallowing correction to each of 
the 234 component B directions (E/I method; 
Tauxe and Kent, 2004). An f factor of 0.7 was 
determined using 1000 bootstrapped data sets 
(average inclination 33.0° with 95% confidence 
bounds at 28.7° and 37.3°). We applied the f 
factor to the individual directions, calculated 
individual sample virtual geomagnetic poles, 
and averaged them to determine a paleopole 
that is in excellent agreement with the Middle–
Late Devonian paleopole from Van der V oo 
(1990; Fig. 15; Table 3).
The component D directions are only found 
in the lower 20 m of the core, which have been 
intruded by both calcite and quartz veins. Evans 
et al. (2014) showed that pyrite precipitated 
along with calcite during early veining, and that 
fluids were locally derived (based on compari-
sons of stable isotopes between the veins and 
undeformed portions of the Marcellus Forma-

tion). We suggest that this process of local, 
perhaps reducing fluid mobilization and rock 
fracturing may have facilitated dissolution of 
detrital magnetite by physically breaking up the 
clay flocs that shielded them, and resulted in a 
separate episode of pyrrhotite formation yield-
ing a Late Jurassic paleopole (with directions in 
geographic coordinates). Note that a paleopole 
from the tilt-corrected component D directions 
falls close to the modern-day north pole. Since 
tilting occurred during the Permian, we know 
this cannot be correct. The conundrum we face 
is that Evans et al. (2014) argued that veining 
occurred in the Permian, when the sediments 
achieved maximum burial. Our results suggest 
a hydrothermal event that occurred much later 
in the Jurassic is necessary to explain the paleo-
magnetic directions. Such an event would be 
contemporaneous with the hydrothermal event 
observed in Newark Basin sediments to the east, 
(Witte and Kent, 1991) and a steep geothermal 
gradient accompanied by kimberlite emplace-
ment along the Alleghany structural front to 
the west (Roden and Miller, 1989). Roden 
and Miller (1989) demonstrated that apatite 
fission-track systems of the Devonian Tioga 
and Kalkberg ash beds were reset ca. 180 Ma 
in some locations within the Valley and Ridge 
Province, which they suggested indicates migra-
tion of hot fluids in the region. Thus, we sug-
gest that geochemical and paleomagnetic data 
extracted from the lower portion of the Oatka 
Creek Member reflect temperature conditions 
caused by Jurassic thermal alteration, rather 
than Permian peak burial as suggested by Evans 
et al. (2014).
Implications for the Middle Paleozoic 
APW Path
High-quality middle Paleozoic paleomagnetic 
poles from the North American craton have, so 
far, been hard to come by. Van der V oo (1990) 
listed only five paleopoles for the Middle–Early 
Devonian, with age brackets as broad as 71 m.y. 
Recent studies omitted altogether or greatly 
limited data from the Early to Late Devonian 
Period. Cocks and Torsvik (2011) extrapolated 
the North American APW path between 340 and 
390 Ma; that is, they included no primary refer-
ence poles to support the path for this period. 
Torsvik et al. (2012) added one reference pole 
to this period at 370 Ma and commented that 
Middle Devonian to Early Carboniferous poles 
are urgently needed for North America. The 
component B direction observed in this study 
is likely a magnetite DRM (detrital remanent 
magnetization), which suggests an age of mag-
netization equivalent to the age of the forma-
tion (388–389 Ma). The paleopole derived from 
these magnetizations adds to the primary data 
for North America and tentatively supports the 
northwest deflection of the North American 
APW path ca. 390 Ma reported by Van der V oo 
(1990) relative to the interpolated paths pre-
sented by Cocks and Torsvik (2011) and Tors-
vik et al. (2012). Further paleomagnetic study of 
increasingly available drill cores through middle 
Paleozoic sedimentary rocks in the Appalachian 
basin may provide the key material necessary to 
further test the results of this study and provide 
a stronger basis for the Devonian portion of the 
North American APW path.

Paleomagnetism of the Oatka Creek Member of the Marcellus Formation
 Geological Society of America Bulletin, v. 128, no. 5/6 717
CONCLUSIONS
The Oatka Creek Member of the Devonian 
Marcellus Formation, sampled in the subsurface 
with a 50.8-mm-diameter drill core, records 
multiple components of magnetization observed 
using AF demagnetization techniques.
(1) Component A is consistently observed 
throughout the entire core, points west and 
steeply down in geographic coordinates, has a 
higher intensity in subspecimens taken near the 
exterior of the core (closest to the cutting sur -
face), and is likely a drilling-induced remanence.
(2) Component B was isolated over an AF 
demagnetization range of 20–50 mT, in the 
upper 100 m of the core, where Lowrie tests 
indicate magnetite is present. SEM observa-
tions indicate the presence of iron oxides with 
detrital textural characteristics, adhering to par-
ticles within clay floccules, supporting the con-
clusion that component B is a magnetite DRM. 
This result yields a paleopole of latitude 29.4°, 
longitude 116.9°, A
95 = 1.3°, with an age of 
388–389 Ma based on conodont biostratigraphy 
of the Oatka Creek Member, from the Appala-
chian foreland. The location of this pole does 
not support the interpolated pole path of Cocks 
and Torsvik (2011) for the Devonian, but it is 
in good agreement with the Late–Middle Devo-
nian paleopole based on the compilation of data 
from Van der V oo (1990).
(3) Component C was isolated over an AF 
range of 50–100 mT, and was infrequently not 
completely demagnetized by fields as high as 
110 mT, although this component did trend 
into the origin. The component is ubiquitous 
throughout the core and yields a Late Permian 
reference pole, consistent with magnetizations 
found in late authigenic pyrrhotite from Man-
ning and Elmore (2012) in the Union Springs 
Member of the Marcellus Formation. We sug-
gest this component is also carried by pyrrho-
tite in the Oatka Creek Member, which formed 
chemically during maximum burial of the Mar-
cellus Formation in the Permian.
(4) Component D was isolated over an AF 
range from 20 to 100 mT and was not always 
completely removed by fields as high as 110 
mT, although it also trended into the origin. This 
direction is confined to the lower 20 m of the 
core, where there has clearly been hydrothermal 
alteration, likely from heating and mobilization 
of locally derived fluids. This component yields 
a Late Jurassic paleopole consistent with ther -
mal events occurring over a wide region encom-
passing the Newark Basin and Alleghanian 
structural fronts.

carbon resources in the Appalachian foreland 
continues, more drill cores containing middle

Paleomagnetism of the Upper Paleozoic
of the Novaya Zemlya Archipelago
V. V. Abasheva, b, *, D. V. Metelkina, b, N. E. Mikhal’tsova, b, V. A. Vernikovskya, b, and N. Yu. Matushkina, b
aNovosibirsk State University, Novosibirsk, 630090 Russia
bTrofimuk Institute of Petroleum Geology and Geophysics, Siberian Branch,
Russian Academy of Sciences, Novosibirsk, 630090 Russia
*e-mail: abashevvv@ipgg.sbras.ru
Received March 10, 2017
Abstract⎯ The rock magnetic and paleomagnetic results from the Upper Paleozoic sedimentary sequences
composing the isles of the Novaya Zemlya Archipelago are presented. The recorded temperature depen-
dences of the magnetic susceptibility, the magnetic hysteresis parameters, and the results of the first-order
reversal curve (FORC) measurements suggest the presence of single-domain or pseudo-single-domain mag-
netite and hematite grains in the rocks. The Upper Paleozoic deposits overall are promising for unraveling the
tectonic evolution of the Barents–Kara region. Together with the rock magnetic data, the positive fold and
reversal tests testify to the primary origin of the indentified magnetization components. However, the inter-
pretation of the paleomagnetic data should take into account the probable inclination shallowing. New sub-
stantiation is offered for the paleomagnetic poles for Early Devonian and Late Permian. For the first time,
paleomagnetic constraints are obtained for the Late Carboniferous boundary. It is shown that the Early Cim-
merian deformation stage within the Paikhoi–Novaya Zemlya region is associated with the sinistral strike slip
displacement along the Baidaratskii suture during which the internal structure of the Southern Novaya Zem-
lya segment could undergo shear in addition to the nappe-thrust transformations. The Northern Novaya
Zemlya segment, which is shifted northwest with respect to the Southern segment, was deformed in the
thrusting mode with an overall clockwise rotation of this segment relative to the East European Craton.
Keywords: rock magnetism, paleomagnetism, Paleozoic, paleomagnetic pole, magnetotectonics, shear defor-
mations, Barents–Kara shelf, Novaya Zemlya Archipelago, the Arctic

A Newly Determined Paleomagnetic Pole for the Late Ordovician
in Siberia and Kinematics of the Siberian Platform 
on the Time Interval of ~505–455 Ma Ago
V. E. Pavlova,*, A. M. Pasenkoa, A. V. Dronovb, and I. V. Fedyukina
Presented by Academician A.O. Gliko March 2, 2021
Received March 2, 2021; revised March 12, 2021; accepted March 12, 2021
Abstract—A paleomagnetic study of the Chertovskii Horizon of the Moyero River valley was carried out.
Based on published and newly obtained data, the sequence of seven reliable determinations of the paleomag-
netic pole position is obtained for Siberia within the time interval of ~505–450 Ma. This sequence makes it
possible to determine with high precision the paleogeographic position of the Siberian platform over a period
of ~50 Ma from the Middle Cambrian until the middle of the Upper Ordovician.
Keywords: Siberian Platform, Ordovician, Paleomagnetism, paleoreconstruction
DOI: 10.1134/S1028334X21060131
INTRODUCTION
Due to their lithological characteristics, relatively
great thickness, excellent exposure, and good biostra-
tigraphic coverage, the Cambrian and Ordovician sed-
imentary sections of the Siberian Platform represent a
unique object for obtaining a detailed paleomagnetic
record, characterizing, in particular, the paleogeo-
graphic position and horizontal movements of the
Siberian Craton during the Early Paleozoic. These
data are necessary for paleotectonic and paleogeo-
graphic reconstructions and for exploring the geody-
namic evolution of the Siberian platform as well as of
the entire crust of the Earth.
Long-term studies of the paleomagnetism of the
Cambrian and Ordovician have already made it possi-
ble to identify reliably a number of paleomagnetic pole
positions with good statistical substantiation, which
are being used widely to solve these problems. Mean-
while, the paleomagnetic data available for the Lower
Paleozoic are incomplete. Until now, there has been
uncertainty about the position of the paleomagnetic
pole of Siberia for the Lower Cambrian [1]. The
paleomagnetic data for the Upper Ordovician is utterly
insufficient: there are only two Siberian pole determi-
nations, performed for the Dolborskii horizon of the
Moyero River section [2] and for the Chertovskii-Bak-
san interval of the Ordovician section of the middle
reaches of the Angara River [3].
Field studies of the section of the Moyero River
(north of the Siberian Platform), carried out in the
summer of 2020 included, among other things, sam-
pling of the deposits of the Chertovskii horizon, corre-
sponding in its stratigraphic position to the lower half
of the Caradoc of the British Stratigraphic Scale and
to the Lower Sandbian of the International Strati-
graphic Scale. This contribution presents the results of
paleomagnetic laboratory studies of a sample collec-
tion from the Chertovskii horizon, which made it pos-
sible to obtain a new paleomagnetic pole position for
the Upper Ordovician of the Siberian Platform and
propose a sequence of paleomagnetic poles describing
the paleogeographic position and horizontal displace-
ments of the Siberian Platform in the time interval of
~505–455 Ma.

cations, usually associated with the intrusion of Perm-

Biostratigraphic data based on the study of conodonts
and macrofossils (brachiopods, cephalopods, etc.)
indicate that the Ordovician section of the Moyero
contains ten horizons out of 12 identified on the Sibe-
rian platform (Fig. 1). The latter suggests that the
Moyero section is one of the most complete strati-
graphic sections of the Ordovician of Northern Eur-
asia, and perhaps the entire planet.
The initial detailed description of the Ordovician
reference section along the Moyero River was given in
the monograph by Myagkova et al. [4]. Modern data
on the stratigraphy, lithology, and formation condi-
tions of the Ordovician deposits of the Siberian plat-
form in general and the section along the Moyero
River in particular were reported in [5–7]. The cor-
relation of regional units (horizons) of the Ordovician
of the Siberian Platform with the International Strati-
graphic Scale was given in [8].
Here we give only a brief description of outcrop 70,
where the rocks of the Chertovskii Horizon are
exposed. The outcrop is located on the left bank of the
Moyero River, 3.5 km above the mouth of the Bug-
arikty River, near the mouth of a small stream. The
deposits of the Moyeronskii (Middle Ordovician) and
Dzheromskii (Upper Ordovician) formations are
exposed in the outcrop on a steep slope up to 80 m high
(Figs. 1, 2).
The Moyeronskii Formation in outcrop 70 is repre-
sented by its upper subformation. Its lower part is
composed of alternating beds of violet–red marls and
beds of gray and yellowish gray bioclastic limestones
with an admixture of quartz sand and/or quartz sand-
stones, and the upper part is represented by a layer of
quartz sandstones with a thin slant and horizontal lay-
ering. The subformation is correlated with the
Kirensko-Kudrinskii Horizon; it is about 30 m thick.
The Dzheromskii Formation comprises the Cher-
tovskii, Baksanskii, and Dolborski horizons and cor-
responds to the Sandbian–Lower Katian stage of the
Upper Ordovician [6]. In outcrop 70, the Dzheromskii
Formation is composed mainly of typical cold-water
carbonates.

The lower boundary of the formation, which is also
the lower boundary of the Chertovskii Horizon, is
unconformable, lithologically expressed as an abrupt
change of light gray fine-grained quartz sandstones
crowning the Moyeronskii Formation to cherry–
brown siltstones and greenish gray bioclastic lime-
stones. This boundary is interpreted as the flood sur-
face and the lower boundary of the Mangazeiskaya
sedimentary sequence [6]. The Chertovskii Horizon is
distinguished by a darker, reddish color and forms a
brow in the relief (see Fig. 2). Its lower part is com-
posed by a thin alternation of cherry–brown siltstones
and greenish gray bioclastic limestones. The upper
part of the Chertovskii Horizon is formed by greenish
gray siltstones with a few interlayers and nodules of
pinkish gray packstones. Deposits of the Chertovskii
Horizon (2.5 m thick) represent the deepest part of the
Mangazeiskaya sedimentary sequence and are inter-
preted as a transgressive system tract [6].
The middle and upper parts of the Dzheromskii
Formation (Baksanskii and Dollyuorskii horizons) are
composed of alternating gray and greenish gray organ-
ogenic–detrital, less often clayey, limestones and
mudstones.
Forty samples were collected from the section of
the Chertovskii Horizon in outcrop 70 with a sampling
step of 5–7 cm for paleomagnetic analysis. The sam-
ples underwent laboratory processing in accordance
with the standard procedure [9] in the laboratory of
the Main Magnetic Field and Petromagnetism of the
Institute of Physics of the Earth, Russian Academy of
Sciences, using modern laboratory equipment
(http://paleomag-ifz.ru/ru/equipment). Magnetic
cleaning was carried out using a TD80 thermodemag-
netizer (manufactured by Magnetic Measuremenets
Ltd., Great Britain) in a special room shielded from an
external magnetic field; the remanent magnetization
was measured in the same room using a cryogenic
magnetometer manufactured by 2GEnterprise
(United States). In total, depending on the nature of
the paleomagnetic recording, from 12 to 18 cleaning
steps were performed up to temperatures correspond-
ing to the hematite Curie point (~670–680°C).
LABORATORY PALEOMAGNETIC STUDY
The values of the magnetic susceptibility and natu-
ral remanent magnetization (NRM) of the rocks stud-
ied varied from 40 to 250 × 10
–6 SI units and from 1 ×
10–3 to 10–20 × 10–3 A/m, respectively.
Thermal magnetic cleaning (see Fig. 3) made it
possible to distinguish either two components of mag-
netization, low-temperature and high-temperature,
or, in some cases, three components of magnetization,
low-temperature, medium-temperature, and high-
temperature. The first, unstable low-temperature
component of the magnetization is usually destroyed
at 200–250°C and corresponds to the direction of the
modern magnetic field. The second, medium-tem-
perature component is close to the paleomagnetic
directions determined in the trap intrusions of the

Since the effect of contamination is opposite for sam-

Thus, there is reason to believe that the calculated

The following arguments support the primacy of
the characteristic magnetization identified: (1) consis-
tency with the more ancient Ordovician directions and
the proximity of the corresponding paleomagnetic
pole to the pole of rocks of the same age from the out-
crops of the valley of the middle reaches of the Angara
River [2, 3]; (2) the presence of both direct and reverse
polarity; and (3) the difference from the poles identi-
fied from younger formations of the Siberian platform
and, in particular, from the pole of the Permian and
Triassic trap rocks. The latter, due to their close loca-
tion to the section studied, could well be a source of
the rock magnetization reversal.
DISCUSSION
The paleomagnetic direction identified in the
Chertovskii Horizon of the Moyero River section was
used to calculate the paleomagnetic pole (see Tables 1
and 2). Together with the poles of the Dolborskii
Horizon, which are close in age [2], and the Moyero
River and Chertovskii–Baksanskii horizons of the
Ordovician in the middle reaches of the Angara River
[3], this pole can be used to determine the position of
the middle paleomagnetic pole of the Upper Ordovi-
cian of the Siberian platform with a conditional age of
~450 Ma [12]. We took the middle poles for Tremado-
cian, Arenig, Llanvirn, and Llandaleo from [13]; to
calculate the middle poles of the Middle and Upper

The poles obtained allow the paleogeographic
position of the Siberian platform to be determined
with great accuracy and its drift to be followed for over
~50 Ma from the Middle Cambrian to the middle of
the Upper Ordovician.
Figure 4 shows that from the middle Cambrian
(~505 Ma ago) to the end of the Early Ordovician
(~473 Ma ago), the northern (in modern coordinates)
part of the platform was located in the southern tropi-
cal latitudes, while the southern (in modern coordi-
nates) part of the platform was located in the southern
near-equatorial latitudes. At the same time, the mod-
ern southern part of the platform was turned towards
the north. The rate of latitudinal movement of the
platform at this time was low and did not exceed 0.3 °
per 1 Ma. By the Darrywilian time (Middle Ordovi-
cian), the latitudinal drift velocity of the Siberian Plat-
form had increased significantly; it began to move rap-
idly northward at a speed of more than 1 ° per million
years, and by the middle of the Late Ordovician, the
middle part of the platform was at the equator. At that
time the platform experienced only minor rotations
relative to the meridian, which slightly accelerated
near the Tremadocian–Floian and Darriwilian–
Sandbian boundaries.

Abstract
We present results of study of the basites of the Vilyui paleorift. Their 40Ar/39Ar isotopic ages were used to establish the sequence of their
intrusion, which lasted ~18 Myr. Dolerite sills of the Kontai–Dzherba zone were the first crystallizing phase (378.0–380.7 Ma), which was
followed by the intrusion of dikes of the Vilyui–Markha zone (372–373 Ma). Dikes of the Chara–Sinsk zone were the last crystalizing phase
(362–364 Ma). The prolonged plume–lithosphere interaction resulted in the successive enrichment of basaltic melt with titanium, phosphorus,
REE, HSFE, and LILE. Accumulation of the melt and formation of a magmatic lens at the crust–mantle boundary led to early crystallization
of the melt at a depth of 35–40 km from the paleosurface under reducing conditions at a temperature of 1450–1470 ºC. We assume that the
inception and sequent opening of the Vilyui paleorift were associated with the relative rotation of 22° of the Angara–Anabar block with respect
to the Aldan block in Early Famennian time. The Euler pole of rotation was located in the southern part of the paleorift, and a melting zone
was directly beneath it.

NEW PALEOMAGNETIC DATA ON THE SILURIAN AND DEVONIAN
SEDIMENTARY ROCKS FROM PODOLIA, SW UKRAINE, AND KINEMATICS
OF THE EAST EUROPEAN PLATFORM IN THE MIDDLE PALEOZOIC
V. G. Bakhmutov, I. B. Poliachenko
Institute of Geophysics, National Academy of Sciences of Ukraine, Kiev, Ukraine
Abstract: Paleomagnetic data are the priority source of information for global paleotectonic reconstructions representing hori­
zontal movements of the crustal blocks. Upon receipt of new paleomagnetic data, kinematic models of the East European
platform in the Paleozoic are regularly revised and improved. The article presents results of the paleomagnetic study of sedi­
mentary gray­colored and red beds of the Silurian and Lower Devonian sequences located in the Dniester river basin, Podolia
region, SW Ukraine. The study covered 17 outcrops that are stratigraphically correlated with the Wenlock, Ludlow, Pridoli
states of the Sillurian and the Lochkovian stage of the Devon. Over 400 samples of grey limestone, argillite, dolomite, red
limestone and sandstone were analyzed, and two components of natural remnant magnetization (NRM) were revealed. The
first component with SSW declination and negative inclination is revealed in the majority of the samples during AF­ and
T­magnetic cleaning. Its pole positions, that are calculated separately for each series, are trending to the Permian segment of
the apparent polar wander path (APWP) published by Torsvik et al. [2012] for Baltica / Stable Europe. Considering its chem­
ical origin, this NRM component is related to formation of authigenic minerals due to rock remagnetization. The second
component is revealed only in some samples taken from the red beds (during thermal demagnetization in the range of un­
blocking temperatures from 590 to 690 °С) and in few samples of grey limestone (in AF fields from 30 to 70 mT or in the
range of unblocking temperatures from 300 to 460 °С). This component has SW declination and positive inclination, goes to
the origin of coordinates of the diagrams, and has all the indicators of primary magnetization of sediments. Calculated posi­
tions of the poles (0 ºS and 329 ºE for grey limestone of the Tiverskaya series, 2.3 °S and 338.4 °E for red beds of the Dnies­
trovskaya series, etc.) are well correlated with the Devonian segments of APWP for Baltica / Stable Europe. The same is true
for the Silurian poles. The new results suggest that in the Ludlow, the East European platform was located at the near­
equatorial latitudes of the Southern Hemisphere, and in the Pridoli, it moved to the north towards the equatorial latitudes of
the Southern Hemisphere. Later on, the drifting mode was changed, and the platform moved to the south. In the Lochkovian,
its position was stabilized at the equatorial latitudes of the Southern Hemisphere. Drifting of the platform can be described by
counterclockwise rotation by 16° around the Euler pole (Φ=34 °S, Λ=247 °E).
Key words: paleomagnetism, Middle Paleozoic, East European platform, apparent polar wander path (APWP), paleotectonic
reconstruction.
