2. Geological setting 
2.1. Regional geology 
The progressive convergence of India and Asia and their collisional 
effects led to the emergence of the Himalayan orogeny ( Yin and Harri -
son, 2000 ), with distinct structures such as the South Tibetan Detach -
ment System (STDS), Main Central Thrust (MCT), Main Boundary Thrust 
(MBT), and Main Frontal Thrust (MFT). Traditionally, the Himalayan 
belt can be divided into the Tethyan, Greater Himalayan, Lesser Hima -
layan, and Sub-Himalayan domains ( Gansser, 1964 ). The Tethyan 
Himalaya is situated between the STDS and the Indus-Tsangpo suture 
zone (ITSZ), encompassing Proterozoic to Eocene sedimentary rocks 
interbedded with Paleozoic and Mesozoic volcanic rocks ( Yin, 2006 ). 
South of the STDS lies the Greater Himalaya, composed of Neo -
proterozoic to Ordovician metasedimentary protoliths, and medium-to 
high-grade metamorphic rocks of upper Paleozoic and Mesozoic 
(Permian-Miocene Gondwana sequence) and Cenozoic foreland-basin 
deposits bearing the Lesser Himalaya extend along the MCT ( Sakai, 
1983, 1989 ; DeCelles et al., 2004 ; Yin, 2006 ; Searle et al., 2009 ; Khatri 
et al., 2021 ). The Neogene clastic rocks of the Siwalik Group or Sub- 
Himalaya, restricted farther to the south, are capped by the MBT at 
the top. The youngest and northerly-dipping MFT runs along the 
northern frontier of the Quaternary Indo-Gangetic plain, separating the 
Siwaliks ( Gansser, 1964 ). 
In western Nepal, the Paleocene to Miocene Tosh Group comprises 
conglomerates, sandstones, and shales with coal seams and fossiliferous 
horizons ( Fig. 1 ), overlying the Proterozoic Gwar Group with a discon -
formity and an erosional surface ( Dhital and Kizaki, 1987 ). The sepa -
ration between the Lesser Himalayan rocks and the Siwaliks is marked 
by the Botechaur Thrust and Main Boundary active fault, commonly 
called the Main Boundary Thrust, extending along the northern slopes of 
the Dang valley ( Dhital, 2015 ). Previously, the Tosh Group in the 
northern part of Dang has been studied based on the lithostratigraphic 
framework ( Frank and Fuchs, 1970 ; Sharma, 1977, 1980 ; Dhital and 
Kizaki, 1987 ; Dhital, 2015 ), preliminary paleomagnetic study ( Pant 
et al., 1992 ) and some detrital zircon U-Pb-Hf isotopic analysis ( Baral 
et al., 2018 ). The age of this group has been assigned as Paleocene to 
Miocene, based on the lithological and fossil assemblages Dhital and 
Kizaki (1987) . However, Sharma (1980) mentioned its age range be -
tween the Cretaceous to Eocene. The Tosh Group has been subdivided 
into the Sattim and Dubring formations. The Sattim Formation is char -
acterized by three members, including a basal member with conglom -
erate beds, a middle member featuring thin coal seams, and thick beds of 
quartzose sandstone and orthoquartzite interbedded with shale. The 
upper member contains gray, gray-green, and gray lenticular limestone 
beds bearing foraminifera ( Nummulites and Assilina ) and bivalves ( Dhital 
and Kizaki, 1987 ; Dhital, 2015 ). The Dubring Formation comprises a 
lower member of foraminifera and bivalves bearing argillaceous lime -
stone and an upper member with green sublitharenite beds alternating 
with red-purple mudstone. Both formations consist of compact lenses of 
bivalves and gastropods, interpreted as tempestites ( Dhital and Kizaki, 
1987 ). 
2.2. Stratigraphy and sedimentology 
A 357 m thick section was measured from the Tulsipur section (28

comprising shale/mudstone interbedded with limestone and basal 
dominant shale; and (b) Unit II characterized by upper shale/mudstone 
and fine-grained sandstone interbedded with limestone (silty/sandy 
type). In the field, we observed fairly distinct lithostratigraphic variation 
in both units and found no evidence of hiatus, suggesting uninterrupted 
sedimentation. Unit I (357 – 84 m) features dark gray-green to yellowish- 
green shale and a very thin marl layer (up to ~50 cm) in the lower part. 
The calcareous content increases gradually in the upper part, forming 
parallel to wavy nature bedding. The gray-green to occasionally dark 
gray shale interbeds with dark gray limestone in 1 – 6 m thick layers, 
suggesting a sudden sea level rise. Shale/mudstone interbedding with 
limestone and mudstone becomes prominent after 300 m, indicating a 
shift from a relatively low-energy to a more efficient sedimentary 
environment. The shale content decreases gradually upward after 150 
m, and the yellowish-green to grayish-green mudstones commonly occur 
in the middle part (130 – 203 m). In the upper part, dark green shale and 
gray fine-grained sandstone interbed in thin layers up to about 98 m, 
which later ended by interbedding with gray-yellow silty limestone. This 
unit is comparable to the Sattim Formation ( Dhital and Kizaki, 1987 ; 
Dhital, 2015 ), as well as the Melpani and Amile formations in western 
and eastern Nepal, respectively, ( Sakai, 1983 ; Kayastha, 1992 ; Khatri 
et al., 2021 ). Unit II (84 – 0 m) is characterized by interbedding of shale, 
mudstone, and silty-sandy limestone. The dark green shale and gray 
fine-grained sandstone in the lower part alternate with dark gray lime -
stone in the upper part, with each layer being 10 – 20 cm thick. Silty to 
sandy limestone beds gradually increase to 15 m in the middle part. The 
deep red-purple mudstone appears to be intermixed with a very thin 
layer of gray-yellow marl ( < 30 cm) in the upper part. Later, they 
interbed with gray-red, fine-grained sandstone and gray-yellow lime -
stone. Asymmetrical wave ripples and horizontal laminations are 
observed in the interbedding of deep purple-red mudstone and gray- 
yellow limestone, with ripple spacing varying from 2 to 6 cm and 
heights reaching up to 2 cm. These wave ripples are straight-crested, 
bifurcated on a bedding surface in the upper part of this unit ( Fig. 1 ). 
This unit concludes with dark green mudstone and gray-yellow lime -
stone, featuring < 1 m thick light gray-red sandy limestone beds. This 
unit is comparable to the Dubring Formation ( Dhital and Kizaki, 1987 ) 
and also to the Swat and Bhainskati formations of the western and 
eastern parts of Nepal, respectively, ( Sakai, 1983 ; Kayastha, 1992 ; 
Khatri et al., 2021 ). 
3. Materials and methods 
3.1. Paleomagnetic sampling 
We conducted magnetostratigraphy to establish a more accurate 
chronological framework for the Tulsipur section. Magnetostratigraphic 
samples were acquired from shale, mudstone, fine-grained sandstone, 
and limestone layers ( Fig. 1 ) using a portable petrol-powered drill. The 
sampling interval varied, typically set at 1 m and occasionally reduced 
to 0.5 m based on the lithology and outcrop conditions. In total, 318 core 
samples were collected from this section during the field work.

5. Discussion 
5.1. Depositional environment and sedimentary evolution of the study 
area 
The Tulsipur section provides valuable insights into the complex 
interplay of tectonic, climatic, and depositional processes in the north -
ern continental margin of the Indian subcontinent during the Late 
Cretaceous to Early Eocene times. This section shows a rapid subsidence 
of a preexisting fluvial regime during the Late Cretaceous ( Figs. 7 and 8 ), 
most likely caused by the rifting of the northern Indian passive margin 
opening. The section unveils distinct sedimentary facies towards a slope 
towards basinal succession inferred by gray, green or black shale 
intercalation with limestone beds between Unit I and Unit II. Unit I 
(68 – 57 Ma), exhibit a shale-dominated deposition with a high sediment 
accumulation rate, indicating that subsidence outpaced sediment supply 
until lithological changes occurred. The basal 357 – 318 m of this unit, 
dated between 68 and 66 Ma, is composed of dark greenish-gray shale, 
evidence of a northern shallow sea from the Tethyan Seaway. The dark 
gray-greenish gray shale intervals followed by yellow-gray-green in -
tervals are caused by weathering or diagenesis processes and are likely 
deposited in the outer shelf (offshore environment) very close to the 
inner shelf during retreated sea level and gradual upward occurrence of 
limestone representing a gradual rise in sea level. Similarly, the lami -
nated dark gray shale (e.g., between 321 and 315 m and 102 – 99 m) is 
well preserved in offshore to nearshore environments ( Blatt and Tracy, 
1996 ). The precise explanation of the depositional environment of shale 
intervals is challenging due to the lack of typical diagnostic character -
istics ( Singh and Chakraborty, 2022 ). However, we interpret that the 
varying shale/mudstone to upward shale/mudstone intercalations with 
limestone and rarely observed marl units indicate a dynamic offshore 
environment below the fair weather wave base but faintly above the 
storm wave base. 
Unit II (57 – 54 Ma) is characterized by mudstone, fine-grained 
sandstone, and silty to sandy limestone. The presence of red-purple 
mudstone and fine-grained sandstone indicates deposition in an arid 
to semiarid, oxidizing environment ( Paik and Kim, 2006 ) of proximal 
offshore to nearshore environments promoting a tidal flat origin ( Fig. 7 ). 
The light green mudstones/shale suggests period of prolonged standing 
water ( Lowenstein and Hardie, 1985 ). In this unit, gray to red mudstone- 
sandstone and limestone (silty to sandy limestone) interbeds frequently 
suggest deposition in proximal shelf (offshore) to tidal flats (nearshore) 
settings, under oxic and redox conditions influenced by tidal actions. 
Furthermore, the horizontally laminated deposition interrupted by wave 
asymmetrical ripples in the fine-grained sandstone under waning-flow 
conditions in the tidal flats ( Lowenstein and Hardie, 1985 ; Paik and 
Kim, 2006 ), suggests low-energy to high-energy settings. It further re -
veals erosion and sediment derivation from the hinterland and addi -
tional flexural subsidence ( Fig. 8 ). The distinct change in sediment 
deposition in the study area was only observed after 59 Ma, attributed to 
modifications and denudation from the adjacent topography that is 
uplifted Tethyan and Higher Himalayan terrane ( Sakai, 1983 ; DeCelles 
et al., 2004 ; Baral et al., 2018 ; Neupane et al., 2018 ), caused by the 
Indian and Eurasian plates convergence ( Lee and Lawver, 1995 ), and the 
onset of monsoon-like rainfall patterns during the Eocene ( Licht et al., 
2014 ; Spicer et al., 2017 ; Teng et al., 2019 ; Fang et al., 2021 ; Wu et al., 
2022 ; Tardif et al., 2023 ). The various limestone beds intercalated with 
shale/mud and sandstone indicate frequent cycles of shallow marine 
transgressions and regressions. Fifteen and seven transgressive- 
regressive (T-R) cycles obtained in Unit I and Unit II are inferred by 
stacked lithofacies and their interrelated depositional settings ( Fig. 6 ). 
Some shelf areas in northeast India display extensive limestone deposits 
during the Paleocene and Late Eocene age, followed by a regressive 
phase ( Tewari et al., 2010 ). 
5.2. Correlations to the geomagnetic polarity timescale 
Out of the total 285 samples, 76.8% (219) were utilized to delineate 
the magnetic polarity zonation, establishing discrete magnetozones as 
intervals in the Tulsipur section. Employing principal component anal -
ysis, the magnetostratigraphic sequence was established from samples 
exhibiting both low and high-temperature stable components ( Fig. 5 ). 
Initially, each polarity zone was defined by at least two or more 
consecutive data points with the same ChRM polarity, either normal or 
reverse in polarity. Subsequently, a total of six normal (N1 – N6) and six 
reversed (R1 – R6) polarity zones were identified from the top to the 
bottom of the sampled sequence. The zones exhibited correlation with 
C25n, C26n, C27n, C28n, C29n, and C30n as well as C24r, C25r, C26r, 
C27r, C28r, and C29r, respectively. Thus, these polarities show chrons 
C25n – C30n and C24r – C29r, respectively, in accordance with the 
geomagnetic polarity timescale (GPTS) of Gradstein et al. (2012) . The 
identified magnetozones aligned seamlessly with six individual mag -
netozones of the GPTS ( Fig. 5 ), with polarity chrons from R1 to R4 
characterized by a major reversed polarity interspersed with some short- 
period normal polarities. The chron N5 was noted as a relatively short- 
term normal polarity, considering the correlation of the stretched 
normal polarity of N3 above R4 with N4 and N6. As observed magne -
tozones in this section are straightforwardly correlated to the GPTS, it 
can be concluded that a relatively continuous depositional sequence 
from the Late Cretaceous (68.19 Ma) to Early Eocene (53.98 Ma) exists. 
In addition, no sedimentary hiatuses were observed during the field 
excursion, suggesting that the absence could be attributed to relatively 
less dense sampling intervals of the paleomagnetic specimens. Based on 
the proposed magnetostratigraphic chronology of the Tulsipur section, 
linear interpolation yielded a youngest age of 53.98 Ma and an oldest 
age of 68.19 Ma. We assume that the conglomerate bed reported by 
Dhital and Kizaki (1987) could be much older than 68 Ma and the age of 
the Dubring Formation could be assigned to be of Eocene age. Marine 
fossils were also reported from this region ( Dhital and Kizaki, 1987 ) 
which could be assigned to the end of Late Cretaceous and Eocene 
respectively. However, these fossils were not observed in this section. A 
linearly extrapolated age range between 68.2 and 54 Ma was obtained 
for the studied Tulsipur section. Consequently, a magnetostratigraphic 
sequence with a thickness of 357 m was constructed ( Fig. 5 ), and reliable 
sediment accumulation rate estimations were determined ( Fig. 6 ). It was 
observed that a plot of magnetostratigraphic ages versus thickness of the

We tested two hypotheses based on the long-term (million-year 
scale) effects of climate fluctuations and tectonic factors using the 
magnetic polarity-based age model of sedimentation. Mishandling in the 
core recovery process sometimes changes the true depth position of 
stratigraphic surfaces and leads to sediment swelling or liquefaction, 
promoting uncertainties in age-depth models ( Scardia et al., 2006 ). 
Overlapping uncertainties also occurred when two ages were very 
narrowly spaced and/or had large uncertainties ( Halverson et al., 2022 ). 
This was carefully avoided by taking precautions on uncertainties in 
identifying precisely the stratigraphic position of polarity reversals 
subject to sampling resolution and interpolating ages between them.

Furthermore, the collision with the Asian plate and successive tectonic 
effects such as deformation, uplift, and volcanism likely influenced the 
sedimentation rates. Convergence was highest at around 68 to 59 Ma 
and later gradually decreased in the basins of the Indian plate ( Alam

increased convergence and subduction rates of the Indian plate and/or 
basin uplift probably intensified sedimentation rates within the periods

these aforementioned factors also led to a marked drop and subsequent 
rise in sedimentation rate between 59.2 and 57.8 Ma and two distinct 
decreasing phases between 66 and 62 Ma. Despite the complexity 
introduced by tectonic effects, the higher sedimentation rates in the 
study area are thus anticipated merely with the Indian plate ’ s vivacious 
shortening rates formed during its northward voyage. 
5.4. Comparison between sedimentation rates, Indian drift rates and 
coeval sedimentation rate variation recorded in Asian basins 
The Tulsipur section witnessed shale/mudstone deposits offshore, 
indicative of a surge in SARs during the Late Cretaceous and Early 
Paleocene, conceivably influenced by the near-field effects of the India- 
Asian convergence ( Figs. 6 and 7 ). The flexural isostatic effects, driven 
by denudational rebound onshore/nearshore and sediment loading 
offshore, likely played a pivotal role in shaping sedimentation patterns 
( Widdowson and Cox, 1996 ; Gunnell and Fleitout, 2000 ). We infer that 
the maximum sedimentation rates may be attributed to rift-flank 
denudation and escarpment production, linked to fragmentation ef -
fects such as those of the India-Seychelles ( Campanile et al., 2008 ). The 
appearance of clastic sediments in the Early Eocene ( Fig. 7 ) suggests a 
swift response following the rifting event associated with seafloor 
spreading, Deccan flood basalt emplacement, and Seychelles micro -
continent rifting ( Fig. 8 ), ( Norton and Sclater, 1979 ; Hooper, 1990 ) 
leading to the creation of the present-day Arabian Sea ( Miles and Roest, 
1993 ). Furthermore, the stratigraphic appearance in the study area can 
be intricately tied to the K/Pg boundary, marking the onset of lower 
sedimentation rates, possibly influenced by tectonic effects, deforma -
tion, uplift, volcanism, and the northward shift of the Indian subconti -
nent. This decrease in sedimentation rate might be one of the reasons 
triggered by the onset of the India-Asia collision. It is consistent with 
studies of the sedimentary rocks of the 90

that show a rapid decline in relative velocity from 18 to 19 cm/yr to 4.5 
cm/yr around 55 Ma ( Klootwijk et al., 1992 ; Chatterjee and Scotese, 
2010 ; Clementz et al., 2011 ; Chatterjee et al., 2013 ; Li et al., 2015 ) and 
9 – 15 cm/yr ( van Hinsbergen et al., 2011a ) or between ~15 – 20 cm/yr 
and ~ 13 – 18 cm/yr around 50 Ma ( Patriat and Achache, 1984 ). Some 
scholars argue that major peninsular rivers were eventually affecting the 
variation of sediment sources and accumulation rates until 65 Ma and 
again between 56 and 34 Ma, usually in the northeast regions of the 
Indian subcontinent ( Krishna et al., 2016 ). Notably, Chen et al. (1993b) 
believe that the soft collision between the northwest corner of the Indian 
Shield and South Tibet at 59 Ma caused a relative upsurge in sedimen -
tation rate. Therefore, tectonic processes such as regional compressional 
events ( Zhang et al., 2012 ), shortening in the Tibetan Plateau ( Kapp 
et al., 2007 ), and escalating magmatism ( Shellnutt et al., 2014 ) played 
crucial roles in the variation of SARs in the region.

related to the mantle plume events caused mountain exhumation around 
the Qaidam Basin, activation of the Liupanshan fault, and strike-slip

and the retreat of the trench around the LingBao basin ( Chen et al., 
2021 ; Jiang et al., 2023 ). Furthermore, this led to higher sediment 
accumulation rates across several basins of the Tibetan Plateau (TP) (e. 
g., Hoh Xil basin) in the northern part ( Jin et al., 2018 ), northeastern 
part (e.g., Xining and Lanzhou basins) ( Dupont-Nivet et al., 2004 ; Fang 
et al., 2019 ; Zhang et al., 2020a ), eastern part (e.g., Nangqian and 
Gongjue basins) ( Zhang et al., 2018 ; Li et al., 2020a, 2020b ), and east- 
central part (Gonjo basin) ( Studnicki-Gizbert et al., 2008 ; Li et al.,

southern part and within these aforementioned regions between 70 and 
55 Ma, followed by rapid exhumation and reactivation of several major 
fault systems between 54 and 47 Ma ( Wallis et al., 2003 ; Hetzel et al., 
2011 ; Jian et al., 2018 ; Jin et al., 2018 ). In fact, these wider basins have 
been generally dominated by basin-bounding and syn -sedimentary 
thrusts since the Late Cretaceous to Paleogene time ( Jin et al., 2018 ; 
Studnicki-Gizbert et al., 2008 ; Li et al., 2020a, 2020b ). Meanwhile, the 
higher sediment accumulation rates within the Hoh Xil and Gongjue 
basins between 69 and 63 Ma can be correlated with a similar trend 
observed in the southernmost part of the TP in this study area ( Fig. 6 ). 
The onset of tectonic events such as crustal thickening and the growth of 
the Longmen Shan Mountain started in the eastern TP during the Late 
Cretaceous to Paleogene period ( Zeng et al., 2004 ; Hubbard and Shaw, 
2009 ; Tian et al., 2016 ; Airaghi et al., 2018 ). 
5.5. Constraints on tectonism between the late cretaceous to early Eocene 
in the Indian subcontinent 
The Indian subcontinent underwent significant tectonic motions 
during its fragmentation from Gondwana, manifesting in three distinct 
phases: ca. 140 – 121 Ma, ca. 100 – 83 Ma, and ca. 73 – 68 Ma respectively, 
( Wu et al., 2023 and references therein). The initial motion (ca. 
136 – 126 Ma) involved the fragmentation of India and Australia- 
Antarctica, followed by the separation of India and Madagascar 
(98 – 84 Ma) ( Gibbons et al., 2013 ) and the breakup of Laxmi-Seychelles 
from India (71 – 62 Ma) ( Collier et al., 2008 ), with Deccan volcanism 
occurring between 69 Ma and 61 Ma ( Sheth et al., 2001 ; Chenet et al., 
2009 ; Jiang et al., 2023 ). The northward movement of the Indian Plate 
led to the continual cessation of the Neotethys Ocean ( Dercourt et al., 
1993 ), and during the passage over plume zones like Kerguelen and 
Crozet (68 – 64 Ma), Deccan volcanism intensified, resulting in signifi -
cant continental flood basalt volcanic events in the Indian subcontinent 
( McLean, 1985 ; Keller et al., 2008 ; Keller and Abramovich, 2009 ; 
Hooper et al., 2010 ; Punekar et al., 2014 ; Gu et al., 2022 ). During this 
period, uplift occurred in the Qiangtang-Lhasa terranes, Shan Plateau (E. 
Myanmar), and the Gaoligong-Baoshan mountain (SW Simao Basin) 
system ( Morley, 2004 ; Kapp et al., 2007 ; Yu et al., 2014 ). It is believed 
that a restructuring and rift shift in the Indian Ocean followed the 
emplacement of Deccan Traps in the Indian subcontinent ( Chatterjee 
and Bajpai, 2016 ). Subsequently, the Indian plate became lighter and 
drifted faster after the fragmentation of microplates such as Madagascar 
and Seychelles ( Fig. 8 ) from the early landmass of Greater India along 
with seafloor spreading ( Schlich, 1982 ; van Hinsbergen et al., 2011a ; 
Chatterjee et al., 2013 ). Campanile et al. (2008) proposed that rift-flank 
denudation and escarpment production during the fragmentation be -
tween western India and the Seychelles enhanced a higher sedimenta -
tion rate. Regardless of these events, the Himalayan Foreland basin was 
formed in the northern margin of the Indian subcontinent due to the 
sequel to the collision effect of the Indian and Eurasian plates and 
stretched out from the Indus Suture to the entire width of the Himalaya 
by shallow sea ( Najman et al., 1993 ; Virdi, 1994 ; Bhatia et al., 2017 ), 
named Subathu Sea in northwest India to Pakistan, and Bhainskati Sea in 
Nepal, and Assam-Arakan Sea in the northeast regions of India such as 
the Yinkiong-Mariang area of Arunachal Pradesh, Meghalaya, Bengal, 
Assam-Arakan and Andaman Islands was dominating in the Himalaya 
( Triphathi and Mamgain, 1986 ; Jafar and Kapoor, 1988 ; Khatri et al., 
2021 ). We proposed that rift-flank denudation and escarpment-forming 
events play a significant role around this section in acquiring a higher 
sedimentation rate at that time ( Fig. 6 ). 
5.6. Constraints of paleoposition and paleomagnetic direction on the size 
of Greater India 
The India-Asia collision led to crustal thickening in the Indian sub -
continent and uplift of the Himalayan terrane in an east-west lineament. 
The Himalayas contain a significant amount of deformed Indian crust, 
providing insight into the extent of the northern Indian plate margin (the 
size of Greater India). In the present context, the size of Greater India can 
be defined as the extension of the north-south region of the Indian 
subcontinent that encroached northward over the Indus-Yarlung suture 
or was subducted into the top mantle layer under the Tibetan Plateau ( Li 
and Tian, 2023 ). Its size is still a topic of debate ( Xu et al., 2022 ); 
however, its established size ranges from a few hundred kilometers to at 
least 3400 km ( Klootwijk and Bingham, 1980 ; DeCelles et al., 2002 ; Ali 
and Aitchison, 2005 ; Yi et al., 2011 ; Ma et al., 2016 ; Meng et al., 2019 ; 
van Hinsbergen et al., 2019 ; Meng et al., 2020 ; Meng et al., 2023 ). 
Indeed, understanding the timing and process of collision requires 
knowledge of the size of Greater India. The Indus-Tsangpo suture serves 
as a geological boundary between the southern Himalayan terrane and 
the northern Lhasa terrane. Various laterally distributed underthrusts/ 
faults (such as the Karakoram fault, Altyn Tagh fault, Kunlun fault, Main 
Central Thrust, and Main Boundary Thrust) are localized beneath the 
Tibetan and Indian lithospheres, likely originating from crustal thick -
ening effects ( Tapponnier et al., 2001 ; Agius and Lebedev, 2013 ).

◦

2021 ). In the central-western part, Zhada extended to 2700 km during 
the Late Cretaceous ( Meng et al., 2020 ; Meng et al., 2023 ), while in the 
western part, Zanskar showed a size of 810 ± 333 km (7.3 ± 2.5
◦
) 
( Dannemann et al., 2022 ). Some recent studies ( Zhao et al., 2021 ; 
Dannemann et al., 2022 ) have raised concerns about the remanence and 
reliability of the Gamba area studied by Patzelt et al. (1996) and Yi et al. 
(2011) . In addition, Xu et al. (2022) questioned the reliability of the 
results for the Zhada section studied by Meng et al. (2020) due to in -
consistencies with earlier studies. Despite these challenges, some 
paleomagnetic investigations, the projected northern extent of Greater 
India is estimated to be ~950 km ( Parsons et al., 2020 ; Lu et al., 2022 ; 
Jin et al., 2023 ) until the Tethyan Himalaya separated from India prior 
to the India-Asia collision ( Jin et al., 2023 ). 
5.7. Insights into the timing of India-Asia collision 
The age of the India-Asia collision still has large uncertainties and 
controversies regarding its timing estimation, as conducted by various 
studies. The collision age ranges from 25 to 20 Ma ( van Hinsbergen 
et al., 2012 ) up to ~70 Ma ( Aitchison et al., 2007 ; Yin and Harrison, 
2000 ; Ding et al., 2022 ); however, the widely accepted collision age is 
~50 – 56 Ma ( Lippert et al., 2014 ; Ding et al., 2017 ; Najman et al., 2017 ; 
Meng et al., 2019 ; Pusok and Stegman, 2020 ; Yuan et al., 2021 ; Meng 
et al., 2023 ; Wu et al., 2023 ). Recent studies propose that the initial 
contact between India and Eurasia occurred in northern Pakistan and 
northern India between 54 and 56 Ma ( Ding et al., 2017 ; Najman et al., 
2017 ). Some believe that the Indian craton collided with the Tethyan 
Himalaya at ~53 – 48 Ma, leading to the disappearance of the northern 
Indian Sea from west to east ( Yuan et al., 2021 ). Others suggest that the 
collision began along the western-central Tibetan boundary at ca. 55 ±
5 Ma and was completed at 40 ± 5 Ma, extending towards the eastern 
boundary around Myanmar ( Wu et al., 2023 ). 
During the Late Cretaceous, a wide Neo-Tethys Ocean covered 
almost 3530 ± 440 km ( Bian et al., 2021 ; Yuan et al., 2021 ), slightly 
contracting to ~2000 km during 62 – 59 Ma ( Jin et al., 2023 ) and not 
ceasing until ~54 Ma ( Burg and Chen, 1984 ; An et al., 2017 ). Some 
scholars suggest that the northern margin of Greater India between the 
Himalayan terrane and the Indian craton was occupied by an intra- 
oceanic basin ( Yi et al., 2011 ; Meng et al., 2012 ) covering ~1800 km 
( Ali and Aitchison, 2008 ; van Hinsbergen et al., 2012 ; Metcalfe, 2013 ). 
Additionally, the Himalayan terrane (Zongpu and Zongshan area) was at 
4.4
◦
± 4.4
◦
S during 68 ± 3 Ma ( Patzelt et al., 1996 ) and moved between 
7.4
◦
± 3.1
◦
N to 8.1
◦
± 1.6
◦
N during 59 ± 4 Ma ( Patzelt et al., 1996 ; 
Yang et al., 2015 ), while the southern margin of the Lhasa terrane was 
still ~7.0
◦
farther north at 59 ± 4 Ma. In the west, the Kohistan Ladakh 
Arc was at 8.3 ± 5.6
◦
N during 66 – 62 Ma and first collided with India at 
60 – 50 Ma, later colliding with Asia between 45 and 50 Ma, indicating a 
probable India-Asia collision at ~50 Ma ( Martin et al., 2020 ). Besides, 
Khan et al. (2009) suggested that the Kohistan-Ladakh arc progressively 
collided around 65 Ma (Early Paleocene), marking a significant 
geological event. During 60 – 50 Ma, the Himalayan terrane was north -
ward drifting with a velocity of~16 cm/yr, proceeding to the collision 
( Klootwijk et al., 1992 ; Copley et al., 2010 ; Torsvik et al., 2012 ), and 
most likely collided with the Lhasa terrane between 55 and 50 Ma 
( Klootwijk et al., 1992 ; Patzelt et al., 1996 ; Guillot et al., 2003 ; Copley 
et al., 2010 ; Najman et al., 2010 ; Meng et al., 2023 ). This collision age is 
consistent with the metamorphic age of ~54 Ma for the eclogite-facies 
rocks in the northwestern Himalaya prior to continental subduction at 
57 ± 1 Ma ( Leech et al., 2005 ; Guillot et al., 2008 ). From the enhanced 
stable sediment accumulation rate (~27 m/Ma) between 62 and 54 Ma 
in the Tulsipur section (this study), we suggest that India and Asia 
collide only after 54 Ma. 
The northern extent of Greater India was still at ~1800 km (~15.9
◦
) 
( Yi et al., 2011 ; Meng et al., 2012 ) during ~54.0 Ma. Jin et al. (2023) 
suggested there is no clear indication of India – Asia collision observed 
between 62 and 59 Ma. The rapid sediment change and provenance 
documented in the trench basins of the Tethyan passive margin of India 
and active margin of Asia could be used to define the collision age be -
tween 59 ± 1 Ma and 61 Ma ( Hu et al., 2016b, 2020 ; An et al., 2021 ), 
which occurred at ~14.1 ± 1.9
◦
N ( Yuan et al., 2021, 2022 ). However, 
the ocean existed until ~54 Ma, as shown by the Maastrichtian- 
Paleocene fossils and the youngest age group of sandstone blocks in 
the Xiukang m ´elange at 54.5 ± 0.6 Ma ( Burg and Chen, 1984 ; An et al., 
2017 ). Parameters such as the timing of sediment provenance alone 
cannot provide significant evidence of the timing of collision ( Jin et al., 
2023 ). Bian et al. (2021) argued that there is no significant paleo -
latitudinal variation at ~51 – 49.5 Ma, and India-Asia likely collided no 
later than this time frame ( Najman et al., 2010 ; Cande and Stegman, 
2011 ; Lippert et al., 2014 ; Li et al., 2020). Recent studies show several 
pieces of evidence demonstrating that the timing of the collision is most 
likely reliable with paleomagnetic data and signifies the possibility of 
the final collision at ~50 Ma: (1) a significant reduction in northward 
drift velocity from ~140 to 40 mm/yr at ~53 – 48 Ma ( Klootwijk et al., 
1992 ; Copley et al., 2010 ; Cande and Stegman, 2011 ; Pusok and

6. Conclusions 
We conducted a magnetostratigraphy study of the Tulsipur area in 
the northern part of the Sub-Himalaya, western Nepal. Initially, a 
continuous chronology was established for this section to examine the 
sedimentation history and compare it with tectonic events in the 
northern Indian passive margin from the Late Cretaceous to the Early 
Eocene. A total of 315 samples were collected, and 268 samples with 
reliable directions were selected to determine virtual geomagnetic pole 
latitudes and construct the magnetic polarity sequence. A 357 m thick 
succession was dated to between ~68 and 54 Ma. The two periods of the 
highest sedimentation rates were identified between 64 and 68 Ma and 
two steady periods between 62 and 57.5 Ma, respectively. The highest 
sedimentation rate in the study area was most likely influenced by rift- 
flank denudation and escarpment expansion caused by the separation of 
microplates such as Seychelles from India. Furthermore, the initiation of 
tectonic subsidence and pronounced tectonic basin uplift also contrib -
uted to the development of the passive margin, with a shallow sea 
extending east and west in the northern part of the Indian subcontinent 
during the Late Cretaceous to Early Eocene. Tectonism likely played a 
more significant role compared to climate change in the region during 
this time. Additional magnetostratigraphic studies are crucial in the 
future from both the western and eastern parts of the Nepal Himalaya to 
strengthen age constraints for the evolution of the northern continental 
passive margin and provide evidence for the Indian-Asian collision 
recorded within the Himalayan orogeny.

ABSTRACT
To constrain the drift history of the Eastern Qiangtang Terrane and the closure time of the Paleo-Jinshajiang 
Ocean, we conducted a paleomagnetic study of Late Triassic limestones in the Qamdo region of the Eastern 
Qiangtang Terrane. The results of the rock magnetic, petrographic, and reversal test indicate the limestones carry 
primary magnetizations. Our new paleomagnetic data provide a Late Triassic paleopole of 30.9
◦
N, 161.4
◦
E (A
95 
= 8.4
◦
), which corresponds to a paleolatitude of 35 ± 8.4
◦
N for the study area. Integrating these data with 
existing paleomagnetic results and geological evidence, we determine that the Eastern Qiangtang Terrane was 
situated at a relatively constant paleolatitudinal position without significant N-S displacements during 
~230 – 209 Ma. We conclude that the Paleo-Jinshajiang Ocean in the Qamdo region had already closed before 
~221 Ma, and likely around ~230 Ma.
1. Introduction
The Tibetan Plateau, a collage of continental fragments that rifted 
from Gondwana and assembled in the Mesozoic-Cenozoic, is an ideal 
natural laboratory from which we may enrich our understanding of a 
variety of plate tectonic processes, including microcontinent formation, 
ocean basin dynamics, and continental assembly ( Meng et al., 2019, 
2020, 2023 ; Metcalfe, 2013 ; Pan et al., 2012 ; S ¸ eng ¨or and Atayman, 
2009 ; Tang et al., 2020 ; Wang et al., 2018 ; Wei et al., 2022, 2023; Xu 
et al., 2015 ; Xu et al., 2024 ; Yan et al., 2016 ; Yan et al., 2019a,b; Yin and 
Harrison, 2000 ; Zhu et al., 2023 ). The north-central Tibetan Plateau is 
crossed by several structural corridors interpreted as oceanic sutures, 
including the Jinshajiang Suture Zone ( Fig. 1 a) that is thought to mark a 
major ocean basin that formerly separated the cratonic blocks of Tarim 
and North China (and related terranes such as Qaidam, Central Qilian 
and Alxa/Alex) in the north from the Eastern Qiangtang (EQT), Indo -
china and South China terranes in the south ( Zhao et al., 2018 ). This 
once immense ( > 5000 km) ‘Paleo-Jinshajiang Ocean ’ shrank with the 
northward migration of the EQT in the late Paleozoic to early Mesozoic, 
and ultimately closed when that block collided with Tarim-North China 
( Song et al., 2015, 2017, 2020 ; Yu et al., 2022a ). However, despite the 
physical magnitude and tectonic significance of this ocean, key details of 
its evolution remain unclear, including the timing of its closure.
The closure of the Paleo-Jinshajiang Ocean has been studied from a 
variety of perspectives (e.g., palaeontologic, paleomagnetic, magmatic, 
sedimentologic, and structural), but large uncertainties remain in its

Ocean ( Guan et al., 2021 ; Song et al., 2015, 2020 ; Yu et al., 2022a ), but 
the exact closure time remains undetermined. More paleomagnetic data 
from the EQT during this interval are thus important to acquire.

2. Geological setting and sampling
The Qiangtang Terrane, one of the major Gondwanan-derived con -
tinental blocks of the Tibetan Plateau, is bounded by the Jinshajiang 
Suture Zone to the north and Bangong-Nujiang Suture Zone to the south 
( Fig. 1 a). The Longmu Co-Shuanghu Suture Zone divides the Qiangtang 
Terrane into the EQT (also called the ‘Northern Qiangtang ’ terrane) and 
the Western Qiangtang Terrane (also called the ‘Southern Qiangtang ’ 
terrane) ( Li et al., 2009 ; Peng et al., 2015 ; Zhu et al., 2013 ) ( Fig. 1 a).
Our study area, Zhiduo, is located in the northwest of the Qamdo 
area in the EQT ( Fig. 1 a). In this region, the major stratigraphic units 
consist of Triassic carbonates and clastic rocks, which are overlain 
(above an angular unconformity) by the late Cenozoic deposits ( Qinghai 
Geological Survey Institute (QGSI), 2005 ; Zhao et al., 2006 ) ( Fig. 1 b). 
The Triassic sequence includes the Jielong Formation (Fm.) (T
1-2
j
2
), the 
Bolila Fm. (T
3
b ), and the Batang Group (T
3
bt ). The Late Triassic Batang 
Group itself contains three divisions: a basal unit of sandstone and silt -
stone (Lower Batang Fm.) overlain by volcanic rocks (basalt, andesite, 
tuff, rhyolite, dacite; Middle Batang Fm.), and then an upper unit mainly 
composed of carbonate rocks (Upper Batang Fm.). The Cenozoic strata 
(the Neogene Quguo Fm.) unconformably overlie the Batang Group, and 
contain sandstone, conglomerate, and minor mudstone ( Fig. 1 b).
In this study, we investigated limestones from the Upper Batang Fm., 
which are well exposed along several regional NW-trending faults 
( Fig. 1 b), where they present a thickness of up to 1500 m in the Zhiduo 
area. The succession consists mainly of massive grey limestone and 
bioclastic limestone, but also includes some intercalated volcanic rocks 
( Qinghai Geological Survey Institute (QGSI), 2014 ). Abundant fossils, 
including brachiopods ( Rhaetinopsis pentagonalis Ching, Oxycolpella 
elongata Ching et Fang, Amphiclina sp., Arcestes sp.), bivalves ( Pteria 
angusta (Saurin), Neomegalodon (N.) sp.), corals ( Montlivaltia norica 
Frech, Thecosmilia sinensis Liao et Li, Pinacophyllum sp.) and ammonites 
( Paratibetites sp.) have been observed within the Upper Batang Fm. 
limestone in the Zhiduo area ( Qinghai Geological Survey Institute 
(QGSI), 2014 ). These fossils constrain the age of the limestone to the 
Late Triassic Carnian-Norian (~237 – 209 Ma) ( Qinghai Geological Sur -
vey Institute (QGSI), 2014 ; Zhao et al., 2006 ).
Additional age constraints on the Upper Batang Fm. are provided by 
isotopic age constraints from the Middle Batang Fm. Within a few km 
from our studied section, where the Upper Batang Fm. sits conformably 
above the Middle Batang Fm., several U
–
Pb (on zircon) age dates have 
been reported from the Middle Batang Fm. volcanics: ~221 ± 1 Ma from 
a dacite ( Zhao et al., 2014 ), ~227 ± 2 Ma from a rhyolite ( Liu et al., 
2019 ) and ~ 227 – 222 Ma from a tuff ( Yu et al., 2022a ) ( Fig. 1 b). These 
results are consistent with the Carnian-Norian biostratigraphic age es -
timates on the Upper Batang Fm. in the Zhiduo region ( Qinghai 
Geological Survey Institute (QGSI), 2014 ; Zhao et al., 2006 ), and so in 
this paper we take the Upper Batang Fm. limestone to be ~221 – 209 Ma.

4. Results
4.1. Rock magnetism
The measured κ -T heating curves show a strong inflection and 
decrease significantly between ~450 
◦

◦

and 4 – 4) or between ~550 
◦

magnetite is the major magnetic mineral constituent ( Fig. 3 a). Hyster -
esis loops display a narrow ‘wasp-waisted ’ appearance for most samples 
( Fig. 3 b, Fig. S1a), which is also reflected by quantitative analysis 
(following Fabian, 2003 ), indicating that E
hys 
is greater than 4MsBc 
(Table S3). This likely suggests the presence of at least two magnetic 
components with distinct coercivities. These could correspond to a 
mixture of magnetic minerals with different compositions, or different 
size fractions of a single mineral ( Jackson and Swanson-Hysell, 2012 ; 
Tauxe et al., 1996 ). In addition, all measured specimens were found to 
be saturated below 0.75 T, and have low coercivity (Bc, 16.11 – 34.64 
mT) and remanent coercivity (Bcr, 41 – 76 mT) ( Fig. 3 b, Fig. S1a), 
reflecting a dominance by low-coercivity components. IRM acquisition 
curves likewise reveal that ~56 – 69 % of the saturation remanence is 
acquired by 0.1 T, and samples almost fully saturate (~88 – 93 %) by 0.3 
T ( Fig. 3 c), again reflecting dominance by a ‘soft ’ magnetic phase, likely 
magnetite. Additional insights are provided by FORC results, which 
exhibit a sharp central ridge that is a hallmark of single-domain (SD) 
grains ( Roberts et al., 2014, 2022 ) ( Fig. 3 d, Fig. S1b), but also a sig -
nificant population of very low-coercivity ( < 10 mT) grains that could 
be close to the superparamagnetic (SP) threshold ( Pike et al., 2001 ; 
Roberts et al., 2017 ).
In Fig. 4 we show the summary hysteresis parameters of 14 repre -
sentative samples on a Day diagram, together with theoretical particle 
size mixing lines from Dunlop (2002) and an empirical range of both 
primary and remagnetized carbonates ( Jackson and Swanson-Hysell, 
2012 ). The majority of our results fall in the border region between 
the ‘SD ’ and ‘PSD ’ fields, overlapping the range of carbonates with 
primary magnetizations. Although these Day diagram fields cannot be 
used for an unambiguous domain state diagnosis without additional 
constraints (e.g., on the magnetic mineralogy and oxidation degree; 
Roberts et al., 2018 ), it remains a common method for remagnetization 
discrimination of carbonate rocks ( Fu et al., 2022, 2024 ; Jackson and 
Swanson-Hysell, 2012 ; Roberts et al., 2019 ; Yu et al., 2022b ). So, we 
here emphasize the relative stability among the samples on this diagram 
and their similarity with primary magnetized carbonates, rather than 
seeking to make firm statements pertaining to domain state ( Fig. 4 ).
In summary, the above-mentioned rock magnetic results suggest that 
SD magnetite is the main magnetic remanence carrier for all represen -
tative samples. Such grains can maintain a stable remanence over long 
intervals of geological time.
4.2. Petrography
EMPA observations of polished thin sections indicate that the mor -
phologies of Fe-oxide minerals are sub-euhedral to euhedral ( Fig. 5 a). 
The sizes of these grains range from a few micrometers to tens of mi -
crometers. Most are irregularly shaped and lack noticeably oxidized 
rims ( Fig. 5 a), suggesting that they were not significantly affected by 
chemical alteration due to fluids, hydrothermal processes, or weathering 
following deposition ( Cao et al., 2019 ; Meng et al., 2022 ). The EDS re -
sults indicate that these grains are predominantly composed of Fe and O 
( Fig. 5 b), and integrated with the rock magnetic results, we interpret 
them to be primarily detrital magnetite. Thus, detrital magnetite is 
inferred to be the main magnetic carrier in the Longyi section.

5. Discussion
Rock magnetic results, EMPA observations and EDS analyses indicate 
that SD magnetite is the main magnetic carrier in the Longyi section of 
the Upper Batang Fm. ( Figs. 3, 4, and 5 , Fig. S1). The low-temperature 
(field) components are likely recent viscous overprints, whereas the 
ChRM is likely to be primary ( Figs. 6 and 7 a). Inclination shallowing is 
commonly observed in sedimentary rocks, and is thought to occur dur -
ing deposition and/or by post-depositional compaction processes ( Tauxe 
and Kent, 2004 ; Yan et al., 2005, 2012 ). However, carbonates are 
generally considered to be less susceptible to inclination shallowing, as 
they experience less compaction (e. g., Cheng et al., 2012 ). Notably, our 
tilt-corrected mean inclination (54.5
◦
) is also broadly consistent with 
some other high quality Late Triassic volcanic-based paleomagnetic re -
sults from EQT (e.g., Song et al., 2015 ; Yu et al., 2022a ) (Table S1), 
which further suggests that our new data have not suffered from sig -
nificant inclination bias. Our new paleopole (30.9
◦
N, 161.4
◦
E (A
95 
=
8.4
◦
)) differs significantly from existing high quality post-Late Triassic 
poles from the EQT (Fig. S3) (e.g., Jurassic, Cheng et al., 2012 ; Yan et al., 
2016 ; Cretaceous, Huang et al., 1992 ; Tong et al., 2015 ; Cenozoic, Li 
et al., 2020 ; Lippert et al., 2011 ; Tong et al., 2017 ; Xiao et al., 2021 ; 
Zhang et al., 2018 ; Zhang et al., 2020 ). Taken together, these findings 
are consistent with the Upper Batang limestone having retained a pri -
mary magnetization. We therefore conclude that this new pole repre -
sents a reliable Late Triassic (~221 – 209 Ma) pole for the EQT.
To better understand the Late Triassic paleogeography of the EQT, 
we collected all the available Late Triassic paleomagnetic data from this 
block. So far, there have been 7 Late Triassic paleomagnetic poles re -
ported from the EQT ( Li et al., 1999 ; Lin and Watts, 1988 ; Song et al., 
2012 ; Song et al., 2015 ; Ye and Li, 1987 ; Yu et al., 2022a ; Zhou et al., 
2019 ) ( Fig. 1 a, Table S6). Due to variable data quality in different 
studies, Guan et al. (2021) , Song et al. (2015) and Yu et al. (2022a) have 
reevaluated the quality of these data according to the criteria of Besse 
and Courtillot (2002) . Only the poles by Song et al. (2015) and Yu et al. 
(2022a) meet these criteria. However, Guan et al. (2021) , by projecting 
all the available paleopoles on the trajectory formed by the Permian to 
Triassic high-quality results, suggested that two paleopoles ( Song et al.,

Our new paleomagnetic result from the Upper Batang Fm. provides a 
direct constraint on the paleolatitude of the EQT during this critical 
interval. At the reference locality (33.8
◦
N, 95.2
◦
E), this result corre -
sponds to a paleolatitude of ~35 ± 8.4
◦
N ( Figs. 8 a, b, pole #7). This 
paleolatitude is indistinguishable from the average Permian-Triassic 
paleolatitude of the Tarim Block ( Huang et al., 2018 ), suggesting that 
the closure of the Paleo-Jinshajiang Ocean by the collision of the EQT 
and the Tarim Block had occurred at least by (but possibly prior to) 
~221 Ma ( Figs. 8 b, c). This constraint further supports our previous 
view that the EQT had collided with the northern block before ~225 Ma, 
most likely at ~230 Ma ( Guan et al., 2021 ; Yu et al., 2022a ), and in -
dicates that the EQT did not experience significant N-S latitudinal 
movement until ~209 Ma, after colliding with the northern terranes at 
~230 Ma ( Figs. 8 b, c).
To further constrain the closure time of the Paleo-Jinshajiang Ocean, 
other lines of related geological evidence can also be considered. Sedi -
mentologically, evidence of the closure of the Paleo-Jinshajiang Ocean 
may be observed in an early Late Triassic shift from marine to terrestrial 
deposition in the EQT foreland ( Fu et al., 2010 ; Wang et al., 2022 ; Zhao 
et al., 2001 ), including molasse deposits in the Jiangda and Gonjo areas, 
as well as the appearance of turbidite deposits (inferred to be collision- 
related) from ~230 Ma in the Western Songpan-Ganzi terrane ( Zhang 
et al., 2008 ). These changes broadly reflect basin inversion driven by 
collisional orogenesis, which is further evident in the extensive un -
conformities seen in Late Triassic strata of the EQT (e.g. Shizhongshan, 
Waigoucun, and Jiapila Formations) ( Wang et al., 2021 ). Late Triassic 
collision-type granites have also been recognized in the EQT (e.g. Yangla 
and Ludian granites; ~236 – 212 Ma), and Middle Triassic eclogites 
(~240 ± 3 Ma and ~ 244 ± 1 Ma; U
–
Pb on zircon) have been 
discovered in the Jinshajiang Suture Zone. Some of the latter eclogites 
are hosted by a ~ 226 Ma adamellite, implying they were rapidly 
exhumed ( Tang et al., 2020 ). Collectively, these geological observations 
are consistent with an early Late Triassic (~230 Ma) closure of the 
Paleo-Jinshajiang Ocean, as inferred from our paleomagnetic analysis.
6. Conclusions
This study presents a new and reliable paleomagnetic pole from Late 
Triassic limestones of the Qamdo area in the Eastern Qiangtang Terrane. 
Detailed rock magnetism, petrographic investigations, stepwise de -
magnetizations, and field stability tests demonstrate the presence of 
stable ChRMs in these Triassic samples. Based on the paleomagnetic 
results from 6 sites (54 samples), we obtained a reliable ~221 – 209 Ma 
paleomagnetic pole of 30.9
◦
N, 161.4
◦
E (A
95 
= 8.4
◦
). This result in -
dicates that the Eastern Qiangtang Terrane was located at a paleo -
latitude of 35 ± 8.4
◦
N (with a reference point at 33.8
◦
N and 95.2
◦
E) 
during the Late Triassic. Integrated with other reliable paleomagnetic 
data and geological evidence, we interpret that the collision of the 
Eastern Qiangtang Terrane with Tarim and the closure of the Paleo- 
Jinshajiang Ocean occurred before ~221 Ma, and most likely at 
~230 Ma.

1. Introduction
The Tibetan Plateau is a complex collage of several terranes that have gradually amalgamated with the stable 
Asian continent since the Paleozoic (Figure 1a). Three terranes including the Qiangtang, Lhasa, and Himalayan 
terranes are traditionally considered to have been derived from Gondwana, and their successive dispersion, subse-
quent northward drift, and eventual Asian amalgamation involved the successive opening and closure of a series 
of Tethys Oceans (e.g., Kapp & DeCelles,  2019; Pan et al.,  2012; Yin & Harrison,  2000). With regard to these 
oceans, the Meso-Tethys Ocean plays a crucial role in understanding the formation and evolution of the Tibetan 
Plateau prior to the India-Asia collision, because its subduction, closure, and subsequent continental collision 
resulted in the initial uplift of the proto-Tibetan Plateau, which influenced the drainage divide and atmospheric 
circulation (e.g., Ding et al., 2022; Lippert et al., 2014). However, the history of the Meso-Tethys Ocean remains 
hotly debated, such as the estimated closure time of the Meso-Tethys Ocean ranging from the Middle Jurassic 
(e.g., Ma, Hu, Kapp, BouDagher-Fadel, & Lai,  2020; Ma, Hu, Kapp, Lai, et al.,  2020; Sun et al.,  2019), Late 
Jurassic to Early Cretaceous (e.g., Fan et al., 2021; Kapp & DeCelles, 2019; Ma et al., 2018; Zeng et al., 2021) to 
the Late Cretaceous (e.g., Li, Lu, et al., 2022; Yang et al., 2022). The Lhasa terrane is separated from the Qiang-
tang terrane to the north by the Bangong-Nujiang suture zone which represents the Meso-Tethys oceanic relict 
(e.g., Metcalfe, 2021). Therefore, the northward drift history during the Jurassic is critical for understanding the 
evolution of the Meso-Tethys Ocean.
Abstract The drift history of the Lhasa terrane is crucial for understanding the tectonic evolution of 
Tethyan Oceans and Jurassic true polar wander. However, high-quality Middle Jurassic paleomagnetic data 
from the Lhasa terrane are limited in number. Here we report a combined paleomagnetic and geochronologic 
study on the Yeba Formation volcanic rocks, dated at ∼170 Ma, from the Lhasa terrane. Robust field and 
reversal tests indicate that the characteristic remanent magnetizations are primary. Our results provide a 
reliable Middle Jurassic (∼170 Ma) paleopole at 29.8°N, 180.7°E with A95 = 5.7° and a paleolatitude of 
14.4 ± 5.7°N for the Lhasa area. Compared with previous paleomagnetic and geologic evidence, we propose 
that the Meso-Tethys Ocean probably began to close in the eastern part at ∼168 Ma and that the Lhasa terrane 
underwent a ∼2,900 km southward “monster shift” during the Late Jurassic.
Plain Language Summary The formation of the Tibetan Plateau followed the breakup of the 
Gondwana supercontinent and was associated with the demise of several Tethyan Oceans. The Lhasa terrane, 
which is a long and narrow continental fragment derived from Gondwana, was isolated in the Tethyan Ocean 
during the Jurassic and finally accreted to the south margin of the Paleo-Asia continent, leading to the closure 
of the Meso-Tethys Ocean. However, when this Meso-Tethys Ocean closed is still controversial. Our new robust 
paleomagnetic result shows that the Lhasa terrane was located at ∼14.4°N at ∼170 Ma. Based on available 
reliable Jurassic paleomagnetic data from the eastern part of the Lhasa and Qiangtang terranes, we suggest that 
the Meso-Tethys Ocean began to close in the eastern part at ∼168 Ma. Integrating our critical Middle Jurassic 
paleomagnetic data with that of the Late Jurassic from the Lhasa terrane, we argue that the Lhasa terrane 
suffered a ∼2,900 km southward latitudinal shift during the Late Jurassic, which is known as true polar wander.

In addition, the Jurassic witnessed a period of a global event, “true polar wander (TPW)” (e.g., Kent & 
Irving, 2010; Torsvik et al., 2012). TPW is the rotation of the entire mantle-crust system with respect to Earth's 
spin axis (Evans, 2003). Although many previous paleomagnetic studies have supported the existence of Jurassic 
TPW (e.g., Fu et al.,  2020; Gao et al.,  2021; Kent & Irving,  2010), its duration and magnitude are still contro-
versial. Based on different statistical criteria, two different models of the Jurassic TPW have been proposed: a 
steady and constant TPW throughout the whole Jurassic (e.g., Torsvik et al.,  2012), or a rapid TPW referred to 
as a “monster shift” during ∼160−145 Ma time interval (e.g., Kent & Irving,  2010). Because the Lhasa terrane 
was located at a relatively low latitude and approximately orthogonal to the rotation axis of the Jurassic TPW, its 
paleolatitudinal displacement history can provide evidence to better constrain the evolution of the Jurassic TPW 
and further test the above mentioned models of Jurassic TPW (Gao et al.,  2021; Ma et al.,  2022; Van der Voo 
et al., 2015).
Paleomagnetic data can be used to estimate the paleolatitudes of terranes to constrain their kinematic processes 
(Butler, 1992), and thus is the most effective method for quantifying the latitudinal drift history of the Lhasa terrane. 
However, only four reliable Jurassic paleomagnetic poles are available for the Lhasa terrane (Li et al.,  2016; Li, 
Ding, et al., 2022; Ma et al., 2022; Otofuji et al., 2007). Notably, three high-quality and well-dated poles based on 
data from volcanic rocks, which include two Early Jurassic (Li et al., 2016; Ma et al., 2022) and one Late Juras-
sic (Li, Ding, et al.,  2022) poles, all provided the near-equatorial and southern hemisphere latitudes. Li, Ding, 
et al. (2022) suggested that the Lhasa terrane remained in a paleolatitudinal stand-still during ∼180−155 Ma due 
to the interaction between its northward plate tectonic motion and the simultaneous southward-directed Jurassic 
TPW. Their interpretation can match both Kent and Irving (2010) and Torsvik et al. (2012) Jurassic TPW models 
because of lacking the Middle Jurassic pole. Furthermore, based on a Middle Jurassic pole from redbeds reported 
by Otofuji et al. (2007) revealing that the northeastern Lhasa terrane had reached a northern hemisphere latitude 
during the Middle Jurassic, Ma et al. (2022) argued that the influence of the TPW during ∼180−170 Ma is insig-
nificant and that the southward shift of the Lhasa terrane during ∼170−155 Ma was caused by a fast Late Jurassic 
TPW. However, the paleomagnetic results from redbeds reported by Otofuji et al. (2007) have no accurate age and 
an inclination shallowing test was not carried out. Therefore, there is an urgent need for reliable Middle Jurassic 
paleomagnetic datasets with accurate ages.
This study presents combined paleomagnetic and geochronologic data from the Middle Jurassic Yeba Formation 
lavas in the Lhasa terrane (Figure 1a). Our new well-dated paleomagnetic data, which satisfy all the seven relia-
bility criteria, as updated by Meert et al. (2020), provide a reliable constraint on the Middle Jurassic (∼170 Ma) 
paleolatitude of the Lhasa terrane and contributes to a better understanding of the closure of the Meso-Tethys 
Ocean and the Jurassic TPW.
2. Geological Background and Sampling
The Lhasa terrane is an east-west trending elongated belt located in the southern Tibetan Plateau (Figure  1a). 
Our study area is located in the Lhasa area of the Lhasa terrane, where Mesozoic arc magmatic rocks associ-
ated with the northward Neo-Tethyan subduction are widely exposed (Figure 1b, 1:250000 scale Lhasa regional 
geological survey report [H46C003001], 2007). The main lithostratigraphic sequence in this area includes the 
Lower-Middle Jurassic Yeba Formation, Upper Jurassic Quesangwenquan Formation, Upper Jurassic Duodigou 
Formation, Lower Cretaceous Linbuzong Formation and Lower Cretaceous Chumulong Formation from bottom 
to top (Figure 1b, H46C003001, 2007).
The Yeba Formation strata are exposed in an area of ∼2,000 km 2 with a thickness of more than 5,000 m, and they 
mainly consist of basalt, andesite, dacite, rhyolite, tuff, and volcanic clastic rocks intercalated with conglomerate, 
sandstone, siltstone, and limestone (H46C003001, 2007). These strata are in normal fault contact with the overly-
ing Upper Jurassic Quesangwenquan Formation and Duodigou Formation (Figure 1b). Abundant bivalve fossils 
have been identified in sedimentary interlayers within the Yeba Formation, such as Cercomya cf. suessi (Oppel),

collected using a portable gasoline-powered drill. All core samples were oriented using both a magnetic compass 
and a Sun compass, and the declination differences between the two oriented methods are less than 3°. Fifteen core

were collected from sites YB1 and YB22, respectively (Figures S1a and S1c in Supporting Information S1). All the

3. Results
3.1. Zircon U-Pb Geochronology
For the basaltic block sample from the YB1 site, the concordance of most dating results is less than 90%, and thus no 
a reliable zircon U-Pb age is available for it. For the rhyolitic sample from the YB22 site, the selected zircon grains are 
mainly euhedral to subhedral with sizes ranging from 50 to 150 μm and clear oscillatory zoning (Figure 2a), and yield 
high Th/U ratios (0.65−1.24, Table S2 in Supporting Information S1), indicating that these zircons should be the 
igneous origin (Hoskin & Black, 2000). After removing 14 dating results whose concordances are smaller than 90%, 
the remaining 12 results provide a weighted mean 206Pb/ 238U age estimate of 170.1 ± 2.2 Ma (Figures 2b and 2c). Our 
new dating result, combined with the previous U-Pb age of ∼172–174 Ma obtained below our sampling stratigraphic 
units (Figure 1c), indicates that our sampling volcanic rocks erupted during the Middle Jurassic (∼170 Ma).
3.2. Petrography and Rock Magnetism
Scanning electron microscopy (SEM) observations indicate that feldspar and quartz suffered from no significant 
deformation and reorientation. Ti-Fe and Fe oxides have euhedral to irregular shapes with sizes ranging from less 
than 1 to more than 50 μm (Figures S2a−S2d in Supporting Information  S1). These magnetic minerals have no 
obvious oxidized rims (Figures S2a−S2d in Supporting Information S1). Energy dispersive spectroscopy (EDS) 
analysis shows that the elements in magnetic minerals mainly consist of oxygen, iron, and titanium, but no sulfur 
(Figures S2e−S2h in Supporting Information S1). Our SEM-EDS analysis, combined with rock magnetic results 
as follows, indicates that the main magnetic phases are primary hematite and magnetite.
The k-T curves and Lowrie  (1990) tests show that most samples, except for YB3, YB9−10, and YB35, have 
unblocking temperatures of ∼680°C (e.g., Figures S3f−S3h and S3j−S3l in Supporting Information S1). The corre-
sponding isothermal remanent magnetization (IRM) curves indicate a steady increase, and saturation is not reached 
at 2.4 T. Backfield demagnetizations show the remanence reduced to zero above 400 mT (e.g., Figures S3b−S3d in 
Supporting Information S1). These results show that high-coercivity hematite is the primary magnetization carrier 
in most samples. For the YB3, YB9−10, and YB35 sites, the k-T curve and the Lowrie (1990) test indicate unblock-
ing temperatures of ∼580°C (e.g., Figures S3e and S3i in Supporting Information  S1). The IRM curve reaches 
saturation at ∼300 mT, and backfield demagnetization indicates a coercivity of remanence below 40 mT (e.g., 
Figure S3a in Supporting Information S1), revealing that the low-coercivity magnetite is dominant in these sites.

ered rocks, exhibit scattered and uninterpretable demagnetization patterns (Figure  2j), and no reliable ChRMs 
can be isolated in these samples.
A total of 24 out of the 35 paleomagnetic sites were accepted provide ChRM directions, yielding the overall 
mean A direction: Dg = 66.6°, Ig = −11.8°, kg = 3.4, α95 = 19.1° in situ, and Ds = 66.5°, Is = +33.7°, ks = 9.6, 
α95 = 10.1° after tilt correction (Table S1 in Supporting Information  S1). Notably, the ChRM estimated means 
from sites YB16−17, YB18−19, and YB31 fall outside of 40° angular deviations from the overall mean A direc-
tion, and these may reflect transitional directions or partial overprints (Yang et al.,  2015). After removing these 
three anomalous site-mean directions, the remaining 21 sites, which include 9 normal and 12 reverse polarity 
estimated directions, provide similar ChRM directions recorded by both magnetite and hematite, yielding an 
overall mean B direction of Dg = 73.0°, Ig = −16.8°, kg = 4.3, α 95 = 17.5° in situ (Figure  2l), and Ds = 64.0°, 
Is = +27.2°, ks = 27.1, α95 = 6.2° after tilt correction (Figure 2m). This direction passes both McElhinny (1964) 
and McFadden (1990) fold tests at the 99% confidence level, as well as the C-class reversal test at the 95% confi-
dence level (Table S1 in Supporting Information  S1; McFadden & McElhinny, 1990). The best grouping of the 
direction-correction test for the accepted 21 site-mean directions is 105% (Figure  2k; Watson & Enkin,  1993). 
Furthermore, eight cobble samples yield reliable ChRM directions and these give a positive conglomerate test: A 
random distribution test gives R = 4.32 (N = 8), which is less than the critical R-value of 4.48 at a 95% confidence 
level (Figure 2n; Watson, 1956). These positive field and reversal tests strongly support that the Yeba Formation 
volcanic rocks record a primary magnetization of ∼170 Ma age.
Given that our new Middle Jurassic data set is obtained from the volcanic rocks that can only record spot read-
ings of the paleomagnetic field, we apply the widely accepted approach proposed by Deenen et al. (2011) to test 
whether it has averaged out the paleosecular variation (PSV). Twenty-one site-level virtual geomagnetic poles 
provide a mean paleopole at 29.8°N, 180.7°E with A95 = 5.7°. The A95 value of 5.7° falls within the A95 envelope 
interval (3.55°, 12.05°) for N = 21, suggesting the PSV has been averaged out (Deenen et al., 2011).
4. Discussion
Because dual polarities and near-equatorial latitude (∼14.4°) were observed in this study, whether the Lhasa 
terrane located in the northern or southern hemisphere at ∼170 Ma needs further discussion. The Lhasa terrane 
would have moved southward from ∼7.7°S to ∼14.4°S during ∼180−170 Ma if it had been in the southern hemi-
sphere, which conflicts with the widely accepted model of its continuous Late Triassic−Middle Jurassic north-
ward drift (e.g., Li et al., 2016; Yin & Harrison, 2000; Zhu et al., 2011). Furthermore, based on the tilt-corrected 
overall mean B direction, the study area would have required a larger vertical-axis rotation (116°) to obtain a 
latitude of the southern hemisphere than that of the northern hemisphere (64°). Moreover, many geologic obser-
vations as listed in the following discussion part support that the Lhasa and Qiangtang terranes collided in the 
northern hemisphere at ∼168 Ma. Hence, we place the Lhasa terrane at 14.4 ± 5.7°N at ∼170 Ma in the following 
discussion.
4.1. The Jurassic Drift History of the Lhasa Terrane
Previous paleomagnetic studies suggested several different kinematic models for the Lhasa terrane due to 
limited Jurassic paleomagnetic results. These included a continuous northward drift throughout the Jurassic (Li 
et al., 2016), a paleolatitudinal stand-still at near-equatorial southern hemisphere latitudes during ∼180−155 Ma 
(Li, Ding, et al.,  2022), and a yoyo-like drift motion near the equator during ∼170−130 Ma (Ma et al.,  2022). 
To better constrain the drift history of the Lhasa terrane during the Jurassic, only paleomagnetic poles including 
either at least a positive fold test or dual polarities in addition to other five criteria proposed by Van der Voo (1990)

4.2. Insights Into the Jurassic TPW
Many paleomagnetic studies have concluded that a TPW with a clockwise rotation around the Euler pole at 0°N, 
11°E for the entire Jurassic (e.g., Torsvik et al., 2008, 2012), or, alternatively, a very fast TPW called a “monster 
shift” during the Late Jurassic based on more strict criteria (e.g., Fu et al.,  2020; Kent & Irving,  2010; Mattei 
et  al., 2014; Muttoni & Kent,  2019). Torsvik et  al.  (2012)'s model suggested a ∼30.5° TPW throughout the 
whole Jurassic (200−140 Ma), yielding a relatively lower TPW rate of ∼0.45–0.8°/Myr. In contrast, Kent and 
Irving (2010)'s model implied a faster rotation velocity of ∼2.0°/Myr during ∼160−145 Ma. Although these two 
TPW models show similar rotational amplitudes, their temporal durations are quite different (Ma et al., 2022). Our 
high-quality ∼170 Ma paleomagnetic result, combined with the reliable ∼155 Ma paleomagnetic result (Li, Ding, 
et al., 2022), reveals that the Lhasa terrane suffered a significant southward shift of ∼26.3° during ∼170−155 Ma 
(Figure 3a), corresponding to an observed plate motion rate of ∼1.75°/Myr. Such a rapid southward latitudinal 
shift can only be explained by the Late Jurassic “monster shift.” Notably, the Late Jurassic TPW of ∼24–30° was 
also observed from reliable Middle−Late Jurassic paleomagnetic studies from North China (Yi et al., 2019), Iran 
(Mattei et al., 2014), Adria (Muttoni & Kent, 2019; Muttoni et al., 2013), North America (Kent & Irving, 2010; 
Kent et al., 2015), the Pacific (Fu & Kent,  2018), and so on, indicating that there was a synchronous and rapid 
clockwise rotation around west Africa. Furthermore, the distribution of climate-sensitive sedimentary facies 
reveals that Iran and Adria transitioned from a temperate humid belt to a tropic arid belt during the Middle to Late 
Jurassic, suggesting the occurrence of the Late Jurassic TPW (e.g., Muttoni & Kent, 2019; Mattei et al., 2014).
In addition, our new results, together with the paleolatitude estimate at ∼180 Ma, indicate that the Lhasa terrane 
experienced a very fast northward movement during ∼180−170 Ma. Because the Jurassic TPW is a southward 
translation in the eastern hemisphere, the northward drift of the Lhasa terrane should decelerate due to their inter-
action. Considering that the observed northward velocity of the Lhasa terrane during 180−170 Ma (∼24.3 cm/
yr or 2.2°/Myr) is consistent with the theoretical speed limits of the modern plates (∼20  cm/yr; Zahirovic 
et al., 2015), we propose that the Jurassic TPW was negligible before ∼170 Ma and that the Lhasa terrane expe-
rienced a “monster shift” of ∼2,900 km to the south during the Late Jurassic (Figure 3).
4.3. Implications for the Closure of the Meso-Tethys Ocean
The paleolatitudinal overlap of two terranes has been widely used to estimate the timing and location of Tethys 
Ocean closure (e.g., Bian et al., 2021; Jin et al., 2023; Sun et al., 2012; Tan et al., 2010; Tong et al., 2022; Wang 
et al., 2022; Yu et al., 2022). Considering that the Lhasa-Qiangtang collision may have been diachronous (e.g., 
Yan et al., 2016; Yin & Harrison, 2000) and the Lhasa terrane is very long and narrow, which may yield signifi-
cantly deviated paleolatitudes for a reference point far away from the sampling area, we only discuss the collision 
of the Lhasa terrane to the east of 87°E (Table S4 in Supporting Information S1). For the Qiangtang terrane, nine 
Jurassic paleopoles fulfill our criteria, and they yield paleolatitudes of 20.7 ± 3.9°N (QMC; Yan et al.,  2016), 
10.8 ± 8.2°N (JQ; Cheng et al., 2012), 34.4 ± 3.8°N (SJ; Cao et al., 2019), 13.4 ± 2.1°N (BQ; Yan et al., 2016), 
17.6 ± 6.8°N (JB; Cheng et al., 2012), 16.3 ± 2.7°N (XL; Yan et al., 2016), 12.0 ± 6.4°N (JX; Cheng et al., 201
2), 17.1 ± 3.9°N (SW; Yan et al., 2016), 23.0 ± 6.1°N (JS; Cheng et al., 2012), respectively.
Given that TPW took place in the Late Jurassic, we divide these nine Qiangtang terrane paleopoles into two groups 
based on their age. Five Middle Jurassic (∼171−163 Ma) paleomagnetic datasets, including 75 sites, provide an 
inclination-only mean of 34.9 ± 3.8° (Table S5 in Supporting Information  S1), corresponding to a paleolatitude 
of 19.2 ± 2.5°N for the reference point (29.7°N, 91.3°E). Other four Late Jurassic (∼163−158 Ma) paleomagnetic 
data, including 55 sites, yield an inclination-only mean of 31.8 ± 3.0° (Table S5 in Supporting Information  S1), 
corresponding to a paleolatitude of 17.2 ± 1.9°N for the reference point (29.7°N, 91.3°E). Comparing the Middle 
Jurassic paleolatitude (19.2 ± 2.5°N) of the Qiangtang terrane with the observed paleolatitude (14.4 ± 5.7°N) of the 
eastern part of the Lhasa terrane (east of ∼87°E) reveals a paleolatitude difference of ∼4.8° (∼530 km), implying 
that the Meso-Tethys Ocean was narrow but did not close at ∼170 Ma. Extrapolating a constant northward velocity 
of ∼24.3 cm/yr during ∼180−170 Ma implies that the Lhasa terrane for the reference point (29.7°N, 91.3°E) would 
need ∼2.2 Ma after ∼170 Ma before it intersects with the Qiangtang terrane at 19.2 ± 5.7°N, supporting the inter-
pretation that the closure of the Meso-Tethys Ocean in its eastern part most likely occurred at ∼168 Ma (Figure 3a).
Many geologic and geochemical observations also support that the Lhasa- Qiangtang collision occurred at ∼168  Ma. 
For example, geologic mapping and zircon U-Pb dating in Xianshuihe area document a suit of syn-kinematic

5. Conclusion
In this study, we report a new paleomagnetic pole of 29.8°N, 180.7°E (A 95 = 5.7°) obtained from the ∼170 Ma 
Yeba Formation in the Lhasa terrane, which satisfies all seven criteria proposed by Van der Voo (1990) and Meert 
et al. (2020). Our new paleomagnetic result indicates that the Lhasa terrane was located at ∼14.4 ± 5.7°N at 
∼170 Ma. Combined with other robust Jurassic paleomagnetic results from the Lhasa and Qiangtang terranes, we 
propose that the closure of the Meso-Tethys Ocean in the eastern part most likely occurred at ∼168 Ma and that 
the Lhasa terrane underwent a southward paleogeographic shift of ∼2,900 km, caused by the Late Jurassic TPW.

New Late Cretaceous paleomagnetic and geochronologic 
results from the southern Qiangtang Terrane: Contributions 
to the reliability of redbed paleomagnetic datasets from the 
Tibetan Plateau and shape of the Qiangtang Terrane
Jiahui Ma1,2, Tianshui Yang1,2,†, Wenxiao Peng1,2, Weiwei Bian1, Suo Wang1,2, Fei Han1,2, Jiacheng Liang1,2, 
Xianwei Jiao1,2, Jingjie Jin2, Shihong Zhang1,2, Huaichun Wu1, Haiyan Li1, and Yiming Ma3
1 State Key Laboratory of Biogeology and Environmental Geology, China University of Geosciences, Beijing 100083, China
2 School of Earth Sciences and Resources, China University of Geosciences, Beijing 100083, China
3 School of Earth Sciences, China University of Geosciences, Wuhan 430074, China
ABSTRACT
To better clarify the reliability of redbed 
paleomagnetic datasets from the Tibetan 
Plateau and shape of the Qiangtang Ter -
rane (QT) prior to the India-Asia collision, 
a combined paleomagnetic and detrital 
zircon U-Pb geochronologic study is con -
ducted on the Upper Cretaceous Abushan 
Formation (Fm) redbeds, dated to be within 
89.1–83.6 Ma, in the Anduo area. The tilt-
corrected grand mean direction for 37 sites 
is Ds = 0.9°, Is = +36.4°, k = 43.6, α95 = 3.6°, 
which provides a paleopole at 78.2 °N, 
266.8°E (A95 = 3.6°), corresponding to a pa -
leolatitude of 20.5° ± 3.6°N for the study area 
(32.3°N, 91.4 °E). Reliable demagnetization 
curves, positive fold, and conglomerate tests 
support the interpretation that characteristic 
remanent magnetization directions recorded 
primary magnetizations carried by detrital 
hematite and did not suffer from the influ -
ence of distortional strains. Our paleomag -
netic results indicate that the mean inclina -
tion observed from the southwest dipping 
limb (Is = +44.2°) is clearly steeper than that 
from the north dipping limb ( Is = +34.2°). 
The results of syntectonic-sedimentation-cor-
rection and the fluvial gravel deposits present 
in the Abushan Fm redbeds sampled support 
the contention that the apparent inclination 
discrepancy is attributed to the syntectonic 
growth strata and that the paleomagnetic da-
tasets observed from two limbs of folds are 
still reliable. Furthermore, reliable Late Cre-
taceous paleomagnetic datasets show that the 
shape of the QT west of the Eastern Hima -
laya Syntaxis (EHS) during the Late Creta -
ceous was similar to its present-day relatively 
E-W alignment, and that around the EHS, 
its shape changed from the Late Cretaceous 
NE-SW alignment to the present-day ap -
proximately NW-SE alignment.
INTRODUCTION
The Tibetan Plateau is regarded as a complex 
tectonic collage of several microcontinents, fly-
sch complexes, and island arcs that have gradu-
ally amalgamated with paleo-Asia since the 
early Paleozoic (e.g., Yin and Harrison, 2000). 
The Qiangtang, Lhasa, and Himalayan terranes 
are traditionally considered to have drifted 
northward from Gondwana in the south, and 
their eventual paleo-Asian amalgamations are 
along the Jinsha suture zone, Bangong-Nujiang 
suture zone, and Indus-Tsangpo suture zone, 
respectively (e.g., Yin and Harrison, 2000; Pan 
et al., 2012; Metcalfe, 2013; Kapp and DeCelles, 
2019; Fig. 1A). Notably, the early Cenozoic 
India-Asia collision led to the closure of the 
Neo-Tethyan Ocean, and the subsequent contin-
ued plate convergence resulted in the extensive 
intracontinental deformation within Asia and the 
uplift of the Tibetan Plateau that changed the 
Asian climatic system (e.g., Yin and Harrison, 
2000; van Hinsbergen et al., 2019). Therefore, 
determining the location of the southern margin 
of paleo-Asia during the late Mesozoic and esti-
mating the intracontinental shortening amount 
within Asia after the early Cenozoic India-Asia 
collision are vital to better understanding the for-
mation and evolution of the Tibetan Plateau and 
the Asian climatic system (e.g., van Hinsbergen 
and Boschman, 2019).
The late Mesozoic Lhasa-Qiangtang and early 
Cenozoic India-Asia collisions together with 
subsequent penetration of the Indian plate into 
Asia generally occurred in a north-south direc-
tion along the Bangong-Nujiang suture zone 
and Indus-Tsangpo suture zone. Paleomagnetic 
is one of the major techniques that can effec -
tively quantify plate paleolatitude to estimate 
kinematic plate movements. Therefore, many 
paleomagnetic studies of Cretaceous rocks have 
been performed in the Lhasa and Qiangtang ter-
ranes (e.g., Pozzi et  al., 1982; Lin and Watts, 
1988; Sun et al., 2012; Chen et al., 2012, 2017; 
Ma et al., 2014, 2017b, 2018, 2022; Yang et al., 
2015; Bian et al., 2017, 2020, 2022a; Cao et al., 
2017a, 2017b, 2020; Li et al., 2017b; Wang et al., 
2022). The paleomagnetic data from the coeval 
rocks yielded significantly different inclinations 
and thus paleolatitudes estimates. For example, 
the Late Cretaceous paleomagnetic data reported 
from both volcanic and sedimentary rocks of the 
Lhasa terrane produced significantly different 
inclinations, ranging from 16.2° to 48.5°, with the 
corresponding paleolatitudes ranging from 6.6°N 
to 25.4°N for a reference latitude of 29.3°N (e.g., 
Bian et al., 2022a). These discrepant paleolati-
tude estimates resulted in a range of India-Asia 
collision ages varying from 65 Ma to 43 Ma, as 
well as the significantly discrepant shortening 
magnitudes, which have been estimated to be 
from 1900 km (e.g., Tang et al., 2013) to only 
a few hundred kilometers (e.g., Tan et al., 2010) 
between the Lhasa terrane and stable Asia.
