The reliability of redbed paleomagnetic datasets from the Tibetan Plateau and shape of the Qiangtang Terrane
 Geological Society of America Bulletin, v. 136, no. 5/6 1771
Gilder et al., 2001; Tan et al., 2003; Yan et al., 
2005; Kodama, 2012; Huang et al., 2013; Ding 
et al., 2015), some researchers suggested that the 
lower paleolatitudes obtained from Cretaceous 
sedimentary rocks could result from inclination 
shallowing (e.g., Tan et al., 2010; Chen et al., 
2017). For example, Chen et al. (2017) carried 
out a combined paleomagnetic and geochrono-
logic investigation on Cretaceous rocks in the 
Gaize area of the southern Qiangtang Terrane 
(QT). The mean inclination of 22 sites from the 
Upper Cretaceous redbeds is 13.1 ° shallower 
than that based on data from 14 sites from the 
underlying ca. 110–100 Ma volcanic rocks. In 
contrast, the mean inclination of ∼47.9° after the 
elongation/inclination (E/I) inclination shallow-
ing correction was consistent with the ∼47.7° 
result from the volcanic rocks (Tauxe and Kent, 
2004). Furthermore, the Late Cretaceous paleo-
magnetic data from the Linzhou Basin of the 
Lhasa terrane (Tan et  al., 2010) also revealed 
the similar result, which indicated that the tilt-
corrected mean inclination (23.5° ± 2.5°) of 43 
redbeds sites was significantly shallower than 
that (41.9° ± 4.4°) of 32 lava flows sites and the 
mean inclination (∼42.0°) of the redbeds after 
the elongation/inclination (E/I) shallowing cor-
rection was similar with the characteristic rema-
nent magnetization (ChRM) mean inclination of 
the lava flows. Tan et al. (2010) proposed that 
the Upper Cretaceous redbeds of the Lhasa ter-
rane experienced ∼18° of inclination flattening. 
However, such an observation is challenged by 
the fact that no significant inclination discrep -
ancy has been recognized between the data from 
redbeds and intercalated volcanic rocks in the 
Tibetan Plateau (Sun et  al., 2006; Cao et  al., 
2017a). The Late Cretaceous paleomagnetic 
result reported by Cao et al. (2017a) from the 
Linzhou Basin of the Lhasa terrane revealed 
that the tilt-corrected mean direction (Ds = 1.7°, 
Is = +17.9°, ks = 38.1, α95 = 7.9°, n = 10) for 
the Shexing Formation (Fm) redbeds was con-
sistent with the one (Ds = 359.4°, Is = +22.5°, 
ks = 18.9, α95 = 10.8°, n = 11) for the interca-
lated basalt flows. Another paleomagnetic study 
on the Early Cretaceous basalt flows intercalated 
with the redbeds from the Qaidam Basin of the 
northeastern Tibetan Plateau also indicated that 
the tilt-corrected site-mean direction for the 
redbeds ( Ds = 18.4°, Is = +55.3°, ks = 69.1, 
α95 = 5.5°, n = 11) and the basalt flows 
(Ds = 16.1°, Is = +52.0°, ks = 42.6, α95 = 8.6°, 
n = 8) are entirely consistent (Sun et al., 2006). 
Furthermore, Yang et al. (2019) summarized the 
available Cretaceous paleomagnetic datasets 
from the Lhasa terrane. They showed that for 
the same reference point (29.3°N, 85.3°E) the 
data from 91 sites in Late Cretaceous volcanic 
rocks yielded a paleolatitude of 14.0° ± 2.1°N, 
which is very consistent with 13.5 ° ± 1.2°N 
deduced from the 118 reliable Late Cretaceous 
sedimentary sites. Therefore, high-quality paleo-
magnetic datasets are still needed to ascertain if 
the compaction-induced inclination shallowing 
is substantial in the Cretaceous redbeds of the 
Tibetan Plateau.
In addition to the deposition and/or com -
paction-induced inclination shallowing, some 
researchers considered the possibility that 
unidentified syntectonic growth strata origi -
nally tilted to the north or south could lead to 
significant inclination deviations if the sampling 
strata were not restored to their originally non-
horizontal orientation at the time of remanence 
acquisition (e.g., Gilder et al., 2001; Tong et al., 
2019; Bian et al., 2020; Bian and Yang, 2021; 
Wang et al., 2022). For example, after analyz -
ing the Cretaceous paleomagnetic data from 
the Lhasa terrane, Tong et al. (2019) found that 
paleomagnetic data obtained from the southern 
limb of folds yielded steeper site-mean inclina-
tions than those from the northern limb of folds, 
and proposed that the significant inclination 
discrepancy obtained from two limbs of folds 
could result from the unidentified syntectonic 
growth strata, which were not restored to their 
original orientation before folding. Bian et al. 
(2020) performed a paleomagnetic study on 
the Upper Cretaceous Jingzhushan Fm red -
beds of the western Lhasa terrane. Though the 
mean direction of all the 54 paleomagnetic sites 
passed positive fold tests, the mean inclination 
(Is = +51.8°) obtained from the southern limb 
of folds is clearly steeper than that (Is = +19.0°) 
observed from the northern limb of folds. After 
analyzing several possible factors, Bian et al. 
(2020) concluded that the ChRM direction 
observed from the Jingzhushan Fm redbeds 
should represent primary magnetization and the 
large inclination discrepancy of the two limbs 
of folds could be attributed to the syntectonic-
sedimentation. Because the steeper inclinations 
obtained from the southern limb of folds can 
reasonably offset the shallower inclinations 
obtained from the northern limb of folds, some 
researchers proposed that paleomagnetic data 
obtained from two limbs of the folded syntec -
tonic strata are still reliable for paleogeographic 
reconstructions (e.g., Tong et  al., 2019; Bian 
et al., 2020; Bian and Yang, 2021; Wang et al., 
2022). However, Zhao et al. (2021) argued that 
the Upper Cretaceous Jingzhushan Fm redbeds 
in the northern Lhasa terrane suffered from post-
depositional tectonic penetrative deformation, 
and thus considered that the tectonic strains led 
to the steeper inclinations found in the southern 
limb of folds and the shallower inclinations of 
the northern limb of folds.
It should be emphasized that sedimentary 
rocks, especially redbeds, have always been the 
most widely used material for paleomagnetic 
studies in the Tibetan Plateau and its adjacent 
areas due to their widespread distribution (e.g., 
Achache et  al., 1984; Sun et  al., 2006, 2012; 
Ding et al., 2014; Yang et al., 2015, 2019; Yan 
et  al., 2016; Chen et  al., 2017; Tong et  al., 
2017, 2022; Bian et  al., 2020, 2022a, 2022b; 
Cao et al., 2020; Li et al., 2020a, 2020b; Yuan 
et al., 2021; Wang et al., 2022; Ma et al., 2022), 
as well as their ability to record nearly continu-
ous geomagnetic fields and, usually, unequivo-
cal paleohorizontal, which are occasionally 
the problem with volcanic rocks. Due to the 
India-Asia collision and subsequent continued 
convergence, post-depositional tectonic strains 
generally have affected the pre-Paleogene strata 
exposed on the Tibetan Plateau. Therefore, it is 
especially important to clarify the reliability of 
ChRM directions recorded in the redbeds of the 
Tibetan Plateau.

netic study on the Upper Cretaceous Abushan 
Fm redbeds in the Anduo area of the QT. Our 
new paleomagnetic datasets are obtained from 
two different limbs of the folded Abushan Fm 
redbeds and provide the opportunity for the 
positive fold and conglomerate tests that are 
essential to evaluate the reliability of paleo -

GEOLOGY AND SAMPLING
The QT is located in the central Tibetan Pla-
teau, and it is separated from the Lhasa terrane 
by the Bangong-Nujiang suture zone on the 
south and from the Songpan-Ganzi terrane by the 
Jinsha suture zone on the north ( Fig. 1A). The 
present-day QT extends from west to east and 
rotates to the N-S trend after passing through the 
Eastern Himalaya Syntaxis (EHS) (Tapponnier 
et al., 1982; Armijo et al., 1986; Royden et al., 
1997; Wang and Burchfiel, 2000; Jessup et al., 
2008). Our study area is located in the southern 
margin of the QT where the Abushan Fm red -
beds are widely exposed (Fig. 1B). Based on the 
1:250,000 scale Anduo (I46C004001, 2003) and 
Zigetangcuo (I46C004002, 2005) regional geo-
logical survey reports, the middle-upper part of 
the Abushan Fm includes purplish-red sandstones 
and siltstones with a fining-upward trend, and 
its lower part mainly consists of gray-red con -
glomerates interbedded with sandstones. In the 
Anduo area, the Abushan Fm is ∼750 m thick, 
and unconformably overlies the Upper Jurassic–
Lower Cretaceous Bangai Fm and underlies the 
Eocene Niubao Fm (I46C004001, 2003; Fig. 2). 
In the Madeng area, this formation is ∼500 m 
thick with volcanic interlayers in the lower part, 
and unconformably overlies the Upper Jurassic 
Suowa Fm and underlies the Eocene Niubao Fm 
(I46C004002, 2005; Fig. 2). Two volcanic inter-
layers located at the bottom of the Abushan Fm

can be restricted within 89.1–83.6 Ma. The 
oldest phase of folding of the Late Cretaceous 
strata occurred in the latest Late Cretaceous

A total of 39 paleomagnetic sites were col -
lected from the middle-upper of the Abushan 
Fm redbeds ( Figs.  1B and 2). Eight sites 
(MD1–MD8) were collected from Section A 
(32°13′47″N, 91 °02′46″E), located ∼5 km 
southwest of the Madeng village, where the 
bedding dips from 55° to 79° toward the south-
west (Figs. 2 and 3). Thirty-one sites were drilled 
from Sections B (AK1-AK15 and AK29-AK31, 
32°16′34″N, 91°47′27″E), C (AK16-AK22, 
32°17′17″N, 91°49′22″E), and D (AK23-AK28, 
32°17′94″N, 91°48′28″E), located ∼15 km east 
of the Anduo county, where the bedding dips 
from 42° to 84° toward the north ( Figs. 2 and 
3). To perform a conglomerate test and assure 
the reliability of the ChRM direction, two sites 
(AK21 and AK22) including 20 oriented cores 
were drilled from redbed cobbles of conglomer-
ate layers that are intercalated with the Upper 
Cretaceous Abushan Fm redbeds. The bedding 
attitudes for the 39 paleomagnetic sites are given 
in Table 1. Generally, each paleomagnetic site 
includes ∼10 cores, and each oriented core of 
the same site was distributed at different strati-
graphic levels (Fig. 3). All cores were collected 
with a gasoline-powered drill and oriented by 
both a sun compass and a magnetic compass. 
The discrepancy between these two oriented 
records was less than 3°, indicating that the local 
magnetic disturbance can be ignored.
Eight hand blocks oriented on the strata bed-
ding plane were collected from Section B for test-
ing the anisotropy-based inclination shallowing. 
Furthermore, one fresh block sample for detrital 
zircon U-Pb geochronology was collected from 
the AK2 site, which is located at the bottom of the 
sampled Abushan Fm redbeds sequence.
METHODS
The standard oriented cores were cut into 
2.2-cm-long cylindrical specimens for subse -
quent analysis. All redbeds specimens were sub-
jected to stepwise thermal demagnetization up 
to 680 °C using an MMTDSC or an ASC-TD 48 
thermal demagnetizer. Remanent magnetization 
was measured using the 2G-755-4 K cryogenic 
magnetometer. The isothermal remanent mag -
netization (IRM), backfield demagnetization of 
the saturation IRM (SIRM), and three-axis IRM 
were performed using an ASC IM10-30 pulse 
magnetizer and measured with a JR-6A spinner 
magnetometer. Three-axis IRM were imparted 
in successively smaller fields of 2.4 T, 0.4 T, and 
0.12 T along three orthogonal directions (Low-
rie, 1990). AMS analysis was carried out using 
an MFK1 Kappabridge (AGICO) before thermal 
demagnetization.
All demagnetization and remanence measure-
ments were performed within the magnetically 
shielded room (<300 nT) at the Paleomagnetic 
and Environmental Magnetism Laboratory of 
the China University of Geosciences, Beijing, 
China. ChRM directions were determined using 
principal component analysis (Kirschvink, 
1980), and site-mean directions were calculated 
using Fisherian statistics (Fisher, 1953). Paleo-
magnetic data were processed using the packages 
developed by Enkin (1990) and Cogné (2003).
A total of eight standard core samples were 
drilled in the direction perpendicular to the strata 
bedding from the oriented hand blocks. These 
standard specimens were subjected to suc -

RESULTS
Detrital Zircon U-Pb Analytical Results
The CL images showed that most of detrital 
zircons are euhedral to subhedral with grain 
sizes ranging from 100 μm to 260 μm with 
clearly oscillatory zoning ( Fig.  4A). These 
features, combined with higher Th/U ratios 
of all zircons compared to metamorphic zir -
cons, suggest that the dated zircons are igne -
ous in origin. A total of 60 of 63 zircon grains 
analyzed provided reliable U-Pb ages, 35 of 
them produced pre-Paleozoic dates, and the 
remaining 25 grains yielded Mesozoic dates. 
Considering that three zircon grains exhib -
ited Late Cretaceous dates of 89.1 ± 0.9 Ma, 
91.5 ± 1.0 Ma, and 95.4 ± 0.9 Ma ( Figs. 4B 
and 4C), we use the youngest zircon age of 
89.1 ± 0.9 Ma to constrain the maximum 
depositional age of the sampled Abushan Fm 
redbeds sequence.
Anisotropy of Magnetic Susceptibility 
Results
The maximum ( Kmax), intermediate ( Kint), 
and minimum (Kmin) principal axes of the AMS 
ellipsoids in equal-area projections show the 
Kmax axes are in bedding planes and slightly 
grouped in an approximately northwest-south-
east direction (Fig. 5). The Kmin axes are roughly 
clustered perpendicular to bedding planes with 
a slight trend to the southwest. Such a distribu-
tion of the principal axes is common in primary 
sedimentary fabrics with weak tectonic fabric 
and comparable with those observed in foreland 
basin sedimentary rocks (e.g., Gilder et al., 2001; 
Parés, 2004; Huang et  al., 2006, 2010; Tang 
et al., 2013). The corrected anisotropy degree 
(Pj < 1.05) is relatively low, and their shape 
parameter (−1 < T < + 1, usually T > 0) indi-
cates a range from obviously oblate to prolate 
(Fig. 5). These AMS characteristics are consis-
tent with the incipient deformation (stage 2) to 
pencil structure (stage 3) as described by Hrouda 
and Chadima (2020), indicating that the studied 
Abushan Fm redbeds did not suffer from strong 
deformation.

Rock-magnetic results show that the Abushan 
Fm redbed specimens have the same rock-mag-
netic characteristics ( Fig. 6). The IRM acqui -
sition curves reveal a gradual increase and the

Microscopic Observations
Microscopic observations show that the red-
bed specimens from the Madeng and Anduo 
areas contain abundant quartz, detrital hema -
tite grains, and pigmentary hematite ( Fig. 7). 
Detrital hematite grains appear as angular to 
subrounded with different sizes ranging from 
a few to tens of microns, whereas pigmentary 
hematite formed as the rims of clasts (Figs. 7C 
and 7F). These detrital hematite particles most 
probably record a detrital remanent magnetiza-
tion (DRM). The random orientation of mineral 
particles supports that the studied redbeds did 
not suffer from significant deformation. These 
petrographic characteristics are similar with 
those observed from the Abushan Fm redbeds in 
the Shuanghu (Meng et al., 2018) and Linzhou 
(Ma et al., 2022) areas.
Paleomagnetic Results
A total of 315 specimens were subjected to 
stepwise thermal demagnetization, and typical 
Zijderveld diagrams are illustrated in Figure 8A. 
Most specimens do not reveal a well-defined low 
unblocking temperature component close to the 
present geomagnetic field direction, but rather 
a well-defined high-temperature component 
(HTC) that decays to the origin, which is defined 
as the ChRM direction, and this can be isolated 
between 300–500 °C and 660–680 °C (Table 
S11). Except for the two sites AK21 and AK22 
drilled from the redbed cobbles, 262 specimens 
yield reliable ChRM directions that provide 37 
site-mean directions. The eight paleomagnetic 
sites including 64 specimens collected from the 
southwest dipping limb of folds provide a mean 
direction (Group A) of Dg = 21.5°, Ig = +1.8°, 
kg = 60.3, α95 = 7.2° in situ, and Ds = 354.0°, 
Is = +44.2°, ks = 80.6, α95 = 6.2° after tilt cor-
rection (Fig. 9A). Group A passes the McFad -
den (1990) fold tests at the 95% confidence level 
(Table 1). The 29 paleomagnetic sites including 
198 specimens distributed at the north dipping 
limb of folds yield a mean direction (Group B) of 
Dg = 122.9°, Ig = +71.8°, kg = 14.3, α95 = 7.3° 
in situ, and Ds = 2.6°, Is = +34.2°, ks = 46.4, 
α95 = 4.0° after tilt correction (Fig. 9B). Group 
B passes both McElhinny (1964) and McFad -
den (1990) fold tests at the 95% and 99% con-
fidence levels (Table 1). The 37 paleomagnetic 
sites collected from the Abushan Fm redbeds 
yield a grand mean of Dg = 74.6°, Ig = +68.3°, 
kg = 4.0, α95 = 13.6° in situ, and Ds = 0.9°, 
Is = +36.4°, ks = 43.6, α95 = 3.6° after tilt cor-
rection (Fig. 9C), corresponding to a Fisherian 
mean paleopole located at 78.2°N, 266.8°E with 
A95 = 3.6° and a paleolatitude of 20.5° ± 3.6°N 
for the study area (32.3°N, 91.4°E). This overall-
mean direction passes McElhinny (1964) and 
McFadden (1990) fold tests at the 99% con -
fidence level ( Table  1), and the Enkin (2003) 
direction-correction (DC) test is also positive 
with the best group at 88.90% ± 5.10% untilt-
ing (Fig. 9C).
The specimens drilled from redbed cobbles 
at the AK21 and AK22 sites show isolation of 
a stable HTC decaying toward the origin. The 
ChRM directions obtained from different cob -
bles at the same site are randomly distributed, 
while the two specimens collected from the 
same cobbles showed similar ChRM directions 
(Fig. 8B). The Watson’s (1956) random distri-
bution test for these two conglomerate sites 
yielded R values of 5.03 and 4.60, respectively, 
which were less than the R 0 value (n = 10) of 
5.94 at the 99% confidence level and 5.03 at the 
95% confidence level. Thus, positive fold and 
conglomerate tests strongly confirm that the 
Abushan Fm redbeds have recorded a primary 
remanent magnetization.

DISCUSSION
The Reliability of the Abushan Fm Redbed 
Paleomagnetic Datasets
Though the positive fold and conglomer -
ate tests indicate that the ChRM directions 
obtained from the Abushan Fm redbeds repre -
sent a primary magnetization, the mean incli -
nation observed from the southwest dipping 
limb (Is = +44.2°) is clearly steeper than that 
of the north dipping limb ( Is = +34.2°). The 
conspicuous inclination discrepancies in the 
Upper Cretaceous redbed paleomagnetic data 
may be explained by some factors such as: (1) 
insufficient averaging of geomagnetic paleos -
ecular variation (e.g., Deenen et al., 2011; Vaes 
et al., 2021); (2) a secondary chemical remanent 
magnetization (CRM) recorded in the redbeds 
that partially or completely overprints the DRM 
(e.g., Kodama, 2012; Jiang et al., 2015, 2022); 
(3) the distortional strains should be taken 
seriously when the remanence directions are 
obtained from two limbs of folds (Cogné et al., 
1991; Kanamatsu and Herrero-Bervera, 2006; 
Kligfield et al., 1983); (4) the depositional and/or 
compaction of redbeds may result in the ChRM 
inclination shallowing (e.g., Tauxe and Kent, 
2004; Tan et al., 2010; Ding et al., 2015); and 
(5) the strata may not have been horizontal at the 
time of magnetization because of unidentified 
syntectonic growth strata (Gilder et al., 2001; 
Sato et al., 2011; Tong et al., 2019; Bian et al., 
2020; Bian and Yang, 2021; Wang et al., 2022). 
These five factors are discussed separately to 
clarify the ChRM inclination discrepancy in the 
Abushan Fm redbeds obtained from two differ-
ent strikes, as well as to assure the reliability of 
the paleomagnetic dataset we report.
Tests for Paleosecular Variation
Deenen et al. (2011) suggested the N-depen-
dent A95 envelope can help ascertain whether 
paleomagnetic datasets have sufficiently aver -
aged out paleosecular variation. Considering 
that each independently oriented core has been 
drilled from different stratigraphic levels, we 
thus assume that each ChRM direction is a spot 
reading of the geomagnetic field, and thus that it 
can be transformed to a virtual geomagnetic pole 
(VGP). For the 37 paleomagnetic sites, the 262 
VGPs yield a Fisherian specimen-mean paleopole 
at 78.6°N, 265.9°E with A95 = 1.8° for the study 
area (32.3°N, 91.4°E). The A95 value of 1.8° is 
within the N-dependent envelope (A95min = 1.3°, 
A95max = 2.5°) for 262 poles (Deenen et  al., 
2011). For the 64 specimens from the south -
west dipping limb and 198 specimens from the 
north dipping limb, their corresponding VGPs 
provide the Fisherian specimen-mean paleo -
poles at 82.4°N, 313.7°E with A95 = 3.5° and at 
76.5°N, 258.0°E with A95 = 2.0° for the study 
area (32.3°N, 91.4°E). These two A95 values of 
3.5° and 2.0° are also within their corresponding 
A95 envelopes of ( A95min = 2.3°, A95max = 6.0°) 
for 64 poles and ( A95min = 1.4°, A95max = 2.9°) 
for 198 poles, respectively (Deenen et al., 2011). 
These tests support the inference that the above-
mentioned three mean directions obtained from

Origin of Hematite
The natural remanent magnetization in most 
redbeds is a mixture of detrital hematite and 
authigenic hematite (Tauxe et  al., 1980). In 
general, a primary DRM is carried by detri -
tal hematite, and it can partially to completely 
be replaced by a secondary CRM, which is 
recorded by authigenic hematite (Collinson, 
1966; Tauxe et al., 1980; Tauxe and Kent, 1984; 
Huang et  al., 2020); to identify the primary 
magnetization, an essential aspect of paleomag-
netic studies on redbeds is to discriminate CRM 
from DRM (Walker et al., 1981; Kodama and 
Dekkers, 2004). Previous studies have suggested 
that the shapes of demagnetization curves and 
the maximum unblocking temperatures can dis-
criminate between these two remanences (Jiang 
et al., 2015, 2022). The thermal demagnetiza -
tion curves of the Abushan Fm redbeds show a 
convex up shape with the maximum unblocking 
temperature at ∼680 °C (Fig. 10). Such demag-
netization characteristics are clearly different 
from the concave shape of the CRM demag -
netization curve, which has a wider laboratory 
unblocking temperature spectrum ∼600–650 °C, 
but are fully consistent with the DRM demagne-
tization curve that displays a convex up shape 
with a confined narrow unblocking temperature 
up to 660–680 °C (Fig. 10). This result, com -
bined with the positive conglomerate and fold 
tests, as well as the petrographic characteristics, 
shows that the ChRM directions obtained from 
the Abushan Fm redbeds is likely a primary 
DRM carried by detrital hematite.
The Effect of Distortional Strains
Although previous studies have shown that 
the distortional strains can reorient the magnetic 
foliations and lineations (Weil and Yonkee, 2009; 
Hrouda and Chadima, 2020; Cao et al., 2022), it 
is still unclear whether the distortional strains 
affect paleomagnetic directions (Bian et  al., 
2020; Bian and Yang, 2021; Zhao et al., 2021). 
According to our AMS analysis, the magnetic 
fabrics observed should belong to the incipient 
deformation (stage 2) to pencil structure (stage 
3) (Hrouda and Chadima, 2020). Noticeably, our 
overall-mean direction passes both the McEl -
hinny (1964) and McFadden (1990) fold tests 
and the Enkin (2003) DC test, as well as the posi-
tive conglomerate tests, which strongly support 
that ChRM directions should be a pre-folding 
primary magnetization, not secondary remagne-
tization as a result of penetrative deformation.
In addition, several studies have shown that 
the primary magnetization can be maintained 
when the deformed magnetic fabrics of the 
redbeds display characteristics of deformation 
stage 2 (incipient deformation) to stage 4 (weak 
cleavage) (e.g., Li et al., 2020a, 2020b; Ma et al., 
2022; Wang et al., 2022). Thus, the effect of the 
distortional strains on remanence directions of 
the Abushan Fm redbeds can be ignored.

Although three available Cretaceous paleo -
magnetic investigations on basalt flows inter -
calated with redbeds demonstrated that the two 
sets of site-mean directions for redbeds and basalt 
flows are quite consistent (Sun et al., 2006; Li 
et al., 2013; Cao et al., 2017a), the depositional 
and/or compaction-induced inclination shallow-

and Kent, 2004; Tan et al., 2010; Kodama, 2012; 
Huang et al., 2013). Therefore, it is necessary to 
carry out inclination shallowing correction for 
the obtained Abushan Fm redbeds paleomagnetic 
datasets. Both the anisotropy-based correction 
method (Hodych and Buchan, 1994) and the E/I 
correction method (Tauxe and Kent, 2004) have 
been used widely to quantitatively test and cor-
rect for inclination shallowing of paleomagnetic 
data obtained from sedimentary rocks. Consider-
ing that the specimens collected from the north 
dipping limb show a shallower mean inclination 
than those from the southwest dipping limb, we 
therefore follow the abovementioned two meth-
ods to test and correct the paleomagnetic data 
obtained from the north dipping limb.
The anisotropy-based correction results of 
the eight specimens from the north dipping 
limb are given in Figure 11. The values of the 
IRMz/IRMx in a field interval of 200–1000 mT 
and the thermal demagnetization temperature 
range of 600–680 °C were 0.900–1.017 and 
0.903–1.021, respectively (Fig. 11). The IRMz/
IRMx values of the eight specimens in the tem-
perature range of 600–680 °C were used to cal-
culate the mean IRMx/IRMz value (0.971) for 
correcting the measured overall-mean direction 
obtained from the north dipping limb. After the 
anisotropy-based inclination shallowing correc-
tion, the measured mean inclination of the 29 
sites changed from 34.2 to 35.3, showing that 
the inclination shallowing is insignificant in the 
Abushan Fm redbeds.

Syntectonic-Sedimentation Correction
The Abushan Fm redbeds were deposited 
in an alluvial fan to braided river environment 
(Zhang et al., 1985; Ma et al., 2017a), which, 
combined with the fluvial gravel deposits 
observed in our sampling sections ( Fig.  3B), 
supports the interpretation that the Abushan Fm 
redbeds are syntectonic growth strata and their 
original bedding might not be horizontal when 
the sediments were magnetized. Therefore, the 
conspicuous inclination discrepancy obtained 
from two different limbs of the folded Abushan 
Fm redbeds may be attributed to syntectonic-
sedimentation (Fig. 13A).
The syntectonic-sedimentation-correction 
of Tong et  al. (2019) suggests that the origi -
nal dip of the sampling Abushan Fm redbeds 
is 7.5° ( Fig.  13B). After the syntectonic-sed -
imentation-correction, the site-mean direc -
tion for the southwest-dip strata is Dc1 = 0.4°, 
Ic1 = +41.2°, kc1 = 81.7, α95 = 6.2°, n = 8, 
and for the north-dip strata it is Dc2 = 5.3°, 
Ic2 = +40.9°, kc2 = 53.3, α95 = 3.7°, n = 29 
(Fig. 13D). The site-mean direction for the total 
37 sites is Dc = 4.2°, Ic = +41.0°, kc = 57.7, 
α95 = 3.1° (Fig. 13D), corresponding to a paleo-
pole at 80.4°N, 247.5°E with dp/dm = 2.3/3.8 
and a paleolatitude of 23.5 ° ± 2.3°N for the 
study area (32.3°N, 91.4°E). This syntectonic-
sedimentation-correction overall-mean direction 
passes both McElhinny (1964) and McFadden 
(1990) fold tests at the 95% and 99% confidence 
levels (Table 1), and the Enkin (2003) direction-
correction (DC) test is also positive with the best 
group at 101.66% ± 7.79% untilting (Fig. 13C). 
Obviously, the site-mean inclination of the 
southwest dipping strata (Ic1 = 41.2°) is similar 
to that of the north dipping strata ( Ic2 = 40.9°) 
after syntectonic-sedimentation-correction and 
the k values increase significantly from 43.6 to 
57.7, indicating that the inclination discrepancy 
obtained from Group A and Group B samples 
should result from the syntectonic sedimentation. 
In addition, considering that the overall-mean 
inclination (Ic = 41.0° ± 3.1°) after syntectonic-
sedimentation-correction is also relatively con-
sistent with the observed overall-mean inclina-
tion (Is = 36.4° ± 3.6°), the paleomagnetic data 
before correction are still credible for paleogeo-
graphic reconstructions. Several paleomagnetic 
datasets of the Cretaceous redbeds obtained 
from two limbs of folds also show that the incli-
nations are generally consistent before and after 
syntectonic-sedimentation-correction (e.g., Bian 
et al., 2020; Wang et al., 2022).
The abovementioned studies demonstrate 
that the conspicuous inclination discrepancies 
in the Upper Cretaceous redbeds of the Lhasa 
and Qiangtang terranes mainly result from the 
lack of correction for syntectonic growth pro -
cesses. Although the syntectonic-sedimentation 
can cause a significant deviation of paleomag -
netic inclinations obtained from monoclinal 
strata, paleomagnetic datasets observed from 
two limbs of folds are still reliable. In addition, 
previous paleomagnetic results obtained from 
the Lhasa and Qiangtang terranes indicated that 
inclination shallowing is negligible within the

The Shape of the Qiangtang Terrane 
during the Late Cretaceous
High-quality paleomagnetic datasets are 
pre-condition for quantitative paleogeographic 
reconstruction. Meert et al. (2020) updated the 
Van der V oo (1990) criteria and proposed the 
“R” reliability indexes, which are listed in the 
notes of Table 2, to evaluate the quality of paleo-
magnetic data. Considering the age range of the 
Cretaceous Normal Polarity Superchron (ca. 
121.4–83.6 Ma; Ogg, 2020) and the insignificant 
inclination shallowing in the central Tibetan Pla-
teau, we require that reliable paleomagnetic data 
should fulfill at least five “R” indexes (1–4 and 
7) with at least a positive field test.
Table  2 summarizes the five available Late 
Cretaceous paleopoles from the QT, and their 
paleolatitudes have been calculated for the indi-
vidual sampling location. The MK1 paleopole 
satisfies all seven “R” indexes, and the other four 
paleopoles (GZ, SH, AD, and MK2) fulfill six 
“R” indexes (except for criteria 6, the presence 
of reversals). Therefore, all five datasets from 
redbeds match our selection criterion (Table 2). 
Three paleomagnetic poles (GZ, SH, and AD), 
which were obtained from the west of the EHS 
(Fig. 1A), yield paleolatitudes of 18.6° ± 3.1°N 
(Chen et al., 2017) for the Gaize area (32.5°N, 
84.3°E), 20.8° ± 2.5°N (Meng et al., 2018) for 
the Abushan Fm of the Shuanghu area (33.2°N, 
88.7°E), and 20.2° ± 2.4°N (this study) for the 
Abushan Fm of the Anduo area (32.3°N, 91.4°E), 
respectively. Comparing these three observed 
paleolatitudes with their sampling latitudes gives 
the latitudinal differences of 13.9° ± 3.1° (GZ), 
12.4° ± 2.5° (SH), and 11.8° ± 3.6° (AD), indi-
cating that the Gaize, Shuanghu, and Anduo sam-
pling areas moved northward 1540 ± 340 km, 
1380 ± 280 km, and 1310 ± 400 km after the 
Late Cretaceous, respectively (Fig. 14). Further-
more, the consistently northward displacement 
distance is within the paleomagnetic resolution 
for these three sampling locations, which span a 
wide longitude ranging from 84.3°E to 91.4°E, 
which supports that the QT shape to the west of 
the EHS was essentially similar to its present-
day relatively E-W alignment during the Late 
Cretaceous.
The other two poles (MK1 and MK2) are from 
the Mangkang area, located to the east of the EHS, 
and provide paleolatitudes of 36.6 ° ± 6.7°N 
(Tong et al., 2015) for the Zonggu Fm in the 
MK1 sampling location (29.7°N, 98.4°E) and 
32.9° ± 10.6°N (MK2; Huang et al., 1992) for 
the Mangkang Fm in the MK2 sampling loca -
tions (29.7°N, 98.7°E). Considering that these 
two redbed poles from the same sampling area 
have been obtained from the same age rocks and 
lithology, we follow the method of Arason and 
Levi (2010) to obtain the inclination-only (cor-
responding to paleolatitude-only) mean and then 
calculate its corresponding paleolatitude. A total 
of 28 paleomagnetic sites yield an inclination-
only mean of 53.3° ± 4.5°, corresponding to a 
paleolatitude of 33.9° ± 4.3°N (Table S2; see 
footnote 1). Comparing this observed latitude 
with the sampling latitude of 29.7°N shows the 
latitude differences of 4.2° ± 4.3°, implying that 
the Mangkang sampling area to the east of the 
EHS moved southward 470 ± 480 km after the 
Late Cretaceous (Fig. 14). The opposite displace-
ments sense between the west and east areas of 
the EHS has led to the QT shape around the EHS 
changing from a Late Cretaceous NE-SW align-
ment to its approximate present-day SE-NW 
alignment. These paleomagnetic observations 
are consistent with the previous geologic stud-
ies that indicate that the southeastern edge of 
the Tibetan Plateau, such as the Indochina and 
Shan-Thai block, has experienced a southward 
displacement from 700 ± 200 km to more than 
1000 km caused by the indentation of India into 
Asia (e.g., Yang and Besse, 1993; Schärer et al., 
1994; Yang et  al., 1995; Leloup et  al., 1995, 
2001; Lacassin et al., 1996, 1997; Sato et al., 
1999, 2007; Otofuji et al., 2007; Li et al., 2017a).
Due to the limited paleomagnetic data 
obtained from the Late Cretaceous rocks of the 
QT, as well as the discrepancy in data quality, 
further paleomagnetic studies from the Late Cre-
taceous rocks are still necessary to accurately 
constrain the shape of the QT prior to the India-
Asia collision.
CONCLUSIONS
We have conducted a combined geochrono-
logic and paleomagnetic study on the Upper Cre-
taceous Abushan Fm redbeds of the Anduo area in 
the QT. These new paleomagnetic data pass both 
positive fold and conglomerate tests, and provide 
an opportunity to evaluate the reliability of redbed 
paleomagnetic datasets from the Tibetan Plateau. 
Based on the paleomagnetic data from the Upper 
Cretaceous redbeds of the QT, the main conclu-
sions can be summarized as follows:
(1) The Anduo area of the QT was located at 
20.2° ± 2.4°N during the Late Cretaceous.
(2) The reliability of redbed paleomagnetic 
datasets is not influenced by the distortional 
strains in the pencil structure magnetic fab -
rics stage.
(3) The conspicuous inclination discrepancies 
observed from the folded Upper Cretaceous red-
beds of the Lhasa and Qiangtang terranes likely 
result from an inability to recognize syntectonic 
growth strata.

Unraveling the Lhasa‐Qiangtang Collision in Western Tibet:
Insights From Geochronological and Paleomagnetic
Analyses
Peiping Song
1
, Lin Ding
1
, Jinxiang Li
1
, Yahui Yue
1
, and Jing Xie
1
1
State Key Laboratory of Tibetan Plateau Earth System, Environment and Resources (TPESER), Institute of Tibetan
Plateau Research, Chinese Academy of Sciences, Beijing, China
Abstract The Lhasa‐Qiangtang collision closed the Meso‐Tethys Ocean, but the exact timing of this event
remains hotly debated. Here, we present geochronological and paleomagnetic analyses conducted on
Cretaceous volcanics from western Qiangtang to constrain the Lhasa‐Qiangtang collision in western Tibet. Our
investigations yield a paleolatitude of ∼ 30.5 ± 5.0°N for western Qiangtang during ca. 110–100 Ma. A
reanalysis of previously acquired Mesozoic‐Cenozoic paleomagnetic data from western Qiangtang suggests a
stationary position during ca. 136–34 Ma. Examination of paleomagnetic data from western Lhasa reveals a
significant reduction in northward paleolatitudinal motion during the Early Cretaceous, dropping from
∼ 12.3 cm /yr to nearly zero. Integration of our paleomagnetic findings with available geological records has led
to conclude that the Lhasa‐Qiangtang collision in western Tibet occurred at ca. 132 Ma. Additionally, we infer
that crustal shortening on the order of ∼ 1,000 km happened between Lhasa and Qiangtang during the Early
Cenozoic.
Plain Language Summary The Tibetan Plateau comprises multiple different blocks, which
originated from the Gondwana in the southern hemisphere. Their convergence histories toward Euraisa have
changed the global land‐sea distributions since the Late Paleozoic. The time at which the Lhasa block, one of the
Tibetan blocks, accreted to the Qiangtang block to the north remains poorly constrained. In this work, we
provide robust data suggesting a latitude of ∼ 30.5 ± 5.0°N for western Qiangtang during the Early Cretaceous
(ca. 110–100 Ma). We also compiled the available latitudinal data from western Tibet in combination with
geological observations. We suggest Lhasa collided with Qiangtang during 132 million years ago in western
Tibet. Significant shortening of the continental crust by ∼ 1,000 km between the Lhasa and Qiangtang blocks
occurred after their collision.
1. Introduction
The evolution of the Tethyan domain during the formation and break‐up of Pangea involved various stages of the
Wilson cycle spanning late Paleozoic‐early Cenozoic eras, characterized by the opening, growth, and closure of
multiple oceans (i.e., the Paleo‐, Meso‐, and Neo‐Tethys oceans) (L. Ding et al., 2022 ; A. Yin & Harrison, 2000 ).
The Meso‐Tethys ocean opened concurrently with the separation of the Cimmerian blocks (e.g., Qiangtang,
Sibumasu) from southernly Gondwana (DeCelles et al., 2014 ; Metcalfe, 2013 ), and was then consumed by
oceanic subduction beneath Qiangtang and /or Lhasa, accompanied by the rifting and northward drift of Lhasa
toward northernly Eurasia (Kapp & Decelles, 2019 ). The Meso‐Tethys eventually closed during the Lhasa‐
Qiangtang collision processes (Hu et al., 2022 ; S. Li et al., 2019 ), with remnants trapped in the Bangong‐
Nujiang suture zone (BNS) (Figure 1a and Figure S1 in Supporting Information S1 ). While central Tibet pre-
serves extensive geological records related to these processes, many fundamental issues regarding the temporal‐
spatial evolution of the Meso‐Tethys remain contentious. The rifting of Lhasa from either Indian (Torsvik &
Cocks, 2013 ) or Australian Gondwana (Q. Wang et al., 2021 ) is interpreted to have occurred either during the
Early Middle Permian (marked by emplacement of significant volumes of mafic rocks, Liao et al., 2015 ), or
during the Middle‐Late Triassic (as suggested by paleolatitudinal reconstructions, Z. Li et al., 2016 ). The sub-
duction of the Meso‐Tethys oceanic crust exhibited either a single polarity beneath Lhasa (Zhu et al., 2009 ) or
Qiangtang (Y. Li et al., 2013 ), or a divergent double polarity beneath both (Kapp & Decelles, 2019 ) during the
Middle Permian‐Early Jurassic. The Lhasa‐Qiangtang collision is suggested to have occurred from the Middle‐
Late Jurassic to the Late Cretaceous (Guynn et al., 2006 ; Kapp et al., 2007 ; S. Li et al., 2019 ; Z. Yin et al., 2024 ).

of Tethyan tectonic evolution and global land‐sea distributions. Paleomagnetism aids in reconstructing latitudinal
plate and block motion (e.g., Huang et al., 2018 ), therefore Mesozoic paleomagnetic data are crucial for un-
derstanding the convergence history of Tibetan blocks. Some suggest western Qiangtang accreted to the Eurasian
margin in the Late Triassic (C. Song et al., 2012 ), and experienced negligible latitudinal motion ( ∼ 28–30°N) from
120 to 30 Ma (W. Chen et al., 2017 ; Cao et al., 2020 ; Lippert et al., 2011 ; P. Song et al., 2022 ). However, others
argue for a more southerly latitude of ∼ 21–22°N, proposing a pre‐120 Ma Lhasa‐Qiangtang collision in western
Tibet (Bian et al., 2017 ; S. Wang et al., 2022 ). Here, we present new geochronological and paleomagnetic data
from Lower Cretaceous lavas from western Qiangtang to determine the paleolatitude, and integrate these findings
with available paleomagnetic and geological data to evaluate the timing of the Lhasa‐Qiangtang collision in
western Tibet.
2. Geological Setting and Sampling
Tibet is subdivided into Tethyan Himalaya, Lhasa, Qiangtang, and Songpan‐Ganzi blocks, separated by the
Indus‐Yarlung‐Zangbo, Bangong‐Nujiang, and Jinsha sutures, respectively (Figure 1 and Figure S1 in Supporting
Information S1 ). Some suggest the large metamorphic belt in the Longmu Co‐Shuanghu region represents an in
situ ophiolite zone separating western and eastern Qiangtang subblocks (e.g., Zhai et al., 2013 ). Others argue it
formed due to thrusting beneath Qiangtang from the Jinsha suture, indicating an intra‐continental setting (e.g.,
Pullen & Kapp, 2014 ). Upper Paleozoic strata containing glacio‐marine sediments crop out extensively in western
Qiangtang (K. J. Zhang et al., 2012 ). Upper Triassic to Middle Jurassic marine sediments unconformably overlie
these strata (A. Ma et al., 2017 ). In the Early Cretaceous, the marine environment transitioned into a continental
environment throughout western Qiangtang (Kapp et al., 2007 ). Magmatism in western Qiangtang is charac-
terized by three main phases: Carboniferous‐Permian rift‐related (Y.‐X. Zhang & Zhang, 2016 ), Late Jurassic‐
Cretaceous syn‐collision (Y. Li et al., 2018 ; Liu et al., 2017 ), and Eocene‐Oligocene post‐collision phases (L.
Ding et al., 2007 ).
The Cretaceous volcanics we investigated in western Qiangtang are mainly gray and dark andesites conformably
overlying sandstones (Figures S2 and S5 in Supporting Information S1 ). We drilled 48 volcanic sites from
monoclinically folded strata near Lumajiangdongco (34.2°N, 81.4°E), using a portable gasoline‐powered driller,
with orientations determined using both magnetic and sun compasses. At each site, 8–10 paleomagnetic samples
were collected, spanning several meters of stratigraphic thickness and /or at least one lava flow. Approximately 25
lava flows were sampled across ∼ 1,500 m. Bedding attitudes were assessed from sandstones and volcanic cooling
margins (Figure S2 in Supporting Information S1 ), with an average dip of 40° toward 175° from nine directional
measurements conducted in the field (Figure 1b ). See Supporting Information S1 for details on the U/Pb dating,
rock magnetism, magnetic petrography, and paleomagnetism analysis methods and the data.

3.3. Reliability of the Characteristic Directions
First, we employed a fold test to compare our paleomagnetic data with that from ∼ 104 Ma Qushenla Formation
lavas in Gerze (W. Chen et al., 2017 ), as our sampled strata exhibit monoclinic folding. Our tilt‐corrected mean
inclination (I = 49.7°) matches that of W. Chen et al. ( 2017 ) (I = 50.66), but a ∼ 100° difference in declination
suggests regional vertical‐axis rotation between Lumajiangdongco and Gerze (Figure 2b ), supported by fault
investigations (Taylor et al., 2003 ; Figure 1a ). We calculated site‐mean inclinations for our studied area (34.2°N,
81.4°E) using the corresponding VGPs from W. Chen et al. ( 2017 ). After rotating W. Chen et al.’s site mean
declinations by 100° clockwise both in geographic and stratigraphic coordinates (see Table S3 in Supporting
Information S1 ), the progressive unfolding correction of all 56 sites yielded a positive result with a highest
precision parameter at 95.2% (Figure 2c ). The tilt‐corrected k increased significantly from 11.2 to 31.2. The
Fisher‐mean inclination (I = 50.0°) matches the inclination‐only mean (I = 49.6 ± 3.1°) using the method of
Arason and Levi ( 2010 ). Second, the HTs are primarily carried by single‐domain and multi‐domain magnetites,
with minor maghemite and hematite (see Supporting Information S1 ). Third, the HTs align with the Cretaceous
Normal Polarity Superchron (126–84 Ma, Gradstein et al., 2012 ). No secondary magnetizations were found for
the HT components, supporting a primary origin (see Supporting Information S1 ). Furthermore, the angular
dispersion (S) value (18.2°) of the 42 site‐mean VGPs matches the PSV10 data set at a similar latitude (de Oliveira
et al., 2021 ). The A
95
value of 5.0° of mean pole falls within the expected interval (2.69°, 7.78°) for the pale-

4. Discussion
Our discussion in this paper focuses on the convergence history between Qiangtang‐Lhasa in western Tibet
(longitudinally from 80°E to 90°E). A summary of available Mesozoic‐Cenozoic paleomagnetic results is pre-
sented in Table S6 of the Supporting Information S1 and Figure 3a . Paleolatitudes have been calculated for a
reference point in our sampling area (34.2°N, 81.4°E).
4.1. Mesozoic‐Cenozoic Paleolatitudes of Western Qiangtang
Paleomagnetic data derived from Xiaochaka (XC) sandstones suggest that western Qiangtang accreted to Eurasia
at 25.6 ± 3.8°N in the Late Triassic (C. Song et al., 2012 ), coinciding with the closure of the Paleo‐Tethys ocean.
However, the interpretation of five available paleomagnetic paleopoles, obtained from Cretaceous sandstones and
volcanic rocks show considerable disparity (Cao et al., 2020 ; W. Chen et al., 2017 ; Y. Chen et al., 1993 ). The
paleolatitudes derived from the Lower Cretaceous Longmucuo (LM) and Tianshuihai (TH) and the Upper
Cretaceous Qushenla (QL) redbeds range from 10.6 ± 5.1°N (Y. Chen et al., 1993 ) to 31.8 ± 3.2°N (W. Chen
et al., 2017 ). In contrast, the paleolatitudes from the ∼ 104 Ma Qushenla (QS) and ∼ 116 Ma Meriqieco (MR)
volcanic rocks yield values of 31.5 ± 5.7°N (W. Chen et al., 2017 ) and 26.4 ± 5.0°N (Cao et al., 2020 ),
respectively. The discrepancy may be contributed to the following factors: (a) Sedimentary paleomagnetic data,
such as those reported by Y. Chen et al. ( 1993 ), may exhibit lower latitudes due to inclination shallowing, and (b)
while volcanic rocks are immune to the inclination shallowing bias, pelaomagnetic data from the QS and MR
volcanic rocks may not sample enough individual VGP readings to average out paleomagnetic virtual secular. S.
Wang et al. ( 2022 ) used small circle and inclination‐only methods on all five paleopoles derived from both
sedimentary and volcanic rocks, obtaining paleolatitudes of 18.9 ± 11.8°N and 21.4 ± 2.9°N, respectively,
including results from the LM and TH redbeds without inclination shallowing correction. Given that the prevalent
sedimentary inclination shallowing observed throughout Central Asia (e.g., Lippert et al., 2011 ; Yan et al., 2005 ),
the Late Cretaceous QL paleomagnetic results from redbeds were subjected to elongation /inclination analysis
(Tauxe & Kent, 2004 ), with corrected inclinations used for subsequent study. Considering that the local vertical‐
axis rotations within Tibet occurred along faults (Figure 1a ; Taylor et al., 2003 ), and that more sites or inde-
pendent readings sampling the time‐varying paleomagnetic field can significantly improve the accuracy of
paleolatitude estimation (Gerritsen et al., 2022 ; Sapienza et al., 2023 ), we applied an inclination‐only method to
paleomagnetic inclinations from the LJ, QS, and MR volcanic rocks and corrected inclinations from the QL
redbeds, recalculated from site VGPs to the reference point, following the method of Arason and Levi ( 2010 ). The
96 Cretaceous inclinations collectively yield a mean of 49.01 ± 2.09 ( α
95
)° (mean‐M1), corresponding to a
paleolatitude of 29.9 [28.1, 31.8]°N (see Table S7 in Supporting Information S1 ). Additionally, two Eocene
paleopoles from central Qiangtang (QT) and Meisu (MS) volcanic rocks indicate paleolatitudes of 29.9 ± 3.7°N
(Lippert et al., 2011 ) and 30.2 ± 5.9°N (P. Song et al., 2022 ), respectively. These results collectively indicate
western Qiangtang experienced no significant latitudinal movement from the Early Cretaceous to the Late Eocene
(Figure 3a ).
4.2. Mesozoic‐Cenozoic Paleolatitudes of Western Lhasa
For western Lhasa, only three Triassic‐Jurassic paleomagnetic studies have been published (Z. Li et al., 2022 ; Y.
Ma et al., 2022 ; Zhou et al., 2016 ). One paleomagnetic study on the Late Triassic Dibuco (DB) limestone yielded
a latitude of 18.4 ± 10.7°S (Zhou et al., 2016 ). Two paleopoles derived from the ∼ 173–183 Ma Bima (XG) and
∼ 153–156 Ma Zenong (XB) volcanic rocks indicate paleolatitudes of 6.9 ± 5.0°S (Y. Ma et al., 2022 ) and
4.6 ± 2.5°S (Z. Li et al., 2022 ), respectively. We note, that a “monster shift” true polar wander (TPW) has been
proposed to have occurred in Late Jurassic‐earliest Cretaceous (ca. 160–145 Ma) (e.g., Fu & Kent, 2018 ; Kent &
Irving, 2010 ; Muttoni et al., 2005 ), characterized by a ∼ 30–20° clockwise rotation with an Euler axis at 0°N, 11°E
and a velocity of ∼ 2°/Myr. Western Lhasa, located to the east of the Euler pole, could have been translated to a
more southernly latitude by this potential TPW. Therefore the Jurassic paleolatitude might reflect the interplay
between the block's northward plate tectonic motion and the simultaneous TPW (Z. Li et al., 2022 ). However, the
existence and speed of this TPW event remain hotly debated and depend on different data filters. A reassessment
of the Eurasian and Indian paleopoles with careful data selection ruled out this anomalously rapid TPW (Kulakov

4.3. Implications for the Lhasa‐Qiangtang Collision in Western Tibet
Our compilation of paleomagnetic data from western Qiangtang indicates that it was situated at ∼ 29.9°N and
underwent negligible latitudinal movement during the period of ca. 116–34 Ma. Furthermore, our findings
suggest that western Lhasa began to rift away from Gondwana during the Late Triassic to Early Jurassic, coin-
ciding with the extension of the Meso‐Tethys Ocean (Figure 3b ). The maximum width of the Meso‐Tethys Ocean
is estimated to have been ∼ 4,000–5,000 km. Western Lhasa exhibited a northward drift at a velocity of ∼ 3.1 cm /
yr from 220 to 180 Ma and ∼ 1.1 cm /yr from 180 to 155 Ma, followed by a rapid increase to ∼ 12.3 cm /yr until
Lhasa reached the northern hemisphere at ∼ 132 Ma. We note that, the Jurassic paleolatitudinal motion of western
Lhasa could be slightly biased by the potential TPW (see Section 4.2 ). Since then, western Lhasa has remained
stationary at ∼ 18.5–21.5°N for ∼ 50 Myr (Figure 3a ).
We then conducted an integrated analysis of ophiolite occurrences, lithostratigraphy, magmatism, and tectonic
events in western Tibet to constrain the Lhasa‐Qiangtang collision. Ophiolites in the western BNS were dated
primarily to ca. 193 and 147 Ma in the Bangongco and Zhongba areas (e.g., Hu et al., 2022 ; S. Li et al., 2019 ;
Shi, 2007 ; Y. Tang et al., 2020 ; B. D. Wang et al., 2016 ), with a youngest age of ∼ 133 Ma, suggesting ongoing
formation of oceanic crust possibly until the late Early Cretaceous. The accretionary emplacement of the Gerze
ophiolites occurred during ∼ 151–168 Ma (S. Li et al., 2019 ), preceding the collision. The marine environment in
western Qiangtang started during the Late Triassic‐Early Jurassic and was ceased by the Late Jurassic, with

the marine environments in western Lhasa continued to develop until Mid‐Cretaceous (Rao et al., 2020 ). The
arrival of Qiangtang detritus into western Lhasa basins at ∼ 111–116 Ma marks a minimum age for the initial
Lhasa‐Qiangtang collision (S. Li et al., 2019 ). The ca. 131–110 Ma Qushenla volcanics in western Lhasa record
first roll‐back and then break‐off of south‐dipping Meso‐Tethys lithosphere following the collision (e.g., S.‐M. Li
et al., 2018 ). The scarcity of magmatic records from ca. 142 to 128 Ma in western Qiangtang has been interpreted
to reflect the termination of subduction and therefore the initial collision (e.g., Kapp et al., 2007 ; Zhu et al., 2016 ).
Overall, these geological observations indicate that the Lhasa‐Qiangtang collision likely occurred during ca. 133–
116 Ma (Figure 3b ). Our paleomagnetic analysis reveals that the Cretaceous standstill of western Lhasa following
rapid northward motion happened after ∼ 132 Ma. In summary, the combination analysis of paleomagnetic data
set and geological records support a ca. 132–133 Ma timing for the Lhasa‐Qiangtang collision in western Tibet
(Figure 3c ). Future research focusing on high‐quality paleopoles from Upper Jurassic‐Lowest Cretaceous units
both in western Lhasa and Qiangtang will further refine the processes involved in the evolution of the Meso‐
Tethys.
The comparison of the calculated paleolatitudes between western Lhasa and Qiangtang suggests a ∼ 9.3°
discrepancy in latitude in 132–67 Ma. Instead of a spatial gap interpretation, we use the crustal shortening model
of P. Song et al. ( 2022 ) to explain this. The latitudinal velocity of western Lhasa was ∼ 3.1 cm /yr during ca. 67–
22 Ma, causing significant crustal shortening ( ∼ 1,000 km) within the western Lhasa and /or BNS during the early
stage of the India‐Asia collision. This estimate is approximately 500–600 km greater than estimates based on
geological records (Murphy et al., 1997 ; Volkmer et al., 2007 ). This discrepancy may be due to either significant,
previously undetected tectonic shortening within the interior of the Lhasa /BNS, or /and the eastward extrusion of
the Indochina block, which originally occupied a position between Lhasa and Qiangtang (Dupont‐Nivet
et al., 2010 ; Otofuji et al., 2007 ).
5. Conclusions
New geochronological and paleomagnetic data obtained from Early Cretaceous volcanic rocks in western
Qiangtang reveal a paleolatitude of 30.5 ± 5.0°N at ca. 110–100 Ma. A comparison of our new data and previous
Mesozoic‐Cenozoic paleomagnetic data from western Qiangtang and Lhasa provides key constraint on the
convergence evolution of the two blocks. We conclude that western Qiangtang occupied a stationary position
( ∼ 29.9°N) during the Cretaceous‐Eocene period. The northward drift velocity of western Lhasa decreased
significantly from ∼ 12.3 cm/yr to standstill during the Early Cretaceous. Based on these findings integrated with
geological records, we propose that the Lhasa‐Qiangtang collision in western Tibet occurred at ca. 132 Ma.

SUMMARY
The extensive Yukon-Tanana terrane (YTT) of the northern Canadian Cordillera has been
considered controversially to be part of the allochthonous ‘Baja BC’ microcontinent or of the
para-autochthonous North American cratonic margin during the Mesozoic. Palaeomagnetic
methods have isolated a very-stable Early Jurassic thermochemical remanent remagnetization
in the terrane’s felsic Tatlmain batholith and maﬁc Ragged stock after correction for: (1)
rotation from northeast-plunging anticlinal deformation, (2) northerly dipping tectonic tilt of
the host rocks and (3) northwestward regional translation on the adjacent Tintina transcurrent
fault zone. The resulting 196 ± 6 Ma Tatlmain and Ragged palaeopoles are 64.9
◦N, 44.8◦E
(A95 = 5.9◦) and 64.2 ◦N, 58.5◦E( A95 = 7.7◦), respectively. The YTT palaeopoles support
para-autochthonous tectonic models that have the YTT: (1) accreting to North America by
the Early Jurassic, (2) undergoing non-signiﬁcant orogen-perpendicular shortening by mid-
Early Cretaceous from thrust-faulting, and, then (3) undergoing signiﬁcant orogen-parallel
northward translation of ∼500 km from mid-Early Cretaceous to the Eocene. In contrast, the
palaeopoles for Stikinia and Quesnellia of the Intermontane Belt show progressive northwest-
ward translation relative to North America by ∼1000 km and a rotation of ∼55
◦ cw since
mid-Early Cretaceous. We speculate that ∼500 km of the northward translation is related to
dextral motion on the Tintina and Northern Rocky Mountain Trench fault in British Columbia,
and that the clockwise rotation is related to upper crustal tectonics in both Yukon and southern
British Columbia.
Key words: North America; Palaeomagnetism; Remagnetization; Continental tectonics:
strike-slip and transform; Folds and folding.
1 INTRODUCTION
The Yukon-Tanana terrane (YTT) of the North American Cordillera
crops out over large areas of east-central Alaska, southwestern
Yukon and northernmost British Columbia (Fig. 1; Colpron et
al. 2006a). As the result of the YTT’s complex deformational
and metamorphic history, understanding the geological evolution
of these mid- to late Palaeozoic rocks has long proven chal-
lenging (Tempelman-Kluit 1976; Colpron et al. 2006a). Thus
hypotheses for the original location of the YTT’s continental
margin, arc and marginal basin assemblages relative to North
America range from autochthonous (e.g. Hansen 1990)o rp a r a -
autochthonous (e.g. Hansen & Dusel-Bacon1998) to allochthonous
(e.g. Mortensen 1992). Early palaeomagnetic work on late Palaeo-
zoic strata in the Slide Mountain terrane and Late Cretaceous strata
in the YTT and overlapping Intermontane Belt (IMB) terranes was
interpreted to show that the YTT was an exotic allochthonous
terrane that was translated some 1500–3500 km northwards rel-
ative to North America before accreting to the continent (e.g.
Richards et al. 1993; Johnston 2001; Enkin et al. 2006). Con-
versely, geologic evidence and palaeomagnetic work on several
Cretaceous plutons have indicated that the YTT is pericratonic,
having travelled ∼500 km northwards relative to North Amer-
ica, mostly as a result of Palaeocene–Eocene dextral transcurrent
fault displacement on the inboard Tintina fault zone (Gabrielse
1985; Symons et al. 2005; 2015, 2017; Gabrielse et al. 2006;M c -
Causland et al. 2006; Symons & Kawasaki 2011). Heretofore, the
three previously published Jurassic YTT palaeopoles from the Big
Creek, Granite Mountain and Taylor Mountain plutons have been
too scattered to reliably locate the YTT during the latest Trias-
sic to mid-Cretaceous interval (Symons et al. 2000; McCausland
et al. 2001, 2009).
When collected in the summer of 2000, the Ragged gabbro-
syenite stock was thought to be Jurassic and to intrude the late

2G E O L O G Y
Ragged stock and Tatlmain batholith intrude the YTT in the Glen-
lyon map area (NTS 105 L/1–7, 11–14; 115I/9, 16) of central Yukon
(Fig. 1). Early geological mapping in the area was done by Camp-
bell (1967), Templeman-Kluit (1984), Oliver (1996)a n dO l i v e r&
Mortensen (1998). The following geological summary of the sam-
pled study area is taken mostly from extensive mapping and geo-
chemical research reported by Colpron et al. (2002, 2005, 2006a,b,
2007a,b, 2016a,b).
2.1 Geology of the study area
In the northern part of the Glenlyon map area, the YTT study
area crops out as a∼50-km-wide northwest-trending tectonic block
(Fig. 2). The block is separated on its northeast side from Cambro-
Ordovician phyllites in the Selwyn basin of ancestral North America
by the dextral transcurrent Tintina fault zone. On its eastern side,
the dextral transcurrent Big Salmon fault separates the block from
the southeastward continuation of the YTT, a thin slice of the Slide
Mountain terrane and the Cassiar terrane. The pericratonic Cas-
siar terrane is represented by Silurian to Mississippian dolomites
of the Askin Group and black shales of the Earn Group. On its
southwestern side, the tectonic block is separated from the Stikine
terrane of the Intermontane Belt (IMB) by the Tadru transcurrent
fault and linked Needlerock northwest-verging thrust fault. The ad-
jacent Stikine terrane contains Early Jurassic basalts of the Semenof
Formation and the mid-Jurassic McGregor and Tachun granodiorite
batholiths.
In the studied tectonic block, psammitic schist of the basal De-
vonian and older (?) Snowcap Assemblage forms the basement of
the YTT (Colpron et al. 2006a; Morneau et al. 2017). The Early
Mississippian Ragged gabbro-syenite stock intrudes the Snowcap
Assemblage, and both units are unconformably overlain by the Early
to Middle Mississippian Finlayson Assemblage (Gradstein et al.
2004). This assemblage contains arkosic grit and psammite of the
basal Drury Formation, quartzite of the overlying Pelmac Forma-
tion, and volcanic rocks of the upper Little Kalzas Formation. Both
the Snowcap and Finlayson assemblages have been intruded by gra-
nodiorite and tonalite of the Early to Middle Mississippian Little
Kalzas plutonic suite and by granite and granodiorite of the Middle
Mississippian Tatlmain plutonic suite.
Ragged stock has a surface area of ∼50 km

(∼70 Ma) Carmacks volcanics outcrop over an area of ∼150 km2
in the study area around the northwest end of the Tatlmain batholith
(Fig. 2). The volcanics unconformably overlie both the batholith
and adjacent Pelmac Formation.
2.2 Metamorphism in the study area
The Snowcap Assemblage typically contains metamorphic rocks
of the amphibolite facies that experienced Devonian or older (?)
metamorphism (Colpron et al. 2006a). In contrast, the rocks of
the overlying Finlayson Assemblage have experienced greenschist
metamorphism only, excluding contact metamorphism associated
with emplacement of the Little Kalzas plutonic suite and Tatlmain
batholith (Colpron et al. 2006a;S t a p l e set al. 2016). The Tatl-
main batholith has also given a
40Ar/39Ar hornblende plateau age
of 343.7 ± 3.2 Ma that indicates rapid cooling to below theca. 530
◦C closure temperature of Ar in hornblende (McElhinny & McFad-
den 2000). However, nine 40Ar/39Ar ages and one K/Ar age with
a mean age of 196 ± 6 Ma have been reported for muscovite and
biotite from the Tatlmain batholith and Finlayson Assemblage in the
study area (Breitsprecher et al. 2004; Colpron et al. 2007b). This
cluster of ages indicates greenschist metamorphism, uplift, erosion
and cooling of the tectonic block from about 500 to 300 ◦Cb e -
tween about 205 and 190 Ma. Also in the Early Jurassic, the Stikine
terrane of the IMB impacted on the southwest side of the YTT,
resulting in regional folding, thrust faulting and the emplacement
of the large Tatchun granitic batholith along the southwest side of
the studied tectonic block (Fig. 2). Tatchun batholith has yielded
seven
40Ar/39Ar biotite dates with a mean of 185 ± 5 Ma (Colpron
et al. 2007b).
2.3 Post-Finlayson assemblages of the YTT
Outside of our study area, the Finlayson Assemblage is uncon-
formably overlain by the Klinkit Assemblage. It includes Middle
Mississippian to Early Permian intermediate to maﬁc volcanoclas-
tic, volcanic and limestone rocks that are deemed to record conti-
nental arc magmatism and intra-arc rifting environments (Colpron
2001; Colpron et al. 2006a). The adjacent oceanic Slide Mountain
Assemblage is composed of Mississippian to Early Permian chert,
argillite and basalt, and hence is about coeval with the Klinquit
Assemblage. Both the Slide Mountain and Klinkit assemblages are
unconformably overlain by the Klondike Assemblage, which con-
sists of Middle to Late Permian calc-alkaline felsic rocks with minor
maﬁc volcanic rocks and comagmatic plutons. This assemblage has
the geochemical signature of continental arc magmatism, and it
corresponds in time to the Klondike orogeny ( ∼275 to ∼260 Ma)
when the Slide Mountain oceanic terrane subducted under the YTT
(Mortensen 1992;N e l s o net al. 2006; Beranek & Mortensen 2011;
Parsons et al. 2019). A cover sequence of calcareous siltstones,
sandstones and shales unconformably overlaps the Yukon-Tanana,
Slide Mountain, Cassiar and Selwyn Basin terranes. Deposition be-
gan in latest Permian but occurred predominantly in the Middle and
Late Triassic (Colpron et al. 2006b). Pressure–temperature–time
(P–T–t) measurements on garnet and monazite crystals associated
with amphibolite-facies metamorphism indicate that ductile defor-
mation of the YTT occurred mostly between ∼264 and ∼254 Ma
in the Klondike orogeny at pressures of ∼9 kbar and temperatures
of ∼600
◦C during plutonism (Berman et al. 2007;S t a p l e set al.
2016).
2.4 Post-Middle Jurassic deformation
About 70 km south of our study area, Lithoprobe ran reﬂection
seismic and gravity proﬁles across the Whitehorse Trough (Calvert
et al. 2017). The proﬁles display a synform that is> 100 km across,
∼18–20 km deep and ﬁlled with deformed Mesozoic strata of the
Intermontane Belt (IMB). The synform overlies about 16–18 km
of YTT rocks in large-scale imbricate structures and the Cassiar
terrane of the North American craton. In the synform are folded
formations of the Triassic Lewes River Group, Lower to Middle
Jurassic Laberge Group and Middle Jurassic to Lower Cretaceous
Tantalus Formation, which suggests signiﬁcant compression after
the mid-Cretaceous (Parson et al. 2018). Further south in Yukon
and northern British Columbia, the Lewes River Group is an overlap
assemblage on the Stikinia, Quesnellia and Cache Creek terranes
(Colpron et al. 2015;S t a p l e set al. 2016).
Three major Cretaceous-to-Eocene plate tectonic processes may
have been important in the evolution of the YTT. One is the easterly
subduction and collision of the Farallon and Kula plates with North
America and the related intrusion of the Coast Plutonic Complex
(CPC) from ∼140 to ∼40 Ma along the western margin of the
YTT (Engebretson et al. 1985). The second process is the counter-
clockwise rotation of the Arctic Alaskan plate to open the Canada
basin in the Arctic Ocean, and to close against the western side of
Yukon from∼150 Ma to ∼80 Ma (Plafker & Berg1994). The third
process is the∼500 to> 1000 km of dextral shear displacement both
along and between the Tintina and Coast Shear Zones on either side
of the YTT from the mid-Early Cretaceous to the Eocene (Gabrielse
et al. 2006; McCausland et al. 2006; Symons et al. 2006; 2017).
2.5 Plate tectonic models for the YTT
Parsons et al. (2019) evaluated and assigned the published tec-
tonic models for the YTT into three categories, i.e. the Klondike
Orogeny, Intra-Oceanic Arc and Cordilleran Ribbon models. The
Klondike Orogeny model and its variants suggest that the YTT is
an allochthonous continental island arc terrane that rifted from the
Laurentian margin in the Devonian-Early Mississippian, travelled
northwestwards (NW) in the Panthalassa Ocean to deposit the Slide
Mountain Ocean on its eastern side, then travelled northeastwards to
close the Slide Mountain Ocean, and ﬁnally obducted onto, and ac-
creted with, the North American plate in the Late Permian Klondike
orogeny with continuing sedimentation and magmatism to the Early
Jurassic (Mortensen 1992; Colpron et al. 2006b, 2007b, 2015; Nel-
son et al.

island arc that formed at 270–280 Ma in the Slide Mountain ocean,
that the YTT subducted eastwards under the arc and accreted to it
in the latter Permian from 272 to 252 Ma, and that the arc then
collided with, and accreted to, the western margin of Laurentia af-

Middle Jurassic (van Staal et al. 2018; Parsons et al. 2019).
The Cordilleran Ribbon model proposes that the YTT and IMB
were part of SA YBIA, an∼8000 km long by ≤600 km wide con-
tinent that formed along and offshore of western North America in
the Panthalassa ocean (Johnston2001). SA YBIA was assembled by
Late Triassic–Early Jurassic accretion of the IMB overthrusting the
YTT and was stitched together by ∼186 Ma plutons at a location
∼3000 km to the south and offshore of Mexico (Johnston & Erdmer
1995; Johnston 2008; Hildebrand 2009). The model proposes that
SA YBIA was translated slowly northwards from the Early Juras-
sic to Early Cretaceous, colliding initially with North America at
∼120 Ma. From ∼120 to ∼40 Ma, dextral transpression on strike-
slip faults moved the YTT and IMB northwards by ∼2000 km,
bulldozed a large region of the continental foreland eastwards on
thrust faults and folds to form the Mackenzie and Rocky Mountains,
and intruded a series of eastward-younging (140–40 Ma) plutons to
create the Coast Ranges.
3 METHODS
3.1 Sampling
The Ragged and Tatlmain intrusions are located in a remote moun-
tainous region of Yukon, requiring helicopter access with few poten-
tial landing locations because of recessive weathering. Therefore,
two well-separated sites were sampled at each landing location. At
each site, six cores were drilled and oriented using a solar compass
in most instances or a magnetic compass with topographic checks
in a few instances. A total of 34 sites were collected with 14 from
the Ragged stock and 20 from the Tatlmain batholith. From 7 to 16
standard paleomagnetic specimens were sliced from the cores for
each site for palaeomagnetic measurement, yielding a total of 412
specimens.
3.2 Measurements
After storage for several months in a magnetically shielded room,
the natural remanent magnetization (NRM) of each specimen was
measured using an automated vertical 2G Enterprises 3-axis DC
SQUID cryogenic magnetometer with a sensitivity of∼2 × 10
−6 A
m−1 for a standard specimen. T wo example specimens per site were
subjected to alternating ﬁeld (AF) demagnetization in 14 steps up to
140 mT using a Sapphire Instruments SI-4 demagnetizer. Next, one
of these two specimens per site was subjected to saturation isother-
mal remanent magnetization (SIRM) tests by pulse magnetizing it
in a direct current (DC) ﬁeld in 13 steps up to 900 mT, which is
taken to give a saturation remanence ( J
900), using a Sapphire In-
struments SI-6 DC pulse magnetizer and then AF demagnetizing it
in eight steps up to 150 mT. A second pair of example specimens
per site were subjected to thermal (TH) demagnetization in 16 steps
up to 600 or 610
◦C using a Magnetic measurements MMTD-80
oven. Following examination of the data from the AF and TH step
demagnetization of the example specimens, up to eight additional
specimens per site were TH demagnetized in 12 steps up to 610
◦C, except that a small number of glued specimens were AF de-
magnetized in 10 steps up to 80 mT. The specimen characteristic
remanent magnetization (ChRM) directions were obtained using
vector density plots (Kamb 1959), orthogonal vector component
plots (Zijderveld 1967) and least-squares vector ﬁtting (Kirschvink
1980) methods. The great-circle technique was not used to obtain
any ChRM directions (Bailey & Halls 1984). The specimen ChRM
directions were then averaged to obtain the site mean ChRM direc-
tions and they in turn averaged to get the unit mean ChRM directions
following Fisher (1953).
4 RESULTS
4.1 Natural remanent magnetization (NRM)
The 173 measured specimens of maﬁc syenite from Ragged
stock have NRM intensities that range between 2.17 × 10
−4 and
5.91 × 100 Am −1 with median ( M) and quartile ( Q)v a l u e so f
M = 2.25 × 10−3 (Q1 = 1.01 × 10−3, Q3 = 2.02 × 10−2)Am −1
(Table 1). In contrast, the 239 measured specimens of granodiorite
from Tatlmain batholith have NRM intensities that are about an or-
der of magnitude weaker with values that range between 3.36× 10−5
and 4.02 × 10−1 Am −1 with M = 1.34 × 10−3 (Q1 = 3.64 × 10−4,
Q3 = 5.67 × 10−3)Am −1 (Table 1).
4.2 Progressive AF demagnetization
On progressive AF step demagnetization, after removal of the vis-
cous remanent magnetization (VRM) by ∼15 mT, the specimens
from both the Ragged and Tatlmain plutons retain a consistent re-
manence direction up to the 20–50 mT step but have lost∼75 ± 10
per cent of their NRM intensity (Fig.4). This behaviour is typically
indicative of titanomagnetite, coarse-grained magnetite or possibly
pyrrhotite (Dunlop & ¨Ozdemir 1997). After this initial intensity
decrease, the specimens of the two plutons behave differently. The
Ragged stock specimens mostly exhibit erratic changes in both re-
manence direction and intensity, which is indicative of the presence
of either titanomagnetite or coarse-grained magnetite with a sig-
niﬁcant initial VRM component (Figs 4a and b). This behaviour is
well illustrated by Kamb (1959) plots where the remanence vectors
for the 15–30 mT steps form a highly coherent population (Fig.5a)
that degrades rapidly by the 40–70 mT steps (Fig.5b) and becomes
entirely scattered by the 80 mT step and above.
After the initial rapid intensity decrease up to 20–50 mT, the
Tatlmain specimens mostly continue on further AF step demag-
netization to decay fairly smoothly in direction but more slowly
in intensity (Figs 4c and d) and to deﬁne a coherent population
of vector directions up to 160 mT (Figs 5c and d). This pattern
of remanence of AF demagnetization suggests that the Tatlmain
specimens retain, in addition to a titanomagnetite or multidomain
magnetite component, a pseudo-single (PSD) or single domain (SD)
magnetite, pyrrhotite or hematite remanence component.

5 DISCUSSION
5.1 Magnetic remanence
Progressive AF and TH demagnetization showed that the ChRM
of both Ragged stock and Tatlmain batholith was carried by PSD-
SD magnetite and titanomagnetite with a composition of about
Fe
2.8Ti0.2O4 ( ¨Ozdemir & O’Reilly1981). In addition, Ragged stock
carries a trace component of hematite and Tatlmain batholith carries
at r a c et o∼25 per cent ChRM component of hematite. Further, the
magnetite, titanomagnetite and hematite give near-collinear ChRM
directions in a given specimen, indicating that all three minerals
were crystallized or recrystallized at the same time.
Magnetite (Fe
3O4) and titanomagnetite (Fez−xTixO4) withx ≈ 0.6
form a solid solution series. Both minerals are common in volcanic
rocks, especially submarine basalts, and give Curie temperatures
of 580 and 150 ◦C, respectively (Dunlop & ¨Ozdemir 1997). Meta-
morphic heating in an oxidizing environment causes the titano-
magnetite to invert irreversibly to titanomaghemite and ultimately
to exsolve to a mixture of magnetite, titanomagnetite, ilmenite,
hematite, titanohematite and pseudo-brookite. With sufﬁcient heat-
ing, any residual primary magnetite and resulting magnetite, titano-
magnetite, hematite and titanohematite acquire a secondary remag-
netization thermochemical remanent magnetization (TCRM) with
a common ChRM direction. Thus, we interpret both Ragged stock
and Tatlmain batholith to retain a secondary TCRM from metamor-
phism. The ﬁnding of a dominant magnetite—titanomagnetite—
hematite remanence association has not been previously reported
in YTT palaeomagnetic studies, however, it is not surprising given
that the lower Finlayson Assemblage is deemed to be a volcanic arc
tectonic assemblage (Colpron et al. 2006b).
When the unit mean ChRM directions for Ragged and Tatlmain
plutons are compared using the correlation test of McFadden &
Lowes (1981), the calculated statistic F = 0.02 is much less than
the 95 per cent conﬁdence comparison statistic of F
2.54 = 3.17,
which indicates that their ChRM’s are not signiﬁcantly different
at 95 per cent conﬁdence and were likely acquired in the same
metamorphic event.
5.2 Tectonic considerations
5.2.1 Study area translation correction
It is necessary to make several tectonic corrections before com-
paring palaeopoles from the Tatlmain and Ragged plutons to the
N o r t hA m e r i c a nA P W Po fT o r s v i ket al. (2012) to test for trans-
lation or rotation of the YTT relative to the North American
craton. First, our study area in the YTT was translated NW by
∼490 km relative to the craton by dextral displacement on the
Tintina fault zone between ∼100 and ∼50 Ma (Gabrielse et al.
2006; McCausland et al. 2006; Symons et al. 2017). This correction
moves the mean location of the study area from 62.7
◦N, 224.2◦E
to 59.6◦N, 231.0◦E relative to North America in the present day
co-ordinates.

5.2.2 Batholith rotation corrections
The Tatlmain batholith has been deformed into a sigmoidal shape
with its northwestern and central limbs giving different ChRM di-
rections (Fig. 2). The northwestern limb trends WNW ( ∼305◦)i n
declination and its seven sites (sites 23, 26, 27, 29–32) give a mean
ChRM direction of D = 353.6◦, I = 69.8◦ (N = 7, k = 60.4,
α95 = 7.8◦), and the central limb trends NNW ( ∼345◦) and its
10 sites (sites 15–22, 33, 34) give a signiﬁcantly different mean
ChRM direction of D = 12.7◦, I = 74.1◦ (N = 10, k = 116.3,
α95 = 4.5◦) at 95 per cent conﬁdence (McFadden & Lowes 1981).
The sigmoid’s vestigial southeastern limb is truncated by the Big
Salmon fault zone (Fig. 2). It is likely that the batholith’s sigmoidal
shape is a response to the two stages of deformation observed in
the lower Finlayson Assemblage host rocks (M. Colpron, personal
communication, 2018). Palaeomagnetic methods have long been
used to demonstrate tectonic rotation in apparently massive plutons
(Symons 1977). Further, a palaeomagnetic fold test can be used to
determine if the ChRM in a deformed rock unit is pre-folding, syn-
folding or post-folding (Graham 1949; McFadden & Jones 1981;
Butler 1992). Thus, tectonic corrections are necessary for the fold-
ing to remove the effects of rotation in the Tatlmain batholith.
The northwestern limb of Tatlmain batholith parallels the re-
gional tectonic trend of folds and faults in the YTT and surround-
ing terranes of central Yukon. The change in tectonic trend is∼40
◦
clockwise (cw) on going from the northwestern limb’s ∼305◦ re-
gional trend to the central limb’s ∼345◦ anomalous trend. Run-
ning a declination-only fold test by rotating Tatlmain’s central limb
counter-clockwise by 19◦ ± 4◦ of the 40◦ trend change brings the
two mean ChRM directions into best alignment. The fold test re-
sult implies that the ChRM is synfolding and was acquired when
rotational deformation was about 50 ± 10 per cent complete. The
result also implies that the ChRM inclination of the central limb
was further steepened by 4.3 ◦ during the original rotation. Given
that Tatlmain’s ChRM is mostly retained in titanomagnetite at un-
blocking temperatures of ≤500
◦C, it is evident that the syndefor-
mational ChRM is probably recording the regional Early Jurassic
metamorphic cooling and deformational episode on average. This
timing suggests that the anomalous central-limb trend was caused
by the bending of the batholith and its host rocks around the north-
west end of the southeastern slice of pericratonic Cassiar terrane
as the IMB impacted on southwest side of the YTT (Fig. 2). The
fold test results suggest that the likeliest estimate for Tatlmain’s
ChRM direction after rotation correction but before tilt correction
is given by (1) accepting the measured ChRM directions for sites on
the regionally trending northwestern limb, (2) fully correcting the
measured ChRM directions of sites on the anomalously trending
central limb by subtracting 40
◦ from the declination and 9 ◦ from
the inclination and (3) combining the resulting 17 site mean ChRM
directions into one unit mean direction. The result of this two-step
correction process gives a unit mean direction before tilt correc-
tion for the Tatlmain batholith of D = 340.9
◦, I = 67.6◦ (N = 17,
k = 54.8, α95 = 4.9◦). Further, Ragged stock is located beside
Tatlmain batholith’s central limb (Fig.2). The stock’s mean ChRM
direction ofD= 13.1◦, I= 74.3◦ (N= 12, k= 45.0,α95 = 6.5◦) is vir-
tually identical to the batholith’s central limb direction ofD = 12.7◦,
I = 74.1◦ (N = 10, k = 116.3, α95 = 4.5◦) before rotation correction.
Therefore, the same correction procedure is used for the Ragged
stock sites as used for the Tatlmain’s central limb sites, giving a
rotation-corrected unit mean ChRM direction for Ragged stock of
D = 333.1
◦, I = 65.3◦ (N = 12, k = 45.0, α95 = 6.5◦) before tilt
correction.
