5.2.3 Tilt corrections
Finally, it is necessary to correct both the Tatlmain and Ragged
ChRM directions for tectonic tilts that postdate the acquisition of the
ChRM. The∼70 Ma Carmacks volcanics unconformably overlie the
Tatlmain batholith and dip at 5◦NE (Tempelman-Kluit 1984). This
tilt postdates the formation of Tatlmain’s and Ragged’s TCRMs but
predates the post-70 Ma tectonic translation of the YTT. Thus 5◦NE
is the initial required tilt correction. Further, the metasediments of
the host lower Finlayson Assemblage outcrop along the northeastern
side of the Tatlmain batholith. These metasediments dip at 20◦–40◦
NE (M. Colpron, personal communication, 2018), or at 30 ◦ ± 7◦
NE assuming a normal distribution of the dip values. The 30◦ ± 7◦
NE value includes the 5◦ NE post-70 Ma tilt, leaving 25◦ ± 7◦ NE
for pre-70 Ma tilt as a maximum value. Guided by the results of
the ‘declination-only’ fold test that shows that Tatlmain batholith’s
synfolding ChRM was acquired when folding was ∼50 per cent
completed of the 25
◦ ± 7◦, the best estimate for tilting at the time
of ChRM acquisition is 13 ◦ ± 7◦ NE. Combining the 5 ◦ NE and
13◦ ± 7◦ NE corrections gives a ‘best estimate’ for tilt correction
of 18◦ ± 7◦ NE. Using the 305◦ regional structural trend for strike
and the 18◦ tilt correction gives an estimated tilt-corrected ChRM
direction of D = 3.2◦, I = 54.1◦ (α95 = 4.9◦) for Tatlmain batholith
and of D = 356.1◦, I = 53.4◦ (α95 = 6.5◦) for Ragged stock.
The combination of a 305 ◦-trending northwestern limb dipping at
18◦N and a 345 ◦-trending central limb dipping at 18 ◦E provides
an estimate that the Tatlmain batholith has been deformed into an
anticlinal shape that plunges at∼22◦ towards N55◦E. Finally, using
a mean site location of 231.0 ◦E, 59.6◦N to correct for post-100
Ma translation on the Tintina fault zone and the tilt-corrected unit
mean ChRM directions, the tectonically corrected palaeopoles are
located at 64.9
◦N, 44.8◦E( A95 = 5.9◦) for the Tatlmain batholith
and at 64.2◦N, 58.5◦E( A95 = 7.7◦) for the Ragged stock.
5.2.4 Fit of the Tatlmain and Ragged palaeopoles to North
America
Given the imprecision of the structural attitudes and the complexity
of the tectonic correction process, it is evident that the Tatlmain
and Ragged palaeopoles may not be deemed to be suitable for use
in the construction of a conventional continental APWP . We ar-
gue, however, that the two palaeopoles are sufﬁciently reliable to
support a number of conclusions. First, the Tatlmain and Ragged
palaeopoles are notably closer to the 190 and 200 Ma palaeopoles
on the North American APWP of Torsvik et al.( 2012)t h a nt oa n y
of the path’s other palaeopoles (Fig. 10). This closeness supports
the conclusion that Tatlmain batholith and Ragged stock acquired
their TCRMs during the Early Jurassic metamorphic and orogenic
event. Thus, the palaeopoles’ ages agree with the 196 ± 6M aa v -
erage of nine Ar/Ar and one K-Ar radiometric determinations from
muscovite and biotite samples from the Tatlmain batholith and Fin-
layson Assemblage reported for the study area (Breitsprecher et al.
2004; Colpron et al. 2007b). Also the closeness supports the con-
clusions that the batholith’s sinusoidal outcrop pattern is structural
in origin, and that the stock was rotated tectonically after ChRM ac-
quisition but during post-emplacement deformation. Second, based
on their ChRM inclinations of 54.1
◦ and 53.4◦, the Tatlmain and
Ragged plutons were located at palaeolatitudes of 35 ◦ ± 5◦ and
34◦ ± 7◦, respectively. Relative to the study area, the 200 and 190
Ma palaeopoles on the North American APWP were similarly lo-
cated at palaeolatitudes of 36◦ ± 3◦ and 38◦ ± 4◦, respectively. This
co-incidence of palaeolatitudes, is independent of the accuracy of
the fold-limb declination estimates, and strongly supports the con-
clusion that the YTT was located close to the translation-corrected
collecting site of 59.6
◦N, 231.0◦E along North America’s cratonic
margin at 196 ± 6M a .
Relative to the 196 Ma reference palaeopole for North Amer-
ica of Torsvik et al. (2012), the Tatlmain and Ragged plutons have
undergone NW translations of 3.1 ◦ ± 5.3◦ and 3.7◦ ± 6.6◦,u s i n g
the calculation method of Demarest (1983), as well as cw rotations
of 18.7◦ ± 6.5◦ and 11.6◦ ± 8.1◦, respectively. The 3.1 ◦ ± 5.3◦
and 3.7◦ ± 6.6◦ estimates support the conclusion that the YTT was
close to the pluton’s pre-70 Ma translation-corrected collecting site
on North America’s cratonic margin or perhaps ∼200 km further
southeast at 196 Ma. Also, the 18.7
◦ ± 6.5◦ and 11.6◦ ± 8.1◦ cw ro-
tation estimates indicate that both the Tatlmain batholith and Ragged
stock underwent about 15
◦ ± 7◦ more cw rotation than accounted
for by the rotation corrections. This rotation undercorrection is not
surprising given the lack of marker horizons in the two plutons.

5.3 Y ukon-Tanana terrane’s palaeowander path
There are 13 palaeopoles from the YTT for the Late Triassic to
present (Table 3). More recent radiometric age dating informa-
tion is now available for some of the older palaeopoles. The Big
Creek batholith has yielded a 206Pb/238U zircon crystallization age
of 185.0 ± 0.1 Ma and four K/Ar hornblende ages of 189 ± 4,
184 ± 7, 152 ± 7 and 142 ± 10 Ma that deﬁne an ∼47 Ma cool-
ing history centred on about 165 Ma (Stevens et al. 1982; Hunt &
Roddick 1987; M. Colpron, personal communication, 2018). The
cooling history is compatible with six Al-in-hornblende geothermo-
barometric determinations that yield a ∼16 ± 2 km emplacement

age groups of 69 ± 1, 101 ± 10, 165 and 198 ± 4M at h a tg i v e
mean translation distances of −1◦ ± 15◦,0 ◦ ± 14◦,2 ◦ ± 10◦
and −2◦ ± 13◦, respectively, relative to their respective North
America reference palaeopoles (Table 3). None of these four age
groups from the Cretaceous and Jurassic are signiﬁcantly differ-

conﬁdence. Overall, the ﬁve YTT palaeopole age groups give an
average translation distance of 1.6
◦ ± 3.4◦ NW or 180 ± 380 km.
This 180 ± 380 km translation distance agrees with the geologi-
cal estimate of 490 ± 30 km of Gabrielse et al. (2006)f o rN W
displacement of the YTT on the Tintina fault zone during mid-
Cretaceous to Eocene time. Further, because the four groups of
Mesozoic palaeopoles ﬁt the North American APWP so closely,
they give errors for the terrane rotation values that are highly vari-
able or even incalculable. Nonetheless, the 3 ◦ ± 4◦ cw average
rotation for the means of the four groups does imply that the YTT
overall in Yukon was not rotated signiﬁcantly with respect to North
America since the Late Triassic. The fact that the 12 Cretaceous and
Jurassic palaeopoles from the YTT yield both non-signiﬁcant ter-
rane translation and rotation on average provides powerful evidence
that the YTT was accreted solidly to North America by the start
of the Jurassic, and that it is para-autochthonous only because of
Cretaceous–Eocene translation on the Tintina fault zone. The para-
autochthonous conclusion further reﬁnes the YTT tectonic model
given by Symonset al.( 2015, 2017) for the Late and mid-Cretaceous
and extends the model back in time to the latest Triassic.
5.4 The YTT-IMB tectonic relationship
It has long been evident that terranes along the southern coast of
Alaska and the western coast of British Columbia, termed ‘Baja
Alaska’ and ‘Baja BC’, respectively, have been rafted northwards
from mid-palaeolatitudes (Stone 1977; Irving 1985). In their sum-
mary of the post-Palaeozoic palaeomagnetic results from the YTT
and IMB terranes, Symons et al. (2005) noted that the two YTT
Jurassic palaeopoles then available (BC and GM in Table 2)i n -
dicated that the YTT had ‘been close to its present position and
unrotated with respect to the craton at least since the Early Juras-
sic’. Palaeomagnetic results from the Taylor Mountain batholith and
now from this study have conﬁrmed that the YTT has been a para-
autochthonous terrane of North America since the Late Triassic
(Symons et al. 2009, 2015), and that is was not part of the hypothe-

Symons & Kawasaki (2011) compared the available palaeopoles

conclude that the YTT was not part of ‘Baja BC’ but was part of
the cratonic marginal ramp since the Early Jurassic.

palaeopole. Lowe et al. (2001) concluded from the study of mostly
deformed and altered rocks in and near the Endako molybdenite
mine that the Jurassic intrusions had suffered Eocene tilting and
remagnetization. Symons et al. (2005) discussed and disputed their
conclusion. Nonetheless, the palaeopole is close to ∼173 Ma on
the North American APWP whereas virtually all other ≤130 Ma
palaeopoles from Stikinia are cw rotated by tens of degrees (Harris
et al. 1997a,b, 1999a). One possible explanation may be that YTT
or equivalent rocks are exposed in a window through the Stikine
terrane. The second deviant Jurassic palaeopole is from the 177± 4
Ma Teslin Crossing pluton, which comes from a small collection of
sites with too large anA
95 value of 16.5◦ to be reliable (Harris et al.
1999b). The third and fourth Jurassic palaeopoles come from the
173 ± 3 Ma dikes and 177 ± 4 Ma host rocks of the Fourth of July
batholith (Table 3). The dikes and batholith belong to the Cache
Creek terrane of the IMB and they give very different translation
and rotation values to those found in either Stikinia or Quesnellia
(Harris et al. 2003).
5.5 Fit of palaeopoles to tectonic models
Coherent terrane APWPs are available for the Canadian Cordillera
for only the YTT back through the Early Jurassic and the IMB back
through the Early Cretaceous. Any acceptable tectonic model for
the Cordillera should give terrane palaeopole locations that align
with these APWPs. Here we evaluate the Klondike Orogeny, Intra-
Oceanic Arc, Cordilleran Ribbon and Orogenic Wedge models.
The ﬁve Jurassic YTT palaeopoles acquired their remanence in
three fashions. The Taylor Mountain and Granite Mountain plutons
(palaeopoles TM and GM) retain dominantly primary Early Juras-
sic TRMs upon intrusion. The Big Creek batholith (BC) retains
a dominantly secondary Middle Jurassic remagnetization TRM or
TCRM of its primary Early Jurassic remanence that was acquired
upon uplift. The Ragged stock’s and Tatlmain batholith’s (RS, TL)
primary TRMs were also remagnetized to secondary TCRMs during
the Early Jurassic. As discussed earlier in Section 2.5, the Klondike
Orogeny model postulates that the YTT collided with the North
American plate in the Late Permian with subsequent deposition
of an Early-Middle Triassic burial sedimentary assemblage and
Late Triassic—Early Jurassic arc sequence that record compression,
metamorphism and magmatism (Colpron et al. 2006b; Beranek &
Mortensen 2011; Nelson et al. 2013). Similarly, the Intra-Oceanic
Arc model proposes that the YTT collided and accreted with the
Slide Mountain terrane in the Middle to Late Permian, that together
they collided with the North American plate in the Middle Triassic,
and that orogenesis continued through the Early Jurassic (van Staal
et al. 2018; Parsons et al. 2019). Thus both the Klondike Orogeny
and Intra-Oceanic Arc models provide the necessary geologic con-
ditions in the Early and Middle Jurassic to yield concordant YTT
palaeopoles to the North American APWP , However, neither model
describes the subsequent geologic evolution of the YTT in either
plate or terrane tectonic terms. We note that the North American
APWP exhibits a major cusp in the Early Jurassic but no cusp in the
Middle Permian (Torsviket al. 2008, 2012). The APWP cusp is in-
dicative that the North American plate was involved in a major Early
Jurassic tectonic collision that caused it to undergo a major change
in its drift direction and velocity, which favours the Intra-Oceanic
Arc model over the Klondike Orogeny model.
To its credit, the Cordilleran Ribbon model attempts to explain
the evolution of the major Mesozoic-Cenozoic tectonic features
of the western North American Cordillera (Ross & Ross 1983).
Unfortunately, Johnston (2001, 2008) chose to base this model for
the Canadian Cordillera solely on the anomalous palaeolatitude of
the Carmacks volcanics’ palaeopole (Symonset al. 2017), and it is
anomalous relative to > 25 Mesozoic-Cenozoic palaeopoles from
the YTT, IMB and Selwyn basin (Symonset al. 2005; Enkin 2006;
Symons & Kawasaki2011; Kawasaki & Symons2012). Overall, the
Cordilleran Ribbon model does not provide a good ﬁt to the APWPs
of either the YTT or IMB terrane for any Mesozoic-Cenozoic time
period.
To summarize, both the Klondike Orogeny and Intra-Oceanic
Arc tectonic models are consistent with the post-Triassic APWP
for the YTT by concluding that the YTT accreted to North Amer-
ica prior to the Jurassic. Other than participating in ∼500 km of
Cretaceous–Eocene dextral displacement on the Tintina and par-
allel fault zones, the exposed YTT remained a stable unrotated-
overall para-autochthonous terrane of North America and provided
the metamorphosed basement for the overlying post-Triassic IMB
strata.
Staples et al. (2014, 2016) have proposed an ‘Orogenic Wedge’
model to explain the Mesozoic tectonic evolution of the northern
Canadian Cordillera. They interpret metamorphism, exhumation
and deformation in Yukon to be diachronous in both the YTT and
IMB strata. They suggest that the YTT and trailing IMB terranes
were carried northeasterly (orogen-perpendicular) on thrust faults
up and over the subducting western marginal ramp of the North
American plate during the Early Jurassic to mid-Cretaceous inter-
val. The ﬁve Jurassic YTT palaeopoles, moving only ∼3
◦ along
the APWP , are quite consistent with the Orogenic Wedge model
(Fig. 10). Staples et al. (2016) suggest that the regional tectonic
kinematics on the YTT changed in the mid-Cretaceous at ∼110
Ma from orogen-perpendicular compression to orogen-parallel ex-
tension. This seems unlikely because plate modelling shows near-
orthogonal compression and closure between the Farallon and North
American plates of ∼150 ± 50 km Ma
−1 from about 125 to 90
Ma (Engebretson et al. 1985; Kelley 1993). Also, the seven mid-
Cretaceous to Palaeocene palaeopoles from the YTT are concordant
with the North American APWP after correction for 490 km of dex-
tral Late Cretaceous to Eocene strike-slip translation on the Tintina
fault zone (Table 3; Symons et al. 2015, 2017).
In contrast to the YTT, the Jurassic palaeopoles from the IMB
terranes—Stikinia, Quesnellia and Cache Creek—are widely scat-
tered with no consistent regional pattern of translation or rotation
(Symons et al. 2005; McCausland et al. 2006), suggesting the IMB
terranes were fragmented and variably rotated upon initial accretion
with each other and/or with the YTT and North America. However,
the Cretaceous and younger IMB palaeopoles, mostly from Yukon
and British Columbia in Stikinia, do show a consistent pattern from
the present back to ∼120 Ma of increasing northward translation
up to ∼10
◦ polewards and steadily increasing rotation up to ∼55◦
cw relative to North America (Table 3). Historically, this pattern
of northward translation and cw rotation has been interpreted by
palaeomagnetists to signify that the IMB was part of ‘Baja BC’,
having been carried northwards along the western margin of North
America during the mid-Cretaceous and then being rotated cw on
accretion (Irving & Wynne 1991; Symons et al. 2005).
However, if the IMB was accreted to North America by the Early
Jurassic as the Klondike Orogeny and Oceanic-Arc models pro-
pose, then the ‘Baja BC’ model is wrong and a new tectonic model
is required to explain the IMB palaeopoles. It is also true to point
out here that no plausible plate tectonic model has been published
yet to explain the Laramide orogeny in the Mackenzie, Ogilvie
and Richardson mountain ranges of Yukon. Recently, Hayward

the ∼55
◦ cw rotation found in the IMB’s Cretaceous palaeopoles
is recording upper-crustal Laramide deformation that is not found
in the lower-crustal rocks of the YTT. From ∼120 to ∼80 Ma the
Yukon region was subject to active Laramide deformation. The
Farallon plate was converging perpendicularly against the western
margin of North America at a rate of ∼150 km Ma
-1, thereby cre-
ating northeasterly directed compression with the intrusion of the
massive plutons of the outer CPC along the margin (Monger et al.

North American plate and rotated by∼66
◦ ccw to open the Canada
basin in the Arctic ocean. Arctic Alaska rotated about a pole located
near the Mackenzie delta, potentially causing an increasingly wide
wedge of Arctic Alaska to compress against, and overlap with, the
western side of Yukon (Fig11), which could generate south-easterly
to easterly compression in Yukon (Carey 1955;G r a n t zet al. 1979;
Plafker & Berg 1994). This kinematic scenario could have caused
upper-crustal IMB rocks to be rotated cw over lower crustal YTT
rocks, and co-incidentally drive the upper crustal rocks easterly to
form the Mackenzie, Ogilvie and Richardson mountains. Evidence
for Eocene to present cw rotation of the upper crust in Yukon with
related shortening and thrust faulting is described in Symons et al.
(2004) and extended to the mid-Cretaceous in Symonset al. (2005).
In these papers Symons et al.( 2004, 2005) also point to evidence
for upper-crustal cw rotation and extension in the IMB in southern
British Columbia. Note also, if the established ∼500 km of dex-
tral displacement on the Tintina fault extends southwards through
British Columbia on the Northern Rocky Mountain Trench fault,
then the ‘translation poleward’ estimates given in Table 3 for the
IMB are all decreased by ∼5
◦ to become non-signiﬁcant, and only
the rotation estimates are signiﬁcant at 95 per cent conﬁdence.
Many papers in Haggartet al.(2006) summarize palaeomagnetic,
palaeontologic, tectonic, sedimentary and other evidence for hun-
dreds to low thousands of kilometres of northward displacement of
the IMB and Insular Belt terranes relative to North America with
cw rotations, and subsequent studies continue to add to the con-
cept (Johnston 2008; Hildebrand 2009; Symons & Kawasaki 2011;
Sz˝ucs et al. 2019)
6 CONCLUSIONS
Palaeomagnetic results from 29 sites have shown that the Missis-
sippian Tatlmain batholith and Ragged stock in the Finlayson As-
semblage of the YTT of the Canadian Cordillera carry a very stable
TCRM that resides in magnetite, titanomagnetite and hematite. A
declination-only palaeomagnetic fold test about a 40
◦ bend in the
batholith’s outcrop pattern shows that the TCRM is ∼50 per cent
synfolding. Multiple 40Ar/39Ar and K-Ar radiometric age deter-
minations date the TCRM at 196 ± 6 Ma during a major Early
Jurassic deformation and metamorphic event. After tectonic cor-
rection for fold rotation, regional dip in the overlying host rocks,

American palaeopoles. The agreement of the YTT and North Amer-
ican palaeopoles since the latest Triassic asserts that the YTT began
accretion to the craton by the Early Jurassic.
Since accretion, the YTT has undergone: (1) Early Jurassic to
mid-Cretaceous orogen-perpendicular compression that resulted
in palaeomagnetically non-signiﬁcant ( ≤ 200 km) northeasterly
shortening on thrust sheets and (2) northwesterly Late Cretaceous
to Eocene dextral orogen-parallel translation of ∼500 km on the
Tintina fault zone. In contrast, the Cretaceous and younger strata
and plutons of the overlying Stikinia, Quesnellia and Cache Creek
(?) terranes of the IMB underwent∼55
◦ cw rotation from the upper-
crust rotation of the IMB over lower crustal YTT rocks (Symonset
al. 2004, 2005) on a recently discovered regional d´ecollement (Hay-
ward 2019) in response to surrounding coeval Laraminde regional
tectonic forces associated with (1) the Laramide subduction of the
Paciﬁc plate under North America and the related intrusion of the
Coast Plutonic Complex; (2) the rotation of the Arctic Alaska plate;
(3) the uplift of the arcuate Mackenzie, Ogilvie and Richardson
mountain ranges; and (4) subsequent modiﬁcation by translation
along the Tintina and Denali faults.

Gondwana reconstructions. However, estimates of Greater India extent have significant discrepancies in the Early 
Cretaceous. Here we report geochronologic and paleomagnetic studies on rocks of the Jiabula Formation in the 
northern subzone of the Tethyan Himalaya. The studied limestones are characterized by two-component mag -

1. Introduction
Greater India ( Argand, 1924 ) refers to a part of continental litho -
sphere that extended farther north from the northern margin of the In -
dian continent in Late Mesozoic East Gondwana reconstructions 
( Veevers et al., 1975 ). Greater India, together with Indian continent, 
rifted away from the Eastern Gondwana during the late Jurassic to early 
Cretaceous ( Powell et al., 1988 ). It moved fast as an individual entity 
with the rest of India, and collided with Asia, and helped to form the 
Tibetan Plateau ( Allegre et al., 1984; Ding et al., 2022 ). Therefore, 
knowledge of the original extension of Greater India in the Early 
Cretaceous is critical for understanding the paleogeography of the East 
Gondwana, the collision process between India and Asia, and the for -
mation of the Tibetan Plateau ( Molnar and Tapponnier, 1975; Yin, 2006; 
van Hinsbergen, 2022; Ding et al., 2022 ).
Paleomagnetism can be used to quantitatively determine the size of 
Greater India ( Yang et al., 2015; Huang et al., 2015; Ma et al., 2016; van 
Hinsbergen et al., 2019; Meng et al., 2019; Yuan et al., 2021, 2023; 
Dannemann et al., 2022; Bian et al., 2021, 2023; Xu et al., 2022; Jin 
et al., 2023 ). Two groups presented Early Cretaceous paleomagnetic 
results from the Lakang Formation lava flows in the southern subzone of 
the Tethyan Himalaya ( Yang et al., 2015; Meng et al., 2019 ). Based on 
the zircon U – Pb dates obtained from the interbedded volcanic rocks 
( Zhu et al., 2009 ), both studies assigned the Lakang Formation lava 
flows to an age of ca. 130 Ma. However, the two estimates of Greater 
India in the Early Cretaceous exhibit significant discrepancies ( Yang 
et al., 2015; Meng et al., 2019 ). Yang et al. (2015) obtained a paleo -
latitude of 52.2
◦
± 5.7
◦
S for the study area, which implied that Greater 
India had an extension of 230 ± 710 km. In contrast, Meng et al. (2019)
acquired a paleolatitude of 39.6 ± 7.6
◦
S for the study area, and suggested 
Greater India at least extended 1,950 ± 970 km. It should be noted that 
both paleomagnetic data sets are derived from lava flows, yet face 
challenges in fully averaging paleosecular variation. It is thus important 
to obtain high-quality Early Cretaceous paleomagnetic data from 
different sedimentary rocks in the Tethyan Himalaya.

2. Geologic setting and sampling
The Himalayan orogen belt consists of four tectonostratigraphic 
units: the Tethyan Himalaya, the Greater Himalaya, the Lesser Himalaya 
and the Sub-Himalaya from north to south ( Fig. 1 a and b). The tectonic 
boundaries of these units consist of the Indus-Yarlung Tsangpo Suture, 
the South Tibet Detachment System, the Main Central Thrust, and the 
Main Boundary Thrust ( Fig. 1 a and b). The Tethyan Himalaya contains 
Proterozoic � Eocene marine sedimentary sequences, as well as Paleo -
zoic and Mesozoic volcanic rocks ( Yin, 2006 ), which can be further 
divided into the southern and northern subzones by the Gyirong- 
Kangmar thrust ( Yin, 1988; Liu and Einsele, 1994 ). The Middle 
Jurassic � Upper Cretaceous strata of the northern subzone, exposed in 
our study region, consist of five formations: the Middle Jurassic Zhela 
Formation, the Upper Jurassic Weimei Formation, the Upper Jurassic �
Lower Cretaceous Sangxiu Formation, the Lower Cretaceous Jiabula 
Formation, and the Upper Cretaceous Zongzhuo Formation ( Fig. 1 c). 
The Sangxiu Formation mainly consists of the dark shale in the lower 
part and the volcanic rock in the upper part. The ammonite species from 
the dark shale in the lower part indicate a Berriasian � Valanginian age 
( Wan et al., 2005 ), while the volcanic rocks in the upper part are dated 
as 133 ± 3 Ma ( Zhu et al., 2005 ). The Sangxiu Formation is thus assigned 
to a Berriasian � Hauterivian age, and the age of the overlying Jiabula 
Formation should be later than the Hauterivian, as suggested by Wan 
et al. (2005) . The Jiabula Formation is well exposed at the Zhangda 
section in Nagarze, about 200 m thick, and mainly consists of grey 
medium bedded limestone in the lower part, and medium bedded 
sandstone intercalated with thin mudstone in the middle part, and basalt 
and andesite lava flow in the upper part ( Fig. 1 d).
We drilled 242 core samples at 27 sites from limestone beds of the 
Jiabala Formation from the lower part of the Zhangda section ( Fig. 1 d �
f), using a gasoline-powered portable drill. The bedding of sites

3. Methods
The U-Pb isotope compositions of zircon were measured in situ using 
an Agilent 7500a Quadrupole-ICP-MS coupled with a GeoLasHD 193 nm 
ArF excimer laser ablation system at Institute of Geology and 
Geophysics, Chinese Academy of Sciences. Backscattered electron (BSE) 
images and energy dispersive spectroscopy analysis were performed 
using a scanning electron microscope (FEI Nova NanoSEM 450) with an 
energy dispersive spectrometer (Oxford X-MAX80) at the Electron Mi -
croscopy Laboratory, Institute of Geology and Geophysics, Chinese 
Academy of Sciences.
Room-temperature magnetic experiments, including hysteresis 
loops, isothermal remanent magnetization (IRM) acquisition curves, and 
backfield demagnetization curves, were carried out using a Princeton 
Measurements Corporation MicroMag 3900 vibrating sample magne -
tometer. Stepwise thermal demagnetization experiments were con -
ducted using a PGL-100 thermal demagnetizer developed by Qin et al. 
(2020) . The specimen remanences were measured on a 2-G Enterprises 
Model 755 cryogenic magnetometer. All the rock magnetic and paleo -
magnetic measurements were performed at the Paleomagnetism and 
Geochronology Laboratory (PGL), Institute of Geology and Geophysics, 
Chinese Academy of Sciences. Demagnetization data were fitted by 
principal component analysis ( Kirschvink, 1980 ). Paleomagnetic data 
were analyzed using the Paleomac software developed by Cogn ´e (2003) . 
The mean directions were analyzed using classic Fisher statistics ( Fisher, 
1953 ).

MS U – Pb zircon dating ( Fig. 2 ; Table S1 ). The zircons are rounded to 
subrounded with clear oscillatory zoning for the most grains in these two 
samples. The Th/U ratios of the zircons (0.2 – 1.58) in these two samples 
are much higher than those of metamorphic zircons (generally < 0.1). 
These features indicate that igneous rocks were the major sources of the 
zircon grains. For the sandstone sample (WMD01), 82 detrital zircon 
ages were obtained (3423 – 126 Ma), with two youngest zircon ages at 
126.2 Ma and 126.7 Ma ( Fig. 2 a). For the andesite sample (SX162-165), 
10 concordant zircon dates range from 2356 Ma to 126 Ma, with the 
youngest zircon date as 125.8 Ma ( Fig. 2 b). The youngest zircon date 
(126.7 � 125.8 Ma) in these two samples is interpreted as the maximum 
allowable depositional age of the Jiabula Formation for this study, 
consistent with the ages in previous study ( Wan et al., 2005 ). We used 
ca. 126 Ma for the Jiabula Formation in further discussion.
4.2. SEM observations
The SEM observations show the presence of magnetite, rutile, and 
pyrite grains in two selected samples of the Zhangda rocks ( Fig. 3 ). 
Magnetite grains exhibit rectangular, rhombic, and other irregular 
shapes with a grain size of 1 � 5 μ m ( Fig. 3 f – i and k � l), which is a 
characteristic feature of detrital grains. Darker rutile particles are 
observed ( Fig. 3 e and j), consistent with the magnetite in shape and size. 
In addition, both samples contain iron sulfides ( Fig. 3 a � c, e, and l). The 
EDS analyses reveal an Fe:S ratio of ~1:2, implying that the iron sulfide 
is pyrite ( Fig. S1 ). The pyrite grains are rounded to subrounded ( Fig. 3 b, 
e, and l) or framboidal ( Fig. 3 a and c) with grain sizes of 2 μ m to 10 μ m. 
Similarly, the mineral assemblage of detrital magnetite and rutile, as 
well as framboidal pyrite in the Lower Cretaceous volcaniclastic sand -
stones were also reported by Huang et al. (2015) .
4.3. Rock magnetic results
All samples show a significant paramagnetic contribution. After 
high-field slope correction, the hysteresis loops for some samples are 
closely saturated by 300 mT ( Fig. 4 a � f), indicating the dominance of 
the low coercivity minerals, such as magnetite. The other samples are 
still not saturated at above 0.5 T ( Fig. 4 g � l), suggesting the presence of 
high coercivity minerals, such as goethite and/or hematite. This is 
consistent with the wasp-waisted hysteresis loops ( Jackson, 1990; 
Roberts et al., 1995 ). On the Day plot ( Day et al., 1977; Dunlop, 2002 ), 
almost all the samples are distributed in the pseudo-single domain (PSD) 
space ( Fig. 4 m; Table S2 ), indicating that the magnetic mineral assem -
blage is dominated by large PSD magnetic grains.

It should be noted that the studied limestones show no clear evidence 
of substantial inclination shallowing, consistent with previously re -
ported E/I correction results, also indicating that inclination shallowing 
is no significant for some Tibetan and Himalayan limestones (e.g., Ma 
et al., 2018; Jiao et al., 2023 ). It is possible that the detrital magnetite 
grains in some limestones are nearly not affected by the depositional or 
post-depositional compaction processes, leading to no significant incli -
nation shallowing.
5. Discussion
Our new paleomagnetic results from the Jiabula Formation lime -
stones in the eastern segment of the Tethyan Himalaya yield a paleo -
latitude of 40.9
◦
± 2.6
◦
S at ca. 126 Ma for the reference point (28.9
◦
N, 
91.1
◦
E) ( Fig. 8 ). India was located at 52.7
◦
± 2.8
◦
S at ca. 130 Ma, and at 
45.2
◦
± 2.6
◦
S at ca. 120 Ma, using its apparent polar wander path 
( Torsvik et al., 2012 ) for the reference point (28.9
◦
N, 91.1
◦
E). Interpo -
lating an average speed of ~0.75
◦
/Ma during ca. 130 � 120 Ma, India 
was located at 49.7
◦
± 2.8
◦
S at ca. 126 Ma. The difference in value 
between this expected paleolatitude (49.7
◦
± 2.8
◦
S) and the observed 
paleolatitude (40.9
◦
± 2.6
◦
S) implies that Greater India had a width of 
968 ± 418 km (8.8
◦
± 3.8
◦
) for the reference point (28.9
◦
N, 91.1
◦
E) at ca. 
126 Ma ( Fig. 8 ). However, the tectonic reconstruction at ca. 126 Ma 
places India as having rotated about 40
◦
clockwise with respect to its 
present N-S orientation ( Torsvik et al., 2012 ). The rotation of India at ca. 
126 Ma indicates that the difference in value between the observed and 
expected paleolatitudes is slightly less than the extent of Greater India in 
the present N-S direction ( Meng et al., 2019 ). Even if we considered the 
effect of the rotation of India on determining the size of Greater India at 
ca. 126 Ma, Greater India would have an extension of 1265 ± 550 km 
(11.5
◦
± 5.0
◦
), which overlapps with the difference value (8.8
◦
± 3.8
◦
) 
between the expected and observed paleolatitudes in this study. 
Therefore, this effect on determining the size of Greater India at ca. 126 
Ma is almost negligible.
India rotated to a closely present N-S orientation after ca. 80 Ma, and 
the effect of the rotation of India on determining the extent of Greater 
India is completely negligible ( Yuan et al., 2023 ). Our previous paleo -
magnetic results from ca. 75 Ma oceanic red beds in the eastern part of 
the Tethyan Himalaya yielded a paleolatitude of 19.3
◦
± 1.8
◦
S ( Yuan 
et al., 2021 ), while an expected paleolatitude of 27.1
◦
± 2.9
◦
S was ob -
tained using the apparent polar wander path of India for the reference 
point (28.9
◦
N, 89.2
◦
E) ( Torsvik et al., 2012 ). The difference value of the 
observed and expected paleolatitudes indicates that Greater India had 
an extension of 858 ± 374 km (7.8
◦
± 3.4
◦
) for its eastern part at ca. 75 
Ma. Recently, we performed a paleomagnetic study on the ca. 75 Ma 
oceanic red beds in the central part of the Tethyan Himalaya, yielding a 
paleolatitude of 16.7
◦
± 1.8
◦
S ( Yuan et al., 2023 ). Correspondingly, an 
expected paleolatitude of 25.0
◦
± 2.9
◦
S is obtained using the apparent 
polar wander path of India for the reference point (29.8
◦
N, 83.6
◦
E) 
( Torsvik et al., 2012 ). The difference value further indicates that Greater 
India had a similar extension of 913 ± 374 km (8.3
◦
± 3.4
◦
) at its central 
part at ca. 75 Ma. Therefore, our new paleomagnetic results in this 
study, in conjunction with our previous results ( Yuan et al., 2021 , 2023) 
indicate that Greater India had a similar extension of ~900 km during 
the time interval between ca. 126 Ma and ca. 75 Ma ( Fig. 8 ).
A relatively small Greater India (~900 km) is consistent with mul -
tiple lines of geologic and geophysical evidence, as addressed by Yuan 
et al. (2023) . For example, this small-sized Greater India is compatible 
with the East Gondwana reconstructions ( Ali and Aitchison, 2005, 2008; 
Gibbons et al., 2012 ), balanced cross section reconstructions in the

logic interpretations ( Zhao et al., 2010; Gao et al., 2016 ). Therefore, our 
reconstruction of the extent of Greater India (~900 km) ( Fig. 8 ) can be 
used to reconstruct the Tethyan paleogeography and the India-Asia 
collision process ( Ali and Aitchison, 2005; Aitchison et al., 2007; 
Jagoutz et al., 2015; van Hinsbergen et al., 2019; Kapp and DeCelles, 
2019; Martin et al., 2020, 2023; Yuan et al., 2021, 2022, 2023, 2024; 
Dannemann et al., 2022; Bian et al., 2021, 2022, 2023; Xu et al., 2022; 
Jin et al., 2023; Jin et al., 2024; Li et al., 2024; Advokaat and van 
Hinsbergen, 2024 ).
6. Conclusions
We report high-resolution thermal demagnetization data from the 
Jiabula Formation limestones in the eastern part of the Tethyan Hima -
laya. Combined petrographic observations, rock magnetic analyses, and 
positive fold tests, suggest that the HTCs are of a primary origin, and that 
the remanence is carried by detrital magnetite. After evaluating the 
possibility of inclination shallowing, we provide a high-quality Early 
Cretaceous paleopole of 11.2
◦
N/300.5
◦
E, A
95 
= 2.6
◦
, with a paleo -
latitude of 40.9
◦
± 2.6
◦
S at ca. 126 Ma. The new results, together with 
our previous results from the Chuangde Formation oceanic red beds, 
lead us to conclude that Greater India had a comparable extension of 
~900 km during the Early Cretaceous to the Campanian. Our estimate of 
the extent of Greater India in this study provides crucial insights into 
paleogeographic reconstructions and the India-Asia collision processes.

Early Cretaceous volcanic 
rocks of West Liaoning: 
Evidence for intracontinental 
rotation

Abstract Detailed rock magnetic studies of 55 lavas from 
Yixian and Fuxin area, West Liaoning, show the primary 
carriers of remanence to be pseudo-single domain ti-
tanomagnetite. K/Ar dating indicates that the volcanic se-
quence spans 93 to 133 Ma. Stepwise thermal demagnetiza-
tion successfully isolated well-defined characteristic mag-
netization (ChRM) in all lavas thermal-treated above 250 ć. 
The mean paleodirections are D/I = 5.9 /58.8 (D95 = 2.9) and 
D/I =179.2/59.9 ( D95 = 5.2) for 27 normally magnetized 
flows and 28 reversibly magnetized flows, respectively. It 
indicates that since the Early Cretaceous there is no signifi-
cant horizontal movement and rotation between the 
Yixian-Fuxin area and Eurasia. However, Korea Peninsula 
may have undergone a clockwise rotation of 33.9 relative to 
the Yixian-Fuxin area during the Cretaceous. On the basis of 
characteristics of hotspot origins (core-mantle boundary or 
upper mantle), the clockwise rotation of Korea Peninsula 
relative to Eurasia is assumed to be mainly caused by an 
extensional force in the crust of eastern China, which was 
corresponding to intensive surface volcanic activities in this 
area. 
Keywords: Cretaceous, paleomagnetism, geodynamics. 
 Eastern China had been undergone tectonic structure 
changes from an E-W pattern in Paleozoic and early 
Mesozoic to a NNE pattern in late Mesozoic, and transi-
tion from a compression system to an expansion system. 
Meanwhile, in this region al so occurred both deep conti-
nental subduction and the crust shortening [1]. Numerous 
metal deposits, oil and gas resources were accumulated, 
which is supposed to be closely related with the in-
tra-continental tectonic processes since the Mesozoic. 
Therefore, investigations on continental tectonic history of 
eastern China are obviously very important for the study 
of continental dynamics. Th is note aims to study the 
kinematics characteristics of intracontinental blocks in 
eastern China since the Mesozoic by means of paleomag-
netism. 
1 Geological settings and sample collection 
 Eastern China underwent frequent intensive volcanic 
eruptions resulting from a complex influence of the west-
ern Pacific plate and deep Earth’s processes during the 
middle to late Mesozoic. It forms a part of the Pacific-rim 
volcanic belt. In the Yixian and Fuxin region, it consists of 
Cretaceous basalts, andesites, trachytes, rhyolites, etc. The 
famous Jehol Fauna, includ ing numerous early birds, 
flowers and mammals
[2,3], which attracts great attention of 
paleobiologists and provides good materials for studying 
the biological massive extinc tions, generations, the deep 
Earth’s processes and ancient environments[4ü7].
 Total 410 orientated basaltic cores were collected 
from 55 lavas at the Zhuanchengzi section in Yixian, the 
Sihetun section at Beipiao, the Hulahada and Wuhuanchi 
in Fuxin, using a portable gasoline drill. All cores were 
orientated in situ using a magnetic compass and/or a sun 
compass. Each core was cut into 3 ü5 samples (1 cm in 
height) in laboratory for rock-magnetic and paleomagnetic 
measurements. In view of the stratigraphical sequence 
relative to the fossil-bearing lake sediments, basaltic lavas 
of the Yixian Formation at th e Sihetun section consist of 
lavas overlying (#Sht1-2), intruded (#Sht3) and under-
lying ones (#Sht5-20); basaltic and andesitic intervals of 
the Yixian Formation at the Zhuanchengzi section 
(#ZCZ1-20). The Hulahada section and the Wuhuanchi 
section in Fuxin are parts of the Tuhulu Formation and the 
Dalinghe Formation, respectively.

Laboratory of the Institute of Geology, China Seismol-
ogical Bureau. Fresh volcanic rocks were crushed and 
sieved to a size range between 0.20 ü0.28 mm. Mineral 
crystals, such as olivine a nd plagioclase, which may con-
tain excess argon, were removed. The sieved samples 
were washed with water, ethanol and acetone, and then 
baked at low temperature.

nique with a 99.98% pure 
38Ar spike, on an MM1200 
mass spectrometer connected to a purification and extrac-

measured by a flame photometer (Model HG-3).

with two vacuum systems: th e inner vacuum system, in-
cluding the Christmas tree, was connected to the purifica-
tion system and mass spectrometer. The outer vacuum 
system was evacuated with a diffusion pump and used for 
electron bombardment heating. The samples were then

4 Discussion and conclusions 
 A compilation of available palaeomagnetic data in-
dicates that the North Chin a block (NCB), South China 
block (SCB) and the Korea block had been completely 
sutured as a whole by the late Jurassic
[8ü11]. Whether there 
are relative intra-plate rotations since then can be revealed 
by means of paleomagnetism. To further this study, pub-
lished palaeomagnetic data for NCB and Korea blocks 
since the Cretaceous (table 3) were compiled according to 
the present international criteria for reliability
[12, 13] . For 
the NCB block and the Korea block, table 3 shows that no 
significant difference exists between their Cretaceous pa-
leolatitudes and present latitudes. Furthermore, results of 
the Cretaceous basalts (for age spans 93 ü113 Ma see 
table 2) from Yixian and Fuxi n indicate that West Liao-
ning has neither significant latitude-directional movement 
nor tectonic rotations relative to the main Eurasia conti-
nent since the Cretaceous (tables 2 and 3). The same fea-
tures are observed for Inner Mongolia from paleomag-
netitic study on the tuff of Pingzhuang. The Korea block 
has no horizontal movement an d rotation relative to Eura-
sia since the Tertiary
[10]. However, it is noted that there was 
a significant clockwise rotation of 33.9° relative to the 
Eurasia during the Cretaceous time
[10] (North and South 
Korea have the same movement characteristic, see table 3). 
 Then what an internal force drives Korea to rotate 
clockwise during the Cretaceous time? West Liaoning and 
its adjacent areas and the Korea Peninsula may provide 
some useful clues. Strong tectonic movements and inten-
sive volcanic activities were then their main characteris-
tics of this region. Especially, in the early Cretaceous 
massive basaltic magma erupted in downfaulted basins
[16]. 
Besides, the difference of the ratio of Ta/Hf and Th/Hf 
(table 4 and fig. 4) suggests that those basalts were formed 
in the expansional rift tectonic environment [17]. Therefore, 
we assume that the clockwise rotation of 33.9° of the 
Korea Peninsula was a result of the continental crust ex-
tension of eastern China, which was manifested by mas-
sive surface volcanic eruptions. Controlled by the

Mongolia may have had no significant effect on the crust 
extensional process. 
 Although most volcanic activities occur at plate 
margins (such as mid-oceanic ridge and subduction zone), 
some basaltic eruptions may happen at intraplates. Mor-
gon (1972) proposed that hotspots are formed as the lower 
mantle-flow upwelling onto the surface, often distributed 
along the extensional plate boundaries and areas with high 
long-wave geoid
[18]. Recently, Zhao (2001) reported that 
the mantle plumes beneath ho tspots in Hawaii, Iceland, 
south Pacific and East Africa originate from the core- 
mantle boundary (CMB); there are also some hotspots 
corresponding to small-scale mantle plumes that originate 
from the discontinuity bounda ries at depths of 410 or 610 
km, and, the western Pacific margin is a zone with a low 
velocity of seismic wave
[19]. Furthermore, computer 
simulation and experimental studies show that the tem-
perature and physical property differences in the mantle 
beneath the edge of thick continental lithosphere and rift 
can produce local mantle convections
[20], which may pro-
duce massive continental volcanic eruptions [21ü23]. Com-
bined with above observations of seismology and experi-
mental simulation, we assume that extensively-distributed 
basalts in West Liaoning may be associated with a small- 
scale mantle plume originated from the upper mantle. The 
mantle plume is generated by an upwelling of local heat 
flow from the discontinuity boundaries at depths of 410 
and 610 km. 
 This study shows that West Liaoning area relative to 
Eurasia has no significant horizontal movement and rota-
tion since the early Cretaceous, but the Korea Peninsula 
had a clockwise rotation of 33.9° relative to Eurasia in the 
early Cretaceous time; in view of geochemistry, those 
basalts were produced in the extensional rift geotectonic 
environment. 
 A full explanation for the clockwise rotation of the 
Korea Peninsula is beyond th e scope of this investigation. 
Remaining questions are if this rotation was related with 
the deep Earth’s extension process, e.g. a plume from the 
discontinuity boundaries at depths of 410 and 660 km or 
from the upper mantle, or with the Mesozoic shear-strike 
slip movements at the East Asia continental margin. The 
fact of a clockwise rotation of 33.9° is clearly contradicted 
to some geological assumptions that sinistral shear move-
ments at this area in Mesozo ic time. To solve the above 
questions, a combined study by different approaches must 
be done.

Middle Triassic paleomagnetic results from central Hubei 
province, China and their tectonic implications 
K. Huang and N.D. Opdyke 
Department of Geology, University of Florida, Gainesville, FL 32611 
Abstract. Twenty one sites consisting of 4 to 7 samples per 
site were drilled from the redbeds of the Middle Triassic Badong 
Formation from central Hubei province, China. These samples 
were subjected to progressive thermal demagnetization which 
revealed two components of magnetization. The low 
temperature (A) component was probably acq at a late 
stage of folding and is similar in direction to the late Mesozoic 
overprint widely observed in the eastern Yangtze Block . The 
high temperature (B ) component is Irefolding with dual 
polarity. Unlike the prefolding paleomagnetic directions 
observed in eastern Sichuan, western Hubei and northwestern 
Hunan, the B component resolved from central Hubei indicates 
no significant rotation with respect to other parts of the 
Yangtze Block. Since one of the two sampled sections is in 
the strongly deformed foreland fold-thrust belt of the Qinling 
Fold Belt, this would seem to negate the possibility that the 
differential rotations observed in the border area between 
Sichuan, Hubei, Hunan and Guizhou are associated with the 
collision of the Yangtze Block with the North China Block. 
Introduction 
We have reported paleomagnetic results from the Middle 
Triassic rocks from western and southeastern Hubei province 
and northwestern Hunan province in the Yangtze Block (YB) 
(Huang and Opdyke, 1996). The results indicate that western 
Hubei and northwestern Hunan have been subjected to 
significant differential rotations but that southeastern Hubei 
may not have been significantly rotated within paleomagnetic 
error limits since the acquisition of the remanence. The 
differential rotations observed in eastern SiChuan and the 
border area between Hubei, Hunan, Guizhou and Sichuan have 
been infen to be due to oroclinal bending in the late 
Mesozoic (Steiner et al., 1989; Huang and Opdyke, 1996). To 
further constrain the extent and cause of such rotations, we 
studied coeval rocks from central Hubei province.

the foreland fold-thrust belt at the northern margin of the YB 
and constitute a bundle of WNW-trending elongate folds. The 
deformation is further intensified as approaching the 
Fangxian-Guang.ji fault to the north, a north-dipping boundary 
thrust between the YB and the Qinling Fold Belt (QFB), and 
the WNW-trending folds become overturned with southward 
vergence (Hubei Bureau of Geology and Mineral Resources, 
1990). Clearly, these folds own their origin to the collision 
of the YB with the North China Block (NCB)and subsequent 
overthrusting of the QFB onto the YB (Mattauer et al., 1985; 
Hsu et al., 1987; Liu and Hao; 1989; Okay et al., 1993). 
Superimposed on the west flank of the ]ingmen-Dangyang 
basin is the Yuan'an graben, a NNW-trending fault depression

Therefore, folding of the Jura-Triassic rocks in the Jingmen- 
Dangyang basin took place sometime in the interval from late 
Jurassic to early Cretaceous (Yanshanian).

been inferred that Sangzhi has been rotated clockwise by

observed at Yuan'an differs by -25.1+8.6 ø from that observed

other parts of the YB (-7.9t:12.?ø). This is also supported by 
the fact that the palcomagnetic pole derived from Yuan'an 
overlaps those from Badong and Sangzhi after correction for 
the local rotations (Fig. 4). As indicated earlier, the northern 
flank of the Jingmen-Dangyang basin is involved in the 
strong deformation of the foreland fold-thrust belt of the QFB, 
and the sampled Liujiatai section is only 100 km south of the 
Fangxian-Guangji boundary thrust. If the differential rotations 
observed in eastern Sichuan (Steiner et al., 1989), western 
Hubei and northwestern Hunan (l-luang and Opdyke, 1996) are 
due to the collision of the YB with the NCB and subsequent 
intracontinental thrusting, significant rotations would be 
expected to take place in the foreland fold-thrust belt. 
Therefore, the palcomagnetic results from the Jingmen- 
Dangyang basin seem to disassociate the differential rotations 
in the above-mentioned area from the collision of the YB with 
the NCB. Finally, a mean Middle Triassic palcomagnetic pole 
for the YB (40.9øN/213.1øE, A95 TM 7.9 ø, N = $) has been 
calculated based upon the poles derived from Guangxi (Gilder et

in the APWP for the YB (Fig. 4)which reinforces the Permo- 
Triassic swing noted by Enkin et al. (1992) and implies about 
9 ø of northward motion and 24 ø of counterclockwise rotation 
of the YB during this time period. 
In conclusion, the palcomagnetic results obtained from the 
Middle Triassic Badong Fm in the lingmen-Dangyang basin 
indicates no significant rotation relative to other parts of the 
YB and thus further delimit the differential rotations to the 
border area between Sichuan, Hubei, Hunan and Guizhou 
provinces (Fig. 1). Since one of the sampled sections is in the 
strongly deformed foreland fold-thrust belt of the QFB, this 
seems to disassociate these rotations from the collision of the 
YB with the NCB. Future work should be focused on the border 
area between Sichuan, Hubei, Hunan and Guizhou, especially 
eastern Sichuan, to establish the correlation between the 
rotation and the trend of the fold and look into possible causal 
relationship of these rotations with the collision of the 
Huanan Block with the YB (Hsu et al., 1990) and/or the 
interaction between the Pacific plate and the Asia continent 
(Sichuan Bureau of Geology and Mineral Resources, 1991).

Heavy mineral provenance and paleomagnetic studies of Mesozoic 
rocks in the Gold Beach terrane, southwestern Oregon, USA
Ericka M. Boudreau1,†, Richard M. Gaschnig1, Jeffrey D. Vervoort2, Joshua J. Schwartz3, Bernard Housen4, and 
Basil Tikoff5
1 Department of Environmental, Earth and Atmospheric Sciences, University of Massachusetts Lowell, 1 University Avenue, Lowell, 
Massachusetts 01854, USA
2 School of the Environment, PO Box 642812, Washington State University, Pullman, Washington 99164, USA
3 Department of Geological Sciences, California State University Northridge, 18111 Nordhoff Street, Northridge, California 91330, USA
4 Geology Department and Pacific NW Paleomagnetism Laboratory, Western Washington University, 516 High Street, Bellingham, 
Washington 98225, USA
5 Department of Geoscience, University of Wisconsin–Madison, 1215 W Dayton Street, Madison, Wisconsin 53706, USA
ABSTRACT
We present detrital mineral and paleo -
magnetic data from the Gold Beach terrane 
of southwestern Oregon, USA, that supports 
its large-magnitude northward translation 
along the North American margin in the Late 
Cretaceous. Detrital zircon and titanite were 
gathered from Late Jurassic–Late Cretaceous 
aged sandstones and indicate a shift in sedi-
ment sources over time. Zircon Hf isotopes in 
Jurassic grains (200–144 Ma) yield positive 
εHf(i) values (+15 to +6), whereas Late Creta-
ceous grains (100–90 Ma) have a wide range 
of values spanning 20 epsilon units ( +11 to 
−12). Trace-element abundances in detrital 
zircons show increasing U/Yb and Eu/Eu* 
with decreasing age. Detrital titanite Nd iso-
topes mimic zircon Hf isotopes and show εNd(i) 
values ranging from +8 to +1 in Jurassic 
aged grains and +5 to −9 in Late Cretaceous 
grains. Gold Beach titanites are primarily of 
magmatic origin and are derived from fel -
sic sources, while others have trace element 
chemistry revealing metamorphic sources.
Paleomagnetic results from the Late Cre-
taceous Houstenaden Creek Formation 
pass fold tests with a tilt-corrected mean 
of D = 130°, I = 70°, n = 12, k = 10, and 
α95 = 14.4°. The directions have a widely 
streaked distribution along a small-circle 
path due to local rotations of blocks between 
sites. The tilt-corrected, inclination-only 
mean is I = 59°, n = 12, k = 58, α95 = 4.4°, 
which yields a Late Cretaceous paleolatitude 
of 41° ± 4°N. Comparing these results with a 
Late Cretaceous reference for North Amer-
ica shows an expected paleolatitude of 47°N, 
resulting in an estimate of 750 ± 500 km of 
displacement and ∼100° of clockwise rota -
tion. This estimate is consistent with detrital 
mineral results that indicate continentally 
derived sources in southern California, as 
well as a western source offshore of the Late 
Cretaceous North American margin. We con-
clude that northward translation of the Gold 
Beach terrane from southernmost California 
occurred during the Late Cretaceous and 
that it was near its present location in south-
western Oregon by the Eocene.
INTRODUCTION
The North American Cordillera contains mul-
tiple terranes, with distinct geological histories, 
that accreted during the Mesozoic (Fig. 1; Coney 
et  al., 1980; Jones et  al., 1983). The accreted 
terranes of western North America are gener -
ally oceanic in nature, characterized by marine 
sedimentation and juvenile magmatism. The 
87Sr/86Sr(i) = 0.706 isopleth is commonly used to 
mark the boundary between these accreted oce-
anic terranes and the Laurentian craton (Arm -
strong et al., 1977; Kistler and Peterman, 1978; 
Burchfiel et al., 1992).
One of the most notable and persistent contro-
versies in the study of the North America Cordil-
lera is the amount and timing of latitudinal move-
ment of these terranes, both prior to and after 
accretion to the continental margin (Busby et al., 
2023). Models proposing large-scale margin-
parallel translation are largely driven by robust 
and internally consistent paleomagnetic datasets 
indicating large portions of the Canadian Cordil-
lera were located up to 3000 km south of their 
current locations prior to ca. 90 Ma (Beck and 
Noson, 1972; Irving et al., 1985; Wynne et al., 
1995; Enkin et al., 2006; Tikoff et al., 2023). The 
Baja–British Columbia hypothesis, utilizing this 
paleomagnetic data, places these terranes off the 
coast of southwestern Laurentia during the Late 
Cretaceous (Irving et  al., 1996; Cowan et  al., 
1997; Umhoefer et al., 2006; Wyld et al., 2006).
Provenance studies are used to indepen -
dently evaluate the margin-parallel movement 
of terranes, motivated by the potential for this 
approach to resolve the controversy (Cowan 
et al., 1997). Unfortunately, the use of detrital 
zircon provenance analysis has not unambigu -
ously resolved this issue. For example, results 
from different detrital zircon investigations of the 
Nanaimo basin of the Insular superterrane were 
used to argue for and against large-magnitude 
translation (Matthews et  al., 2017; Mahoney 
et al., 2021; Boivin et al., 2022). Isotopic trac -
ers—such as Hf in zircon—provide additional 
constraints on depositional source by character-
izing the origins of parent magmas (Gehrels and 
Pecha, 2014). Because of the widespread distri-
bution of detrital zircons in the Cordillera and the 
unknown configuration of paleo-river systems 
(Dumitru et al., 2016), non-unique provenance 
signatures are common; therefore, multi-mineral 
approaches are needed if detrital minerals are 
to provide well defined provenance models that 
constrain paleogeography (O’Sullivan et  al., 
2016; Gaschnig, 2019; Chew et al., 2020).
This study contributes two different datasets 
that support significant northward translation of 
the Mesozoic Gold Beach terrane of southwest-

ern Oregon, USA. First, ages and geochemical 
and isotopic compositions from detrital zircon 
and titanite offer a comprehensive provenance 
evaluation for the Gold Beach terrane, supporting 
a southerly origin. Second, new paleomagnetic 
data presented herein indicate that the terrane 
was located significantly (∼750 km) to the south 
during Late Cretaceous deposition, consistent 
with provenance interpretations from this detrital 
mineral study and previous work done in the area 
(Blake et al., 1985; Bourgeois and Dott, 1985; 
Liner, 2005). Together, these datasets aid in the 
characterization of the motion of displaced ter-
ranes along the western margin of North America 
and support tectonic models requiring margin-
parallel translation in the mid- to Late Cretaceous.
GEOLOGIC BACKGROUND
Structural and Stratigraphic Nature of 
Southwestern Oregon Terranes
The southwestern Oregon coast was the sub-
ject of intensive mapping, sedimentary petrogra-
phy, and isotopic dating that revealed complex 
assemblages of fault-bounded Mesozoic terranes 
that differed markedly from inland Klamath 
Mountains terranes in stratigraphy, tectonic style, 
and metamorphic history (Figs. 1 and 2; Diller, 
1903; Dott, 1971; Bourgeois, 1980a; Roure and 
Blanchet, 1983; Blake et al., 1985; Irwin, 1985). 
Sampled terranes are listed in Table 1, and brief 
descriptions and interpretations of the terranes 
mentioned below are summarized in Table  2. 
Much like the tectonic style of the northern Cali-
fornia Coast Ranges, coastal southern Oregon is 
characterized by near-vertical fault boundaries 
and wide shear zones that trend N-NW, contrast-
ing with the N-NE trend of arcuate inland ter -
ranes that occur as klippe in the Klamath Moun-
tains Province (Dott, 1965; Roure and Blanchet, 
1983). Blake et al. (1985) described six distinct 
tectonostratigraphic terranes in southwestern 
Oregon based on their fault-bounded contacts, 
varying internal stratigraphic records, and dis -
continuity of depositional facies (Figs. 2 and 3; 
Table 2; Table S2 in the Supplemental Material1). 
The tectonic elements represented in Figure 2 are 
either ocean plate mélanges or broken formations 
with coarse boulder conglomerates, chert, lime-
stone blocks, and pillow basalt (Sixes River and 
Western Yolla Bolly terranes), or slices of basinal 
strata composed of greywacke and mudstone tur-
bidite sequences ± ophiolitic basement that are 
related stratigraphically to the Klamath Moun-
tains, Franciscan Complex, and/or Great Valley 
Group in California (Pickett Peak, Eastern Yolla 
Bolly, Snow Camp, and Western Klamath ter -
ranes; Jayko and Blake, 1993). The Gold Beach 
terrane is in westernmost southern Oregon and is 
a hybrid of the contrasting tectonic elements—
broken formation and sandstone turbidites 
together with conglomerate beds, greywacke, 
chert, and pillow lavas overlain by a transgres-
sive marine cover sequence (Bourgeois, 1980a).
The Sixes River terrane marks the northern-
most tectonostratigraphic terrane in southwest-
ern Oregon and is notably the product of ocean 
floor subduction (Blake et al., 1985). The ter -
rane is divided into three fault-bounded belts of 
westward-younging Eocene mélange that con-
tain high-grade blocks of Jurassic age (Coleman 
and Lanphere, 1971) and limestone blocks with 
Cenomanian microfossils ( Diller, 1898 ). The 
eastern and central mélange belts are overlain 
by middle Eocene Tyee Formation sandstones, 
while the western belt is overlapped by the 
sandstones of the Umpqua Group ( Figs. 2 and 
3; see also Wiley et al., 2014). At Cape Blanco 
and Blacklock Point, these sandstones also 
overlie Late Jurassic rocks of the Gold Beach 
terrane, providing a minimum age of juxtaposi-
tion of the Gold Beach terrane with southwest-
ern Oregon (Fig. 3). The Sixes River terrane is 
bounded to the west by the Gold Beach terrane 
along N-NW–trending strands of the Battle 
Rock fault zone ( Fig. 2), a near-vertical shear 
zone several kilometers wide that is marked by 
lensoidal masses of serpentinite and volcanics 
(Dott, 1962).
The Battle Rock fault zone can be traced 
south along the coast as diverging strands: one 
that occurs offshore and is distinguished by 
linear trains of sea stacks and another farther 
inland just south of Port Orford called the Brush 
Creek fault zone (Fig. 2; see also McClaughry 
et al., 2013). The inland strand separates broken 
formation of the Gold Beach terrane from less 
deformed strata to the east in the Elk outlier of 
the Western Klamath terrane; this subterrane 
occurs as an isolated coastal nappe structure, 
detached from the rest of the Klamath Moun -
tains Province ( Koch, 1966; Dott, 1971). The 
Oxfordian Galice Formation occupies the lowest 
structural level of the outlier and is intruded by 
the 148 Ma Pearse Peak diorite (Fig. 3; see also 
Beaulieu, 1976), both of which are unconform-
ably overlain by coarse conglomerates and lithic 
wackes of the Berriasian–Valanginian Humbug 
Mountain and Rocky Point Formations (Fig. 3; 
see also Koch, 1966).
The bulk of the Gold Beach terrane is exposed 
in the central part of the map area, parallel to the 
current coastline (Fig. 2). It is overthrust on its 
eastern boundary by the Colebrooke Formation 
of the Pickett Peak terrane, a northern exten -
sion of the Franciscan Eastern Belt along with 
the eastern Yolla Bolly terrane (not sampled 
in this study). The thrust contact is marked by 
bodies of sheared serpentinite mélange contain-
ing blocks of peridotite derived from oceanic 
mantle ( Fig.  2; see also Henry and Medaris, 
1980). These ultramafic fragments are distinct 
from peridotite occurrences farther east in the 
Snow Camp terrane, which are discussed later. 
The Colebrooke schist was regionally metamor-
phosed under blue-greenschist facies conditions 
between 142 Ma and 125 Ma (Coleman, 1972). It 
experienced several episodes of thrusting before 
being overprinted by a younger phase of defor-
mation, offsetting the terrane along steeply dip-
ping N-NE–trending normal faults and placing 
it structurally below the Humbug Mountain and 
Rocky Point Formations of the Elk subterrane 
(Dott, 1971; Roure and Blanchet, 1983). Struc-
tural nappes associated with the Pickett Peak 
terrane also overlie the northern Gold Beach 
and Sixes River terrane east of Blacklock Point 
(Fig. 2), requiring juxtaposition of the underly-
ing elements prior to the final phases of thrusting 
(Miocene?; see McClaughry et al., 2013).
A N-S–striking group of fault-bounded 
ultramafic rocks belonging to the Snow Camp 
terrane occurs several kilometers east of the 
Gold Beach–Pickett Peak terrane boundary 
(Fig.  2). These rocks consist of dismembered 
ophiolitic slices that preserve a structurally 
coherent sheeted dike complex and constrain 
the age of ophiolite formation to 169–164 Ma 
(Saleeby, 1983). A cover sequence of Titho -
nian–Valanginian flysch-like sedimentary rocks 
(Myrtle Group—Riddle and Days Creek Forma-
tions) overlies the Snow Camp ophiolite along 
an angular unconformity (Fig. 3; see also Imlay 
et al., 1959). Because of its fault-bounded char-
acter and stratigraphic similarities with coeval 
sequences to the south in California, Jones et al. 
(1978) suggested its equivalence to the Coast 
Range ophiolite and overlying Great Valley 
Group; however, notable differences in lithol -
ogy and structure make correlations uncertain 
(Dott, 1971; Blake et al., 1985). Emplacement 
of the Snow Camp outlier above the Pickett Peak 
and Western Klamath terranes of southwestern 
Oregon took place at amphibolite-greenschist 
facies conditions during a 154–148 Ma phase of 
Nevadan thrusting (Schoonmaker et al., 2006).

Provenance of the Gold Beach terrane
 Geological Society of America Bulletin, v. 137, no. 5/6 2569
The Gold Beach terrane terminates at its 
southern end along the Whaleshead fault zone 
that extends from Whaleshead Island north -
ward to Hunters Cove and possibly connects 
to the southern strand of the Battle Rock fault 
zone (Fig. 2; see also McClaughry et al., 2013). 
The Whaleshead fault zone is characterized as a 
N-NW–striking crustal structure that juxtaposes 
basement of the Gold Beach terrane with rocks 
of the western Yolla Bolly terrane just north of 
Brookings (Fig. 2; see also Widmier, 1963). Its 
trace is marked by sheared serpentinite bodies 
that occur in linear distribution with chert pebble 
conglomerates. Along this boundary, the Yolla 
Bolly terrane is characterized by vertical to over-
turned beds of greywacke mélange containing 
olistostrome deposits that record mass wasting 
and collapse of the slope and shelf edge (Blake 
et al., 1985; McClaughry et al., 2013). Dacite 
flows in this area yielded a whole-rock K-Ar 
age of 149 Ma, slightly older than Gold Beach 
terrane basement, supporting the conclusions of 
Dott (1965) that described separate evolutionary 
histories for the two terranes.
Geology of the Gold Beach Terrane
The Gold Beach terrane is the most outboard 
tectonostratigraphic terrane in southwestern 
Oregon and consists of a Late Jurassic volcano-
sedimentary basement complex overlain by a 
relatively thin Cretaceous cover sequence (Bour-
geois and Dott, 1985 ). Stratigraphic units, in 
order of depositional age, include the Tithonian 
Otter Point Formation, the Aptian–Campanian 
Houstenaden Creek and correlative Blacklock 
Point Formations, the Campanian Cape Sebas-
tian Formation, and the Maastrichtian Hunters 
Cove Formation (Fig. 3). All formations belong-
ing to the Gold Beach terrane occur only west of 
high-angle N-NW–trending faults and are strati-
graphically complex, yet unmetamorphosed, 
contrasting with terranes to the east (Fig. 2; see 
also Dott, 1971).
The Otter Point Formation is the most litho-
logically varied unit of the Gold Beach terrane 
and was originally described by Dott (1962) , 
Koch (1966), and Aalto and Dott (1970). The 
formation consists of folded and near-vertical 
beds of volcaniclastic conglomerate, sandstone, 
and mudstone that form resistant coastal head-
lands and sea stacks, and of N-NW–trending 
alignment of ultramafic bodies, pillow lavas, 
and volcanic breccia that are associated with 
pervasively sheared serpentinite; the lensoi -
dal bands of serpentinite are thought to mark 
the traces of intraformational shear zones and 
faults (Dott, 1962). V olcanics in the Otter Point 
Formation have been altered by ocean-floor 
metamorphism and contain prehnite, pumpel -
lyite, and epidote, while alteration of sedimen-
tary rocks is limited to veins of laumontite 
(Koch, 1966 ; Goodfellow, 1987 ). Deposition 
of Otter Point sediments likely occurred as 
turbidity flows with SE-directed paleocurrents 
in a deep-water submarine slope, or fan chan -
nel setting, proximal to an active island arc 
during the Late Jurassic (Tithonian; Walker, 
1977). Bourgeois and Dott (1985) and Blake 
et al. (1985) show results of sandstone petrog -
raphy and preliminary paleomagnetic data that 
support translation of the Otter Point Forma -
tion from southern latitudes, while Seiders and 
Blome (1987) pose an alternative interpretation 
based on Late Triassic–Early Jurassic radiolaria 
in chert pebble conglomerates. They suggest a 
Klamath Mountains source, though Bourgeois 
and Dott reply by highlighting distinct welded 
tuffs in Otter Point conglomerates—lithologies 
not present in the Klamath Mountains ( Bour-
geois and Dott, 1987 ). Additionally, the reply 
addresses limitations of using conglomerate 
clast compositions in regional provenance 
studies, as well as flaws in their discussion of 
the data (Seiders and Blome, 1987 ; Bourgeois 
and Dott, 1987). A number of low-angle thrust 
faults truncate Otter Point strata, followed by 
deposition of the Houstenaden Creek (Albian–
Campanian) and correlative Blacklock Point 
(Aptian–Campanian) Formations along ser -
pentinized fault surfaces (McClaughry et al., 
2013). These mid-Late Cretaceous units are 
characterized by volcaniclastic sandstone and 
plant-rich mudstone turbidite sequences, with 
minor pebble conglomerate deposited as chan-
nelized bodies and slumps. The two formations 
were interpreted as separate lobes of a prograd-
ing suprafan submarine channel system into 
what formerly was a basin-plain environment 
(Bourgeois, 1980a). No identifiable clasts from 
the Otter Point Formation were found in the 
Houstenaden Creek or Blacklock Point Forma-
tion conglomerates, suggesting that the units 
were tectonically superposed after deposition 
during a localized phase of faulting (Bourgeois, 
1980a; Bourgeois and Dott, 1985 ). Episodic 
tectonic activity is supported by the angular 
unconformity between the Houstenaden Creek 
and Cape Sebastian (Campanian) Formations, 
each of which represents different depositional 
environments.
The Cape Sebastian Formation consists of 
a basal conglomerate, containing clasts of the 
Otter Point Formation, that fines into hummocky 
and rippled sandstones, together representing a 
transgressive period where high-energy near -
shore deposits gave way to sedimentation in 
deeper and quieter waters ( Bourgeois, 1980b; 
Howard, 1961). This unit is lighter colored, less 
deformed, and notably lacks the volcanic clasts 
present in conglomerate beds of older units 
(Koch, 1966; Dott, 1971). Importantly, it is in 
depositional contact with the overlying Hunt -
ers Cove Formation (Maastrichtian), another 
feature the older formations lack ( Bourgeois, 
1980a). The Hunters Cove Formation contin -

Cape Sebastian Formation with laminated and 
rippled mudstones. Small-scale slump deposits 
containing clasts of Cape Sebastian, channeled 
coarse-grained sandstone, and a synclinal struc-
ture exposed along the coast in Hunters Cove, 
provide evidence of contemporaneous verti -
cal faulting ( Bourgeois and Dott, 1985 ), later 
overprinted by Eocene–present tectonic activity 
related to the San Andreas fault system.
In summary, the Gold Beach terrane was 
affected by several tectonic events that occurred 
during the later part of the Mesozoic (Dott, 1965; 
Bourgeois, 1980a). First, the sheared nature of 
the Otter Point Formation suggests that it was 
accreted to the margin during a poorly con -
strained Late Jurassic–middle Cretaceous com-
pressional event that juxtaposed Otter Point with 
the overlying Houstenaden Creek and Blacklock 
Point Formations along fault contacts, now ser-
pentinized. Secondly, the Houstenaden Creek 
Formation was deformed, uplifted, and eroded 
prior to the Campanian deposition of the Cape 
Sebastian Formation. The Hunters Cove Forma-
tion was also deposited in a tectonically active 
environment, evidenced by numerous slump 
deposits and small-scale extensional fractures.

Gold Beach terrane was tectonically molded into

METHODS
Sample Processing and Mineral Separation
Twelve samples of sedimentary rocks were 
collected from the Gold Beach terrane with 
lithologies ranging from conglomerate to shale; 
four samples were collected from neighboring 
terranes: the Dothan Formation of the western 
Yolla Bolly terrane, the Myrtle Group–Days 
Creek Formation of the Snow Camp terrane, and 
the Humbug Mountain and Rocky Point Forma-
tions of the Elk outlier in the Western Klamath 
terrane (Figs.  2 and 3). Table  1 contains GPS 
coordinates, locations, formation names, and 
lithologies for each sample; this is expanded 
upon in Tables S1 and S2. Sample and outcrop 
photographs of each formation and representa-
tive stratigraphic columns are also included in the 
Supplemental Material; the stratigraphic columns 
for the Houstenaden Creek and Blacklock Point 
Formations are featured in Figure 4 to highlight 
paleomagnetic sites. Four sandstone samples (suf-
fix “SCJ13”), previously studied by Rivas (2014), 
are evaluated, along with three samples analyzed 
for age and Hf compositions at Washington State 
University (Pullman, Washington, USA).
Each sample was crushed and processed 
through methylene iodide to isolate the heavy 
mineral fraction. Zircons from the 1.8A non -
magnetic fraction were poured onto double-
sided sticky tape and mounted in epoxy for 
analysis. Titanite grains were hand-picked 
from the 1.8A magnetic fraction and mounted 
in epoxy. Facilities at the University of Massa-
chusetts Amherst were used to obtain SEM-CL 
(scanning electron microscope–cathodolumines-
cence) images of all zircon mounts and SEM-
BSE (backscattered electron) images of titanite 
mounts. Detailed sample processing descriptions 
and selected optical and CL images are included 
in the Supplemental Material.
Geochronology, Isotope, and Trace Element 
Analysis of Zircon and Titanite
Detrital mineral simultaneous U-Pb dating 
and trace-element analysis were performed using 
a Teledyne CETAC LSX-213 G2 + 213 nm Nd: 
yttrium aluminum garnet (Y AG) laser ablation 
unit with a HelEx two volume ablation cell cou-
pled to an Agilent 7900 quadrupole inductively 
coupled plasma–mass spectrometry (ICP-MS) in 
the Core Research Facility at the University of 
Massachusetts Lowell (UML), primarily follow-
ing the methods of Gaschnig (2019). Detrital zir-
cons from three samples with prefixes “15GB-” 
were analyzed only for U-Pb ages at Washington 
State University following the methods of Gas-
chnig et al. (2010). All data were reduced using 
Iolite software (Paton et al., 2010), and uncer -
tainties on isotope ratios and ages were derived 
from the internal standard error propagated with 
the excess uncertainty on the primary standard. 
Zircon mineral grains were analyzed in con -
junction with a primary and secondary standard, 
91500 and Plešovice, respectively (Wiedenbeck 
et  al., 1995; Sláma et  al., 2008; Horstwood 
et al., 2016), and a series of alternating tertiary 
standards: FC-1 (Paces and Miller, 1993), Fish 
Canyon ( Schmitz and Bowring, 2001 ), Mud 
Tank (Gain et al., 2019), Zirconia ( Fisher and 
Vervoort, 2018), and Rak-17 (Webb et al., 2020). 
Zircon trace-element concentrations were deter-
mined using 91500 as an external standard and Si 
as an internal standard (set to 15.3% by weight). 
Additional information on methodology can be 
found in the Supplemental Material.
Zircon maximum depositional ages (MDAs) 
were calculated with nine different models using 
DZmda software. Each sample was treated 
individually, the results of which are shown in 
Table 3. These results were then grouped into 
composite samples by formation, a weighted 
mean was calculated, and the results are reported 
graphically in Supplemental Data S2. Compos-
ite samples include all individual samples col -
lected from a particular formation (see Table 1 
for sample list).
Titanite mineral grain analyses were per -
formed at UML on the same instrument as zir-
cons, using MKED1 (Spandler et al., 2016) as 
the primary standard, TH-tnt-1 (Fisher et  al., 
2007) as the secondary standard, and CKHB 
and Mud Tank (Fisher et al., 2020) as tertiary 
standards. Trace-element analyses of titanite 
were conducted simultaneously, using NIST 610 
as the external calibrant and Si as the internal 
standard, assuming a concentration of 14.3 wt%. 
Information on how mineral ages were calcu -
lated can be found in Supplemental Text S1.
Zircon Hf isotope analyses were conducted 
by laser ablation–multicollector (LA-MC)-ICP-
MS Neptune Plus coupled to a Teledyne CETAC 
Analyte Excite ArF 193 nm excimer laser in the 
Radiogenic Isotope Lab at Washington State 
University. Plešovice was used as the primary 
standard and FC-1, R-33, and the MunZirc syn-
thetic zircon series of Fisher et al. (2011) were 
used as secondary standards. Standards were 
measured intermittently throughout the analyti-
cal sessions. Titanite Nd isotope analyses were 
conducted at Washington State University with 
the same instruments as zircon Hf isotope work, 
following the methods of Fisher et  al. (2011, 
2020). A spot size of 40 μm was used. MKED1 
was used as the primary standard, while Mud 
Tank and Tory Hill were used as secondary 
standards.
Paleomagnetism
Paleomagnetic samples were collected from 
12 Houstenaden Creek Formation locations. Sev-
eral of the locations had sections of strata with 
different bedding attitudes; these were subdi -
vided into different paleomagnetic sites: 00Khu 
sites from bioturbated greywacke and intrafor-
mational conglomerate and 00Kh sites from 
calcareous mudstones and turbidite sequences 
(Liner, 2005). At each site, 5–20 oriented cores 
were drilled and cut into standard-sized speci -
mens. The remanent magnetization was mea -
sured using 2G Enterprises 755 single-sample 
superconducting magnetometer, treated with 
either alternating field demagnetization (using 
a D-Tech D2000 af demagnetizer) or thermal 
demagnetization (using an ASC TD-48 thermal 
demagnetizer) housed in the Pacific Northwest 
Paleomagnetism Lab at Western Washington 
University. Details regarding the paleomagnetic 
results, including supporting rock-magnetic and 
magnetic anisotropy results, can be found in 
Liner (2005). For this study, the paleomagnetic 
experiments were reviewed, and new principal 
component analysis was used to define the char-
acteristic remanent magnetization of the samples 
based on methods of Gerritsen et al. (2022). This 
yielded a larger set of directional data than was 
reported in Liner (2005).
RESULTS
Zircon Maximum Depositional Ages 
(MDAs)
Detrital zircon MDAs were calculated for 
each sample using DZmda software devel -
oped by Kurt Sundell and hosted at the GitHub 
repository listed in the Supplemental Material. 
The software employed 10 different MDA cal-
culation methods, the results of which are pre-
sented in Table 3. MDAs for the two Otter Point 
samples fall within the range of the Tithonian 
biostratigraphic age constrained by Koch (1966). 
Houstenaden Creek and Blacklock Point sam -
ples show varied results, with the oldest MDA 
in 42SCJ13 (143.7 Ma) and the youngest in 
15GB03 (88.9 Ma). All results for these samples 
are older than the Campanian biostratigraphic 
ages reported in Bourgeois (1980a) , though 
poorly preserved foraminifera in the basal shales

There is a noticeable increase in the abundance

a fluctuation in the Middle Jurassic age mode 
(Fig. 5). Cape Sebastian and Hunters Cove have 
zircon age distributions that emphasize domi -
