older than peak ages in the underlying units. The 
mid-Cretaceous age mode at ca. 100 Ma is more 
prominent in Cape Sebastian samples relative to 
Hunters Cove samples, though this population 
may be subdued in Hunters Cove by the influx 
of 175 Ma zircons (Fig. 5).
Zircon age distributions from adjacent terranes 
in the Klamath Mountain Province show spectra 
that differ from observations in the Gold Beach 
terrane (Fig. 5). The Early Cretaceous Humbug 
Mountain and Rocky Point Formations show 
peak ages at 202 Ma, 168 Ma, and 146 Ma, and 
178 Ma and 146 Ma, respectively. In the Snow 
Camp terrane, zircons from the Days Creek For-
mation of the Myrtle Group have a spectrum of 
ages comparable to zircons in the Houstenaden 
Creek and Blacklock Point Formations (Fig. 5). 
Mesozoic age populations peak at 173 Ma, with 
minor peaks at 188 Ma, 138 Ma, and 103 Ma. 
The Dothan Formation of the Yolla Bolly (west) 
terrane yielded zircons with peak Mesozoic ages 
at 192 Ma, 167 Ma, and 101 Ma and have a simi-
lar distribution to zircons in the Cape Sebastian 
Formation ( Fig.  5). Several Precambrian zir -
cons obtained from the Dothan Formation share 
overlapping populations with the Cape Sebastian 
Formation (Fig. 5). In summary, the terranes of 
southwestern Oregon have detrital zircon U-Pb 
ages dominated by major Middle–Late Jurassic 
populations, though the exact peak age varies 
spatially. Additionally, strata with mid-Late Cre-
taceous depositional ages have minor zircon age 
populations between 105 Ma and 95 Ma, with 
relative proportions that increase with decreas-
ing depositional age.
Zircon Hf Isotope Geochemistry and Trace 
Element Compositions
Hf isotope compositions of southwestern 
Oregon zircons reflect hybridized source con -
tributions (Fig. 6). The Otter Point Formation 
yielded Late Paleozoic–Late Jurassic aged zir-
cons with εHf(i) values that form two relatively 
equal clusters: one highly juvenile with a range 
between +15 to +10 and another straddling 
chondritic uniform reservoir (CHUR; Fig.  6). 
Houstenaden Creek and Blacklock Point zircons 
lack this signature and instead have εHf(i) values 
that form a broad swath of juvenile grains with a 
minor population of highly evolved 170–80 Ma 
zircons. The small cluster of Rocky Point For-
mation zircons have juvenile εHf(i) values rang-
ing from +14 to +7 (Fig. 6). Late Cretaceous 
deposition of highly juvenile Mesozoic zircon 
grains dominate the Dothan, Cape Sebastian, 
and Hunters Cove Formations. Grains between 
190 Ma and 160 Ma in the Dothan Formation 
drop to more moderately juvenile values ( +7 
to +5) relative to the Gold Beach terrane units, 
but all three formations record deposition of ca. 
100 Ma zircons that yield a broad span of εHf(i) 
values from +14 to −15 (Fig. 6).
Southwest Oregon terranes display signifi -
cant overlap in zircon trace element chemistry 
through time, though some important distinc -
tions are observed (Fig. 7). Late Jurassic Otter 
Point Formation zircons have restricted trace 
element compositions in Triassic grains that 
broaden through time; notably, ca. 160 Ma zir-
cons have U/Yb <0.01, strongly negative Eu 
anomalies, and increasing Nb/Yb. Trace ele -
ment compositions in Early Cretaceous Gold 
Beach units gradually become more restricted 
in Cretaceous grains, an opposing trend com -
pared to Otter Point zircons. Additionally, these 
grains show low U/Yb and a strong Nb deple -
tion (Fig. 7). Cape Sebastian and Hunters Cove

Titanite Geochronology
Titanites in southwestern Oregon terranes 
have U-Pb ages that closely align with zircon. 
Sandstones in the Late Jurassic Otter Point For-
mation generally lack titanite, but grains were 
recovered from diorite cobbles in a conglomer-
ate unit south of the town of Gold Beach. This 
sample was plotted in Tera-Wasserburg space, 
and a discordia line was regressed to determine 
the composition of common Pb to use for age 
corrections ( Fig.  8A; Fig. S8). The corrected 
ages were plotted to determine a weighted mean 
age of 170.9 ± 3.1 Ma, but the true uncertainty 
is much greater resulting from the very low U 
content and should be interpreted with caution.
Titanites in the Houstenaden Creek and 
Blacklock Point Formations are primarily Mid-
dle–Late Jurassic in age (Fig. 8C). Houstenaden 
Creek titanites yield U-Pb ages that form a uni-
modal peak at 173 Ma with a very minor con -
tinuum of Cretaceous grains. Titanite ages in 
the Blacklock Point Formation show modes at 
168 Ma and 150 Ma and, like the Houstenaden 
Creek Formation, have a minor subset of Creta-
ceous ages. Titanite age distributions shift to pri-
marily younger age modes in upper Gold Beach 
terrane strata. Grains in the Cape Sebastian 
Formation yielded ages between 200 Ma and 
82 Ma, with peaks at 175 Ma, 163 Ma, 115 Ma, 
and 92 Ma (Fig.  8B). Titanites in the Dothan 
Formation show a unique population at 192 Ma 
that are not present in the Gold Beach terrane 
(Fig.  7B). When plotted together with zircon 
ages (Fig. 9B), mineral age distributions are dis-
tinctly alike, though the 192 Ma population in 
the Dothan Formation still stands out as unique.

Paleomagnetic Results
Step-wise thermal and alternating field 
demagnetization experiments on sandstones 
from the Campanian Houstenaden Creek Forma-
tion yielded two components of magnetization, 
with the last-removed component considered to 
be the characteristic component of magnetiza -
tion (Fig. 10A). Many of these had well-defined 
vectors with principal component analysis 
(PCA) having mean angular deviation (MAD) 
values of less than 15°. Other results had less 
well-defined vectors with MAD values >15, for 
which the origin was included as an additional 
point in the PCA fits. There were also a number 
of samples whose magnetization vectors were 
too variable to accept. The inclusion of larger 
MAD values follows the recommendations of 
Gerritsen et  al. (2022) who favored a greater 
amount of data with some scatter over too many 
rejected values. This was a departure from prior 
analysis of these data by Liner (2005), who had 
acceptance criteria that were more conservative 
and yielded fewer acceptable data. Site mean 
directions from 11 sites were obtained (Table 4).
The mean directions before correction for 
bedding tilt and after correction for bedding tilt 
(Fig. 10B) indicate that sites have both normal 
and reverse polarity directions. Further, cluster-
ing is improved after correction for bedding tilt.

between sites is large, it is not possible to pro -

that reason we will choose to report a nominal 
estimate of 90° of post-depositional clockwise 
rotation. This correction should be applied when 
considering directions of sediment transport, as it 
would indicate a western source for sediments in 
the Houstenaden Creek Formation.
The question of evaluating inclination error is 
more difficult. The limited magnetic fabric data 
(Liner, 2005) suggested only modest inclination 
error, as there was no good correlation between 
degree of mineral alignment and paleomagnetic 
inclination. The Houstenaden Creek Formation 
has evidence for bioturbation and soft-sediment 
deformation (Bourgeois, 1980a). Experiments 
conducted using stirred sediments to simulate 
bioturbation ( Tauxe, 1993) found that biotur -
bated clastic sediments with magnetite as the 
remanence carrier do not have significant incli-
nation error, so natural sediments with bioturba-
tion such as the Houstenaden Creek Formation 
may be expected to have less inclination error. It 
is possible, due to effects of soft-sediment defor-
mation and bioturbation, that the remanence in 
these sediments may have been acquired as per 
results of “stirred” sediments in experiments 
(see Tauxe, 1993). For purposes of discussion, 
we will use both the observed mean inclina -
tion (I = 59) and an ad hoc 5° inclination error 
(I = 64) in paleogeographic interpretations 
(Figs. 11 and 12).
DISCUSSION
Provenance of Southwest Oregon Terranes
In a general sense, basins located along the 
flanks of mountain chains should accumulate 
sediments eroded from the nearby areas of topo-
graphic relief. Presently, the Gold Beach terrane 
lies at the western boundary of the Klamath 
Mountains Province (KMP), so if the KMP had 
topographic relief at that time and if the ter -
ranes shedding sediment were zircon-rich (and 
titanite-rich), we would expect adjacent basins 
to be dominated by this detritus. Further, this 
region was generally considered contiguous with 
the northern Sierra Nevada until the Late Juras-
sic, after which it moved to a more westward 
position (Ernst, 2013). Importantly, the KMP 
lacks a Cretaceous magmatic arc and the young-
est plutons are ca. 140 Ma (Barnes et al., 1992).
A variety of lithological, geochronological, 
and geochemical observations indicate that the 
Gold Beach terrane did not receive significant 
sedimentation from the Klamath Mountains 
(Dott, 1971; Walker, 1977; Bourgeois and Dott, 
1985). As shown herein, Late Cretaceous aged 
zircon and titanite in Cretaceous Gold Beach 
terrane units cannot have been derived from the 
KMP as magmatism had ceased in the earliest 
Cretaceous; thus, alternative sources must be 
considered. Detrital zircons in the U.S. Cor -
dillera are often inferred to have traveled far 
distances through river systems or along-shore 
current. A critical observation, however, lies in 
the detailed sedimentology. Early work in the 
Gold Beach terrane was focused on conglom -
erate studies that investigated the difficulties of 
long-range transport of coarse sediments and the 
occurrence of clast lithologies along the Cordil-
leran margin ( Walker, 1977; Aalto and Dott, 
1970), which were then combined with estimates 
of plate motions (Jayko and Blake, 1993). Addi-
tionally, the petrographic immaturity of sand -
stones was emphasized by Bourgeois (1980a), 
describing them as lithic- and volcanic-rich with 
ample plagioclase feldspar, implying that much 
of the sediment deposited to this basin could be 
first cycle and locally derived, further support-
ing the proposition of terrane translation (Aalto 
and Dott, 1970; Dott, 1971; Blake et al., 1985;

In conjunction with the original sedimentary 
petrography, Blake et al. (1985) collected recon-
naissance paleomagnetic data from mudstones 
in the Otter Point Formation; although no pre -
cise paleolatitudes or rotations were determined 
(due to uncertainties in the 150 Ma pole at this 
time), the results suggested distinct magnetic 
signatures that would support different geologic 
histories relative to other southwestern Oregon 
terranes. The site means from Blake et  al. 
(1985) were reviewed in Liner (2005) using a 
revised Late Jurassic paleopole from the North 
American craton that yielded well over 1000 km 
of northward displacement. Without the original 
data, precise recalculations were not possible, 
but the exercise added internal consistency 
to the growing body of literature supporting 
northward translation of the Gold Beach ter -
rane. These restorations placed the Otter Point 
Formation of the Gold Beach terrane adjacent 
to Baja, Mexico, during the Late Jurassic, and 
with that in mind, we continue this provenance 
analysis by exploring two different translational 
models (Fig. 12).
Tectonic Model 1—North American 
Reference Frame
In Model 1, the paleolatitude of the 
Houstenaden Creek Formation, including 0°–5° 
of inclination error, was determined using the 
Late Cretaceous reference pole for North Amer-
ica; details of this reference frame are described 
in Tikoff et al. (2023) and Housen (2021). This 
yielded a paleolatitude between 40°N and 46°N, 
reflecting translations of 750 km to 0 ± 500 km. 
The Houstenaden Creek Formation also records 
significant and variable clockwise rotations, 
yielding a tilt-corrected mean direction of 138°; 
however, a unique estimate of rotation is not 
reported here because the range of rotations 
observed between sites is large (previously dis-
cussed with paleomagnetic results). Instead, we 
use a conservative estimate of 90° of post-dep-
ositional clockwise rotation of the Gold Beach 
terrane in the models proposed here ( Fig. 12). 
This places the Gold Beach basin outboard of 
the southern and central Californian margin dur-
ing the Albian–Campanian (100–74 Ma), con-
strained by Albian foraminifera and Campanian 
bivalves (Bourgeois, 1980a), geomagnetic polar-
ity time scales (80.1–74.4 Ma; Malinverno et al., 
2020), and detrital zircon MDAs (100–89 Ma). 
Deposition occurred rapidly along submarine 
canyon slopes in a tectonically active exten -
sional setting similar to the southern California 
borderlands (Busby, 2004) during three distinct 
periods of Cordilleran-wide tectono-magmatic 
evolution: the oblique collision of the Insular 
superterrane with the North American margin 
starting at 100 Ma (Umhoefer et al., 2006; Gior-
gis et al., 2008; Tikoff et al., 2023), voluminous 
arc magmatism from Idaho to Central Mexico 
concurrent with dextral transpression in the arcs 
until ca. 85 Ma (Beck et  al., 1986; De Saint 
Blanquat et al., 1998), and the clockwise rota -
tion of crustal blocks along the North American 
margin (Beck, 1980; Irving et al., 1996).
Outboard Depocenters and Western Sediment 
Sources
Published paleomagnetic data for various 
accreted terranes in the Cordillera show Late 
Cretaceous paleolatitudes comparable to the 
Houstenaden Creek Formation, specifically, 
those belonging to the Insular and southern 
Intermontane superterranes (Tikoff et al., 2023, 
and references therein); paleomagnetic sites 
from displaced terranes include the Nanaimo 
Group ( Kim and Kodama, 2004 ), Methow-
Tyaughton basin (Enkin et al., 2006), and strata 
of the Ochoco basin (Housen and Dorsey, 2005). 
Additionally, prior to 100 Ma, Early-mid Creta-
ceous plutons of the Blue Mountains Province 
(Housen, 2018; Wilson and Cox, 1980 ) yield 
paleolatitudes just north of Gold Beach, suggest-
ing that sedimentary strata may contain detritus 
from similar sources. The previously mentioned 
terranes from both the Insular and Intermontane 
superterranes were likely outboard and/or north 
of the Gold Beach basin from mid-Late Creta -
ceous, acting as northern and western sediment 
sources, as indicated by paleocurrent direc -
tions after restoration of 90° of clockwise rota-
tion (Fig. 12A). In order to evaluate a western 
Insular/Intermontane sediment source, we look 
to Cretaceous aged depocenters within these 
superterranes, particularly those at the southern 
extent bordering the Coast Mountains batholith, 
smaller terranes within the North Cascades–San 
Juan thrust system, and in the Blue Mountains 
Province (Fig. 12A).
A compilation of detrital zircon ages from 
Aptian–Cenomanian (Group 1) and Campan -
ian–Maastrichtian strata (Group 2) in the afore-
mentioned regions shows striking similarity to 
detrital zircon ages in the Houstenaden Creek 
and correlative Blacklock Point Formations 
(Fig. 13). Multidimensional scaling plots (MDS) 
of cross-correlated detrital zircon kernel density 
estimates (KDEs) provide a means to quantify 
intersample similarities with special consid -
eration for the occurrence of age modes and 
changes in their relative magnitudes (Figs. 14A 
and 14B; Saylor et al., 2013; Saylor and Sundell, 
2016); these are complemented by cumulative 
density functions of detrital zircon ages in each 
terrane (Figs. 14C and 14D). In MDS space, ter-
ranes that plot close to each other are considered 
to have similar sediment sources and are identi-
fied by R2 values that approach 1.0.
The Houstenaden Creek and Blacklock Point 
samples plot within MDS cluster 1 (C1), accom-
panied by terranes affiliated with the North Cas-
cades–San Juan thrust system and lower units 
of the Nanaimo and Methow-Tyaughton basins 
(Coutts et al., 2020; Brown, 2012; Brown and 
Gehrels, 2007; Sauer et al., 2017a; DeGraaff-
Surpless et al., 2003; Fig. 14A); R2 values for 
C1 are greater than 0.75. Interestingly, the east-
ern belt of the Franciscan complex (Yolla Bolly–
east) also has a similar detrital zircon distribution 
(R2 = 0.72), characterized by an abundance of 
170–165 Ma grains together with a moderate 
Early Cretaceous age mode (Dumitru et  al., 
2010). Cumulative density functions (CDFs) of 
detrital zircon ages from these terranes support 
MDS comparisons and show a similar grouping 
of terranes that contain very few Precambrian 
detrital zircons, but have an abundance of Juras-
sic grains ( Fig. 14C). The Methow-Tyaughton 
basins, North Cascades thrust system, smaller 
fragmental terranes in the San Juan islands, and 
Cenomanian Ochoco basin strata ( R2 = 0.72) 
also possess this Early-mid Cretaceous peak 
(Fig. 13A), though variations in its magnitude 
may be related to localized thrusting events that 
changed depositional environments (McMechan, 
2000; Wyld et al., 2006). In the Gold Beach ter-
rane, Early Cretaceous sections are missing, and 
the Houstenaden Creek and Blacklock Point 
Formations lie in fault contact with the intensely 
sheared basement unit, the Late Jurassic Otter 
Point Formation (Koch, 1966).

Published detrital zircon Hf isotope data is 
variably available for basinal strata through -
out the Cordillera, leaving our comparisons 
restricted. We incorporate converted whole-rock 
Nd isotope data using the methods of Vervoort 
et al. (2011) and specifically compile data from 
three depositional age ranges: Aptian–Cenoma-
nian (Group 1), Santonian–Campanian (Group 
2A), and Maastrichtian (Group 2B) to compare 
with coeval formations within the Gold beach 
terrane (Fig.  15). Group 1 outboard depocen -
ters include the Methow-Tyaughton, Nanaimo, 
and Ochoco basins, sandstones in the Western 
mélange belt of the North Cascades–San Juan 
thrust system, and high-grade metamorphic 
rocks of the Skagit Gneiss complex, whose 
protoliths were likely forearc or accretionary 
wedge sediments (Surpless and Gulliver, 2018; 
Sauer et al., 2017b). Detrital zircons from the 
Methow-Tyaughton and Nanaimo basins display 
primarily radiogenic Hf isotope trends with εHf(i) 
values between +15 and +5 for both Late Juras-
sic and mid-Cretaceous populations (Fig. 15A). 
Terranes that occupied an outboard or more 
southern location along the margin from the late 
Aptian–Cenomanian also record rapid deposi -
tion of zircons with intermediate to evolved Hf 
isotope compositions: lower Ochoco basin units 
(Surpless and Gulliver, 2018), sandstones from 
the Western mélange belt in the North Cascades–
San Juan thrust system (Sauer et  al., 2017a, 
2017b), and gneissic rocks within the Cascades 
crystalline core (Sauer et al., 2018). The Black-
lock Point Formation displays purely radiogenic 
Hf isotope compositions, while the Houstenaden 
Creek Formation captures the same spread of 
εHf(i) values observed in Ochoco basin zircons 
(Fig. 15A).
Stratigraphic and sedimentological studies of 
the Nanaimo basin and the Houstenaden Creek 
and Blacklock Point Formations suggest broadly 
similar shallow marine depositional environ -
ments during the Campanian (ca. 83 Ma) with 
sediment derived primarily from the southwest 
in Nanaimo and the northeast-southwest in Gold 
Beach; early evolution of the two basins (Albian) 
differs such that sediments of the Comox Forma-
tion were deposited in fluvial/alluvial environ-
ments, and Houstenaden Creek and Blacklock 
Point sediments accumulated in an outer shelf to 
basin plain setting (Girotto et al., 2023; Huang 
et al., 2019; Bourgeois, 1980a). Provenance of 
sediments in the Nanaimo basin have predict -
able spatial and time-dependent shifts that are 
observed in both detrital zircon age spectra 
and in basin morphology (Coutts et al., 2024; 
Mahoney et  al., 2021; Matthews et  al., 2017; 
Kent et al., 2020). Mesozoic zircon age spectra 
for the two basins show less correlation over 
time due to younging of the primary Jurassic age 
mode from 170 Ma to 150 Ma in the Nanaimo 
Basin (Figs. 13A and 13B). This variation has 
been shown to reflect either west-derived sedi-
ments from sources in the Wrangellia terrane, or 
east-derived sediments originating in the Coast 
Mountains batholith, respectively (Mahoney 
et al., 2021; Coutts et al., 2024). Exposures of 
the Nanaimo Group on southern Vancouver 
Island and in the San Juan islands tend to have 
mid-Cretaceous detrital zircon MDAs, fewer 
Late Cretaceous grains, and a Middle Jurassic 
age peak at ca. 170 Ma; these characteristics are 
ubiquitous in Gold Beach terrane samples and 
support MDS analyses and CDF plots that show 
close relationships between the discussed ter -
ranes (Figs. 14A and 14C).
Southeast of basinal strata in the Pacific 
Northwest lies exposures of the Albian–Conia-
cian Ochoco forearc basin, presently in East -
ern Oregon. The Ochoco basin records initial 
deposition of fine-grained sediment, derived 
from metamorphic basement rocks in the Blue 
Mountains Province in a basin plain setting 
with periodic input from turbidity currents car-
rying sediments rich in chert and volcanic and 
plutonic debris ( Dorsey and Lenegan, 2007 ; 
Surpless and Gulliver, 2018). By Coniacian and 
possibly into the Campanian (subsurface reports 
of Thompson et al., 1984, documenting Cam -
panian strata), the depositional environment 
had evolved into a submarine fan setting where 
south-directed paleocurrents (after 37° of clock-
wise rotation) deposited massive conglomerate 
sequences together with medium-coarse grained 
sandstone; these were conformably deposited 
on Albian–Cenomanian mudstones ( Dorsey 
and Lenegan, 2007). The history of deposition 
in the Ochoco basin closely resembles the set -
ting described by Bourgeois (1980a) for the 
Houstenaden Creek and Blacklock Point For -
mations in the Gold Beach terrane. Importantly, 
these terranes show more correlation through 
time. In Group 2 MDS space (Fig. 14B), Coni-
acian and younger strata of the Ochoco basin 
plot together in cluster 2 (C2) with the Cam -
panian Cape Sebastian Formation and coeval 
Hornbrook and San Joaquin Valley sequences, 
the first indication of a potentially unified and 
widespread depositional system ( Surpless and 
Gulliver, 2018). C2 is characterized by detrital 
zircon age spectra that shift from dominantly 
Middle Jurassic to dominantly mid-Cretaceous 
(ca. 100 Ma) modes and yield cross-correlation 
R2 values greater than 0.75; these basins also 
have strikingly similar ranges of εHf(i) values 
through time (Fig. 15).
Inboard Depocenters and Eastern Sediment 
Sources
Inboard depocenters along the central Cordil-
leran margin, such as the Hornbrook and Great 
Valley forearc basins, show coevolving trends 
that reflect latest Jurassic–Early Cretaceous sedi-
mentation in isolated areas along the margin that 
were eventually overtaken by rising Campanian 
seas; this resulted in a more unified distribution 
of sediments and an interconnectedness of drain-
age systems (Surpless, 2015; Orme and Surpless, 
2019). Aptian–Cenomanian strata in the Sacra-
mento Valley of the Great Valley Group show a 
very narrow range of detrital zircon ages from 
150 Ma to 140 Ma, suggesting local sources in 
the northern Sierra Nevada and southern Klam-
ath Mountains (Surpless et al., 2006; DeGraaff-
Surpless et al., 2002; Orme and Surpless, 2019); 
in contrast, the San Joaquin Valley section has 
a more varied distribution of ages ( Fig. 13A). 
Cross-correlation of detrital zircon KDEs from 
inboard depocenters shows a progression from 
disparate Group 1 strata with R2 values less than 
0.50 to Group 2 strata that plot together in C2 
with the Cape Sebastian Formation (Figs. 13B, 
14B, and 14D). Notably, Group 1 detrital zircon 
KDEs of the Albian–Campanian Houstenaden 
Creek and Blacklock Point Formations show 
better comparability to Group 2 Sacramento 
Valley KDEs, as shown in CDF and MDS plots 
(Figs. 14B and 14D). The younger offset of the 
Jurassic age mode combined with moderate 
populations of 100 Ma zircons is likely respon-
sible for the low correlation in Aptian–Cenoma-
nian sequences (Figs. 13A and 14A). Converted 
whole-rock Nd isotopes of Great Valley Group 
sandstones show moderately radiogenic Hf iso-
tope compositions and suggest mixing of both 
juvenile and evolved material ( Figs.  15A and 
15B; Linn et al., 1992), supporting conclusions 
drawn from zircon Hf isotope compositions in 
volcanic roof pendants that yield εHf(i) values 
between +10 and −3 for Jurassic populations 
and +11 to −8 for mid-Late Cretaceous popula-
tions (Attia et al., 2020).

Provenance trends shift in late Campanian–
Maastrichtian strata, with an increase in mid-
Late Cretaceous aged sediment and evidence 
of reworked sedimentary material in the Gold 
Beach terrane (Bourgeois and Dott, 1985); con-
glomerates in the Cape Sebastian Formation 
contain Otter Point Formation clasts and slump 
deposits in the Hunters Cove Formation con -
tain large blocks of Cape Sebastian sandstone 
(Bourgeois, 1980b). The Cape Sebastian For -
mation continues to yield large R2 values (0.86) 
when compared to zircon KDEs from Group 2 
accretionary wedge rocks, such as Nacimiento 
Franciscan samples (Figs. 13B and 14B). The 
mix of both outboard volcanic arc detritus and 
ocean floor sediments, combined with deposi -
tion of continental sources from the east, is likely 
responsible for high degrees of similarity with 
subduction complex rocks. This is observed 
not only in detrital zircon age spectra, but in 
zircon Hf isotopes of the Albian–Cenomanian 
Dothan Formation (Yolla Bolly–west) and from 
zircons in conglomerate clasts of Nacimiento 
block mélanges (Figs. 15A and 15B; Hartford 
and Chapman, 2018 ); Although Gold Beach 
terrane rocks show no evidence of low tem -
perature–high pressure alteration indicative of 
subduction, their intermediate position between 
outboard and inboard crustal components may 
have led to a similar collection of detritus dur-
ing the Campanian (Bourgeois and Dott, 1985; 
Blake et al., 1985).
Maastrichtian deepwater deposition of the 
Hunters Cove Formation was interrupted by epi-
sodes of wrench-faulting that caused sections of 
the Cape Sebastian Formation to be recycled via 
slump deposits ( Bourgeois, 1980b). Paleocur-
rent indicators show both west- and northeast-
directed flow patterns that suggest sources to the 
east and southwest, though their usefulness is 
uncertain due to evidence of local folding and 
faulting (Bourgeois and Dott, 1985; Bourgeois, 
1980a). Detrital zircon age distributions in the 
Hunters Cove Formation differ only slightly 
from Cape Sebastian spectra ( Fig.  13B); the 
increase in Middle Jurassic (ca. 175 Ma) detri-
tus is complemented by a slight decrease of the 
100–85 Ma population. Hunters Cove zircons 
plot outside of cluster 2 in MDS space, but show 
strong similarities with older Gold Beach terrane 
units and Campanian–Maastrichtian strata of the 
southern McCoy-Bisbee backarc basin in Sonora 
Mexico (Figs. 13B and 14B; Lawton et al., 2020; 
Barth et al., 2004). This could be due to long-
range transport of east-derived sediments from 
southwestern Laurentia into the active forearc 
environment during the latest Cretaceous (Shar-
man et al., 2015), or inflation of the Jurassic age 
mode through recycling of Jurassic sediments 
already present in Gold Beach terrane rocks 
(Rivas, 2014).
Tectonic Model 2—Globally Averaged 
North American Paleopole Reference 
Frame
In Model 2, the paleolatitude of the 
Houstenaden Creek Formation, including 0°–5° 
of inclination error, was determined using the 
globally averaged North American paleopole 
for the Late Cretaceous; this reference frame is 
described in both the paleomagnetic compila -
tions of Kent and Irving (2010) and Vaes et al. 
(2023). One of the main features of these ref -
erence frames is that they place North America 
at slightly higher paleolatitudes during the Late 
Cretaceous. Using the Kent and Irving (2010) 
pole for 70 Ma produced an expected paleo -
latitude for the Houstenaden Creek Formation 
between 53°N and 57°N, reflecting translations 
of 1500 km to 900 ± 600 km. This places the 
Gold Beach terrane south of the Transverse 
Ranges extending into the northern Peninsular 
Ranges forearc (Fig. 12C).
To evaluate the larger translation of the Gold 
Beach terrane rocks that would result from 
the global paleomagnetic reference for North 
America, compilations of published detrital 
zircon data for this more southerly region were 
evaluated together with Model 1 compilations 
(Figs.  13–15). Many crustal blocks along the 
North American margin experienced vertical 
axis rotations of varying magnitudes during the 
mid-Late Cretaceous (Beck, 1980; Irving et al., 
1996). A notable example constrained by the ref-
erence frame of Model 2, and similar to the rota-
tions recorded in the Gold Beach terrane, is the 
large magnitude (70°–110°) clockwise rotations 
derived from paleomagnetic studies of Cenozoic 
rocks of the Transverse Ranges, Southern Cali-
fornia (Hillhouse, 2010). This restores the cen-
tral and eastern Transverse Ranges to a coastal 
position between the southern Sierra Nevada 
batholith and northern Peninsular Ranges batho-
lith, where arc magmatism persisted from 90 Ma 
to 70 Ma (Schwartz et al., 2023). Interestingly, 
Campanian–Maastrichtian (85–65 Ma) zircon 
ages are not present in the Maastrichtian Hunt-
ers Cove Formation despite active plutonism 
and high-grade metamorphism, just north of 
the restored Gold Beach location presented in 
Model 2 (Fig. 12; Chapman et al., 2021).
Detrital zircon KDEs of strata constrained by 
Model 2 show increased correlation through time 
in terranes closest to the Mojave desert segment 
of the continental arc ( Fig. 13). Albian–Ceno-
manian members of the McCoy-Bisbee basin 
and coeval Gold Beach sequences have cross-
correlation R2 values = 0.64 that increase to 0.76 
when compared to KDEs of the Cape Sebastian 
Formation, and further increase to 0.91 relative 
to the Hunter Cove Formation (Figs. 13 and 14). 
Zircon Hf isotopes in the Pelona-Orocopia-Rand 
schists of the Mojave Province show εHf(i) val-
ues that fall within the range of compositions 
observed in the Cape Sebastian and Hunter 
Cove Formations and span from +12 to 0 in 
pre-100 Ma grains and from 0 to −28 in post-
100 Ma zircons (Figs. 15B and 15C; Sauer et al., 
2019); these rocks lack the abundance of Juras-
sic detrital zircons that comprise strata in the 
Gold Beach terrane.
Similarly, farther south along the margin, 
Peninsular Ranges forearc basin strata are rich 
in volcaniclastic debris and record sedimenta -
tion within a tectonically active forearc segment 
(Busby, 2004); detrital zircon KDEs and MDS 
plots show increased correlation in Campan -
ian–Maastrichtian strata, but again the lack of 
a Jurassic sediment source is problematic (Kim-
brough et al., 2014; Sharman et al., 2015). Age 
spectra of the Peninsular Ranges and southern 
California forearc share significant overlap in 
the 100 Ma age mode, but it was not until after 
the Maastrichtian that Mojave desert sediments, 
carrying an abundance of Jurassic aged zircon, 
entered the southern Cordilleran forearc (Shar-
man et  al., 2015; Schwartz et  al., 2021). An 
equally puzzling feature is the absence of latest 
Cretaceous (80–65 Ma) detrital zircon grains 
in all Gold Beach terrane units, when coeval 
strata in the southern California forearc and in 
outboard depocenters in the Nanaimo Group 
have an abundance of latest Cretaceous zircons 
derived from volcanism in northern Mexico 
(Lawton et al., 2009) and ongoing magmatism in 
the Coast Mountains batholith (Cecil et al., 2018, 
2021), respectively. Zircon Hf isotopes in Maas-
trichtian Nanaimo basin units have a juvenile

epsilon units) with minor contributions from an 
evolved 75–70 Ma source, much younger than 
the evolved 100 Ma sediment found in depocen-
ters to the north (Fig. 15; Mahoney et al., 2021).
An additional complication with a more 
southerly origin for the Gold Beach terrane is 
the larger magnitude displacements required 
after 70 Ma to bring the Gold Beach terrane to its 
current position in southwestern Oregon by the 
Eocene (Bourgeois, 1980a; Engebretson et al., 
1987). This, combined with Late Cretaceous 
fault orientations in the Southern California 
batholith, show evidence for a period of post-
80 Ma sinistral movement in the region south 
of the Transverse Ranges that would have repo-
sitioned the Gold Beach terrane farther south 
along the western margin (Schwartz et al., 2023; 
Jacobson et al., 2011, 2017). We therefore prefer 
the reconstruction proposed in Model 1, where 
the Gold Beach terrane occupied an intermedi-
ate location outboard of Early Cretaceous accre-
tionary complex rocks, but inboard of the Insu-
lar and Intermontane superterranes, collecting 
eroded island arc sediment from the west, and 
continental detritus from sources in the central 
and southern Sierra Nevada and western Mojave 
desert (Fig. 12A).
Jurassic Basement Correlations
Using the latitudinal constraints provided by 
our preferred Model 1 and interpretations of pre-
vious studies that considered preliminary paleo-
magnetic analyses and sedimentary petrography, 
we investigate Jurassic basement terranes in the 
Central Cordillera and in outboard arc terranes 
that were accreted during the Late Jurassic–
Early Cretaceous (Fig. 12). The Tithonian Otter 
Point Formation is characterized by flysch-like 
sequences of sheared black mudstone, sand -
stone, conglomerate, and mafic-intermediate 
volcanic rocks that represent the exposed base-
ment of the Gold Beach terrane ( Dott, 1971). 
The complex is lithologically varied and struc-
turally complicated by intrusion of gabbroic-
dioritic dikes and flows of volcanic breccia 
and pillow lavas that occur throughout the unit 
showing strong evidence of sea floor volcanism; 
alteration is limited to veins of laumontite (Koch, 
1966). Paleocurrent indicators in volcanic lithic 
sandstones and chert-pebble conglomerates sug-
gest a variety of flow directions from east-west 
to northeast-southwest and are likely of limited 
use due to the chaotic nature of Otter Point rocks 
(Walker, 1977). The complex is bounded to the 
north and east by steeply dipping shear zones 
that are marked with masses of serpentinite and 
is in fault contact with overlying Cretaceous 
units ( Dott, 1971 ). Prior to deposition of the 
Cretaceous formations, the Otter Point Forma-
tion experienced a period of transpression as it 
was accreted to the continental margin ( Roure 
and Blanchet, 1983).
South of Port Orford, Oregon, the inland 
strand of the Brush Creek fault zone separates 
the northern extent of the Gold Beach terrane—
dominantly Otter Point broken formation—from 
less deformed strata to the east in the Elk sub -
terrane (Fig. 2; Wiley et al., 2014). This outlier 
of the Western Klamath terrane is composed of 
the Oxfordian Galice Formation (Surpless et al., 
2024) and Early Cretaceous Humbug Moun -
tain and Rocky Point Formations (Koch, 1966; 
Dott, 1971 ). Before deposition of the coarse 
Early Cretaceous cover sequence, the base of 
the outlier was intruded by the Pearse Peak dio-
rite at ca. 148 Ma (Howard, 1961; Koch, 1966; 
Beaulieu and Hughes, 1976; Blake et al., 1985; 
McClaughry et al., 2013). Intrusive phases were 
accompanied by Late Jurassic mafic-intermedi-
ate volcanism of the Rogue-Chetco arc, all of 
which were located west of the Josephine basin, 
an ophiolite-floored backarc basin that opened 
during the Middle Jurassic (Roure and Blanchet, 
1983; Harper et al., 1994; Grove et al., 2008). 
Galice Formation sediments accumulated from 
both the westward juvenile arc and the eastern 
continental margin into the Josephine basin syn-
chronous with Nevadan deformation that began 
at ca. 157 Ma ( Saleeby, 1983 ; Harper et  al., 
1994). Nevadan thrusting resulted in meta -
morphism of the Galice Formation to prehnite-
pumpellyite and greenschist facies conditions 
(Frost et al., 2006; LaMaskin et al., 2021). Like 
the Josephine basin, the younger Great Valley 
forearc basin is in depositional contact with the 
Coast Range ophiolite at its northwestern end 
and is faulted against the roots of accreted island 
arc terranes to the east, underlying areas of the 
Sacramento Valley (Dickinson and Seely, 1979). 
The basal Great Valley sequence stands apart 
from the Galice Formation because of its less 
deformed strata and virtually unmetamorphosed 
nature (zeolite grade; Wakabayashi, 2017 )—
characteristics that also describe the Otter Point 
Formation (Dott, 1971).
Our preferred Model 1 suggests that Cre -
taceous strata of the Gold Beach terrane were 
deposited along the western margin between the 
Sacramento Valley and the Transverse Ranges at 
paleolatitudes of 40°N to 46°N (Fig. 12). Recon-
naissance paleomagnetic data for the Otter Point 
Formation (Blake et al., 1985), combined with 
conglomerate studies and sandstone petrogra -
phy (Aalto, 1989; Aalto and Dott, 1970; Koch, 
1966), support a similar depositional location for 
the Late Jurassic arc complex. By the Campan-
ian, material eroded from the Otter Point Forma-
tion was being deposited to the Cape Sebastian 
Formation, constraining its paleogeographic 
location to the latitudinal range of Model 1.
Detrital zircon ages in Otter Point rocks are 
compared with other Jurassic and older base -
ment terranes, from the Klamath Mountains 
south to the Jurassic retroarc in SW Laurentia, 
using cross-correlation R2 values and MDS 
plots (Figs. 16B and 16C; Supplemental Data 
S3). Otter Point zircons plot in cluster 3 (C3) 
with Sierran pre-batholithic rocks, Kernville and 
Sierran Foothills terranes, and basal strata of the 
Great Valley Group (Fig. 16B); additionally, C3 
contains samples from the McCoy-Bisbee basin 
and from the Galice Formation. Similarities in 
zircon age spectra from such a wide range of 
terranes is likely a reflection of the inboard posi-
tion they occupied and connections to interior 
drainage systems during the Middle–Late Juras-
sic (Attia et al., 2018, 2021). Deep marine sedi-
mentation in early Mesozoic and Late Paleozoic 
terranes of the southern Sierra Nevada Foothills 
and Central Western Metamorphic belt show 
Early–Middle Jurassic age modes, a domi -
nant Permo-Triassic population, and variable 
amounts of 600–500 Ma zircons (Attia et  al., 
2021) common in the Otter Point Formation 
(Fig.  5). These terranes run along the axis of 
the Sierra Nevada batholith from the foot of the 
Klamath Mountains to the Mojave desert and 
contain ophiolitic complexes, chert, argillite, and 
greenstone packages, subduction mélanges, and 
volcaniclastic turbidity flows (Snow and Ernst, 
2008; Schweickert et al., 1977; Christe et al., 
2018). Cumulative density functions of detrital 
zircon ages in terranes of the Sierra Nevada pre-
batholithic framework show strong correlations 
with Otter Point age spectra ( Figs. 16B–16D), 
especially in the Eastern Sierras proximal to 
the Mojave desert and in the Kernville terrane 
and Southern Western Metamorphic belt of the 
southern Sierra Nevada (Attia et al., 2021).
These metamorphic belts stretch northward 
into the Klamath Mountains terranes and pos -
sibly have correlatives farther north in the base-

for in the Otter Point Formation (Fig. 16A). This 
population is also present in the Late Jurassic 
Galice and Cretaceous Hornbrook Formations, 
suggesting it may be supplied by volcanic island 
arc terranes within the Sierran Foothills terrane 
and in the Western Metamorphic belt.
Provenance and Paleomagnetic Integration
Based on the data presented in this study 
and comparisons made in Models 1 and 2 with 
regions spanning much of the North Ameri -
can Cordillera, we constrain the Late Juras -
sic–Eocene location of the Gold Beach terrane, 
presently located in southwest Oregon, using 
(1) detrital zircon and titanite in sandstones and 
(2) paleomagnetic data from some of the same 
rocks. Deposition occurs in the Gold Beach ter-
rane during the Late Jurassic (Otter Point Forma-
tion), mid-Cretaceous (Houstenaden Creek and 
Blacklock Point Formations), and Late Creta -
ceous (Cape Sebastian and Hunters Cove For -
mations), each phase characterized by different 
depositional patterns.
The basal Otter Point Formation likely 
received sediment from Sierra Nevada pre-
batholithic framework terranes (600–500 Ma 
zircons) that occur as N-S–elongated coastal 
belts from the Klamath Mountains to the Mojave 
desert. Additionally, zircon and titanite from 
early Mesozoic plutons in the Sierra Nevada and 
Middle Jurassic volcanism in the Mojave Desert 
were transported through long-range drainage 
systems to the coastal marine environment along 
the margin. The fault contact between the Otter 
Point Formation and the Albian–Campanian 
Houstenaden Creek and Blacklock Point For -
mations could be a remnant structure caused by 
collision of outboard arc terranes. The angular 
unconformity between the Houstenaden Creek 
and Cape Sebastian Formations is likely a result 
of renewed regional tectonic activity, as sand -
stones comprising the youngest Gold Beach ter-
rane units show evidence of more shallow, high-
energy depositional environments. The Cape 
Sebastian and Hunters Cove Formations pos -
sess significantly more evolved Late Cretaceous 
zircon and titanite, potentially sourced from 
the Sierran-Peninsular continental arc. Deposi-
tion of juvenile Late Cretaceous sediment may 
be related to magmatic activity outboard of the 
margin on the Insular superterrane.
Paleomagnetic evidence suggests that the 
Insular superterrane was outboard of the south-
western Laurentian margin during the Late Cre-
taceous (Irving et al., 1985; Wynne et al., 1995; 
Umhoefer et al., 2006; Tikoff et al., 2023) and 
could have supplied the highly juvenile Early 
Jurassic–Late Cretaceous zircons in the Creta -
ceous Gold Beach units. Having contributions 
from the Insular or some other outboard—i.e., 
located to the west—terrane would be consis -
tent with west-to-east directed sediment trans -
port directions after correction for the significant 
vertical axis rotations observed in the paleomag-
netic data. The observed paleolatitude in Model 
1 places the Gold Beach terrane north of the 
latitude of the Transverse Ranges during the 
Late Cretaceous (Fig. 12); this is consistent with 
detrital mineral provenance interpretations.
The Late Cretaceous Nanaimo Group on 
Vancouver Island, British Columbia, records 
a paleolatitude of 41°N and 46°N, as obtained 
from inclination-error corrected paleomagnetic 
results of Kim and Kodama (2004) and from 
fossil leaf assemblages that range from 41 °N 
to 45°N ( Kodama and Ward, 2001 ; Kim and 
Kodama, 2004). This data places the Nanaimo 
basin at a paleolatitude similar to estimates for 
the Gold Beach terrane. Both basins share a 
comparable mid-Cretaceous depositional envi-
ronment together with detrital zircon spectra 
and Hf isotope compositions that suggest similar 
sediment sources. This emphasizes the idea of 
translation from southern latitudes.
CONCLUSIONS
Taken as a whole, the provenance and paleo-
magnetic results from the Gold Beach terrane are 
consistent with translation from lower paleolati-
tudes in the Late Jurassic, with ∼750 km of trans-
port from a paleolatitude between 40°N and 46°N 
since the Late Cretaceous. The adjacent Klamath 
Mountains—which lack Late Cretaceous gran-
ites—cannot be the sole source for the Gold 
Beach sedimentary rocks that contain abundant 
Cretaceous detrital zircons and titanites. Fur -
ther, sedimentary rocks of different depositional 
ages exhibit different provenance, and no single 
source region contains all the lithologies neces-
sary to satisfy these provenance requirements. 
Paleomagnetic results from the Houstenaden 
Creek Formation pass both fold and reversals 
tests and indicate 750 ± 500 km of northward 
displacement described in Model 1. These data 
are consistent with inferred source areas in the 
Transverse Ranges and southern Sierra Nevada.
The paleomagnetism also shows an ∼90° 
clockwise rotation of the terrane, with the cur-
rently southward paleocurrents indicating an 
original source on its western margin. Thus, 
some deposition must have occurred from rocks 
currently located on its west side. We infer that 
the Insular superterrane was located on the west 
side of the Gold Beach terrane, supported by 
some of the detrital mineral constraints. Overall, 
we prefer Model 1 that shows the Gold Beach 
terrane translated northward from an area just 
north of the Transverse Ranges, and along the 
continental margin during the Late Cretaceous. 
Per paleomagnetic constraints, the Gold Beach 
terrane was accompanied by terranes associated 
with the Insular superterrane that also contain 
evolved detritus sourced from regions in south-
western Laurentia.
